en: From whom this entire world of illusion, fashioned by conceptual proliferation, is born;
in whom it abides and at the time of its end it dissolves again, cycle after cycle;
and meditating upon whom, free from all proliferation, sages find certain liberation—(1.1).
I bow to him who is named Puruṣottama— the stainless, eternal, all-pervading, and immovable one;
whom the wise meditate upon at the time of samādhi as pure as the sky,
consisting of eternal bliss, serene, stainless, the Lord of all, and devoid of qualities.

I bow to that Hari, the destroyer of worldly existence, the ageless bestower of liberation, who is beyond the manifest and the unmanifest, free from conceptual proliferation, accessible through meditation alone, and all-pervading. [In the] most meritorious, pure, and beautiful Naimiṣa forest...
It was crowded with various holy men and adorned with diverse flowers.
With *aśvattha* trees, *pārijāta*s, sandalwood, *aguru*, and *pāṭala*s; with *bakula*s, *saptaparṇa*s, *puṃnāga*s, and *nāgakesara*s.
It was beautified by śāla, tāla, and tamāla trees, as well as by coconut palms, arjuna trees, and many other trees such as the campaka.
It was filled with flocks of various birds, joined by herds of various wild animals,
and adorned with various holy reservoirs such as long ponds and the like.
By Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras, and other castes;
by forest-dwellers, householders, ascetics, and students.
It was adorned everywhere with flourishing herds of cattle,
and with barley, wheat, chickpeas, black gram, mung beans, sesame, and sugarcane.
While that great sacrifice was being performed, with the sacrificial fire blazing brightly, the ground was adorned with grains such as Chinese millet and other pure crops.
While the inhabitants of Naimiṣa were performing the twelve-year sacrificial session (sattra),
sages and other twice-born ones also arrived there.
When those twice-born ones had arrived, they offered them the worship due to them;
and when they, together with the officiating priests, were seated there.
Then the wise Sūta Lomaharṣaṇa arrived there;
seeing him, those best of sages, filled with joy, performed worship for him.
Having honored them in return, he too sat down upon an excellent seat;
then the twice-born ones, together with the charioteer, engaged in conversation with one another.
At the conclusion of the discourse, all of them— initiated together with the officiating priests and the members of the assembly— joyfully asked the disciple of Vyāsa about their doubt.
The sages said:
O best of beings, you know the Purāṇas, the Āgamas, and the Śāstras along with the Itihāsas;
you know the conduct, the births, and the deeds of the gods and the Daityas.
There is nothing unknown to you regarding the Vedas, the Śāstras, the Mahābhārata, the Purāṇas, and the treatises on liberation; O high-minded one, you are omniscient.
Just as before, all this has arisen— the world with its moving and unmoving beings,
including the gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas.
O Sūta, we wish to hear; tell us everything: how the world came to be, and furthermore, O highly fortunate one, how it will come to be.
O Sūta, from whom this world arose, and from whom the mobile and immobile universe proceeded;
that in which it was dissolved, and likewise that wherein it shall go to its dissolution.
Lomaharṣaṇa said: To Viṣṇu, the conqueror of all— the unchanging, the pure, the eternal Supreme Self, whose form is always of one and the same nature.
Homage to Hiraṇyagarbha, to Hari, and to Śaṅkara;
to Vāsudeva, the Savior, whose activity consists of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world.
Salutation to Viṣṇu, the cause of liberation, who possesses both singular and manifold natures, whose essence is both gross and subtle, and who is both unmanifest and manifest.
Salutations to that Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, who is free from old age and death, who is the root cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world.
Having prostrated before the Imperishable, the Supreme Person, who is the support of the universe, subtler than the subtlest, and who dwells within all beings; BrP_1.25.
That which is, in ultimate reality, the very nature of knowledge and absolutely stainless,
appears as the nature of objects due to erroneous perception.
Viṣṇu, the devourer of the universe, the Lord in its maintenance as well as its creation,
the omniscient ruler of the worlds, unborn, undecaying, and immutable.

Having prostrated before the Lord of the Universe, who is primordial and most subtle, and before those beginning with Brahmā, as well as [Vasiṣṭha], who knows the Itihāsas and Purāṇas and has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; BrP_1.28 //
Having bowed to my preceptor, the lord Parāśara’s son, who knows the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures, I shall proclaim this Purāṇa which is equal to the Vedas.
I shall relate how, in the past, when questioned by Dakṣa and other most excellent sages, the Blessed One, the lotus-born Grandfather, spoke.
Listen, for I shall relate a wondrous tale that destroys sin—
a narrative being told by me that is diverse, rich in meaning, and extensive in its scriptural detail.
But whoever should constantly uphold this, or listen to it repeatedly,
having ensured the continuity of his own lineage, is glorified in the heavenly world.
That unmanifest cause is eternal, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent;
from that Pradhāna, the Lord Puruṣa fashioned the universe.
Know him, O best of sages, to be Brahmā of immeasurable splendor,
the creator of all beings, who is devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
From that Mahat, however, came the ego (ahaṃkāra), and from it the elements were born;
from the elements, the various manifestations of beings arose—such is the eternal creation.
Listen as I proclaim in detail, according to my wisdom and according to what I have heard, that which increases the fame of you all.
This has been proclaimed by those of steadfast fame as that which increases the merit of all;
thereafter, the Blessed Self-born One, desiring to create various beings, [proceeded].
In the beginning, he emitted the waters alone; upon them he then emitted his seed.
The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara.
Since they were his first resting place (ayana), he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa;
that egg, resting upon the waters, became golden-hued.
In that place, we have heard, the self-existent Brahmā himself was born;
the golden-hued Lord remained there for a full year.
He divided that egg into two parts, namely heaven and earth;
between those two shells, the Lord created the ether.
In the waters, he established the earth floating about and the ten directions;
therein he placed time, mind, speech, desire, anger, and likewise pleasure.
Desiring to create the world and the Prajāpatis who would be of his own form, he brought forth creation:
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
And that one of great splendor created the seven mind-born sons of Vasiṣṭha;
these are established in the Purāṇas as the "Seven Brahmās."
Then, in the beginning, Brahmā created Rudra, who was born from his own wrath, from among those seven born of Brahmā who were of the nature of Nārāyaṇa.
And Sanatkumāra, the all-pervading lord, the first-born even of the ancients;
from these seven [sages], O twice-born ones, the progeny and the Rudras were born.
Skanda and Sanatkumāra remain with their splendor withdrawn;
from them arise seven great divine lineages, accompanied by hosts of gods.
They were active, possessed of offspring, and adorned by great seers;
they beheld lightning, thunderclouds, and red rainbows.
In the beginning, he created the classes of beings and indeed created Parjanya;
he fashioned the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman verses for the successful accomplishment of sacrifice.
"They gave birth to the Sādhyas and the gods"—thus they recounted;
from his limbs were born various beings, both high and low.
Indeed, when the offspring being created did not increase at all while Prajāpati Āpava was engaged in the creation of progeny, then—
Dividing his own body into two parts, he became a male with one half and a female with the other;
in her, he then produced the two kinds of progeny.
Having pervaded both heaven and earth with his majesty, Viṣṇu remained; he created Virāj, and that Virāj created Puruṣa.
One should know that Manu to be Puruṣa; his period is remembered as a Manvantara. This second Manvantara is said to belong to Mānasa Manu.
That Lord Puruṣa Vairāja brought forth the creation of beings;
and the offspring of that Nārāyaṇa-emanation were likewise not born from a womb.
A man who knows this primary creation shall become long-lived, renowned, and possessed of merit and progeny;
and having understood it, he shall attain his desired goal.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Having thus created living beings, the patriarch Āpava indeed obtained as his wife Śatarūpā, who was not born from a womb. BrP_2.1 //
O best of sages, while Āpava remained pervading the heavens by his own greatness, Śatarūpā was born from him through dharma alone.
Having performed extremely difficult austerities for ten thousand years,
she obtained as her husband a man of radiant asceticism.
O Brahmins, that self-existent person is called Manu;
his period of authority here is said to be seventy-one yugas, known as a manvantara.
From the Puruṣa Vairāja, Śatarūpā gave birth to Vīra;
from Vīra, Kāmyā gave birth to Priyavrata and Uttānapāda.
The excellent daughter of the progenitor Kardama was named Kāmyā;
the sons of Kāmyā were four: Samrāṭ, Kukṣi, Virāṭ, and Prabhu.
The patriarch Atri took Uttānapāda as his son;
and from Uttānapāda, Sūnṛtā gave birth to four sons.
Dharma’s daughter, renowned by the name Sūnṛtā, was fair-hipped and auspicious; she was born from the horse sacrifice as the mother of Dhruva.
The Lord of Creatures, Uttānapāda, begot Dhruva, Kīrtimant, Āyuṣmat, and Vasu upon Sūnṛtā.
O twice-born ones, for three thousand divine years,
the highly fortunate Dhruva performed austerities, seeking great renown.
The Lord Brahmā, the Prajāpati, being pleased, granted him a station equal to his own,
an immovable one situated in front of the Seven Sages.
And having observed his pride, his supernatural power, and his greatness, Uśanas, the preceptor of the gods and asuras, formerly sang this verse: BrP_2.12 //
Oh, the power of his asceticism! Oh, his sacred learning! Oh, how wonderful it is, that the Seven Sages stand today with him placed before them!
From him, Śambhu begot Śliṣṭin and Bhavya from Dhruvā;
Succhāyā bore five faultless sons to Śliṣṭin.
Bṛhatī bore Ripu, Ripuñjaya, Vīra, Vṛkala— who possessed the splendor of a wolf— and Cakṣuṣa, who possessed all-encompassing energy, from Ripu.
He begot Cākṣuṣa Manu upon Vairiṇī, the daughter of the high-souled Prajāpati Vīraṇya, in the lotus-lake.
O tigers among sages, ten sons of great power were born to Manor, the daughter of the Prajāpati Vairāja, by Naḍvalā.
Kutsa, Puru, Śatadyumna, Tapasvin, Satyavāk, Kavi, Agniṣṭut, Atirātra, and Sudyumna—these are the nine. (BrP 2.18)
And Abhimanyu was the tenth; Puru begot six sons of great luster upon Naḍvalā, the daughter of Agni. These were the highly energetic sons of the great-splendored Puru.
From Aṅga were born Sumanas, Svāti, Kratu, and Aṅgiras;
and from the body of Aṅga, Sunītha gave birth to one son, Veṇa.
Due to the misconduct of Veṇa, a very great wrath arose,
he whose right hand the sages churned for the sake of progeny.
When Veṇa’s hand was churned, a great king was born;
seeing him, the sages, being delighted, said: "He shall indeed gladden the subjects."
Possessing great splendor, he will achieve great fame;
born as an archer clad in armor, he will resemble a blazing fire.
Likewise, Pṛthu, the son of Vena and the first-born of the Kṣatriyas, protected this earth;
he was the first lord of the world among those consecrated by the Rājasūya sacrifice.
And from that very [cow] were born the skillful Sūta and Māgadha;
by him, O best of sages, this cow was milked for the crops by the king.
Desiring the livelihood of all creatures, he was [honored] by the gods together with the hosts of sages,
as well as by the ancestors, the Dānavas, the Gandharvas, and the throngs of Apsarases.
The Earth was milked by serpents, Puṇyajanas, as well as by creepers and mountains, from various such vessels.
She gave milk according to their desire, and by that they sustained their lives.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, Pṛthu’s two sons, who were knowers of dharma, vanished from sight.
Śikhaṇḍinī gave birth to Havirdhāna from within her own body;
from Havirdhāna, Dhiṣaṇā, who was of the nature of Agni, gave birth to six sons.
Prācīnabarhis, Śukra, Gaya, Kṛṣṇa, Vraja, and Ajina;
the venerable Prācīnabarhis was a great lord of creatures (prajāpati).
O best of sages, from Havirdhāna were nurtured the offspring who roam the surface of the earth,
namely the venerable Prācīnabarhis.
The Lord Prajāpati, having reached the conclusion of his great asceticism, took Savarṇā, the daughter of the Ocean, as his wife.
Sāmudrī bore ten sons to Prācīnabarhis by Savarṇa;
they were all named Pracetas and were masters of the science of archery.
Practicing their religious duties without deviation, they performed great austerities for ten thousand years while lying within the waters of the ocean.
While the Pracetasas were performing austerities upon the earth, trees overran the unprotected land, and then there occurred a destruction of living beings.
The wind was unable to blow, for the sky became covered with trees;
for ten thousand years, living beings were unable to move.
Having heard that, all the Pracetasas, endowed with ascetic power and filled with wrath,
emitted wind and fire from their mouths.
Then the wind, having uprooted the trees, dried them up;
the terrible fire then consumed them, and thus occurred the destruction of the trees.
Then, perceiving that the trees were being exhausted and only a few branches remained,
Soma approached those Prajāpatis and spoke to them.
"O kings, all you descendants of Prācīnabarhis, restrain your anger!
The earth has been made treeless; let fire and wind be appeased."
And this maiden of excellent complexion is like a jewel among trees;
O father, knowing her future destiny, she was indeed conceived by me in my womb.
"By name she is called Māriṣā, created from the essence of trees;
O highly fortunate ones, let her be your wife, for she shall increase the lineage of Soma."
"By half of your splendor and by half of my own splendor,
a wise Prajāpati named Dakṣa shall be born from her."
He, being himself like fire, shall further cause these creatures— who have been mostly consumed by the fire consisting of your own splendor— to flourish once more.
Then, at the word of Soma, those Pracetasas,
having withdrawn their anger from the trees, took Māriṣā as their wife according to dharma.
O twice-born ones, from the ten Pracetas, the Prajāpati Dakṣa of great splendor was born of Māriṣā through a portion of Soma.
Having created both the immobile and the mobile— both bipeds and quadrupeds—
the skillful Dakṣa subsequently created women by means of his mind.
The Lord gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
and the remaining ones, known as the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), to King Soma.
From them were born the gods, birds, cattle, serpents, sons of Diti and the Dānavas, Gandharvas, Apsarases, and indeed other species as well.
From that time forward, O best of Brahmins, progeny were born from sexual union;
it is said that for those who came before, progeny arose from mere intention, sight, or touch.
The sages said:
"We have heard of the origin of the gods, the dānavas, the gandharvas, the uragas, and the rākṣasas, as well as that of the high-souled Dakṣa."
It is said that Dakṣa, of auspicious vows, was born from the thumb of Brahmā;
likewise, his wife was born from his left thumb.
How did that great ascetic again obtain the state of being a Prācetasa?
O Sūta, you ought to explain this doubt of ours here:
how did he, who was the grandson of Soma, become his father-in-law?
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
O twice-born ones, origination and cessation are constant among all beings;
regarding this, the seers and those people who possess knowledge are not deluded.
In age after age, these kings beginning with Dakṣa come into being again, and they are likewise dissolved again; the wise man is not deluded by this.
O best of the twice-born, among them there was previously no seniority or juniority;
austerity alone was weightier, and spiritual power was the sole cause [of distinction].
He who knows this creation of Dakṣa, together with all that is moving and unmoving,
shall be blessed with offspring, attain a full lifespan, and be glorified in the heavenly world.
The sages said:
O Lomaharṣaṇa, recount in full detail the origin of the gods, the Dānavas, the Gandharvas, the Uragas, and the Rākṣasas.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
O twice-born ones, listen now to how Dakṣa, having been previously commanded by the Self-existent One to "create progeny," brought forth all beings.
In the beginning, the Lord created from his mind alone all beings:
the sages, the gods along with the gandharvas, the asuras, the yakṣas, and the rākṣasas.
O Brahmins, when his mental offspring did not increase,
that righteous-souled Prajāpati then reflected upon the matter for the sake of progeny.
Desiring to procreate various offspring through the law of sexual union,
he took Asiknī, the daughter of the patriarch Vīraṇa, as his wife.
Then the valiant one begot upon Vairaṇī five thousand sons— daughters endowed with great austerity and capable of sustaining the world.
Dakṣa Prajāpati himself begot them upon Asiknī;
and seeing those illustrious ones desiring to multiply their progeny, [he rejoiced].
The celestial sage Nārada,
whose speech is ever agreeable, spoke these words for their destruction and likewise for his own self-curse.
The sage Kaśyapa, the supreme lord, begot that most excellent son upon the daughter of Dakṣa out of fear of Dakṣa’s curse.
For previously that Nārada, the best of divine seers, was born from Parameṣṭhin; then he was born again from Asiknī Vairaṇī.
He brought forth that bull among sages once again, just as a father does;
by him, Dakṣa’s sons became renowned as the Haryaśvas.
"Having been churned up, they were all destroyed by fate; there is no doubt about this.
Then Dakṣa, possessed of immeasurable prowess, rose up for his destruction."
Having placed the brahman-sages before him, he was entreated by Parameṣṭhin;
thereupon, an agreement was indeed made between Dakṣa and Parameṣṭhin.
"Nārada shall become your son," he said to me regarding the maiden;
thereupon Dakṣa gave his beloved daughter to the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin),
and from her the sage Nārada was born once again out of fear of the curse.
The sages said:
"O best of Sūtas, how were the sons of Prajāpati destroyed by the great seer Nārada? We wish to hear this according to the truth."
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
The sons of Dakṣa, the Haryaśvas, being desirous of increasing their progeny, assembled together; those of great prowess were addressed by Nārada.
Nārada said:
"Alas, you are indeed childish, O sons of Pracetas, for you do not know the true extent of this earth while desiring to create living beings."
"How indeed do you create progeny within, above, and below?
Having heard those words, they departed in all directions.
Even now they do not cease, like rivers flowing into the oceans;
and when the Haryaśvas had perished, Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, [procreated] again.
Then the Lord begot a thousand sons upon Vairaṇī;
those Śabalāśvas desired to increase their progeny.
Urged by Nārada, they all spoke these previously mentioned words to one another: "The great seer has spoken correctly."
"We must go to learn the extent of our brothers' domain; there is no doubt about this. Once we have ascertained the dimensions of the earth, we shall happily create progeny. (BrP 3.22)
They too have set out along that very same path in every direction;
even today they do not return, like rivers flowing into the oceans.
O twice-born ones, from that time forward, a brother who sets out in search of his brother perishes quickly; therefore, a wise man should not do so.
Having learned that those sons were lost, Dakṣa Prajāpati then created sixty daughters from Vairiṇī; so we have heard.
O brahmins, the lord Kaśyapa then accepted them as wives for Soma,
Dharma, and likewise for other great ṛṣis.
He gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
twenty-seven to Soma, and four to Ariṣṭanemi.
Two were born to Bahuputra, two likewise to Aṅgiras, and two to the learned Kṛśāśva; hear their names from me.
O twice-born ones, Arundhatī, Vasu, Yāmī, Lambā, Bhānu, Marutvatī, Saṃkalpā, Muhūrtā, Sādhyā, and Viśvā. BrP_3.29.
These ten are indeed the lawful wives; learn now their offspring:
from Viśvā were born the Viśvedevas, and Sādhyā gave birth to the Sādhyas.
From Marutvatī were born the Maruts; from Vasu were born the Vasus as sons;
the Bhānus were the sons of Bhānu; and the Muhūrtas were born of Muhūrtā.
From Lambā was born Ghoṣa, and from Yamī was born Nāgavīthī;
Arundhatī gave birth to the entire domain of Pṛthivī.
From Saṃkalpā, the soul of the universe was born as Saṃkalpa himself;
and from Nāgavīthī, Vṛṣala was born in the night.
Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, gave away those others who were wives of Soma;
they are all known by the name Nakṣatra and are celebrated among the luminaries.
As for those other renowned gods who have light as their precursor—
the eight who are known as the Vasus— I shall describe them in detail.
Āpa, Dhruva, Soma, Dhava, Anila, Anala,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are remembered as the Vasus by name.
Āpasya’s son was Vaitaṇḍya, as well as Śrama and the weary Muni;
Dhruva’s son was the blessed Kāla, the destroyer of the worlds.
From Soma was born the illustrious Varca, who is full of splendor;
likewise from Dhava came Draviṇa and Hutahavyavaha. From Manoharā were born Śiśira, Prāṇa, and Ramaṇa.
Anila’s wife was Śivā, and her son was Manojava;
Avijñātagati was also [his son], making two sons in total for Anila.
The son of Agni was Kumāra, who was endowed with splendor while in a clump of reeds;
his younger brothers were Śākha, Viśākha, and Naigameya.
The offspring of the Kṛttikās is known as Kārttikeya;
they know the son of Pratyūṣa to be the sage named Devala.
Devala also had two sons who were patient and wise;
Bṛhaspati’s sister, however, was an excellent woman and a speaker of Brahman.
Having attained perfection in yoga, she wandered through the entire world unattached;
she was indeed the wife of Prabhāsa, the eighth of the Vasus.
In her was born the illustrious Viśvakarman, the lord of progeny,
the creator of thousands of crafts, and the architect of the gods.
He was the creator of all ornaments and the best among artisans;
he indeed fashioned the celestial chariots for all the deities.
Human beings subsist upon the craftsmanship of that great-souled one;
Surabhi, moreover, brought forth the eleven Rudras from Kaśyapa.
Through the grace of Mahādeva and purified by asceticism,
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Tvaṣṭṛ, and the heroic Rudra [were born].
Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, Aparājita, Vṛṣākapi, Śambhu, Kapardin, and likewise Raivata; BrP_3.48 //
Mṛgavyādha, Śarva, and Kapālī— O best of the twice-born,
these eleven are renowned as the Rudras, the lords of the three worlds.
O tigers among sages, it is thus declared in the Purāṇa that there are one hundred Rudras of immeasurable splendor, by whom the world of moving and non-moving beings is pervaded.
O best of brahmins, hear now the wives of Kaśyapa Prajāpati:
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Ariṣṭā, Surasā, and Khasā.
O brahmins, Surabhi, Vinatā, Tāmrā, Krodhavaśā, Irā, Kadrū, and Muni— learn now of their offspring.
When the immensely illustrious Cākṣuṣa Manu had appeared,
they gathered together with one another for the benefit of all the worlds.
"Come quickly, O gods; having entered into Aditi, let us be born during a Manvantara. That will be for our welfare."
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Having spoken thus, they were all born during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu from Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, and Aditi, the daughter of Dakṣa.
There, Viṣṇu and Śakra were indeed born once again,
as were Aryaman, Dhātṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, and likewise Pūṣan.
Vivasvat, Savitṛ, Mitra, Varuṇa,
Aṃśa, Bhaga, and the exceedingly radiant [Dhātṛ]— these are remembered as the twelve Ādityas.
The twenty-seven wives of Soma who were declared to be of great vows had offspring who were radiant and possessed immeasurable splendor.
The children of the wives of Ariṣṭanemi were sixteen here;
four Vidyuts are recorded as the offspring of the learned Bahuputra.
In the former period of Cākṣuṣa, the Ṛgvedic hymns honored by the Brahman-sages were remembered,
as were the divine weapons of the celestial sage Kṛśāśva.
Indeed, at the end of a thousand yugas, all these hosts of gods, numbering thirty-three and born of desire, are born once again here.
And for them too, O brahmins, cessation and arising are spoken of,
just as here the rising and setting of the sun occur in the sky.
In this way, those hosts of gods arise age after age;
we have heard that two sons were born to Diti from Kaśyapa.
Hiraṇyakaśipu and the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa were born,
and there was also a daughter, Siṃhikā, who became the wife of Vipracitti.
Her sons were known as the Saiṃhikeyas, who were possessed of great strength;
these four sons of Hiraṇyakaśipu were renowned for their prowess.
Hrāda, Anuhrāda, the heroic Prahrāda, and Saṃhrāda as the fourth were born; likewise, Hrāda was the son of Hradu.
Hrada had two heroic sons, Śiva and Kāla;
and from Virocana, the son of Prahrāda, Bali was born.
O ascetics rich in austerity, Bali had a hundred sons with Bāṇa as the eldest:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Sūrya, Candramas, and Candratāpana.
Kumbhanābha, Gardabhākṣa, Kukṣi, and others such as these were his sons;
among them, Bāṇa was the eldest, possessed of exceeding strength, and dear to Paśupati.
In a former kalpa, Bāṇa propitiated the Lord, the husband of Umā, and requested this boon: "I shall sport by your side. (BrP 3.71)
And the sons of Hiraṇyākṣa were indeed wise and possessed of great strength:
Bharbhara, Śakuni, and likewise Bhūtasaṃtāpana.
Mahānābha, Vikrānta, and likewise Kālanābha—
there were also one hundred sons of Danu, possessed of fierce prowess.
I shall describe those ascetics of great power according to their prominence:
Dvimūrdhan, Śaṅkukarṇa, and the all-pervading Hayaśiras.
Ayomukha, Śambara, Kapila, Vāmana, Mārīci, Maghavan, Ilvala, and Svasṛma; ||| BrP_3.75 |||
Vikṣobhaṇa, Ketu, Ketuvīrya, Śatahrada,
Indrajit, Sarvajit, and likewise Vajranābha.
Ekacakra, the long-armed Tāraka of great strength,
Vaiśvānara, Puloman, Vidrāvaṇa, and Mahāśiras.
Svarbhānu, Vṛṣaparvan, and the powerful Vipracitti—
all these were the sons of Danu, born from Kaśyapa.
Those Dānavas, headed by Vipracitti, were possessed of immense strength;
however, O best of the twice-born, it is impossible to enumerate their sons and grandsons.
Because their number was vast, it is impossible to enumerate their endless sons and grandsons;
Svarbhānu’s daughter was Prabhā, while Śacī was the daughter of Puloman.
Upadīpti was Hayaśiras, Śarmiṣṭhā was the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan,
and both Pulomā and Kālikā were the two daughters of Vaiśvānara.
Bahvapatyā and Mahāpatyā were the wives of Marīci;
from them were born sixty thousand sons who brought joy to the Dānavas.
Endowed with great ascetic power, Marīci begot another one thousand four hundred inhabitants of Hiraṇyapura.
The Paulomas and Kālakeyas were Dānavas of great strength;
indeed, those inhabitants of Hiraṇyapura were incapable of being slain by the gods.
After those who were slain by Savyasācin through the grace of his grandfather,
there were yet other Dānavas of great heroism and extreme ferocity.
Then, from Siṃhikā, the sons of Vipracitti were likewise born;
through the union of Daityas and Dānavas, they were born with fierce prowess.
There were thirteen known as the Saiṃhikeyas, who possessed great strength:
Vaṃśya, Śalya, the powerful Nala, and likewise Bala.
Vātāpi and Namuci, as well as Ilvala and Svasṛma, Añjika and Naraka, and likewise Kālanābha; BrP 3.88.
Saramāna, as well as Svarakalpa and Vīryavān—
these indeed were the preeminent Dānavas who increased the lineage of Danu.
Their sons and grandsons numbered in the hundreds and thousands;
for in the lineage of the Daitya Saṃhrāda were the Nivātakavacas.
Born through great asceticism and possessing purified souls,
thirty million sons of theirs resided in Maṇivatī.
Those six highly fortunate sons of Tāmrā, who were likewise invulnerable even to the gods, were struck down by Arjuna; thus they have been proclaimed.
Krauñcī, Śyenī, Bhāsī, Sugrīvī, Śuci, and Gṛdhrikā—
of these, Krauñcī gave birth to the owls (ulūka) and the night-owls (pratyulūka).
Śyenī gave birth to hawks, Bhāsī to bhāsa birds, Gṛdhry to vultures,
Śuci to flocks of aquatic birds, and Sugrīvī, O best of the twice-born, [to the various species of parrots].
Horses, camels, and donkeys are proclaimed as the offspring of Tāmrā;
and Vinatā had two famous sons, Garuḍa and Aruṇa.
Garuḍa, the best of flyers, was formidable due to his own past deeds;
he begot upon Surasā a thousand serpents of immeasurable power.
O Brahmins, there were thousands of powerful sons of Kadrū, great-souled sky-dwellers with many heads and immeasurable splendor.
Under the power of Suparṇa, the Nāgas were born with many heads,
among whom Śeṣa, Vāsuki, and Takṣaka were always the foremost.
Airāvata, Mahāpadma, both Kambala and Aśvatara,
Elāpattra, Śaṅkha, Karkoṭaka, and Dhanañjaya.
Mahānīla and Mahākarṇa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Balāhaka,
Kuhara and Puṣpadaṃṣṭra, as well as Durmukha and Sumukha.
Śaṅkha, Śaṅkhapāla, Kapila, Vāmana,
Nahuṣa, Śaṅkharoman, Maṇi, and others such as these.
Their sons and grandsons numbered in the hundreds and thousands—
fourteen thousand in all— cruel beings who subsist on wind.
O brahmins, his entire host consists of the lineage of Krodha and all fanged creatures;
those born on land, birds, and aquatic beings are known as the offspring of the Earth.
Surabhi gave birth to cows and likewise to buffalo-cows;
Irā produced trees, creepers, climbing plants, and all varieties of grasses in every way.
Khasā gave birth to the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, while Muni gave birth to the Apsarases;
Ariṣṭā, however, gave birth to the great Siddhas and the Gandharvas of immeasurable power.
These descendants of Kaśyapa, both stationary and moving, have been proclaimed;
their sons and grandsons are numbered in the hundreds and thousands.
O Brahmins, this creation is recorded as having occurred during the Svārociṣa Manvantara,
at the vast and extensive sacrifice of Varuṇa in the great Vaivasvata period.
The creation of progeny by Brahmā while performing sacrifice is now described here,
wherein the seven mind-born Brahman-sages were formerly produced.
The Grandfather himself ordained him as his son;
then, O twice-born ones, there arose a conflict between the gods and the Dānavas.
Diti, whose sons had indeed been destroyed, propitiated Kaśyapa;
and Kaśyapa, his mind being pleased, was duly honored by her.
He invited her to choose a boon, and she then chose this boon:
a son of immeasurable splendor, capable of slaying Indra.
And that one of great asceticism, being entreated, granted him a boon;
and having bestowed the boon, the exceedingly fierce Mārīca spoke:
"Your son shall slay Indra for a hundred autumns, provided that you maintain this vow, remaining devoted to purity. (BrP 3.113)
When the husband, that great ascetic, was addressed with "So be it" by the queen,
O best of sages, she, being pure, conceived a fetus.
Then Kaśyapa, having deposited his seed in Aditi, departed,
leaving behind that most excellent host of gods of immeasurable splendor.
Having withdrawn her invincible splendor, which was indestructible even by the immortals,
she went to the mountains for asceticism, firm in her vows.
And Indra, the subduer of Pāka, remained intent on finding a weakness in her;
when a hundred years had passed since her birth, the infallible one perceived an opening.
Without having performed the purification of her feet, Diti lay down upon her bed and fell asleep; having entered her womb, he [Hiraṇyakaśipu] remained there.
Then Vajrapāṇi cut that embryo into seven pieces;
as the embryo was being split apart by the vajra, it wept aloud.
"Do not weep," Śakra said to him again and again;
yet that embryo split into seven parts, and Indra, enraged, [struck] it once more.
The one who draws out his enemies split each one of them into seven pieces with his very thunderbolt;
O best of the twice-born, they became the gods known as the Maruts.
Just as it was spoken by Maghavan, so did the Maruts become;
thus there were forty-nine gods who became the companions of the wielder of the thunderbolt.
O best of the twice-born, while those beings were thus engaged,
he took pleasure in the hosts of gods of immeasurable splendor, who were the foremost among their classes.
O twice-born ones, Hari bestowed those kingdoms, beginning with Pṛthu, upon the various Prajāpatis in each of their respective lineages in due order.
He is Hari, the Puruṣa, the Hero, Kṛṣṇa, the Victorious, the Lord of Creatures, Parjanya, the Sun, and Ananta; this entire world belongs to him.
O best of the twice-born, for one who correctly understands this creation of beings, there is no fear of returning to this world; how then could there be fear of the next world?
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Having consecrated Pṛthu, the son of Vena, as the sovereign lord of kings,
the Grandfather then proceeded to assign the various kingdoms in due order.
He consecrated Soma in the sovereignty over the twice-born, the plants, the lunar mansions and the planets, as well as over sacrifices and ascetic penances.
He appointed Varuṇa to the sovereignty over the waters, Vaiśravaṇa as the lord of kings,
Viṣṇu among the Ādityas, and Pāvaka among the Vasus.
Among the Prajāpatis, he chose Dakṣa; among the Maruts, Vāsava;
and among the Daityas and Dānavas, Prahrāda of immeasurable splendor.
He consecrated Vaivasvata Yama in the sovereignty over the ancestors,
as well as over the yakṣas, the rākṣasas, and likewise the kings of the earth.
Of all spirits and piśācas, he is the Lord of the Mountains (Śiva) who bears the trident;
of mountains, Himavat; and of rivers, the Ocean.
He made Citraratha the lord and sovereign of the Gandharvas;
he made Vāsuki the lord of the Nāgas, and Takṣaka of the serpents.
Then he appointed Airāvata as the king of elephants,
Uccaiḥśravas as the king of horses, and Garuḍa as the king of birds.
Then he consecrated the tiger as the lord of wild beasts, the bull as the master of cattle,
and the Plakṣa tree as the king of the lords of the forest.
Having thus divided the kingdoms in due order, the Grandfather,
the Lord, then established the guardians of the quarters.
In the eastern direction, he consecrated Sudhanvan, the son of the patriarch Vairāja, as the king and guardian of that quarter.
In the southern direction,
he consecrated as king the son of the patriarch Kardama, named Śaṅkhapada.
In the western direction, he consecrated the high-souled King Ketumān, the son of Rajas, as the unshakable sovereign.
Likewise, he consecrated Hiraṇyaroman as the invincible king of Parjanya Prajāpati in the northern quarter.
By them, this entire earth— with its seven continents and its cities—
is even today protected according to their respective regions through righteousness.
Then King Pṛthu, the lord of men, was consecrated in his kingdom by these sovereigns according to the ritual prescribed in the Vedas.
Then, when the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara of immeasurable luster had passed,
he assigned sovereignty over the earth to Vaivasvata Manu.
I shall relate in detail the account of Vaivasvata Manu,
for your benefit, if you desire to hear it here;
this great foundation is established within that Purāṇa.
The sages said:
O Lomaharṣaṇa, recount in detail the birth of Pṛthu,
and how this earth was milked by that high-souled one.
Just as it was milked by men, and by the gods, and by the great seers;
and by the Daityas and the Nāgas, and by the Yakṣas, and by the trees.
Just as the earth was milked by the mountains, the piśācas, the gandharvas, the best of the twice-born,
and the rākṣasas of great being.
O you of noble vows, you should describe to us in due order those particular vessels,
the specific qualities of the calves' milk, and the milker.
And for what reason, my dear, was the hand of Veṇa formerly rubbed by the enraged great sages? Proclaim that cause as well.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
"Listen, O bulls among the twice-born; with one-pointed minds and self-restrained, I shall proclaim in detail the account of Pṛthu, the son of Vena, for the sake of merit."

O Brahmins, I would not proclaim this to one who is impure, nor to one of base mind, nor to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who lacks vows, nor to an ungrateful person, nor to one who acts against my welfare.
Listen now exactly as it is to this secret, proclaimed by the sages, which leads to heaven, brings fame, longevity, and prosperity, and is in perfect accord with the Vedas. BrP 4.26.
Whoever, having paid homage to the Brahmins, should constantly recite this detailed account of Pṛthu, the son of Vena, shall not grieve over what has been done or left undone.
In former times, there was a lord who protected the Dharma, equal to Atri;
born in the lineage of Atri, he was the Prajāpati named Aṅga.
His son was Vena, a lord of creatures who was not particularly skilled in dharma;
he was born of Sunīthā, the daughter of Mṛtyu.
Due to that fault of his maternal grandfather, the son of the son of Time (Yama) cast his own duty behind him and became addicted to lust and greed.
That king broke the bounds established by righteousness;
transgressing the Vedic laws, he became devoted to unrighteousness.
While that Prajāpati reigned, the subjects were devoid of Vedic study and the utterance of "vaṣaṭ," and the deities did not drink the Soma offered in sacrifices.
"One must not sacrifice, nor must one offer oblations"—this was the cruel vow of that Prajāpati when destruction was at hand. (BrP 4.33)
O descendant of Bhṛgu, I am the one to be worshipped, the sacrificer, and the sacrifice itself;
the sacrifice is to be performed in me, and the oblation is likewise to be offered into me.
Then all the great seers, headed by Marīci, spoke to him as he was acting improperly and transgressing the bounds of propriety: BrP_4.35 //
"We shall enter upon initiation for many groups of years;
do not practice unrighteousness, O Veṇa, for this is the eternal dharma."
"Born here in the lineage of Atri, you are undoubtedly a Prajāpati;
'I shall protect the subjects,' such was the vow made by you in this world."
To all those great ṛṣis who were speaking thus,
the evil-minded Veṇa, ignorant of what is beneficial, then laughed and spoke these words.
Veṇa said:
Who else is the creator of dharma, or whose words should I listen to?
For who on earth is equal to me in learning, heroism, austerity, and truth?
"You are indeed deluded and deprived of your senses; you do not know me, the source of all beings and especially of all phenomena."
If I so desired, I could burn the earth or likewise flood it with waters;
I could indeed obstruct both heaven and earth—of this there is no need for deliberation.
When the king could not be dissuaded from his course due to delusion and arrogance,
the great seers then became enraged at Veṇa.
Having restrained that mighty one as he quivered with great strength, those high-souled ones, filled with wrath,
then churned his left thigh.
While that [sacrificial fire] was being churned, indeed, from the thigh of the king there was born a man who was exceedingly short and black in complexion.
O best of the twice-born, he stood there terrified with palms joined in reverence;
seeing him so distressed, Atri then said to him, "Sit down."
O best of speakers, he became the founder of the Niṣāda lineage;
he also created the fishermen (dhīvara) born from Veṇa’s impurity.
And those other Brahmins who dwell in the Vindhyas as well as those who take refuge in the mountains, who delight in unrighteousness, are indeed defiled by the sin of the bamboo-reed (veṇa).
Then once again, those high-souled ones, filled with fury and stirred to action, churned Vena’s right hand as if it were a fire-drill.
From his hand was born Pṛthu, resembling a blazing fire,
shining with his own body like Agni himself in a state of flame.
Then, for the sake of protection, he took up the great-sounding bow named Ajagava,
as well as divine arrows and armor of great luster.
When he was born, all beings were filled with joy on every side;
the highly fortunate ones gathered together, while Veṇa ascended to the third heaven.
O Brahmins, by that high-souled and virtuous son who had been born,
that tiger among men was then saved from the hell named Put.
Then the oceans and the rivers, bringing jewels from every quarter and waters for the purpose of consecration, all approached him.
And the blessed Grandfather, together with the gods and the descendants of Aṅgiras, [beheld] all beings, both stationary and moving, in every way.
Having assembled, they then consecrated the son of Vena as lord of men;
by that great king of kings, the subjects were delighted.
Then that majestic and powerful Pṛthu, son of Vena, was duly consecrated into the supreme sovereignty over kings by those experts in the Dharma.
His subjects were not won over by his father, but they were won over by him;
because of that affection for him, the name "Rāja" (King) originated for him.
As he advanced toward the ocean, the waters solidified for him;
the mountains yielded the way, and his banner suffered no breakage.
The earth yields crops without being ploughed; foods are accomplished by mere thought;
cows grant all desires; and in every leaf-cup there is honey.
At that very time, during the auspicious sacrifice of the Grandfather (Brahmā),
the high-minded Sūta was born at the Sūti ceremony on the day of the Sautya rite.
At that very same great sacrifice, the wise Māgadha was born;
the two of them were summoned there by the great seers for the purpose of praising Pṛthu.
Then all the sages said: "Let this king be praised;
this deed is worthy of you both, and this lord of men is a fitting recipient."
Then the Sūta and the Māgadha said to all those ṛṣis:
"We two please both the gods and the ṛṣis by means of our own duties."
"O twice-born ones, we do not know his deeds, nor his name, nor his characteristics, nor his glory,
by which we might offer praise for this radiant king."
The sages then enjoined them both, saying, "Let that which the mighty Pṛthu later performed be praised through prophecies. (BrP 4.65)
From that time forward, O best of sages, blessings were indeed employed in panegyrics throughout the world by sūtas, māgadhas, and bards.
At the conclusion of their praise, Pṛthu, the lord of subjects, being well-pleased, bestowed the Anūpa region upon Sūta and Magadha upon Māgadha.
Seeing him, the wise subjects, filled with supreme joy, said:
"This lord of men will be the provider of livelihoods for you all."
Then, at the command of the great seers, the subjects approached the high-souled son of Vena, saying, "Provide for our livelihood."
Thus pursued by the subjects, yet desiring to act for their welfare,
the powerful one took up his bow and arrows and rushed toward the earth.
Then, terrified by the fear of Vainya, the Earth fled away, having become a cow;
Pṛthu, taking up his bow, pursued her as she ran.
Having traveled through the worlds beginning with the world of Brahmā out of fear of the son of Vena, she then beheld the son of Vena before her,
holding his bow.
With blazing, sharpened arrows, he [pierced] from all sides that great-souled one of radiant splendor,
a master of great yoga who was unassailable even by the immortals.
Finding no protection,
she then approached the son of Vena with her palms joined in reverence, she who was worthy of worship by the three worlds.
He said to the son of Vena: "Do you not perceive the unrighteousness in the killing of a woman?
O King, how will you sustain the subjects without me?"
The worlds are established in me, O King; this universe is sustained by me. Know this, O ruler of the earth: upon my destruction, all creatures would perish.
"You ought not to kill me, O protector of the earth, if you desire the welfare of all creatures; listen to these words of mine."
All undertakings that are commenced with skillful means succeed;
find a means by which you may sustain this progeny.
"O King, even having slain me, you will not be capable of nourishing your subjects;
therefore, O high-minded one, restrain your anger and I shall become favorable."
They say that a woman is not to be slain even among those born of animal wombs;
if this is so, O protector of the earth, you ought not to abandon righteousness.
Having heard these various words, the high-minded and righteous king restrained his anger and spoke thus to the earth: BrP_4.81 //
Pṛthu said:
"He who, for the sake of one person— whether himself or another—
should kill many living beings, incurs infinite sin in this world."
When that inauspicious being has been slain, many prosper in happiness; O blessed lady, when it is killed, there is neither mortal sin nor minor offense.
Therefore, O Earth, for the sake of all creatures, I shall slay you if you do not today perform what is for the welfare of the world according to my word.
Having slain you today with an arrow for being averse to my command,
I shall manifest myself and personally sustain the subjects.
Therefore, abiding by my command, O best among the upholders of dharma,
restore all living beings to life, for you are indeed capable of sustaining them.
"Moreover, become my daughter; then I shall restrain this arrow of terrible appearance which is raised for the purpose of slaying you."
Vasudhā said:
"O hero, I shall accomplish all this without a doubt;
however, look for a calf for me, so that I, being full of maternal affection, may yield milk."
And make me level everywhere, O best among the upholders of dharma, so that my flowing milk may nourish everything on all sides. (BrP 4.89)
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Then the son of Vena pushed aside mountains by the hundreds of thousands with the tip of his bow; by that means, the mountains were displaced.
Indeed, in the previous dissolution, on this uneven surface of the earth,
there was at that time no distribution of cities or villages.
There were no crops, no cattle-rearing, no agriculture, and no trade routes;
there was neither truth nor falsehood, neither greed nor envy.
O brahmins, since the Vaivasvata interval has now arrived, the origin of all this indeed begins from the son of Vena.
O twice-born ones, wherever that land was level at that time,
there all the subjects chose to make their dwelling.
At that time, the food of living beings consisted of fruits and roots;
we have heard that they were beset by great hardship.
Having then conceived of the lord Svāyambhuva Manu as his calf,
that tiger among men milked the earth into his own hand.
The powerful Pṛthu, son of Vena, [caused] all species of grain to grow;
by means of that food, all creatures subsist even today in every way.
Then the sages, the gods, the ancestors, as well as the reptiles,
the Daityas, Yakṣas, Puṇyajanas, Gandharvas, mountains, and trees [all gathered].
In ancient times, O best of the twice-born, these sages indeed milked the earth;
their milk, calf, vessel, and milker were each distinct.
O twice-born ones, for the sages, Soma was the calf, Bṛhaspati the milker,
their milk was austerity and sacred knowledge, and the Vedic meters were the vessel.
The golden vessel of the gods is their calf, Śatakratu;
the milk is indeed strength-bestowing, and the blessed Sun is the milker.
For the ancestors, the vessel was made of silver, the powerful Yama was the calf,
Antaka was the milker, and their milk is known as nectar (sudhā).
Among the Nāgas, Takṣaka is the calf; the vessel is known as the gourd (alābu);
the milker is the Nāga Airāvata; and their milk is said to be poison.
Madhu was the milker for the Asuras; it is remembered that their milk consisted of illusion (māyā). Virocana was the calf, and the vessel was indeed made of iron.
The raw vessel for the Yakṣas is indeed Vatsa; the lord Vaiśravaṇa is the milker, and Rajatanābha is the milk, which is invisibility itself.
Sumālī was the calf of the lords of the Rākṣasas, blood was the milk,
Rajatanābha was the milker, and the skull was the vessel.
For the Gandharvas, Citraratha is the calf, the lotus is the vessel,
Suruci is the milker, and their milk is known as pure fragrance.
The vessel was the mountain Śaila, and the milk consisted of the mountains, gems, and medicinal herbs;
Himavat was the calf, and the great mountain Meru was the milker.
The Plakṣa tree is the calf among trees, while the flowering Śāla tree is the milker;
the vessel is made of Palāśa wood, and the milk is the regrowth of what was cut or burnt.
This Earth is the nurse, the creator, and the purifier;
she is the foundation and the very source of all that is moving and unmoving.
This earth, renowned throughout the world as far as the ocean's edge, was a cow that milked all desires and caused all crops to grow.
Because she was completely drenched with the fat of Madhu and Kaiṭabha,
this goddess is called Medinī by those who discourse on Brahman.
Then, O twice-born ones, by the acceptance of King Pṛthu, the son of Vena,
she attained the status of his daughter and is called the goddess Earth (Pṛthivī).
The earth was divided and purified by Pṛthu;
it became prosperous, abounding in grain and mines, and adorned with cities and towns.
Such was the power of that king, the son of Vena, the best of monarchs;
he was undoubtedly worthy of homage and worship by all the hosts of living beings.
And by the highly fortunate Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
Pṛthu alone— being the eternal source of the Brahman— is to be saluted.
And by illustrious kings who desire sovereignty here on earth,
the majestic Pṛthu, son of Vena— the first king— must be saluted.
Moreover, even by warriors who are valiant and desirous of victory in battle,
the Primordial King, the first of monarchs, should be saluted.
For whatever warrior goes to battle after having praised King Pṛthu,
he emerges safely from that terrible conflict and becomes possessed of fame.
Even by wealthy Vaiśyas who follow the Vaiśya way of life,
Pṛthu alone— the giver of livelihoods and possessor of great fame— is to be saluted.
In the same way, Śūdras who are pure and serve the three higher castes must likewise pay homage to Pṛthu, if they desire the highest welfare in this world.
These specific calves, the milkers, the milk itself, and the vessels have been described by me; what more shall I describe to you?
The sages said:
O Lomaharṣaṇa of great intelligence, recount in detail all the Manvantaras and their prior creation.
O Sūta, we desire to hear in truth the number of Manus, the duration of time, and the Manvantaras. (BrP 5.2)
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
O brahmins, it is not possible to describe the details of all the Manvantaras even in hundreds of years; therefore, O twice-born ones, listen to them in brief.
First was Svāyambhuva Manu, then Svārociṣa Manu,
as well as Auttami, Tāmasa, Raivata, and Cākṣuṣa.
And, O brahmins, Vaivasvata is currently called Manu; likewise Sāvarṇi, Raibhya, and Raucya are Manus as well. (BrP 5.5)
In the same way, O twice-born ones, four Manus named Merusāvarṇi are recorded as having passed, those who are present, and likewise those who are yet to come.
These Manus have been recounted to you by me exactly as they were heard;
now I shall proclaim their sages, as well as their sons and the hosts of gods.
Marīci, the venerable Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, Kratu,
Pulastya, and Vasiṣṭha— these seven are the sons of Brahmā.
Likewise, O twice-born ones, in the northern direction are the Seven Sages:
Āgneya, Agnibāhu, Medhya, Medhātithi, and Vasu.
Jyotiṣmat, Dyutimat, Havya, Savala, and the one named Putra—
these ten of great prowess were the sons of Svāyambhuva Manu.
O sages, this indeed is declared to be the first Manvantara;
[its seven ṛṣis were] Aurva, the son of Vasiṣṭha, Stamba, and Kaśyapa.
Prāṇa, Bṛhaspati, Datta, Atri, and Cyavana—
these great sages, O Brahmins, are proclaimed by Vāyu as observers of the great vow.
And in the Svārociṣa interval, the gods were known as the Tuṣitas;
Havighna, Sukṛti, Jyotis, Āpas, and Mūrti are also recorded [as their names].
Pratīta, Nabhasya, Nabha, and likewise Ūrja—
these, O Brahmins, were the sons of the high-souled Manu Svārociṣa.
These protectors of the earth, endowed with great heroism and prowess, have been proclaimed;
O brahmins, this second Manvantara has thus been described by me.
I shall now declare this third [topic]; understand it, O best of the twice-born!
There were seven sons of Vasiṣṭha, renowned as the Vāsiṣṭhas. (BrP 5.16)
The sons of Hiraṇyagarbha, born of vigor and possessed of great luster—the sages mentioned here by me—listen as they are being proclaimed. (BrP 5.17)
Śuci, Śukra, Sahas, Nabhasya, and Nabhas—
these are the Bhānus, the gods in that Manvantara, as it has been declared.
O best of the twice-born, I shall now describe to you the fourth Manvantara: Kāvya, Pṛthu, Agni, Jahnu, and Dhātṛ.
O twice-born ones, there were the seven ṛṣis, Kapīvan and Akapīvan;
O brahmins, their sons and grandsons are celebrated in the Purāṇa, O twice-born ones.
Likewise, during the interval of the Manu Tāmasa, there were the hosts of gods:
Dyuti, Tapasya, Sutapas, Tapobhūta, and Sanātana.
Taporatir, Akalmāṣa, Tanvī, Dhanvī, and Paraṃtapa—
these are proclaimed as the ten sons of Tāmasa Manu.
O best of sages, this fourth interval was proclaimed by Vāyu;
Devabāhu, Yadudhra, and the sage Vedaśiras were [the lords] there.
Hiraṇyaroman, Parjanya, and Soma-ja Ūrdhvabāhu,
as well as Satyanetra and Ātreya— these are the other seven ṛṣis.
The gods were the Abhūtarajasas, and the Prakṛtis are likewise remembered;
this interval of Manu is called Vāriplava and Raibhya.
Now, O sons, understand these words as I speak them to you:
he who is steadfast, immutable, disciplined, a seer of reality, and free from worldly longing.
Āraṇya, Prakāśa, Nirmoha, Satyavāk, and Kṛtī were the sons of Raivata Manu; this is the fifth interval (antara).
I shall now fully declare the sixth; understand it, O best of the twice-born:
Bhṛgu, Nabhas, Vivasvat, Sudhāman, and likewise Virajas. (BrP 5.29)
Atināman and Sahiṣṇu— these seven great ṛṣis,
O brahmins, are remembered as the gods during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu.
O Brahmins, those inhabitants of heaven are indeed renowned from childhood as distinct; they are known as the five classes of gods, called by the name Lekhas.
The sons of the seer Aṅgiras were ten highly renowned sons of great soul and great power, the best of sages, born of Nāḍvalā.
The Brahmins beginning with Ruru belong to the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu;
this is declared the sixth Manvantara. Now learn of the seventh.
Atri, the venerable Vasiṣṭha, and Kaśyapa the great ṛṣi;
likewise Gautama, Bharadvāja, and Viśvāmitra.
Likewise, the son of the high-souled Ṛcīka was the blessed Jamadagni; these seven are currently ṛṣis in heaven.
The Sādhyas, the Rudras, the Viśvedevas, the Vasus, and likewise the Maruts;
the Ādityas and also the two Aśvins are recorded as the deities of the Vaivasvata [Manvantara].
These ten sons, headed by Ikṣvāku, belong to the high-souled Manu Vaivasvata in the present interval.
O twice-born ones, the sons and grandsons of these great sages of mighty luster who have been thus glorified dwell in all directions.
In all the Manvantaras, there were previously seven groups of seven [sages] each,
for the purpose of establishing dharma in the world and for the protection of the world.
When a manvantara has passed, four groups of seven,
having performed their duties, go to heaven, to the stainless world of Brahmā.
Furthermore, O twice-born ones, others endowed with austerity fill that station;
both those of the past and those of the present do so in this sequence.
And these seven great sages who are remembered as yet to come,
O twice-born ones, shall appear here upon reaching the interval of Manu Sāvarṇa in heaven.
Rāma, Vyāsa, and likewise Ātreya—these were radiant and deeply learned;
so too was Bhāradvāja’s son, the son of Droṇa, Aśvatthāman, who possessed great splendor.
Gautama and Ajara, Gautama named Śaradvat,
Kauśika, Gālava, Aurva, and Kāśyapa.
These seven great-souled ones will be the best of sages in the future:
Vairī, Adhvarīvan, Śamana, Dhṛtimān, and Vasu.
Ariṣṭa, Adhṛṣṭa, Vājī, and Sumati—
these will be the sons of Sāvarṇi Manu, O best of sages.
By reciting these at dawn, a man’s happiness increases;
he attains great renown and shall become long-lived.
O Brahmins, these seven Manvantaras have thus been described to you in truth; now hear in brief about those that are yet to come.
O wise ones, learn now of those five Sāvarṇa Manus;
one of them is Vaivasvata, while four belong to Prajāpati.
These sons of Parameṣṭhin, who became the Brahmins known as the Merusāvarṇyas,
were indeed the grandsons of Dakṣa and the sons of his beloved daughter, O King.
Endowed with great austerity on the summit of Mount Meru,
the son of the Prajāpati Ruci, possessed of great luster, is known as the Manu named Raucya.
And the son of Ruci, named Bhautya, was begotten by the goddess Bhūti;
these seven are recorded as the Manus in this kalpa who have yet to come.
O best of the twice-born, they must protect this entire earth, with its seven continents and its cities, for a full thousand yugas.
And Prajāpati, through his ascetic power, effects their constant dissolution;
those periods are said to consist of seventy-one full yugas.
The period of a Manu is said to consist of the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages.
These fourteen Manus have been described as the increasers of fame.
In all the Vedas along with the Purāṇas, the lords of creatures and the wise are sovereign; the proclamation of their names is auspicious.
In each Manvantara there are destructions, and at the end of those destructions there are new creations;
indeed, it is impossible to state their limit even in hundreds of years.
O twice-born ones,
O best of the twice-born, the destructions of created beings and of the dissolution itself are heard of throughout the Manvantaras.
The gods remain there together with the seven seers,
endowed with austerity, celibacy, and sacred learning.
When a full thousand yugas have passed, the kalpa is said to be complete;
therein all beings are consumed by the rays of the sun.
Placing Brahmā at their head, O twice-born ones, together with the hosts of Ādityas,
they enter the Lord Hari-Nārāyaṇa, the foremost of the gods.
The unmanifest, eternal God is the creator of all beings again and again at the ends of the kalpas; this entire world belongs to him.
O tigers among sages, here I shall proclaim to you the creation of the present Manu Vaivasvata, who is of great splendor.
In this context, as we speak in connection with the lineage, there is an ancient account told of where that high-souled Hari, the Lord, was born into the Vṛṣṇi clan.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
O best of the twice-born, Vivasvat was born from Kaśyapa through Dākṣāyaṇī;
the goddess Saṃjñā, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, became the wife of that Vivasvat.
Renowned throughout the three worlds as Sureśvarī,
that illustrious lady was indeed the wife of the high-souled Lord Mārtaṇḍa.
Endowed with great splendor through her excellent asceticism, the woman named Saṃjñā was not satisfied with her husband’s form, though he was possessed of beauty and youth.
For that form of the sun’s orb,
scorched by its own intense radiance upon his limbs, indeed did not appear particularly beautiful.
Out of affection, Kāśyapa did not say, "This one is dead," because he was unaware; therefore, he is called Mārtaṇḍa.
But the splendor of that son of Kaśyapa was always even greater than that of Vivasvat, by which he scorched the three worlds.
O Brahmins, the Sun, the best among those who shine, begot three offspring upon Saṃjñā: two lords of progeny and a daughter.
In former times, Manu Vaivasvata was the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) and the deity of the Śrāddha rites;
Yama and Yamunā were born as his twin children.
But having seen that dark-complexioned form of Vivasvat, Saṃjñā, unable to endure her own shadow, then created Savarṇā.
O best of the twice-born, that Saṃjñā was composed of illusion; and Chāyā, having arisen from her shadow, stood with palms joined in reverence, bowing before Saṃjñā.
She said, "Tell me, O lady of pure smiles, what must be done by me? I stand at your command; instruct me, O woman of excellent complexion. (BrP 6.11)
Saṃjñā said:
"I shall go to my own father's abode; may you be blessed.
You must dwell in my house yourself, free from all apprehension."
"These two boys of mine and this slender-waisted girl are to be entrusted to you;
however, this matter must never be told to the Blessed One."
Savarṇā said:
"O Goddess, until my hair is seized and until a curse is pronounced, I shall never speak [of this]. Salutations to you; go, O Goddess, as you please."
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Having thus instructed Savarṇā, and having been told "So be it" by her,
that ascetic woman went into the presence of Tvaṣṭṛ as if filled with shame.
But that auspicious woman, having approached her father, was rebuked by him;
she was repeatedly urged, "Go back to the presence of your husband."
Then, having assumed the form of a mare and concealed her blameless beauty,
she went to the Northern Kurus and began to graze upon the grass.
Then, while reflecting upon the second name,
"He who is to be known," Āditya begot a son equal to himself.
O Brahmins, because this lord was considered similar to his predecessor Manu,
he became Manu by name and is also called Sāvarṇa.
O Brahmins, that second son of hers was to be known as Śanaiścara;
and then Saṃjñā, the daughter of the Earth, [gave] her own son [that name].
Manu indeed showed her even greater affection than he did toward his elder sons;
however, while Manu tolerated that behavior, Yama did not tolerate it.
O sinless one, out of anger, childishness, or perhaps due to the inevitability of what was destined to happen,
Yama, the son of Vivasvat, threatened Saṃjñā with his foot.
Then, out of anger and being deeply distressed, Sāvarṇi’s mother cursed him: "May this foot of yours fall off! (BrP 6.23).
Yama, however, with palms joined in reverence, reported all of that to his father,
being greatly agitated by the fear of a curse and filled with apprehension due to the words of Saṃjñā.
"O twice-born ones, he spoke to his father: 'May this curse be averted;
indeed, one must treat all sons with the affection due to a mother. (BrP 6.25)
This very woman, having cast us out here, desires to unite with Vivasvat;
though my foot was raised against her, it was not brought down upon her body.
Whether out of childishness, or through fickleness, or from delusion, you ought to forgive that.
O Lord of the World, best among those who radiate heat, I have been cursed by my mother;
yet, O Lord of Cows, by your grace, may my foot not fall [to the ground].
Vivasvat said:
"Without doubt, my son, there must be a great cause for this,
by which anger has taken possession of you, who are a knower of dharma and a speaker of truth."
It is not possible to make these words of your mother false;
the worms, having taken the flesh, shall indeed go to the earth.
"Thus your mother’s word shall indeed be made true;
by the averting of the curse, you too shall be saved."
And Āditya said to Saṃjñā: "Why is it that among your children, who are indeed equal, you show such excessive affection toward only one? (BrP 6.31)
But she, avoiding him, did not tell Vivasvat;
and he, concentrating his mind through yoga, perceived the truth.
O best of sages, although the Blessed One desired to curse her, he did not curse her;
instead, that best of sages seized her by the hair.
Then he related everything exactly as it had happened to Vivasvat;
having heard that, Vivasvat became enraged and went to Tvaṣṭṛ.
Having seen him, and having honored the god of fire according to the prescribed rule,
he then pacified him who was desirous of burning everything down in his wrath.
Tvaṣṭṛ said:
"This form of yours, possessed by excessive brilliance, does not shine;
unable to endure it, Saṃjñā wanders in the grassy forest."
For today, O Lord of the Cowherds, by resorting to yoga, you shall behold that wife of yours, who is of auspicious conduct, praiseworthy, and endowed with the power of yoga.
"If it be agreeable to you, O Lord, and if it be my wish,
O subduer of enemies, I shall today transform your form into one that is beautiful."
Then, O twice-born ones, Tvaṣṭṛ, having placed the discus upon a lathe, whetted that brilliance of the sun Vivasvat because he had consented to it.
Then that form, illuminated by the concentrated radiance,
shone even more intensely, appearing far more beautiful than the most beautiful thing.
Then, employing his yogic power, he beheld his own wife as a mare,
invincible to all beings by virtue of her splendor and her self-restraint.
O brahmins, as she was moving about without fear in the form of a mare,
the Blessed One, assuming the form of a horse, united with her at her mouth.
Suspecting her of being unfaithful to another man as she was making amorous gestures,
he expelled that semen from Vivasvat through his two nostrils.
From her were born two gods, the Aśvins, the best of physicians;
Nāsatya and Dasra are remembered as the two Aśvins.
These two were the sons of Mārtaṇḍa, the eighth Prajāpati;
and Bhāskara showed himself to her with his lovely form.
O best of sages, she was delighted merely upon seeing her husband;
Yama, however, had his mind deeply distressed by that deed.
The King of Dharma delighted these subjects through righteousness;
by that auspicious deed, he of supreme luster attained [great renown].
O you whose wealth is asceticism, Manu Sāvarṇi was the sovereign lord of the Pitṛs as well as a world-protector (lokapāla). He was indeed a Prajāpati.
When that Sāvarṇika Manvantara has arrived, he is to be manifested;
indeed, even today he constantly performs penance upon the summit of Mount Meru.
His brother was Śanaiścara (Saturn), who indeed attained the status of a planet;
and with that splendor, Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned the discus of Viṣṇu.
That [bow] was unassailable in battle, intended for the destruction of the Dānavas;
and she too, the illustrious maiden Yamī, was younger [than her].
And she became the Yamunā, the best of rivers, the purifier of the world;
she is called Manu in the world, and she is also called Sāvarṇi.
His second son was Śanaiścara, the brother of Manu;
he indeed attained the status of a planet, being honored by all the worlds.
The best of men who hears this account of the birth of the gods shall be liberated from calamity upon encountering it, and shall attain great renown.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Vaivasvata Manu had nine sons who were indeed equal to him:
Ikṣvāku, Nābhāga, Dhṛṣṭa, and Śaryāti.
Nariṣyanta was the sixth, Prāṃśu was the seventh, and Riṣṭa,
Karūṣa, and Pṛṣadhra— these nine, O best of sages, were his sons.
O sages, the high-minded Manu, the lord of creatures, desiring sons, performed a sacrifice to Mitra and Varuṇa even before this.
O twice-born ones, while those many sons had not yet been born,
and while that sacrifice was still in progress, O best of the twice-born.
In the portion belonging to Mitra and Varuṇa, Manu offered an oblation;
there appeared a woman wearing celestial garments and adorned with divine ornaments.
And according to sacred tradition, Ilā was born with a divine physique;
at that time, Manu, the wielder of the rod of punishment, addressed her simply as "Ilā."
"Follow me, O blessed lady," Ilā replied to that Prajāpati who was desirous of a son, speaking these words consistent with dharma.
She said: "O best of speakers, I was born from the portions of Mitra and Varuṇa;
I shall go back into their presence—do not cause me to be struck down by dharma."
Having spoken thus to the god Manu, Ilā, the woman of beautiful limbs, approached Mitrāvaruṇa and, with palms joined in reverence, addressed these words to them.
She said:
"O gods, I have been born as a portion of you both; what may I do for you? And I was told by Manu: 'Follow after me. (BrP 7.10)
O best of the twice-born, both Mitra and Varuṇa spoke thus to that virtuous Ilā, who was speaking in such a manner and was devoted to dharma.
Mitra and Varuṇa said: "O fair-hipped one of excellent complexion, we are pleased with this righteousness of yours, as well as with your humility, self-restraint, and truthfulness."
"O highly fortunate one, you shall attain fame between us two as our daughter."
"And you yourself, O beautiful one, shall become the son who continues the lineage of Manu,
renowned in the three worlds as Sudyumna."
Beloved by the world, virtuous in character, and the enhancer of Manu’s lineage—
hearing this, she turned back as she was returning from her father’s presence.
O brahmins, having approached her in private, Budha invited her for sexual union; from that son of Soma, Budha, Purūravas was born of her.
Having given birth to him, Ilā then became Sudyumna;
and Sudyumna had three most righteous heirs.
O twice-born ones, Utkala, Gaya, and Vinatāśva [were the sons];
O brahmins, the western regions belong to Vinatāśva, while the land of Utkala belongs to Utkala.
O tigers among sages, the eastern direction is known as Gayā of Gaya;
O brahmins, when Manu had entered [the womb] of the Sun, the subduer of enemies.
Furthermore, Ikṣvāku, the eldest heir, divided this earth into ten parts for that kṣatriya lineage and obtained the Middle Country.
However, because he was a maiden, Sudyumna did not obtain this kingdom;
yet, by the word of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, he resided in Pratiṣṭhāna.
O best of the twice-born, having attained the establishment of the Dharma-king Sudyumna,
that highly illustrious one bestowed the kingdom upon Purūravas.
O best of sages, the son of Manu, endowed with the characteristics of both female and male,
bore that [name] as Ilā and was likewise renowned as Sudyumna.
O twice-born ones, the Śakas were the sons of Nariṣyanta,
while the son of Nābhāga was Ambarīṣa, the most excellent among the best of kings.
From Dhṛṣṭa came the Dhārṣṭakas, a kṣatriya lineage proud in battle;
and from Karūṣa came the Kārūṣas, kṣatriyas intoxicated by war.
The sons of Nābhāga and Dhṛṣṭa were Kṣatriyas who attained the status of Vaiśyas.
Prāṃśu had one son known as Prajāpati.
The heir of Nariṣyanta was King Daṇḍadhara Yama;
Śaryāti, however, had a pair of children, among whom the one named Ānarta became renowned.
There was a son, a daughter named Sukanyā, and she became the wife of Cyavana.
The heir of Ānarta, however, was the highly effulgent one named Raiva.
The realm was Ānarta, and his capital was the city of Kuśasthalī;
Raivata’s son was the righteous Kakudmin.
He had an eldest son who, having obtained the kingdom of Kuśasthalī,
heard the Gāndharva [hymn] from Brahmā in his presence along with his daughters.
O twice-born ones, what was but a moment for the god became many yugas;
then he returned to his own city, which was surrounded by the Yādavas.
He built the delightful city named Dvāravatī, which possessed many gates and was protected by the Bhojas,
Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas, led by Vasudeva.
O best of the twice-born, having understood the matter exactly as it was, Raivata then gave that maiden named Subhadrā, also known as Revatī, to Baladeva.
Having given [the gift], he went to the peak of Meru and remained established in asceticism;
Rāma too, the righteous-souled one, rejoiced happily together with Revatī.
The sages said: O high-minded one, how was it that after so many yugas had passed,
old age did not overtake Revatī or Kakudmin Raivata?
How did the lineage of that Śaryāti remain on earth even until today after he had gone to Mount Meru? We wish to hear this according to the truth.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
"O best of sages, O eternally sinless ones, neither old age, nor hunger, nor thirst, nor death exists there; the wheel of the seasons has no power in the world of Brahmā."
When Kakudmin Raivata had indeed departed for the heavenly world, [the earth remained].
O brahmins, that Kuśasthalī was seized by the Puṇyajanas, the Rākṣasas;
yet that righteous and high-souled one had a hundred brothers.
Being slaughtered by the Rākṣasas, O unshakable ones,
that hundred of brothers fled in all directions, O best of Brahmins, as they were thus put to flight.
O best of the twice-born, their lineage was indeed very great in various places;
for among them, O foremost of sages, were those renowned as the Śaryātas.
Those Kṣatriyas, endowed with virtues and renowned in all directions,
entered every thicket with their great power on all sides.
The two sons of Nābhāga and Ariṣṭa were Vaiśyas who attained the status of Brahmins;
from Karūṣa, however, came the Kārūṣas, Kṣatriyas fierce in battle.
O best of the twice-born, Pṛṣadhra, having harmed his guru’s cow, fell into the state of a Śūdra due to a curse; these nine have thus been proclaimed.
O best of sages,
O brahmins, Ikṣvāku was the son born to the sage Vaivasvata Manu while he was sneezing.
Ikṣvāku had a hundred sons who gave profuse sacrificial fees;
among them, Vikukṣi was the eldest, but because of his lack of physical vigor, he did not inherit the kingdom.
O knower of the supreme dharma, he became the lord and sovereign of Ayodhyā;
it is remembered that he had five hundred sons, headed by Śakuni.
The protectors of the land of Uttarāpatha are of great strength;
there are forty-eight in that same direction, the southern quarter.
And other excellent brahmins, headed by Vaśāti, were appointed as guardians;
then Ikṣvāku commanded Vikukṣi at the Aṣṭakā festival.
"O mighty one, slay deer and bring meat for the sake of the *śrāddha*;
you have been appointed to the *śrāddha* rite, yet the *śrāddha* rite has not yet been performed. (BrP 7.49)
O Brahmins, having eaten a hare, the lord Śaśāda went out hunting;
he was then abandoned by Ikṣvāku at the word of Vasiṣṭha.
O brahmins, when Ikṣvāku had passed away, Śaśāda became the king;
and the heir of Śaśāda was the heroic one named Kakutstha.
From Anenas, Kakutstha was born; Pṛthu is recorded as the son of Anenas;
Viṣṭarāśva was the son of Pṛthu, and from him Ārdra was born.
Ārdra was the son of Yuvanāśva; his son, O twice-born ones, was Śrāvasta. From him was born King Śrāvastaka, by whom the city of Śrāvastī was founded.
The heir of Śrāvasta was King Bṛhadaśva;
his son was King Kuvalāśva, who was supremely righteous.
That king, because of his slaying of Dhundhu, attained the status of Dhundhumāra.
The sages said:
"O one of great wisdom, we wish to hear in truth about the slaying of Dhundhu,
by whose death that Kuvalāśva attained the state of being Dhundhumāra."
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Kuvalāśva had a hundred sons,
all of whom were excellent archers, proficient in the sciences, powerful, and difficult to overcome.
They were all righteous, performers of sacrifices, and givers of abundant sacrificial fees;
Bṛhadaśva, his father, installed Kuvalāśva in the kingdom.
Having transferred his royal fortune to his son, the king indeed entered the forest;
then the brahmin-sage Uttaṅka restrained him as he was departing.
Uttanka said:
"Protection must be provided by you, and it is right for you to perform that task;
O King, I am unable to practice my austerities without being free from anxiety."
Indeed, near my hermitage, in the level desert lands,
there is an ocean filled with sand known as Uddālaka.
Invulnerable to the gods, possessed of a massive body and great strength,
that great being remained there within the earth, hidden beneath the sands.
The son of the Rākṣasa Madhu, a great Asura named Dhundhu,
lies there having undertaken a terrible penance for the sake of destroying the world.
O lord of men, at the end of every year he releases a sigh,
and whenever that occurs, the earth trembles there.
By the wind of his breath, a great cloud of dust is raised,
obscuring the path of the sun for seven days while the earth trembles.
"O father, because it is so terrifying— with its sparks, embers, and smoke— I am unable to remain in my own hermitage there."
"Slay that one of great body out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds;
once he has been struck down by you today, the worlds will become secure."
For you alone, O lord of the earth, are capable of slaying him;
and a boon was granted to me by Viṣṇu in a former age, O King.
"To him who shall slay that fierce and mighty great Asura,
you shall proclaim his splendor by granting him a boon."
O protector of the earth, the immensely powerful Dhundhu cannot be consumed by one of meager splendor, even in the course of hundreds of ages.
"And his prowess was truly great, unassailable even by the gods.
Having been addressed thus by the high-souled Uttaṅka, the royal seer gave his son Kuvalāśva to him for the destruction of Dhundhu.
Bṛhadaśva said:
"O Blessed One, I have laid down my weapons; however, O best of the twice-born, this son of mine will become Dhundhumāra, of this there is no doubt."
Having assigned his son the task of slaying Dhundhu, that royal sage,
the king of rigid vows, departed for the mountain.
Lomaharṣaṇa said: O twice-born ones, Kuvalāśva, accompanied by Uttanka and his hundred sons,
set out for the destruction of that Dhundhu.
Then the Lord, the blessed Viṣṇu, entered him with his splendor at the command of Uttaṅka and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
As that invincible one set forth, a great sound arose in the sky:
"This illustrious one shall today become the slayer of Dhundhu (Dhundhumāra), who is otherwise unslayable."
O best of the twice-born, the gods scattered divine perfumes and garlands over him, and the celestial drums resounded.
Having gone there with his sons, that valiant one, the best among victors,
caused the inexhaustible ocean to be dug out amidst the sands.
O Brahmins, while his sons were digging, Dhundhu, who was hidden within the sands, was then discovered by them as he stood obstructing the western quarter.
As if overturning the worlds with the fire born from his mouth out of anger,
he emitted water with great force, like the great ocean at the time of its rising tide.
O tigers among sages, the great ocean of Saumya was turbulent with excellent waves;
yet his one hundred sons, less three, were consumed by a Rākṣasa.
Then that radiant king, possessed of great splendor and the destroyer of Dhundhu, encountered the exceedingly powerful Rākṣasa Dhundhu.
Having swallowed that torrent of water, the lord of men,
like a yogi, extinguished the fire with water through his yogic power.
Having slain that water-demon of massive body by force,
the king, his task accomplished, showed him to Uttaṅka.
But Uttaṅka granted a boon to that high-souled king:
he gave him inexhaustible wealth and invincibility against his enemies.
May there be constant delight in the Dharma, as well as an imperishable residence in heaven;
and for those sons who were slain by the Rākṣasa, may they attain inexhaustible worlds in heaven.
Three of his sons remained; Dṛḍhāśva is said to be the eldest, while the two younger princes were Candrāśva and Kapilāśva.
Haryaśva is recorded as the son of Dṛḍhāśva, the son of Dhundhumāra;
