Haryaśva’s son was Nikumbha, who was always devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya.
Saṃhatāśva was the son of Nikumbha, skilled in battle;
O twice-born ones, Akṛśāśva and Kṛśāśva were the two sons of Saṃhatāśva.
His daughter was Dṛṣadvatī, the daughter of Himavat, esteemed by the virtuous;
she is renowned throughout the three worlds, and her son was Prasenajit.
Prasenajit obtained a wife named Gaurī, who was devoted to her husband;
however, having been accused by her husband, she indeed became the Bāhudā river.
His son was the great king Yuvanāśva;
Māndhātṛ was the son of Yuvanāśva, the conqueror of the three worlds.
Caitrarathī, the daughter of Śaśabindu, became his wife;
she was a virtuous woman named Bindumatī, peerless on earth in her beauty.
O twice-born ones, Māndhātṛ begot two sons upon her, who was devoted to her husband and the eldest of ten thousand brothers.
[He had] Purukutsa, who knew the dharma, and Mucukunda the king. Purukutsa’s son, however, was Trasadasyu, the lord of the earth.
Then Saṃbhūta was born from Narmadā,
and his son was Tridhanvan, the crusher of enemies, who was the heir of Saṃbhūta.
King Tridhanvan had a wise and powerful lord named Trayyāruṇa;
he had a son, a prince of great strength named Satyavrata.
That evil-minded one created obstacles for the mantras of the marriage ceremony,
by which he both took as his wife the bride who had already been wedded and seized her from another.
Out of childishness, desire, delusion, recklessness, and impulsiveness,
being afflicted by lust, he carried off the daughter of a certain city-dweller.
Filled with anger, Trayyāruṇa abandoned him, saying repeatedly, "Begone, you who are a stake of unrighteousness! (BrP 7.100).
Abandoned, he said to his father again and again, "Where shall I go?
And his father then said to him, "Live together with the dog-cookers."
"I do not desire a son through you as my son, O defiler of the family!"—
having been addressed thus by his father's words, he departed from the city.
But the venerable seer Vasiṣṭha did not restrain him;
rather, O brahmins, Satyavrata [dwelt] near the dwellings of the dog-cookers.
Abandoned by his father, the hero lived on, while his father also went to the forest;
thereafter, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, did not send rain upon that realm.
O brahmins, for twelve years he lived by that very unrighteousness;
meanwhile, Viśvāmitra of great asceticism took his wives into his own domain.
Having renounced his worldly ties at the edge of the ocean, he performed intense austerities;
meanwhile, his wife tied her own biological middle son around her neck.
For the sake of supporting his remaining family, he indeed sold him for a hundred cows;
and the prince saw him bound by the neck for the purpose of sale.
O twice-born ones, the righteous and mighty-armed Satyavrata liberated the son of the great seer and provided for his maintenance.

For the sake of Viśvāmitra’s satisfaction and out of compassion alone, that great ascetic, the wise Kauśika, was released by that hero; because of the binding around his neck, he became known by the name Gālava. (BrP 7.109)
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
But Satyavrata, remaining steadfast in discipline, supported Viśvāmitra’s wife out of devotion, compassion, and his promise.
Having killed deer, boars, and wild buffaloes,
he hung their meat upon a tree near the hermitage of Viśvāmitra.
Having undertaken a silent vow and the twelve-year initiation,
he lived there by his father’s command after the king had gone to the forest.
And because of his relationship as the officiating priest and preceptor, the sage Vasiṣṭha protected Ayodhyā, the kingdom, and likewise the inner apartments.
But Satyavrata, due to his youth and the force of destiny,
constantly harbored an excessive resentment toward Vasiṣṭha.
For at that time, the sage did not restrain his beloved son as he was being expelled from the kingdom by his father, despite many reasons for doing so.
"The completion of the marriage mantras occurs at the seventh step;
therefore, Satyavrata did not kill him until that seventh step had been reached."
"O twice-born ones, Satyavrata then conceived anger toward Vasiṣṭha in his mind, thinking, 'Though he knows the Dharma, Vasiṣṭha does not protect me.'"
Out of regard for his virtues, the venerable Vasiṣṭha acted in that manner;
however, Satyavrata did not perceive that secret act of his.
And because of that, the high-souled father was dissatisfied;
consequently, Pākaśāsana did not send rain for twelve years.
Therefore, O Brahmins, that initiation now ordained by him— which is difficult to bear on earth— has been performed so that the atonement for the lineage may indeed be accomplished.
The venerable sage Vasiṣṭha did not restrain him when he was abandoned by his father; for the mind of that muni was resolved thus: "I shall consecrate his son."
That powerful one carried out that initiation for twelve years,
while meat was unavailable to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.
The prince beheld that cow who milks all desires;
yet, overcome by anger, delusion, fatigue, and hunger, he [treated her] thus.
O best of sages, the king, following the laws of his country, killed him;
he himself ate that meat, as did the sons of Viśvāmitra.
Having heard that, Vasiṣṭha fed him, yet he (Vasiṣṭha) became enraged at him.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O cruel one, I would undoubtedly cause you to fall,
were it not for these two stakes that have been firmly established by you."
"Due to the dissatisfaction of your father, the killing of the cow that yielded for your guru, and the consumption of meat not consecrated by sprinkling— these are your three transgressions."
Seeing that he had three such spikes, the great ascetic said, "He is Triśaṅku";
thus he is remembered as Triśaṅku.
By him, the maintenance of Viśvāmitra’s wives was performed;
therefore, the sage, being pleased, granted a boon to Triśaṅku.
Then, being invited to choose a boon, the prince chose this boon:
"May I go to heaven in my physical body"—thus was the boon requested.
When that twelve-year period of fear caused by drought had passed,
he consecrated him in his father’s kingdom and then performed a sacrifice for the king.
While the deities and Vasiṣṭha were looking on, Kauśika,
the great ascetic, caused him to ascend to heaven in his physical body.
His wife, named Satyarathā, born of the Kaikeya lineage,
gave birth to a sinless prince, Hariścandra.
That King Hariścandra is remembered as Traiśaṅkava;
he was renowned as a sovereign emperor (samrāṭ) who performed the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Hariścandra had a son named King Rohita;
Harita was the son of Rohita, and his son was called Cañcu Hārita.
And Vijaya became the son of Cañcu, O best of sages;
because he was the conqueror of the entire earth, he is known as Vijaya.
Ruruka was his son, a king skilled in dharma and artha;
Vṛka was the son of Ruruka, and from Vṛka, Bāhu was born.
The Haihayas and Tālajaṅghas drove that king away;
taking her fetus with her, his wife entered the hermitage of Aurva.
Nāsatya was indeed righteous, and he flourished during the Age of Dharma;
Sagara, however, was the son of Bāhu, born together with Gara at a sacrifice.
Having reached the hermitage of Aurva and being protected by the descendant of Bhṛgu,
King Sagara obtained the fiery weapon (āgneya-astra) from that descendant of Bhṛgu.
Having slain the Tālajaṅghas along with the Haihayas,
the infallible Acyuta conquered the earth; and that knower of dharma, O best of sages, abolished the religious practices of the Śakas, the Pahlavas, the Kṣatriyas, and the Pāradas.
The sages said:
How was that Sagara born together with poison, O Acyuta?
And for what reason [was he born] among the Kṣatriyas of great luster, such as Śakra and the others?
The steadfast king, filled with rage, cast aside the duties appropriate to his lineage;
O high-minded one, relate all of this to us in detail.
Lomaharṣaṇa said: O best of the twice-born, it is said that in former times, the kingdom of Bāhu was seized by the Haihayas, the Tālajaṅghas, and the Śakas when he was addicted to vices.
The Yavanas, the Pāradas, the Kāmbojas, and the Pahlavas—
these five tribes likewise exerted their prowess for the sake of the Haihayas.
Then, having been deprived of his kingdom, that king Bāhu went to the forest;
followed by his wife, he, being sorrowful, gave up his life there.
His Yādava wife, who was pregnant, followed behind him;
O sinless ones, it is said that poison had previously been administered to her by a co-wife.
Having prepared her husband's funeral pyre in the forest, she was about to ascend it;
but the brahmins, O sages, Aurva of the Bhṛgu lineage, restrained her out of compassion.
And in his hermitage, that embryo was born together with the poison itself;
he became the mighty-armed king named Sagara.
But Aurva, having performed for that high-souled one the birth-rites and other ceremonies,
and having taught him the Vedas and the Shastras, then bestowed upon him the divine weapons.
O highly fortunate ones, that [weapon] was of the nature of fire and difficult even for the immortals to withstand;
endowed with the power of that weapon and with strength, he [fought] in battle.
Enraged, he swiftly slaughtered the Haihayas like Rudra slaughtering animals;
that best among the famous acquired fame throughout the worlds.
Then the king resolved to exterminate without remainder the Śakas, Yavanas, Kāmbojas, Pāradas, and Pahlavas as well.
Being slaughtered by the heroic and high-souled Sagara,
they sought refuge with Vasiṣṭha and prostrated before that wise sage.
Then the immensely radiant Vasiṣṭha, seeing them,
granted them safety and restrained Sagara by means of an agreement.
But Sagara, having heard his own promise and the words of his preceptor,
indeed destroyed their dharma and changed their appearances.
Having shaved half of the heads of the Śakas, he released them;
as did the Yavanas and the Kāmbojas, having shaved their entire heads.
By that high-souled one, the Pāradas were made to have their hair disheveled, the Pahnavas to grow beards, and both were deprived of the study of the Vedas and the utterance of the vaṣaṭ-call.
O best of the twice-born, there are the Śakas, Yavanas, Kāmbojas, Pāradas,
Koṇisarpas, Māhiṣakas, Darvas, Colas, and Keralas.
All those Kṣatriyas became Brahmins; their former dharma was set aside by the high-souled King Sagara at the word of Vasiṣṭha.
That king, victorious through righteousness, having conquered this earth,
released a horse while consecrated for the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
As he was driving it, that horse was carried away near the shore in the south-eastern ocean and made to enter the very earth.
Then that king had that region excavated by his sons;
as the great ocean was being dug there, they reached [the bottom].
Then he [saw] that primordial Person, the divine Hari, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Creatures,
Viṣṇu in the form of Kapila, sleeping as the Puruṣa.
As he awoke, by the splendor arising from his eyes,
all the best of sages were consumed, yet four remained as survivors.
Barhiketu, Suketu, King Dharmaratha,
Śūra, and Pañcanada were the kings who perpetuated his lineage.
And the Blessed Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa granted him a boon:
an imperishable lineage for Ikṣvāku and an undying fame.
The Lord [granted] his son, the ocean, and likewise eternal residence in heaven;
and the ocean, taking up the respectful offering (argha), paid homage to that lord of the earth.
By that very deed of his, he indeed attained the state of being the ocean;
and he recovered from the sea that horse belonging to the horse-sacrifice.
That man of great asceticism performed a hundred horse-sacrifices;
we have heard that he had sixty thousand sons.
The sages said:
O best of beings, by what rite were the sixty thousand heroic sons of Sagara born so exceedingly powerful and valiant?
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Sagara had two wives whose sins were burnt away by ascetic penance;
the elder was the daughter of Vidarbha, known by the name Keśinī.
But the elder wife was the younger one, most virtuous,
the daughter of Ariṣṭanemi, peerless in beauty upon the earth.
Aurva granted a boon to them; understand this, O best of the twice-born:
"Let one of these broad-hipped women take sixty thousand sons. (BrP 8.65)
"Let one of you choose a single lineage-holder as she desires.
Thereupon, one of them chose sixty thousand sons.
Then the Sage said, "So be it; let one [daughter] be the bearer of the lineage," and thus that king of great splendor became known by the name Pañcajana.
The other gave birth to a gourd filled with seeds; so says the sacred tradition.
Within it were sixty thousand embryos, each the size of a sesame seed.
They were conceived at the proper time and grew according to their ease;
she then placed those embryos in jars filled with clarified butter.
The king provided that same number of nurses for each one of them for their nourishment;
then, after ten months, they emerged in due order.
O twice-born ones, those princes, who increased the joy of Sagara, became sixty thousand sons for him in due course of time.
O Lord of the Earth, from the interior of a gourd within the womb were born those great-souled ones, into whom the splendor of Nārāyaṇa had entered.
One son named Pañcajana became king;
Śūra was the son of Pañcajana, and he had a valiant son named Aṃśumān.
Dilīpa was his son, renowned as Khaṭvāṅga,
who, having come here from heaven and obtained life for but a moment, [remained].
O sinless ones, the three worlds were brought into harmony by Dilīpa through his intelligence and truth;
his heir was the great king Bhagīratha.
That Lord, who caused Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, to descend,
led her to the ocean and even adopted her as his daughter.
Therefore, she is called Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā by those who investigate the lineages.
King Śruta, the son of Bhagīratha, was renowned by that name.
Nābhāga had a son named Śruta, who was supremely righteous;
Ambarīṣa, the son of Nābhāga, became the father of Sindhudvīpa.
The valiant Ayutājit was the heir of Sindhudvīpa;
the son of Ayutājit was the highly illustrious Ṛtuparṇa.
The powerful and highly illustrious Ārtaparṇi, son of Ṛtuparṇa, was indeed a friend of King Nala and was well-versed in the secrets of divine dice.
The son of that Sudās was King Indrasakha;
the son of Sudās is declared to be the monarch named Saudāsa.
The king known as Kalmāṣapāda was indeed Mitrashaha;
Kalmāṣapāda’s son was renowned as Sarvakarman.
Anaraṇya was the son of Viśruta, the performer of all rites;
Nighna was the son of Anaraṇya, and from Nighna two sons were born.
Anamitra and Raghu were the two most excellent among the bulls of kings;
the son of Anamitra was the learned King Duliduha.
Dilīpa was his son and the great-grandfather of Rāma;
Dilīpa’s son was Raghu, who was long-armed and known by that name.
He who was formerly the mighty great king in Ayodhyā was born as Aja, the descendant of Raghu;
and from Aja, Daśaratha was likewise born.
From Daśaratha was born Rāma, whose soul was righteous and who possessed great fame;
and from Rāma was born a son known by the name Kuśa.
From Atithi was born the righteous and highly illustrious Kuśa;
and from Atithi there arose a son named Niṣadha, who was endowed with great prowess.
Nala was the son of Niṣadha, and Nabha was the son of Nala; Puṇḍarīka was the son of Nabha, and Kṣemadhanvan is recorded as his successor.
The son of Kṣemadhanvan was the powerful Devānīka;
the lordly son of Devānīka was named Ahīnagu.
The heir of Ahīnagu was the king named Sudhanvan;
and from Sudhanvan was born a son, King Śala.
That righteous-souled one was indeed named Utkya Śalaputra;
Vajranābha was his son, and Nala was the son of that great-souled one.
O best of sages, only two Nalas are renowned in the Purāṇas:
the son of Vīrasena and the one who was the upholder of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
Those born of the Ikṣvāku lineage have been proclaimed as the principal ones;
these kings of great splendor belong to the dynasty of Vivasvat.
By properly reciting this creation of the Sun Vivasvat,
the god Śrāddhadeva, who bestows nourishment upon all creatures,
one becomes possessed of progeny and attains union with the Sun Vivasvat.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
O Brahmins, the venerable sage Atri was born as the father of Soma,
from the mind of Brahmā at the beginning, when he desired to bring forth the creation of beings.
We have heard that there was indeed an unsurpassed austerity practiced by him in the past for three thousand divine years.
His semen ascended upwards and attained the state of Soma;
from his two eyes, water flowed forth, illuminating the ten directions.
Then, commanded by the prescribed rite, ten goddesses took up that embryo;
having come together, they bore it, yet they were not able to sustain it.
When those quarters were no longer able to sustain that embryo,
he was then abandoned by them and fell to the earth.
Beholding Soma fallen, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
placed him upon his chariot out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
When that son of Atri, the Supreme Self, had descended, the gods,
the sons of Brahmā, and other excellent sages offered hymns of praise.
As he was being thus praised, the splendor of that radiant Soma nourished all the worlds on every side for their well-being.
With that preeminent chariot, he of exceeding fame circumambulated the earth, bounded by the oceans,
twenty-one times.
That energy of his which entered the earth emerged as the plants by which the world is sustained.
Having attained splendor through his praises and his own deeds, that illustrious Lord,
endowed with great fortune, performed austerities for the sake of beholding the lotuses.
Then, O best of sages, Brahmā, the foremost among the knowers of Brahman, bestowed upon him sovereignty over seeds,
medicinal herbs, brāhmaṇas, and the waters.
Having obtained that great sovereignty, Soma, the best among those who are gentle,
performed the Rājasūya sacrifice, for which the sacrificial fee consisted of hundreds of thousands.
"O twice-born ones, we have heard that Soma gave the three worlds as a sacrificial fee to those chief brahmin-sages and to the members of the assembly."
Hiraṇyagarbha, Brahmā, Atri, and Bhṛgu became the officiating priests (ṛtvij);
Hari, surrounded by many sages, was the member of the assembly (sadasya) there.
Sinī, Kuhū, Dyuti, Puṣṭi, Prabhā, Vasu,
Kīrti, Dhṛti, and Lakṣmī— these nine goddesses waited upon him.
Having reached the foremost final ablution, the lord of emperors, honored by all the gods and sages,
shone resplendently, illuminating the ten directions.
O dear one, having obtained that sovereignty so difficult to attain and honored by the sages, his mind wandered astray, led away from right conduct by a lack of discipline.
Intoxicated by the pride of his own power, Soma indeed forcibly abducted the wife of Bṛhaspati, disregarding the son of Aṅgiras.
Though he was repeatedly entreated by the gods and likewise by the celestial rishis,
he did not at that time release Tārā to Aṅgiras.
Then Uśanas took up the rear-guard of that descendant of Aṅgiras,
and Rudra also took up the rear-guard after seizing the Ājagava bow.
By that high-souled one, the supreme weapon named Brahmaśiras was discharged against the gods, by which their glory was destroyed.
There, that great battle known as the Tārakāmaya took place between the gods and the Dānavas, causing the destruction of the worlds.
Thereupon, those disciplined gods and the Tuṣitas, O twice-born ones,
went for refuge to Brahmā, the primordial and eternal god.
Then, having restrained both Uśanas and Rudra Śaṅkara,
the Grandfather himself gave Tārā back to Aṅgiras.
Seeing her pregnant, Bṛhaspati said in anger:
"By no means should this embryo be retained by you in my womb."
Having approached a clump of reeds, she gave birth to the embryo;
as soon as he was born, that Blessed One eclipsed the splendor of the gods.
Then, fallen into doubt, those best of gods said to Tārā:
"Tell the truth; whose son is he—Soma’s or Bṛhaspati’s?"
When she did not speak to the gods even though she was questioned by them,
Kumāra, the greatest slayer of enemies, began to curse her.
Having restrained him, Brahmā then asked Tārā about his doubt:
"O Tārā, tell me what is the truth in this matter; whose son is this? (BrP 9.30)
With palms joined in reverence, she said to her grandfather, "It is for Soma.
Then King Soma, having smelled his son upon the head, [spoke] regarding him.
He gave the name Budha to that wise boy;
and in the sky, the planet Budha rises in a favorable manner.
Then he begot a son who was the offspring of Vairāja;
his offspring was the highly resplendent Purūravas, also known as Vaila.
From Urvaśī were born the seven sons of that great-souled one;
thus has this birth of Soma, which increases fame, been recounted to you.
O best of sages, listen now as his lineage is being proclaimed—
a lineage that is auspicious, life-prolonging, health-bestowing, meritorious, and the means for the fulfillment of one's intentions.
Merely by hearing of the birth of Soma, one is liberated from sins. (BrP 9.36)
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
O best of sages, the son of Budha was the learned Purūravas,
who was radiant, charitable by nature, a performer of sacrifices, and a giver of abundant sacrificial fees.
A proponent of Brahman, valiant and difficult for enemies to subdue in battle,
he was a lord of the earth who maintained the sacred fire and performed sacrifices.
Truthful, virtuous-minded, and perfectly restrained in sexual conduct,
he was always peerless in fame throughout the three worlds.
The illustrious Urvaśī, casting aside her pride, chose that teacher of the Veda, who was peaceful, a knower of dharma, and a speaker of truth.
O twice-born ones, the king lived with her for ten and five years,
and six, five, seven, eight, ten, and eight years.
In the delightful Caitraratha forest, likewise on the banks of the Mandākinī,
in the vast city of Alakā, and in the Nandana, the most excellent of groves.
Having reached the Northern Kurus, where the trees bear delightful fruits,
he likewise stayed at the foot of Mount Gandhamādana and on the northern peak of Meru.
In these preeminent forests frequented by the gods,
the king, accompanied by Urvaśī, took delight with supreme joy.
In that most meritorious region, praised by the great seers,
that lord of the earth established his capital at Prayāga.
Such was the power of King Aila, that best of men;
the highly illustrious one resided on the northern bank of the Ganges at Pratiṣṭhāna.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
The sons of Aila were seven, resembling the sons of gods;
they were renowned in the world of the Gandharvas as Āyu, Dhīmān, and Amāvasu.
Viśvāyu, the righteous Dharmāyu, and another, Śrutāyu,
as well as Dṛḍhāyu, Vanāyu, and Bahvāyu— these were the sons of Urvaśī.
The heir of Amāvasu was King Bhīma, a sovereign of kings;
the heir of the illustrious Bhīma was King Kāñcanaprabha.
The learned Suhotra was also very powerful;
from Suhotra was born Jahnu, conceived in the womb of Keśinī.
He who performed the great sacrificial session, the serpent-sacrifice, a grand festival,
for which Gaṅgā indeed flowed as his wife out of desire for a husband.
Then the Gaṅgā flooded his assembly hall against his will;
seeing the sacrificial enclosure thus inundated on all sides by her, [he was filled with anger].
O best of the twice-born, the son of Suhotra, the king, being enraged, cursed the Gaṅgā:
"I shall render your effort fruitless by drinking up your water. (BrP 10.17)
"O Gaṅgā, receive immediately the fruit of this arrogance!
For the great seers, having seen the Gaṅgā drunk by the royal sage Jahnu," BrP_10.18 //
The highly fortunate Jahnu brought the daughter of Yuvanāśva, Kāverī, as his own daughter;
he took Jāhnavī as his daughter as well.
By the curse of Yuvanāśva, she emerged from half of Gaṅgā,
the blameless wife of Jahnu, into Kāverī, the best of rivers.
Jahnu, however, begot upon Kāverī a beloved and righteous son named Sunadya,
and Ajaka was his son.
The heir of Ajaka was the lord of the earth Balākāśva, who was devoted to hunting; his son was Kuśa.
Kuśa had four sons of divine splendor:
Kuśika, Kuśanābha, Kuśāmba, and Mūrtimat.
Having grown up together with cowherds, the king was always a forest-dweller;
meanwhile, the lord Kuśika performed austerities, seeking a son equal to Indra.
Thinking "May I obtain it," Śakra approached him out of fear;
and when a full thousand years had passed, Śakra indeed beheld him.
Seeing his exceedingly fierce asceticism, the thousand-eyed Purandara himself,
the eternal one, became capable of fathering a son for him.
For the sake of obtaining a son, Maghavān, the lord of the gods and best of deities,
himself became King Gādhi Kauśika.
The citizens had a wife, and from her Gādhi was born;
Gādhi’s daughter was the highly fortunate and auspicious Satyavatī by name.
The lord Gādhi gave her to Ṛcīka, the son of Kāvya;
that descendant of Bhṛgu, the joy of the Bhṛgus, was indeed pleased with her as her husband.
In the same manner, he prepared a sacrificial oblation (caru) for Gādhi for the sake of obtaining sons;
then Ṛcīka, the descendant of Bhṛgu, called his wife and spoke to her.
"O auspicious lady, you yourself must consume this sacrificial porridge with your mother;
from her shall be born a radiant son, a bull among Kṣatriyas."
Invincible by the kṣatriyas in this world, O slayer of the bull among kṣatriyas,
he shall have a son for you as well, O auspicious lady— one who is steadfast and rich in asceticism.
"O best of the twice-born, this sacrificial oblation shall produce one whose nature is tranquility.
Having spoken thus to his wife, Ṛcīka, the descendant of Bhṛgu—
Constantly devoted to austerity, Gādhi entered the forest;
accompanied by his wife, he then went to the hermitage of Ṛcīka.
Then, on the occasion of a pilgrimage to sacred fords, that lord of men took two portions of sacrificial charu from the sage Satyavatī in order to see his daughter.
Having taken the sacrificial oblation with care, she presented it to her mother;
but the mother, by the power of fate, gave her own oblation to her daughter.
Then, out of ignorance, she prepared that sacrificial pap (caru) for herself;
thus, Satyavatī then made it all [destined] to be the ender of the Kṣatriyas.
She of terrible appearance held it with her blazing body;
then Ṛcīka, seeing her, approached her through the power of yoga.
Then that best of the twice-born said to his own wife of excellent complexion:
"O blessed lady, you have been deceived by your mother because of the exchange of the sacrificial porridge."
"For your son will be born a man of cruel deeds and exceedingly terrible;
yet a brother shall also be born who is a treasury of asceticism and has become one with Brahman."
"For the entire universe, through my ascetic fervor, has been entrusted by me to him.
Thus was the highly fortunate Satyavatī addressed by her husband at that time.
He propitiated his husband, saying, "May my son not be such as this—a low-born offspring of a Brahmin from you. Thus addressed, the sage replied:
Ṛcīka said:
"O blessed lady, this desire was not intended by me to be fulfilled in that way;
for the sake of both father and mother, the son would become one of fierce deeds."
Having spoken these words, Satyavatī further said this:
"O Sage, if you so desired, you could even create worlds; how much more so a son?"
"You ought to grant me here a son who is peaceful in nature and upright;
O Lord, may I have such a grandson as this, and you likewise."
"O best of the twice-born, if this cannot indeed be done otherwise,
then he granted her favor by the power of her asceticism."
"O woman of excellent complexion, there is no distinction for me between my son and my grandson;
O blessed lady, it shall be exactly as you have spoken."
Then Satyavatī gave birth to a son of the Bhṛgu lineage,
Jamadagni, who was devoted to austerity, self-controlled, and equanimous in soul.
In this lineage of Bhṛgu on earth, Jamadagni was born;
for she, Satyavatī, was virtuous and devoted to truth and righteousness.
This great river has come forth and is known as Kauśikī.
There was a lord of men named Reṇu, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
His highly fortunate daughter was named Kāmalī Reṇukā;
and upon Reṇukā Kāmalī, [he begat a son] endowed with asceticism and sacred knowledge.
Ārcīka begot the most formidable son of Jamadagni,
who had reached the furthest limit of all sciences and was the preeminent master of the science of archery.
Thus was the highly illustrious Rāma, the slayer of Kṣatriyas and like a blazing fire, born to Satyavatī from Aurva’s son Ṛcīka.
From the power of his asceticism, Jamadagni was born as the best among the knowers of Brahman;
his middle son was Śunaḥśepha, and the youngest was Śunaḥpuccha.
Gādhi, the son of Kuśika, begot upon his wife a son, Viśvāmitra, who was his heir and whose nature consisted of austerity, knowledge, and tranquility.
Having attained equality with the Brahman-sages, this righteous Viśvāmitra reached the status of a Brahman-rishi; he is remembered by the name Viśvaratha.
By the grace of Bhṛgu, he was born from Kauśika as the increaser of the lineage;
and the sons of Viśvāmitra are recorded as Devarāta and others.
They are renowned throughout the three worlds; hereafter are their names:
Devarāta and Kati, from whom the Kātyāyanas are said to have descended.
From Śālāvatī were born Hiraṇyākṣa, Reṇu, and then Reṇuka,
as well as Sāṃkṛti, Gālava, and the renowned Mudgala.
Madhucchandas, Jaya, Devala, as well as Aṣṭaka,
Kacchapa, and Hārita— these were the sons of Viśvāmitra.
The renowned lineages of those high-souled Kauśikas are the Pāṇinas, the Babhruvas, and likewise the Dhyānajapyas.
The Pārthivas, Devarātas, Śālaṅkāyanas,
Bāṣkalas, Lohitas, Yamadūtas, and likewise the Kārūṣakas are recorded [as the divisions].
O best of sages, even within this lineage, the connection between the Brahmanical seer Kauśika and the Paurava— representing the union of the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya— is well known.
Among the sons of Viśvāmitra, Śunaḥśepha is remembered as the eldest;
that best of sages, though born of Bhṛgu, indeed attained the status of a Kauśika.
It is said that Viśvāmitra had a son named Śunaḥśepha,
who was appointed as the sacrificial animal at the sacrifice of Haridaśva.
Śunaḥśepha was indeed given back to Viśvāmitra by the gods;
because he was given by the gods (devaiḥ), he therefore became Devarāta.
Devarāta and the others were the seven sons of Viśvāmitra;
likewise, Aṣṭaka was the son of Dṛṣadvatī and thus a descendant of Viśvāmitra.
I have described to you the group of Jahnu, beginning with Lauhi, the son of Aṣṭaka.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the lineage of the high-souled Āyu.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Āyu’s sons were five, all of them heroic great chariot-warriors;
they were born as kings from Prabhā, the daughter of Svarbhānu.
Nahuṣa was born first, and after him Vṛddhaśarmā;
then Rambha, Raji, and Anenas, who were renowned throughout the three worlds.
Raji indeed begot five hundred sons here,
known as the Rājeyas, a warrior class that struck fear into Indra.
When a most terrible war between the gods and the asuras had broken out,
both the gods and the asuras then spoke to the Grandfather (Brahmā).
The gods and asuras said: "O Blessed One, who will be the victor in the battle between us two?
Tell us, O Lord of all beings; we wish to hear this according to the truth."
Brahmā said:
"Those for whose sake the lord Raji, having taken up his weapons, shall fight in battle, they will conquer the three worlds; of this there is no doubt."
Where there is fortitude, there is sovereignty; where there is fortitude, there is prosperity.
Where both fortitude and prosperity reside, there is righteousness, and likewise victory.
Then those gods and Dānavas, delighted by what the god had said, approached Raji, seeking victory and choosing that bull among men.
For he was born to Prabhā as the grandson of Svarbhānu;
he was a king of supreme splendor who caused the lineage of Soma to flourish.
All those gods and dānavas, with joyful minds, said to Raji:
"Take up your excellent bow for our victory!"
Then Raji, who understood the matter, spoke there to those two— the god and the daitya— aiming at his own interest while manifesting his own glory.
Raji said:
"If, having conquered all the hosts of Daityas through my prowess,
I become Indra by means of righteousness, then I shall fight in battle."
O King, let the gods and the foremost sages, with delighted minds,
grant that your desire be fulfilled exactly as you wish.
Having heard the words of the hosts of gods, King Raji then questioned the leaders of the Asuras just as he had questioned the gods.

The Dānavas, filled with pride and perceiving only their own self-interest, replied with these words of arrogance to that best of kings: BrP_11.15: "The Dānavas, filled with pride and perceiving only their own self-interest, replied with these words of arrogance to that best of kings."
The Dānavas said:
"Prahlāda is our Indra, for whose sake we fight;
therefore, O King, best of monarchs, stand with us in this battle."
Even though he was urged by the gods, that king said "So be it," and was told by the gods: "Having conquered him, you shall become Indra. (BrP 11.17)
He, the self-controlled one of supreme glory, slew all the Dānavas who were otherwise invincible even to the wielder of the thunderbolt; he restored to the gods their lost prosperity.
Having slain all the Dānavas, the lord Raji took possession [of the world];
then Śatakratu, together with the gods, [approached] the immensely powerful Raji.
Having said, "I am the son of Raji," he spoke these words once more:
"O father, you are Indra among all the gods; there is no doubt about this."
"I am your son, Indra, and I shall attain fame through my deeds.
But he, having heard Śakra’s words, was deceived by that illusion.
"So be it," the king replied with joy to Śatakratu;
and when that lord of the earth, who was equal to the gods, had ascended to heaven, [the king departed].
From Indra, his sons took possession of the inheritance and the kingdom of Raji;
his five hundred sons indeed occupied that very station of Śatakratu.
They repeatedly ascended to the heavenly world, Triviṣṭapa;
yet when they became utterly deluded, intoxicated by passion, and unrighteous, [they fell].
Having become haters of Brahman and having had their vigor and prowess destroyed,
Indra then regained his own sovereignty as well as that supreme station.
Having slain all the sons of Raji, who were devoted to lust and anger—
he who hears or even retains this account of the displacement from his station of Śatakratu shall not encounter misfortune.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Rambha was indeed childless; I shall now describe the lineage of Anenas.
The son of Anenas was the highly illustrious king Pratikṣatra.
And the son of Pratikṣatra was the renowned Saṃjaya;
Saṃjaya’s son was Jaya, and Vijaya was his offspring.
Vijaya’s son was Kṛti, and his son was Haryatvata;
the son of Haryatvata was the powerful King Sahadeva.
The righteous son of Sahadeva was known as Nadīna;
Nadīna’s son was Jayatsena, and Jayatsena’s son was Saṃkṛti.
The righteous and highly illustrious Kṣatravṛddha was also born from Saṃkṛti;
and another son of Kṣatravṛddha was known as Anenas.
There, the son of Kṣatravṛddha was the highly illustrious Sunahotra;
Sunahotra had three heirs who were supremely righteous.
Kāśa and Śala—these two—and likewise the lord Gṛtsamada;
the son of Gṛtsamada was Śunaka, from whom Śaunaka descended.
The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and likewise the Śūdras;
Śalātmaja was the son of Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, and his son was Kāśyapa.
The king of Kāśī was Kāśya, and his son was Dīrghatapas; Dhanu was the son of Dīrghatapas, and from him came the learned Dhanvantari.
At the conclusion of his great asceticism, the wise and aged Dhanvantari was born again here among humans in this birth as a god.
Then, O Great King, the god Dhanvantari was born in his house as the great king of Kāśī, the destroyer of all diseases.
Having received Āyurveda from Bharadvāja, that physician,
having divided it again into eight parts, imparted it to his disciples.
The son of Dhanvantari was renowned as Ketumān;
now, the son of Ketumān is remembered as the heroic Bhīmaratha.
The son of Bhīmaratha was Divodāsa, a lord of subjects;
the righteous Divodāsa became the sovereign of Vārāṇasī.
At that very time, O twice-born ones, a Rākṣasa named Kṣemaka caused the city of Vārāṇasī to be laid waste and became its inhabitant.
"For she has been cursed by the high-souled Nikumbha, who is possessed of great intelligence;
she shall indeed remain desolate for a thousand years, of this there is no doubt."
As soon as she had been cursed, Divodāsa, the lord of subjects,
established a beautiful city on the banks of the Gomati at the edge of his territory.
Formerly, the city of Vārāṇasī belonged to Bhadraśreṇya;
Bhadraśreṇya had a hundred sons who were supreme archers.
Having slain him, King Divodāsa established that kingdom of Bhadraśreṇya, which had been seized by the more powerful one.
The son of Bhadraśreṇya was the renowned Durmada; he was released by Divodāsa out of compassion because he was but a child.
That lord of the earth indeed seized the inheritance of Haihaya and forcibly took back his paternal inheritance which had been taken by Divodāsa.
O fortunate ones, the end of the enmity was brought about by the high-souled Durdamana, the son of Bhadraśreṇya, through his own splendor.
From Divodāsa, by the Dṛṣadvatī river, the hero Pratardana was born;
with that son, though still a child, he struck back at the army.
Pratardana had two very famous sons, Vatsa and Bharga.
Alarka was indeed the son of Vatsa, and Saṃnati was his offspring.
Alarka was his son, devoted to Brahmanas and true to his promise;

regarding the royal sage Alarka, an ancient verse has been sung: BrP_11.51: "He who would give away the whole earth, filled with gold, to one who asks, but does not restrain himself from anger when his head is being split—of what use is that earth to him?"
For sixty thousand years and sixty hundred years,
that upholder of the lineage was formerly a youth endowed with beauty.
By the grace of Lopāmudrā, he attained a supreme lifespan;
endowed with beauty and youth, his kingdom was exceedingly great.
At the end of the curse, the mighty-armed one, having slain the Rākṣasa Kṣemakara,
once again established the beautiful city of Vārāṇasī.
The heir of Saṃnati was the righteous one named Sunītha;
the heir of Sunītha was the highly illustrious Kṣema.
Kṣema’s son was Ketumān, and his son was Suketu;
the son of Suketu is likewise known as Dharmaketu.
The heir of Dharmaketu was the great chariot-warrior Satyaketu;
and the son of Satyaketu was the lord of creatures named Vibhu.
Ānarta was the son of Vibhu, and Sukumāra was his son;
the son of Sukumāra was the very righteous Dhṛṣṭaketu.
The heir of Dhṛṣṭaketu was Veṇuhotra, a lord of creatures;
and the son of Veṇuhotra was the lord of creatures named Bhārga.
Vatsa’s son was Vatsabhūmi, while Bhārgaja was born from Bhārgu;
these were the sons of Aṅgiras, born thus in the lineage of Bhṛgu.
"Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas—these three sons were born by the thousands.
These are declared to be the descendants of Kaśyapa; now learn of those of Nahuṣa."
Lomaharṣaṇa said: Six sons of great prowess, whose splendor was equal to that of Indra, were born to Nahuṣa by Virajā, the daughter of the Pitṛs; they were his heirs.
Yati, Yayāti, Saṃyāti, Āyāti, and Pārśvaka were born; among them, Yati was indeed the eldest, and after him came Yayāti.
The most righteous one obtained the daughter of Kakutstha named Gā;
but the ascetic, having established himself in liberation, became a sage who had become Brahman.
Having conquered this earth, Yayāti took Devayānī, the daughter of Uśanas, as his wife among those five sons.
Devayānī gave birth to Yadu and Turvasu, and Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan and an Asura, likewise bore sons.
To him, Śakra, being pleased, gave a most resplendent chariot, along with Druhyu, Anu, and Puru, and Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan.
He bore that divine golden armlet, drawn by celestial, supreme horses,
bright and swift as thought, with which he was to accomplish his purpose.
With that preeminent chariot, the invincible Yayāti conquered the earth in six nights,
as well as the gods along with the Dānavas in battle.
At that time, Saratha was the king of all the Kauravas,
descending from Janamejaya of the Kuru line, who was named Saṃvarta-Vasu.
O king of kings, that chariot of the son of Kuru, King Pārīkṣita, was utterly destroyed by the curse of the wise Garga.
For that King Janamejaya caused the death of Garga’s young son in the course of time; he thereby incurred the sin of killing a Brahmin.
That royal sage, smelling of iron, ran hither and thither;
abandoned by the people of the city and the countryside, he found no peace anywhere.
Then, tormented by grief and finding no peace anywhere,
the king sought refuge with Śaunaka, the best of brahmins.
And Śaunaka, the knower of wisdom, O best of the twice-born, caused King Janamejaya to perform the horse sacrifice for the sake of his purification.
That iron-like odor vanished as he reached his ritual bath,
and that divine chariot then came under the control of the king, the lord of Cedi.
Śakra, being pleased, gave it to him; from him Bṛhadratha received it, and from Bṛhadratha it passed in due succession to the king who was the descendant of Bṛhadratha.
Then, having slain Jarāsaṃdha, Bhīma, the joy of the Kurus, out of affection gave that excellent chariot to Vāsudeva.
Having conquered the earth together with its oceans consisting of seven islands, Yayāti,
the son of Nahuṣa, then divided the kingdom into five parts for his sons.
Yayāti appointed his eldest son Yadu in the eastern quarter;
and that son of Nahuṣa consecrated Puru as king in the middle region.
In the southeastern direction, the wise king Turvasu [ruled];
by them this entire earth, with its seven continents and its cities, was governed.
Even today, the people are protected according to their respective regions by means of Dharma;
O best of sages, I shall speak of them before you.
Having laid aside his bow and arrows, and having entrusted the burden to those five bulls among men,
the king became subject to old age.
Having laid down his weapons, the lord of the earth wandered over the world;
King Yayāti, the unconquered, became filled with joy.
Having thus divided the earth, Yayāti said to Yadu:
"O son, accept my old age in exchange for your youth."
"Endowed with your beauty, I would roam this earth as a youth, having transferred my old age onto you. To him, Yadu replied:
Yadu said:
"O King, alms were promised to me by a Brahmin without being specifically designated. Without having fulfilled that obligation, I will not accept your old age."
"In old age there are many defects caused by eating and drinking;
therefore, O King, I am not able to accept old age."
"O King, you have many sons who are dearer to you than I;
O knower of dharma, choose indeed another son to accept [the kingdom]."
Thus addressed by Yadu, King Yayāti, the best among speakers, filled with anger, spoke while censuring his son.
Yayāti said:
"O evil-minded one, what other stage of life do you have, or what duty is prescribed for you, that you disregard me, who am your guide?"
Having spoken thus to Yadu, O Brahmins, he, filled with wrath, cursed him:
"O fool, your progeny shall not possess sovereignty; of this there is no doubt. (BrP 12.31)
O best of the twice-born, the king spoke in this very same manner to Druhyu, Turvasu, and Anu, and he was likewise rejected by them as well.
The unconquered Yayāti, filled with great rage, cursed them;
O best of the twice-born, I have related all of this to you exactly as it happened.
O brahmins, having thus cursed all four sons born before Puru,
the king spoke those same words to Puru as well.
"If you agree, O Puro, I shall wander this earth in my youth, having transferred my old age onto you. (BrP 12.35)
The powerful Puru accepted his father’s old age, and Yayāti,
endowed with Puru’s youth, traversed the earth in his beauty.
Seeking the end of desires, that best of kings,
the lord, took his pleasure in the Caitraratha forest together with Viśvācī.
And when the lord of men was satiated with desires and enjoyments,
he then received back his own old age from Puru.
Therein are the verses sung by Yayāti, the best of sages,
by which one should withdraw all desires from every side, just as a tortoise draws in its limbs.
Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of sensual pleasures;
like a fire fed with clarified butter, it only increases all the more.
Whatever rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women exist upon the earth—all that is not enough for even one person; having realized this, one does not become deluded.
When one does not commit any evil toward any living being through action, mind, or speech, then one attains Brahman.
When one does not fear them, when they do not fear him,
and when one neither desires nor hates, then one attains Brahman.
That which is difficult for the wicked-minded to abandon, which does not decay even as one decays,
and which is a disease that ends only with life— that craving, when one renounces it, brings happiness.
The hair of an aging person decays; the teeth of an aging person decay;
but the hope for wealth and the hope for life do not decay even as one ages.
Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine pleasure there is—
these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the bliss that comes from the destruction of craving.
Having spoken thus, that royal sage entered the forest with his wife;
and after a long time, he performed extensive austerities.
At the end of his ascetic penance on Bhṛgutuṅga, the highly illustrious one attained the goal;
casting off his body by fasting, he reached heaven together with his wife.
In his lineage, O best of sages, there were five most excellent royal seers by whom the entire earth was pervaded, just as by the rays of the sun.
Now I shall describe the lineage of Yadu, honored by kings; listen, for it was therein that Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the upholder of the Vṛṣṇi clan, was born.
O best of the twice-born, that man who constantly hears this account of Yayāti’s life shall become healthy, possessed of offspring, long-lived, and renowned.
The Brahmins said:
"O Sūta, we wish to hear in truth the lineage of Puru,
and separately those of Druhyu, Anu, Yadu, and Turvasu."
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Listen, O tigers among sages, as I first describe in detail and in due order the lineage of the high-souled Puru.
Puru’s son was Suvīra, and his son was Manasyu;
the son of Manasyu was the king named Abhayada.
In the same way, Abhayada had a son named Sudhanvan;
Sudhanvan’s son was Subāhu, and Raudrāśva was his son.
The sons of Raudrāśva were Daśārṇeyu, Kṛkaṇeyu,
Kakṣeyu, Sthaṇḍileyu, and likewise Sannateyu.
Ṛceyu, Jaleyu, the mighty Sthaleyu,
Dhaneṣu, and Vaneṣu were his ten sons, and he had ten daughters.
Bhadrā, Śūdrā, Madrā, Śaladā, Maladā, Khaladā, Naladā, and Surasā, O brahmins, were likewise born. (BrP 13.7)
Likewise, Gocapalā and Strīratnakūṭā—these were the ten;
and Prabhākara, born in the lineage of Atri, was the husband of them all.
Upon Bhadrā he begot a son, the illustrious Soma,
at the time when Sūrya was struck by Svarbhānu and was falling from the great sky.
And when the world was overwhelmed by darkness, he by whom light was set forth;
saying "May it be well with you," the Sun indeed fell [from the sky].
At the word of that brahmin seer, he did not fall from heaven to earth—
he who, possessed of great ascetic power, established the most excellent lineages of the Atris.
In the sacrifices of Atri, his strength was established by the gods;
he begot upon those daughters sons born according to his own desire.
Likewise, there were ten sons, great beings devoted to fierce asceticism;
those brahmins were founders of lineages, seers who had mastered the Vedas.
Known as the Svastyātreyas, they were moreover devoid of the three types of wealth;
yet Kakṣeyu had exactly three sons who were great chariot-warriors (mahārathas).
Sabhānara, Cākṣuṣa, and likewise Paramanyu;
the son of Sabhānara was the learned king Kālānala.
O knower of dharma, the son of Kālānala was indeed named Sṛñjaya;
the son of Sṛñjaya was the heroic King Purañjaya.
O best of sages, Janamejaya was the son of Purañjaya;
the royal seer Janamejaya had a son named Mahāśāla.
Among the gods he was well known, and his fame was established upon the earth;
he was the renowned son of Mahāśāla, named Mahāmanas.
A hero was born, honored by the hosts of gods and possessed of great magnanimity;
O twice-born ones, that Mahāmanas begot two sons. (BrP 13.19)
And [he begat] Uśīnara, who was a knower of dharma, and the very powerful Titikṣu;
moreover, Uśīnara had five wives born from the lineages of royal sages.
Nṛga, Kṛmi, Navā, Darvā, and Dṛṣadvatī as the fifth—
these were the five sons of Uśīnara, the perpetuators of his lineage.
And through great ascetic penance, sons were born to the aged king;
Nṛga was the son of Nṛgā, while Kṛmi was born to Kṛmī.
Navā had a son named Nava, and Suvrata was born of Darvā;
furthermore, Śibi Auśīnara, the king, was born of Dṛṣadvatī.
The Śibis, O brahmins, were the descendants of Śibi; the Yaudheyas were those of Nṛga;
Navarāṣṭra belonged to Nava; and the city of Kṛmilā belonged to Kṛmi.
Likewise, the Ambaṣṭhas were the sons of Suvrata; now learn of the sons of Śibi.
Śibi’s sons were four, world-renowned as the Śibis.
Vṛṣadarbha, Suvīra, Kekaya, and likewise Madraka—
their prosperous territories were known as Kekaya and Madraka.
The Vṛṣadarbhas and the Suvīras were the offspring of Titikṣu;
O twice-born ones, Titikṣu became the king in the eastern quarter.
Uṣadratha was possessed of great heroism; his son was Phena.
From Phena was born Sutapas, and from Sutapas came Bali.
Born into the human womb as King Kāñcanaiṣudhi,
he was formerly that great yogi, King Bali.
He begot five sons who established lineages upon the earth:
Aṅga was born first, and likewise Vaṅga and Suhma.
Puṇḍra and Kaliṅga are likewise called the Bāleya Kṣatriyas;
the Bāleya Brāhmaṇas were the progenitors of his lineage upon the earth.
O twice-born ones, a boon was granted to Bali by the pleased Brahmā:
the state of a great yogi and a lifespan equal to the duration of a kalpa.
In strength, indeed, there shall be incomparability; the vision of the true meaning of the nature of reality (dharmatattvārtha);
invincibility even in battle; and preeminence in righteousness (dharma).
"You shall behold the three worlds, as well as preeminence in procreation;
you shall also establish the four fixed social classes."
Thus addressed by the Lord, O brahmins, King Bali attained supreme peace; and after a long time, he returned to his own abode.
Their five provinces were Aṅga, Vaṅga, along with Suhma, Kaliṅga, and Puṇḍraka; these are now the subjects of Aṅga.
Aṅga’s son was the great lord of kings, Dadhivāhana;
and Dadhivāhana’s son was King Diviratha.
The son of Diviratha was named Dharmaratha, a learned man whose prowess was equal to that of Śakra; his son was Citraratha.
Then, on Mount Kālañjara, while performing a sacrifice together with Śakra, that high-souled Dharmaratha drank the Soma.
Now, Citraratha also had a son named Daśaratha,
who was renowned as Lomapāda, whose daughter was Śāntā.
To him was born, by the grace of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, the heroic and highly illustrious son of Daśaratha, who increased his lineage with a fourfold army.
The son of Caturaṅga was known as Pṛthulākṣa;
the son of Pṛthulākṣa was the highly illustrious king named Campa.
The city of Campa was formerly called Mālinī;
by the grace of Pūrṇabhadra, Haryaṅga became his son.
Then Vaibhāṇḍaki, by means of mantras, brought down to the earth that supreme mount, the elephant of Śakra.
There, the son of Haryaṅga is remembered as King Bhadraratha;
the son of Bhadraratha was Bṛhatkarman, a lord of subjects.
Bṛhaddarbha was his son, from whom Bṛhanmanas was born;
and that lord of kings, Bṛhanmanas, indeed begot a son.
From him was born one named Jayadratha; from him came King Dṛḍharatha, and from Dṛḍharatha came Viśvajit Janamejaya.
Vaikarṇa was his heir, and Vikarṇa was his son;
he had a hundred sons who increased the lineage of the Aṅgas.
All these kings born of the Aṅga lineage have been described by me;
they were high-souled, devoted to truth, possessed of progeny, and great chariot-warriors.
O best of sages, O twice-born ones, listen as I shall fully declare the lineage of Ruceyu, the son of Raudrāśva, that king. BrP 13.50.
The son of Ṛceyu was King Matināra, the lord of the earth;
and the sons of Matināra were three, who were supremely righteous.
Vasurodha, Pratiratha, and the righteous Subāhu—
all were knowers of the Vedas, devoted to Brahman, and speakers of truth.
O best of sages, he had a daughter named Ilā, who was a woman devoted to the sacred word; Taṃsu approached her.
Then the son of Taṃsu was the powerful royal sage Dharmanetra, a proclaimer of the Veda and one of great prowess; his wife was Upadānavī.
From him, Upadānavī then gave birth to four auspicious sons:
Duṣyanta, Suṣmanta, Pravīra, and Anagha.
The heir of Duṣyanta was the powerful Bharata;
he was great, known by the name Sarvadamana, and possessed the strength of ten thousand elephants.
A son was born to the high-souled Duṣyanta by Śakuntalā, the universal monarch Bharata, after whose name the Bhāratas are so called.
I have previously related how the sons of King Bharata were destroyed due to the wrath of their mothers.
The powerful sage Bharadvāja, a wise and great seer who was the son of Bṛhaspati Aṅgiras, performed sacrifices for him with grand rites.
But previously, when his son's birth had indeed proved futile,
a son named Vitatha was then born to him from Bharadvāja.
Then, when Vitatha was born, Bharata ascended to heaven;
having consecrated Vitatha as king, Bharadvāja then departed for the forest.
And he, though himself false, begot five sons:
Suhotra, Suhotṛ, Gaya, and likewise Garga.
And the high-souled Kapila, the two sons of Suhotra,
the very truthful Kāśika, and likewise King Gṛtsamati.
Likewise, the sons of Gṛtsamati were Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas;
and the son of Kāśika was Kāśeya, as well as Dīrghatapas.
To Dīrghatapas was born a learned son named Dhanvantari;
and the son of Dhanvantari was renowned as Ketumān.
Likewise, the son of Ketumān is remembered as the learned Bhīmaratha;
the son of Bhīmaratha, moreover, became the sovereign of Vārāṇasī.
Known as Divodāsa, he was the destroyer of all the kṣatriyas;
the son of Divodāsa was the heroic king Pratardana.
Pratardana had two sons, Vatsa and Bhārgava;
and the prince Alarka became a king of great wisdom on earth.
That lord of the earth indeed seized the inheritance of Haihaya and forcibly took back his paternal inheritance which had been taken by Divodāsa.
By the high-souled Divodāsa, the son of Bhadraśreṇya known as Durdamana, he was released out of compassion because he was but a child.
O twice-born ones, there was indeed a king named Aṣṭāratha, the son of Bhīmaratha; by that son, a blow was struck against him while he was still a child.
O best of sages, Alarka, the king of Kāśī— who was devoted to Brahman and true to his promise— desired to bring an end to enmity by means of a kṣatriya.
For sixty thousand years and sixty hundred years,
that upholder of the Kāśi lineage remained young and endowed with beauty.
O best of sages, at the end of his life, by the grace of Lopāmudrā, he attained supreme longevity after slaying the Rākṣasa Kṣemakara.
The king established the beautiful city of Vārāṇasī.
The heir of Alarka was the monarch named Kṣemaka.
The son of Kṣemaka was indeed Varṣaketu;
and the heir of Varṣaketu was the lord of subjects named Vibhu.
Ānarta was the son of Vibhu, and from him Sukumāra was born;
the son of Sukumāra was Satyaketu, a great chariot-warrior.
From Vatsa was born the highly resplendent and most righteous King Vatsabhūmi,
and from Bhārgava came Bhargabhūmi.
But these sons of Aṅgiras were born in the lineage of Bhṛgu as Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, O best of sages.
O best of the twice-born, let another lineage, that of Ājamīḍha, be heard:
Suhotra’s son was Bṛhat, and Bṛhat had three sons.
Ajamīḍha, Dvimīḍha, and the heroic Purumīḍha were born;
Ajamīḍha had three wives who were endowed with great fame.
Nīlī, Keśinī, and Dhūminī were the excellent wives;
from Ajamīḍha and Keśinī was born the powerful Jahnu.
He who performed the great sacrificial session, the Sarvamedha sacrifice, the all-pervading Lord,
for whom Gaṅgā flowed as if led away by the desire for him as her husband.
And though he did not wish it, the Gaṅgā flooded that assembly hall of his;
seeing that sacrificial enclosure inundated on all sides by her, [he was filled with wonder].
Then, O Brahmins, King Jahnu, being enraged, spoke to Gaṅgā:
"I shall now drink up these waters of yours, having drawn them together from the three worlds.
O Gaṅgā, receive immediately the fruit of this arrogance!"
Then, seeing that the Gaṅgā had been taken up, the great-souled and highly fortunate maharṣis offered Jāhnavī to him as a daughter.
Jahnu married Kāverī, the daughter of Yuvanāśva,
whose body was later turned into a river by the curse of Gaṅgā.
Jahnu’s beloved son was the powerful Ajaka;
the heir of Ajaka was the lord of the earth, Balākāśva.
Kuśika became devoted to hunting, and his son grew up among the Pahlavas and forest-dwellers.
Kuśika, however, performed austerities with the thought, "May I obtain a powerful son equal to Indra"; and Śakra, out of fear, approached him and was born [as his son].
He became King Gādhi; Maghavan himself was Kauśika; Viśvāmitra was the son of Gādhi, and likewise Aṣṭaka was born from Viśvāmitra.
I have described to you the lineage of Jahnu, beginning with Lauhi, the son of Aṣṭaka;
now listen, O best of sages, to the other lineage, that of Ājamīḍha.
From Ajamīḍha and Nīlī was born Suśānti;
from Suśānti came Purujāti, and from Purujāti came Bāhyāśva.
The five external sons were Mudgala, Sṛñjaya, and King Bṛhadiṣu; they were prosperous and inhabited by many people.
Yavīnara the valiant, and Kṛmilāśva as the fifth—
these five were renowned as being capable of protecting the regions.
Those five [sons] became the Pañcālas, prosperous regions filled with people;
they were renowned as the Pañcālas because they were capable of protecting them.
The heir of Mudgala was the highly illustrious Maudgalya,
from whom Indrasenā conceived Vadhnya.
Pañcajana was the son of the high-souled Sṛñjaya;
and the son of Pañcajana was the lord of the earth, Somadatta.
The heir of Somadatta was the highly illustrious Sahadeva;
and the son of Sahadeva was the renowned one named Somaka.
When the lineage had declined, Somaka was born as the son of Ajamīḍha;
Somaka’s son was Jantu, whose hundred sons shone forth.
The youngest among them was Pṛṣata, the father of Drupada and their lord;
these high-souled Somakas are known as the descendants of Ajamīḍha.
O best of sages, Dhūminī, the queen of Ajamīḍha, was devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, of noble birth, and eager for sons.
And that queen, desiring a son, was devoted to the practice of vows;
then, for ten thousand years, she performed austerities that were exceedingly difficult to endure.
Having offered oblations into the fire according to the rules, that pure woman, who ate sparingly,
slept upon the very kusha grass used for the Agnihotra sacrifice, O best of sages.
Having united with that queen Dhūminī, Ajamīḍha begot Ṛkṣa, who was smoke-colored, handsome, and of beautiful appearance.
From Ṛkṣa was born Saṃvaraṇa, and from Saṃvaraṇa likewise came Kuru,
who, having gone beyond Prayāga, established Kurukṣetra.
Meritorious, delightful, and frequented by those who perform virtuous deeds, his lineage was exceedingly great; it is after his name that they are called the Kauravas.
And Kuru had four sons: Sudhanvan, Sudhanu, the mighty-armed Parīkṣit, and the preeminent Arimejaya.
The heir of Parīkṣit was the righteous Janamejaya,
as well as Śrutasena, Agrasena, and Bhīmasena by name.
All these were highly fortunate, valiant, and endowed with great strength;
likewise, Janamejaya’s son was the wise Suratha.
To Suratha was born a valiant son, Vidūratha;
the heir of Vidūratha was the great chariot-warrior Ṛkṣa.
But the second was known by that very name, Bharadvāja;
there were two Ṛkṣas in this Lunar dynasty, and likewise two Parīkṣits.
There were three Bhīmasenas who were Brahmins, and two Janamejayas;
furthermore, the son of the second Ṛkṣa was Bhīmasena.
From Bhīmasena came Pratīpa; from Pratīpa came Śāntanu, Devāpi, and Bāhlika—these three were indeed great chariot-warriors.
O best of the twice-born, Bhīṣma was born into that lineage of Śāntanu;
now, O brahmins, hear the lineage of the royal seer Bāhlika.
And the highly illustrious Somadatta was born as the son of Bāhlīka;
from Somadatta were born Bhūri, Bhūriśravas, and Śala.
The sage Devāpi was the preceptor of the gods;
Kṛtaka, the son of Cyavana, was the beloved priest of that high-souled one.
Śāntanu, however, became the king and the leader of the Kauravas;
I shall now proclaim the lineage of Śāntanu, which is renowned throughout the three worlds.
That lord begot a son named Devavrata of the Ganges;
he was known as Bhīṣma, the grandfather of the Pāṇḍavas.
O twice-born ones, Kālī gave birth to Vicitravīrya,
the beloved son of Śāntanu, who was righteous-souled and stainless.
And from Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, in the field of Vicitravīrya,
she gave birth to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and Vidura.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra begot one hundred sons by Gāndhārī;
of them all, Duryodhana was the eldest and their sovereign.
Dhanañjaya was the son of Pāṇḍu, and Saubhadra was his son;
Parīkṣit was the son of Abhimanyu, and he was indeed the father of Pārīkṣita.
Two sons were born to Pārīkṣita in Kāśī:
King Candrāpīḍa and Sūryāpīḍa, who was a knower of liberation.
Candrāpīḍa had one hundred sons who were supreme archers;
thus, the Kṣatriya lineage known as Jānamejaya became renowned upon the earth.
Among them, the eldest was Satyakarṇa, the mighty-armed, who performed sacrifices and gave abundant sacrificial fees; he resided there in that city named Vāraṇasāhvaya.
The powerful Śvetakarṇa was the heir of Satyakarṇa;
being childless, that righteous-souled one entered the forest of asceticism.
Therefore, having gone to the forest, the daughter of Sucāru, the fair-browed Mālinī— so called because she wore a garland of crocodiles— conceived a child.
While he was still in the womb, Śvetakarṇa, the lord of subjects,
followed his father’s previous and infallible resolve to set out on the Great Journey.
But having seen her beloved, the virtuous, lotus-eyed Mālinī, the daughter of Sucāru, followed after him into the forest.
On the road, that young woman gave birth to a delicate boy;
having abandoned him right there, she followed after the king.
Like the virtuous Draupadī of old, who was devoted to her husband and highly blessed,
that delicate youth wept upon the mountain ridge.
For the sake of that high-souled one, clouds appeared for the purpose of rain;
and there were two sons of Śraviṣṭhā: Paippalādi and Kauśika.
Seeing this, the two, filled with compassion, took him and washed him in water;
his sides, which were smeared and drenched in blood, were rubbed upon a stone.
He, who was dark as a goat, remained perfectly composed as his two flanks were rubbed;
indeed, those two flanks of his became dark like goats through the action of the god.
Then those two gave him the name Ajapārśva;
he was raised by the two brahmins in the dwelling of Remaka.
Remaka’s wife bore him for the sake of obtaining a son;
that son was born of Rematī, while those two brahmins were his ministers.
Their sons and grandsons lived simultaneously and for equal spans of life;
such was this lineage of the Pauravas, the high-souled Pāṇḍavas.
And on this subject, this verse was also sung long ago by the wise Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, when he joyfully transferred his old age [to another].
Without doubt, this earth would become devoid of the moon, the sun, and the planets;
yet the earth will never be without the lineage of Puru.
This renowned lineage of yours, the Pauravas, has been recounted by me;
now I shall proclaim the lineages of Turvasu, as well as those of Druhyu, Anu, and Yadu.
The son of Turvasu was Vahni, and his son was Gobhānu;
the son of Gobhānu was King Aiśānu, who was unconquered.
Karaṇdhama was the son of Aiśāna, and Marutta was his son;
however, another king named Marutta, the son of Avikṣita, has been mentioned by me.
The king, a performer of sacrifices who gave profuse sacrificial fees, remained childless;
that lord of the earth had a daughter named Saṃyatā.
She was given as a sacrificial fee to the great-souled Saṃvarta;
she also obtained Duṣyanta, a descendant of Puru, as her son, who was free from all taint.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, when the transfer of old age occurred through the curse of Yayāti, Turvasu’s lineage entered that of the Pauravas.
The heir of Duṣyanta was Karūroma, a lord of subjects;
from Karūroma came Ahrīda, who had four sons.
O King, there were Pāṇḍya and Kerala, as well as Kāla and the monarch Cola;
and the son of Druhyu, O King, was the monarch Babhruketu.
His son was Aṅgārasetu, who is called the lord of the Maruts;
that powerful one was slain with great difficulty by Yauvanāśva in battle.
There was also a very great war that lasted for ten months;
the heir of Aṅgārasetu was a king named Gāndhāra.
Indeed, by his name alone the great region of Gāndhāra is known,
as well as the horses born in the land of Gāndhāra, the best among steeds.
Anos’s son was Dharma, and Dyūta was his son;
from Dyūta was born Vanaduha, and Pracetas was his son.
Thus have the Anus, including Pracetas and Sucetas, been described by me;
moreover, Yadu had five sons who were like the children of gods.
Sahasrāda, Payoda, Kroṣṭā, Nīla, and Añjika—
these three were the heirs of Sahasrāda, and they were exceedingly righteous.
Haihaya, Haya, and likewise King Veṇuhaya;
Haihaya’s son was known as Dharmanetra.
The son of Dharmanetra was Sāhañja, and his son was [Sāhañjaya];
by that king, the city named Sāhañjanī was founded.
The powerful Bhadraśreṇya was the son of Mahiṣmat;
the heir of Bhadraśreṇya was the renowned Durdama.
The wise son of Durdama was known by the name Kanaka;
Kanaka’s heirs were four, world-renowned.
Kṛtavīrya, Kṛtaujas, and likewise Kṛtadhanvan; Kṛtāgni was the fourth, and from Kṛtavīrya came Arjuna.
He who, with his thousand arms, became the lord of the seven continents,
alone conquered the earth on a chariot possessing the splendor of the sun.
For having performed extremely difficult austerities for ten thousand years, Kārtavīrya propitiated Datta, who was born of Atri.
To him, Datta granted four boons of immense splendor;
first, he requested the very great boon of a thousand arms.
The virtuous should restrain one who is engaged in unrighteousness;
having conquered the earth by forceful means, he should then win over his subjects through righteousness alone.
Having conquered many battles and slain enemies by the thousands,
he met his death in battle at the hands of one superior to him while engaged in combat.
O twice-born ones, it is said that as he fought, a thousand arms appeared through his illusory power (māyā), like those of the Lord of Yogins manifesting through yoga.
Thus, by means of fierce rites, he conquered this entire earth with its seven islands, its ports, its oceans, and its cities.
O best of sages, it is heard that by means of that [charity], the king duly performed seven hundred sacrifices across the seven continents.
O best of sages, all those sacrifices involved hundreds and thousands of sacrificial fees;
all had sacrificial posts of gold, and all had altars of gold.
O best of sages, all those [worlds] are constantly adorned by gods seated in decorated celestial chariots, as well as by gandharvas and apsaras.
At whose sacrifice the wise Gandharva Nārada, the son of Varīdāsa, sang this song,
being struck with wonder by his greatness.
Nārada said:
Surely no kings shall ever attain the state of Kārtavīrya,
whether by means of sacrifices, gifts, austerities, valor, or sacred learning.
For he, the yogi, is seen by men as he wanders through the seven continents, equipped with shield, sword, and bow, and mounted on a chariot.
No property was ever lost, nor was there any grief or confusion,
because the great king protected his subjects with righteousness through his sovereign power.
He became a universal monarch (cakravartin), a sovereign possessing all jewels;
he himself was the protector of cattle, and he himself was the guardian of the field.
Through his rain-giving power, he became Parjanya; through his state of yoga, he became Arjuna.
Indeed, with his thousand arms, the skin of which was hardened by the striking of bowstrings, [he appeared].
He of great splendor shone with a thousand rays like the sun in autumn;
for he was among men in Māhiṣmatī as a leader of the Nāgas.
Having conquered the sons of Karkoṭaka, that lotus-eyed one established them in that city during the rainy season, when the ocean's current was at its height.
As if playing, he sent the river flowing upstream with his arms;
as he sported there, the river that garlands that village was tossed about by him.
The Narmadā approaches, filled with apprehension at the sight of his thousand arms as he tosses the great ocean with their thousands of surging waves.
The gods of the earth, remaining motionless and hidden out of fear,
stayed in the underworld [watching] that ocean whose great waves were pulverized and which contained moving fish and great sea-monsters.
Then the king, with his thousand arms, set in motion that ocean whose mass of foam was driven by the winds and which was agitated by the turbulence of whirlpools.
Like Mount Mandara when hurled by the gods and asuras into the Ocean of Milk,
they were terrified by the agitation caused by Mandara and apprehensive that the nectar of immortality was about to be produced.
Suddenly springing up in terror upon seeing the formidable and supreme king,
those great serpents bowed with their heads motionless.
In the evening, the plantain groves seemed as if shaken by the wind;
he indeed fixed his uplifted bow with its strings and [aimed] five arrows.
Having forcibly deluded the lord of Laṅkā, Rāvaṇa, along with his army,
and having conquered him and brought him under his control, he bound him in Māhiṣmatī.
Having heard that Rāvaṇa, the descendant of Pulastya, had been bound by Arjuna,
Pulastya then went there and personally beheld that Arjuna.
Entreated by Pulastya, he released the Rākṣasa descendant of Pulastya;
the sound of whose thousand arms striking the bowstring was like the roar of thunder.
Oh, how marvelous was the prowess of Bhārgava in battle, which severed [the head] like the bursting of a cloud at the end of an eon, or like a crashing thunderbolt!
Once, when King Bāhusahasra was thirsty, he was asked for alms by the Fire-god, who was like a grove of golden palm trees.
That hero gave alms to the Fire-god: the seven continents, as well as cities, villages, cowherd settlements, and entire provinces in their entirety.
The fire blazed up with the desire to consume all his [possessions] by the power of that high-souled lord of men.
He burned the mountains and forests of Kārtavīrya,
as well as the lovely, deserted hermitage of Varuṇa’s son.
Fearing that powerful one, Citrabhānu, the son of the Haihaya, burned him down—
he whom Varuṇa had formerly obtained as his most excellent and radiant son.
That sage was known by the name Vasiṣṭha, and also as Āpava;
it was there that the powerful Āpava, out of anger, cursed Arjuna.
"O Haihaya, because this forest was not spared by you for me,
therefore another shall slay you for the difficult deed you have committed."
The mighty-armed and powerful son of Jamadagni named Rāma,
having crushed you with his strength, swiftly severed your thousand arms.
But that ascetic Brahmin, the descendant of Bhṛgu, who possessed the power of never losing his wealth, O subduer of enemies, shall slay you.
While that lord of men was protecting his subjects through righteousness by means of his majesty,
his death came from the curse of that great sage.
O brahmins, in former times Varas was likewise chosen by himself;
that high-souled one had a hundred sons, of whom five remained.
Skilled in weapons, powerful, heroic, righteous,
and illustrious were Śūrasena, Śūra, Vṛṣaṇa, and Madhupadhvaja.
And there was a great king of Avanti named Jayadhvaja;
the sons of Kārtavīrya were heroic and possessed of great strength.
The son of Jayadhvaja was the very powerful Tālajaṅgha;
his hundred sons were renowned and remembered as the Tālajaṅghas.
In the lineage of those high-souled Haihayas, O best of sages,
the Vītihotras, Sujātas, Bhojas, and Āvantyas are recorded.
The Tauṇḍikeras are well-known, as are the Tālajaṅghas;
the Bharatas and the Sujātas have not been enumerated individually due to their great number.
The Brahmins beginning with Vṛṣa were Yādavas of meritorious deeds;
among them, Vṛṣa was the sustainer of the lineage, and his son was Madhu.
Madhu had a hundred sons, but Vṛṣaṇa was the founder of his lineage;
from Vṛṣaṇa all were called Vṛṣṇis, while from Madhu the Mādhavas are remembered.
Those known by the name of Yadu are called Yādavas, and so too are the Haihayas;
for him [who recites this], there shall be no loss of wealth, and he shall recover whatever has been lost.
O best of the twice-born, he who here constantly recounts the birth of Kārtavīrya [shall attain merit]; these are the five lineages of the sons of Yayāti.
O best of sages, those who are celebrated as the heroes of the world indeed sustain the worlds, just as the five elements sustain all beings, both stationary and moving.
Having heard these five excretions, the king, who is skilled in dharma and artha,
becomes the master and lord over his five sons.
One shall obtain five boons that are difficult to attain in this world:
long life, fame, sons, sovereignty, and prosperity.
O twice-born ones, O best of sages, by means of both retaining and hearing this account of the five groups, listen as I speak of the lineage of Kroṣṭu. BrP 13.212.
Now, by merely hearing of the lineage of Kroṣṭu— the progenitor of the Yadu dynasty, a performer of sacrifices and a doer of meritorious deeds— one is liberated from all sins;
for Viṣṇu, Hari, the upholder of the Vṛṣṇi clan, was born in his lineage.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Gāndhārī and Mādrī were the two wives of Kroṣṭu.
Gāndhārī gave birth to Anamitra, who was possessed of great strength.
Mādrī [gave birth to] another son, Yudhājit, and Devamīḍhuṣa;
their lineage, which increased the Vṛṣṇi clan, became divided into three branches.
Two sons were born to Mādrī, both renowned as Vṛṣṇi and Andhaka;
likewise, two sons, Śvaphalka and Citraka, were born to Vṛṣṇi.
O best of sages, wherever the righteous-souled Śvaphalka dwells,
there is no fear of disease, nor drought, nor even excessive heat.
Once, O best of sages, in the kingdom of the King of Kāśī, Indra,
the subduer of Pāka, did not send rain for three full years.
There he brought forth Śvaphalka, who was highly honored;
through the intervention of Śvaphalka, Indra, whose vehicle is green horses, sent down rain.
Śvaphalka took as his wife the daughter of the King of Kāśī, named Gāndinī; she, for her part, used to give a cow daily to a brahmin.
From that Śvaphalka was born Akrūra, a donor, a sacrificer, a hero, learned in the scriptures, fond of guests, and one who bestowed abundant sacrificial fees.
Upamadgu, Madgu, Medura, Arimejaya,
Avikṣita, Akṣepa, Śatrughna, and Arimardana.
Dharmadhṛk, Yatidharman, Dharmokṣa, Andhakaru, as well as Āvāha and Prativāha, and the beautiful woman Sundarī.
O best of the twice-born, from Akrūra and Ugrasenā,
who was of beautiful limbs, Prasena and Upadeva were born, both possessing the splendor of gods.
Citraka had sons, namely Pṛthu and Vipṛthu,
as well as Aśvagrīva, Aśvabāhu, Svapārśvaka, and Gaveṣaṇa.
Ariṣṭanemi and Aśva, Sudharmā and Dharmabhṛt, as well as Subāhu and Bahubāhu; Śraviṣṭhā and Śravaṇā were the two women.
He begot the heroic Devamīḍhuṣa upon Asiknī;
ten heroic men were born to Bhojyā, the chief queen.
The mighty-armed Vasudeva was born first as Ānakadundubhi;
at the moment of his birth, kettledrums resounded in the heavens.
A great clamor of kettledrums arose in the sky,
and a vast rain of flowers fell during the birth of the hero.
Even in the entire world of men, there was no one on earth equal in beauty to that foremost of persons, whose splendor was like that of the moon.
From him were born Devabhāga, and likewise Devaśravas,
Anādhṛṣṭi, Kanavaka, Vatsavān, and Gṛñjama.
Śyāma, Śamīka, and Gaṇḍūṣa were his sons, and he had five excellent daughters:
Pṛthukīrti, Pṛthā, Śrutadevā, and Śrutaśravā.
And likewise Rājādhidevī; these five were the mothers of heroes.
From Śrutaśravā was born King Śiśupāla, the ruler of Cedi.
He who was formerly the king of the Daityas, Hiraṇyakaśipu,
was born as the son of Vṛddhaśarman by Pṛthukīrti.
The heroic and mighty Dantavakra, the lord of Karūṣa, took Pṛthā as his daughter; Kunti gave her away, and Pāṇḍu married her.
In her was born that king Yudhiṣṭhira, who knew the dharma,
as well as Bhīmasena from Vāta and Dhanañjaya from Indra.
In this world, a hero who was a peerless warrior and equal to Śakra in prowess was born as Śani from Anamitra, the youngest son of the Vṛṣṇi delighter.
From him came Śaineya Satyaka, and from him Yuyudhāna Sātyaki;
the highly fortunate Uddhava was the son of Devabhāga.
They say that among the wise, Devaśravas was the most excellent;
Anādhṛṣṭi obtained from Aśmaki a glorious son.
Śrutadevā gave birth to Śatrughna, whose enemies had been turned back;
the sons of Śrutadevā were those who are celebrated as the Naiṣādas.
O best of sages, Ekalavya was raised among the Niṣādas; however,
the powerful Vasudeva,
the descendant of Śūra, gave his own heroic son Kauśika to the childless Vatsavat by means of a formal water-consecration.
Indeed, Viṣvaksena gave his sons— Cārudeṣṇa, Sudeṣṇa, Pañcāla, and Kṛtalakṣaṇa— as a mouthful to Aputra.
O best of the twice-born, that mighty-armed son of Rukmiṇī, the youngest brother, was never one to turn back from battle as long as he was not engaged in combat.
Thousands of crows followed behind him as he went, thinking,
"Today we shall feast upon the beautiful ones slain by Cārudeṣṇa."
Tantrija and Tantripāla were the two sons of Kanavaka; Vīru and Aśvahanu were likewise the two heroic sons of Gṛñjima.
Śyāmaputra was Śamīka; Śamīka, however, ruled the kingdom, and loathing the status of a Bhoja, he performed the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Ajātaśatru was born as the destroyer of his enemies;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the heroic sons of Vasudeva.
Thus, by upholding the vast and highly energetic lineage of Vṛṣṇi, which has three branches and many offshoots, one is not joined with misfortunes in this world.
Vasudeva had fourteen excellent wives,
the foremost of whom were Pauravī, Rohiṇī by name, and Madirā.
Vaiśākhī, Bhadrā, Sunāmnī, Pañcamī, Sahadevā, Śāntidevā, Śrīdevī, and Devarakṣitā. (BrP 14.37)
Vṛkadevī, Upadevī, and Devakī as the seventh;
Sutanu and Vaḍavā—these two were her female attendants.
O best of sages, Pauravī, named Rohiṇī, was the daughter of Bāhlika; she was the eldest wife and the beloved of Ānakadundubhi.
He obtained as his sons the eldest, Rāma; Śaraṇya; Śaṭha;
Durdama; Damana; Śubhra; Piṇḍāraka; and Uśīnara.
