O best of sages, the daughter of Rohiṇī was nine years old and named Citrā; she was later renowned as Subhadrā.
And from Vasudeva, the highly illustrious Śauri was born of Devakī;
and from Rāma, his beloved son Niśaṭha was born of Revatī.
From Subhadrā, the charioteer Abhimanyu was born of Pārtha;
from Akrūra, Satyaketu was born of the daughter of Kāśī.
Learn now of all those heroic sons who were born from the seven highly fortunate wives of Vasudeva.
Both Bhoja and Vijaya were the two sons of Śāntideva;
Vṛkadeva and Gada were both the two sons born of Sunāmā.
Vṛkadevī,
the daughter of the king of Trigarta and the wife of Śiśirāyaṇi, gave birth to the high-souled Agāvaha.
He exerted human effort in his desire for knowledge, yet that effort did not succeed;
thus, in his twelfth year, he appeared like black iron.
But Gārgya, falsely accused and driven by intense fury,
took a girl from a cowherd settlement and proceeded to have sexual intercourse with her.
And the Apsaras Gopālī, assuming the guise of a cowherd woman,
bore for Gārgya that difficult-to-bear and infallible embryo.
By the command of the trident-wielder Śiva, he was born as the exceedingly powerful king named Kālayavana from Gargī, the wife of a human.
With the upper half of his body well-proportioned, possessing the sturdy build of a lion,
that youth grew up in the inner apartments of the childless king.
O best of sages, that Yavana became Kālayavana;
while fighting, the king questioned the most excellent of the twice-born.
The powerful Nārada then described to him the lineage of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas;
with an army consisting of one akṣauhiṇī, he then marched toward Mathurā.
He dispatched a messenger to the abode of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas;
then the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, placing the high-minded Kṛṣṇa at their head, [set out].
Then, gathered together out of fear of the Yavana, they took counsel;
having reached a decision, they all favored flight.
Leaving the beautiful city of Mathurā while honoring the wielder of the Pināka bow,
they desired to establish their residence in Kuśasthalī-Dvāravatī.
Thus, the wise man who, being pure and with senses restrained, recites this account of Kṛṣṇa’s birth on the sacred festival days, shall become free from debt and happy.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Now, Kroṣṭu had a son named Vṛjinīvān, who was highly illustrious;
they call him Vārjinīvata, and Svāhi was the best among those who offer oblations with the *svāhā* cry.
Svāhi’s son was King Uṣadgu, the best among speakers,
who performed various great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Then, desiring offspring, Uṣadgu begot an eldest son;
his son was Citraratha, who was endowed with meritorious deeds.
The heroic Śaśabindu, ruler of Caitraratha, was a performer of sacrifices who bestowed abundant sacrificial fees; he followed the supreme conduct practiced by the royal sages.
Pṛthuśravas, of wide renown, was the king Śaśibindu;
those learned in the Purāṇas declare that Antara was the son of Pārthaśravas.
Suyajña was the son of Antara;
he performed every sacrifice completely and was devoted to his own duty.
Śineyu was the son of Uṣata, the scorcher of his enemies;
his son was Maruta, who became a royal seer and a king.
Maru obtained as his eldest son Kambalabarhiṣ;
though he had been excluded from his share due to resentment, he practiced extensive dharma.
Desiring a virtuous offspring,
he became Rukmakavaca, the son of Śataprasava, who was himself the son of Kambalabarhiṣ.
Having slain a hundred armored archers in battle with his sharpened arrows, Rukmakavaca attained supreme glory.
And from Rukmakavaca was born Parājita, the slayer of enemy heroes;
five sons of great prowess were born to Parājita.
Rukmeṣu, Pṛthurukma, Jyāmagha, Pālita, and Hari—
his father gave both Pālita and Hari to the Videhas.
Rukmeṣu became king through his alliance with Pṛthurukma;
having been exiled by those two, King Jyāmagha lived in a hermitage.
Then the king, having been pacified and enlightened by the brahmins,
took up his bow and, with his banner and chariot, went to another land.
Having conquered the banks of the Narmadā, the solitary Mṛttikāvatī, and Mount Ṛkṣavanta, he dwelt alone at Śuktimatī.
Jyāmagha’s wife was Śaibyā, a powerful and virtuous woman;
although that king was indeed childless, he did not take another wife.
He achieved victory in that battle and obtained a maiden there;
trembling, that lord of men said to his wife, "She is my daughter-in-law."
Having heard this, the queen asked, "O Lord, whose daughter-in-law is she?
Upon hearing that, Jyāmagha, the best of kings, replied.
The king said:
"The wife who has been provided for you shall belong to the son who will be born to you."
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Through her fierce asceticism, that fortunate Śaibyā, having reached maturity, gave birth to a son, Vidarbha. 15.20.
Later, Vidarbha begot upon his daughter-in-law, the princess of Kratha and Kaiśika, two wise and heroic sons who were skilled in battle.
Bhīma was the son of Vidarbha, and Kunti was his son.
From Kunti was born a son, Dhṛṣṭa, who was powerful and bold in battle.
To Dhṛṣṭa were born three heroic sons, supremely righteous:
Āvanta, Daśārha, and the powerful Viṣahara.
Vyoma was the son of Daśārha; Jīmūta is said to be the son of Vyoma;
Vikṛti was the son of Jīmūta, and Bhīmaratha is recorded as his [Vikṛti’s] son.
Now Bhīmaratha had a son named Navaratha;
his son was Daśaratha, and Śakuni was his son.
From him was born Karambha; Karambha’s son was King Devarāta; his son was Devakṣatra, and from him came the highly illustrious Vṛddhakṣatra.
Born like the offspring of a god, the delighter of the divine kṣatriyas was King Madhu,
the founder of the Madhu lineage, who was also sweet of speech.
Then Purudvān, the best of men, was born to Madhu by the princess of Vidarbha;
and Aikṣvākī became the wife of that Madhu, and by her he begot [a son].
Endowed with all virtues, the protector of beings and increaser of fame,
having understood this creation of the high-souled Jyāmagha,
one becomes joined with supreme joy and shall always possess progeny. (BrP 15.29)
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Kauśalyā gave birth to sons endowed with goodness from Satvata:
Bhāgin, Bhajamāna, Divya, and King Devāvṛdha.
And Andhaka, the mighty-armed, and Vṛṣṇi, the joy of the Yadus—
the four lineages of these have been described here in detail.
Bhajamāna had two wives, Sṛñjayī, Bāhyakā, and Upabāhyakā; from them were born many sons.
Krimi, Kramaṇa, Dhṛṣṭa, Śūra, and Purañjaya—
these were born to Bhajamāna from Bāhyakāsṛñjayī.
Āyutājit, Sahasrājit, Śatājit, and Dāsaka were born from Bhajamāna by Upabāhyakā, the daughter of Sṛñjaya.
The king, a performer of sacrifices and a promoter of the gods, practiced extensive austerity,
resolved that he would have a son endowed with all virtues.
As he was engaged in ascetic penance and constantly touching the water of the Parṇāśā river,
that river performed what was pleasing for him as he performed his ritual ablutions.
Overwhelmed by anxiety, that best of rivers did not reach a decision,
because of the excellence of that king.
But she did not find that woman from whom such a son might be born;
therefore, having gone there myself, I shall become his companion.
Then, having become a young maiden and possessing a most excellent form,
she chose the king as her husband, and that lord desired her.
In her, that noble-minded one conceived a radiant embryo;
then, in the tenth month, she, the best of rivers, gave birth.
"O twice-born ones, it is heard that those who know the Purāṇas sing of Babhru, the son of Devāvṛdha, endowed with all virtues, as belonging to this lineage. (BrP 15.41)
Proclaiming the virtues of that high-souled Devāvṛdha,
we see him from afar just as clearly as if he were right before us.
Babhru is the best among men; he is equal to the gods who increase the divine power.
There are sixty-six thousand and seven hundred men.
These indeed attained immortality from Babhru, the son of Devāvṛdha—
he who was a sacrificer, a lord of charity, wise, devoted to Brahman, and possessed of very firm weapons.
His lineage was very great, consisting of those Bhojas who dwell at Sārtikāvatī.
Andhakā obtained four sons from the daughter of Kāśya.
Kukura had a son named Bhajamāna, and [Bhajamāna] had a son named Sasaka Balabarhiṣa; Vṛṣṭi was the son of Kukura, and likewise, the son of Vṛṣṭi was [Pratiṣṭha].
Then Kapotaroman’s son was Tiliri;
from him Vasu was born, and from Vasu, in turn, was born Abhijit.
In that manner, it is said, a pair of sons was born to Abhijit;
they were Āhuka and Śrāhuka, renowned as the best among those who possess fame.
And regarding that Āhuka, they cite this verse here:
"Surrounded by a white retinue, the great man was like a young colt. (BrP 15.49)
Equipped with eighty pieces of armor, Āhuka should go first;
he must not be one who has no son, nor one who has not given a hundred gifts, nor one whose life does not extend for ten thousand years.
Neither one of impure conduct nor one who has not performed sacrifice should go toward the Bhoja;
it is said that they departed for the eastern direction, toward the Bhoja, in the presence of the Nāgas.
There were indeed ten thousand chariots belonging to Soma, drawn by teams of horses, adorned with banners and protective fenders, and possessing a roar like that of clouds.
There are twenty-one thousand girdles of silver and gold;
likewise, there are that many thousands in the northern direction.
The Bhojas were protectors of the earth, equipped with bows and small bells;
they said, moreover, that the Andhakas gave their sister to the Avantis.
To Āhuka, by his wife Kāśyā, two sons were born:
Devaka and Ugrasena, both equal to the offspring of gods.
Devaka had four sons who were like the gods:
Devavān, Upadeva, Saṃdeva, and Devarakṣita.
Then he gave seven maidens to Vasudeva:
Devakī, Śāntidevā, Sudevā, and Devarakṣitā.
Vṛkadevī, Upadevī, and Sunāmnī as the seventh—these were the nine daughters of Ugrasena; among them, Kaṃsa was the eldest.
Nyagrodha, Sunāman, as well as Kaṅka, Subhūṣaṇa, Rāṣṭrapāla, Sutanu, Anāvṛṣṭi, and Puṣṭimat.
They had five sisters: Kaṃsā, Kaṃsavatī, Sutanū, Rāṣṭrapālī, and the beautiful woman Kaṅkā.
Ugrasena, born of the Kukura lineage, has been described along with his offspring;
he maintained this dynasty of the Kukuras, who possessed immeasurable splendor.
A man possessing offspring shall attain a vast lineage for himself. (BrP 15.62)
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
The son of Bhajamāna was Vidūratha, a preeminent chariot-warrior;
Rājādhideva was Śūra, and he was the son of Vidūratha.
To Rājādhideva were born sons of exceeding prowess:
the mighty Datta and Atidatta, Śoṇāśva, and Śvetavāhana.
Śamī, Daṇḍaśarman, and Dantaśatru were born as Śatrujit;
and Śravaṇā and Śraviṣṭhā became sisters.
Śamīputra was the son of Pratikṣatra, and Svayaṃbhoja was the son of Pratikṣatra;
from Svayaṃbhoja, Bhadika was born.
He indeed had sons, all of whom were of terrible prowess;
Kṛtavarman was the eldest among them, while Śatadhanvan was the middle one.
Devānta, Narānta, the physician Vaitaraṇa,
Sudānta, Atidānta, Nikāśya, and Kāmadambhaka.
The learned Devānta was the son of Kambalabarhiṣ;
his son was Asamaujas, and both of them were named Asamaujas.
To Ajātaputra he gave two sons, Sudaṃṣṭra and Sucāru; and Asamaujas had a son named Kṛṣṇa—these are remembered as the Andhakas.
Gāndhārī and Mādrī both became the wives of Kroṣṭu;
Gāndhārī gave birth to the exceedingly powerful Anamitra.
Then Mādrī [gave birth to] the son Yudhājit, as well as Devamīḍhuṣa,
Anamitra— the unconquered conqueror of his enemies.
Nighna was the son of Anamitra, and from Nighna two sons were born:
Prasena and Satrājit, both of whom conquered the armies of their enemies.
But Prasena, while residing in Dvāravatī, obtained from the Sun a great divine jewel named Syamantaka.
The Sun became a friend of that Satrājit, equal to his very life-breath.
Once, at the end of the night, that best of chariot-warriors [set out] with his chariot.
He went to the water’s edge to touch the waters and to worship the Sun;
as he was standing there worshipping Sūrya, Vivasvat stood before him.
Then the Lord Vivasvat, whose form was clearly manifest and who possessed a circle of splendor, being all-pervading,
spoke to the King as he stood before him.
Just as I always behold you in the sky, O Lord of lights, as the divine one encircled by a halo of splendor, even so do I see you standing right before me.
"What distinction is there for me, who have approached you as a friend?
Having heard this, the Blessed One [offered] the Syamantaka jewel.
Then the Lord, having unfastened it from his own neck, placed it aside;
thereupon the king beheld it in embodied form.
Then, having seen him, Satrajit was filled with joy and conversed with him for a moment; he spoke again to Vivasvat as he was about to depart.
O Lord, that by which you constantly illumine all the worlds—
that very jewel, O Blessed One, you ought to give to me.
Then the Sun-god gave him the Syamantaka jewel;
having fastened it on, the lord of the earth entered the city.
The people ran after him, crying out, "This is Sūrya who is going! But the king, as well as his inner apartments, remained bewildered within his own city.
Out of affection, King Satrājit gave that supreme, divine Syamantaka jewel to his brother, Prasenajit.
That jewel emitted gold in the dwelling of Vṛṣṇi and Andhaka;
the rain-cloud poured forth at the proper time, and indeed there was no fear of disease.
Govinda desired Prasena’s jewel-gem, the Syamantaka;
yet, though he was capable, he did not seize it, nor did he obtain it.
Once, while out hunting adorned with that [jewel],
Prasena met his death at the hands of a forest-dwelling lion on account of the Syamantaka.
Then the mighty king of bears, having struck down the charging lion and seized that jewel-gem, entered his cave.
Then all the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, having bound themselves with that request for the jewel because of the killing of Prasena, were filled with apprehension regarding Kṛṣṇa.
Suspected [of the crime], that righteous-souled one,
having made the vow, "I shall recover the jewel," departed for the forest without having committed that deed.
Then, having followed the tracks of Prasena with trustworthy men, [he went] to the place where Prasena had been roaming for game.
Seeking Mount Ṛkṣavanta, the best of mountains, and the supreme mountain Vindhya,
that high-minded one, exhausted from his search, beheld them.
He found Prasena killed along with his horse, but he did not find that jewel;
then, the lion was not far from Prasena’s body.
He saw that [the demon] had been slain by a bear, and the tracks of the bear were indicated by footprints;
then Mādhava followed those footprints to the cave of the bear.
O twice-born ones, he indeed heard a voice uttered by a female monkey at the bear’s cave,
while the nurse was carrying the infant son of Jāmbavat.
And while she was playing with a jewel, he said to her, "Do not cry. (BrP 16.35)
The nurse said: "The lion killed Prasena; the lion was slain by Jāmbavān.
Do not weep, my dear child; for this Syamantaka belongs to you."
From that very moment, the Lord quickly went to the cave;
having entered there, he proceeded straightway into that bear’s den.
Having stationed the Yadus at the entrance of the cave along with Balarāma,
the wielder of the Śārṅga bow beheld Jāmbavān staying within the cave.
Vāsudeva, however, fought with Jāmbavanta inside the cave;
Govinda fought with his two arms alone for twenty-one days.
Then, once Kṛṣṇa had entered the cave, those preceded by Baladeva arrived at the city of Dvāravatī and announced that Kṛṣṇa was slain.
Vāsudeva, having also conquered the mighty Jāmbavanta,
obtained the maiden Jāmbavatī, who was highly esteemed by the king of the bears.
He took the Syamantaka jewel for the sake of his own purification;
then, having conciliated the king of the bears, he emerged from the cave.
By this means, Kṛṣṇa returned to Dvārakā with humble attendants preceding him;
thus, having recovered the jewel, the infallible Acyuta purified himself.
Thus, by Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of enemies, who had been falsely accused, that jewel was indeed given to Satrājit in the assembly of all the Sātvatas.
Having conquered the Syamantaka jewel, he purified himself of sin;
Satrājit had ten wives, and they had one hundred sons.
Among them, three were renowned: Bhagakara was the eldest, as well as Vira, Vatapati, and Vasumedhas.
O best of the twice-born, there were also three maidens renowned in the quarters; among them, Satyabhāmā was the most excellent, being observant of vows and firm in her resolve.
Likewise, he gave his wife Prasvāpinī to Kṛṣṇa;
and Sabhākṣa and Bhaṅgakārin were the two best of men who were the boatmen.
Two sons endowed with virtues and renowned for their excellence of form were born;
then a son was born to Mādrī, and then a son of Vṛṣṇi, Yudhājit, was born.
Two sons were born to Vṛṣṇi: Śvaphalka and Citraka.
Śvaphalka took as his wife the daughter of the King of Kāśī.
Her father always gave cows named Gāndinī;
from her was born the mighty-armed Śrutavat, who was fond of guests.
Then the highly fortunate Akrūra was born, as well as Vipuladakṣiṇa,
Upamadgu, Madgu, Mudara, and Arimardana.
Ārikṣepa, as well as Upekṣa, Śatruhā, and Arimejaya;
Dharmabhṛt, Dharmā, Gṛdhrabhoja, and Andhaka likewise.
Āvāha and Prativāha, as well as the beautiful woman Sundarī, were the daughters;
Sundarī became the queen of Viśrutāśva, and his daughter was Vasuṃdharā.
Endowed with beauty and youth, and captivating the hearts of all beings,
Akrūra begot two sons upon Ugrasenā who were the delight of their lineage.
Vasudeva and Upadeva, both possessing divine luster, were born;
Citraka’s sons were Pṛthu and Vipṛthu.
Aśvagrīva, Aśvabāhu, Supārśvaka, Gaveṣaṇa,
Ariṣṭanemi, Suta, Dharma, and Dharmabhṛt were his sons.
Subāhu, Bahubāhu, Śraviṣṭhā, and Śravaṇā— these two women [are present]—
[hear] this false accusation which has been uttered against Kṛṣṇa.
False accusations never touch him; this is what the Vedas declare.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Regarding the jewel-syamantraka that Kṛṣṇa had given to Satrājit,
Babhru caused it to be seized by Śatadhanvan, the Bhoja king.
For Akrūra had always longed for the blameless Satyabhāmā,
seeking an opportunity, as well as the Syamantaka jewel.
Then, having slain Satrājit at night, the mighty Śatadhanvan took that jewel and gave it to Akrūra.
But then, O Brahmins, Akrūra, taking that most excellent jewel, made an agreement, saying: "I must not be revealed by you. (BrP 17.4)
"We shall spring forward to rescue you when you are assailed by Kṛṣṇa;
today, the entire city of Dvārakā undoubtedly remains under my control. (BrP 17.5)
When her father was dead, the high-minded Satyabhāmā, afflicted with grief,
ascended a chariot and departed for the city of Vāraṇāvata.
But Satyabhāmā, having informed her husband of that deed of Śatadhanvan the Bhoja, stood by his side, afflicted with grief, shedding tears.
And having performed the water-libation rites for the deceased Pāṇḍavas, Hari appointed Sātyaki to the task of constructing a funeral mound for them.
Then, having arrived swiftly at Dvārakā, the glorious Madhusūdana spoke these words to his elder brother, the wielder of the plow: BrP_17.9 //
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Prasena was killed by a lion, and Satrājit by Chatadhanvan;
but the Syamantaka jewel is mine, O Lord, for I am its master."
Therefore, mount the chariot quickly; having slain the great car-warrior Bhoja, O mighty-armed one, that Syamantaka jewel shall belong to us.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Then a tumultuous battle commenced between the Bhoja king and Kṛṣṇa;
thereafter, Śatadhanvan gazed in every direction for Akrūra.
Seeing both those tormentors of the Bhojas enraged there,
Akrūra, though capable, did not intervene with the son of Hṛdika due to the curse.
Then, afflicted by fear, the Bhoja king set his mind on retreat;
he retreated from his heart for more than a hundred yojanas.
O brahmins, Bhoja’s mare, renowned by the name Hṛdayā and capable of traveling a hundred yojanas, was the one with whom Kṛṣṇa fought.
Seeing that his own speed had diminished after traveling a hundred yojanas and observing the superior progress of the chariot, he afflicted Śatadhanvan.
Then, O twice-born ones, when she had been slain, her life-breaths rose up into the sky due to exhaustion and fatigue; thereupon Kṛṣṇa spoke to Rāma.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Stay here, O mighty-armed one; the faults of the horses have been seen by me.
I shall go on foot and take back the Syamantaka jewel."
Then, O brahmins, having gone on foot from there, Acyuta, the supreme knower of weapons, slew Śatadhanvan in the vicinity of Mithilā.
Having slain the mighty Bhoja, he did not see the Syamantaka;
and as Balarama returned, he said to Krishna, "Give me the jewel."
"It does not exist," Kṛṣṇa replied; thereupon Rāma, filled with rage, responded repeatedly to Janārdana with the exclamation, "Fie! (dhik).
Balarāma said:
"Out of brotherhood, I forgive you; may it be well with you, for I am departing.
I have no concern with Dvārakā, nor with you, nor with the Vṛṣṇis."
Then Rāma, the crusher of enemies, entered Mithilā,
honored by the King of Mithilā with all desired offerings.
At that very time, Babhru, the best among the wise,
performed all kinds of various sacrifices without restraint.
For the sake of the Syamantaka jewel, the wise and highly illustrious son of Gāndinī entered that armor consisting of initiation for the purpose of protection.
Then, for sixty years, that righteous-souled king employed various other jewels and diverse kinds of wealth solely for the sake of sacrifices.
Those sacrifices of that great-souled one were known as the Akrūra-yajñas;
they all provided abundant food and sacrificial fees, and granted every desire.
Then King Duryodhana, having gone to Mithilā,
that lord obtained divine instruction in the mace from Baladeva.
Then, having been reconciled by the great chariot-warriors of the Vṛṣṇi and Andhaka clans, Rāma was brought back to Dvārakā itself by the high-souled Kṛṣṇa.
And Akrūra, that bull among men of great strength, arrived together with the Andhakas;
having slain the sleeping Satrājit along with his kinsmen.
Out of fear of causing a rift among his kinsmen, Kṛṣṇa then remained indifferent toward him; and when Akrūra had departed, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, ceased to send rain.
Then, due to a drought, the kingdom became impoverished in many ways;
thereupon, the Kukuras and Andhakas sought to appease Akrūra.
Then, when that lord of donors had arrived again at Dvāravatī,
the thousand-eyed Indra rained down upon the shore of the ocean.
O best of sages, the wise Akrūra gave his sister Kanyā, who was highly esteemed for her virtue, to Vāsudeva out of affection.
Then, having discerned through his yogic power that the jewel had gone to Babhru, Janārdana Kṛṣṇa, standing in the midst of the assembly, spoke to Akrūra.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Lord, worthy of honor, give me that jewel, the best of gems, which is in your hand; do not show me disrespect.
O sinless one, the anger that arose within me during the sixty years has repeatedly grown; therefore, a great lapse of time has occurred.
Then, at the word of Kṛṣṇa, the high-minded Babhru gave that jewel without any difficulty in the assembly of all the Sātvatas.
Then Kṛṣṇa, the subduer of enemies, with a joyful mind, gave back that jewel to Babhru from the hand of Babhru, as it had been received through straightforwardness.
Having fastened the Syamantaka jewel, that precious gem obtained from the hand of Kṛṣṇa,
the son of Gāndinī shone like the sun.
The sages said:
"Oh, a most magnificent narrative has been recounted by you,
concerning all the descendants of Bharata as well as the kings!"
Of the gods and the dānavas, of the gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas,
as well as of the daityas, siddhas, and likewise of the guhyakas.
Most wonderful deeds, heroic exploits, firm resolutions regarding dharma, various divine narratives, and his foremost, unsurpassed birth.
O high-minded one, you have correctly described the creation of Prajāpati,
as well as that of all the Prajāpatis, the Guhyakas, and the Apsarases.
O illustrious one, you have described the entire manifold world of beings, both stationary and moving; this which has been heard by me is truly captivating. (BrP 18.5)
This ancient narrative, which bestows the fruit of merit, was told with gentle speech;
it perfectly delights the mind and ears, being as sweet as nectar.
Now we wish to hear about the entire mandala of the earth;
you ought to speak, O Omniscient One, for our curiosity is indeed great.
O Mahāmati, as many oceans, islands, regions, mountains, forests, rivers, and [abodes] of the meritorious gods and others as there may be—
You ought to explain correctly the extent of this entire world, its foundation, its essential nature, and the configuration of this universe.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
O sages, listen to this as I speak it in brief;
its extreme detail could not be told even in a hundred years.
O twice-born ones, the islands named Jambū and Plakṣa, and another called Śālmala,
as well as Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara is the seventh.
These continents are surrounded by seven oceans,
equal [in number], consisting of salt water, sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and water.
Jambūdvīpa stands in the center of all these;
and in its center, O best of Brahmins, is Meru, the golden mountain.
Its height is eighty-four thousand yojanas;
it enters sixteen thousand yojanas below and is thirty-two thousand yojanas wide at its summit.
At its base, this mountain stands sixteen thousand [yojanas] in circumference on all sides;
it is shaped like the pericarp of this earth-lotus.
To its south are Himavat, Hemakūṭa, and Niṣadha;
to the north are the mountain ranges Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgin.
Two of them in the middle are one hundred thousand [yojanas] in measure, while the others are ten less;
they are two thousand [yojanas] in height and of the same extent.
O twice-born ones, Bhārata is the first region, then Kiṃpuruṣa is recorded, and likewise Harivarṣa is another; these are situated to the south of Meru.
The northern region is Ramyaka, and its very next is Hiraṇmaya;
and the Northern Kurus are just as [the land] of Bhārata is.
O best of the twice-born, each of these [regions] measures nine thousand [yojanas];
and in their midst is Ilāvṛta, where Mount Meru rises, made of gold.
O fortunate ones, there, extending nine thousand [yojanas] in each of the four directions from Meru, lies Ilāvṛta;
and here there are four mountains.
The supporting pillars extending from Meru are ten thousand yojanas wide;
on the east is the one named Mandara, and on the south is Gandhamādana.
Vipula is situated on the western side, and Supārśva stands on the north;
among them are the Kadamba, the Jambū, the Pippala, and the Vaṭa trees.
O best of the twice-born, the trees that serve as the banners of the mountains are eleven hundred *yojanas* in height; that *jambū* tree is the cause of the name of Jambūdvīpa.
Indeed, the fruits of that Jambu tree, as large as great elephants,
fall upon the back of the mountain, shattering on all sides.
From their juice, the river known as Jambūnadī flows there; it is indeed that stream which is drunk by the inhabitants of that place.
Neither fatigue nor foul odor, neither old age nor the decay of the senses arises for those people there whose minds are healthy from drinking that [water].
Having reached that soil on the bank and its essence, and being dried by a pleasant breeze,
it becomes the gold known as Jāmbūnada, the ornament of the Siddhas.
O best of sages, Bhadrāśva is to the east of Meru and Ketumāla is to the west; between those two regions lies Ilāvṛta.
The Caitraratha forest is in the east, Gandhamādana in the south,
Vaibhrāja likewise in the west, and Nandana is recorded as being in the north.
Aruṇoda, Mahābhadra, Asitoda, and Samānasa—
these are the four lakes that are always enjoyed by the gods.
Śāntavan, Cakrakuñja, Kurarī, and Mālyavat—
these are the filament-mountains (kesarācala) surrounding Meru, with Vaikaṅka at their head, situated to the east.
Trikūṭa, Śiśira, Pataṅga, Rucaka,
Niṣadha, and others are the Kesara mountains to its south.
Śikhivāsa, Savaidūrya, Kapila, and Gandhamādana—
likewise, the Kesara mountains beginning with Jānudhi are situated in the west.
And those situated immediately adjacent to Meru, located within the Jaṭhara and other regions,
are Śaṅkhakūṭa, Ṛṣabha, Haṃsa, Nāga, and others.
Likewise, there are the Kālañjara and other Kesara mountains to the north;
the great city extends for fourteen thousand yojanas.
O best of Brahmins, it is said that above Mount Meru, in the sky, is the abode of Brahmā;
and all around it, in the eight cardinal and intermediate directions, there are [other worlds].
The renowned and preeminent cities of Indra and the other world-protectors are flooded by [the waters] that have issued from Viṣṇu’s feet and bathe the lunar orb.
The Gaṅgā indeed falls from the sky all around the city of Brahmā;
having fallen there, she divided herself into four directions.
The Sītā, the Cālakanandā, and the Cakṣurbadhra follow in sequence;
the Sītā, moving through the atmosphere, flows from mountain to mountain toward the east.
Then, by means of the eastern region, Bhadrāśva, it flows toward the ocean;
likewise, the Alakanandā flows southward, reaching Bhārata.
O best of the twice-born, having divided into seven streams, it flows toward the ocean;
and its current then passes beyond all the western mountains.
The Bhadrā likewise flows toward the western region called Ketumāla, reaching as far as the ocean,
and similarly toward the northern mountains and the Northern Kurus.
O best of the twice-born, having passed beyond the northern ocean,
it flows toward the Mālyavat and Gandhamādana mountains, which extend as far as the Nīla and Niṣadha ranges.
Situated between those two, Mount Meru stands in the form of a pericarp;
there are the Bhāratas, the Ketumālas, the Bhadrāśvas, and likewise the Kurus.
The leaves of the world-mountain are outside the boundary mountains;
Jaṭhara and Devakūṭa are both boundary mountains.
Those two, Gandhamādana and Kailāsa, extend from south to north, reaching as far as Nīla and Niṣadha, and both stretch from east to west.
The Niṣadha and Pāriyātra mountains, both eighty yojanas in extent, are situated within the ocean as boundary mountains.
Those two, extending from south to north and reaching as far as Nīla and Niṣadha,
are situated on the western side of Meru just as the two [eastern mountains] are on the eastern side.
Triśṛṅga and Jārudhi are the two northern mountain ranges;
these two extend from east to west and are situated within the ocean.
Thus, O twice-born ones, these boundary mountains have been described by me;
situated within the belly of Meru, there are two of them in each of the four directions.
O twice-born ones, those Kesara mountains that have been described as being in the four directions of Meru, beginning with Śītānta, are indeed exceedingly beautiful.
In the valleys between the mountains frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
there were likewise most delightful forests and cities.
O best of sages, within those [mountains] are the most excellent abodes of Lakṣmī, Viṣṇu, Agni, Sūrya, and Indra,
frequented by men and kinnaras.
Gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, as well as daityas and dānavas,
sport day and night in those delightful mountain valleys.
O twice-born ones, these are remembered as terrestrial heavens, the abodes of the righteous;
those who commit evil deeds do not go there even in hundreds of births.
O twice-born ones, in Bhadrāśva the Blessed Viṣṇu dwells as Hayaśiras;
in Ketumāla he is Vārāha, and in Bhārata he assumes the form of the Tortoise.
And Govinda, the eternal one, dwells among the Kurus in the form of a fish;
Hari, the Lord of all and the All, exists everywhere in his universal form.
O twice-born ones, he who is the soul of all remains as the support of everything;
O best of the twice-born, there are eight regions, beginning with Kimpuruṣa.
Among them there was no sorrow, no exertion, and no agitation, nor hunger, fear, and the like;
the subjects were well-situated, free from affliction, and devoid of all suffering.
O twice-born ones, their lifespan is fixed at ten thousand or twelve thousand years; among them there are no other earthly conditions such as hunger, thirst, and the like.
In those regions, there is no conception of the Kṛta, Tretā,
and other ages. In all these varṣas, O best of the twice-born, there are seven principal mountain ranges each, and from them flow rivers by the hundreds.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
To the north of the ocean and to the south of the Snowy Mountains lies that land named Bhārata, where the lineage of the Bhāratas resides.
O best of the twice-born, this land of action, nine thousand yojanas in extent, exists for those who inquire about heaven and liberation.
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, Ṛkṣaparvata,
Vindhya, and Pāriyātra— these seven are the principal mountain ranges here.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, heaven is attained from this, and liberation indeed proceeds from this; likewise, men go to the state of animals or even to hell because of this.
From here one goes to heaven, to liberation, and to the intermediate state;
indeed, nowhere else among mortals is the field of action ordained.
Listen to the nine divisions of this land of Bhārata: Indradvīpa, Kaserumān, Tāmraparṇa, and Gabhastimān; 19.6.
Nāgadvīpa, Saumya, Gandharva, and Vāruṇa;
this, however, is the ninth among them, surrounded by the ocean.
This island extends for a thousand yojanas from south to north;
the Kirātas dwell in the east, and the Yavanas are situated in the west.
The Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras were established in their respective portions in the midst [of society],
possessing their livelihoods such as sacrifice, warfare, and trade.
O Sage, the Śatadrū, Candrabhāgā, and others flow forth from the foothills of the Himavat; and other rivers, such as the Vedasmṛti and so on, originate from the Pāriyātra mountains.
The Narmadā, the Surasā, and other rivers that flow from the Vindhya mountains,
as well as the Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, Nirvindhyā, Kāverī, and other principal rivers.
For these rivers, originating from the foot of Ṛkṣa, are heard to remove sin,
as are the Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Kṛṣṇaveṇī, and others.
The rivers originating from the foothills of the Sahya mountains are remembered as destroyers of sin and fear;
those originating from the Malaya mountains have the Kṛtamālā and Tāmraparṇī as their foremost.
The rivers beginning with the Trisāṃdhyā and Ṛṣikulyā are known to originate from Mount Mahendra;
those beginning with the Ṛṣikulyā and Kumārī originate from the foot of Mount Śuktimat.
There are thousands of other rivers and tributaries besides these;
in them dwell these people, such as those of Kuru, Pañcāla, Madhyadeśa, and so forth.
Those from the eastern regions and so forth, the inhabitants of Kāmarūpa, the Pauṇḍras, Kaliṅgas, Magadhas, and all those from the south; BrP 19.16.
Likewise, the Parāntyas, the Saurāṣṭras, the Śūdras, the Ābhīras, as well as the Arbudas, the Mārukas, the Mālavas, and those dwelling on the Pāriyātra mountains; BrP_19.17 //
The Sauviras, those who have reached Saindhava, the Śālvas, the inhabitants of Śākala,
the Madrārāmas, as well as the Ambaṣṭhas, the Pārasīkas, and others.
O highly fortunate one, they always drink the water of these rivers and dwell there,
filled with joyful and well-nourished people.
O great sage, the ages— Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali— dwell here in Bhāratavarṣa, but they exist nowhere else.
There, ascetics perform austerities and sacrificers offer oblations;
and there, gifts are bestowed with devotion for the sake of the world beyond.
In Jambūdvīpa, Viṣṇu, who consists of sacrifice, is worshipped by men as the Sacrificial Person (Yajñapuruṣa) through sacrifices; in other dvīpas, however, he is worshipped in other ways.
Even here, O great sage, Bhārata is the most excellent in Jambūdvīpa;
for this is the land of action (karmabhūmi), whereas all others are lands of enjoyment (bhogabhūmi).
In this regard, O best of beings, even after thousands upon thousands of births,
a living being may perhaps at some time obtain a human birth through the accumulation of merit.
The gods indeed sing these songs:
"Blessed are those who dwell in the region of Bhārata,
which serves as the cause for attaining both heaven and liberation."
Men become human beings once again when they renounce actions— the fruits of which were not intended— into Viṣṇu, who is the form of the supreme self.
Having reached that infinite ground of karma,
those who are stainless attain dissolution within it; yet we do not know what happens when that itself has dissolved.
Blessed indeed are those men who, through the *Bhārata*, remain free from the impairment of their senses even while undergoing bodily bondage during actions that lead to heaven.
And thus, O brahmins, this Jambūdvīpa, nine thousand yojanas in extent, has been described by me in brief, O twice-born ones. (BrP 19.28)
O twice-born ones, surrounding Jambūdvīpa, the Ocean of Milk stands outside it, a hundred thousand yojanas in extent and shaped like a ring.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Just as the continent named Jambū is surrounded by the salt ocean (Kṣāroda),
so too is Plakṣadvīpa situated, encircling the salt sea.
The extent of Jambūdvīpa is measured at one hundred thousand [yojanas];
O Brahmins, that same measure is declared to be double in Plakṣadvīpa as well.
Medhātithi, the lord of Plakṣadvīpa, indeed had seven sons:
the eldest was named Śāntabhaya, and after him was Śiśira.
Sukhodaya, Ānanda, Śiva, Kṣemaka,
and Dhruva as the seventh— these indeed were the lords of Plakṣadvīpa.
First was the year Śāntabhaya, then Śiśira which likewise bestows happiness;
then Ānanda, Śiva, Kṣemaka, and Dhruva.
O best of sages, there are others, the boundary-making mountain ranges of those [continents]; hear their seven names.
Gomeda, Candra, Nārada, Daṇḍubhi, Somaka, Sumanas, and Śaila; Vaibhrāja is the seventh.
O sinless ones, in these delightful mountain ranges of the Varṣas,
the subjects dwell together with the gods and Gandharvas.
In those regions, the lands are meritorious and heroic; no person dies there, nor do mental afflictions or physical diseases exist, for that place is happy at all times.
I shall now declare by name the seven rivers that flow from those regions into the ocean; when heard, they remove all evil.
Anutaptā, Śikhā, Viprāśā, Tridivā,
Kramu, Amṛtā, and Sukṛtā— these seven rivers flow there.
O twice-born ones, these mountains and principal rivers have thus been described;
there are likewise thousands of small rivers and mountains there.
Those people of the countryside always drink from those rivers with joy;
O twice-born ones, for them the rivers never diminish nor do they ever swell.
O best of the twice-born, in those seven regions there is no state of the Yuga; the time there is always equal to the Tretā Yuga.
O brahmins, in the regions beginning with Plakṣadvīpa and ending with Śākadvīpa,
people live for five thousand years free from disease.
Among them, Dharma is fourfold, arising from the divisions of caste and stage of life;
and there are four castes therein—those I shall proclaim to you, O wise ones.
O best of sages, those who were Āryakas, Kurus, Viviṣvas, and Bhāvins— those were the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
In its center, O best of the twice-born, there is a very great tree equal in size to the Jambu tree; because of that tree, which is named Plakṣa, this is called Plakṣadvīpa.
There, the Blessed Lord Hari— the creator of the world, the all-pervading Lord of all— is worshipped by those castes, beginning with the Āryakas, in the form of Soma.
Plakṣadvīpa is surrounded by an ocean of sugarcane juice that matches its size, forming as it were a surrounding rim.
Thus, O best of sages, this Plakṣadvīpa has been described by me to you in brief; now learn further of that Śālmala [dvīpa].
The hero who is the lord of Śālmaladvīpa is Vapuṣmān; his sons, O twice-born ones, are the names by which those seven regions are indeed known.
O best of the twice-born, they were Śveta, Harita, Jīmūta, Rohita, Vaidyuta, Mānasa, and Suprabha.
And that ocean of sugarcane juice, belonging to Śālman, stands completely surrounded on all sides by a continent twice its extent.
There too, seven mountain ranges are to be known as the sources of jewels;
they likewise manifest the [seven] regions, and there are exactly seven rivers as well.
Kumuda and Unnata, and the third is Balāhaka;
where the great medicinal herbs are found, that is the fourth mountain, Droṇa.
Kaṅka was the fifth, Mahiṣa the sixth, and likewise Kakudmān, the best of mountains, was the seventh; O twice-born ones, the names of the rivers follow from this.
Śroṇī, Toyā, Vitṛṣṇā, Candrā, Śukrā, Vimocanī, and Nivṛtti is the seventh among them; these are remembered as bestowing the pacification of evil.
Śveta, Lohita, Jīmūta, Harita,
Vaidyuta, Mānasa, and the seventh named Suprabha.
These seven regions are indeed inhabited by the four castes;
O best of the twice-born, such are the castes that dwell within these lands of Śālmala.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras— tawny, ruddy, yellow, and black respectively— each individually worship him.
The sacrificers worshipped the Blessed One, Viṣṇu himself, the imperishable Self,
who had become the wind and was established within the sacrifice through the most excellent of rituals.
The presence of the gods is exceedingly enchanting here;
and there is a great śālmali tree, which gives its name to this place.
This continent is surrounded on all sides by the Suroda ocean, which is equal in extent to Śālmala itself.
The Surodaka ocean is surrounded on all sides by Kuśadvīpa,
which is twice the extent of Śālmala [dvīpa] in every direction.
Listen now, O sons, to the names of the sons of Jyotiṣmān in Kuśadvīpa:
Udbhida, Veṇumān, Svairatha, Randhana, and Dhṛti.
Then there is Prabhākara and Kapila; the sequence of regions is named after them.
In that region dwell Daityas and Dānavas together with human beings.
In that very same way, the gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Kiṃpuruṣas, and others—
there too, there are four castes, devoted to their own respective duties.
O best of the twice-born, the *daminas*, the *śuṣmiṇas*, the *snehās*,
and the *māndahās* were the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, respectively, as declared in due order.
Because they performed the actions as prescribed, their own offices were brought to an end;
there, in that Kuśadvīpa, they beheld Janārdana in the form of Brahmā.
Those who sacrifice exhaust that fierce [karma] which yields the fruit of their specific entitlement;
likewise, Vidruma, Hemaśaila, Dyutimān, and Puṣṭimān [are situated there].
Kuśeśaya, Hari, and Mandarācala as the seventh—
these, O best of the twice-born, are the seven mountain ranges of the rain there on that island.
And there are seven rivers; I shall state their names in order:
Dhūtapāpā, Śivā, Pavitrā, and likewise Saṃmati.
Lightning, water, and the earth—these others are removers of all sins;
there are also thousands of other small rivers and mountains there.
In Kuśadvīpa there is a clump of kuśa grass; it is known by that name.
That island is equal in extent to that [clump] and is surrounded by the Ghṛtoda ocean.
And the ocean of clarified butter is indeed surrounded by Krauñcadvīpa;
O best of sages, hear now of another great island, Krauñcadvīpa.
The extent of Krauñcadvīpa is twice that of Kuśadvīpa;
there, the seven high-souled sons of Dyutimat [reigned].
The high-minded one gave names to those regions:
Kuśāva, Mandagā, Uṣṇa, Pīvara, and Andhakāraka.
Muni and Dundubhi—these seven, O twice-born ones, were their sons;
even there, they were exceedingly beautiful and frequented by gods and gandharvas.
O twice-born ones, the best of sages are the Varṣācalas;
their names are Krauñca, Vāmana, and the third is Andhakāraka.
Devavrata, Dharma, another named Puṇḍarīkavān,
Dundubhi, and Mahāśaila— these are each twice the size of the preceding one.
Those mountains which exist on each island, as well as those islands themselves,
are likewise situated within these delightful regions and upon the preeminent mountain ranges of those regions.
The subjects dwell there free from fear along with hosts of gods;
they are prosperous, lotus-like, blessed, and renowned as the best of the twice-born.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are mentioned there in their proper order;
O best of sages, they always drink from the rivers that flow there.
There are seven principal rivers, as well as hundreds of others that are small streams;
namely, Gaurī, Kumudvatī, Saṃdhyā, Rātri, and Manojavā.
Khyāti, Puṇḍarīkā, and these seven are the rivers of those regions;
there too, the Blessed Janārdana resides with his attendants, Puṣkara and the others.
In the vicinity of the sacrifice, he who is the form of Rudra is worshipped through the yoga of meditation;
Krauñcadvīpa is surrounded by an ocean of whey (*dadhimaṇḍodaka*).
Enclosed on all sides by Śākadvīpa, which is equal in extent to Krauñcadvīpa,
the sea of curd-water is likewise surrounded.
O best of the twice-born, the territory of Bhavya, the noble and great-souled lord of Śākadvīpa, is twice the extent of Krauñcadvīpa.
He gave seven regions to those seven sons:
Jalada, Kumāra, Sukumāra, and Manīraka; // BrP_20.60 //
Kusumoda, Modāki, and the seventh, Mahādruma—
there too, the seven regions are named after these very [mountains] in succession.
There too, there are seven mountains that serve as the dividers between the regions:
the first among them is Udayagiri, and the next is Jaladhāra.
Likewise, O twice-born ones, there are Raivataka, Śyāma, Ambhogiri,
the delightful Āstikeya, and Kesara, the best of mountains.
And there is a great tree there called Śāka, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas,
from the touch of the wind from whose leaves supreme delight arises.
There, the lands are auspicious and inhabited by people belonging to the four castes;
high-souled beings dwell there, free from fear and free from disease.
And here are rivers of great merit that remove all sins and fears:
Sukumārī, Kumārī, Nalinī, and Reṇukā.
O best of the twice-born, there are the Ikṣu, the Dhenukā, and likewise the Gabhastī as the seventh; furthermore, there are tens of thousands of other small rivers there.
Likewise, there are mountains by the hundreds and thousands;
those situated among the clouds and other such places drink from them with joy.
In those regions, the inhabited lands possess the fourfold aims of human life,
and there are rivers of great merit that have descended from heaven to the earth.
In those seven regions, there is no decline of the Dharma, nor is there excessive joy or grief, nor even any transgression of the bounds of propriety.
The Magas, the Māgadhas, the Mānasas, and likewise the Mandagas—
the Magas were for the most part Brahmins, while the Māgadhas were Kṣatriyas.
The Vaiśyas among them are known as Mānasas, while the Śūdras are those who move slowly;
by those residing in Śākadvīpa, Hari Viṣṇu, who bears the form of the sun, is worshipped.
O brahmins, Śākadvīpa is surrounded on all sides by the Ocean of Milk, where those of self-restraint duly worship with the aforementioned rituals.
O Brahmins, the Ocean of Milk, surrounded on all sides by the continent named Puṣkara, is encircled by it as if by a ring the size of Śākadvīpa.
From Śākadvīpa, the continent was twice as large on all sides;
and from Savana, Mahāvīta became the son of Puṣkara.
Likewise, Dhātaki is the name of those two regions;
there is another region called Mahāvīta, as well as the one known as Dhātakīkhaṇḍa.
And here, O fortunate ones, there is one famous mountain range known as Mānasottara, which forms a circular ring in the middle.
It rises fifty thousand yojanas in height and is of the same extent in width, being perfectly circular on all sides.
Standing as if dividing the circular Puṣkara-dvīpa through its center, that [mountain] exists; indeed, by it those two regions have become separated.
Each of these two is ring-shaped, and between them lies a great mountain;
there, human beings live for ten thousand years.
O twice-born ones, they were free from disease and sorrow, devoid of passion and hatred; among them there was neither inferiority nor superiority, nor were there those to be slain and those who slew.
Therein, there is no envy, malice, fear, anger, fault-finding, greed, or the like;
the great outer region is Dhātakīkhaṇḍa at its edge.
On that island named Puṣkara, which is frequented by gods, Daityas, and others, neither truth nor falsehood exists near the Mānasottara mountain.
In that island, which consists of two regions, there are neither rivers nor mountains;
the men there are of uniform appearance, being identical in form to the gods.
It was devoid of the conduct of the castes and stages of life, bereft of the practice of dharma, and lacking in the pursuit of the three Vedas, commerce, civil law, and service.
Then, O Brahmins, for two years this supreme earthly heaven exists—
a time that bestows happiness upon all and is free from old age and disease.
O twice-born ones, in Puṣkara, Dhātakīkhaṇḍa, and Mahāvīta— indeed,
in Puṣkaradvīpa, there is a banyan tree, the supreme abode of Brahmā.
While Brahmā dwells there, being worshipped by gods and asuras,
the Puṣkara ocean is surrounded by the sea of sweet water.
Just as Puṣkara is equal in its extent and its circumference,
so too are the seven continents surrounded by seven oceans.
The continents and the oceans increase twofold respectively;
indeed, the waters in all the oceans are always equal.
No deficiency or excess ever arises in them,
just as water contained in a pot increases when it comes into contact with fire.
Likewise, O best of sages, as the moon waxes, the waters in the ocean increase;
yet those waters neither diminish nor exceed their measure, for they only swell and subside accordingly.
At the rising and setting of the moon during the bright and dark fortnights,
[the shadow] increases by exactly five hundred and ten finger-breadths.
O best of the twice-born, the increase and decrease of the waters of the ocean are observed;
in that Puṣkara-dvīpa, food is provided spontaneously.
Indeed, the brahmins and all creatures always enjoy food of six flavors;
the arrangement of the world is seen on all sides around this sweet water.
Twice as large is the golden land, devoid of all living beings;
beyond that is the Lokāloka mountain, ten thousand yojanas in extent.
He was as many thousands of yojanas in height;
then darkness, enveloping him, stood all around that mountain.
And this earth, O best of the twice-born, is fifty koṭis in extent and is surrounded on all sides by the shell of the cosmic egg and darkness.
Together with the shell of the cosmic egg, including the islands and the mountains,
this very earth is the sustainer and the creator, superior in qualities to all beings;
she is the support of all worlds, O best of the twice-born.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
O best of sages, this extent of the earth has been described;
its height, moreover, is said to be seventy thousand [yojanas].
O best of sages, each of the netherworlds— Atala, Vitala, Nitala, and likewise Sutala— is ten thousand [yojanas] in extent.
Talātala, Rasātala, and Pātāla as the seventh;
[their grounds] are black, white, reddish, yellow, gravelly, rocky, and golden.
O best of Brahmins, those grounds are adorned with magnificent palaces,
and within them dwell hundreds of various classes of Dānavas and Daityas.
And Nārada said that for the great-bodied Nāgas and their kinsmen, O best of the twice-born, the netherworlds (pātālas) are even more delightful than the heavenly realm (svarloka).
Having gone from the netherworlds to heaven, he spoke in the midst of the assembly of the gods:
"Therein are white, radiant jewels that produce great delight."
And adorned with ornaments of serpents, what is equal to Pātāla,
which is beautified here and there by the daughters of the Daityas and Dānavas?
In Pātāla, who would not feel delight, even one who is liberated?
For there, the rays of the sun spread light by day, but no heat.
And for the moon, there was no cold at night; it served only for illumination, while the serpents were intoxicated by the pride of their great consumption of food, edibles, and drinks.
There, even though time passed, it was not perceived by the Danujas and others;
there were forests, rivers, delightful lakes, and lotus-pools.
The warbling of male cuckoos and other birds, charming garments, most beautiful ornaments, perfumes, and unguents; BrP 21.11.
O twice-born ones, there are always the sounds of lutes, flutes, and drums;
these and other delightful things are to be enjoyed by the Dānavas through their good fortune.
The Daityas and Uragas dwelling within the depths of Pātāla consume [the offerings],
and beneath those netherworlds resides that tamasic form of Viṣṇu.
He whom the Daityas and Dānavas, known as the "Remnant," are unable to describe by his qualities—
he who is recited as Ananta by the Siddhas and worshipped by the gods and divine seers.
Manifested with a thousand heads and adorned with pure svastika ornaments,
he illuminated the quarters of the sky with a thousand jewels upon his hoods.
He whose eyes are ever rolling with intoxication and who always wears but a single earring renders all the asuras powerless for the welfare of the world.
Wearing a crown and bearing a garland, he shone like a white mountain with fire;
clad in blue garments, intoxicated with pride, and adorned with a white necklace.
With the waterfall of the Ganges falling from the clouds, he was like the supreme Mount Kailāsa;
with the tip of his hand resting on his plough, he bore his excellent mace.
He who is himself worshipped by the splendor of Varuṇa’s own form, from whose mouths at the end of the eon there issues forth a fire blazing with tongues of poisonous flame; ||| BrP_21.19 |||
Rudra, whose essence is Saṃkarṣaṇa, emerges and devours the three worlds,
bearing upon him the entire circle of the earth as if it were a mountain peak.
Śeṣa, who is worshipped by all the gods, dwells at the base of Pātāla;
[I shall describe] his heroism, his power, his true nature, and his very form.
It cannot be described or even known, even by the gods,
he for whom this entire earth is reddened by the tips of the jewels on his hoods.
He remains like a garland of flowers; who will speak of his prowess when Ananta unfolds himself, his eyes rolling with intoxication?
Then this earth, together with its mountains, waters,
forests, Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, Kinnaras, Uragas, and elephants, trembles.
One does not reach the end of his qualities; therefore, he is infinite and imperishable, whose body is anointed with yellow sandalwood paste by the hands of the wives of the Nāgas.
Exhausted by the wind of his frequent sighs, he becomes the fragrance for the garments of the quarters;
it is by propitiating him that the ancient seer Garga truly understood the luminaries.
Having understood the entire fruit as declared by the signs,
this earth was supported on his head by that best of Nāgas;
it sustains all the worlds together with their gods, asuras, and humans.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
O brahmins, O best of the twice-born, listen now to those hells, Raurava and the rest, into which sinners are cast immediately thereafter.
Raurava, Śaukara, Rodha, Tāna, Viśasana,
Mahājvāla, Taptakuḍya, Mahālobha, and Vimohana.
Rudhirāndha, Vasātapta, Kṛmīśa, Kṛmibhojana,
Asipattravana, Kṛṣṇa, and the terrible Lālābhakṣa.
Likewise, there are Pūyavaha, the sinful Vahnijvāla, Adhaḥśiras, Sadaṃśa, Kṛṣṇasūtra, Tamas, and Avīci as well.
Śvabhojana, Apratiṣṭhoma, and likewise Āvīci—
these and other such hells are exceedingly terrible.
In the realm of Yama, there are terrible places where weapons, fire, and poison appear;
into these fall those men who were devoted to evil deeds.
A false witness, as well as one who speaks correctly out of partiality,
and he who speaks any other untruth— that man goes to Raurava.
O best of sages, the killer of an embryo, the destroyer of a city, the slayer of a cow,
and he who obstructs the breath— all these go to the terrible Raurava hell.
The drinker of liquor, the slayer of a Brahmin, and the stealer of gold go to the Śūkara hell,
as does he who indeed enters into association with them.

The slayer of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, likewise one who violates the teacher’s bed, one who has sexual intercourse with his sister, and he who kills a king’s soldier— all these go to the Taptakumbha hell.
The seller of honey, the keeper of executioners, the seller of saffron,
and he who abandons his food— these fall into the Taptaloha hell.
Having gone to his daughter or even his daughter-in-law, he is cast into Mahājvāla;
so too is that lowest of men who insults his elders or who is a reviler.
O twice-born ones, he who defiles the Vedas, he who sells the Vedas, and he who approaches those who should not be approached— these go to the Śabala hell.
A thief falls into delusion, as does one who violates the bounds of propriety,
one who hates the gods, the twice-born, and the ancestors, and he who defiles precious gems.
That lowest of men who eats while bypassing the ancestors, the gods, and guests goes indeed to the realm of Kṛmīśa, where he is devoured by worms for having performed improper sacrifices.
The man who fashions arrows goes to the fierce Śarakarta hell, as does the man who makes barbed shafts or who crafts swords and other such weapons. He goes to the Vaidhaka hell for consuming saliva.
These go to the exceedingly dreadful Viśasana hell;
and one who accepts gifts from the wicked goes to the Adhomukha hell.
In that place, one who sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, as well as one who indicates the constellations [for profit],
and a man who always eats sweet food, goes alone to the Kṛmipūya hell.
O twice-born ones, a Brahmin who sells lac, meat, juices, sesame seeds, and salt goes to that very same hell.
O best of the twice-born, by rearing cats, cocks, goats, dogs, pigs, and birds, one goes to that very same hell.

One who lives by painting, a fisherman, one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa*-born son, a poisoner, a spy, a keeper of buffalo-cows, and that twice-born man who approaches his wife on forbidden days; BrP 22.21.
The arsonist of a house, the betrayer of friends, the fowler, the village priest,
and those who sell the Soma— all these fall into the Rudhirāndha hell.
The man who steals honey, the destroyer of a village, those who drink semen and the like, and those who violate established boundaries, all go to the Vaitaraṇī river.
Those who live by deceit and those who are impure go to a state of suffering;
he who cuts down a forest in vain goes to the Forest of Sword-Leaves (Asipattravana).
Shepherds and deer-hunters indeed fall into Vahnijvāla; O Brahmins, those who give fire to those who have not yet cooked their food go to that very same place.
Both he who violates his vows and he who has fallen away from his own stage of life fall into the midst of the *saṃdaṃśa* (tongs) torment.
Those men who, though practicing celibacy, discharge semen during the day while dreaming,
and those who are taught by their own sons, fall into the Śvabhojana hell.
These and other hells exist by the hundreds and thousands,
wherein those who have performed evil deeds are cooked, having undergone their torments.
In that very same way, these and thousands of other evils are experienced by men born into various births who have the intermediate states of hell as their domain.
Those men who perform actions contrary to the duties of their caste and stage of life—
whether by deed, thought, or word— fall into the hells.
The gods in heaven are seen by the denizens of hell with their heads downward;
likewise, the gods look down from below at all the hell-beings who face downward.
Immobile beings, worms, fish, birds, domestic animals,
humans, the righteous gods, and likewise those seeking liberation [attain their states] in due order.
The second is a thousandth part of the first, and so on in succession;
for all these are highly fortunate, up to those who have taken refuge in liberation.
As many beings as there are in heaven, so many are the inhabitants of hell;
the evildoer who turns his back on expiation goes to hell.
The supreme sages, having recollected them accordingly, have prescribed penances that correspond to each respective sin.
O best of Brahmins, those who know the truth—beginning with Svāyambhuva—have declared that for great sins there are great penances, and for minor sins, minor ones. (BrP 22.36)
Of all the various penances without exception, which consist essentially of ascetic practices,
the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa is the supreme among them all.
For that man in whom remorse indeed arises after a sin has been committed,
the one supreme expiation is the remembrance of Hari.
By recollecting Nārāyaṇa in the morning, at night, during the twilights, at midday, and so forth, a person immediately attains the destruction of their sins.
O Brahmins, through the constant remembrance of Viṣṇu, one whose entire accumulation of afflictions has been exhausted attains liberation by the recitation of that Viṣṇu's names.
O best of Brahmins, for one whose mind is fixed on Vāsudeva during recitation, fire-offerings, worship,
and so forth, even the fruit of lordship over the gods constitutes an obstacle.
Where is the ascent to the summit of heaven, which is characterized by returning once more;
and where is the recitation of "Vāsudeva," the unsurpassed seed of liberation?
Therefore, a twice-born man who constantly remembers Viṣṇu day and night goes to no hell, being purified and with all his sins utterly destroyed.
Heaven is that which brings joy to the mind; hell is the opposite of that.
O best of the twice-born, indeed, merit and demerit are what are designated as heaven and hell.
Since a single object leads to suffering, to pleasure, to the arising of envy,
and to anger, how can that object be of the nature of suffering?
That very same thing, having become a source of pleasure, arises again as suffering;
that very same thing arises as a cause of serenity for one who dwells within anger.
Therefore, nothing exists that is essentially suffering, nor does anything exist that is essentially happiness;
this is merely a transformation of the mind characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Knowledge alone is the supreme Brahman; ignorance is held to lead to bondage.
This entire universe is of the nature of knowledge; nothing exists beyond knowledge.
"O Brahmins, let knowledge and ignorance indeed be understood as such;
thus has this mandala of the earth been described by me to you."
O twice-born ones, all the subterranean realms as well as the hells,
the oceans, the mountains, the islands, the regions, and the rivers—
all this has been told in brief; what more do you wish to hear?
The sages said:
"Everything has been told by you to us in its entirety;
now we wish to hear about the worlds, beginning with Bhuvarloka."
O illustrious Lomaharṣaṇa, describe exactly as they are the positions and dimensions of the planets, according to their true nature.
Lomaharṣaṇa said: As far as the earth is illuminated by the rays of the sun and the moon— including its oceans, rivers, and mountains— so great is it said to be.
To whatever extent the earth extends in its width and circumference,
to that same extent indeed does the sky extend in its width and circumference.
O Brahmins, the solar orb is situated one hundred thousand yojanas from the earth,
and the lunar orb is likewise situated one hundred thousand yojanas from the sun.
At a full hundred thousand yojanas above the moon,
the entire circle of constellations shines forth.
O Brahmins, two hundred thousand yojanas above the stellar sphere is Budha;
at a distance equal to that same measure, Uśanas is situated above Budha as well.
Aṅgāraka is situated at that same distance from Śukra;
and the preceptor of the gods (Bṛhaspati) is situated two hundred thousand [yojanas] from Bhauma.
O best of the twice-born, Saturn is situated two hundred thousand [yojanas] above Jupiter;
the circle of the Seven Sages is one hundred thousand [yojanas] beyond that.
Situated more than a hundred thousand yojanas above the ṛṣis,
Dhruva stands as the central pivot of the entire circle of luminaries.
O best of the twice-born, this triple world has been described in brief;
it is the ground for the fruit of sacrifice, and within it, sacrifice is established.
Above Dhruva is Maharloka, where those who dwell for an eon reside;
Maharloka is ordained to be one crore yojanas [above].
But there are two other realms, Jana and Loka, where those sons of Brahmā—
Sanandana and the others— are said to dwell, O Brahmins, they who possess stainless minds.
Above Janaloka, Tapoloka is said to be four times greater;
there dwell those Vairāja deities who are devoid of physical bodies.
Sixfold in extent above the world of austerity (tapas), the world of truth (satya) shines forth;
there, free from rebirth, it is inhabited by perfected beings and other sages.
Whatever object made of earth exists that can be traversed on foot is designated as the Bhūrloka; its extent has been described by me.
O best of sages, that which lies between the earth and the sun, frequented by the Siddhas and other holy men, is called Bhuvarloka; it is the second world.
The distance between Dhruva and the Sun is fourteen hundred thousand [yojanas];
that is called Svarloka by those who contemplate the structure of the worlds.
This triple world is declared by the brahmins to be created,
while the triad consisting of Jana, Tapas, and Satya is uncreated.
The Maharloka is known as being between the created and the uncreated;
it becomes empty at the end of a kalpa, yet it does not perish at the ultimate end.
O twice-born ones, these seven great worlds have been described by me to you;
likewise, there are exactly seven netherworlds (pātālas). This is the extent of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
This [egg] is completely enclosed on all sides— horizontally, above, and below— by its shell, just as the seed of a wood-apple fruit is enclosed.
The twice-born [egg] was enveloped by that water increased tenfold;
and that [egg], surrounded by water, was itself encircled on the outside by fire.
Fire is enveloped by wind, O brahmins, and wind is enveloped by space;
even space, O best of sages, is surrounded by the Great Principle (mahat).
O Brahmins, these seven [worlds], each tenfold greater than the last and including all their parts,
indeed abide encompassing the Great One (Mahat), which itself rests within Pradhāna.
There is no end to that which is infinite, nor is there any calculation of it;
for it is indeed infinite and incalculable, even by means of measurement.
O twice-born ones, she is the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti), the cause of everything without exception;
she is the source of thousands, tens of thousands, and millions of cosmic eggs.
In that same way, there are hundreds of millions upon millions of such [beings] there;
as fire exists in wood and oil in sesame seeds, so does the Puruṣa exist here.
Established in the Pradhāna, all-pervading, and manifesting his conscious self,
he perceives both the Pradhāna and the Puruṣa through the experience of all beings.
O best of the twice-born, by the power of Viṣṇu, those two possess the nature of dependence and are sustained;
that very power is the cause of both their separation and their union.
And at the time of creation, O best of the twice-born, it becomes the cause of agitation,
just as the wind carries coolness within the droplets of water.
Likewise, the power of Viṣṇu is the world, consisting of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa;
just as a tree is composed of roots, trunk, branches, and so forth.
From the original seed, other seeds indeed arise;
from those, yet other supreme trees come into being.
O twice-born ones, following that same sequence of characteristics, substances, and causes,
the Great One (mahat) and the other principles likewise arise from the unmanifest (avyākṛta).
From them, the gods and others arise, ending with the Viśeṣas;
from them come their sons, and from those sons, the supreme grandsons.
Just as there is no depletion of a tree by the growth of a tree from its seed,
so too there is no depletion of the primary elements by the creation of beings.
Just as space, time, and so forth are the causes of a tree due to their mere proximity,
in that very same way, the Lord Hari is the cause of the universe through non-transformation.
Just as in a grain of rice there is the root, the stalk, the leaf, and the sprout,
so too are the stem, the husk, the flower, the milk, and likewise the grain itself.
O best of sages, even husks and chaff, being existent, indeed manifest their own nature once they encounter the totality of causes for growth.
Likewise, within manifold karmas, the bodies of gods and others remain;
having attained the power of Viṣṇu, they indeed attain growth.
And that Viṣṇu is the Supreme Brahman, from whom this entire world arises,
who is the world, in whom this world exists, and into whom it shall go to its dissolution.
That is Brahman, the supreme abode, the highest state of both being and non-being,
from which this entire world of moving and unmoving things is inseparable.
He alone is the root-primal nature (mūlaprakṛti) and he is the manifest form; he is the universe. Everything goes to dissolution in him alone, and in him it abides.
He is the agent of all actions and he is the sacrifice;
he alone is that fruit of action which belongs to him,
from whom the beginning of the age arises in its entirety.
"There is nothing whatsoever that exists apart from Hari.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
"The form of the Lord, the Master, is composed of stars and has the shape of a porpoise."
That form of Hari which is in heaven—Dhruva is situated at its tail.
This very [wind], as it revolves, causes the planets such as the moon and the sun to revolve;
and following that revolving [wind], the constellations move like a wheel.
The sun and moon, the stars, and the constellations together with the planets are indeed bound to Dhruva by bonds consisting of the hosts of winds.
The form of the luminaries in the sky that is described as having the shape of a crocodile is Nārāyaṇa, the supreme abode; he himself is its support within the heart.
Having propitiated that Prajāpati, Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda,
became established at the tail of the stellar crocodile.
Janārdana, the supervisor of all, is the support of the Śiśumāra;
the Śiśumāra is the support of Dhruva, and the Sun is established upon Dhruva.
Now listen from me at this moment to that method by which this world—including gods, asuras, and humans—is supported. BrP 24.7.
For eight months, Vivasvat swallows the waters whose essence is sap;
from that he rains down water, and from that comes food, and from food, the entire world of eaters.
Vivasvat, having drawn up the water of the world with his sharp rays, nourishes the moon;
and the moon, in turn, [nourishes it] in the sky through channels consisting of wind.
The waters are cast into the clouds, which consist of smoke, fire, and wind;
since the waters do not fall away from them, they are therefore called *abhra* (clouds).
Just as waters situated in the clouds, impelled by the wind, fall down,
so too the pure Brahmins, having attained the refinement produced by time, descend.
O twice-born ones, the Blessed Sun absorbs four kinds of water: those from rivers and oceans, those belonging to the earth, and likewise those originating from living beings.
Having thus drawn up the water of the celestial Gaṅgā,
the Sun immediately casts it upon the earth from the cloudless sky by means of his rays.
O best of the twice-born, a mortal whose stain of sin has been washed away by contact with that [water] does not go to hell; for that is remembered as a divine bath.
For that water, having seen the sun, falls from the sky without clouds;
it is the water of the celestial Gaṅgā, cast down by the rays of the sun.
When water from the sky falls upon the odd-numbered lunar mansions beginning with Kṛttikā after seeing the sun, it should be known as the Ganges-water brought down by the elephants of the quarters.
But as for the water that falls from the sky during the twin constellations when the sun has risen,
it is immediately drawn up by the rays of the sun and cast down again.
O twice-born ones, both are exceedingly meritorious and destroy the sins of men;
O best of the twice-born, bathing in the divine waters of the Ākāśagaṅgā is likewise so.
O twice-born ones, that water which is released by the clouds nourishes all plants; for it is indeed the nectar of life for living beings.
By him, the entire collection of medicinal herbs was brought to supreme growth;
yet it arises for living beings as something that culminates when its fruit ripens.
Therefore, those humans who possess the eye of the scriptures perform the sacrifices as they have been prescribed;
day after day, they thereby cause the gods to swell with nourishment.
In this way, the sacrifices and the Vedas, the castes beginning with the twice-born,
all the hosts of gods, and the multitudes of animals and spirits— BrP_24.22.
O best of sages, this entire world, both stationary and moving, is sustained by rain; and that rain, in turn, is produced by the Sun.
O best of eminent sages, Dhruva is the support of the sun;
that Śiśumāra is the support of Dhruva, and he too has Nārāyaṇa as his support.
Within the heart of that Śiśumāra resides Nārāyaṇa,
the eternal, primordial source, and the sustainer of all beings.
Thus, O best of sages, have I described the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) as it is joined with the earth, oceans, and other elements; what else do you wish to hear?
The sages said:
"O knower of dharma, you ought to describe those holy fords and sacred abodes that exist upon the earth; our minds are intent on hearing them."
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
He whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained,
and who possesses knowledge, austerity, and fame— he enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.
The pure mind is a person’s sacred ford,
as are the restraint of speech and the control of the senses;
these are the sacred fords born of the body.
They reveal the path to heaven:
"A corrupted mind within is not purified by bathing at sacred fords;
even if washed with water hundreds of times, it remains as impure as a vessel that once held liquor. (BrP 25.3d–4)
Neither sacred fords, nor gifts, nor vows,
nor stages of life can purify one who is evil-minded, fond of hypocrisy, and whose senses are wayward.
Wherever a man may dwell after bringing his senses under control,
there is Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, and likewise Puṣkara.
Therefore, listen, O best of sages; I shall describe in brief all the sacred fords (tīrthas) and shrines that exist anywhere upon the earth.
Even in hundreds of years, it is not possible to describe them in detail—
the first sacred site, Puṣkara, and Naimiṣāraṇya as well.
