The Śatadruhas, the Kaliṅgas, the Pāradas, the Hārabhūṣikas,
the Māṭharas, the Kanakas, the Kaikeyas, and the Dambhamālikas.
O best of Brahmins, there are lands comparable to those of the Kṣatriyas, as well as the families of Vaiśyas and Śūdras;
and also the Kambojas, Barbaras, and Laukikas.
The Vīras, the Tuṣāras, the Pahlavas, the Ādhāyatas,
the Ātreyas, the Bharadvājas, the Puṣkalas, and the Daśerakas.
The Lampakas, Śunaśokas, Kulikas, along with the Jāṅgalas,
the Auṣadhyas, the Calacandras, and the various tribes of the Kirātas.
The Tomaras, Haṃsamārgas, Kāśmīras, Karuṇas, Śūlikas, Kuhakas, and likewise the Māgadhas.
These are the northern regions; now learn of the eastern regions:
the Andhas, Vāmaṅkurakas, Vallakas, and Makhāntakas.
Likewise, there are others: the Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Maladas, Mālavartikas, Bhadratuṅgas, Pratijayas, Bhāryāṅgas, and Cāpamardakas.
The Prāgjyotiṣas, the Madras, the Videhas, the Tāmraliptakas,
the Mallas, the Magadhas, and the Nandas— these were the eastern provinces.
Then there were other peoples dwelling in the southern region (Dakṣiṇāpatha),
namely the Pūrṇas, the Kevalas, and likewise the Golāṅgūlas.
The Ṛṣikas, the Muṣikas, the Kumāras, the Rāmaṭhas, the Śakas, the Mahārāṣṭras, the Māhiṣakas, and the Kaliṅgas from all sides; BrP_27.55 //
The Ābhīras along with the Vaiśikyas, those from the Aṭavī and Sarava regions,
as well as the Pulindas, Mauleyas, and Vaidarbhas together with the Daṇḍakas.
The Paulikas, Maulikas, Aśmakas, Bhojavardhanas,
Kaulikas, Kuntalas, Dambhakas, and Nīlakālakas.
These are the southern regions; now learn of those in the western borderlands:
Śūrpāraka, Kālidhana, and Lolā, together with Tālakaṭa.
Thus, O dwellers of the Vindhya, hear about these others from the western regions:
the Malajas, the Karkaśas, the Melakas, along with the Colakas.
The Uttamārṇas, the Daśārṇas, the Bhojas along with the Kiṣkindhakas, the Toṣalas, the Kośalas, as well as the Traipuras and the Vaidiśas; BrP_27.60 //
The Tumburus and the Caras, as well as the Yavanas together with the Pavanās, the Abhayas, the Ruṇḍikeras, the Carcaras, and the Hotradhartayas; BrP_27.61 //
All these regions are inhabitants of the Vindhya;
therefore, I shall now describe those countries which are situated upon the mountains.
The Nīhāras, Tuṣamārgas, Kuravas, Tuṅgaṇas, Khasas,
Karṇaprāvaraṇas, Ūrṇas, Darghas, and Sakuntakas;
The Citramārgas, Mālavas, and Kirātas, along with the Tomaras, are here;
and the ordinance established for the four ages, beginning with the Kṛta and Tretā, is also present.
Thus, the land of Bhārata-varṣa is situated in nine divisions;
to its south and east lies the great ocean.
To the north of this bow is the Himavat mountain, which serves as its string;
O best of the twice-born, this is the land of Bhārata-varṣa, containing all seeds.
The state of being a Brahmā, the lordship over the immortals, and likewise divinity among the Maruts;
as well as birth among the Mṛgas, Yakṣas, and Apsarases, and similarly among the serpents and reptiles.
O Brahmins, for all stationary beings as well, [the results] are measured by their auspicious and inauspicious deeds;
O Brahmins, this land of action exists, and no other such place is found in the worlds.
"O Brahmins, this has always been the desire even of the gods:
'May we, having fallen from our divine state, attain human birth upon the earth.'"
Whatever a human being performs cannot be performed by gods or asuras,
for they are bound by the shackles of their own karma and are intent solely on exhausting that karma.
O twice-born ones, there is no land on earth equal to Bhārata,
wherein the social classes, beginning with the Brahmins, attain their desired goals.
Blessed are those best of men who are born in the land of Bhārata;
they obtain the great fruit of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Wherein is obtained the fruit of austerity, which is exceedingly difficult to attain,
as well as the fruit of all acts of giving and likewise the fruit of all sacrifices.
O twice-born ones, [I shall describe] the fruit of pilgrimage to sacred fords, as well as the fruit of service to the guru,
the fruit of propitiating the deities, and the fruit of self-study of the Vedas.
Where the gods, ever joyful, desire a beautiful birth,
as well as the fruit of various vows and the fruit of various scriptures.
The fruit of non-violence and other virtues is the perfect fruit of all that is desired;
likewise, there is the fruit of celibacy and whatever fruit is obtained through the life of a householder.
Whatever fruit is obtained through dwelling in the forest and through renunciation,
as well as the fruit of sacrificial rites and charitable works, and likewise that of other auspicious deeds— [all that is attained by this].
O best of the twice-born, this is attained in Bhārata-varṣa and nowhere else;
O brahmins, who is able to describe all the virtues of Bhārata?
Thus have I correctly described the supreme Bhārata-varṣa,
which removes all sins, is meritorious, auspicious, and increases the intellect.
Whoever, with senses restrained, should constantly hear or recite this,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Brahmā said: There, in the land of Bhārata, situated by the southern ocean,
lies the region renowned as Oṇḍra, which bestows both heaven and liberation.
Extending as far as the dustless realm beyond the ocean,
that land is adorned with every virtue by those of meritorious conduct.
In that regard, those Brahmins born in that land who have their senses restrained and are devoted to austerity and Vedic study are always to be saluted and honored.
In ancestral rites, in giving gifts, in marriage, in sacrifice, and in the duties of a preceptor—
in all such activities, the twice-born born in that region are highly commended.
There, the Brahmins were devoted to the six duties, masters of the Vedas,
knowers of the Itihāsas, and experts in the meaning of the Purāṇas.
Some were skilled in the meaning of all the scriptures, performers of sacrifices, and free from envy;
some were devoted to the *agnihotra* fire-sacrifice, while others were intent upon the fires prescribed by the *smṛtis*.
Endowed with sons, wives, and wealth, being generous and truthful in speech,
they dwell in the meritorious land of Utkala, which is adorned with sacrifices and festivals.
The other three castes as well— the Kṣatriyas and the rest— remaining well-restrained,
devoted to their own duties, peaceful, and righteous, abide there.
Known as Koṇāditya, he is established in that region;
by beholding that Sun, a mortal is liberated from all sins.
The sages said:
"O best of gods, we wish to hear; tell us now about that field of the Sun, in which region that Maker of Day resides."
Brahmā said:
On the shore of the salt ocean, in a pure and very beautiful place,
strewn everywhere with sand and endowed with all excellent qualities.
With *campaka*, *aśoka*, and *bakula* trees, with *karavīra* and *pāṭala*, with *puṃnāga*, *karṇikāra*, *bakula*, and *nāgakesara*— BrP_28.12 //
With *tagara*, *dhava*, and *bāṇa* trees, with *atimuktas* and *kubjakas*,
with *mālatī* and *kunda* flowers, as well as other varieties such as *mallikā*.
And with groves of *ketakī* flowers radiant with blossoms of every season,
as well as *kadamba*, *lakuca*, *śāla*, *panasa*, and *devadāru* trees.
With *sarala* trees, *mucukunda*, and white as well as black sandalwood;
with *aśvattha*, *saptaparṇa*, mangoes, and likewise *āmra-ātaka* trees.
It was adorned on all sides with palmyra palms, betel-nut trees, coconut trees, wood-apple trees, and various other kinds of trees.
There lies the sacred field of the Sun, renowned throughout the world;
extending for more than a yojana in every direction, it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
There dwells the Lord himself, the thousand-rayed maker of day,
renowned as Koṇāditya, the bestower of the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In the month of Māgha, during the bright fortnight, on the seventh lunar day, one who has restrained the senses and observed a fast,
having gone there and bathed in that abode of sea-monsters (the ocean), [attains merit].
Having performed his purification, with a cleansed soul, and remembering the divine Sun,
he bathed according to the rules in the ocean at the end of the night, composed in mind.
O twice-born ones, having gratified the gods, the sages, humans, and the ancestors,
and having emerged from the water, he should put on two clean and perfectly spotless garments.
Having sipped water and become purified on the shore of that great ocean,
he then sat down at sunrise, facing east toward the sun.
The wise man, having drawn an eight-petalled lotus with red sandalwood water— abounding in filaments, circular, and with an upward-pointing pericarp— BrP_28.23.
One should place sesame seeds, rice grains, water mixed with red sandalwood,
red flowers, and *darbha* grass into a copper vessel.
O best of sages, in the absence of copper, having placed sesame seeds and other offerings within a cup made of arka leaves and covering it, one should set that vessel upon another vessel.
Having performed the ritual placement of the hands and the assignment of the limbs with the heart-mantra and the others,
and having meditated upon himself as the Sun, he should do so perfectly, endowed with faith.
The wise one should worship [the deity] in the center on the fire-petal, in the southwest on the wind-petal,
in the domain of Kāmāri, and again in the center.
Having worshipped the lotus— which is abundant, stainless, essential, and worthy of attainment— and having invoked the Sun from the sky into it, one should worship that supreme bliss.
Having placed it upon the pericarp, one should then display the mudrā;
having performed all the rites such as bathing, one should meditate upon him with a well-composed mind.
Upon a white lotus, situated within a solar orb of radiant light,
he is tawny-eyed, two-armed, red in complexion, and wears garments as crimson as a lotus petal.
Endowed with all the primary marks, adorned with every ornament,
beautiful in form, the granter of boons, peaceful, and graced by a halo of light.
Then, seeing the rising sun resembling thick vermilion,
he took that vessel and knelt upon the ground with his knees.
Having placed that vessel upon his head, with a one-pointed mind and restrained speech,
he should present the *arghya* offering to the Sun with the three-syllabled mantra.
But one who is uninitiated offers the arghya with the name of that [deity] alone,
because the Sun is to be grasped through devotion by one endowed with faith and pure intent.
One should worship the Heart, the Head, the Crest, the Armor, the Eyes, and the Weapon in the directions of Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, Īśa, the center, and the east, respectively.
Having offered the arghya, as well as incense, perfume, a lamp, and food offerings,
and having recited the mantra, praised [the deity], bowed down, and formed the mudrā, one should perform the dismissal.
With constant devotion and a perpetually pure inner self,
they enjoy their desired objects and attain the supreme goal.
Those men who take refuge in the god Bhāskara, the lamp of the three worlds who moves through the sky, shall become vessels of happiness.
As long as the arghya offering is not presented to the Sun-god as prescribed,
one should not worship Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, or the Lord of the Gods.
Therefore, having become pure, one should exert effort day after day to offer the *arghya* to Āditya with beautiful flowers and fragrances.
Thus, he who, being pure and having bathed, offers the arghya with great concentration to Āditya on the seventh lunar day, shall obtain his desired fruit.
The sick person is freed from disease; one who seeks wealth obtains riches;
the seeker of knowledge attains learning; and one who desires a son shall possess a son.
Whatever desire a wise man contemplates while offering the arghya water to Sūrya, he fully attains the fruit of that very desire.
Having bathed in the ocean, offered the arghya water to the Sun, and prostrated,
whether a man or a woman, one shall obtain the fruit of all desires.
Then, taking a flower and restraining his speech, he should go to the abode of the Sun;
having entered, he should perform three circumambulations and worship Bhānu.
O best of sages, one should worship Koṇārka with supreme devotion,
using perfumes, flowers, lamps, incense, and even food offerings.
Having thus worshipped that god, the thousand-rayed lord of the world, with prostrations like a staff, shouts of victory, and hymns of praise, [he spoke].
A man obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices;
freed from all sins, he becomes a youth with a divine body.
O twice-born ones, having rescued seven generations of descendants and seven of ancestors,
he shall travel by means of a radiant celestial chariot, sun-colored, moving at will.
Being sung to by Gandharvas, he goes to the world of the Sun;
having enjoyed excellent pleasures there until the dissolution of all beings.
Having come here due to the exhaustion of his merit, he shall be born into an eminent family of yogins as a Brahmin learned in the four Vedas, pure and devoted to his own duty.
Having attained the yoga of Vivasvat, one shall thereafter obtain liberation;
in the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, one should perform the pilgrimage known as Damanabhañjikā.
Whatever man performs [this rite] there, he shall obtain the previously mentioned fruit during the Sun’s awakening and rising, at the solstice, and at the equinoxes.

O twice-born ones, those who perform a pilgrimage there with faith and with their senses restrained, whether on a Sunday, on the lunar day (tithi), or during a festival (parva) time; ||| BrP_28.55 |||
By means of a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun, they go to the world of the Sun;
there dwells Mahādeva on the shore of the lord of rivers and streams.
Known as Rāmeśvara, he bestows the fruits of all desires;
those who, having properly bathed in the great ocean, behold that enemy of Kāma (Śiva), [attain their goals].
With perfumes, flowers, as well as incenses, lamps, and excellent food offerings;
with prostrations, as well as hymns of praise, songs, and captivating musical instruments.
Those high-souled ones fully obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice as well as the fruit of the Vājimedha,
and likewise attain supreme perfection.
Being sung to by Gandharvas, they go to the world of Śiva in a celestial chariot that moves at will and is adorned with garlands of networks of tinkling bells.
Having enjoyed delightful pleasures until the dissolution of the world (saṃplava),
they return here upon the exhaustion of their merit and become masters of the four Vedas.
Resorting to the yoga of Śaṅkara, they then attain liberation—
that man who gives up his life-breaths there in the field of the Sun.
Having ascended to the world of the Sun, he rejoices in heaven like a god;
returning again to human state, he becomes a righteous king.
Having attained union with the Sun, one shall thereafter obtain liberation.
Thus, O best of sages, has this most difficult-to-attain sacred field been described by me.
On the shore of the ocean at Koṇārka, it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The sages said:
O best of gods, we have heard that supreme field of the Sun-god, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, as described by you.
We do not reach satiety while listening to this merit-bestowing story arising from your mouth— a narrative that grants happiness and destroys the sins of even the Sun.
Beyond this, O best of gods, O foremost of speakers, tell us, O Lord,
what is the fruit of worshiping the gods and what is the fruit of giving.
Whatever [merit] is gained in prostration, in salutation, likewise in circumambulation, in the offering of lamps and incense, and in the rite of sweeping; BrP_29.4 //
What merit is there in fasting, and what merit in eating only at night? What kind of *argha* offering is prescribed, and where is it to be presented?
And how is devotion performed? How does the God become pleased?
O Best of Gods, we wish to hear all of this.
Brahmā said: O best of the twice-born, listen as I describe the water-offering (arghya), all the rites of worship for the Sun,
as well as devotion, faith, and meditative concentration.
Mental cultivation is called devotion (bhakti), and faith (śraddhā) is likewise proclaimed;
meditation (dhyāna) is said to be concentration (samādhi)—listen with well-composed minds.
He who causes the discourse on that [Lord] to be heard, or honors His devotees,
and likewise serves the sacred fire— he indeed is an eternal devotee.
He whose mind and thought are fixed on that, who is always devoted to the worship of the Divine,
and who performs those very actions— he indeed is the eternal devotee.
O Brahmins, that man who approves of the rites being performed for the sake of the gods, or who praises them, is indeed the most devoted of all.
One should not be envious of his devotees, nor should one revile other deities;
such a man, practicing the vow of the Sun, is indeed the most devoted of all.
Whether walking, standing, sleeping, smelling, or even opening and closing his eyes,
the man who constantly remembers the Sun-god is indeed the most devoted of devotees.
One who possesses discernment should always practice this kind of devotion—
through devotion, through meditative concentration, through hymn of praise, and likewise through the mind.
Whatever restriction is observed when a gift is given to a Brahmin,
the gods, humans, and likewise the ancestors accept that [gift].
The gods accept whatever leaf, flower, fruit, or water is offered with devotion, and they shun those who are atheists.
Purity of intention should be practiced, conjoined with the observance of restrictive rules;
whatever is performed with purity of intention shall all become fruitful.
By means of praise, recitation, offerings, and worship of Vivasvat,
as well as through fasting and devotion, one is indeed liberated from all sins.
He who, placing his head upon the ground, performs a prostration, is liberated at that very moment from all sins; of this there is no doubt.
That man who, endowed with devotion, performs a circumambulation of the Sun,
has thereby circumambulated the earth with its seven continents.
He who, having placed the sun in his mind, performs a circumambulation of the sky,
has indeed circumambulated all the gods.
Having taken only one meal a day on the sixth lunar day, he who worships the Sun,
observing the rules of his vow and endowed with devotion, [attains the fruit].
Or on the seventh [lunar day], O highly fortunate ones, he who worships the Sun while fasting for a day and night shall obtain the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha).
On the seventh or the sixth lunar day, he attains the supreme goal;
having fasted on the seventh day of the dark fortnight, with his senses subdued.
Whoever worships the Sun with an offering of all kinds of jewels goes to the world of the Sun by means of a lotus-glittering celestial vehicle.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight, a man devoted to fasting who worships the Sun with entirely white offerings— BrP_29.26 —
Freed from all sins, he goes to the world of the Sun;
one should drink a handful of water mixed with *arkasaṃpuṭa*.
By increasing the practice step by step, one should again diminish each [period] until it reaches twenty-four;
thus, within two years, the observance will be completed.
For this Arkasaptamī is indeed praised as the granter of all desires;
it occurs when the seventh lunar day of the bright fortnight falls on a Sunday.
The seventh is named Vijayā; whatever is given there yields great fruit—whether it be bathing, giving, austerity, burnt offerings, or likewise fasting.
On the Vijayā-saptamī, everything destroys even the greatest sins;
and those men who perform a śrāddha when the day of the Sun has arrived, [attain the same].
And those who perform all their righteous rites always directed toward the Sun sacrifice the Great White One (Mahāśveta), and they obtain whatever they desire.
In their family, no one is born poor or even diseased;
[this applies] whether with white, red, or even yellow clay.
But the one who performs the smearing obtains the fruit of his desires by worshipping Citrabhānu with various fragrant flowers.
He who, while observing a fast, performs worship shall obtain his desired objects;
furthermore, having lit a lamp with ghee or with sesame oil.
He who worships the Sun is never deprived of his sight;
the man who constantly gives lamps shines with the lamp of knowledge.
Sesame seeds are pure, as is sesame oil; the gift of sesame seeds is supreme.
In the fire-ritual and in the lighting of lamps, it destroys even the greatest of sins.
He who constantly offers lamps in temples,
at crossroads, and on roads, shall become handsome and fortunate.

The first method is with sacrificial offerings (havir); the second is with the juices of medicinal herbs; [the third is] with the extracts of fat, marrow, and bone; but it must never be given by any means [with the fourth].
A lamp moves upward and never downward;
likewise, a donor shines brightly and does not go to a state of rebirth as an animal.
One should never remove or extinguish a lamp that is burning;
a man who steals a lamp shall go to bondage, destruction, wrath, and darkness.
The giver of lamps shines in the heavenly world like a garland of lights;
so too does he who constantly anoints [the deity] with saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood.
A pure man, having offered red flowers mixed with red sandalwood, attains wealth, fame, and splendor after passing away.
By always offering the arghya water at sunrise, one shall obtain success within a year;
one should remain performing this from sunrise until the setting of the sun.
Reciting some mantra or even a hymn while facing the sun—
this is the vow of the Sun, which destroys even the greatest sins.
One should cause everything, including the *arghya* offering and all its constituent parts, to be presented;
endowed with faith at sunrise, one is liberated from all sins.
The giver of the guest-offering (arghya) who presents it together with a golden cow, a bull, land, and clothing, obtains a fruit that follows him for seven births.
The arghya offering should be diligently presented in fire, in water, in the atmosphere, as well as on pure ground, and likewise upon an image or a funeral cake (piṇḍa).
One should always offer [the oblation] facing [the deity], neither to the right nor to the left;
filled with devotion to the Sun, one may also offer guggulu resin mixed with ghee.
At that very moment, one is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt about this.
Likewise, [one should offer] śrīvāsa, caturasra, and devadāru.
Having offered incense of camphor and agallochum, they indeed go to heaven,
whether during the northern course of the sun or the southern course.
Having performed worship especially at the equinoxes, during eclipses, and at the beginnings of the six-aśīti periods, one is liberated from all sins.
By worshipping with special devotion, a person is liberated from all sins at all times and during every period. // BrP_29.53 //
He who worships the Sun with devotion is honored in the world of the Sun,
offering kṛsara, milk-rice, cakes, fruits, roots, ghee, and cooked rice.
By making an offering to the Sun, one shall obtain all desires;
by performing a libation with clarified butter, a man shall become accomplished in all things.
Having performed a libation with milk, one is not afflicted by mental torments;
but having performed a libation with curd, a person shall obtain the accomplishment of his purpose.
He who, being composed and having attained purity at sacred fords, fetches water for the purpose of bathing the Sun, goes to the supreme goal.
By giving with faith an umbrella, a banner, a canopy, a flag, or chowries to the Sun, one shall attain the desired goal.
Whatever substance a person offers with devotion to Āditya,
the Maker of Light multiplies that for him a hundred-thousandfold.
Whatever misdeed has been committed through mind, speech, or body—
all that, without exception, he removes by the grace of the Sun.

The fruit that is obtained from the worship of the Sun in even a single day cannot be attained even by hundreds of sacrifices, even when performed by Brahmins who provide the prescribed sacrificial fees.
The sages said:
"O Lord of the World, O best of gods, we have thus heard the majesty of the Sun-god as you described it to them— a thing difficult to obtain."
Speak further, O Lord of Gods, regarding that which we ask, O Master of the World;
we wish to hear it, O Brahman, for our curiosity is great.
Whether one is a householder, a student, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant—
whoever desires to abide in liberation, which deity should he worship?
For from what source does his imperishable heaven come, and from what his supreme beatitude?
And having reached heaven, what should he do so that he does not fall away from there again?
And among the gods, who is the god here? And among the ancestors, who is the father?
O Lord of the Suras, tell me that than which there is nothing higher.
From what was this entire universe, both the stationary and the moving, created? And unto whom does it go at the time of dissolution? You ought to explain that.
Brahmā said:
"As he rises, he makes the world free from darkness with his rays;
O best of the twice-born, there is no other god superior to him."
For this Puruṣa is without beginning or end, eternal and immutable;
becoming fierce with his rays, he heats the three worlds.
For he is composed of all the gods, the best of those who scorch,
the lord of the entire world, the witness of all, and the master of the universe.
He withdraws all beings and likewise emits them again;
he shines, he burns, and he rains with his rays.
He is the Ordainer and the Disposer, the source of all beings and the creator of all creatures;
for he never undergoes decay, possessing an eternally imperishable sphere.
For he is indeed the father of the ancestors and the deity of the deities;
this is remembered as his eternal station, from which he never again falls away.
At the time of creation, the entire world is brought forth from the Sun;
and at the time of dissolution, it returns to that radiant Bhāskara.
And countless yogins, having abandoned their bodies and homes,
become like the wind and enter this sun, that mass of splendor.
Upon his thousands of rays, like birds upon branches,
perfected sages dwell together with the deities, taking refuge in him.
Householders such as Janaka and other kings who followed the path of yoga,
as well as the Vālakhilyas and other sages who were exponents of Brahman.
The forest-dwellers, and others such as Vyāsa and the rest, as well as the mendicants—
all of them, having established themselves in yoga, entered the solar disc.
The illustrious Śuka, son of Vyāsa, having attained the dharma of yoga,
went to the rays of the sun and established himself in the state beyond rebirth.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others are known through the gateway of hearing mere words;
this supreme deity, the Sun who destroys darkness, is directly perceptible.
Therefore, one who desires auspiciousness should not direct devotion elsewhere;
for those gods, led by Viṣṇu, are inaccessible to the physical eye.
Therefore, you must constantly worship the Blessed Sun;
for he is indeed the mother, the father, and the teacher of the entire world.
O best of the twice-born, that Lord of the World, the Master of the Universe, who is garlanded with rays, is without beginning; yet, because he abided in friendship, he performed austerities.
Brahmā is without beginning or end, eternal and indeed imperishable;
having created the fourteen worlds, including the islands and the oceans.
For the benefit of the worlds, he remained on the bank of the Candrasarit river after having created all the Prajāpatis and having created various kinds of progeny.
Then, having again divided himself twelvefold, the unmanifest one himself becomes the Sun, the possessor of a hundred thousand rays.
Indra, Dhātṛ, Parjanya, Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, Aryaman, Bhaga,
Vivasvat, Viṣṇu, Aṃśa, Varuṇa, and Mitra.
O best of the twice-born, by these twelve forms, as well as by that Sun, the Supreme Self, this entire world is pervaded.
Of him, that first form of Āditya known as Indra,
established in the sovereignty of the gods, is the destroyer of the enemies of the deities.
His second form, celebrated by the name Dhātr,
abides in the state of Prajāpati and creates various offspring.
The form of the third sun, renowned as Parjanya,
resides within the clouds and rains down by means of its rays.
His fourth form, renowned by the name Tvaṣṭṛ,
is stationed everywhere within trees and among all medicinal herbs.
His fifth form, renowned by the name Pūṣan, is established in food;
it constantly nourishes all creatures.
The sixth form of the Sun, which is renowned as Aryaman, is that of Vāyu’s Saṃsaraṇa; it is indeed established among the gods.
That seventh form of the Sun, renowned by the name Bhaga,
is situated abundantly within the bodies of embodied beings.
His eighth form, renowned as Vivasvān, is established in fire;
it digests the food of embodied beings.
That form of the Sun which appears on the ninth day, known by the name Viṣṇu,
constantly manifests as the destroyer of the enemies of the gods.
His tenth form, renowned as Aṃśumān,
is established in the wind and indeed brings delight to all creatures.
The eleventh form of the Sun is named Varuṇa;
situated within the waters, it constantly nourishes all creatures.
That form of the Sun which is the twelfth, known by the name Mitrā,
stands upon the bank of the Candrasarit for the benefit of the worlds.
Subsisting on air, he performed austerities while remaining with a friendly gaze,
constantly favoring his devotees with various kinds of boons.
Thus was that form, beneficial to the worlds, established in ancient times;
because Mitra was stationed there, it is therefore remembered as the supreme Mitra.
O best of the twice-born, by means of these twelve forms, that Savitṛ, the Supreme Self, pervades this entire universe.
Therefore, he should be constantly meditated upon and worshipped by devoted men in his twelve forms, with their inner selves entirely absorbed in him.
Thus, having paid homage to the twelve Ādityas,
a person who constantly hears and recites this is glorified in the world of the Sun.
The sages said: "If this Sun is indeed the primordial, eternal God,
then why did he perform austerities, desiring a boon, like an ordinary man?"
Brahmā said:
I shall declare to you this supreme secret of the Sun,
which was previously asked by Mitra of the high-souled Nārada.
The twelve forms of the Sun were previously described by me to you;
among them, both Mitra and Varuṇa are established in austerity.
Varuṇa remained in the western ocean subsisting on water alone,
while Mitra, in this forest of Mitra, then subsisted on air.
Then the great yogi Nārada, having descended from the peak of Mount Meru and from Gandhamādana, wandered through all the worlds, having mastered his senses.
Then he came to that very place where Mitra was performing austerities;
seeing him engaged in penance, curiosity indeed arose within him.
He who is imperishable and indeed undecaying, both manifest and unmanifest, eternal—
the Great-Souled One by whom the three worlds, consisting of a single essence, are upheld.
Reflecting in his mind, "He who is the father of all the gods and who is even beyond the supreme— what deities did he worship, or which ancestors did he sacrifice to? Nārada spoke thus to that god.
Nārada said:
You are praised in the Vedas, along with the Purāṇas, together with their limbs and sub-limbs;
you are the unborn, the eternal, the sustainer, and the unsurpassed treasure.
The past, the future, and the present—all are established in you alone, O God;
likewise, the four stages of life, beginning with that of the householder, are likewise established in you.
Day after day they worship you, who have assumed embodied form;
for you are the father and mother of all, the eternal deity.
Whom do you worship as a father, or which god? We do not know.
Mitra said:
"O Brahmin, although this is unspeakable, it must be told; it is the supreme, eternal secret. Since you are devoted, I shall declare it to you exactly as it is."
That which is subtle, unknowable, unmanifest, immovable, and eternal,
devoid of the senses, the objects of the senses, and all elemental beings;
For he is indeed called the inner self of all beings and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña);
he is distinct from the three qualities (guṇas) and is conceived as the Puruṣa.
The Lord Hiraṇyagarbha is remembered as being that very intellect;
in the systems of yoga, he is called the "Great One" (Mahat) and is described as the "Primal Matter" (Pradhāna).
In Sāṃkhya and Yoga, he who possesses many forms is described by various names;
he is remembered as the threefold universal soul, Śarva, and the Imperishable (Akṣara).
By him this triple world is sustained as a single essence through his own self;
bodiless, he dwells within all bodies.
"Though dwelling within bodies, my inner self, as well as yours and those of others who are situated in bodies, is not stained by actions."
He is the witness of all; he cannot be grasped by anyone anywhere.
He is both possessed of qualities and devoid of qualities, the universe itself, and is remembered as being accessible only through knowledge.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces on all sides,
and possessing ears everywhere in the world, He stands encompassing everything.
With the universe as his head, the universe as his arms, and the universe as his feet, eyes, and nose,
he indeed moves alone within the field (kṣetra), wandering at will according to his pleasure.

In this world, bodies are the fields (*kṣetra*); he knows them and their respective pleasures according to his will. Because that one whose self is yoga knows them, he is therefore called the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*).
And because he lies within the unmanifest city, he is called Puruṣa;
the manifold universe is to be known as his, and he is said to be everywhere.
Therefore, because he possesses many forms, he is remembered as Viśvarūpa (the Universal Form);
for that one alone has greatness, and he is remembered as the one Puruṣa.
For the one eternal Being alone bears the title of "Great Person" (mahāpuruṣa);
yet, dependent upon the performance of ritual action, he creates himself by means of himself.
In a hundred ways, in a thousand ways, and likewise in a hundred-thousand ways,
he makes himself into millions by means of his own self.
Just as water fallen from the sky acquires a sweet taste through the particular quality of the earth, so too does he [attain his nature] through the quality of the *guṇas*.
Just as the single wind indeed becomes fivefold within bodies,
so too its unity and its diversity are beyond doubt.
And just as fire receives a supreme designation due to its specific location,
O Sage, so too does this [Self] attain such designations among Brahmā and the others.
Just as a single lamp produces thousands of lamps,
so does that one being produce thousands of forms.
When he realizes the Self, then he becomes solitary;
and upon the dissolution of his unity, multiplicity proceeds for him.
For there is nothing eternal in this world, whether stationary or moving;
he alone is said to be imperishable, immeasurable, and all-pervading.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, that which has arisen from the unmanifest and consists of the three qualities (guṇas),
abiding in the state between the unmanifest and the manifest, is called Prakṛti.
Know that womb of Brahmā to be that which consists of both being and non-being,
and which is worshipped in the world in rites for the gods and the ancestors.
"Therefore, O twice-born ones, there is no other father superior to him, not even a god;
he is to be known as the Self, and for that reason I worship him."
For even among those embodied beings in the heavens, O celestial sage, whoever pay him homage go by that very act to the destination whose fruit has been ordained by him.
The gods and those established in their own hermitages, resorting to various forms, worship that Primordial One with devotion; and He grants them their goal.
For he is indeed described as being omnipresent and devoid of qualities;
having understood this according to my knowledge, I worship the Maker of Day.
And those who, permeated by that, have taken refuge in the single reality—
this too is superior for them, namely that they enter into the One.
Thus, O Nārada, this secret summary has been proclaimed to you;
and because of your devotion to us, O divine sage, it has also been remembered by you as supreme.
Whether by the gods or by the ancient sages, he is remembered as the bestower of boons;
and all worship the Sun, who is the Supreme Self.
Brahmā said:
"O best of the twice-born, this was indeed related in the past by Bhānu to Nārada; and I too have fully recounted this story of Bhānu."
O best of the twice-born, this narrative which has been told by me is to be recounted;
for this should never be given to one who is not devoted to the Sun.
The man who constantly causes this to be heard and he who listens to it himself shall enter the god of a thousand rays; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, one who is afflicted shall be freed from disease by hearing this narrative from the beginning;
and one who desires knowledge shall obtain it, as well as his desired goal.
O Sage, whoever recites this attains their path in an instant;
whatever desire one may long for, one obtains it without a doubt.
Therefore, you must constantly remember the Blessed Lord Ravi;
he is the sustainer, the ordainer, and the sovereign lord of the entire world.
Brahmā said:
O best of sages, the entire three worlds have the Sun as their root;
from him arises this whole universe, including the gods, asuras, and humans.
This is the universal splendor of Rudra, Upendra, and Mahendra, of the foremost of Brahmins and the inhabitants of heaven,
and of all those possessed of great luster.
The soul of all, the lord of all worlds, the god of gods, the progenitor of creatures—
the Sun alone is the root of the three worlds and the supreme deity.
An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings.
Everything is produced from the Sun and into him alone it is dissolved;
for the existence and non-existence of the worlds have issued forth from the Āditya since of old.
This indeed is the meditation of meditators, and this is the liberation of those seeking liberation;
therein they go to nirvāṇa, and from it they are born again and again.
Moments, instants, days, nights, fortnights, and always months, years, seasons, and the ages (yugas).
For without the sun, no reckoning of time exists for these [beings];
without time, there is no regulation, nor is there the act of maintaining the sacred fire.
And because there would be no division of the seasons, whence could there be flowers and fruits?
Whence indeed would be the production of grain, and whence the multitude of grasses and medicinal herbs?
Due to the power of the world, there is an absence of all worldly activities for living beings both in heaven and here on earth; they enter into the sun, which acts as a thief of the waters.
The sun does not burn because of drought, nor does it wither due to drought;
it does not form a halo because of drought, for the sun shines by means of water.
In spring the sun is tawny; in summer it resembles gold;
in the rainy season it is white in color; and in autumn the sun is pale.
In the winter the sun has the luster of copper, and in the cool season it is red;
thus are declared the colors of the sun arising according to the seasons.
And by the colors corresponding to the nature of the seasons, the Sun brings about security and abundance;
now, O best of the twice-born, are the general names of Āditya.
I shall describe those twelve [names] individually and in their entirety:
Āditya, Savitṛ, Sūrya, Mihira, Arka, and Prabhākara.
Mārtaṇḍa, Bhāskara, Bhānu, Citrabhānu, Divākara, and Ravi—
these twelve should be known as his common names.
Viṣṇu, Dhātṛ, Bhaga, Pūṣan, Mitra, Indra, Varuṇa, Aryaman,
Vivasvat, Aṃśumat, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Parjanya is remembered as the twelfth.
Thus these twelve Ādityas are established as distinct;
indeed, they always rise in succession according to the twelve months.
Viṣṇu shines in the month of Caitra, and likewise Aryaman in Vaiśākha;
Vivasvat is known to shine in the month of Jyeṣṭha, and Aṃśumat in Āṣāḍha.
Parjanya blazes in the month of Śrāvaṇa, Varuṇa in the month known as Prauṣṭhapada,
Indra in the month of Āśvayuja, and Dhātṛ in Kārttika.
Likewise, Mitra shines in Mārgaśīrṣa; Pūṣan, the maker of day, in Pauṣa;
Bhaga is to be known as shining in Māgha; and Tvaṣṭṛ in Phālguna.
Viṣṇu always shines with twelve hundred rays;
Aryaman shines with a thousand cows and three hundred rays.
Vivasvān [ruled] for twice seven [ages], while Aṃśumān ruled for five and three;
Vivasvān was like Parjanya, and Varuṇa as well as Aryaman were likewise.
Tvaṣṭṛ was like a friend to the Blessed One with one thousand and one hundred;
Indra, however, with twelve hundred; and Dhātṛ with eleven hundred.
At the commencement of the sun's northern course, its rays increase accordingly: Mitra indeed with a thousand, and Pūṣan with nine hundred.
As the sun begins its southern course, its rays diminish further;
thus, from the world of the Sun, a thousand rays descend in grace.
Thus, twenty-four names of these have been proclaimed;
furthermore, another thousand have been proclaimed in detail.
The sages said:
O Prajāpati, O Supreme Lord, what merit and what destination belongs to those who praise the Sun with his thousand names?
Brahmā said:
Listen, O tigers among sages, to this eternal essence;
there is no need for the thousand names—simply recite this auspicious hymn in this manner.
I shall proclaim to you those names of the Sun which are secret, purifying, and auspicious; listen indeed!
Vikartana, Vivasvat, Mārtaṇḍa, Bhāskara, Ravi,
Lokaprakāśaka, Śrīmat, Lokacakṣus, and Maheśvara.
The witness of the world, the lord of the three worlds, the creator and the destroyer, the dispeller of darkness;
the scorching one, the burner, the pure one, whose vehicle is drawn by seven horses.
Gabhastihasta, Brahmā, and he who is saluted by all the gods—
this praise consisting of twenty-one names is always desired for the Sun.
Bestowing physical health and increasing wealth and fame,
it is renowned as the "King of Hymns" (Stavarāja), celebrated throughout the three worlds.
O best of the twice-born, he who, having become pure, praises the Sun with this [hymn] at the two twilights— at both sunset and sunrise— is liberated from all sins.
Whether mental, verbal, or born of the body, as well as that born of action—
all that perishes by a single recitation in the presence of the Sun.
The single recitation, the fire-oblation, and the twilight worship;
likewise, the mantra for incense, the mantra for the water-offering, and the mantra for the food-oblation.
In the giving of food, in charity, in prostration, and in circumambulation,
this great mantra— auspicious and the remover of all sins— is honored.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, you should with great effort praise the boon-granting God, who bestows the fruit of all desires, by means of this very hymn.
The sages said:
"O Sun, you have described the Lord as being without qualities (nirguṇa) and eternal;
yet we have heard from you that he has again become manifest in twelve forms."
How did that highly resplendent ray of light, possessing great luster, come to be conceived in the womb of a woman and born as the Sun? In this matter, we have a great doubt. (BrP 32.2)
Brahmā said:
"Dakṣa had sixty excellent and beautiful daughters, namely Aditi, Diti, Danu, Vinatā, and others."
Dakṣa gave those thirteen daughters to Kaśyapa;
Aditi gave birth to the gods, the lords of the three worlds.
Diti gave birth to the Daityas, Danu to the fierce Dānavas who were arrogant in their strength,
and Vinatā and others likewise gave birth to various beings, both stationary and moving.
Then, O Sage, this entire world was filled with their sons, daughters' sons, grandsons, daughters' grandsons, and so forth— both of those men and of those women.
Among those sons of Kaśyapa, the principal ones are known as the hosts of deities;
others are remembered as the Sāttvika, Rājasa, and Tāmasa groups.
The creator Parameṣṭhin, Prajāpati, the best among the knowers of Brahman, likewise made the gods the partakers of sacrifice and the lords of the three worlds.
The Daityas and Dānavas, acting together out of rivalry, oppressed them;
thus were the sons driven away by the Daityas and the Dānavas.
O best of sages, seeing the three worlds destroyed and being intensely oppressed by hunger, Aditi deprived [the gods] of their sacrificial portions.
To propitiate Savitṛ, she exerted supreme effort;
with one-pointed mind, restricted in her diet, and established in the highest discipline,
she praised the Sun, the mass of splendors stationed in the sky.
Aditi said:
Homage to you, who bear the supreme, subtle, and most meritorious, incomparable abode; O Lord, the sovereign of those who possess abodes, and the eternal support of all abodes.
O Lord of the Cow, I praise you for the benefit of the worlds;
I bow down to that fierce form of yours which you assume when taking [the world] up.
I bow to that form of yours, which is exceedingly intense, as you bear the watery essence for a period of eight months in order to take it up.
Salutations to that one whose nature consists of qualities, who is united with Agni and Soma;
for your form shines through the unity of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
O Radiant One, salutations to You who are this entire universe known as the Triple Veda;
salutations to that eternal, stainless One, whose form beyond that [universe] is designated by the syllable "Om," which is both subtle and yet manifest.
Brahmā said: O twice-born ones,
thus that goddess, self-restrained and abstaining from food, performed hymns of praise day and night,
desiring to propitiate Vivasvat.
Then, after a long time, O best of the twice-born,
the blessed Sun appeared before her, the daughter of Dakṣa.
She beheld a great peak of light enveloping the sky,
resting upon the earth, radiant and exceedingly difficult to look upon because of its flames;
and having seen it, the goddess then fell into a state of supreme terror.
Aditi said:
"O Primordial One of the World, be gracious! O Lord of Rays, I do not see you;
show me favor so that I may behold your form, O Maker of Day."
O All-pervading Lord, compassionate toward your devotees, protect my sons, who are your devotees.
Brahmā said:
Then, from that splendor, the lord Vibhāvasu appeared; he was seen as the Sun, resembling molten copper.
Then, O twice-born ones, as that goddess bowed before him while he remained invisible, the radiant one said: "Choose from me a single boon, whatever you desire."
Bowing her head and pressing her knees against the earth,
she replied to Vivasvat, the granter of boons, who stood before her.
Aditi said:
"O God, be gracious! My three worlds and the sacrificial portions have been seized from my sons by the Daityas and Dānavas, who are superior in strength."
O Lord of the Cowherds, show me favor for that reason:
having entered into brotherhood with them through a portion of yourself, destroy those enemies.
O Lord, O Maker of Light, act so that my sons may once again become partakers of sacrificial offerings and sovereigns of the three worlds.
O Ravi, being well-pleased with your sons, act accordingly;
O remover of the distress of those who seek your grace, you are said to be the performer of what must be done.
Then, O brahmins, the Lord Bhāskara, the stealer of waters, being well-disposed with favor toward her, spoke to Aditi as she bowed before him.
Sūrya said:
"By a thousandth part of myself, I shall be born as your embryo in its entirety;
being capable, I shall swiftly destroy your son's enemies and bring you peace."
{Brahmā said:} Having spoken thus, the radiant Lord vanished;
she too, having attained all her desires, desisted from her ascetic penance.
Then, from among those thousands of rays, the ray of the sun known as Suṣumṇā [emerges];
at the end of that year, it proceeds for the fulfillment of his desires.
Then Savitṛ made his dwelling within the womb of the Mother of the Gods;
she, being perfectly composed, performed the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other penances.
"O twice-born ones, she said, 'I bear this divine embryo with purity.
Then Kaśyapa spoke to her, his words slightly overflowing with anger."
Kaśyapa said:
"Why do you kill the embryo? Thus spoke she who was constantly observing fasts.
Brahmā said:
And she, becoming angry, said to him: "Look at this egg of a fetus!
It has not been killed by our enemies; it will surely become their death. (BrP 32.35)
Having spoken thus, the source of the gods, provoked by her husband's words, then cast out that embryo, which was blazing with splendors.
Seeing that embryo, which possessed the splendor of the rising sun, Kaśyapa bowed down and praised it with reverence using primordial words.
Being thus praised, he then emerged manifest from the cosmic egg,
possessing a luster like the petals of a lotus and pervading the quarters of the sky with his splendor.
Then, from the intermediate space, an incorporeal voice, deep as a water-laden cloud, addressed Kaśyapa, the best of sages.
Speech said:
"O Sage, this egg of Aditi was spoken of by you as 'māritaṃte';
therefore, this son of yours shall be known by the name Mārtaṇḍa."
"He shall slay the Asuras, those enemies who seize the sacrificial portions"—
having heard these words that had come from the sky, the gods [were reassured].
The Dānavas attained incomparable joy, while their vital energy was destroyed;
then Śatakratu summoned the Daityas for battle.
Accompanied by the gods and filled with joy, the Dānavas also advanced toward him;
a terrible battle then ensued between those gods and the Asuras.
In that battle, where the interior of the entire world was set ablaze by a rain of weapons and missiles,
they were gazed upon by the Blessed Mārtaṇḍa.
Being consumed by that splendor, those great asuras were reduced to ashes;
thereupon, all the inhabitants of heaven attained incomparable joy.
They praised Mārtaṇḍa, the source of splendors, as well as Aditi;
thereafter, they regained their respective offices and their sacrificial shares as before.
The Blessed One Mārtaṇḍa also then performed his own office;
like a kadamba flower, the radiant one, surrounded by rays above and below,
resembled a mass of fire and assumed a form that was not overly distinct.
The sages said:
"O Lord of the World, tell me how the Sun later obtained a form so exceedingly beautiful, shaped like a cluster of Kadamba flowers."
Brahmā said:
Having prostrated himself and offered his grace, Viśvakarman Prajāpati gave his daughter named Saṃjñā to Vivasvat.
That lord of cattle begot three offspring upon her:
two highly fortunate sons and a daughter, Yamunā.
By that excessive splendor of the sun-god Vivasvat,
he scorched the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
Seeing that form of Vivasvat, which was shaped like a sphere, Saṃjñā, unable to endure his great brilliance, spoke these words to her own shadow: ||| BrP_32.52 |||
Saṃjñā said:
"I shall go to my own father's abode; may you be blessed.
O auspicious one, by my command you must remain right here without any change of state."
"These two children of mine and this maiden of excellent complexion must not be revealed by you to the Blessed One."
Chāyā said:
"O Goddess, until my hair is seized and until a curse is pronounced, I shall never reveal your secret thought; you may go wherever you desire."
Having been addressed thus, the ashamed Saṃjñā went to her father’s abode;
she remained in her father’s house for a thousand years.
Told repeatedly by her father, "Go to your husband's side," she returned again and again,
having become a mare, and then went to the northern Kurus.
There, O best of the twice-born, that virtuous woman performed austerities without food,
intent on her words, while Saṃjñā had gone to her father’s presence.
A shadow assuming that form approached the Sun;
and the Blessed Lord Sūrya, thinking of her, "This is Saṃjñā," [approached her].
In that same manner, she gave birth to two sons and a daughter;
and Saṃjñā, the daughter of the Earth, likewise provided for those children of hers.
She did not show such affection toward her elder brothers as she did toward Manu;
Manu forgave that behavior of hers, but Yama did not tolerate it.
Being tormented in many ways by his father’s wife, he was deeply distressed;
out of anger, childishness, and the force of destiny,
he indeed threatened her with his foot, yet did not strike her body.
Chāyā said:
"Since you have threatened your father’s most venerable wife with your foot, therefore this foot of yours shall fall; of this there is no doubt."
Brahmā said: But Yama, his mind deeply distressed by that curse,
reported everything to his father along with Manu, the righteous-souled one.
Yama said:
"O God, our mother does not behave with equal affection toward us;
having abandoned the elder out of partiality, she desires to favor the younger."
I raised my foot against her, but it was not brought down upon her body;
whether out of childishness or delusion, you ought to forgive that.
"O dear one, O best of ascetics, since I was cursed by my mother in her anger as her son,
I therefore do not consider her to be my true mother."
O Blessed One, O Lord of the Cowherds, please think of such a way that, through your grace, this foot of mine may not fall today due to my mother’s curse.
Ravi said: "Without doubt, my son, there must be a great cause for this,
by which anger has taken possession of you, who are a knower of dharma and of virtuous character."
Indeed, a counteraction exists for all curses;
however, there is never any reversal of a curse for those cursed by their own mothers.
"It is not possible to make this word of your mother false;
however, out of affection for my son, I shall grant you some favor."
Worms shall take away her flesh and depart for the surface of the earth;
thus her word will be made true, and you shall be saved.
Brahmā said:
"The Sun then spoke to Chāyā: 'Why indeed, among your children who are all equal, has such excessive affection been shown by you toward only one?'"
Surely you are not their mother; you must be some *saṃjñā* who has come here.
A mother would never utter a curse even upon her own children, however devoid of virtue they may be.
Avoiding that [act] and fearing the curse of Ravi, she then related the account;
having heard it, he went to his father-in-law.
And he, having honored Ravi according to custom,
spoke to him as he desired to consume [the world] with his wrath, seeking to appease him.
Viśvakarman said:
"This form of yours, pervaded by excessive splendor, is very difficult to endure;
unable to bear it, Saṃjñā indeed practices penance in the forest."
Today you shall see your own wife of virtuous conduct,
who is performing great asceticism in the forest for the sake of your beauty.
"I have heard the word of Brahmā regarding the obstruction of your splendor;
O Lord of Heaven, I shall today restore your beloved form."
Brahmā said:
Then the Blessed Sun said "So be it" to Tvaṣṭṛ.
Thereupon, the form of Vivasvat was previously circular.
Then Viśvakarman, permitted by Vivasvat in Śākadvīpa,
placed [the sun] upon a lathe and proceeded to whet its brilliance.
As the sun, which pervades all wandering worlds, was not eclipsed,
the earth— with its oceans, mountains, and forests— ascended into the sky.
O brahmins, O highly fortunate ones, the entire sky, along with the moon, planets, and stars,
fell downward, tossed about and thrown into turmoil.
All the oceans became agitated with their waters tossed about,
and the great mountains were rent asunder, their peaks and foundations shattered.
O best of sages, all the celestial abodes supported by Dhruva,
whose binding rays were snapping asunder, fell downward.
Tossed by the winds produced by the impact of their rapid whirling,
thousands of great clouds, resounding with terrible roars, were shattered to pieces.
O best of sages, the world— comprising the earth, the sky, and the netherworld— became utterly agitated at that time, bewildered by the blazing whirlwind.
Beholding the three worlds agitated and wandering in confusion, the celestial sages and the gods,
together with Brahmā, offered praise to the Radiant One.
You are the primordial god among the gods; you were born for the welfare of the world. At the times of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, you abide in a threefold division.
"May it be well with you, O Lord of the World, O Sun who brings heat and rain!
Then the gods, headed by Indra, praised him as he was being depicted.
"Victory, O God, Lord of the World! Victory, O Sovereign of the entire world!
Then the seven sages, led by Vasiṣṭha and Atri, [spoke].
They praised him with various hymns, uttering "May there be well-being! May there be well-being!
And the Vālakhilyas also offered praise with the most excellent declarations of the Vedas.
Agni and the other [guardians] joyfully depicted the radiant one;
"O Lord, you are the liberation of those seeking liberation, and you are the supreme object of meditation for meditators."
You are the refuge of all beings who abide within the ritual section of the Veda;
you alone are to be fully worshipped, O Lord of Gods. May there be peace for us, O Lord of the worlds! (BrP 32.94)
"May there be constant welfare for our bipeds, and may there be welfare for our quadrupeds.
Then the hosts of Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas [spoke].
With palms joined in reverence, they all bowed their heads to the Sun and spoke various words that brought pleasure to the mind and the ear.
"O Creator of beings, may your splendor be bearable for all creatures.

Ṣaḍja, Madhyama, and Gāndhāra.
And with modulations (*mūrchanās*), rhythms (*tālas*), and musical combinations that bestow happiness,

Menakā, Sahajanyā, and Rambhā, the best among the Apsarases,

Then, while they performed many gestures such as *bhāva*, *hāva*, and *vilāsa*,

Paṇavas, puṣkaras, mṛdaṅgas, paṭahas, ānakas,

With gandharvas and throngs of apsaras singing and dancing,

Then, amidst that clamor in the assembly of all the gods,
