He was skillfully carved down to his knees by Viśvakarman;
however, he did not approve of being carved, and therefore he was lowered down by him.
But her form was not diminished by the suppression of her splendor;
rather, from that point on, her beauty shone forth even more intensely, becoming more lovely than the most lovely.
Thus, having heard of the Sun’s inscription above [the world], which is praised by Hara, Kamalāsana, and Viṣṇu as the cause of the seasons of snow, water, and heat—
At the end of his life, he goes to the world of the Sun;
thus, O best of sages, was the former birth of Ravi,
and his supreme form has been fully described by me.
The sages said:
"Tell us once more a story concerning the Sun;
we do not reach satiety while listening to that auspicious tale."
"O Lord, we wish to know this: from where does the power of this one come, who is blazing, possessed of great splendor, and radiant like a mass of fire?"
Brahmā said:
When the worlds had become shrouded in darkness and all things, both stationary and moving, had perished,
Intellect (buddhi) first arose from the causal qualities of primordial nature (prakṛti).
From that, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) was born, which sets the great elements into motion;
from it arose wind, fire, water, space, and earth, and from those the cosmic egg was produced.
Within that egg, these worlds are established,
including the earth with its seven continents and its seven oceans.
Remaining right there, I am indeed Viṣṇu, the Great Lord;
all those deluded ones, characterized by darkness (tamas), meditate upon that Lord.
Then indeed, the one of great splendor, the dispeller of darkness, appeared;
and at that time, we recognized him as the Sun through the practice of meditative concentration.
And having each individually realized the Supreme Self,
we all praised that Lord, the God, with divine hymns of praise.
You are the primordial god among the gods, and you are the Lord by virtue of your sovereignty;
you are the first creator of all beings, the god of gods, the maker of day.
He is the life-force of all beings—of gods, gandharvas, and rākṣasas;
likewise of sages, kiṃnaras, and siddhas, as well as of uragas and birds.
You are Brahmā, you are Mahādeva, you are Viṣṇu, and you are Prajāpati;
you are Vāyu, Indra, Soma, Vivasvat, and likewise Varuṇa.
You are Time, the creator of the universe, its destroyer, its sustainer, and likewise its Lord;
you are the rivers, the oceans, the mountains, and the lightning and rainbows.
Dissolution and manifestation, the manifest and the unmanifest, and the eternal;
beyond the Lord is Knowledge (vidyā), and beyond Knowledge is Śiva.
There is no god higher than Śiva; you alone are the Supreme Lord, with hands and feet everywhere, and eyes, heads, and faces on every side.
He has a thousand rays, a thousand mouths, and a thousand feet and eyes;
he is the source of all beings, and the worlds Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Mahaḥ, Satyam, Tapaḥ, and Janaḥ.
Salutation to you whose form is blazing, illuminating, divine, and the light of all the worlds, which is difficult even for the lords of the gods to behold.
Salutations to you whose form is the supreme unmanifest, frequented by hosts of gods and siddhas such as Bhṛgu, Atri, and Pulaha, and praised by them.
Salutations to that form of the one who transcends all gods, which is eternally to be known by those who know the Vedas and is endowed with all knowledge.
Salutation to that form of yours which is the creator of the universe, the source of all beings, worshipped by Vaiśvānara and the gods, abiding within the world, and inconceivable.
Salutation to that form of yours which is known as the Supreme Self— beyond sacrifice, beyond the Vedas, beyond the worlds, and beyond heaven.
Salutations to you whose form is unknowable, without defining marks, beyond the reach of meditation,
imperishable, and indeed without beginning or end.
Homage, homage to the cause of all causes; homage, homage to the liberator from evil; homage, homage to you, the destroyer of the sons of Diti.
Homage, homage to the one who liberates from disease; homage, homage to the bestower of all boons;
homage, homage to the bestower of all happiness.
Homage, homage to the bestower of all wealth; homage, homage to the bestower of all intelligence.
Thus praised, the Blessed One assumed his fiery form.
He spoke with auspicious words: "What boon may be granted to you?"
The gods said: "O Lord, no one would be able to endure your exceedingly brilliant form;
let it become endurable for the welfare of the world."
Saying "So be it," that Blessed One, the primordial creator and Lord,
who bestows heat, rain, and snow, [proceeded] for the sake of accomplishing the purposes of the worlds.
Then the followers of Sāṃkhya, the followers of Yoga, and others who long for liberation,
being meditative, meditate upon the Sun-god dwelling within the heart.
Even if one is devoid of all auspicious marks or joined with all manner of sins,
one who has taken refuge in the Sun-god crosses over every evil.
The Agnihotra fire-sacrifice, the Vedas, and sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees,
do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of a single act of devotion and prostration to the Sun.
They take refuge in the Sun, the supreme sacred ford among all sacred fords, the most auspicious among all auspicious things, and the purest among all purifiers.
Those who bow down to the Sun-god, who is praised by Śakra and the other deities,
are liberated from all sins and go to the world of the Sun.
The sages said:
"O Brahmin, for a long time now a desire has arisen in us to hear that hundred-and-eight names of Ravi which were previously spoken by you."
Brahmā said:
O twice-born ones, listen as I recite the one hundred and eight names of Bhāskara, which are supremely secret and bestow both heaven and liberation.
Oṃ: Sūrya, Aryaman, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, Arka, Savitṛ, Ravi, Gabhastimān, Aja, Kāla, Mṛtyu, Dhātṛ, and Prabhākara.
Earth, water, fire, ether, and wind are the ultimate refuge;
as are Soma, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Budha, and Aṅgāraka.
Indra, Vivasvat, Dīptāṃśu, Śuci, Śauri, Śanaiścara,
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Skanda, Vaiśravaṇa, and Yama.
He is the fire of lightning and the digestive fire within the body; he is the lord of all luminous energies.
He is the banner of dharma, the author of the Vedas, the embodiment of the Vedāṅgas, and the vehicle of the Vedas.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages, as well as all the abodes of the immortals;
the divisions of time such as kalā, kāṣṭhā, and muhūrta, as well as nights, watches, and moments.
The Ashvattha tree that marks the year, the wheel of time, the consumer of oblations;
the eternal Person, the Yogi, both manifest and unmanifest, the primeval one.
The overseer of time, the overseer of creatures, the architect of the universe, the dispeller of darkness, Varuṇa, the ocean, Aṃśa, the cloud, the life-giver, and the slayer of enemies.
The abode of the elements, the lord of beings, honored by all the worlds;
the creator, the fire of dissolution, the origin of all, and free from greed.
Ananta, Kapila, Bhānu, Kāmada, Sarvatomukha,
Jaya, Viśāla, Varada, and he who is served by all beings.
He is the mind, the one with beautiful wings, the source of all beings, the swift-moving, the sustainer of life;
he is Dhanvantari, the smoke-bannered, the primordial god, and the son of Aditi.
The twelve-fold Sun is Dakṣa, the father, the mother, and the grandfather;
he is the gate of heaven, the gate of progeny, the gate of liberation, and the celestial realm.
The creator of the body, the tranquil self, the soul of the universe, facing in all directions,
the soul of the moving and the unmoving, the subtle self, Maitreya, endowed with compassion.
O best of the twice-born, this beautiful hundred-and-eight names of the Sun, who is worthy of praise and possesses immeasurable splendor, has indeed been proclaimed by me.
It is indeed frequented by hosts of gods, ancestors, and yakṣas;
it is venerated by asuras, the moon, and siddhas;
and it possesses the luster of excellent gold and fire.
I have prostrated before the Sun for my own welfare.
He who, being well-composed, recites this at sunrise shall obtain sons, a wife, and an accumulation of wealth and jewels.
That man shall obtain the recollection of his past births;
he attains supreme memory and intelligence. That man who [recites] this hymn to the best of gods...
One who recites this with a pure mind and concentrated focus is liberated from the ocean of the forest-fire of grief and shall obtain all desires as wished for by the mind.
Brahmā said:
That god who is omnipresent, the enemy of Tripura, the three-eyed one, Rudra who acts for the pleasure of Umā, and whose crest is adorned with the crescent moon; ||| BrP_34.1 |||
Having put to flight all the gods, the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Ṛṣis,
as well as the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Nāgas, and others who had assembled there.
Formerly, on the surface of the earth, he destroyed the prosperous sacrifice of Dakṣa as he was performing it—
a sacrifice rich in jewels and provided with every necessary material.
O Brahmins, terrified by his majesty, the gods of the three heavens, headed by Śakra,
found no peace and went to Kailāsa for refuge.
There sits the boon-granting Lord, wielder of the trident, whose banner bears the bull;
the Blessed One holds the Pināka bow in his hand and is the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
O best of sages, at Ekāmra, in an extraordinary place, Mahādeva— the wearer of animal skins, whose banner bears the bull—
is Hara, the granter of all desires.
The sages said:
For what reason did that Lord Bhava, who is devoted to the welfare of all beings,
destroy the sacrifice of Dakṣa, which was adorned by all the gods?
"O Lord, we do not consider the cause for this to be insignificant;
we wish to hear it, for our curiosity is great. Please speak."
Brahmā said:
Dakṣa had eight daughters who were thus united with husbands;
having brought them from their own homes, their father honored them in his own house.
Then, having been honored, those brahmin women dwelt in their father’s house;
among them, the eldest was indeed Satī by name, the wife of Tryambaka.
Hating Rudra, Dakṣa did not indeed invite that daughter of his;
nor did Maheśvara offer any salutation to Dakṣa.
The son-in-law remained naturally steadfast in his splendor toward that father-in-law;
then Satī, having understood everything, [realized] that they had all arrived at her father's house.
Then Satī, though uninvited, went to her father’s house;
however, her father offered her a disrespectful honor that was inferior to that given to the others.
Thereupon, the goddess, overwhelmed with anger, spoke to her father: BrP 34.13.
Satyuvāca:
"O Lord, I am the eldest among my younger sisters; why do you not honor me?
You have brought me to this contemptible state, one that is devoid of respect."
"I am the eldest and the most excellent; you ought to honor me."
Brahmā said:
Thus addressed, Dakṣa, his eyes bloodshot with rage, spoke to her.
Dakṣa said:
"O virtuous lady, my young daughters are superior, most excellent, and worthy of worship compared to you;
and their husbands, likewise, are highly esteemed by me."
O virtuous lady, they were all devoted to Brahman, established in their vows, great yogis, and highly righteous; they were praiseworthy and superior in their qualities because of Tryambaka.
Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Pulastya, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, Kratu,
Bhṛgu, and Marīci— these, likewise, are my most excellent sons-in-law.
Śarva competes with them all, and they likewise compete against him;
therefore, I do not wish for you, for Bhava is adverse to me.
When Dakṣa had spoken thus with a completely deluded mind—
having addressed the great ṛṣis for the purpose of cursing himself—
the goddess, becoming enraged at what he had said, spoke to her father.
Satyā said:
"Since you reproach me, who am faultless in speech, thought, and deed,
therefore, my dear, I shall abandon this body born of you."
Brahmā said: Then, due to that insult, Satī, indignant with grief,
spoke these words after bowing to the Self-Existent One (Svayaṃbhū).
Satyā said:
"By that [merit], even though I was indeed bodiless, I have now been born again with a radiant body;
moreover, I am born once more as a virtuous woman, free from delusion."
May I become the lawful wife of the wise Tryambaka himself.
{Brahmā said:} Then,
seated right there, she composed her agitated mind and maintained within herself the fire-element concentration (dhāraṇā) directed toward the Self.
Then, having raised himself up, the fire, impelled by the wind,
issued forth from all his limbs and reduced her to ashes.
Having heard of that death of the goddess Satī and having understood their conversation exactly as it was, the Lord Śaṅkara, the wielder of the trident,
became enraged for the sake of Dakṣa’s destruction.
Śrī Śaṅkara said:
O Dakṣa, because Satī was insulted and departed in haste,
while all your other daughters were praised by their husbands.
Therefore, when the Vaivasvata Manvantara has arrived, these great ṛṣis shall indeed be born again in your second sacrifice, for they will not be born from a womb.
During the sacrificial session of Brahmā Cākṣuṣa Manu,
having addressed the seven ṛṣis, he cursed Dakṣa once again.
In the interval of Manu Cākṣuṣa,
there will be a human king who is the grandson of Prācīnabarhis and the son of Pracetas.
O worthy one, you shall be born of Māriṣā by the name Dakṣa himself,
from a maiden of the Śākhis, when the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara has arrived.
"O evil-minded one, I shall create obstacles for you even there,
again and again, in these actions joined with the pursuit of dharma, kāma, and artha."
Then, having been thus addressed, Dakṣa cursed Rudra in return.
Dakṣa said:
"O cruel one, because you have insulted the sages on my account,
therefore the twice-born shall no longer sacrifice to you in the ritual together with the gods."
"O cruel one, having offered an oblation to you in their rituals, people shall touch water;
you shall dwell in this very world, having abandoned heaven, until the end of the age (yuga).
After that, there will be no worship for you even together with the gods."
Rudra said:
"The fourfold order belongs to the gods, and they eat together in one place;
I shall not eat together with them, but rather I shall eat separately."
Of all the worlds, Bhūrloka is said to be the first;
I alone sustain it by my own will, not by your command.
When that is upheld, all the worlds remain eternally stable;
therefore, I dwell here constantly, not by your command.
Brahmā said:
Then Dakṣa, addressed by Rudra of immeasurable splendor,
abandoned his body born of Svayambhū and was reborn here among human beings.
When the householder Dakṣa, the lord and master of sacrifices,
performed a complete sacrifice here together with the deities.
Then, when the Vaivasvata interval had arrived, the king of mountains begot that goddess Umā upon Menā; she was the very same goddess Satī.
That goddess Satī existed previously, and afterwards she became Umā;
she shares the same vows as Bhava, and Bhava is never released from her.
In this world, during the various Manvantaras, the Lord assumes whatever form he desires,
just as the goddess Aditi was devoted to Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci.
Śrī was with Nārāyaṇa, just as Śacī is with Maghavan;
Kīrti with Viṣṇu, Uṣas with Sūrya, and Arundhatī with Vasiṣṭha.
But these goddesses never abandon their husbands under any circumstances;
thus was Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, born during the Cākṣuṣa interval.
O King, he was the grandson of Prācīnabarhis and the son of the Pracetas; furthermore, O noble one, he was born again from the ten Pracetas through Māriṣā.
We have heard that he was born a second time due to the curse of Rudra;
and all those great seers, Bhṛgu and the others, were likewise born.
Formerly, in the first Tretā age, during the great sacrifice of the god Vaivasvata Manu, he assumed the form of Varuṇa.
Thus, this latent tendency (anuśaya) persisted between them as they passed into another birth—
between Prajāpati Dakṣa and the wise Tryambaka.
Therefore, one should never harbor resentment toward those who grant boons here;

for even a being who has passed into another birth, though conditioned by good and evil deeds, does not achieve prosperity through fame. Thus, that [resentment] should not be practiced by one who possesses discernment.
The sages said: O Lord,
how was it that Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, having previously cast off her body out of anger,
was born again in the house of the King of Mountains?
How did her former body come to exist within another body?
How was there a union with Bhava, and how did their conversation take place?
O Lord of the World, how did the svayaṃvara take place during that great birth, and how did the marriage occur, endowed with every wonder?
O Brahmin, you should now relate all of that in detail;
we wish to hear this meritorious and most enchanting story.
Brahmā said:
Listen, O tigers among sages, to this meritorious story of Umā and Śaṅkara, which destroys sins and bestows the fruits of all desires.
Once, when Kaśyapa, the best among men, had arrived at his own home,
Himavat asked him about events in the world that were both beneficial and conducive to renown.
O Sage, tell me how the worlds may become inexhaustible, how supreme renown may be attained, and likewise how one may be worthy of worship among the virtuous.
Kaśyapa said:
"O mighty-armed one, all this is obtained through offspring;
through offspring, my fame is established along with that of Brahmā and the ṛṣis."
"Do you not see, O Lord of Mountains, that you ask me this? O Mountain, I shall relate to you what was seen by me in the past, exactly as it occurred."
While traveling toward Vārāṇasī, I beheld a celestial chariot stationed in the sky— divine, well-constructed, incomparable, and possessed of great majesty.
Beneath it, in the place of a pit, I heard a cry of distress;
having recognized him through my ascetic power, I remained there, invisible.
Then, O Lord of Mountains, a brahmin arrived there— one who was observant of his vows, pure,
whose soul was purified by ablutions at sacred fords, and established in supreme austerity.
Then, as that twice-born man was traveling along, being pursued by a tiger,
he entered that region where the mountain cave was located.
Then that twice-born man, distressed, saw those sages hanging from a clump of *vīraṇa* grass in a pit; afflicted with grief, he questioned them.
The twice-born said: "Who are you that hang head-downwards from this stalk of vīraṇa grass?
By what cause are you suffering, O sinless ones, and how will your liberation come about?"
The ancestors said: "We— your father, grandfather,
and great-grandfather— are suffering because of your wicked deed, even though you have performed meritorious acts."
"O illustrious one, this hell exists here in the form of a pit;
and you are a clump of vīraṇa grass, upon which we hang ourselves. (BrP 34.67)
"O Brahmin, as long as you live, so long shall we remain;
once you have died, we, being evil-minded, shall go to hell."
If you, having entered into marriage, procreate a son of superior qualities,
by that means we shall be released from our sin.
"O son of great intelligence, this cannot be achieved by any other austerity nor by the fruit of visiting sacred fords; therefore, do this and deliver your ancestors from fear."
Kaśyapa said:
Having promised "So be it," and having propitiated the bull-bannered god (Śiva),
he raised his ancestors from the pit and made them leaders of the Gaṇas.
He was personally beloved by Rudra, known by the name Suveśa;
esteemed and powerful, he became a leader of Rudra’s hosts.
Therefore, O Lord of Mountains, having performed severe austerity, produce a daughter of excellent complexion and most virtuous offspring.
Brahmā said:
Having been thus addressed by the seer, the lord of mountains remained established in his observances and performed incomparable austerity, by which I was gratified.
Then I leapt up toward him and said, "I am the granter of boons;
speak, O Lord of Mountains, observer of noble vows, for I am pleased with this asceticism of yours."
Himavat said:
"O Blessed One, I desire a son adorned with all virtues;
O Lord, if you are pleased with me, grant me this boon."
{Brahmā said:} O twice-born ones, having heard those words of the king of mountains, I then granted him the boon desired by his mind. BrP_34.77 //
"O Lord of Mountains, O observer of noble vows, by this asceticism a daughter shall be born to you,
through whose power you will attain auspicious fame everywhere."
Worshipped by all the gods and surrounded by ten million sacred fords,
he is indeed purifying through his merit for all the gods as well.
And she shall be your eldest, O auspicious one, and others as well shall follow thereafter.
In due time, that lord of mountains also begot upon Menā three daughters:
Aparṇā, Ekaparṇā, and likewise Ekapāṭalā.
Having eaten a single leaf of the nyagrodha tree and a single trumpet-flower of the pāṭala tree, he practiced austerities without a fixed dwelling.
For a hundred thousand years, Ekaparṇā practiced a difficult austerity that was hard for even gods and dānavas to perform,
subsisting on a single leaf as her food.
Likewise, with a single *pāṭala* flower, she became Ekapāṭalā;
and when a full thousand years had passed, those two took food.
But Aparṇā, who was fasting, her mother addressed, forbidding her with the words "No! and distressed by maternal affection.
Having been addressed thus by her mother, that goddess, who had performed difficult austerities,
became renowned in the worlds by that very name as one worshipped by the gods.
This entire world, both stationary and moving, consists of these three maidens;
their ascetic practice shall endure as long as the earth shall remain.
All three of them were embodied asceticism, devoted to yoga;
all were highly fortunate and likewise possessed of perpetual youth.
They are indeed the mothers of the world and practitioners of celibacy;
they always sustain the worlds through their own ascetic power.
Umā was the most excellent among them, the eldest, and possessed of the finest complexion;
endowed with the power of great yoga, she attended upon Mahādeva.
Dattaka was his son, and he was the joy of the Bhṛgu lineage;
he had a wife named Ekaparṇā, who gave birth to a son, Devala.
Among those maidens, the third was indeed Ekapāṭalā;
she attended upon Jaigīṣavya, the son of Alarka.
And Śaṅkha and Likhita were her two sons, born not from a womb;
as for Umā, that woman of excellent complexion whom I have described to you— ||| BrP_34.93 |||
Then, perceiving that the entire three worlds were being scorched by the power of her asceticism, I spoke these words to her.
"O Goddess, O beautiful one, why will you torment the worlds with penance?
All this has been created by you; do not destroy what you have made."
For you indeed sustain all these worlds by your own splendor;
tell us now, O Mother of the World, what is it that you desire from us here?
The Goddess said:
"O Grandfather, you yourself already know the purpose for which I am performing this austerity; why then do you ask?"
Brahmā said:
Then I spoke to her, "O auspicious one, he for whose sake you perform these austerities will come here himself and choose you as his bride."
Śarva alone is the supreme lord, the sovereign of the lords of all worlds;
O auspicious lady, we are always his submissive servants.
O Goddess, that God of gods, the Supreme Lord, the Self-born One, will himself come into your presence,
possessing both a noble form and forms such as the deformed.
Though he is of uniform form, Maheśvara belongs to no one; he dwells in the world of the mountains,
the Lord of the moving and the unmoving, the primordial and immeasurable.
He who, with his teeth like moons and possessing a splendor equal to Indra,
had assumed a terrifying form—
Brahmā said:
Then the gods, having gone there, spoke to that beautiful woman:
"O Goddess, in a short time Dhūrjaṭi, Nīlalohita [will come]."
"That Lord of Gods shall be your husband; do not perform further penance.
Then the gods and the brahmins circumambulated the daughter of the mountain.
They departed from her sight, and she too ceased [speaking];
that goddess, having thus spoken this hymn, remained in her own auspicious hermitage.
And having taken refuge by the aśoka tree that had grown at the gate, she remained there;
then Hara, the destroyer of the suffering of the thirty gods, arrived, bearing the mark of the moon.
Assuming a deformed appearance, he became short and thin-armed;
his nose was broken, he was hunchbacked, and the tips of his hair were tawny.
And with a distorted face, he said, "O Goddess, I choose you as my bride.
Then Umā, perfected in yoga, recognized that Śaṅkara had arrived.
With his inner being purified, and desiring to perform acts of compassion,
he addressed him with offerings of water for the hands (*argha*), water for the feet (*pādya*), and the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*).
Having honored that brahmin with flowers, she who was dear to brahmins [spoke].
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, I am not independent; my father is the leader in my household.
He is indeed the master over my giving away, for I am a maiden, O bull among the twice-born."
"Go and beg my father, the imperishable Lord of Mountains;
O Brahmin, if he gives me to you, that will be fitting for me."
Brahmā said:
Then that blessed Lord, the powerful one, remaining in that very same deformed state, spoke to the king of mountains: "O king of mountains, give me your daughter."
Recognizing him as the imperishable Rudra in his transformed form, he became afraid of the curse and, with a dejected mind, spoke these words: BrP_35.12.
The Lord of Mountains said:
"O Blessed One, I do not hold the Brahmins in contempt, for they are deities upon this earth;
however, O Great-minded One, hear that which was previously desired by me."
"A svayaṃvara for my daughter shall take place, honored by the brahmins;
whoever she herself chooses there shall become her husband."
Having heard those words of Śaila, the high-minded Lord whose banner bears the bull approached the Goddess and said this:
Śiva said:
"O Goddess, it is heard that you have been authorized by your father to choose a husband in a svayaṃvara;
whoever you choose there shall be your husband."
Therefore, having taken my leave, I shall depart; for how could you, O fair-faced one, abandon a handsome man like me to choose one who is unworthy?
Brahmā said: Then,
having been addressed by him there, she contemplated what he had spoken,
as well as the disposition placed within Rudra and the grace of his mind.
Having approached the Lord of Gods, he said: "Let not your mind be otherwise;
I shall choose you as my boon, for this is by no means a wonder."
Or if you have some doubt regarding me in any way, O Brahmin,
then right here, O illustrious one, I choose you according to your heart's desire.
Brahmā said:
Taking a cluster of flowers with both hands,
the Goddess stood there, placed it upon the shoulder of Śambhu, and said, "You have been chosen by me."
Then that Blessed Lord, chosen by that goddess, spoke to Aśoka as if reviving him with his speech: BrP_35.22.
Śiva said:
"Since I have been covered by this cluster of your great merit,
you shall be abandoned by old age and become immortal."
He who can assume any form at will, whose flowers are desire, who grants desires, and who is dear to me;
he who is enriched with the flowers of all ornaments and who possesses all flowers and fruits.
You shall be the consumer of all foods and possess the taste of nectar;
you shall be the possessor of all fragrances among the gods and remain steadfastly beloved.
"You shall be fearless in all worlds and perfectly at peace;
[go to] this hermitage known as Citrakūṭa, which is exceedingly famous. (BrP 35.26)
For whoever goes there seeking merit shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
and whoever dies there shall go to the world of Brahmā.
And he who, endowed with the prescribed observances, here completely renounces his life-breaths,
shall become a great lord of the Gaṇas, joined with the ascetic power of the Goddess.
{Brahmā said:} Having spoken thus, the god, the creator of the world, the lord and protector of all beings, took leave of the daughter of Himavat and vanished.
When that Blessed One of immeasurable self had departed, the goddess also turned her face upward toward him from that very spot and became established upon the stone.
With her face turned toward that Maheśa, the lord of the worlds,
she then did not shine, dejected like a night devoid of the moon.
Then Śailajā heard the sound of a distressed child near the hermitage and by a lake filled with water.
Then Śiva himself, the God of gods, having assumed the form of a child for the sake of sport, became seized by a crocodile in the middle of the lake.
Resorting to his yogic power (yogamāyā), which is the cause of the emergence of the phenomenal world,
he placed that form in the middle of the lake and spoke thus.
The boy said:
"May someone save me," he cried, his mind seized by the crocodile;
"Alas, what misery! I am but a child, my desires for worldly goals unfulfilled. (BrP 35.35)
I am going to my death in the mouth of this evil-minded crocodile;
seized by the crocodile and deeply distressed, I do not grieve for my own body.
Just as I grieve for my father and my ascetic mother, who,
upon hearing that I have been seized by a crocodile and have met my death, will be filled with anxiety.

"My two beloved sons, my only children, will surely give up their lives. Alas! What a great calamity it is that I, a mere child who has not yet entered the stages of life, shall indeed meet my death while seized by the crocodile."
Brahmā said:
Having heard that cry of the distressed Brahmin, the beautiful goddess rose up and set out for the place where that twice-born man was staying.
The moon-faced woman saw the boy of beautiful form,
trembling as he stood having entered the mouth of the crocodile.
That illustrious and excellent crocodile, seeing that the goddess had approached,
seized her and quickly went into the very middle of the lake.
As he was being dragged away, that radiant youth let out a cry of distress;
then the goddess, afflicted with grief upon seeing the boy seized by the demon, spoke.
Pārvatī said:
O King of Crocodiles, O being of great courage, O you with mighty tusks and fearsome prowess, release this boy, my only son, immediately!
The demon said:
"O Goddess, he who first comes to me on the sixth day is my food, as ordained of old by the creators of the world."
Therefore, O illustrious daughter of the king of mountains, on this sixth day, he has surely been impelled by Brahmā; I shall not release him by any means whatsoever.
The goddess said:
"O King of Grāhas, release this child by virtue of the supreme austerity I performed on the peak of the Himalayas; homage be unto you."
The demon said: "O goddess, O young woman of beautiful countenance, do not waste your ascetic merit.
O most excellent lady, do as I say, and you shall likewise attain liberation."
The goddess said:
"O Lord of the Grāhas, speak quickly that which is not censured by the virtuous;
that has been done, there is no doubt here, for Brahmins are dear to me."
The demon said:
"Whatever penance you have performed, whether it be small or great, give all of that to me immediately; then you shall obtain liberation."
The Goddess said:
"O great Grāha, whatever merit has been earned by me since birth—all that I give to you; release the child, O great Grāha!"
Brahmā said:
Then the crocodile, adorned by that asceticism, blazed forth;
like the sun at midday, he then became difficult to behold.
And with a satisfied soul, he spoke thus to the Goddess, the sustainer of the world:
The demon said:
"O Goddess of great vows, what is this that you have so firmly resolved to do?
Even the acquisition of ascetic merit is painful; its abandonment is not praised."
"Accept penance itself, O slender-waisted one, and this boy as well;
I am pleased with your devotion to the brahmins, and therefore I grant you a boon.
Thus addressed by the crocodile, she of the great vows spoke these words.
The goddess said:
"O crocodile, even at the cost of my own body, I must protect this brahmin with great effort;
for while I may regain my ascetic power, I can never again obtain a brahmin."
O great crocodile, having reflected well, you have brought about the liberation of the child;
there is no austerity superior to that of the Brahmins—indeed, the Brahmins are considered by me to be supreme.
"O Lord of Grāhas, once given, I do not take back what has been bestowed by you;
for no man, O Grāha, would ever reclaim that which has already been given. (BrP 35.56)
"This has been given by me to you; I shall certainly not take it back.
Let this remain with you alone, and let this boy be set free."
Brahmā said:
Having been addressed thus, he then praised her, released the child, and paid homage to the goddess; then, shining like the sun, he vanished right there.
Then the boy, released by the crocodile on the shore of the lake,
vanished right there like a mass of wealth obtained in a dream.
Perceiving that her ascetic merit was diminishing, the goddess, daughter of the Lord of the Snowy Mountains,
began once again to perform penance, established in her observances.
O brahmins, knowing that she desired to perform further asceticism, Śaṅkara himself spoke these words: "Do not perform penance. (BrP 35.61)
"O Goddess of great vows, this ascetic merit which was given by you to me shall become yours a thousandfold and inexhaustible through that very act. (BrP 35.62)
Having thus obtained this supreme and inexhaustible boon from her asceticism, the goddess remained there,
joyful and filled with delight, awaiting the svayaṃvara.
Indeed, that man who always recites this account of Śambhu’s conduct as a child shall become purified upon the dissolution of the body.
Gaṇeśa would indeed become equal to Kumāra.
Brahmā said:
On the vast expanse of the Himalayas, crowded with hundreds of celestial chariots...
In the course of time, however, the self-choice marriage (svayaṃvara) of the daughter of the Mountain took place.
Then Himavat, the king of mountains, skilled in meditation,
understood that his daughter had been consecrated by the God of gods.
Although he was aware of this, the Great Mountain, desiring to protect the agreement,
then proclaimed the self-choice marriage of the goddess throughout all the worlds.
If my daughter should choose the Supreme Lord in the presence of the gods, dānavas, siddhas, and all the inhabitants of the world; BrP_36.4 //
"Only that is well-done, praiseworthy, and conducive to my prosperity,"—
having reflected thus, the Lord of Mountains placed Maheśvara in his heart.
Among the gods up to the realm of Brahmā, that best of mountain lords,
having made the region filled with jewels, caused the Goddess to choose her own husband.
Then, as soon as the svayaṃvara of the daughter of the Lord of Mountains had been thus proclaimed,
the gods and all other inhabitants of the world gathered there.
They arrived there, having assumed their respective guises;
he was seated upon a full-blown lotus throne,
surrounded by immeasurable siddhas and yogins.
Requested by that king of mountains,
I then arrived accompanied by the gods,
bearing a thousand eyes, O Lord of the Suras.
Possessing a magnificent form with divine gestures, movements, and garlands,
he mounted Airāvata, the foremost of all lordly elephants, from whose temples flowed streams of trickling ichor.
Having ascended, the king of all the immortals, bearing his thunderbolt and possessing a form equal to and exceeding them in splendor and power, came before the gods.
Illuminating all directions like the sun,
he arrived swiftly with speed, mounted upon a golden celestial chariot adorned with fluttering banners.
And the sole son of Kaśyapa, wearing earrings blazing with the brilliance of jewels, arrived in a celestial chariot resembling the splendor of fire and the sun.
Born from the midst of the sun, he bore the name Bhaga; his body was a stout pillar, his limbs were graced with elegant gestures,
and his majesty was equal to splendor, strength, and sovereign command.
Seizing his staff, Kṛtānta arrived, swiftly mounted upon a terrifying buffalo,
his massive limbs as lofty as a great mountain.
Adorned with beautiful garments studded with gold and other jewels,
Samīraṇa, the sustainer of the entire world,
indeed approached having ascended his celestial chariot.
Scorching all the lords of the gods and asuras,
and established in a splendor exceeding that of splendor itself,
Vahni approached the midst of the lords of the gods.
Blazing forth and wearing magnificent attire,
his slender body illuminated by various jewels,
he set out toward that foremost, divine celestial chariot, the best in the world.
Having ascended, that lord of all masters of wealth,
the king of kings, proceeded swiftly,
gladdening all the lords of the gods and asuras.
Beautiful in form through both his radiance and his attire,
the Moon arrived, ascending a celestial chariot (vimāna) that was brilliant and variegated with great jewels.
With a dark-limbed body, wearing most wonderful attire,
and with fragrant garlands bound upon all his limbs,
he mounted Tārkṣya, who was like unto a mountain.
Then Gadādhara arrived swiftly,
and the two Aśvins, the best of physicians,
also quickly ascended a single celestial chariot.
The two most excellent and heroic gods, charming and clad in brilliantly shining, beautiful attire, arrived;
[he] possessed a thousand serpents and was the color of a flickering fire.
Then, possessing the brilliance of fire and the sun,
that great-souled one, together with other nāgas, ascended a celestial chariot and approached.
Having assumed attire befitting his excellent form, he appeared like the sons of Diti, the great Asuras, whose splendor was equal to that of fire, the sun, Indra, and the wind.
Then the king of the Gandharvas, of beautiful form, adorned with divine armlets and traveling in a celestial chariot, arrived before the assembly of the gods.
Accompanied by hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases,
he arrived there at the command of Śakra;
and other gods also came from the triple heaven at that time.
And the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Kiṃnaras, having each assumed beautiful attire, arrived having mounted the backs of celestial chariots.
There, in the midst of the lords of the gods, Śacīpati shone with a form that was the supreme object of royal splendor,
his joy produced by the power of his command and sovereignty.
He adorned that svayaṃvara as the cause of the three worlds and of the birth of the universe;
and she was the mother of them all, including the gods and the asuras.
And she who is the supreme Prakṛti, sung of in the Purāṇa as the consort of the wise Puruṣa Śambhu,
went to the house of Himavat due to the anger of Dakṣa.
For she was seated upon the back of a celestial chariot belonging to the gods who had arrived for the sake of their mission— a chariot adorned with jewels and gold—
her body fanned by waving yak-tail whisks.
Taking a very fragrant garland of flowers from all seasons,
the goddess set out forcefully.
{Brahmā said:}
While the goddess stood holding the garland in the assembly of the gods,
Śakra and the other deities arrived, and the svayaṃvara commenced.
Out of a desire to test the Goddess, the omnipresent Lord Śambhu suddenly became a five-crested infant and lay down upon her lap.
Then the goddess saw that infant standing there with five tufts of hair;
recognizing him through meditative concentration, she took him up, filled with joy.
Then she, whose resolve was pure, having obtained her desired and virtuous husband,
stood there withdrawn, holding that all-pervading Lord within her heart.
Then, seeing the infant resting in the lap of the goddess, the gods consulted among themselves, "Who is this? and cried out, utterly bewildered.
Raising up his arm, the slayer of Vṛtra brought down the thunderbolt upon him;
that arm of his remained fixed exactly as it had been raised.
Paralyzed by Śambhu, the God of gods, who had assumed the form of a child,
the slayer of Vṛtra was unable to hurl his thunderbolt nor even to move.
Then the powerful god Āditya, named Bhaga and belonging to the lineage of Kaśyapa,
raised his blazing weapon, desiring to strike, yet he was utterly bewildered.
Then the Blessed One likewise paralyzed his arm; the All-pervading Lord likewise paralyzed his strength, his splendor, and his yogic power.
Shaking his head, Viṣṇu gazed intently at Śaṃkara while those gods remained thus filled with indignation.
Deeply agitated, I respectfully took recourse in meditation and beheld the Lord of the Gods of gods seated upon the lap of Umā.
O twice-born ones, having recognized the Supreme Lord, I rose quickly and with reverence prostrated at the feet of Śambhu and praised him.
Through the ancient Sāman chants and the meritorious, secret names [of the Lord],
you are the unborn, the undecaying God, the creator, the all-pervading one, both the supreme and the non-supreme.
You are the Pradhāna, the Puruṣa, that Brahman which is to be meditated upon, the Imperishable,
the Immortal, the Supreme Self, the Lord, and the Great Cause.
Brahmāsṛk is the creator of primordial nature (prakṛti), the maker of all, and beyond primordial nature;
and this Goddess Prakṛti is always the cause of your creation.
Having assumed the form of a wife, you have come as the cause of the world;
salutations to you, O Mahādeva, together with the Goddess.
O Lord of Gods, by your grace and at your command, these creatures beginning with the gods have been created by me; yet they are deluded by your power of yoga-illusion.
"Grant them your favor so that these may become as they were before.
Having thus petitioned the Supreme Lord, O brahmins, I [acted].
When all those gods had been paralyzed, I then said this:
"O foolish deities, you do not recognize this Śaṅkara."
Go quickly for refuge to this very Maheśvara,
the Lord of Gods, the Supreme Self, the Imperishable, together with me alone.
Then all those inhabitants of heaven were likewise paralyzed;
with minds purified by their inner disposition, they bowed mentally to Śarva.
Then Maheśvara, the God of gods, became gracious toward them;
he then swiftly restored the bodies of the deities as they had been before.
Then, while all the gods were thus engaged in their efforts to ward him off,
the Lord of Gods assumed a most wonderful three-eyed form.
Overwhelmed by his splendor, they all closed their eyes;
he then bestowed upon them the supreme vision, endowed with the power to behold his own form.
Then they beheld the Lord of the supreme gods, the all-pervading one;
having seen the Supreme Lord bearing the third eye.
Then all the gods, the lords of the immortals, beginning with Śakra,
and his goddess as well, were delighted in the presence of the inhabitants of the third heaven.
The one of immeasurable luster placed a garland of flowers at his feet;
then all the gods said again to the Lord, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Together with the Goddess, they paid homage with their heads touching the ground;
meanwhile, O Brahmins, I [stood] there along with the deities.
And he spoke to the immensely radiant Himavat, the great mountain:
"You are praiseworthy, worthy of worship, and venerable; you are the greatest of all."

"Since you have this great prosperity through your alliance with Śarva, let a beautiful marriage be performed; why do you remain in such a state? Then Himavat, having bowed to me, replied: ||| BrP_36.56 ||| "O Lord of the Gods, I am indeed fortunate that my daughter has been chosen by you for your son. However, O Lord of the Gods, she is still a mere child; how can she be fit for marriage? She is not yet capable of understanding the duties of a wife, nor does she know how to serve her husband. Therefore, let her first be instructed in the duties of household life. ||| BrP_36.57 ||| Hearing these words of his, I said, "Let it be so," and then departed from that place. Having gone there, I spoke to Śarva: "O Lord of the Gods, Himavat has spoken thus regarding your daughter. He says that she is still a child and not yet capable of performing the duties of a wife. ||| BrP_36.58 ||| Hearing my words, Śarva, the Lord of the Gods, laughed and said, "She shall become capable of performing the duties of a wife. Go now, O Lord of Mountains, and perform the marriage of your daughter according to the prescribed rites. ||| BrP_36.59 ||| Having heard the words of Śarva, I returned to Himavat and told him everything exactly as it had been spoken by Śarva. Then Himavat, together with his wife, went to the presence of Śarva and performed the marriage of his daughter according to the prescribed rites. ||| BrP_36.60 ||| Then, having honored Śarva, the Lord of the Gods, he took leave of him and departed. After some time, the daughter of Himavat became pregnant by Śarva. When she was eight months pregnant, she gave birth to a son endowed with all auspicious marks. ||| BrP_36.61 ||| When the birth ceremony had been performed, the gods, led by Brahmā, arrived at that place. They were accompanied by the hosts of sages, the Gandharvas, the Apsarases, the Yakṣas, the Rākṣasas, the Kinnaras, and the serpents. ||| BrP_36.62 ||| The gods, having seen that infant who shone like the rising sun, were filled with joy and praised him with various hymns. Then the gods, led by Brahmā, spoke to Śarva: "O Lord of the Gods, grant a name for this son of yours. ||| BrP_36.63 ||| Hearing those words of the gods, Śarva, the Lord of the Gods, reflected for a moment and then spoke to them: "Because he was born from the womb of Pārvatī, let him be known by the name Kumāra. ||| BrP_36.64 ||| Having bestowed this name upon him, the gods, led by Brahmā, took their leave of Śarva and departed. Then, after some time, the son of Śarva grew up and became proficient in all weapons. ||| BrP_36.65 ||| He was surrounded by a multitude of attendants and became the leader of the Gaṇas. Then, having obtained his father's permission, he set out to conquer the three worlds. Having conquered the three worlds, he returned to his father's presence. ||| BrP_36.66 ||| Then the gods, led by Brahmā, approached Śarva and spoke these words: "O Lord of the Gods, Kumāra has conquered the three worlds. Grant him a boon. Hearing the words of the gods, Śarva, the Lord of the Gods, spoke to them: "Let him be the commander-in-chief of my Gaṇas. ||| BrP_36.67 ||| Having granted him this boon, Śarva, the Lord of the Gods, took his leave of the gods and departed. Then Kumāra, having received the command of the Gaṇas, set out to conquer the Daityas. Having conquered the Daityas, he returned to his father's presence. ||| BrP_36.68 ||| Then the gods, led by Brahmā, approached Śarva and spoke these words: "O Lord of the Gods, Kumāra has conquered the Daityas. Grant him another boon. Hearing the words of the gods, Śarva, the Lord of the Gods, spoke to them: "Let him be
Himavat said:
"O Lord, you alone are the cause for my every success;
your grace has suddenly arisen within me, and you indeed are the reason as well."
O Grandfather, ordain whatever marriage is appropriate for him.
{Brahmā said:} O twice-born ones, having heard these words of the King of Mountains, I then spoke to the Lord: "O God, let the marriage be performed. (BrP 36.58)
"O Brahmins, the god Śaṅkara, the protector of the world, said to me, 'As you wish. And at that very moment, a city was created by us there."
For the sake of Maheśa’s wedding, there were various jewels for adornment:
diverse gems and precious stones, as well as gold and pearls.
Approaching in embodied form, they adorned that supreme city;
its ground was variegated with emeralds and beautified by pillars of gold.
And at that gate in the lovely city, a wall of shining crystal was constructed for the sake of the wedding, adorned with hanging strings of pearls.
There, the two great jewels, the Moon and the Sun, shone together, heating [the world] for the sake of Maheśvara, the high-souled God of gods.
Taking up a delightful fragrance from the cattle, the wind blew with a pleasant touch, manifesting devotion to Bhava.
There are the four oceans, Śakra and the other foremost gods,
the celestial rivers and great rivers, as well as the perfected ones and the sages.
All the Gandharvas and Apsarases, the Nāgas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas;
those dwelling in the water, those moving in the sky, and others—the Kinnaras and the celestial Cāraṇas.
Tumburu, Nārada, Hāhā, and Hūhū— these singers of the Sāman hymns—
then came to that city, bringing delightful musical instruments.
But the sages there, whose wealth was their asceticism, with joyful minds recited the sacred wedding mantras sung in the Vedas.
All the mothers of the world and all the daughters of the gods,
entirely filled with joy, sing at the wedding of the Supreme Lord.
There, the six seasons, bringing various fragrances and pleasures,
stood present in embodied form as the wedding procession of Śaṅkara.
With peacocks resembling dark blue clouds, delighted by the sound of the mantras, crying out their "kekā" calls and dancing on all sides; BrP 36.71.
She was made to smile by the clearly flickering streaks of tawny lightning,
and she was graced by cranes as white as a cluster of water-lilies.
With fresh *śilīndhra* mushrooms and *kandalī* sprouts, and with the auspicious foliage emerging from creepers and trees,
it was made beautiful by those awakened by the affectionate pouring of auspicious rain-showers.
Resounding with large frogs and groups of toads,
[it was filled with] even high-minded women who, though their hearts were puffed up with pride toward their lovers, [were nonetheless moved].
In an instant, by means of the enchanting cries of peacocks— which cause the breaking of pride—
and likewise by his own complexion, radiant and beautiful form, [he captivated her].
She was resplendent on all sides with the bow of Indra, which resembled the curved line of the moon and hovered near the mass of clouds.
With winds arising from various flowers and water, fragrant and made very cool by contact with dense clouds, she was causing [the trees] to tremble with those enchanting breezes.
The beautiful rows of curls on the celestial women’s hair were like the orb of the moon obscured by thundering clouds; the lovely *dūrvā* grass was as if sprinkled with fresh water.
Gazed upon with longing by the wives of travelers who sighed like smoke,
she was rich with the sound of swans for her anklets and possessed uplifted breasts like clouds.
Wearing a necklace of shimmering lightning-streaks, with eyes like clearly blooming lotuses.
The swans were terrified by the deep rumbling of the dark clouds;
the tips of the lotuses were bent down by the falling torrents of pure water;
and the beauty of their entire bodies was fashioned from the pollen of fragrant flowers.
At the wedding of the Mountain’s Daughter, the rainy season appeared,
divested of its mantle of clouds, with breasts emerging from the calyxes of lotuses;
it resounded with the anklets of swans and filled the quarters of the sky with all manner of crops.
Her broad hips were like a wide riverbank, her girdle was the warbling of cranes,
and she was enchanting with eyes as dark as blooming blue lotuses.
Her lips were like ripe bimba fruits, her teeth smiled like kunda flowers,
and she was graced by a line of body hair as dark as a fresh, young vine.
With a multitude of necklaces like moonbeams resting upon her throat and chest,
she gladdened the hearts of all the inhabitants of heaven.
She speaks with a sweet voice, sung forth by the hosts of *samādāli* bees;
she is adorned with beautiful earrings that resemble clusters of swaying white water-lilies.
She bears fingers of sprouts arising from the branches of the red Aśoka tree,
and she is beautifully adorned with garments made from a collection of its flowers.
Her feet were like the tips of red lotuses, her rows of nails like jasmine flowers,
her beautiful thighs like the trunks of plantain trees, and her face was like the moon.
Endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament,
she was as delightful as a beloved woman, touching him with affection and full of passion.
Her body was like a garment freed from the shroud of dark clouds; her face was like the orb of the full moon;
her eyes were like blue lotuses; her breasts were like lotuses blossomed by the rays of the sun;
and she delighted the minds with a breeze fragrant with the pollen of various flowers.
There, at the wedding of the Goddess, was the autumn season with the sound of swans and anklets;
and the two seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira, exceedingly radiant, arrived, constantly flooding the quarters with extremely cool waters.
By those two seasons, that Himavat, the best of mountains,
which quickly rained down a powder of frost, shone as if it were made of silver.
By that dense shower of frost,
the Himalaya then shone like the unfathomable ocean Kṣīroda.
That great mountain, having reached the turn for drinking the seasonal nectar,
suddenly became as if its purpose were fulfilled through the hospitable treatment of the virtuous, like a wicked man.
With its peaks covered by layers of frost,
the mountain shone like a lord of the earth with magnificent, white parasols.
The breezes repeatedly stirred the hearts of the gods and the celestial nymphs,
and likewise there were lotus ponds filled with clear water.
Endowed with blossoms of lotuses and water-lilies, the spring season arrived for the marriage of the preceptor’s daughter. (BrP 36.94d–95)
Just as women become more beautiful when the tips of their breasts have slightly begun to emerge,
so too were the lakes of water neither too hot nor too cold.
Made tawny by the pollen of filaments,
resounded by pairs of cakravāka birds,
the preeminent celestial elephants went forth, filled with joy.
The *priyaṅgu* trees and the mango trees, and the mango trees and the *priyaṅgu* trees as well,
shone as if threatening one another with their flower-clusters.
Upon the white, snow-capped peaks, clusters of flowers shone like elders who had gathered together for a specific purpose.
There, flowering *aśoka* creepers clinging to the *śāla* trees shone like amorous women with their arms thrown around the necks of their lovers.
In that season, there were white kadamba and nīpa trees, palms, tamāla, sarala, and kapittha trees,
as well as aśoka, sarja, arjuna, and kovidāra trees.
Puṃnāgas, nāgeśvaras, and karṇikāras; lavaṅgas, tālas, agarus, and saptaparṇas; nyagrodhas, śobhāñjanas, and nārikelas.
Likewise, other trees, laden with fruits and flowers,
appeared most enchanting to the eye;
and the reservoirs of water possessed waters of gold.
Frequented by *cakrāṅga*, *kāraṇḍava*, and *haṃsa* birds,
and joined by *koyaṣṭi*, *dātyūha*, and *balākā* birds,
they were visible, filled with lotuses, water-lilies, and fish.
And birds with variously adorned limbs and most variegated wings were seen upon the trees,
threatening those engaged in their sports.
On that mountain, during the wedding of the Mountain’s Daughter, they made sounds with their limbs stirred by intoxication,
and winds blew with pleasantly cool limbs.
Gently shaking even white flowers from the trees born on Mount Malaya,
all the auspicious seasons likewise [appeared].
They shone there with their limbs intertwined with one another;
those whose auspicious marks have been proclaimed were of most pleasing form.
With heaps of stone-flowers sung forth by the assembly of *samādāli* bees,
the *mālatī* vines shone as they seemed to nourish one another.
The waters were made blue by blue lotuses, white by white lotus stalks,
and intensely red by red ones.
In some places, there were golden lotuses with petals frequented by swarms of intoxicated bees amidst the vast waters;

O Mahādeva, because of your anger they did not find peace;
and this man who was born from your sweat, O bull among the gods.
"O Knower of Dharma, this one named Jvara will spread throughout the worlds;
for it is impossible for his unified splendor to be contained, O Lord."
"The entire earth is capable; let this [universe] be created in many ways.
Thus was that Lord addressed by me, even as the portions were being assigned.
The Blessed One, the god of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow, said to me, "So be it," and that wielder of the Pināka himself attained supreme delight.
Dakṣa also mentally sought refuge with the god Bhava,
diligently restraining his prāṇa and apāna breaths at the location of the eyes.
Restraining his gaze in every direction, the many-eyed conqueror of enemies smiled and spoke these words: "Tell me, what shall I do for you?"
When this great narrative had been proclaimed by the Pitṛs together with the gods,
Dakṣa, the lord of progeny, having joined his palms in reverence, spoke to the god;
he was terrified, his mind filled with apprehension, and his face and eyes were bathed in tears.
Dakṣa said:
"If the Blessed One is pleased, if I am dear to you,
if I am worthy of your favor, and if a boon is to be granted to me..."

Whatever food was eaten, whatever drink was drunk, whatever was terrified away, and whatever was destroyed; whatever sacrificial materials were ground to powder or cast aside—such was the state of the preparations for the sacrifice.
"O Maheśvara, by your grace, may that which has been accumulated over a long time and with great effort not become false for me."
Brahmā said:
"So be it," said the Blessed One, Hara, the destroyer of Bhaga's eyes;
the Lord of Creatures [then addressed] Mahādeva, the three-eyed one, the overseer of dharma.
Having gone to the earth on his knees and obtained a boon from Bhava,
Dakṣa praised the bull-bannered god with eight thousand names.
{Brahmā said:} O best of the twice-born, having thus witnessed the power of Śambhu at that time, Dakṣa,
with palms joined in reverence and bowing down, began to offer praise. (BrP 40.1)
Dakṣa said:
Homage to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; homage to you, O slayer of Andhaka!
You are the Indra of the gods, the most powerful, worshipped by both gods and dānavas.
O thousand-eyed one, O Virūpākṣa, O three-eyed one, beloved of the lord of Yakṣas!
You have hands and feet everywhere; you have eyes, heads, and faces on every side.
Possessing ears everywhere in the world, you stand encompassing all;
you have spike-like ears, great ears, pot-shaped ears, and your abode is the ocean.
O Gajendrakarṇa, O Gokarṇa, O Śatakarṇa, homage be to you!
You are the hundred-bellied, the hundred-whirled, the hundred-tongued, and the eternal.
The singers of the Gāyatrī hymns sing of you; the reciters of praises worship you as the Sun;
you are the protector of both gods and demons, and you are Brahmā and Śatakratu.
You are the embodied Great Form, the ocean, the treasury of waters;
for all the deities dwell within you, like cattle in a cow-pen.
Within your body, I behold Soma, Agni,
Varuṇa, Āditya, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā together with Bṛhaspati.
Action, the instrument, and the effect, as well as the agent and the cause;
likewise, the non-existent, the existent, and the both-existent-and-non-existent, as well as origination and dissolution.
Homage to Bhava, to Śarva, to Rudra, and to the Giver of Boons;
homage indeed be to the Lord of Creatures and to the slayer of Andhaka!
Salutations indeed to Trijaṭa, to the three-headed one, to the bearer of the excellent trident,
to the three-eyed one, to Tryambaka, and to the destroyer of Tripura.
Salutations to the Fierce One, to the Shaven-headed One, and to the one who bears universal ferocity;
salutations indeed to the staff-bearer, to the spike-eared one, and to the one whose staff is a staff.
Homage to the one with half-staff-like hair, to the emaciated and the deformed;
homage indeed to the deep red, to the smoke-colored, and to the blue-necked one.
Homage be to the Peerless One, to the Deformed One, and to Śiva;
to the Sun, to the Lord of the Sun, who possesses the sun as his banner and flag!
Homage to the destroyer of obstacles, and indeed homage to him whose shoulders are like those of a bull;
homage to Hiraṇyagarbha and to him who possesses golden armor.
Salutation to the one with a crest made of gold, to the Lord of Gold;
to the slayer of enemies, to the fierce one, and to the one who lies upon a bed of leaves.
Salutations to the one who has been praised, to praise itself, and indeed salutations to the one being praised; salutations to the All, to the consumer of all, and to the inner self of all beings.

Homage to the sacrificial fire, to the mantra, and to him who possesses the white banner and pennant; homage to the one who is not to be bowed to, to the one who is to be bowed to, and homage to Kilakila.
Salutations to you while lying down, to you who have already lain down, and to you who have arisen; to you standing, to you running, to you hunchbacked, and to you crooked.
Homage to the one whose nature is dancing, who plays wind instruments from the mouth,
who removes affliction, who is greedy, and who performs singing and instrumental music.
Homage to the eldest, to the most excellent, and to the subduer of strength;
homage ever to the fierce one, and homage to the ten-armed one.
Homage to him who holds a skull in his hand, who is fond of white ashes,
who is terrifying, who is formidable, and who observes fearsome vows.
To him with various distorted faces, with a sword for a tongue and fierce fangs;
to him whose half-month is his month, and who is fond of the gourd-lute.

Salutation to the one whose form is both non-terrible and terrible, and who is more terrible than the terrible; salutation to Śiva, the peaceful, and salutation to him who is most profoundly peaceful.
Homage to the Buddha, the pure one, who delights in sharing;
homage to Pavana, to Pataṅga, and to the supreme Sāṃkhya.
Homage to Caṇḍaikaghaṇṭa, to Ghaṇṭājalpa, to Ghaṇṭin,
to Sahasraśataghaṇṭa, and to him who is fond of garlands of bells.
Salutations to you, the eternal one who wields the staff of life, and to the Red One;
salutations to Rudra, who utters the sounds *hūṃ* and *hūṃ*, and who is beloved by her whose form is *bhaga*.
Homage always to the one who has no further shore, and to him who is fond of mountains and trees;
homage to the Lord of Sacrifice, to the Being, and to the one who is well-pressed.
Salutation to the carrier of sacrifice, to the self-controlled, to the one who undergoes austerity, and to the blessed one;
salutation to the shore, to that which belongs to the shore, and to the lord of the rivers.
Salutations to the giver of food, to the Lord of food, and to the eater of food;
salutations to the one with a thousand heads and to the one with a thousand feet.
Salutation to the one who has raised a thousand tridents, and to the thousand-eyed one;
salutation to the one with the color of the rising sun, and to the one who assumes the form of a child.
Homage to the one in the form of the rising sun, and to the one who plays as a child;
homage to the pure Buddha, the agitator, and the destroyer.
Salutations indeed to the one whose hair is marked by waves and to the one with disheveled hair;
salutations to the one devoted to the six duties and to the one restrained by the three duties.

Salutations to the one who causes the distinct duties of the castes and stages of life to proceed according to rule; salutations to the most excellent and the eldest, and salutations to the source of all sound.
To the one with white and tawny eyes, and to the one with black and red eyes;
to the one who is dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation; to Kratha and to Krathana.
Salutation to the follower of Sāṃkhya, the foremost of the Sāṃkhyas, the Lord of Yoga;
salutation to him who is on the carriage-road, on the main highway, and at the crossroads and paths.
Obedience be to you, O Harikeśa, who are clothed in a black antelope skin as an upper garment, who wear a snake as a sacred thread,
and who are the sovereign lord of the host of Rudras!
O Tryambaka, O Lord of Ambikā, O You who are both manifest and unmanifest, salutations be unto You!
O Destroyer of Time, of Desire, and of the Unwilling, O Slayer of the wicked and the arrogant!
O you who are censured by all, the destroyer of all, Sadyojāta, homage be to you!
O Unmādana, Śatāvarta, whose hair is moistened by the waters of the Gaṅgā!
Homage be to you, who possess the whirlpool of the joined crescent moon and the whirlpool of clouds;
homage to the giver of food, and homage to the source of the giver of food.
O Fire of Dissolution, you alone are the consumer and the protector of food;
you are indeed the womb-born, the egg-born, the sweat-born, and the soil-born.
O Lord of the gods of gods, you alone are the fourfold collection of beings;
you are the creator of all that is moving and unmoving, and you alone are its destroyer.
You alone are Brahmā, O Lord of the Universe; they call you Brahmā within the waters.
You are the supreme source of all, the moon of nectar, and the treasury of lights.
The exponents of the Veda call you the Ṛg, Sāman, and the syllable Oṃ;
they repeatedly utter "Hāyi hāyi hare hāyi huvāhāva."
The best of the gods, the chanters of the Sāman, and those who discourse on Brahman, sing of you as consisting of the Yajus,
the Ṛk, and likewise the Sāman and the Atharvan in their thousands.
You are studied by those who know Brahman through the collections of Kalpa and Upaniṣads;
likewise by the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and all those belonging to the various castes and stages of life.
You alone are the various stages of life (āśramas), as well as lightning and thunder;
you are the year, the seasons, the months, and even the half-months.
You are the divisions of time—kalās, kāṣṭhās, and nimeṣas—as well as the lunar mansions and the ages;
you are indeed the hump of bulls and the peaks of mountains.
The lion is the lord of wild beasts, Takṣaka of the serpents with infinite coils,
the Ocean of Milk of the seas, and likewise the syllable Om (praṇava) of mantras.
Among weapons, you are the vajra; among vows, you are truth itself.
You alone are desire and hatred, passion and delusion, tranquility and forgiveness.
You are resolve, fortitude, greed, desire, anger, victory, and defeat;
you are the wielder of the mace, the wielder of the arrow, the wielder of the bow, as well as the wielder of the khaṭvāṅga staff and the mallet.
"You are considered by us to be the cutter, the breaker, the striker, the leader, and the thinker;
you are Dharma endowed with the ten characteristics, as well as Artha and Kāma."
The moon, the ocean, rivers, ponds, and lakes;
creepers, climbing plants, grasses, herbs, domestic animals, wild beasts, and birds.
The commencement of substances, actions, and qualities; the bestower of time, flowers, and fruits;
the beginning, the end, and the middle; and indeed the Gāyatrī and the syllable Oṃ—[all these are the Supreme].
Harita, Lohita, Kṛṣṇa, Nīla, Pīta, as well as Kṣaṇa,
Kadru, Kapila, Babhru, Kapota, and likewise Macchaka.
He is renowned as Suvarṇaretas, and he is also considered Suvarṇa;
likewise, he is named Suvarṇanāman and is indeed Suvarṇapriya.
You are Indra and Yama, Varuṇa, Dhanada, and Anala;
you are Utphulla, Citrabhānu, Svarbhānu, and Bhānu as well.

O Brahman, the Hotṛ priest, the oblation, the act of offering, and likewise the one who has offered, as well as the Trisauparṇa and the Śatarudriya among the Yajus formulas, are all under his control.
You are the purifier of purifiers and the most auspicious of auspicious things;
you are the vital breath, you are passion (rajas), and likewise you are darkness (tamas) joined with goodness (sattva).
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
as well as the opening and closing of the eyes, hunger, thirst, and yawning.
Lohitāṅga, Daṃṣṭrin, Mahāvaktro, Mahodara,
Śuciroma, Haricchmaśru, Ūrdhvakeśa, and Calācala.
He whose limbs consist of song, instrumental music, and dance; who is fond of singing and playing instruments;
the fish, the net, the water, the unconquerable, the aquatic serpent, and the dweller in a hut.
He is the untimely hour and the auspicious time, the bad season and the destroyer of time;
he is death itself, the inexhaustible, and the end; he is the mass of patience, illusion, and creative power.
Saṃvarta, Vartaka, Saṃvartaka, Balāhaka,
Ghaṇṭākī, Ghaṇṭakī, Ghaṇṭī, Cūḍāla, and Lavaṇodadhi.
He is Brahmā, he whose mouth is the fire of time (Kālāgni), the bearer of the staff (Daṇḍin), the shaven-headed one (Muṇḍa), the bearer of the triple-staff (Tridaṇḍadhṛk);
he is the four ages (Caturyuga), the four Vedas (Caturveda), the four officiating priests (Caturhotra), and the crossroads (Catuṣpatha).
He is the leader of the four stages of life and the creator of the four social orders;
he is both the perishable and the imperishable, the beloved, the rogue, the one counted among the hosts, and the lord of the hosts.
Wearing red garlands and garments, the Lord of the Mountain, beloved of the Daughter of the Mountain,
is the Master of Artisans, the foremost of craftsmen, and the initiator of all artisans.
The fierce destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, the crusher of Pūṣan’s teeth,
you who are Svāhā, Svadhā, Vaṣaṭkāra, and the act of salutation— homage be to you!
He is the one of secret vows, the hidden one, and the one practiced in secret vows;
he is the one who crosses over, the one who causes others to cross, and the savior of all beings.
He is the Ordainer, the Disposer, the Uniter, the Depositor, the Sustainer, and the Supporter;
he is austerity, the Veda, truth, celibacy, and likewise uprightness.
He is the self of all beings, the creator of beings, the being himself, and the source of the past, the future, and the present;
he is indeed the earth, the atmosphere, and the heavens, the manifested fire, the Great Lord.
O Brahmāvarta, O Surāvarta, O Kāmāvarta, homage be to you!
You are the destroyer of the form of desire and the lover of garlands of Karṇikāra flowers.
The leader of cows, the one who wanders with the cattle, whose vehicle is the bull-lord;
the protector of the three worlds, Govinda, the guardian, and Gogarga.
Facing the full moon, he is fair-faced, yet difficult to face;
he is faceless, four-faced, and many-faced, always facing forward in battles.
Hiraṇyagarbha, Śakuni, Dhanada, Arthapati, Virāṭ, Adharmahā, Mahādakṣa, Daṇḍadhāra, and Raṇapriya.
He stands firm, stable, and motionless, perfectly immovable;
he is difficult to restrain, difficult to withstand, difficult to endure, and difficult to overcome.
Durdhara, Durvaśa, Nitya, Durdarpa, Vijaya, Jaya,
Śaśa, Śaśāṅkanayana, Śītoṣṇa, Kṣut, Tṛṣā, and Jarā.

He is both mental afflictions and physical diseases, yet he is the destroyer of disease and the lord of disease; he is the hunter of the sacrifice-deer who is capable of being endured, the source of all maladies, and yet the one who is without a source.
Śikhaṇḍin, Puṇḍarīka, Puṇḍarīkāvalokana,
Daṇḍadhṛk, Cakradaṇḍa, and Raudrabhāgavināśana.

The drinker of poison and the drinker of nectar, the drinker of wine and the drinker of milk and soma, the drinker of honey and the drinker of water, and the drinker of all things, who possesses both strength and weakness.
He whose body is marked by the bull, the Bull itself, and likewise the one with the eyes of a bull;
he who is renowned as the Bull and is the sanctifier of the worlds.
The moon and sun are your two eyes, and the Grandfather (Brahmā) is your heart;
likewise, your body is the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, perfected through righteous deeds.
"Neither Brahmā, nor Govinda, nor even the ancient seers are able to know your majesty as it truly is, O Śiva."
May those subtle forms of Śiva come into my sight;
through them, protect me from all sides, as a father protects his own biological son.
Protect me, protect me; I am worthy of your protection, O sinless one! Homage be to you!
The Blessed One is compassionate toward his devotees, and I am forever devoted to you.
May he who stands alone at the edge of the ocean, having encompassed many thousands of men difficult to behold, be my protector forever.

Salutation to that Self of Yoga, whom those who are sleepless, who have conquered their breath, who are established in purity, and who perceive with equanimity, behold as a light while practicing yoga.
I take refuge in Him who lies within the waters, having consumed all beings when the end of the age has arrived.
Having entered the mouth of Rāhu, he who drinks the moon at night becomes Svarbhānu and likewise Somāgni, and swallows the sun.
May those persons, the size of a thumb, who reside within the bodies of all embodied beings,
protect me always and may they constantly nourish me.
For those by whom the waters were produced in the womb and those which have reached their allotted portions, for them there is *svāhā* and *svadhā*; they obtain these and they relish them.
Salutations eternally to those by whom embodied beings grow, by whom they are made to weep, by whom they are gladdened, and by whom they are drawn away.
Those who [reside] in the ocean, in river-fords, on mountains, in caves,
at the roots of trees, in cow-pens, and in the depths of dense forests;
At crossroads, on main roads, in squares, and in assembly halls;
in stables for elephants, horses, and chariots, and in ruined gardens and dwellings.
Those who are among the five elements, in the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions,
those situated between Indra and Arka, and those within the rays of the moon and the sun;
To those who have gone to the subterranean realm (rasātala) and to those who have gone beyond that—to them, salutations; to them, salutations; to them, salutations from every side!
"You are everything, the all-pervading God, Bhava, the lord of all beings, and the inner self within all beings; therefore, you were not invited."
O God, you alone are worshipped with sacrifices accompanied by various sacrificial fees;
you alone are the creator of everything, and for that reason, you were not invited.
Or perhaps you have been deluded by your own subtle illusion (māyā), O Lord;
for that reason, indeed, I did not invite you.
Be gracious to me, O Lord of Gods; you alone are my refuge. You are my goal and you are my foundation; it is my conviction that there is no other.
{Brahmā said:} Having thus praised Mahādeva, that high-minded one fell silent;
the Blessed One, being well-pleased, spoke again to Dakṣa.
The Blessed One said: "I am well pleased with you, O Dakṣa of noble vows, by this hymn.
But what is the use of much speaking? You shall come into my presence."
Brahmā said: Thus spoke Bhava, the sovereign of the three worlds,
the omniscient one, having uttered words that provided consolation and were consistent with his speech.
Śrī Śiva said:
O Dakṣa, you should not feel grief regarding the destruction of the sacrifice;
O sinless one, I am the destroyer of your sacrifice—this was seen by you long ago.
Furthermore, O observer of noble vows, receive this boon from me;
becoming gracious and cheerful of countenance, listen to me with a one-pointed mind.
"O Prajāpati, by my grace, you shall indeed partake in the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices."
"Understand the Vedas along with their six auxiliary limbs, as well as Sāṃkhya and Yoga in their entirety;
and having performed extensive austerity that is difficult even for gods and dānavas to practice."
It was endowed with twelve ages, profound, and censured by those lacking wisdom;
it was never anywhere subdued by the duties (dharma) created for the social classes and stages of life.
I have attained and resolved upon the Pāśupata vow, which effects liberation from the bonds of the individual soul for all stages of life.
O skillful one, this auspicious [rite] has been performed, which liberates from all evil;
may the abundant fruit that comes from its correct practice belong to you,
O highly fortunate one, and let the fever of your mind be abandoned.
{Brahmā said:} Having spoken thus, the Lord of Gods, together with his wife and his followers,
vanished from the sight of Dakṣa of immeasurable splendor.
And having thus obtained his share as it was described by Umā,
Bhava, the knower of all dharmas, then divided the fever into many parts.
O twice-born ones, listen now to that which serves for the pacification of all beings:
the heat from the crests of serpents and the bitumen of mountains.
One should know that *nīlikā* is among the waters, as is the sloughing of snakes;
*khoraka* is among the cattle, and *ūkhara* is upon the surface of the earth.
Furthermore, O knowers of dharma, the obstruction of the vision of even dogs,
the appearance of a wound on horses, and the bursting of the crest-feathers of peacocks [are ill omens].
The redness of the eyes of cuckoos is said to be hatred toward great-souled ones, and likewise the division among people; so we have heard from all.
For all parrots as well, O brahmins, hiccup is said to be fever;
furthermore, among tigers, exhaustion is here called fever.
Among human beings, this one is celebrated by the name Jvara;
he is established at birth, at death, and likewise in the interval between them.
This is the splendor of Maheśvara, known as Jvara, most terrible;
he is the Lord who is to be saluted and honored by all living beings.
That man who, with a mind free from dejection and well-composed, should constantly recite this account of the origin of fever,
shall be freed from disease and filled with joy.
Whoever recites or hears this hymn proclaimed by Dakṣa shall obtain all desires according to their wish;
they shall encounter no inauspiciousness whatsoever and shall attain a long life.
Just as the Blessed Lord Bhava is the most excellent among all the gods,
so too is this hymn composed by Dakṣa the most excellent among all hymns.
Those who desire fame, heaven, sovereignty over the gods, wealth, and victory,
as well as those who seek knowledge, should diligently praise [him] by resorting to devotion.
A man who is diseased, suffering, miserable, or seized by fears and the like,
or one appointed to royal service, is liberated from great danger.
And with this very body, having obtained happiness in this world from Maheśvara, he is born as a leader of the Gaṇas.
Neither yakṣas nor piśācas, neither nāgas nor vināyakas,
shall create obstacles in the home where Bhava is praised.
Or if a woman, imbued with devotion and purified by her being, should listen to this with faith,
she indeed becomes worthy of honor on both the side of her paternal kin and the side of her husband.
Whoever should hear all of this, or should recite it repeatedly,
all of his undertakings shall reach fulfillment without obstacle.
Whatever has been thought by the mind and whatever has been uttered by speech—
all that comes to pass for one through the recitation of this hymn.
Then, having performed the distribution of the sacrificial offering (bali) for the god along with Guha, for the goddess, and for Nandīśvara, he did so with self-restraint and religious observance.
Then, having applied himself, a person should quickly grasp the names in their proper order;
he obtains his desired objects, as well as his wishes and enjoyments.
And when dead, he attains heaven, surrounded by thousands of women,
whether he was devoted to all his desires or burdened with all manner of sins.
By reciting this hymn composed by Dakṣa, one is liberated from all sins;
and upon death, being honored by gods and demons alike, one attains union with the Gaṇas.
He shall shine in a celestial chariot drawn by a bull as appointed,
