and he shall become an attendant of Rudra, remaining there until the dissolution of all beings.
Thus spoke the Lord Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara:
"No one truly understands this, and this should not be heard by anyone."
Having heard this supreme secret, even those who are of sinful birth—
whether Vaiśyas, women, or Śūdras— shall attain the world of Rudra.
And the twice-born who always causes it to be heard by Brahmins on every festival day attains the world of Rudra; of this there is no doubt.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
O twice-born ones, having thus heard from Vyāsa as he spoke this meritorious narrative, which destroys sin and arose from the wrath of Rudra, the best of sages were filled with wonder.
[He told] likewise of Pārvatī’s wrath and Śambhu’s unbearable anger,
the birth of Vīrabhadra, and the manifestation of Bhadrakālī.
And the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, as well as the wonderful power of Śambhu,
and again the grace of the great-souled god toward Dakṣa.
They were joyful, delighted, and filled with wonder again and again at the sacrificial portion of Rudra and the fruit of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
And so the twice-born asked Vyāsa for the remainder of the story;
being thus questioned, Vyāsa spoke to them once more concerning the sacred field of Ekāmraka.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard this meritorious narrative spoken by Brahmā, those bulls among sages then praised it, joyful and with the hair on their bodies standing on end.
The sages said:
"O best of gods, you have proclaimed the majesty of Lord Śambhu,
as well as the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice."
O Brahmin, you should now describe Ekāmraka, the most excellent of sacred fields; for we desire to hear it, as our curiosity is great.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of theirs, the four-faced Lord of the World spoke regarding that sacred field of Śambhu on earth, which wipes away evil deeds.
Brahmā said:
Listen, O tigers among sages; I shall describe in brief that meritorious field which removes all sins and is extremely difficult to attain.
Endowed with ten million lingas, as auspicious as Vārāṇasī,
it is renowned as Ekāmra and is possessed of eight sacred fords (tīrthas).
O best of the twice-born, in a former kalpa there was a single mango tree there;
because of that very name, that sacred field became known as Ekāmra.
It was crowded with happy and well-nourished people, filled with men and women,
abounding in throngs of learned men, and endowed with wealth, grain, and other riches.
It was crowded with house-towers, adorned with triple-storied gateways,
filled with various merchants, and embellished with diverse jewels.
It was equipped with city walls and watchtowers, adorned by chariot-warriors,
and graced by white palaces resembling royal swans.
It was provided with gateways along the roads, beautified by white walls,
protected by multitudes of weapons, and adorned with moats.
It was adorned with banners fluttering in the wind, colored white, red, yellow, black, and dark blue.
It was perpetually joyful with constant festivals, resounding with the sounds of various musical instruments—
lutes, flutes, drums, and cymbals— and was beautifully adorned.
It was adorned everywhere with divine temples for the deities, embellished with walls and gardens, and arranged with various kinds of offerings.
There, slender-waisted women were seen, joyful,
their necks adorned with necklaces and their eyes as broad as lotus petals.
They had full and elevated breasts, were youthful, and possessed faces resembling the full moon;
their locks of hair were steady, their cheeks were beautiful, and they resounded with the tinkling of waist-bands and anklets.
They possessed beautiful hair and lovely hips, with eyes extending as far as their ears;
they were endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every kind of ornament.
Wearing divine garments, some were radiant and others resembled gold;
they moved with the gait of swans and elephants, their bodies bent by the weight of their breasts.
Their limbs were anointed with divine perfumes, they were adorned with earrings,
languid with passion, possessed of beautiful hips, and always had smiling faces.
With teeth slightly visible, bimba-red lips, and sweet voices, their mouths were stained with betel; these clever women were lovely to behold.
They were all fortunate, sweet-spoken, and ever proud of their youth;
they wore divine garments and were always adorned with virtuous conduct.
Those women, resembling apsarases with their beautiful faces, always sport there in their respective homes, rejoicing by day and by night.
There, men are seen who are proud of their beauty and youth,
endowed with all auspicious marks, and wearing highly polished jeweled earrings.
O best of sages, Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras,
all very righteous and devoted to their own duties, dwell there.
And other beautiful-eyed courtesans also reside there,
equal to Ghṛtācī and Menakā, as well as Samatilottamā.
Some were like Urvaśī, others resembled Vipracitti;
some had the appearance of Viśvācī and Sahajanyā, and others were like Pramlocā.
They were all sweet-spoken, all possessed smiling faces;
they were all endowed with skill in the arts and all possessed of virtuous qualities.
O best of sages, courtesans skilled in dance and song, proud of all feminine charms, dwell there.
They were skilled in gazing and conversation, beautiful and pleasing to behold;
they were not lacking in beauty, nor were they ill-behaved or intent on harming others.
By the falling of whose sidelong glances men fall into delusion—
among them there are none who are poor, none who are foolish, and none who are hostile toward others.
They were neither diseased, nor filthy, nor miserly, nor deceitful;
they were neither lacking in beauty, nor of evil conduct, nor doers of harm to others.
Young men dwell there in that field renowned throughout the world,
where movement is easy everywhere and which brings happiness to all beings.
It was crowded with various people and endowed with all kinds of crops,
[and adorned] with *karṇikāra*, jackfruit, *campaka*, and *nāgakesara* trees.
With *pāṭala*, *aśoka*, and *bakula* trees, with many *kapittha* and *dhava* trees,
and with *cūta*, *nimba*, *kadamba*, as well as other species of flowering plants.
It was resplendent with *nīpaka*, *dhava*, and *khadira* trees, as well as creepers,
and with *śāla*, *tāla*, *tamāla*, coconut, and auspicious *añjana* trees.
With *arjuna* trees, *samaparṇa*, *kovidāra*, and *pippala*;
with *lakuca*, *sarala*, *lodhra*, *hintāla*, and *devadāru* trees; ||| BrP_41.41 |||
With *palāśa*, *mucukunda*, and *pārijāta* trees along with *kubjaka* shrubs,
as well as groves of plantain trees and the fruits of *jambū* and *pūga* trees.
With *ketakī* and *karavīra* flowers, with *atimukta* and *kiṃśuka*,
with *mandāra* and *kunda* blossoms, and likewise with other varieties of flowers.
It was graced by gardens comparable to the Nandana grove, frequented by the warbling of various birds,
with trees bent low under the weight of fruit and abounding in clusters of flowers from every season.
With cakoras, śatapatras, bhṛṅgarājas, and cuckoos;
with sparrows, peacocks, priyaputras, and likewise parrots.
With jīvañjīvaka birds, hārītas, and cātakas surrounded by the forest, and with various other flocks of birds warbling with sweet voices; BrP_41.46 //
With long ponds, lakes, lotus-pools,
and reservoirs, as well as various other bodies of water adorned with clusters of lotuses.
With white water-lilies, lotuses, and beautiful blue lotuses,
as well as with kādamba birds, ruddy geese, and water-fowls.
With kāraṇḍavas, water-fowls, swans, and other aquatic birds,
as well as with various kinds of trees and diverse, excellent flowers.
Adorned on all sides by various meritorious reservoirs of water,
the Lord himself dwells there— the one clad in animal skins, whose banner bears the bull.
Śiva, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation for the welfare of the entire world,
[is present] along with all the sacred fords (tīrthas), rivers, and lakes that exist upon the earth.
Having previously collected drops of water individually from lotus ponds, lakes, large tanks, wells, and oceans; BrP_41.52.
O best of the twice-born, for the sake of the welfare of the entire world, Rudra, together with all the gods,
[established] the sacred ford named Bindusaras in that field.
O best of the twice-born, he performed [this] together with the sages on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa; therefore, it is remembered as Bindusaras.
He who, having conquered his senses and being endowed with faith, performs a pilgrimage there at the equinox after bathing according to the prescribed rites in Bindusaras;

Having gratified the gods, the sages, humans, and the ancestors with water mixed with sesame seeds according to the prescribed rite, he who knows the rules for names and lineages should remain restrained in speech.

Having bathed there according to the prescribed rite during a lunar or solar eclipse, at the equinoxes, at the sun's passage into a new sign, or likewise at the solstices, he shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
On the beginnings of the Yugas, on the day of the sixty-fourth [day], and likewise on other auspicious lunar days,
those who bestow gifts such as wealth and other things there upon the Brahmins— BrP_41.58 //
Those who offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to their ancestors on the bank of the Sarasvatī indeed obtain a hundredfold more merit than from any other sacred ford.
They provide inexhaustible satisfaction to the ancestors; of this there is no doubt.
Then, having gone to the abode of Śambhu, one should remain silent with senses restrained.
Having entered, one should worship Śarva after circumambulating him three times;
being pure, one should cause Bhava to be bathed with ghee, milk, and other substances.
Having anointed [the image] with fragrant sandalwood and saffron,
one should then worship the god who bears the moon upon his crest, the Lord of Umā.
With various kinds of pure flowers, such as bilva, arka, and lotus,
one should worship Śaṅkara with the mantras declared in the Āgamas and those declared in the Vedas.
But one who has not been initiated should worship by name alone and with the root mantra;
having thus worshipped that deity with perfumes and flowers that are pleasing to it, [he should proceed].
With incense, lamps, food offerings, and likewise with gifts and hymns,
with prostrations like a staff and with enchanting songs and musical instruments;
Having thus worshipped the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, according to the prescribed rite with dances, recitations, prostrations, shouts of victory, and circumambulations; ||| BrP_41.66 |||
Completely liberated from all sins, proud of their beauty and youth,
they rescued twenty-one generations of their lineage and were adorned with divine ornaments.
Adorned with a golden celestial chariot garlanded with networks of tinkling bells,
he was celebrated in song by Gandharvas and graced by Apsarases.
Illuminating all directions, he goes to the world of Śiva;
having enjoyed there, O Brahmins, that happiness which bestows delight upon the mind.
He remained there together with the inhabitants of that world until the dissolution of all beings;
then, when his merit was exhausted, he returned from that place to this earth.
O best of the twice-born, one who has mastered the four Vedas is born in the home of yogins;
having attained the Pāśupata yoga, he shall thereafter obtain liberation.
Likewise on the occasion of rising from sleep, at the transit of the sun, at the solstice, on the eighth day known as Aśoka, and at the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa).
And those who behold that supreme god clad in animal skins go to the world of Śiva by means of a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
At all times, those of wise intellect who behold that deity are indeed liberated from evil and go to the world of Śiva.
To the west, east, south, and likewise north of the deity,
that sacred field extending for two and a half yojanas bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In that excellent field, those who bathe in the pool and behold that god Maheśvara, known by the name Bhāskareśvara, [attain the highest state].
Having previously worshipped the three-eyed God of gods, who was honored by Āditya,
they were liberated from all sins and ascended to an excellent celestial chariot.
Being sung to by Gandharvas, those best of the twice-born go to the world of Śiva; they remain there, filled with joy, for one kalpa.
Having enjoyed extensive and delightful pleasures in the world of Śiva,
they return here upon the exhaustion of their merit and are born into an excellent family.
Alternatively, in the homes of yogins, the best of the twice-born are born— those who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and who delight in the welfare of all beings.
Skilled in the meaning of the scriptures on liberation and possessing equanimity toward all things,
they attain the supreme yoga of Śambhu and thereby proceed to liberation.
O twice-born ones, whatever linga is seen in that meritorious, excellent field—
whether it be worthy of worship or unworthy of worship, whether in the forest or even in the middle of a street— [is sacred].
Whether at a crossroads, in a cremation ground, or wherever else it may stand,
one should behold that linga with an undistracted mind, full of faith and well-composed.
Having bathed him with devotion, one should worship him with fragrances, beautiful flowers,
incense, lamps, along with food offerings, prostrations, and likewise with hymns of praise.
By prostrating like a staff and likewise by means of dance, song, and so forth,
a man who worships according to this procedure shall go to the world of Śiva.
Or a woman, O tigers among the twice-born, having worshipped with faith, obtains the previously mentioned fruit; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
O best of sages, who is able to describe all the qualities of that supreme field, except for the gods and Maheśvara?
Having gone to that most excellent field during the months beginning with Mādhava, whether with faith or even without faith, a man or a woman—
On whichever lunar day, O brahmins, having bathed in the waters of Bindusaras,
one should behold the god Virūpākṣa and the goddess Śivā, the bestower of boons.
He goes to the world of Śiva, [having seen] Gaṇa, Caṇḍa, Kārttikeya, Gaṇeśa, as well as Vṛṣabha, the Kalpa-tree, and Sāvitrī.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rites at the Kāpila-tīrtha, which destroys all sins,
one attains one's desired objects and goes to the world of Śiva.
He who, with his senses restrained, duly performs the rite of the pillar there,
uplifts twenty-one generations of his lineage and goes to the world of Śiva.
Whoever performs a ritual bath there in the auspicious Ekāmra, the field of Śiva, which is equal to Vārāṇasī, certainly attains liberation.
Brahmā said:
In Virajā is established the mother Virajā, who is Brahmāṇī;
by the sight of her, a mortal purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation.
But having seen that goddess even once, and having worshipped and bowed down to her with devotion,
a man, having uplifted his own lineage, goes to my world.
And other mothers of the world, who remove all sins, bestow boons, and are affectionate toward their devotees, dwell there in that stainless place.
There flows the river Vaitaraṇī, which removes all sins;
by bathing in it, O best of men, one is liberated from all evils.
The Self-born One, Hari himself, dwells right there in the form of a boar;
having seen him and bowed with devotion, they go to the Supreme Viṣṇu.
At Kāpila, Gograha, Soma, and the tīrtha known as Cālābu;
at Mṛtyuñjaya, Kroḍatīrtha, Vāsuka, and Siddhakeśvara.
Having gone to these sacred fords at Virajā, the wise man, with his senses restrained,
should duly bathe in the eight holy sites and bow down to the gods.
Completely liberated from all evil, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot and being sung of by Gandharvas, he is honored in my world.
Whoever indeed offers the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) in my field, Viraja, provides inexhaustible satisfaction for the ancestors; there is no doubt about this.
O best of sages, those men who cast off their bodies in my field, Viraja,
indeed attain liberation.
That mortal who, having bathed in the ocean and beheld Hari in the form of Kapila,
should also behold the goddess Vārāhī, goes to the abode of the gods.
There are other sacred fords and holy shrines as well;
however, O best of sages, those indeed should be known [as such] at that specific time.
O best of the twice-born, on that shore of the ocean, in that region,
there lies a supreme secret field that grants liberation and destroys all sins.
Everywhere strewn with sand, pure, and granting all desires,
that field ten yojanas in extent is exceedingly difficult to attain.
With *aśoka*, *arjuna*, and *puṃnāga* trees, with *bakula* and *sarala* trees, with *panasa*, *nārikela*, *śāla*, *tāla*, and *kapittha* trees.
With *campaka*, *karṇikāra*, mango, and *bilva* trees, along with *pāṭala*, *kadamba*, *kovidāra*, *lakuca*, and *nāgakeśara* trees; ||| BrP_42.16 |||
With *prācīnāmalaka*, *lodhra*, *nāraṅga*, *dhava*, and *khadira* trees; with *sarja*, *bhūrja*, *aśvakarṇa*, *tamāla*, and *devadāru* trees.
With mandāra and pārijāta trees, with nyagrodha, aguru, and sandalwood,
with excellent kharjūra and āmrātaka, and with mucukunda and kiṃśuka;
With *aśvattha* trees, *saptaparṇa*, and auspicious *madhudhāra-añjana*; with *śiṃśapā*, *āmalaka*, *nīpa*, *nimba*, *tindu*, and *vibhītaka*.
Rich with the fragrance of fruits of all seasons, radiant with flowers of every season,
delightful to the mind, pure white, and resounding with the songs of various birds;
With sounds uttered by birds— delightful to the ear, very sweet, produced by the play of their strength, and generating joy for the mind.
With cakoras, śatapatras, bhṛṅgarājas, as well as parrots,
cuckoos, sparrows, hārītas, and jīvajīvakas;
It was graced by the presence of beloved young *cātaka* birds and others with sweet voices—
delightful to the ear, pleasing, and warbling beautifully.
And with groves of *ketakī* flowers, *atimuktas*, and *kubjakas*,
as well as *mālatīs*, *kunda*s, *bāṇas*, and *karavīras* that were not white.
With *jambīra*, *karuṇa*, and *aṅkola* trees; with pomegranates, *bījapūraka* citrons, *mātuluṅga* fruits, betel nuts, *hintāla* palms, and groves of plantains.
And with various other trees and other captivating flowers,
with canopies of creepers, shrubs, and diverse reservoirs of water.
With long ponds, lakes, lotus-pools,
and reservoirs— various meritorious bodies of water adorned with clusters of lotuses.
And there were delightful lakes with clear waters,
adorned with white water-lilies, lotuses, and beautiful blue lotuses.
They were covered on all sides with white water-lilies and lotuses,
as well as with *kādamba* ducks, ruddy geese, and water-fowls.
It was filled with *kāraṇḍava* ducks, water-fowls, swans, tortoises, fish, and cormorants;
it was crowded with *dātyūha* cranes and *sārasa* cranes, and adorned by *koyaṣṭi* birds and herons.
And by these and other water-dwelling birds chirping on all sides,
as well as by other aquatic birds and water-born flowers.
Thus, with various kinds of trees and flowers born of both land and water, and with celibate students, householders, forest-dwellers, and mendicants; ||| BrP_42.32 |||
It was adorned by the social classes devoted to their own duties as well as others,
crowded with people who were joyful and well-nourished, and teeming with men and women.
The abode of all sciences without exception, a mine of the qualities of all dharmas—
such a field, endowed with every excellence, is exceedingly difficult to attain.
O best of sages, the renowned Puruṣottama resides there,
as far as the region of Utkala has been described in sequence.
Indeed, by the grace of Kṛṣṇa, that region is most meritorious,
for therein dwells the Soul of the Universe, that Supreme Person.
The Lord of the Universe, who pervades the world, is established there;
in him abide I, Rudra, Śakra, and the gods led by Agni.
O best of sages, we— all the Gandharvas, Apsarases, Pitṛs, gods, and humans— always dwell in that region.
Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, Siddhas, and sages of rigid vows;
the Ṛṣis, the Vālakhilyas, and the lords of progeny such as Kaśyapa and others.
The Suparṇas, Kinnaras, Nāgas, and likewise other inhabitants of heaven;
the four Vedas with their auxiliary limbs, and various Śāstras as well.
The Itihāsas and Purāṇas, sacrifices with excellent sacrificial fees, various holy rivers, sacred fords, and shrines; BrP_42.41 //
The oceans and likewise the mountains are situated in that region;
such is that most meritorious land, frequented by gods, sages, and ancestors.
To whom would dwelling in a place provided with every enjoyment not be pleasing?
What excellence does any other region possess that is superior to this?
Blessed are those men, renowned like the gods, who dwell in Utkala, where the Lord Puruṣottama himself, the bestower of liberation, resides.
Having bathed in the waters of the king of holy fords (Tīrtharāja) and beheld Puruṣottama, those mortals dwell in heaven; they do not go to the abode of Yama.
The lives of those wise inhabitants of Utkala, in the sacred field of Śrī Puruṣottama, are truly fruitful.
Those who behold the best of gods, with his gracious, wide eyes, his beautiful brows, hair, and crown, and his lovely earrings; ||| BrP_42.47 |||
With a beautiful smile and beautiful teeth, adorned with beautiful earrings,
he possessed a fine nose, beautiful cheeks, a lovely forehead, and auspicious marks.
The lotus-face of Kṛṣṇa, which generates joy for the three worlds.
Brahmā said: O brahmins, formerly in the Kṛta age, there was a glorious king renowned as Indradyumna, whose prowess was equal to that of Śakra.
He was truthful, pure, and skillful, learned in all the scriptures;
he was handsome, fortunate, heroic, a giver, an enjoyer, and sweet-spoken.
He was the performer of all sacrifices, devoted to Brahmanas, and true to his word;
he was skilled and accomplished in the science of archery, the Vedas, and the sacred treatises.
He was beloved by men and women like the moon on a full-moon night;
yet he was as difficult to gaze upon as the sun, striking fear into the hosts of his enemies.
A Vaiṣṇava endowed with the quality of purity (sattva), who has conquered anger and subdued his senses,
who studies Yoga and Sāṃkhya, who seeks liberation, and is devoted to dharma.
While that king, a mine of all virtues, was thus protecting the earth,
the thought of propitiating Hari arose within him.
"How shall I propitiate Janārdana, the God of gods?
In which sacred field, holy ford, riverbank, or hermitage [shall I do so]?"
Thus absorbed in thought, he then surveyed the earth with his mind,
beholding all the sacred fords (tīrthas), as well as the holy fields (kṣetras) and cities.
Having abandoned all those things, he went again to the sanctuary,
the famous and supreme sacred field, Puruṣottama, which bestows liberation.
Having gone to that excellent field with his abundant forces and vehicles,
he performed the horse sacrifice according to the rules, bestowing profuse sacrificial fees.
Having caused a magnificent and world-renowned palace to be built,
the valiant one installed Saṃkarṣaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, and Subhadrā there.

And having duly performed the rite of the five sacred fords (pañcatīrtha) there, the lord of the earth likewise performed bathing, giving gifts, austerity, burnt offerings, and the beholding of the deities.
Having worshipped Puruṣottama daily according to the rules with devotion,
he then attained liberation through the grace of the God of gods.
O twice-born ones, having seen Mārkaṇḍeya, Kṛṣṇa, and Rāma,
and having bathed in the ocean known as Indradyumna, one will certainly attain liberation.
The sages said: Why did that king Indradyumna, formerly the lord of the world,
go to the supreme sacred field of Puruṣottama, which bestows liberation?
O best of gods, having gone there, how did that most excellent of kings duly worship Puruṣottama with the horse sacrifice?
How did he cause a desired palace to be built upon that field which grants all fruits and is most difficult to attain— a monument renowned throughout the three worlds?
O Lord of Creatures, how did that tiger among kings fashion Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Subhadrā, and how did he protect the field?
How did the wise protector of the earth establish Kṛṣṇa and the others, who are worshipped by the gods, in that palace, the most excellent in the world?
O best of gods, you ought to relate all this— the life-story of that wise one— in its entirety, in detail, and exactly as it happened.
We truly do not reach satiety with the nectar of your words;
O Brahmin, we wish to hear more, for our curiosity is great.
Brahmā said: "Excellent, excellent, O best of the twice-born, that you inquire about this ancient,
auspicious, and meritorious account, which removes all sins and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
I shall relate his life story exactly as it occurred in the Kṛta Yuga;
listen, O tigers among sages, being attentive and with senses restrained.
There was a city named Avantī, renowned throughout the land of Mālava;
it was like the preeminent peak of that king's dominion over the earth.
It was crowded with joyful and well-nourished people, possessing firm walls and gateways,
with doors secured by strong mechanical bolts, and adorned with moats.
Crowded with various merchants, well-stocked with the sale of diverse goods,
it was delightful, possessing thoroughfares and marketplaces, with well-proportioned crossroads.
The city was crowded with gate-towers and beautifully adorned with streets filled with white,
charming peacocks that resembled royal swans and possessed variegated necks.
It was adorned with many hundreds of thousands of palaces,
gladdened by sacrifices and festivals, and filled with the sounds of singing and musical instruments.
It was beautifully adorned with banners and flags of various colors,
crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, and teeming with throngs of foot soldiers.
It was crowded with various warriors and joined by people from many different regions,
including Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and other twice-born classes.
That city, O best of sages, was prosperous and adorned with learned men;
there were no impure people there, nor any fools, nor any who were destitute.
Neither the sick, nor those with missing limbs, nor those addicted to gambling were seen;
rather, men and women were always joyful and of cheerful mind.
They played there day and night, joyful and individually engaged;
well-attired men were seen there, wearing polished earrings.
Handsome and virtuous, adorned with divine ornaments,
they resembled the god of love and were endowed with all auspicious marks.
They possessed beautiful hair, handsome cheeks, and lovely faces;
they bore beards, were knowers of all the scriptures, and were destroyers of enemy armies.
O best of sages, there women are seen who are exceedingly beautiful, givers of all jewels and enjoyers of every prosperity.
They walk with the gait of swans and elephants, their eyes are like blossoming lotuses;
they possess slender waists, shapely hips, and full, elevated breasts.
They had beautiful hair, lovely faces, and handsome cheeks; their locks were thick and steady, their necks were bent with graceful gestures and emotions, and they were adorned with earrings.
With lips reddened by betel, they shone with their faces colored by it;
endowed with golden ornaments, they were adorned with every kind of finery.
Dark-complexioned yet radiant, with beautiful hips, they resounded with the tinkling of waist-bands and anklets;
they wore divine garlands and garments, and were anointed with celestial perfumes.
They were clever, fortunate, lovely, with beautiful limbs and pleasing appearance;
endowed with both form and grace, they all had smiling faces.
And those women, intoxicated with passion, were sporting in the assembly halls and at the crossroads,
delighting themselves with song, instrumental music, storytelling, and conversation.
And courtesans were seen there, skilled in dance and song, adept at performance and conversation, and endowed with all the qualities of women.
And there were seen other noble ladies, teachers of virtue,
devoted to their husbands, fortunate, and adorned with every excellence.
With sacred groves, pleasure gardens, and delightful parks,
and with divine temples adorned with various kinds of flowers.
With *śāla*, *tāla*, *tamāla*, *bakula*, and *nāgakeśara* trees;
with *pippala*, *karṇikāra*, *candana*, *aguru*, and *campaka* trees.
With *puṃnāga* trees, coconut palms, jackfruit trees, and *sarala* trees;
with oranges, *lakuca*, *lodhra*, *saptaparṇa*, and auspicious *añjana* trees.
With mango, bilva, and kadamba trees, with śiṃśapa, dhava, and khadira,
with pāṭala, aśoka, and tagara, and with karavīra flowers both white and non-white;
With yellow arjuna, bhallātaka, and prepared āmrātaka,
as well as with nyagrodha, aśvattha, kāśmarya, palāśa, and devadāru;
With *mandāra* and *pārijāta* trees, with *tintiḍīka* and *vibhītaka*,
with *prācīnāmālaka* and *plakṣa*, and with *jambū* and *śirīṣa* trees;
With *kāleya*, *kāñcanāra*, *madhu*, *jambīra*, and *tinduka*; with *kharjūra*, *agastya*, *bakula*, *śākhoṭaka*, and *harītaka*.
With *kaṅkola*, *mucukunda*, *hintāla*, and *bījapūraka* trees; with groves of *ketakī* forests, and with *atimukta* and *kubjaka* shrubs.
And with *mallikā*, *kundabāṇa*, and *kadala* trees, adorned with groves of plantains,
along with *mātuluṅga*, betel nuts, *karuṇa*, and *sindhuvāraka* trees.
With many *kovidāra* trees, *badara* trees, and *karañjaka* trees,
as well as various other flowering trees and other beautiful ones.
With creepers and shrubs, with canopies, and with gardens resembling the Nandana grove—
always rich with the fragrance of flowers and always bowed down by the weight of fruit.
It was delightful with the various songs of birds, filled with diverse herds of deer,
and frequented by *cakoras*, *śatapatras*, *bhṛṅgāras*, and *priyaputrakas*.
With kalaviṅkas, peacocks, parrots, and cuckoos, as well as pigeons, wagtails, hawks, and doves; BrP 43.57.
With various other birds, many kinds of pleasing to the ear and delightful to the mind,
there were rivers, lotus ponds, and very many lakes.
[He was surrounded] by other sacred reservoirs adorned with night-lotuses and blue lotuses,
with white and other-colored lotuses, and with fragrant kahlāra flowers.
With various other kinds of flowers, most enchanting aquatic blooms,
divine scents that fill the air with fragrance, and blossoms radiant from every season;
It was filled with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, adorned with ruddy geese, cranes,
herons, and storks, and abounded with tortoises, fish, and crocodiles.
With water-fowls, kadamba birds, water-cranes, water-hens,
and other aquatic birds adorned with various cries;
They were adorned on all sides with various colors and ever-joyful [beings],
likewise with many kinds of flowers and diverse bodies of water.
It was graced by various sacred trees, diverse gardens,
and birds of beautiful appearance dwelling upon both land and water.
That great city was adorned with divine temples of the deities;
there dwells the Blessed Lord, the three-eyed God, the enemy of Tripura.
Śiva, renowned as Mahākāla, is the bestower of all desires;
having bathed according to the prescribed rites in the sin-destroying Śivakuṇḍa, a man [attains his goal].
Having duly gratified the gods, the ancestors, and the sages, the wise man should then go to the abode of Śiva and circumambulate it three times.
Having entered, being self-restrained, wearing clean garments, and having conquered his senses,
he should worship with devotion using baths, flowers, perfumes, incense, and lamps.
One should worship Śaṅkara with food offerings and gifts, with songs and instrumental music, with circumambulations, with prostrations like a staff, and with dances and hymns of praise.
Having worshipped Mahākāla, who is Śiva, even once with devotion according to the prescribed rite,
a person obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Completely liberated from all sins, he ascends celestial chariots that fulfill every desire and goes to the third heaven, where the abode of Śambhu is located.
Possessing a divine form, glorious, and adorned with celestial ornaments,
he enjoys excellent pleasures there until the dissolution of all beings.
O best of sages, having been free from old age and death in the world of Śiva,
he has returned here to an eminent brahmin family upon the exhaustion of his merit.
A Brahmin may become a master of the four Vedas and an expert in all the scriptures;
yet, having attained the Pāśupata Yoga, he shall thereafter obtain liberation.
There dwells a holy river renowned by the name Śiprā;
having bathed in it according to the prescribed rites and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, [one attains merit].
Completely liberated from all evil, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot,
that best of men enjoys manifold pleasures in the heavenly world.
Right there dwells the Blessed One, Janārdana, the God of gods;
he is Hari, known by the name Govinda-svāmin, the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Upon seeing him, one attains liberation together with twenty-one generations of one's lineage,
traveling by means of a sun-colored celestial chariot garlanded with networks of tinkling bells.
Sung by Gandharvas who have attained all their desires, travel at will, and are themselves unsteady, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Free from fear and with his afflictions gone, he enjoys various desires until the dissolution of all beings,
remaining handsome, fortunate, and happy.
In due time, an intelligent Brahmin, who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and Shastras, shall appear on this earth in the preeminent home of the yogins.
O twice-born ones, having resorted to Vaiṣṇava yoga, one shall then attain liberation from Viṣṇu,
who is named Vikramasvāmin, right there.
Whether a man or a woman, upon seeing it, shall obtain the fruit previously described;
other gods as well, led by Śakra, abide there.
And having seen those mothers, the best of sages, who grant the fruits of all desires, he should worship them according to the rules with devotion and prostrate before them.
Freed from all sins, a man goes to the third heaven;
such is that delightful city protected by the lion among kings.
It was ever-rejoicing in perpetual festivals like Indra’s Amarāvatī,
endowed with eighteen cities and possessing very extensive crossroads.
Resounding with the twang of bowstrings, adorned by the assemblies of Siddhas,
abounding in hosts of Vidyādharas, and echoing with the chanting of the Vedas.
O twice-born ones, the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, various Śāstras, and even poetic narratives and stories are heard by them day and night.
Thus have I described that city, rich in virtues,
in which the high-minded King Indradyumna formerly reigned.
Brahmā said:
Formerly, while exercising supreme sovereignty,
that wise king protected his subjects like his own biological sons.
He was a speaker of truth, possessed of great wisdom, a hero, a mine of all virtues,
intelligent, endowed with righteousness, and the best among all wielders of weapons.
Truthful, virtuous, self-controlled, glorious, and a conqueror of enemy cities,
he was like the sun in his splendors and like the two Aśvins in his physical forms.
Increasing in marvelous divinity and possessing prowess equal to Śakra,
he shines like the autumnal moon, adorned with all the auspicious marks.
He was the performer of all sacrifices, including the horse sacrifice and others;
indeed, there is no king equal to him in terms of gifts, sacrifices, and ascetic penances.
At every sacrifice, the lord of the earth bestowed great wealth— gold, jewels, pearls, elephants, and horses— upon the foremost of the brahmins.
There was no end to his preeminent elephants, horses, and chariots; to his woolen blankets, deerskins, and garments; nor to his jewels, wealth, and grain.
Thus, endowed with all wealth and adorned with all virtues,
his soul fulfilled by every desire, he ruled his kingdom free from thorns.
This thought arose in him: "How shall I propitiate Hari, the Lord of all yogis, the Master who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation?"
Having thoroughly examined all the scriptures, the tantras, the extensive Āgamas,
the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, and all the Vedāṅgas in their entirety.
All the treatises on Dharma, the rules spoken by the sages,
the Vedāṅgas, the technical sciences, and whatever other branches of knowledge there may be.
Having diligently served his guru and the Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas,
and having attained the supreme goal, he then became one who had fulfilled all his duties.
Having attained the supreme reality known as the imperishable Vāsudeva,
the seeker of liberation, whose senses are restrained, transcends erroneous cognition.
How shall I propitiate the eternal God of gods,
who is clad in yellow garments, possesses four arms, and bears the conch, the discus, and the mace?
His chest was covered by a forest garland, his eyes were as broad as lotus petals,
his breast was marked with the Śrīvatsa, and he was adorned with a crown and armlets.
But that Prajāpati departed from his own city of Ujjayinī,
accompanied by a great force, along with his servants and his domestic priest.
All the chariot-warriors, weapons in hand,
followed him on chariots resembling celestial palaces, adorned with banners and flags.
And likewise all the horsemen, with spears and javelins in their hands,
followed that king on horses resembling the wind.
With mountain-like elephants born in the Himalayas, ever-intoxicated, possessing tusks as long as plow-poles, fierce, and sixty years of age; ||| BrP_44.19 |||
And all those skilled in elephant warfare followed him, riding elephants with golden girths, adorned with banners and decorated with the ringing of bells.
And there were innumerable foot-soldiers, holding bows, spears,
and swords in their hands, wearing divine garlands and garments, and anointed with divine perfumes.
And all those youths followed him— wearing polished earrings,
skilled in all weapons, heroic, and ever eager for battle.
All the women dwelling in the inner apartments were well-adorned,
with beautiful lips and lovely teeth, and decorated with every kind of ornament.
All of them wore celestial garments, were adorned with divine garlands,
had their limbs anointed with divine perfumes, and possessed faces resembling the autumnal moon.
They were of slender waist, elegantly dressed, with beautiful ears adorned by locks of hair;
their mouths were stained red with betel, and they were well-guarded by protectors.
They all proceeded in various splendid vehicles adorned with jewels and gold,
while being serenaded by singers and reciters of hymns of praise.
Surrounded by those with weapons in their hands, the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, whose eyes were as broad as lotus petals, followed that king.
All the guilds and assemblies of merchants dwelling in various cities,
together with their wives and retinues, [followed him] with wealth, jewels, and gold.
Those who sell weapons, those who live by the trade of betel, those who sell grass, and those who sell wood; BrP 44.29.
All those who live by the stage, as well as meat-sellers, oil-sellers, and cloth-sellers; BrP 44.30.
There were thousands of fruit-sellers, as well as leaf-sellers, horse-merchants, and washermen.
Cowherds, barbers, as well as others who work with cloth, shepherds, goat-herders, deer-keepers, and swan-keepers; BrP 44.32.
Those who sell grain, those who sell roasted flour (saktu), those who sell molasses, and likewise those who live by selling salt; BrP 44.33.
Singers and dancers, as well as reciters of auspicious hymns, actors, storytellers, and those proficient in the meaning of the Purāṇas; 34.
Poets who compose poetry and are experts in various poetic forms;
those who neutralize poison and are masters of the science of Garuḍa; and those who examine various kinds of gems.
Ironworkers, copper-smiths, bell-metal workers, and those who fashion *rūṭhaka* ornaments;
makers of *kauṣa* vessels, painters, makers of *kundaka* bowls, and smiths.
The staff-bearers, the sword-bearers, those who live by the distillation of liquor, wrestlers, messengers, scribes, and whatever other laborers there may be; BrP 44.37.
Weavers, image-makers, leather-workers, oil-pressers, those who live by quails, those who live by partridges, and those who subsist on deer and birds; (BrP 44.38)
Those who are elephant physicians, physicians, and those men who are physicians for humans;
those who are tree physicians, cow physicians, and others who perform cutting and burning [of trees].
All these citizens, as well as others not specifically mentioned,
followed the king, together with all the inhabitants of the city.
Just as anxious sons follow their father when he departs for another village, so too did those citizens follow him.
Thus that illustrious king, surrounded by all the great people—
elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry— proceeded very slowly.
Having thus gone to the shore of the southern ocean,
that lordly king was followed by all those armies over a long period of time.
He beheld the beautiful ocean standing as if dancing,
agitated by many hundreds of thousands of waves.
It was a repository of various jewels, filled and teeming with diverse living beings,
abounding in ripples and waves, and endowed with great wonders.
The king of holy fords, of great roar, boundless and most terrifying,
resembling a mass of clouds, unfathomable, and the abode of sea-monsters.
It was filled with fish, tortoises, conchs, pearl oysters, crocodiles, and porpoises; with crabs and highly venomous serpents.
The salt-water ocean, the lord of rivers, is the abode of Hari and his resting place;
it is meritorious, the remover of all sins, and the bestower of the fruits of all desires.
He is the one with many whirlpools and profound depths, the refuge of the Dānavas,
the divine source of the nectar of immortality, the womb of the gods, and the lord of the waters.
It is the most distinguished among all beings and living creatures for sustaining life;
it is the most pure among purifiers and the most auspicious among auspicious things.
The Lord of aquatic creatures is the supreme and imperishable shrine among all shrines;
his measure is established according to the waxing and waning of the moon.
Impenetrable by all beings, the immortal abode of the gods,
it is the eternal cause of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution [of the world].
Seeing that lord of rivers and streams, which is the source of livelihood for all and a field of merit,
that best of kings was filled with supreme wonder.
Having reached the shore of the ocean, he made his dwelling there in a holy and enchanting region endowed with all the virtues of the earth.
It was surrounded by *śāla*, *kadamba*, *puṃnāga*, and *sarala* trees,
as well as by *panasa*, coconut, *bakula*, and *nāgakesara* trees.
With *tāla*, *pippala*, *kharjūra*, *nāraṅga*, and *bījapūraka* trees;
with *śāla*, *āmrātaka*, *lodhra*, *bakula*, and *bahuvāraka* trees.
With *kapittha* trees, *karṇikāra*, *pāṭala*, *aśoka*, and *campaka*;
with *dāḍima*, *tamāla*, *pārijāta*, and likewise *arjuna* trees.
With *prācīnāmalaka*, *bilva*, *priyaṅgu*, *vaṭa*, and *khadira*; with *iṅgudī*, *saptaparṇa*, *aśvattha*, *agastya*, and *jambuka* [trees].
With madhuka, karṇikāra, bahuvāra, and tinduka trees;
with palāśa, badara, and nīpa; and with the efficacious nimba and auspicious añjana.
With *vāraka*, *kovidāra*, *bhallātaka*, and *āmalaka* fruits, as well as with *hintāla*, *kāṅkola*, *karañja*, and *vibhītaka* fruits.
It was strewn with *sasarja*, *madhuka*, and *kāśmarya* trees; with *śālmalī* and *devadāru*; with *śākhoṭhaka*, *nimba*, and *vaṭa* trees; and with *kumbhī*, *kauṣṭha*, and *harītaka*.
With *guggulu* trees, sandalwood trees, as well as *aguru* and *pāṭala* trees;
with *jambīra* and *karuṇa* trees, *tintiḍī* and red sandalwood trees.
Thus, with various kinds of trees and other many plants,
including wish-fulfilling trees that bear fruit eternally and abound in blossoms of every season;
With the divine sounds of various birds, resounding with the cries of intoxicated cuckoos,
echoed by excellent peacocks, and filled with parrots and mainas;
With hārītas, bhṛṅgarājas, cātakas, bahuputrakas,
jīvaṃjīvakas, kākolas, kalaviṅkas, and pigeons;
And by various other birds, pleasing to the ear and captivating to the mind,
who were perched beautifully upon the flowering treetops and warbling.
And with groves of white ketakī plants that always bear flowers,
as well as with mallikā, kunda blossoms, yūthikā, and tagara.
With *kuṭaja* trees, *bāṇa* flowers, *atimukta* and *kubjaka*,
as well as with *mālatī*, *karavīra*, and golden plantain trees.
With various other flowers— fragrant, beautiful to behold,
grown in forests, gardens, and groves, multicolored, and sweet-scented.
It was crowded with hosts of Vidyādharas, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
and filled with Gandharvas, Uragas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Apsarases, and Kiṃnaras.
It was crowded with hosts of sages and yakṣas, frequented by various creatures,
and teeming with deer, monkeys, lions, boars, and buffaloes.
Likewise, it was adorned everywhere by other deer such as the black antelope,
by tigers, by radiant elephants, and by other forest-dwelling creatures.
Thus, with various kinds of trees, gardens resembling the Nandana grove,
canopies of creepers and shrubs, and diverse reservoirs of water;
[The lakes] were crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, adorned with clusters of lotus ponds,
and graced by *kādamba* geese, water-fowls, swans, and ruddy geese.
With lotuses, hundred-petaled lilies, white water-lilies, night-blooming lilies, and blue lotuses;
with birds and other aquatic creatures, and with various flowers born of the water.
With mountains possessing blazing peaks, adorned with beautiful caves, filled with various trees, and embellished by diverse minerals; BrP_44.76 //
With peaks consisting of all wonders, auspicious abodes of all beings, endowed with all medicinal herbs, and possessing vast, variegated ridges; BrP_44.77 //
Thus the protector of the earth beheld that place, honored by the three worlds, adorned with all those most enchanting [features] gathered together.
Ten yojanas in width and five yojanas in length,
that field, endowed with various wonders, is exceedingly difficult to attain.
The sages said:
"O Lord, why was there no image of Viṣṇu previously situated in that most excellent, meritorious, Vaiṣṇava sacred field of Puruṣottama?"
Having gone there with his army and vehicles,
that king established Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and the auspicious Bhadrā who bestows blessings.
O Lord of the World, we have a great doubt and wonder in this matter;
we wish to hear everything—tell us the cause of it.
Brahmā said:
Listen to this ancient tale that destroys all sins;
I shall relate it in brief, as Hari was formerly questioned by Śrī.
On the golden peak of Sumeru, which is endowed with every wonder and graced by Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, and Kinnaras;
By the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, nāgas, hosts of apsarases, sages, guhyakas, siddhas, suparṇas, and the hosts of maruts; 45.6.
It was beautiful and most enchanting, adorned with other celestial abodes to be attained by Kaśyapa and other lords of progeny, as well as by the Vālakhilyas and others.
It was adorned with divine groves of *karṇikāra* trees, which resembled gold and were like the sun, bearing an abundance of blossoms from every season.
And with many other trees such as *śāla* and *tāla*,
and groves of *puṃnāga*, *aśoka*, *sarala*, *nyagrodha*, *āmra*, *ātaka*, and *arjuna*.
With *pārijāta*, *āmra*, *khadira*, *nīpa*, and clusters of *bilva* and *kadamba*;
with *dhava*, *khadira*, *pālāśa*, *śīrṣa*, *āmalaka*, and *tinduka* trees.
With oranges, *kola*, *bakula*, *lodhra*, pomegranates, and *dāruka*;
with *sarja*, *karṇa*, *tagara*, *śiśu*, *bhūrja*, and *nimba* trees; || 45.11 ||
And it was adorned with flowering trees bent down by the weight of their fruits— some made of gold— and rich with the fragrance of various blossoms.
With *mālatī*, *yūthikā*, *mallī*, *kunda*, *bāṇa*, and *kuruṇṭaka*;
with the flowers of *pāṭalā*, *agastya*, *kuṭaja*, *mandāra*, and others.
And with various other flowers that grant delight to the mind, and with flocks of diverse birds warbling with sweet voices; BrP_45.14 //
With the divine songs of male cuckoos, the cries of intoxicated peacocks,
and likewise with various kinds of trees and various kinds of flowers.
In that place, adorned by various kinds of birds and frequented by the gods,
he beheld the Lord of the World, the imperishable creator of the universe, stationed there.
Having bowed her head to the imperishable Vāsudeva, the creator of all worlds, the goddess born from the lotus, desiring the welfare of the worlds, asked him this great and unsurpassed question.
Śrī said:
"Speak, O Lord of all worlds, regarding the doubt residing in my heart concerning this mortal world— this most wondrous realm of action so difficult to attain."
O Lord of Gods, by what means may one who is seized by the crocodiles of greed and delusion, and caught in the great ocean of desire and anger, be liberated from this sea of saṃsāra?
Speak, O Lord of all gods, if you consider me worthy of your favor;
for apart from you, there is no one in this world capable of resolving my doubts.
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of hers, Janārdana, the God of gods,
spoke with supreme affection that which was the highest essence, like nectar.

The Blessed One said: O Goddess, Puruṣottama, who is easy to worship, easy to accomplish, delightful, and yielding excellent fruit, dwells in that preeminent sacred site, renowned throughout the world.
There is no one equal to him to be found in the three worlds, O Goddess of the Gods; by chanting his name, one is liberated from all sins.
It was not known by all the immortals, nor by the Daityas, nor by the Dānavas;
it has been kept secret from me by the best of sages, beginning with Marīci, O fair-faced one.
I shall now fully describe that king of holy fords to you; listen with single-minded devotion, O lady of beautiful hips, O woman of excellent complexion.
When the kalpa had arisen and the world of moving and stationary beings had perished,
the gods, gandharvas, daityas, vidyādharas, and uragas were all dissolved.
All this was enveloped in darkness; nothing at all could be discerned.
Within that, the Soul of Beings, the Supreme Self, the Teacher of the World, remained awake.
The glorious Lord Maheśvara, the creator of the three forms and the maker of the universe, is renowned as Vāsudeva; he is Hari, the Lord whose essence is yoga.
At the end of his yogic sleep, he created the imperishable being Brahmā, who emerged from the center of the lotus from his navel and resembled the filaments of a lotus.
Then Brahmā, the great lord of all the worlds, being of such a nature,
gradually creates that which is composed of the five elements.
All beings born from a womb, whether gross or subtle,
all fourfold kinds, both stationary and moving.
Then Prajāpati Brahmā, having reflected upon himself with his mind, created all things moving and unmoving, and brought forth various kinds of progeny.
All the sages beginning with Marīci, as well as the gods, asuras, and ancestors,
the yakṣas, vidyādharas, and others, and likewise the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā— [all these were seen by him].
O Goddess, [he saw] men, monkeys, lions, and various birds—
those born from the womb, those born from eggs, as well as those born from sweat and those born from sprouts.
He created the fourfold order of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, as well as the various outcaste tribes and Mlecchas, each distinct from the others.
Having become Brahmā, he created the entire world, including all that moves and is immobile, as well as everything designated as living beings, from grass and shrubs down to ants.
Having likewise conceived himself as a male being on his right side and as a female on his left, he fashioned that which had become twofold.
From that time forward, the offspring in this world were born through sexual union;
they were inferior, superior, and middling, according to whichever of my fields they entered.
Having reflected thus, that god, who was formerly born from the waters,
entered into meditation, assuming a body whose essence was Vāsudeva.
By the mere power of meditation, at that very moment, Janārdana himself appeared there,
possessing a thousand eyes and a thousand feet.
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads; his eyes resemble lotuses;
he has the luster of water, darkness, and clouds; he is glorious and bears the Śrīvatsa mark.
Then Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, suddenly beheld him and greeted him with seats, water for the hands and feet, and unbroken grains of rice.
Viriñci, being well-composed, praised him with supreme hymns.
Then I said to the god Brahmā, who was born from the lotus:
"O Father, tell me now the reason for my meditation."

Brahmā said: O Lord of Gods, for the welfare of the world, [I shall describe] the paths to the gateway of heaven, which are difficult for those in the mortal world to attain— namely, sacrifices, gifts, and vows.
Yoga, truth, austerity, faith, and various sacred fords—
setting all these aside, tell me that which is happiness and its means.
O Lord of the World, tell me, O Supreme Person, of that place on earth which is said to be preeminent— the highest station among all.
Having heard the words of the Creator, I then said, "O beloved, listen, O Brahmā; I shall proclaim that which is stainless and difficult to find on earth."
It is the most excellent of all fields, auspicious, a means of crossing over saṃsāra,
beneficial to cows and Brahmins, meritorious, and the source of happiness for the four castes.
This field, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men, is extremely difficult to attain;
it is a source of great merit for all and indeed grants spiritual perfection at Pitāmaha.
From that, the eternal king of holy fords arose;
it is the celebrated and supreme sacred field, frequented throughout the four ages.
Of all the gods, sages, and celibate students,
as well as the Daityas, Dānavas, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
Since he is the supreme person among the Nāgas, the Vidyādharas, and all things both stationary and moving, he is therefore called Puruṣottama.
On the shore of the southern ocean stands a banyan tree;
the sacred field where it resides, ten yojanas in extent, is exceedingly difficult to attain.
But he who, when the destruction of the world has arisen in the form of a great falling meteor,
does not meet his end in that manner, remains there established in himself.
Merely by seeing that banyan tree and repeatedly entering its shade, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin; what need is there to mention other sins?
Those living beings who performed circumambulations and offered salutations have all shaken off their sins and gone to the abode of Keśava.
To the north of the nyagrodha tree and slightly to the south of Keśava, a temple stands there; for that is indeed the abode consisting of Dharma.
Having seen the image there, fashioned by the God himself,
men then go to my world without any effort.
O beloved, once, seeing them as they were departing, the King of Dharma approached me,
bowed his head, and spoke.
Yama said:
Homage to you, O Blessed One, O God, Lord of the worlds, Master of the universe—
the God who dwells in the Ocean of Milk and reclines upon the coils of Śeṣa.
To Viṣṇu— the best, the most excellent, the giver of boons, the uncreated creator, the Lord, the Sovereign of the Universe, the unborn, the omniscient, and the unconquered.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, with eyes like white lotuses,
the omniscient, beyond attributes, peaceful, the imperishable sustainer of the world.
The creator of all worlds, the bringer of happiness to all worlds,
the ancient Person, the one to be known, both manifest and unmanifest, the eternal.
To the creator of the high and the low, the lord of the world, the teacher of the universe,
who is endowed with the Śrīvatsa upon his chest and adorned with a garland of forest flowers.
Clad in yellow garments, four-armed, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
he is adorned with necklaces and armlets, and wears a crown and bracelets.
Complete with all auspicious marks, yet devoid of all sense organs;
immovable, unshakable, subtle, consisting of the nature of light, and eternal.
I bow to the Lord of the World, the Sovereign and the Bestower of Bliss, who is free from existence and non-existence, all-pervading, and beyond primordial nature.
Thus, in former times, the King of Dharma, having praised [him] with various hymns in the vicinity of the banyan tree, then prostrated himself.
O highly fortunate lady, having seen him prostrate with palms joined in reverence,
O Goddess, I asked Antaka the reason for his hymn of praise.
"O mighty-armed son of Vivasvat, you are indeed the foremost of all the gods;
for what purpose have you praised me? Tell me that in brief."
The King of Dharma said:
"In this meritorious and renowned sanctuary of Puruṣottama,
there is an excellent image made of sapphire that fulfills all desires."
O lotus-eyed one, having seen her with single-minded devotion and faith,
men who are free from desire go to the abode known as Śveta.
Therefore, O slayer of enemies, I am unable to perform this task;
be gracious, O Great God, and withdraw this image, O All-pervading Lord.
Having heard these words of Vaivasvata, he spoke this:
"O Yama, I shall conceal her on all sides with sands."
Then, O Goddess, that image was concealed by me with creepers,
so that men desiring heaven did not see it there.
Having covered him with creepers and cloths of gold, O Goddess,
he dispatched Yama toward his own city in the southern direction.
Brahmā said:
O twice-born ones, when the image of sapphire had vanished,
in that most excellent and meritorious field renowned as Puruṣottama, [the Lord remained].
The Blessed Lord Janārdana, the God of gods, previously related to her that entire account of what had occurred there in the past.
The journey of Indradyumna, the sight of the sacred field,
the description of the field, and likewise the construction of the temple.
The performance of the horse sacrifice, the vision in a dream,
and likewise the sight of a log on the shore of the salt ocean.
O twice-born ones, there was the vision of Vāsudeva and the king of artisans,
as well as the specific construction of the image according to its description.

O best of Brahmins, there is likewise the installation of all [the deities] in the temple, the most excellent abode in the world, as well as the proclamation of the ritual manual at the time of the festival procession.
The life story of Mārkaṇḍeya, the installation of Śaṅkara, the majesty of the five sacred fords (pañcatīrtha), and the vision of the Trident-bearer; BrP_45.83 //
O twice-born ones, there is the sight of the banyan tree and its auspicious fruit,
as well as the sight of Baladeva and especially that of Kṛṣṇa.
And there itself is the greatness of Subhadrā in every respect,
as well as the vision of Narasiṃha and the proclamation of his glorious deeds.
The vision of Ananta-Vāsudeva, the glorification of his qualities,
the majesty of Śveta-Mādhava, and the vision of Svargadvāra.
O twice-born ones, [the account includes] the sight of the ocean, as well as bathing and the offering of libations;
furthermore, the majesty of bathing in the ocean and that of Indradyumna.
The fruit of the five sacred fords (pañcatīrtha), as well as that of Mahājyeṣṭha,
and likewise the fruit of the festival pilgrimage to the abode of Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma.
That Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) previously described to her again and again the entire description of Viṣṇuloka and the sacred field (kṣetra).
The sages said:
"O God, we wish to hear the remainder of the story of the lord of the earth;
having gone to that most excellent sacred field, what did the king do?"
Brahmā said:
Listen, O tigers among sages; I shall describe in brief both the sight of the sacred field and the duty of that king.
Having gone there to that field renowned throughout the three worlds, the protector of the earth beheld delightful places as well as rivers.
There is a most meritorious river there, flowing from the foothills of the Vindhya mountains;
renowned as the Svittropalā, it is auspicious and removes all sins.
Equal to the Gaṅgā, with a great current flowing toward the southern ocean,
that best of rivers, possessing meritorious waters, is known by the name Mahānadī.
Situated within the womb of the southern ocean and adorned with whirlpools,
on both its banks are villages and cities.
The tigers among sages are seen there, possessing excellent crops and being most enchanting;
they are crowded with people who are joyful and well-nourished, and adorned with garments and ornaments.
There, Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras were seen separately,
each devoted to their own duty, peaceful, and endowed with auspicious marks.
With their mouths full of betel, adorned with garlands and wreaths,
the Brahmins had their faces filled with the Vedas, including the six auxiliary sciences and the methods of Pada and Krama recitation.
Some were devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice, while others performed the Aupāsana rites;
they were all skilled in the meaning of every scripture, performers of sacrifices, and givers of abundant sacrificial fees.
On the four royal highways, in the forests and groves,
in the assembly halls, circular courtyards, and palaces, as well as in the temples of the deities.
There, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs and auspicious marks,
as well as poetic works, treatises, and narratives, are heard by great men.
The women dwelling in that region were proud of their beauty and youth;
they were endowed with all perfect characteristics and possessed broad, rounded hips.
With faces like lotuses, dark-complexioned, and countenances resembling the autumnal moon,
they all had full and elevated breasts and were beautiful to behold in every perfection.
Adorned with golden bracelets and decorated with divine garments,
they resemble the interior of a plantain tree and possess the luster of lotus filaments.
The beloved women had lips like the bimba fruit, eyes extending to their ears, beautiful faces, and lovely hair; they were bent with gestures of amorous play and emotion.
Some had eyes like lotus petals, some had eyes like blue water-lilies;
others were slender-limbed women with teeth as bright as lightning.
Adorned with curved locks of hair, they shone with parted hairlines;
they were equipped with neck-ornaments and decorated with garlands of flowers.
Adorned with earrings set with jewels and captivating ear-ornaments,
they appeared like celestial women, endowed with auspicious marks.
The excellent women were sporting with divine, most auspicious songs,
and with lutes, flutes, mṛdaṅga drums, paṇavas, and gomukhas.
Always joyful and playful with one another, those graceful women sported amidst the sounds of conchs and kettledrums, and various captivating musical instruments.
In this manner, there were many such excellent women, skilled in various songs and instrumental music, who,
intoxicated by passion, remained joined together day and night.
It was frequented by monks, forest-dwellers, perfected beings, those who have completed their studies, and celibate students;
by those perfected through mantras, perfected through austerity, and perfected through sacrifice.
Thus the king beheld that most beautiful sacred field, thinking:
"Right here I shall propitiate the eternal Blessed One."
To Viṣṇu, the preceptor of the world, the supreme deity, the ultimate shore, the highest state, the Lord of all lords, the infinite, and the unconquered.
This is that mental holy site known to me as Puruṣottama,
where the great-bodied Nyagrodha tree stands, like a wish-fulfilling tree.
The image known as Indranīla was hidden by the Lord himself;
no other auspicious Vaiṣṇava image is seen here.
"I shall make such an effort that Lord Viṣṇu,
the master of the world whose valor is truth, will come before my very eyes."
Through sacrifices, gifts, austerities, burnt offerings, meditations,
as well as worship and fasts performed according to the rules, may I practice this supreme vow.
With a mind focused on nothing else, with my thoughts fixed on Him and no other in mind,
I now undertake the construction of this abode for Viṣṇu.
Brahmā said:
O best of the twice-born, having reflected thus,
that protector of the earth then began the construction of a temple for Hari there.
Having summoned all the astrologers and teachers who had mastered the scriptures,
the king, with supreme joy, diligently purified the ground.
[He was accompanied] by Brahmins endowed with knowledge who had mastered the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras,
as well as by ministers and counselors skilled in the science of architecture.
Having deliberated with them, on an auspicious day at a favorable moment,
when the moon and stars were in conjunction and the planets were in a state of favorability, [he acted].
With sounds of "Victory! and "Auspiciousness!", with various charming musical instruments, with the resonant chanting of the Vedas, and with songs of most sweet melody.
Then the king, with great faith and well-composed mind, offered the *arghya* oblation with flowers, parched grain, unbroken rice, perfumes, full water-pots, and lamps.
Having thus offered the guest-water (arghya) according to the prescribed rite,
that lord of the earth summoned the heroic ruler of Kaliṅga, as well as the ruler of Utkala and the ruler of Kośala; then the king spoke to them.
The king said:
"Go all together, with full concentration, for the sake of the stone,
taking along the foremost artisans who are experts in stonework."

"Having surveyed the vast Vindhya mountain, adorned with many caves, and having cleared all its plateaus and cut away the auspicious stones, let them be transported by carts and boats; do not delay! (BrP 47.9)
{Brahmā said:} Having thus commanded those kings to depart, that lord of the earth spoke these words once more to his ministers and his domestic priests.
The king said:
"Let messengers go everywhere and proclaim my command;
let them travel very swiftly to wherever the kings on earth reside."
"By the command of Indradyumna, all of you go together with the elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, along with the ministers and the family priests."
Brahmā said:
Thus commanded by that high-souled king,
the messengers went and spoke these words of that monarch to the other kings.
Having heard those words of the messengers, all those kings then arrived in haste, each surrounded by his own armies.
Those kings who reside in every direction, those situated to the south, those situated in the west, and those established in the northern region; // BrP_47.15 //
Those who dwell in the borderlands, those who dwell in the vicinity, those who are mountain-dwellers, as well as those who inhabit the islands; BrP_47.16 //
Having heard the command of Indradyumna, many brahmins arrived there in great numbers with chariots, elephants, foot soldiers, horses, and abundant wealth.
Seeing those kings who had arrived, together with their ministers and domestic priests,
the king, with a joyful heart, spoke respectfully regarding the matter at hand.
The king said:
Listen, O tigers among kings, to what I shall say regarding this auspicious and most excellent holy field, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
"My mind is agitated with the thought: 'How shall I be able to perform the great horse-sacrifice and the Vaiṣṇava temple? (BrP 47.20)
"With you as my good companions, I shall accomplish all this,
provided that you, O best of kings, become my helpers."
{Brahmā said:} As the wise king of kings was speaking thus,
all those monarchs were delighted and rejoiced at his command.
They showered wealth and jewels, with gold, gems, and pearls;
with precious blankets and skins, and auspicious rugs made of *rāṅkava* wool.
With diamonds, lapis lazuli, rubies, emeralds, and sapphires;
with elephants, horses, wealth, and other things, as well as chariots and female elephants.
With countless and manifold kinds of substances, both high and low, as well as with rice, paddy, barley, beans, mung beans, and sesame seeds; BrP 47.25.
With *siddhārtha* seeds, chickpeas, wheat, lentils and the like, *śyāmāka*, *madhuka*, wild rice (*nīvāra*), and horse gram (*kulattha*).
And with thousands of various other grains, both cultivated and wild,
and with heaps of many thousands of grains of rice.
With jars of cow-derived oblation by the hundreds and thousands, as well as with various other substances such as foods to be chewed and eaten, and unguents; BrP 47.28.
The kings fulfilled whatever was required through their available wealth; seeing those sacrificial materials, endowed with every excellence, [he was amazed].
[He invited] Brahmins who were knowers of sacrificial rites, who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
who were proficient in the scriptures, and skillful and dexterous in all tasks.
And likewise the ṛṣis, the great ṛṣis, and the divine ṛṣis, as well as ascetics;
those who are celibate students, householders, forest-dwellers, and renunciants.
[He gave gifts] to Snātaka Brahmins and others who were constantly engaged in the Agnihotra sacrifice,
as well as to excellent teachers and sub-teachers endowed with Vedic study and austerity.
Seeing those members of the assembly who were skilled in the scriptures, as well as many other purifiers, the illustrious king spoke to his own domestic priest:
The king said:
"Therefore, let the learned Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas set forth;
for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the horse sacrifice, let them seek out a land fit for the rite."
Brahmā said:
Thus addressed, the royal priest, together with his ministers, joyfully did as he was told by that king.
Then the wise domestic priest departed together with the architects,
placing before him the Brahmins who were skilled in the performance of sacrificial rites.
That brahmin had that region— a fisherman's village complete with main streets and watchtowers—
constructed as a sacrificial enclosure according to the prescribed rules.
It was crowded with hundreds of palaces, adorned with the finest jewels,
as delightful as the abode of Indra, and embellished with gold and gems.
Having provided pillars variegated with gold and massive archways at the sites of the sacrificial grounds, he offered pure gold as well.
The righteous-souled king had inner apartments constructed for the rulers dwelling in various lands at their respective locations, according to the prescribed rites.
And for the Brahmins and Vaiśyas who had gathered from various lands,
he likewise caused many dwellings to be constructed there according to the prescribed rites.
For the sake of pleasing that king, the best of monarchs arrived, bringing many jewels; women also came to the festival.
As those great-souled ones were entering their own camps,
a sound arose that reached the heavens, like the roaring of the ocean.
O best of sages, when they had arrived, that king assigned them dwellings and beds with due hospitality.
Then the best of kings himself approached and ordered various foods consisting of rice, sugarcane, barley, and cow's milk.
Likewise, at that great sacrifice, there were many exponents of the Veda who were the most eminent among the twice-born and the best of the twice-born.
Accompanied by their disciples, they arrived; the king received them, and he escorted them all as far as their dwellings.
Then that best of kings, possessed of great splendor, having himself abandoned deceit,
performed his own craft, as did the other artisans at that time.
Then they reported the entire sacrificial procedure to that king;
having heard that everything had been completed without negligence, the best of kings,
the steadfast Acyuta, along with his ministers, became thrilled, his hair standing on end.
Brahmā said:
When that sacrifice had commenced, eloquent speakers, desiring to defeat one another, uttered many arguments based on logic.
O twice-born ones, they beheld there archways made of gold, fashioned by that lion among kings just like those of the Lord of the Gods.
And many varieties of beds and seats, heaps of jewels,
jars, bowls, cauldrons, pitchers, and vardhamānaka vessels.
The lord of the earth did not see anything that was not made of gold,
nor even the sacrificial posts prescribed by the scriptures, which were made of wood and adorned with gold.
O twice-born ones, at the appropriate time and according to the prescribed rites, those of great luster presented whatever animals there were— both those born on land and those born in water.
There, those kings beheld all who had been brought together:
cows, buffaloes, and likewise aged women as well.
And aquatic beings, beasts of prey, and birds;
those born from a womb, those born from an egg, those born from sweat, and those born from sprouting.
They beheld the mountains, the things to be stored, and all living beings; thus everything was exceedingly joyful, abounding in cattle, wealth, and grain.
Having seen the sacrificial enclosure, filled with abundant and opulent choice food for the Brahmins and the Vaiśyas, the kings were struck with the utmost wonder.
When a full hundred thousand Brahmins had finished eating there,
a drum then repeatedly sounded with the roar of thunderclouds.
And as each day passed, he repeatedly caused it to resound;
in this manner, the sacrifice of that wise king continued to grow.
The brahmins beheld very many offerings of food that appeared like flowing streams, as well as channels of curd and lakes of milk.
Indeed, the entire Jambūdvīpa, filled with various provinces,
was present there at that great sacrifice of the king, and brahmins were seen there as well.
There, O best of the twice-born, many thousands of men took up vessels from here and there and departed.
And all those heralds, adorned with well-polished jeweled earrings,
served the twice-born by the hundreds and thousands.
The various kinds of beverages and the attendants who followed the man gave those items fit for the king's consumption to the brahmins together with him.
Then, that king who bestowed abundant sacrificial fees performed the worship, according to the prescribed rites, of the assembled knowers of the Vedas and the lords of the earth.
He [received] actors, dancers, and others who had come from various regions to the king, who was engaged in a great war, as well as those skilled in song and praise.
His wives were enchanting, with full and elevated breasts,
eyes like the petals of blue lotuses, and faces resembling the autumn moon.
Endowed with noble lineage, virtuous conduct, and excellent qualities— numbering one thousand and more than a hundred—
thus was he accompanied by that multitude of the king’s supreme wives.
It was divine, filled with garlands of jewels, adorned with banners and flags,
graced with strings of pearls, delightful, and possessed of a radiance equal to the luster of the moon.
He [mounted] hundreds of elephants, mountain-like in form, dripping with rut, possessed of great strength, and accompanied by hosts of millions of tuskers adorned with ivory ornaments.
With many millions of beautiful horses born in the Indus region, swift as the force of the wind—
white horses with dark ears and endowed with great speed.
And likewise, there were countless foot soldiers, resembling sons of gods, who were armored with their girdles fastened and brandished various weapons.
Thus did the king behold the vast array of sacrificial preparations;
then the king attained great joy, and being thrilled, he spoke these words.
The king said:
"O princes, bring the best of horses, endowed with all auspicious marks; let it be grazed upon the earth by you, remaining well-restrained."
"Let the learned ones who know the Dharma perform a fire sacrifice here,
[offering] a black goat, a buffalo, and a black antelope, O twice-born ones."
Let the oxen, the cows, and all the herdsmen be provided for;
let the sacrificial rites proceed, and thereafter let the Vaiṣṇava temple be constructed.
And let all of this that is desired by their hearts be given to the Brahmins:
women, crores of jewels, villages, and cities.
Likewise, for those who desire them, there were lands of perfect abundance,
as well as many other delightful varieties of objects.
Indeed, this [request] should not be spoken to any of those who beg;
let the sacrifice proceed for as long as the God does not yet approach here visibly in the presence of this sacrifice. (BrP 47.80)
{Brahmā said:} Having spoken thus, O brahmins, that lion among kings, the mighty-armed one,
then gave a heap of gold and ornaments numbering ten million.
A hundred thousand female elephants, millions of horses, a hundred million bulls, and cows with golden horns.
Filled with joy, he gave to the Brahmins learned in the Vedas cows that were beautiful, fragrant, yielding plenty of milk, and provided with bronze milking vessels.
And costly garments, blankets made of ranku-deer hair, very white and bright cloths, and the finest coral and gems.
At that great sacrifice, he bestowed various kinds of jewels.
Whatever there may be of diamonds, lapis lazuli, rubies, pearls, and the like, as well as radiant maidens with lotus-like eyes adorned with ornaments; [all these he gave].
The king, filled with joy, bestowed five hundred women upon the brahmins—
women with full breasts, their own bosoms covered by bodices.
And there were many women with beautiful hips, eyes as long as lotus petals,
necks graced with graceful gestures and expressions, and adorned with bracelets.
Adorned with anklets on their feet and dressed in fine silk garments,
he presented many desirable women one by one to him.
O best of the twice-born, for the Brahmins and others who were petitioners at the horse sacrifice,
there was an abundance of food and edibles provided with various kinds of provisions.
Various kinds of sweets such as *khaṇḍaka*, steamed and baked flour-cakes,
other pure foods, *ghṛtapūra* cakes, and *khāṇḍava* confections.
Sweet cakes, threatened sweets, and well-cooked, delicious food—
food is given again and again for the sake of pleasing all sentient beings.
There is no end to wealth that has been given or is being given;
seeing this great sacrifice, the gods and daityas, along with Vāraṇa, [were amazed].
The Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, Ṛṣis,
and lords of creatures were filled with supreme wonder upon seeing that auspicious, excellent sacrifice.
The royal priest, the ministers, and the king were all there, filled with joy;
therein, no one was soiled, none was dejected, and none was afflicted by hunger.
There is neither affliction nor exhaustion, nor mental anxieties or physical diseases;
there is no untimely death there, nor biting insects, nor seizing spirits, nor poison.
In that great festival of the king, all the people were joyful and well-nourished,
as were the long-lived sages there who had attained perfection through asceticism.
