O best of the twice-born, such a sacrifice, endowed with wealth and grain, had never been performed before;
thus did that king duly complete the horse sacrifice (vājimedha) as well as the Vaiṣṇava temple.
The sages said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, tell us that which we ask concerning the ancient past—
how those images were formerly fashioned by Indradyumna."
And by what manner was Mādhava pleased with him?
Tell us all that, for our curiosity is indeed great.
Brahmā said:
Listen, O tigers among sages, to this ancient account equal to the Vedas;
I shall relate the events of old and the origin of the images.
When the great sacrifice had commenced and the palace was completed,
he then became consumed with thought day and night regarding the matter of the images.
I do not know by what means I may behold the Supreme Person, the Lord of gods, the Lord of all, the purifier of the worlds, and the author of creation, preservation, and destruction.
But the king became possessed by anxiety; he neither slept at night nor during the day, nor did he enjoy various pleasures, nor did he engage in bathing or personal adornment.
Neither by musical instruments, nor by perfumes, nor even by singers or cosmetics;
neither by rutting elephants, nor by numerous chariots drawn by horses.
Not with sapphire or great-blue gems,
nor with those made of ruby, nor with gold, silver, and the like, combined with diamond and crystal.
Neither by those with many passions seeking wealth and desire, nor by forest-dwellers moving through the air,
was there any increase of satisfaction for that king’s mind.
On the surface of the earth, what material produced from stone, clay, or wood is recommended for an image of Viṣṇu that is endowed with all auspicious characteristics?
"Among these three, that which is dear and honored by the gods should be established; once established, it will bring about satisfaction. Thus he became absorbed in thought. (BrP 48.11)
Having worshipped Puruṣottama according to the ritual of the Pañcarātra,
the protector of the earth, overcome with anxiety, began to offer praise.
O Vāsudeva, homage be unto you; homage be unto you, the cause of liberation!
Protect me, O Lord of all worlds, from the ocean of birth and saṃsāra.
O you who resemble the stainless sky, salutations to you, O Supreme Person!
O Saṃkarṣaṇa, let there be salutations to you; protect me, O upholder of the earth!
Homage to you, who shine like the interior of gold; homage to you, whose banner is the sea-monster;
homage be to you, O beloved of Rati; protect me, O Destroyer of Saṃvara!
Homage to you, who resemble collyrium; homage to you, who are affectionate toward your devotees.
O Aniruddha, let there be homage to you; protect me and become the granter of boons.
Homage to you, O abode of the wise; homage to you, O beloved of the wise.
O Nārāyaṇa, let there be homage to you; protect me, who have come to you for refuge.
Homage to you, O best of the mighty; homage to you, whose weapon is the plow!
O four-faced one, abode of the world, protect me, O Great-Grandfather!
Homage to you, who resemble a dark blue cloud; homage to you, worshipped by the thirty gods.
O Viṣṇu, Lord of the World, protect me who am submerged in the ocean of existence!
O you who resemble the fire of universal dissolution, salutations to you, the destroyer of the sons of Diti;
O Narasiṃha of great heroism, with blazing eyes, protect me!
Just as in the past the earth was lifted from the netherworld by you with your tusk,
so may you, as the Great Boar, protect me from the ocean of suffering.
O Kṛṣṇa, these forms of yours, which grant boons, have been praised by me;
these [forms] beginning with Baladeva exist as separate manifestations of you.
O Lord of Gods, O Master, Garuḍa and the others are your limbs; likewise, O Acyuta, the guardians of the quarters with their weapons, Keśava and the rest, are yours as well.
And whatever other manifestations of yours, O Lord of Gods, have been proclaimed by the wise— those too, O Lord of the World, O you with gracious, wide eyes, [are present].
All of you have been worshipped and praised by me, and likewise saluted;
grant me a boon that bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa.
Those manifestations of yours, O Hari, such as Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others,
which have arisen for the purpose of your worship, are therefore fully dependent upon you.
O Lord of Gods, no distinction exists for you from the perspective of ultimate reality;
that which has been described as your manifold form is merely figurative.
How can a human being speak of duality regarding you who are non-dual?
For you alone, O Hari, are all-pervading, of the nature of consciousness, and stainless.
That which is your supreme form is devoid of both existence and non-existence;
it is untainted, free from qualities, most excellent, immutable, immovable, and eternal.
"O Lord, even the gods do not know that which is liberated from all limiting adjuncts and established as pure existence alone; how then could I know it?"
Furthermore, that form of yours which wears yellow garments, has four arms, holds a conch, a discus, and a mace in its hands, and bears a crown and armlets; // BrP_49.19 //
The gods and others who take refuge in you worship him, who is endowed with the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest and adorned with a forest garland.
O God of gods, best of deities, granter of fearlessness to your devotees!
Protect me, O lotus-petal-eyed one, for I am submerged in the ocean of sense-objects.
O Lord of the World, I see no other to whom I may go for refuge; O Beloved of Kamalā, O Madhusūdana, be gracious to me! BrP_49.22 //
Endowed with hundreds of old age and diseases, oppressed by various sufferings,
possessed of joy and grief, the fool is tightly bound by the snares of karma.
I have fallen into the great, fierce, and terrible ocean of saṃsāra,
which is difficult to cross due to its treacherous waters and teeming with the predatory fish of passion and hatred.
In this [ocean] which is deep with the whirlpools of the senses, crowded with the waves of craving and grief,
without support, without refuge, devoid of essence, and utterly unstable;
Deluded by Māyā there, O Lord, I have wandered for a very long time,
being born again and again among thousands of different species.
O Janārdana, throughout this saṃsāra, I have experienced many thousands and tens of thousands of various births.
The Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs have been studied by me, as well as various treatises,
the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, and numerous arts and crafts.
O Lord of the World, I have experienced dissatisfaction and contentment, accumulation and depletion, expenditure, decline, growth, and that which is neither.
I have witnessed separations and reunions with wives, enemies, friends, and kinsmen;
likewise, I have seen various fathers and mothers.
And sufferings have been experienced, as well as manifold pleasures;
and kinsmen, sons, brothers, and likewise relatives have been obtained.
Likewise, O Lord, I have dwelt within the womb of women, which is slippery with feces and urine;
thus have I experienced great suffering while residing in the womb.
O Hṛṣīkeśa, those many sufferings that exist within the domains of childhood, youth, and old age— indeed, all of them have been experienced by me.
Whatever sufferings exist at the time of death, on the path of Yama, and in the abode of Yama—
those I have experienced, as well as the torments in hell.
Of worms, insects, and trees; of elephants, horses, deer, and birds;
of buffaloes, camels, and cows; and likewise of other forest-dwellers.
Among all the twice-born, as well as among Śūdras in their wombs,
among wealthy Kṣatriyas, and among poor ascetics.
O Lord, I have been born again and again in the houses of kings, royal servants, and other embodied beings.
O Lord, I have repeatedly fallen into the state of servitude among men;
likewise, I have experienced poverty, lordship, and mastery over others.
"I have killed, and others have been killed by me; I have caused to be killed, and likewise others have been caused to be killed.
I have given to others many times, and I have been given to by others many times."
And for the sake of fathers, mothers, friends, brothers, and wives;
and for the wealthy, the Vedic scholars, the poor, and the ascetics.
O Janārdana, having cast aside the various forms of wretchedness and shame among gods, animals, humans, and among both the stationary and the moving, [one attains this state]. (BrP 49.41)
"O Lord, there is no place where I have not gone;
O Master of the World, when was my dwelling in hell, and when was it in heaven?"
Sometimes in the worlds of humans and sometimes among the animal realms,
it is like a water-wheel where a jar is bound by a rope.
It moves upward and downward, and sometimes it remains in the middle;
likewise, O best of gods, I am bound by the rope of karma.
"Moving by means of yoga, I travel below, above, and likewise in the middle;
thus I move within this wheel of saṃsāra, which is Bhairava and hair-raising."
I have wandered for a very long time, yet I never see an end;
O Hari, with my senses overwhelmed, I do not know what I should do today.
Overcome by grief and thirst, bewildered and not knowing where to turn,
I have now come to you for refuge, O Lord, in my agitation.
Save me, O Kṛṣṇa, for I am suffering and submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra;
have mercy, O Lord of the World, if you consider me your devotee.
"Other than you, I have no kinsman who will care for me;
O Lord, having obtained you as my protector, I have no fear anywhere."
O Lord, O God, those lowest of men who do not worship you according to the prescribed rites, whether in life or in death, or even in the pursuit of security and prosperity— [they are lost].
But how could there be a happy rebirth for them from the bondage of saṃsāra?
What is the use of their lineage, conduct, learning, or even life itself?
Those who, having fallen into a demonic nature, do not develop devotion for Keśava, the sustainer of the world, and instead, being deluded, revile you; [they are lost].
They fall again and again into the terrible hell as they are born;
for them, there is no deliverance from that ocean of hell.
O Lord, those of evil conduct and lowest among men who revile you—
wherever my birth may occur due to the bondage of karma, [may they never exist].
O Hari, may there always be firm devotion toward you in every place;
having propitiated you, the gods, the Daityas, humans, and others as well, have become self-controlled.
They have attained supreme perfection; O God, who would not worship you?
O Hari, even the thirty gods, beginning with Brahmā, are unable to praise you.
How can I praise you, who are beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), with a human intellect? Thus, O Lord, have you been praised by me through a state of ignorance.
Therefore, forgive my offense if you have compassion for me;
for the virtuous, O Hari, grant forgiveness even to one who has committed an offense.
Therefore, be gracious, O Lord of Gods, taking refuge in your affection for your devotees;
since you have been praised by me with a mind full of devotion, O God,
may all that [be accomplished] along with its constituent parts— O Vāsudeva, salutations be unto you!
{Brahmā said:} O best of sages, being thus praised by him at that time, the one whose banner is Garuḍa was pleased and granted him everything desired by his mind.
The wise man who, having fully worshipped the Lord of the World, praises Him every day with this hymn, certainly attains liberation.
The wise man who, being pure, recites this supreme hymn at the three junctions of the day,
obtains virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
Whoever should read, or hear, or cause others to hear this with a concentrated mind,
shall go to the eternal world of Viṣṇu, cleansed of all impurities.
This auspicious [teaching] is blessed, it removes sin, and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is secret, very difficult to obtain, and meritorious, and should not be given to just anyone.
One should never give this to an atheist, a fool, an ungrateful person, one who is conceited, one of wicked intellect, or one who lacks devotion.
It should be given to one endowed with devotion, possessed of virtue and good character,
a devotee of Viṣṇu, peaceful, and distinguished by faith and the performance of religious observances.
This is the cause for the destruction of all sins,
known as Compassion; it bestows happiness and liberation,
grants the fruits of every desire, and is most excellent.
This hymn to Puruṣottama has been spoken by me. Those pure ones who constantly meditate upon that most subtle, ancient Person, Murāri, [attain liberation].
Those who possess liberation enter Viṣṇu,
just as clarified butter offered with mantras enters the sacrificial fire;
He is the one God, the destroyer of the suffering of worldly existence.
There is nothing higher than him, nor anything else beyond him;
he is the seer, the protector, and the agent of destruction— Viṣṇu, who is the essence of all things without exception.
Of what use is sacred knowledge, of what use are their own virtues, and of what use are sacrifices, gifts, and fierce austerities for those who possess no devotion here to Kṛṣṇa?
In this world, he who [serves] the Teacher of the World, the bestower of the bliss of liberation, is blessed, he is pure, he is wise; by sacrifices,
by austerities, and by virtues, he is most excellent.
"He is the knower, he is the giver, and he is the speaker of truth—
he who possesses devotion for the one named Puruṣottama.
Brahmā said:
Having thus praised and bowed down to the eternal Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, who bestows the fruits of all desires, those tigers among sages— [continued].
Overcome with anxiety, the protector of the earth spread kusha grass upon the ground and,
having clothed himself and become single-mindedly intent on that, he slept upon the surface of the earth.
"How shall the God of gods, Janārdana, come before my very eyes? How shall that Lord then be the remover of my distress?"—thus he reflected.
While that king was asleep, Vāsudeva, the teacher of the world,
revealed himself bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
With love, he beheld the God of gods, the teacher of the world—
the Lord bearing the conch and the discus, with mace and discus held in his formidable hands.
The god who holds the Śārṅga bow and arrows, whose orb of blazing splendor is like the sun at the end of an aeon, and who resembles blue lapis lazuli.
To him, as he sat upon the shoulder of Suparṇa—auspicious, with eight arms—the wise one said: "Excellent, O King, O high-minded one! (BrP 50.7)
"O protector of the earth, I am pleased with you because of this divine sacrifice, as well as by your devotion and faith; why do you grieve in vain?"
O King, regarding this eternal image which is worshipped by the world,
I shall tell you the means by which it is obtained, O ruler of the earth.
When this night has passed and the stainless sun has risen,
at the edge of the ocean's waters, adorned with various trees—
Likewise,
O King, the vast waters of the salt ocean are seen there at the shore, completely overwhelmed by waves.
For at the edge of the shore stands a great tree, situated both on land and in the waters;
though struck by the tides, that tree does not tremble.
Taking an axe in your hand, go from there into the midst of the ocean;
wandering alone, O King, you will see that tree. (BrP 50.13)
Having observed such a sign, cut it down without hesitation;
for when that tree is being cut, it will present a wondrous sight in the morning.
Having seen it and reflected upon it by that very means, O protector of the earth, fashion that divine image from the sight [of it]; abandon your delusive anxiety.
Brahmā said:
Having spoken thus, the illustrious Hari vanished from sight;
and he too, having beheld the dream, was filled with supreme wonder.
Having observed that night, he remained with his mind fixed upon her,
reciting Vaiṣṇava mantras and hymns dedicated to her.
When the night had passed, he rose with a focused mind;
having bathed properly in the ocean according to the prescribed rite, he then [proceeded].
Having given gifts to the Brahmins, including villages and cities,
and having performed his morning rites, that best of kings departed.
Neither with horse nor foot-soldier, neither with elephant nor charioteer,
did that lord of the earth enter the great ocean shore alone.
He beheld that great tree, a majestic and mighty forest tree, with an exceedingly vast trunk,
holy and truly immense.
Of great height and massive body, it was sleeping near the water,
possessing the dense hue of madder-red, and devoid of name or caste.
O brahmins, at that time the lord of men, filled with joy upon seeing the tree,
felled it with a sharp and sturdy axe.
And Indra’s friend (Agni) became intent on splitting it asunder there;
yet, while the wood was being examined, a wondrous sight appeared.
Then both Viśvakarman and Viṣṇu, those two highly fortunate ones, assuming the forms of Brahmins and equal in their status as twice-born, arrived there.
Then, blazing with their own splendors and adorned with divine garlands and unguents,
the two approached that king, the friend of Indra.
They both said, "O Great King, what will you do here?
And for what purpose, O mighty-armed one, has this lord of the forest been felled? (BrP 50.27)
How indeed was that tree felled while you were alone in a great wilderness, in a desolate and dense forest, and on the bank of a mighty river?
{Brahmā said:} O brahmins, having heard their words, that king was filled with joy and spoke to them words that were both gentle and sweet. BrP_50.29 //
Having seen those two brahmins arrived there like the moon and the sun,
he paid homage to the lords of the world and stood with his face cast downwards.
The king said:
"It is my intention to fashion an image in order to propitiate the God of gods, who is without beginning or end, the infinite Lord of the worlds."
"I was pointed out by the supreme Great-Souled God of gods at the end of a dream, and I have now related it to you both."
Brahmā said:
Having heard the words of the king, who was like Indra himself,
the Lord of the Universe, being pleased, smiled and spoke these words to him.
Viṣṇu said:
"Excellent, excellent, O protector of the earth, that this supreme resolve has been formed by you regarding this terrible ocean of worldly existence, which is like the leaf of a plantain tree."
In this world which is devoid of essence, abounding in suffering, agitated by desire and anger,
turbid with the whirlpools of the senses, difficult to cross, and hair-raising;
In this world which whirls with hundreds of various diseases and resembles a bubble on the water,
it was for the sake of propitiating Viṣṇu that your resolve indeed arose.
Blessed are you, O tiger among kings, adorned with all virtues;
blessed is the earth, along with its subjects, mountains, forests, and groves.
Together with its villages and cities, adorned by the four castes—
therein you, O tiger among kings, shall be the sovereign protector of the subjects.
"Come, come, O highly fortunate one! Stay with us two upon this tree, which is pleasant and cool, engaged in discourses based on the Dharma."
"But this companion of mine has arrived, the best among artisans, equal to Viśvakarman himself, truly skilled in all crafts. He shall fashion the image as I have directed; leave the bank. (BrP 50.40)
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of that twice-born man, the king then left the shore of the ocean and went into his presence.
That best of kings stood in the cool shade of a tree;
then, in the form of a twice-born brahmin, the Soul of the Universe gave him a command.
"O best of Brahmins, have an image made for the chief of artisans—
a supreme form of Kṛṣṇa, profoundly peaceful, with eyes as broad as lotus petals."
He bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, and holds the conch, the discus, and the mace;
his body is fair-limbed with the luster of milk, and he is marked with the second [sign], the Svastika.
The god named Ananta, possessed of great strength and bearing the plow as his weapon,
[was honored] by gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, vidyādharas, and uragas.
For its end is not known; therefore it is remembered as "infinite" (ananta).
[He saw] the sister of Vāsudeva, golden-hued and most beautiful.
And indeed, the third was Subhadrā, who was endowed with all auspicious marks.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of his, Viśvakarman, the performer of noble deeds,
immediately had images endowed with auspicious characteristics fashioned.
First, [he saw him] with the luster of a white color, possessing a radiance like the autumnal moon,
with reddish eyes, a massive body, and a head formidable with its protruding crest.
He was fierce, wearing blue garments, possessed of great strength and arrogant with power,
divine, adorned with a single earring, and bearing a mace and a club.
The second has lotus-eyes, resembles a dark blue cloud,
is like the *atasī* flower, and has long eyes like lotus petals.
[One should meditate upon] Hari, who is clothed in yellow garments, exceedingly fierce, auspicious, marked with the Śrīvatsa,
divine, holding a discus in his hand, and the remover of all sins.
The third [face] has the luster of gold, with eyes as broad as lotus petals;
it is covered with variegated garments and adorned with necklaces and armlets.
Viśvakarman fashioned her, adorned with various ornaments, draped with necklaces of jewels, possessing full and elevated breasts, and truly beautiful.
But that king, having witnessed this wonder, saw in a single moment [beings] created,
covered with pairs of divine garments and adorned with various jewels.

The statues, endowed with all the auspicious marks and exceedingly beautiful, having reached a state of supreme wonder, spoke these words: ||| BrP_50.56 ||| "Endowed with all the auspicious marks, the statues were most enchanting; having attained a state of supreme wonder, they spoke these words. ||| BrP_50.56 |||
Indradyumna said:
"O two gods, why have you both arrived here assuming the forms of brahmins?
You are both performers of wondrous deeds, possessing divine conduct and superhuman power."
Are you two gods or humans, or perhaps yakṣas and vidyādharas? Are you Brahmā and Viṣṇu, or the Vasus, or even the Aśvins?
I do not know whether you two exist as reality or as illusion;
I have come to you for refuge—let my own self be revealed to me.
The Blessed Lord said: "I am neither a god, nor a yakṣa, nor a daitya, nor the king of the gods;
I am neither Brahmā nor Rudra—know me as Puruṣottama."
The remover of the suffering of all worlds, possessing infinite strength and prowess,
he is to be propitiated by all beings, for whom no end is known.
He is recited in all the scriptures, proclaimed in the Vedāntas,
and whom the yogis call Vāsudeva, saying that he is attainable through knowledge.
I alone am Brahmā himself; I am Viṣṇu and I am Śiva as well;
I am Indra, the king of the gods, and Yama, the restrainer of the world.
O King, the elements such as earth and the rest, the three sacrificial fires, the consumer of oblations,
Varuṇa the lord of waters, and I myself am the supporter of the earth, O mountain-dweller.
Whatever consists of speech in the world, the universe of moving and unmoving beings, and whatever exists as the totality of the animate and inanimate— nothing whatsoever exists apart from me.
"I am pleased with you, O best of kings, O observer of noble vows; choose a boon.
Whatever is desired and established in your heart, that I shall grant."
The sight of me does not arise even in a dream for those devoid of merit;
you, however, because of your firm devotion, have seen me directly before your eyes.
{Brahmā said:} O twice-born ones, having heard these words of Vāsudeva,
the king, his body covered in horripilation, sang this hymn of praise. (BrP 51.9)
The King said:
O Beloved of Śrī, homage be unto you! O Lord of Śrī, wearer of yellow garments;
O Giver of Śrī, Lord of Śrī, Abode of Śrī, homage to you, O Sanctuary of Śrī!
I bow down to the primordial Puruṣa, the Lord, the Master of all, whose face is turned in every direction, the partless, supreme, eternal God.
Beyond sound, beyond qualities, devoid of existence and non-existence,
untainted, devoid of attributes, subtle, all-knowing, and the source of all beings.
Resembling a monsoon cloud, devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins,
the protector of all, all-pervading, and present in every state of being.
I bow to the God who bears the conch and the discus, who holds the mace and the club,
the boon-granting Lord whose complexion is like the petal of a blue lotus.
I bow to Hari, Hṛṣīkeśa, who reclines upon the serpent-couch and sleeps upon the ocean of milk, the remover of all sins.
Again I bow to you, the Lord of the gods of gods, the all-pervading bestower of boons,
Viṣṇu, the Lord of all worlds, the imperishable cause of liberation.
Brahmā said:
Having thus praised that god, having prostrated with palms joined in reverence,
he spoke while bowing down and falling upon the surface of the earth.
The king said:
"If you are pleased with me, O Lord, I choose this supreme boon:
that the gods, asuras, along with gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and mahoragas [shall be under my power]."
The Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Sādhyas, Kinnaras, and Guhyakas, as well as those highly fortunate Ṛṣis who are experts in various scriptures; BrP_51.19 //
Wandering mendicants engaged in yoga, those who contemplate the true meaning of the Vedas,
and others who know the path to liberation— all these meditate upon the supreme state.
Through your grace, I desire to attain that state which is devoid of qualities, stainless, and peaceful, which the wise behold, yet which is so difficult to reach.
The Blessed One said:
"May all be well with you; may you obtain everything according to your desire.
By my grace, it shall be exactly as you wish; of this there is no doubt."
O best of kings, rule over a great kingdom for ten thousand and nine hundred years without interruption.
You shall go to that divine state, difficult for even gods and asuras to attain—
fulfilling all desires, peaceful, secret, unmanifest, and imperishable.
Higher than the highest, subtle, untainted, partless, and eternal;
it is completely free from anxiety and sorrow, and devoid of both action and its cause.
Therefore, I shall show you that supreme state called the Knowable,
by attaining which you will reach the highest bliss and the ultimate goal.
And your fame, O Indra among kings, shall endure here upon this earth as long as the clouds are in the sky, and as long as the moon, the sun, and the stars exist.
As long as the seven oceans exist, as long as Mount Meru and the other mountains remain,
and as long as the gods abide in heaven, so long shall it endure everywhere, immutable.
There is a sacred ford named Indradyumna-saras, born from the components of a sacrifice;
by bathing there even once, a person shall attain the world of Śakra.
Whoever shall offer alms-food on this auspicious shore of the lake,
having delivered twenty-one generations of his family, shall go to the world of Śakra.
Honored by apsarases and by the melodic songs of gandharvas,
he shall dwell there in a celestial chariot for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras.
To the south of the lake, situated in the south-western direction, stands a banyan tree; near it is a pavilion.
It was covered with groves of *ketakī* plants, crowded with various trees,
and filled with countless coconut palms, *campaka* trees, and *bakula* trees.
With Aśoka, Karṇikāra, Punnāga, and Nāgakesara trees;
with Pāṭala, Āmrātaka, Sarala, sandalwood, and Devadāru trees.
With nyagrodha, aśvattha, and khadira trees, along with pārijātas and arjunas,
as well as hintālas, tālas, śiṃśapas, and likewise badaras;
It was beautified and adorned with karañjas, lakuca trees, plakṣas, panasa trees, bilvas, dhātukis, and many other kinds of trees.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, under the constellation presided over by the ancestors (Maghā), they will lead us away;
having taken us there, they will indeed remain for seven days.
They shall establish him in the pavilion with beautiful courtesans,
amidst many special diversions, enchanting with dance and song.
Fanning us with yak-tail whisks having golden handles, with fans adorned with jewels,
those auspicious ones will likewise establish us [in our positions].
Brahmacārins, ascetics, and Snātakas— the best of the twice-born—
as well as forest-dwellers, householders, Siddhas, and other Brāhmaṇas.
Furthermore, O King, they will again offer praise to Rāma and Keśava with hymns consisting of various colored words, and with the sounds of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Then, having praised, beheld, and bowed down with devotion,
a person shall dwell for ten thousand divine years in the glorious city of Hari.
Honored by apsarases and by the melodic songs of gandharvas,
that follower of Hari sports there indeed with Keśava.
In a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun, shining with necklaces of jewels,
he dwells in that supreme world, possessing all desires and great enjoyments.
Having returned here from the exhaustion of his merit, that man shall become a Brāhmaṇa;
he will certainly become a glorious lord of ten million in wealth and a master of the four Vedas.
Brahmā said:
O Brahmins, having thus granted him the boon and established the agreement, Hari vanished from sight along with Viśvakarman.
Then that king, thrilled and with the hair on his body standing on end,
considered himself as one who had accomplished his purpose through the sight of Hari.
Then, [he departed] with Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Subhadrā— the bestower of boons—
by means of chariots resembling celestial palaces (vimānas) and adorned with jewels and gold.
Then, having had them massaged amidst the sounds of great auspicious instruments,
the wise king, together with his ministers and his domestic priest, brought them forward.
Having established it in an auspicious, pure, and very beautiful location, amidst the sounds of various musical instruments and the auspicious chanting of the various Vedas.
Then, on an auspicious lunar day, at a favorable time, under a constellation marked by auspicious signs,
and during a propitious moment, he had the consecration performed together with the twice-born.
Having performed everything according to the prescribed method and the ritual seen in the injunctions, with the approval of the preceptor, the lord of the earth—
Then the Lord, having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor according to the rules,
likewise gave wealth to the officiating priests and others in accordance with the prescribed rites.
Having performed the consecration according to the rules in that most excellent palace,
he established them all through the ritual procedures prescribed by the ordinances.
Then, having worshipped him according to the prescribed rite with various fragrant flowers,
gold, gems, pearls, and other such items, as well as various beautiful garments;
With various divine jewels, seats, villages, and towns,
he also gave other territories, cities, and fortresses.
Having thus bestowed many kinds of gifts, having ruled the kingdom as was fitting,
and having performed various sacrifices and given gifts on numerous occasions;
Then the king, having accomplished his purpose and renounced all possessions,
went to that supreme station, the highest abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus, O best of sages, I have related to you this most excellent of kings and the majesty of the sacred field; what else do you wish to hear?
Viṣṇu said:
Having heard these words of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest,
the brahmins considered it a marvel and questioned him again with joy.
The sages said:
"O best of gods, at what time should one go to Puruṣottama?
O Lord, by what rite should the five sacred fords (pañcatīrtha) be performed?"
And tell me, one by one, the specific fruit of bathing and giving gifts at each individual sacred ford (tīrtha), as well as the fruit of beholding the deities.
Brahmā said:
He who, having conquered his senses and subdued his anger, performs penance for seventy thousand years at Kurukṣetra on a single foot while abstaining from food; BrP_51.63 //
Having seen Puruṣottama on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha while observing a fast, one obtains a fruit even greater than that.
Therefore, O best of sages, those brahmins and others who desire the heavenly world must, with great effort and well-restrained senses, behold Puruṣottama during the month of Jyeṣṭha.
Having duly performed the fivefold ablution (pañcatīrtha) in the month of Jyeṣṭha, O best of men,
one should behold that Puruṣottama on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight.
Those who behold the imperishable God, Puruṣottama, on the twelfth day,
reach the world of Viṣṇu and never fall from it again.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, one should go with great effort to Jyeṣṭha;
having performed the five sacred fords (pañcatīrtha) there, Puruṣottama is to be beheld.
Even one who stands at a great distance, if they glorify Puruṣottama with devotion day after day, that pure-souled person shall go to the city of Viṣṇu.
The man who, with faith and a concentrated mind, undertakes a pilgrimage to Kṛṣṇa,
shall be liberated from all sins and go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having seen the discus of Hari situated atop the palace from afar,
a man is suddenly released from sin by bowing down to it with devotion.
Brahmā said:
O best of sages, when the great dissolution had set in during that kalpa,
the sun, the moon, and the wind had perished, and all things mobile and immobile had been destroyed.
When the fierce sun of universal dissolution had risen amidst the roar of thick clouds,
and when trees and mountains were shattered by masses of lightning portents;
And when the world had been destroyed, with all great meteors extinguished, and all waters in the lakes and rivers dried up; ||| BrP_52.3 |||
Then, O twice-born ones, the Saṃvartaka fire, together with the wind,
entered the entire world which was adorned by the suns.
Afterwards, having split the earth and entered the subterranean realm (rasātala),
he produced great terror among the gods, dānavas, and yakṣas.
O tigers among sages, burning the world of the Nagas and whatever else exists here upon the earth, it destroys everything below in an instant.
Then the swift-moving wind and that Saṃvartaka fire burn for thousands and hundreds of twenty-yojana distances.
Then the Lord, fully ablaze, consumes the entire world, including the gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas.
Blazing, he is renowned as the Great Terrible Fire at the End of the Aeon;
possessing great flames and great radiance, he is intensely ignited with a mighty roar.
Resembling ten million suns and blazing as if with splendor,
he swiftly scorched the three worlds, including the gods, asuras, and humans.
In such a state, most terrible and as dreadful as the great dissolution,
the sage, whose soul was supremely devoted to dharma, became intent on the yoga of meditation.
O Brahmins, there remains alone one renowned as Mārkaṇḍeya;
he is bound by the snares of delusion, his senses agitated by hunger and thirst.
O Brahmins, having seen that great fire, his throat, lips, and palate became parched; afflicted by thirst and overwhelmed by fear, he then began to stumble.
Confused and fleeing in all directions, he wandered over the entire earth; finding no protector indeed, he ran hither and thither.
O twice-born ones, he did not find peace anywhere where he might rest; "What shall I do? I do not know whom I should go to for refuge. (BrP 52.15)
"How may I behold that god, the eternal Lord of Men?"—
thus he meditated one-pointedly upon the eternal God.
He attained that divine state, the cause of the great dissolution,
the eternal King of Banyan Trees (Vaṭarāja) known as Puruṣeśa.
In haste, that sage went to the vicinity of the banyan tree;
having reached it, O best of sages, he sat down at its root.
There is no fear of the fire of time there, nor is there a rain of burning coals; there is no arrival of the world-destroying dissolution there, nor likewise any thunderbolt or lightning strike.
Brahmā said:
Then, great clouds resembling herds of elephants, adorned with garlands of lightning and wonderful to behold, rose up in the sky.
Some clouds were dark like blue lotuses, some resembled white water-lilies; some were like the filaments of a lotus, and some were yellow.
Some were greenish in appearance, others resembled the eggs of crows;
some had the luster of lotus petals, and others were like vermilion.
Some have the form of excellent cities, some resemble great mountains;
some are like collyrium, and some possess the luster of emeralds.
Great clouds, their bodies entwined with garlands of lightning, rose up—
formidable in appearance, highly majestic, and resounding with terrible roars.
Then all the clouds completely covered the surface of the sky;
by them, this entire earth, along with its mountains, forests, and mines, was enveloped.
O best of sages, all the quarters were filled and inundated by a flood of water;
then those terrible clouds [discharged] their water, O most excellent of ascetics.
Impelled by the Supreme Lord, they flooded everything,
raining down vast waters and filling the earth.
They extinguished that most terrible, inauspicious, and fierce fire;
thereafter, for twelve years, clouds gathered during the deluge.
Being impelled by that Great-Souled One, the oceans indeed fill themselves with torrents and,
O twice-born ones, then overstep their own shores.
The mountains shattered and the earth sank into the waters;
those great clouds, wandering everywhere, filled the vault of the sky.
Having been enveloped and struck by the force of the wind, they perish;
then, O best of sages, Viṣṇu [encounters] that terrible wind.
O twice-born ones, having drunk [the waters], the god whose seat is the primordial lotus sleeps within that terrible single ocean when all things mobile and immobile have perished.
When the world had perished— devoid of gods, asuras, and humans, and abandoned by yakṣas and rākṣasas—
the sage, having meditated upon Puruṣottama, then rested.
Opening his eyes, he beheld the earth filled with water;
he saw neither that banyan tree, nor the ground, nor the directions and so forth, nor the sun.
In that single, terrible ocean, which had become one mass of darkness and was without refuge, there were neither moon, sun, fire, nor wind, nor gods, asuras, or serpents.
O brahmins, sinking then, he proceeded to swim across;
that distressed sage wandered here and there, wallowing in the water.
O brahmins, he then sank down and found no protector;
seeing him thus distressed, O tigers among sages, the Supreme Person, gratified by his meditation, spoke out of compassion. (BrP 53.18)
The Blessed One said:
"O child, you are weary; you are but a boy, yet you are devoted to me, O observer of noble vows. Come, come quickly to my presence, Mārkaṇḍeya!"
Do not be afraid; you have come before me.
O sage Mārkaṇḍeya, you are steadfast, yet you are but a child, oppressed by fatigue.
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of his, the sage became exceedingly incensed;
O brahmins, he then spoke, and was repeatedly struck with wonder.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Who is this that proclaims his name as if to slight my asceticism,
and as if to challenge my body which has endured many thousands of years?
For such conduct is not even found among the gods;
even Brahmā, the lord of the gods, addresses me as "Long-lived One."
"Who is this ascetic who, having cast off his life today before me, Ghoraśiras,
and calling out 'Mārkaṇḍeya,' desires to go to my death here?"
Brahmā said:
Having spoken thus, O brahmins, the sage then became overcome with anxiety:

As he was reflecting in this way, there arose within him an insight that destroys suffering:
"With devotion, I go for refuge to the God, the Supreme Person."
Having gone for refuge to the god with his mind fixed upon him,
that sage beheld once again that vast banyan tree above the water.
Upon its vast branch, a great and wonderful,
beautiful, divine couch had been fashioned by Viśvakarman out of gold.
It was fashioned from diamond and lapis lazuli, adorned with gems and coral,
graced with rubies and other jewels, and embellished with various precious stones.
It was covered with various carpets, adorned with various jewels,
endowed with various wonders, and graced by a circle of radiance.
Above him stood the god Kṛṣṇa, assuming the form of a child,
resembling ten million suns, blazing and full of splendor.
The god has four arms and beautiful limbs, with eyes as broad as lotus petals;
on his chest is the Śrīvatsa mark, and he holds the conch, the discus, and the mace.
His chest was covered by a forest garland, he wore divine earrings,
his neck was graced with the weight of necklaces, and he was adorned with celestial jewels.
Then, seeing the god, the sage’s eyes blossomed with wonder;
his body bristling with horripilation, he prostrated before the god and spoke as follows.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:

Brahmā said:
Although the great sage knew the past, the present, and the future,
he did not recognize the God at that time, being deluded by His illusory power (māyā).
When he did not perceive him, then, out of distress, he spoke.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"In vain is the power of my asceticism, in vain is my knowledge, in vain are my ritual acts;

I, who do not recognize this divine child sleeping upon the couch.

Brahmā said:
Having entered the belly of that child, that best of sages beheld the entire earth, filled with various provinces.

He beheld Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara,
as well as the regions beginning with Bhārata and all the mountains.
And he beheld Meru, the golden mountain, enriched with all kinds of jewels,
adorned with peaks composed of various gems and possessing many caves.
It was crowded with various holy men, filled with forests of diverse trees,
inhabited by various creatures, and endowed with many wonders.
It was adorned with tigers, lions, boars, yak-tails, buffaloes, elephants, deer,
monkeys, and other creatures, making it exceedingly beautiful.

Himavān, Hemakūṭa, Niṣadha, Gandhamādana,

Kurukṣetra, the Pañcālas, the Matsyas, the Madras along with the Kekayas,

Whatever sacred fords, villages, and cities exist upon the earth, as well as agriculture, cattle-rearing, trade, and likewise buying and selling; [all these are found there].
Śakra and the other preeminent gods, as well as other celestial dwellers,

O best of sages, [he slew] the hosts of Daityas and Dānavas, the Nāgas,

O best of the twice-born, whatever moving or unmoving thing he had previously seen anywhere in this world, he then beheld it all within his belly.
Or rather, what is the use of speaking at length or proclaiming it again and again?
Whatever exists, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, including all that is moving and unmoving—[all this is pervaded by Him].
O best of the twice-born, [he traversed] Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka,

O best of the twice-born, his movement was then unimpeded by the grace of that god, and no loss of memory occurred.
O twice-born ones, while wandering at that time within the belly,
he never reached the end of the body of that Viṣṇu, even though he traversed this entire world.
O brahmins, when he had reached the end of that body,
the sage then sought refuge in that god who grants boons.
Then, O Brahmins, he suddenly emerged with the speed of the wind from the open mouth of that great-souled Puruṣa.
Brahmā said:
O best of sages, having emerged from the belly of that child,

And he beheld that same god as seen before, in the form of a child,
seated upon a lotus posture on a branch of a banyan tree.
The god, whose chest bears the śrīvatsa mark, who wears yellow garments, who has four arms,
and whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals, stands holding the entire world.

to the beloved of Śrī, the self-controlled, the yogi who is contemplated by yogis.
Oṃ, salutations to the one whose form is the Sāman, and to the one who possesses the most excellent sound of the Sāman;
Oṃ, salutations to the one who is gentle through the Sāman, and salutations to the knower of the yoga of the Sāman.
Oṃ, salutations to the Sāman and to the one for whom the Sāman is sung;
salutations to the upholder of the Sāman, to the knower of the Sāma-yajña, and to the creator of the Sāman.
Salutations to the Atharvaśiras; salutations to him whose nature is the Atharva;
let there be salutations to the feet of the Atharva, and salutations also to the hands of the Atharva.
Oṃ, homage to Vajraśīrṣa, the slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha,
who dwells within the waters of the great ocean and who brought forth the Vedas.
Salutations to you whose nature is radiant; salutations indeed to Hṛṣīkeśa.
Salutations to you, the Blessed One; salutations to you, Vāsudeva.
O Nārāyaṇa, salutations to you; salutations to the benefactor of the world!
Oṃ, salutations to the destroyer of delusion and the shatterer of worldly existence!
Salutations and salutations to the bestower of states of existence, and to the remover of bonds;
salutations to the creator of the splendors of the three worlds, who is the very embodiment of splendor.
Salutation to the Lord of Yogins, the pure one, to Rāma, the deliverer,
to the source of happiness, to the one with auspicious eyes, and to the upholder of meritorious deeds.
Salutations indeed to Vāsudeva, who is worthy of worship, to Vāmadeva,
the creator of the bodies of embodied beings, and the destroyer of the sense of duality.
Salutations to you whose body is worshipped by the gods, who wear a divine crown;
salutations to the abode of all latent impressions and to the one who conducts the affairs of the world.
Oṃ, salutations to the maker of wealth and the bestower of the abode of wealth;
salutations to the one whose nature is sacrifice, to the Lord of sacrifice, and to the yogin.
Salutation to the Lord who performs the yoga of asceticism, the bearer of the limbs of sacrifice;
salutation to Saṃkarṣaṇa and to the slayer of Pralamba.
Homage be to you, who possess the speed of a plow-bearer emerging from the resonance of the sound of clouds;
O Narayana, supreme refuge of the wise, homage to your wisdom!
"O Lord, I have no kinsman other than you for crossing over hell;
therefore, O you who are compassionate toward those who bow, I prostrate before you with my whole being."
O Keśava, O Lord of Gods, O Acyuta, there is no one other than you who can cleanse the impurity born of body or mind.
"Having abandoned all associations, I have approached you;
O Keśava, may I have union with you for the sake of attaining my true self."
"Alas, O Keśava, I know this saṃsāra to be a painful calamity difficult to cross;
afflicted by the three types of suffering, I have therefore come to you for refuge."
The entire world is deluded by your illusory power through its various cravings and drawn away by greed and other passions; therefore, I have taken refuge in you.
O Viṣṇu, there is no happiness whatsoever for an embodied being dwelling in saṃsāra;
for in whatever measure the mind is directed toward you, O Lord of Sacrifice, [in that same measure does happiness arise].
In that way, one may obtain absolute happiness devoid of fruit;
yet I am seen to be ruined, empty of discernment, and the world appears afflicted.
O Govinda, save me from saṃsāra;
you ought to uplift me, who am submerged in the flood of delusion within the shoreless ocean of existence.
O lotus-eyed one, there is no other savior to be found but you.
{Brahmā said:} O twice-born ones, having been thus praised by King Śveta in that divine and most excellent sacred field renowned as Puruṣottama, [Brahmā spoke].
Reflecting upon his devotion, Hari, the God of gods and Preceptor of the World,
arrived before the king, surrounded by all the deities.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, with eyes as broad as lotus petals,
the wise one held at the tip of his hand the Sudarśana, its orb blazing.
Resembling the waters of the Ocean of Milk, stainless and like the moon,
the immensely radiant Pāñcajanya shone upon his left hand.
The glorious Lord, whose banner bears the king of birds and who wields the mace, the Śārṅga bow, and the sword, said:
"Excellent, O King, you whose mind is so supreme!
Whatever boon you desire, may it be auspicious for you; I am pleased with you, O sinless one."
{Brahmā said:} Having heard those words of the God of gods, which were like supreme nectar,
Śveta, with his mind fixed upon that, bowed his head and spoke. (BrP 59.78)
Śveta said: "O Blessed One, if I am your devotee, grant me this supreme boon:
the imperishable station of Viṣṇu, situated above even the abode of Brahmā."
O Lord of the World, through your grace, I desire to go to that state which is stainless, free from passion, pure, and devoid of attachment to saṃsāra.
The Blessed Lord said: That delightful, supreme, and stainless state which all the gods, sages, and perfected yogis do not attain— BrP_59.81.
Having partaken of the nectar of sovereignty, you shall go to the supreme abode;
having transcended all worlds, you will go to my world.
O Indra among kings, your fame shall spread here through the three worlds,
and my presence shall always abide right here.
"O Indra among kings, all those gods and dānavas shall sing, 'This is the White Gaṅgā,' and even the water of the White Gaṅgā [shall be known] by the tip of a blade of kuśa grass."
My devotees who are composed in mind shall go to heaven after touching it;
and whoever should go to this image named Mādhava, which possesses the luster of the moon, [shall likewise attain that state].
Having bowed even once with devotion to her who resembles a conch shell or cow’s milk, who destroys all sins without exception, and whose eyes are like lotuses; BrP_59.86.
Having indeed abandoned all worlds, he is honored in my own world;
there, surrounded by celestial maidens, he remains for many Manvantaras.
Being sung to melodiously and attended by Siddhas and Gandharvas,
he enjoys vast pleasures at his will together with my [ancestors].
Having passed away from there and come here, he becomes a human being, a brahmin,
learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, illustrious, possessed of enjoyments, and long-lived.
Rich in elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles, surrounded by wealth and grain, pure,
handsome, highly fortunate, and endowed with sons and grandsons.
Furthermore, having reached Puruṣottama at the foot of the banyan tree by the ocean, one should cast off the body while remembering Hari; thereafter, one shall go to the state of peace.
Brahmā said:
Having beheld Śvetamādhava nearby, [he saw] Matsyamādhava,
who formerly had assumed the form of Rohita in the waters of the single ocean.
Having reflected thoroughly upon the earth situated at the bottom of the netherworld (rasātala) for the purpose of seizing the Vedas, he established himself in that place.
Having bowed down and become prostrate before Mādhava in his form as the Fish, which was his first incarnation, one is liberated from all suffering.
He goes to the supreme abode where the Lord Hari himself resides;
returning here again in due time, he shall become a king upon the surface of the earth.
Having approached Vatsamādhava, a man becomes invincible;
he becomes a donor, an enjoyer, a performer of sacrifices, a devotee of Viṣṇu, and true to his promise.
Having attained union with Hari, one shall thereafter obtain liberation.
This majesty of Matsya-Mādhava has been fully proclaimed by me;
having seen it, O tigers among sages, one shall obtain all desires.
The sages said:
"O Blessed One, we wish to hear about the purification performed in the abode of Varuṇa;
tell us the complete fruit of the bathing, giving of gifts, and other rites performed there."
Brahmā said:
Listen, O tigers among sages, to the ritual procedure for the *mārjana* rite;
by performing it with devotion and a focused mind, one attains supreme merit.
Bathing in the Mārkaṇḍeya lake is praised as being performed during the earlier part of the day;
it especially destroys all sins on the fourteenth lunar day.
In the same way, bathing in the ocean is praised at all times;
especially on the full moon day, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Mārkaṇḍeya, the banyan tree, Kṛṣṇa, the son of Rohiṇī, and the great ocean,
as well as the lake of Indradyumna— this is recorded as the procedure for the five sacred sites (pañcatīrthī).
When the full moon of the month of Jyeṣṭha coincides with the Jyeṣṭhā asterism,
one should especially go to that supreme and most auspicious king of holy places.
Pure in body, speech, and mind, his being is not of another intent;
he is liberated from all dualities, free from passion, and devoid of envy.
Having bathed there at the beautiful Vaṭa tree, which is like a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), one should perform the circumambulation of Janārdana three times with a well-composed mind.
O twice-born ones, by seeing which one is liberated from the sins accumulated over seven births,
and one obtains vast merit as well as a desirable destination.
O Brahmins, I shall declare his names and his measure in each age, according to their respective order in the Kṛta and subsequent ages.
O twice-born ones, Vaṭa, Vaṭeśvara, Kṛṣṇa, and Purāṇapuruṣa—
these are the names of the Banyan tree proclaimed throughout the ages beginning with Kṛta.
One yojana, three-quarters of a yojana, half a yojana, and half of that again—
these are proclaimed as the measurements of the Kalpavṛkṣa tree in the Kṛta and subsequent ages.
Having paid homage to that banyan tree with the aforementioned mantra,
one should proceed facing south for three hundred *dhanvantaras*.
There Viṣṇu is seen at the delightful Gateway to Heaven,
a piece of wood endowed with all excellent qualities, which was drawn forth from the waters of the ocean.
Then, having prostrated before him and honored him again, O sir,
one is liberated from all diseases and the like, as well as from sins, malevolent planets, and so forth.
Having previously seen Ugrasena at Svargadvāra, one should go to the ocean,
perform ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and, being pure, meditate there upon the supreme Nārāyaṇa.
Thereafter, one should assign the eight-syllable mantra— “Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya,” which the wise call *yam*— to both the hands and the body.
What is the use of many mantras that cause the delusion of the mind?
The mantra "Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya" is the accomplisher of all goals.
Because the waters are the offspring of Nara, they are here called "Nārāḥ";
since those waters were formerly the place of Viṣṇu's movement (ayana), he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
The Vedas have Nārāyaṇa as their supreme goal; the twice-born have Nārāyaṇa as their supreme goal;
the sacrifices have Nārāyaṇa as their supreme goal; and all ritual acts have Nārāyaṇa as their supreme goal.
The earth is devoted to Nārāyaṇa; the water is devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
the fire is devoted to Nārāyaṇa; and the sky is devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
The wind is devoted to Nārāyaṇa; the mind is devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
both the ego-sense and the intellect have Nārāyaṇa as their very essence.
Whatever exists— past, present, and future— that which is designated as a living being,
whether gross, subtle, or supreme, all has Nārāyaṇa as its self.
All objects of the senses, beginning with sound, as well as the sense organs, beginning with hearing,
and both primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa)— all these have Nārāyaṇa as their essence.
In water, on land, in the netherworld, in the heavenly realm, in the sky, and on the mountain—
the Lord Nārāyaṇa remains, having pervaded all this.
Moreover, what is the use of saying more here? This entire world, both moving and non-moving, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is entirely of the nature of Nārāyaṇa.
"O twice-born ones, I do not see anything here superior to Nārāyaṇa;
by him all this—visible and invisible, moving and unmoving—is pervaded. (BrP 60.33)
For water is indeed the abode of Viṣṇu, and he alone is the lord of the waters;
therefore, one should always remember Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of sins, within the waters.
Especially at the time of bathing, having approached the water and become pure,
one should remember Nārāyaṇa, meditate upon him, and perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the hands and the body.
One should place the syllable *oṃ* and the syllable *na* on the two thumbs of the hands;
with the remaining [syllables], one should assign them to the fingers beginning with the index finger, extending as far as the palms of the hands.
One should place the syllable Oṃ on the left foot and the syllable Na on the right;
one should place the syllable Mo on the left hip and the syllable Nā on the right.
One should place the syllable *rā* at the region of the navel, the syllable *ya* on the left arm,
the syllable *ṇā* on the right, and place the syllable *ya* upon the head.
Having meditated upon Nārāyaṇa below, above, in the heart, at the sides, behind, and in front, the wise man should thereafter begin the armor-rite (kavaca).
May Govinda protect me in the east, Madhusūdana in the south,
the divine Śrīdhara in the west, and Keśava likewise in the north.
May Viṣṇu protect [the deity] in the southeast, the imperishable Mādhava in the southwest,
Hṛṣīkeśa in the northwest, and Vāmana in the northeast.
May Varāha protect [him] on the surface of the earth, and likewise may Trivikrama protect him above;
having thus performed this armor-rite (kavaca), one should thereafter meditate upon the Self.
"I am the god Nārāyaṇa, the bearer of the conch, the discus, and the mace";
having thus meditated upon oneself as that very self, one should then utter this mantra.
You are Agni, the lord of bipeds, the depositor of seed, and the kindler of desire;
you are the primary principle of all beings, the imperishable master of living souls.
O Lord of the Waters, you are indeed the source of nectar and the womb of the gods;
O King of Tīrthas, take away all my wickedness; homage be unto you!
Having recited thus according to the prescribed rule, one should then perform the bath;
otherwise, O best of the twice-born, bathing there is not commended.
Having performed the consecration and the ritual sprinkling with Vedic mantras,
one should then recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times while submerged within the water.
O Brahmins, just as the horse-sacrifice is a rite that removes all sins,
so too is the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn here the destroyer of all evil.
Having emerged from the water and put on two clean, pure, washed garments,
he should restrain his breath, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and worship the Sun at the twilight devotions.
Then, having cast a handful of flowers and water,
he should perform the ritual attendance (upasthāna) to the Sun with his arms raised, using its specific mantras.
Standing with a concentrated mind, one should recite the purifying goddess Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times, as well as other solar mantras.
Having circumambulated the sun, paid homage, and sat down,
and having performed his private recitation while facing the east, he should offer libations to the deities and the sages.
And the knower of mantras, being well-composed, should duly offer water mixed with sesame seeds to humans, the ancestors, and others by their names and lineages.
Having first performed the libation for the deities with a concentrated mind,
the twice-born becomes qualified thereafter for the libation to the ancestors.
At a śrāddha ceremony and at the time of the fire-oblation (havana), one should offer with a single hand;
however, in the libation (tarpaṇa), one should use both hands—this is the rule that always applies.
With his left hand held back and his right hand [extended],
he should pour water while restrained in speech, saying "May they be satisfied," using the [deceased's] name and lineage.
If one, out of delusion, performs the libation for the ancestors with hairs from the body or sesame seeds,
his ancestors are satisfied by means of skin, flesh, blood, and bone.
One should not perform the libation for the deities and ancestors with sesame seeds that remain on one's limbs;
that water would become blood, and the giver would become a sinner.
O tigers among sages, if water is given on the ground while the giver stands in the water, that gift is in vain; it does not reach anyone.
If a man, standing on dry land, offers water into the water, that water does not reach the ancestors; it is useless.
One should never offer water for libation to the ancestors while still standing in water;
rather, having emerged from the water, one should perform the water-libation (udakatarpaṇa) in a clean place.
Water that is not poured upon the ground does not reach [the ancestors], whether it is in other waters, in vessels, offered while angry, or with only one hand. BrP 60.62.
"O twice-born ones, the earth has been given by me as an imperishable abode for the ancestors;
therefore, one who desires the gratification of the ancestors should give there itself."
Produced upon the surface of the earth, established indeed within the earth,
and returning to dissolution within the earth— therefore, one should offer water upon the earth.

Having spread out those *kuśa* grasses with their tips intact, he should invoke the deities with his own respective mantras upon those whose tips point eastward, and likewise the ancestors upon those whose tips point southward.
Brahmā said:
Having gratified the gods, the ancestors, and others, and having sipped water while restraining his speech,
[he should prepare] a square space measuring one cubit, with four doors, most beautiful.
O Brahmins, having drawn the city on the shore of that great ocean,
one should draw there in its center a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp.
Having thus drawn the mandala, O twice-born ones,
one should worship there the unborn, all-pervading Nārāyaṇa according to the rite of the eight-syllable mantra.
Hereafter, I shall explain the supreme purification of the body:
having meditated upon the syllable *A* in the heart, accompanied by a line of a wheel.
One should contemplate the syllable *rā* upon the crown of the head, blazing with three points, burning away evil,
and situated in the center of the lunar disc.
Raining down white-colored nectar and flooding the earth,
one whose sins have thus been shaken off shall thereafter possess a divine body.
Then the wise one should assign the eight-syllable mantra to himself,
beginning from the left foot and placing it in successive order.
The practitioner should perform the purification of the hands using the five-limbed Vaiṣṇava rite, as well as the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha), with the root mantra.
One should place each letter individually upon the fingers;
one should then place the syllable Oṃ and the white Earth upon the left foot.
The syllable *na*, which is of the nature of Śambhu and dark in color, is situated on the right;
they say the syllable *mo* is Time itself, and one should place it upon the left hip.
The syllable *nā* is the seed of all, situated in the south;
they say the syllable *rā* is fire, situated in the region of the navel.
This letter *ya* belongs to Vāyu and is situated on the left shoulder;
the letter *ṇa* is to be known as all-pervading and is established on the right shoulder.
This letter *ya* is located in the head, wherein the worlds are established.

Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu—this is for the head. Oṃ, obeisance to Jvalana—this is for the crest-lock (śikhā). Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu—this is the armor (kavaca). Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu—this is for the radiating binding of the directions.
Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ—the weapon (astra). Oṃ, Vāsudeva, white in color, is in the head.
Oṃ Āṃ: on the forehead is the red Saṃkarṣaṇa, Garuḍa, fire, splendor, and the sun.
Oṃ Āṃ: on the neck is the yellow Pradyumna, wind, and clouds.
Oṃ Āṃ: in the heart is the black Aniruddha, endowed with all powers.
Having thus manifested himself in four forms, he should then perform his ritual action:
"Viṣṇu stands before me, and Keśava behind;
Govinda is on my right side, and Madhusūdana on my left. (BrP 61.14)
Above is Vaikuṇṭha, and on the surface of the earth is Vārāha;
as for those intermediate directions, Mādhava is present in all of them.
Whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping,
I am indeed composed of Vāsudeva, protected by Narasiṃha.
Having thus become one with Viṣṇu, one should then commence the ritual action;
just as in the body, so too in the deity, one should unite all the principles (tattvas).
Then, one should perform the sprinkling with the syllable Om (praṇava), ending with the word "phaṭ"; this is declared to be auspicious and the remover of all obstacles.
Therein, one should contemplate the mandalas of the Sun, Moon, and Fire;
one should place Viṣṇu in the center of the lotus, as well as those of Wind and Space.
Then, having meditated upon the syllable *oṃ* in his heart as being of the nature of light—
seated upon the pericarp, eternal, and of the nature of light.
Then one should assign the eight-syllable mantra according to the proper sequence; worship performed with that mantra, both individually and collectively, is considered supreme.
One should worship the eternal God with the twelve-syllable mantra;
then, having fixed him in the heart, one should place him externally upon the pericarp.
Having visualized the Great Being with four arms, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
as the eternal form of light through the great yoga,
one should then invoke the mantra in due order within the inconceivable mind.
The invocation mantra:
"May the boon-granting Lord Nārāyaṇa— in the forms of the Fish, the Boar, the Man-lion, and the Dwarf— come before me."
Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, salutations!
The mantra for installation:
Upon this excellent pedestal, here in the pericarp, is a seat fashioned from a lotus.
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, remain here, O Madhusūdana!
Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, salutations!
The mantra for the water offering (argha):
Oṃ, salutations to Viṣṇu, Hṛṣīkeśa, the God of gods, the Lord of the lords of the three worlds.
Oṃ, salutation to Nārāyaṇa; salutation!
The mantra for the water for the feet:
Oṃ, O eternal God Padmanābha, [this is] the water for the feet for your two feet.
O Viṣṇu, whose eyes are like lotus petals, O Madhusūdana, accept [this].
Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, salutations!
The mantra for the honey-mixture (madhuparka):
"O Mahādeva, this honey-mixture has been prepared for you by Brahmā and the other gods."
"O Puruṣottama, accept this which has been offered by me with devotion."
Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, salutations!
{The mantra for the water for sipping:} The white water of the Mandākinī is auspicious and removes all sins.
Please accept this water for sipping, which has been offered by me with devotion.
Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, obeisance!
{The bathing mantra:} You are the waters and you are the earth; you are indeed light and you are the wind.
O Lord of the World, I bathe you with water merely by way of this ritual act.
Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, salutations!
{The mantra for the garment:} O you who are united with the reality of the deity, endowed with the colors of the sacrifice!
O Lord Keśava, these two garments of yours possess a golden-hued luster.
Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, salutations! [This is the mantra for anointing:
O Keśava, I do not know your body nor even your movements.
"The fragrance offered by me has been accepted; please apply it as anointment."
Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, salutations!
{The mantra for the sacred thread:} With the mantras of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, [the thread] was made threefold by the Lotus-born One.
I offer you this sacred thread, joined with the Sāvitrī-knot.
Oṃ, salutation to Nārāyaṇa, salutation! [The Ornament Mantra:
O you who are endowed with divine jewels, whose radiance is equal to fire and the sun!
O Mādhava, may your limbs shine forth adorned with ornaments.
Oṃ, salutation to Nārāyaṇa; salutation!
One should worship with "Oṃ, salutation" for each syllable, or with the entire root mantra.
{The incense mantra:}
This divine incense, the essence of the forest trees, rich in fragrance and sweet-smelling, has been offered by me with devotion; please accept it.
Oṃ, homage to Nārāyaṇa, homage!
{The Lamp Mantra:} His light is equal to the sun and the moon, and likewise to lightning and fire.
O God, you alone are the lamp among all lights; may this [lamp] be accepted.
Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, salutations!
{The mantra for the food offering:} Food of four kinds, endowed with the six flavors, [is offered].
O Keśava, this food offering has been presented by me with devotion unto you.
Oṃ, salutation to Nārāyaṇa, salutation!
One should place Vāsudeva on the eastern petal, Saṃkarṣaṇa on the southern,
Pradyumna on the western, and likewise Aniruddha on the northern.
Likewise, he should place Vārāha in the southeast, Narasiṃha in the southwest,
Mādhava in the northwest, and Trivikrama in the northeast.
Likewise, one should place Garuḍa in front of the eight-syllabled deity;
similarly, one should place the discus on the left side and the conch on the right.
Likewise, one should place the great mace on the right side of the deity;
then, the wise one should place the Śārṅga bow on the left side of the deity.
One should place two divine quivers on the right and a sword on the left;
having stationed Śrī on the right, one should place Puṣṭi on the left.
Then, one should place the forest garland in front, followed by the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha;
and one should assign the heart-mantra and the others to the four directions starting from the east.
Then one should place the weapon of the God of gods in the corner,
as well as Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛta, and Varuṇa.
One should worship Vāyu, Dhanada, Īśāna, Ananta, and Brahmā,
both below and above, with Tantric mantras.
Having thus worshipped Janārdana, the Lord of Gods, who resides within the mandala, a person shall obtain their desired objects; of this there is no doubt.
Whoever beholds Janārdana, worshipped within the maṇḍala according to this very procedure, shall enter the imperishable Viṣṇu.
He by whom Keśava has been worshipped even once according to this rite shall cross over birth, death, and old age, and attain the abode of Viṣṇu.
For one who, unwearied, constantly remembers Nārāyaṇa with devotion day after day, Śvetadvīpa is prepared as his dwelling place.
That name of all the principles (tattvas), which is joined with the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and illuminated by the word *namaḥ* at the end, is designated as a mantra.
By this very procedure, one should present fragrant flowers;
one should perform [this] for each [deity] individually, according to the prescribed sequence.
Then the knower of mantras should bind the mudrās as impelled by the prescribed sequence,
and he should perform the recitation with the root mantra.
Concentrated and according to his capacity, he should perform twenty-eight, eight, one hundred, or likewise one hundred and eight repetitions regarding the objects of desire, as has been prescribed.
The lotus, the conch, the śrīvatsa, the mace, Garuḍa,
the discus, the sword, and the Śārṅga bow— these are proclaimed as the eight mudrās.
{The mantra for dismissal:} Go, go to the supreme abode, O Ancient Puruṣottama,
where Brahmā and the other gods attain the highest state. (BrP 61.56)
Those who do not know the worship of Hari according to the mantras as they have been declared,
let them always worship Acyuta there with the root-mantra (mūlamantra).
Brahmā said:
Having thus worshipped that Puruṣottama according to the rules with devotion,
and having bowed his head, he should afterwards propitiate the Ocean.
O Lord of rivers, you are the life-breath of all beings and their source;
O King of Tīrthas, beloved of Acyuta, salutations to you—protect me!
O twice-born ones, having thus properly bathed in that ocean within that most excellent sacred field,
and having duly worshipped the healthy Nārāyaṇa on the shore, they remained there.
By prostrating before Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Subhadrā, and the ocean,
a person obtains the fruit of a hundred horse-sacrifices.
Completely liberated from all evil and entirely freed from all suffering,
he was as glorious as a celestial being, proud of his beauty and youth.
Having uplifted twenty-one generations of his lineage, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu by means of a celestial chariot, sun-colored and resounding with divine gandharvas.
Having enjoyed excellent pleasures there and sported with the Apsarases for more than a hundred Manvantaras, he remains free from old age and death.
Having come here due to the exhaustion of his merit, he was born into a family endowed with every virtue;
he was handsome, fortunate, illustrious, truthful, and a master of his senses.
A Brahmin who knows the meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras should be a performer of sacrifices and a devotee of Vishnu;
having attained Vaishnava Yoga, he shall thereafter obtain liberation.

During an eclipse of the planets, at the transit of the sun, at the solstices, as well as at the equinoxes, on the anniversaries of the Yugas, at the sixty-fourth day (ṣaḍaśīti), during the Vyatīpāta yoga, and on the day of the loss of a lunar day (dinakṣaya); // BrP_62.10 //
On the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, or Māgha, or on any other auspicious lunar day,
those wise ones who bestow gifts there upon the Brahmins— BrP_62.11 //
Those who offer the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) to their ancestors there according to the prescribed rite obtain a fruit a thousand times greater than that obtained at other sacred fords.
Their ancestors indeed attain inexhaustible satisfaction;
thus has the full fruit of bathing in the ocean been declared by me.
O Brahmins, the fruit of giving and indeed of the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) bestows the fruits of dharma, wealth, and liberation, and it increases longevity, renown, and fame.
It yields the fruits of enjoyment and liberation for men; it is auspicious, the destroyer of evil dreams, meritorious, the remover of all sins, and the bestower of the fruits of all desires.
O best of the twice-born, the Purāṇa must not be spoken to an atheist;
for as long as [the Purāṇa is withheld], the sacred fords continue to roar with their respective greatnesses individually.
O twice-born ones, as long as the majesty of the king of holy places is not described,
Puṣkara and the other sacred sites yield only their own respective fruits.
Furthermore, that king of holy fords bestows the fruits of all holy fords;
whatever holy fords, rivers, and lakes exist upon the surface of the earth, [are present there].
All those [other holy places] enter into the ocean; therefore, it has attained preeminence as the king of all sacred fords (tīrtha), the ocean, the lord of rivers.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, this place is superior to all holy fords and grants all desires; just as darkness comes to an end when the sun has risen.
By bathing in the King of Tīrthas, there is likewise the complete destruction of sin;
a tīrtha equal to the King of Tīrthas has never existed, nor will it ever exist.
O twice-born ones, who is able to describe the virtues of the King of Tīrthas, which is indeed the abode of the Lord Nārāyaṇa?
O twice-born ones, ninety-nine million sacred fords (tīrthas) are indeed located there;
therefore, whatever bathing, giving, fire-offering, recitation,
or worship of the gods is performed there, it becomes inexhaustible.
Brahmā said:
O best of the twice-born, from there one should go to the sacred ford born of the limbs of sacrifice,
named Indradyumna-saras, where that purifying and auspicious lake is situated.
Having gone there, the wise man, being pure, should sip water, meditate upon Hari in his mind, and after performing the ritual worship of the water, he should utter this mantra: BrP_63.2 //
O Tīrtha born from the constituent parts of the Aśvamedha sacrifice, destroyer of all sins!
I perform my ablution in you today; take away my evil. Salutations be unto you!

Having recited thus and bathed according to the prescribed rule, he should satisfy the gods, the sages, the ancestors, and others with water mixed with sesame seeds; then, having sipped water, he should remain silent.
Having offered rice-balls to the ancestors and having worshipped Puruṣottama,
a person obtains the full fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
Having uplifted seven generations of descendants and seven generations of ancestors like a god,
he goes to the world of Viṣṇu by means of a celestial chariot that moves at will.
Having enjoyed pleasant pleasures there for as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure,
he falls from that state and, having come here, certainly attains liberation.
Having thus performed the pilgrimage to the five sacred sites and fasted on the eleventh day,
whoever beholds Puruṣottama on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, [attains the supreme goal].
Having obtained the aforementioned fruit and having sported in the abode of Acyuta,
he goes to the supreme station from which he does not return again.
The sages said:
"O Great-grandfather, O Lord, why do you praise Jyeṣṭha while setting aside the other months beginning with Māgha? Tell us the reason for that."
Brahmā said:
Listen, O tigers among sages; I shall explain in brief why I praise the month of Jyeṣṭha to you again and again.
Whatever sacred fords, rivers, lakes, lotus ponds, tanks, oblong ponds, wells, and pools there are upon the earth—
From the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha onwards, various rivers and oceans always visibly flow toward Puruṣottama for seven days.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, whatever is performed there at that time— such as bathing, giving gifts, or beholding the deity— that becomes inexhaustible.
O best of the twice-born, the tenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha removes ten sins; therefore, it is known as Daśaharā.
The man who, being well-restrained, beholds the plow-bearer Kṛṣṇa and Bhadrā at that [shrine],
shall be liberated from all sins and go to the world of Viṣṇu.
O Brahmins, by beholding Puruṣottama, Rāma, and Subhadrā during either the northern or southern solstice, a man shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having seen Govinda, the Supreme Person,
mounted upon the swing on the full moon day of Phālguna, a man who has become self-restrained shall go to the city of Govinda.
O twice-born ones, when the day of the equinox has arrived, one should perform the Pañcatīrthī according to the prescribed rite, and having seen Saṃkarṣaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, and Bhadrā.
A man obtains the fruit of all sacrifices, which is difficult to attain;
liberated from all sins, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
He who beholds Kṛṣṇa anointed with sandalwood paste on the third day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha goes to the abode of Acyuta.
He who beholds Puruṣottama on the full moon day of Jyeṣṭha when it is conjoined with the Jyeṣṭhā nakṣatra,
having delivered twenty-one generations of his lineage, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Brahmā said:
When the Mahājyaiṣṭhī occurs through the conjunction of the zodiac sign and the lunar mansion,
mortals should then go to Puruṣottama with great effort.
O twice-born ones, having seen Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Bhadrā on the full moon of the month of Jyeṣṭha,
a man obtains the fruit of twelve pilgrimages and even more.
At Prayāga, Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, and Gayā;
at Gaṅgādvāra, Kuśāvarta, and the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
