At Kokāmukha, at Śūkara, at Mathurā, in Marusthala, at Śālagrāma, at Vāyutīrtha, on Mandara, and at the ocean of the Sindhu; BrP_64.4 //
O twice-born ones, [one should visit] Piṇḍāraka, Citrakūṭa, Prabhāsa, Kanakhala,
Śaṅkhoddhāra, Dvārakā, and likewise Badarikāśrama.
At Lohakuṇḍa and at Aśvatīrtha, which liberates one from all sins;
at Kāmālaya, Koṭitīrtha, and likewise at Amarakaṇṭaka.
At Lohārgala, Jambumārga, Somatīrtha, Pṛthūdaka, Utpalāvartaka, Pṛthutuṅga, and Sukubjaka; BrP_64.7 //
O twice-born ones, [these are] Ekāmra, Kedāra, Kāśī, Virajā,
Kālañjara, Gokarṇa, Śrīśaila, and Gandhamādana.
On Mahendra, Malaya, Vindhya, Pāriyātra, and Himālaya;
on Sahya, Śuktimant, Gomanta, and likewise Arbuda.
O twice-born ones, [one obtains merit] at the Gaṅgā, at all the tīrthas on the Yamunā,
at those on the Sarasvatī, at the Gomatī, and at the seven sons of Brahmā.
O twice-born ones, the Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Tuṅgabhadrā, Narmadā, Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, Kāverī, Śiprā, and Carmaṇvatī [are there]. BrP_64.11 //
The Vitastā, the Candrabhāgā, the Śatadrū, the Bāhudā,
as well as the Ṛṣikulyā, the Kumārī, the Vipāśā, and the Dṛṣadvatī.
The Śarayū, the celestial Gaṅgā, the great river Gaṇḍakī,
the Kauśikī, the Karatoyā, the Trisrotā, and the Madhuvāhinī.
There is the great river Vaitaraṇī and those others which have not been mentioned;
or rather, O best of the twice-born, what is the use of speaking at length?
On the earth, in all sacred fords, in all shrines,
and in oceans, mountains, rivers, and lakes;
Whatever fruit is obtained by bathing and giving gifts when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, that same fruit a man obtains by beholding Kṛṣṇa on the day of Mahājyaiṣṭhī.
Therefore, O best of sages, those who desire the fruit of all their wishes should go with every effort to Puruṣottama on the day of Mahājyaiṣṭhī.
Having seen Rāma, the great eldest, along with Kṛṣṇa and Subhadrā,
a man goes to the world of Viṣṇu, having uplifted his entire lineage.
Having enjoyed excellent pleasures there until the dissolution of all beings,
he shall return here upon the exhaustion of his merit and become a twice-born master of the four Vedas.
Devoted to his own duty, peaceful, a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, and having conquered his senses,
one who relies upon Vaiṣṇava yoga shall thereby attain liberation.
The sages said:
"O Lotus-born One, at what time should the bath of Kṛṣṇa be performed, and by what rite? Tell us that, O best among those who know the ritual procedures."
Brahmā said:
Listen, O sages, as I describe the meritorious bathing of Kṛṣṇa,
Rāma, and Subhadrā, which destroys all sins.
O twice-born ones, when the month of Jyeṣṭha has arrived, on the full moon day under the lunar asterism [Jyeṣṭhā],
that is the time for bathing at Hari at all times.
O twice-born ones, there stands a pure and stainless well containing all sacred fords; at that time, Bhogavatī becomes manifest there.
Having prepared a very beautiful couch, adorned with banners, firm and easy to traverse, and decorated with cloths and flowers; BrP_65.6 //
It was spacious, perfumed with incense for the bathing of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
draped with white cloths, and hung with strings of pearl necklaces.
There, O twice-born ones, having placed Kṛṣṇa, who is clad in blue garments, amidst various kinds of musical instruments,
and having seated Subhadrā in the center amidst the sounds of victory and auspiciousness;
O twice-born ones, he was surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of men and women belonging to the brahmin, kṣatriya, vaiśya, and śūdra castes, as well as other classes.
Then householders, graduates, ascetics, and celibate students bathe Kṛṣṇa, who is on the bier along with Balarāma.
Likewise, O best of the twice-born, all the sacred fords mentioned previously bathe him individually with their own waters mixed with flowers.
Thereafter, with the sounds of kettledrums and conchs, the resonances of large drums and clay drums, as well as with trumpets, cymbals, mṛdaṅgas, and jharjharas; ||| BrP_65.12 |||
And with various other musical instruments adorned with the ringing of bells,
with the auspicious sounds of women, and with enchanting words of praise.
With shouts of victory and hymns of praise, accompanied by the sounds of lutes and flutes,
a very great noise was heard, like the roar of the ocean.
With the words of the sages, with Vedic utterances, as well as with other mantra-sounds, and with various meritorious sounds of hymns augmented by the chanting of Sāman verses; ||| BrP_65.15 |||
O best of gods, at the time of bathing, ascetics, those who have completed their Vedic studies, householders, and celibate students praise you with supreme joy.
And with dark-complexioned courtesans, bent down by the weight of their breasts,
wearing yellow and red garments and bending under the weight of their garlands.
Rāma and Keśava were fanned with divine whisks adorned with jeweled handles and golden clusters, and set with precious gems.
Surrounded by yakṣas, vidyādharas, siddhas, kinnaras, and hosts of apsarases, as well as gods, gandharvas, and cāraṇas moving through the sky;
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, and the hosts of Maruts,
as well as the guardians of the worlds and others, praise the Supreme Person.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, O Ancient One, O Supreme Person; O God who effects creation, preservation, and destruction, O Protector of the worlds, O Lord of the universe!
We bow with devotion to that God who sustains the three worlds, who is devoted to Brahman, who is the cause of liberation, and who bestows the fruit of all desires.
Having thus praised Kṛṣṇa, the exceedingly powerful Rāma,
and Subhadrā, O best of sages, the gods then remained stationed in the sky.
The gods and gandharvas sang, and the apsarases danced;
divine instruments were played, and cool breezes blew.
Then the clouds moving through the sky rained down a shower mixed with flowers, while the sages, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas raised shouts of "Victory! (Jaya).
All the gods beginning with Śakra, the sages, the ancestors,
the lords of creatures, the nāgas, and whoever else dwells in heaven.
Then, having taken the substances for the consecration accompanied by auspicious materials and preceded by ritual mantras, the hosts of deities [prepared].
Indra, Viṣṇu of great prowess, as well as the sun and the moon,
Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, and likewise wind and fire.
The wise Pūṣan, Bhaga, Aryaman, Tvaṣṭṛ, Aṃśu, and Vivasvat,
together with his two wives, as well as Mitra and Varuṇa.
The Lord was surrounded by the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas, and the two Aśvins,
together with all the Viśvedevas, Maruts, Sādhyas, and Pitṛs.
By Gandharvas and Apsarases, by Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas,
by innumerable celestial sages (devarṣis), and likewise by the most excellent Brahman-sages (brahmarṣis).
By the Vaikhānasas, the Vālakhilyas, those who subsist on air, those who drink the rays of the sun,
and by the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases, all of whom were thoroughly established in every branch of knowledge.
Surrounded by all the meritorious vidyādharas and those perfected in yoga,
there were the Grandfather (Brahmā), Pulastya, and Pulaha of great austerity.
Aṅgiras, Kaśyapa, Atri, Marīci, Bhṛgu, Kratu, Hara, Pracetas, Manu, and likewise Dakṣa; BrP_65.34 //
O best of the twice-born, the seasons, the planets, the luminaries,
the rivers in embodied form, and the eternal gods were also present.
The oceans and lakes, various sacred fords,
the earth, the sky, the directions, and the trees, O best of the twice-born.
Aditi, the mother of the gods, Hrī, Śrī, Svāhā, Sarasvatī,
Umā, Śacī, Sinīvālī, as well as Anumati and Kuhū.
Rākā and Dhiṣaṇā were the wives, as were the other wives of the celestial dwellers;
and there were Himavat, Vindhya, and Meru with its many peaks.
Airāvata with his followers, as well as the divisions of time known as kalās and kāṣṭhās,
half-months, months, seasons, nights, days, and years.
Uccaiḥśravas, the best of horses; Vāmana, the king of elephants;
Aruṇa and Garuḍa; and the trees together with the medicinal herbs.
The Lord Dharma, the god, arrived together with them all assembled;
and Kāla, Yama, Mṛtyu, and those who were the followers of Yama also came.
And because they are so numerous, the various hosts of deities who have not been mentioned are arriving from here and there for the sake of the god’s consecration.
Then all those brahmins, as well as the gods who dwell in heaven, took up the materials for the consecration and all the auspicious items in their entirety.
O twice-born ones, with golden jars endowed with divine materials, filled with the holy waters of the Sarasvatī and indeed with divine waters; BrP_65.44 //
Standing upon the earth, they bathed Kṛṣṇa, who was joined by Rāma, with water from the celestial Gaṅgā using golden jars filled with flowers.
Likewise, the celestial palaces of the gods move through the sky—
divine, of various heights, moving at will, and stable.
Variegated with divine jewels, they were frequented by throngs of apsaras and adorned on all sides with songs, musical instruments, and banners.
Thus, at that time, O best of sages, having bathed Kṛṣṇa who was united with Rāma, as well as Subhadrā, they praised them, filled with joy.

Victory, victory to you, O Guardian of the World, protector of devotees! Victory, victory to you, who are affectionate toward those who bow before you! Victory, victory to you, whose feet are worshipped by all beings! Victory, victory to you, the primordial God, the cause of many things! Victory, victory to you, O Vāsudeva! Victory, victory to you, the destroyer of the asuras! Victory, victory to you, the divine Fish!
Victory, victory to you, the best among the thirty gods! Victory, victory to you, who recline upon the ocean!
Victory, victory to you, O best of yogis! Victory, victory to you, O sun-eyed one! Victory, victory to you, O king of gods! Victory, victory to you, O enemy of Kaiṭabha!

Victory, victory to you, O supreme Veda! Victory, victory to you, O one in the form of a tortoise! Victory, victory to you, O supreme sacrifice! Victory, victory to you, O lotus-navelled one! Victory, victory to you, O dweller upon the mountain!

Victory, victory to you who recline in yoga! Victory, victory to you, the bearer of speed! Victory, victory to you, whose form is the universe! Victory, victory to you, the wielder of the discus! Victory, victory to you, the lord of beings! Victory, victory to you, the upholder of the earth! Victory, victory to you who recline upon Śeṣa! Victory, victory to you, clad in yellow garments!
Victory, victory to you, beloved of Soma!

Victory, victory to You who dwell in yoga! Victory, victory to You whose face is fire! Victory, victory to You who are the abode of dharma! Victory, victory to You, the treasury of virtues! Victory, victory to You, the abode of Śrī! Victory, victory to You who ride upon Garuḍa! Victory, victory to You, the dwelling place of happiness! Victory, victory to You, the banner of dharma! Victory, victory to You, the refuge of the earth! BrP 65.49.4.
Victory, victory to you of profound conduct! Victory, victory to you accessible to yogis! Victory, victory to you who dwell in the sacrifice! Victory, victory to you known through the Vedas!

Victory, O bringer of peace! Victory, victory to you contemplated by yogis! Victory, victory to you who bestow nourishment! Victory, victory to you, the embodiment of knowledge! Victory, victory to you, the source of the lotus!

Victory, victory to you, O one perceivable through devotion! Victory, victory to you, O granter of liberation! Victory, victory to you, O one of pure body! Victory, victory to you, O abode of all beings!

Victory, victory to you, O one enriched with qualities! Victory, victory to you, O performer of sacrifice! Victory, victory to you, O one devoid of qualities! Victory, victory to you, O granter of emancipation! Victory, victory to you, O refuge of the earth!

Victory, victory to you endowed with splendor! Victory, victory to you, the refuge of the world! Victory, victory to you joined with Lakṣmī! Victory, victory to you, lotus-eyed one! Victory, victory to you, the creator! Victory, victory to you endowed with yoga! Victory, victory to you whose body is dark like the *atasī* flower! Victory, victory to you whose body is immersed in the ocean!
Victory, victory to you, the bee to the lotus of Lakṣmī!

Victory, victory to you who are subject to your devotees! Victory, victory to you, the beloved of the world! Victory, victory to you, the supremely peaceful one! Victory, victory to you, the supreme essence!
Victory, victory to you, the wielder of the discus! Victory, victory to you, endowed with enjoyments! Victory, victory to you, clad in blue garments! Victory, victory to you, the bringer of peace!
Victory, victory to you, the bringer of liberation! Victory, victory to you, the remover of impurity!
Victory to you, O Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the World! Victory to you, younger brother of Saṃkarṣaṇa!
Victory to you, whose eyes are like lotus petals! Victory to you, the bestower of the fruits of all desires!
Victory to you, whose chest is adorned with a garland; victory to you, the wielder of the discus and the mace;
victory to you, the beloved of Padmālayā; victory to you, O Viṣṇu—homage be unto you!
{Brahmā said:} Having thus offered praise, the gods headed by Śakra, with joyful minds,
as well as the hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas and others who dwell in heaven, [remained there].
And the Vālakhilya sages, those best of seers, having prostrated before Kṛṣṇa who was joined with Rāma, as well as Subhadrā, remained stationed in the sky.
Having seen, praised, and paid homage to Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Subhadrā, those dwellers of the third heaven then departed for their respective abodes.
Then the celestial palaces of the gods, both high and low, divine, moving at will, and stable, traveled through the sky.
Variegated with divine jewels and frequented by hosts of apsarases,
they were adorned on all sides with songs, musical instruments, and banners.
At that time, those mortals who behold Puruṣottama,
Balabhadra, and Subhadrā, go to the imperishable state.
Having seen the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) seated upon his couch together with Subhadrā and Rāma, one goes to the state free from affliction; of this there is no doubt.

O best of sages, that fruit which is remembered as resulting from the gift of a hundred tawny cows at Puṣkara, a man who performs auspicious deeds obtains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa on his bed with Sātyaki and Subhadrā.
Whatever fruit is declared to result from the gift of a hundred maidens,
a man obtains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa seated upon the couch.
Whatever fruit is remembered as resulting from the gift of a hundred gold *niṣkas*,
a man obtains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa upon his bed.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed to result from the gift of a thousand cows,
a man obtains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa seated upon the couch.
Whatever fruit is declared to result from the ritual gift of land,
a man obtains that same fruit simply by beholding Kṛṣṇa seated upon the couch.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed for the gift of food and for the hospitable reception of guests,
a man obtains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa seated upon the couch.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed to be obtained through the ritual release of a bull according to the rules,
a man obtains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa seated upon the couch.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed for the gift of water during the summer or at other times,
a man obtains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa seated upon the couch.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed to result from the gift of a sesame-cow,
a man obtains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa seated upon the couch.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed to result from the gift of elephants, horses, and chariots,
a man obtains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa seated upon his couch.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed to result from the gift of a cow with golden horns,
a man obtains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa seated upon the couch.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed to result from the gift of a water-cow,
a man obtains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa seated upon the couch.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed to result from the gift of a cow filled with ghee,
a man obtains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa seated upon the couch.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed to be obtained by performing the Cāndrāyaṇa penance,
a man obtains that same fruit simply by beholding Kṛṣṇa seated upon his couch.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed to be obtained through month-long fasts performed according to rule,
a man obtains that same fruit simply by beholding Kṛṣṇa upon his bed.
Now, O best of the twice-born, what is the use of speaking at length or repeating it again and again? Such is the majesty of that deity while situated upon the couch.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed for all sacred fords through vows and gifts,
that fruit is obtained by beholding Kṛṣṇa on his palanquin together with Halāyudha.
O best of sages, a man who performs auspicious deeds attains Subhadrā;
therefore, whether a man or a woman, one should behold that Puruṣottama.
Then, one obtains the fruit of bathing and other rites at all sacred fords;
by the water remaining from Kṛṣṇa’s own bath, one sprinkles oneself.
A barren woman, one whose children have died, one who is unfortunate, one afflicted by planetary influences, one seized by Rākṣasas and the like, or those overwhelmed by diseases; BrP_65.78 //
Immediately consecrated with the water remaining from their bath,
they obtain all desired objects, whatever cherished things they may wish for.
One desiring a son shall obtain sons; one desiring happiness shall obtain good fortune;
one afflicted by disease shall be freed from disease; and one longing for wealth shall obtain wealth.
Whatever meritorious waters exist upon the surface of the earth,
they do not equal even a sixteenth part of the water remaining after his bath.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, one should sprinkle one's limbs with that water which remains after Kṛṣṇa’s bath; for it bestows all desires.
Those who behold Kṛṣṇa after he has bathed and as he proceeds facing the south are liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt.
O Kṛṣṇa, by beholding You walking while facing south, a man obtains that fruit which is proclaimed in the scriptures as resulting from three circumambulations of the earth.
Whatever fruit of pilgrimage on earth has been proclaimed,
a man obtains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa facing the south.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed for beholding Nara and Nārāyaṇa at Badarī,
a man obtains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa facing the south.
Whatever fruit is obtained by bathing and giving gifts at Gaṅgādvāra and Kurukṣetra,
a man obtains that same fruit simply by beholding Kṛṣṇa facing southward.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed to be gained at Prayāga on the great Māghī day,
a man obtains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa facing the south.
Whatever fruit is obtained by bathing and giving gifts at Śālagrāma during the Mahācaitrī festival,
a man obtains that same fruit simply by beholding Kṛṣṇa facing the south.
O Kṛṣṇa, by beholding you facing southward, a man obtains that same fruit which is traditionally said to be gained at Puṣkara on the great full moon day of Kārttika.
O Kṛṣṇa, whatever fruit a man obtains by bathing and giving gifts at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, he obtains that same fruit simply by seeing Kṛṣṇa facing southward.
Whatever fruit is obtained by bathing and giving gifts at Kurukṣetra when the sun is eclipsed,
a man obtains that same fruit simply by seeing Kṛṣṇa facing the south.
O twice-born ones, [one obtains the same merit] at the Gaṅgā, at all the tīrthas along the Yamunā,
at the tīrthas of the Sarasvatī, and likewise at other lakes.
Whatever fruit is declared to result from bathing and giving gifts performed according to the rules,
a man obtains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa facing the south.
And also at Puṣkara, at the sacred fords of Gayā and Amarakaṇṭaka,
at the holy sites such as Naimiṣa, and in sacred fields and shrines.
O Kṛṣṇa, whatever fruit a man obtains by bathing and giving gifts when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, that same fruit he obtains by beholding you facing the south.
Now, what is the use of speaking further again and again? Whatever fruit of meritorious action has been described here [is the result].
O best of the twice-born, [this has been declared] by the wise in the Vedas, the Śāstras, the Purāṇas, the Mahābhārata,
in all the Dharmaśāstras, and likewise elsewhere.
Having seen Kṛṣṇa together with Sahalāyudha, Bhadra, and his entire retinue proceeding toward the south, a person shall obtain that same fruit.
Brahmā said:
Those who behold Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma, and Subhadrā seated upon the chariot as they proceed to the Guḍivā pavilion, go to the abode of Hari.
Those who then behold Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma, and Subhadrā staying in the pavilion for seven days go to the world of Viṣṇu.
The sages said:
"O Lord of the World, by whom was that pilgrimage in the south established?
And what fruit is obtained there by men? Please tell us."
For what purpose, O Lord of the World, did you go to the bank of that lake, to that pure and solitary place, and there into the pavilion belonging to that king?
Kṛṣṇa, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and Subhadrā, having completely abandoned their own abode, indeed dwell for seven nights with you in this chariot.
Brahmā said: O brahmins, in former times Hari was indeed entreated by Indradyumna, saying,
"May my festival take place for seven days on the shore of this lake."
"O Lord of Gods, [the place] named Guḍivā bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
To him, indeed, that Puruṣottama granted a boon.
The Blessed One said:
"O King, for seven days on the shore of your lake,
there shall be my festival named Guḍivā, which bestows the fruits of all desires."
O King, Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, and Śūdras indeed [should worship] with flowers,
perfumes, incense, lamps, and excellent food offerings.
With various kinds of offerings, prostrations, and circumambulations;
with shouts of "Victory!", as well as hymns, songs, and enchanting musical instruments.
O best of kings, by my grace there will be no fruit whatsoever that they desire which shall not be attained; of this there is no doubt. (BrP 66.12)
Brahmā said:
Having spoken thus to him, the god vanished right there;
and that illustrious, best of kings then felt his purpose was fulfilled.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, with every effort one should behold that Supreme Person, the God who grants all desires, at Guḍivā.
One without a son obtains sons; one without wealth obtains wealth;
the sick are freed from disease; and a maiden finds a virtuous husband.
A man obtains longevity, renown, fame, intelligence, strength, knowledge, fortitude, cattle, progeny, and the perfection of beauty and youth.
Whatever enjoyments a man or even a woman desires upon seeing that Supreme Person, they obtain them all without a doubt.
Having performed the pilgrimage known as Guḍī according to the rules and with a well-composed mind,
whether it be a man or even a woman, during the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha—
O best of the twice-born, having seen Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Subhadrā,
one obtains the fruit of fifteen horse-sacrifices and even more.
Having uplifted seven generations of descendants and seven generations of ancestors from his own lineage,
he shall travel in a celestial chariot that moves at will and is adorned with every kind of jewel.
Served by Gandharvas and Apsarases according to his merit,
that handsome, fortunate, and heroic man shall go to the city of Viṣṇu.
There, having enjoyed excellent pleasures until the dissolution of all beings,
his self fulfilled with every desire, he is exempt from old age and death.
Having returned here due to the exhaustion of his merit, he shall become a twice-born master of the four Vedas;
then, by resorting to Vaiṣṇava yoga, he shall attain liberation.
The sages said:
"Tell us separately the fruit of each individual pilgrimage—
that which a man, or a self-controlled woman, obtains by performing it there."
Brahmā said:
O Brahmins, listen as I describe the fruit of the return-journey (pratiyātrā),
which a man who is well-restrained obtains by performing it in that sacred field.
Likewise, on the full moon of Phālguna, at the equinox, and at the rising of the sun,
having performed the pilgrimage according to the prescribed rite, and having beheld Kṛṣṇa and bowed down to him—
One who visits Saṃkarṣaṇa and Subhadrā shall indeed obtain the fruit everywhere;
such a person shall go to the world of Viṣṇu for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
As long as a man performs the pilgrimage in the month of Jyeṣṭha according to the prescribed rites, for that long he enjoys happiness in the world of Viṣṇu for an eon; of this there is no doubt.
In that most excellent, meritorious, and beautiful field, Śrī Puruṣottama,
which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men and brings happiness to all living beings.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, a man or a woman who has controlled their senses, being composed, should undertake the pilgrimage according to the prescribed injunctions for twelve years.
He who performs the consecration, free from deceit and hypocrisy,
shall enjoy various pleasures and, at the end, will certainly attain liberation.
The sages said:
"O God, we wish to hear from you as you speak of the installation [of the image],
the ritual procedure, the worship, the gifts, and the fruit thereof for the Lord of the World."
Brahmā said:
Listen, O tigers among sages, to the installation rite as enjoined by the sacred law,
performing which with devotion a man or a woman obtains the fruit.
O best of the twice-born, when the twelve-year pilgrimage is completed,
one should then perform, according to the rules, the sin-destroying consecration.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the bright fortnight, on the eleventh day, being composed,
having gone to a sacred body of water, and having sipped water for purification, one should remain restrained and pure.
Having invoked all the sacred fords (tīrthas) and likewise meditated upon Nārāyaṇa,
one should then perform the ritual bath according to the rules with a well-concentrated mind.
Whatever procedure has been prescribed by the sages for the act of bathing,
by that very rule is his bathing ordained.
Having bathed according to the proper ritual procedure, he who knows the rules for names and lineages should then satisfy the gods, the sages, the ancestors, and others with libations.
Having crossed over and put on two clean, stainless washed garments,
he should then perform the ritual sipping of water according to the rules while facing the sun.
One should mentally recite one hundred and eight times the purifying goddess Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas, who is meritorious and the remover of all sins.
Then, with faith and well-composed mind, having performed three circumambulations clockwise, he should bow down to the Sun and recite meritorious solar mantras.
For the three [upper] castes, bathing and the recitation of mantras as declared in the Vedas are prescribed;
for women and Śūdras, bathing and recitation are performed excluding the Vedic rites.
Then, remaining silent, he should go home and worship Puruṣottama,
having washed his hands and feet and performed the ritual sipping of water according to the rules.
One should bathe the deity with ghee, immediately thereafter with milk,
and likewise with honey, fragrant water, and water from sacred bathing-places mixed with sandalwood.
Then, with devotion, one should clothe him in a pair of excellent garments and anoint him with sandalwood, agalloch, camphor, and saffron.
One should worship Puruṣottama with supreme devotion using lotuses,
and one should honor him with other Vaiṣṇava flowers such as jasmine and the like.
Having thus worshipped Hari, the Lord of the World who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
one should burn incense mixed with agallochum (aguru) before the God.
O best of sages, one should burn fragrant guggulu resin;
and with devotion, according to one's ability, one should indeed light a lamp with ghee.
Furthermore, O best of sages, one who is composed should offer twelve other lamps,
using either ghee or sesame oil.

For the food offering (naivedya), one should present milk-rice (pāyasa), cakes (apūpa), fried pastries (śaṣkulī), and dumplings (vaṭaka), as well as sweetmeats (modaka), molasses (phāṇita) in small quantity, and fruits.
Having thus worshipped Puruṣottama with the fivefold offerings,
one should mutter the mantra "Obeisance to Puruṣottama" one hundred and eight times.
Then, with devotion, one should propitiate that God, the Supreme Person:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of all worlds, bestower of fearlessness upon your devotees! (BrP 67.29)
O Supreme Person, save me who am submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra;
O Lord of the World, those twelve processions which were performed by me for you—BrP_67.30.
"O Govinda, by your grace, may those [desires] of mine be fulfilled.
Having thus propitiated that god and prostrated himself like a staff, he spoke.
Then one should worship the Guru with devotion using flowers, garments, and ointments;
for, O best of sages, no difference exists between these two.
O best of sages, with faith and well-composed mind, one should construct a variegated pavilion of flowers above the deity using various kinds of blossoms.
Having made this resolution, he should thereafter keep watch during the night;
he should also have stories of Vāsudeva and songs sung.
Meditating upon, reciting, and praising the God, the wise man should pass the night;
then, at the clear dawn of the twelfth day (dvādaśī), he should perform twelve [rites].
One should invite Brahmins who have bathed after their vows, who have mastered the Vedas,
who are learned in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, who are well-versed in the scriptures, and whose senses are restrained.
Having bathed according to the proper rite, wearing clean garments and with his senses subdued,
he should bathe Puruṣottama there as before and worship Him.
With perfumes, flowers, offerings, food oblations, and likewise with lamps, with manifold services, prostrations, and circumambulations; BrP_67.38 //
Having thus worshipped the Lord of the World with recitations, hymns, prostrations, and captivating songs and instrumental music, one should then worship the Brahmins.
Endowed with faith and devotion, he should give them twelve cows, as well as gold, an umbrella, and a pair of sandals.
O twice-born ones, one should give them gifts such as clothing and other requisites with devotion,
for Govinda is truly pleased when worshipped with a sincere heart.
Then, with devotion, he should give to the teacher a cow, clothing, gold, as well as an umbrella,
a pair of sandals, and another vessel made of bell-metal.
Then one should feed those Brahmins food beginning with milk-rice (pāyasa),
as well as cooked grains, various kinds of eatables and foods, accompanied by molasses and clarified butter.
Then, once those Brahmins have been satisfied with food and are of tranquil mind,
one should give them twelve water-pots, each filled with water.
And one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to them according to one's ability, free from envy;
and one should present both the water-pot and the sacrificial fee to the preceptor (ācārya).
O best of the twice-born, having thus honored those brahmins, one should worship with supreme devotion the preceptor who imparts knowledge, regarding him as equal to Viṣṇu.
Having honored him with gold, garments, cows, grain, and other excellent articles, and having paid homage to him, the wise man should recite this mantra: BrP_67.47 //
May the Lord of the Universe, the all-pervading one who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace—
the God who is without beginning or end, the Supreme Person— be pleased.
Having uttered this, and having circumambulated the Brahmins three times,
he should then respectfully bow his head to the preceptor and bid him farewell.
Then, one should follow those brahmins with devotion as far as the boundary;
having followed them all and paid homage, one should turn back.
Then, accompanied by his kinsmen and relatives, he should eat while remaining restrained in speech,
along with other humble lay-devotees and mendicants who are desirous of food.
By acting thus correctly, a man or a woman obtains the fruit of thousands of horse-sacrifices and a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices.
O Brahmins, having taken with him a hundred ancestors and a hundred future descendants, that best of men,
possessing a divine form, shall go to heaven.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, adorned with every ornament,
his self fulfilled in all desires, he was like a god, free from all affliction.
Endowed with beauty and youth, adorned with all virtues, being praised by the Apsarases, and graced by the Gandharvas; ||| BrP_67.55 |||
Adorned with all kinds of jewels, he shall travel in a celestial chariot that is sun-bright, moves at will, is stable, and is equipped with banners and flags.
Illuminating all directions in the sky, free from fatigue,
that youth— possessed of great strength and wisdom— goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
There, for as long as a hundred kalpas, he enjoys desired pleasures together with perfected beings,
apsarases, gandharvas, gods, vidyādharas, and uragas.
Being praised by the best of sages, he remains free from all feverish distress,
like the Lord of the World, the God who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Likewise, O brahmins, that delighted one, having assumed a four-armed form,
enjoyed excellent pleasures there and sported together with the gods.
At the end of that [time], he comes to the abode of Brahmā, which grants all desires and is adorned by perfected *vidyādharas*, gods, and *kiṃnaras*.
O best of Brahmins, having enjoyed happiness there for ninety kalpas,
that man returns from that place which bestows the fruits of all desires.
The world of Rudra, frequented by hosts of gods and bestowing happiness and liberation,
is adorned with many hundreds of thousands of celestial chariots.
Adorned by accomplished Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, Daityas, and Dānavas,
a man enjoys happiness there for the duration of eighty kalpas.
At the end of that, he goes to Goloka, which is endowed with all enjoyments,
beautified by gods, siddhas, and apsarases, and is exceedingly enchanting.
There, having enjoyed unsurpassed pleasures for seventy kalpas—
pleasures difficult to find in the three worlds— he remains with a steady mind like an immortal.
Therefore, he comes to the unsurpassed world of Prajāpati,
surrounded by Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, Munis, and Vidyādharas.
Having joyfully enjoyed various kinds of pleasures there for sixty kalpas, at the end of that time he reaches the abode of Śakra, which is endowed with many wonders.
Surrounded by Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Siddhas, gods, Vidyādharas, and Uragas,
as well as Guhyakas, Apsarases, Sādhyas, and other supreme deities.
Having come there and enjoyed happiness for fifty kalpas,
that man then goes to the world of the gods, adorned with celestial chariots.
Having enjoyed exceedingly rare pleasures for forty kalpas,
he then comes to the world called Nakṣatra, which is very difficult to attain.
Thereafter, O best of the twice-born, he enjoys excellent enjoyments as he desires for thirty kalpas; from there, he returns to the world of Śaśāṅka.
Where that Soma dwells, adorned by all the gods,
there he enjoys exceedingly rare pleasures for twenty kalpas.
From there, he goes to the world of Āditya, which is honored by the gods,
filled with various wonders, meritorious, and frequented by Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Having enjoyed auspicious pleasures there for ten kalpas, O best of the twice-born,
he comes from there to the world of the Gandharvas, which is very difficult to attain.
Having enjoyed all pleasures there for one kalpa at his ease, he returns to the earth and becomes a righteous king.
The universal monarch, possessed of great heroism and adorned with all virtues,
having ruled his kingdom according to his own dharma and performed sacrifices with excellent sacrificial fees, [attained this state].
At the end of that, having gone to the auspicious world of the yogins which bestows liberation,
he shall enjoy excellent pleasures there until the dissolution of all beings.
Therefore, O Brahmins, he comes here and is born into a preeminent family of Vaiṣṇava yogins, which is difficult to attain and esteemed by the virtuous.

An excellent Brahmin learned in the four Vedas, having performed sacrifices accompanied by the distribution of sacrificial fees and having resorted to the Vaiṣṇava yoga, shall thereafter attain liberation.
Thus, O Brahmins, the fruit of this pilgrimage has been correctly described by me, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men; what else do you wish to hear?
The sages said:
"O Lord, we wish to hear about the world of Viṣṇu, which is free from suffering,
a source of joy for the worlds, beautiful, and endowed with every wonder."
O Lord, by what action do those devoted to dharma attain the lifespan, enjoyment, splendor, and strength of that world? BrP_68.2 //

Tell us in detail and according to the truth whether [liberation comes] from seeing [the deity], or from touching [it], or even by bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha) and so forth; for our curiosity is indeed great.
Brahmā said:
Listen, all you sages, to that which is the supreme, highest state—
the auspicious, meritorious desire of devotees, which brings about the destruction of saṃsāra.
As I speak of that which is the most excellent for all the worlds, known by the name of Viṣṇu—
a meritorious site consisting of every wonder and worshipped by the three worlds— listen.
With Aśoka trees, Pārijātas, Mandāras, and Campaka trees;
with Mālatī, Mallikā, and Kunda, as well as Bakulas and Nāgakesaras.
With *puṃnāga*, *atimukta*, *priyaṅgu*, *tagara*, and *arjuna* trees; with *pāṭala*, mango, and *khadira* trees, radiant with groves of *karṇikāra*.
With orange trees, jackfruit trees, *lodhra* trees, neem, pomegranates, and *sarjaka*;
with grapevines, *lakucha*, dates, *madhuka*, and trees bearing excellent fruits.
With wood-apples, coconuts, palmyra palms, and bilva fruits, with countless kalpa-trees and other beautiful wild trees; BrP_68.9 //
With straight-sounding *candana* trees, *nīpa*s, auspicious *devadāru* and *añjana* trees, and with *jātī*, cloves, and *kaṅkola* trees, all permeated with the fragrance of camphor; ||| BrP_68.10 |||
With heaps of betel leaves, as well as areca-nut trees and various other trees adorned with fruit in every season.
With various kinds of flowers arising from clusters of creepers, with various meritorious reservoirs of water, and with the excellent songs of various birds; ||| BrP_68.12 |||
With hundreds of charming oblong ponds filled with water, and with white water-lilies, blue lotuses, and excellent red lotuses; 68.13.
With lovely red and blue lotuses, fragrant white water-lilies, and other beautiful aquatic flowers of various colors; ||| BrP_68.14 |||
It was filled with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, adorned with ruddy geese,
and crowded with *koyaṣṭika* birds, *dātyūha* cranes, and excellent *kāraṇḍava* ducks.
With cātaka birds, with their dear young ones, with species of jīvañjīvaka birds, and with other divine water-dwelling creatures whose songs were sweet during their play; ||| BrP_68.16 |||
Thus it was adorned with various kinds of divine trees and meritorious water-bodies, endowed with many wonders and exceedingly beautiful.
There, with celestial chariots adorned with various jewels, moving at will, golden and brilliant, and resounding with divine gandharvas; ||| BrP_68.18 |||
Adorned by Apsarases who resemble the rising sun,
they are provided with golden beds and seats and endowed with various objects of enjoyment.
With celestial beings bearing banners, adorned with hanging strings of pearls,
of various colors, innumerable, and clad in garments of gold;
Rich with the fragrances of various flowers, adorned with sandalwood and agallochum,
they were filled with pleasant movements and the sounds of various musical instruments.
And with [vehicles] equal to the wind of the mind, crowded with clusters of tinkling bells,
they roam in that city of Viṣṇu, which is honored by the world.
It was constantly frequented by various women, such as Gandharvas and Apsarases—
lovely ladies with moon-like faces who were most enchanting.
On all sides were women with full and elevated breasts, slender waists,
complexions ranging from dark to fair, and the gait of elephants in rut.
Surrounding that best of men, those women fanned him with whisks having golden handles,
adorned with various jewels.
With songs, dances, and instrumental music, the yakṣas, vidyādharas, siddhas, gandharvas, and hosts of apsaras rejoiced, languid with intoxication.
And with hosts of gods and sages, that best of worlds shone;
having reached it, the wise obtain great enjoyments.
Near the king of banyan trees, on the shore of the southern ocean,
those by whom the blessed Kṛṣṇa— the lotus-eyed Lord of the World— was beheld.
They sport together with the Apsarases as long as the heavens endure with the moon and stars,
resembling molten gold and free from old age and death.
Devoid of all suffering and free from the exhaustion of craving,
they have four arms, possess great heroism, and are adorned with garlands of forest flowers.
Adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark and bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
some were dark as blue lotuses, while others resembled gold.
Some resemble emeralds, some are like lapis lazuli;
others are dark-complexioned and wear earrings, while yet others are like diamonds.
O best of the twice-born, the worlds of all the gods do not shine as brightly as the world of Hari,
which is endowed with every wonder.
O twice-born ones, because of the power of that deity, there is no returning from that place again until the dissolution of all beings.
Proud of their beauty and youth, they wander about in that divine city;
there, in the presence of Puruṣottama, they behold Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Subhadrā.
In the center of the city shines the temple of Hari, adorned with jewels, resembling molten gold and like the rising sun.
It was adorned with hundreds of thousands of banners,
ten thousand yojanas in extent, and encircled by a golden wall.
With various colored, variegated, and beautifully fashioned banners,
it shines like the autumnal moon together with the stars.
It had four wide gates, was well-guarded by chamberlains,
possessed seven surrounding walls, and was magnificent and enchanting.
The first there is made of gold; the second is joined with emeralds;
the third is of sapphire, and after that, of great-blue gemstone.
The fifth city is radiant and made of rubies;
the sixth, O brahmins, is made of diamond; and the seventh city is made of lapis lazuli.
That great palace shines with pillars made of various jewels, adorned with sprouts of gold and coral, appearing truly marvelous.
And there the perfected ones (siddhas) are seen, illuminating the ten directions,
like the moon shining with its constellations on the night of the full moon.
There the Blessed One, Janārdana, together with Lakṣmī, ascended;
he was dark-complexioned, clad in yellow garments, and marked with the Śrīvatsa sign.
Hari held in his right hand the blazing Sudarśana discus, the terrible leader of all weapons, which consists entirely of splendor.
Taking that [discus], which resembled a jasmine flower, silver, or a conch shell, and was like a pearl necklace or cow’s milk,
Keśava held it in his left hand, O best of sages.
By the sound of which the entire world is thrown into agitation—
that [conch] renowned as Pāñcajanya, adorned with a thousand coils— [is held by him].
She brings an end to evil deeds, she is fierce, the destroyer of Daityas and Dānavas;
she has the form of a blazing flame of fire, unbearable even for the gods.
He held the Kaumodakī mace in his right hand,
while in his left, the Śārṅga bow, radiant as the sun, gleamed.
With his excellent arrows, which resemble the sun and are wreathed in flames,
that god destroys the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
The glorious one who brings joy to all, proficient in all scriptures,
the divine teacher of all the worlds, is saluted by all the gods.
The Lord of gods has a thousand heads, a thousand feet and eyes;
he is named "Thousandfold," possessing a thousand limbs and a thousand arms, the Sovereign.
Seated upon his throne, the Lord, whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals,
who resembles lightning in its brilliance, is the Master of the World and the Teacher of the World.
He was surrounded by gods and siddhas, by hosts of gandharvas and apsaras,
by yakṣas, vidyādharas, and nāgas, and by sages, perfected beings, and cāraṇas.
Being praised by the Suparṇas, Dānavas, Daityas, Rākṣasas, Guhyakas, Kinnaras, and other divine hosts of gods, he shines resplendently.
Established there eternally are Fame, Wisdom, Intelligence, Sarasvatī, Intellect, Thought, as well as Forbearance, the Embodiment of Success, and Splendor.
Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Maṅgalā, Sarvamaṅgalā,
Prabhā, Mati, and likewise Kānti— Nārāyaṇī is established there.
Śraddhā and the goddess Kauśikī, as well as Vidyut and Saudāminī; Nidrā, Rātri, and Māyā, and other celestial women.
All those [goddesses] are established in the abode of Vāsudeva;
now, what is the use of saying more? Everything is established there.
Ghṛtācī, Menakā, Rambhā, Sahajanyā, Tilottamā,
Urvaśī, Nimlocā, as well as others such as Vāmanā.
And Mandodarī, the fortunate Viśvācī, Vipulānanā,
Bhadrāṅgī, Citrasenā, and the most enchanting Pramlocā.
She who deludes the sages, the beautiful woman with a waist like the moon and a lovely face;
she with beautiful hair and dark locks, who likewise kindles the god of love.
Alambuṣā, Miśrakeśī, as well as another, Muñjikasthalā, Kratusthalā, Varāṅgī, and likewise the other, Pūrvacitti.
Parāvatī, Mahārūpā, Śaśilekhā, and Śubhānanā—
walking with the grace of swans and the gait of elephants in rut.
Bimbauṣṭhī and Navagarbhā are renowned as celestial women;
these and other Apsarases are proud of their beauty and youth.
They had slender waists and beautiful faces, were adorned with all kinds of ornaments,
were endowed with the sweetness of song, and possessed every auspicious mark.
And the wives of the gods and gandharvas, skilled in song and instrumental music,
dance there every day where that Supreme Person resides.
Therein there is no disease, nor sickness, nor death, nor cold or heat;
there is no hunger, no thirst, no old age, no deformity, and no unhappiness.
O twice-born ones, I do not see any world superior to this one, which generates supreme bliss and bestows the fruit of all desires, even beyond the world of Viṣṇu.
O brahmins, those worlds in the heavenly realm that are heard of as belonging to those of meritorious deeds do not equal even a sixteenth part of the world of Viṣṇu.

Śiva said:
"O Gautama, what shall I grant you for your auspicious devotion, hymns of praise, and vows?
I am well-pleased; ask for even that which is difficult for the gods to attain."

Having heard these words of the Embodiment of the Universe, Gautama, who was skilled in speech, his limbs overwhelmed with tears of joy, reflected thus: {Brahmā said:} Having heard these words of the Embodiment of the Universe, Gautama, who was skilled in speech, his limbs overwhelmed with tears of joy, reflected thus: (BrP 75.28)
Oh, the power of destiny! Oh, the power of dharma! Oh, indeed, the worship of brahmins!
Oh, how wondrous is the course of the world! Oh, Creator, let there be salutation to you!
Gautama said:

O Lord of gods, worshipped by the thirty [deities], if you are pleased, grant me the auspicious Gaṅgā who resides within your matted locks; O abode of the three Vedas, salutations be unto you! (BrP 75.30)
Īśvara said: "That which you have requested for the benefit of the three worlds,
request that now for your own benefit, free from fear on any side."
Gautama said:
"Those devotees who indeed praise you, the Goddess, with this hymn, shall have all their desires fulfilled; this is the boon I choose."
Brahmā said:
"So be it," the Lord of the Gods, being well-pleased, spoke these words:
"Free from all anxiety, ask for other boons from me as well."
Thus addressed with joy, Gautama spoke to Śaṅkara.
Gautama said:
O Lord of the World, release this goddess on the mountain of Brahmā— she who dwells in matted locks, who is purifying, the sanctifier of the world, and your beloved.
Indeed, she who is the embodiment of all sacred fords flows as far as the ocean;
[she purifies] sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, as well as those committed through mind, speech, and body.
O Śaṅkara, by the mere act of bathing,
may all [sins] go to dissolution during an eclipse of the moon or sun, as well as at the solstices and the equinoxes.
O Hara, may that merit which arises from [visiting] sacred fords at the time of the sun's transit or during the Vaidhṛti yoga be produced by the mere remembrance of this [river].
In the Kṛta age, austerity is said to be praiseworthy; in the Tretā, sacrificial rites;
in the Dvāpara, both sacrifice and charity; and in the Kali age, charity alone.
Whatever duties pertain to the ages (yugas) and likewise those pertaining to the regions (deśas),
whatever duty is praised in a particular place when there is a conjunction of place, time, and so forth— [that is what should be observed].
O Hara, may that merit which is produced elsewhere through bathing, giving, self-restraint, and other such practices arise simply from the remembrance of this [river].
"Wherever this river flows as it proceeds toward the ocean, there you must be present; let this be your supreme boon."
Even for those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin), once they have entered within that space extending upwards to ten times ten million yojanas in number, [they do not suffer].
O Śiva, may those ancestors and their descendants, as they come for the bath,
indeed become partakers of liberation even during the interval between baths and death.
On one side are all the sacred fords in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld;
yet this [river] is superior to them all. O Śambhu, enough! Salutations be unto you!
{Brahmā said:} Having heard those words of Gautama, Śiva replied, "So be it. "There has never been, nor will there ever be, a holy place (tīrtha) superior to this one."
"Truth, truth, and again truth—this is firmly established in the Vedas:
for all, the Gautamī is meritorious. Having said this, she vanished.
Then, after the Blessed One, who is honored by the world, had departed,
Gautama Pūrṇabala, at his command, took up his matted locks and went to that best of rivers.
Surrounded by the gods, he entered Brahmagiri.
Then, when Gautama had arrived, Nārada took up his matted locks;
a rain of flowers fell there, and the lords of the gods assembled.
And the highly fortunate sages, as well as the Brahmins and Kshatriyas,
filled with joy, honored that brahmin with shouts of victory.
Nārada said:
Having taken the Gaṅgā from the matted locks of Maheśvara,
what did Gautama do next after arriving at the holy mountain of Brahmā?
Brahmā said:
Having taken up the Gaṅgā, Gautama, pure and with a restrained mind,
was honored by the gods, the Gandharvas, and likewise by those dwelling on the mountain.
Placing his matted locks upon the summit of the mountain and meditating on the three-eyed God,
that best of the twice-born, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to Gaṅgā.
Gautama said:
O Mother, born from the matted locks of the Three-eyed One, bestower of all desires, forgive me; you are peaceful, go in happiness and grant us well-being.
{Brahmā said:} Having been addressed thus by Gautama, the goddess Gaṅgā, assuming a divine form and adorned with celestial garlands and unguents, spoke to Gautama.
Gangā said:
"I would go to the abode of the gods, or even to my water-pot;
I would go to the netherworld (rasātala), for you have become one whose word is true."
Gautama said:
"O Goddess, for the sake of benefiting the three worlds, I requested this, and it was likewise granted by Śambhu; therefore, it shall not be otherwise."
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of Gautama spoken by the twice-born, Gaṅgā then divided herself threefold— into heaven, the mortal world, and the netherworld.
In heaven she was divided fourfold, and in the mortal realm sevenfold;
likewise in the netherworld (rasātala) she was fourfold—thus she exists in fifteen forms.
She alone, who exists everywhere as all beings and is the destroyer of all sins,
is eternally praised in the Veda as the bestower of all desires.
Mortals see only those who have gone to the mortal realm, not those who have gone to the netherworld;
mortals of ignorant intellect do not see those who have gone to heaven at all.
As long as she was the goddess Sāgaragā, she was considered divine;
once released by Gautama himself, she departed toward the eastern ocean.
Then Gautama, that tiger among sages, performed a circumambulation of his auspicious mother, who was cherished by the celestial rishis and the entire world.
Having first worshipped the three-eyed Lord of the Gods, Gautama formed the resolve: "I shall perform my ablutions on both banks."
Then, as soon as he was remembered, the Ocean of Compassion appeared there;
he spoke thus to Śarva: "How can bathing be accomplished here? (BrP 76.15)
Having joined his palms in reverence, he bowed with devotion before the Three-eyed One.
Gautama said: O God of gods, O Great Lord, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, tell me correctly the procedure for bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha), O Maheśāna.
Śiva said:
"O great sage, listen to the entire procedure originating from the Godāvarī.
Having first performed the *nāndīmukha* rite and having effected the purification of the body," [BrP 76.18]
Having fed the Brahmins and having received their command,
they proceed in a state of celibacy, avoiding conversation with those who have fallen from their status.
He whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained,
and who possesses knowledge, austerity, and fame— he enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.
Abandoning malice in his heart and remaining steadfast in his own duty,
he should provide food as is appropriate while massaging those who are weary.
One should give garments and woolen blankets to virtuous people who possess nothing;
likewise, while listening to the divine stories of Hari and those concerning the origin of the Gaṅgā,
one who travels according to this rule shall properly obtain the fruit of the sacred ford.
Brahmā said:
"And Tryambaka," he said to Gautama, who was surrounded by sages.
Śiva said:
"O Gautama, holy fords (tīrthas) shall come into existence within a space of two cubits;
I am present everywhere, likewise bestowing all desires."
Brahmā said:
At Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, and likewise at the confluence of the ocean,
that Bhāgīrathī bestows merit upon men and grants them liberation.
The Narmadā, the best of rivers, is on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka;
there the Yamunā joins it, while at Prabhāsa it is the Sarasvatī.
O Nārada, where the Kṛṣṇā, the Bhīmarathī, and the Tuṅgabhadrā meet— that sacred ford (tīrtha) bestows liberation upon men.
Wherever the Payoṣṇī river flows, that place bestows liberation;
but this Gautamī, O child, [is sacred] wherever it may be by my command.
It will grant liberation through bathing to all men at all times; however, according to the arrival of the gods, a certain sacred ford becomes most meritorious for a limited period.
For everyone and at all times, the Gautamī is a sacred ford; of this there is no doubt.
It extends for three and a half crores of yojanas within two hundred [yojanas].
O Gautama, tiger among sages, sacred fords will come into being;
this [river] shall be known as the Māheśvarī Gaṅgā and the Vaiṣṇavī Gautamī.
Brāhmī, Godāvarī, Nandā, Sunandā, and Kāmadāyinī—
brought here by the splendor of Brahmā, they destroy all sins.
"Merely by being remembered, she is my eternal beloved who destroys the flood of sins;
among even the five elements, water has attained the state of preeminence."
Even among those, the waters are remembered as supreme because they constitute sacred fords;
of them, the Bhāgīrathī is the best, and likewise, the Gautamī is superior even to her.

O Sage, Gaṅgā, together with her matted locks, has been brought here; there is nothing else that brings such auspiciousness, whether in heaven or on the surface of the earth—a sacred ford that grants all goals.
Brahmā said:
"O son, this which was told to the high-souled Gautama by Hara himself out of satisfaction has now been related by me to you."
Thus, that Gautamī Gaṅgā is considered superior even to all others;
her true nature has been described, so what further desire could there be for hearing more?
Nārada said:
O best of gods, although that [knowledge] is indeed one, it is said to be twofold;
for one variety has been described as that which was brought by the Brahmin.
"O Kṣatriya, another portion of Bhava, the God of gods, was also deposited within the matted locks; tell me how that was brought forth."
Brahmā said:
"In the lineage of Vaivasvata, born in the family of Ikṣvāku,
there was formerly a king named Sagara who was exceedingly righteous."
He was a performer of sacrifices, constantly devoted to giving, and possessed of reflection upon the practice of dharma;
he had two wives who were entirely devoted to their husband.
Thinking, "He indeed has no progeny," he became absorbed in anxiety;
then, having summoned Vasiṣṭha to his home, he honored him according to the prescribed rites.
The king spoke these words concerning the cause of progeny;
having heard those words and reflected upon them, [the sage] addressed the king.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O King, always remain devoted to the worship of the ṛṣis together with your wife.
Brahmā said:
O Brahmin, having spoken thus, that sage departed for his own abode;
then, on one occasion, that treasury of asceticism came to the house of that royal seer.
He performed the worship of that ṛṣi, who, being well-pleased, spoke these words:
"Choose a boon, O highly fortunate one. When this was said, he chose sons.
That sage said to the king: "May there be one son who shall uphold the lineage for one [queen], and likewise sixty thousand sons for the other."
When the sage had departed after granting the boon, thousands of sons were born;
he performed very many sacrifices, including horse-sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees.
Once, having been duly consecrated for a horse sacrifice,
the king appointed his sons, together with their armies, to guard the horse.
Having found an opening somewhere, Śatakratu seized the horse;
and though they searched for it, his sons could not find the horse at that time.
Likewise, sixty thousand [demons], experts in various modes of warfare,
were among those sons of Sagara while they watched the rākṣasas.
Having taken that consecrated horse, the serpents went to the subterranean realm (rasātala);
yet, though joined with their powers of illusion, they did not see the rākṣasas there.
Not seeing the horse of the powerful Sagara, those sons wandered here and there,
yet they did not find the horse at that time.
Then they went to the world of the gods, searching through the mountains, the lakes,
and the forests, yet they did not see the horse at all.
Having had the rites for a successful journey performed by the officiating priests and having had auspicious ceremonies conducted,
the king nevertheless fell into anxiety because he did not see the beautiful sacrificial animal.
Wandering through all the oceans, they approached the world of the gods;
yet even there, while searching for that horse, the horse was not to be found.
Then they traversed the earth, including its mountains and forests;
yet even there, the princes did not see the horse at all.
In the meantime, a divine voice then arose there:
"The horse remains bound in the subterranean realm (rasātala); it is nowhere else but in the oceans."
Having heard these words, they then desired to go to the netherworld (rasātala);
thereupon, the oceans dug up the entire earth on all sides.
Afflicted by hunger, they ate dry clay day and night;
they dug into the earth and proceeded swiftly toward the subterranean realm (rasātala).
Hearing that those powerful and skillful sons of the ocean-king had arrived,
the *rakṣasas* were terrified and fled to the presence of Kapila.
The immensely wise Kapila also lies there in the netherworld (rasātala);
formerly, he accomplished the supreme task for the gods.
Then, when his task toward the gods was accomplished, the illustrious Kapila, weary and sleepless, said: "Grant me a place for sleep."
The sage gave the netherworld (rasātala) to him, and then spoke again to the gods:
"May that dull-witted one who attempts to raise me up be reduced to ashes immediately."
"Then I shall lie down upon the surface; otherwise, it is not even a dream.
Having been told "So be it" by the hosts of gods, he lay there in Rasātala.
Having recognized his power, the rākṣasas, endowed with illusory powers (māyā),
devised a means for the slaughter of all the oceans.
Then those Rākṣasas, terrified and without fighting,
quickly went to where that great and wrathful sage Kapila was.
Having tied the horse by its head, they stood at a distance, filled with haste and observing in silence, wondering what might happen.
Then all the ocean-dwellers, entering the subterranean realm of Rasātala,
beheld the horse tied up and likewise the man lying there.
And they thought of him as a thief and a destroyer of the sacrifice:
"Having slain this great sinner, let us lead the horse back to the presence of the king."
Some said, "What is the use of leading away this bound animal?
To that, other brave men replied, "We are kings and rulers."
"Let us rouse this great sinner and slay him with our kṣatriya prowess!
Saying these harsh words, they struck that sage with their feet.
Then, out of great wrath, Kapila, the best of sages,
looked upon those oceans with anger, intending to reduce them to ashes.
Then all those oceans indeed blazed up there;
however, King Sagara, being initiated for the sacrifice, did not know any of that.
Nārada related to the high-souled Sagara the location of Kapila as well as the state of the horse.
But seeing the transformation of the Rākṣasas and the destruction of the oceans,
the king became lost in thought and did not know what ought to be done.
There was yet another son known as Asamañjas;
out of folly, he would cast children and citizens alike into the water.
Then King Sagara, having been informed by the assembled citizens and having learned of that misconduct, became enraged and spoke.
Then the king said to his own ministers,
"Let this Asamañja, who has abandoned the duty of a Kṣatriya and is a slayer of children, undergo exile from the country."
Having heard those words of Sagara, the ministers, filled with haste,
abandoned the king’s son Asamañja, who had gone to the forest.
"All the Sāgaras have perished in the netherworld due to Brahmā’s curse;
even one has reached the forest—what is my fate now?"
The son of that Asamañjas was renowned as Aṃśumān;
having summoned the boy, the king informed him of the task to be done.
And having propitiated Kapila, the young Aṃśumat also gave the horse back to Sagara; thus, the sacrifice was completed.
His son was the radiant and righteous Dilīpa;
his son, likewise, was known as the wise Bhagīratha.
Having heard of the fate of all his grandfathers, he was deeply distressed;
full of humility, he questioned Sagara, that tiger among kings.
"But how can there be atonement for all these oceans?
The king said to Bhagīratha, "O son, Kapila knows."
Having heard those words of his, the boy departed for the netherworld (rasātala);
and having paid homage to Kapila, he reported everything to him.
O best of kings, that sage, having meditated for a long time and propitiated Śaṅkara through austerity,
bathed his ancestors with the water from his matted locks.
"Then you and your ancestors will have achieved their purpose.
"I shall do so," he said, bowing again to the sage.
"O best of sages, where should I go? Tell me also what must be done."
Kapila said:
"O best of men, go to that Kailāsa and praise Maheśvara;
perform penance according to your ability, and then you shall obtain your desire."
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of the sage and having bowed to the sage,
that boy, becoming pure and engaged in boyish activities, went to Mount Kailāsa.
Having made a firm resolve for asceticism, that Bhagīratha spoke.
Bhagīratha said:
"O Lord who bears the young moon, I am but a child, with the intellect of a child;
I know nothing at all. Therefore, O Lord, be pleased."
O Lord of the Chamaras, those who are devoted to my welfare may at times assist me through their speech, thoughts, and deeds; for their benefit, I shall speak here.
I bow to Soma, who is worshipped by the gods and others;
he by whom [the lineage] was produced and increased,
who is of the same lineage and the same dharma.
May Śiva grant their desires;
I am eternally prostrate before Him who bears the crescent moon upon His crest.
(Brahmā said:)
As he was speaking thus, Śiva appeared before him;
desiring to grant him a boon, he spoke to Bhagīratha.
Śiva said:
"O high-minded Bhagīratha, whatever cannot be accomplished even by the hosts of gods, that I shall surely grant to you; speak without fear."
Brahmā said:
Having prostrated before the Lord, the delighted Bhagīratha spoke to Śaṅkara.
Bhagīratha said:
"O Lord of Gods, grant me that very best of rivers which resides within my matted locks for the purification of my ancestors; by that, everything will be attained."
Brahmā said:
Then Maheśa, having laughed, spoke to Bhagīratha.
Śiva said:
"O son of noble vows, this has been granted to you by me; praise her once again."
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of the gods, he performed great penance for that purpose and,
with a disciplined mind, offered praise to Gaṅgā with devotion.
Having obtained her favor as well, even though he was a child, he acted like one who was not;
taking the Gaṅgā, whom he had received from Maheśvara, he went down to the netherworld (rasātala).
Having diligently established Gaṅgā according to the manner previously described, he reported [the matter] to the high-souled sage Kapila.
Then, having performed a circumambulation, he spoke with his palms joined in reverence: (BrP 78.68)
Bhagīratha said:
"O Goddess, my ancestors have fallen into ruin due to the curse of the great sage Kapila;
therefore, O Mother, you ought to save them."
Brahmā said:
Having said, "So be it," the celestial river, who benefits all,
descended for the sake of assisting the worlds and for the purification of the ancestors.
The celestial river is especially for the refilling of the ocean drunk by Agastya,
and for the destruction of sins through mere remembrance.

He performed what was requested by Bhagīratha for the sake of the sons of the king who had been reduced to ashes while dwelling in the depths of the netherworld, and especially for the sake of the oceans.
Then, having flooded those who were completely consumed by fire, he filled up the excavated pits;
thereafter, having flooded even Mount Meru, the boy king stood there and spoke.
"You must remain in the land of action," he said; "So be it," she replied, and she went to the Himalayas.
From the sacred Himavat mountain, she arrived in Bhāratavarṣa.
From the midst of that, the Puṇyanadī flowed toward the eastern ocean;
thus, O great sage, has this Gaṅgā Kṣātrā been described to you.
She is indeed Māheśvarī, Vaiṣṇavī, and that very same purifying Brāhmī;
she is Bhāgīrathī, the river of the gods, who takes her refuge on the peak of the Himalayas.
Thus, the water from the matted locks of Maheśvara has come to be twofold:
on the south of the Vindhya it is called the Gautamī Gaṅgā,
and on the north of the Vindhya it is designated as the Bhāgīrathī.
Nārada said:
My mind finds no satisfaction while listening to the stories narrated by you;
my heart is now intent on hearing about the specific fruits of each sacred ford (tīrtha).
First, tell me about the Gaṅgā as brought by the Brahmins in due order,
along with the merit and the fruit of each sacred ford (tīrtha) individually, together with its history, according to sequence.
Brahmā said:
"I am unable to describe the individual nature, the fruits, and the majesty of all the sacred fords (tīrthas), nor are you capable of hearing it all."
Nevertheless, O Nārada, listen attentively as I shall say something regarding those sacred fords that have been mentioned and those scriptural passages that have been cited.
Having paid homage to the Three-eyed One, I shall relate those [events] in brief,
wherein that Blessed Lord Tryambaka was personally manifest, O Sage.
That sacred ford named Tryambaka bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
there is another sacred ford, Vārāha, which is renowned throughout the three worlds.
I shall describe his form and how the name of Viṣṇu came to be;
long ago, a Rākṣasa, having defeated the gods, seized the sacrifice.
One known as Sindhusena reached the subterranean realm (rasātala);
when he reached that realm during a sacrifice, the earth indeed became devoid of sacrifice.
"This world does not exist, nor the next, for the sacrifice has perished"— thinking thus, the short-lived gods entered that very Rasātala, free from enmity.
But the gods, led by Indra, were unable to defeat him;
they went to Viṣṇu, the Ancient Puruṣa, and made their request to him.
Then the Blessed One, having assumed the form of a boar, spoke regarding that deed of the Rākṣasa which had completely destroyed the sacrifice.
"Having gone to the netherworld with conch, discus, and mace in hand,
I shall bring back the sacred sacrifice after slaying the foremost of the Rākṣasas."
"May all the gods go to heaven; let the fever of your minds depart.
By the very same path by which Gaṅgā reached the surface of the earth, the Wielder of the Discus [shall follow]."
O son, that glorious one in the form of a boar swiftly went to the netherworld (rasātala) after piercing through the earth, [there to confront] those who dwell in the netherworld.
Having slain the Rākṣasas and Dānavas and held them in his mouth,
the Blessed One, in the form of a boar, took the great sacrifice and became the enjoyer of the sacrifice.
By the very same path by which Viṣṇu reached the bottom, the conqueror of enemies,
having placed the Great Sacrifice in his mouth, emerged from the netherworld.
There, on Mount Brahmagiri, the gods waited for Hari;
having emerged from that path, he went to the Gaṅgāsravaṇa.
And he washed his limbs, which were smeared with blood, with the waters of the Gaṅgā, O Nārada; thereupon, that pool became the Vārāha Kuṇḍa.
Hari, the foremost of the thirty gods, placed the great sacrifice into the mouth [of Brahmā] before the deities;
from his mouth, the sacrifice was born.
From that time forward, the sacrificial ladle (sruva) is called the primary limb of the sacrifice;
indeed, it assumed the form of a boar due to another cause.
Therefore, Vārāha is the most meritorious of sacred sites, granting all desires;
bathing and giving gifts there bestow the fruit of all sacrifices.
Even while staying there, if any meritorious person remembers his ancestors,
the ancestors, being liberated from all sins, shall attain heaven.
Brahmā said:
I am not capable of describing to you the majesty of Kuśāvarta;
by the mere remembrance of it, a man becomes one who has accomplished all his duties.
Known as Kuśāvarta, it grants all desires to men;
it was there that the high-souled Gautama turned the sacred grass (kuśa) into a whirlpool.
Having caused it to be brought by Kuśa, the sage brought that [river] there;
bathing and giving gifts therein bestows satisfaction upon the ancestors.
The Nīlagaṅgā, the best of rivers, has issued forth from the Nīla mountain;
whatever a self-restrained man performs there, such as bathing and other rites, [yields great merit].
One should know that all of this is inexhaustible and bestows satisfaction upon the ancestors;
the supreme sacred site of Kapota is renowned throughout the three worlds.
O Sage, listen as I describe its form and its great fruit:
on that Brahma-mountain, there was a certain hunter who was extremely cruel.
He harms brahmins, virtuous men, ascetics, cattle, birds, and deer;
such is that evil-souled one, wrathful and a speaker of falsehoods.
He was of terrifying form, extremely fierce, with blue eyes and short arms;
he had protruding teeth, a missing nose and eyes, short feet, and a broad belly.
With a short belly and short arms, deformed and with the voice of a donkey, he held a noose in his hand; evil-minded and most wicked, he was always armed with a bow.
O Nārada, his wife was likewise so disposed, as were their children;
yet, urged on by her, he entered the dense forest.
That wicked man killed deer and birds of many forms;
he cast some into a cage while others were still alive.
With his limbs tormented by hunger and likewise distressed by thirst,
having wandered through many lands, he returned more frequently toward his home.
Then, when the afternoon had arrived and the month of Madhava had passed,
suddenly there arose thunder and lightning accompanied by clouds.
A wind blew, accompanied by a rain of stones and terrifying torrents of water;
exhausted from his journey, that hunter could no longer discern the path.
Then that sinner, exhausted, could no longer distinguish water from land, a pit from a path, or even the directions; he could not even find a place of refuge.
"Where shall I go? Where shall I stay? What shall I do? he thought, "I am the one who takes away the lives of all living beings, just like the Ender."
A being that brings about my end has arrived, along with a rain of stones;
I see no protector at all nearby, neither a rock nor a tree.
Having reflected thus in many ways, the hunter saw nearby in the forest one like a lord of the woods, or as Atri was among the stars.
Like a lion among deer, like a householder among hermitages,
like the mind among the senses, he was a protector of living beings, like a mountain.
Taking refuge in that excellent, bright tree adorned with branches and sprouts,
the hunter sat down, his garments drenched.
Remembering his wife and children, he thought, "They may live or they may not";
in that very interval, the sun set there.
Resorting to that very mountain, the pigeon dwelt there on that best of mountains together with his wife and surrounded by his sons and grandsons.
Having become fearless through happiness, well-satisfied and truly joyful,
many years passed for that bird as he lived there.
His wife was devoted to her husband and was indeed very pleased with him;
she resided in that excellent hollow, which was devoid of water, wind, and fire.
The pigeon always remained surrounded by his wife and sons;
on that day, however, by the power of fate, both the male pigeon and the female pigeon— BrP_80.25 //
Both of them went for the sake of food; the pigeon reached a tree, while she, my son, remained within her cage by the power of fate.
Then, though seized by the hunter, the female pigeon continued to live as if she were still alive,
even as she looked upon her offspring who were now deprived of their mother.
A terrifying year had arrived and the sun had set;
seeing his own hollow devoid of her, he lamented.
The king of pigeons did not realize that she was bound within a cage;
indeed, he continued to recite the praises of his beloved pigeon.
"Even now the auspicious lady who increases my joy has not arrived—
she who is the mother of my dharma and the mistress of my body."
She alone is my constant companion in the pursuit of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
when pleased she smiles, and when angry, she wipes away my sorrow.
That auspicious friend of mine, who was always devoted to my words and constantly intent upon our secret counsels,
has not yet returned even though the sun has already set.
She knows nothing of religious vows, mantras, the divine, nor even the purpose of dharma;
she is devoted to her husband, her very life is her husband, her mantra is her husband, and her beloved is her husband.
"The auspicious lady has not yet arrived; what shall I do, or where shall I go?
For neither my home nor the forest appears the same when deprived of her."
"Endowed with her, whether she be terrifying or beautiful,
my beloved endowed with splendor has not yet come to the house, as she was described."
"Without her I shall not live, or else I shall cast off this dear body; what can my children do? As for me, I have lost my dharma."
Hearing these words of her husband as he was thus lamenting, she,
remaining within the cage, spoke these words to her husband:
The female dove said:
"O best of birds, I am right here, bound and helpless;
I have been brought here by a hunter, O high-minded one, having been caught in snares."
"I am blessed; I am favored, for my husband speaks of my virtues, whether they be real or unreal. I have achieved my purpose; of this there is no doubt."
When the husband is pleased, all the deities are pleased with women;
but in the opposite case, women will inevitably meet with destruction.
You are my destiny, you are my lord, you are my friend, and you are my ultimate refuge;
you are the vow, you are the supreme Brahman, and you alone are heaven and liberation.
"Do not worry, O auspicious one; make your mind firm in the Dharma.
For it is through your grace that I have indeed enjoyed various pleasures. Enough of this distress and despondency; make your mind firm in the Dharma."
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of his beloved, he quickly climbed down from that best of mountains to where the female dove remained within her cage.
Having approached her and seen his beloved, and seeing that the hunter was as if dead, he said to her, "I shall release him; the hunter is now motionless."
O illustrious one, do not release me, knowing that all relationships are unstable;
for among those who prey upon others, the food of sky-dwellers is indeed living beings, and one living being is the food of another.
I do not recall any offense on his part; maintain a firm resolve toward righteousness.
Fire is the preceptor of the twice-born, and the Brahmin is the preceptor of all social classes.
The husband alone is the teacher of women; every guest is a teacher.
Those who satisfy with their words a guest who has arrived—that is, one who has reached them—[attain merit]. (BrP 80.48)
The goddess Vāgīśvarī certainly becomes satisfied with them;
by the offering of that food, Śakra attains satisfaction.
The ancestors [are pleased] by the washing of the feet and by food; Prajāpati [is pleased] by that service, and through such worship, Lakṣmī attains delight with Viṣṇu.
Since all the gods reside in the guest, therefore the guest is most worthy of worship.
One who has arrived weary from the road, brought by the sun, having come to one's house—
one should know him to be the very form of a god, for he is indeed the fruit of all sacrifices.
All the gods, the ancestors, and the sacred fires follow after a weary guest;
for when he is satisfied, they attain joy.

Even though you have gone away, they remain hopeless; therefore, O beloved, abandon sorrow with all your heart and attain tranquility. Establish a virtuous mind and perform your duty according to dharma.
Beneficence and malevolence are both considered to be excellent;
