however, everyone returns a favor only to those who have previously helped them.
He who acts virtuously toward those who do him harm is declared a partaker of merit.
The dove said: "What you have spoken is appropriate for us, and you consider it well;
however, there is something more that must be said, so listen to it, O fair-faced one."
One person supports a thousand, another a hundred, and yet another ten;
still another supports himself with ease, while we are merely those who toil to fill our bellies.
Some have grain and wealth stored in pits; others possess wealth in granaries;
some have wealth placed in jars, and we have wealth placed in our beaks.
O auspicious lady, how shall I honor this weary guest who has arrived?
The female dove said:
"Fire, water, auspicious speech, and even grass, wood, and the like—these too should be given to one who asks; yet this hunter is afflicted by the cold."
Brahmā said:
Having heard these affectionate words, the king of birds climbed the tree and looked out;
he then saw the fire at a great distance.
Having gone to the place of the fire, that pigeon took up a burning brand with his beak and kindled the fire before the hunter.
Again and again, at midnight, that king of pigeons cast dry wood, leaves, and grasses into the fire.
Seeing that fire blazing, the hunter, suffering from the cold,
warmed his own limbs— which were beyond his control— and attained comfort.
Seeing the hunter being consumed by the fire of hunger, the female dove said to her husband, "O illustrious one, do not release him! (BrP 80.65)
With my own body, I shall satisfy that hunter who is afflicted by suffering;
O you of noble vows, may you attain those worlds reserved for those who honor their guests.
The dove said:
"While I am present, this duty of yours is not ordained;
I am a guest you desire here, so grant me permission, O auspicious one."
Brahmā said:
Having spoken thus and having circumambulated the fire three times, he meditated upon the four-armed Lord,
the Great Viṣṇu, the soul of the universe, the refuge, who is affectionate toward his devotees.
Saying, "Enjoy it as you please," he entered the fire accordingly;
seeing him with his life-force cast into the fire, the hunter spoke these words:
The hunter said:
"Alas! Fie upon this human life of mine, since this king of birds has performed such a reckless act for my sake!"
Brahmā said:
To that hunter who was speaking thus, the female bird spoke these words.
The female dove said:
"O illustrious one, release me; my husband is going far away."
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of hers, the fowler then quickly released the female dove from her cage, as if struck with fear.
She too, having circumambulated her husband and the fire, then spoke.
The female dove said:
"This is the supreme duty of women, that they follow after their husband;
this path is ordained in the Veda and honored throughout all the worlds."
Just as a snake-catcher forcibly draws a serpent out from its hole,
even so a devoted wife shall go to heaven together with her husband.
For as many hairs as there are on a human being— three and a half crores—
so long shall she who follows her husband dwell in heaven.
Having paid homage to the earth, the gods, the Gaṅgā, and the lords of the forest,
and having comforted those children, he spoke these words to the hunter:
The female dove said:
"O illustrious one, by your grace such a thing has come to pass for me.
Forgive my offspring here; I am going to heaven with my husband."
Brahmā said:
Having spoken thus, that virtuous female bird entered the fire.
As she had entered the sacrificial flame, the sound of "Victory! ceased.
Then, in the sky, he beheld a most splendid celestial chariot resembling the sun,
and upon it, a divine-looking couple.
Both, filled with joy and wonder, spoke to the hunter.
The couple said:
"We two shall go to the abode of the thirty gods; you have been asked for leave, O high-minded one. You are a guest upon the stairway to heaven for us; salutations be unto you!"
Brahmā said:
Seeing those two mounted upon that excellent celestial chariot, even that hunter,
casting aside his bow and cage, spoke with palms joined in reverence:
The hunter said:
"O illustrious ones, you must not abandon me; something should be given to one who knows nothing.
I am a guest here worthy of honor; you ought to tell me the means of atonement."
The couple said:
"Go to Gautamī; may it be well with you. Report your sin to her.
By bathing there for a fortnight, you will be liberated from all evils."
Having been freed from sin by bathing there again in the Gaṅgā,
you will obtain the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and become purified.
By bathing once again in the Gautamī, the best of rivers, which is the source of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Sambhu,
he shall cast off his defiled body.
Having ascended a supreme celestial chariot, you will go to heaven without a doubt.
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words from the two of them, that hunter acted accordingly;
ascending an excellent celestial chariot, he assumed a divine form.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, and being honored by throngs of apsarases—
the pigeon, the female pigeon, and the hunter as the third—
all indeed ascended to heaven through the power of the Gaṅgā.
From that time forward, that sacred ford became renowned as Kāpota;
there, bathing, giving gifts, and the worship of the ancestors [should be performed].
Ritual acts such as the sacrifice of recitation lead to infinity.
Brahmā said:
Kārttikeya is a supreme sacred site, renowned as Kaumāra;
by merely hearing its name, one becomes possessed of noble lineage and beauty.
When the Daitya Tāraka had been slain and the celestial realm had become secure,
Pārvatī spoke with affection to her eldest son, Kārttikeya.
"Enjoy at your pleasure the objects of enjoyment in the three worlds that are dear to your heart,
with a joyful mind, by my command and through the grace of your father."
Thus addressed by his mother, Viśākha took his pleasure at will with the celestial women; even the wives of the gods took their delight.
Then, O Nārada, while the wives of the gods were being enjoyed by him,
the inhabitants of heaven were unable to restrain Kārttikeya.
Then they reported that act of patricide to Pārvatī;
though he was repeatedly forbidden by his mother and by the gods, that wielder of the spear [remained firm].
But the six-faced one, being attached to women, did not heed her words;
fearing the threat of a curse, Pārvatī reflected: BrP_81.7 //
Likewise, out of affection for their sons and for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods,
the goddesses repeatedly considered that the wives of the gods must be protected for a long time.
In that same manner in which Skanda took his pleasure,
Pārvatī likewise assumed that very form and conducted herself in such a way.
Having summoned the wives of Indra and Varuṇa as well, the six-faced one looked at them,
but he saw in them only the form of his mothers.
Having dismissed her, he then bowed and summoned another;
but upon seeing her in the form of a mother, he was overcome with shame.
Having thus seen that form in many [beings] and reflected that "the world consists of mother," the son of Gaṅgā then attained detachment.
"But having realized that my mother's purpose was to turn me away from what I had undertaken, [I thought:
'If I am to be restrained from enjoyment, why was I previously incited to it?'"
"Therefore, everything done by my mother is an object of my laughter," he said,
and filled with supreme shame, he then went to Gautamī.
And may this one, who has the form of my mother, hear what I say;
she who bears the name of woman here and is considered by me to be equal to a mother.
Knowing this, Śaṅkara, the Lord of the World, together with Pārvatī, restrained his son; thus spoke the Guru: "This is the way things are. (BrP 81.16)
Then the Lord of the Gods, being pleased and wondering "What shall I give?", Skanda, with his palms joined in reverence, spoke again to his father: BrP_81.17 //
Skanda said:
"I am the commander-in-chief, the lord of the gods, and your son—enough of this, O Lord of Devas; what further boons are needed, O you who are worshipped by the gods?"
Or, O Lord, if you desire to give out of a wish for the welfare of the worlds, I beg you; you ought to grant me permission for this, and not for my own sake.
May those who are great sinners, even those who have approached the wives of their gurus,
become cleansed of their sins merely by bathing here.
O Lord of the Gods, even animals shall attain the highest birth;
one who is ugly shall obtain perfection of form by bathing here.
Brahmā said:
"So be it," Śambhu replied in assent to what was spoken by his son.
From that time forward, that sacred ford became known as Kārttikeya.
There, bathing and giving gifts bestow the fruit of all sacrifices.
Brahmā said:
Regarding that which is known as Kṛttikātīrtha, situated immediately after [the shrine of] Kārttikeya—
one obtains the fruit of drinking Soma merely by hearing of it.
Long ago, for the sake of destroying Tāraka, the Sage (Bṛhaspati) drank the seed of Bhava;
O Muni, seeing the Sage pregnant with that seed, the wives of the sages felt desire for him.
Among the wives of the seven seers, excluding Arundhatī who had bathed after her menses, a conception occurred through Agni in those six women at that time.
But as they were performing their austerities, O sage, those most beautiful women, having bathed after their menstrual periods, said:
"What shall we do? Where indeed shall we go? By doing what would it be well-done?"
Having said this, they went in haste to the Gaṅgā and oppressed her;
from them, those embryos then emerged from her into the water in the form of foam.
Indeed, when all of them had attained oneness with the water and the wind,
they then became one in form, and from them the six-faced one was born.
Having caused those embryos to flow out, the wives of the sages went to their homes;
seeing their deformed forms, those sages said:
"Go, go quickly! It is not fitting for women to act according to their own will. Thus, O child, they were dismissed by their husbands.
Then, seeing those six who were overcome by suffering and abandoned by their husbands, Nārada said: "Kārttikeya is born from Hara."
Known as Gāṅgeya, Agnibhava, and Tārakāntaka, he will go to him before long; being pleased, he will grant him enjoyment.
At the very word of the celestial sage, the Kṛttikās approached the six-faced one in person and reported this exactly as it had happened.
Having assented to those words of the Kṛttikās, Kārttikeya said:
"Let all of them go to the Gautamī, where, having bathed and worshipped Maheśvara, they shall attain their goal."
"I shall come back to that very place and go to the abode of the gods.
Having said, "So be it," the Kṛttikās bathed in the Gaṅgā and the Gautamī.
Having worshipped Deveśvara at the command of Kārttikeya,
they proceeded to the abode of the gods by the grace of Deveśvara.
From that time forward, that sacred ford is called Kṛttikātīrtha;
whoever performs a ritual bath there on the full moon day of Kārttika when the moon is in conjunction with the Kṛttikās, [attains great merit].
Having obtained the fruit of all sacrifices, he becomes a righteous king; moreover,
whoever remembers that holy site or hears of it shall be liberated from all sins and attain a long life.
Brahmā said:
O great sage, listen to that holy ford known as Daśāśvamedhika,
by the mere hearing of which one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
The illustrious Viśvarūpa, son of Viśvakarman, was possessed of great strength;
his first son was Bhauvana, the all-pervading lord.
His family priest was Kaśyapa, who was proficient in all branches of knowledge; the mighty-armed Bhauvana, the sovereign of the whole world, questioned him.
"O Sage, I shall sacrifice with ten horse-sacrifices simultaneously;
thus he asked his brahmin preceptor, 'Where shall I sacrifice to the gods? (BrP 83.4)
He said, "O best of kings, there was a sacrificial ground for the gods here and there,
wherever the most excellent of the twice-born performed great sacrifices."
There, in the sacrificial arena, groups of sages served as officiating priests; ten sacrifices were performed simultaneously by the family chaplain.
Seeing that those sacrifices had not reached completion, the king became lost in thought;
he abandoned the sacrificial ground for the gods and performed those rites again elsewhere.
As he proceeded there in that manner, obstacles and defects assailed him;
seeing the sacrifices thus incomplete, the king then spoke to his preceptor.
The king said:
"Whether due to a defect of the land, a defect of the time, a defect of my own, or even yours,
these sacrificial horses have not attained their full measure in ten sacrifices."
{Brahmā said:} Thereupon, the king, being distressed, together with his domestic priest Kaśyapa, went to Saṃvarta, the elder brother of Bṛhaspati, and spoke to him. BrP_83.10 //
Kaśyapa and Bhauvana said:
"O Blessed One, O giver of honor, tell us of that place and that preceptor where ten horse-sacrifices may simultaneously reach completion."
Brahmā said:
Then, having meditated upon Bhaumana, Saṃvarta, the best of sages, said:
"Go to Brahmā; he will tell you the place."
The highly wise Bhauvana also, having arrived with the great-souled Kaśyapa, spoke to me regarding my preceptor and the region and so forth.
Then I said, "O son, go to Gautamī, O Indra among kings; that region is meritorious through sacrifices. (BrP 83.14)
This very Kaśyapa, who has mastered the Vedas, is the most excellent teacher;
by the grace of this teacher and by the grace of Gautamī, [all this was attained].
By means of a single horse-sacrifice or by bathing there once more,
the sacrifices and the ten horse-sacrifices of the steeds will be accomplished.
Having heard that, King Bhauvana went to the bank of the Gautamī,
consecrated for the horse sacrifice with Kaśyapa as his assistant.
Then, when the great sacrifice, the horse-sacrifice of the Lord of Sacrifice,
had commenced and was completed, the king prepared to give away the earth as a gift.
Then, from the sky, a voice spoke loudly to that best of kings,
who stood there having honored the brahmins, the officiating priests, and the presiding masters of the assembly.
The Voice of Space said:
"O King, everything— including the mountains, forests, and groves— was given by you to the priest Kaśyapa when you desired to bestow the entire earth upon him."
Abandoning the desire for the gift of land, give food, which yields great fruit;
no merit equal to the gift of food is found in the three worlds.
Especially on the sandy bank of the Gaṅgā with faith, O Sage,
this horse sacrifice has been performed by you with abundant sacrificial fees;
you have accomplished your purpose— blessings be upon you— and there is no need for further deliberation in this matter.
Brahmā said:
Nevertheless, the Earth spoke to that son of Bhūvana, who was desirous of giving.
The Earth said:
"O son of Viśvakarman, O sovereign of the whole earth, do not give me back again and again!
I shall sink into the midst of the waters; therefore, let me not be given."
Brahmā said:
Thereupon Bhauvana, being terrified, asked, "What should be given?
And Pṛthvī spoke again to Bhauvana, who was surrounded by the brahmins.
The Earth said:
"Sesame seeds, cows, wealth, grain—whatever is given on the bank of the Gautamī, all that gift becomes inexhaustible; what then will you give me, O Bhauvana?"
"O Bhauvana, he who takes refuge on the banks of the Gaṅgā and offers even a single morsel of food has, by that act, given me in its entirety; what more then can you give me?"
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of Bhuva, Bhauvana, the lord of all beings, agreed,
saying "So be it," and bestowed food upon the brahmins in great abundance.
From that time forth, they have known that sacred ford as Daśāśvamedhika;
by bathing there, the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices is obtained.
Brahmā said:
There is another sacred site, Paiśāca Tīrtha, honored by those who discourse on Brahman.
I shall describe its nature; it is located on the southern bank of the Gautamī.
"O Nārada, on the side of Mount Brahmagiri is a mountain named Añjana;
O best of sages, upon that mountain dwells a supreme Apsaras who was cast down by a curse."
There was a female monkey there named Añjanā, who was excellent in her physical form;
her husband was named Kesari, and there was another woman named Adrikā.
That excellent Apsaras, the wife of Kesarin, who had fallen due to a curse,
remained on Mount Añjana as a female cat with her head [transformed].
The world-renowned lion arrived at the southern ocean;
in the meantime, Agastya went to Mount Añjana.
Both Añjanā and Ādrikā honored Agastya, the best of sages,
according to tradition and to their satisfaction.
Then the blessed Lord, being pleased, said: "O both of you, let a boon be chosen. They both replied to Agastya: "O Lord of Sages, grant us two sons."
"Stronger and more excellent than all others, and benefactors of the entire world"—
having said "So be it," the best of sages departed toward the southern direction.
Then, at one time,
Añjanā and Ādrikā were performing song, dance, and laughter upon the summit of the mountain.
And Vāyu and Nirṛti, seeing those two gods smiling,
both of them with minds overcome by desire, then departed in haste.
"O gods who grant boons, may we both become the wives of these two. They too replied, "Let it be so," and they took their pleasure upon the mountain peak.
Likewise, from Añjanā and Vāyu, Hanumān was born;
and from Adrikā and Nirṛti, the king of the Piśācas named Adri was born.
Again, both of them said: "By the boon of the sage, two sons have been born;
our deformed appearance has been marred by our heads."
"Because of the curse of the Lord of Śacī, you two ought to recognize him there.
Then the Blessed One Vāyu and Nirṛti likewise spoke.
"By bathing and giving gifts at Gautamī, there shall be liberation from the curse.
Having said this, those two, being pleased, vanished right there.
Then the mountain, assuming the form of a piśāca, took up some collyrium and bathed his mother for the pleasure of his brother Hanumān.
In that very manner, Hanumān, taking up the Gaṅgā and moving with great haste,
brought her who was in the form of a cat to the bank of the Gautamī.
From that time forth, having reached the auspicious Brahmagiri, which grants all desires, that holy place became known as Paiśāca and likewise Añjana.
Fifty-three yojanas to the east of Mārjāra would be Dhanumān Vṛṣākapi; from that place known as Mārjāra, [he proceeds].
The auspicious Phenāsaṅgama is declared to be the bestower of all desires;
its true nature and its auspicious benefits are described right there.
Brahmā said:
O Nārada, listen with a focused mind to that which is known as Kṣudhātīrtha;
I shall describe it, for it is highly meritorious and bestows all desires upon men.
In ancient times, there was a seer named Kaṇva, an ascetic and the foremost among those who know the Vedas;
while wandering through hermitages, he was tormented by hunger.
He saw Gautama’s holy hermitage, abundant with food and water,
and he saw himself afflicted by hunger, while Gautama was likewise well-provided for.
Then, having observed this disparity, Kaṇva attained a state of detachment;
Gautama, the best of the twice-born, likewise thought, "I am indeed firmly established in asceticism."
Therefore, because begging would be inconsistent with my vow, I shall not eat in the house of Gautama, even though I am afflicted by hunger and my body is suffering.
"I shall go to the Ganges, O Gautamī, and acquire spiritual merit";
having thus resolved, the wise man went to the purifying Gaṅgā.
Having bathed, purified, and composed his mind, he sat upon a seat of kuśa grass and offered praise to the Gaṅgā of Gautama, as well as to Hunger and Supreme Misfortune.
Kaṇva said:
Homage be to Gaṅgā, the remover of supreme distress;
homage to Hunger, the cause of suffering for all people.
Homage to the auspicious one born from the matted locks of Maheśāna;
homage to her who has emerged from the mouth of Great Death—
she who possesses a peaceful form for the virtuous and a wrathful form for the evil-minded.
In the form of a river, you remove the heat and the sins of all beings.
Salutations to you who bestow suffering and sin upon all in the form of hunger;
salutations, O auspicious Goddess; salutations, O tormentor of sins! Salutations, O Goddess who brings peace; salutations, O destroyer of poverty!
Brahmā said:
As he was thus offering praise, two things appeared before him:
one was the heart-stealing [form] of Gaṅgā, and the other was of terrifying appearance.
Again, having joined his palms in reverence and paid homage, that best of the twice-born—
Kaṇva said:
O you who are the most auspicious among all that is auspicious, O Brāhmī, O Māheśvarī, O Śubhā,
O Vaiṣṇavī, O Tryambakā, O Goddess Godāvarī, salutations be to you!
O Godāvarī, born from the matted locks of Tryambaka, destroyer of the sins of Gautama,
you who flow sevenfold toward the ocean— salutations be to you!
O Goddess Hunger, who causes the destruction of dharma, desire, and wealth for all evildoers, and who consists of suffering and greed— to you, salutations again and again!
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of Kaṇva, the two of them, being well-pleased, spoke to the twice-born man.
The two Gaṅgākṣudhas said:
"Speak what you desire, O auspicious one; choose boons, O observer of noble vows."
Brahmā said:
Kaṇva, having bowed down, spoke to Gaṅgā regarding hunger in due order.
Kaṇva said:
"O Goddess Gaṅgā, grant me my heart's desires and my prosperity; bestow upon me longevity, wealth, worldly enjoyment, and liberation."
{Brahmā said:} Having spoken thus to Gaṅgā Gautamī, the best of the twice-born spoke also to Hunger.
Kaṇva said:
O Hunger and Thirst, you who are most wicked and harsh, go away from me and from those born of my lineage; may you never exist again.
For those who, afflicted by hunger, praise you with this hymn, may the sufferings of poverty not befall them; this is another boon.
May those men who, with devotion, perform bathing, giving, recitation, and other rites at this highly meritorious sacred site, become possessors of fortune.
Whoever recites this hymn, whether at a sacred pilgrimage site or in their own home, shall have no fear of poverty or suffering; this is another boon.
Brahmā said:
Having said, "So be it," they departed for their own abode. From that time forward, that sacred ford was known as Kāṇva, Gāṅga, and Kṣudhābhidha.
O child, it removes all sins and increases the satisfaction of the ancestors.
Brahmā said:
O Brahmin, there is a great sacred site (tīrtha) known as Cakratīrtha;
by bathing there with devotion, a person shall attain the world of Hari.
O Lord of the Earth, having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight and bathed at Gaṇikāsaṅgama, one shall attain the imperishable state.
Listen as I relate what occurred there in the past:
there was a Vaiśya named Viśvadharā who possessed great wealth.
O Sage, in his later years, he had an excellent son who was virtuous, endowed with beauty, playful, and of auspicious appearance.
A son, dearer even than one's own life, has met his death in due time;
seeing their son thus, the husband and wife were oppressed by grief.
At that time, they both resolved to die together with him, crying out:
"Alas, my son! O, by wicked and evil-souled Time!"
"O ocean of virtues, although you were still in the prime of youth when you were led away,
you are likewise even more difficult for us two to obtain than our own lives."
Having thus heard the piteous lamentation of the couple, Yama,
his mind overcome with compassion, quickly abandoned his own city.
Staying on the auspicious bank of the Godāvarī and meditating upon Janārdana,
even in a short time his offspring increased on all sides.
"Tell me how large this earth is, and by whom it has been filled;
for no living being dies, yet the earth is overwhelmed by its burden."

Then, O best of sages, the goddess Earth went quickly to where Śakra, the conqueror of enemy cities, was joined by the gods. Seeing Vasundharā, Indra prostrated himself and spoke this: Br̥hatkathāślokasaṃgraha 86.11: tato devī gatā tūrṇaṃ vasudhā munisattama / yatrāsti surasaṃyuktaḥ śakraḥ parapuraṃjayaḥ // dṛṣṭvā vasuṃdharām indraḥ praṇipatyedam abravīt // BrP_86.11 //
Indra said:
"O Earth, tell me: what is the purpose of your coming?"
Dhara said:
"O Śakra, oppressed by a heavy burden, I have come to ask about the cause without having caused slaughter; tell me, what is this?"
{Brahmā said:} Having heard these words of the Earth, Indra spoke this speech: (BrP 86.14)
Indra said:
"If there were indeed a cause for this, it would then be known by me;
for I am the lord of the gods over all the earth."
Brahmā said:
Then, having heard those words, the Earth spoke to the Lord of Śacī: "In that case, let Yama be commanded as to how he shall withdraw the subjects."
Having heard these words of Mahī, O great sage, the Siddhas and Kinnaras were commanded by Mahendra to bring Yama quickly.
Then they all went quickly to the city of Vaivasvata;
however, there they, along with the Siddhas and Kinnaras, did not see Yama at all. Having returned, they again reported the news to Śakra with great speed.
The Siddhas and Kinnaras said: "O Lord, Yama was not seen by us in the city of Yama,
even though we searched everywhere with great effort."
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of theirs, Savitṛ was then questioned by Śakra, who asked, "Where indeed is his father Yama? (BrP 86.20)
Sūrya said:
O Śakra, Kṛtānta is now present on the bank of the Godāvarī, performing intense austerity there; I do not know what the cause could be.
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of the Sun, Śakra fell into a state of doubt.
Śakra said:
"Alas, what a tragedy! What a great tragedy! My lordship over the gods is lost, for Yama of wicked conduct is performing penance at the Godāvarī!"
"It is my conviction that the gods surely desire to seize my position."
Brahmā said:
Having spoken thus, the host of Apsarases was summoned by Indra.
Indra said:
"Among you, who is capable of destroying the asceticism of Kāla, who stands firm in his penance and is my enemy? Let this be told to me quickly."
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of Śakra, O great sage, not one of them spoke;
then Śakra, in a fit of rage, replied to the host of Apsarases.
Indra said:
"He did not say anything further regarding our destination; therefore, let us go ourselves. O gods, prepare yourselves and come with your armies without delay."
"We shall cause our enemy, who desires heaven through asceticism, to be destroyed."
Brahmā said:
When this had been spoken, the army of the gods appeared;
for Hari, the sustainer of the worlds, having thus understood the heart of Indra, [acted accordingly].
Indeed, the discus was sent by the Wielder of the Discus for the protection of Yama;
wherever that discus came to rest, there arose the unsurpassed Cakratīrtha.
Then Menakā, feeling apprehensive, spoke these words to Indra.
Menakā said:
"O Lord of the Gods, there is no one capable of predicting the time of death;
and O God, death at your hands is better than at the hands of Yama."
"O Lord, this courtesan is intoxicated by her beauty and youth;
she requests a boon from you. Grant her that very thing—she considers it to be lordship over you."
{Brahmā said:} Having heard these words of hers, Śakra, the lord of the foremost gods,
honored that emaciated woman and likewise commanded the courtesan.
Śakra said:
"O Gaṇikā, go; perform my task, O beautiful one, without delay.
Having accomplished your purpose, you shall once again become as dear to me as Śacī."
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words from Śakra, the courtesan of beautiful form rose up and, in an instant, arrived in the presence of Yama.
Having reached the presence of Yama, illuminating the ten directions,
the young woman sang the *hindolakaṅkala* melody with playful grace.
Then the fickle and ever-shifting mind of Kāla wavered;
thereupon Yama opened his eyes, which were filled with the fire of desire.
O great sage, he directed it toward that enemy of his welfare;
then, having instantly dissolved, she immediately became a river.
Having come together at Gautamī with her courtesans and attendants,
she went to heaven while songs were being sung, through the power of that sacred ford.
Seeing the courtesan departing toward heaven, seated upon a celestial chariot, Kāla, whose eyes were trembling, was struck with the utmost amazement.
Then, having approached, Āditya spoke thus to Yama at that time: Br̥hatkathāślokasaṃgraha 86.40.
Sūrya said:
"O son, perform your own duty;
behold the constant blowing of the wind that creates offspring for all beings."
Carrying me as I wander through the three worlds, you carry the earth and its creatures.
{Brahmā said:} Having heard these words, Yama spoke the speech of his father. (BrP 86.42)
Yama said:
"I would certainly not perform this censurable deed;
you ought not to command me in such a most cruel act."
Having heard those words, Bhānu spoke these words:
"O Yama, what indeed is that censurable deed which you are capable of doing?"
Have you not seen a courtesan,
while being carried away by her attendants and singing of heaven, who immediately plunged into the waters of the Gautamī?
"And here, O son, you have performed intense and most difficult penance;
I do not see its end at all. Therefore, go to your own city."
Having spoken thus, the Lord Bhānu bathed there and went to heaven;
Yama also, having bathed at the confluence, then departed for his own city.
Then, O great sage, Bhūtahā abandoned his apprehension;
seeing Yama thus departing, he prepared his chariot for the journey.
That mortal who, with a concentrated mind, should either hear or recite: "Where the Blessed One Govinda is adorned with a forest garland."
His calamities perish, and he shall attain a long life.
Brahmā said:
O best of sages, listen properly to this account of how it occurred there at the Ahalyāsaṃgama, a sacred ford that purifies the three worlds. BrP_87.1 //
O Lord of Sages, in the past, out of great curiosity, I created many kinds of beautiful maidens endowed with excellent qualities.
From among them, he fashioned one who was most excellent and possessed auspicious marks;
seeing that young woman, whose every limb was beautiful and who was endowed with the qualities of form, [he was struck with wonder].
The thought entered my mind: "Who indeed is capable of nourishing her?
Neither among the Daityas nor the Suras, and likewise not even among the sages."
It was my conviction that she lacked the power to nourish him—
a wise Brahmin, preeminent in virtue and endowed with ascetic power.
To Gautama, who was endowed with all auspicious marks, a knower of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and possessed of great wisdom, I gave her for his nourishment.
"O best of sages, protect her until she attains youth;
once she is established in her youth, you may bring that virtuous woman back to my presence."
Having spoken thus, O Gautama, I gave that slender-waisted maiden to him;
taking her, that best of sages, whose sins were destroyed by austerity, [departed].
Having raised her according to the prescribed rites and having adorned her,
that best of sages, remaining free from all agitation, then brought Ahalyā into my presence.
Seeing her, all the gods—Śakra, Agni, Varuṇa, and the others—said individually, "O Lord of the Gods, she should be given to me. (BrP 87.10)
In the same way, the sages, the Sādhyas, the Dānavas, and the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas—
all of them having arrived and gathered together for the sake of the maiden— were seen by him.
At that time, however, Indra’s seizure became particularly intense;
yet Gautama’s greatness, profundity, and fortitude remained steadfast.
Having remembered this, I became greatly amazed, and this thought occurred to me, O wise one:
"This fair-faced girl is to be given to Gautama alone; she is not fit for anyone else."
Therefore, I shall indeed give her to him; nevertheless, I thought thus:
"The courage of everyone has been shattered by this young girl."
Then, when "Ahalya" was uttered by the gods, by me, and by the sages, I looked at the gods and the sages there and spoke aloud:
BrP_87.15: "Ahalya! it was said by the gods, and by me and the sages then; having looked at the gods and the sages, I then spoke there loudly.
That fair-browed woman is given to him who first circumambulates the earth and worships her, and not to anyone else, again and again.
Then, having heard the words spoken by Maya, all the hosts of gods went for the sake of Ahalya on their circumambulation of the earth.
When the hosts of gods had departed, Gautama, the lord of sages,
likewise made some effort for the sake of Ahalyā in this manner.
In the meantime, O Brahmin, Surabhi, the cow who milks all desires, was half-given birth; Gautama beheld her.
He performed a circumambulation of it, recollecting the thought,
"This is the Earth," and then he likewise performed a circumambulation of the Linga of the Lord of the Gods.
Having performed a circumambulation of those two, Gautama, the best of sages,
also performed a single circumambulation of all the gods.
"Two things have arisen for me: neither [of them] was previously present for one who travels upon the earth.
Having thus resolved, that sage then approached my presence.
Having paid homage, the high-minded Gautama spoke these words to me:
"O Lotus-seated One, Soul of the Universe, let there be salutation to you again and again."
"O Brahman, this entire earth has been circumambulated by me;
O Lord of Gods, you yourself know what is appropriate in this matter. (BrP 87.24)
Having learned this through the practice of meditation, I said to Gautama:
"O fair-browed one, she is given to you alone; this circumambulation has been performed."
"O brahmin-sage, know that Dharma is difficult to comprehend even by the Vedas;
Surabhi has given birth but half, and the earth consists of seven continents."
By circumambulating that [image], one has effectively circumambulated the entire earth;
by circumambulating the Liṅga, one obtains that very same fruit.
Therefore, O Sage Gautama of noble vows,
I am pleased with all your effort, as well as by your fortitude, your knowledge, and your austerity.
"O tiger among sages, this daughter, the best in the world, is given by me";
having said this, O sage, I gave Ahalyā to Gautama.
When the marriage was completed, all those gods, having performed the circumambulation of Ilā, returned very slowly and beheld her.
Then those gods, having arrived and seeing Gautama and Ahalyā— a couple who increased their mutual affection— were filled with wonder.
When the marriage was concluded, all the gods departed for heaven;
and Śacī’s husband, filled with jealousy upon seeing her, also went to heaven.
Then, with a joyful mind, I gave to that high-souled Gautama the auspicious and holy Brahmagiri, which grants all desires.
There, that Gautama, the best of sages, took pleasure with Ahalyā;
and having heard this meritorious story of Gautama in heaven, Śakra [was moved].
Assuming the guise of a brahmin, Śatakratu came to see that hermitage, that sage, and his blameless wife.
Having seen his palace, his wife, and his wealth,
he formed an evil intent and set his eyes upon Ahalyā.
O child, at that time, Śatakratu, drawn away by passion, was not aware of himself, nor of the other, nor of the place, nor of the time, nor even of his fear of the sage’s curse.
Constantly devoted to that meditation and proud of his sovereignty over the gods, he thought:
"With my limbs thus tormented, what shall I do? How can my entry [into heaven] be accomplished?"
Living thus in the form of a brahmin, he did not perceive any difference;
once, that man of great wisdom, having performed his morning rites, [proceeded].
Accompanied by his disciples, Gautama went out from the hermitage;
O brahmins, he [bestowed] the Gautamī hermitage, various grains, and other things.
Having gone to see that best of sages, Indra gazed upon him;
saying, "This is the opportunity," he performed a deed pleasing to his mind.
Having assumed the form of Gautama, Śatakratu, desiring to please him,
beheld Ahalyā, whose every limb was beautiful, and spoke these words.
Indra said:
"I am drawn by your virtues; remembering your form, my steps falter.
Speaking thus and smiling, he took her hand and entered within.
Ahalyā did not recognize him as her paramour, but thought him to be Gautama;
while she was enjoying herself with him at her pleasure, Gautama returned accompanied by his disciples.
Ahalyā, speaking ever so sweetly, would always go out to meet him as he approached,
addressing him with endearing words and pleasing him with her virtues.
Not seeing her, the highly wise one considered that a great marvel;
O Nārada, everyone saw the best of sages standing at the door.
The guards and household attendants of the Agnihotra hall,
filled with fear and wonder, spoke to Gautama, the best of sages.
The guards said:
"O Blessed One, what is this wonder? You are seen both outside and inside;
you have entered within with your beloved, and yet you remain likewise outside."
"Oh, how great is the power of this asceticism, that you have assumed these various forms!"
Brahmā said:
Having heard that, he was struck with wonder within himself and thought, "Who indeed stays here?
O dear Ahalyā, why do you not answer me?"
Having heard these words of the ṛṣi, Ahalyā spoke to her lover.
Ahalyā said:
"Who are you that have committed this sin in the guise of a sage?
Speaking thus, she rose quickly from her bed out of fear.
And that evildoer Śakra became a cat out of fear of the sage;
for he had then seen his own beloved wife terrified, disfigured, and defiled.
That sage spoke out of anger, "What is this rash act that has been committed?
To her husband who was speaking thus, she too said nothing, being overcome with shame.
While searching for that paramour, the sage saw the cat;
he said to him, "Who are you? I shall reduce you to ashes for speaking falsely! (BrP 87.54)
Indra said: With palms joined in reverence,
the Lord of Śacī, the husband of Śacī, the destroyer of cities, the one whose wealth is asceticism, and who is praised by many, spoke thus.
"O sinless one, what I have spoken is the truth: this evil has come upon me;
O sage, I have committed a great and censurable deed."
What will those whose hearts are pierced by the arrows of Love not do?
O Brahman, O ocean of compassion, forgive me, a great sinner! (BrP 87.57)
"The virtuous never exhibit harshness even toward one who has committed an offense.
Having heard those words, the brahmin, filled with rage, spoke to Hari.
Gautama said:
"O Bhava, you who possess a thousand phalluses, may the sin committed through devotion to the phallus be yours!
At this, the sage spoke to her in anger: "And you, become a dry river! (BrP 87.59)
Then, describing his appearance, she sought to appease him.
Ahalyā said:
Even those most sinful women who desire another man in their minds cause all their ancestors to go to inexhaustible hells.
"O Blessed One, having become gracious, please attend to my words;
he came to me in your form, and these [beings] here are witnesses."
"So be it," the guards replied; Ahalyā spoke the truth.
Having understood this even through meditation, the tranquil sage spoke to the devoted wife.
Gautama said:
"But when you have united, O blessed one, with the river Gautamī,
the lord of rivers, you shall become a river and then regain your original form, doing what is pleasing to me."
Having heard these words of the seer, the devoted wife acted accordingly;
thus Ahalyā, the beloved of Gautama, was united with that goddess.
It then became that very form which had been previously created by me;
thereupon, with palms joined in reverence, the king of the gods spoke to Gautama.
Indra said:
"Protect me, O tiger among sages, who have come to your house as a most sinful man. Seeing him fallen at his feet, Gautama spoke out of compassion.
Gautama said:
"Go to Gautamī; may it be well with you, O Purandara! Perform your ablutions there, and in an instant you shall be cleansed of sin and become thousand-eyed."
"O Nārada, I have seen both things that cause wonder:
the restoration of Ahalyā and the thousand-eyed husband of Śacī."
From that time forward, that auspicious holy site known as Ahalyā-saṅgama became famous as Indratīrtha, bestowing all desires upon men.
Brahmā said:
Beyond that is another sacred site known as Janasthāna;
it extends for four yojanas and grants liberation to men through mere remembrance.
In ancient times, there was a king named Janaka born in the lineage of Vaivasvata;
he married the daughter of the Lord of Waters, who was an ocean of virtues.
King Janaka was the progenitor of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
and because of his corresponding virtues, his wife was an ocean of qualities.
And Yājñavalkya, the best of Brahmins, was the domestic priest of that king;
the most excellent of monarchs questioned that priest, Yājñavalkya.
Janaka said:
Both enjoyment and liberation have been determined by the best of sages to be supreme;
yet, enjoyment is considered excellent when it consists of female and male servants, horses, chariots, and so forth.
However, enjoyment is ultimately insipid, whereas liberation alone is free from all harm;
liberation is far superior to enjoyment—how, then, can one attain liberation through enjoyment?
"Since the attainment of liberation through the renunciation of all attachments is so extremely difficult, tell me, O tiger among the twice-born: how can liberation come about from happiness?"
Yājñavalkya said:
"The lord of the waters is your preceptor, as well as your father-in-law and one who does what is pleasing to you.
Go to him, O King, and ask; he will instruct you in what is beneficial."
Then Yājñavalkya and King Janaka went to Varuṇa and, remaining composed, spoke to him in due order concerning the path to liberation.
Varuṇa said:
Liberation is established in two ways, both through action and through inaction;
this is the path determined in the Veda, for action is indeed superior to inaction.
And since all four aims of human life are bound to action,
it is falsely said that the path to liberation is attained through inaction alone.
O best of kings, all grains will be produced through ritual action;
therefore, men should perform Vedic rites with their whole being.
By means of that, men in this world attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
[they attain] merit through action even for one who is inactive, and likewise through action within the stages of life (āśramas).
And regarding that which depends on birth, O Indra among kings, listen to that as well, O knower of dharma;
there are four stages of life, O giver of honor, which are the gateways to action.
Among the four stages of life, the householder stage is remembered as the bestower of merit;
therefore, it is my conviction that both worldly enjoyment and liberation arise from it.
Brahmā said:
Having heard this, the wise Janaka and Yājñavalkya,
after honoring Varuṇa, spoke these words once again.
"O best of gods, what land and what sacred ford (tīrtha) bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation? Tell me that, for you are omniscient; salutations be unto you! (BrP 88.17)
Varuṇa said:
On earth, there is Bhāratavarṣa, and within it, the merit-bestowing Daṇḍaka;
any action performed in that sacred field grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation to men.
Among all sacred fords, the Gaṅgā at Gautamī is the most excellent, bestowing liberation upon men;
there, through sacrifice and charity, one shall attain both worldly enjoyments and liberation.
Brahmā said: Having heard the words of the Lord of Waters, Yājñavalkya and Janaka,
being duly permitted by Varuṇa, then departed for their own city.
King Janaka performed rituals such as the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha),
and Yājñavalkya, the best of Brahmins, officiated as the priest for that monarch.
Resorting to the bank of the Gaṅgā, the king attained liberation through sacrifices;
likewise, many kings of the Janaka lineage attained it there through ritual action.
Those highly fortunate ones attained liberation through the grace of Gautamī;
from that time forward, that sacred ford became renowned as Janasthāna.
Janasthāna is proclaimed as the sacrificial assembly of the Janakas;
it extends for four yojanas and destroys all sins through mere remembrance.
There, by means of bathing, giving gifts, and the libation to the ancestors, or even by remembering the sacred ford, by going there, or by serving it with devotion; // BrP_88.25 //
One obtains all desires and shall likewise attain liberation.
Brahmā said:
O best of sages, there are two most meritorious and auspicious rivers, Aruṇā and Varuṇā; their confluence with the Gaṅgā is likewise sacred.
Listen here to its origin, which destroys all sins:
the eldest son of Kaśyapa was Āditya, renowned throughout the world.
The Eye of the Three Worlds, the Sharp-rayed One, the Seven-horsed, honored by the world—
his wife is known as Uṣā, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, the most beautiful woman in the three worlds.
Unable to endure the intensity of her husband's prowess, the slender-waisted and passionate woman reflected, "What ought I to do? (BrP 89.4).
Her two sons were the great kings Manu Vaivasvata and Yama, and [her daughter was] the holy river Yamunā; hear now the cause of wonder.
She diligently created her own shadow in her own form; then Uṣā spoke to it: "And you shall become like me."
"Protect your husband and your offspring by my command;
remain devoted to your husband until my return."
"O beloved, this must not be told by you anywhere, even to your own children.
And Chāyā said, "So be it," and Uṣā departed from the house.
Having spoken thus, she departed quickly, desiring a peaceful form. Having gone to the house of Tvaṣṭṛ, Uṣā reported everything to her father.
Tvaṣṭṛ, who was deeply affectionate toward his daughter, spoke to her in astonishment.
Tvaṣṭṛ said:
"It is not fitting for a woman who has a husband to act according to her own will. How shall there be a livelihood for your offspring, or for your husband, the Sun?"
"I am afraid, O blessed lady; I am bound by duty. Return once more to your husband's house."
Brahmā said:
Having been addressed thus by her father, she repeatedly replied,
"No," and departed in haste for the region of Uttarakuru to perform austerities.
There, Uṣā, assuming the form of a mare, performed intense penance,
meditating motionless upon her own beloved, who was difficult to behold.
In the meantime, dear one, Chāyā, assuming the form of Uṣas,
remained devoted to her husband, and then offspring were born.
Sāvarṇi, Śani, and Viṣṭi— that evil woman— she,
being Chāyā, constantly acted with intentional malice.
Yama then became enraged at his own offspring, Uṣā,
because his mother Chāyā was behaving with partiality toward them.
Yama, the lord of the southern quarter, struck with his foot;
due to the agitation caused by his son's wickedness, Chāyā struck Yama, the son of Vivasvat.
He cursed him, saying, "O sinner, by my command let your foot fall apart!
With his foot shattered, he went to his father weeping out of grief,
and reported that entire incident to Savitṛ in its entirety.
Yama said:
"O best of gods, she by whom I have been cursed in this manner is not my mother;
for a mother does not become angry even when her children act perversely."
Whatever I may have spoken out of childishness, or whatever evil deed I may have committed, that mother does not become angry; therefore, she is not my mother.
Whatever is done by her offspring, whether good or bad, in whatever manner it may be—all that is attributed to her; therefore she is celebrated as "Mātā" (the Mother).
"O dear one, she seems as if she would burn me; she constantly gazes at me with her eye and speaks with a voice like that of fire or the hour of death. This is not my mother. (BrP 89.21)
{Brahmā said:} Having heard those words of his son, Savitṛ then reflected:
"This Chāyā is not his mother; Uṣas is his mother, but she is elsewhere."
Desiring peace for me,
the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, assuming the form of a mare, is devoted to asceticism in another region, in Uttarakuru.
Knowing that she was there, the Lord Divākara went to where his beloved was staying, having himself assumed the form of a horse.
Seeing her in the form of a mare, he, who was in the shape of a horse, ran after her;
for upon seeing the horse overcome by passion and hearing the sound of its neighing, he pursued her.
Uṣā, endowed with devotion to her husband and intent on meditating upon him,
was terrified by the assault of the horse and did not know who this being could be.
When her husband arrived, she fled in haste toward the south, thinking:
"Who indeed might be my protector here—be they sages or even gods?"
Assuming the form of a horse himself, he ran after that beloved mare as she fled, following wherever Uṣas went, just as the sun follows her.
Who, having fallen under the power of the planet of lust, does not perform wicked deeds—
whether by the river Bhāgīrathī, other rivers, or in forests and groves?
Then, having crossed both the Narmadā and the Vindhya while facing southward,
the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, agitated by fear, reached the Gautamī.
"It has been heard that there are sages who are protectors in Janasthāna;
together with the horse, she entered the hermitage of the seers, Gautamī."
Then the horse arrived, possessing the form of the sun;
thereupon, the sons of sages from Janasthāna tried to restrain the horse.
Then, out of anger, the lord Uṣāpati cursed those sages.
Bhānu said:
"Since you have restrained me, you shall become banyan trees."
Brahmā said:
With their vision of knowledge, the sages perceived the horse as the Lord of Uṣas;
praising that Sun, the Lord of the gods of gods, the sages rejoiced with joy.
Then, being praised by hosts of sages, Bhānu arrived on his horse;
his own face was fixed upon the mouth of the mare, who was in the form of a horse.
Having learned of her husband, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ discharged her seed from her mouth;
by that seed, the two Aśvins were born in the Gaṅgā.
Thereupon, hosts of gods, perfected beings (siddhas), and likewise sages arrived;
as did rivers, cows, medicinal herbs, deities, and the hosts of luminaries.
The chariot has seven horses and is holy; Aruṇa is its driver, and Bhānu is its guide.
Yama, Manu, Varuṇa, Śani, and likewise Vaivasvata [are its attendants].
O Sage, the holy river Yamunā and the great river Tāpī likewise assumed those respective forms out of wonder at those rivers.
Filled with wonder, they came to see him, as did his father-in-law;
but having understood his intention, Bhānu spoke to his father-in-law.
Bhānu said: "O Tvaṣṭṛ, while Uṣā performs supreme austerity for my sake,
place me upon a mechanical device and divide my splendors into many parts."
O Prajāpati, cut it off while there is still happiness for her.
Brahmā said:
Having said "So be it," Tvaṣṭṛ then, in the presence of Somanātha, performed the cutting away of the splendors; therefore, they know that place as Prabhāsa.
Where she, in the form of a mare, united with her husband on the Gautamī,
and where the Aśvins were born— that is called Aśvatīrtha.
That place was declared to be Bhānutīrtha, as was the hermitage of Pañcavaṭa;
both the Tāpī and the Yamunā arrived there to see their father.
The confluence of the Aruṇā and Varuṇā rivers with the Gaṅgā is auspicious;
there, the various deities and sacred bathing places (tīrthas) have arrived individually.
There are nine thousand meritorious holy sites (tīrthas);
bathing and giving gifts there bestow inexhaustible merit.
O Nārada, by remembering it, by reciting it, or even by hearing it,
one shall be liberated from all sins, become endowed with dharma, and attain happiness.
Brahmā said:
O Nārada, listen attentively as I describe the power of that sacred ford named Gāruḍa, which grants the pacification of all obstacles.
There was indeed one named Maṇināga, the son of Śeṣa and possessed of great strength;
out of devotion and fear of Garuḍa, he propitiated Śaṅkara.
Then the blessed Lord Parameṣṭhin Maheśvara, being pleased, said to that great serpent: "O serpent, choose a boon."
The Naga said, "O Lord, grant me freedom from fear of Garuḍa.
Śambhu said to him, "So be it; you shall have no fear of Garuḍa."
The fearless elephant has emerged from Aruṇānuja, the Garuḍa,
where the one who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk dwells in the vicinity of that milk-ocean.
This elephant roams here and there in that pleasant and cool place;
even Garuḍa goes to that very region where he dwells.
Seeing the serpent moving about fearlessly, Garuḍa seized that great nāga and cast him into his own abode.
While Garuḍa was binding that best of serpents with his Garuḍa-nooses,
Nandin spoke at that moment to Īśa, the Lord of the World.
Nandikeśvara said: "Surely the Naga has not returned, O Lord of the Gods; he must have been either eaten or bound by Garuḍa, for a Naga would not return alive."
Brahmā said:
Having heard the words of Nandin and understood them, Śambhu then spoke.
Śiva said:
"A serpent remains bound in the house of Garuḍa;
go quickly and praise Viṣṇu, Janārdana, the Lord of the worlds."
"Bring the bound Naga yourself at my word, as Kāśyapa has done. Having heard those words of his lord, Nandin went to the Lord of Śrī.
He himself addressed these words to Viṣṇu, the refuge of the worlds;
Nārāyaṇa, with a pleased mind, spoke these words to Garuḍa.
Viṣṇu said:
"O son of Vinatā, at my word, give a serpent to Nandin.
Hearing that, the bird, trembling, replied, "No."
Out of anger, Suparṇa spoke even to Viṣṇu in the presence of Nandin.
Garuḍa said:
Whatever most beloved thing powerful lords may give to their servants, others will give; but you shall certainly not take back what has been brought by me.
"Behold, O Lord, how the three-eyed god will release the serpent provided by me;
you, however, shall give the serpent to Nandin."
"I always carry you, O Lord; therefore, you must always give me what is due to me.
It is not fitting for you to say 'give' regarding the elephant provided by me."
This would not be the conduct of virtuous masters who act with integrity;
for the virtuous give to their servants, whereas you are one who seizes what has been acquired by me.
"O Keśava, you conquer the Daityas in battle solely by my power;
yet you boast in vain, thinking, 'I am the one of great strength.'"
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of Garuḍa, the wielder of the discus and mace laughed while standing beside Nandin, as the world-protectors looked on.
The one of great intelligence said this to me: "O best of birds, you have become emaciated;
by your strength, I shall conquer all the asuras."
Having spoken thus, O Brahmā, the Lord of Śrī, his anger appeased, said this:
"Quickly extend the little finger of your hand toward Nandin."
Then, placing this upon the head of Garuḍa, he spoke again:
"O bird, you always carry me truthfully; behold the Dharma!"
Then, as soon as his finger was placed [there], his head entered his belly;
and his belly entered the interior of his foot and was crushed to powder.
Thereupon, he stood with palms joined in reverence, dejected, pained, and filled with shame.
Garuḍa said:
"Save me, save me, O Lord of the World! I am your servant and have committed an offense.
You are the sovereign of all worlds; you alone are the sustainer and the one who is to be sustained."
The powerful forgive thousands of offenses;
indeed, they possess great compassion even toward a person who has committed a transgression.
"All the sages proclaim you alone to be the source of compassion;
O Mother of the World, dweller in the lotus, protect me who am afflicted! O Kamalā, you who are affectionate toward your children, [protect] this miserable, suffering child."
Brahmā said:
Then the goddess Śrī, filled with compassion, also spoke to Janārdana.
Kamalā said:
"O Lord, protect your own servant Garuḍa, who has fallen into calamity.
Janārdana spoke thus to Nandin, the vehicle of Śambhu:
Viṣṇu said:
"Take the serpent, along with Garuḍa, into the very presence of Śambhu;
for by his grace, Garuḍa, being gazed upon by Maheśvara, [shall attain immortality]."
Furthermore, Garuḍa shall obtain his own form.
Brahmā said:
Having said, "So be it," Vṛṣabha, together with the Nāga and Garuḍa,
approached Śaṅkara slowly and reported everything to him.
Śaṅkara, the moon-crested Lord, also spoke to Garuḍa.
Śiva said:
"Go, O mighty-armed one, to the Gaṅgā, the Gautamī, the purifier of the world; having bathed in that peaceful river which grants all desires, you shall regain your body."

And you shall obtain all your desires a hundredfold and even a thousandfold. O bird, for those living beings who are tormented by every sin and whose efforts have been uprooted by ill fortune, the Gautamī is their refuge, bestowing their heart's desires.
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words, Garuḍa bowed down and approached;
having bathed in the Gaṅgā, that Garuḍa paid homage to Śiva and Viṣṇu.
Then, O best of sages, that wise one, possessing a golden body, a diamond-like frame, and great strength, became swift and once again approached Viṣṇu.
From that time forth, that sacred site became known as Gāruḍa, granting all desires.
Whatever a self-restrained man performs there, such as bathing and other rites,
O child, all of that becomes inexhaustible and brings pleasure to Śiva and Viṣṇu.
Brahmā said:
Then there is the sacred ford of Govardhana, which destroys all sins,
generates merit for the ancestors, and removes evil even by its mere remembrance.
O Nārada, this is the power of that [place] which was seen by me:
there was a certain Brahmin farmer well-known as Jābāli. (BrP 91.2)
He does not let go of the two oxen even when the sun has reached the meridian;
he prods them with a goad from behind as well as from both sides.
Seeing those two cows with eyes filled with tears,
Surabhi— the wish-fulfilling milch-cow and mother of the worlds— told everything to Nandin.
And he, becoming distressed, reported that to Śambhu;
and Śambhu said to the bull, "May all your words be fulfilled."
Accompanied by Śiva’s command, Nandin brought back all the cattle that had been born from the cows;
when all the cattle had vanished from both heaven and the mortal world, he then acted with haste.
The hosts of gods said to me, "We cannot live without cows.
I replied to all those gods, "Go to Śaṅkara and beg him."
Having likewise praised the Lord, they all reported their business to him;
the Lord also said to the gods, "The Bull [Nandin] knows my intention."
The immortals said to Vṛṣa, "Give us the cows, for they have been our benefactors.
Vṛṣa also said to the gods, "Let the Gosava sacrifice be performed."
"Then you shall obtain all cattle, both those that are divine and those that are human;
from that, the god-ordained Gosava sacrifice shall proceed."
Then, on the auspicious flank of Gautamī, the cows flourished;
that sacred ford is known as Govardhana, which increases the joy of the gods.
O best of sages, bathing there yields the fruit of a thousand cows;
we do not know what fruit might be obtained through some small gift or other offering.
Brahmā said:
O Nārada, listen attentively as I declare the name of the sacred ford (tīrtha) called Pāpapraṇāśana, which removes the fear of sin. BrP_92.1 //
There was a world-renowned Brahmin known as Dhṛtavrata;
his wife was named Mahī, a young woman who was the most beautiful in the world.
O Sage, his son was known as Sanābjāta, who was like the sun; while he was thus upholding his vows, Death, impelled by Time, approached him.
Then that beautiful young widow with a young son,
seeing no protector at all, went to the hermitage of Gālava.
Then, having handed over her son to him, that wanton woman, deluded by sin and driven by lust,
wandered through many lands, acting according to her own will.
His son, though born in the house of Gālava as one who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas,
became a man whose mind was led astray by the fault of his mother and was reduced to the state of a commoner.
Known as Janasthāna, it is filled with various species;
there he dwells upon the earth in the guise of a merchant.
His son, too, being lustful, wandered through many lands;
he also, by the power of time, was then dwelling there in Janasthāna.
A twice-born man who has maintained his vows desires a courtesan as a woman;
and the earth, too, awaits men who are givers of wealth.
He did not recognize his own son, nor did he recognize his mother;
nevertheless, by the power of destiny, the reunion of that mother and son took place.
Thus, after much time had passed as the son went about his business and the mother her own,
there was no mutual recognition whatsoever between that mother and son.
O Nārada, listen to how even that man of evil conduct, while acting according to the duty of a father, came to possess right-mindedness in a most wonderful manner.
Living according to his own will, he did not neglect this;
having performed the Vedic twilight devotions (*brāhmī saṃdhyā*), he thereafter engaged in the acquisition of wealth.
Having acquired vast riches through the power of his knowledge, he gives them away;
likewise, rising early in the morning, he goes to the Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rite.
Having performed all duties such as purification, bathing, and the twilight prayers in their proper order,
and having bowed to the Brahmins, he then proceeds to his own tasks.
At dawn, when the deformed man went to the Gautamī river— his entire body afflicted with leprosy, his limbs loosened, and pus and blood flowing from him—
Having bathed in the Gautamī Gaṅgā, he who assumes a beautiful form proceeds,
peaceful yet resembling the sun and fire, like the Sun-god himself in embodied form.
That twice-born Gālava, devoted to austerity and knowledge, did not perceive these two forms of his own while he was there where the Blessed One resided.
Having taken refuge in Queen Gautamī, he dwells there surrounded by sages;
and even the Brahmin, having regularly visited that very sacred ford, remains right there.
Then, having paid homage to Gālava, he proceeds to his own abode;
[he assumes] that body which was born from the ancient practice of serving the Gaṅgā.
Furthermore, O twice-born one, whatever occurs after the time for bathing and the twilight prayers—that too is his very form; Gālava says this is indeed eternal.
Seeing this, he was filled with wonder and thought, "There must be some cause for this.
Having thus become amazed, Gālava spoke to that twice-born man:
Then, as he was departing for his home, the wise preceptor, out of compassion, wonder, and with great effort, called out to him who had been born from the sacrificial fire and paid him homage.
Gālava said: Who are you? Where are you going? What are you doing? Where will you eat?
What is your name? Where is your bed? Who is your wife? Tell me.
Brahmā said:
Having heard the words of Gālava, the brāhmaṇa also spoke to that sage.
The Brahmin said:
"Tomorrow I shall tell you everything, having ascertained the decision regarding what must be done."
Brahmā said:
Having spoken thus to Gālava, he who was born from the eternal [lotus] went to his home;
having eaten well that night with her, he approached the bed with the harlot.
Remembering the words of Gālava, he spoke in agitation.
The Brahmin said:
"Though you are a harlot, you are endowed with all virtues and are devoted to your husband;
may our mutual affection continue as long as we live."
Nevertheless, I ask you something: what is your name, or what is your lineage?
What is your dwelling place, or where are your kinsmen? Let everything be told to me.
The harlot said: "There was a pure Brahmin known as Dhṛtavrata who had been initiated for a vow;
his wife was Mahī, and I am she, and my son is in the hermitage of Gālava."
"The wise youth known as Sanātjāta has been abandoned;
but I, due to my former fault, have cast aside the dharma inherited from my family and now live here as a wanton woman— know me, O twice-born one, to be a Brāhmaṇī."
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of hers, he felt as if pierced in his vital organs;
the courtesan suddenly fell to the ground and spoke these words to him.
The courtesan said:
"But what has happened, O best of the twice-born, and where has your affection gone?
What words have I spoken that cause such opposition in your heart?"
Having comforted himself by means of his own self, the brahmin spoke these words:
The Brahmin said:
"O sage, my father was one firm in his vows; I am his son from time immemorial.
This earth is my mother, who has come to me through destiny."
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of his, she too became exceedingly distressed.
Then, while the two of them were grieving, at dawn when the sun had become bright, [he spoke].
Having gone to Galava, that tiger among sages, the brahmin made his request known.
The brāhmaṇa said:
"O Brahman, the son of Dhṛtavrata was previously protected by you;
and by you, O Lord, my mother Mahī was also initiated."
What shall I do, and by doing what might there indeed be atonement for me?
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of the brahmin, Gālava replied, "Do not grieve;
I behold this twofold form of yours as something eternally unprecedented."
Then you were questioned regarding the events as they were heard and known by me;
whatever was your duty, all of that has reached its end in the Gaṅgā.
"By the greatness of this sacred site and by the grace of this goddess, you are purified every day, my child; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter."
At dawn, I shall again behold your forms, which are full of sin day and night,
as well as your form of supreme virtue.
I see you constantly coming yoked to a cow and going free from blame; therefore, O Goddess, you have now been made pure.
Therefore, O Brahmin, no further task will remain for you; and this mother of yours, whom you know to be an unchaste woman, shall also be recognized.
She then became utterly remorseful and desisted from her sinful act;
for, my child, affection toward living beings is natural.

Through association with the virtuous and by the power of destiny, there may arise a turning away from worldly life; yet this [turning away] occurs only for one who has previously performed great merit and feels profound remorse.
"Having performed a bath here at this sacred ford, she will then become purified.
And so, O Nārada, both the mother and son did exactly that.
Through that bath, both of them undoubtedly became free from sin;
from that time forward, they call that sacred ford Dhautapāpa (the Washer-away of Sins).
Known as Pāpapraṇāśana and Gālava, this [tīrtha] is renowned;
it destroys all sins, whether they be major (mahāpātaka), minor (alpa), or secondary (upapātaka). This Dhautapāpa bestows great merit.
Brahmā said:
O twice-born one, where Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, together with Sītā,
gratified the ancestors, they therefore know that place as Pitṛtīrtha.
There, bathing, giving gifts, and likewise the libations for the ancestors—all these attain imperishability; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
There, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha and lord of kings, honored the great sage Viśvāmitra along with sages who perceive the ultimate truth.
I shall now describe the true nature of that most meritorious tīrtha frequented by sages, known as Viśvāmitra, as it has been recited by the exponents of the Vedas.
In former times, there occurred a most terrifying drought for the subjects;
then the highly wise Viśvāmitra, together with his disciples, went to the Gautamī river.
Seeing his disciples, sons, and wife emaciated and afflicted by hunger,
the illustrious Kauśika was deeply distressed and spoke thus to his disciples:
Viśvāmitra said:
"In whatever way, whatever it may be, wherever, and however it may be—let some food, whether hard or soft, be brought; do not delay!"
One must go and fetch it this very moment, indeed in an instant.
Brahmā said:
At the word of the sage, the hungry disciples went in haste;
wandering here and there, they saw a dead dog.
Taking him, they hurriedly presented him to the teacher;
he, having said "Welcome," accepted him with his hand.
"Carve the dog's flesh and wash it with water;
then cook it, having offered oblations into the fire according to the prescribed rite while reciting mantras."
"Having gratified the gods, the sages, the ancestors, others, the guests, and our elders,
we shall all eat the remainder," so said that Kauśika.

Having heard the words of Viśvāmitra, the disciples did exactly so. While the dog-meat was being cooked, the messenger of the gods, Agni, arrived at the assembly of the gods and reported all of that to the deities.
Agni said:
"In times of distress, the gods must eat even dog-meat prepared by a sage."
Brahmā said: At those words of Agni, Indra, having become a hawk,
then carried off from the sky the vessel full of meat, which was covered over.
Having seen that deed, those disciples reported it to the seer:
"O best of sages, the vessel has been carried off by a hawk of undisciplined mind."
Then the Blessed One became enraged, desiring to curse Hari;
thereupon the Lord of the Gods, having understood this, prepared a vessel overflowing with honey.
The bird Hari placed them back into the very torches; however, seeing the vessel filled with honey, Viśvāmitra became enraged,
and out of that anger, Kauśika spoke these words.
Viśvāmitra said:
"Give us dog-meat; we shall take the supreme nectar of immortality.
Otherwise, I shall reduce you to ashes. Then Indra, being afraid, spoke thus.
Indra said:
"Having offered the honey according to the rule, drink it together with your sons.
O great sage, what is the use of this impure dog-meat?"
Brahmā said: Viśvāmitra also replied, "No; what is the fruit of eating alone?
All subjects are perishing; what use is that honey to you, O Hari?"
"If it were nectar for all, I would eat this pure nectar;
otherwise, let the gods and ancestors eat this dog-meat."
"Afterwards, I shall eat that meat; there is no falsehood in my word.
Then, terrified, the thousand-eyed Indra immediately summoned the clouds.
He rained down the water of nectar, for the subjects were offered with nectar;
thereafter, that meritorious nectar was given by Hari according to the prescribed ritual.
Having first gratified the gods and having gratified the three worlds,
the brahmin Viśvāmitra partook of food together with his disciples and his wife.
From that time forward, that sacred ford (tīrtha) became renowned as bestowing great merit,
where the Lord of the Gods arrived to bestow the nectar of immortality upon the worlds.
That sacred ford (tīrtha), which is devoid of flesh, bestows merit upon men;
bathing and giving gifts there yield the fruit of all sacrifices.
From that time forward, that holy ford was known as Viśvāmitra;
then there were Madhutīrtha, Aindra, Śyena, and Parjanya.
Brahmā said:
There is a holy place known as Śvetatīrtha, auspicious and renowned throughout the three worlds;
by merely hearing of it, one is liberated from all sins.
In ancient times, there was a brahmin named Śveta, a dear friend of Gautama;
devoted to the hospitality and worship of guests, he resided on the bank of the Gautamī.
Devoted to the worship of Śiva through mind, deed, and speech,
he was constantly meditating upon and honoring that best of the twice-born.
Then, messengers from the Lord of the Southern Quarter arrived to lead away that best of the twice-born, who had reached the full span of his life and was devoted solely to the worship of Śiva.
O Nārada, they were not even able to enter his house;
then, when that time had passed, Citraka spoke to Mṛtyu.
Citraka said:
"O Death, why does Śveta not come, his life exhausted? Why is it that even now your messengers have not arrived? This is truly not fitting for you."
Brahmā said:
Then Mṛtyu, becoming enraged, went in person to the White House,
seeing his messengers standing outside, afflicted by fear.
He asked, "What is this? and the messengers spoke of death to him.
The messengers said:
"We are not able even to look upon Śveta, who is protected by Śiva.
For those with whom Giriśa is pleased, what indeed can cause fear?"
Brahmā said:
Then Death, with noose in hand, entered where that twice-born man was;
yet that brahmin did not perceive either Death or the servants of Yama.
While Śiva was being worshipped with devotion near Śveta,
Daṇḍin, having seen Mṛtyu holding a noose, spoke in astonishment.
Daṇḍin said: "O Death, what do you see here? Death replied. *BrP 94.11*
Death said:
"I have come here to lead Śveta away; therefore, I am looking for that best of the twice-born."
Brahmā said: "Go! Death, holding his staff, then cast his nooses;
O tiger among sages, he then became enraged at Śveta. (BrP 94.13)
With a staff bestowed by Śiva, Daṇḍin struck Mṛtyu;
thereupon Mṛtyu, the bearer of the noose, fell to the surface of the earth.
Then those messengers, having quickly seen that Death had been slain,
reported everything to Yama regarding the killing of Death by Daṇḍin.
Then Dharma, enraged, mounted upon his buffalo-vehicle,
summoned Citragupta of great strength and the protector Yamadaṇḍa.
[He destroys] the Mahiṣa [demon], spirits, and vetālas, as well as mental and physical ailments,
diseases of the eyes, diseases of the belly, and likewise earaches.
Having said to them, "Let them hasten [to their respective punishments]— the threefold fever, sin, and the various hells"— Yama departed in haste.
Surrounded by these and others where Śveta, the best of the twice-born, was located,
Nandin, bearing his weapons, spoke upon seeing Yama approaching.
There, that battle took place between Vināyaka, Skanda, and Daṇḍin, the lord of spirits, bringing fear to all the worlds.
Kārttikeya himself, with his spear,
pierced the servants of Yama and also struck down the lord of the southern quarter along with his army.
Those who remained after being slain reported it to Yama;
and Āditya, having heard of that great marvel together with the gods, [acted accordingly].
Followed by the world-protectors, he approached my presence;
so did I, the blessed Viṣṇu, Indra, Agni, and Varuṇa.
The Moon and the Sun, the Aśvins, the world-protectors, and the hosts of Maruts—
these and many others have gone into the presence of Yama, as have we.
The powerful Dakṣiṇeśa lies dead on the bank of the Gaṅgā,
along with the oceans, rivers, nāgas, and numerous various beings.
There they went to see Yama, the son of Vivasvat and lord of the gods.
Having seen Yama with his army destroyed, all the gods, afflicted by fear,
spoke repeatedly to Śambhu with their palms joined in reverence.
The gods said:
O you who are eternally fond of devotion and the slayer of the wicked, salutations to you, the primordial creator; O Blue-throated One, let there be salutations to you!
O beloved of Brahmā, let there be salutation to you; O beloved of the gods, let there be salutation to you.
Yama and all the others were unable to lead away that white twice-born devotee who was devoid of life;
they attained supreme satisfaction upon seeing him.
O Lord, your fondness for those devoted to you is true;
even Kṛtānta is not able to look upon those who have sought refuge in you, the compassionate one.
Knowing this, all [beings] are indeed Śiva;
they worship you alone with supreme devotion.
O Lord of the worlds, O Śaṅkara, do you not remember?
"Who else besides you is capable of establishing order here, O Lord?"
Brahmā said:
As they were thus offering praise, Śiva appeared before them. "What shall I give? he asked them; and the gods replied as follows.
The gods said:
"This Vaivasvata Dharma is the restrainer of all embodied beings; established as the arbiter of righteousness and unrighteousness, he is the protector of the world."
He does not deserve death, for he is neither an offender nor an evildoer;
without him, nothing at all will remain for the Sustainer of the World.
Therefore, O Lord of Gods, restore Yama to life along with his army and his vehicles;
O Protector, let this prayer bear fruit, for among the great, a request does not go in vain.
Brahmā said:
Then the Blessed One spoke: "I shall undoubtedly bring him back to life, provided that the deities grant my word today to Yama."
Then all the gods said: "We shall carry out the word spoken by you, who, together with Hari, Brahmā, and the others, have the entire world under your control."
Then the Blessed One spoke to the immortals who had assembled there:
"Let my devotee not suffer death. The immortals replied once more, "No. (BrP 94.37)
Then, O God, all the worlds, including the moving and the unmoving, would become immortal;
O God, who pervades the universe, this distinction between the mortal and the immortal would not exist.
Again Śambhu said to them: "Listen to my speech concerning those Vaiṣṇavas devoted to me who dwell along the Gautamī."
"We are indeed the eternal masters; death does not deserve mastery over us.
Not even a word regarding them should ever be spoken by Yama."
One should never be overcome by mental or physical ailments and the like at any time;
those who have gone for refuge to Śiva are liberated even at that very moment.
"Therefore, all of you must pay homage to Yama along with his followers.
To the God of gods, Śiva, the hosts of deities replied, "So be it."
Then the Blessed Lord spoke to his mount, Nandin:
Śiva said:
"Sprinkle the deceased Yama with the water of the Gautamī."
Brahmā said:
Then all of them, headed by Yama, having been consecrated by Nandin,
rose up with their lives restored and departed toward the southern direction.
On the northern bank of the Gautamī, Viṣṇu and all the other deities were stationed, worshipping Maheśvara, the God of gods.
Therein, there were eight times ten thousand, fourteen thousand,
as well as six thousand, and again another six thousand.
Likewise, on the southern bank, there are thirty thousand holy fords (tīrthas).
O Nārada, this is indeed the meritorious narrative of Śvetatīrtha.
Wherever that Death fell, that place is called Mṛtyutīrtha;
by the mere hearing of its name, one lives for a thousand years.
In that regard, bathing and giving gifts there destroy all sins; likewise,
hearing, reciting, and even remembering it effects the destruction of impurities for all people and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Brahmā said:
There is a place renowned as Śukratīrtha, which bestows all perfections upon men,
pacifies all sins, and destroys all diseases.
Aṅgiras and Bhṛgu were two sages of supreme righteousness;
their sons were highly wise and distinguished by their beauty, intellect, and charm.
Seeing their two sons, Jīva and Kavi by name, who were devoted to the authority of their parents and had been initiated, the two parents spoke to one another.
The two sages said: "Let there be only one teacher for us both, and always for our two sons.
Therefore, let there be one ruler; let the other remain as he pleases."
Brahmā said:
Having heard this, Aṅgiras then quickly spoke to the descendant of Bhṛgu:
"I shall teach you; let the descendant of Bhṛgu remain at ease, for you are worthy."
Having heard these words of Aṅgiras, the descendant of Bhrigu,
considering it so, offered Śukra to him.
He used to teach both sons separately at all times;
however, after some time, Śukra spoke this to those two boys out of a sense of partiality.
Śukra said:
"O Teacher, you instruct me constantly with partiality;
such partiality between a son and a pupil is not fitting for teachers."
