Furthermore, foolish teachers behave with partiality toward their disciples;
there is no limit to the sin of those who possess such uneven minds.
"O Teacher, you have been rightly known; I bow to you again and again.
I shall indeed go to another guru; you ought to grant me permission."
"O Brahmin, I would go to my father if he were in distress;
otherwise, I shall go elsewhere. My lord, you have been asked; now let us depart."
Brahmā said:
Having seen his preceptor Bṛhaspati, he departed from there with his permission;
having acquired all knowledge, he thought, "I shall go to my father."
"Therefore, whom should I question? Who might be the most excellent teacher? Thinking thus, he questioned the highly wise Vṛddhagautama.
Śukra said:
"O best of sages, tell me who might be my guru;
I shall go to him who is the guru of even the three worlds."
Brahmā said:
He spoke to Śambhu, the Lord of the worlds, the God and Teacher of the universe:
"Where shall I worship Giriśa? Thus addressed, Gautama replied.
Gautama said:
Having become pure at the Gautamī river, propitiate Śaṅkara with hymns of praise;
then the Lord of the World, being pleased, will bestow that knowledge upon you.
Brahmā said:
At those words of Gautama, that descendant of Bhṛgu went to the Gaṅgā;
having bathed and become thoroughly pure, the boy offered a hymn of praise.
Śukra said:
"O Lord who bears the young moon, I am but a child, possessed of a child's intellect;
I do not know anything to offer as praise for you—salutations be unto you!"
Abandoned by my preceptor, I have no friend or companion; you are my lord through all my being. O Lord of the World, homage be to you!
O God, you are the teacher of those who possess great wisdom, and the greatest among the great;
I am but a small child—homage be to you, O one who pervades the universe!
O Lord of the gods, for the sake of knowledge I do not know your course;
look upon me with compassion, O witness of the world—salutations be to you!
Brahmā said:
As he was thus offering praise, the Lord of the Gods became pleased.
Śiva said:
"Choose a boon, may it be well with you—even one that is difficult for the gods to obtain."
Brahmā said:
The noble-minded sage, with palms joined in reverence, also spoke to the Lord of Gods.
Śukra said:
"O Lord, I shall beg for that knowledge which is not within the reach even of the sages beginning with Brahmā; you are my guru and my deity."
Brahmā said:
The best of the gods gave that science of reviving the dead, which was unknown even to the thirty deities, to Śukra when he requested it.
Other worldly knowledge and Vedic knowledge have other spheres of application;
but when Śaṅkara is pleased, what remains to be deliberated?
Having obtained the great lore (mahāvidyā), he went to his father, who was his guru;
and Kavi, by virtue of that lore, became the preceptor of the Daityas and was honored by them.
Then once, for a certain reason,
Kaca, the son of Bṛhaspati, obtained that science from Kavi.
From Kaca, Bṛhaspati also received it, and from him the gods each individually obtained the great science which they call "the reviver of the dead."
Where that sage attained [his goal] after worshipping Maheśvara,
on the northern bank of the Gautamī, that place is called Śukratīrtha.
The Mṛtasaṃjīvinī Tīrtha increases longevity and health;
whatever bathing or giving is performed there bestows inexhaustible merit.
Brahmā said:
There is a place renowned as Indratīrtha, which destroys the sin of killing a Brahmin;
by its mere remembrance, it destroys the multitude of afflictions arising from the flood of sins.
O Nārada, long ago, when the slaying of Vṛtra had occurred, the sin of Brahman-murder followed Śacī’s husband; seeing her, Hari became as if terrified.
Then Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, ran hither and thither;
wherever he went, that slaughter followed after him, pursuing Indra.
Having entered that great lake, he approached the lotus stalk;
there, having become like a thread, the Lord of Śacī took up his residence.
O Sage, even on the shore of that lake, there was a slaughter for a thousand divine years;
during this interval, the gods were indeed deprived of Indra.
They deliberated with undistracted minds as to how Indra might come to be;
there, having prepared a place for the slaughter, I spoke to the gods.
For the sake of purifying Indra, let him be consecrated at Gautamī;
there, having been consecrated, he will become Indra again with a purified soul.
Having thus made their resolve, they quickly went to Gautamī;
there the gods and the sages saw the Lord of the Gods having bathed.
Desiring to consecrate him, they all stood before the beloved of Śacī;
but as Indra was being consecrated, Gautama spoke to him out of anger.
Gautama said:
"They shall consecrate the most wicked Mahendra, who has violated his guru’s bed;
I shall reduce them all to ashes, so let the enemies of the Asuras depart quickly."
{Brahmā said:} Having heard those words of the sage and having left Gautamī,
they all went quickly to the Narmadā, taking Indra with them.
On the northern bank of the Narmadā, they stood ready for the consecration;
there the venerable seer Māṇḍavya [saw] that Indra, who was about to be consecrated.
"I would have reduced you to ashes had there been this consecration," he said;
then the immortals honored Māṇḍavya with reasoned arguments and hymns of praise.
The gods said:
"O Sage, in whatever place this thousand-eyed Indra is consecrated, a most terrible obstacle arises there."
O auspicious one, bring peace; be gracious and become a granter of boons.
Grant us many boons for that purpose toward which we offer this atonement for our impurity.
"We shall all give [it] in that region; you should grant permission for that place where the consecration of the Lord of the Gods will take place."
It shall grant all desires to men and be endowed with grain, trees, and fruits;
there shall never be irregular rain nor famine here.
Brahmā said: Then the best of sages, Māṇḍavya, who is honored by the world,
considered that his consecration had been performed there as well as the removal of his impurity.
Then, having been addressed by the gods and the sages, that region was called Mālava;
at that time, when the Lord of the Gods had been consecrated and Vimala had come into being.
Having brought Gautamī and Gaṅgā, the gods, the sages, as well as I and Viṣṇu, consecrated him for the sake of merit.
Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, Agastya, Atri, and Kaśyapa—
these and other sages, as well as gods, yakṣas, and pannagas.
They performed their ablutions and consecrations with those holy waters;
furthermore, I myself consecrated the husband of Śacī with the water from my own water-pot.
And there, the river became meritorious by being sprinkled with water;
thus it was known as Siktā where it meets the Gaṅgā.
The two confluences there are renowned and always frequented by sages;
from that time forward, that sacred ford has been called Puṇyasaṅgama.
The merit of bathing at the confluence is said to be equal to that of Indra;
there, seven thousand auspicious sacred sites (tīrthas) existed.
Bathing and giving gifts at those places, especially at their confluence, one should know all that to be inexhaustible; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
Whoever reads or hears this meritorious narrative shall be liberated from all sins born of the actions of mind, speech, and body.
Brahmā said:
The sacred ford known as Paulastya is proclaimed to bestow all perfections upon men;
I shall describe its power, which grants back a lost kingdom.
In former times, he was the lord of the northern quarter, endowed with prosperity and supernatural powers;
he was formerly the lord of Laṅkā and the eldest son of Viśravas.
He had these brothers, powerful and of immeasurable splendor:
the stepbrothers Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, and Vibhīṣaṇa.
Those sons of Viśravas were indeed Rākṣasas born of a Rākṣasī;
together with his brothers, Dhanada [Kubera] ascended the celestial chariot granted by me.
Filled with devotion, he constantly comes and goes to my presence;
however, Rāvaṇa’s mother, becoming enraged, spoke to her sons.
Rāvaṇa’s mother said: "O son, I shall die and not live on because of this disfigurement;
even the gods and the dānavas have been enemies to one another as brothers."
Driven by the power of victory and sovereignty, they desire to kill one another;
therefore, you are neither true men, nor capable, nor seekers of victory.
For him who consents to such rivalry, life is meaningless.
Brahmā said:
O sage, having heard those words of their mother, those three brothers went to the forest for the sake of asceticism and performed great penance.
And these three Rākṣasas obtained boons from Mātali,
as well as from their maternal uncle Marīci and their maternal grandfather.
And at his mother's word, he then requested Laṅkā;
due to the nature of the Rākṣasas and the fault of his mother, a great enmity arose between the two brothers.
Then that battle took place like the one between the gods and the Dānavas;
having defeated his elder brother, the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), the conflict likewise subsided.
He seized the Puṣpaka chariot, the city of Laṅkā, and everything else;
Rāvaṇa then made a proclamation throughout the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile.

"He who provides refuge for my brother shall be put to death by me. Thus rejected by his brother, Vaiśravaṇa did not find refuge anywhere. Having gone to his grandfather Pulastya and bowed down, he spoke these words: ||| BrP_97.13 ||| He who would provide shelter for my brother, he too would deserve to be slain by me. Having been cast out by his brother, Vaiśravaṇa found no refuge anywhere; having approached his grandfather Pulastya and paid homage, he spoke these words. ||| BrP_97.13 |||
Dhanada said:
"I have been cast out by my wicked brother; tell me, what should I do? What would be a refuge or a shelter for me—whether it be destiny or even a sacred ford?"
{Brahmā said:} Having heard those words of his grandson, Pulastya spoke these words: *BrP_97.15*
Pulastya said:
"Go, my son, to the Gautamī river and praise the god Maheśvara;
there he shall have no entry into the midst of the waters of the Gaṅgā."
"You shall attain auspicious success; act accordingly with me."
Brahmā said:
Having said "So be it," that lord of wealth, the giver of riches, departed together with his wife and his aged father and mother, Pulastya.
Having gone to the Gautamī-Gaṅgā, purified and firm in his vows,
he praised Śiva, the Lord of the gods of gods, the bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Dhanada said:
O Śambhu, you alone are the lord of this entire universe of moving and unmoving beings; there is no other superior to you.
If anyone, out of delusion, acts with arrogance here even after disregarding you, that person alone is to be pitied;
for you, through your eightfold form, sustain the entire universe.
Everything indeed proceeds according to your command;
nevertheless, the wise man knows you as such, but one who is ignorant never knows your ancient greatness.
"O Lord, that which my mother spoke, born of impurity, was said out of jest: 'This son of yours shall be a hero;
and he whom you look upon shall be the Lord of Obstacles.'"
But alas, the activity of one whose vision is directed by the Lord was born [of this].
Seeing the Mountain-Daughter with her limbs drenched in tears, she spoke thus to the Lord regarding the separated couple: "Alas! (BrP 97.22d–23b).
Manobhava became Madana,
and Rati attained preeminence in beauty from Soma.
{Brahmā said:}
While he was thus offering praise, the three-eyed Lord appeared before him;
out of joy, he invited him to choose a boon, but [the sage] said nothing at all.
When Dhanada, Pulastya, and Maheśvara had become silent,
Śiva, filled with joy, spoke again and again, saying, "Choose a boon!"
In the meantime, an incorporeal voice spoke there, saying this to Maheśvara: "The status of a guardian of wealth (Dhanapāla) is to be attained."
Having understood the thought of his father Pulastya Vaiśravaṇa, a voice then spoke these auspicious words.
"What is to be will become as if it has already happened; what is being given shall be as if already given;
and what is to be attained shall be as if already attained"—such were the auspicious divine words that occurred there.
Having worshipped the Someśvara Liṅga, he who had many enemies and suffered humiliation attained lordship over the quarters and mastery over wealth.
Having heard those words regarding his wife and sons who were unable to cross over [the ocean], the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada) spoke these words to the God of Gods, the wielder of the trident:
"Let it be so."
"So be it," the Lord of the Gods thus assented to the divine speech,
as well as to Pulastya and the sage Viśravas with holy boons.
Having greeted Dhanapāla, Śiva, the lord of gods, departed;
from that time forth, they have known that holy ford as Paulastya and Dhanada.
Likewise, Vaiśravaṇa is meritorious, auspicious, and the granter of all desires;
whatever acts such as bathing are performed in those [tīrthas], all of them bestow great merit.
Brahmā said:
There is a place renowned as Agnitīrtha, which bestows the fruits of all sacrifices and pacifies all obstacles; hear now the fruit of that tīrtha.
Known as Jātavedas, he was the brother of Agni and the carrier of oblations;
while carrying the offerings of the gods, he was indeed on the bank of the Gautamī.
In the sacrificial session of the seers, Madhu, the powerful son of Diti, [slew] the supreme brother of Agni,
who was as dear to his brother as Dakṣa himself.
While the foremost of sages and even the gods looked on, he struck him down;
indeed, as long as Jātavedas was dead, the gods did not receive their sacrificial offerings.
When his brother Jātavedas had died, that Agni,
overcome by great anger, entered the waters of the Gaṅgā.
When the waters of the Gaṅgā had entered the fire, both gods and humans cast off their lives,
for they were considered to have their very life in the fire.
All those gods, sages, and ancestors likewise came to that place where fire had entered the water.
"We cannot live without fire; we especially praise Agni. Having seen Agni situated within the water, the inhabitants of heaven spoke these pleasant words.
The gods said:
"Sustain the gods with sacrificial offerings (havya) and the ancestors with ancestral offerings (kavya);
sustain humans with cooked food and by the moistening of seeds."
Brahmā said:
Agni also said to those gods, "My younger brother who went [to you] was capable;
whatever fate befell Jātavedas while your task was being performed, [that shall be his]."
Even if that liquor were mine, I would not venture to accomplish this task;
for the business of Jātavedas must be carried out by you in every way.
Having reached this state, I do not know how it might be for me;
even the power to pervade both this world and the next would not exist here.
"Moreover, even while this task is being performed, that same course of action shall be mine.
To him, all the gods and likewise the sages spoke with their whole heart: ||| BrP_98.13 |||
"O Havyavāhana, may longevity, merit, joy, and pervasive power be granted;
we shall offer the fore-sacrifices and the after-sacrifices."
"You are the supreme mouth of the gods; the first oblations belong to you.
O best of deities, we shall eat whatever substance is offered by you."
Brahmā said:
Then, by the word of the gods, Vahni became satisfied according to the proper order,
both in his pervasion here and in the hereafter, as well as in the sacrificial oblation and in worldly fire.
By the command of the noble king, the fire became everywhere fearless and capable;
Jātavedas, Bṛhadbhānu, Saptārcis, and Nīlalohita were all present.
He is called the womb of the waters, the womb of the *śamī* tree, and the womb of sacrifice;
for having drawn Agni from the waters and consecrated him, the gods [established him].
In both places there was a dwelling, and from that Agni became all-pervading;
the gods departed as they had come, and that is called Vahni-tīrtha.
There were seven hundred meritorious holy fords (tīrthas) there;
he who, having conquered his self, performs bathing and giving of gifts in them, [attains great merit].
One obtains the full and auspicious fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice without deficiency;
and right there is the Devatīrtha, which belongs to Agni and is known as Jātavedasa.
A linga established by Agni resides there, appearing in many colors;
by merely beholding that deity, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
Brahmā said:
Those who know the Vedas recognize a sacred ford named Ṛṇapramocana (the Release from Debt).
I shall describe its true nature; listen with a focused mind, O Nārada.
There was a son of Kakṣīvat named Pṛthuśravas who was dear to his father;
out of world-weariness, he neither took a wife nor performed the worship of the sacred fires.
But the younger brother, O Sage, although capable, did not perform marriage rites and the like, nor did he attend to the sacred fires, out of fear of being superseded by his elder brother.
Then the hosts of ancestors spoke these words individually to the auspicious son of Kakṣīvat, both the eldest and the youngest.
The ancestors said:
"To discharge the three debts, let the taking of a wife be performed."
Brahmā said: Then the eldest replied, "No. "What debt is incurred by whom? he asked. But the younger brother said to the ancestors, "Marriage is not appropriate for me. (BrP 99.6)
"Since the elder brother exists, O one of great wisdom, [one fears] becoming a *parivitti*.
Thus did both of them speak again, those indeed who were their grandfathers.
The ancestors said:
"O two sons of Kakṣīvat, go both of you to the holy Gautamī;
perform the bath in the Gautamī, which bestows all desired objects."
"Let them go to the Gautamī Gaṅgā, which purifies the three worlds,
and let them perform ablutions and libations there, endowed with faith."
Gautamī, when seen, saluted, or meditated upon, grants all desires;
there is no restriction here regarding place, time, caste, or the like for her immersion.
Therefore, the elder brother shall be free from debt, and not the other, who would otherwise be a *parivitti*.
Brahmā said:
Then the eldest, Pṛthuśravas, having performed his ablutions and the libations,
became free from debt toward the three worlds on behalf of Kākṣīvat.

From that time forth, O Nārada, that sacred ford is called Ṛṇamocana; for by bathing and giving gifts there, one who is burdened by debts— whether those arising from the Śruti and Smṛti or others— is liberated and becomes happy.
Brahmā said:
There is the place named Suparṇāsaṃgama and likewise Kādravāsaṃgama,
where the god Maheśvara resides, having taken refuge on the sandy bank of the Gaṅgā.
And right there were sacrificial fire-pits (agnikuṇḍa) belonging to Rudra, Viṣṇu,
Sūrya, Soma, Brahmā, Kumāra, and likewise Varuṇa.
Where the river Apsarā likewise meets the Gaṅgā,
by the mere remembrance of that sacred ford (tīrtha), a man becomes one who has accomplished his purpose.
Listen with diligence, O Nārada, to that which pacifies all sins.
Formerly, the great sages known as the Vālakhilyas were harmed by Indra;
having been deprived of half their ascetic merit, they all spoke to the sage Kāśyapa.
The Vālakhilyas said:
"Procreate with him a son who shall be auspicious and the destroyer of Indra's pride;
we will give you half of our ascetic merit. The sage, however, said to them, "So be it."
Then, O Brahmin, that Prajāpati slowly deposited his seed in Suparṇā and also in Kadrū, the mother of the serpents.
Desirous of departing, Prajāpati said to both of those pregnant women:
"No offense whatsoever should be committed, and you must simply go."
"If you go elsewhere, there will be a curse; of this there is no doubt. (BrP 100.8)
Brahmā said:
Having spoken thus, he departed; and when their husband had gone, those two wives immediately went to the sacrificial session of the seers of purified souls.
Crowded with hosts of Brahmins and situated on the banks of the Gaṅgā,
those two women were perpetually intoxicated and proud of their abundant youth.
Though repeatedly restrained by sages who perceive the truth,
the two of them continued to act with hostility toward that sacrificial session, both the participants and the oblations.
"Who is able to restrain the wicked conduct of women?
Having seen those two women devoted to improper paths, the brahmins were agitated."
"Since you two shall indeed become rivers situated along the Apāmārga, you have both been born as the two rivers Suparṇā and Kadrū."
Then, on one occasion, Kaśyapa, the lord of creatures, returned home and related there to the sages the account of the curse pronounced upon those two in full detail.
Having heard this, he was filled with wonder and thought, "What shall I do?
He then spoke to the sages, who were known as the Vālakhilyas.
They went to the Brahmin Kaśyapa at the Gautamī river and said to him:
"Go there and praise Maheśāna; then you two shall have wives again."
Out of fear of the sin of killing a Brahmin, the Lord Maheśvara always resides there in the middle of the Gaṅgā, known by the name Madhyameśvara.
Having said "So be it," Kaśyapa, firm in his vows, bathed in the Gaṅgā and praised Maheśvara, the God of gods, with meritorious hymns.
Kaśyapa said:
Of him who is the sole sovereign of the three worlds, there is not even a trace of egoism regarding any object whatsoever.
May that Siddhanātha, the creator of the entire universe and the husband of Śivā,
be gracious toward those scorched by the heat of the threefold afflictions.
For embodied beings, both stationary and moving, who run hither and thither,
you alone are skilled in dispelling their suffering.
Even the threefold yoga of *sattva* and the other qualities,
which is impossible for Śakra and the others to describe, belongs to that Soma when one contemplates his manifold activity.
"Always happy, devoted to giving, and most excellent"—with such hymns of praise was the god Śiva, the lord of Gaurī, extolled.
(Brahmā said:
"Thus, by these and other praises, the god Śiva, the husband of Gaurī, was lauded."
For Śambhu, being pleased, granted many boons to Kaśyapa.
To him who desired a wife, he said:
"You shall have two wives in the form of rivers, those two who, having reached Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, [shall become yours]."
By the mere act of uniting with him, they both regained their own bodies;
through the grace of Gaṅgā, those two women were born once again as pregnant.
Then the high-minded Prajāpati, having regained his two wives,
was pleased and summoned those brahmins who were dwelling on the banks of the Gautamī.
The delighted Prajāpati performed the parting-of-the-hair ceremony for the two of them and honored the Brahmins with rites prescribed by rule.
Then, after the brahmins had finished eating in the palace of Kaśyapa, Kadrū,
seated near her husband, looked at the brahmins.
Then Kadrū laughed at the sages with one eye, and they were provoked;
[they said], "O sinful woman, since you have laughed with this eye, let that eye of yours, O wicked one, be destroyed!"
Then Kadrū became one-eyed, she who is called the mother of the serpents;
thereafter, the venerable seer Kaśyapa propitiated the rishis.
Then, being pleased, they said: "Gautamī, the best of rivers, shall protect you from thousands of offenses through her service."
Kaśyapa, the best of sages, did likewise together with his wife;
from that time forth, they have known that sacred ford as the "Confluence of Both," which pacifies all sins and bestows the fruit of all sacrifices.
Brahmā said:
Those who know the Vedas recognize the sacred site known as Purūravas;
it destroys sins merely by being remembered, but even more so by being seen.
Having reached the abode of Brahmā, Purūravas beheld there the river Sarasvatī,
the celestial stream, who was laughing spontaneously in the presence of Brahmā;
seeing her endowed with such beauty, the lord of the earth spoke to Urvaśī.
The king said:
"Who is this virtuous and beautiful woman standing near Brahmā,
the most excellent of all women, illuminating this assembly?"
Brahmā said: Urvaśī spoke to the king: "This auspicious celestial river Sarasvatī, the daughter of Brahmā, is constantly coming and going."
Having heard that, the king was amazed and said, "Bring her here into my presence."
Brahmā said:
Urvaśī spoke once more to the king who bestows abundant sacrificial fees.
Urvaśī said:
"O Great King, having reported everything concerning her, she shall be brought here."
Brahmā said:
Then the king affectionately sent Urvaśī there;
having gone, Urvaśī then delivered the king's message.
Sarasvatī also accepted what had been reported by Urvaśī;
having promised "So be it," she departed for where Purūravas was.
Then he dwelt for many years on the bank of the Sarasvatī;
his son was Sarasvant, whose son was Bṛhadratha.
Knowing that Sarasvatī was constantly going to the king’s palace,
and seeing the same mark made on others, he then [recognized] Sarasvant.
I gave her a curse, saying, "Become a great river! Fearing my curse, Vāgīśā went to the goddess Gautamī.
[He saw] his mother, born from a water-pot, pure, the purifier of the world,
the quencher of the three-fold suffering, and the bestower of both worldly and otherworldly fruits.
Having gone there, she spoke to Queen Gautamī about her curse from the beginning;
Gaṅgā also said this to her: "You ought to release me from the curse."
It was not right that you bestowed a curse upon Sarasvatī;
for this is indeed the nature of women, since women are desirous of men.
O Brahman, all women are by nature fickle;
how is it that you, the lotus-seated creator of the world, do not know this? (BrP 101.15)
"Or whom indeed does desire not mock by its very nature?
Therefore, I spoke the curse: 'Even Sarasvatī shall become visible.'"
Therefore, due to that curse, the river Sarasvatī became visible and invisible among mortals;
there, the goddess, overwhelmed by the curse, joined the Gaṅgā.
There, that virtuous and excellent king Purūravas,
having performed austerities and propitiated the god Hara, the Lord of Siddhas, attained his goal.
Then, by the grace of the Gaṅgā, he obtained all his desires;
from that time forward, that sacred ford (tīrtha) is called Purūravasa.
And the confluence of the Sarasvatī is called Brahmatīrtha;
where the god Siddheśvara resides, that place indeed grants all desires.
Brahmā said:
Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Śraddhā, Medhā, and Sarasvatī—
these five sacred fords (tīrthas) the sages know.
Having bathed there and having drunk [the water], one is liberated from all impurity;
for there dwell Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Śraddhā, Medhā, and Sarasvatī.
"These are my eldest daughters, the causes for the establishment of dharma;
among them all, he fashioned one who was the most excellent, the beauty of the world."
O best of sages, upon seeing her, my mind became agitated;
that young woman, being pursued by me, fled when she saw me.
That young woman became a doe, and I then became a deer;
and Śambhu became a hunter for the sake of protecting righteousness.
Terrified of me, those five sons went to the great river Gaṅgā;
thereafter, Maheśvara set out for the sake of protecting righteousness.
Then Hara, though the Lord himself, took up his bow and arrow and said to me in the form of a deer: "O hunter, I shall kill you. (BrP 102.7)
Having desisted from that act, I gave my daughter to Vivasvat;
her five sons, Sāvitrī and the others, became united with the form of rivers.
O Nārada, they returned once more to my presence in the heavenly world, where those five goddesses were united with the Tīrthas.
The five rivers and the Sarasvatī converge there;
whatever bathing or giving a man performs at those places, [it becomes inexhaustible].
That [place] bestows all desires and is remembered as granting liberation through the cessation of worldly action (naiṣkarmya).
Therein was the Mṛgavyādha-tīrtha, which grants all goals to men;
another is known to yield the fruit of heaven and liberation, and the fruit of the Brahmatīrtha.
Brahmā said:
There is a place renowned as Śamī-tīrtha, which grants the pacification of all sins.
I shall recount its history; listen with care, O Nārada. (BrP 103.1)
There was a Kṣatriya named Priyavrata, the best among victors;
on the southern bank of the Gautamī, he underwent initiation with his family priest.
When the horse sacrifice had commenced, chosen by the ṛṣis as the officiating priests,
Vasiṣṭha was the family priest of that mighty-armed king.
Then the Dānava Hiraṇyaka went to that sacrificial enclosure;
and seeing that Dānava, the gods, led by Indra, [approached].
Some, being terrified, went to heaven; the bearer of oblations entered the Śamī tree;
Viṣṇu went to the Aśvattha; Bhānu went to the Arka; and Śiva went to the Vaṭa.
Soma went to the Palāśa tree, Havyavāhana to the waters of the Gaṅgā, while the two Aśvins, having seized the horse, became a crow themselves; and Yama likewise [became so].
In the meantime, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha,
taking up his staff, then restrained the Daityas by his command.
Then the sacrifice commenced once again;
the Daitya, endowed with his own power,
departed for these auspicious holy sites (tīrthas).
They would grant the fruits of ten horse-sacrifices.
First, they know the Śamī-tīrtha; second is the Vaiṣṇava;
then the Ārka, the Śaiva, the Saumya, and the Vāsiṣṭha, which grants all desires.
When the extensive sacrifice had concluded, all the gods and sages,
being gratified, spoke to Vasiṣṭha, the sacrificer who was devoted to his vows.
Filled with joy, they went here and there again and again toward those trees and that Ganges for the successful completion of the horse sacrifice.
"The sacred fords shall yield the fruit of a horse sacrifice," so the gods declared.
Therefore, O Nārada, by bathing and giving gifts at those sacred fords, one obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice; these words are not false.
Brahmā said:
[He spoke of] Viśvāmitra, Hariścandra, Śunaḥśepa, and Rohita;
[and of the mantras] belonging to Varuṇa, Brahmā, Agni, Indra, the Moon, and Īśvara.
Maitra, Vaiṣṇava, Yāmya, Āśvina, and Auśana—
listen to me as I recite the names of these meritorious tīrthas.
There was once a king named Hariścandra, born of the lineage of Ikṣvāku.
Into his house arrived two sages, Nārada and Parvata;
having properly offered them hospitality, Hariścandra spoke to those two ṛṣis.
Hariścandra said:
People suffer for the sake of a son; what will be gained by a son, whether he be wise or ignorant, or whether he be of the highest or middling sort?
O two best of sages, please resolve this constant doubt of mine.
Brahmā said:
Then Parvata and Nārada spoke thus to Hariścandra.
Nārada and Parvata said: "O King, although the answer exists perfectly in one way, ten ways, a hundred ways, and a thousand ways,
it is nevertheless declared thus."
"O best of kings, there is no world beyond for one who has no son;
O lord of men, when a son is born, the father who performs the ritual bath [attains that world]."
One shall obtain the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices through the consecration;
from one's son, there shall arise a self-established installation, and he shall be born as the best of immortals.
Through nectar the gods became immortal, and through a son, the Brahmins and others [attain their goal];
a son liberates his father and grandfathers from the three debts.
But what is the root, what is water, what are the beard, and what is austerity?
O Indra among kings, heaven and liberation are said to be attained through a son.
The son alone is the supreme world, as well as virtue, pleasure, and wealth;
the son is liberation, the highest light, and the savior of all embodied beings.
O Indra among kings, heaven and liberation are very difficult to attain without a son;
indeed, a son alone is supreme in this world for the accomplishment of dharma, pleasure, and wealth.
Whatever is given without a son, whatever is offered in sacrifice without a son,
and whatever birth occurs without a son— all that appears to me as futile.
"Therefore, there is nothing in the three worlds as desirable as a son.
Having heard that, the king, filled with wonder, spoke to them again.
Hariścandra said:
"Tell me truly how I might have a son,
by whatever means possible and wherever it may be, having exerted some measure of human effort."
"By means of mantras, sacrifices, and gifts, this son must be produced by me."
Brahmā said:
Having meditated for a moment, they both spoke to Hariścandra, the best of kings, who was seeking a son: "O giver of honor, go in the proper manner to the Gautamī."
There, Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, bestows that which is most excellent and desired by the mind;
indeed, he is proclaimed by the sages as the giver of all things.
"Being pleased, he will gradually give you a son in due time.
Having heard these words of the sage, the best of kings acted accordingly.
Having taken refuge on the bank of the Gautamī, he gratified Varuṇa;
and then Varuṇa, being pleased, spoke to Hariścandra.
Varuṇa said:
"O King, I shall grant you a son who will be an ornament to the three worlds;
provided that you worship with him alone, a son shall certainly be born to you."
Brahmā said: Hariścandra also said to Varuṇa, "I shall sacrifice for you.
Then, having gone there, Hariścandra prepared a sacrificial oblation (caru) dedicated to Varuṇa.
The king gave [the child] to his wife; then a son was born from the king.
Once the son was born, the Lord of Waters, the best among speakers, spoke:
Varuṇa said:
"This very day your son must be sacrificed; do you remember your former word?"
Brahmā said:
Hariścandra also spoke these words, which had come down through tradition, to Varuṇa.
Hariścandra said:
"A sacrificial animal becomes fit for sacrifice after ten days have passed; therefore, I shall indeed perform the sacrifice."
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of the king, Varuṇa went to his own abode;
then, returning after ten days had passed, he said to that monarch, "Perform the sacrifice."
The king also said to Varuṇa: "A beast that is toothless is useless;
now that teeth have grown on the beast, come, O Lord, let us go."
Having heard those words of the king, O Nārada, the Lord of Waters set out once more when the teeth had grown and seven years had passed.
Again he said to the king, "Perform a sacrifice.
Then the king spoke to Varuṇa: "O Lord of Waters, these [sacrifices] will bring me destruction."
"Others will likewise succeed; therefore, I shall sacrifice now.
O Nārada, Varuṇa went back again and said to the king, "Sacrifice! The king, however, spoke to the Lord of Waters.
The King said:
"O guardian of the waters, when a Kṣatriya becomes the sacrificial animal at a sacrifice,
and when he knows the science of archery (Dhanurveda), then he would be the most excellent of animals."
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of the king, Varuṇa returned to his own abode once Rohita had become proficient in missiles and weapons.
That subduer of enemies became a knower of all the Vedas and the Shastras when Rohita reached his sixteenth year and attained the status of crown prince.
Full of joy, he went to where King Sarohita was;
having arrived, Varuṇa said, "Sacrifice your own son today."
Having said "Om," the king, the best of monarchs, spoke to the officiating priests,
and to his eldest son Rohita, while Varuṇa was listening.
Hariścandra said:
"Come, my son, O great hero; I shall indeed sacrifice you to Varuṇa."
Brahmā said:
"What is this? Rohita then spoke thus to his father;
and the father also related that event to him in full detail, exactly as it had occurred.
Rohita spoke to his father while Varuṇa was listening.
Rohita said:
"O great king, previously, together with the officiating priests and the family priest, I,
being purified, intended to swiftly perform a sacrifice for Viṣṇu, the Lord of the worlds."
Therefore, you ought to grant permission for this animal sacrifice to Varuṇa.
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of Rohita,
the Lord of Waters was then overcome by great anger and caused him to suffer from dropsy.
Having taken up his divine bow and mounted his chariot, Rohita, free from distress, went to the forest with King Hariścandra.
And Rohita also went to that place where Hariścandra, the lord of men, having propitiated Varuṇa, obtained a son on the banks of the Gaṅgā.
Then, after five years had passed and the sixth was underway,
the prince, remaining there, heard of the king's illness.
"Since I have been born as a son who causes my father distress,
what fruit or what purpose would there be?"— thus he reflected.
On its bank, the king’s son beheld holy seers;
there, situated on the shore of the Gaṅgā, he saw the most excellent of sages.
Seeing Ajīgarta by name, the son of the sage Vaya,
who was followed by three sons and his wife and whose means of subsistence were exhausted,
the king’s son bowed to him and spoke these words: BrP_104.45.
Rohita said:
"Why do you appear emaciated, with your means of subsistence exhausted, as if you are dejected in mind?"
Brahmā said:
Ajīgarta also spoke to Rohita, the son of the king.
Ajīgarta said:
"There is no means of sustenance for my body, and those who must be fed by me are many.
We shall die without food; tell us, what shall we do?"
{Brahmā said:} Having heard that, the prince then spoke again to the sage. *Brahmapurāṇa* 104.49.
Rohita said:
"O best among speakers, tell me what is in your mind."
Ajīgarta said:
"O tiger among kings, I possess no gold, silver, cattle, grain, clothing, or the like; therefore, I have no means of subsistence."
"I have sons, I have a wife, and I myself am the fifth;
O best of kings, there is no one among them who would sell even one of us for food."
Rohita said:
"O highly intelligent Ajīgarta, what indeed do you wish to buy? Tell me the truth;
nothing else should be spoken, for Brahmins are surely speakers of truth."
Ajīgarta said:
"Of my three sons, take one—or even me—or likewise this wife; having purchased her, let us live."
Rohita said:
"O one of great intelligence, what use have I for a wife, and what use have you for this aged form?
Give me a young son—one whom you yourself desire among your sons."
Ajīgarta said:
"O Rohita, I will not sell my eldest son, Śunaḥpuccha; nor will his mother sell her youngest. Therefore, I cannot sell these two."
"But I shall buy Śunaḥśepa for a middling price; tell me what that wealth shall be."
Rohita said:
"An animal is to be prepared for Varuṇa, and a man is even more excellent as an offering.
If you wish to purchase it, O great sage, tell me the price truthfully."
Brahmā said: Having said, "So be it," Ajīgarta determined the price for his son to be a thousand cows, grain, gold coins, and garments.
"O prince, grant me a boon; I shall give my own son to you."
Brahmā said:
Having replied, "So be it," Rohita gave him wealth along with clothing;
having given it, Rohita went to his father together with the son of the ṛṣi.
He presented to his father the son of the sage, whom he had purchased by means of a trade.
Rohita said:
"Sacrifice to Varuṇa with an animal; may you yourself be free from disease."
Brahmā said:
Hariścandra spoke thus immediately after his son's words.
Hariścandra said:
"It is the sacred tradition that Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are to be protected by the king;
indeed, among the castes, the best of the twice-born are especially the gurus."
For even those like me are worthy of worship by Viṣṇu himself; how much more so, then, by kings, for even by showing them contempt, the destruction of one's own lineage may occur.
Having made those animals [sacrificial], how could I bear to protect them so piteously?
Furthermore, that I should make a Brahmin an animal is certainly not fitting.
"Indeed, death is better than ever sacrificing a Brahmin as an animal;
therefore, my son, go happily with the Brahmin."
{Brahmā said:} In that interval, an unembodied voice spoke there.
The Voice of Space said:
"O Indra among kings, go to Gautamī together with your officiating priests and family priest,
accompanied by a sacrificial animal, the son of a Brahmin, Rohita, and your own son."
"You must perform a sacrifice without the slaughter of Śunaḥśepa; in that way, the sacrifice will be complete. Therefore, go there, O high-minded one! (BrP 104.68)
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words, the best of kings quickly went to the Gaṅgā,
accompanied by the seer Viśvāmitra and his domestic priest Vasiṣṭha.
Having reached that Gaṅgā, known as Gautamī, together with the sage Vāmadeva and other sages, he was initiated for a human sacrifice.
He constructed the sacrificial altar, the pavilion, the fire-pits, and so forth, as well as the sacrificial post and the animal victim;
having performed everything according to the prescribed rule, that sacrifice was set in motion.

Having bound the sacrificial animal Śunaḥśepa to the sacrificial post according to the mantras, and seeing him sprinkled with water, Viśvāmitra spoke these words: BrP_104.72: "Having bound the sacrificial animal Śunaḥśepa to the sacrificial post according to the mantras, and seeing him sprinkled with water, Viśvāmitra spoke this."
Viśvāmitra said:
"May all the gods, the sages, Hariścandra, and especially Rohita,
grant permission for this Śunaḥśepa, the best of the twice-born."
"May all those gods to whom this oblation is to be given individually grant their permission, especially for Śunaḥśepa."
O best of the twice-born, this animal Śunaḥśepa, consecrated with mantras, is to be offered as an oblation into the fire at the sacrifice along with its fat, hair, skin, and flesh.
"O best of Brahmins, having been served by me, may you all grant me your permission;
let these foremost of sages go to the Gautamī river and, after bathing, worship the gods individually."
Praising him with mantras and hymns, let those who delight in Śiva attain joy;
and let the sages and the gods who consume oblations protect him.
Brahmā said:
"So be it," the sages replied, and the best of kings agreed.
Then Śunaḥśepa went to the Gaṅgā, the purifier of the three worlds.
Having bathed, he praised those gods who partake of the oblation there;
then, O Sage, the hosts of gods were pleased, and all those deities spoke to Śunaḥśepa while Viśvāmitra was listening.
The gods said:
"Let this sacrifice be complete without the slaughter of Śunaḥśepa."
Brahmā said:
Then Varuṇa spoke specifically to that best of kings;
thereupon, King Nṛmedha, world-renowned, became fulfilled.
Through the grace of the gods, through the favor of the sages,
and through the power of the sacred ford, the king’s sacrifice was brought to completion.
Viśvāmitra honored Śunaḥśepa in the assembly;
having honored him, he made him his own son in the presence of the gods.
That Kauśika made him the eldest of his sons;
however, those sons of the wise Viśvāmitra did not accept this.
And because they claimed the primogeniture of Śunaḥśepa, Kauśika cursed them;
however, he honored those sons who recognized his primogeniture.
O tiger among sages, by virtue of that boon, all of this has been described by me;
it is there, on the southern bank of the Gautamī, where all this was born.
In that place, there are many meritorious and renowned sacred fords (tīrthas) celebrated by the gods and others; O high-minded one, hear their names from me.
Hariścandra, Śunaḥśepa, Viśvāmitra, Sarohita,
and so forth— these are the eight thousand sacred sites (tīrthas), as well as fourteen others.
O best of sages, bathing and giving gifts at those [sites] bestow the fruit of a human sacrifice; and the greatness of this sacred ford has been declared.
Whoever should read it, cause it to be read, or even listen to it with devotion—
being childless, he obtains a son, as well as whatever else is dear to his heart.
Brahmā said: O Nārada, listen with care to that which occurred there, a story of great merit, concerning the place renowned as Somatīrtha, which increases the satisfaction of the ancestors.
In former times, King Soma was composed of nectar for the Gandharvas;
at that time, the gods did not approach me, but rather spoke thus to me.
The gods said:
"In former times, the Soma that gives life to the gods was carried away by the Gandharvas.
Thinking of it, the hosts of gods and the sages were exceedingly distressed."
Let policy be so ordained that Soma shall indeed remain ours.
Brahmā said:
There, Vāk spoke to the gods: "The Gandharvas are lustful toward women;
having given me to them, O gods, you ought now to bring back Soma."
The immortals replied to Vāc: "We are not able to give you away;
for it is impossible to exist even without him, nor indeed without you."
Again Speech said to the gods: "I shall indeed return here;
let wisdom be applied to this matter, and let the supreme sacrifice be performed."
If the gods should come to the southern bank of the Gautamī,
let the best of the deities come, making the sacrificial ground their domain.
"Gandharvas, who are always fond of women, bargain with me!
Having said "So be it," the hosts of gods remained obedient to the words of Sarasvatī.
Then, by means of divine messengers, they issued invitations there on the holy Devagiri to the various gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, and pannagas.
Then, O sage, there arose a mountain named Devagiri;
there the hosts of gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, and kiṃnaras arrived.
The gods, the Siddhas, and the Ṛṣis— likewise the eight classes of divine beings—
were present while the great sacrifice was being performed by the Ṛṣis on the banks of the Gautamī.
There, surrounded by the gods, the thousand-eyed one spoke.
Indra said:
"Then, having honored the Gandharvas in the vicinity of Sarasvatī,
bargain with us for Sarasvatī as your immortal self."
Brahmā said: At those words of Śakra, those Gandharvas, who were lustful toward women,
gave Soma to the gods and took that Sarasvatī for themselves.
Soma became the lord of the Cāmaras, and Sarasvatī,
the mistress of speech, likewise dwelt there among the Gandharvas and in the presence of the gods.
And he always comes in secret, saying, "Let it be done in private.
For this very reason, O Nārada, the purchase of Soma takes place.
"One must proceed with whispered recitation (upāṃśu) at the very moment of the purchase of Soma;
from that [act], Sarasvatī became a deity among the gods, as did Soma."
Neither Soma nor Sarasvatī herself was present for the Gandharvas;
nevertheless, they all went to the bank of the Gautamī for the sake of Soma.
The cows, the gods, the mountains, the yakṣas and rākṣasas, the siddhas, the sādhyas, the sages, the guhyakas,
the gandharvas, those maruts, and the pannagas— BrP 105.19abc.
All medicinal herbs, the Mothers, the world-protectors,
the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the two Aśvins—
whatever other gods are worthy of a share in the sacrifice.
O Sage, twenty-five rivers indeed converge with the Gaṅgā;
because the *pūrṇāhuti* offering was given there, it is called *Pūrṇā*.
O Nārada, hear in brief the names of those holy fords (tīrthas) which are all situated at Gautamī, exactly as they have been described.
Then there is Somatīrtha, Gāndharvatīrtha, and beyond that Devatīrtha;
after that, Pūrṇātīrtha, Śālatīrtha, and likewise the confluence of the Śrīparṇā.
The conjunction with Svāgatā is meritorious, as is the conjunction with Kusumā;
the conjunction with Puṣṭi is proclaimed [to be auspicious], and the conjunction with Karṇikā is auspicious.
Vaiṇavīsaṃgama, Kṛśarāsaṃgama,
Vāsavīsaṃgama, Śivaśaryā, and likewise Śikhī.
Then Kusumbhikā, Upārathyā, Śāntijā, and Devajā,
along with Aja, Vṛddha, Sura, and Bhadra, were united with Gautamī.
These and many others, accompanied by rivers and streams,
went from all the sacred fords on earth to the Mountain of the Gods.
Likewise, others also came to the sacrificial pavilion for the sake of Soma;
those sacred bathing places (tīrthas) on the Gaṅgā had assembled there in due order.
Some here take the form of rivers, some the form of streams; some exist in the form of lakes, and others in the form of hymns of praise.
Those very places are renowned as individual holy fords (tīrtha);
in them, one should perform bathing, recitation, fire-offerings, and the libation to the ancestors.
It bestows all desires upon men, grants worldly enjoyment, and is a vessel for liberation.
Any person who either recites or even remembers these [names] becomes completely freed from all sins and goes to the city of Viṣṇu.
Brahmā said:
There is a great river named Pravarasaṅgama, which is most excellent,
where the god Siddheśvara resides, performing benefit for all the worlds.
O great sage, there occurred a most terrible encounter between the gods and the dānavas, yet among them there was also mutual affection.
Having reached Mount Meru, those gods and dānavas, desiring each other's welfare, consulted with one another in this manner.
The gods and daityas said:
"By means of the nectar, immortality shall be attained; having produced the supreme nectar, let us all drink it and become immortal."
Having become one, let us protect the worlds and attain happiness;
let us abandon strife, for strife is the cause of suffering.
And with affection, free from envy, we shall enjoy the wealth we have acquired;
for that livelihood which proceeds with love always grants us happiness.
But whatever has occurred in opposition [to dharma] should never be remembered;

nor is there even the slightest happiness in the sovereignty over the three worlds or in absolute liberation (kaivalya), compared to that which is attained beyond even those, through freedom from enmity.
Brahmā said:
Thus, the gods and the Dānavas, being mutually affectionate and becoming one, were well-pleased as they churned the abode of Varuṇa.
Having made Mount Mandara the churning stick and Vāsuki the rope,
all the gods and Dānavas churned the abode of Varuṇa.
Then, the merit that was produced became nectar, beloved by the gods;
and when that meritorious nectar was perfected, they spoke to one another:
"Having accomplished our task and reached exhaustion, let us each go to our own respective abodes;
let everything be distributed equally among all of us, according to what is appropriate."
"O best of gods, let this merit, which is like nectar, be distributed at that auspicious moment when all the scriptures converge."
Having spoken thus, all those Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas departed;
and when the hosts of Daityas had gone, all the gods took counsel together.
The gods said:
"O subduer of enemies, those foes of ours have perished through the turn of fate;
for under no circumstances should the nectar of immortality be given to our enemies."
Brahmā said: Bṛhaspati replied, "So be it," and spoke this again to the gods.
Bṛhaspati said:
"The wicked do not know how you drink this nectar;
this alone is the appropriate mantra: that there shall be the defeat of our enemies."
Those who know the principles of statecraft understand that those who are hateful must be hated with one's whole being;
enemies are not to be trusted, nor should secrets be told to them, nor should counsel be shared with them.

The nectar must not be given to them, for they would then become immortal. And if those Daityas, our enemies, were born as immortals, we would certainly not be able to conquer them; therefore, the nectar must not be given.
Brahmā said:
Having deliberated thus, those gods then spoke to Vācaspati.
The gods said: "Where shall we go? Where might there be counsel? Where shall we drink? Where is our place of rest?
O Lord of Speech, first tell us what we should do accordingly."
Bṛhaspati said:
"O immortals, go to Brahmā and ask him about the supreme course here;
for he, the Grandfather, is the knower, the speaker, and the giver."
Brahmā said:
Having heard the words of Bṛhaspati, all the gods came into my presence; having paid homage to me, they reported everything that had occurred.
Therefore, O son, at the word of the gods, I went to Hari; everything was related by them to Viṣṇu, the destroyer of poison, for the sake of Śambhu.
I, Viṣṇu, and Śambhu, having come to a cave on Mount Meru along with the gods, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras, did not know [the situation] as the Asuras did.
Having appointed Hari as their protector, they stood ready for the drinking of the Soma;
there, the Sun distinguished those who were to partake of the Soma from the others.
Soma was the giver of the portion of nectar, and Cakradhṛk was the protector;
neither the Daityas, nor the Danujas, nor the Rākṣasas knew this at all.
Except for the highly wise Rāhu, the son of Siṃhikā and drinker of Soma,
Rāhu, assuming any form at will, entered into the midst of the Maruts.
Assuming the form of a Marut and likewise holding a drinking vessel,
Divākara recognized that Daitya and reported him to Soma.
Then, having given that nectar to the Daitya who was in the form of a Daitya,
Soma presented that Soma to Viṣṇu.
O child, Viṣṇu, having raised the Daitya who had drunk the nectar with his discus, swiftly cut off his head;
yet that head became immortal.
That body, deprived of its head alone, fell to the earth;
that body, touched by the nectar, fell upon the southern bank.
O tiger among sages, Gautamī’s body—and her son as well—became immortal, causing the earth to tremble; it was truly like a marvel.
The body depends on the head, and the head depends on the body;
both have become immortal, and this Daitya is possessed of great strength.
"The head has entered the body and is devouring all the gods;
therefore, let us first destroy this body upon the earth.
Then all the gods, filled with agitation, spoke to Śaṅkara.
The gods said:
"O best of gods, destroy the Daitya's body that has entered the earth!
O Lord, you are an ocean of compassion and the protector of those who have come for refuge."
It would not even be joined with its head; act in such a manner toward the body of the Daitya.
Brahmā said:
The Lord also dispatched his own supreme power,
the Goddess who is the Mother and protector of the worlds, together with the Mothers.
The goddess, bearing the weapons of Īśa and endowed with the power of Īśa,
went to where the body lay upon the earth, desiring to devour it.
All the gods remained right there on Mount Meru, consoling her head alone;
meanwhile, the goddess’s body fought there once more for many years.
There Rāhu said to the gods: "Formerly, having pierced my body, [the nectar] stayed here;
therefore, extract that excellent essence from my body."
When the supreme and excellent nectar has departed from the body, it will be reduced to ashes in an instant; therefore, let them perform that [rite] beforehand.
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of Rāhu, all the enemies of the asuras were pleased;
they consecrated him, saying, "May you become the foremost among the planets, filled with joy."
At those words of the god, the power known as Īśvarī,
joined with the divine energy (suraśakti), pierced the body of the lord of the Daityas.
Having quickly drawn out the supreme and excellent nectar from his body and placed it outside,
Ambikā then devoured that body.
She who is called Kālarātri and Bhadrakālī, possessed of great power,
established the supreme mercury, the most excellent of all essences.
That which was established flowed forth, and it became the river Pravarā;
she also drank the nectar that had been drawn out and established there.
Then there arose the most excellent river, preeminent, immortal, and auspicious;
born from the body of Rāhu and endowed with the power of Rudra.
The most excellent and beautiful river Amṛtā was sent forth there;
in that place, there are five thousand meritorious holy fords (tīrthas).
There Śambhu himself remained forever, worshipped by the gods;
and all the gods, being pleased with her, offered their salutations individually to that goddess, the river.
Filled with joy, they granted boons so that you might receive worship in the world just as Śambhu, the lord of the gods, receives worship.
O Goddess, establish your residence here out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds;
remain forever, O Mistress of the Essence (Raseśānī), bestowing all accomplishments upon everyone.
By praising, chanting, and meditating upon you, you grant all desires; those who always bow to you with devotion, seeking nothing else at all, [attain their goals].
By the command of the deity, all their tasks shall be accomplished,
since the eternal abode of Śiva and Śakti is situated therein.
Therefore, the sages call this place "Nivāsapura";
for in ancient times, the gods, being well-pleased with Pravarā, granted her boons.
O beloved of the gods, at that confluence of the Gaṅgā which is renowned as dear to the deities,
for all who have bathed there, there is either enjoyment of worldly pleasures or indeed liberation.
Whatever was desired by their minds, even that which is difficult for the gods to obtain—all this they received here; having thus given it, the deities departed.
From that time forward, they have known that sacred ford as Pravarasaṅgama;
for it was Śakti herself who, impelled by the God of gods, was sent forth there.
That very river is renowned as Amṛtā; thus is the preeminent great river.
Brahmā said:
I shall relate the narrative of Vṛddhāsaṃgama, where Śiva is present as Vṛddheśvara; listen to this account which destroys all sins.
Long ago, when Gautama’s son was still a boy, O twice-born one, there lived a sage of great asceticism who was called Gautama because he was old.
Born before [his time], he was therefore one who bore a deformed appearance;
then, out of detachment, he wandered from here and there to various sacred fords (tīrthas).
The preceptor did not associate with one who was ashamed,
nor did he engage in study together with other disciples who were ashamed.
And having been somehow brought back by his father Gautama,
Gautama himself also departed outside for the sake of performing his religious observances.
Thus, after a great deal of time had passed while the twice-born was maintained by Brahmā’s allowance,
no study whatsoever had been accomplished by that Gautama.
At that time, Gautama had no practice of studying the scriptures;
instead, being firm in his vows, he performed the fire-ritual constantly.
By the mere practice of the Gāyatrī, one is a Brahmin in name only;
likewise, the mere worship of the sacred fire and the mere practice of the Gāyatrī [are insufficient].
To this extent, O sage, the state of being a brahmin arose for the high-souled Gautama as he worshipped the fire according to the rules and [recited] the Gāyatrī.
O son, the life of that long-lived Gautama increased;
yet he did not take a wife, nor was there anyone who gave him a daughter.
Wandering thus through sacred sites, various forests,
and holy hermitages, that Gautama remained traveling about.
Wandering in this manner, that Gautama took refuge on the Snowy Mountain (Himavat);
there he saw a delightful cave, adorned with garlands of creepers and branches.
Having sat down there, the best of Brahmins resolved to stay;
while reflecting as he entered, he beheld an excellent woman.
Then [he saw her] with relaxed limbs, emaciated, aged, and established in austerity;
living in celibacy, free from passion, and situated in solitude.
Upon seeing her, that best of sages stood to offer his salutation;
as he, the best of sages Gautama, was bowing in reverence, she restrained him.
The elder said:
"You shall be my guru; you ought not to bow down to me.
Longevity, learning, wealth, fame, righteousness, and whatever else such as heaven—"
Everything belonging to him indeed perishes whom the Guru pays homage to.
Brahmā said:
With palms joined in reverence, Gautama, filled with wonder, spoke to her.
Gautama said:
"You are an ascetic, aged, and preeminent in virtue, O beautiful lady;
whereas I am of little learning and young in years—how can I be your teacher?"
The elder said: "O dear son of Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, he is known as Ṛtadhvaja;
he is virtuous, wise, heroic, and devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya."
Once, his mind drawn by the hunt, he went to the forest;
there, Ṛtadhvaja took rest in this cave.
Then an apsaras beheld that best of kings, who was young, wise, skillful, and endowed with great strength, as he lay there resting.
The daughter of the Gandharva king, renowned as Suśyāmā, saw him; the king desired her, and she desired the king.
Thus, O Great-minded One, that play took place with her for the king;
his desire having ceased, the lord of kings took leave of her and went home.
Then, O Mahāmati, I was born from that Suśyāmā;
as I was departing at that time, my mother said this to me, O ascetic.
Suśyāmā said:
"O blessed lady, whoever enters this [cave] shall become your husband."
The elder said:
"Having spoken thus, O high-minded one, my mother then departed;
therefore, you who have entered here are a man and never anyone else."
Having ruled the kingdom for eighty thousand years, my father performed austerities right here and subsequently ascended to heaven.
O tiger among sages, even after his father had gone to heaven, he likewise ruled the kingdom for another ten thousand years.
"My brother has gone to heaven, while I remain right here;
O Brahmin, I have no other occupation, nor do I have a mother or a father."
"O Brahmin, I am a Kṣatriya maiden named Ātmeśvarī, established here;
therefore, O Brahmin, accept me, who am observing a vow and seeking a husband."
Gautama said:
"O blessed lady, my lifespan is but a thousand years, whereas you are superior to me in age;
I am a child while you are old, so this union between us is not fitting."
The elder woman said:
"In former times you were ordained as my husband; no other husband is recognized by me.
Since you were bestowed upon me by the Creator, you ought not to reject me."
Or, if you do not desire me, though I am faultless and devoted to you,
then I shall give up my life right now while you look on.
For embodied beings, death is better than the failure to obtain what is desired;
there exists no sin greater than the abandonment of devoted people.
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of the old woman, Gautama spoke these words.
Gautama said:
"I am devoid of asceticism, lacking in learning, and truly possessing nothing.
I am neither a suitable bridegroom for you, being ill-favored and destitute of enjoyments."
"I am noseless; what can I do? Moreover, I possess no knowledge of asceticism.
Therefore, O auspicious lady, first acquire a beautiful form and excellent knowledge;
only after that should my word be carried out. Then the old woman spoke to the twice-born man.
The elder said:
"O twice-born one, by means of ascetic penance I gratified the goddess Sarasvatī,
as well as the Waters who grant beauty, and Agni himself."
Therefore, the goddess Vāgīśvarī will grant you knowledge,
and the god Agni, endowed with beauty, will grant you a beautiful form.
Having spoken thus to Gautama, the aged Brahmā addressed Vibhāvasu;
after making his request, he made that sage highly learned and handsome.
Then, being well-learned, fortunate, and handsome, he, full of affection, made his aged wife his partner; he took delight with her,
who was many years old yet charming.
Once, while the joyful couple were dwelling happily and contentedly in their mountain cave,
O tiger among sages, certain stainless sages arrived at that cave.
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, and other great ṛṣis,
while wandering among sacred pilgrimage sites, reached that cave of his.
Knowing that those sages had arrived, Gautama, together with his wife, offered them hospitality; yet some among them laughed at him.
Some there— children intoxicated by youth, those who were middle-aged, and even the elderly—
laughed upon seeing Gautama.
The sages said: "O old woman, is this your son or your grandson? Who was Gautama?
Speak the truth, O blessed one!"—thus the twice-born ones laughed.
"To an old man, a young woman is poison; to a young man, an old woman is nectar.
Alas, after a long time, we have witnessed the union of the desirable and the undesirable! ||| BrP_107.47 |||
Brahmā said:
While the couple were listening, some spoke thus;
having spoken in this manner and having offered hospitality, all the great ṛṣis departed.

Having heard the words of the sages, both of them— Gautama and his wife— were deeply distressed and filled with shame; yet, being possessed of great wisdom, Gautama questioned Agastya, the tiger among sages and the best of seers.
Gautama said:
O one of great wisdom, what is that land or what is that sacred ford (tīrtha) where the highest good is attained swiftly, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation?
Agastya said: O Brahmin, while the sages were speaking, I heard these words:
"All desires are fulfilled there at the Gautamī; of this there is no doubt. (BrP 107.51)
Therefore, O one of great intelligence, go to Gautamī, the destroyer of sins;
I shall follow you—do as you wish.
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of Agastya, Gautama went there with his aged wife;
and there, that venerable ṛṣi performed intense austerities together with his consort.
The venerable sage offered praise to the god Śambhu and likewise to Viṣṇu,
and he propitiated Gaṅgā for the sake of obtaining her as his wife.
Gautama said:
"In this worldly existence, you alone, O Śiva, are the refuge for those whose souls are weary,
like a tree laden with fruit for travelers in a desert."
O Kṛṣṇa, you are in every way the dispeller of the sins of beings high and low,
just as a rain-cloud relieves crops withered by drought.
O Gautamī, you are the ladder to the fortress of Vaikuṇṭha and a river of nectar; be the refuge for those who have fallen low and are tormented.
Then Brahmā spoke these words with joy to Gautama, who was accompanied by his aged wife;
and the refuge-giving Gautamī, seeing him distressed and seeking protection, spoke with delight.
Gautamī said:
"Consecrate your wife with waters mixed with mantras using jars and ritual offerings; then your beloved wife [will be restored]."
Beautiful, with lovely limbs on every side, fortunate and fair-eyed,
she shall attain a charming form, complete with all auspicious marks.
Furthermore, having been consecrated by your wife Rūpavatī,
you shall attain a beloved form, complete with all auspicious marks.
Brahmā said: "So be it," and at the word of Gaṅgā, the two performed exactly as instructed;
by the grace of Gautamī, they both attained a beautiful form.
O best of sages, that water used for the consecration became a river, and it became famous by the name of Vṛddhā.
The river was renowned as Vṛddhā, and Gautama was likewise so called;
thus he was addressed by the resident sages as Vṛddhagautama.
Then Vṛddhā spoke to Gautamī, who appeared before her in visible form.
Vṛddhā said: "O Goddess, let this river be called by my name, Vṛddhā;
and because of its union with you, it shall be an unsurpassed sacred ford."
It brings about the perfection of physical beauty and good fortune, the increase of sons and grandsons,
longevity, health, and auspiciousness; it increases victory and joy,
and through bathing, giving, and fire-offerings, it is the supreme purifier of the ancestors.
Brahmā said:
"So be it," Gaṅgā replied to that aged wife of Gautama;
the Liṅga installed by Gautama became celebrated by the name Vṛddheśvara.
And right there, that best of sages attained joy through his prosperity;
bathing and giving gifts there bestows all desired objects.
From that time forward, that sacred ford has been called Vṛddhāsaṃgama.
Brahmā said:
There is a place renowned as Ilātīrtha, which bestows all perfections upon men;
it purifies even such sins as the killing of a Brahmin and grants all desires.
Born in the lineage of Vaivasvata, a lord of men named Ila went to the hunting forest together with a great army.
He wandered through the dense forest, which was teeming with many predatory beasts,
filled with birds of various kinds, and adorned with spreading branches.
The best of kings, Ila, whose mind was intent on hunting, set his thoughts upon that very forest-dweller and then spoke to his ministers:
Ila said:
"Let everyone go to the city protected by my son;
let them once again govern that kingdom, its territory, its treasury, and its army."
"Let Vasiṣṭha also go in that manner, taking our sacred fires like a father;
then I, accompanied by my wives, shall dwell in the forest, O wise one."
Let all those who enjoy the forest, including horses, elephants, and men, as well as those addicted to hunting, depart from here for the city.
Brahmā said:
Having said, "So be it," they departed; he himself went slowly to the mountain Himavat, which is composed of jewels, where King Ila was dwelling.
There he beheld a cave variegated with various jewels;
therein dwelt a certain lord of the yakṣas, renowned as Samanyu.
His wife, who bore the same name and was devoted to her husband's vows,
lived with him— that Yakṣa— in that delightful, excellent mountain.
In the form of a deer, that high-minded yakṣa roamed with his wife at will in his own forest, sporting in dance and song.
In this way, that yakṣa, even while assuming the form of a deer, recognized [the place],
but Ila did not know that the cave was guarded by the yakṣa.
The king sat there in the vast mansion of the Yakṣa, which was adorned with various jewels, surrounded by a great army.
He took up residence right there in the house of that wise Yakṣa;
meanwhile, that Yakṣa, out of anger at unrighteousness, had his wife assume the form of a deer.
"I am unable to conquer Ila, yet he does not give when asked;
my home has been seized by him—what shall I do? he thought. (BrP 108.15)
Thinking, "How can I slay him while he is intoxicated in battle? the king of the yakṣas remained there and dispatched his own brave yakṣas, who were skilled archers.
The yakṣa said:
"After you have defeated King Ilā, whose tuskers are uplifted, in battle,
you ought to do for me that which causes him to depart from his palace to another place."
Brahmā said:
At those words of the Lord of the Yakṣas, all those Yakṣas, intoxicated by battle, went to Ilā and said, "Come out from this cave-dwelling!"
"If you do not fall away from battle, where will you go after fleeing?
At these words of the Yakṣa, that king of kings fought out of anger.
Having conquered various kinds of yakṣas, the lord of the yakṣas lived for ten nights in the forest,
having become a deer while dwelling there with his wife.
Having lost his home and reached the forest, with his servants gone, he became consumed by anxiety and spoke to his beloved Yakṣiṇī, who had assumed the form of a doe.
The yakṣa said:
"O lovely one, this king is dejected, his mind obsessed by calamity;
consider what means there is to prevent him from falling into disaster."
O fair-browed one, having become a charming deer, lead the kingdoms of all the kings— which end in the vice of hunting— to the forest of Umā.
"O King, whoever enters there will undoubtedly become a woman. O auspicious lady, you must do this; yet it is not fitting for me, for I am a man while you are a woman and a yakṣiṇī."
The Yakṣiṇī said:
"Why must you not go to the unsurpassed Umāvana?
Even if you were to go there, what fault would there be? Tell me that in truth."
The yakṣa said:
On Himavat, the best of mountains, Śiva, accompanied by Umā and followed by the gods and their hosts, wandered about as he pleased.
Once, Pārvatī spoke to Śaṅkara as he was staying in private.
Pārvatī said:
"This is the nature of women: that sexual pleasure must be kept secret.
Therefore, by your command, let a fixed place for me be protected."
"O Lord of the Thirty-three, grant me the grove of Umā, which is renowned;
for without you, O Gaṇeśa, Kārttikeya, and Nandin, it cannot be obtained."
"But whoever should enter here, O Lord, would become a woman. (BrP 108.29)
The yakṣa said:
"Thus has this command been granted in Ājñovana by the gracious moon-crested Lord.
O beloved, what shall I do, a man tormented by your love?"
Therefore, I must not go to Umā’s excellent forest.
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of her husband, the Yakṣiṇī, who could assume any form at will,
became a large-eyed doe and appeared before Ila.
But that yakṣa, stationed there with his mind intent on hunting, beheld the doe at that time, especially upon seeing her.
Mounted on a single horse, he set out after that doe;
she, however, gradually drew the king, who was intent on the hunt, along with her.
She went slowly to that place which is called Umāvana,
while remaining invisible to him, appearing here and there like a deer.
Standing still, walking, and running as if in terror,
that fawn-eyed and restless woman dragged him toward the forest of Umā.
Mounted upon his horse, he reached that Umāvana forest;
and when the yakṣiṇī learned that he had entered Umāvana, she then [acted].
Having cast off her form as a doe, the Yakṣiṇī, who can assume any form at will,
assumed a divine form and stood near the Aśoka tree.
Then, with her hand resting upon that branch, anointed with divine perfumes,
possessing a celestial form, slender, and having accomplished her purpose, she stood poised.
Then, seeing the king mounted on his horse,
weary and gazing with restless eyes at that doe, Ila laughed.
Remembering her husband’s words in their entirety, she spoke to the lord of the earth.
She said:
"O slender woman, why do you go alone, mounted upon a horse? And in the guise of a man, whom will you follow, O Śilā? (BrP 108.41)
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words, the king, overcome with anger,
rebuked the yakṣiṇī and questioned the doe once again.
Nevertheless, the yakṣiṇī said, "Ile, what are you looking for?
Hearing the word "Ile," he stood upon his horse, holding his bow.
Enraged, the conqueror of the three worlds displayed his bow;
then she herself spoke again to the high-souled king: "Ile. (BrP 108.44)
"Look at me from behind and tell me if I am a liar, though I speak the truth.
Then the king looked at her high breasts between her arms.
"What has happened to me?"—thus he became alarmed.
She said: "What is this that has happened to me? You clearly know;
tell me everything exactly as it is, or tell me who you are, O lady of virtuous vows."
The yakṣiṇī said:
"In a most excellent cave of the Himavat, my husband dwells, the glorious lord of the yakṣas; I am his wife, a yakṣiṇī."
O King, you are seated here upon this very cool mountain cave,
where you have slain the Yakṣas out of delusion, indeed without any formal combat.
Then, for the sake of your departure, I became a doe and entered the Umā forest; you entered as well, as Maheśvara had previously declared.
"Any dull-witted man who enters here shall attain womanhood;
therefore, since you have attained womanhood, you ought not to grieve. For even one who is mature does not understand the strange course of destiny in this world."
Brahmā said:
Having heard the words of the yakṣiṇī, he then rushed forward mounted on his horse;
having comforted him, that very yakṣiṇī spoke these words again.
The yakṣiṇī said: "Womanhood is born again and again; you ought not to strive for manhood.
Accept instead the knowledge appropriate for women: dance, song, and adornment."
All that—feminine grace, feminine charm, and feminine activity—is indeed hers alone.
Brahmā said:
Having obtained everything, Ilā spoke these words to the Yakṣiṇī:
She said: "Who indeed is my husband, and what must be done? Furthermore, how may manhood be restored? O auspicious lady, tell me this, especially since I am afflicted by grief."
There is nowhere anything superior to the alleviation of the suffering of those who are afflicted.
The yakṣiṇī said:
"O fortunate one, to the east of this forest is the hermitage of the one named Budha, the son of Soma; he will come constantly to see his father."
By this very path, that wise planet goes constantly to see his father Soma, and likewise to pay him homage.
When that wise one goes forth in peace, then show yourself to him;
for upon seeing you, O fortunate lady, he shall obtain all his desires.
Brahmā said:
Having comforted her, that fair-browed Yakṣiṇī then vanished;
that Yakṣiṇī told him [her story], and the Yakṣa also attained happiness.
His army was there, having gone as they pleased;
and Celā, staying in Umā’s grove, was singing and dancing again.
While performing the movements of a woman and mindful of the course of karma,
she was once engaged in the act of dancing by Ilā.
The wise and intelligent Budha, who was prepared to depart for his father's world, saw her;
having seen Ilā, he abandoned his course, returned, and spoke to her.
Budha said:
"Become my wife; remain well-disposed toward me, and be dearer to me than all others."
Brahmā said:
O Sage, having joyfully welcomed the words of Budha with devotion, Ilā acted accordingly; and remembering the speech of the Yakṣiṇī, she then became satisfied.
Budha took her to his own excellent abode and rejoiced with that love;

she, too, gratified her husband with her whole being. Then, after a long time had passed, Budha, being pleased, spoke to his beloved: BrP_108.65: "Budha took her to his own excellent abode and rejoiced with that love; she, too, gratified her husband with her whole being. Then, after a long time had passed, Budha, being pleased, spoke to his beloved."
Budha said:
"O blessed lady, what dear thing that resides in your heart should I give to you?"
Brahmā said:
At the very moment those words were spoken, Ilā addressed Budha, the son of Soma— affectionate and dear to her— saying, "Grant me a son."
Budha said:
"This seed of mine is unfailing, as is the joy from which it arose;
therefore, you shall have a son who will be a kṣatriya renowned throughout the world."
The illustrious founder of the lunar dynasty was like the sun in brilliance,
equal to Bṛhaspati in intellect, and equal to the earth in forbearance.
In valor he was like Hari in battle, and in wrath he was like the fire-god.
Brahmā said:
As that great-souled son of Budha was being born, a cry of "Victory! arose everywhere throughout the abode of the gods.
When the son of Budha was born, the lords of the gods arrived there;
I too, O high-minded one, came there filled with joy.
As soon as he was born, the son let out a loud cry;
because of that, all the assembled ṛṣis and gods indeed spoke.
Because he has many voices (*purūravaḥ*), they all, with contented minds, gave him the name Purūravas. Thus they named him.
Budha also taught his son the auspicious science of the Kṣatriyas;
Budha then bestowed upon his son the science of archery along with its practical application.
He grew rapidly, like the moon in the bright fortnight.
Beholding his mother Ilā filled with sorrow, the high-minded Aila,
humble in spirit, paid homage to her and spoke these words.
Aila said:
"O mother, my father is wise, your husband is likewise dear to you, and I am a dutiful son; why then do you suffer this mental anguish?"
She said: "It is true, my son, that your husband is wise and you, my son, are a mine of virtues;
I have never had any anxiety on account of my husband or my son."
Nevertheless, O one of great intelligence, remembering some former suffering again and again, I reflected; then I spoke to my mother.
Aila said:
"O mother, tell me that very thing first."
Brahmā said:
Ilā spoke this to him: "How can I speak these words in secret?
Nevertheless, my son, I shall tell you, for a son is the refuge of his parents."
For those who have fallen into the great ocean of suffering, a son is the supreme vessel.
{Brahmā said:} Having heard those words of his mother, the humble one prostrated at her feet and spoke to his mother: "Tell me, Mother, exactly as it is. (BrP 108.82)
Brahmā said:
She spoke to Purūravas concerning the lineage of the Ikṣvākus,
his own birth therein, the acquisition of his kingdom, and his beloved sons.
