Then [he spoke of] his family priest Vasiṣṭha, his beloved wife, his own position,
his departure for the forest, and [the grief of] his ministers and priest.
And [he related] his dispatching [of messengers] to that city, as well as his addiction to hunting,
his journey to the caves of the Himalayas, and his arrival at the abode of the Lord of the Yakṣas.
And [she told him] in full about the entry into Umā’s grove and her attainment of womanhood,
as well as the fact that, by the command of Maheśvara, no man was permitted to enter there.
He also [attained] the speech of the yakṣiṇī, as well as the granting of boons,
the attainment of wisdom, joy, and the birth of a son, and so forth, in their entirety.
Having heard all that, he spoke to his mother; Purūravas said, "What shall I do? By doing what would it become a virtuous deed?"
O Ambikā, if you are satisfied with this much, then enough of this;
yet, whatever else dwells in your mind, please command that as well from me.
She said: "I desire supreme manhood; I desire an excellent kingdom;
and I desire the consecration of my sons, and especially yours."
O son, by your grace, I desire to give gifts, to perform sacrifices, to behold the path to liberation, and to accomplish all these things.
The son said:
"I ask you for a means by which you may regain manhood;
whether it be through austerity or by some other way, tell it to me in truth."
She said: "O son, go and ask your father Budha as is fitting;
he knows everything and will instruct you in what is beneficial."
Brahmā said: At his mother’s word, Aila went straight to his father and,
having bowed down, spoke of his mother’s purpose as well as his own.
Buddha said: "O one of great wisdom, I know of Ilā, and how she was born again as Ilā; I also know of her entry into Umā’s forest and likewise Śambhu’s command."
Therefore, O son, by the grace of Śambhu and the grace of Umā, you shall be freed from the curse after having propitiated them; it cannot be otherwise.
Purūravas said:
"O Father, tell me first: how might I see that god, or how might I see my auspicious mother? Is it through a sacred ford or through ascetic penance?"
Bṛhaspati said:
"Go to Gautamī, my son; there Śiva always dwells together with Umā—the illustrious one who destroys curses and bestows boons."
Brahmā said:
Having heard his father’s words, the wise Purūravas became joyful; he went to the Gautamī, a branch of the Gaṅgā that purifies the three worlds, in order to perform austerities.
Desiring manhood from his mother, he then went quickly to the Himavat mountain for asceticism,
having paid homage to his mother, his father, and his guru.
Likewise, Ilā, the daughter of Soma, followed her son as he went;
they all reached the Gautamī from Himavat, the best of mountains.
Having bathed there and performed some austerity, they offered supreme praise to Bhava, the God of gods; hear now this sequence of his praise.
Buddha first offered praise, and after him, Ilā;
then his son Purūravas praised Gaurī the goddess and Śaṅkara.
Buddha said:
Those two, who were of identical form, resembling natural gold, [anointed] with saffron produced from their own bodies—
"May those two, who have been honored by Skanda and Gaṇeśvara, be my refuge as they are the ones worthy of providing shelter. [The Lord said:
"He spoke:"
Embodied beings, scorched by the forest fire of the threefold afflictions of saṃsāra, attain supreme bliss immediately upon reflecting on these two.
May those two Śaṅkaras be my refuge;
for I am distressed, with a tormented mind,
and there is no other protector against afflictions and the like.
"O Lord, may those two most meritorious feet of yours,
which are worthy of refuge, be my protection.
Purūravas said:
From whom this entire world arises and into whom it finally goes to dissolution— those two who are the refuge of the world and whose very nature is the world.
May Gaurī and Hara be my refuge—
those two whose feet, O Lord, you should grasp during the great festival among the hosts of gods, as the son of the Mountain Lord’s daughter.
"Out of affection for Dhṛti, Śiva has declared:
'May those two be my refuge; may they become my protection. [The Goddess said:]
"Tell me what desired object I shall grant to you;
you have accomplished your purpose—blessings be upon you—for this is difficult even for the gods."
Purūravas said:
"O Ambikā, King Īla entered the forest without knowing [your power].
Therefore, O Sovereign of the Gods, forgive him; you ought to grant him manhood."
Brahmā said:
"So be it," he said to them all, remaining in accordance with the will of Bhava.
Then the Blessed One, who is ever devoted to the words of the Goddess, spoke.
Śiva said:
"By this very consecration, let this king attain manhood."
Brahmā said:
From the body of Budha’s wife, who had bathed, water flowed forth—
the very dance, song, and beauty that the Yakṣiṇī had acquired.
All that entered the waters of the Gaṅgā as streams of water;
through her dancing and singing, these rivers became endowed with auspicious beauty.
And those three holy confluences also join the Gaṅgā;
bathing and giving gifts at them bestow the fruit of sovereignty over the gods.
Then, having attained manhood through the grace of Gaurī-Śambhu,
Ilā performed a horse sacrifice for the sake of achieving great prosperity.
Having summoned his family priest Vasiṣṭha, as well as his wife, sons,
ministers, army, and treasury, that best of kings—
Then he established his fourfold army and kingdom in Daṇḍaka;
that city there is said to be renowned by the name of Ila.
Having consecrated his previously born sons in the kingdom according to the succession of the Solar dynasty, he subsequently anointed that Aila out of affection.
"O Sage, may this illustrious king become the founder of the lunar dynasty;
thus he became the eldest and most excellent among all the wise. (BrP 108.120)
And where the auspicious sacrifices of King Ilā were performed, where he attained manhood, and where his sons were assembled; ||| BrP_108.121 |||
O Nārada, those places where rivers— possessing the auspiciousness and blessings of song and dance bestowed by Yakṣiṇīs— become the Gaṅgā and merge with her, [are sacred].
There were sixteen thousand auspicious sacred fords (tīrthas) on both banks, O dear one; there, Śambhu is known as Īśvara. Bathing and giving gifts at those sites bestow the fruit of all sacrifices.
Brahmā said:
There is a place renowned as Cakratīrtha, which destroys sins such as the killing of a Brahmin;
it is there that the Lord Hari obtained his discus from the god Cakreśvara.
Where the Lord Viṣṇu himself, having stayed there, worshipped the Lord Śaṅkara for the sake of the discus— that sacred site is called Cakratīrtha.
By the mere hearing of which one is liberated from all sins,
when the sacrifice of Dakṣa had commenced and the assembly of the gods was gathered.
When the god Śiva, Sarva, Maheśvara, had been insulted by Dakṣa,
and while the lord of the gods was not invited, Dakṣa’s mind became defiled.
When the daughter of Dakṣa had heard the words regarding the reason for not being summoned,
and when Ahalyā had spoken, the Queen of the Gods became enraged.
"I shall destroy my father's sin; I will never forgive it, even as I hear the words of reproach spoken by my father to my husband."
For those women who listen to the censure of their husband, how can there be an end to their sin?
Whether he be such or even otherwise, the husband is the supreme refuge for women.
How much more so, then, for Mahādeva, the sovereign of all and the teacher of the world?
If I have heard his censure, then I shall no longer sustain this body.
"Therefore, having said, 'I shall cast off this body,' that great virtuous lady,
the queen of the gods, was overcome by great anger and blazed with fury."
With her mind fixed solely on Śiva, she abandoned her body by force through yoga;
Maheśvara, for his part, heard the entire account from Nārada.
Seeing this, he became enraged and questioned Jayā and Vijayā;
both of them spoke to the god regarding the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Having heard [the words] "of Dākṣāyaṇī," Maheśvara set out for the sacrifice;
surrounded by his terrifying Gaṇas, he went together with the lords of the Bhūtas.
Makha was entirely surrounded by them, with the gods and Brahmins placed at his head,
and protected by Dakṣa, the sacrificer, who was pure in intent.
Surrounded by extremely formidable sages such as Vasiṣṭha and others,
he was protected on all sides by Indra, Āditya, and the Vasus.
Adorned with the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas and the utterance of "svāhā," [he was accompanied by] Faith, Nourishment, Contentment, Peace, Modesty, and Sarasvatī.
The earth, the sky, the night, patience, the dawn, hope, victory, and intelligence—
with these and other such [qualities], he was adorned on all sides.
And she was fashioned by the high-souled Tvaṣṭṛ, the architect of the universe (Viśvakarman):
the cow Surabhi, Nandinī, the wish-fulfilling cow, who milks all desires.
Through these showers of desires, he possesses the fulfillment of all wishes;
[he becomes] the wish-fulfilling tree Pārijāta and the creepers such as the Kalpalatā.
Whatever was most cherished and whatever was present at that sacrifice was personally protected by Maghavan, Pūṣan, and Hari.
"Let it be given, or let it be eaten; let it be done, or let one remain at ease"—by all such words was Dakṣa’s sacrifice honored on every side.
At first, that Vīrabhadra went forth accompanied by Bhadrakālī;
thereafter, his soul overwhelmed by grief and anger, he followed, bearing the trident and the Pināka bow.
Mahādeva, adorned by the great elements, approached;
those elements surrounded Maheśvara on all sides at the sacrifice.
They destroyed the sacrifice; there was great commotion there.
Some fled from that place, while others, having gone to Śiva, [sought refuge].
Some praised the Lord of Gods, while others grew angry with Śaṅkara;
having seen the sacrifice thus destroyed, Pūṣan approached.
Then, having uprooted the teeth of Pūṣan, he put Indra to flight in an instant;
O Brahmin, Vīrabhadra gouged out the eyes of Bhaga.
Then, having whirled Divākara around with his two arms, he hurled him away;
thereupon, all the hosts of gods went to Viṣṇu for refuge.
The gods said:
"Save us, save us, O mace-wielder, from the fear created by the Lord of Beings!
He is a certain leader of the Pramathas, a host of Maheśvara."
By him, while Hari was looking on, the entire sacrifice dedicated to Viṣṇu was consumed by fire.
Brahmā said:
Hari discharged his discus for the purpose of slaying Bhūtanātha;
but Bhūtanātha, as it was falling upon him, swallowed that very discus.
When his discus had been swallowed, the world-protectors then fled out of fear of Viṣṇu.
Seeing them standing there in such a state, as well as the gods and the sacrifice,
Dakṣa Prajāpati praised the god Śaṅkara with devotion.
Dakṣa said:
Victory, O Śaṅkara, Lord of Umā! Victory, O omniscient Śambhu!
Victory, O Śambhu, bearer of auspiciousness! Victory! Salutations to you, whose nature is Time.
Salutations be to you, the Primordial Creator; O Blue-throated One, salutations be to you!
Salutations be to you, beloved of Brahmā; salutations be to you, whose form is Brahman!
Obeisance to the threefold form, O God, O Supreme Lord of the three abodes;
obeisance be to you, O embodiment of all, the support of the three worlds and the granter of desires.
Salutations to the one known through the Vedānta; salutations to you, the Supreme Self.
O you whose form is sacrifice, salutations be to you; O abode of sacrifice, salutations be to you.
O sacrifice and gift, homage be to you; O carrier of oblations, homage be to you.
Homage be to you, the receiver of the sacrifice; homage be to you, the giver of its fruit.
Save me, save me, O Lord of the World, you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge!
O Lord, you alone are the refuge for both the devoted and the undevoted.
Brahmā said:
As he was thus offering praise, Maheśvara became pleased with him and said to him, "What shall I give? [Kratu replied,] "O Lord, may my sacrifice be complete."
"So be it," said the Blessed One, Maheśvara, the God of gods,
Śaṅkara, the soul of all beings, and the ocean of compassion.
O sage, having thus spoken and completed the sacrifice for Dakṣa, the Blessed One vanished along with his attendants.
The gods departed for their own abodes just as they had come;
then, at one time, a great conflict arose between the gods and the Daityas.
There, the gods, terrified of the Daityas,
praised Janārdana, the Lord of Śrī, with all their being through these words.
The gods said:
"Even Śakra and the other thirty-three deities perform austerities merely by catching a side-glance from her."
And I take refuge in him who has become Brahman, in whom Lakṣmī delights at his feet,
and than whom there is no other superior or equal in the three worlds.
And may that God of gods— who is superior even to the Man-lion with his chariot drawn by Tārkṣya— protect us all out of compassion when we have sought refuge from great terrors.
Brahmā said:
Then the Blessed One, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, being pleased, said to them, "For what purpose have you all come? I shall accomplish that."
The gods said:
"O Madhusūdana, there is intense fear of the Daityas for the gods;
therefore, O Janārdana, devise a means for the protection of the gods."
Brahmā said:
Hari spoke to those who had arrived: "My discus has been swallowed by Hara;
what shall I do? The discus is gone, and you have come to me in distress."
May all the hosts of gods depart; protection for you is being provided by me.
Brahmā said:
Then, after the gods had departed, Viṣṇu, intent on obtaining the discus,
went to the Godāvarī and began the worship of Śambhu.
With devotion, Viṣṇu constantly performed worship of the Lord of Umā with one thousand divine, fragrant golden lotuses.
While they were being honored in this manner, listen to this truth regarding them:
even when a thousand lotuses are offered, not even one is ever completed.

Then the enemy of the Asuras, Hari, having no other refuge, plucked out his own eye and prepared it as an *arghya* offering; taking the *arghya* vessel in his hand, which was adorned with a thousand lotuses, he meditated upon Śambhu and offered the *arghya*.
Viṣṇu said:
"O God, you alone know the inner disposition of men;
you alone are the refuge and the sovereign lord here—what need is there for further deliberation?"
Brahmā said:
As he spoke with eyes full of tears, saying "He has vanished into the Lord," Śambhu, accompanied by Bhavānī, then appeared before him.
Embracing Hari firmly, she gratified him with various excellent things;
that very discus became his eye once again, just as it was before.
Then all the hosts of gods praised Hari and Śaṅkara,
as well as Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, and the bull-bannered god.
From that time forward, that sacred ford has been known as Cakratīrtha;
by the mere hearing of its name, one is liberated from all sins.
Whoever performs bathing, giving, and the libation for the ancestors there shall be liberated from all sins and, together with the ancestors, become a partaker of heaven;
that holy site, marked by the discus, is visible even today.
Brahmā said:
Pippala Tīrtha is proclaimed as being immediately after Cakratīrtha;
it is there that the god Cakreśvara and Hari obtained the discus.
Where Viṣṇu himself, having stayed there, worshipped the omnipresent Śaṅkara for the sake of the discus— that sacred site is proclaimed as Cakratīrtha.
They know that Pippala tree to be where Śambhu took delight in Viṣṇu;
even the Lord of Serpents is not capable of describing its greatness.
Listen with devotion, O Nārada, to the reason for the names Cakreśvara and Pippaleśa, as they have been declared by me directly from the Vedas. BrP_110.4.
There was a celebrated sage named Dadhīci, endowed with all virtues;
his wife was highly wise, of noble birth, and devoted to her husband.
She who was known as Lopāmudrā had a sister named Gabhastinī,
who was also celebrated by the name Vaḍavā.
Dadhīci’s beloved wife constantly performed great asceticism;
Dadhīci, however, was always possessed of the sacred fire and devoted to the duties of a householder.
Resorting to the Bhāgīrathī, devoted to gods and guests,
content with his own wife, and tranquil, he was like another Agastya.
O tiger among sages, by his power, neither enemies nor Daityas or Dānavas came to that region where the hermitage of Agastya was located.
There the gods assembled—the Rudras, the Ādityas, and likewise the two Aśvins;
Indra, Viṣṇu, Yama, and Agni, having conquered the Daityas who had approached them.
Filled with joy at the victory and being praised by the hosts of Maruts,
the lords of the gods, upon seeing Dadhīci, that tiger among sages, bowed down before him.
Dadhīci, filled with joy, honored each of the gods individually and then attended to his domestic duties together with his wife.
When asked about his welfare by him, even the gods engaged in conversation;
the gods spoke again to Dadhīci, asking whether he was happy with his wife.
Having bowed down again and again to the seer who was seated with a joyful mind, [they spoke].
The gods said:
"O Sage, what in this world will today become difficult for us to obtain, since we possess a compassionate sage such as you, who is like a wish-fulfilling tree at the end of an eon?"
O best of sages, this alone is the fruit for living men:
bathing at sacred fords, compassion for all beings, and the sight of those such as you.
O Sage, pay heed to that which we say out of affection:
having conquered the Daityas and slain the foremost of the Rākṣasas, we have arrived here.
O Brahmā, we are happy, especially now that you have been seen;
we are truly not capable of bearing the burden of weapons or their fruit.
"O Lord of Sages, we do not see the place where these weapons were deposited;
having learned that the enemies of the gods have placed them in heaven, they are now taking them away."
Thinking, "They shall lead away the weapons," they likewise [placed them] in the netherworld;
therefore, O giver of honor, these missiles are being kept in your meritorious hermitage.
O Brahmin, there is no fear whatsoever here from Dānavas or from terrible Rākṣasas;
for this holy land is protected by your command.
There is no one equal to you in austerity;
you have conquered your enemies and are the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman.
As for us, the hosts of Daityas were already slain long ago.
"Enough with these missiles that have become a burden; they have served their purpose.
O Lord of Sages, let your station be established near me, along with divine enjoyments accompanied by beautiful women."
"Let us enjoy ourselves in the Nandana grove of the gods;
then, having accomplished our task, we shall go together with Indra to our respective abodes and to the protection of our weapons."
"Let that which was created by you come into being; rule over it, for you are capable both of protecting and sustaining it.
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words, Dadhīci spoke this speech to the gods: "So be it," even though he was being dissuaded by his wife of pleasing character.
What is the use of divine rites for one who acts in opposition [to them],
for those who have mastered the scriptures, are established in the ultimate truth,
and have lost all attachment to the activities of worldly existence?
O Sage, what is the use of their devotion to the welfare of others, since they find no happiness here or in the hereafter,
and instead give rise to hatred toward the enemies of the gods?
O best of brahmins, O lord of sages, listen to this regarding that situation: when weapons are lost or stolen,
the gods become angry and turn into one's enemies.
Therefore, O best of those who know the Vedas,
it is not proper to have a sense of ownership over another's property;
for as long as there is friendship, so long does the state of [true] possession exist.
When [wealth] is lost or stolen, those [who do not give] become your enemies.
If you have the power to bestow wealth, then it must certainly be given to the seeker; what need is there for deliberation?
If the virtuous would not perform the tasks of others through their speech, thoughts, and deeds,
this alone would be the upholding of another's property.
"O beloved, abandon immediately that which has been rejected by the virtuous.
[Brahmā said: Thus did that brahmin respond to the words of his beloved.
Having heard this, Dadhīci spoke thus to his fair-browed wife:
"O blessed lady, in former times, having obtained the consent of the gods..."
"The word 'no' does not bring me happiness," [Brahmā said:
having heard these words spoken by her husband regarding his beloved wife.
"Nothing other than destiny is capable [of stopping this] for men. While they remained silent, those best of gods set aside their exceedingly radiant weapons.
Having bowed to the Lord of Sages, the enemies of the Daityas, having laid down their weapons and accomplished their purpose, departed for their worlds;
and when the gods had gone, the preeminent sage—
Endowed with righteousness, he lived happily with his wife;
and when a very long time had passed—
a thousand divine years by calculation— BrP 110.34d–35b.
O Lord of Munis, those gods did not follow the command of their weapons, nor did they obey his word or mind;
then Dadhīci spoke to Gabhasti with vigor.
"O blessed lady, the enemies of the gods hate me here; they do not wish to take you away. Tell me what has been established here that is appropriate."
And she, out of modesty, said to her beloved:
"O Lord, you yourself know what is appropriate here;
the greatly increased Daityas will seize [them]."
Endowed with ascetic power and strength, he took up his weapons; for the sake of protecting the weapon, he purified them with mantras and with holy waters.
Dadhīci then drank that water, which consisted of all the divine weapons, was highly meritorious, and was endowed with splendor; thereby,
those weapons became rendered powerless.
In the course of time, they gradually went to ruin; then the gods, having come together, said to Dadhīci:
"A great fear has indeed come upon us from our enemy."
"O hero among sages, grant those weapons which were deposited with you by the gods at your request," Dadhīci said, out of fear of the enemies of the gods.
"Since you have not come here, your weapons residing within your bodies will soon be drunk [by me].
What you have said is appropriate; tell me what is fitting for me."
Having heard those words spoken by him, the gods, bowing low with humility, spoke thus to him: "Grant us the weapons," they said. 110.41c–110.42a.
O Lord of Sages, we are unable to offer any other reply;
without them, we are constantly being humiliated by our powerful enemies. O Master of Munis, where shall we go?
"O dear one, today there shall be no dwelling for the gods in the world of mortals, nor in the underworld, nor in heaven;
for you are the best of brahmins and are endowed with ascetic power."
"Nothing else is fitting for you to say before me," [the Lord said].
Then the Brahmin replied: "Let them take up the weapons residing within my bones; there is no doubt in this."
The gods said to him, "What is this to us? For the lords of the gods, deprived of their weapons, have attained womanhood.
Then the preeminent sage spoke again.
"Endowed with yoga, I shall cast off my bodily life-breaths;
let my bones become weapons,
unsurpassed and of excellent form."
"Perform it," they said to Dadhīci, whose courage was undaunted; he, who was like fire itself, then spoke words that were pleasing to them.
"O Lord of Sages, she did not show hospitality while you were present.
And those gods, having failed to see her, quickly spoke to the brahmin out of fear: 'Do it!'"
Filled with affection, he abandoned his life-breaths so difficult to give up; enjoy this body at your pleasure,
and may you find satisfaction in my bones.
"O gods, what indeed is to be done with this body?
Having spoken thus, he sat down in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana). (Brahmā said: BrP_110.49a.
With the light of his gaze fixed on the tip of the nose and serene,
he should slowly lead the wind, together with the fire, through the yoga of the central upward-thrust into the interior of the space within the heart.
Having fixed his intellect precisely upon that immeasurable supreme state, which is the form of Brahman and that which is to be worshipped, the Great-Souled One—
He attained union with Brahman. Seeing that his body had become lifeless, the gods and the celestial beings [prepared] it thoroughly.
Hurrying, they also said to Tvaṣṭṛ:
"Produce many weapons immediately.
And he said to them: "How indeed should it be done?"
"O gods, I am afraid to fashion the body of this Brahmin here; I am incapable of performing such a terrible task,
and my supreme weapons have been shattered."
"I shall immediately turn them into bones.
Then the gods, hurrying, spoke to the cows.
(The gods said:)
For the sake of your welfare, the gods shall in an instant turn you into vajras for the purpose of weapons; having torn apart the body of Dadhīci, you [shall become so]. (BrP 110.54)
"Give me these pure bones today," Brahmā said;
and they did exactly so at the word of the god.
Having licked the bones, they gave them to the gods;
the gods, undaunted in spirit, departed in haste for their own abode, and the cows did likewise.
Having thus fashioned the weapons of the deities, Tvaṣṭṛ then departed at the command of the gods; thereafter, after a long time, Śīlavatī Subhadrā—
The beloved of her husband, pregnant with a child, hastening and holding a water-filled jar in her hand,
approached Umā after bowing before her with fruits and flowers.
Desiring to see both her husband Agni and the hermitage, she then arrived quickly;
at that time, as the daughter-in-law was approaching, [she saw] her.
She warded off that falling meteor;
having returned to her own hermitage in great agitation,
she did not see her husband there before her.
Then the daughter of Pratīpa, filled with wonder, asked the fire, "Where has he gone? And the fire then spoke to her in detail.
Having heard everything— the arrival of the gods, the request, the extraction of the bones from her body, and then her departure— she became utterly distressed.
Then, out of agitation from her suffering, she fell upon the earth; and being very gently comforted by the fire,
Prātitheyī said:
"I am not capable of pronouncing a curse upon the immortals;
what then would be my purpose?
[Brahmā said:]"

Restraining both her anger and her grief, the virtuous woman then spoke words consistent with dharma to her husband; [Prātitheyī said: The virtuous Prātitheyī, restraining both her anger and her sorrow, then spoke words endowed with righteousness to her husband.
Whatever arises is perishable;
there is nothing in the world of men that should be grieved for.
In this world, people sacrifice even their lives for the sake of cows, Brahmins, and gods.
Human beings, who partake in merit, cherish their dear lives;
yet as they revolve upon the wheel of saṃsāra,
they may sometimes obtain a capable body endowed with dharma.
Those living beings who renounce their dear lives for the sake of gods and brahmins are indeed blessed;
for all life belongs to one who possesses a body.
There is indeed not even a trace of doubt in this matter;
knowing this, those lords bestow these things for the sake of the Brahmins, cows, gods, the poor, and others.
Even though he was being restrained by me as I sought refuge,
he took up the divine weapon;
or perhaps he knows the intent of the Creator.
[Brahmā said: "Who [is capable] of [fathoming] the deeds that transcend the world of mortals?
Having spoken thus, he worshipped the fires according to the prescribed rule.
Prātitheyī entered her husband’s skin and hair; then, having torn open the belly of the child situated in the womb, she took him in her hand.
Having bowed to the Gaṅgā, the earth, the hermitage,
the trees, and the medicinal plants situated in the hermitage,
Prātitheyī said:
May all the hosts of beings protect one who is deprived of father, kinsmen, and relatives of the same lineage, as well as every child deprived of his mother.
Likewise, the medicinal herbs and the world-protectors [protect] the child;
those who [protect] the child abandoned by mother and father [do so] without distinction, with [their own bodies] grown forth from their own forms.
They surely behold and protect [all beings],
and they are indeed worthy of worship even by Brahmā and the other gods.
{Brahmā said:}
Having spoken thus, she who was devoted to her husband’s will abandoned the child;
having placed the child near the *pippala* trees, she paid them homage.
Having circumambulated the fire, Prātitheyī, accompanied by the sacrificial vessels,
entered the fire and went to heaven together with her husband.
And those trees dwelling in the hermitage and living in the forest wept,
as did the sage Dadhīci, by whom they had been nurtured like sons.
"Without him we do not live, nor do we live without that mother," so said all the deer, birds, and trees to one another.
The trees said:
"Those men alone are truly successful who constantly maintain genuine affection for their parents' offspring once those parents have ascended to heaven."
"Neither our father nor our mother looks upon us as Dadhīci or Prātitheyī used to look upon us in the past; fie on us, we are sinners! (BrP 110.76)
From this day forward, it is resolved for all of us as well:
the child Dadhīci is the guest-reception, and the child Dharma is the eternal law.
{Brahmā said:} Having spoken thus, the medicinal herbs, together with the forest trees,
approached King Soma and begged for the supreme nectar of immortality.
And Soma also gave them the unsurpassed nectar;
they, in turn, gave that nectar, so dear to the gods, to the boy.
Satisfied by that, he grew like the moon in the bright fortnight;
because he was nourished with *pippala* fruits, that boy was named Pippalāda.
Having grown up, he spoke thus to the *pippala* trees, being greatly amazed: [BrP 110.80]
Pippalāda said: "From humans, humans are born; from birds, birds;
from seeds, creepers arise in the world—no inequality is seen at all."
But how was I born from a tree, possessing hands, feet, and other organs of life?
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words, the trees all spoke in due order concerning the death of Dadhīci and likewise the virtuous woman’s entry into the fire.
Having heard all this in detail— the collection of the bones by the gods— he was overcome with grief and then fell to the ground.
Comforted once more by the trees with words endowed with dharma and artha,
he, being reassured, spoke again to the medicinal herbs and forest lords.
Pippalāda said:
"I shall slay those who killed my father; I am not able to live otherwise.
A son follows the same path toward his father's friends and enemies alike."
He alone is a son; any other is considered an enemy in the form of a son.
They say that the friends of one's father rescue even those who are harmful.
Brahmā said:
Then the trees, taking that boy, went to the presence of Soma;
and those trees reported the words of the boy to Soma.
Having heard that, Soma also spoke to the boy Pippalāda.
Soma said:
"Accept in its entirety, according to the prescribed rite, knowledge,
the perfection of asceticism, and auspicious speech."
"O son, by my command you shall obtain heroism, beauty, strength, and intelligence.
Brahmā said:
Pippalāda also spoke to that Lord of Herbs with humility.
Pippalāda said:
"I consider all this to be in vain as an atonement for killing my father;
I will not perform it here until [you provide the means]. Therefore, speak first of that."
O best of gods, in which country, at what time, with which deity and mantra,
and at which sacred ford (tīrtha) shall my resolve be fulfilled?
Brahmā said: Candra, having reflected for a long time, replied: "Whether it be worldly enjoyment or even liberation, everything arises from the god Maheśvara; there is no doubt in this."
He spoke again to Soma: "How shall I behold Maheśvara?
I am but a child, with a childish intellect, and I lack the capacity for such asceticism."
Candra said:
"Go to Gautamī, my dear boy; praise Hara, the Lord of the Discus. For the Lord, being pleased with you, will grant your desire with little effort."
The great god Śiva, the compassionate one, would become pleased;
Śambhu himself was directly perceived by the powerful Viṣṇu.
And he granted a boon to Viṣṇu, as well as the discus worshipped by the gods:
"Go there, O one of great intelligence, to the Gautamī river in Daṇḍaka."
The medicinal herbs know that sacred ford named Cakreśvara;
go there and praise Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, with your whole being.
My dear son, he, with a pleased mind, will grant you all your desires.
Brahmā said: O Brahmin,
at those words of the king, the great sage Pippalāda came to where Rudra, the Lord of the World, was roaring.
Filled with compassion for that child, the Pippalas went to their own hermitages.
Then, having bathed in the Godāvarī and bowed to the Lord of the Three Worlds,
the pure Pippalāda praised Śiva with his whole being.
Pippalāda said:
"The wise, having abandoned all actions,
having relinquished their desires, and having conquered the winds of the mind,"
I bow down to that primordial god Śambhu, the witness of all and the inner self of all, whom those seeking liberation take as their refuge with great effort.
May that enemy of Smara, the Lord of All and the treasury of all arts, who has perceived everything residing in my mind, show compassion toward me.
Having conquered the lords of the quarters, as the Enemy of the Cities— who is worshipped by the gods—
shook Mount Kailāsa, [the earth] sank below the netherworld by the mere action of his big toe.
Having heard the words of that very Daśānana, whose body was mangled,
he laughed and granted a desired boon together with the Goddess.
Just as he was pleased with him, so too, O Maheśvara, you were angry; though you are one who bestows what is improper,
he brought the prosperity of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice to an end.
Bāṇa, who had performed worship of Hari constantly and most excellently, offered high praise and a beautiful, pleasing, and lofty adoration to the One whose crest is the crescent moon.
Having conquered his enemies and honored the hosts of gods,
Viśākha went to pay homage to his preceptor;
seeing that the Lord of the Gaṇas was married, he became enraged.
Placing him on his lap, Soma laughed;
though seated upon the lap of Īśa, the boy did not release his mother’s lap due to his childhood nature.
Unable even to awaken his son who was thus enraged,
Soma then attained the state of being half-woman.
(Brahmā said:)
Then the Self-Existent One, being well-pleased, addressed Pippalāda:
Śiva said:
"Choose a boon, O Pippalāda, may it be well with you, according to your desire."
Pippalāda said:
"O Great God, my father, who was highly illustrious, free from hypocrisy, and truthful in speech, has been slain by the gods; likewise, my mother was devoted to her husband."
And having heard from the gods, O Lord, the detailed account of their destruction, I am overcome with grief and anger; I have no desire to live.
Therefore, grant me the power so that I may destroy the gods;
O Moon-crested One, you alone are the one who cannot be slain and is worthy of service throughout the three worlds.
Ishvara said:
"O sinless one, if you are able to behold my third eye,
then you will become capable of cutting off the gods."
Brahmā said:
Then the mind of the Lord turned toward creating a third eye;
he was unable to do so, and thereupon he said to Śaṅkara, "I am not capable."
The Lord said:
"O child, perform some austerity; when you behold the third eye, you shall then obtain your desire—of this there is no doubt."
Having heard these words of Īśāna, the righteous son of Dadhīci, having resolved upon asceticism,
remained right there for many years.
Devoted solely to the meditation on Śiva, even a child becomes like one who is powerful;
rising every day at dawn, having bathed, and having bowed to his gurus in due order.
Seated comfortably, having fixed his mind upon the *suṣumnā* with undistracted intellect,
and placing his hands in the *svastika* posture at the navel, he forgets the cycle of worldly existence.
The eater of *pippala* fruits beheld the splendor of Śambhu, which, by its excellence, surpassed one station after another;
he saw the third eye of the God, and with palms joined in reverence, he spoke these words in humility: BrP_110.118 //
Pippalāda said:
"In former times, a boon was granted to me by Śambhu, the God of gods:
'At the very moment you behold the light of the third eye, [you shall attain success].'"
"Everything you have requested shall be accomplished," said the Lord of the Thirty-three;
therefore, grant me that which will serve as the cause for the destruction of my enemies.
At that very moment, O one of great splendor, the Pippalas and even Vaḍavā said:
"Your mother Prātitheyī has gone to heaven, speaking thus."
Men who delight in harming others, who have forgotten their own welfare,
and whose minds wander here and there, fall into the pit of hell.
Hearing those words of his mother, Pippalāśana was incensed;
for when pride burns within, praise from the virtuous is meaningless.
"Give! Give! the Kṛtyā, who had emerged from his eye, said to him;
and the Brahmin, remembering "Vaḍavā," became a Vaḍavā in form, while the Kṛtyā likewise took the form of a Vaḍavā.
She who contains a vast fire within her for the destruction of all beings,
Gabhastinī, whose womb holds a child, is the mother of the Pippalāśins.
Through the power of that meditation, a Kṛtyā was born, containing fire within her;
once produced, she was exceedingly fierce and terrifying, like the very tongue of Death.
She said to Pippalāda, "Tell me what I must do.
Pippalāda also said to her, "Devour my enemies, the gods."
Having said "So be it," she took hold of Pippalāda who stood before her;
he asked, "What is this task? and she replied, "It is what you have spoken."
Having created that body by means of the gods, he then became afraid and went to Śiva;
that sage praised the god, and then Śiva spoke to Kṛtyā.
Śiva said:
"By my command, do not seize the living beings situated within a distance of one yojana.
Therefore, go far from there; once you have reached that place, perform whatever task is required."
Brahmā said:
From the Pippala Tīrtha, extending forward for a distance of one yojana,
that Kṛtyā created by the Ṛṣis stood there in the form of a mare.
From her was born a great fire capable of destroying the world;
seeing it, all the gods were terrified and approached Śambhu.
Praising Cakreśvara, the Lord of the Pippala tree, who had been propitiated by Pippalāda, the gods, with hearts filled with fear, spoke to Śambhu: BrP_110.133 //
The gods said:
"O Śambhu, protect us; that Kṛtyā afflicts us like fire.
O Lord of All, grant fearlessness to those who are afraid; be our refuge."
O Auspicious One, you alone are the refuge for all living beings who are everywhere despised, afflicted, and weary in mind.
Requested by the Ṛṣi, the Kṛtyā has emerged from the fire of your eye;
she seeks to destroy the three worlds, and you alone are our protector, none other.
Brahmā said:
The Lord of the World spoke to those dwelling within a league [of distance]:
"This *kṛtyā* does not afflict you; therefore, you must [protect her] day and night."
Stay right here, O immortals; you shall have no fear of him.
Brahmā said:
They spoke again to the Lord of the Gods: "O Lord, honored by the thirty deities, how shall we dwell here, having abandoned the heaven (triviṣṭapa) granted by you?"
Brahmā said:
Having heard the words of the gods, Śiva then spoke these words.
Śiva said:
That god has eyes on all sides; that god has faces on all sides.
He who constantly blows with his rays is considered the progenitor.
Let that Sun alone always remain here visibly in his own form; all others who exist shall abide within his manifestation.
Brahmā said:
"So be it. Then, at the word of Śambhu, the gods made the Pārijāta tree their sun; Tvaṣṭṛ spoke to Bhāskara: *Br̥had-Āraṇyaka Purāṇa 110.143*
Tvaṣṭṛ said:
"O Lord of the World, remain right here yourself and protect these gods;
we too shall stay here in the presence of Śambhu with our own portions."
The supreme gods took their seats, having reached both banks of the Gaṅgā, extending for a distance of many yojanas all around the Lord of the Discus.

O best of sages, three crores, five hundred, and half of a half-finger’s breadth of land along the banks of the Gaṅgā are filled with sacred fords; who can hear of, or even describe, their manifold benefits?
Brahmā said:
Then all the hosts of gods, being humble, spoke to Śiva.
The gods said:
"O Lord of the gods, O you who pervade the universe, bring peace to Pippalāda!"
Brahmā said:
Having uttered "Om," the Lord of the World spoke to Pippalāda.
Śiva said:
"Even if the gods were destroyed, your father would not have come;
your life was given by your father for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods."
For who indeed could be such a kinsman of compassion for the wretched and the distressed?
O dear one, your mother, devoted to her husband, has likewise gone to heaven.
In this regard, Lopāmudrā and Arundhatī are equal in my estimation,
since by means of their bones all the gods have become victorious and forever happy.
By this, you have acquired abundant fame that shall never diminish;
by you, as a son, nothing greater has been accomplished anywhere than this.
Out of fear of your majesty, they have fallen from heaven; you ought to protect them.
Fleeing in all directions out of terror of you, you ought to save these immortals.
Nowhere does a greater merit exist than the protection of those in distress.
For as long as one's beautiful fame resounds in the world of men,
for that many days does one reside in heaven;
day by day, the number of years increases in the other world.
One who dwells in the world becomes changeless;
those for whom there is no fame are as if dead here;
and those who are devoid of sacred learning are truly blind.
Those who are devoted to generosity and virtue are not eunuchs;
those who are devoted to the Dharma are not to be pitied.
{Brahmā said:}
Having heard what was spoken by the God of Gods, the sage became tranquil;
then, with palms joined in reverence and bowing to the Lord, he spoke.
Pippalāda said:
Those who are devoted to my welfare may at times benefit me through their words, thoughts, and deeds.
For their benefit and for the sake of others here, I pay homage to Soma, who is worshipped by the gods and other beings,
and who was protected and nourished by them.
May Śiva grant the desired objects to those who share his lineage and his nature;
I bow eternally to him whose crest is the crescent moon.
O Lord, O God of gods, let there arise in the three worlds a sacred ford (tīrtha) by their names— those by whom I have been constantly nourished like a mother and like a father.
But their fame shall be great, and through them I shall be free from debt;
for whatever sacred fields belong to the gods and whatever holy places exist upon the earth, [they shall possess them].
May the deities grant me permission for whatever among these is excessive;
then, being stainless, I shall forgive the offense of the gods.
Brahmā said: Then,
in the presence of the thousand-eyed Indra and others, he spoke these words in the language of the gods.
The gods also reflected with reverence upon the words spoken by the son of Dadhīci,
[considering] the child’s intelligence, discipline, and learning.
Having recognized his heroism, strength, daring, truthful speech, devotion to his parents, and purity of heart,
Śaṅkara then spoke to Pippalāda.
Śaṅkara said:
"O child, whatever dear desire you have, and whatever is beloved by the gods—speak that auspicious thing; you shall obtain it. Do not set your mind on anything else."
Pippalāda said:
O Maheśa, those who are devoted to dharma and have bathed in the Gaṅgā behold your lotus feet.
May they forcibly attain all desires,
and at the end of their bodies, may they reach the state of Śiva;
my father has attained your state, as has Ambikā, my mother.
O Lord, Pippala and the immortals have arrived;
having beheld you, the protector of protectors, they have attained happiness. May they behold you and may they proceed to your state.
Brahmā said: Having said "So be it" to Pippalāda, Maheśvara, the God of gods,
greeted him and then spoke these words along with the deities.
Even the gods, filled with joy and freed from the fear caused by him, all spoke thus to Dadhīca in the presence of Śiva: BrP_110.169 //
The gods said: "Without doubt, that which was desired by the gods has been accomplished by you;
the command of the God of gods, the ornament of the three worlds, has been upheld."
"O twice-born one, previously you requested for the sake of others and not for yourself;
therefore, ask for something else, and we shall grant it to you."
Brahmā said:
Having first bowed with palms joined in reverence, Śambhu spoke this to the hosts of gods and the best of the twice-born, who were saying the same thing again and again.
And Pippalāda, having bowed to Umā and to the pippala trees, spoke.
Pippalāda said:
"I am always desirous of seeing my parents, for their voices remain within the range of my hearing.
Blessed are those living beings in this world who abide under the authority of their mother and father."
Constantly devoted to service, they await his commands from his feet;
[so too do] the senses, the body, the family, power, the intellect, and the physical form.
Having obtained these two, one becomes personally fulfilled in their purpose;
for beasts and even birds, the sight of their mother is easily attained.
That [result] is difficult for me to obtain; shall I ask what the fruit of my sin is?
If it were likewise difficult for anyone at all to obtain, then it would belong to everyone.
"O best of gods, it would not be possible for anyone else to be a doer of evil as easily as I; and if I were to obtain even a mere sight of those two," BrP_110.177.
The fruit of the actions of mind, speech, and body will surely be obtained.
As for those who, having been born into this cycle of existence, do not honor their parents—
who is capable of calculating the number of such great sins?
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of the sage and consulted with one another, those gods [departed],
while the auspicious couple, the parents, ascended their excellent celestial chariot.
Desiring a sight of you, you shall certainly see him today;
casting off despondency, greed, and delusion, bring your mind to tranquility.
"Look! Look! the best of the gods said to Dadhīca, as two celestial beings, adorned with golden ornaments, ascended an excellent celestial chariot.
Your auspicious parents, a husband and wife, long for the sight of you;
they are being fanned by celestial women and praised by kinnaras.
Having seen his parents in the presence of Śiva, he bowed down;
with eyes filled with tears of joy, he spoke to them with some difficulty.
The son said:
"Other sons who uphold the lineage truly deliver their parents;
I, however, was merely a cause of destruction within my mother's womb."
Even though I am such as this, through delusion that exceedingly foolish-minded one might still see those two.
Brahmā said:
Beholding those two, he was then unable to speak out of grief;
and the gods spoke then to Pippalāda and his parents.
"Blessed are you, my son, among all in the worlds, for your fame has reached the heavens.
You have directly beheld the Three-Eyed God, and the gods have been comforted by you.
With you as their son, these worlds shall never perish."
Brahmā said:
Then, O great sage, a shower of flowers fell from heaven upon his head, and the cry of "Victory! uttered by the gods manifested there.
Having bestowed his blessing upon his son, Dadhīci, together with his wife,
bowed to Śambhu, Gaṅgā, and the gods, and then spoke these words to his son:
Dadhīci said:
"Having obtained a wife, cultivate devotion to Śiva and serve the Gaṅgā;
having procreated sons according to the rules and performed sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees."
"Therefore, my child, having accomplished your purpose, ascend to heaven for a long time."
"Brahmā said:
'I shall do so,' replied Pippalāśana to Dadhīci,
after Dadhīci had consoled his son and his wife again and again."
Permitted by the hosts of gods, he ascended once more to heaven;
and all the gods, filled with agitation, spoke to Pippalāda.
The gods said:
"Quell the *kṛtyā*; may it be well with you; that great conflagration has arisen. (BrP 110.192)
Brahmā said:
Pippalāda, however, said to them, "I am not capable of warding them off;
I shall certainly not speak an untruth, but you must tell them of that Kṛtyā."
"Upon seeing me, that most fierce woman will act perversely.
Having gone to her, the gods spoke for the sake of bringing about peace.
"Fire and Wind said to him, 'We two shall not go according to your pleasure;
for I was created by the twice-born one solely for the consumption of all. (BrP 110.195)
And likewise, fire was produced from me; otherwise, how could the five great elements, as well as all things stationary and moving, have come into being?
"Everything that ought to be said is known within our mouths; nothing remains for us to say.
Having consulted with me, those gods spoke thus once more to both of them.
Both of them consumed everything in due order;
likewise, the mare spoke thus to the gods: "Listen, O Nārada! (BrP 110.198).
The mare said:
"O best of gods, by your will, everything shall be my food."
Brahmā said:
O sage, that mare became a river and merged with the Gaṅgā;
as for the great fire that had been so terrifying, it was [extinguished].
The immortals say of him: "They know Vahni to be the first of all beings."
The Suras said:
"Water should be known as the eldest; likewise, you are the first among them. Furthermore, make the ocean, the lord of waters, the eldest and your food."
But just as we say, "Go and eat as you please," so it is here.
Brahmā said: Fire then spoke to the immortals, "How indeed may I go there,
if they cause me to reach the great water?"
They too said to him, "O Agni, how can there be a way for you?
And Agni also said to those gods, "A maiden endowed with excellent qualities [has chosen me]."
"Having placed it in a golden pitcher, one should carry it to wherever my destination lies.
Hearing those words of his, they spoke to the maiden Sarasvatī.
The gods said:
"Take this Anala quickly by the head to the abode of Varuṇa."
Brahmā said:
Sarasvatī spoke to the gods: "I am not alone capable of bearing [the weight];
joined by four others, I shall quickly carry [you] to the abode of Varuṇa."
Having heard the words of Sarasvatī, as well as those of Gaṅgā, Yamunā,
Narmadā, and Tapatī, the gods spoke to each of them individually.
Accompanied by them, he carried the fire in a golden vessel;
having placed it upon his head and supported it, they went to the abode of Varuṇa.
There, the Lord of Gods, Somanātha, the Master of the World adorned with the moon, established himself and resides at Prabhāsa together with the gods.
The five rivers and the Sarasvatī reached the fire;
and the great Agni sat there, drinking the water very slowly.
Then all the hosts of gods spoke to Śiva, the supreme among the gods.
The gods said:
"Tell us the means of purifying bones, as well as those for ourselves and for cows."
Brahmā said:
Śiva then declared to all: "Having diligently bathed in the Gaṅgā, gods and cows alike are liberated from their sins; of this there is no doubt."
Then those bones originating from the body of the Ṛṣi were washed;
by that very washing, they attained purity right there.
Where the gods dwell, freed from sin, that is a sacred ford (tīrtha) which destroys evil;
bathing and giving gifts there destroy even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Where there is that purifier of cows called Gotīrtha,
by bathing there, one of great intelligence obtains the fruit of a Gomedha sacrifice.
O Nārada, where those sacred bones of the brāhmaṇas lay,
that place should be known as Pitṛtīrtha, which increases the delight of the ancestors.
The ashes, bones, nails, and hair of any living being that may enter that sacred bathing place shall remain there as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure.
"Even for one who has committed evil deeds, there shall be residence in heaven by virtue of that Tīrtha Cakreśvara. O Nārada, there are three other Tīrthas [there];
purified by them, the hosts of gods and the cows then spoke to Śambhu: *Brahmapurāṇa* 110.219.
The gods said:
"We shall go each to our own abode; here the sun is established.
When this maker of day is present, all the gods are established."
O Lord of the worlds, you ought to grant permission for this;
for the Sun is indeed the eternal self of this world, both that which moves and that which is stationary.
There, we have installed the divine Divākara;
where the world-sustainer Gaṅgā flows, where Tryambaka himself resides,
and where there is the abode of the gods, Pratiṣṭhāna, which is sacred to Tryambaka.
Brahmā said:
Having taken leave of that Pippalāda, the gods went to their own abode;
then, in the course of time, the Pippalas themselves ascended to the imperishable heaven.
The powerful brahmin Pippalāda,
having established himself as the lord of the trees, worshipped Śaṅkara.
The sage Dadhīcisūnu, possessed of fierce splendor,
having obtained as his wife the daughter of Gautama,
and having further obtained sons, prosperity, and fame—
The wise man attained heaven along with his friends.
From that time forth, that holy site is called Pippaleśvara;
it is meritorious, yielding the fruit of all sacrifices, and it destroys sins through mere remembrance.
Furthermore, through bathing and giving gifts, as well as from the sight of the Sun, one obtains the two names of the God of gods:
Cakreśvara and Pippaleśa.
Having understood the secret doctrine, one shall obtain all desires.
Because it is the established abode of the Sun,
that field— established as the residence of the gods— is beloved even by the deities.
Whoever should read, hear, or remember this exceedingly meritorious narrative shall be long-lived, wealthy, and endowed with righteousness.
And at the end, remembering Śambhu, he attains the eternal state.
Brahmā said:
There is a holy place known as Nāgatīrtha, auspicious and the granter of all desires.
Listen also to the detailed account of that place where the god Nāgeśvara resides.
In the city of Pratiṣṭhāna, there was a king renowned as Śūrasena;
born of the Lunar dynasty, he was illustrious, wise, and an ocean of virtues.
Together with his beloved wife, he made a great effort for the sake of a son;
after a long time, a son was born to him who was indeed a serpent of terrifying appearance.
King Śūrasena protected that son [in secret],
so that no person knew him as "the king's son Sarpa."
Whether he be an insider or even an outsider, no one— neither a nurse nor a minister nor a priest— knows the mother or the father, except for the child itself.
Seeing that terrifying serpent, the best of kings, together with his wife, constantly experienced great distress; indeed, he considered childlessness to be better than having such a serpent.
This great serpent always speaks like a human;
that serpent said to his father, "Perform even the rite of tonsure."
Likewise, the initiation ceremony and even the study of the Vedas [are required];
as long as he has not studied the Veda, the twice-born is equal to a Śūdra.
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of his son, Śūrasena was deeply distressed;
he brought a certain Brahmin and then performed the funeral rites and other ceremonies for him.
Having mastered the Vedas, even the serpent spoke this to his father:
The serpent said:
"O King, O best of monarchs, perform a marriage for me; for I am desirous of a wife.
Otherwise, it is my conviction that your purpose will not be accomplished."
A father who, having procreated sons, does not perform for them all the purificatory rites according to the Vedic injunctions, finds no atonement for his sin; there is no escape from hell for him.
Brahmā said:
Astonished, that father spoke to his son who was in the form of a serpent.
Śūrasena said:
"O son, tell me, what can I do? To whom even the sound of whose name causes even brave men to tremble with fear—to such a person, who would give his daughter?"
{Brahmā said:} Having heard those words of his father, the wise serpent spoke. (BrP 111.14)
The serpent said:
"O King, O lord of men, there are many forms of marriage for kings:
abduction by force, marriage by weapons, and the [conventional] wedding ceremony."
Once the marriage of my son has been performed, that father shall have fulfilled his duty;
otherwise, I shall die right here in the Gaṅgā—of this there is no doubt.
Brahmā said:
Having learned of that resolve regarding a son, the best of kings, though childless,
summoned his ministers for the sake of marriage and spoke these words.
Śūrasena said:
My son Nāgeśvara is the crown prince;
he is a mine of virtues, endowed with merit and intelligence, heroic, invincible, and a scorcher of his enemies.
He is not equaled on chariot, elephant, bow, or upon the earth;
his marriage must be performed, for I am likewise old.
"Having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to my son, I shall therefore be free from anxiety;
until I have taken a wife, this son alone is dear to me."
"He does not abandon his state of childhood; therefore, all of you, having given your consent, should now make an effort toward my marriage, being devoted to my welfare."
At that time, I had no concern whatsoever that my son was married;
for virtuous men, having entrusted the burden of their family to their sons, go to the forest for asceticism.
Brahmā said:
Having heard the king’s words, all the ministers,
with palms joined in reverence, spoke joyfully to the monarch of immense splendor.
The ministers said:
"Your son is preeminent in virtues and you yourself are renowned everywhere;
regarding the marriage of your son, what counsel is needed, and what is there to deliberate?"
{Brahmā said:} When the ministers had spoken thus, the profound and best of kings did not disclose to his ministers that his son was a serpent; nor did they know it.
The king spoke to them again: "Which maiden would be superior in virtue?
And which king, born of a great lineage and endowed with splendor, would be a repository of virtues?"
Having heard those words of the king— "He is worthy of alliance and heroic, such that an alliance with him is praised"— the high-minded [minister] addressed the ministers.
Noble by birth, exceedingly virtuous, and devoted to the welfare of the king's affairs,
he who understood gestures spoke these words after discerning the king's intention.
The minister said:
"O Great King, in the eastern region there was a monarch named Vijaya,
for whom there was no counting of his horses, elephants, and jewels."
The wise great king had eight sons who were mighty archers; their sister was Bhogavatī, like another Lakṣmī in person. O King, she whom I have described is a fitting wife for your son.
Having heard the words of the aged minister, the king replied to him.
The king said:
"Tell me how I might have a daughter from this son of mine."
The elder minister said:
"O Great King, you have been observed; whatever is in your mind, and whatever task must be performed by Śūra, then grant me permission for that."
Brahmā said:
Having heard the words of the aged minister, and having honored him with gifts of ornaments and clothing, he sent him forth accompanied by a great army.
Having come to the eastern region and approached the great king,
he honored him with various words and means born of political wisdom.
And Mahāmati was born of Bhogavatī, the daughter of the great king,
and of the wise Nāga, the son of King Śūrasena.
He made an agreement for the sake of marriage through false and deceitful words;
he honored the king with ornaments, garments, and other such gifts.
Having received the honor, the king then said, "I shall give it.
Thereupon, that high-minded elder minister returned to the king.
He reported that account of the wedding to Śūrasena;
then, after a long period of time had passed, the high-minded elder minister—
Furthermore, adorned with garments and ornaments, he went swiftly with great force, surrounded by all his other ministers.
Accompanied by his ministers, that wise and aged great minister reported everything regarding the marriage to the Great King.
The elder minister said:
"The son of King Śūrasena, known as Nāga— wise and an ocean of virtues— does not come here to visit."
O King, O high-minded one, the marriages of Kṣatriyas may take many forms; therefore, their marriage should be performed with weapons and ornaments.
For both Kṣatriyas and Brāhmaṇas indeed speak truthful words;
therefore, let the marriage be permitted with weapons as ornaments.
Brahmā said:
Having heard the words of the aged minister, Vijaya, the best of kings, then considered that speech to be true, regarding the minister as his sovereign.
The king performed the marriage with Bhogavatī in full detail,
and then, according to the scriptures, he sent her away once more by means of a weapon.
Then Vijaya, filled with great joy, gave away his own ministers, cattle, gold, horses, and so forth, in great abundance.
Then, taking her with them, the ministers, led by the senior counselors,
arrived at Pratiṣṭhāna and presented that daughter-in-law to Śūrasena.
They reported this and spoke at length regarding the words of Vijaya,
as well as the various ornaments, maidservants, garments, and other such things.
Having offered [the tribute] to Śūrasena, those ministers of Vijaya who had come with Bhogavatī became fulfilled in their purpose.
Having honored them with great respect, the king,
acting according to his pleasure for the sake of victory, dismissed them.
Vijaya’s daughter was a young woman endowed with beauty and youth;
the slender-waisted girl constantly served her mother-in-law and father-in-law.
And the husband of Bhogavatī, a most terrifying great serpent,
was in a secluded, solitary place within a house beautifully adorned with jewels.
There, upon that pleasant and cool ground strewn with fragrant flowers,
the serpent spoke again and again to his mother and father.
"My wife is a princess; why does she not approach me at all?
Having heard those words of her son, the mother of the serpent spoke this:
The king’s wife said:
"O Dhātrikā, O fortunate one, go quickly to Bhogavatī and say, 'Your husband is a serpent'; then tell me what she will say."
Brahmā said:
Having replied, "So be it," Dhātrikā then went to Bhogavatī;
having gone there in private, she spoke these words with humility, as if she were a stranger.
The nurse said:
"O fortunate one, O blessed lady, I know your husband to be a deity;
you must not mention this anywhere, for he is certainly neither a serpent nor a man."
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of hers, Bhogavatī spoke this.
Bhogavatī said: "For among human women, a man would generally be a husband;
how much more so for one of divine birth, who is obtained as a husband through merit?"
Brahmā said:
She then reported all those words of Bhogavatī to the serpent,
to the mother of the serpents, and to the king, each in their proper order.
At those words, the king wept, remembering the course of that deed;
Bhogavatī also spoke again to her friend whom she had addressed before.
Bhogavatī said:
"Show me my beloved—blessings be upon you—for my youth is passing away in vain."
Brahmā said:
Then, having gone into seclusion, she showed him that most terrifying serpent upon a bed strewn with fragrant flowers.
Seeing her husband, who was adorned with jewels, as that terrifying serpent, she immediately spoke these words to her beloved with palms joined in reverence: ||| BrP_111.65 |||
Bhogavatī said:
"I am blessed, I am favored, for my husband is my deity."
Brahmā said:
Having spoken thus, the slender-limbed woman remained upon the bed and, perceiving the serpent through her own serpent-like nature, she played with him by means of songs and physical embraces.
She gratified her husband with fragrant flowers and drinks;
and by his very grace, O sage, the serpent regained his memory.
Having remembered everything ordained by fate, the serpent spoke to his beloved at night.
The serpent said:
"O beloved, why were you not afraid upon seeing me, even though you are a princess? She replied: "Who is capable of transgressing what is ordained by fate?"
The husband alone is the refuge of women at all times, and especially so.
Brahmā said:
Having heard this, the Nāga, delighted and with a smiling face, spoke to her.
The serpent said:
"I am pleased with your devotion; what desired thing shall I give you?
O lady of beautiful limbs, through my grace, this recovery of all your memories has occurred."
"I was cursed by the enraged Pinākin, the God of gods;
I am the mighty serpent Śeṣaputra, who was placed in the hand of Maheśvara."
Thus I am your husband, and you were formerly my wife named Bhogavatī;
pleased by the words of Umā, Śambhu laughed aloud while remaining in private.
"O blessed lady, a laugh also came to me in the presence of that god;
thereupon, Śambhu became enraged and pronounced this curse upon me."
Śiva said:
"In a human womb, you shall become a serpent endowed with knowledge."
The serpent said:
"Then, O blessed lady, Śambhu was propitiated by you along with me;
and then he spoke to me, 'O blessed one, my worship shall take place at Gautamī.'"
"When you perform this for me, who am in the form of a serpent, I shall bestow knowledge upon you;
then, by the grace of Bhogavatī, you shall be freed from the curse."
Therefore, this has befallen both me and you as well, O fair-faced one;
so, taking Gautamī with me, perform the worship together with me.
Then we two shall be freed from the curse and go once more to what is auspicious;
for the auspicious alone is the supreme refuge for all who are afflicted by suffering at all times.
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of her husband, she went with her husband to the Gautamī;
then, having bathed in the Gautamī, she performed worship to Śiva.
Then, O sage, the gratified Blessed One granted him a divine form;
having taken leave of his parents, the serpent was preparing to depart for Śivaloka with his wife, whereupon his high-minded father, learning of this, spoke.
The father said:
"Since you are my eldest son and the sole heir to the status of crown prince,
therefore, having ruled the kingdom in its entirety and having procreated many sons,"
When I have gone to the supreme abode, then you too shall go to the auspicious city.
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of his father, that king of the Nāgas, firm in his vows, replied, "So be it," and then, having assumed a form at will, he went together with his wife.
Having ruled the kingdom most extensively with his father, mother, and sons,
and having established his sons in his own position, the father departed for the heavenly world.
Then, accompanied by his wife, ministers, and others, he went to the city of Śiva;
from that time forward, that sacred ford has been known as Nāgatīrtha.
Where the god Nāgeśvara is established at Bhogavatī,
bathing and giving gifts there bestow the fruit of all sacrifices.
Brahmā said:
Known as Mātṛtīrtha, it bestows all perfections upon men; even by the mere remembrance of that sacred site, a living being is liberated from mental afflictions.
A most terrible conflict arose between the gods and the asuras;
at that time, the gods were unable to conquer the host of dānavas.
Then, accompanied by the gods, I approached the trident-wielder as he stood there;
with palms joined in reverence, I slowly praised him with various words.
O Maheśa, when all the gods and asuras had deliberated together, they brought forth the Kālakūṭa poison from the ocean in order to churn it.
Who else but you is capable of swallowing it—
[you] who are capable of bringing the three worlds under your own control with a mere blow of a flower?
Even Māra, who is worshipped by other gods and others,
went to his destruction while being spread abroad;
O enemy of the bodiless one, even after churning the ocean.
O Blue-throated One, having given that which is supreme to the dwellers of heaven and withdrawing the poison,
who indeed besides you would be capable of bearing it?
And then the Blessed One, the three-eyed primordial creator, was pleased.
Śiva said:
"O best of gods, speak what you desire; I shall grant it to you."
The gods said:
"O Bull-bannered One, come here from that place where there is terrible fear from the Dānavas; slay our enemies, protect the gods, and grant us a protector, O Lord."
O Śambhu, if you had not been a friend without motive,
then what indeed would all embodied beings, afflicted by suffering, have done?
Brahmā said:
Having been addressed thus, he departed at that very moment to where those enemies of the gods were;
there, a battle took place between Śaṅkara and the adversaries of the deities.
Then, as Śiva, the three-eyed one, who had assumed the form of darkness,
grew weary while fighting, drops of sweat fell from his forehead.
Assuming a dark form (*tāmasī mūrti*) as he was annihilating the hosts of Daityas,
the Asuras, upon seeing that form, fled from the summit of Mount Meru to the earth.
Then Hara, withdrawing all the Daityas, came to the earth;
terrified, they fled here and there across this entire world.
In that very same way, Rudra also pursued those enemies out of anger;
likewise, as Śambhu fought, drops of sweat fell from him.
O Sage, wherever the drop (bindu) of Maheśvara reached the earth,
there the Mothers were born in the form of Śiva.
"Let us all procure Maheśvara and devour the Asuras!
Then the Blessed One, surrounded by all the hosts of gods, spoke.
Śiva said:
"Those Rākṣasas have descended from heaven to earth, and from there they have reached the netherworld (rasātala);
therefore, let them all hear my speech."
"Wherever the enemies go, there let the Mothers go;
now that the enemies have reached the netherworld (rasātala) out of fear of me,
may you also follow after the enemies to the netherworld."
Brahmā said:
Piercing through the earth, they went to where those Daityas and Dānavas were;
having slain all those most terrifying enemies of the gods, the Mothers departed.
The mothers returned to the gods by that very same path;
and as far as the mothers had gone, so far did they return.
Meanwhile, the gods remained stationed there on the bank of the Gautamī,
from the time of the departure [of the Mothers] until the installation of the deities.
That sacred field is Pratiṣṭhāna, which increases merit and victory;
there, moreover, is the origin of the Mothers, with their respective Mātṛ-tīrthas.
In various places there were caves leading down to the subterranean realm (rasātala);
from them the gods requested boons, that they might receive worship in the world just as Śiva does.
"May worship always be offered to the Mothers in that same manner.
Having spoken thus, the gods vanished; the Mothers remained right there.
Wherever the goddesses are situated, there they know to be Mātṛtīrtha; it is to be resorted to even by the gods, let alone by humans and others.
Bathing in them, as well as giving gifts and the libation to the ancestors—
all that is to be known as inexhaustible, according to the word of Śiva.
Whoever should constantly hear this narrative of the Mātṛtīrthas, or likewise remember it or recite it, shall become long-lived and happy.
Brahmā said:
This is yet another sacred ford (tīrtha), difficult even for the gods to attain,
renowned as Brahmatīrtha, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men.
O best of sages, while the divine armies remained stationed and the Daityas had entered the subterranean realm (rasātala), as did the Mothers who followed them.
"My fifth face, which is of the form of a donkey and terrifying—that face spoke while I remained among the armies of the gods. (BrP 113.3)
"O Daityas, why do you flee? Let there be no fear for you; come quickly!
I shall devour all the gods in an instant. Thus he spoke.
Seeing him thus restraining me as I was intent on devouring [him], all the gods were terrified and spoke to Viṣṇu.
"Save us, O Viṣṇu, Lord of the World! Cut off the mouth of this Brahmā!
Holding his discus, he said to the gods, "I shall indeed sever his head with my discus."
But rather, this very [mantra], once severed, shall withdraw all that is moving and unmoving;
O wise ones, listen now to the entire mantra in its entirety.
The three-eyed one, the slayer of Kāśī, he indeed upholds [it], there is no doubt;
Śambhu was thus praised and addressed by me and by all.
Thinking that a sacrifice, being momentary, is incapable of producing a visible result and thus does not bear fruit for the performer,
[the world] considers the matted-haired ascetic to be a guarantor for the granting of that fruit.
Having reached this certainty, the world proceeded with its respective rites.
Then the Lord of the Gods, satisfied for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods and for the benefit of the worlds, said "So be it" to the deities.
"That mouth, which was of the nature of sin, terrifying and hair-raising—having cut it off with his nail-weapons, where should it be placed? he then asked.
Thereupon Ilā said to the gods, "I am not able to carry your head;
I shall go to the netherworld (rasātala). Then the ocean also spoke.
"I shall wither away in an instant," they said; then the gods spoke again to Śiva:
"Out of compassion for the worlds, this Brahma-head must be borne by you alone."
"If it is not severed, there will be the destruction of the worlds; if it is severed, there is such a fault.
Having reflected thus, Someśa then held the head of Ka.
Having witnessed that difficult feat performed by the purifying Gautamī,
the gods praised the Lord of the worlds with affection and devotion.
The moon-crested Lord, having cut with the needle-like tip of his claw that most terrifying Kaśīra, who was an enemy among the gods and had approached to devour them, [protected them].
Even though he was inclined toward renunciation due to his aversion to faults, he maintained his resolve out of compassion.
Then all those gods who were present near Brahmā praised the Lord of the Gods, having witnessed that super-divine deed.
From that time onwards, that sacred ford has been known as Brahmatīrtha;
even today, the four-faced form of Brahmā remains established there.
But he who should see only the head would go to the station of Brahmā,
where Rudra himself, having stood there, severed the head of Brahmā.
That very place shall be Rudratīrtha; for the Sun-god himself resides there in person, and because he stands there in the form of the gods, it is most excellent.
That sacred ford (tīrtha) is declared to belong to Sūrya; it bestows the fruit of all sacrifices.
Having bathed there and beheld the Sun, rebirth no longer exists.
When the fifth head of Brahmā was severed by Mahādeva,
it was placed in the sacred field of Avimukta, thereby securing the welfare of the deities.
He who, having seen only the head at the Brahmatīrtha on the bank of the Gautamī,
subsequently beholds the meritorious skull of Brahmā established in that very field of Avimukta, shall attain purification even if he is a slayer of a Brahmin.
Brahmā said:
This sacred ford (tīrtha) is proclaimed to be free from obstacles and the destroyer of all impediments;
I shall relate what occurred there as well—listen with devotion, O Nārada.
But while the sacrifice for the gods was underway on the northern bank of the Gautamī,
the completion of the sacrificial session did not occur at all due to the fault of obstacles.
Then all the hosts of gods spoke to me regarding Hari;
thereupon, having entered into meditation and perceived the underlying cause, I spoke to them.
"This sacrificial session will not be completed due to the obstacles created by Vināyaka;
therefore, let them all praise the Primordial God, Vināyaka."
Having said "So be it," the hosts of gods bathed on the bank of the Gautamī and,
with devotion, the deities praised Gaṇeśvara, the Primordial God.
The gods said:
He who is always the master in all undertakings of the gods— even of Śiva,
Viṣṇu, and the Lotus-born Brahmā— BrP_114.6a–6b.
He is worthy of worship, worthy of salutation, and worthy of deep reflection;
we go for refuge to that King of Obstacles (Vighnarāja).
There is no one whatsoever who is equal to the King of Obstacles.
Having resolved that the god was the granter of his heart’s desire, even the Destroyer of Tripura honored him for the sake of slaying the cities.
May that son of Ambikā quickly grant us freedom from obstacles in this great sacrifice—
by whom, when meditated upon, [the welfare] of all embodied beings [is secured].
The desires of the mind will be fulfilled;
a great festival arose for everyone when a son was born to the Goddess as soon as he was merely thought of.
Therefore, the hosts of gods, their purpose accomplished,
spoke while bowing to the newly born King of Obstacles (Vighnarāja),
who had then been placed upon his mother’s lap by her.
Even though he was being forcibly restrained, he hid the moon within the matted locks of his father,
the Lord of the Gaṇas; this was for the sake of diversion.
Even though you have drunk at your mother’s breast and are satisfied,
yet because your mind is stained by envy toward your brother,
may you become Lambodara, the King of Obstacles (Vighnarāja).
Śambhu gave him the name Lambodara;
surrounded by the hosts of gods, Maheśa said,
"Let the dance proceed."
Satisfied by the mere sound of his anklets,
he consecrated his son in the position of Lord of the Gaṇas;
he who carries the noose of obstacles in his hand.
He wields an axe against the very shoulder of another;
when even his mother is not honored,
who else is equal to him, the Lord of Obstacles?
Among dharma, artha, kāma, and the rest, he who is worthy of worship first is indeed eternally worshipped by gods and asuras; for him, there is no destruction of his worship.
I first bow to that one who is worthy of worship from of old,
by whose adoration and prayer one beholds the attainment of every fruit according to its nature.
I praise that Akhuratha, who was dear to his brother and possessed extreme pride born from his own independent prowess,
yet who [honored] his mother with delightful dances and songs.
Thus, with all his desires and diversions,
he then gratified that most highly pleased Śrī Gaṇeśa; him I take refuge in.
It was always prosperous through the assistance of the gods, battles with the asuras,
hymns of praise, prostrations, and mantras,
and by the grace of the ancestors.
I take refuge in that Śrī Gaṇeśa,
who in ancient times brought victory against his adversaries,
and who was honored with joy even by his father.
He also ensured his freedom from obstacles;
I pay homage to that Gaṇeśa.
(Brahmā said:)
Thus praised by the hosts of gods, Vighneśa spoke to them again:
Gaṇeśa said:
"From me, the enemy of the Asuras shall obtain freedom from obstacles for this sacrificial session."
Brahmā said:
When the sacrifice of the gods had concluded, Gaṇeśa spoke to those deities.
