Those who, firm in their vows, shall praise me with devotion by means of this hymn—
for them, the miseries of poverty shall never arise.
Let it be understood that for those who, free from sloth, perform bathing and giving here with devotion,
all their undertakings shall be successful.
Brahmā said:
At the very moment of those words, the gods also said, "So be it.

From that time forth, that sacred site has been called Avighna;
it bestows all desires upon men and destroys all obstacles.
Brahmā said:
I shall describe the form of that which is known as Śeṣatīrtha, the bestower of all desires, as it has been explained by me.
The great Naga named Śeṣa, the lord and master of the netherworld (rasātala),
surrounded by all the Nagas, then approached the netherworld.
The Rākṣasas, Daityas, and Danujas who had entered the netherworld (rasātala) drove out the Lord of Serpents, who,
being overwhelmed, then spoke to me.
Śeṣa said:
"Rasātala has been given by you both to the Rākṣasas and to me;
yet they will not grant me a place there, and therefore I have come to you for refuge."
Then I said to the Naga, "O serpent, go to Gautamī;
having praised Mahādeva there, you shall obtain your heart's desire."
"There is no one else in the three worlds who can fulfill this desire.
Impelled by my words, the Naga bathed diligently in the Gaṅgā and,
with palms joined in reverence, praised the Lord of the Thirty-three."
Śeṣa said:
Homage to the Lord of the three worlds, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice;
homage to you, the primordial creator; homage to you who embody the three worlds.
Salutations to the thousand-headed one; salutations to the agent of dissolution;
salutations to you who take the form of the moon, the sun, and fire, and who take the form of water.
Salutations to you who are always all forms, whose form is time!
Protect me, O Śaṅkara, Lord of All; protect me, O Someśa, you who go everywhere! O Lord of the World, salutations to you; grant me that which is desired by my mind.
Brahmā said:
Then Maheśvara, being pleased, granted the boons desired by the Nāga for the destruction of the enemies of the gods— the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas.
He gave the trident to Śeṣa, saying, "Slay the foremost of your enemies with this. Then Śiva spoke to that Śeṣa regarding the trident and the serpents.
Then, having gone to the netherworld (rasātala), the elephant struck his enemies in battle;
having slain the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas with his tusk, he destroyed them.
The god turned back again toward where Śeṣeśvara Hara was,
by the same path by which that king of serpents had come to see the god.
Where the god [Śiva] emerged from the subterranean realm (rasātala), there a cave was formed;
from that cavity flows the water of the Gaṅgā, which bestows supreme merit.
That water went to the Gaṅgā; from there it reached the confluence of the Gaṅgā, and also a very extensive pool in front of the deity.
The Naga performed his fire sacrifice there where the sacred fire was ever present;
consequently, the water of the Ganges became warm at that confluence.
Having propitiated the God of gods, the highly illustrious Nāga was pleased;
then, having obtained from Śiva his desired destination, he went to the subterranean realm of Rasātala.
From that time forward, that sacred ford has been called Nāgatīrtha;
it is meritorious, bestows all desires, and destroys both disease and poverty.
This meritorious [account] bestows long life and prosperity, and through bathing and giving gifts, it grants liberation;
whoever hears it, reads it with devotion, or even remembers it, [attains these benefits].
O tiger among sages, there is the holy site of Śeṣeśvara where Śiva bestows his power; there, on both banks, are twenty-one hundred sacred sites that grant all forms of prosperity.
Brahmā said:
That which is known as Mahānala is called the Vaḍavānala;
where the deity Mahānala is, there that river Vaḍavā is located.
"O son, I shall describe that sacred ford which removes death, defects, and old age.
Formerly, in the Naimiṣa forest, there were sages performing a long sacrificial session (sattra)."
The ascetic seers made Death the immolator while the sacrificial session was underway,
as Death stood there established as the immolator.
At that time,
O best of sages, nothing died— neither the stationary nor the moving— with the exception of animals and mortals who had attained immortality.
Then, while heaven was empty and the world of mortals was exceedingly crowded,
and Death remained indifferent, the gods spoke to the Rākṣasas at that time.
The gods said:
"Go! Destroy that sacrificial session of the sages, that great ritual.
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of the gods, those Rākṣasas spoke to the deities.
The Asuras said:
"We shall destroy that sacrifice; what fruit could arise from it for us?
For nothing ever occurs anywhere without a cause."
Brahmā said:
The gods also said to the Asuras, "Half of the sacrifice shall belong to you as well;
therefore, go to the supreme sacrificial session (sattra) of the Ṛṣis."
Having heard this, they all went in haste to where the sacrifice was being performed;
especially at the word of the gods, they went there for the purpose of destruction.
Having learned of that death, the sages said, "What shall we do?
At the command of the gods, the Rākṣasas who destroy sacrifices have arrived."
O Nārada, after consulting with Death, all the inhabitants of the Naimiṣa forest abandoned their own hermitage along with Śamitra.
Taking only the fire and leaving behind their vessels and other belongings, they went in haste toward Gautamī in order to complete the sacrifice.
Having bathed there, they stood before Maheśāna for his protection;
with their palms joined in reverence, they praised the Lord of the Thirty-three.
The sages said:
He who by his mere sport created this universe,
the sustainer and ordainer of the three worlds.
We go for refuge to that Someśvara, who is multiform, who is beyond both being and non-being. {Mṛtyu said:}
I seek refuge in that Śaṅkara, the lord of the thirty gods, who by his mere will destroys, protects, and creates everything.
I go for refuge to Śaṅkara, the god who possesses a great flame, a great body, and the ornaments of a great serpent; he who bears a magnificent form.
Brahmā said:
Then the Blessed One spoke: "O Mṛtyu, what pleasure shall there be for you?"
Death said:
"O Lord of the Thirty-three, a terrible fear has come upon us from the Rākṣasas;
protect our sacrifice and ourselves until the sacrificial session is completed."
Brahmā said:
Thus did the Blessed One, the three-eyed one whose banner is the bull, perform the sacrifice;
with Mṛtyu as the slaughterer, it reached completion for the sages.
The immortals arrived in succession for their share of the oblations;
the hosts of sages, agitated by Death, spoke to them.
The sages said:
"Since the Rākṣasas were dispatched for the destruction of our sacrifice,
therefore let the most wicked Rākṣasas be the enemies of you all."
Brahmā said:
From that time forward, the Rākṣasas became the enemies of the gods;
and there, the gods and the stainless sages [confronted] the Kṛtyā Vaḍavā.
"Become the wife of Death," they said to her, and having consecrated her,
the water used for that consecration became the river Vaḍavā.
The linga established by Mṛtyu is known as Mahānala;
from that time onwards, they have known that sacred site as Vaḍavāsaṃgama.

Where the god Mahānala resides, that sacred ford (tīrtha) bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. There, on both banks, are a thousand sacred fords that grant all desired objects and destroy sins through mere remembrance.
Brahmā said:
I shall describe the power of that which is renowned as Ātmatīrtha, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men, and wherein Śiva resides as Jñāneśvara.
He was also renowned as Datta, the son of Atri and beloved of Hara;
he was the dear brother of Durvāsas and an expert in all branches of knowledge.
Having approached his father, he bowed with humility and said: *Br̥hatpārāśarīya Purāṇa 117.2*
Datta said:
"How may I attain the knowledge of Brahman? Whom shall I ask, and where shall I go?"
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of his son and having reflected upon them, Atri spoke these words.
Atri said:
"O son, go to Gautamī and there praise Maheśvara;
when he becomes pleased with you, then you shall attain knowledge."
Brahmā said:
Having said, "So be it," Ātreya then went to the Gaṅgā; being pure and self-restrained, he joined his palms in reverence and praised Śaṅkara with devotion.
Datta said:
By fate, I have fallen into the well of saṃsāra,
hidden by delusion in the mire of worldly suffering.
"O Lord of the Gods, shrouded by the darkness named ignorance, I do not find the Supreme;
I have been pierced by a most powerful trident."
Torn by the arrow-like thoughts of evil,
I am tormented by the intense heat of the five senses;
I am exhausted— O Somanātha, carry me across!
I am bound by the fetters consisting of poverty; I am struck by the intense heat of the fire of disease;
I am trampled upon by the serpent of death.
"O Śambhu, being greatly afraid, what shall I do?
I am intensely tormented by existence and non-existence, as well as by thirst and hunger, and by passion and darkness."
Overcome by such old age as this,
O Lord, behold my condition today;
[I am tormented] by desire, anger, and envy.
"By deceit, by pride, and by many other such means,
I have been pierced one by one and have fallen into distress; O Lord, like a protector, ward off these enemies!"
It is true,
O Somanātha, that for anyone who has fallen, there is no dispeller of suffering except for you.
Nowhere is there even a word of compassion;
meanwhile, there exist anger, fear, delusion, and suffering,
as well as ignorance, poverty, and disease.
Desire and the like, as well as death itself, persist here as long as I do not utter the words "Obeisance to Śiva.
For me there is no dharma, nor is there any devotion.
"I am not one who practices detachment; how could there be compassion for me? Therefore, O refuge-giver, quickly place the word 'Soma' within my heart."
I do not beg for the sovereignty of the gods, O Somanātha; my only prayer is for proximity to the lotus feet of Śrī Soma within the lotus of my heart.
Having reflected upon this, do as you have requested; O sinner, even though I am already known to you,
nevertheless, listen to my petition.
O Somanātha, Lord of Gaurī, O Śaṅkara Somanātha, wherever the word "Śiva" is heard, there may my dwelling be. (BrP 117.16c–117.17a)
O Lord of the Universe, O treasury of compassion, O Soul of all!
Wherever you are constantly praised, there may the abode of certain perfected ones be found.
Brahmā said:
Having heard this praise of Ātreya, the blessed Hara was pleased;
the creator of the universe, Bhava, said to that yogin, "I am the granter of boons."
Ātreya said:
"Self-knowledge, liberation, and abundant worldly enjoyment,
as well as the majesty of this sacred ford— this is the boon [I seek], O you who are worshipped by the gods."
Brahmā said:
"So be it," Śambhu replied to him and vanished.
From that time forward, the wise have known that sacred ford as Ātmatīrtha.
O Nārada, by bathing there and by giving gifts, liberation shall be attained in this world.
Brahmā said:
Aśvatthatīrtha has been described, and after that, Pippala;
to the north is Mandatīrtha—now hear from me about the merit (vyuṣṭi) therein.
Formerly, the venerable Lord Agastya, the master and lord of the southern quarter,
was urged by the gods to request the Vindhya mountain [to stop its growth].
Surrounded by a thousand sages, he slowly approached the Vindhya,
that best of mountains, which was densely crowded with many trees.
The steadfast sage, the husband of Lopāmudrā, [dwelt upon] that exceedingly lofty mountain, the Vindhya, which was covered with hundreds of peaks and rivaled Meru and Mānasa in splendor.
Having been hospitably received by the twice-born and having praised the mountain once more,
that best of sages spoke these words for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods' mission.
Agastya said:
"O best of mountains, I am going; accompanied by sages who perceive the truth, I shall perform a pilgrimage to the holy fords and proceed toward the southern quarter."
"O Lord of Mountains, give way; grant hospitality to one who begs for it.
You must indeed remain here until my arrival."
"It must not be otherwise for you; so be it," said the Best of Mountains.
Surrounded by those sages, the Sage set out toward the southern direction.
Having been initiated for a sacrificial session (sattra), he slowly arrived at the Gautamī;
surrounded by sages, he performed that sacrificial session for the duration of a year.
The two wicked sons of Kaiṭabha were Rākṣasas who were thorns to righteousness;
they were renowned in the abode of the gods as Aśvattha and Pippala.
Aśvattha in the form of Aśvattha and Pippala, assuming the form of Brahmā—
both of them sought an opportunity for the destruction of the sacrifice.
"Let the two evil-minded Dānavas assume their desired forms:
let Aśvattha take the form of a tree, and Pippala the form of a Brāhmaṇa. (BrP 118.12)
O ascetic, both of those two constantly afflict the Brahmins;
moreover, that tree devours each and every one who sacrifices an *aśvattha* tree.
The Rākṣasa Pippala, having become a Sāmaga, devoured his disciples;
therefore, even today, the Sāmaga among Brahmins is exceedingly merciless.
Seeing the twice-born being diminished, the highly wise sages realized, "These two are Rākṣasas," and took refuge on the southern bank.
Having gone to Sauri Śanaiścara, who was performing austerities, slow-moving and firm in his vows,
all the hosts of sages reported the deed of the Rākṣasa.
Sauri said to the hosts of sages:
"O twice-born ones, when my ascetic penance is complete, I shall slay the two Rākṣasas; for as long as it is incomplete, I am indeed incapable."
Again the hosts of sages said, "We shall grant you great ascetic power.
Thus addressed by the brahmins, the son of Sura said to them, "It is done."
Sauri, having assumed the guise of a brahmin, approached the Rākṣasa who was in the form of an Aśvattha tree;
then, becoming a brahmin himself, he performed a circumambulation.
The wicked Rākṣasa perceived him as a Brāhmaṇa indeed as he was performing a circumambulation, yet by means of his illusory power, he devoured him as if it were an ordinary meal.
Having entered his body, he saw the intestines with his own eyes;
that wicked Rākṣasa was seen by the dull-witted son of the Sun.
In an instant, he was reduced to ashes like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt;
having turned the peepal tree to ash, he assumed another form as a brahmin.
He approached that Rākṣasa, the abode of evil, all alone,
like a disciplined Brahmin student intent on his studies, appearing in the form of a disciple.
And Pippala also ate the son of Bhānu as before;
having been eaten, he saw the entrails within his belly just as previously.
Merely looked upon by him, that Rākṣasa was reduced to ashes;
having slain both, the son of Bhānu said, "Tell me now, what remains to be done?"
Then all the sages and ascetics were filled with joy; indeed, the seers, led by Agastya, became truly serene.
The powerful Śani, son of the Sun, being pleased, granted boons according to their desires to the slow-moving Sauri and then spoke to the brahmins.
Sauri said: "And those who, being self-restrained, perform the ritual of hanging from the *aśvattha* tree at my gateway—
for them, all their undertakings shall succeed, and no suffering shall arise from me."
For those men who perform their ablutions at the sacred ford known as Aśvattha, all their undertakings shall succeed; this is another boon.
May the affliction of the planets be dispelled for those men who, having risen early on a Saturday, touch the holy fig tree (aśvattha).
Brahmā said:
From that time forward, they have known that sacred site as Aśvattha and Pippala;
there is the Śanaiścara-tīrtha, and there also is the Sāttvika-tīrtha of Agastya.
There was also the Yājñika Tīrtha and the Sāmaga Tīrtha;
thus there were sixteen thousand and eight such [sacred sites].
Bathing and giving gifts at them bestow the fruit of a Sattra sacrifice.
Brahmā said:
That which is known as Somatīrtha has also been described by the high-souled ones;
by bathing and giving gifts there, one obtains the fruit of drinking the Soma juice.
In the beginning, the medicinal herbs were the mothers of the worlds, esteemed as living beings;
even for me, these goddesses are my mothers, being more ancient than those former ones.
Upon these is established Dharma, as well as Vedic study and sacrificial rites;
by these alone is all the triple world, with its moving and unmoving beings, sustained.
"By these [herbs], there is undoubtedly the alleviation of all diseases;
by these alone, food shall be provided for the protection of all living beings.
Thus spoke the world-worshipped herbs to me, free from egoism. (BrP 119.4)
The medicinal herbs said:
"O best of gods, grant us a husband who shall be our king."
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of theirs, I spoke this to the medicinal herbs:
"You shall all obtain a husband, a king who increases your joy."
O Sage, having heard that [the king was dead], they spoke to me again: "Where must we go? and being told once more, "The mothers should go to Gautamī," they departed.
When she was thus gratified, O King, you would have become honored by the world;
and so, O best of sages, they went and offered praise to the river Gautamī.
The medicinal herbs said:
"What would people following the ways of worldly existence do, being afflicted by the overwhelming burden of various evils?"
And if you, O Gautamī, beloved of Śambhu, had not come to this earth with its meritorious waters,
who could have known the fortune of those who possess a human body?
O Mother Gaṅgā, sovereign of the rivers that flow upon the earth, you are always easily accessible to these people as the destroyer of the multitude of great sins.
Indeed, O Gaṅgā, Mother of the World, who is not aware of your majesty, you who are worshipped by the three worlds—
even Śiva, whose body is embraced by Gaurī?
Even the enemy of Smara bears you upon his head;
salutations to you, O Mother, bestower of desired boons! Salutations to you, who are composed of Brahman and the destroyer of sins!
Homage be to you, who have issued from the lotus-foot of Viṣṇu;
homage be to you, who have issued from the matted locks of Śambhu.
{Brahmā said:}
When they had praised him in this manner, the Lord said, "What shall I give?"
The medicinal herbs said:
"O Mother of the World, grant us a husband, a king of exceeding splendor."
Then the river Gaṅgā spoke these words to those medicinal herbs: Brahmā said: 119.15. Then the river Gaṅgā spoke these words to those medicinal herbs.
Gaṅgā said:
"I am of the nature of nectar, and the medicinal herbs are my immortal mothers;
I give you Soma as a husband, who is likewise of the essence of nectar."
Brahmā said:
The gods, the sages, Soma himself, and even the medicinal herbs accepted those words; thereafter, they departed for their own abodes.
And there, the great medicinal herbs [honored] King Soma, who is of the nature of nectar and the dispeller of the entire multitude of fevers and sins.
That place is renowned as Somatīrtha, which bestows the fruit of drinking the Soma juice;
by bathing and giving gifts there, the ancestors attain heaven.
Whoever should constantly hear this, or recite it with devotion, or remember it, shall obtain long life; he shall be blessed with sons and become wealthy.
Brahmā said:
Known as Dhānyatīrtha, it grants all desires to men;
it bestows abundance and security upon people, and wards off all calamities.
Having obtained Soma as their king and husband, the herbs were filled with joy and spoke words desired by the entire world and by Gaṅgā.
The medicinal herbs said:
There is a meritorious Vedic verse known by those who know the Vedas,
which speaks of the earth as being rich in crops, like a mother, equal to a mother.
Whoever, filled with joy, should give land abounding in crops, cows, and medicinal herbs near the Gaṅgā, shall obtain all his desires.
Whatever a devoted person may give to one who possesses the forms of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Īśa, know that all of it becomes inexhaustible; he shall obtain all his desires.
"Herbs have Soma as their king, and Soma is the lord of herbs.
Knowing this, the knower of Brahman who shall bestow herbs [attains merit].
He attains all desires and is glorified in the world of Brahmā;
those very goddesses, whose king is Soma, being pleased, spoke thus again and again.
The medicinal herbs said:
"O King, we shall carry across that person who gives us to the Gaṅgā.
You are the most excellent among the lords of herbs; the world of moving and unmoving beings is dependent upon you."
The herbs converse together with Soma, the king:
"O King, we deliver him who gives us to the learned brahmins."
O King, we are of the nature of Brahman and indeed of the nature of vital breath;
he who gives us to the Brahmins, him we deliver across [to safety].
O King, we rescue that man who, having mastered his vows, constantly gives us to the Brahmins; such is our service to him.
"O King, whatever in this world—whether stationary or moving—is occupied by us, we deliver that person to the Brahmins who gives us to them. (BrP 120.12)
O King, whatever sacrificial offering for the gods or the ancestors, whatever nectar, or anything whatsoever is consumed—
if one should give that which is most excellent, we shall deliver him.
O King, whoever hears, remembers, or recites this Vedic verse with devotion, him we deliver.
Brahmā said:
Where this verse was recited by King Soma together with the medicinal herbs on the bank of the Gaṅgā, that is called Dhānyatīrtha.
From that time forward, that sacred ford (tīrtha) was known as Auṣadhya, Saumya,
Amṛta, Vedagātha, and likewise Mātṛtīrtha.
Bathing, recitation, burnt offerings, giving gifts, libations to the ancestors, and the gift of food— whosoever performs these among these [sites] leads to infinity.
On both banks, there are one thousand six hundred sacred fords that destroy all sins and increase all prosperity.
Brahmā said:
I shall relate that meritorious account of the confluence at Vidarbha and likewise the confluence at Revatī,
concerning which those who know the Purāṇas are aware of what occurred there in the past.
There was a sage renowned as Bharadvāja, preeminent in asceticism;
his sister was named Revatī, who was ill-favored and possessed a distorted voice.
Seeing her thus transformed, his powerful brother Bharadvāja stood on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā, overcome with profound anxiety.
"To whom shall I give this maiden, my sister of terrifying appearance?
No one accepts her; yet a sister must likewise be given away."
Alas! For no one is a daughter merely a cause of sorrow;
rather, for this living being, death exists at every step even while he still lives.
As he was reflecting thus in his own most beautiful hermitage,
the best of sages set out to see Bharadvāja, who was firm in his vows.
At sixteen years of age, possessing an auspicious body, peaceful, self-controlled, and a mine of virtues,
he who was known by the name Kaṭha bowed down to Bharadvāja.
Having duly honored that Brahmin Kaṭha at that time, Bharadvāja,
standing before him, inquired about the purpose of his arrival.
Kaṭha also said to Bharadvāja: "I have come as a seeker of knowledge;
likewise, desiring a vision of you, let that which is appropriate be performed."
Bharadvāja said to Kaṭha: "Study that which you desire—the Purāṇas, the Smṛtis, the Vedas, and the various authorities on dharma."
"I know everything, O one of great wisdom; speak what is pleasing without delay.
A disciple who is well-born, devoted to righteousness, intent on serving his teacher, free from pride, and a retainer of sacred learning is obtained through meritorious deeds. (BrP 121.11)
Kaṭha said: "O Brahmin, please instruct me, your disciple, who am free from taint,
devoted to service, faithful, of noble birth, and truthful."
Brahmā said:
Having said, "So be it," Bharadvāja imparted the knowledge in its entirety.
Having acquired the knowledge, Kaṭha was pleased and then spoke to Bharadvāja.
Kaṭha said:
"O Guru, I wish to give you a sacrificial fee that is pleasing to your heart.
Speak, O Guru—even if it be difficult to obtain—and salutations be unto you."
Even after receiving knowledge, those who out of delusion do not bestow a gratuity upon their own teacher go to hell for as long as the moon and stars endure.
Bharadvāja said:
"Accept this maiden according to the prescribed rites and make her your wife; you must treat her with affection. This is the fee (dakṣiṇā) I request."
Kaṭha said:

"A disciple should always behave toward his teacher as toward a brother or even a son; and the teacher should behave toward him as toward a father. What kind of relationship exists between them in this regard?"
Bharadvāja said:
"Make my word true; this command of mine is your sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having remembered everything, O Kaṭha, bring Revatī today with your mind fixed upon her."
Brahmā said:
Having said "So be it" at the word of his guru, Kaṭha took Revatī by the hand as she was given according to the prescribed rites; then, having gazed upon her, Kaṭha—
Then, for the sake of perfecting her beauty through Revatī and for the pleasure of Śiva, Revatī worshipped Śaṅkara, the Lord of the Gods, right there.
She was beautiful, with lovely limbs; her form could not be compared to anything else.
There, the consecration water that had issued forth from Revatī remained.
She became there in the Gaṅgā; therefore, that river is known by her name as Revatī, the bestower of beauty and good fortune.
Furthermore, Vidarbha performed an ablution with various kinds of darbha grass for the sake of attaining a state of merit; from that [act], she became a river.
Having bathed with faith at the confluence of the Revatī and the Gaṅgā, a man,
liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Likewise, O Sage, he who performs a bath with faith at the confluence of the Vidarbha and Gautami attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation at that very moment.
There, on both banks, are one hundred supreme holy fords (tīrthas) that destroy all sins and bestow all spiritual accomplishments.
Brahmā said:
On the northern bank of the Gaṅgā, there is a place renowned as Pūrṇatīrtha;
by bathing there, a person obtains auspiciousness even if it was done through ignorance.
By what living being can the majesty of Pūrṇatīrtha be described,
where the wielder of the discus and the wielder of the Pināka bow reside in person?
In ancient times, at the beginning of the Kalpa, Dhanvantari, the son of Āyus, having performed various kinds of sacrifices, foremost among them the Aśvamedha; ||| BrP_122.3 |||
Having given many gifts and enjoyed abundant pleasures,
and having realized the instability of such enjoyments, he took recourse in supreme dispassion.
On a mountain peak, on the far shore of the ocean, likewise on the bank of the river Gaṅgā,
or even in the abode of Śiva or Viṣṇu— especially at a confluence of sacred waters.
Whatever has been performed as austerity, offered in sacrifice, or recited as mantra shall all become inexhaustible;
knowing him to be Dhanvantari, he performed great penance there.
Endowed with knowledge and detachment, and taking refuge at the feet of Bhīmeśvara,
he performed extensive austerities at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
And formerly, having been defeated by the king and abandoning the battle, that great asura entered the ocean out of fear for a thousand years.
When Dhanvantari had reached the forest and his son had obtained the kingdom,
and when the king had become detached from worldly life, he then departed from the ocean.
O sage, while he was performing austerities on the bank of the Gaṅgā, the powerful Asura named Tamas approached, since King Dhanvantari was there.
"Devoted to constant recitation and burnt offerings, and intent upon the knowledge of Brahman,
I shall destroy that enemy"— thinking thus, Tamas emerged from the ocean.
"I have been defeated many times by this powerful king;
I shall destroy that enemy! Thinking thus, he then emerged from the ocean, shrouded in darkness.
Having assumed the form of a young woman through her illusory power, she approached the king;
that fair-browed one, beautiful to behold, began to dance and sing while smiling.
Having gazed upon her for a long time— she whose every limb was beautiful,
who was disciplined, peaceful, devoted, and faithful— the king spoke out of compassion.
The king said:
"Who are you, and for what reason do you dwell in this dense forest?
Seeing whom do you seem so joyful? O auspicious lady, tell it to me who asks."
Brahmā said:
And the woman, having heard those words, spoke to the king.
Pramadā said:
"While you remain in this world, what cause for joy could there be for me? For I am the very splendor of Indra, yet upon seeing you filled with desire, [I am overcome]."
"O King, out of joy I run before you again and again;
yet, due to my lack of innumerable merits, I am difficult for anyone else to attain."
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words, he immediately abandoned his most difficult ascetic penance;
meditating upon her alone in his mind, he became fixed in her and devoted solely to her.
O Brahmin, when that darkness had vanished after having destroyed his great ascetic power, the king became solely devoted to him.
In the meantime, I indeed arrived to grant boons;
seeing him thus overwhelmed, fallen from his asceticism as if dead, [I spoke].
Then, having consoled that best of kings with various reasons, he said,
"Your enemy named Tamas has caused this fall from your asceticism."
"O King, he has departed having accomplished his purpose; you ought not to grieve.
Women gladden men and cause them suffering as well."
"All these [beings] are indeed characterized by particularity; how much more so she who is composed of illusion?
Then the king, his delusion dispelled, spoke to me with palms joined in reverence."
The king said:
"O Brahmin, what shall I do, and how may I reach the further shore of asceticism?"
Brahmā said:
Then I gave him this reply: "Praise Janārdana, the God of gods, with all your effort; thereby you shall attain success."

For he is the creator of the entire world without exception, the ancient one to be known through the Vedas, the bestower of the fulfillment of all goals for men; there is no other such being in the three worlds.
That best of kings went to Himavat, the foremost of mountains,
and with palms joined in reverence, he praised Viṣṇu with devotion.
Dhanvantari said:
Victory to you, O Viṣṇu! Victory, O Inconceivable One! Victory, O Conqueror! Victory, O Acyuta!
Victory, O Gopāla, Lord of Lakṣmī! Victory, O Kṛṣṇa, who pervades the universe!
Victory to you, O Lord of beings, O Protector! Victory to you who recline upon the serpent!
Victory to you, all-pervading Govinda! Victory to you, the creator of the universe; salutations!
Victory to you, O God whose arms are the universe; victory to you who sustain the universe; salutations!
O Lord, you are indeed both the existent and the non-existent; victory to you, Mādhava, the upholder of dharma!

Victory to you, O Kāma, the fulfiller of desires; victory to you, O Rāma, ocean of virtues! Victory to you, O bestower of nourishment, Lord of nourishment; victory to you, the giver of auspiciousness!
Victory to you, O Lord of beings, O protector of beings! Victory to you, the ordainer of human destiny!
Victory to you, the giver of the fruits of action, O Karmada! Victory to you, who are clothed in yellow garments!
Victory to you, O Lord of all; you are everything. Victory to you, whose form is auspiciousness!
Victory to the sovereign lord of all beings; victory to the knower of the Vedas; salutations to you!
Victory to You, O Supreme Self, who are born from birth and abide in birth; salutations be unto You!
Victory to You, O Giver of Liberation, for You are liberation itself; victory to You, O Keśava, Giver of worldly enjoyment!
Victory to you, O Giver of the World, Lord of the World! Victory to you, Destroyer of Sins!
Victory to you, who are affectionate toward your devotees! Victory to you, the Wielder of the Discus; homage to you!
Victory to you, O giver of honor; you are the mind. Victory to you, O one honored by the worlds!
Victory to you, O giver of dharma; you are dharma. Victory to you, O one who has gone to the further shore of saṃsāra!
Victory, O Giver of Food! You are food; victory, O Lord of Speech, salutations to you!
Victory, O Giver of Power! You are power; victory, O Bestower of the boon of victory!
Victory to you, O giver of sacrifice; you are the sacrifice itself. Victory to you, O lotus-petal-eyed one!
Victory to you, O giver of gifts; you are the gift itself. Victory to you, O slayer of Kaiṭabha!
Victory to you, O giver of fame, for you are fame itself; victory to you, O giver of form, for you are the bearer of all forms!
Victory to you, O giver of happiness, whose very self is bliss; victory to you, the purifier of the purifiers!
Victory to you, O bestower of peace; you are peace. Victory to you, O source of Śaṃkara!
Victory to you, O giver of drink; you are drink. Victory to you, whose nature is light!
Victory to you, O Vāmana, Lord of Wealth! Victory to you, whose banner is smoke!
Victory to you, the embodiment of the giver of all to the entire world; let there be salutation unto you!
O Śrī Puṇḍarīkākṣa, O ocean of compassion, you alone are skilled in destroying the afflictions of the multitude of living beings dwelling in the three worlds.
"Place your hand upon my head, O Viṣṇu!
[Brahmā said:
To him who was thus praising him, the Blessed One, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, spoke.
He, the granter of the fulfillment of all desires, invited him to choose a boon.
Dhanvantari, his mind pleased by the granting of a boon from the wielder of the discus,
stood before Govinda, the Lord of Gods, in order to request a boon.
Bowing low, the king said to him: "O Viṣṇu, sovereignty over the gods was my desire, and that has been granted by you; I have attained the fulfillment of my purpose."
Having been praised and fully honored, Viṣṇu vanished right there;
and in that very manner, the king gradually attained the lordship of the thirty gods.
Then, due to the ripening of many karmas accumulated in the past,
the thousand-eyed one fell from his own position three times.
[He was cursed] by Nahuṣa for the slaying of Vṛtra, then for the killing of Sindhuṣeṇa,
and for his approach to Ahalyā, or for whatever other reason.
Remembering each of those things again and again, Indra became dejected with a mind tormented by anxiety;
then the Lord of the Gods spoke these words to Vācaspati: BrP_122.50 //
Indra said:
"O Lord of Speech, by what cause am I deprived of my kingdom?
For men, even a lack of fortune is better than the intermittent loss of one's position."
Who truly knows the course of living beings through their intricate karmas?
No one else is capable of understanding the secret of all states of existence.
Brahmā said:
Bṛhaspati spoke to Hari, "Go and ask Brahmā;
he indeed knows what has been, what is yet to be, and how things proceed."
But he will say this, O Mahāmati:
"Those two of great wisdom, having arrived and paid homage in my presence, stood with palms joined in reverence and spoke these words to me. (BrP 122.54)
Indra and Bṛhaspati said:
"O Blessed One, by what fault is the noble-minded husband of Śacī deprived of his kingdom? O Lord, you ought to sever our doubt."
Brahmā said:
O Brahman, having reflected for a long time upon Bṛhaspati, I then spoke:
"Because of that fault known as the violation of partial duties (khaṇḍadharma), he has been fallen from his royal station."
Due to defects of place, time, and so forth; from a lack of faith or errors regarding the mantra;
from not giving the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) properly; and from the offering of improper substances.
And especially due to the sin of contempt for the gods and the celestial deities, that which arises as a fragmentation of one's own dharma among embodied beings; (BrP 122.58)
Therefore, the torment of excessive pride and the loss of one's station are difficult to abandon;
even dharma performed by one with a disturbed mind results in what is undesirable.
For that reason, [the world] would not succeed in its purpose, nor would it be free from agitation;
indeed, when one's own duty is incomplete, what undesirable consequence does not arise?
O sinless one, I have also related to you that former account concerning those two;
furthermore, the illustrious and noble-minded Dhanvantari was the son of Āyus.
The obstacle created by Tamas was destroyed by Viṣṇu;
thus the events of his previous births and so forth have been fully narrated.
Having heard that, both of them were struck with wonder and spoke to me once again.
Indra and Bṛhaspati said:
"O best of gods, by what means could there be an obstruction to that fault?"
Brahmā said:
Having meditated again, I spoke to those two: "Listen to that which causes faults [to cease], which is the cause of all perfections, and the means of crossing over the suffering of saṃsāra."
Nirvāṇa is the refuge even for those who are living but whose minds are tormented;
having approached Queen Gautamī, Hari and Śaṅkara should be praised.

"O best of sages, there is no other means for complete purification in the three worlds than those two; having abandoned them, [the gods] went at that very moment to the Gautamī. Having bathed and prepared themselves, both gods joyfully offered praise."
Indra said:
Homage to the Fish, to the Tortoise, and repeated homage to the Boar;
homage and homage to the divine Man-Lion and to the Dwarf.
Homage be to you in the form of a horse; O Trivikrama, homage be to you!
Homage be to you in the form of a Buddha, in the form of Rāma, and as Kalki!
O Lord, salutations to you who are Ananta and Acyuta; salutations to you who are the son of Jamadagni;
salutations to you who possess the nature of Varuṇa and Indra, and who possess the form of Yama.
Salutations to the Supreme Lord, the God whose form is the three worlds;
you who bear Sarasvatī in your mouth, you are omniscient—salutations be to you!
You are possessed of fortune; therefore, O sinless one, you bear fortune upon your chest. You have many arms, thighs, and feet, and many ears, eyes, and heads.
Having found you alone, who are truly happy, many others have become happy.
Men remain devoid of splendor, stained with impurity, or even in a state of wretchedness only so long as they do not seek refuge in you, O Hari, the ocean of compassion.
Bṛhaspati said:
It is the subtle, supreme light, whose form is infinite;
it is the mere syllable *oṃ*, which is beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
O Lord, those seeking liberation worship you here, the Sovereign, declaring that everything is of the nature of consciousness and consists of bliss.
Even those who are free from desire enter your divine abode, having attained their desires and crossed beyond the ocean of saṃsāra by means of even the five great sacrifices— such is your form.
Having perceived all beings with an attitude of equanimity, those who have attained a state of peace regarding the six paths of existence abandon the fruits of their actions through knowledge.
O Śambhu, they enter into you through meditation;
neither the laws of birth, nor the Vedas and scriptures,
nor the yoga of meditation, nor the practice of concentration [can do so].
With devotion, I bow to the god Soma— Rudra, Śiva, Śaṅkara, whose mind is peaceful; O Śambhu,
even though I am a fool, through devotion to your feet...
One would attain your body consisting of liberation through [the practice of] knowledge, sacrifices, austerities,
meditations, and highly fruitful fire-offerings.
This is the attainment of the supreme fruit:
that there is devotion day and night toward Someśvara,
who is always dear to every living being.
O Abode of the World, this devotion of yours is a flight of stairs leading to the fruits already seen and heard, as well as to heaven and liberation.
But for the sake of attaining the fruit of reaching Your feet, the wise do not speak of a flight of stairs;
therefore, O Compassionate One, may devotion to You be mine.
O Lord, there is no means for you to favor beauty;
having beheld your own greatness,
show grace toward us who are sinful.
You are the gross and the subtle, the beginningless and eternal;
you are the father and the mother, that which is non-existent and that which is existent—
thus have you been praised by the Vedas and the Purāṇas.
"I bow to Someśvara, the Lord.
Brahmā said:
"Then Hari and Hara, the lords of the thirty gods, being pleased, spoke:"
Hari and Hara said:
"Choose whatever is desired by your heart, even that boon which is exceedingly difficult to obtain."
Brahmā said:
Indra spoke to the Lord of the Gods: "My kingdom arises and falls again and again;
let that sin be pacified."
"If the two lords of the gods are well-pleased, so that I may remain firm in my kingdom and everything may be stable for me, then everything shall always be secure."
"So be it," they said, welcoming Hari's words;
having attained supreme grace and beholding him with smiling faces, they spoke as follows.
Free from misfortune and without support, whose very nature is changeless,
both are the refuge for all worlds and the bestowers of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Hari and Hara said:
"The Gautamī is a great sacred ford (tīrtha) presided over by three deities and bestows all desires;
let them both perform their ablutions therein with devotion using this mantra."
May Bṛhaspati perform the consecration of Mahendra for his auspiciousness,
keeping us both in mind for the sake of achieving stability in prosperity.
Whatever merit has been performed by me in this life or in previous ones—may all that reach fulfillment; O Godāvarī, salutations be unto you!
Whoever, having remembered this, performs a ritual bath at Gautamī,
shall attain the perfection of Dharma through our grace;
freed from the defects committed in previous births, he shall become a possessor of merit.
Brahmā said: "So be it," and then the preceptor of the celestial dwellers, Śakra and Bṛhaspati, joyfully performed the great consecration of Indra.
Because of that, there was a sacred river called Maṅgalā;
and its confluence with the Gaṅgā is meritorious and bestows auspiciousness.
Praised by Indra, Viṣṇu, who pervades the universe, became manifest;
Śakra obtained from the Lord of the World a portion of the earth equal to the three worlds.
And he became renowned there by that name as Govinda;
moreover, by him, the wielder of the thunderbolt, cows equal to the three worlds were obtained.
And there Govinda was given by Hari;
thus he became Hari, O Sage, since the sovereignty over the three worlds was obtained by Hari from Hari.
From Maheśvara, the God of gods, that which is immovable was born;
there, Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, praised Maheśvara.
For the sake of the stability of the kingdom of the high-souled Lord of the Gods,
the god Siddheśvara, whose linga is worshipped by the thirty deities, resides there.
From that time forward, that holy ford became renowned as Govinda;
and beyond it are Maṅgalāsaṃgama and Pūrṇatīrtha.
It is renowned as Indratīrtha and celebrated as Bārhaspatya,
where the god Siddheśvara and Viṣṇu himself, Govinda, reside.
One should know that whatever bathing, giving, or accumulation of merit is performed in those places is all inexhaustible and exceedingly dear to the ancestors.
Whoever hears, reads, or constantly remembers this greatness of the sacred ford (tīrtha), which bestows the recovery of a lost kingdom, [shall attain his desire].
O tiger among sages, there are thirty-seven thousand holy fords on both banks, which bestow all spiritual perfections.
There is no sacred ford equal to Pūrṇatīrtha that yields such great fruit;
the birth and life of that man who does not resort to it is fruitless.
Brahmā said:
There is a place renowned as Rāmatīrtha, which destroys the sin of killing an embryo;
by the mere hearing of its name, one is liberated from all sins.
Born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, he was a world-renowned kṣatriya,
powerful, wise, and heroic, like Śakra Puraṃdara.
He remained ruling the kingdom inherited from his father and grandfather, just like Bali;
for King Daśaratha indeed had three principal queens.
O Great-minded One, Kauśalyā, Sumitrā, and Kaikeyī—
these women are of noble birth, fortunate, and endowed with beauty and auspicious marks.
O Sage, while that king, the lord of Ayodhyā, remained in his kingdom,
and especially while Vasiṣṭha, the best among the knowers of Brahman, served as his domestic priest.
There shall be no disease, no famine, no drought, and no mental anxieties,
constantly for the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, and especially for the Śūdras.
While he, the upholder of the Ikṣvāku lineage, was ruling, O Indra among kings, there arose joy in each and every one of the hermitages.
A conflict arose between the gods and the dānavas for the sake of sovereignty;
in some instances there the gods achieved victory, and likewise in others the others did.
While things were proceeding in this manner, O Nārada, the three worlds became utterly oppressed; then I spoke there to the Daityas and Dānavas.
Even the gods, in particular, did not carry out what was commanded by me;
furthermore, a very great conflict arose among them once again.
Having approached Viṣṇu, the gods spoke, and likewise to Īśāna, who is identical with the universe;
both of them spoke to the gods, the asuras, the daityas, and the dānavas.
"Let them go forth strengthened by asceticism and wage battle once more.
"So be it," they said, and all departed, their vows restrained for the sake of penance.
But the gods, filled once again with indignation, went against the Rākṣasas;
a most terrible conflict then broke out between the gods and the Dānavas.
Neither the gods, nor the Daityas, nor the Dānavas were victors there;
yet, while the battle was underway, an incorporeal voice spoke.
The Voice of Space said:
"Those for whom Daśaratha is king shall be victors, and not others."
Brahmā said:
Having heard this, both the god and the dānava set out for victory;
there, Vāyu arrived in haste and then spoke to the king.
Vāyu said:
"O King, you must come to the battle between the gods and the dānavas;
it is well known that wherever King Daśaratha is, there victory lies."
Therefore, you should be on the side of the gods; thus the deities shall be victorious.
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of Vāyu, King Daśaratha, the monarch, replied:
"I shall truly come; go, O Vāyu, as you please."
When the wind had departed, the Daityas then approached the lord of the earth and said,
"O Blessed One, you ought to grant us your assistance."
"O glorious King Daśaratha, victory rests in you;
therefore, you ought indeed to provide assistance to the lord of the Daityas."
Then the king, having been entreated by Vāyu in the past, spoke:
"That was promised by me; let the Daityas and Dānavas depart."
The king did exactly so; having gone to heaven, he waged war against the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas.
While the hosts of gods were looking on, the brothers of Namuci then pierced the axle of the king with sharpened arrows.
O Nārada, due to his agitation, the king did not notice that the chariot had its axle broken;
meanwhile, the fair-browed Kaikeyī, who was standing near the king, was perceived by him.
Having personally observed it and seeing that the axle was broken, Suvratā did not inform the king herself; instead, she then placed her own hand upon it.
O tiger among sages, this is a great marvel, like a game of dice:
that you, the best of chariot-warriors, have been defeated by her who has surrendered her hand as a stake.
Having conquered the Daityas and Danujas after receiving many boons from the gods,
he was then permitted by the gods and returned once more to Ayodhyā.
But that great king, seeing his beloved on the road in the midst of it all,
was struck with supreme astonishment upon witnessing that deed of Kaikeyī.
Then, O Nārada, he granted her three boons;
she, in turn, having honored the words spoken by the king, Kaikeyī spoke these words.
Kaikeyī said:
"O Indra among kings, let these boons granted by you remain with you."
Brahmā said:
Having bestowed the ornaments upon him, the king of kings,
victorious and joyful, departed for his own city with his beloved in a chariot.
For what indeed is not to be given by women to those they love when the occasion for favor arises?
Once, that Daśaratha was surrounded by those fond of the hunt.
While wandering in the forest during the night, he then constructed a water-dam;
for a king must remain free from the seven vices.
Although he knew this, by the power of fate he nevertheless did so;
having entered a pit, he struck with sharp arrows those who had come there for the purpose of drinking.
The mighty-armed one slays deer; hear now of this reversal of time:
while that king has entered a pit in that very same excellent mountain.
An old man named Vaiśravaṇa neither heard nor saw;
his wife was likewise so. Then the two of them spoke to their son.
The parents said:
"We are tormented by thirst, and the night is darkening;
our entire lives have passed while you, dear son, remain but a child."
Fie on the life of the blind, the deaf, and the aged;
fie, fie, my dear son, on the life of those whose bodies are shattered by old age!
Men should live only so long as their fortune, their body, and their unimpeded authority remain firm;
otherwise, it is death at a sacred ford or the like.

Having heard these words of the two elders, the son, who was devoted to his gurus, spoke to alleviate their sorrow with sweet speech: {Brahmā said:} Having heard these words of the two elders, the son, who was devoted to his gurus, spoke to alleviate their sorrow with sweet speech. (BrP 123.41)
The son said:
"While I am alive, what indeed is this kind of suffering for you two?
For a son does not remove the mental anguish of his parents through his own conduct."
What is the use of that son born here who causes distress to his family?
Brahmā said:
Having spoken thus, the high-minded one bowed to his parents, comforted them,
and then placed his aged parents upon the branch of a tree.
Taking the water-pot in his hand, the son of the seer departed;
that seer did not recognize the king, nor did the king recognize the twice-born man.
Both of them being impetuous there, the twice-born one entered the water and quickly seized the water with his swift arrows as it was being poured into an overturned jar.
Thinking the twice-born man to be an elephant, the king pierced him with sharp arrows;
yet the wild elephant, though knowing this, remained invulnerable to kings.
"What would the king not do, being thus deceived by fate?
Pierced in his vital organs, he spoke these words in his suffering."
The twice-born one said:
"By whom was this deed, which causes such suffering, committed against me, a virtuous Brahmin?
A Brahmin is called a friend to all; there is no offense whatsoever on my part."
{Brahmā said:} Having heard these words of the distressed sage, the king,
motionless and devoid of energy, slowly approached that place.
But upon seeing that best of the twice-born blazing, as it were, with splendor,
he too became there as if pierced by a thorn and fell into a swoon.
Having steadied himself by means of his own self, the king spoke these words.
The king said:
"Who are you, O tiger among the twice-born, and for what purpose have you come here?
Tell me, for I am a doer of evil; tell me the supreme means of atonement."
O one of great intelligence, a slayer of a Brahmin must never be touched by those who follow the stages of life (varṇins), nor even by outcastes (śvapacas); he must never be looked upon.
Having heard those words of the king, the son of the sage spoke these words: {Brahmā said:} "BrP_123.55 //"
The son of the Sage said:
"My vital breaths are about to depart; therefore, I shall say something more.
Know that the knowledge of acting according to one's own will is the ripening of karmas."
But I do not grieve for my own sake; rather, I grieve for my parents who have grown old. Who would be their attendant when they are blind and have but this one son?
"How will those two live in the great forest without me?
Oh, what a misfortune for me! What a loss to the service of my parents! (BrP 123.58)
"Alas, O Fate! What have you done today? You have brought me to birth only to be deprived of my life.
Nevertheless, go there quickly, taking the water-pot with you."
Give them water from that well, so that the two of them shall not die.
{Brahmā said:} While he was speaking thus in the great forest, his life-breaths departed;
having cast aside his bow and arrow, the king took up a water-pot.
He went with great speed to where the two elders were in the great forest;
and then, during that night, those two elders spoke to one another.
The two elders said:
"Is he anxious, or perhaps angry, or has he been devoured?
Why have we not received our staff? What shall we do, and what will our fate be?"
In the entire world of the moving and the unmoving, there is no son such as that who,
even when censured, does not act contrary to the words of his parents.
Harder even than a diamond is the life of those two who, not seeing him,
do not quickly depart from this world, their very existence depending solely upon him.
{Brahmā said:} While the two elders were thus speaking many kinds of words in the forest,
King Daśaratha then slowly approached that place.
By the sound of his footsteps, they recognized that their son had arrived.
The two elders said:
"Why have you returned after so long, my child? You are our sight and our refuge.
Why do you not speak? Are you angry with us, your blind parents?"
Brahmā said: Then, O Nārada, that lord of kings, afflicted by grief as if pierced by a thorn and lamenting his own misdeed, spoke to those two as if terrified.
Having heard those words spoken by the king, they said, "Construct a well;
this speaker is not our son. Tell us first, who are you?"
"Afterwards, let us both drink water"; then the king spoke to them both.
The king said:
"Your son stays there, where he has taken refuge in the water."
Brahmā said:
Having heard that, those two, being distressed, said, "Speak the truth and not otherwise.
Thereupon, the king related everything exactly as it had happened.
"Therefore, take us two who have fallen there; do not touch us!
The sin of touching a killer of a Brahmin is never destroyed."
The best of kings led the aged Śravaṇa together with his wife to the place where their son had fallen; upon touching him, the two of them lamented.
The two elders said: "O wicked one, just as death was ordained for us through separation from our son,
so too shall you meet death through separation from your son."
Brahmā said:
O Brahmin, while they were thus conversing, the king’s life-breaths departed;
he then had the two elders and the son of the sage cremated with fire.
Then, O Sage, the king went to the city in distress and reported all of that to Vasiṣṭha in its entirety.
"For the kings of the Solar dynasty, Vasiṣṭha is indeed the supreme refuge.
Then Vasiṣṭha, having consulted with the best of the twice-born, declared the means of atonement.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having diligently summoned Gālava, Vāmadeva, Jābāli, Kaśyapa, and others, [he prepared] for the horse sacrifice.
Perform sacrifices with many horse-sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Brahmā said:
King Daśaratha performed horse sacrifices with the twice-born;
in the midst of this, an incorporeal voice spoke there.
The voice from the sky said:
"Indeed, the body of King Daśaratha has become purified;
he shall be fit for social interaction, and his sons likewise shall be so."
"By the grace of his eldest son, the king shall become free from sin."
Brahmā said:
Then, after a long period of time, from the lord of sages, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga,
there were born sons resembling the gods for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the deities.
Likewise, Rāma was born of Kauśalyā, Lakṣmaṇa of Sumitrā,
and the most intelligent Bharata, as well as Śatrughna, were born of Kaikeyī.
All of them were wise and remained under the control of their beloved king;
having approached that king, the seer Viśvāmitra, who was like Prajāpati, [spoke].
And the sage, who was well aware of their greatness, requested both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa for the sake of protecting the sacrifice, O high-minded one.
The aged king, who had finally obtained a son after a long time, replied, "Not at all."
The king said:
"O sage, through some great stroke of fate,
in my old age, two children have somehow been born to me who bestow a mass of joy."
"I shall give away this kingdom along with my very body, but never these two sons."
Brahmā said:
Then King Daśaratha was addressed by Vasiṣṭha in this manner.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O King, the descendants of Raghu have never been taught anywhere to reject a request.
Brahmā said:
The king somehow spoke to both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
The king said:
"Perform the protection of the sacrifice for the brahmin-sage Viśvāmitra."
Brahmā said:
Speaking thus with a sigh of heat and his lower lip parched,
the author of the scriptures handed over his two sons to Viśvāmitra.
Having said "So be it" and having paid homage to Daśaratha again and again,
the two of them joyfully departed with Viśvāmitra for the purpose of protection.
Then, being greatly delighted, that sage joyfully bestowed upon both of them the great lore of Maheśvara, preceded by the science of archery.
He mastered the science of chariots— both that taught in the scriptures and that which is worldly— as well as the science of elephants,
the science of horses, the science of the mace, and the invocation and dismissal of mantras.
Then, having acquired all branches of knowledge, both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa slew Tāṭakā in the forest for the sake of the welfare of the forest-dwellers.
They freed Ahalyā from the curse by the touch of their feet,
and they slew the Rākṣasas who had come there to destroy the sacrifice.
Having mastered their sciences and with bows in hand, they performed the protection of the sacrifice;
then, when that great sacrifice was concluded, Viśvāmitra, the lord of sages, [departed].
Accompanied by his two sons, the prince went to see King Janaka;
there, in the midst of the kings, he displayed the wonderful painting.
Accompanied by the son of Sumitrā, Rāma mastered the science of archery as taught by his preceptor;
pleased with him, Janaka gave him Sītā, the Lakṣmī not born from a womb.
In the same manner, for Lakṣmaṇa, for Bharata’s younger brother,
and for Śatrughna, Bharata, and the others, Vasiṣṭha remained established in his doctrine.
O Sage, the illustrious King Daśaratha performed the marriage ceremony;
then, after a long period of time had passed, he bestowed the kingdom upon him.
With the consent of the king of all the worlds and even that of her guru,
she was impelled by ill fortune and a malicious nature, and became agitated by envy.
Kaikeyī thus created obstacles for his departure to the forest, as well as for Bharata’s receiving that kingdom; yet the king did not grant it at all.
Fulfilling that promise of truthful speech to his father, Rāma entered the great forest together with Sītā and likewise with the son of Sumitrā.
And he entered the pure minds of the virtuous by means of his own qualities,
once Rāma had departed for the forest, having been initiated into the vow of exile.
Together with Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā, who were free from any thirst for sovereignty—
[he beheld] that Rāma, the son of Sumitrā, and the virtuous Sītā.
Overcome by great sorrow and remembering the curse of Brahmā,
King Daśaratha then gave up his life in distress.
O one of great wisdom, by the ripening of his own past actions, the king was led away by the followers of Yama, extending as far as all things stationary and moving.
O Nārada, in the abode of Yama there are many hells, such as Tāmisra and others— numerous, terrible, and fearsome.
Then, having been cast there, the king is cooked in various individual hells;
the king is cut, crushed, and likewise ground to powder.
He is dried up, bitten again and again, burned, and submerged;
thus he is cooked in such terrible hells as these.
Rāma, too, as he traveled along the road, arrived at Citrakūṭa;
there, O high-minded one, three years passed away.
Again, he proceeded toward the southern direction to the Daṇḍaka forest,
which is renowned throughout the three worlds as a land that bestows merit.
He entered that great forest, terrifying and inhabited by Daityas, which had been abandoned by the sages out of fear of them; having slain the Daityas and Rākṣasas, he entered it.
While wandering through the Daṇḍaka forest, he then made it a place frequented by sages;
I shall relate what occurred there—listen attentively, O Nārada.
Rāma proceeded slowly for five yojanas until he reached the Gautamī river; meanwhile, the king remained in hell.
Yama said to his own servants: "Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, is proceeding toward Gautamī; he is going to the father of that wise man."
Then they shall drag the king from the hells; of this there is no doubt, as he proceeds for five yojanas after crossing the Gautamī.
"Let Rāma’s father not be cooked in hell at all,
provided that these messengers do not carry out my meritorious word."
And then you shall all sink into a terrible hell;
for whatever supreme power (parā śakti) has been described as being inherent (samavāyinī) to Śiva, [that very power you have disregarded].
The virtuous call that very Gautamī the embodiment of water,
for she alone is worthy of honor and worship by Hari, Brahmā, and Maheśa.
No one can escape the sin born of transgressing her;
yet even for a sinner, there may be some son who shall remember the Gaṅgā.
Having emerged from many difficult hells, he would attain liberation;
how much more so for a son such as this, who remains in the presence of Gautamī?
Having heard the words of the Lord of the Southern Quarter, whose cooking in hell cannot indeed be prevented by anyone, the servants of Yama [acted].
Having rescued that king, the lord of Ayodhyā, who was being cooked in hell from that terrible infernal realm, they spoke these words:
The Yama-kiṅkaras said:
"O tiger among kings, you are blessed, for you have such a son;
by whom can a truly good son be obtained, who brings rest both in this world and the next?"
Brahmā said:
Having rested, the king slowly spoke these words to his servants:
The king said:
"Being cooked again and again in the terrible hells, how was he quickly drawn out? You ought to tell me that here."
{Brahmā said:} Thereupon, a certain man of tranquil mind spoke this to the king: *BrP_123.133*
The messenger of Yama said:
"This [truth] is to be guarded with great effort in the Vedas, Śāstras, Purāṇas, and other texts;
nevertheless, it is being revealed to you because of the power of your son and your pilgrimage."
"O best of men, your illustrious son Rāma has arrived at the bank of the Gautamī; therefore, you have been drawn out from that terrible hell."
O best of kings, if Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa, should remember you there at Gautamī and, having performed his ablutions, offer you the funeral cakes and other rites, then you,
liberated from all sins, shall go to the third heaven.
The king said:
"Having gone there, I shall relate your words to my two daughters;
you alone are my refuge, and it behooves you to grant me permission."
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of the king, the servants of Yama out of compassion granted him permission; the king then went toward his two sons.
Having attained a terrifying body of torment, sighing repeatedly,
he looked upon himself with shame, recollecting the deeds he had committed.
Wandering at his own will, Rāghava reached the Gaṅgā;
both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa took their stand upon the bank of the Gautamī.
Together with Sītā Vaidehī, he bathed according to the prescribed rites;
however, there was no food to be eaten or chewed on the bank of the Gautamī.
On that day, while they were staying there on the banks of the Gautamī,
Lakṣmaṇa, his brother, became distressed upon seeing that and spoke to Rāma.
Lakṣmaṇa said:
"We two are the sons of Daśaratha, and even for you, such strength as this does not exist;
furthermore, there is no food for us who dwell on the banks of the Gaṅgā."
Rāma said:
"O brother, that which is ordained by destiny cannot be otherwise.
Even though the earth is filled with food, we are still desirous of food."
O Saumitri, surely we have not offered oblations into the mouths of Brahmins;
out of contempt, we have neither gratified nor honored the gods on earth.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, those who are born always hungry must bathe, worship the gods, and offer oblations into the sacrificial fire; thereafter,
at the proper time, the Lord will provide food for us both."
While the two brothers were thus conversing and observing the course of their actions,
King Daśaratha slowly approached that place.
Seeing him, Lakṣmaṇa quickly cried out, "Stay! Stay!
and drawing his bow in anger, he said, "Are you a Rākṣasa or perhaps a Dānava?"
Moreover, seeing that he is nearby, go, go there; you shall share in the merit.
King Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, who partakes in righteousness, is present here—behold him!
Devoted to his guru, true to his word, and a servant of the gods and brahmins—
this Rāghava, who is skilled in protecting the three worlds, dwells wherever he may be.
"There is no entry for those of sinful deeds like you there;
if you enter, O sinner, then you shall meet your death."
Having heard those words of his son, he slowly summoned her with his voice and,
bowing his head with palms joined in reverence, spoke to his daughter-in-law while repeatedly reflecting inwardly upon the destiny of one who has performed evil deeds: BrP 123.152.
The king said:
"I am King Daśaratha; my two sons, listen to my words.
Overwhelmed by three instances of the sin of killing a Brahmin, I have fallen into misery."
Behold my body cut asunder and cast down into the hells!
Brahmā said:
Then Rāma, along with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, all with palms joined in reverence,
prostrated themselves on the ground and spoke these words.
Sītā, Rāma, and Lakṣmaṇa said:
"O dear one, O best of kings, whose action is this the fruit of?"
Brahmā said:
And he related exactly what had occurred regarding those three acts of Brahman-slaughter.
The king said:
"O sons, no atonement whatsoever exists for those who have killed a Brahmin."
Brahmā said:
Then, overwhelmed by great sorrow, they all went to the earth to see the king, as well as their mother and father, who were living in the forest.
Reflecting thus upon the onset of suffering, the course of karma, and his fall into hell, the king’s son fell into a swoon. Seeing the king unconscious, Sītā then spoke these words: BrP_123.159.
Sītā said:
"Noble souls such as you do not grieve when calamity arrives;
they contemplate the remedy, whether it be divine or human."
Even after grieving for a thousand yugas, they do not cross over their calamity;
yet the wise in this world never fall into delusion.
"O Lord of Men, what is the use of this fruitless suffering here?
Grant first the death-blow for that most terrifying [sin] which was committed at the very beginning."
A Brahmin who was devoted to his father, virtuous in character, a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
and free from fault— since he has been slain, what atonement is there for this sin?
"I act according to the scriptures; do not both of you grieve.
Let Lakṣmaṇa take one death, and you, sir, take the other."
Brahmā said:
"These words spoken firmly by Sītā were consistent with righteousness;
both [her parents] replied, 'So be it,' and then Daśaratha spoke."
Daśaratha said:
"Since you are the daughter of Janaka, a knower of Brahman, and were not born from a womb,
what is surprising in the fact that you speak words so fitting for Rāma’s wife?"
There is no [sin] whatsoever for you, yet there remains even a slight exhaustion from bathing and giving gifts in the Gautamī, as well as from the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
"Released from three murders of a Brahmin, I am going to heaven;
you, O daughter of Janaka, have spoken what is worthy of your own lineage."
By the grace of the Godāvarī, women of noble family reach the further shore of the ocean of existence; what indeed is difficult to attain here?
Brahmā said:
When he had agreed, saying "So be it," the slayer of enemies, while preparing to offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas), did not see any food to eat; thereupon, he spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
Lakṣmaṇa spoke with humility: "There are fruits of the iṅgudī tree, and their oil-cake has been brought here as if at that very moment. (BrP 123.171)
Then, intending to offer a funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his father in the Gaṅgā with oil-cake (piṇyāka),
Rāma’s mind became sluggish and he was then overcome with grief.
Divine speech arose there: "Abandon your sorrow, O son of a king!
Having been deprived of your kingdom and having reached the forest, why indeed are you so destitute?"
Being free from deceit and devoted to the Dharma, you ought not to grieve here;
for he who performs a religious duty with deceit regarding his wealth is indeed a sinner.
It is heard in all the scriptures, O Rāma; listen to it with diligence:
"O King, whatever food a person eats, his deities eat that same food."
When the funeral cake had fallen upon the ground, he did not see his father there,
but only the corpse where that unsurpassed Śavatīrtha was located.
The recollection [of the Lord] destroys the accumulation of great sins;
there the world-protectors, the Rudras, the Ādityas, and likewise the two Aśvins arrived.
Having each mounted their own celestial chariot, he, most radiant among them,
ascended a preeminent vimāna while being praised by the kinnaras.
In their midst, his father shone with a form resembling the sun;
not seeing his own father, but seeing the gods, they became arrogant.
With palms joined in reverence, Rāma asked, "Where is my father?
To which a divine voice, addressing Rāma in the presence of Sītā, replied.
"O dear one, King Daśaratha was freed from three murders of Brahmins;
behold him surrounded by the gods, for even the deities spoke thus to him."
The gods said:
"O Rāma, you are blessed; you have accomplished your purpose, for your father has gone to heaven—he who rescues his ancestors from the multitude of various hells."
By that virtuous one, the three worlds have been sufficiently adorned;
behold him, O mighty-armed one, freed from sin and radiant as the sun.
Even one endowed with every prosperity is like a scorched tree if he is a sinner;
yet even one who possesses nothing is seen to be virtuous, like the moon-crested Lord Śiva.
Brahmā said:
Having seen him, the king greeted his son with blessings and spoke.
The king said:
"You have accomplished your purpose; may it be well with you. I have been delivered by you, O sinless one. Blessed is that son in this world who delivers his ancestors."
Brahmā said:
Then the hosts of gods spoke for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the deities:
"O dear one, go as you please to Rāma, the best among men."
Then, having heard those words, Rāma spoke to those gods.
Rāma said:
O gods, what remains for me to do toward my guru, my father?
The gods said:
"No river is equal to the Gaṅgā; no son is like you;
there is no god equal to Śiva; and no Manu is equal to Tāra."
"O Rāma, you have performed every duty toward your elders;
O Rāma, bestower of honor, you have delivered your ancestors by being their son.
Let everyone go to their own abodes, and you too may depart as you please."
Brahmā said:
Then, emboldened by those words of the gods and having witnessed that majesty of the Gaṅgā, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa was filled with wonder and spoke these words to Sītā.
Rāma said:
"Oh, this power of the Gaṅgā is incomparable even in the three worlds! We are blessed, since we have beheld the Gaṅgā, who purifies the three worlds."
Brahmā said: Filled with great joy, having installed the god Maheśvara,
he diligently worshipped that Īśāna with sixteen types of offerings.
Having worshipped the Lord, who is endowed with his retinue and consists of thirty-six kalās,
Rāma, with palms joined in reverence, praised Śaṅkara.
Rāma said:
I bow to Śambhu, the ancient Puruṣa;
I bow to the omniscient one of boundless nature.
I bow to that Lord Rudra, the imperishable;
I bow my head to Śarva;
I bow to that supreme, undecaying God.
I bow to Umāpati, the teacher of the world;
I bow to him who shatters poverty;
I bow to the remover of disease; I bow to him.
I bow to the auspicious one of inconceivable form;
I bow to him who is the seed-form of the origin of the universe; I bow to him, the cause of the sustenance of the universe.
I bow to the one who effects withdrawal;
I bow to him, the imperishable beloved of Gaurī;
I bow eternally to him, the perishable and the imperishable.
I bow my head to Him who is the form of consciousness, whose nature is immeasurable; I bow my head to that Three-eyed One;
I bow to the one who brings about compassion for the world of existence.
I always bow to the Terrifier; I bow to the giver of all desired things;
I first bow to Someśa, the Lord of Umā.
I bow to him whose eye is the three Vedas;
I bow to him who is devoid of the three forms;
I bow to the auspicious one who transcends both being and non-being.
I bow to him who removes sin;
I bow to him who is devoted to the welfare of the universe;
I bow to him who assumes many forms.
I bow to him who is the protector of all, the leader of both the existent and the non-existent; I bow to that Lord of the Universe,
the Master of Sacrifice, to whom the offerings to gods and ancestors are now presented.
I bow to that Lord Sadāśiva, who is the goal of the world,
who grants everything when propitiated,
and who is fond of giving— my chosen deity.
I bow to Someśvara, who is not independent;
I bow to that Umāpati, Vijaya;
I bow to Vighneśvara and Nandinātha.
I bow my head to him who is dear to his son;
I bow to the God who destroys the sorrow and grief of existence; I bow to the wearer of the moon.
I bow to the Lord who bears the Gaṅgā, the one worthy of praise;
I bow to Umā’s husband, the best of gods.
I bow to him who is the beginning of Brahmā, Śiva, Indra, and the rest.
I bow to him whose lotus-feet are worshipped by the gods and asuras, who desired a triad of eyes for the purpose of beholding the musical instruments in the mouths of the goddesses.
With the five nectars, perfumes, excellent incense, and lamps; with various flowers and diverse mantras;
with varieties of food and all ritual services (upacāras).
"I bow to Soma, who has been fully honored.
[Brahmā said:
Then the Blessed Lord Śambhu spoke to Rāma, who was accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa.
"Choose boons; may prosperity be yours," Rāma said to the bull-bannered god.
Rāma said:
O Maheśvara, O Supreme God of gods, may all the undertakings of those who satisfy you with devotion by means of this hymn attain success.
And those whose fathers have fallen into the ocean of hell, O Śambhu— may they,
purified by the offering of funeral cakes and other rites, go to the third heaven.
Whatever sins have been committed since birth— whether mental, vocal, or physical transgressions—
all those shall attain immediate destruction merely by bathing here.
In this regard, O Śambhu, whatever— even if it be minute— those who give with devotion to supplicants may offer,
all of that shall become inexhaustible and yield fruit for the donors.
"Brahmā said:
'So be it,' Śaṅkara, delighted, said to that Rāma.
When that best of gods had departed, Rāma also, together with his followers," [BrP 123.212]
Gautamī gradually approached that place where she had arisen;
from that time forth, that sacred ford has been called Rāmatīrtha.
There, an arrow fell from the hand of the compassionate Lakṣmaṇa;
it became that sacred ford of arrows (*bāṇatīrtha*), which wards off all calamities.
Where the son of Sumitrā performed his ablutions and the worship of Śaṅkara,
that sacred ford became known as Lakṣmaṇa as well as Sītāsamudbhava.
Through contact with his feet, she became the Gaṅgā, the purifier of the three worlds, capable of uprooting the entire multitude of various and inexhaustible sins.
What can be said of the excellence of that place where he performed his ablutions? Nowhere else is there to be found a sacred ford equal to Rāmatīrtha.
Brahmā said:
That meritorious sacred site (tīrtha) is called Putratīrtha;
by merely hearing of its greatness, one obtains all desires.
I shall describe its true nature; listen with diligence, O Nārada. When the sons of Diti, the Danujas, had become utterly diminished, the sons of Aditi became the eldest in every respect, O Nārada.
Then Diti, out of grief from the separation from her sons, approached Danu while competing with her. [Diti said:]
"O blessed lady, our sons alone have perished;
what weightier deed can we perform in this world? Behold the unbroken and most excellent lineage of Aditi."
Endowed with good governance, possessed of fame and the glory of victory, having conquered his enemies, and characterized by exalted renown and righteousness—
he was capable of destroying the joy of my heart.
Even though she shares the same husband, the same dharma,
the same lineage, and the same form,
I shall not restore her fortune or her prosperity.
Having seen those born of Aditi, I am worn out; I have fallen into some wretched state. And now, having beheld the supreme prosperity of Aditi, I am distressed.
"Even entering a forest fire is surely for one's happiness;
the fortune of a rival must not be looked upon even in a dream.
Brahmā said:
To her who was speaking thus with an exceedingly dejected face,
sighing deeply, the son of Parameṣṭhin—
having offered worship and being free from fatigue— [spoke].
Consoling her who was beautiful to the mind,
the son of Parameṣṭhin said:
"You should not feel distress regarding that which you so greatly desire."
"That is attained through merit alone, O blessed lady;
the high-souled Prajāpati knows the means for that, and he will explain it to you."
"O virtuous lady, being bowed down with humility, you have spoken this with your whole being."
While Diti was speaking thus, Danu spoke to her, O Nārada.
Danu said:
"O blessed lady, gratify your husband Kaśyapa with your own virtues;
if your husband should be pleased, then you will obtain your desires."
Brahmā said:
Having said, "So be it," she gratified Kaśyapa with all her being.
Then the blessed Prajāpati Kaśyapa spoke to Diti.
Kaśyapa said:
"O Diti of virtuous vows, tell me what you desire; choose a boon."
Brahmā said:
Diti also spoke to her husband for a son endowed with many virtues,
a conqueror of all the worlds, and one who would be honored by all the worlds.
"O Father of the Gods, may I choose as my husband him by whose birth I shall become a mother of a hero in this world," she said with humility.
Kaśyapa said:
"I shall instruct you in the most excellent vow, which yields the fruit of twelve years;
then, having returned, I will place within your womb that which is desired by your mind."
For when freedom from sin has been attained, one's desires are indeed fulfilled.
Brahmā said:
Delighted by her husband’s words, the large-eyed Diti bowed to him and performed the vow instructed by her husband according to the prescribed rules.
