Deprived of visiting sacred fords, giving to worthy recipients, and the practice of vows,
how shall living beings here attain their heart's desires?
Then, when her vow had been completed, Diti conceived a fetus;
Kaśyapa spoke again in private to that lovely Diti.
Kaśyapa said:
O lady of pure smiles, even sages established in austerity do not obtain those desires by means of contempt for the limbs of action as they have been prescribed.
One should not perform any censurable act during either of the two twilights;
one should not sleep, nor go about, and one should not have disheveled hair.
O fortunate one, one must not eat, nor indeed sneeze or yawn,
during the time of twilight, which is crowded with hosts of spirits.
One should always remain concealed, especially when laughing;
one should never stay in the interior of a house during the twilight hours.
O beloved, the pestle, the mortar, and so forth, as well as the winnowing basket, the seat, and the lid, must never be stepped over, whether by day or by night.
One should not sleep with the head toward the north, especially during the twilights;
nor should one speak any falsehood, nor wander about the houses of others.

"If you comply with such restrictive rules as, 'No man other than my beloved shall ever be looked upon even with effort,' then a son shall be born to you who will be the recipient of sovereignty over the three worlds."
Brahmā said:
"So be it," she promised her husband, who is honored by the worlds;
and Kaśyapa, O Brahmin, departed from here and there toward the gods.
The embryo, born of merit, grew strong within Diti;
the Daitya Maya knew all this in its true essence through his power of illusion.
Indra’s friendship with Maya was formed out of affection;
having gone into private, Maya spoke to Indra with humility.
Diti related to Indra her intention, the vow for the growth of the embryo,
and its various powers, out of affection.
If that friend who is the sole abode of trust, who is free from fear of misfortune,
and who has acquired various kinds of merit is obtained, [then all is gained].
Nārada said: O Lord of the Gods, how did friendship exist between Maya, the exceedingly powerful Daitya who was the beloved brother of Namuci, and the slayer of his brother?
Brahmā said: In ancient times, there was a powerful lord of the Daityas named Namuci;
he had a terrifying and hair-raising enmity with Indra.
Once, O friend, having abandoned the battle and seeing Śatakratu departing, the heroic lord of the Daityas, Namuci, followed behind him.
Beholding him approaching, Indra, the lord of Śacī, overcome with fear,
abandoned his elephant Airāvata and entered into the foam.
Vajrapāṇi swiftly struck the enemy with foam alone;
Namuci perished, as did his younger brother Maya.
For the destruction of his brother’s slayer, Maya performed great austerities and acquired various illusions that were most terrifying even to the gods.
Having obtained boons through ascetic penance from Viṣṇu, the supreme refuge of the world,
that Maya then became one who was liberal in giving and pleasant in speech.
Having honored the sacred fires and the Brahmins, and having made his preparations to conquer Indra,
he was praised by bards as he bestowed gifts upon those who sought them.
Having learned that the illusory Maya was his enemy and had approached for a fair fight, Maghavan, becoming a Brahmin, went toward him;
the husband of Śacī spoke thus to the Daitya Maya again and again.
Indra said:
"O Lord of the Daityas, grant me, who am a petitioner, the boon I desire.
Having heard that you are the preeminent giver, I have come as a foremost among the twice-born."
Brahmā said:
Maya, too, considering him to be a brahmin, said, "I have given it to you.
The wise deliberate long upon whether what is offered to a petitioner is much or little.
When this was said, Hari replied, "I indeed desire friendship with you.
Maya spoke again to Indra: "O best of the twice-born, what is the use of him?"
"O sir, I have no enmity toward you; may it be well with you," Hari said to Maya.
When the Daitya asked him, "Tell me the truth," that Hari revealed his own form.
He revealed to the Daitya that which is called the Thousand-eyed One;
then the Daitya Maya, filled with wonder, spoke to Hari.
Māyā said: "What is this? You are Vajrapāṇi; this action is unworthy of you, my friend."
Brahmā said:
Having embraced him and smiled, Hari then spoke thus regarding what had transpired:
"In this world, even the wise accomplish their desired aims by some means or other."
From that time forth, O tiger among sages, there arose a great affection between Śakra and Maya; for Maya was always devoted to the welfare of Indra.
Having gone to the abode of Indra, he reported everything to him;
Hari then said to the illusory Maya, "What is my task? (BrP 124.49).
Maya then affectionately bestowed his *māyā* upon Hari, and likewise Hari, being well-pleased, said to Maya: "I have arrived; tell me, O Maya, what task is to be done."
Māyā said:
"Go to the hermitage of Agastya; there Diti dwells, pregnant.
Remain there for some time, performing service for her."
O Maghavan, having entered her womb on those days, you who wield the thunderbolt must cut him as he grows, with your vajra, until he either becomes submissive or meets his death; thereafter,
there shall be no enemy remaining.
Brahmā said:
Having said, "So be it," and having honored Maya, Maghavan alone then departed quickly toward his mother Diti with humble demeanor.
While serving that goddess,
Diti, the mother of the Daityas, Śakra did not perceive the mind of his enemy; for Diti was unaware of the being situated in her womb who was acting as the Lord of the Gods.
That splendor of the sage Kaśyapa is unfailing and difficult to approach.
Then, grasping his thunderbolt, the thousand-eyed Purandara dwelt there for a long time, desiring to enter within.
Observing her sleeping with her head toward the north during the twilight hour, the wielder of the thunderbolt said,
"This is the opportunity," and entered the womb of Diti.

And seeing Indra within, bearing his weapon and desiring to kill him, that being spoke again and again, as if undaunted: antarvarti ca yad bhūtam indraṃ dṛṣṭvā dhṛtāyudham / hantukāmaṃ tadovāca punaḥ punar abhītavat // BrP_124.57 //
The one dwelling in the womb said:
"O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, why do you not protect me? You seek to kill your own brother.
There is no greater sin than killing one who does not fight."
"O mighty-armed Śakra, fight without resorting to battle; fight once I have departed. Therefore, this [course of action] will not be appropriate for you."
O Lord, you are Śatakratu, Sahasrākṣa, the husband of Śacī, Purandara, Vajrapāṇi, and Surendra; it would not be fitting for you to act thus.
Or, O mighty-armed one, if you desire battle, act so that my departure may proceed; withdraw from this path.
Even those who are great do not turn toward the wrong path when fallen into calamity;
they possess neither ignorance as their weapon nor any collection of arms.
O Vajrapāṇi, you who possess knowledge, are you not ashamed to strike me down?
Those of noble birth never perform a despicable deed.
What glory or merit indeed could arise from killing?
Brothers are slain out of lust; what manliness is there even in those still in the womb?
"O brother, if you have an undoubted devotion to battle with me, then stand firm against the wielder of the thunderbolt, having placed your fist forward. BrP 124.65.
O Śakra, why are you intent on killing me—one who has killed a child, killed a Brahmin, and likewise betrayed trust? Such is the fruit [of such deeds].
By whose command all this, including the moving and the unmoving, exists—he indeed slays me, a mere child; what fame is there in that, and what manliness?
Brahmā said:
As the embryo was speaking thus, he cut it apart with his thunderbolt;
for those blinded by anger and possessed by greed, no compassion exists anywhere.
He did not die from that suffering; then his brothers said, "We [are here]," but he cut them into pieces again, and they cried out, "Do not kill us! (BrP 124.69).

O Śatakratu, not even a single grain of compassion arose in the hearts of those whose intellects were destroyed by hatred toward their own brothers, who were trusting and dwelling within their mothers' wombs.
Thus, seeing each severed limb— like a living being with hands, feet, and so forth— remaining entirely without change, he was utterly amazed at every seven [pieces].
"Though they are many forms, they are as one; though staying in the womb, they are auspicious.
These many forms are weeping; 'Do not weep! thus Hari spoke."
Then those Maruts were born, powerful and of great energy;
while still in the womb, free from delusion, they spoke to one another regarding Śakra.
"Agastya, that tiger among sages, in whose hermitage our mother resides—
your brother and our father— holds your friendship in high regard."
O Sage, we know that your mind is full of affection toward us,
for even the wielder of the thunderbolt does not act in such a way toward one who is engaged in the killing of a dog-eater.
Having heard these words, Agastya went there in great haste and consoled Diti, who was distressed by the pangs of labor.
There, Agastya, being greatly provoked, cursed the beloved of Śacī.
Agastya said:
O Hari, may your enemies always see your back in battle;
for this indeed is the death of the living for those who possess self-respect.
That which enemies see on the backs of those fleeing in battle.
Brahmā said:
Diti also, out of anger, cursed that Indra who was situated within her womb.
Diti said:
"Since you have not acted with manly prowess, this curse shall befall you:
having suffered humiliation at the hands of women, O Hari, you shall be cast down from your kingdom."
Brahmā said:
In the meantime, Kaśyapa, the lord of creatures,
became distressed upon hearing from Agastya about the actions of Śakra, and he went there.
Having entered into the womb, Śakra spoke to his father like one who was terrified.
Śakra said:
"I am afraid to step outside because of Agastya and Diti."
Brahmā said:
In the meantime, Kaśyapa, the lord of creatures, arrived;
having seen that act of procreation and the very state of the embryo remaining within the womb.
Having heard this curse of Diti regarding Agastya, he became sorrowful.
Kaśyapa said:
"Go forth, Śakra, my son! What evil deed have you committed?
Those born of a stainless lineage do not set their minds upon sin."
Brahmā said:
Having emerged, Vajrapāṇi, filled with shame and with his face cast down, spoke;
for it is the very form of that [deity] which declares the good and evil conduct of men.
Śakra said:
"Whatever is declared here to be for one's welfare, that I shall undoubtedly perform."
Brahmā said:
Then Kaśyapa, together with the world-protectors and the gods, approached me; he related everything that had occurred and questioned me once again.
He indeed granted peace to the womb of Diti, the thousand-eyed Indra’s sovereignty over the quarters,
and friendship with Indra for all those remaining in the womb.
[He recounted] their recovery of health, the faultlessness of the Lord of Śacī, and how, in due course, he became free from the leprosy resulting from the curse of Agastya.
Then I spoke these words to Kaśyapa with humility:
"O Prajāpati Kaśyapa, together with the Vasus and the world-protectors..."
Accompanied by Indra, O giver of honor, go quickly to the Gautamī;
having bathed there, offer praise to Maheśāna together with all [your followers].
"Then, by the grace of Śiva, everything will become auspicious.
Having said, "So be it," Kaśyapa then went to the Gautamī river.
Having bathed, he praised the Lord of Gods with these very words;
for the removal of all suffering, only two are proclaimed:
either the holy river Gautamī or Śiva, the mine of compassion.
Kaśyapa said: Protect me, O Śaṅkara, Lord of Gods; protect me, O you who are saluted by the worlds! Protect me, O Purifier, Master of Speech; protect me, O you whose ornament is the serpent!
Protect me, O Dharma, mounted upon the bull; protect me, O you whose eyes are the three Vedas;
protect me, O Lord of Lakṣmī, who wears a hide; protect me, O Śarva, whose garment is the elephant.
Protect me, O Lord of the three cities; protect me, O one adorned with the crescent moon.
Protect me, O Lord of sacrifice, O Lord of Soma; protect me, O bestower of desired boons.
Protect me, O abode of compassion; protect me, O bestower of auspiciousness!
Protect me, O source of all; protect me, O guardian Vāsava!

Protect me, O Bhāskara; protect me, O Lord of Wealth; protect me, O Brahman, who art saluted by all; protect me, O Lord of the Universe, O Lord of the Siddhas; protect me, O Perfect One—homage be to you!
O Ocean of Compassion, O Auspicious One, you alone are the refuge for embodied beings whose minds are distressed by wandering through the terrible wilderness of saṃsāra.
Brahmā said:
As he was thus offering praise, the bull-bannered Lord appeared before him and invited Kaśyapa, that lord of creatures, to choose a boon.
Kaśyapa also spoke these words to Śiva in a humble manner;
he then related in detail the deeds of Indra.
[He told them] of the curse and the destruction of his sons, their mutual enmity,
the attainment of sin by Śakra, and likewise the receipt of a curse;
then Vṛṣākapi spoke to Diti and to Agastya.
Śiva said:
"May those Maruts who are your sons, numbering forty-nine,
all become fortunate and partakers in the sacrificial offerings."
Together with Indra, they should always dwell there, filled with joy.
In whatever sacrifice there may be a portion of the oblation for Indra, the Maruts must be present there first; of this there is no doubt.
They could never defeat Śakra even when he is accompanied by the Maruts;
he shall always be the victor. Remain at ease, O Lord of Creatures!
From this day forward, those who commit the murder of a brother through injustice shall suffer the extinction of their lineage and constant misfortune.
Brahmā said:
Śambhu also spoke with great effort to Agastya, that tiger among sages.
Śambhu said:
"O sage, you must not harbor anger toward the husband of Śacī;
attain tranquility, O highly wise one, for the Maruts shall become immortal."
Brahmā said:
And Śiva, the bull-bannered one, being pleased, spoke also to Diti.
Śiva said:
"May I have one son who is adorned with the sovereignty of the three worlds"—
thinking thus, you became disciplined for the sake of asceticism.
Thus, this has borne fruit for you today: your sons have become auspicious, endowed with many virtues, powerful, and heroic; therefore, destroy the pain of your mind.
O lady of beautiful brows, free from agitation, ask for other boons as well.
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of the God of gods,
Diti bowed to Śambhu with her palms joined in reverence and then spoke these words.
Diti said: "O you who are worshipped by the gods, in this world, the sight of one's children is the supreme joy for parents; indeed, it is especially dear to the mother."
Even in that case, he should possess beauty of form, heroism, and valor;
yet even if there is but one son, how much more so if there are many?
"By my power, those sons of mine will certainly be victorious and strong;
they are truly the brothers of Indra and the sons of Prajāpati."
Through the grace of Agastya and through the favor of the Gaṅgā, wherever you, O Lord, bestow your grace, that shall be auspicious; what doubt can there be in this?
I have already achieved my purpose; nevertheless, out of devotion, I address you.
Listen, O Lord, to my words and act for the welfare of the world.
Brahmā said:
"Speak," was addressed by the Sustainer of the World; Diti, bowing low, spoke this.
Diti said:
"O one worshipped by the gods, the attainment of progeny is difficult to achieve in this world;
especially since a son is dear to a mother, how can it even be described?"
And if he is born virtuous, illustrious, and long-lived,
O Lord of Gods, what need has he for heaven or even for the station of Brahmā?
"For all beings here and in the hereafter who desire fruits,
the attainment of a virtuous son is always their cherished goal.
Therefore, let this favor be granted here by means of the ritual ablution."
Śaṅkara said:
This state of childlessness, whether it occurs for a woman or for a man, is the fruit of great sin; indeed, it is the condition of being barren that arises.
Therefore, by merely bathing here, that fault shall go to destruction;
and whoever bathes there and recites this hymn, he shall receive the fruit [of his merit].
He indeed obtains a son through bathing and giving gifts for three months;
moreover, a woman without a son, having performed the bath here, shall obtain a son.
Any woman who has bathed after her menses and bathes there shall obtain sons;
likewise, one who is pregnant within three months may do so here through devotion.
Having bathed with fruits, one should behold me and likewise praise me with a hymn;
to her, a son equal to Śakra is born—of this there is no doubt.
O Diti, listen: for those who do not obtain a son due to the faults of their ancestors, or due to the sins of misappropriating wealth, this is the supreme expiation.
In that regard, by means of offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and by pleasing the ancestors (pitṛs),
and furthermore by the gift of some gold, a son will certainly be born thereafter.
The lineage of those who steal deposits and the like, who conceal precious gems,
and who neglect the performance of ancestral rites (śrāddha), does not flourish.
"May this be the destiny of those deceased who were guilty;
meanwhile, let the lineage of the living flourish through their devotion to sacred fords."
Having bathed at the confluence of the Diti and the Gaṅgā, [one should worship] the Lord Siddheśvara,
who is without beginning or end, undecaying, and whose form consists of consciousness, existence, and bliss.

Mahādeva, who consists of the *liṅga*, is composed of light and is free from all affliction; he is served by the celestial sages (*devarṣi*), the perfected ones (*siddha*), the gandharvas, and the lords of yogins.
Having worshipped with ritual services daily and with devotion, one who is restrained in their vows and praises [him] with this hymn on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days; BrP_124.134 //
Whoever performs the gift of gold according to their ability and provides food for Brahmins here at the Gaṅgā shall obtain a hundred sons.
Having attained all desires, he shall at the end go to the city of Śiva;
whoever praises me with this hymn, wherever they may be,
shall obtain a son within six months— even a barren woman will undoubtedly do so.
Brahmā said:
From that time forward, that sacred ford has been called Putratīrtha;
by bathing, giving gifts, and other rites there, one shall obtain all desires.
Because of his friendship with the Maruts, it is called Mitratīrtha;
and because of Indra’s freedom from sin, it is called Śakratīrtha.
The sacred ford where she obtained the splendor of Indra is named Kamalā;
indeed, all these holy fords bestow every desired object.
Having said, "Everything shall come to pass," Śiva vanished;
and all of them, their purpose accomplished, returned as they had come.
It is proclaimed that one hundred thousand holy fords (tīrthas) bestow merit there.
Brahmā said:
It is renowned as Yamatīrtha, which increases the satisfaction of the ancestors;
it grants all desired things, both seen and unseen, and is frequented by hosts of gods and sages.
I shall describe his power, which destroys all sins:
there was a powerful pigeon known as Anuhrāda.
His wife was a bird named Heti, capable of assuming any form at will;
and Anuhrāda was the grandson of Mṛtyu, while Heti was indeed his daughter.
In the course of time, they had sons and grandsons;
and his enemy was a powerful one, a king of birds named Ulūka.
His sons and grandsons were the Āgneyas, fierce in their strength;
and between those two twice-born men, a feud persisted for a long time.
On the northern bank of the Gaṅgā there was the hermitage of a pigeon;
and on its southern shore lived a king of birds named Ulūka.
O best of the twice-born, he made his dwelling there with his sons and grandsons;
and a battle took place between those two adversaries for a long time.
When two powerful parties, surrounded by sons and grandsons and accompanied by their own strong forces,
contend with one another, neither the owl nor the pigeon attains either victory or defeat.
Having propitiated Yama, Mṛtyu, and likewise the Grandfather (Brahmā),
Kapota obtained the weapon of Yama and thereafter became superior even to all others.
Likewise, having propitiated the fire-god, Ulūka became exceedingly powerful;
and by virtue of their boons, a most terrifying battle took place between the two intoxicated ones.
There, the owl discharged the fiery weapon at the pigeon;
then the pigeon, having hurled the nooses of Yama at his enemy, discharged them.
Then Ulūka hurled a staff and the nooses of Death;
once again, that battle became like the one between Purā and Āḍibaka.
Seeing the fire approaching nearby, Heti’s wife Kapotakī,
devoted to her husband, was overwhelmed with grief during that great battle.
Seeing her sons especially being enveloped by the fire,
Heti went toward the blazing flames and praised it with various words.
Hetu said:
There is no form, no gift, and nothing hidden that is not already one's own self among the multitude of existing things.
I bow to the Lord of Svāhā, the consumer of sacrifice, by whom the gods partake of the oblations;
he who is the mouth of the gods and the bearer of their offerings.
And also as the invoker of the gods, and indeed as the messenger of the gods.
I go for refuge to that god, the primordial deity Vibhāvasu,
who dwells within as the form of vital breath and who bestows food from without;
I go for refuge to that Dhanañjaya, the means of accomplishing sacrifice.
Agni said:
"O pigeon, this weapon of mine is unfailing;
tell me, O devoted wife, where I may lay it down in battle."
The female dove said:
"Let your weapon rest upon me; not upon my son, nor upon my husband.
O Lord of Oblations, Jātavedas, be true to your word; homage be unto you!"
Jātavedas said:
"I am pleased with your words and with your devotion to your husband, O devoted wife;
I grant you, as well as your husband and sons, freedom from weapons and security."
"This weapon of mine is of the nature of fire; it shall not burn my husband nor even my sons, nor you. Therefore, go in peace, O little dove."
Brahmā said:
In the meantime, an owl there beheld her husband being bound with the nooses of Yama and struck by the staff of Yama.
The female owl, having become distressed and overcome with fear, approached Yama.
Ulūka said:
"Terrified of you, people run away;
terrified of you, they practice celibacy."
Fearing you, the wise practice virtue;
fearing you, they become devoted to their duties;
fearing you, they practice fasting unto death.
Those who go from the village to the forest out of fear of you take refuge in gentleness;
those who fear you partake in the drinking of Soma.
Fearing you, they are devoted to the gift of food and cows;
fearing you, they discourse upon the Brahman.
(Brahmā said:)
While she was speaking thus, the Lord of the Southern Quarter said to her:
Yama said:
"Choose a boon—may prosperity be yours—and I shall grant you whatever is dear to your heart."
Having heard these words of Yama, that devoted wife spoke to him.
Ulūka said:
"My husband has been bound with snares and struck by your staff;
therefore, O best of gods, protect my sons and my husband as well."
At those words, Yama, filled with compassion, spoke again and again.
Yama said:
"O lady of auspicious countenance, tell me also the location of the nooses and the staff."
Brahmā said:
She spoke to the god Yama: "O Lord of the World, let the nooses dispatched by you enter into me; let the rod of punishment descend upon me alone."
Then the Blessed One spoke again to Yama out of compassion:
Yama said:
May your husband and all your sons live free from distress.
Brahmā said:
Yama restrained his nooses, while the Fire-god withdrew his fiery weapon;
furthermore, the two gods brought about a state of friendship between the pigeon and the owl.
And the two twice-born ones said: "Let the desired boon be chosen."
The two birds said:
"O best of gods, we have obtained the sight of you, which is difficult to achieve even through the pretext of enmity. And since we are sinful birds, what need have we of a boon?"
"Now, if a boon is to be granted to us by you both out of affection, we do not ask for a boon for our own sake; rather, let a auspicious boon be given."
O lords of the gods, he who begs for his own sake is indeed to be pitied;
however, fruitful is the life of him who is always striving for the sake of others.
Fire, water, the sun, the earth, and various kinds of grain exist for the sake of others; this is especially true of virtuous people.
For even Brahmā and the others are joined with death;
knowing this, O lords of the gods, the exertion for one's own sake is in vain.
Whatever has been ordained by the Supreme Lord for men at the time of their birth never turns out otherwise; indeed, living beings suffer in vain.
Therefore, let us both request something auspicious for the welfare of the worlds;
may you two grant that which bestows virtue upon everyone.
Brahmā said:
Both those gods, renowned throughout the worlds as birds,
spoke thus for the sake of attaining dharma and fame, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
The two birds said:
"O Lords of the worlds, let hermitages be established by us on both banks of the Gaṅgā at the sacred ford; this alone is our supreme boon."

Whether one is virtuous or even a wrongdoer, whatever bathing, giving, recitation, fire-offering, or worship of the ancestors one performs in any manner whatsoever— all that shall become inexhaustible merit; this is the supreme boon.
The two gods said:
"So be it; likewise, being well-pleased, we shall speak further."
Yama said:
Those who recite the hymn to Yama on the northern bank of the Gautamī shall not meet with untimely death within seven generations of their lineage.
A person who,
having conquered their own self, constantly recites this hymn to Death, shall always be a vessel for all perfections.
O best of the twice-born, at this sacred ford, a pregnant woman shall not be afflicted by the eighty-eight thousand diseases for three months.
If she is barren, she shall bathe for seven days within six months;
that woman will become one who gives birth to a hero, and her son shall live for a hundred years.
One becomes prosperous, wise, and heroic, increasing one's sons and grandsons;
there, by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and other rites, the ancestors attain liberation,
and a man is freed from the sins born of mind, speech, and body through bathing.
Brahmā said:
Following the words of Yama, the bearer of oblations likewise spoke to the two birds.
Agni said:
To those who, restrained in their vows, recite my hymn of praise on the southern bank,
I grant health, sovereignty, fortune, and beauty.
Whatever man recites this hymn anywhere at all,
he shall have no fear of fire, even if it remains written within his home.
Any pure man who performs bathing and giving at Agnitīrtha shall undoubtedly obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Brahmā said:
From that time forward, the wise have known that sacred ford as Yāmya, Āgneya, Kapota, Ulūka, and Hetulūka.
Therein, there are three thousand and as many hundreds more;
furthermore, there are ninety sacred fords (*tīrtha*), each of which is a vessel for liberation.
By bathing and giving gifts at those [sites], even those men who have become ghosts (pretas) shall be purified; endowed with sons and wealth, they, being auspicious, shall ascend to heaven.
Brahmā said:
There is a great place known as Tapas-tīrtha, which increases ascetic merit,
bestows all desires, is holy, and augments the satisfaction of the ancestors.
Hear now what occurred at that sacred ford, which destroys all sins:
the conversation between the waters and the fire, and among the sages, with one another.
Some considered water to be the eldest, while others considered fire to be so;
thus did the sages speak, recounting the dialogue between fire and water.
Without fire, how could there be life, since fire is the very essence of living beings?
Everything is born from fire, which is both the self and the sacrificial oblation.
For the world is sustained by fire; indeed, fire is the light of the universe.
Therefore, there is no great purifying deity superior to fire.
He alone is said to be the inner light, for he indeed is the supreme light;
without him, there is nothing whose abode is the three worlds.
Therefore, there is nothing superior to fire as a recipient of the primacy among the elements;
for just so is the seed deposited by a man in the field of a woman.
His power over the body and so forth belongs only to Agni and not otherwise;
for Agni is indeed the mouth of the gods, and therefore they know nothing higher than him.
But others, proponents of the Vedas, indeed considered water to be the eldest;
for food is produced by water, and the pure is born from water.
"Everything is supported by water alone; indeed, the waters are remembered as mothers.
Those who know the ancient lore declare that water is the life of the three worlds. (BrP 126.10)
For the nectar was produced from the waters, and from those waters comes the origin of medicinal herbs;
they say that fire is the eldest, but the waters are the eldest of all.
While reflecting thus, those sages who proclaim the Vedas, being proponents of conflicting doctrines, approached me and spoke as follows.
The sages said:
"Tell us which is superior, fire or water; you are the lord of the three worlds."
Brahmā said:
I also spoke to all the sages who had arrived, who were firm in their vows:
"Both are most worthy of worship in the world; from both the universe is born."
From both [the father and the mother] arises the oblation for the gods and the ancestors, as well as immortality itself;
from both comes life in this world and the sustenance of the body.
And there is no distinction between these two; therefore, their seniority is considered equal.
Consequently, according to my word, seniority belongs to neither of them.
"The most excellent sages considered that seniority belonged to one or the other;
yet, unsatisfied with my words, those ascetics departed for Vāyu."
The sages said:
"O Vāyu, whose seniority is it that you have attained? Truly, truth resides within you."
Brahmā said:
"Vāyu is the eldest; fire is the consumer; everything is established in fire.
Having said this to one another, those sages went to the earth.
The sages said:
"O Earth, speak the truth; you are the eldest, for you are the support of all that is moving and unmoving."
Brahmā said:
The Earth also spoke these words to those sages who had approached her with humility.
The Earth said:
"May the eternal divine Waters also be my support;
for everything is born from the Waters, and preeminence is established in the Waters."
Brahmā said:
Having said "No" to one another, the sages went to the one who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk;
they praised the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace with various hymns.
The sages said:
He who knows the entire world— what is yet to be,
what is being born, and that which is hidden in the cave of the heart.
That which has entered all the three worlds— which possess manifold and diverse forms— at the end,
that which is imperishable, eternal, and immeasurable; (BrP 126.24c–25a)
That which the seers declare to be known through the Vedas,
that which they rely upon to obtain their desired goals— to that true reality we go for refuge.
The true nature of the great elements and the primary source of the world,
which is the form of Viṣṇu, yogis do not perceive;
it is for the sake of explaining that which these sages have come here.
Speak the truth here, O Abode of the World! You are the inner self of all embodied beings;
you alone are everything, and everything is in you, O Lord.
Nevertheless, alas, no one anywhere knows you, who exist everywhere— both within and without— by virtue of your innate power.
As he was revolving with the universal self, Brahmā spoke; then a divine, bodiless voice, the sustainer of the world, spoke: Brahmā said:
Then a divine, incorporeal voice, the sustainer of the world, spoke.
The divine voice said:
"Having propitiated both through austerity, devotion, and self-restraint,
whichever one first attains perfection— that being is called the elder."
Brahmā said:
"So be it," saying this, all those sages honored by the world departed;
they were weary, their inner selves distressed, having resorted to supreme dispassion.
Restraining their vows, they all went to the Gautamī river— the sole mother of all the worlds and the purifier of the three realms— in order to perform austerities.

Then Sarasvatī, the divine mother of the Vedas, spoke there as the goddess of speech: "Those who were then intent on worshipping Agni, whose deity is the waters, and those who remained engaged in the worship of the waters. The divine voice said:
"Water is the womb of fire; purity is attained through water.
And for those who worship fire, how can there be worship without water?"
As long as all the waters have not been purified, a man remains unfit for ritual action— impure and defiled— and thus lacks authority to perform sacred rites.
As long as one who knows the Vedas has not submerged himself in cold waters with faith,
therefore water is the most excellent, since it is remembered as being like a mother;
thus, the preeminence belongs to the waters alone, for they are specifically the mothers of Agni.
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words, those sages who were exponents of the Vedas reached a conclusion: that the preeminence belongs to the waters.

O Nārada, that sacred ford where this took place during the sacrifice of the sages is declared to be the Tīrtha of Penance (Tapas-tīrtha); it is also called the Tīrtha of the Sacrificial Session (Sattra-tīrtha).
That is declared to be Agnitīrtha, and they know it likewise as Sārasvata;
bathing and giving gifts at those places bestows all auspicious desires.
There are fourteen hundred holy sites here that bestow merit;
bathing and giving gifts at them grant both heaven and liberation.
Where Sarasvatī became united with the river Gaṅgā, dispelling the doubts of the sages through her speech— what man is capable of describing the majesty of that confluence?
Brahmā said:
On the northern bank of the Gaṅgā, there is a place renowned as Devatīrtha;
I shall describe its power, which destroys all sins.
There was a king renowned as Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, endowed with all virtues;
his wife was named Jayā, who was like another Lakṣmī herself.
His son was named Bhara, wise and devoted to his father;
he was proficient in both the science of archery and the Vedas, as well as being highly capable.
His wife was the beautiful Suprabhā, renowned by that name;
then King Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, having established his son in the kingdom, [departed].
Then, with his chief priest, the lord of men underwent the initiation on the bank of the Sarasvatī, being intent upon the horse sacrifice.
That best of kings was consecrated by officiating priests and eminent sages devoted to the Vedas and Shastras, in the presence of the Brahmanas and the sacred fires.
The heroic and powerful king of the Dānavas, Mithu, who was evil-minded,
having destroyed the sacrifice, [seized] the monarch along with his wife and his family priest.
Taking him with speed, O Sage, he went to the depths of the netherworld;
when that best of kings had been led away and the sacrifice was thus ruined, the immortals [were distressed].
Then all the officiating priests departed from the sacrifice to their respective places;
and there was the son of the king’s domestic priest, renowned as Devāpi.
Seeing her as his mother and not seeing his father,
the boy was filled with wonder and became exceedingly distressed.
He then asked his mother: "O Mother, where has my father gone?
Bereft of my father, I cannot live; O Mother, tell me the truth."
"Fie, fie upon the life of those who have lost their father and are performers of evil deeds!
O mother, had you not spoken thus to me, I would have entered either water or fire."
That mother, the wife of the king and the priest, said to her son:
"Your father has been struck down by the Dānava along with the king."
Devāpi said: "Where was he taken? By whom was he taken? How was he taken? In what action and where?
While whom did he see? Tell me, what is the abode of the Dānava?"
The mother said:
"While that king was consecrated in the sacrificial assembly together with his wife and his domestic priest, the Daitya Mithu led him away to the subterranean realm (rasātala)."
While the hosts of gods were looking on, in the presence of the fire and the brahmin.
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of his mother, Devāpi remembered his duty:
"I shall see either the gods, or Agni, or the officiating priests, or likewise the Asuras."
"My conviction is that the father must be sought among these very people and nowhere else";
having thus resolved, Devāpi spoke to the prince Bharata.
Devāpi said:
"By means of austerity, celibacy, vows, and self-restraint,
I must bring back all those who have been led to the netherworld."
When a terrible defeat has occurred, what is the use of that lowest of men who does not take retaliatory action— whether he be alive or dead?
"Rule the entire earth as your father Ārṣṭiṣeṇa did;
O King, my mother must be protected by you until my return.
And when my purpose is accomplished, permit me to depart; support me now."
Brahmā said:
Thus addressed by Bhara, that Devāpi, having deliberated upon everything with great effort, [spoke].
Bhara said:
"Accomplish your goal, go in happiness; do not indulge in even the slightest anxiety."
Brahmā said: Then Devāpi, intent on meditating upon the feet of the king of the immortals,
sought out the officiating priests with great effort and bowed down to each of those priests individually.
With palms joined in reverence, the boy Devāpi spoke these words.
Devāpi said:
"The sacrifice must be protected by you, as must the sacrificer who has been consecrated,
the domestic priest, and likewise the wife of the one who has been consecrated."
While you were looking on there, the king of the Daityas destroyed the sacrifice and carried away the King and the others; that would not have been most appropriate.
Moreover, I consider this: you ought to grant them all their health; otherwise, you deserve a curse.
The officiating priests said:
"In a sacrifice, Agni is to be honored first, for Agni alone is the deity here;
therefore, we, who are the attendants of the fires, do not know [anything else]."
He alone is the giver and the enjoyer, the taker and the doer, and the bearer of the oblation.
{Brahmā said:} Having placed the officiating priests behind him and having worshipped the sacrificial fire according to the prescribed rule, Devāpi offered that [oblation] to Agni.
Agni said:
"Just as the officiating priests, so am I the attendant of the gods;
I carry the oblation to the gods, while they are the enjoyers and the protectors."
Devāpi said:
"Having summoned the gods with effort, I shall give them their respective portions of the sacrificial oblation;
this is my fault, therefore go toward the gods."
Brahmā said:
Having approached the gods and bowed down to each of them individually, Devāpi reported the words of the officiating priests, the words of Agni, and the curse as well.
The gods said:
"O best of the twice-born, having been summoned by the officiating priests with Vedic mantras in due order, we shall consume our portions of the sacrificial oblation; we are not independent."
Therefore, O Brahmin, we always follow the Vedas and are impelled by the Veda; thus, we are dependent upon them. Explain that to us from the Vedas.
Brahmā said:
Having purified himself, that Devāpi diligently summoned the Vedas;
endowed with meditation and austerity, the Vedas appeared before him.
Devāpi, bowing again and again,
spoke to the Vedas and presented the words of the officiating priests, the words of Agni, and the words of the gods.
The Vedas said:
"O Father, we are dependent, following the will of the Lord;
[He is] the support of the entire world, yet Himself without support and untainted."
He is the sole abode of all power, the treasury of all prosperity;
he is Mahādeva, the creator, and he is Maheśvara, the destroyer.
O Brahmin, we are composed of sound; we speak and we indeed know.
This is our duty—that which you ask us, we shall speak.
"By whom were they led away? What was his name, what was that city, and likewise what was his army? We know only this: we have been devoured and destroyed."
We shall also know what your capability is, whom you must propitiate, and where it must be done, so that you may attain those cities.
Brahmā said:
Having heard this, he reflected for a very long time within his heart and spoke concerning the Vedas.
Devāpi said:
"Let the Vedas declare all this exactly as it is;
I shall reach every single one of them once they have been brought down to the ground. Sufficient! Let there be salutations to you."
The Vedas said:
"O Devāpi, go to Gautamī and praise Maheśvara there;
being well-pleased, that compassionate one will surely grant you your desire."
O high-minded one, it is true that when praised, the god Śiva becomes pleased;
and King Ārṣṭiṣeṇa’s wife was the virtuous Jayā.
"Your father Upamanyu also stands at the base [of the mountain] in good health;
by the boon of Maheśvara, you shall obtain fame and merit after slaying the Rākṣasa couple— this is possible, and nothing else."
Brahmā said:
Then, by the word of the Veda, the young Devāpi went to Gautamī;
having bathed and made his resolve, the brahmin praised Maheśvara.
Devāpi said:
"I am but a child, O Lord of the gods; you are the teacher of my teachers.
I have no power to offer praise to you; O Śambhu, salutations be unto you!"
Neither the Vedas, nor the gods, nor the sages know you;
neither Brahmā nor even Vaikuṇṭha knows you. Whatever you are, that you are—salutations be unto you!
O Maheśvara, you protect those in the world who are without a protector, those who are wretched, those who are poor and diseased, and those whose natures are sinful.
O Lord of the worlds, the inhabitants of heaven, when worshipped by you with austerities, observances, and mantras, will bestow upon them the fruit granted by you.
It would not be surprising if those who ask were the givers and whatever they desired came to pass for them; you, however, act quite the opposite.
O Lord, O Teacher of the World, you protect those who are ignorant, those who are sinful, and those who are submerged in the ocean of hell, by the mere utterance of the word "Śiva."
{Brahmā said:} As he was thus offering praise, the Three-eyed One spoke before him.
Śiva said:
"Choose a boon, O Devāpi; enough of this wretchedness, my boy."
Devāpi said:
"O Lord of the World, I desire to obtain the king, the queen, and my father— who was my preceptor— and also the death of my enemy."
Brahmā said:
Having heard the words of Devāpi, the Lord of All replied, "So be it. By the command of Śaṅkara, all that was accomplished by Devāpi.
Furthermore, O Nārada, Śambhu, the source of compassion for the gods, spoke to him again and dispatched Nandin with his trident.
Having slain the Asura leaders in the netherworld (rasātala),
Nandin brought their fathers and others together and presented them to him.
And there occurred the horse sacrifice of the wise Ārṣṭiṣeṇa;
and Agni, the officiating priests, the gods, the Vedas, and the sages spoke.
Agni and the others said: "Where Śambhu himself, the God of gods, the Lord of the universe, who is compassionate toward his devotees, was present— O Devāpi— that place became a divine tirtha."
This sacred ford (tīrtha) shall cause the destruction of all sins, bestow all perfections upon men, grant merit, and your fame shall be eternal.
Brahmā said:
When the horse sacrifice had concluded, the gods granted them boons;
having bathed in the Gaṅgā and achieved their purpose, they then ascended to heaven.
From that time forward, fifteen thousand and eight hundred holy fords (tīrthas) came to exist there on both banks;
they know that bathing and giving gifts in them yield exceedingly great fruit.
Brahmā said:
There is the place known as Tapovana, as well as the confluence with the Nandinī;
there is also the Siddheśvara tīrtha on the southern bank of the Gautamī.
And there is the one known as Śārdūla; hear this account of them, by the mere hearing of which one is liberated from all sins.
In former times, Agni was the Hotṛ priest of the gods, the bearer of their oblations;
he obtained as his wife the daughter of Dakṣa, named Svāhā, who was endowed with beautiful form.

In former times she was childless, and for the sake of a son she entered upon ascetic penance. As she was performing intense austerity, pleasing the Consumer of Oblations (Agni), that husband, the Fire-god, spoke to his blameless wife Svāhā.
Agni said:
"Offspring shall come to be; do not practice austerities, O beautiful one."
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of her husband, she desisted from her ascetic penance;
for there is nothing anywhere that grants women their desired objects except the word of a husband.
Then, after some time had passed, when fear of Tāraka had arisen, and while Kārttikeya was not yet born, having remained in seclusion for a long duration; ||| BrP_128.7 |||
Terrified by Maheśvara and Bhavānī, the gods assembled together;
for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods, the denizens of heaven spoke to Agni.
The gods said:
"O illustrious god, go to Śambhu, who is worshipped by the three worlds;
report this fear arising from Tāraka to Śambhu."
Agni said:
"One must not go to that place where a married couple remains in private;
this is the rule by general principle alone—how much more so in the case of the wielder of the trident?"
If one should overhear the words of a couple who are standing in private, speaking freely and full of passion, there shall be no deliverance for that person from hell.
He is the lord of all worlds, Mahākāla, the bearer of the trident;
by whom could he be beheld when he stands in private with Bhavānī?
The gods said:
"When great danger has arrived, what principle can be cited here?
Since fear has arisen from Tāraka, you yourself must go and become Tāraka."
Since the lives of the virtuous in this ocean of great fear exist for the sake of others,
go with whatever form you have, or speak words however you may.
"Having proclaimed the word of the gods, come quickly to Śambhu;
then, O sage, we shall offer worship to both of you in both worlds."
Brahmā said:
Having become a parrot, the consumer of oblations (Agni) went swiftly at the word of the god to where the Lord of the worlds was sporting with Umā.
Then, becoming a parrot, that fire fled as if in fear;
however, the carrier of oblations was unable to enter at the gateway.
Then he stood at the window, shaking his head with his face cast downward;
seeing him, Śambhu laughed and spoke to Umā in private: Br̥hatprokta Purāṇa 128.18.
Śambhu said:
"Behold, O Goddess, the parrot who has arrived from the word of the gods like a fire."
Brahmā said:
Embarrassed, Pārvatī said to the god, "Enough,
O Lord," to that Agni, the lord of gods, who was moving before him in the form of a brahmin.
Having summoned him many times, you have been recognized here, O Agni; do not speak!
Tear open your own mouth, seize this [child], and take him away.
Having said this, he cast much semen into Agni's mouth;
then Agni, containing that seed within him, was not at all able to move.
Then, exhausted, Agni approached the bank of the celestial river (Suranadī);
and because that seed was cast into the Kṛttikās, he became Kārttikeya.
And whatever remained of the Śambhu-nature within Agni’s body,
that very semen Agni cast in two parts into his own wife.
Long ago, when Svāhā was his beloved and especially desirous of a son, she was reassured by him: "You shall have offspring."
Then, O Lord of Fire, having recollected that, the Śāmbhava light was cast into that semen of Agni;
from it, an excellent pair was born.
Suvarṇa and Suvarṇā were peerless on earth in beauty;
they were a constant source of delight to Agni and increased the joy of all the worlds.
Out of affection, Agni gave that golden [daughter] to the wise Dharma;
then he made Saṃkalpā the beloved wife of his son Suvarṇa.
In this manner, the sage Kavi performed the marriage of both his son and his daughter.
Due to the fault of the mutual intermingling of their seed,
both were likewise the offspring of Agni;
thus the son was Suvarṇa, possessing many forms.
Having assumed the forms of the best of the gods—
the wives of Indra, Vāyu, and Kubera, as well as those of the Lord of Waters and the lords of sages— BrP 128.29d–128.30b.
O son of Kavi, Suvarṇa constantly goes to his wife,
assuming whatever form she desires; and having done so, he departs for some other place.
And having assumed the form of their husbands among those devoted wives, he of noble nature took delight with them, making Madana’s purpose fulfilled by acting incessantly.
Having done so, Suvarṇā departed for some unknown place; likewise, Dharmas wife, named Suvarṇā,
the daughter of Svāhā, became a wanton woman.
Whosoever had a woman in their mind, she herself, having assumed the form of a wife, being golden-hued, took pleasure with those husbands— whether they were human or asuras.
The gods, the sages, those in the form of ancestors, and others endowed with beauty, magnanimity, steadfastness, and profundity— whichever deity’s intended wife she was; BrP 128.33c–34a.
Taking on that form, she delights with him through various means and many instruments,
attracting his mind toward the fulfillment of desire.
Having thus observed the behavior of Suvarṇa,
as well as that of Agni’s daughter and Agni himself,
they all then became enraged at Agni and reviled him.
The gods and asuras said: "O son and daughter,
this which has been done by you is of a transgressive nature."
"O Havyavāha, because you lived under a disguise in a sinful form, may your son be unfaithful, wandering everywhere."
Likewise, O Agni, even gold is not fixed to a single state; it does not find satisfaction in one thing alone, yet it transforms into many beings of various kinds, some of whom are contemptible.
"And this fault shall belong to your daughter. Having heard these words of the curse, Agni became as if terrified.
(Brahmā said: 128.37d. Thus spoke Brahmā.
128.37d. [The text continues: "Having heard this speech of the curse, Agni became as if extremely afraid."
Approaching me, he then said: "Tell me the means of atonement for my two sons."
Then I said, "O Vahni, go to Gautamī and Śaṅkara;
having praised him there, O mighty-armed one, report this to the Lord of the World."
O Vahni, because of the power of Maheśvara residing within your body, such offspring as this was born to you; therefore, you have become [as you are].
Report such a curse of the gods to the God;
for his protection of his own offspring, Śambhu will bring about what is beneficial.
"Praise the God and the Goddess with devotion; Śiva will become pleased, and then you shall obtain your beloved desires regarding offspring."
Then, at my command, Agni went to Gaṅgā and, being self-restrained, praised Maheśvara with words and hymns equal to the Vedas.
Agni said:
I bow to that Lord of the World, the creator of the entire universe, whose form is the universe itself, who is untainted, the primordial maker, and the self-existent one.
I bow to that Tryambaka, who, having become fire, withdraws the world, who indeed creates it in the form of water, and who protects it in the form of the sun.
Brahmā said:
Then the blessed, infinite, and imperishable Śambhu was pleased and invited Pāvaka, who is worshipped by the gods, to choose a boon.
That disciplined one said to Śiva, "Your virility resides within me;
by it, a beautiful son has been born, Suvarṇa, renowned throughout the world."
Likewise, O Lord of the World, Suvarṇā was born as his daughter;
and from the mutual union of their vital energies, both of these [qualities] arose due to that defect.
O Śiva, because of their transgression, the offspring became tainted with fault;
all the gods pronounced a curse upon them, so bring about peace for them, O Lord. (BrP 128.49)
Then, at the word of Agni, Śambhu spoke these words of auspicious outcome.
Śambhu said: "From my seed, through you, Suvarṇa of great prowess was born;
all perfections in their entirety are concentrated within this Suvarṇa."
They will come to pass, O Fire, have no doubt; listen to my words:
he shall become the purifier of even the three worlds.
He alone is the nectar in the world; he alone is beloved by the gods;
he alone is both worldly enjoyment and liberation; he alone is the sacrificial fee.
He alone is the form of everything; he is the teacher even of teachers. One should know that vigor is most excellent—that vigor which is superior even to me.
Especially since it has been cast upon you, what need is there for further deliberation?
Without him, everything is deficient; with him, all prosperities are complete.
Even while living, all men are as good as dead without gold;
a man with wealth is honored even if he lacks virtues, whereas one without wealth is not honored even if he possesses them.
Therefore, there shall be nothing superior to this gold;
yet even this gold, though excellent, may be fickle.
"Everything seen by her, whether deficient or complete, shall become perfect;
she is the one who is to be attained through austerity, recitation, and oblations throughout the three worlds."
O Agni, her power and excellence are proclaimed in part;
she who abides everywhere shall come and move about.
From this day forward, Kamalā shall be manifest as Suvarṇā and become pure for her two sons as they act according to their own will.
Nevertheless, the merit of these two has neither been nor will it ever be.
Brahmā said:
Having spoken thus, Śambhu, the auspicious one, then appeared there in person in the form of a *liṅga*, out of a desire for the welfare of all the worlds.
Then, having obtained boons from his two sons, Agni became satisfied;
and Suvarṇā, the daughter of Agni, was likewise delighted by her husband Dharmasuta.
O Sage, in the meantime, the son of Agni also joyfully brought forth his daughter, Suvarṇā, by means of his mental resolve.
And having disregarded that Dharma, Śārdūla, the lord of the Dānavas,
deceitfully carried off her who was the abode of fortune, good luck, and splendor.
By him, Suvarṇā, renowned throughout the world, was led to Rasātala;
he was the son-in-law of Agni and the embodiment of Dharma, and he was indeed Agni, the bearer of oblations.
Having praised Viṣṇu, the Lord of the worlds, again and again,
both of them made their request known to the Almighty.
Then Hari severed the head of Śārdūla with his discus;
the goddess Suvarṇā, the beauty of the world, was brought back by Viṣṇu.
O Nārada, Viṣṇu showed her to Maheśvara— she who was the daughter of Maheśvara and likewise the beloved of Agni.
Maheśa was also delighted and embraced her again and again,
where the radiant discus that had destroyed the tiger had been washed.
That place is renowned as Cakratīrtha, and they know it as Śārdūla,
where that Suvarṇā was led by Viṣṇu into the presence of Śaṅkara.
That sacred ford (tīrtha) should be known as belonging to Śaṅkara, yet it is indeed established as belonging to Viṣṇu;
for there Agni and the eternal Dharma attained supreme bliss.
O best of sages, where the tears of joy fell from Agni,
there the river was born as Ānandā, and likewise as Nandinī.
And the confluence of that river with the Gaṅgā is indeed auspicious; there Śiva himself resides, and at that very confluence, Suvarṇā remains present even today.
She alone is known as Dākṣāyaṇī, Śivā, and Āgneyī;
she is Ambikā, the support of the world, Śivā, and the sovereign Kātyāyanī.
Constantly bestowing the desired objects of its devotees, having adorned both its banks, Agni performed penance there; that sacred site is indeed Tapovana.
O Sage, such are the sacred fords on both banks;
bathing and giving gifts at them bestow all desires and are auspicious.
On the northern shore there are fourteen thousand,
and likewise on the southern shore there are sixteen thousand.
In each of those places, there are indeed sacred fords (tīrthas) possessing their own identifying marks;
they have distinct names, which I shall now state in brief.
Whoever hears these, whoever recites them, or whoever remembers them,
that person shall become fully successful in all their desired aims.
Whoever, having learned this account, performs bathing and other rites there,
shall always become possessed of fortune and especially endowed with righteousness.
To the west of Abjakā is the sacred ford known as Śārdūla;
it is indeed superior to all the sacred fords beginning with Vārāṇasī.
Having bathed there, one honors and gratifies the ancestors and the gods;
liberated from all sins, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
And from the penance grove, tigers [emerge] amidst all the sacred fords without exception;
the majesty of each one of them cannot be described here by anyone.
Brahmā said:
Right there is the one known as Indratīrtha, and also Vṛṣākapa;
where the confluence of the Phena river occurs, there likewise is Hanūmata.
And regarding that which is called Abjaka, where the god Trivikrama resides—
there, bathing and giving gifts result in the difficulty of returning [to this world].
In that regard, I shall now describe the sacred sites on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā;
listen with devotion and restrained vows to those on the northern bank as well, beginning with Indreśvara.
Namuci was powerful, the enemy of Indra, and intoxicated with pride;
a battle took place between him and Indra, and Indra struck off his head with foam.

And having severed the head of the enemy Namuci, who was the lord of the waters, by means of that foam which had assumed the form of a thunderbolt, he cast that foam upon the southern bank of the Gaṅgā.
Having pierced the earth, it fell and entered the subterranean realm (rasātala)—
that water of the Gaṅgā born from the subterranean realm, which purifies the entire universe.
By the path indicated by Vajra, that water reached the circle of the earth;
it is known as the river Phena because of its name "foam."
The confluence of that river with the Gaṅgā is world-renowned and holy;
it causes the destruction of all sins, just like the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Indeed, it was there that Hanūmat’s mother, by the mere act of bathing,
was liberated from her state as a cat through the grace of Viṣṇu and the Gaṅgā.
And that sacred ford was previously called Mārjāra by me to you;
it is also called Hanūmata, and the narrative concerning it has been told before.
Listen now with a disciplined mind to this account of Vṛṣākapi and Abjaka:
there was a powerful one known as Hiraṇya, the first-born among the Daityas.
Having performed austerities, he became exceedingly terrible and invincible to all the gods;
his son was likewise powerful and always difficult for the gods to conquer.
He was known as Mahāśani, and his wife was Parājitā;
with him, Indra fought a continuous battle for a long time.
The great thunderbolt, possessed of great heroism, having constantly conquered Śakra together with his elephant at the forefront of battle, announced it to his father.
Having bound her and brought her along with the elephant, the Daitya then beheld his sister; abandoning his cruelty, he presented her to Hiraṇya.
The Daitya Mahāśanipitā, the most ancient of the ancients,
stationed Śacī’s beloved on the ground and then provided him with protection.
Having conquered Hari, Mahāśani went forth to conquer Varuṇa;
but Varuṇa, who possessed great wisdom, gave his daughter to Mahāśani.
Varuṇa gave the ocean as his own abode to Mahāśani;
thus, a friendship arose between Varuṇa and Mahāśani.
And the maiden Vāruṇī also became the beloved of Mahāśani,
on account of his heroism, fame, valor, and strength.
The great Daitya Mahāśani was peerless in the three worlds;
when Indra had lost his sovereignty over the world, all the gods invited him [to assume it].
The gods said:
"Viṣṇu alone shall be the giver of Indra, and he alone shall be the slayer of the Daityas;
or he alone shall be the seer of the mantra, and he will appoint another as Indra."
Brahmā said:
Having deliberated thus, those gods reported the counsel of Viṣṇu,
saying, "The great Daitya Mahāśani is incapable of being slain by me."
Then Viṣṇu went to Varuṇa, his father-in-law, the lord of the waters;
having approached Varuṇa, Keśava announced the defeat of Indra.
"O Sage, you must act in such a way that Purandara comes;
for this reason, at the word of Viṣṇu, the Lord of Waters went quickly."
Varuṇa, the lord, was highly honored by that son-in-law, who was the husband of his daughter, born of Hiraṇyakaśipu, valiant, and like a great thunderbolt.
Then the Daitya asked his father-in-law about the reason for his arrival with humility;
Varuṇa told that Daitya the purpose of his coming.
Varuṇa said:
"O mighty-armed friend, give back Indra, that lord of the gods who was previously conquered by you and bound while he dwelt in the netherworld."
O slayer of my enemies, grant us that which is always worthy of honor;
for the release of an enemy once captured brings great glory to the virtuous.
Brahmā said:
Having said "So be it," that lord of the Daityas somehow gave Indra, the beloved of Śacī, together with his elephant, to Varuṇa.
Shining most brilliantly in the midst of the Daityas,
he then addressed Hari in the presence of the Lord of Waters,
having honored him with great offerings.
The Great Thunderbolt spoke to Maghavan:
"By whom have you been made Indra today? By whom?"
Your vigor is such that you speak much,
yet you are oppressed by enemies in battle;
nevertheless, that you remain Indra is truly marvelous.
Furthermore, it is logical that if a woman has been bound by a man, her husband should release her;
for women are not independent and have men as their primary authority.
"O virtuous Śakra, you shall indeed become a man;
bound by me in combat with my mount, your weapon, the thunderbolt of unrestrained power, [shall be taken away]."
The wish-fulfilling gem, the Nandana grove, those women, fame, strength, and even that which is enjoyed by the King of the Gods—
all this indeed belongs to you; yet, why have you been released from the Lord of the Waters?
You desire life—fie on this life of yours! That alone is true living which is a repository for fame; that which is contrary to fame is death itself.
Knowing this, O Śakra, how can you not feel shame that you have attained liberation from the lords of the waters while remaining in heaven, surrounded [by your retinue]? (BrP 129.34c–35a)
Fanned by all the gods with their beloveds and likewise praised by the Apsarases,
I think that surely it is shame itself that fears you.
"You are the slayer of Vṛtra and the killer of Namuci; you are the breaker of forts, the piercer of mountain-cows, with the thunderbolt in your arm.
Thus do the gods worship you.
Therefore, O Jiṣṇu, abandon all this modification that arises from what is harmful;
those who live thus enter into the worlds.
"How was it that the Creator— the lotus-born Brahmā, who is difficult even for those like you to dislodge— did not cause your heart to break? {Brahmā said:}
Having spoken thus to the high-souled Varuṇa, the lord of the Daityas gave back Indra and addressed him with these words:
Mahāśani said: "From this day forward, this Indra shall be your disciple and Varuṇa your teacher;
he is my father-in-law, by whom you have attained liberation, O Vāsava."
Therefore, you must conduct yourself toward Varuṇa with the attitude of a servant;
otherwise, having bound you, I shall indeed cast you back down into the netherworld.
{Brahmā said:} Having thus rebuked Śakra and laughing at him again and again, he said, "Go, go! and then dismissed Varuṇa as well.
Having returned to his own abode, he was overwhelmed with shame and told Paulomī everything regarding that defeat by his enemy.
Indra said:
"O fair-faced one, O fortunate lady, since I have been treated thus by my enemy,
tell me how I may extinguish myself."
Indrāṇī said:
"O Śakra, O slayer of Bala, I know the rise of the Dānavas, their illusory powers, their defeat, the granting of boons, and likewise their death."
Therefore, listen as I shall tell you everything for your pleasure: from what cause his death or even his defeat might arise.
The son of Hiraṇya was a heroic and powerful man; he was the son of my paternal uncle, and by virtue of a boon he had received, he became arrogant and thus became my brother.
He gratified Brahmā through austerity and self-restraint;
what cannot be accomplished by austerity when one has attained such power?
Therefore, you must not entertain any passion for the mind or any sense of wonder in any way; listen rather to this which is to be done, as it has come down in due order.
{Brahmā said:} Having spoken thus, Paulomī, filled with humility, addressed Indra.
Indrāṇī said:
"There is nothing unattainable through austerity, nothing unattainable through the performance of sacrifice,
and nothing unattainable through devotion to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, or to Hara."
Furthermore, O beloved lord of the gods, I have heard this most excellent truth: that women alone understand the true nature of women.
Therefore, O Lord, there is nothing unattainable for the earth or likewise for the waters,
since asceticism, sacrificial rites, and so forth, arise from those two alone.
Even there, you should go to that ground which has become a sacred ford (tīrtha);
having worshipped Viṣṇu and Śiva there, you will obtain all your desires.
Furthermore, it has been heard that those women who are devoted to their husbands know everything; by them, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is sustained.
Among the essences of the earth, there is the Daṇḍaka forest;
therein flows the Gaṅgā, the mother of the world. There, O Lord, worship the Master.
Or Viṣṇu, the Lord of the worlds, the all-pervading one who removes the suffering of the distressed and the afflicted,
for those men here who are without a protector and are sinking in the ocean of misery.
Neither Hara, nor Hari, nor Gaṅgā, nor indeed any other refuge exists anywhere;
therefore, with all effort and a concentrated mind, satisfy these [deities].
Perform [this] with devotion, through hymns of praise, and through austerity, together with me;
then you shall obtain the auspiciousness born from the grace of the Lord Viṣṇu.
If one performs an action without knowing its single quality, it will yield fruit for the doer;
but if performed with knowledge, it shall be a hundredfold, and through a wife, that becomes inexhaustible.
In all undertakings, a wife alone is a man’s companion in this world;
for even the accomplishment of the smallest tasks does not occur without her.
O Lord, a man shall receive half the fruit of a deed performed by one person alone;
however, he shall obtain the full merit of that which is performed with his wife.
Therefore, this is well known from the Vedic revelation that "the wife is half [of the husband]";
it is heard that in the Daṇḍaka forest there is the Gautamī, the best of rivers.
It pacifies all sins without exception and bestows all desired objects;
therefore, go there with me and perform meritorious deeds that yield great fruit.
Then, having slain your enemies in battle, you will obtain great happiness.
Brahmā said:
Having said "So be it" to his preceptor and his wife, Śatakratu went to the Gaṅgā, the sustainer of the world, who is renowned as the Gautamī.
The joyful Hari went to the midst of the Daṇḍaka forest and set his mind upon performing austerities for Śambhu, the God of gods.
Having first bowed to the Gaṅgā and bathed there with palms joined in reverence,
he took refuge solely in Śiva and then recited this hymn of praise.
Indra said:
He who, by his own creative power (māyā), creates, protects, and devours the entire world of moving and non-moving beings, yet remains unattached to it— [he is the Lord].
May that Pinākapāṇi— the one who is independent, non-dual consciousness, and whose nature is bliss— be gracious toward us;
he whose true essence even Sanaka and the other sages do not know.
May that Lord of Pārvatī, who knows the secret wisdom of the Vedānta, the granter of all desires, and the slayer of Andhaka, be gracious unto me.
Having himself created Viriñci, the Lord Svayambhū beheld his terrifying head;
having severed it with the tips of his nails, he [cast] it away as it clung to his claws.
From that [desire], he cast [the other qualities] away, and thus the triad of aims (trivarga) arose;
then, from that [triad], sin, poverty, greed, begging,
delusion, and discord emerged, followed by infinity (ananta).
Seeing that this entire world had become pervaded by them— possessing the nature of the suffering of existence and having manifested its power— the Lord of the Gods was struck with awe.
He said to the Goddess: "The world is coming to its end;
protect the world, O Sovereign of the World, Mother of the World!
O Umā, O Refuge, O Auspicious One, O Subhadrā!"
O foundation of the world, O bestower of boons, be victorious! You are worldly enjoyment, meditative absorption, and supreme liberation;
you are Svāhā, Svadhā, Svasti, and primordial perfection.
You are speech and intellect, O undecaying and immortal one;
in the form of knowledge and so forth, you shall indeed provide protection throughout the three worlds by my command.
"The three worlds must have been created by you alone,
since they are inherently so diverse by their very nature.
Thus was his beloved addressed by Hara.
Intent on embracing and conversation,
she became weary while firmly clinging to half of Bhava’s body,
and she wiped away the sweat from her fingertips.
From that, first there arose Dharma, then Lakṣmī, then charity, then well-timed rain,
and lakes possessing abundant purity.
Grains, flowers, and fruits;
articles of good fortune, a beautiful body, fine attire,
and great medicinal herbs that partake of the erotic sentiment.
Dances, songs, the ancient nectar [of the Purāṇas], the Śruti and Smṛti, ethics, as well as food and drink,
weapons, treatises, and articles useful for the household; BrP 129.77c–78a.
Weapons, sacred fords, and forests; sacrifices, charitable works, and auspicious rites; vehicles, bright ornaments, and seats—BrP_129.78b–d.
Through the intense laughter arising from contact with the limbs of existence, and through various secret forms of perspiration and conversation,
the entire world of moving and non-moving beings was likewise brought into being.
And from that, O Goddess, there arose what is free from evil—
abundant happiness, auspiciousness, and constancy;
and this, O Goddess, shines forth through your power.
Therefore, O Mother of the World, foremost among all beings, protect me who am terrified of fears;
for some are bewildered by logical arguments, while others dissolve into that very state.
I bow to that beautiful form, the non-duality of Śiva and Śakti at that time.
Brahmā said:
As he was thus offering praise, Śiva appeared before him.
Śiva said:
"O Hari, tell me what desired boon you seek; speak your ultimate goal."
Indra said:
"I had a powerful enemy who was like Saturn in appearance;
by him I was bound, brought to the ground, and humiliated in many ways."
"Pierced by the arrows of speech, this work has been composed for his destruction;
O Lord of the worlds, O Master, it is for that purpose that I shall conquer my enemy."
Grant me that very vigor and whatever else may destroy my enemies; for once that defeat from which I have arisen is undone,
I consider it better than the birth of fame or the splendor of victory.
Brahmā said:
That Śiva spoke this to Śakra: "Your enemy will not meet his death by me alone;
therefore, you [must also approach] Viṣṇu, the imperishable Hari."
With single-minded devotion, propitiate the god Janārdana Nārāyaṇa, the sole refuge of the three worlds, together with Paulomī.
"Then you shall obtain what is dear from him and from me as well, O Hari.
Thus spoke again the Blessed One, Maheśvara, the primordial creator.
The sages know that the practice of mantras, austerity, or even the practice of yoga bestows perfection at any place whatsoever where there is a confluence [of these].
How much more so, O Brahmin, at the confluence of the Gautamī and the foam of the Sindhu,
or in the caves of mountains, or indeed at the junction of rivers?
A Brahmin becomes wise through his mind alone when it is fixed upon the feet of Mukunda;
such was the lordly sage Āpastamba on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā.
I also attained his favor, O slayer of Bala;
therefore, you too, along with your wife, should propitiate the wielder of the mace.
Brahmā said:
Together with Āpastamba, having bathed with self-restraint at the holy confluence on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā, he then offered praise to the God.
Then, at the confluence of the Phena and the Gaṅgā, he propitiated the god Janārdana with various Vedic mantras and through ascetic penance.
Then Viṣṇu became pleased and asked, "What should be given?
The Blessed Lord Hari replied, "Give me a slayer of my enemies. (BrP 129.96)
"Know that it has been given," so Janārdana said to him;
there, by the grace of both Gaṅgā and Viṣṇu, it belonged solely to Śiva.
Born from the waters, bearing the forms of Śiva and Viṣṇu,
with the discus in his hand and holding a trident, he went to the netherworld (rasātala).
Then he struck down the Daitya Indraśatru with a great thunderbolt;
that Vṛṣākapi, born from the lotus, became a friend of Indra.
Even while staying in heaven, Indra always followed that Vṛṣākapi.
Seeing him attached to another woman, Śacī became angry out of love;
then Śatamanyu, smiling, spoke these words to her as he was consoling her.
Indra said:
"O Indrāṇī, I am not a refuge for anyone except my friend Vṛṣākapi,
whose water or oblation is always pleasing to Agni."
"I shall not go elsewhere, my dear; I swear this to you by your own body.
Therefore, O beautiful woman, you ought not to speak to me with suspicion regarding another."
"You are my devoted wife, dear to me, my companion in dharma and counsel;
you have noble offspring and are of high birth—what other woman could be dearer to me than you?"
Therefore, by your instruction, having reached the great river Gaṅgā through the grace of Viṣṇu, the god of gods, who holds the discus in his hand—
Likewise, by the grace of the god Śiva, Vṛṣākapi,
and from my friend Jalodbhava, who is world-renowned as Abjaka.
"O fortunate one, I am Indra, the imperishable, who has crossed over suffering from here;
what is there that cannot be accomplished when one's wife follows the heart of her husband? (BrP 129.106)
Liberation from that is difficult for us; however, in this auspicious state, the triad beginning with wealth is present, and birth itself is the supreme friend, desiring our welfare in both worlds.
If she is of noble birth, speaks kindly, is devoted to her husband, beautiful, rich in virtues,
and remains the same in both prosperity and adversity—
"For what indeed is impossible for her here in the three worlds?
Therefore, O beloved, through your wisdom this auspicious thing has come to me;
from now on, you alone must carry out what has been spoken by me, for there is nothing else for me to do."
In the next world and in matters of dharma, there is nothing like a virtuous son;
yet in this world, for a man who is afflicted, there is no medicine like a wife.
For the attainment of the state of supreme bliss and likewise for liberation from sin, there is nothing equal to the Gaṅgā; listen to another [truth], O fair-faced one.
For the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, and for liberation from sin,
there is no [other means] for liberation here than the knowledge of the non-difference between Śiva and Viṣṇu.
Therefore, O virtuous lady, all this that has been in your mind has been attained through your own intellect and by the grace of Śiva, Viṣṇu, and the Gaṅgā.
"O beautiful lady, I consider my lordship over Indra to be secure once again through the power of Mitra;
for Vṛṣākapi is my friend, he who was born from the waters."
And you are my constant dear friend; nothing else is more beloved to me than you.
Among sacred fords, Gautamī-Gaṅgā is supreme, and among gods, Hari and Śaṅkara.
Therefore, through faith in these [deities], one obtains everything desired;
and this sacred ford (tīrtha), renowned throughout the three worlds, brings me great joy.
Therefore, I shall indeed request this from all the gods in due order;
may the sages, Gaṅgā, Hari, and Śaṅkara grant their approval.
On both banks of the Indreśvara and Abjaka [rivers], there are gods;
on one side is Lord Śaṅkara, and on the other is Janārdana.
Purifying the Daṇḍaka forest, he is Viṣṇu Trivikrama in person;
and whatever holy fords exist within it, they bestow all merit.
But here, by the mere act of bathing, they shall all attain liberation;
both the most sinful shall obtain release from their sins, as well as those who are righteous.
But their supreme liberation is achieved through the five-times-five ancestors;
and in this regard, even those who give as much as a mere sesame seed to those in need [attain it].
For those who give, that [gift] shall be inexhaustible, bestowing both desires and liberation;
it is auspicious, conducive to fame, long life, and health, and it increases merit.
Having understood this narrative of Viṣṇu and Śambhu, which grants liberation through bathing,
those who hear and recite the majesty of this sacred site (tīrtha) [attain the same].

May they become partakers of merit; may mindfulness toward Śiva and Viṣṇu arise for them right here, which severs the entire multitude of sins and which sages whose senses and minds are conquered pray for.
"Brahmā said:
"The gods and sages said to him, 'It shall be exactly so.
On the northern bank of the Gautamī, there is a place among the holy fords that bestows liberation. (BrP 129.125)
Then, there are indeed seven thousand sacred sites frequented by celestial sages and perfected beings,
and likewise, there are eleven sacred fords on the southern bank.
The lotus-born [Abjaka] is declared by the lords of sages to be the heart of Godāvarī,
the place of rest for Īśa, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā alike.
Brahmā said:
There is a sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Āpastamba, renowned throughout the three worlds,
which is capable of destroying the entire multitude of sins even by its mere remembrance.
The highly wise sage Āpastamba was possessed of great renown;
his wife, named Akṣasūtrā, was entirely devoted to the duties toward her husband.
Then his son, named Karka, who was highly wise and a knower of reality,
had an ashram which Agastya, the best of sages, reached.
Having honored that Agastya, the wise Āpastamba, the lord of sages,
followed by his disciples, proceeded to question him.
Āpastamba said:
O best of sages, among these three—who is indeed worthy of worship?
From whom do both worldly enjoyment and liberation arise, and who might be without beginning?
"O Brahmin, who is infinite? Who is the deity even of the gods?
Which god is worshipped with sacrifices? And who is celebrated in the Vedas?
