O great sage Agastya, please speak to cut through this doubt of mine."
Agastya said:
"Sound is said to be the authority for dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
even among those, the Vedic sound is considered the supreme authority."
That person who is sung of by the Veda is higher than the highest;
he who has died is to be known as the lower, while the other is called the immortal.
That which is formless is to be known as the Supreme (para), while that which is formed is called the Non-Supreme (apara).
Due to the differentiation of the pervasion of the qualities (guṇas), this formed [Non-Supreme] becomes threefold.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are said to be one alone, expressed in three ways;
for that which is to be known is indeed the single supreme reality among all three gods.
The single [Being] manifests in many ways through the differentiation of qualities and actions;
for the sake of benefiting the worlds, there arise three types of forms.
He who knows the supreme reality is a wise man, and no other;
he who speaks of duality therein is called a breaker of the [spiritual] marks.
There is no atonement for one who would speak of division among these three;
for the three gods are each a distinct manifestation of the same form.
The Vedas are authoritative in all respects regarding those things that possess form, each in its own distinct way;
however, that which is formless and one is considered by you to be superior to them.
Āpastamba said:
"No certain conclusion has been reached by me in this matter.
Therefore, let that secret which lies therein be quickly deliberated upon and declared."
Free from doubt and free from conceptual construction, one is a vessel for all prosperity.
Having heard this, the venerable Agastya spoke these words: [BrP 130.16]
Agastya said:
Although there is no mutual distinction among these gods,
nevertheless, all success is attained only through Śiva, whose nature is bliss.

O sage, that which is the cause of phenomenal proliferation is the light, the supreme Śiva; seek refuge in that very Hara with supreme devotion at the Gautamī river and in the Daṇḍaka forest, for he is the destroyer of the entire flood of sins.
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of the sage, he attained supreme joy;
he who bestows enjoyment and liberation upon men, both with form and without form.
From that [source], he is capable of the form of creation and indeed the form of preservation;
he is the giver and the destroyer of all, since everything is concluded within him.
Agastya said:
She is described in all the Vedas as having the form of Brahmā, acting as the creator; likewise as Vaiṣṇavī, acting as the protector; and as having the form of Rudra, acting as the destroyer.
Brahmā said:
Then Āpastamba, having gone to the Gaṅgā and bathed while restrained by his vows,
praised the god Śaṅkara with this hymn, O Nārada.
Āpastamba said:
Fire resides in wood, fragrance in flowers,
trees and the like in seeds, and gold in rocks.
I go for refuge to that Somanātha who exists thus within all beings,
he who by his mere sport created this entire universe.
I go for refuge to that Someśvara, the creator and ordainer of the three worlds, who is the universal form, who transcends both being and non-being.
Remembering whom the embodied being is not touched by poverty, the great curse, nor by diseases and the like;
and relying upon whom they obtain their desires.
I go for refuge to that Someśvara,
by whom Brahmā and the others were formerly favored there after he had observed the dharma of the three Vedas.
Thus, I go for refuge to that Someśvara by whom the body was fashioned in two ways,
to whom the salutation purified by mantra is offered.
I go for refuge to that Someśvara, by whom the oblation has been offered, the worship performed, and the sacrificial gift bestowed, so that the gods partake of it. (BrP 130.27bcd)
Than whom there is nothing else more praiseworthy;
than whom there is nothing else more exceedingly subtle;
than whom there is nothing else greater among the great.
I go for refuge to that Someśvara,
by whose command this universe is variegated,
of inconceivable form, manifold, and vast.
Just as [the world] follows that which performs a single action,
I go for refuge to that Someśvara,
in whom reside all-pervading power and universal sovereignty.
I go for refuge to that Someśvara, who possesses the greatness of being the agent and the giver, whose nature is beginningless, and who is love, fame, and happiness.
He who is eternally the refuge of all and eternally worthy of worship;
he who is eternally dear to those who have come for shelter;
he who is eternally auspicious and the form of everything.
"I go for refuge to that Someśvara.
Brahmā said:
"Then the Blessed One, being pleased, spoke to that sage, Nārada."
Āpastamba has declared this auspicious teaching for the sake of oneself and for the sake of others.
"May they all obtain every desire who, having bathed, behold the Lord Īśvara, the Master of the worlds; so be it," Śiva said to the sage.
From that time forward, that sacred ford was called Āpastamba,
capable of uprooting the mass of beginningless darkness of ignorance.
Brahmā said:
Listen to this account of what occurred at that place renowned as Yamatīrtha, which increases the satisfaction of the ancestors and pacifies all sins without exception. (BrP 131.1)
In this regard, O Sage, there was this ancient historical narrative:
there is a divine dog well-known by the name Saramā.
Her two sons were two great dogs, who constantly followed people,
subsisted on wind, possessed four eyes, and were dear to Yama.
She was guarding the cattle intended for the sacrifice of the gods;
as she was protecting them, those Rākṣasas, Daityas, and Dānavas pursued her.
The highly wise ones, having diligently enticed that female dog— the mother of the two dogs— who was guarding her [the child],
with various words and gifts, [acted as follows].
"The auspicious cows were abducted by wicked Rākṣasas and intended for slaughter as sacrificial animals;
then, having arrived, that dog spoke this to the gods in due order."
Saramā said:

"O gods, having bound me with the nooses of the Rākṣasas and beaten me with their clubs, the cows have been led away for the sake of completing the sacrifice; they have been prepared as sacrificial animals."
{Brahmā said:} Having heard her words, Bṛhaspati quickly spoke to the gods: *BrP_131.8*
Bṛhaspati said:
"This woman has a deformed appearance, and I perceive evil in her.
It was by her consent that those cows were taken, and for no other reason."
This sinful woman appears, by her bodily gestures, as if she were a doer of good deeds.
Brahmā said:
Then, at the word of his preceptor, Śakra struck that bitch with his foot;
from the blow of his foot, milk then flowed forth from her mouth.
Again the husband of Śacī said: "O dog, milk was drunk by you, and it was given by the Rākṣasas; therefore, my cows have been led away."
Saramā said:
"O Lord, there is no fault on my part, nor on that of anyone else;
O Lord of the Thirty-three, there is neither offense nor negligence on my part."
Therefore, O Lord, why are you angry? For those enemies of yours are indeed powerful.
Brahmā said:
Then, having meditated and understood her conduct, the preceptor of the gods realized,
"O Śakra, this woman is truly wicked and acts as a partisan of our enemies."
Then Śakra cursed her: "O most wicked one, you shall become a bitch in the world of mortals, a sinful being who has committed evil through ignorance."
Thus, by the curse of Indra, she was born among humans;
for she, who had been cursed by Maghavan on account of her sin, was indeed exceedingly terrifying.
And making an effort to bring back those cows that had been carried off by the Rākṣasas,
the Lord of the Gods reported the matter to Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu made an effort to slay the Daityas, the Danujas, and the Rākṣasas who had stolen the cows, and he took up his great bow.
Janārdana himself remained there, honored by the gods; he is the conqueror of enemies and the one who, with his world-renowned Śārṅga bow, brings about the destruction of the Daityas.
In that very Daṇḍaka forest where the Lord of the World, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
resides, [he slew] the powerful Daityas, Danujas, and Rākṣasas stationed there.
Furthermore, that Viṣṇu, heard of as the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, slew those Rākṣasas by whom the cows had been led away there in the Daṇḍaka forest.
Then, O great sage, as Viṣṇu was fighting with the sons of Diti and the Rākṣasas,
they fled toward the southern direction out of fear of Viṣṇu.
Then Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, followed after them;
having overtaken them on Garuḍa, he pursued them with arrows released from the Śārṅga bow that were as swift as thought.
Viṣṇu struck them down with arrows on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā;
the enemies of the gods were brought to destruction by the powerful Viṣṇu.
Then those enemies of the gods met their destruction by Viṣṇu’s arrows, which were released from the Śārṅga bow with great velocity, accompanied by beautiful sounds, and well-aimed.
Where the cows were recovered by the gods, that place is called Bāṇatīrtha;
it is known throughout the world as Vaiṣṇava and is celebrated as Gotīrtha.
Cows intended for the sake of the sacrificial animals were on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā;
all those gods fled and settled them along the Gaṅgā.
In the midst of that, they caused an island to be made as a refuge for the cows;
with those cows there, the sacrifice to the gods was performed upon the Gaṅgā.
That is declared to be Yajñatīrtha, situated in the middle of the Gaṅgā within Godvīpa;
it is an auspicious place for the sacrifice of the gods that grants all desires.
O one of great splendor, the power of Gaṅgā herself has become incarnate;
she is the boat for crossing the essence-less and shoreless ocean of saṃsāra.
The Sovereign of All, the Yogamāyā who bestows fearlessness upon true devotees, [resides there];
and then there is the Gorakṣa Tīrtha on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā.
Those two dogs, the sons of Saramā, four-eyed and dear to Yama,
[related] their mother’s curse, their own transgression, and everything else in full detail.
Having offered [the oblation] according to the rule and performed the rite that bestows happiness,
they both questioned Yama regarding the removal of the curse as well.
Accompanied by those two, the son of Sūri spoke to his father, Sūrya;
having heard him, Sūrya said to his son, "O best of gods, [go] to the Gaṅgā."
O child, having bathed well and being perfectly composed with supreme faith at the Gautamī river in the Daṇḍaka forest— the sole purifier of the three worlds— [one should perform this].
"Praise Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and me, the Lord, in due order; with your whole being, you shall cause these two servants to attain delight."
Having heard those words of his father, Yama was then pleased in mind;
for the sake of pleasing those two who were offering libations to the gods, Yama set forth.
With his mind perfectly concentrated, he likewise gratified the best of the gods at the Aghahāriṇī on the Gautamī as well as at the Gaṅgā.
Accompanied by two dogs, the illustrious lord Yama, the master of the southern quarter,
gratified Brahmā on the southern bank.
To Īśāna in the north and to Viṣṇu himself, the powerful Dharma granted an excellent boon that removed the curse from Saramā;
she then requested many boons that would be beneficial to the worlds.
Yama said:
Those who perform ablutions in these [tirthas]— whether for their own sake or for the sake of others— even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara shall attain their auspicious desires.
Those who, having bathed at Bāṇatīrtha, indeed remember the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
for them there shall be no miseries of poverty in age after age.
Having bathed at Gotīrtha or Brahmatīrtha while restrained by his vows,
he should then pay homage to Brahmā and perform a circumambulation of the island.
Whoever should give even a small amount of wealth to a twice-born man, by him the earth, the sustainer of all things with its seven continents, has been circumambulated.
Having reached that sacrificial ground of the gods and having offered even a little into the fire,
one obtains the full fruit of sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha.
Whoever recites there even once the Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas, has indeed studied all the Vedas; free from desire, he becomes a vessel for liberation.
Having bathed on the southern bank and having worshipped the goddess Śakti with devotion according to the prescribed rule, one shall obtain all desires.
The Mother, who consists of the three Vedas, is the power (śakti) of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa;
she fulfills all desires, and one becomes possessed of sons and wealth.
That self-controlled man who, having bathed, beholds the Sun with devotion on the right side, has thereby performed sacrifices accompanied by various sacrificial fees.
Whoever bathes at the northern bank of the Gaṅgā and beholds the Slayer of Daityas, having bowed to him, attains the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, he who, having bathed with a disciplined mind, beholds Yameśvara, who is worshipped at the Yamatīrtha, indeed accomplishes [his goal] without delay.
There, through bathing, giving, recitation, and praise, the ancestors obtain inexhaustible merit that yields fruit and increases fame;
even those ancestors who have performed evil deeds shall attain liberation.
Brahmā said:
"O Nārada, there are eight thousand and three such sacred fords (tīrthas);
bathing and giving gifts in them all bestow inexhaustible merit."
The recollection of these is meritorious, destroying the sins of various births;
by hearing them, one is joined with the ancestors, and by reciting them, one is joined with one's own lineage.
Even their most heinous sins go to destruction by my command;
for one who, being self-restrained, performs bathing and other rites there and gives even a small gift.
Having performed the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and other rites for the ancestors, and having bowed to these deities,
[one obtains] wealth, grain, fame, valor, long life, and the perfection of health.
Having obtained sons, grandsons, a beloved wife, and whatever else he desired,
he remained inseparable from his kinsmen, joyful in mind, and highly honored by them.
Having delivered even his ancestors dwelling in hell and having purified his lineages,
being united with beloved ones, he should at the end remember Viṣṇu and Śiva;
then, according to the word of the gods, he shall go to the state of liberation.
Brahmā said:
There is a sacred ford named Yakṣiṇīsaṃgama, which bestows all fruits;
by bathing and giving gifts there, one shall obtain all desires.
Where the god Yakṣeśvara resides, who grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon being seen,
there one obtains the fruit of performing three great sacrifices merely by bathing.
Viśvāvasu’s sister, named Pippalā, who possessed a radiant smile,
went to the sacrificial session (*sattra*) of the seers dwelling on the banks of the Gautamī.
Seeing the emaciated sages there, she, being exceedingly arrogant, laughed;
she who had gone [there] spoke firmly, saying, "Let there be *vauṣaṭ*, let there be *śrauṣaṭ*! (BrP 132.4).
Speaking with a loud voice, they cursed her, saying, "Become one who discharges [fluids].
Thereupon, she became a river there, very well known as the Yakṣiṇī.
Then Viśvāvasu, having honored the sages and the three-eyed god,
and having approached Gautamī, brought about her release from that curse.
From that time forward, that sacred ford has been known as Yakṣiṇīsaṃgama;
by bathing and giving gifts there, one shall attain all desires.
Where Śambhu, accompanied by Śivā, became pleased with Viśvāvasu,
that supreme Śaiva tīrtha is renowned as Durgātīrtha.
O great sage, that indeed is the essence of all the foremost holy places; it removes the flood of all sins, destroys all miserable rebirths,
is celebrated by the best of sages as a sacred ford, and bestows all spiritual perfections upon men.
Brahmā said:
There is a place renowned as Śuklatīrtha, which bestows all perfections upon men;
by the mere remembrance of it, one shall attain all desires.
There was a sage renowned as Bharadvāja, supremely righteous;
his wife was named Paiṭhīnasī, adorned with excellent virtues.
Dwelling on the bank of the Gautamī, devoted to her husband,
she prepared a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) for Agni and Soma, and one for Indra and Agni.
While the sacrificial cake was being cooked, a certain being was born from the smoke;
having devoured the cake, he became a terror to the three worlds.
"Why do you destroy my sacrifice here out of anger? the sage Bharadvāja, the best of the twice-born, spoke quickly and wrathfully to him.
Having heard those words of the seer, the Rākṣasa replied to him.
The Rākṣasa said:
"O Bharadvāja, know me as the one renowned as Havyaghna;
I am the son of Saṃdhyā and the eldest son of Prācīnabarhis."
"Brahmā granted me a boon: 'Devour the sacrifices at your pleasure.
And my younger brother Kali is also powerful and exceedingly terrifying."
"I am Kṛṣṇa; my father is Kṛṣṇa, my mother is Kṛṣṇā, and likewise my younger brother.
I shall destroy the sacrifice and, as the bringer of the end, I shall cut down the sacrificial post."
Bharadvāja said:
"Let my sacrifice, the beloved and eternal dharma, be protected by you.
I know you to be a destroyer of sacrifices; though you are a virtuous twice-born, protect my ritual."
Yajñaghna said:
O Bharadvāja, listen briefly to these words of mine;
formerly, I was cursed by Brahmā in the presence of the gods and the Dānavas.
Then the god, the Grandfather of the worlds, was propitiated by me:
"When the best of sages sprinkle you with nectars (amṛta), [you shall be restored]."
"Then, O destroyer of the oblation, your curse shall be lifted, and not otherwise;
when you act in this manner, then everything will come to pass."
Brahmā said: Bharadvāja spoke again: "O high-minded one, you are my friend;
tell me how the protection of the sacrifice may be secured, so that I may perform it."
The gods and the Daityas joined together and churned the ocean of milk;
they obtained the nectar of immortality with great hardship—how could that be easily accessible to us?
"If you are pleased with me out of affection, then speak that which is easy to obtain.
Having heard those words of the sage, the Rākṣasa then spoke joyfully.
The Rakṣasa said: "The waters of the Gautamī are nectar; gold is called nectar;
clarified butter produced from cows is nectar; and Soma itself is indeed nectar."
Consecrate me with these, or likewise with these three:
the water of the Gaṅgā, clarified butter, and gold;
yet the water of the Gautamī is divine and superior even to all of them—immortal nectar itself.
Brahmā said:
Having heard this, that sage attained supreme satisfaction;
he respectfully took the nectar-like water of the Gaṅgā into his hand.
Therefore, the sage then consecrated the Rākṣasa at the sacrifice— at the sacrificial post,
with the victim, among the officiating priests, and within the entire sacrificial circle.
Everything indeed became white due to the consecration of the Great-Souled One;
even that Rākṣasa, having become white at that time, was born possessed of great strength.
He who had previously been of a dark complexion became white in an instant;
then the powerful Bharadvāja completed the entire sacrifice.
Then, having dismissed the officiating priests as well, he cast the sacrificial post into the waters of the Gaṅgā;
for that post remains even today in the middle of the Gaṅgā, O high-minded one.
And having been consecrated with nectar, that great sign appeared;
then, at that sacred ford, the Rākṣasa spoke again to Bharadvāja.
The Rākṣasa said:
"O Bharadvāja, I have been made pure by you once again;
therefore, whatever bathing, giving of gifts, and worship you perform here at this sacred ford [shall be fruitful]."
May they perform their desired rites, and may whatever fruit is obtained from a sacrifice always accrue to them; O Sage, by mere remembrance, may their sins go to destruction.
From that time forward, that sacred ford (tīrtha) has been known as Śuklatīrtha;
it is the open gateway to heaven on the Gautamī within the Daṇḍaka forest.
O tiger among sages, on both banks there are seven thousand other sacred fords that bestow all spiritual perfections.
Brahmā said:
"It is renowned as Cakratīrtha, which destroys sins through mere remembrance.
I shall describe its power; listen with care, O Nārada. (BrP 134.1)
O sage, the seven renowned ṛṣis, headed by Vasiṣṭha,
have taken refuge on the bank of the Gautamī and are performing a sacrificial session (sattra).
Then, while that most terrifying obstacle was being undertaken by the Rākṣasas,
the sages approached me and reported the deed of the Rākṣasa.
Then, O Nārada, having created the form of a woman through my power of illusion— by the mere sight of whom the Rākṣasas meet their destruction— I [approached them].
Having spoken thus, O sage, I gave that woman to the ṛṣis;
and at my word, the ṛṣis, taking the illusion (māyā), returned once more.
She who is known as Ajaikā, possessing a dark-red form and called by the name Muktakeśī, remains even today in her own true form.
She who bestows delusion upon the three worlds and can assume any form at will— by her power, all those foremost of sages have their minds rendered unsteady.
Having consecrated themselves again for sacrifice at Gautamī, the best of rivers,
the Rākṣasas once more approached her with the intent to destroy that sacrifice.
Having seen the illusion near the Yakṣa grove, those foremost of Rākṣasas then danced, sang, laughed, and wept.
The daughter of Maheśvara, Mahāmāyā, was exceedingly arrogant due to her power;
among them was a heroic lord of the Daityas named Śambara.
O Nārada, he devoured a woman who was a mere illusory form;
that was truly a great marvel for those who witnessed the power of his illusion.
While the sacrifice was being destroyed, they went to Viṣṇu for refuge;
then Viṣṇu gave his discus for the protection of the sages.
That discus cut down the Rākṣasas, Daityas, and Danujas in battle;
indeed, it was out of fear of it that the foremost of the Rākṣasas died.
Then that great sacrificial session was completed by the sages;
Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana discus was washed by the waters of the Gaṅgā.
From that time forward, that sacred ford has been called Cakratīrtha;
by bathing and giving gifts there, one obtains the fruit of a sacrificial session (sattrayāga).
There were five hundred holy bathing places (tīrtha) there that remove sin;
bathing and giving gifts at each of them bestows liberation.
Brahmā said:
That sacred ford known as Vāṇīsaṅgama, where Hara is the Lord of Speech,
liberates one from all sins and grants all desires.
In that regard, through bathing and giving gifts, there is the destruction of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin;
and [this was told] in the dialogue between Brahmā and Viṣṇu concerning their mutual greatness.
Between those two, Mahādeva indeed appeared as a form of light;
right there, the auspicious divine voice spoke these words to them: "O son!"* *The vocative "putra" (son) is addressed to one of the two, likely Nārada.
"I am great there" and "I am [great] here"—thus indeed did the divine voice speak to those two in turn; but he who perceives its end [is liberated].
"He indeed would be the eldest; therefore, you two should not engage in dispute. By his word, Viṣṇu went downward and I went upward.
Then Viṣṇu, arriving swiftly, sat down beside the light;
O sage, not reaching its end, I traveled further and further away.
Then, exhausted, I turned back desiring to see that Lord, the Master;
at that moment, my mind was thus resolved, for the end had been clearly seen by me.
"Then my preeminence over this god Viṣṇu would become manifest.
Furthermore, O high-minded one, such was my thought once again.
"With truthful mouths, how could I speak a falsehood even when tormented?
Among various kinds of sins, there is no transgression greater than untruth."
Thinking, "How shall I speak words that are untrue with mouths that are truthful?
I then produced a fifth mouth, terrifying in the form of a donkey.
Having thought for a long time, "I shall speak an untruth by means of this," I then spoke to that Hari, the Lord of the worlds, as he sat there.
"And its end was seen by me; therefore, O Janārdana, Hari and Śaṅkara were both at my side as I declared, 'This is mine' regarding my seniority. (BrP 135.12)

Having attained a single form like the sun and the moon, he beheld them both; struck with wonder and fear, he offered praise to them. Then the two Lords of the World, becoming enraged, spoke these words to him: BrP_135.13 //
Hari and Hara said:
"O wicked woman, may you become a river; there is no sin greater than falsehood."
Brahmā said:
Then, becoming overwhelmed, she turned into a river;
seeing that, I was struck with wonder and fear, and I spoke to her at that time.
"Since you have spoken untruth while remaining established in the speech of a Brahmin,
therefore you shall become invisible and undoubtedly take on a sinful form."
Having understood this curse, those two goddesses then bowed down and,
desiring the status of a queen, praised them again and again.
Then, being pleased and having been entreated by the thirty gods, Hari and Hara, the gods of gods worshipped by the immortals, spoke these words with affection: Thus they spoke.
Hari and Hara said:
"O auspicious one, when you are united with the Gaṅgā, you shall regain your body; for it shall indeed be pure, O most beautiful one. (BrP 135.19)
Brahmā said:
Having said, "So be it," that goddess also united with Gaṅgā;
she then became Bhāgīrathī and Gautamī, and assumed her own form once more.
O Brahmin, that goddess went to Gautamī, which is difficult even for the gods to attain; she herself became renowned there by the name Vāṇī, bestowing merit.
That very goddess is called Sarasvatī on the Bhāgīrathī;
the confluence of both, renowned in both places, is worshipped by the world.
The confluence of Sarasvatī is indeed the confluence of Vāṇī;
the goddess Vāṇī has united with the Gautamī, being Sarasvatī in speech.
Everywhere that holy place is honored; there, having worshipped the Lord Śiva, the Sovereign of the Gods, with speech, he was released from his curse.
Having shaken off the corruption of his speech, Brahmā returned once more to his own abode;
therefore, having become pure and bathed there at that confluence, one should remain so.
Then, having seen Vāgīśvara, one shall attain liberation by that alone;
[there is no need for] any other act such as giving gifts, performing fire-sacrifices, or observing fasts.
Whoever should perform [this] at the meritorious confluence shall not be born again in saṃsāra.
On both banks, there are one hundred and nineteen holy fords (*tīrtha*) which effect the destruction of all sins accumulated over various births.
Brahmā said:
Listen to what occurred there at the place renowned as Viṣṇutīrtha.
There was a famous ṛṣi named Maudgalya, the son of Mudgala.
His wife was renowned by the name Jābālā and was blessed with many sons;
likewise, his father was the world-famous sage Mudgala, who was advanced in years.
His wife was likewise known as the auspicious Bhāgīrathī by name;
that Maudgalya, firm in his vows, would bathe in the Gaṅgā every morning.
O best of sages, he performed this ritual constantly,
day and night, on the bank of the Gaṅgā with kuśa grass, earth, and śamī flowers.
Following the path taught by his guru, that son of Mudgala performed the daily invocation of Viṣṇu within the lotus of his own mind.
Summoned by him, the Lord of the World and Master of Fortune,
bearing the conch, discus, and mace, hastens forward after mounting Vainateya.
Having been diligently honored by that sage Maudgalya,
the Lord of the World recounted various wonderful stories to Maudgalya.
Then, in the afternoon, Viṣṇu said to Maudgali again and again: "Go, my child, to your own abode; you are weary."
Having been addressed thus by the god Viṣṇu, that twice-born man proceeds;
then, accompanied by the gods, he goes to his own abode, the Lord of the World.
Maudgalya also, having approached in that same manner and taking something for himself every day,
the wise man brought the wealth he had earned to his own home for his wife.
He, who was devoted to the lotus feet of Mahāviṣṇu, gave [it];
and she, the beloved of Maudgalya, was likewise devoted to her husband.
Whether it be vegetables, roots, or even fruits, whatever has been brought with effort by her husband,
she should prepare it well for the guests, the children, and for her husband himself.
Having given food to them, that woman of firm vows would eat afterwards;
and once they had all finished eating, Maudgali would always [do so] at night.
Then, delighted, he would recount to them the wonderful stories of Viṣṇu that he had heard;
and when much time had passed in this way, Maudgalya’s wife, filled with great wonder, spoke these words to her husband in private.
Jābāli said:
"Even if Viṣṇu, who is worshipped by the thirty gods, approaches you, our distress remains; why is that, O Lord of the World? (BrP 136.15)
Therefore, O one of great wisdom, ask him when Viṣṇu arrives;
for as soon as he is remembered, old age, birth, disease, and death go to their destruction—how much more so when he is seen? Therefore, ask that Lord of the World.
Brahmā said:
Having said "So be it" in response to the words of his beloved, Maudgalya,
being humble, worshipped Hari as usual and questioned him with palms joined in reverence.
Maudgalya said:
O Lord of the World, when you are remembered, my sorrow, poverty, and evil deeds are destroyed;
yet how can misfortune remain when you are beheld?
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
"All beings everywhere and at all times experience what they themselves have done;
herein, no one ever brings about anything, whether beneficial or harmful, for another."
Whatever kind of seed is sown, such is the fruit that arises;
a mango tree can never, under any circumstances, come from the seed of a neem tree.
Those by whom service to Gautamī was not performed, by whom Hari and Śaṅkara were not worshipped,
and by whom gifts were not given to the Brahmins— how can they be vessels of prosperity?
Nothing has been given by you to the brahmins, nor even to me;
for whatever is given, that alone stands by one in this world and in the next.
Because he always performs acts of purification with earth, water, kusha grass, and mantras,
his soul becomes pure through the drying up of the body.
Without giving, men can never obtain enjoyments anywhere;
through the performance of virtuous deeds, a man becomes pure and then dispassionate.
From that, one becomes liberated while living, possessing unimpeded knowledge;
through devotion to me and the fulfillment of duties in this world, liberation is easily attained by all.
Through giving and other such acts, you shall attain worldly enjoyment by dispelling the suffering of all beings;
or else, through devotion, you shall attain liberation, but you will not attain worldly enjoyment.
Maudgalya said:
How can liberation come through devotion? Liberation from worldly enjoyment is very difficult to attain;
if liberation has already arisen for embodied beings, what need is there for anything else?
"O you who pervade the universe, I desire that liberation which is worshipped by all through devotion."
Viṣṇu said:
O Brahman, this very same interval [of time] is granted when one gives while recollecting me;
whether given to a Brahmin or to those who seek it, that gift shall indeed become inexhaustible.
If one should give anything after having meditated upon me, that yields only a result corresponding to its measure;
furthermore, that which is given in this manner does not lead to enjoyment here.
Therefore, O one of great intelligence, grant me some food as a certainty;
or else, [grant it] to the foremost of Brahmins who has taken refuge on the banks of the Gautamī.
Brahmā said:
Maudgalya replied to Viṣṇu, "There is nothing remaining to be given to me;
there is nothing else, such as my body and so forth, that has not already been surrendered to you."
Then Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, said quickly to Garuḍa:
"Bring the grain-husk here; he shall offer it to me."
"Then he shall obtain suitable enjoyments that are dear to his heart";
having heard what was commanded by his master, the king of birds acted accordingly.
While that Maudgalya, firm in his vows, was placing the grains into the hand of Viṣṇu,
in that interval Viṣṇu spoke to Viśvakarman.
Viṣṇu said:
O one of great intelligence, for as many as seven generations in his lineage, there shall be [prosperity], and for that long his desires shall be fulfilled.
Cows, gold, grains, garments, and ornaments.
Brahmā said:
Whatever ornament exists in the world that brings delight to the mind,
all of that Maudgalya obtained through the power of Viṣṇu and the Gaṅgā.
"Go home," Viṣṇu said to Maudgalya, and he departed;
seeing all the prosperity in his own hermitage, the sage spoke:
The sage said:
"Oh, what power this gift possesses! Oh, what remembrance of Viṣṇu!
Oh, what power the Gaṅgā holds! By whom can this greatness be fully comprehended?"
Brahmā said:
Maudgalya, together with his wife, sons, grandsons, kinsmen,
and parents, enjoyed worldly pleasures and attained both enjoyment and liberation.
From that time forth, that sacred ford was known as Maudgalya and Vaiṣṇava;
bathing and giving gifts there bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
If there should be any sacred scripture or traditional law regarding that holy place, Viṣṇu will be pleased with it; one shall be liberated from sins and become happy.
There are eleven thousand sacred fords on both banks,
which bestow all desired objects through bathing, giving, recitation, and other such acts.
Brahmā said:
O Nārada, listen to this meritorious narrative known as Lakṣmītīrtha, which visibly increases prosperity, destroys misfortune, and is sacred. BrP_137.1 //
And formerly, O son, there was a conversation between Lakṣmī and Poverty;
though both were mutually antagonistic, they came together to pervade the entire universe.
There was nothing in the three worlds that was not occupied by those two;
they both spoke to one another, "My seniority! My seniority!
Then, by her splendor, Śrī declared, "I was manifested first."
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"I alone am the lineage, the character, and the very life of embodied beings;
without me, those who possess a body are like the dead, even though they are living."
Brahmā said: "And she was told by Poverty: 'I am indeed superior to all; liberation is eternally dependent upon me. Thus spoke Daridrā."
Lust, anger, greed, pride, and envy—
these never abide where I am.
Fear, the arising of madness, envy, and unruly conduct—
these never abide where I am.
Having heard the words of Daridrā, Lakṣmī replied to her.
Lakṣmī said:
"Every living being adorned by me becomes honored;
even one who is as poor as Śiva is overcome by everyone."
Upon the utterance of the word "Give," the five deities residing within the body—
Intellect, Prosperity, Modesty, Peace, and Fame— immediately depart and go away.
Virtues and dignity endure only so long as one does not seek anything from another;
once a man has become a petitioner, where are his virtues and where is his dignity?
A living being remains the most excellent of all and the abode of all virtues,
worthy of homage by all the worlds, as long as he does not seek anything from another.
Alas, this poverty of embodied beings is a great evil;
people do not honor the poor, they do not speak to them, and they do not even touch them.
"I alone am superior to her; O poor woman, listen to my words. (BrP 137.14)
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of Lakṣmī, the poor woman spoke these words.
Dāridrya said:
"O Lakṣmī, you are truly ashamed to say repeatedly, 'I am the elder';
yet you constantly delight in sinful men, having abandoned Puruṣottama."
You are a constant deceiver of those who trust you; how can you boast?
There is no such pleasure in attaining you as there is the heavy remorse that follows.
Such a fierce intoxication does not arise in men from liquor as that which occurs even for the learned merely by your presence.
"Lakṣmī always delights, for the most part, with those who commit evil deeds;
I, however, always dwell among those who are worthy and virtuous in character."
Among those devoted to Śiva and Viṣṇu, the grateful, the great-souled,
those of virtuous conduct, the peaceful, and those diligent in service to their gurus;
"Lakṣmī always dwells among those who are learned, heroic, wise, and virtuous; therefore, preeminence resides in me."
I shall dwell among the pure Brahmins who observe their vows and among the fearless mendicants; O Lakṣmī, listen to the conditions of your stay.
Among kings, the wicked, the cruel, the villainous,
the slanderers, the greedy, the deformed, and the deceitful;
You always abide among those who are ignoble, ungrateful, destroyers of dharma,
betrayers of friends, undesirable, and those whose resolve has been shattered.
Brahmā said:
While they were thus disputing, both of them came to me;
having heard their words, I spoke to both of them.
The earth existed even before me, and the waters existed even before that;
only women themselves, and no others, understand the disputes among women.
Furthermore, among those [waters], especially those originating from the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu),
the goddess Gautamī will declare the definitive conclusion in that regard.
She alone is the destroyer of all suffering; she alone is the cutter away of doubt.
By my word, you two, having gone to the earth, shall dwell there together with the Earth herself.
Accompanied by all the waters, they went to the river Gautamī;
then Earth and Water spoke their words clearly and in due order to Gautamī.
Having bowed to her, they then reported everything exactly as it had happened—
the words of both the poor woman and Lakṣmī— with impartiality.
While the world-protectors were listening, O Nārada, and while the Earth was listening,
and while the Waters were listening, that Gaṅgā spoke these words to Daridrā;
likewise, having praised Lakṣmī, Gautamī spoke these words.
Gautamī said:
"Brahmaśrī, Tapaḥśrī, Yajñaśrī, she who is named Kīrti,
Dhanaśrī, Yaśaḥśrī, as well as Vidyā, Prajñā, and Sarasvatī."
Then there were Bhuktiśrī, Mukti, Smṛti, Lañjā, Dhṛti, Kṣamā,
Siddhi, Tuṣṭi, as well as Puṣṭi, Śānti, Āpaḥ, and Mahī.
I am power, as well as medicinal herbs, sacred revelation, purity, the night,
the sky, moonlight, blessings, well-being, pervasiveness, illusion, the dawn, and the auspicious one.
Whatever exists in the world, whether moving or unmoving, is pervaded by prosperity when it resides in Brahmins who are steadfast, patient, and virtuous.
And in others who are endowed with knowledge and follow the path toward worldly enjoyment and liberation,
whatever is delightful or beautiful— that is all the manifestation of Lakṣmī.
What is the use of saying more here? This entire world consists of Lakṣmī;
whatever excellent thing is seen anywhere at all, it is she.
All that consists of Lakṣmī, yet devoid of her, is nothing at all;
are you not ashamed to vie with this goddess Sundarī in this regard?
"Go! Go! Gaṅgā said to that poor woman.
From that time forth, the water of the Gaṅgā became the object of enmity for the poor.
Poverty continues to afflict one as long as the Gaṅgā is not resorted to;
from that point on, that auspicious holy ford (tīrtha) becomes the destroyer of misfortune.

By bathing and giving gifts there, O high-minded one, one becomes possessed of fortune and merit; for six thousand sacred fords (tīrthas), frequented by gods, sages, and seers, and bestowing all perfections, are located within that single tīrtha.
Brahmā said:
There is a place renowned as Bhānutīrtha, which bestows all perfections upon men;
there I shall relate this account, which destroys even the greatest sins.
There was a king renowned as Śaryāti, most righteous;
his wife was Sthaviṣṭhā, who was peerless on earth in her beauty.
The best of the twice-born, known as Madhucchandas, the son of Viśvāmitra,
was the domestic priest of that king— a Brahmanical seer and a master among those who have subdued their passions.
To conquer the quarters, that king, a hero among monarchs, set forth with that priest;
then he spoke to the high-souled priest.
Having conquered the quarters and being encamped on his journey, he asked him: "O noble one, tell me the reason why you have come to such distress."
You alone are the most honored in my entire kingdom, possessing faultless knowledge of all sciences;
you are cleansed of sin and free from all distress.
Why do you appear as if your mind were elsewhere?
This earth has been conquered and the lords of men have been subdued;
since this great cause for joy has arisen here.
"Tell me the truth, why are you so emaciated? Having thus addressed Śaryāti, the brahmin, O best of the twice-born and most exalted one, spoke.
Madhucchandas said:
"O protector of the earth, listen to my words regarding that which was spoken by your wife."
When one watch has passed, we shall go; the night is now half-way spent.
"The mistress of this body, my beloved, awaits me;
remembering those words of my beloved, my frame withers away. When the transformation born of love has arisen, that lotus-faced woman is the very medicine for life."
Brahmā said:
Smiling, the king, the subduer of enemies, spoke to the family priest.
The King said:
"You are my preceptor and my friend; why do you mock yourself?
O man of great wisdom, O giver of honor, what is the use of this to me?"
What reliance can great-souled ones have on pleasure that perishes in an instant?
Having heard this, the wise Madhucchandas spoke these words: {Brahmā said:} [BrP 138.12]
Madhucchandas said:
"O King, where there is harmony between husband and wife, the three goals of life flourish;
do not consider this a defect, O King, but rather regard it as an ornament."
Brahmā said:
Surrounded by a vast army, he returned to his own country;
and in order to test that love, he spread a report throughout the city.
When Śaryāti had gone forth to conquer the quarters,
that bull among Rākṣasas killed the king along with his family priest and went down to the subterranean realm (rasātala).
O best of sages, having heard the news from the mouth of the messenger, the king’s wife, the beloved of Madhucchandas, again set about making a firm resolve.
At that very moment she became lifeless; it was as if a marvel had occurred.
Having witnessed her fate, the messengers reported it to the king.
"What has been done by the king's wives and by the beloved wife of the priest?"—
astonished and distressed, the king spoke again to his messengers.
The king said:
"O messengers, go quickly! Guard the body of the Brahmin woman and report back that the king is coming with his priest."
Brahmā said:
While the king was thus consumed by anxiety, an incorporeal voice spoke.
The Voice of Space said: "O King, Gaṅgā— the purifier on earth known as Gautamī, who quells all afflictions— will accomplish everything you desire."
Brahmā said:
Having heard this, Śaryāti took refuge on the bank of the Gautamī;
he gave wealth to the Brahmins and gratified the ancestors and the twice-born.
Having dispatched the family priest, the best of the twice-born, along with wealth,
give gifts diligently at other sacred fords and on pilgrimages.
The royal priest did not know all this, the duty of the king;
when that high-souled preceptor Vaiśvāmitra had departed, the king [acted].
"Having dispatched his entire army, he entered the fire on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Having said this, that lord of kings [addressed] the Gaṅgā, the Sun, and even the gods.
If I have given gifts, if I have offered oblations, and if I have protected my subjects,
by that truth, may that virtuous woman live through the span of my own life.
When Śaryāti, that best of kings, had spoken thus and entered the fire,
at that very moment the wife of that king’s domestic priest returned to life.
Having heard that the king had entered the fire for a cause of wonder,
as well as that his devoted wife had likewise died and then been restored to life, [the people were amazed].
And for that purpose, the king’s preceptor, having especially abandoned his own life for the sake of the king,
did not remember his own duties toward the monarch.
"Either I shall enter the fire and go to the presence of my beloved, or else I shall perform austerities here; thus the twice-born man resolved."
I consider this alone to be my duty and indeed a well-performed deed:
that I restore the king to life and then go back to my beloved.
"May this alone be auspicious for me," he thought, and then he praised the Sun;
for there is no other deity who bestows all desired objects like Ravi.
Madhucchandas said:
Homage be to that Sūrya, the liberated one of immeasurable splendor;
homage to you, the god consisting of the Vedas, the very meaning of the syllable Om.
To the one who is both formless and beautifully formed, to the one consisting of the three qualities and the triple manifestation,
to the sovereign cause of the preservation, creation, and destruction [of the world].
Brahmā said:
Thereupon the Sun became gracious and spoke, saying, "Choose a boon."
Madhucchandas said:
"O Lord of Gods, grant me a king and a sweet-speaking wife;
grant me auspicious sons for myself and auspicious boons for the king."
Brahmā said:
Then the Lord of the World gave Śaryāti ornaments made of jewels,
that wife, other boons, and likewise everything conducive to well-being.
Then, filled with affection for his beloved and accompanied by the gratified priest, he departed happily for his own country; that place is remembered as a sacred site (tīrtha) of auspiciousness.
There are three thousand meritorious sacred fords (tīrthas) there;
from that time forth, that sacred ford has been called Bhānutīrtha.
O Sage, the Mṛtasaṃjīvana, the Śāryāta— which is well-known— and that which is called the Mādhucchandasa, are renowned as destroyers of sin through mere recollection.
Bathing and giving gifts at those places bestow the fruit of all sacrifices;
they are the reviver of the dead and increase longevity and health.
Brahmā said:
On the northern bank of the Gautamī, there is a place renowned as Khaḍgatīrtha;
by bathing and giving gifts there, a man shall become a partaker of liberation.
In this regard, I shall proclaim the account; listen with diligence, O Nārada.
There was a twice-born man renowned as Pailūṣa, the son of Kavaṣa.
Indeed, burdened by the weight of his family, he ran about everywhere seeking wealth;
yet he attained nothing at all, and consequently, he took recourse in detachment.
When fate is utterly averse and human effort has become futile,
there is no other support for a wise man than dispassion.
Thus he reflected, sighing repeatedly:
"I possess no wealth inherited through my lineage, yet those whom I must support are many."
"Proud as he was, this soul did not deserve such suffering; alas, fie upon the workings of ill fortune!
Once, provided with a livelihood, he was occupied with his means of subsistence."
He did not obtain that wealth; consequently, he became detached from his livelihood.
Any service whatsoever is forbidden; it is profound penance that is difficult to perform.
"This craving drags me away by force everywhere toward misdeeds;
you have caused harm through ignorance—therefore, O Craving, homage be to you! (BrP 139.8)
Having reflected thus, the wise Pailūṣa considered, "What might lead to the cutting off of craving? and then spoke these words to his father.
Pailūṣa said:
"O father, O Lord, tell me that means by which one may cut down with the sword of knowledge both anger and greed, as well as this most difficult-to-cross cycle of worldly existence."
Kavaṣa said:
"One should seek knowledge from the Lord; such is the Vedic revelation. Therefore, worship Īśāna, and from him you will obtain knowledge."
Brahmā said:
Having said, "So be it," that Pailūṣa worshipped the Lord for the sake of knowledge.
Then Maheśāna, being pleased, bestowed knowledge upon the twice-born man.
Having attained knowledge, the one of great intelligence spoke verses that grant liberation.
Pailūṣa said:
Anger is indeed the first enemy; it is fruitless and brings about the destruction of the body.
Having severed it with the sword of knowledge, one shall attain supreme happiness.
Craving is manifold, deceptive, binding, and a doer of evil;
having severed this with the sword of knowledge, a person dwells in happiness.
"Attachment is the supreme unrighteousness for the gods and others; such is the sacred tradition.
For this very Self, which is by nature unattached, attachment is its greatest enemy."
Having severed this with the sword of knowledge, one may attain oneness with Śiva;
for doubt is the supreme destruction, the cause of the ruin of dharma and worldly goals.
Having severed this doubt, a person shall attain the highest desire.
Like a female demon, hope enters and utterly consumes all happiness;
having severed it with the sword of full self-awareness (pūrṇāhaṃtā), one attains liberation while living.
Brahmā said:
Then, having attained knowledge, he took refuge on the bank of the Gaṅgā;
through the sword of knowledge, he became free from delusion and thereby attained liberation.
From that time forward, that sacred ford has been known as Khaḍgatīrtha;
it is also called Jñānatīrtha, Kavaṣa, and Pailūṣa, and it grants all desires.
The great seers say that there are six thousand such sacred fords (tīrthas),
which remove the entire flood of the heat of sin and bestow all desired objects.
Brahmā said:
There is an excellent sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Ātreya, situated along the Indrāṇī;
I shall describe its power, which bestows back a lost kingdom.
On the northern bank of the Gautamī, the venerable sage Ātreya,
surrounded by officiating priests and sages, then commenced the sacrificial sessions.
Agni himself became his Hotṛ priest as the bearer of oblations;
and when that sacrificial session (sattra) was thus completed, he performed once more the sacrifice dedicated to Maheśvara.
Having attained sovereignty, the brahmin reached his destination everywhere:

"That action which is not a cause of happiness either in the future or even today—

Ātreya said:
Oh, the power of delusion! Even my mind has become bewildered.

"O Indra, those who remember you shall indeed partake in happiness;

And those [tirthas] celebrated by the names of Indra, Ātreya, and Daiteya—

{Brahmā said:} Having spoken thus, the gods departed, and the sage became satisfied.
Brahmā said:
O Nārada, there is a sacred ford named Kapilā-saṅgama, renowned throughout the three worlds; there I shall relate a meritorious and unsurpassed narrative.
There was a sage named Kapila, a knower of reality, possessed of great fame;
he was both stern and gracious, devoted to asceticism and vows.
Approaching that high-souled one, the best of sages, who was performing austerities on the bank of the Gautamī, Vāmadeva and the others spoke to him.
When Vena had been slain by the curses of the Brahmins and the dharma was lost in that kingless state,
the hosts of sages then spoke to the perfected master Kapila.
The hosts of sages said:
"O Lord of Sages, when the Veda has departed and Dharma has departed, what ought to be done?"
Brahmā said:
Then the sage Kapila, having meditated, spoke to the sages who had arrived.
Kapila said:
"The thigh of Vena was churned; from that, someone will come into being."
Brahmā said:
In that very manner, the sages churned Vena’s thigh;
from it was born a man of great sin, Kṛṣṇa, of fierce prowess.
Seeing him, the sages were afraid and said, "Sit down!
Because he sat down (niṣasāda), he became a Niṣāda, and from that, the Niṣādas came into being.
They churned his right arm, which was endowed with righteousness;
from that was born Pṛthusvara, who was marked by all the auspicious signs.
The illustrious Pṛthu became king, endowed with the power of Brahmā;
having approached him, all the gods congratulated him and requested auspicious boons.
They gave him the weapons and the efficacious mantras;
then the hosts of sages, along with Kapila, spoke to that Pṛthu.
The sages said:
"Give food to living beings; let the earth swallow even the medicinal herbs."
Brahmā said:
Then that best of kings, having taken up the bow, spoke to the Earth.
Pṛthu said:
"Give me those medicinal herbs that were swallowed [by the earth] out of a desire for the welfare of all creatures."
Brahmā said:
The Earth, being afraid, spoke to that large-eyed Pṛthu.
Mahī said:
"The great medicinal herbs have withered within me; how am I capable of giving them?"
Brahmā said:
Then the king, filled with anger, spoke again to that Earth.
Pṛthu said:
"If you do not give them today, I shall indeed kill you and take the great medicinal herbs myself."
The Earth said:
"O King, O best of monarchs, having become a man of wisdom, how can you kill a woman?
And how will you sustain these subjects without me?"
Pṛthu said:
"O Earth, where the benefit of many will arise from the destruction of one, there is no fault; by means of ascetic power, I shall sustain the subjects."
I see no fault in this, nor do I consider it a meaningless word;
for when one is struck down, the happiness of many arises.
The sages declare that such a killing is superior to a hundred horse-sacrifices.
Brahmā said:
Then the gods and the sages, having consoled that best of kings and the goddess Earth,
their mother, spoke to the hosts of deities at that time.
The gods said:
"O Earth, having assumed the form of a cow and consisting of milk, bestow great medicinal herbs upon King Pṛthu; by that, the king will become pleased."
There shall be protection of the subjects, and from that, security will arise.
Brahmā said:
Then, having assumed the form of a cow, she stood before Kapila on the earth;
and the king born from the womb of Vena milked the great medicinal herbs.
O great sage, it was there on the Narmadā that the gods, along with the Gandharvas and the sages, including the sage Kapila, [beheld] the Earth who had assumed the form of a cow.
In the Sarasvatī, the Bhāgīrathī, and especially in the Godāvarī,
as well as in all the great rivers, she milked forth the great milk.
As she was being milked by Pṛthu, she became a river of holy waters;
having joined with the Gautamī, it was like a marvel.
From that time forward, they have known that sacred ford as Kapilāsaṃgama;
there, O high-minded one, are eighty-eight thousand sites worthy of worship.
O Nārada, the hosts of sages declare that all the sacred fords (tīrthas) in this world are purifying even by mere remembrance; I shall describe them all in due order.
Brahmā said:
There is a sacred ford (tīrtha) renowned as Devasthāna, famous throughout the three worlds;
I shall describe its power—listen with care, O Nārada.
Long ago, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, when a conflict between the gods and the Dānavas had commenced,
there was a beautiful Daitya woman renowned as Siṃhikā.
Her son was the great Daitya named Rāhu, possessed of great strength,
who was born when the nectar had been produced and Siṃhikā had been torn asunder.
His son was a great Daitya known as Meghahāsa;
having heard that his father had been slain, he performed austerities, being deeply distressed.
To the son of Rāhu, who was performing austerities on the bank of the Gautamī,
all the gods and sages spoke with great trepidation:
The celestial sages said:
"O mighty-armed one, abandon the ascetic penance that resides in your mind;
by the grace of Śiva and Gaṅgā, let all this indeed come to pass."
By the grace of Śivagaṅgā, what indeed is difficult to obtain here?
Meghahāsa said:
"My father, who is to be honored by you as my deity, has been insulted;
yet, if you would also show him—and me—extreme affection," (BrP 142.7)
"I shall turn you away from this asceticism because of my enmity;
for a son must diligently carry out the requital of his father's enmity.
If you all pray for this, my desires will be fulfilled."
Brahmā said:
Then all the hosts of gods made Rāhu a follower of the planets,
and they also made that bull among Rākṣasas, Meghahāsa, one as well.
Then there arose the son of Rāhu, the powerful lord of the Nairṛtas;

"It is my intention that the power of this sacred ford (tīrtha) must be bestowed.
Having said, "So be it," the gods granted everything exactly as they had intended.
O divine sage, that place is called a *tīrtha* by the name of the lord of the Daityas,
because all the gods came to be present at that spot, O high-minded one.
That sacred ford is the abode of the gods, difficult even for the gods to attain;
because the Lord of Gods resides there, it is therefore known as Devatīrtha.
In that place, O Nārada, there are eighteen sacred fords (tīrthas) worshipped by the Daityas;
bathing and giving gifts at those sites destroys even the most heinous sins.
Brahmā said:
I shall describe the power of that place known as Siddhatīrtha, where Hara is present as Siddheśvara; it bestows all perfections upon men.
Born in the lineage of Pulastya, Rāvaṇa, the one who made the worlds cry out,

I said to the ten-faced one as he was about to fight with Soma:

For men who are bereft of fortune, fallen, and afflicted by various sufferings, Śiva alone is the refuge here in this saṃsāra; there is no other whatsoever.
Then, having turned back from that world of Soma along with his ministers, that Rākṣasa,

The ten-faced one swiftly regained the worlds;

the earth, the serpents, the elephants, and the brahmins, O sages.
He gazed upon the great mountain Kailāsa, the abode of Umāpati;

Rāvaṇa said to his two ministers:
"Who could this great-souled one be who dwells here on the mountain?"
"I shall carry this mountain from the earth;

Brahmā said:
Having thus heard these words of the two ministers of the Rākṣasa, and having understood the intention of the lord of the Rākṣasas, [he spoke].
"It is not right," they said with the intent of what was desired;
the night-stalker did not heed those words,
and the Rākṣasa quickly set down that Puṣpaka.
At the foot of Mount Kailāsa,
the ten-faced Rāvaṇa caused the mountain to tremble;
having perceived this deed, Bhava acted accordingly.
Having conquered the lords of the quarters,
that arrogant enemy of the gods shook Mount Kailāsa,

And having heard the words of the ten-headed Rāvaṇa as he departed for the worlds with his body mangled,

Whether Śambhu is pleased with him or even angry, he is one who bestows what is improper; there is no doubt in this matter.
Therefore, having obtained boons from him, this very heroic man—
Through the grace of Bhava, he reached a flower;
while proceeding toward Laṅkā to worship Bhava,

Having worshipped Śambhu with various mantras and with the waters of the Gaṅgā, he of undaunted spirit obtained that sword from the one adorned with the crescent moon.
Having worshipped Bhava, he accomplished the mantra granted by me for the protection of Śaśin, seeking success, all supernatural powers, and his desired goal.
When the mantra was accomplished, that lord of the Rākṣasas returned once more to Laṅkā, being well-pleased;

This sacred ford (tīrtha) bestows great accomplishments and grants one's desires; it destroys the entire flood of sins and is frequented by all the perfected ones (siddhas).
Brahmā said:
There is also the holy site known as Paruṣṇī-saṃgama, renowned throughout the three worlds.
I shall describe its true nature; listen to this destroyer of sins.
Atri propitiated Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
when they were pleased, he said to them, "You shall become my sons."
And so, O gods, let there be for me one beautiful daughter;
thus did Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara attain the state of being my sons.
And he begot a daughter named Śubhātreyī;
furthermore, Datta, Soma, and Durvāsas were the sons of that great-souled one.
Since Agni was born from Aṅgiras and Aṅgiras arose from the embers,

By the power of Agni, he always spoke harshly to Ātreyī,
yet Ātreyī remained constantly devoted to serving him.
From her were born the sons of Aṅgiras, endowed with great strength and prowess;
among them, Aṅgiras would always speak harshly to the daughter of Atri.
The sons of Aṅgiras always pacified their father;
once, however, distressed by her husband's harsh words, she,
dejected and with palms joined in reverence, spoke to her father-in-law, her guru.
Ātreyī said: "O Havyavāha, I am indeed the daughter of Atri and the wife of your son;
I am constantly devoted to the service of my sons and of my husband."
"My husband speaks harshly to me and looks upon me with anger for no reason;
O Supreme Lord, instruct me, for my husband is my deity."
Jvalana said:
"O blessed lady, your husband is indeed the sage Aṅgiras, born from the embers;
let such a course of action be undertaken so that he may become pacified."
O fair-faced one, when your husband Āgneya arrives at Agni,
you must then flood him with the form of water by my command.
Ātreyī said:
"I would endure harsh words rather than that my husband enter the fire.
What is the use of life for women who are hostile toward their husbands?"
I desire words of peace; may she likewise obtain a husband.
Jvalana said:
"Fire resides within the waters, in bodies, and likewise in all things stationary and moving;
I am considered the eternal abode and the progenitor of your husband."
"Knowing that 'I am who I am,' you ought not to worry.
Furthermore, water is indeed a divine mother and fire is a father-in-law;
having ascertained this through such understanding, do not be despondent, daughter-in-law."
The daughter-in-law said:
"Regarding what you said— that 'the waters are the mothers'— I am the wife of your son, Agni."
"How is it that you, having been my mother, have now become my wife?
This is contradictory, O Lord, since you exist in the form of water. Fire replied:

O blessed lady, you bear such names as *patnī* because of your support [of the husband], *bhāryā* because of your nourishing [him], *jāyā* because of your giving birth, and *kalatra* because of your own virtues. (BrP 144.18)
Do what I have spoken;
he who is born from her is indeed his son,
and she is his mother— of this there is no doubt.
