Having heard those words of her father-in-law, Ātreyī at that very moment assumed a fiery form and drenched her husband with water.
O Brahmin, when that couple was touched by the water of the Gaṅgā,
both husband and wife became endowed with peaceful forms.
Just as Viṣṇu is joined with Lakṣmī, as Śaṅkara is with Umā,
and as the Moon is with Rohiṇī, so too was that couple at that time.
Flooding her husband, she assumed a watery form;
thus she became the river celebrated as the Paruṣṇī, which has merged with the Gaṅgā.
The merit arising from the gift of a hundred cows is obtained by bathing in the Paruṣṇī;
and there, the descendants of Aṅgiras performed sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Regarding that, those who recite the Purāṇas say there are three thousand sacred fords (tīrthas) on both banks; O dear one, they know that the fruit of sacrifice is distinct for each.
Bathing and giving gifts at those places are considered superior even to the Vājapeya sacrifice;
this is especially true at the confluence of the Gaṅgā with the Paruṣṇī.
The merit that arises from bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts cannot be fully described.
Brahmā said:
There is a sacred site named Mārkaṇḍeya, which liberates one from all sins;
it is meritorious, yielding the fruit of all sacrifices, and warding off the flood of misfortunes.
I shall describe its power; listen with diligence, O Nārada!
Mārkaṇḍeya, Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, and Gautama— BrP_145.2 //
Yājñavalkya, Jābāli, and other sages such as Nārada—
these were the authors of the Śāstras, who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas).
"Those learned men, thoroughly established in the discourses on the Purāṇas, Nyāya, and Mīmāṃsā,
spoke among themselves regarding liberation according to their respective understandings."
Some praise knowledge, some action, and others both;
thus disputing among themselves, they said to me, "Both are considered [necessary]."
Having learned my intention, they went to the wielder of the discus and mace;
and having also learned his intention, those sages of great luster departed.
Again, disputing among themselves, they prepared to question Śaṃkara;
having worshipped Bhava at the Gaṅgā, they explained that very matter to him.
But the Destroyer of Tripura declared that action is indeed primary;
for that knowledge is of the nature of action, and it is said that action itself is that [knowledge].
Therefore, all beings attain success through action;
action alone pervades the universe, for nothing exists without it.
The practice of knowledge, the performance of sacrifice, the practice of yoga, and the worship of Śiva—all these are indeed action;
there is no living being here who exists without action.
Therefore, anything other than karma as the cause is the behavior of a madman—
whether it be where sages agree or where the god Maheśvara resides.
He made this determination: "Everything is attained by men through action.
Having placed Mārkaṇḍeya at the forefront, it is therefore called the Mārkaṇḍeya [Purāṇa].
On the northern bank of the Gaṅgā is a sacred ford (tīrtha) crowded with hosts of sages;
it is purifying for the ancestors and meritorious even by constant remembrance.
In that regard, dear one, the Lord who pervades the universe has declared ninety-eight sacred sites;
this has been proclaimed by the Veda, and the sages have likewise accepted it as such.
Brahmā said:
"Go to another sacred site where Śiva Kālañjara resides;
that which pacifies all sins shall be described by me."
King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, was like a second Indra in person;
he had two wives who were adorned with the auspicious marks of noble lineage.
The eldest was the auspicious Devayānī, the daughter of Śukra by name;
the second was she who was Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan.
The Brahmin woman Devayānī, who was highly wise and slender-waisted,
became the wife of Yayāti through the grace of Śukra.
And Śarmiṣṭhā, the wife of that very king who was born of Vṛṣaparvan,
gave birth to two sons together with Devayānī, the daughter of Śukra.
O King, Śarmiṣṭhā obtained three sons who resembled gods— Yadu and Turvasu, both equal to the sons of the gods.
O Brahmin, Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru were the two sons of Devayānī born to Yayāti, the best of kings; they were equal to him in their brilliance and form.
The sons of Śarmiṣṭhā, however, possessed the splendor of Indra, Agni, and Varuṇa.
Once, Devayānī, distressed, spoke to her father.
Devayānī said:
"O descendant of Bhṛgu, I, unfortunate as I am, have only two children;
whereas my servant, who is fortunate, has three children, O father."
Reflecting upon this, O teacher of the Dānavas, I have come to the ultimate misery; I shall die because of the unpleasantness caused by Yayāti.
For to high-minded men, O father, death is better than the shattering of one's honor.
{Brahmā said:} Having heard these words of the daughter, the powerful Śukra became enraged and quickly approached Yayāti, saying this to him: BrP_146.11 //
Śukra said:
"O Indra among kings, because you have done this unpleasant thing to my daughter, being intoxicated by her beauty, you shall therefore become old."
Afflicted by the objects of the senses, he is unable either to enjoy them or to renounce them;
longing for them with his mind alone, he remains there, his intellect destroyed by incessant sighing and gasping.
For embodied beings who are still living, old age itself is death;
therefore, O King, proceed quickly toward that decrepitude which is so difficult to withstand.
Brahmā said:
Having heard this curse from the wise Śukra,
King Yayāti, with his palms joined in reverence, spoke to Śukra.
Yayāti said: "I do not offend, I do not become angry, nor do I ever practice unrighteousness;
those who commit unrighteous acts, being sinful, are indeed to be punished by the high-souled."
"O best of the twice-born, how could you have cursed me while I was practicing only dharma? Why does Devayānī say anything at all to me in vain?"
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, you ought not to cast a curse upon me;
for even if the learned, being deluded, should become angry with one who is faultless,
that is no fault of fools whose minds are scorched by the fire of hatred.
Brahmā said:
At the word of Yayāti, Śukra also remembered the repeated offenses committed against him by his daughter,
who was fierce both by day and by night.
Having said, "My anger has passed," Kāvya spoke to the king.
Śukra said:
"I have understood that this unpleasant act was done by her; I shall not speak a falsehood.
O King, listen as I shall impose this curse, yet grant you this favor."
O giver of honor, O King, by my boon let this old age go instead to that son for whom you desire to transfer it.
Brahmā said:
Again, Yayāti spoke humbly to his father-in-law, Śukra.
Yayāti said:
"O preceptor of the Daityas, let him who, filled with devotion, accepts the old age given by me, become the king; please grant your consent to this."
"O preceptor of the Daityas, if my son should not firmly accept my words, I would curse him; therefore, O Guru, you must certainly grant me permission for this."
"Brahmā said: 'So be it,' the descendant of Bhṛgu replied to the king.
Then Yayāti, having summoned his own son, spoke these words."
Yayāti said:
"O Yadu, take upon yourself this old age born of my curse;
you are my eldest son, mature, knowledgeable in all matters, and established at the head of my sons."
By that very act, the father becomes the son who remains subject to his command.
Brahmā said:
Yadu replied "No" to his father Yayāti, who had bestowed abundant sacrificial fees;
and Yayāti, having cursed Yadu, spoke to Turvasu according to his desire.
Turvasu also did not accept the old age given by his father at that time;
having cursed him, [the father] said to Druhyu, "Accept this old age of mine."
And Druhyu did not desire that old age which destroys beauty;
the king spoke even mildly to him, "Accept this old age of mine."
"No," he replied; having cursed him, he spoke to Pūru.
Then Pūru, having welcomed that old age, took it upon himself from his father.
For a thousand years his father remained pleased with him,
[providing] all those various objects of enjoyment that are appropriate for youth.
Contented with his sons' youth, Yayāti enjoyed happiness;
then King Nahuṣa’s son became satiated with all pleasures.
Then, out of joy, he summoned his son Pūru and spoke to him.
Yayāti said: "O sinless one, I am satiated with all enjoyments through your youth;
O son, take my youth and give me back my wretched old age."
Brahmā said: Pūru then replied, "No; by me, O dear one, the transformations of states that afflict embodied beings are being worn away by old age, yet they are difficult to ward off."
Even old age, which arrives by the force of time, must be endured by all embodied beings;
if it has been accepted for the sake of serving one's elders, how can it be abandoned?
"O King, death is indeed better for embodied beings than the sin of having accepted what was to be renounced;
or else, I shall destroy old age through my ascetic power."
Brahmā said:
Having spoken thus to his father, he went to the unsurpassed Gaṅgā;
then, on the southern bank of the Gautamī, he performed great penance.
Then, after a long time, the god Śiva became pleased;
that best of deities said to Pūru, "What shall I give? to him who was adorned with the excellent jewels of qualities that were transcendent and most noble in the world.
Pūru said:
"O Lord, O Sovereign of the Gods, destroy this old age that has come upon me through my father's curse;
O Lord of Devas, [destroy] that which was inflicted by my father out of anger."
O you who are worshipped by the gods, release my brothers from the curse.
Brahmā said:
Having said, "So be it," the Lord of the World likewise caused the old age born from the curse to vanish;
the Lord of the World then made his brothers free from the curse.
From that time forward, that sacred ford (tīrtha) became the destroyer of old age and disease; by its mere remembrance, even untimely decrepitude and other such ailments are destroyed.
It is also renowned by that name and is called Kālañjara; it is known as Yāyāta, Nāhuṣa, Paura, Śaukra, and Śārmiṣṭha.
O one of great intelligence, one should know that there are exactly one hundred and eight such sacred fords (tīrthas) there, which likewise bestow all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis).
Bathing in them, giving gifts, as well as listening to or reciting [the accounts of] them,
shall pacify all sins and bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Brahmā said:
Next is the pair of Apsarases known as Apsarasaṅgama;
it is meritorious on the southern bank, and by remembering it, one becomes fortunate.
O Nārada, by bathing and other rites there, a man becomes liberated without a doubt; and a virtuous woman who has bathed after her menses at that confluence [attains the same].

Even a barren woman shall give birth to a son within three months together with her husband, provided she remains engaged in ritual bathing and giving gifts; otherwise, my word shall not come to pass.
The reason why this sacred ford (tīrtha) is called Apsaroyuga shall now be told; listen attentively, O Nārada, to this cause.
O Brahmin, there was a great rivalry between Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha concerning the son of Gādhi,
who was performing austerities with firm vows for the sake of attaining the status of a Brahmin.
"O blessed lady, at my command, go to him who is seated at Gaṅgādvāra and cause him— who has been incited by Indra— to fall away from his asceticism."
Then, having spoken thus to Viśvāmitra, who had fallen from his asceticism,
Menā gave her daughter away and returned once more to the city of Indra.
When she had departed, the son of Gādhi remembered everything he had done,
having abandoned that region and the sacred ford beloved by the gods.
He went to the southern Gaṅgā, where Hara is at Kālañjara;
there Indra, the thousand-eyed one, spoke again to him as he was performing austerities.
Then, to Urvaśī, Menā, Rambhā, and Tilottamā, they said, "Not at all," trembling with fear; the Lord of Śacī spoke to them again.
Then both Gambhīrā and Atigambhīrā, who were both proud,
spoke to the thousand-eyed god Purandara.
Deeply and exceedingly profound, they said:
"Let us go and, by means of dance, song, and our perfection of beauty and youth, cause the son of Gādhi— that one of great splendor who is practicing austerities— to fall away from his resolve."
Who here is not conquered by those women, in whose sidelong glances, smiles, speech, and perfection of graceful movement the five-arrowed god of love eternally dwells?
Brahmā said:
When the thousand-eyed one had said, "So be it," they both approached the great river and beheld the great sage Viśvāmitra performing austerities.
Invincible even to Death, like Śiva standing upon the earth,
they were unable to gaze upon him for even a single thousand years.
Then, seeing him standing at a distance, delighting in dance, song, and flattery,
that tiger among sages became overwhelmed with anger.
Seeing such contrary conduct, in whom would anger not arise?
Yet the mighty-armed one, though free from desire, seemed as if laughing at that Indra.
Released from these two Apsarases, the thousand-eyed Indra, as it were speaking, cursed Gādheya: "You two shall become liquid in form."
Since they had come here quickly to propitiate me,
he was pleased by them and granted their release from the curse.
When they were united with Gaṅgā, they both became divine in form;
yet by her curse, they instantly assumed the forms of rivers.
From that, two rivers arose, said to be a pair of Apsarases;
and from those two, there was a most auspicious confluence with the Gaṅgā.
Śiva, renowned throughout all the worlds and the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, resides there; indeed, upon being seen, he is the granter of all spiritual perfections.
Having bathed there and beheld him, one is released from all bonds.
Brahmā said:
On the southern bank of the Gaṅgā is the place renowned as Koṭitīrtha;
by the mere remembrance of it, one is liberated from all sins.
Where the god Koṭīśvara resides, everything becomes ten-millionfold;
there, two crores of auspicious-bestowing holy fords are fully present.
In this regard, I shall proclaim the prosperity [to follow]; listen with a focused mind, O Nārada.
Kaṇva’s eldest son was renowned as Bāhlīka.
Known among the people as Kāṇva, he was a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
together with his wife, that master of the Vedas performed the Pārvaṇa and Āgrayaṇa sacrifices.
Performing his duties, he remained on the bank of the Gautamī, honored by the world;
at the time of dawn, he, together with his wife, offered oblations into the fire with a concentrated mind.
He remained always engaged in this way, though at times he would prepare for a sacrifice;
having offered a single oblation into the kindled fire, he would then proceed.
He took the sacrificial substance in his hand in order to offer another oblation;
in that interval, the fire then became extinguished.
Then Kaṇva, overcome with anxiety and having fallen into great despondency, reflected within himself as to what ought to be done.
And between the two oblations, the sacrificial fire has been extinguished;
another fire must be taken, whether it be Vedic or likewise worldly.
"Where might a second oblation be offered? And where indeed would there be another sacrifice? While he was reflecting thus, a divine voice then spoke:
"You shall not need to fetch another fire here;
whatever wood chips are nearby there will suffice."
"O king of brahmins, let the oblation be offered while the wood is half-burnt.
To this Kāṇva replied, "No. Then that very voice spoke again:
Hiraṇya is the son of Agni, yet he is also his father;
what is given to the beloved son will indeed result in the pleasure of the father.
"What should be given to the father, one should give to the son; it shall result in ten million times the merit of affection.
Thus spoke the divine voice, and then all the great seers [responded].
Having ascertained the entire essence of Dharma, they acted exactly as it had been declared.
Knowing this, one should understand that in this world, what is given by a father becomes the property of his son.
Just as the joy of parents arises through the assistance rendered by their offspring and so forth,
it is well known throughout this world that such [joy] cannot be produced by anything else.
This is well-known throughout the world and honored by all people;
when that is given, O son, the merit becomes ten millionfold.
"The cessation of mental distress occurs and great happiness arises;
furthermore, that voice spoke again regarding this most excellent tirtha of Kaṇva."
By the power of the merit of Kāṇva, that great sacred site (tīrtha) came into being,
yielding greater fruit than all other sacred sites throughout the three worlds.
O Sage, by performing even some small act such as bathing or giving with devotion and a concentrated mind, you will obtain the entire fruit in its totality, multiplied ten millionfold.
Whatever is performed here by men, such as bathing, giving gifts, and so forth, one should know that all of it becomes ten millionfold; therefore, they know it as Koṭitīrtha.
Where this Vṛtta— namely Āgneya, Kāṇva, Pautra, Hiraṇyaka,
and that known as Vāṇī— is located, it is Koṭitīrtha, because from it one obtains the fruit of ten million sacred fords (koṭitīrtha).
The greatness of Koṭitīrtha cannot be described here even by Vācaspati and other gods, nor indeed by anyone else.
For whatever action is performed there, in whatever manner,
by the grace of the Godāvarī, it all becomes ten millionfold.
He who bestows a single cow upon the foremost of the twice-born at Koṭitīrtha enjoys the fruit of ten million cows through the majesty of that sacred site.
Whoever, having become pure at that sacred ford, makes a gift of land with a mind endowed with faith, shall obtain a reward a hundred million times greater.
Everywhere along the banks of the Gautamī, giving gifts for the ancestors is supreme;
it is especially so at Koṭitīrtha, where it yields infinite fruit.
Here, the sages know there are forty-nine sacred sites (tīrthas).
Brahmā said:
On the northern bank of the Gaṅgā, there is the place renowned as Nārasiṃha;
I shall describe its power, which provides protection from all dangers.
In former times there was Hiraṇyakaśipu, the best among the strong;
by means of his asceticism and prowess, he was unconquered even by the gods.
His mind defiled by hatred for the son of Haribhakta,
he manifested from a pillar in the assembly hall, demonstrating his nature as the soul of the universe.
Having slain him, that lion among men then put his army to flight;
having slain all the great daityas in battle, the Great Deer proceeded in due order.
Having conquered the enemies dwelling in the netherworld (rasātala), he went to the heavenly realm (svarloka);
having conquered there as well, he went to the earth and slew the Daityas stationed upon the mountains.
Taking the form of a deer, he slew the Daityas who dwelt by the ocean, those situated by the rivers, those living in villages, and those inhabiting the forests, as they assumed various forms.
Moving through the sky, established in the wind, and having reached the realm of light, he—
whose claws were stronger than the fall of a thunderbolt and whose great mane was tossed upward— [roared].
He roared, causing the embryos of the Daityas to miscarry, having conquered all the Rākṣasas with great shouts and glances resembling the fire of universal destruction.
He pulverized the Asuras with slaps and the tossing of his limbs;
having thus slain them in many ways, Hari went to Gautamī.
There, an enemy of the lord of Daṇḍaka, known as Tāmrārya, [sought] her who was born from his own lotus feet and who delighted his mind and eyes.
That warrior, invincible to the gods and endowed with great strength,
caused a most fierce, terrifying, and hair-raising conflict to arise.
In a battle involving a rain of weapons and missiles fought with the son of the Daitya,
the glorious Hari struck down that enemy on the northern bank.
On the Gaṅgā is the Nārasiṃha Tīrtha, renowned throughout the three worlds;
bathing, giving gifts, and other rites performed there destroy all sins and planetary afflictions.
It is eternally the provider of all protection and the warder-off of old age and death;
just as among all the gods, there is no one equal to Hari.
Among all holy places without exception, that holy place is likewise the most excellent;
having bathed in that holy place, a man should perform the worship of Nṛhari.
"Whether in heaven, on earth, or even in the netherworld, nothing at all is difficult for him to attain," and so forth; O Sage Nārada, there are eight great holy places (tīrthas) there.
The wise have declared that the merit of ten million separate holy places is obtained when even one who lacks faith remembers his name, whereby all evil is utterly destroyed.
Wherever he is ever present, that place becomes Nṛsiṃha himself;
by whom can the fruit born from serving that sacred ford (tīrtha) be described here?
Just as there exists nowhere a god superior to Nṛhari,
so too there is no sacred ford anywhere equal to Nṛsiṃhatīrtha.
Brahmā said:
O high-minded one, the Paiśāca Tīrtha is declared to be on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā; there, in ancient times, a brahmin attained liberation from his state as a piśāca.
In this world, Suyavasa’s son was renowned as Jīgarti;
he was afflicted by the suffering of maintaining a family and tormented by famine.
But he sold his middle son, Śunaḥśepa— the best among the knowers of Brahman— to a Kṣatriya for execution in exchange for abundant wealth.
What sin indeed would even a wise man not commit when fallen into calamity?
For even the Sage accepted abundant wealth while acting as a priest.
And that lowest of brahmins took wealth for the purpose of tearing [the earth apart];
thereafter, he was afflicted by a great disease that could not be cured.
When he died in the course of time, he was cast into the hells;
for there is no exhaustion here of past sins except through their experience.
By the command of Yama, he was sent by the servants through many different wombs;
thereafter, he indeed became a Piśāca, fierce and of terrible appearance.
Furthermore, in the summer, when the forest is parched with dry wood, devoid of water, and desolate, he is cast there by the servants of Yama amidst the spreading forest fires.
Those who sell a maiden, a son, land, a horse,
or a cow do not return from hell until the dissolution of all beings.
Being cooked in the Saṃghāta hell by the terrible servants of Yama as a result of the ripening of his own committed sins, he cried out loudly, remembering what he had done.
Once, while traveling on the road, the middle son of Jīgarta heard the voice of a Piśāca weeping again and again.
Then, for the father Jīgarti, who was a seller of his son, a killer of a Brahmin,
and a sinner, she [the sin] belonged to that father, the seller of his son and the slayer of a Brahmin.
Then Śunaḥśepa said: "Who are you, so deeply distressed?
Jīgarti replied out of sorrow: "I am indeed the father of Śunaḥśepa."
"Having committed an evil deed, I have entered this dreadful womb;
I was cooked in the hells and have now reached this intermediate state.
Such is the destiny of all those who have performed wicked actions."
Jīgartiputra said to him out of sorrow:
"O father, I am your son; having sold me through my own fault, you have thus reached the hells."
"Therefore, I shall now make you go to heaven. Having thus made this promise, that foremost of sages, the son of Gādhi, then attained the state of being his son.
Meditating upon the Gaṅgā and longing for the unsurpassed worlds of his father, he departed from those scorched by the fire of all-encompassing suffering.
For embodied beings sinking into the great ocean of delusion, alas, there is no other support in the three worlds except for the river of Viṣṇu’s feet.
Having thus resolved, the high-souled sage,
desiring to rescue his father from misfortune,
then went quickly and purely to the Gautamī river.
Having bathed there while recollecting Śambhu and Viṣṇu,
he offered water to his father, who had assumed the form of a preta,
appearing as a pīśāca and deeply distressed.
By that mere act of giving, Jīgarti was purified at that very moment; endowed with a most meritorious body,
he ascended a celestial chariot frequented by hosts of gods.
By the power of his own merit, through the influence of the Gaṅgā, and by the grace of Viṣṇu, Śambhu, and Brahmā, he attained the station of Viṣṇu,
possessing a splendor equal to ten thousand suns.
From that time forward, this has become exceedingly famous for the destruction of the Piśācas, for the great disease,
and for the swift destruction of great sins.
By the mere remembrance of this sacred ford (tīrtha), men attain [liberation]; and today this greatness of it has been recounted to you, wherein there are three hundred [deities].
Furthermore, there are other sacred fords (*tīrtha*) that bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation; what else is there here?
It has been declared that this [place] grants all perfections (*sarvasiddhi*); thus begins a section of three hundred verses.
Even by the mere remembrance of sacred fords frequented by sages, one's desired goals are granted.
Brahmā said:
On the northern bank of the Gaṅgā is the sacred ford (tīrtha) renowned throughout the three worlds as Nimnabheda, which destroys all sins.
By the mere remembrance of whom all sins are destroyed,
and by the sight of whom one becomes a knower of the Vedas— that very island of the Vedas is located right there.
The most righteous King Aila desired Urvaśī;
for who would not fall into infatuation upon beholding a woman with intoxicating eyes? (BrP 151.3)
The king set a time limit for her until she could no longer see the fire, and she departed for the place where that king consumed only a small amount of ghee.
He took that woman, who was ever-new and delightful to young men;
while she slept upon the bed, Purūravas rose up.
Upon seeing him naked, she departed at that very moment;
indeed, where is there stability for women whose minds are as flickering as lightning?
At nightfall, that great being, naked and filled with wonder, cast his gaze about;
in the meantime, the king advanced against his enemies for battle.
Having conquered them, he returned once more to the well-honored world of the gods;
and having arrived there, the great king [consulted] Vasiṣṭha, his domestic priest.
Having heard of Urvaśī’s departure, he was thereafter overcome with grief;
he neither offered oblations, nor ate, nor listened, nor looked upon anything.
In the meantime, the family priest awakened that best of kings, who was in a state of death, with words based on logical reasoning.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Great King, she has died today; do not grieve, O high-minded one.
Let not those inauspicious and swift-moving [afflictions] touch you who are thus established."
"O high-minded one, you do not truly know the hearts of women; they are like those of hyenas. Therefore, O King, do not grieve."
O Indra among kings, who in this world has not been deceived by women?
Their deceptive nature, cruelty, fickleness, and lack of virtue [are well known].
Thus, how can those things which are by their very nature [transient] be causes of happiness?
Who has not been struck down by time, and what seeker of wealth has attained lasting dignity?
O King, who has not been deluded by prosperity, or who has not been shattered by women? To those whose minds are overwhelmed by intoxication, all things are like dreams and illusions.
Knowing this— that for whom woman is a source of pleasure— be free from the fever of passion;
O high-minded one, apart from Śaṅkara, Viṣṇu, or Gautamī,
no other refuge exists in the three worlds for those who suffer.
Brahmā said:
Having heard this, King Aila, the most righteous of men, then diligently suppressed his grief and stood in the midst of the Gautamī river.
And there he diligently propitiated the god Śiva, Janārdana, Brahmā, Bhāskara, Gaṅgā, and the other gods.
What state will that creature fall into, who, having fallen away from his path, serves neither sacred fords nor deities, and is subject to the power of time?
Taking refuge solely in the Lord, eager to serve the daughter of Gautama,
he attained supreme faith and turned his back on all attachment to saṃsāra.
He performed many sacrifices with numerous sacrificial fees through the officiating priests;
because he was an island of the Vedas, he is called Yajñadvīpa.
On the night of the full moon, Urvaśī comes there;
and whatever man should perform a circumambulation of that lamp, [he shall attain his desire].
By him the earth, clothed by the oceans, was circumambulated;
there, the Vedas were recollected, and likewise the sacrifices were recollected.
Whoever, being virtuous, performs [rites] there shall obtain the fruit of Vedic sacrifices;
that should be known as Aila-tīrtha, and it is indeed the same as Purūravas.
That which belongs to Vasiṣṭha is called *nimnabheda*;
under King Aila, there would be no deficiency whatsoever in any of his ritual acts.
This inclination toward Urvaśī that existed with his whole being was also split apart by Vasiṣṭha and Gaṅgā.
By that [act], there occurred a breaking open of the lowlands, which grants the attainment of desired goals both seen and unseen;
they say there are seven hundred meritorious sacred sites (tīrthas) therein.
Bathing and giving gifts at those places bestow the fruit of all sacrifices.
Having bathed at Nimnabheda, he who beholds these deities—
In this world or the next, there is nothing low for him;
having attained the highest elevation, he rejoices in heaven like Śakra.
Brahmā said:
Those who know the Vedas recognize the sacred ford known as Nandītaṭa;
O Nārada, listen attentively as I describe its power.
The son of Atri was of great splendor and renowned as Candramas;
he mastered all the Vedas according to rule, as well as the science of archery (Dhanurveda) according to the prescribed method.
"O Great-minded One, having studied all other sciences as well,
I shall perform worship of my guru"— thus did that Moon speak to Jīva.
Then Bṛhaspati, filled with joy, spoke to his disciple Candra.
Bṛhaspati said:
"Tārā, whose radiance is equal to that of Rati, knows my secret."
Brahmā said:
Then, desiring to question her, that Moon entered the inner chamber;
seeing Tārā, whose face was like a star, he seized her by the hand.
Then, out of greed, he tried to drag her by force toward his own home;
meanwhile, [the other] was a treasury of fortitude, wise, intelligent, and one who had conquered his senses.
As long as one is not ensnared by the nets of the eyes of a lustful woman—
especially a long-eyed, passionate woman situated in private.
Upon seeing her, whose mind would not fall under the sway of desire?
For this very reason, she must never behold another man.
Having learned from his attendants that the noble lady, fearing a violation of her virtue, had performed her private duty in secret, he rose up suddenly and departed.
Having seen that evil deed, the noble-minded Bṛhaspati,
casting aside his composure, cursed him in anger with words that were unpleasant to hear.
Seeing his beloved overcome by another, who would be able to endure it?
Even the god Jīva, the Moon, fought with him in anger.
The moon is not slain by curses, nor by weapons consecrated by the gods' mantras;
the hare-marked one is not slain even by the mantras composed by Bṛhaspati.
Then Candra, having taken Tārā and established her in his palace,
enjoyed her for many years, as did Rohiṇī, being fearless from every quarter.
Then he could not be overcome by the gods, nor by the wrathful ones with their curses and mantras;
neither by kings, nor by sages, nor by conciliation, sowing dissension, or punishment.
When that preceptor could not obtain a wife despite every effort,
and when all other means had failed, Jīva then called to mind a stratagem.
Placing dishonor before him and casting pride behind his back, the wise man secures his own interest; for the loss of one's own interest is indeed folly.
Those men who, though knowing that a goal can be achieved by some means,
possess vain pride and are deluded, quickly come to ruin.
Having thus resolved, the wise one went to Śukra and informed him;
knowing that he had arrived, the sage welcomed him with great honor.
When he was seated, well-rested, and honored according to tradition,
the preceptor of the Daityas then questioned him regarding the purpose of his arrival.
"Even enemies who turn their faces away when one has come to their home are not truly superior;
therefore, he related to him in detail, from the beginning, the abduction of his wife."

O Nārada, having heard those words of Bṛhaspati, the sage Kavi was filled with anger; he considered it an offense by his disciple Candra. Having heard of this transgression, the sage then spoke out of wrath: BrP_152.21 //
Śukra said:
"Then I shall eat, then I shall drink, then I shall sleep, then I shall speak—
only when I have brought back your beloved wife, O brother, who is so deeply afflicted."
"O mighty-armed Lord, having brought her here and honored you, I shall curse Candra for his betrayal of his preceptor and afterwards partake of her; O Lord of Planets, listen to my words."
Brahmā said:
Having spoken thus, that teacher of the Daityas departed with Jīva;
having propitiated Śiva with great effort, he attained supreme power.
Having obtained various boons from Śaṅkara, who is worshipped with devotion, what indeed is difficult for embodied beings to attain here through the grace of Śiva?
Śukra went with Jīva and Tārā to where the Moon was staying;
he cursed him loudly: "Listen to my words, O Moon!"
"O wicked one, since you have committed a most sinful deed out of intoxication,
may you become a leper!"— thus did the sage Kavi curse the Moon in his wrath.
At that very moment, the moon was consumed by the poet’s curse;
indeed, who does not meet their destruction when they betray their guru, master, or friend?
Candra abandoned her, and Śukra, the poet, seized Tārā;
he then summoned the gods, the sages, and the hosts of ancestors.
Then she began to question the rivers, the various streams, and the plants— women devoted to their husbands— concerning the release of Tārā from her captivity.
Then Śruti said to the gods: "Let her perform her bath with devotion in the Gautamī; by means of that life-force, Tārā will become purified."
This is a supreme secret that must not be told to just anyone;
in all circumstances here on earth, Gautamī is the refuge for men.
And Tārā performed the bath with her husband according to the prescribed rite;
there a rain of flowers fell and shouts of "Victory! arose.
The gods gave her back again, and the men as well;
the kings, making their word true, restored the wife of the Brahmin.
Furthermore, O great sage, after the sinless Brahmajāyā had been restored by the gods, everything there became secure; therefore, that place is a sacred ford (tīrtha).
When the sinless Brahmajāyā, fashioned by the gods, was given back once more,
everything there became secure; therefore, O great sage, that place became a sacred ford (tīrtha) that destroys the flood of all sins and grants all desires.
There was joy and security for the gods, the enemies of the asuras,
and especially for Bṛhaspati, Śukra, and Tārā.
Having attained supreme bliss, the Preceptor addressed Gaṅgā.
The Guru said:
"O Gautamī, you are always worthy of worship by all as the bestower of liberation;
especially so while I am situated in the sign of Leo, for you are the purifier of the three worlds."
"O best of rivers, you shall become endowed with all sacred fords;
whatever holy sites there are in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld,
they shall go to bathe in you, O Mother, when I am seated upon the lion."
Brahmā said:
The sacred ford named Ānanda bestows merit, fame, and long life; it increases health and prosperity, and generates good fortune and sovereignty.
Therein, Gautama has spoken of five thousand sacred fords (tīrthas);
by either remembering or reciting [their names], one is always united with one's beloved desires.

Because Nandin constantly attends to Śiva who is established here on the bank of the Gaṅgā, he is Dharma manifest; therefore, it is remembered as Nandītaṭa. That sacred ford is also called Ānanda, because it increases all forms of bliss.
Brahmā said:
It is called Bhāvatīrtha, where Bhava himself resides—
the Self of all beings, whose form is existence-consciousness, dwelling within the entirety of the universe.
In this regard, listen as I relate this most meritorious and auspicious story concerning the illustrious upholder of the burden of the Kṣatriyas, the founder of the Solar dynasty.
Known as Prācīnabarhis, he was one who had reached the further shore of all dharmas;
he remained in the kingship for three and a half crores of years.

Near the hermitage of Vālmīki, the foremost of sages,

then, after several days had passed, the prince—

He was meditating on something within himself and sighing repeatedly;
in that interval, the Rākṣasas dwelling in Laṅkā arrived.
Sugrīva, Hanumān, Aṅgada, and likewise Jāmbavat,

"Where has her mother gone, who was not born from a womb? Only Rāma is seen here.

While the world-protectors were looking on and the noble lady was speaking there, Sītā had attained purification in the fire; yet the king remained unrestrained.
With these worldly words that had arisen, Rāma abandoned his beloved;

Rāma, having followed after those two together with the inhabitants of Ayodhyā,

Remembering again and again that Sītā, the mother of the world, they sighed; devoid of any attachment to worldly existence, they were eager to serve Gautamī.
Rāma himself, the lord of the three worlds, accompanied by his younger brother,

Surrounded by a thousand [attendants], he abandoned all his distress;
and the place where that event occurred is called Sahasrakuṇḍa.
There are ten other sacred fords there that grant all desires;
bathing and giving gifts there yield a thousandfold fruit.
On the banks of the Śrīgautamī, where the lords of sages such as Vasiṣṭha performed a fire-sacrifice that delivers one from all calamities and destroys all sins.
Through a stream of wealth poured into sacrificial pits numbering in the thousands,
that great ascetic obtained all the desired objects of his longing.
By the grace of Gautamī, the mother river, that holy site named Sahasrakuṇḍa became one that destroys Rākṣasas and yields great fruit.
Brahmā said:
That which is called Kapila-tīrtha is remembered as Aṅgiras;
that very same place is called Āditya, and it is also termed Saiṃhikeya.
O best of sages, on the southern bank of the Gautamī,
the Aṅgirasas performed a sacrifice for the Ādityas and gave the earth as their sacrificial fee.
Then the Ādityas went to the Aṅgirasas for the sake of performing penance;
that earth, having become Sairihikī, devoured all people.
Thereupon, all those people, being terrified and having realized through their knowledge that the earth was indeed Sairihkī, reported it to the Aṅgirases.
Then, having followed after the Ādityas, the Aṅgirases said to Vāc, "Let them accept the earth that was given"; but the Ādityas then replied, "No."
The wise do not accept a gift that has been turned back;
whoever seizes land, whether given by himself or given by another, [commits a grave sin].
For sixty thousand years, one is born as a worm in excrement;
there is no punishment greater anywhere than for the seizure of land given by oneself or by another.
"Sin is indeed most terrible, yet we do not accept her back;
if this is so, what then would happen in the case of seizing a woman given by herself? (BrP 155.8)
"Nevertheless, we shall accept the earth as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in the form of a purchase price.
When they had said "So be it," those gods [received] Kapilā, who possessed auspicious marks.
On the southern bank of the Gaṅgā, in that place on earth, they gave it;
there Viṣṇu himself, the bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation, dwells in embodied form.
And that confluence with the Kapilā destroys the flood of all sins;
there, from the waters of her gift, arose the river named Kapilā.
The sage performed the gift of the earth as superior even to the gift of cows,
for he protected the world by making an exchange.
The sacred ford where that event occurred is declared to be Gotīrtha;
it bestows merit there, and a hundred [other] sacred fords have been spoken of by the wise.
By bathing and giving gifts there, one obtains the fruit of a gift of land;
that confluence with the Gaṅgā is known as Kapilā-saṃgama.
Brahmā said:
There is a sacred ford named Śaṅkhahrada, where the wielder of the conch and mace resides;
by bathing there and beholding him, one is liberated from the bonds of worldly existence.
In this regard, I shall relate this narrative which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it occurred in the past, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, concerning Brahmā as he was chanting the Sāmaveda.
Born from the abode of the cosmic egg, the Rākṣasas, assuming many forms,
intoxicated by their strength and bearing weapons, arrived to devour Brahmā.
Then I spoke to Viṣṇu, the teacher of the world, for the sake of protection;
that Viṣṇu prepared his discus to slay those Rākṣasas.
Having cut down the Rākṣasas with his discus, he then blew his conch shell;
having made the earth free of thorns, heaven itself became devoid of enmity.
Then, with the utmost joy, Hari blew his conch shell;
thereupon, all the Rākṣasas were utterly destroyed without exception.
Where this entire event occurred through the power of Viṣṇu’s conch,
that place is called Śaṅkhatīrtha, which brings security to all men.
It bestows all that is desired, is meritorious, and grants auspiciousness upon being remembered;
it generates long life and health, and increases fortune and progeny.
O Sage, by either remembering or reciting it, one shall obtain all desires;
ten thousand sacred fords (tīrthas) are present there, which dispel all sins.
There are tens of thousands of sacred fords that remove all sins,
the power of which even the Lord Maheśvara knows how to describe.
There is no other substitute for the destruction of evil anywhere besides these.
Brahmā said:
The Kiṣkindhā Tīrtha has been described, which grants all desires to men,
pacifies all sins, and where Bhava is ever present.
I shall describe its true nature; listen attentively, O Nārada.
Formerly, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, [slew] Rāvaṇa, the one who made the world cry out.
Together with the inhabitants of Kiṣkindhā, he fought at the head of the battle;
having slain him along with his sons and his army, the slayer of enemies took Sītā.
Accompanied by his brother Saumitri, the mighty monkeys,
the powerful Vibhīṣaṇa, and the gods, the king returned.
Having performed the rites for auspiciousness, the illustrious one, resplendent upon the Puṣpaka chariot—
which moves at will and travels swiftly— set out as he had previously belonged to the King of Wealth.
They all went to Ayodhyā; on the way, Rāma—the restrainer of his enemies and the refuge for those seeking shelter—beheld the Gaṅgā.
Gautamī, who is meritorious for the whole world, the bestower of all desires,
and devoted to dispelling the distress of the mind and the eyes.
Having seen her, the illustrious king then went to the bank of the Gaṅgā;
having seen her, O Sage, the king addressed all the monkeys, headed by Hanumān, with a voice faltering with joy.
Rāma said:
"By the power of this [river], my father, the lord of the monkeys,
was liberated from all sins and thereafter went to the third heaven."
This [river] is the mother of every living being; she bestows enjoyment and may even grant liberation,
and she destroys even the most terrible sins.
What other river here is equal to this?
By its power, sins are constantly destroyed, and enemies become friends.
Vibhīṣaṇa constantly approaches with friendliness; Sītā has been recovered, Hanumān is a kinsman,
and Laṅkā, along with the host of Rākṣasas, has been shattered.
For by serving her,
Gautama, having worshipped that best of gods, obtained Śiva— the refuge-giver— who wears matted hair and by whom [all] is destroyed.
She is the mother of all desired things,
the destroyer even of inauspiciousness,
and uniquely skilled in purifying the world.
Today I have seen her directly, the mother of all rivers;
with body, speech, and mind,
I always go for refuge to this Gaṅgā, the worthy refuge.
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of the king,
all the monkeys bathed there.
They performed worship according to the rules, both individually and with many flowers and offerings from all the worlds;
having worshipped Śarva duly, the king [proceeded].
Having praised him with words suited to every emotion,
all those monkeys were filled with joy;
they likewise performed both dance and song.
Having passed that night in comfort, the high-souled one,
attended by his beloved ones and surrounded by those full of affection,
cast off all the suffering born of his enemies.
"What is not obtained by serving Gautamī?
[he asks]. Full of wonder, he gazes upon his circle of attendants;
and greatly rejoiced, he praises the Godāvarī.
Honoring his entire circle of servants, Rāma experienced an indescribable joy; then,
at the clear dawn when the sun had risen, [he set out].
Vibhīṣaṇa spoke to the son of Daśaratha:
"Even now, we are not yet satiated at this sacred ford."
We shall dwell here for some time;
we will stay right here for four more nights, and then we shall go to Ayodhyā, surrounded [by our attendants].
Brahmā said:
Then the monkeys assented to his words,
and likewise for another four nights.
Having worshipped that Lord, the sovereign of all,

By whose power the ten-faced Rāvaṇa became so mighty;

There, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, followed as an attendant, performing service for the king;

Abandon all the lingas established by me by those who know the supreme mantras,

They remain well-established even through that disregard.

He was unable to uproot it with his two arms;

It was not at all difficult; that would have been a great marvel for the lords of the monkeys, O King, and likewise for you. For who could shake one who has attained such great majesty?
Seeing that motionless Maheshvara-linga, the wise and high-souled hero among kings suddenly departed.
Then, having addressed the brahmins and performed worship,
Rāmacandra circumambulated them all with a heart of supreme purity.
Rāma bowed down to all the sacred emblems (liṅgas); therefore,

In this place, even great sins go to destruction simply by bathing; there is no doubt about this.

How much more so, then, through bathing and giving gifts, does it destroy evil?
Brahmā said:
Beyond this is the one known as Vyāsatīrtha, belonging to Pracetas.
There is nothing higher than this, which is purifying and bestows all perfections.
I had ten mind-born sons who were the creators of the worlds;

Having been granted permission by Aṅgiras, those ascetics, rich in penance, bowed to their teacher;

"For indeed, a mother is superior to all others in terms of the respect due to her.
Then, out of anger, Nārada cursed her sons.
The mother said: "Those sons who have set out to practice asceticism in disregard of me—

Brahmā said:
"Gathering [knowledge] from various lands, they do not attain perfection through austerity;

In some places that obstacle arose from Rākṣasas, in others from humans;

Wandering in this manner, they all went to Agastya, the storehouse of asceticism,
the best among those who practice austerities, the jar-born preceptor of the world.
Having paid homage to the peaceful lord of the southern quarter, those born of the lineage of Agni, the descendants of Aṅgiras, being humble, prepared to question him.
The Āṅgirasas said:
"O Blessed One, by what defect does our asceticism not succeed,

"What shall we do? What is the way here? Shall we simply remain engaged in asceticism?
Tell us a means, O best of Brahmins; you are surely foremost in ascetic power."
O Brahmin, you are the knower among the wise; you are the best of speakers among those who speak;
you are eternally tranquil among the self-controlled, and likewise compassionate and a doer of what is pleasing.
Free from anger and without hatred, speak therefore what you wish to say.
Those who possess egoism, who are devoid of compassion, who have abandoned service to their gurus,
