Brahmā said:
Agastya, having meditated for a moment, spoke slowly to them all.
Agastya said:
"O you of tranquil souls, you were indeed created as progenitors by Brahmā;
yet your ascetic power was not sufficient. Remember the cause of your pride."
Those who were created by Brahmā in the past and have attained happiness prosper;
those who went forth again to seek [the truth] became the Āṅgirasas.
And you all, having gone again at the proper time, proceeding slowly and steadily,
will undoubtedly become even greater than Prajāpati.
"Let them go from here to perform austerities at the Gaṅgā, the purifier of the three worlds;
for there is no other means in this cycle of existence except for the Gaṅgā, who is dear to Śiva."
In that hermitage, in that sacred place, you shall worship the Giver of Knowledge;
that one of great intelligence will sever all your doubts,
for nowhere is there success for anyone without a true guru.
Brahmā said:
They said to that best of sages, "Who is designated as the giver of knowledge?
Is it Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, or perhaps Āditya or Candramas?"
"O best of sages, who might be Agni and Varuṇa as the givers of knowledge?
Agastya spoke again: 'Listen to this one who gives knowledge.'"
That which is water is said to be fire; that which is fire is called the sun. That which is the sun is indeed Viṣṇu, and that which is Viṣṇu is the radiant one (Bhāskara).
He who is Brahmā is indeed Rudra; he who is Rudra is everything itself.
He whose knowledge is all that exists is celebrated here as the giver of knowledge.
There are many gurus who provide instruction, inspiration, commentary, and even their very bodies; among them, he who bestows knowledge is the greatest.

That very knowledge is said here by which duality is destroyed: Śambhu is indeed one and non-dual, yet the learned speak of him in many ways under the names Indra, Mitra, and Agni for the sake of assisting those who are deluded.
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of the sage, they departed singing songs;
five went toward the northern Gaṅgā, and five went toward the southern.
Worshipping the gods as they were proclaimed by Agastya according to the prescribed rites,
those contemplators of reality sat down specifically upon their seats.
O Sage, all the hosts of gods became joyful toward them regarding that creative power which was ordained by the Source of the Universe at the beginning of the age.
For the purpose of turning away from unrighteousness, for the establishment of the Vedas,
for the benefit of the worlds, and for the attainment of dharma, pleasure, and wealth.
"In determining the meaning of the Purāṇas, Smṛtis, Vedas, and Dharmaśāstras, you shall be recognized as the creators of the worlds; you shall become such as that."
Indeed, they will gradually attain the status of Prajāpatis when unrighteousness prevails and there is the decline of the Vedas.
From them shall come the future Vyāsas; whenever a decline of Dharma and of the Vedas is observed, from them [the Vedas] shall arise.
At each such time, those Vyāsas will be benefactors;
their place of austerity shall be the most excellent bank of the Gaṅgā.
In each and every place, Śiva, Viṣṇu, I myself, and Āditya,
as well as fire, water, and everything else, are always present there.
There is nothing purer than these, nor is there anything superior to them anywhere;
it is only the Supreme Brahman itself that has attained those various forms.
Śiva is all-pervasive, the soul of all, and the sustainer of the essential nature of all beings;
he is especially present at that sacred site out of compassion for all living creatures.
Followed by all the gods and bestowing grace upon them,
they should be known as the Vyāsas of Dharma as well as the Vyāsas of the Vedas.
The holy ford (tīrtha) of those [sages] was designated by that name throughout the three worlds;
it is a water that washes away the mire of sin, removes the intoxication of the darkness of delusion,
and bestows all perfections upon men— the unsurpassed Vyāsatīrtha.
Brahmā said:
There is a sacred ford (tīrtha) named Vañjarāsaṃgama, renowned throughout the three worlds,
which is constantly frequented by sages, as well as by perfected beings (siddhas) and royal seers (rājarṣis).
In former times, Garuḍa, the bird of the sky, fell into servitude to the Nāgas;
then, his mind tormented by suffering due to that slavery to his mother,
he once stood in solitude and, sighing deeply, reflected.
Garuḍa said:
"They alone are blessed in this world, they alone have truly performed meritorious deeds,
by whom no service has been rendered to others and for whom no calamity has arrived."
Fortunate are those who dwell in happiness, sing, sleep, and laugh, arising from their own bodies; fie, fie upon those who remain under the control of another!
Brahmā said:
Thus overcome with anxiety and distressed,
the immeasurable-souled Vainateya then approached his mother and questioned her.
Garuḍa said:
"O Mother, for whose offense—whether that of my father, myself, or another—have you attained this state of slavery? Tell me the cause of it as I ask you."
Brahmā said:
She spoke to her own son, the beloved younger brother of Aruṇa.
Vinatā said:
"There is no fault of anyone else; my own fault has been declared by me.
She whose word is proven false shall become a slave—this was what I stated."
Kadrū likewise said the same, and she went along with me; however, a dispute arose between Kadrū and me, and I was defeated by her through deceit.
For destiny, O dear one, is powerful; what action does it not compel?
Thus, O son of Kaśyapa, I fell into the state of a slave to Kadrū;
when I became a slave, you too, O twice-born one, became a slave.
Brahmā said:
Then Garuḍa became silent, exceedingly distressed;
he said nothing to his mother, reflecting upon the inevitability of destiny.
Once, Kadrū, desiring the welfare of her sons and seeking her own prosperity, spoke to Vinatā, the mother of the birds.
Kadrū said:
"Your son goes unimpeded to pay homage to the Sun;
oh, in these three worlds, even though you are but a slave, you are indeed blessed! (BrP 159.13)
Brahmā said:
Concealing her own sorrow, she, greatly amazed, spoke to Kadrū.
Vinatā said:
"But why do your sons not go to see the sun?"
Kadru said:
"O fortunate one, lead my sons toward the abode of the Nāgas;
near the ocean there lies a cool lake."
Brahmā said:
Suparṇa carried the serpents, as well as Kadrū and Vinatā;
then, being delighted, she spoke to the mother of Vainateya.
"Garuda is taking my sons to the abode of the gods," said the mother of the serpents again to Garuda with humility.
The mother of the serpents said: "My sons wish to see the swan, the teacher of the three worlds;
having paid homage to the Sun, they will then return to my abode."
"Come now, you must lead my sons daily toward the solar orb."
Brahmā said:
Trembling and distressed, Vinatā spoke to Kadrū.
Vinatā said:
"O mother of snakes, I am not patient; my son shall not carry your sons.
Having seen the divine Sun, let them return once again."
Brahmā said: Vinatā spoke to her son, the sovereign of birds:
"The Nāgas, having attained lordship, now desire to pay you homage."
"This mother of serpents has forcibly said to me, 'O Radiant One,' and I replied, 'So be it. Therefore, O Garuḍa, let the snakes mount upon me. (BrP 159.23)
Then the serpent army, mounted upon Garuḍa, the lord of birds,
slowly approached the place where the divine Sun was;
scorched by the sharp heat of the sun, they were greatly distressed.
The serpents said:
"Turn back, O one of great wisdom! Homage, homage to the moth!
Enough of going to the abode of the sun; we have been scorched by the splendor of the sun."
Whether it be Yama, or Garuda, or even you yourself, O Garuḍa, [I shall abandon them].
Brahmā said:
"While being addressed thus by the Nāgas, [Viṣṇu] said, 'I shall show the Sun to you,' and having spoken, he quickly went through the sky toward the face of the Sun."
With their enjoyments consumed, those many hundreds of thousands, tormented and with their bodies burnt, fell toward that Vīraṇa island.
Distraught with grief, Kadrū arrived to console her sons who had fallen upon the earth and were crying out in distress.
Kadru said to Vinata: "Your son, being exceedingly wicked-minded, has committed a most grievous wrong against those for whom there is no peace."
The lord of serpents, that Kāśyapa of vast splendor, cannot act otherwise than as his master commands; may all be well in this matter.
"And how, O beautiful lady, can there be peace for my sons?
Having heard those words from Kadrū, Vinatā was indeed struck with great fear.
He spoke to his high-souled son Garuḍa, the lord of birds.
Vinatā said:
"O son, this is not more appropriate; for it has been said that it is proper to conduct oneself with humility. To act otherwise is not fitting."
The virtuous should never act with deceit, even toward enemies;
the moon shines equally upon both a learned Brahmin and an outcaste.
O my dear son, those very lowest of men who are unable to act by force commit undesirable deeds through deceits.
Brahmā said:
Then Vinatā spoke to Kadrū, the mother of the serpents.
Vinatā said:
"By doing what will peace come to your sons? I shall do that for you.
Tell me how they have been seized by old age, and I shall bring about that peace."
Brahmā said:
Kadrū also said to Vinatā, "By means of the water located in the subterranean realm (rasātala),
peace will come to my sons once they have been consecrated with it."
Having heard those words, Kadrū brought water from the subterranean realm (rasātala) in an instant and consecrated those Nāgas. Then Garuḍa spoke to Maghavan Śatakratu:
Garuḍa said:
"And let the clouds rain here, bringing benefit to the three worlds."
Brahmā said:
Thus the rain-cloud poured down, and there was well-being for the nāgas;
the water born from the depths of Rasātala, the Gaṅgā’s own, became a life-restoring draught for the nāgas.
That which was brought by Garuḍa for the purpose of destroying old age and grief,
where the Nāgas were consecrated— that is called the abode of the Nāgas.
Since the water was brought by Garuḍa from that netherworld (rasātala),
that water of the Gaṅgā destroys all the sins of everyone.

Because the water from the Ganges, originating in the subterranean realm (rasātala), brought about the warding off of old age for the nāgas and was auspicious for them, it became known as "Nāgasaṃjīvana" (the reviver of the nāgas).
For the sake of destroying old age and sorrow, on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā,
that river Vañjarā appeared, which directly carries the nectar of immortality.

She who removes the torment of old age and poverty, she who is a river for those in distress— she is the Gaṅgā born from the subterranean realm (rasātala), while that which arises in the world of mortals is [the earthly Gaṅgā].
And what more need be said of their union,
by the mere remembrance of which the accumulations of sin go to destruction?
And who is capable of describing the fruit of bathing and giving gifts there?
The wise say that there are one hundred and twenty-five thousand sacred fords (*tīrtha*) at that place.
There is no sacred ford (tīrtha) anywhere equal to the union with Vañjarā, which bestows all prosperity and removes the flood of all sins;
by the mere remembrance of it, even calamities perish.
Brahmā said:
There is a holy ford named Devāgama, which is auspicious and grants all desires;
it bestows worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men and brings satisfaction to the ancestors.
In this regard, O Nārada, I shall relate to you with care the conduct [of those days]:
there was a rivalry between the gods and the asuras for the sake of wealth.
Heaven became the domain of the gods, while Ilā became the domain of the asuras;
having seized the land of action (karmabhūmi), the asuras prevailed everywhere.
Then the Asuras killed the donors of the sacrificial portions belonging to the gods;
consequently, all the hosts of gods were deprived of their shares in the sacrifice.
Distressed, they approached me and asked, "What must be done?
I, for my part, spoke to the hosts of gods after having forcibly conquered the asuras in battle.
"You shall obtain the earth, as well as ritual actions, oblations, and glories.
Having said, "So be it," the gods departed for the earth, seeking battle.
The Daityas, the Dānavas, and the Rākṣasas, arrogant in their strength,
also united and marched forth as victors, desiring battle.
Ahi, Vṛtra, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, Bali, Namuci, Śambara, Maya—
these and many other warriors, arrogant in their strength, [were slain].
Agni, Indra, Varuṇa, Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, as well as the two Aśvins,
the Maruts, and the world-protectors, all skilled in various modes of combat.
All those Dānavas, stationed at the southern ocean, exerted a great effort in battle toward the southern quarter.
In former times, Trikūṭa was the preeminent mountain of the Rākṣasas;
through that forest, they all went together with them to the southern ocean.
That mountain where all of them met was Malaya;
at that time, even the region of Malaya became a place for the enemies of the gods.
"Śiva is present there on the banks of the Gautamī for the sake of the gods"—
thus, it is said, the assembly of those gods took place.
The gods, having mounted their celestial chariots and being pure in intention, assembled here and there upon the sandy bank of Gautamī, the mother river.
"She who is gracious and grants the desires of all the ancestors"—
having thus praised the god Maheśvara, all the hosts of deities then reflected among themselves on how to grant them freedom from fear.
The gods said:
"What means is there for us who have been forcibly conquered by our enemies?
In this situation, there is only one thing beneficial for us: either victory or death."
Fie on the life of those high-minded men who are overwhelmed by their rivals!
Brahmā said:
In the meantime, my son, an incorporeal voice spoke.
The Voice of Space said: "O hosts of gods, enough with this distress! Go quickly to Gautamī and worship Hari and Hara, the two lords, there with devotion."
But by the grace of Godāvarī and of those two, what indeed is difficult to achieve?
Brahmā said:
Having obtained their desired victory from the gratified Viṣṇu and Śiva,
the gods departed in all directions, protecting the inhabitants of heaven.
The sacred ford where the arrival of the gods occurred became renowned by that name;
the sages who perceive the truth praise Devāgama.
There, O Nārada, are eighty thousand Śiva-liṅgas;
that mountain is called Devāgama and also Priya.
From that time forth, they have known that sacred site as Devapriya.
Brahmā said:
Kuśatarpaṇa has been described, as well as Praṇītāsaṃgama—
a holy ford that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation in all the worlds.
I shall describe its true nature; listen to this auspicious account that removes all sins.
On the southern side of the Vindhya mountains lies a great mountain named Sahya.
From his feet there arose rivers headed by the Godāvarī and the Bhīmarathī,
where that Virajā was, and where that Ekavīrā was.
No one is able to fully describe its greatness;
listen attentively, O Nārada, to what exists on that mountain in that holy region.
I shall declare that which is more secret than the secret, auspicious, and directly proclaimed in the Vedas— something which neither sages, nor gods, nor ancestors, nor asuras know.
Therefore, for your pleasure, I shall speak that which grants all desires upon hearing;
for that Supreme Person is to be known as indeed unmanifest and imperishable.
And another [principle] was the perishable; from that, the Puruṣa, endowed with primordial nature (prakṛti), was born—formless yet possessed of parts.
From that the waters were produced, and from the waters likewise the Puruṣa;
from those two the lotus was produced, and therein I came into being, O Sage.
O sage, earth, wind, space, water, and likewise light—
these were born from me all at once, even earlier than before.
I beheld only these, and nothing else, whether stationary or moving;
at that time, the Vedas did not exist, nor was I a seer of anything at all.
If I, from whom I have arisen, were not to see him even then,
while I remained silent, I would have heard a supreme voice.
The Voice of Space said:
"O Brahman, perform the creation of the world, both the stationary and the moving."
Brahmā said:
Then, O Nārada, I spoke these harsh words there:
"How shall I create this world? Where shall I create it? And by what means shall I create it?"
That very divine speech, which is called Prakṛti, spoke;
she is the Mother, impelled by Viṣṇu, the sovereign of the world, who consists of the world.
The Voice of Space said:
"Perform a sacrifice; then power will be yours, of this there is no doubt.
For 'Sacrifice is indeed Viṣṇu'—this is the eternal Vedic revelation, O Brahmin. (BrP 161.15)
What could be unattainable for those who perform sacrifices, both in this world and in the next?
Brahmā said:
I spoke again to that goddess, "Tell me, where or by whom [is this]?
"O highly fortunate one, the sacrifice must be performed," she then said to me.
The Goddess of Space said: "O Lord of Sacrifice, O Supreme Person of Sacrifice, you who have become the syllable Om, who are like a mother and consist of the universe—
perform the sacrifice here in this land of action."
That itself shall be your means of accomplishment; with that, O observer of noble vows, perform that sacrifice.
The sacrifice consists of *svāhā*, *svadhā*, mantras, Brahmins, the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), and so forth.
Hari alone is everything; through him, everything belonging to Viṣṇu is attained.
Brahmā said:
I spoke again to that goddess: "Where is the land of action ordained?
At that time, O Nārada, neither the Bhāgīrathī nor the Narmadā existed.

"Neither the Yamunā nor the Tāpī, nor the Sarasvatī, nor the Gautamī, nor the ocean, nor any river, nor any lake—none of these pure streams [are like her]; she is Śakti herself. Thus she spoke to me again and again.
The divine voice said:
"On the southern side of Mount Sumeru, likewise on the south of the Himavat mountain,
and also on the south of the Vindhya, as well as on the south of the Sahya."
But for everyone, at all times, the land of action is the source of auspicious arising.
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words, I left the great mountain Meru and,
arriving at that region, reflected, "Where should I stay?"
Then that very same incorporeal voice of Viṣṇu spoke to me.
The Voice of Space said:
"Go from here, stay here, or sit down right here;
perform the mental resolve for the sacrifice, and that sacrifice of yours shall be completed."
O best of gods, O Creator, once the resolve for the sake of sacrifice has been made,
perform all those things which the entire Vedas declare.
Brahmā said: The Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and whatever else falls within the domain of speech issued spontaneously from my mouth and became the object of my memory.
And at that very moment, the entire meaning of the Vedas was known to me;
thereafter, I recollected that Puruṣasūkta which is renowned throughout the world.
I prepared all the implements for the sacrifice as they were described;
in the manner prescribed, I arranged the sacrificial vessels.
In whatever region I have stayed, having become pure and self-controlled,
that place of the Brahmins is proclaimed by my name as being consecrated.
O great sage, my meritorious sacrificial ground is known by the name Brahmagiri,
extending for eighty-four yojanas.
My meritorious sacrificial ground is to the east of the mountain of Brahmā;
there, in its center, shall be the altar, and the Gārhapatya fire shall be to its south.
And there I prepared the sacred fires, including the Āhavanīya;
for according to the injunctions of the Śruti, a sacrifice cannot be accomplished without a wife.
"O sage, I indeed divided my own body into two parts;
from the first half, a wife was then created for me for the accomplishment of sacrifice."
Likewise, O Nārada, according to the Vedic revelation, I am the northern half, while my wife is the southern; and the preeminent spring season is Time, appearing in the form of clarified butter.
O son, I then conceived of the summer as the fuel, the autumn as the oblation,
and the rainy season as the sacrificial grass.
At that time, the seven Vedic meters indeed became the enclosing sticks (paridhi);
for the divisions of time—kalā, kāṣṭhā, and nimeṣa—are remembered as the fuel, the vessels, and the kuśa grass.
O divine sage, he who was himself time— both beginningless and endless— then became the sacrificial post in the form of a pillar, as well as the tethering rope for binding the animal.
The three qualities, beginning with *sattva*, are the fetters; there was no bound soul (*paśu*) there at all.
Then I spoke these words, which were Viṣṇu’s own and bodiless: BrP_161.39.
"This sacrifice cannot be completed without an animal," said that very goddess to me, she who is eternally incorporeal.
The Voice of Space said:
"Now, praise that Supreme Puruṣa with the Pauruṣa Sūkta."
Brahmā said:
Having said "So be it," while Janārdana, the god of gods and my progenitor, was being praised with devotion by means of the Puruṣa-sūkta, [he spoke].
And that goddess said to me, "O Brahmin, make me an animal";
then I recognized him as my father, the imperishable Puruṣa.
Beside Kālayūpa, I sprinkled that Puruṣa who stood upon the sacrificial grass, bound by the cords of his qualities, and born from the beginning.
In the meantime, from him everything here came into being;
from his mouth the Brahmins were born, and from his arms the Kṣatriyas.
From his mouth came Indra and Agni; from his breath arose Vāyu;
from his ears the directions emerged, and from his head all of heaven then came into being.
The moon was born from his mind, and likewise the sun from his eye;
the intermediate space from his navel, and the Vaiśyas from his thighs.
From his feet the Śūdra was born, and likewise the earth arose;
the sages were produced from the pores of his skin, and the medicinal herbs emerged from his hair.
Domestic and wild animals emerged from all his nails;
and worms, insects, moths, and the like were born from his anus and generative organ.
Whatever is stationary or moving, visible or invisible—
all that has arisen from me, and from me the gods have also come forth again.
In this interval, that very voice of Viṣṇu spoke to me once more.
The Voice of Space said:
"Everything has become complete; the creation has arisen exactly as desired.
Now, indeed, offer oblations into the fire, along with the sacrificial vessels and the ladles."
Likewise, dismiss the sacrificial post, the *praṇītā* water-vessel, and the *kuśa* grass;
as well as the form of the officiating priests, the form of the sacrifice, the object of reference, and that which is to be meditated upon.
O Brahman, release the sacrificial ladle, the person, the nooses, and everything else.
Brahmā said:
At the very moment of those words, O great sage, they entered the sacrificial hearths in due order— namely, the Gārhapatya fire and likewise the Dakṣiṇāgni.
And then, as he offered oblations sequentially into the eastern fire as well,
he focused his mind upon the Puruṣa, the source of the world, in each respective instance.
There, in the vicinity of the sacrificial pits, stood Yajñadeva, purified by mantras, pure, identical with the universe, the lord of the worlds, and the creator of all.
Viṣṇu, assuming a white form, resides in the Āhavanīya fire;
Viṣṇu is dark-complexioned in the Dakṣiṇāgni, and yellow in the Gārhapatya fire of the wise one.
Viṣṇu is present in all those regions at all times;
there is nothing whatsoever devoid of Viṣṇu, the source of the universe.
Then, with sacred mantras, I performed the ritual pouring of the *praṇītā* water;
moreover, this river of auspicious waters is called *Praṇītā*.
Then, having purified it with *kuśa* grass, I discharged that consecrated water;
while the purification was being performed, drops of the consecrated water [fell].
O tiger among sages, the sacred fords that fell there became endowed with virtues; through bathing in them, they bestow the fruit of sacrificial rites.
Adorned at all times by the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
that flight of stairs serves as the means for everyone to ascend to Vaikuṇṭha.
Where auspicious kusha grasses, having been swept clean, have fallen upon the ground,
that is declared to be the "libation of kusha grass," which bestows the fruit of great merit.
All were gratified with *kuśa* grass, and thus it is called the *kuśatarpaṇa*;
afterwards, Gautamī arrived there for another reason.
O Great Buddha, at the place called Praṇītā, there was a gathering of the refined; and at the site of the Kuśa libation, that sacred ford is known as Kuśatarpaṇa.
Right there, to the north of the Vindhya mountains, I fashioned a sacrificial post;
that post, honored by the world, was released and became the refuge of Viṣṇu.
The glorious one became imperishable, and that banyan tree became imperishable;
he is eternal and the very form of time, bestowing the merit of sacrifices upon those who remember him.
This Daṇḍaka forest is called my own sacrificial ground;
there, Viṣṇu was propitiated by me with devotion when the sacrifice was completed.
He who is called Virāj in the Veda, from whom the formed world was born,
from whom my own origin arose, and whose this transformed universe is.
Having paid homage to that Lord of the Gods of gods, I dismissed him;
my auspicious sacrificial ground extends for twenty-four yojanas.
Therefore, O Nārada, even today there exist three sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) which are the very embodiments of Viṣṇu, the Lord of Sacrifice, who wields the discus.
From that time forward, it has been known as my sacrificial ground;
even a worm or an insect dwelling there becomes a recipient of liberation in the end.
The Daṇḍaka forest is said to be the seed of Dharma and the seed of liberation;
especially because it was embraced by Gautamī, that region became most meritorious.
Furthermore, whoever performs bathing, giving of gifts, and other rites at the confluence of the Praṇītā, or even merely offers libations with *kuśa* grass, shall go to the supreme state.
They know that remembering, reciting, or even listening with devotion bestows all desires upon men and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The wise say that there are eighty-six thousand sacred fords (tīrthas) on both banks; the merit found therein has been described previously.
O Sage, even for Vārāṇasī, the libation with kusa grass is supreme;
there is no sacred ford equal to this one in the world of the moving and the unmoving.
"O Sage, this sacred ford on the surface of the earth is called Svargadvāra; it destroys even such sins as the killing of a Brahmin through the mere act of remembering it."
Brahmā said:
There is a place renowned as Manyutīrtha, which destroys all sins,
grants all desires to men, and annihilates evil merely by being remembered.
O Sage, listen attentively as I shall describe its power:
in ancient times, there was a mutual conflict between the gods and the dānavas.
There, the gods were not victorious; rather, the Dānavas became the victors.
The hosts of gods turned their backs upon the battle, their hearts having departed from it.
Approaching me, they said, "Grant us the means for our safety.
I replied to them, "Go all of you to the Gaṅgā."
There, indeed, on the bank of the Gautamī, having praised the god Maheśvara—
who is beautiful with innate bliss, free from decline, and devoid of exertion— [one attains the goal].
"All the gods shall obtain from Maheśvara the cause of victory";
having said "So be it," the hosts of deities praised Maheśvara.
Some indeed performed austerities, while others danced;
some bathed, and others likewise offered worship.
Then the blessed Maheśvara, the wielder of the trident, being pleased, spoke to the gods: "Being satisfied, let that which you desire be chosen."
The gods said: "O Lord of the Suras, grant us for victory that most praiseworthy Puruṣa, who stands at the forefront in battles."
"Relying upon the strength of whose arms we have become happy," thus spoke the Blessed Maheśvara to the gods.
By his own splendor, the Supreme Lord created one named Manyu,
who was exceedingly fierce and led the vanguard of the divine army.
Having bowed to him and, after bowing to Śiva, all the gods returned to their own abodes;
then, returning with Manyu, they stood ready once more for battle.
Standing in battle against the Danujas and the exceedingly powerful Daityas,
the gods, fully prepared for combat, stood before Manyu and spoke.
The gods said:
"We shall observe your power; afterwards we will fight with the enemies.
Therefore, O Manyu, reveal yourself to us who are desirous of battle."
Having heard those words of the god, Manyu spoke as if smiling: Brahmā said: {brahmovāca:} Having heard those words of the god, Manyu spoke as if smiling. (BrP 162.15)
Manyu said:
"The Lord of the gods, the omniscient, all-seeing Master, is my progenitor—
he who knows everything that resides in the minds of all beings within their abodes."
And no one at all knows him who always knows everything;
yet the Creator, who is identical with the universe, knows this [universe] both as formless and as having form.
That Blessed One is supreme; he is manifest as such, moving through the heavens and the firmament.
Who knows his true form? He who is composed of the universe is the creator of all.
"I am born from one such as this; how can you possibly know me? Or rather, if you truly desire to see me, then look upon me! (BrP 162.19)
Brahmā said:
Having spoken thus, he displayed his own great form of wrath,
which had arisen from the third eye of Bhava, the Supreme Lord.
Since all form is sustained by splendor, it is called "pauruṣa" (pertaining to the Puruṣa);
and egoism exists only among living beings within the Puruṣas.
He who is the terrible wrath of all, the bringer of destruction,
blazing with his own splendor— that representative of Śaṅkara— [he saw].
Seeing him bearing all weapons, all the deities prostrated;
the Daityas and Danujas were terrified, while the gods stood with their palms joined in reverence.
Having become enraged, they then said to Manyu: "O Lord, become our commander-in-chief!
O Manyu, we shall enjoy this kingdom granted by you."
Therefore, in all undertakings, you are the victor, the increaser of victory;
you are Indra, you are Varuṇa, and you alone are the guardians of the world.
"Enter into all of us gods for the sake of victory," Manyu said to them all, "for without me, nothing at all exists."
I have entered within all, yet no one knows me;
that very Lord Manyu has thus been born separately from each.
He himself would become Rudra in form; Rudra became Manyu and Śiva.
Indeed, all that is stationary and all that is moving is pervaded by Manyu.
Having obtained him, all the gods achieved victory in battle;
for victory, wrath, and valor arise from the splendor of the Lord.
Having achieved victory through wrath and having formed an alliance with the Daityas,
they all departed as they had come, protected by that very wrath.
On that bank of the Gautamī, where those gods, having propitiated Śiva,
attained both fury and victory, it is called Manyutīrtha.
And that man who, being self-restrained, should remember the origin of wrath in this manner,
shall achieve victory and shall not be overcome by anyone.
O great sage, there is indeed no purifier equal to the Tīrtha of Manyu,
for there Śaṅkara himself always resides in person in the form of Manyu;
bathing, giving gifts, and even remembering him there grants all desires.
Brahmā said:
There is an auspicious sacred ford named Sārasvata, which grants all desires;
it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men, and destroys all sins.
It pacifies all diseases and bestows all perfections;
listen now, O Nārada, to this account in detail.
To the east of Puṣpotkaṭā is a mountain world-renowned as Śubhra,
the best of peaks, situated on the southern bank of the Gautamī.
The sage known as Śākalya, who was supremely devoted to the life of a perpetual student,
performed unsurpassed austerities on that bright and holy mountain.
All the hosts of beings constantly bow down to and praise that best of the twice-born as he performs austerities, having taken refuge on the bank of the Gautamī.
On that mountain, frequented by sages, gandharvas, and celestial flowers, he was devoted to the service of the sacred fire and intent upon the study of the Vedas.
On that mountain of great merit lived a Rākṣasa named Paraśu, who struck fear into gods and twice-born men,
who was a hater of sacrifices and a slayer of Brahmins.
Moving through the forest, he wanders at will, assuming various forms;
in one moment he takes the form of Brahmā, and at another time he bears the form of a tiger.
Sometimes in the form of a god, sometimes assuming the form of an animal,
sometimes in the form of a woman, and sometimes in the form of a deer.
Sometimes that evildoer wanders about in the form of a child,
wherever the learned Brahmin Śākalya, the best of sages, resides.
That great sinner, the lowest of Rākṣasas, approaches him;
and that axe always approaches Śuciṣmat, the best of the twice-born.
Although that evildoer set out to seize and kill him, he was unable to do so;
once, that best of the twice-born, having diligently worshipped the gods, [proceeded].
O Sage, it is said that one desiring to eat arrived there;
having assumed the form of a Brahmin—loose-limbed, grey-haired, and frail—he brought along a certain maiden and spoke these words to Śākalya: BrP_163.13 //
The ascetic said: "O twice-born one, know me to be a seeker of food, as well as this maiden;
we have arrived at the time for hospitality, so fulfill your duty, O giver of honor."
Those alone are blessed in this world from whose homes guests depart with their desires fulfilled; all others, though living, are as if dead.
But when one has sat down for a meal, whatever has been prepared for oneself—
should he give that to guests, by him the entire earth has been given.
Brahmā said:
Having heard this, Śākalya replied, "I shall give it.
Then, having seated that twice-born man upon a seat, he [prepared] that axe out of ignorance.
Having honored him according to the prescribed rule, Śākalya gave him food;
having performed the *āpośana* rite with his hand, Paraśu spoke these words.
Paraśu said:
The deities follow one who has come from afar and is weary;
when he is satisfied, they too shall be satisfied, but if he is unsatisfied, the opposite occurs.
The guest and the slanderer—these two are friends to all the world;
the slanderer takes away one's sin, while the guest is a bridge to heaven.
If one looks with contempt upon a weary traveler who has arrived on the road,
his merit, fame, and prosperity perish at that very moment.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, I have come to you as a weary guest and I beg of you:
if you will grant my wish, then I shall eat; otherwise, I will not.
Brahmā said:
Śākalya said, "It is given," and he told the Rākṣasa, "Eat.
Then the axe spoke: "I am a supreme Rākṣasa."
"O twice-born one, I am not your enemy, nor am I an old man, grey-haired and emaciated;
many years have passed while I have been watching you."
"My limbs are withering like a small pool of water in the summer;
therefore, O best of the twice-born, I shall take you along with your followers and devour you."
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of Paraśu, Śākalya spoke these words.
Śākalya said:
Those who are born of noble lineage and have mastered all the scriptures—what they promise is fulfilled; there is never any deviation in this matter.
Do as you see fit, my friend; nevertheless, hear my words:
even when others are prepared to strike, the virtuous must speak what is beneficial.
"I am a Brahmin, whose body is adamantine, the all-protecting Hari;
may Viṣṇu protect my feet, and may the god Janārdana protect my head."
May Varāha protect my arms; may the King of Tortoises protect my back;
may Kṛṣṇa protect my heart, and may Mṛga protect my fingers.
May Vāgīśa protect my mouth; may Pakṣiga protect my eyes;
may Vitteśa protect my ears; may Bhava protect me from all sides.
In times of various calamities, Lord Nārāyaṇa himself is the sole refuge.
Brahmā said:
"O Lord of Rākṣasas, having spoken thus, you may now, unwearied, either lead me away or devour me at your pleasure."
At his word, the Rākṣasa prepared himself to devour him;
indeed, there is surely not even a grain of compassion in the hearts of sinners.
Then, with his face made terrifying by his fangs, he went into his presence;
and upon merely beholding that brahmin, Paraśu spoke these words: BrP_163.34 //
Paraśu said:
O best of the twice-born, I behold you, the omnipresent Lord, holding the conch, the discus, and the mace in your hands,
possessing a thousand feet, heads, eyes, and arms.
O Brahmin, today I behold you as the sole abode of all beings, whose form is the Vedic meters, and who consists of the entire universe; your former body no longer exists.
Therefore, O Brahmin, I implore you: be my refuge yourself.
Grant me knowledge, O one of great intelligence; tell me of the sacred ford that effects the expiation of sin.
O Brahmin, the sight of the great never arises without fruit;
even if it occurs through hatred, ignorance, attachment, or negligence.
The touch of iron results in nothing but the production of gold.
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words uttered by the Rākṣasa,
Śākalya spoke out of compassion— that Sarasvatī who is the giver of boons.
Therefore, O Lord of Daityas, praise Janārdana before long;
for in the attainment of the fruits of one's desires, there is nothing else superior to the praise of Nārāyaṇa.
"Listen, O Rākṣasa, there is indeed some cause for this in this world:
at my word, that goddess will become well-disposed toward you."
Brahmā said:
Having said, "So be it," that supreme axe, having bathed in the Gaṅgā who purifies the three worlds,
stood facing the Gaṅgā, pure and with a restrained mind.
There he beheld Sarasvatī, the sustainer of the world, who possessed a divine form and was anointed with divine perfumes, abiding by the words of Śākalya.
To her, the Mother of the Universe, the Sovereign of the World who removes the world's dullness, he—
whose soul was humble and whose impurities had vanished— spoke with his axe.
The other sage said: "The preceptor Śākalya has told me: 'Praise Mākānta, the one who bears the thunderbolt.
By your grace, act in such a way that I may possess that power."
"So be it," Śrī Sarasvatī replied to Brahmā;
and by the grace of Sarasvatī, the axe [struck] that Janārdana.
He praised him with various words, and then Hari became pleased;
Janārdana, the ocean of compassion, granted a boon to the Rākṣasa.
Janārdana said:
Whatever is in the mind of the Rākṣasa, all that shall come to pass.
Brahmā said:
"By the grace of Śākalya, by the grace of Gautamī,
by the grace of Sarasvatī, and by the grace of Narasiṃha."
Then, by the grace of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, whose lotus feet are all sacred fords, even that most wicked Rākṣasa ascended to heaven with his axe.
From that time forth, that sacred ford has been known as Sārasvata;
by bathing and giving gifts there, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Indeed, many sacred fords (tīrthas) originating from Vāgjava, Vaiṣṇava, Śākalya, and Paraśu existed on that Śveta mountain.
Brahmā said:
It is called Ciccikātīrtha; it destroys all diseases, removes all anxieties, and brings peace to all men.
I shall describe its true nature on that bright, best of mountains,
on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā, where the god Gadādhara resides.
There, on the White Mountain (Śvetaparvata), dwells the king of birds, Ciccika, who is called Bheruṇḍa; he is a flesh-eater who always resides right there.
It was frequented by trees laden with various flowers and fruits and blossoming in all seasons,
served by the foremost of the twice-born, and graced by the Gautamī river.
In that vicinity, crowded with Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Kiṃnaras, and gods,
there was a certain mountain frequented by both bipeds and quadrupeds.
On this mountain, endowed with such virtues and filled with various hosts of sages, one is not a vessel for disease, suffering, hunger, thirst, anxiety, or death.
There was a certain ruler of the eastern region known as Pavamāna;
he was illustrious, devoted to the dharma of the kṣatriyas, and a protector of the gods and brāhmaṇas.
Endowed with great power, he went to the forest accompanied by his domestic priest;
there he took delight in the company of beautiful women and in the pleasures of dance and music.
And thus, with bow in hand and surrounded by those whose habit was hunting,
he wandered about until, becoming weary at one point, he approached a tree.
Grown on the banks of the Gautamī and surrounded by flocks of various birds,
it was like the lord of hermitages, served by those who know the Dharma.
Having taken refuge upon that best of mountains, O best of kings,
that wind-god rested surrounded by people and gazed upon the preeminent mountain.
There, that best of kings saw a stout, two-faced Brahmin of handsome appearance, who was both filled with anxiety and exhausted; he questioned him.
The king said:
"Who are you, a two-faced bird, who appear as if burdened by anxiety?
No one here is afflicted by sorrow; why have you come to grief?"
Then the bird Ciccika, his mind somewhat comforted though sighing repeatedly, spoke slowly to King Pavamāna.
Cicika said:
"There is no fear for me from others, nor is any harm brought upon me by another.
This place is strewn with various flowers and fruits and is frequented by sages."
I see this mountain as nothing but empty; therefore, I grieve for myself. I do not obtain any happiness, nor am I ever satisfied.
Nowhere do I find sleep, nor rest, nor peace.
Brahmā said:
Having heard what was spoken by the twice-born Dvimukha, the king was greatly amazed.
The king said:
"Who are you? What sin was committed? Why is the mountain empty?
And how is it that living beings here on this best of mountains are satisfied with a single mouth?"
How much less will you find satisfaction with this non-dual [state]?
Or what evil deed have you committed here in this life, or perhaps in the past?
Tell me all that truly; I shall protect you from great fear.
Brahmā said:
Then the twice-born Cicchika, sighing deeply, spoke to that king.
Cicika said:
"O Pavamāna, listen as I relate to you an ancient account.
I am the foremost among the twice-born, one who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas."
Of noble birth and known for his wisdom, yet a destroyer of tasks and fond of strife,
he speaks one thing in the presence of others and another behind their backs among living beings.
He is always miserable at the prosperity of others, a deceiver of the world through illusion,
ungrateful, devoid of truth, and skilled in censuring others.
A betrayer of friends, masters, and gurus, practicing deceitful conduct and being exceedingly cruel, I torment many people through my mind, actions, and speech. (BrP 164.25)
This alone is my constant delight: the harming of others, the sowing of discord between couples, the destruction of communities, and the perpetual violation of boundaries.
"I am devoid of discernment and have turned my back on the service of the wise;
there is no sinner like me anywhere in the three worlds."
Therefore, I have become two-faced; through that torment, I am fated to suffering. Thus, scorched by misery, this mountain is empty for me.
Moreover, O protector of the earth, hear another word consistent with dharma and artha:
without that [virtuous conduct], a sin equal to the murder of a Brahmin is incurred.
A Kṣatriya, having entered into battle, or even elsewhere than in battle,
[should not strike] one who is fleeing, one who has laid down his weapons, one who is trusting, or one who has turned his back.
If a Kṣatriya should kill one who has sat down unawares and says, "I am afraid," he would indeed be a slayer of a Brahmin.
He who forgets what he has studied,
acts with arrogance, and shows disrespect toward his teachers— him they call a slayer of Brahman.
He who speaks kindly in one's presence but harsh words in one's absence, and who always says one thing while thinking another in his heart and doing yet another— [he is a wicked person].
One who utters curses against gurus, one who hates them, one who reviles Brahmins,
one who is falsely humble, and one who is evil-minded— he indeed shall be a slayer of a Brahmin.
He who, out of hatred, reviles the gods, the Vedas, the inner self (adhyātma), and the harmony between Dharma and the Brāhmaṇas— he indeed shall be a slayer of Brahman (brahmaghātaka).
"Even though I am such a person, O King, I conduct myself as if I were of virtuous character for the sake of hypocrisy and out of shame; therefore, O King, I became a twice-born."
"Even though I have become such as this, O King, I shall perform some virtuous deed somewhere;
by that deed, I shall remember of my own accord what was done in the past."
Having heard those words of Cicika, Pavamāna was greatly amazed; he said to the twice-born man, "By what deed will you attain liberation? {Brahmā said:} BrP_164.38.
Having heard these words of his, the king of birds spoke to the monarch:
Ciccikā said:
"O you of noble vows, lead me to that sacred ford named Gadādhara, which is on this very best of mountains, on the northern bank of the Gautamī."
For that sacred ford is most meritorious, the destroyer of all sins, and the granter of all desires; so it has been heard by the great sages.
"O Gautamī, there is no other destroyer of afflictions like Viṣṇu;
it is my conviction that I must behold that sacred ford with my whole being."
"By any effort made by me, this can never be possible;
how could those who have performed evil deeds ever attain what they desire?"
"O Hero, even with great effort, I do not see that which is so difficult to behold;
therefore, by your grace, may I indeed behold the Wielder of the Mace."
He who knows suffering even when it is unmanifested, the oceanic abode of compassion,
upon seeing whom men no longer perceive the afflictions of existence.
"O observer of noble vows, upon merely seeing you, I shall go to heaven through your grace."
Brahmā said:
Having been addressed thus by the twice-born Ciccika,
the king showed that god and the Gaṅgā to the twice-born one.
Then that Cicchika, having bathed in the Gaṅgā, the purifier of the three worlds, [proceeded].
Cicika said:
O Gaṅgā, O Gautamī, as long as a person does not behold you, the purifier of the three worlds, they are called a sinner both in this world and the next.

Therefore, O best of rivers, deliver me even though I am full of every fault; for embodied beings in this cycle of existence, there is no other refuge anywhere whatsoever except you, O you who have arisen from the lotus-feet of Viṣṇu.
Brahmā said:
Thus, with a soul purified by faith and taking sole refuge in Gaṅgā, the twice-born man performed his bath while inwardly remembering, "O Gaṅgā, save me! (BrP 164.51).
Then, having bowed to Gadādhara while the mountain-dwellers looked on,
he ascended to heaven at that very moment, permitted by Pavamāna.
Then Pavamāna departed for his own city accompanied by his followers;
from that time forth, that sacred bathing place (tīrtha) was known as Pāvamāna, along with Ciccika.
Those who know the Vedas recognize Gadādhara as Koṭitīrtha;
there, the merit of any action performed by men becomes multiplied ten million-fold.
Brahmā said:
It is proclaimed as Bhadratīrtha, which wards off all misfortunes,
pacifies all sins, and bestows great peace.
Uṣas, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ and devoted wife, was the beloved wife of Āditya; Chāyā also was a wife of Savitṛ, and her son was Śanaiścara.
His sister was named Viṣṭi, terrifying and of sinful form;
Savitṛ pondered to whom he should give that maiden in marriage.
"Whomever the Sun, the Lord and Teacher of the World, desires to give [to], she will give to him.
Hearing this, Bhīṣaṇā said, "What shall we do with this wife? While things were thus proceeding, she, being distressed, spoke to her father: BrP_165.4 //
Viṣṭi said:
"If a father gives his daughter while she is still a child to one who is handsome,
that father shall have achieved his purpose in this world, provided he has not been a doer of evil."
From the fourth year onwards, until the end of the tenth year,
the father must make every effort to arrange the marriage of his daughter.
A daughter should indeed be given to a bridegroom who is illustrious, learned, young, of noble birth, renowned, generous, and well-supported.
If a father should act otherwise than this, O Bāskara, he shall dwell eternally in hell;
for a daughter is the means for accomplishing dharma even for the wise.
For fools whose minds are struck by desire, the entire earth with its mountains, forests, and groves is equal to hell.
On one side is a well-adorned maiden who is free from blemishes;
on the other is he who sells a daughter, or even a horse, a cow, or sesame seeds.
There shall never be any deliverance for him from the Raurava and other hells;
one must never commit the transgression of marrying off a maiden.
When that has been done, who can describe the sin that belongs to the father?
[It occurs] as long as he does not know shame, and as long as he plays with dust.
A daughter must be given away in marriage at that time; otherwise, there is a downward path for her parents.
The son should possess the very nature of his father; he who is the father is indeed the son.

Who in this world would not desire their own happiness, and who indeed does not act for it? Yet, regarding a daughter, a father may perform acts such as giving her away in marriage, honoring her, or even looking at her [with improper intent]. (BrP 165.15)
One should know that whatever is done for them is truly done; what is given to them is inexhaustible.
What is given to those maidens conduces to infinity.
O Ravi, who would not bring happiness to his sons and grandsons?
He who acts for the sake of his daughters shall become a vessel of prosperity.
Brahmā said:
To that maiden Viṣṭi, who was speaking thus, the Sun-god spoke.
Sūrya said:
"What can I do? No one accepts you, for you possess a terrifying appearance;
[they disregard] your lineage, form, age, wealth, learning, conduct, and excellent character."
"In matters of mutual alliance, marriage, and regarding women and men, we possess everything—even without your virtues, O auspicious lady!
What shall I do? To whom shall I give you? Fie on me for my uselessness; why do you treat me thus? (BrP 165.20)
{Brahmā said:} Having spoken thus, the Sun-god spoke again to that Viṣṭi.
Sūrya said:
"O Viṣṭi, if you agree, you are indeed to be given away to whomever I choose.
Since you are being given by me today, then grant me your permission."
Brahmā said:
That destiny (viṣṭi) spoke to her father: "A husband, sons, wealth, happiness, long life, beauty, and affection arise as a consequence of one's past deeds. (BrP 165.23)
Whatever action— whether good or evil— was previously performed by a living being,
its fruit is obtained in accordance with that very action, even in another existence.
That very fault must be diligently avoided by the father;
for the fruit will surely be exactly as that which was practiced in the past.
Therefore, the father performs that connection with the gift which follows his own lineage;
as for the remainder, whatever is to be by destiny shall come to pass.
Having heard those terrifying words of his daughter, Brahmā gave that service, which causes fear to the worlds, to Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ.
Viśvarūpa was likewise terrifying with a fearsome form;
thus they wandered together, equal in their conduct and appearance.
At one time, a discord arose between the husband and wife;
they had two sons named Gaṇḍa and Atigaṇḍa.
Raktākṣa, Krodhana, Vyaya, and Durmukha;
the youngest among them was named Dharṣaṇa, who was a partaker of merit.
Suta was well-behaved, fortunate, peaceful, pure-minded, and clean;
once, he went to see his maternal uncle at the abode of Yama.
He beheld many beings who, though situated in heaven, were as if suffering;
having bowed, he questioned his maternal uncle regarding the eternal Dharma.
Harṣaṇa said:
"Who, O dear one, are these who are happy, and who are those who are cooked in hell?"
Brahmā said:
Thus questioned, Dharmarāja spoke everything exactly as it was;
he explained the entire course of those actions in their full detail.
Yama said:
Those men who never commit a transgression against what has been ordained do not see hell even at any time.
Those who do not honor the scriptures, nor proper conduct, nor those who are deeply learned,
and who commit transgressions against what is ordained— they are destined for hell.
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of Dharma, Harṣaṇa spoke again.
Harṣaṇa said:
Your father is Bhīṣaṇa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, and your mother is the formidable Viṣṭi;
your brothers are high-souled beings by whom your intellects have been stilled.
"They shall be handsome, faultless, and bestowers of auspiciousness;
therefore, O best of gods, tell me that rite today, for I shall perform it."
"If it were otherwise, I would not go to them," said Dharmarāja when addressed thus; he spoke to Harṣaṇa of pure intellect: "You are Harṣaṇa (the Delighter), there is no doubt."
Some may have many sons, yet they are not the continuers of the lineage;
there may be only one son by whom that family is sustained.
He who is the support of the family, he who does what is pleasing to his parents, and he who rescues his ancestors—he alone is a son; any other is merely a disease.
"Since you have spoken what is appropriate and pleasing to me, O maternal grandfather,
therefore go to the Gautamī river, having bathed with a restrained mind."
Praise Viṣṇu, the source of the universe, with a heart full of devotion;
for if he is pleased, he will grant all that is desired.
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of Dharma, Harṣaṇa went to Gautamī;
Śuci praised Hari, the Lord of Gods, and Hari became pleased.
Then, for the sake of his joy, he gave Kulabhadra to him, saying:
"May there be welfare for you, preceded by the pacification of all misfortune."
Therefore, that Viṣṭi is called Bhadrā, and his father and sons were likewise called Bhadra;
from that time forth, that sacred ford is called Bhadratīrtha.
There, Hari is the Lord of Bhadra, bestowing all auspiciousness upon men;
for those men who serve that sacred ford, he is the granter of all perfections.
Janārdana, the God of gods, is himself the manifest treasure-house of all auspiciousness.
Brahmā said:
The holy ford known as Patatri-tīrtha is declared to be the destroyer of disease and the annihilator of sin;
by the mere hearing of its name, a man becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done.
Two sons of Kaśyapa, the lords Aruṇa and Saṃpāti,
as well as Jaṭāyu, were born in that lineage.
The two sons of the Prajāpati Tārkṣya were Aruṇa and Garuḍa;
and born in their lineage was Saṃpāti, the best of birds.
For there was another younger brother, renowned as Jaṭāyu;
possessed by a mutual rivalry, the two were intoxicated with their own strength.
Those two best of birds flew together through the sky to pay homage to the maker of day,
until they reached the vicinity of the sun.
Seeing both his kinsmen fallen on the mountain peak, their wings burnt, exhausted, motionless, and deprived of consciousness, [he was overcome with grief].
Overwhelmed by such suffering, Aruṇa spoke to Bhāskara:
"Beholding those two fallen upon the earth,
O Tigmāṃśu, console them until they shall no longer die."
Brahmā said:
Having said, "So be it," the Maker of Day restored those two birds to life;
and Garuḍa, having heard their condition, [acted] together with Viṣṇu.
Nārada arrived, comforted them, and brought them peace;
then they all went to the Gaṅgā to dispel their distress.
Jaṭāyu, Aruṇa, Saṃpāti, Garuḍa,
Sūrya, and Viṣṇu likewise went to that holy place which bestows great merit.
The sacred ford known as Patatritīrtha is said to destroy poison and grant all desires;
there, Sūrya himself, as well as Viṣṇu, along with Suparṇa and Aruṇa, [are present].
Likewise, the bull-bannered Lord Śiva resides on the bank of the Gautamī;
that sacred ford is the supreme station for all three gods.
Having bathed there and become pure, one should pay homage to these deities;
freed from mental and physical ailments, he shall attain supreme happiness.
Brahmā said:
It is renowned as Vipratīrtha, and likewise they know it as Nārāyaṇa;
I shall recount its history, which is full of wonder—listen!
Within the sacrificial altar (antarvedi) there was a certain twice-born Brāhmaṇa who had mastered the Vedas;
his sons were highly wise and endowed with virtue, beauty, and compassion.
Their youngest brother was Śānta, endowed with a multitude of virtues;
he was renowned as Āsandīva, possessed of all knowledge and great intelligence.
In the meantime, during that night, while the son of the twice-born was asleep, his father made an effort to provide him with a palanquin for the wedding.
O gentle one, she who does not remember Viṣṇu, whose head is unsteady, who is undisciplined,
and who is of cruel form, a Rākṣasī capable of changing her shape at will, [reaches] as far as heaven.
Taking him with her, she went quickly to the southern bank of the Gautamī,
on the northern side of Śrīgiri, a place frequented by many Brahmins.
There was a city that was an abode of Dharma and a very dwelling place of prosperity;
there dwelt a king of great fame, endowed with all the virtues of a kshatriya.
At the end of the night, that Rākṣasī, accompanied by the two sons of the Brahmin, reached that city which was endowed with boundless security and abundance.
She always assumes pleasing forms;
together with that twice-born man, she wanders throughout this entire earth, assuming whatever form she desires.
On the southern bank of the Godāvarī,
the terrifying one in the form of an old woman spoke to that twice-born man.
[The Rākṣasī said:]
"O foremost of the twice-born, let this Gaṅgā Sandhyā be worshipped by the best of Brahmins having assembled together at the proper time, as is fitting. BrP 167.10a–10c.
Those who do not diligently perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) are declared by the lords of the gods to be base;
they are the foremost among those of the lowest castes (antyāvasāyin).
"You must say, 'I am your mother,' otherwise you will meet your destruction this very moment,
O best of the twice-born, if you do not carry out my word."
"I shall bring you happiness and whatever is dear to you; furthermore, I shall surely restore you to your country, your home, and your elders—
this is the truth."
Brahmā said:
He asked, "Who are you? And that Rākṣasī, who could assume any form at will, replied to that bull among the twice-born.
Consoling that prince of sages, whose mind was bewildered, with many oaths,
she who was world-renowned by the name Kaṅkālinī— (BrP 167.13c–14a)
The Brahmin also said to her: "I shall do exactly what has been requested; there is no doubt in this matter. Whatever is pleasing, I both speak and perform."
{Brahmā said:} Having heard those words of the Brahmin, the Rākṣasī, who could assume any form at will, though old, possessed lovely limbs and was adorned with divine ornaments.
Taking the brahmin with her everywhere, she went, spoke, and acted in every place, saying, "This son of mine is Guṇākara."
They regarded that brahmin, adorned with beauty, good fortune, youth, and learning,
as her husband, and that aged woman, endowed with virtues, as his mother.
There, a certain excellent brahmin, placing that rākṣasī before him, gave his own daughter, adorned with ornaments, to that twice-born man.
Having obtained him as her husband, that maiden thought, "I have achieved my purpose";
but that twice-born man, seeing his wife endowed with such virtues, was deeply distressed.
The twice-born said: "This Rākṣasī, whose form is sinful, will surely devour me.
What shall I do? Where shall I go? Or to whom shall I tell this?"
"Who here will protect me when I have fallen into such great danger?
This is my auspicious wife, endowed with virtue, beauty, and youth;
yet this Rākṣasī will suddenly devour her as well."
Brahmā said:
In the meantime, that virtuous wife,
though aged and exceedingly difficult to overcome, had gone somewhere at that time.
Bowing down with humility, the young woman, though devoted to her husband,
perceiving her lord to be distressed, spoke softly to her husband in private.
The wife said:
"O Lord, why has this suffering come upon you? Tell me the truth."
Brahmā said:
He spoke slowly to his wife, in due order and with full detail as before:
"O beloved, what is there that should not be told to a friend or to a woman of noble birth?"
Having heard these words of her husband, she, the best among speakers, replied:
The wife said:
For those who lack self-mastery, there is fear from every direction, even within their own homes;
but whence can there be fear for those who possess the Self? How much less so on the banks of the Gautamī?
For those devotees of Viṣṇu who dwell here— detached and discerning—
having bathed in this place and become pure, praise the Lord who is free from all ailment.
Brahmā said:
Having heard this and bathed in the Gaṅgā, the twice-born man, freed from all impurity,
likewise praised Nārāyaṇa on the bank of the Gautamī.
The twice-born said: O Lord, you are the inner self of this world;
O Mukunda, you alone are its creator and its destroyer.
"You are the protector; why do you not protect the wretched one, O Kinsman of the helpless, O Lion among Men?
Having heard this supplication of his, the remover of the world's sorrow—
Nārāyaṇa also slew that wicked Rākṣasī.
With his radiant, thousand-spoked Sudarśana discus,
the Lord granted him his desired boons and brought his preceptor back to life.
From that time forth, they have known that sacred site as Vipranārāyaṇa;
there, through bathing, giving gifts, worship, and other rites, one's desires are fulfilled.
Brahmā said: There is the one known as Bhānutīrtha, as well as the Tvaṣṭra, Māheśvara,
Aindra, Yāmya, and Āgneya tīrthas, which destroy all sins.
There was a king known as Abhiṣṭuta, who was pleasing to behold;
he began to sacrifice to the gods with the meritorious horse-sacrifice.
In that sacrifice, there should be sixteen officiating priests (ṛtvij) led by Vasiṣṭha and Atri;
but when a Kṣatriya is the sacrificer, how should the sacrificial ground be prepared?
"When a Brahmin is consecrated for initiation, the king will give him the earth fit for sacrifice;
but when a king is consecrated for initiation, who would be the giver, and who indeed would be the supplicant?"
This begging, which produces all manner of misfortune and is the very form of sin,
must therefore never be practiced by anyone, and especially not by a Kṣatriya.
While the Brahmins were thus deliberating among themselves,
the immensely wise Vasiṣṭha, the foremost knower of dharma, spoke there.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Queen, while you are being initiated, the Sun should be entreated regarding the earth:
'O God Savitṛ, grant me a place for sacrifice worthy of the deities.'"
"O Brahmin, you are the divine sovereignty; O Lord of Beings, let there be salutation unto you!
Being entreated by the king, Savitṛ [performed] the auspicious sacrifice for the gods."
Therefore, O King, one certainly gives; thus I pray to the Lord Divākara.
Brahmā said:
Having said "So be it," even though he had already been praised, he prayed with faith to the Sun, the god of gods, who is the source of Hari, Īśa, and the Self.
The king said:
"Grant me the sacrifice for the gods; O Savitṛ, homage be unto you!"
Brahmā said:
"Since the solar deity is the source of the kṣatriya power, the earth was granted to the lord of the earth;
therefore, Savitṛ, the Lord of the gods of gods, declared, 'I give it.'"
For one who performs the sacrifice in this manner, there shall be no misfortune whatsoever,
even during the Vājimedha sacrifice when it is performed as a long-term session by Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas.
Where the Sun-god went to the king, having been praised by the monarch when the sacrifice had commenced,
in order to grant the gods their sacrificial offerings— that is called Bhānutīrtha.
The Daityas, the Danujas, and other destroyers of sacrifices [attacked] that supreme horse-sacrifice (hayamedha) of the gods, which was joined by the deities.
All of them, wearing the garb of Brahmins and singing like chanters of the Sāmaveda,
those highly wise ones also entered there unimpeded.

The *camasa* cups and vessels, the *soma*, the *caṣāla* [sacrificial headpiece], the drinking of *soma*, the oblation (*havis*), the ritual offering (*tyāga*), the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and likewise the lord of the earth; BrP 168.17.
O Sage, some revile him and others cast him down, while other asuras laugh; they do not understand his activity without knowing his universal form.
Viśvarūpa also said to his father, "These are Daityas.
Having heard those words of his son, Tvaṣṭṛ spoke this to the gods.
Tvaṣṭṛ said:
"Taking water and *darbha* grass, sprinkle everywhere those who revile the meritorious sacrifice, the sacrificial cup, and the soma."
Having said, "But all of them have been struck down by me," sprinkle [the water] around.
Brahmā said:
The hosts of gods acted accordingly, and Tvaṣṭṛ did likewise; thereupon they were all reduced to ashes and became utterly bewildered as to what to do.
Having said, "The great sinners have been slain by me," he threw water [upon them];
then the Daityas, their lifespans exhausted, departed from there in anger.
Where Tvaṣṭṛ, the Prajāpati of the world, poured forth that water,
that place is known as the Tīrtha of Tvaṣṭṛ, which destroys all sins.
Then Yama struck down the Daityas who had fallen at the word of Tvaṣṭṛ with his staff of time,
his discus, his noose of time, and his wrath.
The sacred ford where those Daityas were slain is called Yāmya;
it was there that the sacrifice was completed after offering much nectar into the fire.
At that great sacrifice, he was praised with unbroken, continuous streams of oblations,
by which the bearer of the sacrificial offerings became truly satisfied.
That place is declared to be Agnitīrtha, which bestows the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice; there, Indra, together with the Maruts, spoke these auspicious words to the king: BrP_168.28.
"O King, you shall become the sovereign ruler of both worlds;
you will always be my dear friend—of this there is no doubt."
Having accomplished his purpose, he should perform libations for the ancestors at Indratīrtha in the world of mortals, and especially so at Yamatīrtha, for the sake of their gratification.
That sacred ford belongs to Maheśvara; there Śiva was worshipped and praised by Brahmins endowed with devotion and skilled in all ritual acts.
One should worship Maheśvara with Vedic and worldly mantras,
as well as with dances, songs, musical instruments, and the fivefold nectars.
And with many ritual services, such as prostrations and circumambulations,
with incense, lamps, food offerings, flowers, and fragrant perfumes.
With single-minded devotion, he worshipped Viṣṇu and Śambhu, the lords of the gods;
thereupon, the two lords of the gods, being pleased, granted him boons by their power.
When the lord of men was thus praised, both worldly enjoyment and liberation were granted;
such is the supreme majesty of this sacred ford.
From that time forward, that sacred ford is called both Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava;
they know that bathing and giving gifts there bestows all desires.
One who either remembers or recites these names of all the holy fords (tīrthas) shall be liberated from all sins and go to the city of Śiva and Viṣṇu.
A bath specifically at Bhānutīrtha grants the accomplishment of all goals;
for in that most meritorious tīrtha, there are indeed a hundred other tīrthas.
Brahmā said:
It is renowned as Bhillatīrtha, which destroys diseases and annihilates sins;
it bestows devotion to the pair of lotus feet of Mahādeva.
In that regard, O Mahāmati, listen to such a meritorious narrative:
on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā and on the northern slope of Śrīgiri.
Known as Ādikeśa and worshipped by the sages,
Mahādeva, in the form of a liṅga, dwells there eternally, granting all desires.
The sage known as Sindhudvīpa was supremely righteous;
his brother, named Veda, was likewise a supreme ṛṣi.
When the sun has reached its meridian, she constantly worships with devotion that primordial Lord, the three-eyed enemy of Tripura.
Even the learned Veda went to the village for the sake of begging alms;
when that best of the twice-born had departed, the hunter was supremely righteous.
On that meritorious, excellent mountain, he used to go hunting constantly;
having roamed through various regions and slain deer at his pleasure, he returned.
Taking water in his mouth for the ablution of the Trident-bearer,
and placing the meat upon the tip of his bow, the exhausted hunter [approached] the Lord Śiva.
Having approached Ādikeśa and offered meat outside of it,
he went to the Gaṅgā, took water in his mouth, and returned to that Śiva.
Taking the leaves of any plant whatsoever with one hand and the meats with the other, he should offer them as a sacrificial oblation (naivedya) with single-minded devotion.
Having approached Ādikeśa, who was worshipped with the Veda through his vital energy,
he struck down that worship with his foot using water brought from his mouth.
Having bathed the god Śiva and worshipped him with leaves, and having prepared that meat [as an offering], one should say: "May Śiva be pleased with me."
Without auspicious devotion to Śiva, he knows nothing at all;
therefore, he goes to his own place by way of flesh, just as he came.
Day after day he performed such [deeds] upon coming again and again;
nevertheless, the Lord was pleased with him—for the disposition of the Lord is indeed wondrous.
As long as that Bhilla does not arrive, Śiva does not partake in happiness;
for who can truly know Śambhu’s compassion for his devotees, which transcends all measure?
He worshipped Ādikeśa Śiva together with Umā every day;
thus, when much time had passed, Veda became enraged.
"Who indeed, being a sinner, would destroy this manifold worship accompanied by mantras and endowed with devotion to Śiva? Such a person shall meet his death at my hands."
One who betrays his guru, a deity, a brahmin, or his master deserves to be executed even by a sage;
indeed, that man who commits treachery against Śiva deserves death at the hands of everyone.
Having thus resolved, the wise Veda and his younger brother, Sindhu, reflected:
"Whose evil deed could this be? It must belong to some most wicked and evil-minded person."
He who, having destroyed an offering made with divine flowers grown in the wild, as well as auspicious bulbs, roots, and fruits, performs another offering instead; ||| BrP_169.20 |||
"He shall be slain by me with my flesh and the leaves of trees";
having reflected thus, the wise one then concealed his body.
"I shall see that wicked man who offers worship to the Lord.
In the meantime, the hunter approached the God just as he had before.
To him who was worshipping as if it were his daily duty, Ādikeśa then spoke.
Ādikeśa said:
"O hunter of great intelligence, you have grown weary, as I have said again and again;
how is it that you have not come for so long, O dear one, and why are you so distressed without me?"
"I do not find any happiness at all; take heart, my dear son."
Brahmā said:
Having heard the god speaking thus and having looked upon him,
Veda became enraged and filled with astonishment, yet he said nothing at all.
The hunter, having performed his worship as usual, went to his own home;
but Veda, becoming enraged, came and spoke to the Lord.
The Veda said:
This hunter is devoted to sin, devoid of ritual action and knowledge;
he delights in harming living beings, being cruel and merciless toward all creatures.
Of low birth, knowing nothing, and devoid of the succession of gurus; always performing what is improper, he has not conquered the entire host of his senses.
He showed himself to him, saying: "You shall say nothing to me;
O Lord, I shall perform worship according to the ritual of mantras, firm in my vows."
"Having you alone as his eternal refuge, though deprived of wife and son,
this hunter performs worship for you with the meat of his own wickedness."
"It is most wonderful that the Blessed One is pleased with him and not with me!
I shall indeed mete out punishment to this Bhilla who has done me harm. (BrP 169.31)
Someone might be pleased with a mild person, and likewise someone with an evil-minded one;
therefore, I would undoubtedly cast a stone upon his head.
