Ādikeśa said:
"Wait until tomorrow; afterwards, hurl the stone at my head."
Brahmā said:
Having said "So be it," that Veda also, casting aside the stone with his arm and withdrawing his anger, said, "I shall do so tomorrow."
Then, having returned in the morning and performed his ablutions and other rites,
Veda also, while performing his daily worship, beheld [the Lord] upon his head.
Seeing the terrible, blood-soaked stream of the wounded Liṅga,
Veda was struck with wonder and thought, "What is this upon the top of the Liṅga?"
He thought, "Whose great calamity is this that it portends?
and with earth, cow dung, kusha grass, and the waters of the Ganges, [he prepared for purification].
Having washed that offering, he then performed the worship as usual;
in the meantime, the hunter departed, his taints gone.
Then he saw within the head of Śaṅkara, whose hair is primordial, his own head joined with a wound and marked by blood at its crown.
Upon seeing him, he exclaimed, "What is this wonder? and pierced himself with sharp arrows in a hundred and a thousand ways.
Seeing such a transformation in his master, who of noble disposition could have endured it?
He repeatedly censured himself, saying, "While I was alive, this has come to pass."
"Alas, what a calamity has occurred! Oh, how terrible is the destruction wrought by adverse fate! Having observed that deed of his, Mahādeva was greatly amazed;
then the Blessed One spoke to Veda, the best among the knowers of the Vedas.
Ādikeśa said:
"Behold this hunter, O one of great intelligence, who is endowed with devotion through his inner feeling;
yet you have merely touched your head with earth, kusha grass, and water."

"By this, O Brahmin, you have even offered yourself to me impetuously. Wherever there is devotion, love, power, or discernment, I shall grant boons to him first; afterwards, O best of the twice-born, I shall grant them to you."
Brahmā said:
The divine Maheśvara invited the hunter to choose a boon.
The hunter spoke to the Lord of Gods: "Whatever remains as your discarded offering (nirmālya)..."
Therefore, O Lord, let a sacred ford (tīrtha) be established for us and called by my name;
may that ford yield the fruit of all sacrifices merely through its being remembered.
Brahmā said:
"So be it," replied the Lord of the Gods; thereafter that supreme holy site became known as Bhillatīrtha, the cause of the severance of the entire multitude of sins.
It brings about great devotion to the feet of Śrī Mahādeva;
through bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Moreover, Śiva granted many various boons even to the Veda itself.
Brahmā said:
There is a sacred ford known as Cakṣus, which bestows beauty and good fortune,
where the Lord Yogeśvara resides on the southern bank of the Gautamī.
The city known as Bhauvana is said to be situated upon the summit of a mountain,
where that King Bhauvana, who was devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya, resided.
In that excellent city, there was a certain Brahmin named Vṛddhakauśika;
his son was known as Gautama, the most eminent among those learned in the Vedas.
Due to a defect in his mother's mind, that twice-born one was born deformed;
he had a certain merchant friend who was called Maṇikuṇḍala.
Thus, there was an extraordinary friendship between that brahmin and the vaiśya;
though one was illustrious and the other poor, they were constantly seeking each other's welfare.
Once, Gautama, standing in private, spoke these words repeatedly with affection to the Vaiśya Maṇikuṇḍala, the lord of wealth: BrP_170.6 //
Gautama said:
"Let us go to gather wealth, even from mountains and oceans;
for that youth should be known as in vain which is devoid of happiness and favorable conditions."
Without wealth, how could that be possible? Alas, fie upon the man who is destitute!
Brahmā said: Kuṇḍala said this to the twice-born man: "This wealth was acquired by my father;
it is abundant. O best of the twice-born, what shall I do with so much wealth today?"
The twice-born one spoke again these words with vigor to Maṇikuṇḍala:
Gautama said:
"Among those who pursue dharma, artha, jñāna, and kāma, who indeed is praised as being satisfied?
O friend, for embodied beings, only the attainment of excellence among these is worthy of praise."
Fortunate are those beings who live by their own exertion;
those who are content with wealth given by others truly lead a life of misery.
O Kuṇḍala, that son is praised in the world and is welcomed by his ancestors, who desire him to uphold the ancestral heritage, even if only in speech.
The son who acquires wealth by relying on the strength of his own arms shall be one who has achieved his purpose in this world; he need not touch the paternal inheritance.
One who, having earned wealth himself, gives it to his father and kinsmen, should be known as a true son; any other is merely a worm born from the womb.
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of the desiring brāhmaṇa,
and accepting his speech with the thought "So be it," he quickly took the jewels.
He offered his own wealth to Gautama, saying,
"With this wealth, travel through the countries as you please."
"Taking our wealth and riches, we shall return home once more;
a merchant speaks only the truth, but that brahmin is a deceiver. (BrP 170.16)
The evil-souled merchant and the evil-minded brahmin did not recognize one another;
they conversed with each other without their mother and father knowing.
Having traveled from one country to another for the sake of wealth, those two—the merchant and the brahmin—[arrived];
the brahmin desired to seize the wealth held in the hands of the merchant.
The Brahmin said:
"By whatever means possible, you must indeed recover that wealth!
Aha! There are thousands of beautiful cities upon this earth."
Women who grant desired objects like deities of love,
captivating the mind here and there— what can I do about them?
If wealth is acquired with effort and given to women, they will then enjoy it perpetually; indeed, that life is truly fruitful.
Constantly devoted to dance and song, adorned by courtesans, how indeed shall I enjoy that wealth which has come from the Vaiśyas into my hands? (BrP 170.22)
Brahmā said:
While reflecting thus, Gautama, as if smiling, spoke this to Maṇikuṇḍala: "Living beings [suffer] solely because of unrighteousness."
Those who are most righteous in this world are seen to experience suffering; yet those who follow their own desires undoubtedly attain prosperity, happiness, and their cherished goals. (BrP 170.24)
Therefore, what is the use of that dharma which has nothing but suffering as its fruit?
Brahmā said:
"No," the Vaiśya then replied, "Happiness is established in righteousness (dharma);
in sin there is suffering, fear, grief, poverty, and indeed affliction."
Since liberation comes from dharma, why should one's own dharma perish?
Brahmā said:
As they were thus disputing there, a trial by ordeal took place between them;
whichever side should prove superior would attain the supreme goal.
"Let us ask whose power is greater: that of the righteous or even the unrighteous?
For in this world, worldly success arises from the Veda, while happiness arises from dharma."
Thus disputing, those two spoke to all the people:
"Which of these two is more powerful on earth, dharma or adharma?"
"Let them speak according to what actually occurred. Thus they spoke with vigor; in that manner, some who were followers of dharma spoke there.
"Those most wicked people experience suffering while virtuous people are happy.
Having said this, he offered all his wealth to the brahmin in the next world.
Maṇimān, the most excellent among those who discern the Dharma, again praised the Dharma. The twice-born [Brahmā] said to Maṇimān: "Why do you praise the Dharma?
Brahmā said:
"So be it," said the Vaiśya; the Brāhmaṇa spoke again.
The Brahmin said:
"O Vaiśya, I have won the wealth; why do you speak so shamelessly? By me alone has Dharma been conquered, since my soul acts according to its own will."
Having heard those words of the Brahmin, the Vaiśya spoke with a smile.
The Vaiśya said:
"O friend, I consider those in whom dharma is not found to be like shriveled grain among crops, or like gnats among birds."
Among the four aims of human life, Dharma is said to be the first;
after that come Artha and Kāma. That Dharma resides within me.
O best of the twice-born, why do you say this: "I have conquered"? BrP_170.36.
Brahmā said:
The twice-born spoke again to the Vaiśya, "Let a wager be made with our hands.
The Vaiśya agreed, saying, "So be it. Having gone there, the two spoke once more.
As before, having gone to the world of mortals, the twice-born said, "I have conquered.

Then, having had his hands cut off, he asked, "How then do you consider righteousness? Thus addressed by the Brahmin, the Vaiśya spoke these words: BrP 170.38: "Having gone to the world of mortals as before, the twice-born said, 'It is won. Then, after his two hands had been severed, he asked, 'But how do you regard dharma? Being thus rebuked by the Brahmin, the Vaiśya spoke this speech."
The Vaiśya said:
I consider dharma alone to be supreme, even when one's life-breaths have reached the throat;
for embodied beings, mother, father, friend, and kinsman are nothing but dharma itself.
Brahmā said:
While they were thus disputing, the Brahmin became wealthy,
while the Vaiśya there was deprived of both his arms and his wealth.
Wandering in this manner, O best of sages, they both reached the Gaṅgā and Hari, the Lord of Yoga; there, by chance, they spoke to one another once again.
The Vaiśya, however, praised Gaṅgā, the Lord of Yoga, and Dharma itself;
then the twice-born man, provoked by excessive anger, reviled the Vaiśya and spoke again.
The Brahmin said:
"My wealth is gone, my hands are severed, and you remain with your life.
If you speak otherwise, I shall take your head with this sword."
Brahmā said:
Laughing, the Vaiśya again spoke these words directly to Gautama.
The Vaiśya said:
I consider dharma alone to be supreme; do as you wish regarding the Brahmins, the gurus, the gods, the Vedas, dharma, and Janārdana.
But that sinner who reviles [the righteous] is not to be touched by the doer of good;
rather, that evil-doer, the wicked-souled defiler of dharma, is to be ignored.
Brahmā said:
Then, out of anger, he spoke to Dharma: "O sage, if you praise [your own side], let there be a wager here between the lives of us two."
When Gautama had spoken thus, the merchant then said, "So be it. Both spoke again, and the worlds likewise replied.
Having struck down that Vaiśya on the southern bank of the Gautamī in front of the Lord of Yoga,
the Brahmin plucked out his eye and said:
The Brahmin said:
"O Vaiśya, by your constant praise of dharma, you have reached this ultimate state:
your wealth is gone, your sight is lost, and your two sprout-like hands have been cut off."
"You have been questioned, O friend; I am going, so do not speak thus in the midst of our conversation."
Brahmā said:
When he had departed, that Vaiśya reflected in his mind:
"Alas, what a tragedy has befallen me, O Hari, whose sole intent is righteousness!"
That eminent merchant Kuṇḍala, now destitute, deprived of his arms,
and deprived of his eyes, fell into grief as he constantly recollected the Dharma.
Thus reflecting in many ways, he sat upon the ground,
motionless and devoid of energy, fallen into an ocean of grief.
At the end of the day, during the night when the lunar disc has risen,
on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, Vibhīṣaṇa arrives there.
Having worshipped the Lord, the Master of Yoga, according to the prescribed rites,
he bathed in the Gautamī-Gaṅgā together with his son, surrounded by Rākṣasas.
Indeed, he saw the son of Vibhīṣaṇa, known as Vaibhīṣaṇi, who was like another Vibhīṣaṇa, and spoke to him.
Having heard the words of the Vaiśya exactly as they had occurred, that knower of dharma reported them to his high-souled father, the Lord of Laṅkā;
and that Lord of Laṅkā spoke with affection to his son Guṇākara.
Vibhīṣaṇa said:
The illustrious Rāma is my guru, and his respected friend is the one renowned as Hanumān; it was by him that this great mountain was brought here.
Formerly, when another task had arisen, the mountain, the refuge of all medicinal herbs,
took them with him and went to the Himavat once that business was accomplished.
Then, having brought the Viśalyakaraṇī and the Mṛtasaṃjīvanī,
the one of great intelligence [gave them] to Rāma of unwearied deeds.
Having reported that which was to be accomplished once it was finished, he returned;
taking up the mountain once more, he came to Devaparvata.
"Bring her and place her upon his heart while remembering Hari;
then this noble-minded one shall obtain everything he desires."
As he was traveling with great speed, the Viśalyakaraṇī [plant] fell again upon the bank of the Gautamī, where Hari, the Lord of Yoga, resides.
Vaibhīṣaṇi said:
"O my father, show me that herb quickly; do not delay.
There is no greater good in the three worlds than the alleviation of another's suffering."
Brahmā said:
Vibhīṣaṇa, having said "So be it," showed her to his son;
then his son cut a branch from that tree with the mantra "For food, thee! (iṣe tvā).
And indeed, out of affection for the Vaiśya as well, the virtuous who delight in the welfare of others [bestow their favor].
Vibhīṣaṇa said:
"Upon that mountain where they fell, there was a powerful tree;
taking a branch from it, place it upon his heart."
As soon as he is touched by that, he shall regain his own form.
Having heard these words of his father, the noble-minded son of Vibhīṣaṇa acted accordingly;
he properly prepared a piece of wood and placed it [in the fire].
In his heart, even that Vaiśya became possessed of sight and hands;
for no one truly understands the potency of gems, mantras, and medicinal herbs.
Taking that very wood and recollecting only the Dharma,
he bathed in the Gautamī and the Gaṅgā, as well as before Hari, the Lord of Yoga.
Having paid his respects, the Vaiśya returned with a piece of wood,
wandering through the king’s city known as Mahāpura.
There was a king there known as Mahārāja, who possessed great strength;
he had no son at all, only a daughter named Naṣṭalocanā.
She herself was his daughter, and her son likewise observed such a vow;
whether he be a god, a dānava, a brāhmaṇa, or a kṣatriya.
Whether he be a Vaiśya or born of a Śūdra womb, whether he possesses qualities or is devoid of them—
to him who shall extract these eyes, this daughter of mine is to be given.
"Indeed, the king proclaimed: 'This [daughter] shall be given away along with the kingdom.
Having heard this proclamation day and night, that Vaiśya then spoke."
The Vaiśya said:
"I shall undoubtedly fetch the eyes of the princess."
Brahmā said:
Having quickly seized that Vaiśya, he presented him to the great queen;
by the mere touch of his wood, the princess regained her sight.
Then the king, filled with wonder, asked, "Who are you?
and the Vaiśya reported everything that had occurred to the king in its entirety.
The Vaiśya said:
"By the grace of the Brāhmaṇas, as well as through righteousness, austerity,
the power of giving, and various sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees."
By the power of divine herbs, my capability is such as this.
{Brahmā said:} Having heard these words of the Vaiśya, the lord of the earth was struck with wonder. (BrP 170.79)
The king said:
"Aha! This person must surely be a great-souled deity;
otherwise, how could such power be seen in another?"
Therefore, I shall bestow that maiden upon him, preceded by the granting of the kingdom.
Brahmā said:
Having thus resolved in his mind, he gave away his daughter and his kingdom;
having gone at will for the sake of recreation, he fell into great distress.
"Without a friend there is no kingdom, and without a friend there is no happiness";
thus did the son of the Vaiśya constantly reflect upon that very Brahmin.
This indeed is the characteristic of well-born beings on this earth:
that their minds are always moist with compassion, even toward those who wish them harm.
That great king, Maṇikuṇḍala, went to the forest;
while he was ruling the kingdom, on one occasion [he encountered] the twice-born Gautama.
Seeing that his wealth had been seized by wicked gamblers, Maṇikuṇḍala,
who knew the dharma, took that brahmin friend and honored him.
He then reported to him the entire power of the dharmas and caused him to bathe in the Gaṅgā for the removal of all evil.
That Brahmin was chosen by all those kinsmen of his own lineage,
as well as by the Vaiśyas born in his own country who were the relatives of the Brahmin.
And having performed sacrifices and worshipped the gods in the presence of that Lord of Yogins, along with Vṛddhakauśika and other leaders, he then ascended to heaven.
From that time forth, they have known that sacred ford as Mṛtasañjīvana;
it is the Cakṣus-tīrtha, which possesses Yogeśa, bestowing merit even through mere remembrance,
generating clarity of mind, and destroying all evil inclinations.
Brahmā said:
Urvaśī-tīrtha is proclaimed as bestowing the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice through bathing,
giving gifts, and the worship of Mahādeva and Vāsudeva.
Where the god Maheśvara resides and where Hari, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, resides,
there was a powerful universal monarch named Pramati.
Having conquered his enemies, he went quickly to the realm of Indra, which was filled with gods;
there, O Nārada, he beheld the lord of the gods together with the Maruts.
Just as Pramati, the bull among kṣatriyas, looked upon Indra with noose in hand,
Hari, observing that Pramati was laughing, then spoke to him.
Indra said: "O one of great intelligence, enough with sporting with the Maruts in the abode of the gods;
having conquered the quarters and reached heaven, sport with me."
Brahmā said:
Having heard the words of Hari, which were tinged with resentment, King Pramati said "So be it" to the lord of the gods, and then asked, "What atonement do you consider appropriate?"
Having heard those words of Pramati, the king of the gods spoke to the monarch.
Indra said:
"Urvaśī herself is our prize, she who is to be attained through all sacrificial rites."
Having heard these words of Indra, Pramati spoke with pride:
"O King, I consider Urvaśī to be the atonement; what do you think?"
"O Lord of the Gods, O Śatakratu, I consider what you say to be true; just as Pramati spoke to Indra for the sake of atonement:
'Give me your righteous right hand, along with its armor and arrow, and let us play. (BrP 171.9)
Brahmā said:
Having thus made this agreement, the two approached the goddess;
there, Pramati won Urvaśī, the celestial woman.
Having conquered her, Pramati spoke with vehemence to that Śatakratu:
Pramati said:
"O Lord, for the sake of atonement, I shall gamble with you again later."
Indra said: "O King, I shall gamble with that supreme, victorious thunderbolt, fit for the gods and equipped with its chariot, without hesitation, even at the cost of my hand."
Brahmā said:
Then Pramati, taking up other nooses adorned with jewels, laughed and said to Śakra, "Victory! (BrP 171.13).
In the meantime, Nārada, the knower of the senses, arrived there—
the lord of the Gandharvas, renowned as Viśvāvasu.
Viśvāvasu said:
"O King, let us play with you using this Gandharva-science.
Having said, "So be it," the king then declared, "I have won."
Having defeated them, the king, out of folly, spoke these dejected words to the Lord of the Gods:
Pramati said:
"O Mahendra, you can never be victorious over me in battle or even in gambling; therefore, always remain a devotee who worships us."
Tell me, by what means was this status of yours as the Lord of the Gods attained?
Brahmā said: "Out of pride, Urvaśī spoke thus: 'Go! Become a servant. Urvaśī replied: 'As I behave toward the gods, so shall I behave toward you.'"
I act with my whole being; you ought not to reproach me.
Brahmā said: Then Pramati spoke to her: "There are wandering women like you;
why are you ashamed, O blessed lady? Go and become a servant."
Having heard what was spoken by the king, the powerful lord of the Gandharvas,
known as Citrasena, the son of Viśvāvasu, [then spoke].
Citrasena said:
"O King, O lord of the earth, I shall indeed play with you for all of this—
both my kingdom and my life, as well as yours."
Brahmā said:
Having said, "So be it," both Citrasena and the excellent king played again with great intensity; then Citrasena was victorious.
Then Citrasena bound the king with great snares provided by the Gandharvas;
he won everything, staking Urvashi as the foremost prize.
The kingdom, the treasury, the army, and whatever other wealth there was—
all that became the property of Citrasena, which had formerly been the wealth of Pramati.
His son, while still a boy, spoke with vigor to the family priest,
the highly wise Madhucchandas, the son of Viśvāmitra.
Pratītiputra said:
"What sin has been committed by my father? Where is the high-minded one bound?
How will he go to his own place, and how will he be released from the snares?"
{Brahmā said:} Having heard the words of Sumati and having reflected upon them, that best of sages, Madhucchandas, then spoke this concerning the conduct of Pramati. BrP_171.27 //
Madhucchandas said:
"O high-minded one, your father remains bound in the world of the gods;
having lost his kingdom through deceit and many vices, he has indeed fallen."
He who goes to a gambling hall shall also become a partaker of afflictions;
gambling, wine, meat, and the like are vices, O Prince.
For indeed, these [qualities] always arise from sinners alone as being sinful in nature;
even each one individually leads to misfortune, to evil, and to hell.
When even those of noble birth become defiled by engaging in deceitful conduct through vehicles, seats, speech, and the like, how much more so must the common gambler?
The wife of a gambler suffers constantly,
and that wicked gambler, too, suffers whenever he beholds another woman.
Seeing her, that evildoer, his joy vanished, constantly says:
"Alas! In this wheel of saṃsāra, there is no sinner equal to me."
For him who possesses not even the slightest pleasure born of sense-objects in this world,
no gambler is seen to be happy even in both worlds.
And thus he always shines, his mind consumed by shame;
with his dharma gone and devoid of joy, he wanders about with his pride swallowed up.
That conduct which is free from deceit is praised for the twice-born;
they may engage in agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade, but not with deceit.
But he who desires to acquire wealth through deceitful means is deprived of virtue,
purpose, pleasure, noble lineage, and manly effort.
"Even an action censured in the Vedas was undertaken by your father;
therefore, my child, what can we do? Whatever you have said shall be carried out."
"What wise person indeed would overstep the path ordained by the Creator? (BrP 171.39)
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of the family priest, Sumati spoke.
Sumati said:
"O father, by doing what might Pramati regain the kingdom?"

Madhucchandas said:
"Go to Gautamī, my child; there worship Śaṅkara, Aditi, Varuṇa, and Viṣṇu; then you will be released from the noose."
Brahmā said:
Having said, "So be it," she quickly went to Gaṅgā after bowing to Janārdana;
she worshipped Śambhu and performed austerities with restrained vows.
Having bound his own father for a thousand years,
he caused him to be released from the gods and regained his kingdom once again.
Released from his bonds by Śiva and Īśā, he obtained a kingdom through his own son;
having acquired the Gāndharva science, he became dear to Indra.
The Śāmbhava, the Vaiṣṇava, and the Urvaśī-tīrtha—
since that time, that sacred site has been renowned as Kaitava.
What is not obtained through the grace of Śiva, Viṣṇu, and the Mother of the World?
There, bathing and giving gifts bestow the fruit of great merit;
they grant liberation from the bonds of sin and destroy all miserable rebirths.
Brahmā said:
The Sāmudra Tīrtha has been described as bestowing the fruits of all holy sites.
I shall describe its true nature; listen with a focused mind, O Nārada.
Released by Gautama for the benefit of the worlds, that Gaṅgā, the destroyer of sins, flowed toward the eastern ocean.
The celestial river was coming along, held by me in a water-pot,
and the Goddess was carried on the head by Śambhu, the Supreme Self.
Born from the foot of Viṣṇu, brought to the mortal realm by the high-souled Brāhmaṇa, remember her who destroys sins through mere remembrance.
Seeing the ocean, the most venerable of his gurus, he reflected upon what ought to be done:
"She who is the sovereign of the worlds, worthy of worship, and saluted by Brahmā, Śiva, and the other gods."
I would go to her, lest there be a violation of dharma;
for he who, out of delusion, does not attend upon a high-souled one who is approaching [is at fault].

"There is no savior for that sinner in either of the two worlds. Having reflected thus, Ratneśa, the lord of rivers, appearing in embodied form and full of humility, spoke these words to Gaṅgā with his palms joined in reverence: BrP_172.7: "There is no savior for that sinner in either of the two worlds. Having reflected thus, Ratneśa, the lord of rivers, appearing in embodied form and full of humility, spoke these words to Gaṅgā with his palms joined in reverence.
Sindhu said:
"Let the water that is in the subterranean realm, on the earth, and in the vault of heaven enter into me alone here; I shall not say anything further."
The jewels, the nectar, the mountains, the Rākṣasas, and the Asuras— I support all these and other such formidable things as well.
Within me, Viṣṇu, joined with Kamalā, sleeps eternally;
there is nothing whatsoever impossible for me in this world of moving and unmoving beings.
He who, out of pride, does not rise to greet a great person when they have arrived shall fall away from dharma and other virtues, and will surely reach hell.
"I feel no weariness in carrying them, except for the humiliation caused by Agastya;
however, because you surpass them in dignity, I am superior to them on that account."
"I say this, O Goddess Gaṅgā: you become united with me through equanimity;
for I am not able to unite with you in your many forms if you remain manifold."
"O Goddess, you shall come to my union; I shall unite with you, and not otherwise.
O Gaṅgā, if you will come to me, I shall deliberate upon that in many ways."
Brahmā said:
To that Ocean, the lord of waters, who was speaking thus, the goddess Gaṅgā Gautamī then said: "Do this word of mine."
"And you must then bring all the wives of the seven ṛṣis, headed by Arundhatī, together with their husbands."
"I shall become small in size, and then I will be united with you.
Having said "So be it," he was escorted by the seven ṛṣis, who were the husbands of the ṛṣi's wives.
He brought that goddess there, and she divided herself into seven parts;
she is this Gautamī Gaṅgā, who has gone to the ocean in seven streams.
From the names of the seven sages, seven Gaṅgās then came into being;
there, bathing, giving gifts, listening, and likewise reciting [the scriptures] [bring great merit].
Even the mere remembrance of it with devotion shall grant all desires.
There is no other sacred site (tīrtha) superior to this in the three worlds than the ocean,
for the destruction of sins, the attainment of enjoyment and liberation, and the delight of the mind.
Brahmā said:
O Nārada, it is known as the Ṛṣisattra; there the seven sages sat down for the sake of austerity, where Śiva is present as Bhīmeśvara.
In this regard, I shall relate this narrative augmented by the gods, sages, and ancestors;
listen attentively as I speak this auspicious account that grants all desires.
O Nārada, the seven sages divided the Gaṅgā into seven streams:
that which belongs to Vasiṣṭha flows southward, and that belonging to Viśvāmitra flows to the north of it.
The Vāmadevī is to be known as the last, the auspicious Gautamī is in the middle;
another is remembered as the Bhāradvājī, and yet another is the Ātreyī.
Likewise, the descendant of Jamadagni and others were designated there in seven ways;
all those high-souled sages were desirous of performing sacrifices there.
The great sacrifice was completed by the seers who have seen the further shore;
meanwhile, there appeared there a powerful enemy of the gods.
Known as Viśvarūpa, he approached the sacrificial session of the sages;
having propitiated them through celibacy, austerity, and according to the prescribed rites,
he then questioned all the ṛṣis in due order with humility.
Viśvarūpa said: "Certainly, through my well-being as the cause, may you all have a son according to your desire— one who is powerful and difficult even for the gods to withstand."
O sages, you ought to tell us whether it is by means of sacrifices or even by means of austerity.
Brahmā said:
Thereupon, the high-minded Viśvāmitra, possessed of great intelligence, spoke.
Viśvāmitra said:
"O dear one, various fruits are obtained through action;
and among the three causes, action is the primary cause."
Therefore, the wise do not know karma to be the cause, the agent, or anything else distinct from it; likewise, they do not know it to be the material cause or the seed.
The causality of actions is observed when the cause is complete; the presence or absence of the fruit is seen accordingly. Therefore, the fruit is dependent upon action.
Action, too, should be known to be twofold: that which is being performed and that which has been performed;
and whatever is called the means for that which is being performed is what ought to be done.
The states resulting from that [meditation] are the cause for the accomplishment of action in both cases;
whatever state a wise person meditates upon while performing an action, [that state he attains].
It is said that the accomplishment of the fruit occurs in accordance with the cultivation of that [intention];
if one performs an action according to the rule without such cultivation, [the result will not correspond].
Otherwise, all the fruit would be in accordance with his state of being;
therefore, [one should practice] austerity, vows, charity, and rites such as recitation and sacrifice.
But they will grant the fruit of action according to its nature and one's inner disposition;
therefore, indeed, action will yield its fruit in accordance with that disposition.
Existence should be known as threefold: sattvic, rājasic, and likewise tāmasic; the fruit [of existence] follows according to one's karma.
And because it conforms to one's cultivation, the state of actions is manifold;
therefore, a wise person should cultivate their disposition according to their desire.
Thereafter, karma must also be performed, for the giver of its fruit is likewise of that same nature;
he bestows the fruit upon those who possess it, provided they are engaged in the fruit.
There is no artisan there who performs the action by its own nature;
rather, it is that very [action] which arises from the distinctions of the qualities such as *sattva* and the like, beginning with the primary material cause (*upādāna*).
In the same way that one begins from existence, the fruit is obtained through existences;
for indeed, action is the cause of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
Action established in its true state is the cause of liberation, yet it is also the cause of bondage;
action that conforms to one's own nature leads to one's own [result] both in this world and in the next.
It swiftly produces various fruits while conforming to a state of equality;
though it is but a single entity, its differentiation is perceived through diverse manifestations.
Therefore, existence (bhāva) is distinguished [as the primary factor], whether an action is performed or experienced;
perform your actions according to your state of being, and you shall obtain whatever you desire.
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of the wise sage Viśvāmitra,
he practiced asceticism for a long time, having resorted to a state of darkness (tāmasa).
Viśvarūpa committed a terrible and most fearsome deed,
even though he was constantly being restrained while the foremost of sages looked on.
In accordance with his own agitation, he performed that terrifying deed within the fearsome sacrificial pit and amidst the fearsome fire.
Having meditated upon himself as a terrifying, fierce being dwelling in the cave of the heart,
and perceiving him thus performing penance, an incorporeal voice spoke.
Without his mass of matted hair, Vṛtra could not have been conquered;
Viśvarūpa would have offered his soul in vain into the sacrificial fire.
He alone is Indra, he is Varuṇa, and he may indeed be everything;
having abandoned his own self, Vṛjinodbhava offered even his matted locks as an oblation.
In the Veda he is called Vṛtra, and he indeed became a sinner;
who can know the majesty of Bhīma, the Lord of the World?
"O lords of sages, that voice proclaimed of him: 'He creates everything without remainder, yet he is not stained by attachment; therefore, he has desisted.'"
Having paid homage to Bhīmeśvara, Viśvarūpa, Mahābhīma, Bhīmakarman, and likewise Tathākṛti, they each departed for their own hermitages.
Having meditated upon himself as having a terrifying form and a terrifying nature, he offered himself as a sacrifice;
therefore, the god Bhīmeśvara is recited in the Purāṇa.
There, bathing and giving gifts bestow liberation; of this there is no doubt.

Thus, whoever recites or hears with devotion this account of Śiva, the Lord of the Gods, who here assumes a formidable form and is known throughout the world as the remover of all sins— BrP 173.36a–36c.
The Godāvarī is the refuge for those who take shelter in the words of mindfulness, the bestower of liberation, the destroyer of the entire multitude of sins, and the giver of the supreme truth.
Always and everywhere, but especially where she has entered the ocean,
a virtuous embodied being, having bathed there, [attains the highest goal].
He who, at the confluence of the Godāvarī and the ocean,
rescues his ancestors from every intense hell, goes to the city of the Enemy of Pura.
That Brahman which is to be known through the Vedānta and which is to be meditated upon— that indeed is Bhīmanātha manifest;
for when He is seen, they do not enter [into rebirth] again.
Brahmā said: "She, who possessed a body and was tormented by intense suffering, remembered him,
the Lord of Waters, whom she had previously united with."
The Gaṅgā is worthy of worship even by the gods;
she is followed by all the deities and praised by the sages and the Maruts.
Vasiṣṭha, Jābāli, Yājñavalkya, Kratu, Aṅgiras, Dakṣa, Marīci, Vaiṣṇava,
Śātātapa, Śaunaka, and Devarāta.
Bhṛgu, Agniveśya, Atri, Marīci, and other leaders;
Manu, Gautama, and others whose sins were thoroughly cleansed;
along with Kauśika, Tumburu, Parvata, and the rest.
Agastya, Mārkaṇḍeya, Pippalāda, and others,
along with Gālava, were devoted to yoga;
as were Vāmadeva, Aṅgiras, and the Bhārgavas.
Skilled in mindfulness, pleasing to the mind through their learning,
all of them were knowers of the meaning of the Purāṇas and possessed of great knowledge; having gone to the Gautamī, that divine river—
Seeing her united with him, Śiva and Hari will praise her with abundant mantras and Vedic hymns, their hearts satisfied and gladdened.
As they revealed themselves to the sages,
those two were likewise seen by the immortals and the ancestors;
all praised the two gods who remove every affliction.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, and the guardians of the worlds—
all with palms joined in reverence— praise Hari and Śaṅkara.
O Nārada, at the seven famous confluences,
the two gods are eternally established at the meeting of the ocean and the Gaṅgā.
It is called Gautameśvara, where the god Maheśvara is eternally present, and there Mādhava dwells together with Ramā.
The Śiva known as Brahmeśvara was established by me alone for the benefit of the worlds and for my own particular purpose.
Known as Cakrapāṇi, Viṣṇu was praised there by the gods along with me; he remained present there together with the gods and the hosts of Maruts.
That very place is known as Aindratīrtha, which is Hayamūrdhaka;
there Viṣṇu is Hayamūrdhā, and even the gods [reside] upon his head.
There is also the place known as Somatīrtha, where Śiva is Someśvara.
Requested by Indra, by Somaśravas, by the gods, and likewise by the sages, O Soma, flow forth for Indra from the very beginning, O Indu!
The seven directions have their various suns; there are seven hotṛ-priests as officiants;
and those who are the seven divine Ādityas—with them, O Soma, protect us.
Flow around for Indra, O Indu!
O King, with that oblation of yours which has been prepared, protect us, O Soma!
Let not the hostile one overcome us, nor let anything whatsoever afflict us.
O Indu, flow around for Indra;
O Sage Kaśyapa, you who increase the songs with the hymns of the mantra-composers,
pay homage to King Soma, who was born as the Lord of Plants.
Flow around for Indra, O Indu! I am a poet, a physician, and the daughter of Upala-prakṣin;
with various thoughts and seeking wealth, we have followed [thee] like cows.
"O Indu, flow around for Indra!
Having spoken thus, and having obtained the Soma for the wielder of the thunderbolt through the sages,
the sacrifice of Śatakratu then became complete once it had been given to them.
That is known as Somatīrtha, and Agneya is situated to its east;
there, Agni, having worshipped me with great sacrifices, obtained his heart's desire.
By my grace, he attained it; I remain there eternally for the sake of benefiting the world, as do Viṣṇu and Śiva.
Therefore, the region of Agni has been described, and immediately after that, the region of Āditya,
where the Sun, who consists of the Vedas, eternally goes to perform worship.
At midday, one should always bow down there to me, Śaṅkara, who is Hari, in my other form; all people should do so at that time.
Because it is uncertain with which form Savitṛ arrives,
therefore that which is called Āditya follows immediately after the Bārhaspatya.
Bṛhaspati received worship from the gods at that sacred ford;
he performed various sacrifices there, and therefore they know it as Bārhaspatya.
Merely by remembering that sacred ford (tīrtha), the pacification of planetary afflictions (graha-śānti) shall occur;
even more excellent than that is another sacred ford at Indragopa on the best of mountains.
Because a great liṅga was established there for a certain reason by Himālaya, that sacred site is called Adritīrtha.
There, bathing and giving gifts bestow all desires and are auspicious;
thus is that Gautamī Gaṅgā, which has issued forth from the Mountain of Brahmā.
Thus far, O Goddess who dwells in the ocean, I have briefly described to you certain sacred fords (tīrthas) and auspicious secrets.
How can one describe that Gautamī of exceeding power, who is celebrated by the seers in the Vedas and Purāṇas and honored by the world?
O Nārada, who has the power to describe this in its entirety?
For one who proceeds with devotion in whatever manner possible, there is no fault; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, having indicated only a mere direction of it with great effort for the benefit of the world,
who is capable of describing its power in full detail?
Even Viṣṇu, the Lord of Lakṣmī, and Śiva, the Lord of Umā, are fully capable [of this].
O highly wise one, while sacred fords (tīrthas) indeed become meritorious at certain times and in certain places, the Gautamī is always so for human beings.
Meritorious everywhere and at all times—who indeed is able to proclaim her virtues? Therefore, it is only fitting to say "Salutation to her."
Nārada said:
O Lord of the Gods, O Sovereign of the Suras, you speak of Gaṅgā as having three deities—
she who was brought down by a Brahmin, the meritorious, the purifier of the world, and the auspicious one.
O best of gods, since this [world] is pervaded by Viṣṇu, Īśa, and you at its beginning, middle, and end, as well as on both its shores,
speak again in brief; I am not yet satiated.
Brahmā said:
She who was formerly situated in the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), and then followed the foot of Viṣṇu, she alone is now stationed in the matted locks of Maheśvara; to her, salutations.
Having diligently propitiated Śiva through the power of Brahmanic splendor,
they then reached the sacred mountain and from there proceeded toward the eastern ocean.
Having arrived, the goddess, who embodies all sacred fords, has united with men;
she is likewise the bestower of desired objects, and her power is preeminent.
I do not consider there to be any sacred site in the three worlds superior to this;
and by its very power, whatever is held in the mind shall come to pass.
Even today, her majesty cannot be fully described by anyone;
yet she who is, in the ultimate sense, Brahman itself will be constantly spoken of with devotion.
It is my conviction that there can be no sacred ford superior to her;
it would in no way be fitting for her to share the same nature as any other sacred ford.

"O Sage, having heard the praise of the virtues of the Gaṅgā through the nectar of my words, why has the intellect of everyone not come to rest in her alone? This truly appears strange to me within the three worlds. (BrP 175.9)
Nārada said:
You are the knower and the instructor of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation;
you know the Vedas along with their secret Upaniṣads, as well as the Purāṇas and the Smṛtis.
The treatises on dharma and whatever else is established in your word,
as well as the sacred fords, gifts, sacrifices, and likewise ascetic penances— [all these are rooted in you].
"O Lord, tell me what is superior among the service of deities and mantras;
for whatever you say, O Blessed One, out of devotion, must be so and not otherwise."
"O Brahmin, you ought to sever this doubt of mine by means of your words;
having heard what is desired in my mind, I have therefore come to a state of wonder. (BrP 175.13)
Brahmā said:
Listen, O Nārada, I shall declare the supreme secret of dharma;
there are four kinds of sacred fords (tīrtha) and likewise as many yugas.
The three qualities (guṇas), the three Puruṣas, the three eternal gods,
and the four Vedas together with the Smṛtis— these are proclaimed [to be the four].
O Nārada, the four aims of human life, the fourfold speech, and indeed the four qualities are all equal.
Since the eternal Dharma is common to all,
it is considered manifold through the relationship of the goal and the means.
Its substratum is twofold: space and time, which is always present;
and there is that phenomenon which, depending on time, is always subject to decrease and increase.

O one of great wisdom, in accordance with the ages, one quarter after another of this Dharma declines; thus, both [the decline of the Dharma and its dependence on place] are contingent upon the country.
The Dharma, having been resorted to at the proper time, is eternally established in that land;
even as the ages decline, it does not perish in that land.
And when both are abandoned, there would be an absence of Dharma;
therefore, Dharma is based on place and is well-established with four feet.
And that Dharma also exists in various regions in the form of sacred sites;
having occupied a specific place and time, Dharma remains established there.
In the Tretā age, Dharma is established in a place that is deficient by one quarter;
in the Dvāpara age, it is established in a place where it occupies only half.
In the Kali age, Dharma moves with only a single foot;
yet for one who understands Dharma in such a manner, it does not perish.
By the power of the ages (yugas), the distinctions between castes are established;
from the qualities (guṇas) and the agents of those qualities, the manifold order of dharma is maintained.
Through the influence of the qualities (guṇas), there likewise occurs the manifestation and suppression of the sacred fords (tīrthas),
the castes (varṇas), the Vedas, as well as heaven and liberation.
But by such a manifestation, that very [time] is distinguished;
time is declared to be the manifestor, while space is said to be the manifested.
Whenever time brings about manifestation, at that very moment that [manifested form] is Brahman; O Brahmin, therefore there is no doubt in this matter.
Likewise, the form of the gods according to the Vedas should be in accordance with the age (yuga),
as it is for ritual acts, sacred sites, castes, and stages of life.
In the Satya Yuga, a sacred ford (tīrtha) dedicated to three deities is honored in the worlds;
in another age, the Tretā, it is dedicated to two deities; and in the Dvāpara, it is dedicated to a single deity.
In the Kali age, nothing at all is to be known; furthermore, hear this other [teaching]:
they know the divine to be the sacred ford in the Kṛta age, and the demonic in the Tretā age.
In the Dvāpara age, the teaching is said to be that of the Ṛṣis, while in the Kali age, it is said to be human;
furthermore, O Nārada, listen as I explain another reason for this.
O great sage, I shall explain to you in detail that which was asked of you by Gautamī regarding how this Gaṅgā reached the head of Hara.
From that time forward, Gaṅgā became even more beloved by Śambhu;
and having understood the deity's intention, she spoke to the elephant-faced one.
Umā, the sovereign of the three worlds and the mother who benefits the universe, is known as Śāntā and Śruti; she bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having heard those words of his mother, the elephant-faced one replied: [BrP 175.36]
Gajavaktra said:
"O Mother, instruct me as to what must be done; I shall perform it without doubt."
Brahmā said:
Umā, residing within the matted locks of Maheśvara, spoke this to her son:
"O Satī, beloved of the Lord, let Gaṅgā be brought down by you; it is the truth."
Moreover, O son, the Lord Śiva always dwells there in manifold splendor;
wherever he is, there are the gods and the eternal Vedas.
Right there are all the sages, humans, and likewise the ancestors;
therefore, let us turn back Īśāna, the God of gods, Maheśvara.
"When the god has turned back from her, all those [who follow him] will indeed turn back;
listen to these words of mine:
therefore, entreat Śaṅkara with your whole being to turn back from her."
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of his mother, the Lord of the Gaṇas spoke again.
Gaṇeśvara said:
"I am not at all able to turn Lord Śiva away from her;
as long as Śiva has not turned back, even the gods cannot turn her away."
O Mother of the worlds, it is not possible [to describe this] for another reason as well:
the Gaṅgā was previously brought down by the great-souled Gautama.
By the sage, who is honored by the world, who acts for the welfare of the three worlds,
and who is worthy of worship through his words and his Brahmanic splendor, [he was addressed] with the means of conciliation.
Having propitiated Bhava, the Lord of Gods, with austerities and hymns of praise,
Gautama was then addressed by the gratified Śaṅkara as follows:
Śaṅkara said:
"Choose meritorious boons that are dear to you and desired by your mind;
O high-minded one, whatever you wish for, all of that I shall grant to you today."
Brahmā said:
Thus addressed by Śiva while I was listening, Gautama then spoke these very words: "O Śaṅkara, give me the matted locks."
He asks me for the holy Gaṅgā; what need have I for any other boon?
Brahmā said:
Śambhu, the benefactor of all the worlds, spoke to him again: *BrP 175.49*
Śambhu said:
"Nothing has been requested by you for yourself; therefore, ask for something difficult to obtain."
Brahmā said:
Gautama, his spirit undaunted, spoke to that Bhava with palms joined in reverence.
Gautama said:
"And this very vision of yours is the most difficult for all to attain;
yet today it has been obtained by me through your grace, O Śaṅkara."
Merely by remembering you, wise men become fulfilled;
how much more so when the Great Lord, you yourself, is seen in person?
Brahmā said:
When this was spoken by Gautama, Bhava was filled with joy:
"That which has been requested by you is for the benefit of the three worlds."
"O one of great intelligence, the Self does not beg," Śiva said to the twice-born man.
Thus addressed, the brahmin reflected once more and spoke likewise to Śiva.

Modest yet undepressed in spirit and endowed with devotion to Śiva, Gautama spoke these words for the benefit of all the worlds, while the world-protectors were listening: "Once again, he requested this. (BrP 175.56)
Gautama said:
O Bull-bannered One, as long as the goddess who flows to the ocean was released from the mountain of Brahmā, you must remain there at all times and in every place.
O Lord of the world, O Lord of gods, you alone are the giver of fruit to those who desire it;
other holy places are auspicious only here and there.
They know that very place where you are eternally present to be the bestower of auspiciousness; for wherever the Gaṅgā was placed by you within your matted locks and crown,
O Śaṅkara, all sacred fords (tīrthas) exist there everywhere due to your presence.
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of Gautama, Śiva spoke again out of joy.
Śiva said: Wherever, whatever, and whoever performs with devotion a pilgrimage, a ritual bath, a gift, or even the libation for the ancestors; ||| BrP_175.61 |||
O Gautama, whatever man, restrained in his vows, performs with devotion the hearing, the recitation, or even the remembrance [of this] at the Godāvarī, [attains the highest goal].
The earth, adorned with dharma, consisting of seven islands, along with its mountains, forests, and groves, its jewels, medicinal herbs, and oceans, was beautiful.
Whatever merit arises from giving [a gift] becomes, according to the Gautamī-smṛti,
the merit of such a woman, O Brahmin, who is called "Ilā" because of her gift of a cow.

During an eclipse of the moon or sun, at a time when I am present, the wise man who is restrained in his vows and has always performed [worship] with devotion for Viṣṇu, the supporter of the earth, [attains this].
O best of the twice-born, whatever merit one may obtain who gives beautiful cows along with their calves at that world-renowned confluence— [that merit one obtains there].
Therefore, by bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts performed with devotion at the Gautamī— the great river venerated by the whole world— a man attains excellent merit.
Therefore, the Godāvarī shall be brought by you;
it will be the destroyer of all sins and the bestower of all desired objects.
Gaṇeśvara said:
"O Mother, I have heard this from Śiva as he was speaking to Gautama;
for this reason, Śambhu remains constantly established in the Gaṅgā."
O Mother, who is able to turn back that ocean of compassion?
Nevertheless, O Mother, it may be that men [are hindered] by the snares of obstacles.
Bound by attachment, they do not go even to the nearby Godāvarī;
they do not bow to the auspicious Lord Śiva, nor do they remember or praise him.
"O Mother, I shall act accordingly for the sake of your satisfaction;
however, my affliction prevents me from obeying your word—please forgive me."
Brahmā said:
From that time forward, Vighneśa creates some obstacle for those humans who proceed toward their goals without having worshipped him.
Moreover, disregarding obstacles, he who proceeds with devotion to Gautamī shall achieve his purpose in this world; no further duty remains for him.
Many obstacles arise for that lowest of men who desires to depart from his home;
having placed his foot upon the head of that man, [the deity] proceeds.
What fruit has he not obtained from the Gaṅgā? Even Sadāśiva himself could not describe her power;
thus, I have spoken in brief, following the accounts of the Itihāsas.
Whatever means for achieving dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa exist among the moving and the unmoving,
all that is found here in this detailed Itihāsa.
This has been declared as the truth revealed by the Vedas, the secret of all the Śrutis; it is the true cause, correctly expressed, and always rightly perceived for the benefit of the worlds.
This Purāṇa, which contains manifold dharmas, has been proclaimed.
One should listen to even a single verse or a single word of it with devotion, or recite it;
or, by uttering the words "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā," one shall obtain merit.
This [work] is capable of destroying the stains of the Kali age;
it bestows all perfections, grants auspiciousness,
is honored in the world, and yields desired fruits.
This supreme teaching of the Gaṅgā has been uttered;
well done, Gautama, may it be well with you! Who else is there who is your equal, who could reach this Ganges of Gautamī in the Daṇḍaka forest?
Whoever should utter "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā," even from a distance of hundreds of yojanas,
is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Three and a half crores of sacred fords in the three worlds come to bathe in the Gaṅgā when Jupiter enters Leo.
Bathing in the Bhāgīrathī for sixty thousand years is equal to bathing once in the Godāvarī when Jupiter is conjoined with Leo.
But this Gautamī, O son, by my command, shall grant liberation through bathing to all men at all times and in every place.
Whatever fruit one obtains by performing thousands of horse sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices, that shall be attained simply by hearing this.
O Nārada, for him in whose house this ancient [text] spoken by Brahmā remains, no fear of the Kali age exists.
This supreme Purāṇa must not be told to anyone at all,
except to one who is faithful, tranquil, a devotee of Viṣṇu, and high-souled.
This is glorious, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and destroying all sins;
by merely hearing this, a man shall have accomplished his life's purpose.
Having written this book, he gives it to a Brahmin;
liberated from all sins, he shall not enter a womb again.
The sages said: "We are not yet satiated while listening to the discourse of the Blessed One;
you ought to speak once more, in its entirety, of that which is the supreme secret."
"O God, you have not described Ananta-Vāsudeva correctly;
we wish to hear it—please tell us in detail."
Brahmā said:
O best of sages, I shall proclaim the supreme majesty of Ananta-Vāsudeva, which is more essential than the essence itself and difficult to find on earth.
O brahmins, in the first kalpa of old, I, whose birth is unmanifest,
summoned Viśvakarman and spoke these words.
"O most excellent one, you who are the sovereign of divine artisans and the foremost craftsman of Viśvakarman,
fashion an image of Vāsudeva out of stone upon this earth."
Beholding her according to the prescribed rites, humans and others, including Indra, became devoted;
and having recognized a very great danger from the Dānavas and Rākṣasas, they [sought refuge].
Having reached the third heaven and the summit of Mount Sumeru, they dwell there for a long time,
free from all fear, having propitiated Vāsudeva.
Having heard those words of mine, Viśvakarman instantly fashioned a pure image bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, with eyes as long as lotus petals,
marked with the Śrīvatsa sign, she was an exceedingly formidable and supreme image.
Her chest was covered by a forest garland; she wore a crown and armlets, was clad in yellow garments, possessed full shoulders, and was adorned with two earrings.
Thus, having reached the time for its consecration, that divine image was fashioned by me in the past through secret mantras. 176.11.
At that time, Śakra, the king of the gods, mounted his excellent elephant and went to the abode of Brahmā along with the sky-dwellers.
Having propitiated the image with repeated baths and offerings, Śakra,
having worshipped that image, returned once more to his own city.
Having propitiated her for a very long time with his speech, body, and mind restrained,
he [conquered] the cruel asuras, Vṛtra and others, headed by Namuci.
Having slain the terrible Dānavas, he enjoyed the three worlds;
and when the second age, the Tretā, had arrived, there was a lord of the Rākṣasas.
The ten-necked one, possessed of great heroism and majesty,
remained without food for ten thousand years, having conquered his senses.
He performed a most fierce vow, an ascetic practice exceedingly difficult to perform;
pleased by that austerity, I granted him a boon.
He was invincible to all the gods, as well as to the Daityas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas;
he was unslayable by fierce weapons of curses and by the servants of Yama.
Having obtained that boon, the Rākṣasa then, having utterly defeated these Yakṣas and all their hosts as well as the Lord of Wealth,
prepared to conquer Śakra.
Having waged a most terrible battle with the gods and having utterly defeated the king of the gods, that Rākṣasa was then indeed known as Indrajit.
His son, the Rākṣasa named Meghanāda, having obtained [the boon],
then reached Amarāvatī, the auspicious abode of the king of the gods.
But Rāvaṇa, endowed with great strength, beheld an image of Vāsudeva, resembling collyrium and possessed of all auspicious marks.
She was endowed with the Śrīvatsa mark, possessed eyes as broad as lotus petals,
her chest draped with a forest garland, and adorned with a crown and armlets.
She holds a conch, a discus, and a mace in her hands, wears yellow garments, possesses four arms,
is adorned with all ornaments, and bestows the fruits of all desires.
Leaving behind the heaps of jewels and the image endowed with auspicious marks,
he quickly dispatched [them] to Laṅkā by means of the Puṣpaka aerial chariot.
The illustrious and righteous Vibhīṣaṇa, the younger brother and minister of Rāvaṇa, who was devoted to Nārāyaṇa, stood as the superintendent of the city.
Having seen that divine image fallen from the abode of the Lord of the Gods,
his body became covered in horripilation and he was filled with wonder.
Having bowed my head to the God with a joyful inner soul, today my birth has become fruitful; today my asceticism has become fruitful.
Having spoken thus, that righteous-souled one, having repeatedly prostrated himself and approached his elder brother, spoke with palms joined in reverence.
"O King, you ought to show me favor through an image of yourself,
by propitiating which, O Lord of the World, I may cross over the ocean of worldly existence."
Having heard his brother's words, Rāvaṇa then said to him:
"O hero, take the image; what shall I do with this?"
"Having propitiated the Self-Existent One— the god who consists of manifold wonders and is the source of the existence of all beings— I shall conquer the three worlds."
Then the highly intelligent Vibhīṣaṇa,
having propitiated Janārdana with that auspicious image for one hundred and eight years, [attained his goal].
Having attained freedom from old age and death, endowed with the supernatural powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and others,
he enjoys sovereignty over Laṅkā and all desired pleasures.
The sages said:
"Aha! Great wonder has arisen in us upon hearing this supreme nectar—the account of the birth of Ananta-Vāsudeva, which is difficult to obtain on earth."
O God, we wish to hear in detail and exactly as it is;
you ought to recount the majesty of that deity in its entirety.
Brahmā said:
Then that cruel, evil-doing Rākṣasa [assailed] the gods, Gandharvas, and Kiṃnaras, as well as the world-protectors, the sages, and the Siddhas.
Having conquered all in battle, he then seized their women;
having established them in the city of Laṅkā, he was once again deluded by his longing for Sītā.
Then Rāvaṇa, having been struck with fear by the golden deer-form,
was confronted in battle by the enraged Rāma together with the son of Sumitrā.
For the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa, having killed Vālin, who was as swift as thought,
Sugrīva was consecrated [as king] and Aṅgada likewise as the crown prince.
Hanumān, Nala, Nīla, Jāmbavān, Panasa,
as well as Gavaya, Gavākṣa, and Pāṭhīna, all possessed supreme energy.
Surrounded by these and many other monkeys of great strength and formidable appearance, the lotus-eyed Rāma stood there.
Having built a bridge across the great ocean with the combined masses of all the mountains,
Rāma crossed over the vast sea by means of his great army.
Accompanied by hosts of Rākṣasas, he waged an incomparable battle against Yamahasta,
Prahasta, Nikumbha, and Kumbha.
Having slain the highly heroic Narāntaka as well as Yamāntaka,
Mālāḍhya, and Mālikāḍhya, the valiant Rāma prevailed.
Furthermore, having slain Indrajit, as well as Kumbhakarṇa along with Rāvaṇa,
and having purified Vaidehī by means of fire, he bestowed the kingdom upon Vibhīṣaṇa.
Taking Vāsudeva with him, he ascended the Puṣpaka chariot and reached the previously protected Ayodhyā with effortless ease.
Then Rāma, who is affectionate toward his devotees, out of love consecrated his youngest brother Bharata and Śatrughna as sovereigns over the entire kingdom, like a supreme monarch.
Then Hari, having propitiated his own ancient form for ten thousand years and ten hundred years, [remained there].
Having enjoyed the earth bounded by the oceans and having attained his kingdom, that descendant of Raghu entered the auspicious state, the station of Viṣṇu.
And Rāma gave that image to the Lord of the Ocean, saying:
"Blessed are you; may you be its protector, endowed with the waters and jewels."
When the Lord, the Master of the World, reached the Dvāpara age,
it was due to the request of the Earth and because of the resulting laxity of being.
That Lord, the Master, has descended into the family of Vasudeva,
accompanied by Saṃkarṣaṇa, for the purpose of slaying Kaṃsa and the others.
Then, O Brahmins, for some other reason and for the sake of the welfare of all the worlds, they [concealed] that image which grants the fruits of all desires.
In that most excellent, meritorious field, difficult to attain and presided over by the Supreme Person,
the ocean, the lord of rivers, himself drew it forth from the water.
O twice-born ones, from that time forward, that god, who bestows the fruits of all desires, has remained in that very field which grants liberation for the sake of the gods.
Those who constantly take refuge in the infinite Lord, the Sovereign of All, with devotion through speech, mind, and action, go to the supreme state.
Having seen Ananta even once with devotion, having worshipped him and prostrated before him,
one obtains ten times the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Upon a celestial chariot that fulfills all desires, moves at will, possesses great splendor, is the color of the sun, and is adorned with garlands of networks of tiny bells.
Having delivered twenty-one generations of his lineage, served by hosts of celestial women and praised by Gandharvas, that man shall go to the city of Viṣṇu.
Having enjoyed excellent pleasures there, free from old age and death, he,
glorious and possessing a divine form, remains until the dissolution of all beings.
Having arrived here due to the exhaustion of his merit, that best of the twice-born, a knower of the four Vedas,
shall attain liberation by resorting to the Vaiṣṇava yoga.
Thus, O best of sages, have I recounted this infinite [account] of him;
who is able to describe his virtues even in hundreds of years?
Brahmā said:
Thus have I described to you the infinite majesty of this Puruṣottama-kṣetra, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men, and which is exceedingly difficult to attain.
There dwells the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa, the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace,
clad in yellow garments, the slayer of Kaṃsa and Keśin.
Those who behold there Kṛṣṇa, who is honored by gods and asuras, as well as Saṃkarṣaṇa and Subhadrā—they are blessed; of this there is no doubt.
Those who always meditate upon Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the three worlds, the god who bestows the fruit of all desires, are liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Those who are devoted to Kṛṣṇa remember Kṛṣṇa;
those who, having risen again at night, [remember] Kṛṣṇa,
enter into Kṛṣṇa once their bodies have perished.
Just as an oblation offered with mantras reaches the fire, so too,
O best of sages, the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa should always be visited with great effort in that sacred field by those who desire liberation.
Those wise ones who behold Kṛṣṇa upon his rising from rest,
as well as Halāyudha and Subhadrā, go to the abode of Hari.
Those who, at any time, behold Puruṣottama with devotion,
as well as Rauhiṇeya and Subhadrā, go to the world of Viṣṇu.
He who dwells for four months of the rainy season at Puruṣottama obtains the fruit of a pilgrimage to all the sacred sites on earth, and even more.
Those wise ones who dwell there at all times,
having conquered their senses and subdued their anger, obtain the fruit of their ascetic penance.
Whatever a man obtains by performing austerities at other sacred sites for ten thousand years,
he obtains that in a single month at Puruṣottama.
The wise who dwell there constantly obtain that fruit which is the result of austerity, celibacy, and the renunciation of attachment.
Whatever merit is proclaimed to come from bathing and giving gifts at all sacred fords (tīrthas),
wise men constantly obtain that fruit there.
Whatever has been declared regarding the proper ford, the vow, and the observance,
one who is self-restrained and pure obtains that fruit there every single day.
Whatever fruit a man obtains through various kinds of sacrifices,
he obtains that same fruit there every day, provided his senses are restrained.
Those men who cast off their bodies there at Puruṣottama, having reached the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), are liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Those who cast off their bodies between the Vaṭa and the Sāgara attain the supreme liberation, which is difficult to obtain; of this there is no doubt.
Even that man who, though unwilling, gives up his life there,
is liberated from suffering and attains liberation, which is difficult to obtain.
Worms, insects, moths, and others who belong to the animal realm—
having cast off their bodies there, they go to the supreme goal.
O twice-born ones, behold the delusion of the world regarding other religious systems—
that which is obtained from other systems, such as the fruit [of liberation], is attained through what is called the Supreme Person (puruṣa).
That mortal who beholds Puruṣottama even once with faith shall become the most excellent person among thousands of men.
Since he is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti) and is even superior to the Puruṣa,
he is therefore called Puruṣottama in the Veda, in the Purāṇa, and in this world.
He who is proclaimed in the Purāṇas and Vedānta as the Supreme Self (Paramātman) dwells for the benefit of the universe; therefore, he is the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Whether in a sacred recitation hall, a cremation ground, a house pavilion, or even on the streets— wherever it may be, whether he desires it or not, there he [should cast off] his body.
By abandoning [all else], a human being attains liberation;
therefore, O best of the twice-born, men who truly desire liberation should, with every effort, cast off their bodies in that sacred field.
The majesty of the place called Puruṣa has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again;
for there, having cast off the body, a person attains liberation that is otherwise difficult to obtain.
This is but a single portion of its qualities that has been proclaimed by me;
who is able to describe all its qualities, even in hundreds of years?
O best of sages, if you desire eternal liberation,
dwell without weariness in that most meritorious and excellent field.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest,
they took up residence there and attained the supreme state.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, you should dwell with great effort in that excellent field called Puruṣa, if you desire liberation.
Vyāsa said:
O best of sages, in that field which brings happiness to all beings and bestows the fruits of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, [there is] Puruṣottama.
There was a great seer named Kaṇḍu, possessed of immense splendor and supreme righteousness;
he was truthful, pure, self-controlled, and devoted to the welfare of all beings.
Having conquered his senses and subdued his anger, and having mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
he attained supreme perfection by propitiating Puruṣottama.
Other sages as well, firm in their vows, were perfected there;
they were intent on the welfare of all beings, self-controlled, having conquered anger, and free from envy.
The sages said:
Who was this Kaṇḍu, and how did he attain the supreme goal there?
O best of beings, we wish to hear his life story; please tell it to us.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O tigers among sages, to his captivating story;
I shall relate in brief the deeds of that sage.
On the sacred bank of the Gomatī, in a secluded and very charming place,
filled with bulbs, roots, and fruits, and provided with sacrificial fuel, flowers, and kuśa grass.
It was filled with various trees and creepers, adorned with various flowers,
delightful with the songs of various birds, and frequented by various herds of wild animals.
O best of sages, there was the hermitage of Kaṇḍu,
rich in fruits and flowers of every season and adorned with groves of plantain trees.
There the sage performed a most great and supremely wonderful austerity through vows,
fasts, observances, ritual bathing, silence, and perfect self-restraint.
In summer he practiced the penance of the five fires, during the rains he slept on the bare ground, and in winter he wore wet clothes; thus he performed most intense austerity.
Having witnessed the power of that sage’s asceticism,
the gods, gandharvas, siddhas, and vidyādharas were utterly amazed.
O best of sages, by the power of his asceticism, Kaṇḍu scorched the earth, the atmosphere, and the heavens— the three worlds.
"Oh, what supreme fortitude he possesses! Oh, what supreme austerity!"—thus the gods spoke upon seeing him established in penance.
Then, agitated by fear of him and desiring to obstruct his asceticism, they deliberated together with Śakra, remaining undistracted.
Having understood their intention, Śakra, the lord of the three worlds,
[summoned] the woman of noble form named Pramlocā, who was proud of her beauty and youth.
To her, who had a slender waist, lovely shanks, and full hips and breasts,
and who was endowed with all auspicious marks, the slayer of Phala spoke:
Śakra said:
"O Pramlocā, go quickly; when that sage is performing his ascetic penance, O Suprabhā, agitate him at once for the purpose of obstructing his austerity."
Prāmloca said:
"O Lord, O best of gods, I shall always carry out your word;
however, I have a doubt here, for there is uncertainty regarding my very life."
I fear that best of sages, who stands firm in the vow of celibacy,
who is exceedingly fierce, whose ascetic heat is blazing, and whose radiance is equal to fire and the sun.
"Once that sage Kaṇḍu, who possesses supreme splendor, realizes that I have come here out of anger for the purpose of creating an obstacle, he will utter an unbearable curse."
Urvaśī, Menakā, Rambhā, Ghṛtācī, Puñjikasthalā,
Viśvācī, Sahajanyā, Pūrvacitti, and Tilottamā.
Alambuṣā, Miśrakeśī, Śaśilekhā, and Vāmanā—
there are also other Apsarases who are proud of their beauty and youth.
Appoint there those women who have slender waists, lovely faces, and full, elevated breasts,
and who are skilled in the primary arts of love.
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of hers, the Lord of Śacī spoke again:
"Let the other women remain aside; you alone, O auspicious one, are skilled in this matter."
"I give you Kāma, Vasanta, and Vāyu as companions;
go with them, O lady of beautiful hips, to where that great sage dwells."
Having heard the words of Śakra, that lovely-eyed woman then traveled through the path of the sky together with them to the hermitage of the sage.
Having gone there, she beheld a most excellent and beautiful forest,
and a sinless sage of radiant asceticism dwelling in a hermitage.
Together with them, she beheld a delightful forest, comparable to the Nandana grove,
rich with the finest flowers of every season and teeming with troops of monkeys.
It was meritorious, endowed with the strength of lotuses, and possessed the great power of its sprouts;
it heard the very sweet sounds, pleasing to the ear, uttered from the mouths of birds.
He saw trees rich with the weight of fruit in every season, radiant with blossoms in every season, and made resonant by the songs of birds.
Mangoes, hog-plums, bhavyas, coconut palms, and tinduka trees;
then wood-apples, as well as jīvas, pomegranates, and citron fruits.
Panasa fruits, lakucas, nīpas, and beautiful śirīṣas;
likewise pārāvatas, kolās, arimeda, and amlavetasas.
Bhallātaka, āmalaka, śataparṇa, and kiṃśuka;
iṅguda, karavīra, harītakī, and vibhītaka.
The large-eyed lady beheld these and other trees,
as well as Aśoka, Puṃnāga, Ketakī, and Bakula trees.
Pārijāta trees, kovidāras, as well as mandāras and indīvaras,
lovely blooming pāṭalas, and likewise devadāru trees.
He beheld śāla, tāla, and tamāla trees, as well as nicula and lomaka trees, and other excellent trees, all laden with flowers and fruit.
With cakoras, śatapatras, bhṛṅgarājas, as well as parrots,
cuckoos, sparrows, green pigeons, and jīvajīvaka birds;
It was also inhabited by dear young *cātaka* birds and various other kinds of birds,
who were warbling very sweetly and pleasantly to the ear.
And there were delightful lakes with clear waters,
adorned with white water-lilies, lotuses, and beautiful blue lotuses.
They were covered on all sides with white water-lilies and lotuses,
as well as with kādamba ducks, ruddy geese, and water-fowls.
It was filled on all sides with water-fowls such as kāraṇḍavas, cranes, swans, tortoises, and cormorants, as well as other aquatic creatures.
In this manner, she wandered through the forest with them in due order;
thus she beheld that most wonderful and delightful forest together with them.
O best of the twice-born, that excellent woman, her eyes wide with wonder,
spoke to Vāyu, Kāma, and Vasanta.
Prāmloca said:
"All of you together, each individually, provide me with assistance."
{Brahmā said:} Having been addressed thus by the gods, O twice-born ones, she replied, "So be it," and then said,
"Today I shall go to where that sage is staying. BrP_178.46.
Today, I shall make that driver of the body— whose senses are like spirited horses— with its reins slipping away from the weapons of Love, a wretched charioteer.
Whether it be Brahmā, Janārdana, or even Nīlalohita,
nevertheless today I shall make my inner being wounded by the arrows of desire.
Having spoken thus, she then departed for the place where that sage resided—
an hermitage where wild beasts had been pacified by the power of the sage’s asceticism.
Standing on the riverbank amidst the sweetness of the male cuckoo's song,
that excellent apsaras remained there for a short while and sang.
Then, at that moment, Spring suddenly brought forth its power—
sweet with the warbling of cuckoos and enchanting beyond all seasons.
And the wind, whose abode is the Malaya mountain,
blew gently, causing various pure flowers to fall one after another.
And Kāma, bearing his flower-arrows, having approached the sage's presence, agitated even the mind of that ascetic.
Then, hearing the sound of singing, the sage, his mind filled with wonder and tormented by the arrows of Kama, went to where that fair-browed woman was.
Having seen her, he, filled with joy, his eyes wide with wonder,
his upper garment fallen, agitated, and his body bristling with horripilation, spoke.
The Ṛṣi said:
"Who are you, and to whom do you belong, O lady of beautiful hips, blessed one with a lovely smile?
You steal my heart, O fair-browed one; tell me the truth, O slender-waisted one."
Prāmlocā said:
"I am your servant, and I have come for the sake of flowers;
give me your command quickly—what shall I do at your bidding?"
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of hers, he lost his composure and, being utterly deluded,
took the young woman by the hand and entered his own hermitage.
Then, O best of the twice-born, Kāma, Vāyu,
and Vasanta all returned to heaven as they had come, having accomplished their purpose.
Having gone to Hari, they reported her conduct and his;
and having heard it, Śakra and the gods then became pleased and well-disposed.
And as Kaṇḍu was entering the hermitage together with her,
he assumed his own supreme form, possessing the appearance of Madana.
Endowed with beauty and youth, exceedingly captivating,
adorned with divine ornaments, and having the appearance of a sixteen-year-old.
By the power of his asceticism, he suddenly became beautiful, wearing divine garments and adorned with celestial garlands and perfumes, endowed with every object of enjoyment.
Having witnessed that prowess of his, she was struck with great amazement;
saying, "Oh, the power of this asceticism! she became filled with joy.
O best of sages, [one should perform] bathing, the twilight prayers, recitation, fire-offerings, self-study of scripture, worship of the deities, vows, fasting, observances, and meditation.
Having abandoned [his asceticism], he rejoiced with her day and night, his heart possessed by the god of love; he did not perceive the exhaustion of his penance.
With his mind attached to sense objects, he did not perceive the passing of time— neither the twilight, night, day, fortnights, months, seasons, solstices, nor years.
And she, O twice-born ones, being inflamed by states born of desire and skilled in amorous discourse, then chose him in secret, she of the beautiful hips.
Thus Kaṇḍu,
the sage devoted to worldly pleasures, remained with her for more than a hundred years in the valley of Mount Mandara.
She said to that illustrious one, "O Brahmin, I wish to go to heaven; you ought to grant me permission, being well-disposed toward me with favor."
Thus addressed by her, that sage, his mind attached to her, said:
"O blessed lady, please stay for a few days."
Having been addressed thus by him, that slender woman then enjoyed the objects of the senses together with that great-souled one for more than a hundred years.
"Grant me permission, O Blessed One; I am going to the abode of the thirty gods. When he had spoken thus, she replied to him, "Stay yet awhile. (BrP 178.73)
Furthermore, O Brahmin, when more than a hundred years have passed, that lady of auspicious countenance shall go to the third heaven, which is beautiful with the smiles of affection.
Having been addressed thus by her, that sage spoke again to the lotus-eyed woman: "O fair-browed one, please sit here with me; you shall depart after a long time."
Fearing that curse, the fair-hipped woman remained with that ṛṣi for a little less than two hundred years.
Though repeatedly urged by that slender woman to go to the residence of the king of the gods, the illustrious one replied, "Stay."
Terrified by the fear of his curse, yet courteous and sensitive to the pain of a breach in affection, the southern quarter did not abandon the sage.
And as that supreme ṛṣi took his pleasure with her day and night, his love became ever new, for his mind was entirely absorbed in the god of love.
Once, however, the sage emerged from his hut in a hurry;
as he was departing, that auspicious woman asked, "Where are you going?"
Thus addressed by her, he said: "O auspicious lady, the day has turned;
I shall perform the twilight worship, otherwise there would be a lapse in my ritual duties."
Then, laughing with joy, she said to that great sage:
