"O knower of all dharmas, why has today become a day of transformation for you?
This [news] that has passed by does not cause wonder to anyone; of what is it being told?"
The sage said:
"O blessed lady, you came to this auspicious riverbank at dawn;
you were seen by me, O fair-hipped one, as you entered my hermitage."
This twilight has arrived and the day has come to an end;
for what purpose is this laughter? Let my true intention be told to me.
Prāmlocā said:
"O Brahmin, it is true that I arrived at dawn; this is not a falsehood on my part.
However, hundreds of years have passed for you since that time."
Then, filled with trepidation, the brahmin asked that large-eyed woman:
"Tell me, O timid one, what time has passed while I have been constantly enjoying your company?"
Prāmloca said:
Nine hundred and seven years have passed,
as well as six months, and another three days have likewise elapsed.
The Ṛṣi said:
"O timid one, you speak this truth, or perhaps it is a jest, O auspicious lady;
I believe that I have dwelt here together with you for but a single day."
Prāmlocā said:
"O Brahmin, how could I speak an untruth here in your presence,
especially since I have been questioned today by you who follow the path?"
Vyāsa said:
O best of the twice-born, having heard those words of hers, that sage censured himself for his improper conduct, saying, "Fie, fie upon me! BrP_178.90.
The sage said:
"My ascetic merits have been destroyed; the wealth of those who know Brahman has been stolen;
my discrimination has been taken away by someone who has fashioned this woman for the sake of delusion."
"Brahman, which transcends the six waves, is to be known by me through self-conquest; fie upon that great crocodile of desire by whom this path was abandoned! (BrP 178.92)
Today, by means of desire, my vows, all the Vedas, and all causes have been destroyed on the path to the village of hell.
Thus censuring himself by himself, that knower of dharma spoke these words to the Apsaras who was seated there. [The Rishi said:]
"Go, O wicked woman, as you desire! That which was to be done has been done by you, who caused agitation to the King of the Gods through your emotional gestures.
Yet, I shall not reduce you to ashes with the fierce fire of my wrath."
"Friendship with the virtuous is formed by walking seven steps together; I have dwelt with you for that duration."
Or rather, what fault is yours, or what could I possibly do to you?
The fault is entirely mine, since I have failed to conquer my senses.
Just as the expenditure of my ascetic penance was made by her who desired the favor of Śakra,
so have I been reviled by you, who are like a fool deluded by the great delusion of false views.
Vyāsa said:
While that brahmin-sage was thus speaking to the slender-waisted woman,
she began to tremble violently, with drops of perspiration trickling from her.
And that best of sages, to her who was trembling and whose vine-like limbs were perspiring, spoke with anger: "Go! Go! (BrP 178.99).
Rebuked by him, she departed from that hermitage;
moving through the air, she wiped away her sweat with the tender leaves of trees.
The young woman went from tree to tree with their lofty, reddish shoots,
and she indeed wiped her limbs from which perspiration was dripping.
The embryo that had then been deposited in her body by the sage emerged from her limbs in the form of sweat accompanied by horripilation.
The trees received that embryo, and the Wind made it one;
nourished by the Moon and by the rays of light, it then grew gradually.
O twice-born ones, there was a beautiful-eyed maiden named Māriṣā who belonged to the trees;
she became the wife of the Pracetases and the mother of Dakṣa.
And that blessed Kaṇḍu, O best of men, when his ascetic penance was exhausted,
went, O brahmins, to the abode of Viṣṇu known as Puruṣottama.
He beheld the supreme sacred field, which bestows liberation and is difficult to find on earth,
situated on the shore of the southern ocean and granting the fruits of all desires.
It was most beautiful, strewn with sand and adorned with groves of ketaka trees;
it was auspicious, filled with various trees and creepers, and resounded with the songs of diverse birds.
It is a place where one may wander happily everywhere, endowed with flowers in every season;
it bestows all happiness upon men, auspicious, and a mine of all virtues.
It was formerly frequented by Bhṛgu and others, as well as by the best of sages and perfected beings (siddhas),
by gandharvas, kinnaras, yakṣas, and others who long for liberation.
And there he beheld Hari, adorned by all the gods and attended by the castes beginning with the Brahmins, as well as those established in the stages of life (āśramas).
Upon seeing that sacred field and the god Puruṣottama,
that best of sages then considered himself as one who had accomplished all his goals.

There, having become one-pointed in mind, that best of sages, a great yogi, stood with his arms raised and performed the worship of Hari, reciting the *japa* consisting of the *Brahmapāra* with a concentrated mind.
The sages said:
O sage, we wish to hear about the supreme and most auspicious Brahmapāra,
by which Lord Keśava was propitiated through the recitation of prayers by Kaṇḍu.
Vyāsa said: Viṣṇu is the further shore, the supreme, whose own shore is shoreless; he is beyond all that is beyond, having the form of the Supreme Self.
He has reached the further shore of Brahman, having become the further shore beyond; he is the supreme, the shore beyond even the shores of the supreme.
Though he is the cause, he rests upon causes as well.
Its cause is the cause of another cause; and this effect, together with its various forms of action and agent, descends here as everything.
He is the Lord Brahmā, he is Brahmā who has become all beings; he is the imperishable Lord of creatures,
that Viṣṇu is the eternal, immutable, and unborn Brahmā.
Just as that Puruṣottama is unattached to all things such as decay and is the imperishable, unborn, and eternal Brahman,
so may my defects, such as passion and the like, come to rest.
Vyāsa said:
O best of the twice-born, having heard that sage’s recitation of the *Brahmapāra* and having recognized his supreme and very firm devotion, Puruṣottama [acted].
Then that god Madhusūdana, who is compassionate toward his devotees, went near him and spoke with supreme affection.
O brahmins, having mounted Garuḍa, the delight of Vinatā’s lineage, he seemed to make the quarters of the sky resound with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
The Blessed One said:
"O sage, speak the supreme purpose that dwells in your mind.
I have arrived as a giver of boons; choose a boon, O you of noble vows."
Having heard these words of the God of gods, the wielder of the discus,
he suddenly opened his eyes and beheld Hari before him.
Resembling the flax flower, with eyes as broad as lotus petals,
holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, and wearing a crown and armlets.
He has four arms and noble limbs, wears yellow garments, and is auspicious;
he is endowed with the Śrīvatsa mark and adorned with a forest garland.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, adorned with every kind of jewel,
his limbs anointed with divine sandalwood paste and decorated with celestial garlands.
Then, overcome with wonder, his hair standing on end,
he prostrated himself upon the earth like a staff and offered his salutation.
"Today my birth has become fruitful; today my ascetic toil has become fruitful.
Having said this, those tigers among sages began to offer praise to him.
Kaṇḍu said:
O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord marked with the Śrīvatsa, O Master of the world,
O Seed of the world, O Abode of the world, O Witness of the world— salutations be unto You!
O Unmanifest One, O Victorious One, O Source, O Supreme Person,
O Lotus-eyed One, O Govinda, O Lord of the World— homage be to You!
O Hiraṇyagarbha, Śrīnātha, Padmanātha, Sanātana,
Bhūgarbha, Dhruva, Īśāna, Hṛṣīkeśa— salutations be unto you!
O you who are without beginning or end, immortal and unconquerable, conquer! O best among victors, O unconquered and indivisible Śrī Kṛṣṇa, abode of Śrī, homage be to you!
O performer of the rain-rite, O one difficult to cross, O you who are difficult to master,
O destroyer of the pain of suffering, O Hari who reclines upon the waters— salutations be unto you!
O Purifier of beings, Unmanifest One, Lord of beings, unperturbed by the principles of being,
abode of beings, soul of beings, womb of beings— homage be to you!
O performer of sacrifice, upholder of sacrifice, bestower of sacrifice, giver of fearlessness;
O womb of sacrifice, golden-limbed one, born from the speckled cloud—salutations be unto you!
O Knower of the Field, Sustainer of the Field, Owner of the Field, Destroyer of the Field, Maker of the Field, the Subduer;
O Soul of the Field, Free from the Field, Creator of the Field—homage be to You!
O abode of qualities, dwelling place of qualities, refuge of qualities, bringer of qualities;
O enjoyer of qualities, delighter in qualities, renouncer of qualities—homage be to you!
You are Viṣṇu, you are Hari, the wielder of the discus; you are Jiṣṇu, you are Janārdana;
you are the past, you are the *vaṣaṭ* call, you are the future, and you are the Lord of all that exists.
You are the creator of beings, you are the unmanifest;
you are existence, the sustainer of beings, and the divine Lord. They call you the unborn Sovereign.
You are Ananta, you are the Knower of All, you are Prakṛti, you are Vṛṣākapi;
you are Rudra, you are the Unassailable, you are the Infallible, you are the Lord.
You are Viśvakarman, you are the Victorious One; you are Śambhu, you are Vṛṣākṛti;
you are Śaṅkara, you are Uśanas; you are Truth, you are Penance, and you are the People.
You are the conqueror of all, you are the refuge, you are the protector, you are the imperishable;
you are the source of bliss, you are the self-born, you are the eldest, and you are the ultimate resort.
You are Āditya, you are Oṃkāra, you are Prāṇa, you are the destroyer of darkness;
you are Parjanya, you are the celebrated one, you are the Ordainer, and you are the Lord of the Gods.
You are the Ṛg, the Yajus, and the Sāman; you are the esteemed Self.
You are fire, you are the wind, you are the waters, and you are the earth.
You are the creator, you are likewise the enjoyer, you are the priest, and you are the oblation and the sacrifice;
you are the lord, you are the all-pervading one, you are the most excellent, and you are the imperishable Lord of the worlds.
You are the all-seeing, the glorious one; you are the subduer of all and the slayer of enemies.
You are the day and likewise the night; the wise call you the year.
You are time; you are the divisions of time—kalā, kāṣṭhā, muhūrta, kṣaṇa, and lava.
You are the child, as well as the old man; you are male, female, and neuter.
You are the source of the universe, you are the eye, you are the pillar, you are the one of pure fame;
you are the eternal, you are the unconquered, you are Upendra, and you are the supreme.
You are the giver of happiness to the entire universe; you are the limb of the Vedas, you are the imperishable;
you are the knower of the Vedas, you are the sustainer, the ordainer, and you are the one who is perfectly composed.
You are the ocean from its very depths; you are the Sustainer, and you are again the Wealth-giver;
you are the Physician, you are the one whose self is steadfast, and you are the one whose sphere of perception transcends the senses.
You are the leader, you are the village headman; you are the fair-winged bird, you are the primordial one;
you are the gathering, you are the very great, you are the self-sustained, and you are the infallible.
You are Yama, you are Niyama; you are the lofty one, and you are the four-armed one.
You alone are the inner self of food, and you are called the supreme self.
You are the teacher, you are the supreme teacher; you are the left, you are the right;
you are the Pippala tree, you are the unapproachable, you are the manifest, and you are Prajāpati.
You are the god Hiraṇyanābha, you are the moon, and you are Prajāpati;
you indeed possess an indescribable form, you are Yama, and you are the slayer of the enemies of the gods.
And you are the god Saṃkarṣaṇa; you are the creator, you are the eternal one;
you are Vāsudeva, the immeasurable self; you alone are devoid of qualities (guṇa).
You are the eldest, you are the most excellent, and you are the patient Mādhava;
you are the thousand-headed god, you are the unmanifest, and you are the thousand-eyed one.
You are the thousand-footed god; you are the Virāj; you are the lord of the gods.
You alone, O God of gods, remain further as the ten-fingered one.
That which has been is said to be you alone, O Śakra, the supreme Puruṣa;
that which is to be is you, the Lord (Īśāna); you are the Cosmic Order (Ṛta), and likewise you are the Immortal (Amṛta).
From you this world grows; you are the most great, the unsurpassed;
you are the elder, the Puruṣa, and you, O God, abide in ten forms.
The universal being consists of four parts; one part is immortal in heaven, and nine parts reside in the intermediate space as the eternal, spiritual essence.
Two parts were established upon the earth, and here too there was a fourth part;
from you the sacrifices arise, which are the cause of rain for the world.
From you was born Virāṭ, that Puruṣa who dwells in the heart of the world;
he excelled all beings in splendor, fame, and glory.
From you was produced the ghee mixed with curds, the food of the gods;
from you came the plants of the village and the forest, as well as the domestic animals, wild beasts, and the rest.
Devoted to meditation upon the object of thought, you have created medicinal herbs;
O God of gods, you are the seven-faced one known as Time (Kāla), possessed of a radiant form.
This entire world, both moving and unmoving, all that is animate and inanimate—this whole universe has arisen from you; everything is established in you.
You are Aniruddha, you are Mādhava, you are Pradyumna, the slayer of the enemies of the gods;
O Lord, the most excellent of all deities, the ultimate refuge of all the worlds.
Save me, O lotus-eyed one; Nārāyaṇa, homage be to you!
Homage to you, Blessed Viṣṇu; homage to you, Supreme Person!
Homage to you, Lord of all worlds; homage to you, whose abode is the lotus.
Homage be to you, the abode of virtues; homage be to you, the mine of virtues.
O Vāsudeva, homage be unto you; homage be unto you, O best of gods!
O Janārdana, homage be unto you; homage be unto you, O eternal one!
Salutations to you, who are accessible to yogins; salutations be to you, O abode of yoga!
O Lord of the Cowherds, O Lord of Śrī, O Viṣṇu, salutations be to you, O Lord of the Maruts!
O Lord of the world, O Progenitor of the world, salutations to you, O Lord of the wise!
O Lord of heaven, let there be salutation to you; let there be salutation to you, O Lord of the earth!
Salutations to you, the slayer of Madhu; salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one;
salutations be to you, O destroyer of Kaiṭabha; salutations be to you, O Subrahmaṇya.
Homage be to you, O Great Fish, unfallen one who bears the Vedas upon your back;
you who cause the agitation of the ocean's waters and bring delight to the Lotus-born One.
O horse-headed one, with the great snout and the body of the Great Puruṣa;
salutations to you, the slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, O horse-faced one!
Salutations to you, the Great Tortoise, who possesses the body of a massive tortoise, who lifted up the earth, and who bore the form of a mountain.
Homage to Mahāvarāha, who performed the lifting up of the earth;
homage to Ādivarāha, the creator of all forms, the omniscient one.
Homage to the infinite, the subtle, the primary, and the most excellent;
homage to you whose nature is that of the atom, who are accessible only to yogis.
Salutation to him, the cause of all causes,
whose abode is the conduct of the lords of yogis, who is difficult to know,
and who reclines upon the serpent-couch resting on the Milk Ocean.
"Salutations to you, who wear beautiful earrings of gold and jewels.
Vyāsa said:
Thus praised by him at that time, Mādhava was pleased and spoke.
Speak quickly, O best of sages, what it is that you desire from me.
Kaṇḍu said:
O Lord of the World, in this transmigratory existence— which is difficult to cross, hair-raising,
impermanent, full of suffering, and like the leaf of a plantain tree— BrP_178.179 //
It is without support, without foundation, as flickering as a bubble on water,
joined with all manner of calamities, difficult to cross, and exceedingly terrifying.
Deluded by your māyā, I have wandered for a very long time;
with my mind attached to sense objects, I do not reach the end [of saṃsāra].
O Lord of Gods, O Kṛṣṇa, today I, afflicted by the fear of saṃsāra, have come to you for refuge; deliver me from the ocean of existence.
O Lord of Gods, by your grace, I desire to go to that supreme, eternal state of yours, from which a return is difficult to attain.
The Blessed One said:
"O best of sages, you are my devotee; worship me constantly.
By my grace, you shall surely attain the liberation you desire."
My devotees—whether Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, Śūdras, or those born of the lowest castes—attain supreme perfection; how much more so then you, O best of the twice-born?
Even a dog-cooker (outcaste), if he is my devotee and endowed with perfect faith, attains his desired perfection; what then need be said of others?
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus to him, O brahmins, that god Viṣṇu, who is affectionate toward his devotees and whose course is difficult to comprehend, vanished right there.
O best of sages, when he had departed, Kaṇḍu, his mind filled with joy,
abandoned all desires and once again became composed in heart.
Having restrained all the senses, free from the sense of "mine" and devoid of egoism,
with a one-pointed mind, he meditated correctly upon that Supreme Person.
Stainless, devoid of qualities, peaceful, and established as pure existence alone,
he attained the supreme liberation that is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Whoever reads or even hears this story of the high-souled Kaṇḍu,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the heavenly world.
Thus, O best of sages, have I described the land of action,
the supreme field of liberation, and the God who is the Supreme Person.

Those who behold the All-pervading Lord, praise the Giver of Boons, and meditate with devotion upon Him known as Śrī Puruṣottama— the undecaying one who bestows liberation and removes the suffering of saṃsāra— [attain the highest goal].
Having enjoyed the pleasures of a lord of men and divine happiness in heaven, those stainless ones,
freed from all defects, subsequently go to the imperishable abode of Hari.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Having heard the words of Vyāsa, the sages, whose senses were restrained,
became pleased, thrilled, and filled with wonder again and again.
The sages said:
"O Puruṣottama, you have indeed proclaimed the virtues of Bhāratavarṣa;
likewise, [tell us] of that sacred field known as Śrīpuruṣa."
O best of speakers, upon hearing of the supreme majesty of that field known as Puruṣa, there arises both wonder and joy in one who hears it alone.
For a long time now, a doubt has resided within our hearts;
other than you, there is no one else on earth who can dispel this doubt.
O great sage, we ask you about the birth of Baladeva and Kṛṣṇa upon the earth, as well as that of Bhadrā, in its entirety.
O Sage, for what purpose were both those heroes, Kṛṣṇa and Saṃkarṣaṇa, born as the sons of Vasudeva, yet remained in the house of Nanda?
In this essence-less world of death, which is full of suffering, exceedingly fickle,
resembling a bubble on water, terrifying, and hair-raising;
How could they have found pleasure in that most terrible dwelling in the womb, which is slippery with excrement and urine, painful, cramped, and a source of suffering? (BrP 179.8)
O Sage, best among speakers, tell us in detail those actions which they performed when they were born upon the surface of the earth.
[Relate] their entire conduct, which is wonderful and superhuman;
how that Blessed One, the god, the lord of the gods, the best of deities, [acted].
In the lineage of Vasudeva, the wise one attained the state of Vāsudeva;
he was surrounded by immortals and adorned by those who have performed meritorious deeds.
Why have you abandoned the world of the gods and come here to the mortal world—
you who are the leader of both gods and men, the source of heaven and earth, and the imperishable one?
For what purpose did he, who alone sets in motion the wheel of well-being for human beings, apply his divine self among mortals?
How did he who bears the discus and mace, and who provides protection for the entire world of living beings, apply his mind to human existence?
How did that Lord Viṣṇu, having entered the earth, assume the state of a cowherd—
he who is the soul of all beings and who both sustained and created the great elements?
How was that Śrīgarbha, who by his three strides conquered the worlds out of a desire for the state of the Thirty-three gods, held in the womb of a woman who wanders upon the earth?
The paths of the world were established, and the three aims of life (trivarga) came into being;
he who, at the time of the end, having drunk up the world, assumed a body composed of water.
He who is the ancient one, the soul of all that is ancient, assumed the form of a boar and, with his body both visible and invisible, turned the world into a single ocean.
The slayer of enemies, who in former times for the sake of Indra raised up this imperishable triple world with the tip of his tusk; BrP_179.19 //
Having conquered the earth, that best of gods gave it to the deities; for which purpose he had assumed the form of a lion and then divided that body into two parts.
The former Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, who possessed great heroism, was slain—
he who in ancient times became the all-pervading Aurva fire, the Saṃvartaka blaze.
Hari, staying in the netherworld (pātāla), drank the excellent water consisting of the ocean;
he is Brahman with a thousand feet, the giver of a thousand rays and a thousandfold gifts.
They call him the thousand-headed God in age after age,
from whose navel the lotus arose, the abode of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
In the world of the Nagas, amidst the single vast ocean, there was an excellent golden lotus by which you slew those Daityas in the Tārakāmaya battle.
By whom, having assumed a divine body bearing all weapons while stationed in a cave, the arrogant Kālanemi was struck down.
At the northern edge of the ocean, in the Ocean of Milk, the sea of nectar,
he who lies down, having resorted to eternal yoga, [subdues] the great darkness.
Surāraṇī conceived a divine embryo,
and through the excellence of her asceticism, Aditi [conceived] the ancient Śakra, who had been obstructed by the hosts of Daityas.
Having entered the womb, he performed [his deeds]; having made his strides through the power of yoga, he cast the Daityas down into the depths of the ocean.
And having made the gods the lords of the thirty-three, he established Puruhūta as the lord of the gods by means of the gārhapatya rite and the anvāhārya ritual.
The Āhavanīya fire, the Veda, the initiation, the sacrificial fuel, and the Dhruva vessel.
He likewise made the vessel for sprinkling, the *sruva* ladle, and the *āvabhṛthya* vessel;
he, with his hands turned downwards, fashioned those who consume the sacrificial portions.
He then made the gods consumers of the *havya* offerings and the ancestors consumers of the *kavya* offerings;
for the sake of enjoyment, he engaged them in the ritual of sacrifice according to the rules of sacrificial procedure.
The sacrificial vessels, the priestly fee, the initiation rite, the cooked offerings, and the mortars;
the sacrificial post, the fuel, the dipping-spoon, the Soma, the strainers, and even the enclosing sticks.
And the sacrificial materials, as well as other vessels such as the *camasas*,
the members of the assembly (*sadasyas*), the sacrificers, and the highest sacrifices beginning with the *medha*.
He who, in former times, having performed his duties as the supreme lord in accordance with the age, divided the worlds through his prowess; ||| BrP_179.34 |||
Moments, eye-winks, *kāṣṭhās*, *kalās*, as well as the three divisions of time;
*muhūrtas*, lunar days, months, and likewise the day and the year.
The seasons and the conjunctions of time, the threefold measure in the three [realms],
lifespan, fields, accumulation, characteristics, and the excellence of form.
The three worlds, the three gods, the triple Veda, the three fires,
the three times, the three types of action, the three social classes, and the three qualities.
By whom all worlds were created in the past through infinite action—
he is the creator residing within all beings, whose essence consists of the qualities of all beings.
And he who delights in the yoga preceded by the senses of men,
and who is the Lord (Īśvara) himself through the yoga of going and returning— that very same rule applies.
He who is the destination for those endowed with righteousness and the non-destination for those of evil deeds;
he who is the source of the four castes and the protector of the four castes.
He who knows the fourfold knowledge, who takes refuge in the four stages of life, and who is like the various quarters of space, the sky, the earth, the wind, or even fire— [he is the knower].
He is the light consisting of the moon and sun, the Lord of the Yugas, and the wanderer by night;
he who is heard of as the supreme light, and he who is heard of as the supreme austerity.
He whom they call the Supreme yet the Non-Supreme, who is the Supreme Being possessed of the Self;
he who is the deity among the Ādityas and the all-pervading Lord who is the destroyer of the Daityas.
He who is the Ender at the close of the ages, and he who is the destroyer of the destroyers of the worlds;
he who is the bridge for those who are bridges for the world, and he who is the pure one among those whose deeds are pure.
He who is to be known by those who know the Vedas, who is the Lord of the self-born,
who has become the Soma for the gentle, and who has become the sacrificial fire for those possessing the luster of fire.
He who was the lord of the Śakras, the embodiment of asceticism among ascetics,
the discipline of those who follow the path of policy, and the splendor even of the splendid.
He is the physical form of those worthy of form, and the goal of those who possess a goal;
from space arises wind, and from the vital breath of wind arises fire.
The consumer of oblations is the breath from heaven, and Agni is Madhusūdana, the breath;
from essence (rasa) blood is produced, and from blood flesh is said to arise.
From flesh, however, fat is born; from fat, bone is said to arise;
from bone, marrow was produced; and from marrow, semen originates.
From semen the embryo was produced through action rooted in [bodily] fluids;
therein, the first portion of the waters is called the lunar aggregate (saumya-rāśi).
The second aggregate is said to be known as that which arises from the heat of the womb;
one should know that the semen is of the nature of Soma, and the menstrual blood is of the nature of Agni.
The emotional states (bhāvas) follow the aesthetic sentiments (rasas), and within these, the moon and fire reside in the seed;
semen arises in the category of phlegm (kapha), and blood in the category of bile (pitta).
The heart is the seat of phlegm (kapha), and bile (pitta) is established in the navel;
the heart is situated in the middle of the body, and that is recorded as the seat of the mind (manas).
Within that space between the navel and the abdomen resides the god Hutāśana;
the mind should be known as Prajāpati, and phlegm is conceived of as Soma.
Bile is indeed known as fire; thus the world consists of the nature of both fire and moon.
When the embryo has thus been set in motion and has grown to resemble a *arbuda* (a tumor-like mass), [it develops further].
The wind entered in union with the Supreme Self;
residing within the body, it is divided fivefold and functions again.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna—
prāṇa, increasing the supreme self (paramātman), circulates throughout him.
Apāna [governs] the posterior part of the body, while Udāna governs the upper half of the embodied being; Vyāna, however, pervades [the whole], and Samāna is that which circulates through the center.
From that, his attainment of the elements occurs, which are within the range of the senses:
earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth.
The senses, established within him, each took its own respective portion;
they say the earthly body belongs to the earth, while the vital breath (prāṇa) belongs to the wind.
The apertures have space as their source; from water, the flow proceeds;
light is the eyes and their brilliance, while the mind is known as their self (ātman).
"By whose power villages and territories were set in motion—thus the eternal Puruṣa, creating all these worlds... (BrP 179.62)
O Brahman, how did Viṣṇu come to attain human status in this world of mortals?
This is our doubt, O Brahman; this is our great wonder.
How did Viṣṇu, the goal of those who seek their goal, assume a human body? He is described by both gods and demons as the supreme wonder.
O great sage, tell me the wondrous account of the birth of Viṣṇu,
who is renowned for his strength and heroism and possesses immeasurable splendor.
Let the true nature of Viṣṇu, who is wondrous through his actions, be told here:
how is that god Puruṣottama the remover of the suffering of the gods?
The Lord of the universe is all-pervading, the Great Sovereign of all worlds;
he is the God who effects creation, preservation, and dissolution, bringing happiness to all the worlds.
He is imperishable, eternal, infinite, and devoid of decrease or increase;
he is untainted, beyond qualities, subtle, changeless, and stainless.
The eternal Supreme Self is liberated from all limiting adjuncts, established in pure existence alone, changeless, all-pervading, and everlasting.
In the Kṛta Yuga, his state as Hari is heard to be immovable, stainless, all-pervading, eternally satisfied, independent, and pure.
His state as Vaikuṇṭha among the gods and his state as Kṛṣṇa among humans—
such is the profound course of the actions of that Lord.
A desire to hear about the past and the future arises in me regarding this Lord,
the Master, who is unmanifest yet abides in manifest forms.
For Nārāyaṇa is the infinite self, the source and the imperishable;
having become this Nārāyaṇa, he was the eternal Hari.
Brahmā, Śakra, Rudra, Dharma, Śukra, and Bṛhaspati—
indeed, in ancient times, this Lord, the Pradhānātman, created Brahmā.

Thus that primordial Being created the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis) in a former aeon; yet for what purpose did the Blessed Viṣṇu, the Great Lord of all worlds, become Hari and enter this mortal world in the lineage of the Yadus?
Vyāsa said: Having paid homage to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the gods, the sovereign, the primordial Puruṣa, the eternal and the immutable; 180.1.
Salutation to Him who is the soul of the fourfold manifestation, who is both devoid of qualities and possessed of qualities,
the most excellent, the most venerable, the most worthy of choice, and the immeasurable.
To Him whose limbs are the components of sacrifice, who is the complete embodiment of all limbs, and who is desired by the gods and others;
than whom there is nothing subtler, and than whom there is nothing greater.
By whom this entire universe, including the moving and the unmoving, is pervaded— that Unborn One who is distinct from manifestation and disappearance, and from the seen and the unseen.
Having paid homage with meditative concentration to Brahmā, the primordial god, they speak of that which was created and likewise of that which was withdrawn.
Salutation to Viṣṇu, the victorious one, who is changeless, pure, eternal, the Supreme Self, whose form is always of a single nature.
Homage to Hiraṇyagarbha, to Hari, and to Śaṅkara; to Vāsudeva, the Savior, the author of creation, preservation, and destruction.
Salutation to Viṣṇu, the cause of liberation, who possesses both singular and manifold natures, whose essence is both gross and subtle, and who is both unmanifest and manifest.
Salutations to that Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, who is the root cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world, and who is himself composed of the world.
Having prostrated before the Imperishable, the Supreme Person, who is the support of the universe, subtler than the subtlest, and abiding within all beings;
In ultimate reality, it is of the nature of knowledge and absolutely stainless;
yet, due to erroneous perception, it appears to abide in the form of an object.
Viṣṇu, the devourer of the universe, the Lord of its maintenance and creation,
the beginningless Master of the worlds, unborn, undecaying, and immutable.
I shall relate how, in former times, when questioned by the Yakṣas and other foremost sages,
the Blessed One, the Grandfather born from the lotus, spoke.
Having prostrated before the Lord who emerged from the single ocean, he who purifies the three worlds by emitting the Ṛg and Sāman verses from his mouths; BrP_180.14.
I shall proclaim in its entirety the doctrine of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, according to which the hosts of Asuras do not plunder the sacrifices of those who perform them.
By him, for the sake of creation, dharma and the other [purposes] were made manifest;
water was called *nārā* by the sages who perceive reality.
Since they were his primordial abode (ayana), he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa;
that divine Lord, the all-pervading and omnipresent Nārāyaṇa, pervades everything.
Brahmā is established in four ways: as possessing qualities (saguṇa) and likewise as devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
One form is beyond designation; the wise behold it as white.
Her limbs are enveloped in garlands of flames; she is the ultimate goal of yogis.
She should be known as both far away and yet near at hand, transcending all qualities.
This one, designated as Vāsudeva, is perceived through the state of being free from the sense of "mine-ness";
its forms, colors, and so forth are not real entities, but are composed of conceptual construction.
And she always remains pure, firmly established and of a single form;
while a second one, known as Śeṣa, supports the earth from below with his head.
That is declared to be tāmasī, having entered into the state of animals;
the third performs action, being intent upon the protection of subjects.
She should be known as one in whom the quality of sattva predominates, the establisher of dharma;
she is the fourth [form], who reclines upon the coils of the serpent in the midst of the waters.
Indeed, that which is the third form of Hari, ever intent on the protection of subjects, always effects creation through its quality of *rajas*.
She establishes the order of dharma firmly upon the earth;
she slays the arrogant asuras who cause the destruction of dharma.
He protects the gods along with the Gandharvas who are devoted to the preservation of Dharma,
whenever and wherever a decline of Dharma occurs.
When unrighteousness arises, he creates himself anew;
having previously become a boar, he cast away the waters with his snout.
With a single tusk, he uprooted the earth like a lotus;
and having assumed the form of a man-lion, Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain.
And other Dānavas, headed by Vipracitti, were struck down;
having assumed the form of a dwarf, he bound Bali through his illusory power.
Having utterly conquered the sons of Diti,
the powerful Jāmadagnya, born in the lineage of Bhṛgu, traversed the three worlds.
Remembering the slaughter of his father, the powerful Rāma,
having become the son of Atri as Dattātreya, slew the Kṣatriyas.
Having become Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, that powerful deity taught the eightfold yoga to the high-souled Alarka.
He slew Rāvaṇa, the terror of the three worlds, in battle,
when the God of gods, the Lord of the universe, was sleeping upon the single ocean.
At the end of a thousand yugas, the omnipresent Lord, seated upon the serpent-couch and established in his own majesty, remains absorbed in yogic sleep.
Having placed the three worlds, including the entire universe of moving and stationary beings, within his belly,
he was praised by the great ṛṣis and the Siddhas residing in Janaloka.
From his navel arose a lotus, adorned with petals in the form of the directions,
joined with filaments in the form of the winds— the excellent abode of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
When Brahmā, the four-faced god of gods, was born,
at that time the two Dānavas Madhu and Kaiṭabha arose from the wax of his ears.
Those two of great strength and great heroism, intent on slaying Brahmā,
rose from the ocean of their bed and struck those two who were difficult to overcome.
I am not able to enumerate here other [incarnations] such as these;
for this present incarnation of the Unborn One in Mathurā is indeed that one.
Thus, that sattvic form takes an incarnation and is known as Pradyumna, established in the work of protection.
Whether established in the state of a deity, a human, or an animal womb,
she always assumes that very nature by the will of Vāsudeva.
When worshipped, O best of the twice-born, she grants all desired objects.
Thus has been related by me how Viṣṇu, though his purpose was already accomplished, assumed human form; now listen further to what follows.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O tigers among sages; I shall describe in brief the incarnation of Hari here, occurring through his desire to remove the earth's burden.
Whenever, O twice-born ones, there is an increase in unrighteousness and righteousness undergoes decline, then the Lord Janārdana [manifests].
He effects an incarnation here by dividing his own body into two parts,
for the sake of protecting the virtuous and for the establishment of Dharma.
For the sake of restraining the wicked and other enemies of the gods,
and for the sake of protecting living beings, he is born age after age.
O brahmins, it is said that in ancient times the Earth, oppressed by an excessive burden,
went to Mount Meru at the assembly of the inhabitants of heaven.
Then the Earth, speaking with piteous words out of distress, prostrated herself before all the gods including Brahmā and related everything that had occurred.
Dharaṇī said:
Agni is the preceptor of gold, and the Sun is another preceptor of cows;
likewise, for me and for all the worlds, Nārāyaṇa is the venerable preceptor.
Therefore, at present, these Daityas, led by Kālanemi,
having arrived in the world of mortals, oppress the subjects day and night.
That great asura Kaṃsa, the son of Ugrasena, who was slain by the powerful Viṣṇu, has been born [again] as Kālanemi.
Ariṣṭa, Dhenuka, Keśin, Pralamba, and likewise Naraka; the extremely fierce Asura Sunda, and Bāṇa, the son of Bali.
Likewise, there were others of great prowess who, having been born as evil-minded men in the palaces of kings, I do not venture to enumerate.
For there are many Akṣauhiṇīs of gods possessing divine forms,
and [the forces] of the haughty lords of the Daityas, who are endowed with great strength, are arrayed against me.
"O lords of the immortals, afflicted by the pain of that heavy burden, I am unable to sustain myself;
thus do I inform you."
"O highly fortunate ones, let that which shall relieve my burden be performed,
so that I, utterly overwhelmed, may not go to the netherworld."
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of the Earth, Brahmā was then impelled by all the gods and spoke for the purpose of removing the burden of the world.
Brahmā said:
"O dwellers of heaven, everything that the Earth has said is true;
I, Bhava, and you—all are essentially Nārāyaṇa."
But as for those powers (vibhūtis) belonging to him, it is among them alone that superiority and inferiority exist by way of mutual sublation and sublatedness.
Therefore, come, let us go to the excellent shore of the Ocean of Milk;
having propitiated Hari there, we shall indeed inform him of everything.
At all times, for the sake of the world, he who is the soul of all and consists of the world descends to earth with even a small portion of himself to establish the dharma.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the Grandfather (Brahmā) departed for that place together with the gods;
then, becoming composed in mind, he praised the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
Brahmā said:
Homage, homage be to you, O thousand-formed one; O thousand-armed one, with many faces and feet!
Homage, homage to you, the source of the world's activity, its destruction, and its maintenance, O immeasurable one! You are subtler than the subtlest and yet of vastest dimension.
O Blessed One, whose nature is supreme gravity even toward those most venerable, who are the primary essence of the intellect, senses, and speech— O Supreme Self, the root of all, be gracious!
O God, this earth, whose mountain fastenings are oppressed by the great asuras born of the earth,
approaches you for refuge, the ultimate resort of all worlds.
For the purpose of removing the burden, [he is] the shore beyond the shoreless;
we here, as well as this enemy of Vṛtra, these two Nāsatyas (the Aśvins), and likewise this Varuṇa— BrP_181.23d, 181.24a, 181.24b.
And these Rudras, Vasus, along with Sūrya,
as well as others headed by Samīraṇa and Agni— all the gods together, O Lord of the Gods, [must perform] their duty.
O Lord, whatever has been done by us through these [senses], we shall carry out all that; obeying your command, we shall remain ever under your authority, free from fault.
Vyāsa said:
O best of the twice-born, while being thus praised, the Blessed Lord Parameśvara plucked out two hairs from his own body, one white and one black.
And he said to the gods: "These two, my hairs, having descended upon the surface of the earth, will effect the removal of the burden and the suffering of the world."
And let all the gods descend to the surface of the earth with their own portions and wage war against the intoxicated great asuras born in former times.
Then, crushed by various weapons, all those Daityas will undoubtedly go to their destruction upon the surface of the earth.
O gods, this eighth embryo of Devakī, the wife of Vasudeva who is like a goddess, shall be my hair (Keśava).
Having descended there, Hari said, "He shall slay Kaṃsa on earth,
born from Kālanemi," and then vanished.
Then, having prostrated before that invisible Great Soul,
those gods went to the summit of Mount Meru and descended to the surface of the earth.
The venerable sage Nārada declared: "A eighth conception for Kaṃsa from Devakī shall take place upon the surface of the earth."
Having heard that from Nārada, Kaṃsa then became enraged and placed Devakī and Vasudeva under guard in his own house.
O twice-born ones, as he had previously declared to Kaṃsa regarding every child born,
Vasudeva likewise delivered each son to him.
The sons of Hiraṇyakaśipu were renowned as the Ṣaḍgarbhas;
at the command of Viṣṇu, sleep (Nidrā) sequentially placed them within the womb.
The Blessed Lord Hari spoke to that Yoganidrā Mahāmāyā Vaiṣṇavī, by whom the entire world is deluded through ignorance.
Viṣṇu said: "Go, O Nidrā, by my command, and lead the six embryos, one by one, from their dwelling in the depths of Pātāla into the womb of Devakī."
When those haters have been slain by Kaṃsa, then that sinless portion known as Śeṣa shall become the seventh [son] in her womb through a portion of a portion.
"Rohiṇī, the wife of Vasudeva, is staying at Gokula;
at the time of her delivery, you must bring the fetus into your own womb."
"The world will say that the seventh embryo of Devakī has fallen due to the siege and confinement caused by the fear of King Bhoja."
Then, because he draws forth the embryo from the womb, that hero, who resembles the peak of a white mountain, shall indeed receive the name Saṃkarṣaṇa in the world.
Then I shall come into being within the auspicious womb of Devakī;
you must enter the womb of Yaśodā without delay.
And during the rainy season, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhas, I shall be born at night;
and on the ninth day, you shall obtain my birth.
O blameless one, Vasudeva, his mind impelled by my power, will take me from Yaśodā’s bed and you from Devakī’s.
And Kaṃsa, O Goddess, having taken you, shall throw you onto the surface of a mountain rock; and you shall attain a station in the intermediate space.
Then, out of respect for me, Śakra will bow to you in a hundred ways and,
with his head bowed in prostration, accept you as his sister.
Then, having slain Śumbha, Niśumbha, and thousands of other Daityas,
you shall adorn the entire earth with many sacred sites.
You are prosperity, humility, fame, splendor, the earth, and fortitude; you are modesty, nourishment, and the dawn—whatever else exists, that too is you alone.
Those who address you as Āryā, Durgā, Vedagarbhā, Ambikā, Bhadrā, Bhadrakālī, Kṣemyā, and Kṣemaṃkarī; ||| BrP_181.50 |||
In the morning and in the afternoon, they shall offer praise with bodies bowed low;
for by my grace, every desire of theirs shall be fulfilled.
When you are worshipped with offerings of liquor and meat, as well as various kinds of food and edibles,
being thus propitiated, you shall grant all the desires of men without exception.
"By my grace, they shall all undoubtedly and without doubt be auspicious at all times; go, O Goddess, as has been told."
Vyāsa said:
Just as it was previously declared by the God of gods, that Mother of the World (Jagaddhātrī) performed the placement of the embryos within the six [beings] and the extraction of another.
When the seventh conception had reached the Rohiṇī asterism, Hari then indeed entered Devakī’s womb for the benefit of the three worlds.
On that very day, likewise, yogic sleep (yoganidrā) arose within the womb of Yaśodā,
exactly as had been declared by the Supreme Lord.
Then, O twice-born ones, the host of planets moved properly in the sky; and when Viṣṇu had descended to earth as a partial incarnation, the seasons also became auspicious.
No one was able to look upon Devakī because of her excessive splendor;
seeing her blazing so intensely, their minds were thrown into agitation.
The hosts of deities praised Devakī day and night— she who was unseen by men or women— as she bore Viṣṇu within her body.
The gods said:
You are Svāhā, you are Svadhā, you are knowledge, and you are nectar; you are indeed light itself.
For the sake of protecting all the worlds, you have descended upon the surface of the earth.
Be gracious, O Goddess; bring welfare to the entire world.
For the sake of our pleasure, support Īśāna, by whom the whole universe is sustained.
Vyāsa said:
Being thus praised by the gods,
she bore the god within her womb— the lotus-eyed one who is the cause of the protection of the worlds.
Then, for the sake of awakening the lotus of the entire world, the high-souled Acyuta-bhānu appeared to Devakī during the morning twilight.
At midnight, as Janārdana— the support of all— was being born,
the clouds rumbled softly and the gods released a rain of flowers.
Beholding him who had appeared, possessing four arms and the luster of a full-blown blue lotus petal,
with the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, Ānakadundubhi offered praise.
And having praised him with pleasing words, O best of the twice-born, the high-minded one then made his request, being afraid of Kaṃsa.
Vasudeva said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, O wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace, you are known.
O God, withdraw this divine form by your grace."
"O Lord, this very day Kaṃsa inflicts torment upon me,
having learned that you have descended into this temple of mine."
Devakī said:
He who is of infinite form and whose form is the entire universe,
who even within the womb sustains the worlds with his body.
May this God of gods be gracious,
he who has manifested the form of a child through his own māyā; O Soul of All, withdraw this four-armed form.
O destroyer of the sons of Diti, let this Kaṃsa not discover your descent.
The Blessed Lord said:
O Goddess, that which was previously praised by you while desiring a son has today become fruitful for you, since I have been born from your womb.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, O best of sages, the Blessed One became silent;
Vasudeva also, taking him with him, went outside during the night.
And there, the guards and the gatekeepers of Mathurā were deluded by yogic sleep as Ānakadundubhi was departing.
And as the clouds rained down that fierce water at night, Śeṣa went forth, covering Ānakadundubhi with his hoods.
Carrying Viṣṇu, Vasudeva went along the Yamunā, which was exceedingly deep, agitated by hundreds of various whirlpools, and flowing only knee-deep.
Taking Kaṃsa’s hand, he saw Nanda and the other elderly cowherds who had arrived right there on the bank of the Yamunā.
At that time, O sages, Yaśodā too was deluded by yogic sleep; while the people were thus bewildered, she gave birth to that very girl.
Vasudeva, of immeasurable splendor, having placed the boy down and taken up the girl,
quickly returned to Yaśodā’s bedchamber.
And having awakened, Yaśodā beheld her newborn son,
dark as the petal of a blue lotus, and thereupon she attained exceeding joy.
Vasudeva, too, having taken the girl to his own residence,
placed her on Devakī’s bed and remained there as before.
Then, O twice-born ones, hearing the cry of the infant, the guards rose up suddenly and informed Kaṃsa of Devakī’s delivery.
Kaṃsa quickly approached and seized the girl;
though he was restrained by Devakī with a choked voice crying, "Release her! Release her! [he did not let her go].
And she hurled it onto the surface of a rock; yet, once thrown, it remained suspended in the sky,
assumed a massive form with eight great arms bearing weapons,
and laughed loudly while speaking thus to the enraged Kaṃsa.
Yogamāyā said:
"O Kaṃsa, what is the use of me being cast aside? He who was born to kill you was already your death long ago, for he was the very self of all the gods."
Therefore, having reflected upon this, let that which is beneficial for yourself be done quickly.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the goddess— adorned with divine garlands, perfumes, and ornaments—
departed through the sky while being praised by the Siddhas, even as the King of the Bhojas looked on.
Vyāsa said: Then Kaṃsa, with an agitated mind, summoned all the great Asuras— the preeminent among the demons headed by Pralamba and Keśin— and spoke to them.
Kaṃsa said:
"O Pralamba of mighty arms, O Keśin, Dhenuka, Pūtanā,
Ariṣṭa, and the others as well— let my words be heard!"
"Indeed, an effort was made by the wicked immortals to kill me;
yet I do not take any account of these heroes who have been scorched by my prowess."
"O best of Daityas, it is a marvel that this was spoken by a girl;
O heroes, laughter arises within me even though they are so intent on their efforts. (BrP 183.4)
Nevertheless, O lords of the Daityas, I must indeed strive even more to bring about the ruin of those wicked and evil-minded ones.
"Even though death has arisen for me, he is the lord of the past, the future, and the present"—
this is what the young girl born from the womb of Devakī said.
Therefore, the greatest effort must be exerted against fools on this earth;
wherever a fool possesses excessive power, he must be slain with diligent care.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus commanded the Asuras, Kaṃsa then entered his own palace and spoke to Vasudeva and Devakī without opposition.
Kaṃsa said:
"These children of yours have been killed by me in vain;
some other boy alone has arisen for my destruction."
Therefore, enough with this lamentation; for that which is destined to be yours will surely come to pass. Who indeed is not slain at the end of their lifespan, even if they are but children?
Vyāsa said: O best of the twice-born,
having thus consoled Kaṃsa, released him, and gratified him,
he entered his own inner apartments once again.
Vyāsa said:
Vasudeva, having been released, went to Nanda’s cart and saw Nanda rejoicing, thinking, "A son has indeed been born to me!"
Vasudeva also said to him respectfully, "By good fortune! By good fortune!
Even in old age, this son has now been born to you."
"For the entire annual tribute has already been paid by you to the king;
since you have come for that purpose, O high-souled one, you should not remain here."
"The purpose for which you have come has been accomplished; why do you remain?
O Nanda, you should go quickly back to your own Gokula."
My own young son, who was born of Rohiṇī,
must also be protected by you, just like this, your own biological son.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus, the mighty cowherds, led by Nandagopa, departed after paying the tax and loading their goods onto carts.
While they were dwelling in Gokula, Pūtanā, the slayer of children,
took the sleeping Kṛṣṇa at night and offered him her breast.
To whichever child Pūtanā offers her breast at night,
that child’s body is destroyed in an instant.
Filled with rage, Kṛṣṇa seized her breast, which was firmly pressed by his hands, and drank from it along with her very life-breath.
With her great screams released and the bonds of her sinews severed,
the most terrifying Pūtanā fell to the ground while dying.
Awakened by the terror of hearing that roar,
the inhabitants of Vraja saw Kṛṣṇa in Pūtanā’s lap and her herself cast down.
Then, O twice-born ones, Yaśodā, filled with terror, took Kṛṣṇa and removed the infant's affliction by means of brandishing a cow’s tail and other such rites.
Taking cow dung, Nanda the cowherd also placed it upon Kṛṣṇa’s head, uttering this while performing the protective rite: ||| BrP_184.13 |||
Nandagopa said: May Hari, the source of all beings without exception, protect you—
he from whose navel-born lotus the universe arose.
May that Lord Keśava, who assumed the form of a boar and by whom the earth was supported— held up by the tip of his tusk— protect you.
May Viṣṇu protect your secret parts and belly, and Janārdana protect your shanks and feet;
may Vāmana, who became so in an instant, always protect you.
May Govinda, whose weapons flash across the three worlds as he strides his three steps, protect your head; may Keśava guard your throat.
May the imperishable Nārāyaṇa, whose sovereignty is unimpeded, protect your face, arms, forearms, mind, and all your senses.
May Vaikuṇṭha protect you in the cardinal directions, Madhusūdana in the intermediate directions,
Hṛṣīkeśa in the sky, and Mahīdhara protect you upon the earth.
Vyāsa said:
Thus, having had the rite for averting evil performed by the cowherd Nanda,
the infant was laid beneath the wagon on the surface of a small cradle.
And those cowherds, seeing the massive corpse of the dead Pūtanā,
were then struck with supreme terror and amazement.
Once, while lying beneath a cart, Madhusūdana,
desiring the breast, thrust his feet upward and wept.
By the blow of his foot, the cart was overturned;
with its jars and vessels shattered, it indeed fell upside down.
Then, O twice-born ones, all the cowherds and cowherdesses, crying out in lamentation,
arrived there upon learning that the boy was lying on his back.
"By whom was the cart overturned? the cowherds asked. Thereupon, the boys said, "It was overturned by this boy. (BrP 184.25)
"While we were crying, we saw a cart overturned by the trampling of a footstep; this was certainly not the work of anyone else."
Then once again the cowherds were filled with extreme wonder in their hearts;
Nanda the cowherd also, utterly amazed, took up the child.
Yaśodā, overcome with wonder, worshipped the cart and the shards of the broken pot with curds, flowers, fruits, and unbroken grains of rice.
And Garga, urged by Vasudeva, remained hidden there in Gokula and performed the sacraments for the two of them among the cowherds.
The highly intelligent Garga, the best among the wise, gave them names, calling the elder Rāma and the other Kṛṣṇa.
O brahmins, in a very short time, both of those mighty ones became such that their knees and hands were calloused.
With their limbs smeared with cow-dung and ashes, wandering here and there,
neither Yaśodā nor Rohiṇī was able to restrain them.
Playing in the midst of the cow-pen and having entered the calf-pen again,
they were intent on pulling the tails of the calves born that very day.
When Yaśodā was unable to restrain those two boys, who were both moving about in the same place, playing with extreme restlessness; ||| BrP_184.34 |||
Then, having bound him with a rope, she tied Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless, to the middle of a mortar; and being indignant, she spoke this to him.
Yaśodā said:
"If you are capable, then go, O you of most fickle conduct!"
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, that housewife performed her own duties;
meanwhile, while she was busy, he began dragging the mortar.
The lotus-eyed one went between the twin *arjuna* trees,
dragging the mortar sideways between the two trees.
By him those two twin *arjuna* trees, with their lofty branches broken, were shattered;
then, terrified by the sound of the cracking, [he fled].
The people of Vraja arrived and beheld the two great trees,
their trunks broken and their branches shattered, fallen upon the surface of the earth.
And he saw a boy with few teeth in his mouth, smiling and laughing,
standing between the two of them and bound tightly by a rope around his belly.
And from that binding with ropes, he attained the name Dāmodara;
then all the elder cowherds, led by Nandagopa, [honored him].
Distressed and terrified by these great portents, they consulted one another:
"We must not remain here; let us go to another great forest."
For many portents are seen here that are causes of destruction:
the death of Pūtanā and the overturning of the cart.
Just as the falling of two trees occurs without any fault such as wind, so too shall it be with Vṛndāvana; therefore, let us go from this place without delay.
"Until the fault of this great terrestrial portent overcomes Vraja"—
thinking thus, all those inhabitants of Vraja set their minds on departing.
They said, "Let each of you go quickly to your own family; do not delay.
Then, in an instant, they departed with wagons and herds of cattle.
Then, as the inhabitants of Vraja were driving the herds of calves and cowherdesses back in groups,
that [dust] was shaken off from every limb in a mere instant.
O twice-born ones, the cow-pen area of Vṛndāvana became crowded with crows and female crows by the Blessed Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless.
O best of the twice-born, he meditated with a pure mind, desiring the increase of his cattle; consequently, even during that most harsh season of the year, O brahmins.
And like the rainy season, fresh grass appeared everywhere;
then that entire settlement of cowherds took up residence in Vṛndāvana.
Then Rāma and Dāmodara became like two young calves, their forms arranged in the shape of a half-moon at the edge of the wagon-pasture.
Remaining there in that cow-pen, the two of them engaged in childish play,
wearing crests made of peacock feathers and ornaments of wild flowers.
Making sounds with flutes fashioned from cowherd-reeds and leaf-instruments,
the two boys, wearing side-locks of hair, were like the twin fires of Kumāra.
Laughing and taking delight, they wandered through that great forest;
in some places laughing with one another, and likewise playing with others.
Tending the calves together with the sons of the cowherds, they wandered about;
as time passed, they both became seven years of age.
While the two cowherd boys were protecting the entire world in the great forest retreat,
the rainy season then arrived, with the sky completely shrouded by masses of clouds.
The earth, rich with newly sprouted flowers and covered with *śakragopa* insects, became as if one with the quarters of the sky through the streams of rain.
Just as a garment of emerald might be adorned with rubies,
so too did the waters of the rivers flowing everywhere along their downward paths carry away [the ornaments].
Having gained control over the minds of the ill-behaved as if they were new-found wealth,
and having returned at will to Vraja at an unconventional hour, the two mighty ones,
accompanied by the cowherds of equal status, sported like two immortals.
Vyāsa said:
Once, Kṛṣṇa went to Vṛndāvana without Rāma;
surrounded by cowherds and radiant with garlands of wild flowers, he wandered about.
Then he went to the Kālindī, which was graced by rolling waves and seemed to laugh on all sides with masses of foam clinging to its banks.
And there he beheld the exceedingly terrifying lake of the serpent Kālīya, which was most fearsome and defiled by sparks of poisonous fire.
Its great trees on the banks were scorched by the spreading fire of poison;
its birds were burnt by the touch of the spray of water driven by the wind.
Beholding him, who was exceedingly fierce and like another mouth of Death,
the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana reflected.
In this place dwells that evil-minded Kālīya, whose weapon is poison;
he who was defeated by me fled to the ocean, having abandoned his wickedness.
Thus, this entire Yamunā, which flows to the ocean, has been defiled;
it is not utilized by men or even by herds of cattle afflicted by thirst.
Therefore, I must carry out the subjugation of this king of serpents,
so that the inhabitants of Vraja, who are constantly terrified, may live in peace.
For this purpose I have taken incarnation in this world of men:
that these evil-minded ones, who stand upon the wrong path, should be disciplined.
Therefore, having climbed this large-branched kadamba tree standing not far away, I shall leap into this lake that destroys life.
Vyāsa said:
Having reflected thus and having tightly girded his loins,
he then plunged with speed into that lake belonging to the king of serpents.
As it fell there, that great lake was agitated by it,
and it drenched those trees growing at an exceedingly great distance.
Sprinkled by the heated water from the blazing flames of the venom of those wicked serpents,
the trees immediately burst into flame, their fire spreading through the quarters of the sky.
Then Kṛṣṇa slapped the serpent pool with his arms;
and upon hearing that sound, the king of the serpents arrived.
With eyes copper-red from anger, he was surrounded by other highly venomous, wind-eating serpents with hoods filled with the flames of poison, all of which were crimson in hue.
And hundreds of Naga wives, adorned with captivating necklaces,
their beauty enhanced by earrings swaying as their trembling bodies moved.
Then Kṛṣṇa was encircled by serpents with their coils as bonds;
they bit Kṛṣṇa as well, with mouths filled with the flames of poison.
Seeing him fallen there, crushed by the coils of the serpent,
Gopā returned to Vraja and wailed, overwhelmed with grief.
The cowherds said:
"Kṛṣṇa has gone there, submerged in delusion within the lake of Kāliya;
he is being devoured by the king of serpents, so come quickly, do not delay!"
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words, which were like the fall of a thunderbolt,
the cowherds and the cowherd women, led by Yaśodā, then went quickly to the lake.
"Alas, alas! Where is he? crying thus, the people of the cowherds, overcome with extreme agitation, ran along with Yaśodā, stumbling as they went.
Nandagopa, the cowherds, and Rāma of wondrous prowess,
longing for a sight of Kṛṣṇa, quickly went to the Yamunā.
And there they also beheld Kṛṣṇa, who had fallen under the power of the king of serpents, rendered motionless and encircled by the serpent’s coils.
O best of sages, Nandagopa became motionless as he gazed intently at his son’s face, and the highly fortunate Yaśodā likewise remained so.
But other cowherd women, weeping and overwhelmed by grief,
beheld him and spoke with affection to Keśava, their voices faltering with fear and distress.
"Let us all enter this great lake together with Yaśodā; it is not appropriate for us to go to Vraja, O King of Nagas."
"What is a day without the sun? What is night without the moon? What are cows without milk? What is Vraja without Kṛṣṇa?
Deprived of this Kṛṣṇa, we shall not leave Gokula."
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of the cowherd women, the mighty son of Rohiṇī,
looking at the distressed cowherds with fixed eyes, spoke.
And he saw Nanda, who was exceedingly dejected with his gaze fixed upon his son’s face,
and Yaśodā, who was overwhelmed by fainting due to her consciousness of Kṛṣṇa’s greatness.
Balarāma said:
O Lord of the gods of gods, why is this human state manifested by you? Do you not know that very Self, who are yourself, as being something else?
You are the navel of this world and the refuge of the gods;
you are the creator, the destroyer, and the protector of the three worlds, consisting of the triple Veda.
O Kṛṣṇa, for those of us who have descended here, the cowherds alone are our kinsmen, as are the cowherd women;
why do you neglect your kin as they languish?
Human nature has been displayed, and childish behavior has been shown;
therefore, O Kṛṣṇa, let this evil-souled one whose weapons are his fangs be subdued.
Vyāsa said:
Thus reminded, Kṛṣṇa, with his lips parted by a smile,
struck his body and released it from the bondage of its coils.
Bending down the middle hood with both hands and mounting it, he of great prowess danced while keeping his head bowed.
Wounds appeared on his hood from Kṛṣṇa’s trampling of his feet; wherever he raised his head, Kṛṣṇa’s head bowed down there.
The serpent fell into a swoon from the confusion caused by Kṛṣṇa’s blows;
from the impact of the falling staff, he vomited much blood.
Beholding him with his head and neck bent back and blood flowing from his mouth,
his wives sought refuge with Madhusūdana.
The wives of the Nāgas said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, you are known; you are the Lord of all, the unsurpassed.
You are that supreme, inconceivable light of which the Supreme Lord is a portion."
Even the gods are not capable of praising that Lord who has no other source of birth;
how then shall a woman describe his true nature?
How shall we praise him, of whom the entire universe— composed of earth, sky, water, fire, and air— is but a minute fraction of a fraction?
Therefore, O Lord of the World, show favor to this one who is despondent;
this elephant is giving up his life—grant him the boon requested by his master.
Vyāsa said:
When they had spoken thus and comforted him, the serpent, though his body was exhausted, spoke these words slowly and softly: "Be gracious, O God of gods!"
Kālīya said:
O Lord, Your supreme sovereignty possesses the eightfold qualities and is innate; for one such as You, from whom all excellence has been surpassed, what indeed can I possibly praise?
You are the beyond; you are the first of that which is beyond; you are the supreme, whose very nature is that which is supreme;
what indeed shall I praise of You, who are higher than the highest?
"Just as I was created by you as a lord in terms of birth, form,
and inherent nature, so too has this action been performed by me."
O God of gods, if I were to act otherwise,
then the infliction of punishment upon me by you would be just, according to your own word.
Nevertheless, this excellent punishment which the Lord of the World has inflicted upon me has been endured;
let there be no other boon for me than this from you.
My vigor is destroyed, my poison is neutralized; I have been subdued by you, O Acyuta.
Grant me my life for a moment; give your command, what shall I do?
The Blessed One said: "O serpent, you must never remain here in the waters of the Yamunā;
together with your servants and retinue, go to the waters of the ocean."
And seeing my footprints upon your head in the ocean, O serpent,
Garuḍa, the enemy of the pannagas, will not strike you.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Hari released the king of serpents;
and he too, having bowed down to Kṛṣṇa, departed for the ocean.
While all living beings were looking on, together with his servants, children, and kinsmen,
and accompanied by all his wives, he abandoned his own lake.
Having embraced the serpent that had departed, as if it had returned from the dead,
the cowherds drenched Govinda on the head with tears from their eyes.
Seeing the river of auspicious waters, other cowherds, their minds filled with wonder, joyfully praised Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are untiring.
Then, being sung of by the cowherd girls for his charming deeds and graceful movements,
and being praised by the cowherds, Kṛṣṇa returned to Vraja.
Vyāsa said:
While again tending the cows together, Rāma and Keśava,
wandering there in the forest, went to a beautiful palm grove.
And that palm grove was constantly inhabited by a Dānava named Dhenuka,
who had the form of a donkey and whose diet consisted of the flesh of men and cattle.
There, having seen a delightful palm grove endowed with an abundance of fruit, the cowherds were filled with longing and spoke these words regarding the gathering of the fruit.
The cowherds said: "O Rāma, O Kṛṣṇa, since this region of the earth is always protected by Dhenuka alone, these [cows] have indeed been abandoned."
"Behold the fruits of the palmyra trees, indeed endowed with a delightful fragrance;
we desire these—if it pleases you, let them be felled."
Having heard these words of the cowherd boys, Saṃkarṣaṇa and Kṛṣṇa indeed caused the palm fruits to fall upon the ground.
Then, hearing the sound of the falling palm fruits,
that evil-minded king of the asuras, the donkey of the Daityas, arrived there in a rage.
Then that powerful one struck him in the chest with both his hind legs, and he was seized by those two as well as by him.
Having seized him and whirled him around in the air until he was lifeless,
he hurled him with great force right there upon the king of grasses (the Śāla tree).
Then, leaping from the tops of the palmyra trees, Khara caused many fruits to fall upon the earth,
just as a great wind causes clouds to fall.
Kṛṣṇa and Balabhadra also effortlessly cast down other Daityas who had arrived there disguised as donkeys, hurling them onto the tops of palm trees.
At that moment, O sages, the earth was adorned with ripe palm fruits and the carcasses of the donkey-like Daityas, and it shone exceedingly.
Then, O twice-born ones, the cows wandered happily and without hindrance in that palm grove,
grazing on fresh grass where they had previously fed.
Vyāsa said:
When that Daitya in the form of a donkey had been struck down along with his younger brother,
the beautiful Tālavana forest shone forth for all the cowherds and cowherd girls.
Then those two high-souled sons of Vasudeva, filled with joy,
shone like two bulls with newly sprouted horns.
Driving the cows to a distance and calling them by their names,
those two, adorned with forest garlands, had ropes for their tasks slung over their shoulders.
Then, adorned with gold and powdered collyrium,
their garments shone like the bow of Indra, appearing like white and black clouds.
Having descended to the earth as the lords of all the lords of the world, they sported with one another in games well-known among people.
Delighting in human pleasures and honoring their human state,
they roamed the forest with amusements suited to their kind and qualities.
Then those two of great strength engaged in exercise there by means of swings, wrestling matches, and likewise with projectiles and stones.
While the two were thus enjoying themselves, an Asura named Pralamba, desiring to seize them and disguised in the dress of a cowherd, arrived there.
Assuming a human form, that supreme Dānava Pralamba, though not a human, plunged fearlessly into their midst.
Seeking a vulnerability between the two of them, he considered himself exceedingly swift;
then he set his mind upon killing Kṛṣṇa and the son of Rohiṇī.
Then, they engaged in a children's game called "Playing with Hari," and they all played together, leaping up two by two at once.
Govinda leaped together with Śrīdāman, Balarāma likewise with Pralamba,
and the other cowherds leaped together with yet other cowherds.
Then Kṛṣṇa, the son of Rohiṇī, defeated Śrīdāman and Pralamba;
the other cowherds who sided with Kṛṣṇa were victorious, while the others were defeated.
Driving one another along, they all reached the trunk of the Bhāṇḍīra tree and then turned back— whosoever among them had been defeated there.
But the Dānava, quickly lifting Saṃkarṣaṇa upon his shoulder,
did not remain still but moved away like a cloud carrying the moon.
Unable to carry him, that best of Dānavas grew to a truly massive body out of fury, like a rain-cloud in the monsoon season.
But Saṃkarṣaṇa, seeing him with a form like a scorched mountain,
adorned with hanging garlands and necklaces, and with a head crowned by a magnificent diadem, [was struck with wonder].
Fierce, with eyes like the wheels of a cart, and making the earth tremble with his tread, he was then carried away and spoke these words to Kṛṣṇa: BrP_187.18 //
Balarāma said:
"Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! Look, he is being carried away by some Daitya in the guise of a cowherd, possessing a form as lofty as a mountain!"
"O Slayer of Madhu, tell me what must be done by me here at this moment;
for this evil-minded one is departing with extreme haste."
Vyāsa said:
To that Rāma, Govinda— the Great Soul who knew the measure of the strength and heroism of Rohiṇī’s son— spoke with his lips parted by a smile.
Kṛṣṇa said: Why is this human state being so clearly assumed by you, O Soul of All, whose nature is more secret than the secret of all secrets?
Remember me, O Lord of the entire world, the cause, the first-born of causes;
remember the one Self who exists both now and when the world has become a single ocean.
O Soul of the Universe, you and I are indeed one and the same cause;
for the sake of this world, we are established in distinct forms.
Therefore, O immeasurable-souled one, remember your true self and slay the Dānava;
by thus assuming this human form, let the welfare of your kinsmen be accomplished.
Vyāsa said:
O brahmins, having been thus reminded by the high-souled Kṛṣṇa,
the powerful Balarāma laughed and began to crush Pralamba.
With eyes bloodshot with rage, he struck him on the head with his fist;
by that blow, his two eyes were forced out.
With his brain forced out and vomiting blood from his mouth,
that best of Daityas fell upon the surface of the earth and died.
Seeing Pralamba slain by Bala of wondrous deeds, the cowherds were delighted; they praised him and exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! (BrP 187.29).
While being praised by the cowherds after the demon Pralamba had been struck down, Rāma,
together with Kṛṣṇa, returned once more to Gokula.
Vyāsa said:
While Rāma and Keśava were thus sporting in Vraja,
the rainy season passed away and autumn arrived, with its blooming lotuses.
When the time had arrived, under the stars of the stainless sky,
he saw the inhabitants of Vraja engaged in the commencement of the festival for the Moon.
Seeing those cowherds eager and longing for the festival, the high-minded Kṛṣṇa spoke these words out of curiosity to the elders.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"What is this so-called Śakramaha festival, because of which joy has come upon you?
And Nanda the cowherd spoke to him as he asked with great respect.
Nanda said:
"The king of the gods, Śatakratu, is the lord of the clouds and the waters;
impelled by him, the clouds rain down the essence consisting of water."
Sustaining ourselves by consuming the crops produced by that rain, we and other embodied beings likewise satisfy the deities.
These cows are full of milk and accompanied by their calves, living in peace;
nourished by the crops raised by him, they indeed become well-fed and contented.
In that place, no land is seen to be uncultivated or in debt, nor is any person seen afflicted by hunger;
there, only rain-bearing clouds are seen.
The cloud, the giver of water, draws this earthly moisture from the sun by means of its rays;
Parjanya rains down upon the earth for the welfare of the entire world.
Therefore, during the rainy season, all kings, filled with joy,
as well as we and other embodied beings, honor Śakra, the lord of the gods, with great ceremony.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of Nanda the cowherd regarding the worship of Śakra,
Dāmodara then spoke for the purpose of inciting the anger of the Lord of the Thirty-three.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"We are not cultivators of the soil, nor do we live by trade;
O dear one, since we are forest-dwellers, the cows are our deity."
Logic, the three Vedas, economics, and likewise the science of government—this is the fourfold group of sciences; now hear from me concerning economics among them.
Agriculture, trade, and likewise thirdly, cattle-rearing—
these indeed, O highly fortunate one, are the sciences that constitute the threefold basis of the livelihood of Vārttā.

Agriculture is the livelihood of farmers, while trade is that of those who live by commerce; for us, cattle are the supreme livelihood—this is the science of economics (vārttā) divided into these three branches.
Whichever knowledge a person is endowed with, that alone is his great deity;
it alone is to be honored and worshipped, and it alone is his benefactor.
O dear one, that man who, while enjoying the fruit of one woman, honors another both in this world and after death, does not obtain anything auspicious.
Let the celebrated boundaries be honored, as well as the forest at the edge of those boundaries;
let all the mountains at the edge of the forests be honored, for they are our ultimate refuge.
"Therefore, let this mountain-sacrifice and the cow-sacrifice be commenced;
what need have we for Mahendra? Cows and mountains are our deities."
The Brahmins are devoted to sacrifices of mantras, the farmers to sacrifices of the plow,
and we, who dwell in mountains and forests, are habituated to sacrifices of the mountain-cows.
Therefore, let Mount Govardhana be honored and worshipped by you with various offerings, having slaughtered a pure animal according to the prescribed rite.
Let the entire collection of sounds be grasped; let there be no hesitation.
Let the Brahmins and others who desire it be fed by that very means.
When that [fire] has been honored after the oblation is performed and the twice-born have been fed,
let herds of cows, adorned with wreaths made of autumn flowers, attend upon it.
O cowherds, if this, which is my opinion, is carried out with affection,
then joy will have been bestowed upon the cows, the mountain, and likewise upon me.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, O brahmins, Nanda and the other inhabitants of Vraja, their faces blossoming with joy, then exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!"*BrP_187.55*
"Your thought is excellent, my child, that which has been spoken by you;
I shall do all of that. Let the mountain sacrifice be commenced."
And so, having performed the mountain sacrifice (giriyajña), those inhabitants of Vraja then offered a mountain-oblation consisting of curd, milk-rice, meat, and other foods.
They fed the twice-born by the hundreds and thousands;
then the cows, having been honored, performed a circumambulation of that mountain.
And bulls bellowed like water-laden clouds;
on the mountain peak, Govinda stood in embodied form, thinking, "I am the mountain."
O twice-born ones, Kṛṣṇa, together with the cowherds, ate various kinds of food brought by the best of the cowherds upon the mountain peak, while remaining in that very same form.
Having ascended, he worshipped his own second form;
