when that [form] had vanished, the cowherds, having obtained boons from him,
performed a mountain festival and returned once more to their own cow-pen.
Vyāsa said:
When his pride was humbled, Śakra, filled with intense anger,
then spoke to the host of clouds known as Saṃvartaka.
Indra said:
"O clouds, having heard these words of mine as I speak them, let this be carried out immediately and without hesitation, following my command at once."
The foolish Nandagopa, supported by other cowherds and puffed up by the strength derived from Kṛṣṇa’s protection, brought about the great destruction of the Bhaṅgas.
"Let those cows, whose livelihood is supreme among them and which are the cause of my state as a cowherd, be afflicted by a downpour of rain at my command."
I too, having mounted a lofty elephant resembling a mountain peak,
shall provide you assistance by means of the gathering of the winds.
Vyāsa said:
Thus commanded by the lord of the gods,
O twice-born ones, those clouds released a most terrifying wind and rain for the destruction of the cows.
Then, O twice-born ones, in an instant the earth, the quarters, and even the sky became one through the filling [of space] by the great torrent of falling rain.
But the cows, shaken by that swift, falling wind of the rain,
all lost their lives with their faces and necks turned sideways.
O best of the twice-born, others stood there having seized their calves with their chests,
while still other cows were deprived of their calves by the flood of water.
And the calves, with dejected faces and necks trembling in the wind, seemed to cry out to Kṛṣṇa in their distress with faint voices, "Save us! Save us!"
Then, seeing that entire Gokula, crowded with cows, cowherd women, and cowherds,
to be in extreme distress, Hari reflected upon how to protect it.
This was accomplished by Mahendra, who is opposed to the great destruction;
now, this entire cow-pen must be protected by me.
Having uprooted this mountain with its broad rocky surface by my own prowess,
I shall hold it over the cow-pen like a large umbrella.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus resolved his mind, Kṛṣṇa uprooted Mount Govardhana with a single hand and held it up effortlessly as if in play.
Having uprooted the mountain, the Lord of the World said to the cowherds: "Enter here together; a protection against the rain has been prepared."
"Stay here in these windless places as is appropriate;
having entered, you who are fearless need not fear the falling of the mountain."
Having been addressed thus by him, those cowherds entered together with their herds of cattle, while the cowherd women,
oppressed by the rain, entered with their goods loaded upon carts.
Kṛṣṇa likewise held that mountain perfectly motionless,
while he was gazed upon by the inhabitants of Vraja with eyes wide with joy and wonder.
While his deeds were being extolled by the joyful cowherds and cowherdesses, whose eyes were wide with affection, Kṛṣṇa supported the mountain.
For seven nights, great clouds rained down upon Nanda’s cowherd settlement,
sent by Indra, who intended to bring about the destruction of the cowherds.
Then, once the great mountain had been held up and Gokula had been rescued,
the slayer of Bala, having made a false vow, restrained those clouds.
When the sky was cloudless and the counsel of Śakra had proved futile, Devendra,
having departed from Gokula, returned joyfully to his own abode.
Then Kṛṣṇa also released the great mountain Govardhana back to its own place,
as he was watched by those inhabitants of Vraja with faces full of wonder.
Vyāsa said:
Once Mount Govardhana had been held up and Gokula had been protected, Indra,
the subduer of Pāka, desired a vision of Kṛṣṇa.
Having mounted the great elephant Airāvata, the conqueror of enemies,
the lord of the thirty gods beheld Kṛṣṇa on Mount Govardhana.
He saw the one of great heroism tending the cows while assuming the form of a cowherd,
the protector of the entire world, surrounded by cowherd boys.
And the twice-born ones beheld Garuḍa, the bull among birds, who had gone high into the sky and remained invisible,
casting a shadow over the head of Hari with his two wings.
Having descended from the king of serpents, Śakra, his eyes wide with joy, spoke these words with a smile to Madhusūdana in a secluded spot.
Indra said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, listen to this for which purpose I have come into your presence, O mighty-armed one; this must not be considered by you otherwise."
O Supreme Lord, you alone— the support of all— have descended to the surface of the earth for the sake of relieving the burden of the world.
By me, who am opposed to great destruction, the great clouds that destroy Gokula were commanded; by them, this slaughter was performed.
"O Hero, by uprooting the great mountain, you have rescued the cattle from their torment;
therefore, I am gratified by this most wonderful deed of yours."
O Kṛṣṇa, I believe the purpose of the gods has been accomplished today,
since this best of mountains was lifted up by you with a single hand.
O Kṛṣṇa, urged by the cows, I have come here into your presence;
I have been exceedingly protected by you who were rescued for the sake of you yourself.
Impelled by the words of the cows, I shall consecrate you as Kṛṣṇa;
as the Indra of the cows in the state of Upendra, you shall become Govinda.
Then, taking a bell from Airāvata, his mount,
he performed the consecration with it, which was filled with pure water.
While the consecration was being performed, at that very moment, the cows made the earth instantly moist with the milk flowing from their udders for Kṛṣṇa.
Having consecrated Janārdana at the word of the cows, the Lord of Devas,
the husband of Śacī, spoke again to Kṛṣṇa with affection and humility.
Indra said:
"This has been done for the sake of the cows at my word; now hear from me something else as well, O illustrious one, which I speak with the desire to remove the earth's burden."
O upholder of the earth, that tiger among men named Arjuna, who is a portion of myself, has descended upon the earth; he must always be protected by you.
O Madhusūdana, that hero will become your friend in the removal of the burden; he must be protected by you as you would yourself.
The Blessed One said:
"I know that Pārtha, born in the lineage of Bhārata, is from a portion of you;
I shall protect him for as long as I remain upon the earth."
O Śakra, subduer of enemies, as long as I remain upon the surface of the earth,
no one, O Lord of the Gods, shall defeat Arjuna in battle.
The mighty-armed Daitya named Kaṃsa, as well as another, Ariṣṭa;
Keśin, Kuvalayāpīḍa, Naraka, and others besides—BrP_188.44.
O Lord of the Gods, when those [asuras] are slain, there will be a great battle;
know, O Thousand-eyed One, that in that [battle] the removal of the burden shall be accomplished.
Therefore, go; you ought not to feel distress on account of your son.
No enemy of Arjuna shall prevail in my presence.
But for the sake of Arjuna, once the Bhārata war has ended, I shall deliver all those wounded men, led by Yudhiṣṭhira, to Kuntī.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus, the king of the gods embraced Janārdana and,
mounting the elephant Airāvata, departed once again for heaven.
Kṛṣṇa also, accompanied by the cows and the cowherds,
returned once more to Vraja by the path purified by the gaze of the gopīs.
Vyāsa said:
When Śakra had departed, the cowherds spoke with affection to Kṛṣṇa, the performer of effortless deeds,
seeing that he had held up Mount Govardhana.
The cowherds said:
"O highly fortunate one, we and the cows have been saved by you from great danger through your deed of supporting the mountain."
"This incomparable childhood play and this loathsome state of being a cowherd, as well as your divine deeds—what is this, O Father? Please tell me."
Kāliya was subdued in the water, Pralamba was struck down, and this Govardhana was held up; our minds are filled with apprehension.
"Truly, truly, O you of immeasurable prowess, we take refuge at the feet of Hari,
since, having beheld your valor, we no longer consider you a mere man."
Are you a god, a dānava, a yakṣa, or even a gandharva?
What is the use of our deliberation? You are a kinsman; homage be to you!
O Keśava, there is joy for Vraja, including its women and children, because of this deed of yours, which is impossible even for all the thirty gods combined.
O Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable soul, our childhood, our excessive vigor, and our birth among these people— when reflected upon, cause me anxiety.
Vyāsa said:
Having remained silent for a moment, feeling a slight touch of affectionate anger at being addressed in this way by those cowherds, O best of the twice-born, Kṛṣṇa spoke.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O cowherds, if you feel no shame on account of my relationship with you, then I am indeed praiseworthy; what need have you for further deliberation?
O kinsmen, if you have affection for me, and if I am worthy of your praise, then let a guest-offering be made to me that is befitting our relationship.
"I am neither a god, nor a gandharva, nor a yakṣa, nor a dānava;
I have been born as your kinsman, so there is no need to think otherwise than this."
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of Hari, the illustrious cowherds then departed for Balarāma while observing a vow of silence, even though he was angry out of affection.
Kṛṣṇa, however, beheld the stainless sky, the moonlight of the autumnal moon,
and likewise the blossoming night-lily that perfumed the intermediate quarters.
Beholding the forest grove, so enchanting with its rows of humming bees, he set his mind upon amorous pleasure together with the cowherd girls.
There, having undertaken his vow, that Kamalapāda sang very sweetly along with Rāma— a song most pleasing to women— while chanting the Name.
Then, hearing the delightful sound of singing, the cowherd women abandoned their dwellings and came in haste to where Madhusūdana was staying.
A certain cowherd girl, following after him, sang very softly;
and another, having fixed her attention, remembered him alone in her mind.
One girl, having cried out "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! repeatedly, was overcome with shame;
yet another, blinded by love, went to his side without any embarrassment.
A certain woman, remaining inside her dwelling and seeing her guru outside,
meditated upon Govinda with her eyes closed, being completely absorbed in him.
Surrounded by the gopīs, Govinda, eager for the delight of commencing the rāsa dance, honored the night made beautiful by the autumn moon.
And the cowherd girls, their very forms dependent upon Kṛṣṇa’s activities,
wandered within Vṛndāvana in groups when Kṛṣṇa had gone to another land.
Then those gopīs, longing for the sight of Kṛṣṇa, wandered about;
O twice-born ones, they saw Kṛṣṇa’s footprints in Vṛndāvana during the night.
Thus, amidst those various kinds of dark deeds,
the gopīs moved about together, busily engaged, in the delightful forest of Vṛndāvana.
O twice-born ones, having returned from there, those gopīs, despairing of seeing Kṛṣṇa, went to the bank of the Yamunā and sang of his deeds.
Then the cowherd women beheld Kṛṣṇa, the protector of the three worlds who acts without effort, approaching with his lotus-face in full bloom.
Seeing Govinda approaching, a certain woman, filled with great joy, spoke with wide-open eyes: "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! (BrP 189.27)
One woman, having made her forehead-plate furrowed by a knitting of the brows,
gazed at Hari with her bee-like eyes and drank in the lotus of his face.
Upon beholding Govinda, one woman closed her eyes;
meditating upon his very form, she shone like one who had ascended to the heights of yoga.
Then Mādhava brought some to compliance with endearing words, some with glances and the knitting of his brows, and others with the touch of his hand.
Together with those cowherd girls whose minds were full of devotion,
Hari, whose conduct is noble, joyfully sported in respectful rāsa-dances.
Although they were arranged in a circular dance formation, the group of cowherd women did not move away from Kṛṣṇa’s side, nor did they remain with their minds fixed on a single spot.
Taking each gopī by the hand one by one, Hari led them into the circle of the rāsa dance, as their eyes were closed by the touch of his hand.
Then there commenced a delightful succession of songs, accompanied by the tinkling of moving bracelets,
which followed the melodies of autumnal poetry.
While Kṛṣṇa sang of the autumn moon, the moonlight, and the lily pond,
the group of cowherd women, however, repeatedly sang only the single name "Kṛṣṇa."
One cowherd girl, exhausted and with her bracelets jingling as she turned around,
placed her vine-like arm upon the shoulder of the slayer of Madhu.
A certain cowherd girl, her arms outstretched, embraced and kissed Madhusūdana under the pretext of being skilled in singing his praises.
Having come into contact with the cheeks of the gopīs, Hari’s two arms became like clouds of perspiration-water for the crop of rising horripilation.
As long as Kṛṣṇa sang the Rāsa-song in a very high-pitched voice, they sang "Well done, Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! with a voice twice as loud.
When he went forth, the cowherd women followed him; when he turned back, they went toward him; thus the cowherd women attended upon Hari both in the contrary and in the natural order.
Then Madhusūdana sported with the cowherd girls;
for him, a moment spent without her was equal to ten million years.
Though restrained by their fathers, husbands, and brothers,
those cowherd women, who were fond of pleasure, took delight with Kṛṣṇa at night.
Even at the age of youth, Madhusūdana,
whose soul is immeasurable and who has destroyed all enemies, took delight with them during the nights, honoring them.
Likewise, in their husbands, in those women, and in all beings, this Lord,
whose form is the nature of the Self, remains pervading everything.
Just as ether, fire, earth, water,
and air exist within all beings, so too does that Self abide, pervading everything.
Vyāsa said:
Once, at the midpoint of the evening while Janārdana was absorbed in the *rāsa* dance,
Ariṣṭa arrived, maddened and terrifying the cow-pens.
Having the appearance of a water-laden cloud, with sharp horns and sun-like eyes,
he tore the surface of the earth excessively with the tips of his hooves.
Licking his lips repeatedly with his tongue with a grinding sound,
his tail tossed in fury, and the muscles of his shoulders hardened, he stood there.
With the fullness of his lofty hump, difficult to surpass in size,
his back and limbs smeared with dung and urine, he causes distress to the cows.
With a long-hanging neck and a face marked by the wounds of trees,
that Daitya, assuming the form of a bull, stood facing him and causing the calves of the cows to miscarry.
He who always roams through the forests, subduing all by his might—
seeing him with his exceedingly terrible eyes, they were overcome with great fear.
The cowherds and the cowherd women cried out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa!
Then Keśava let out a lion's roar and made a sound by clapping his hands.
Upon hearing that sound, he went toward the face of Dāmodara,
with the tips of his horns thrust forward and his eyes fixed upon Kṛṣṇa’s belly.
The evil-minded Daitya, assuming the form of a bull, rushed forward;
seeing that mighty Daitya-bull approaching, Kṛṣṇa [prepared himself].
Madhusūdana did not move from that spot, but with a playful smile of contempt, he seized the approaching [demon] like a crocodile.
He struck with his knee at the belly of that elephant, which was as immovable as a mountain due to its grasping of the tusks;
having destroyed its pride and strength while it was held by the tusks, he subdued it.
He squeezed Ariṣṭa’s neck as if it were a wet garment,
and then, having uprooted one of his horns, he struck him with that very same horn.
That great Daitya died, vomiting blood from his mouth.
When that Daitya was slain, the cowherds praised Janārdana,
just as the hosts of gods once praised the Thousand-eyed One when Jambha was killed.
Vyāsa said:
When Kakudmin had been slain, Ariṣṭa struck down, Dhenuka brought to his end,
and Mount Govardhana held aloft, [the demons were destroyed].
When the serpent Kāliya was subdued, the pair of lofty trees broken, Pūtanā slain, and the cart overturned; // BrP_190.2 //
Nārada related to Kaṃsa everything exactly as it had happened in due order, including in its entirety the exchange of the embryos of Yaśodā and Devakī.
Having heard all that from Nārada, who has the vision of the gods,
the evil-minded Kaṃsa then directed his wrath toward Vasudeva.
Out of great anger, having reproached him in the assembly of all the Yādavas,
he censured the Yādavas as well and reflected upon this matter.
"As long as the two very young ones, Bala and Kṛṣṇa, have not attained full strength, they must be slain by me; once they have reached maturity, they will be invincible."
"Cāṇūra is here, possessed of great heroism, and Muṣṭika is of great strength;
through these two, I shall cause those two intoxicated ones to be slain in a wrestling match."
"Under the pretext of the great Dhanur-mahāyāga sacrifice, I will bring those two from Vraja and act in such a way that they shall go to their destruction."
Vyāsa said:
Having reflected thus, the evil-minded Kaṃsa, resolved to kill Rāma and Janārdana, spoke these words to the heroic Akrūra.
Kaṃsa said:
"O Lord of Generosity, let my words be carried out for my pleasure;
mounting a chariot from here, go to Nanda’s cowherd settlement."
The two sons of Vasudeva there, born from portions of Viṣṇu, have indeed arisen for my destruction; those two wicked ones are growing in power.
"The great Dhanur-mahāyāga will take place on the fourteenth day;
you must indeed bring those two there for the wrestling match."
"Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika are my wrestlers, skilled in hand-to-hand combat;
let all the world here witness the battle between them and these two."
The elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa, urged on by his mahout,
shall slay those two wicked children, the sons of Vasudeva.
Having slain both Vasudeva and the wicked-minded Nandagopa,
I shall also slay my father and the evil-minded Ugrasena.
Then I shall seize all the cattle-wealth and the property of all the wicked cowherds who desire my death.
"O Lord of Charity, without you these Yādavas are wicked toward me;
I shall endeavor to slay them one after another in due order."
"Therefore, I shall rule this entire kingdom, free from thorns and devoid of Yādavas, with your assistance; for that reason, O hero, go out of affection for me."
And just as the cowherds quickly bring buffalo ghee and curd as offerings, you must speak to them in such a manner.
Vyāsa said:
O twice-born ones, having been thus commanded, the highly fortunate Akrūra became filled with joy and, eager to see Kṛṣṇa, thought, "I shall see him tomorrow."
Having said "So be it" to the king, Madhupriya quickly mounted his chariot and then departed from the city of Mathurā.
Vyāsa said:
Keśin, too, formidable in his strength and dispatched as Kamsa’s messenger,
arrived at Vṛndāvana, desiring the death of Kṛṣṇa.
With his hooves scarred by the surface of the earth, shaking the clouds with the tossing of his mane,
he returned to the presence of the cowherds, once again traversing the paths of the sun and the moon.
At the sound of that neighing, the cowherds and the cowherd girls, terrified by the Daitya’s horse, went to Govinda for refuge.
Having heard their cry, "Save us! Save us!", Govinda spoke these words, as deep as the roar of a water-laden cloud: BrP_190.25 //
Govinda said:
"Enough with this fear, O cowherds! Why are you so overcome by dread?
By you, who belong to the caste of cowherds, the prowess of heroes is being lost."
What is the use of this wicked horse, which possesses little strength, causes distress through its neighing, is driven by the power of the Daityas, and prances about?
"Come, come, you wicked one! I am Kṛṣṇa; like Pūṣan when he was struck by the wielder of the Pināka, I shall cause all the teeth in your mouth to fall out."
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, Govinda went toward Keśin;
and that son of Diti, with his mouth wide open, rushed at him.
Then Janārdana, having extended his arm,
thrust it into the mouth of that wicked horse Keśin.
As that arm of Kṛṣṇa entered Keśin’s mouth,
his teeth were shattered like fragments of white clouds.
O twice-born ones, Kṛṣṇa’s arm that had entered Keśin’s body grew,
like a disease neglected by physicians for the sake of its own destruction.
With his lips split open, he vomited copious amounts of frothy blood;
his cheeks were distended, and his eyes were wide open with their lashes disheveled.
He walked upon the earth on his feet, discharging excrement and urine;
with his limbs moist with sweat and exhausted, he then became devoid of effort.
With his mouth wide open, that most terrible asura fell, split in two by Kṛṣṇa’s arm, like a tree struck by lightning.
Keśin’s two halves— consisting of half a foot, half a back, half a tail, one ear, one eye, and one nostril—
shone brightly as they lay split apart.
Having slain Keśin, Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by the joyful cowherds,
remained right there, his body unwearied and at ease, smiling.
Then, Keśin having been slain, the cowherds and cowherdesses were filled with wonder;
they praised the lotus-eyed one, who is enchanting through his affection.
Seeing Keśin slain, the brahmin Nārada, his mind overflowing with joy, arrived swiftly while stationed upon a cloud.
Nārada said:
"Excellent, excellent, O Lord of the World! O Acyuta, it is by mere sport that this Keśin, the bringer of distress to the inhabitants of heaven, has been slain by you."
O Madhusūdana, my heart was indeed struck with wonder by the noble deeds performed during your incarnations; through this, my mind has now attained satisfaction.
O Kṛṣṇa, even Śakra and the gods are afraid of this horse when he whinnies while looking toward the clouds, his mane bristling.
"O Janārdana, because this evil-souled Keśin has been slain by you,
you shall therefore be celebrated in the world by the name Keśava."
"May it be well with you; I shall now depart for the battle with Kaṃsa.
O slayer of Keśin, I will return with you again the day after tomorrow."
O Upholder of the Earth, you have brought about the removal of the burden of the world by striking down Kaṃsa, the son of Ugrasena, along with his followers.
In that regard, O Janārdana, I must witness the various kinds of battles of the rulers of the earth as they are directed by you.
Therefore, O Govinda, I shall depart; the great task for the gods has been accomplished by you.
Honored by you, may it be well with you; I am now going.
Vyāsa said:
When Nārada had departed, Kṛṣṇa, unperplexed,
entered Gokula with the cowherds— he who is the sole vessel for the drinking of the eyes of the gopīs.
Vyāsa said:
Akrūra also, having set out in his swift-moving chariot and being intent on beholding Kṛṣṇa, proceeded to Nanda’s cowherd settlement.
And Akrūra thought: "There is no one more fortunate than I, for I shall behold the face of the Wielder of the Discus who has descended as a partial incarnation."
Today my birth has become fruitful and my night has turned into a beautiful dawn,
since I shall behold the face of Viṣṇu, whose eyes are like the petals of a blossoming lotus.
I shall behold that lotus-eyed face of Viṣṇu, which, when remembered or even conceived in thought, removes the evil of men.
And from which the Vedas and all the Vedāṅgas emerged;
that supreme abode of the gods, the mouth of the Blessed One, I shall behold.
I shall behold that Lord of the Universe, the support of all, who, as the Person of Sacrifice and the Supreme Person, is worshipped by men in sacrifices.
Having worshipped with a hundred sacrifices, Indra attained the sovereignty over the immortals;
I shall behold that Keśava, who is without beginning or end.
Neither Brahmā, nor Indra, Rudra, the Aśvins, the Vasus, the Ādityas, nor the hosts of Maruts know His true nature; may that Hari touch me today.
He who is the self of all, all-pervading, all-encompassing, and established within all beings—
he who is imperishable and omnipresent— is indeed beheld by me today.
"Abiding in the forms of a fish, a tortoise, a boar, a lion, and so forth,
he will employ his yoga through yogic power and address me."
And now the Lord of the World, the imperishable one who assumes a body by his own will, has attained human form in order to establish himself among the multitude of tasks in Vraja.
He who is infinite and supports the earth established upon its peaks has descended for the sake of the world; he will address me as "Akrūra."
Salutations again and again to Him, whose māyā— consisting of fathers, kinsmen, friends, brothers, mothers, and relatives— the world is unable to overcome.
Salutation to that Self of Knowledge, by whose being established in the heart mortal beings cross over this widespread ignorance and this illusory power (māyā).
I bow down to him who is called Yajñapuruṣa by eternal sacrificers, Vāsudeva, and Viṣṇu by those who know the Vedāntas.
Likewise, may that Being, in whom this world— both existent and non-existent— is sustained and established within His abode, attain gentleness toward me through His very essence.
I constantly go for refuge to Hari, the foremost of men, by whose remembrance one becomes a vessel for all auspiciousness.
Vyāsa said:
Thus, with his mind and heart bowed down by devotion as he meditated upon Viṣṇu,
Akrūra reached Gokula while the sun was still shining brightly.
Then he saw Kṛṣṇa there at the milking place of the cows,
standing in the midst of the calves, with the complexion of a blooming blue lotus petal.
With eyes like the petals of a full-blown lotus, his chest marked with the Śrīvatsa, possessing long arms and a broad, high-chested torso, and a prominent nose; BrP_191.20 //
He bore a lotus-face that was the locus of a playful smile,
and with his feet, he stood firmly established upon the earth, his high, reddish nails visible.
Wearing two yellow garments, adorned with wild flowers,
holding a thick blue creeper in his hand, and having a white lotus as an ear-ornament.
O twice-born ones, he then beheld the joy of the Yadus, Balabhadra, who was as white as a swan, the moon, or a kunda flower, and who wore blue garments.
Tall with uplifted arms and a blossoming lotus-face,
he was like another Mount Kailāsa encircled by a garland of clouds.
O brahmins, upon seeing them, that great-minded Akrūra’s lotus-like face blossomed and his entire body was covered with horripilation.
He who is this supreme abode, this supreme state,
that Vāsudeva has become manifest in a twofold manner.
May there be success for my pair of eyes simultaneously upon seeing the Creator of the World; and by the grace of the Blessed One, may this body [of mine] break into loud laughter.
When contact with my limbs has been granted, that shall become the path to the fruit;
this very day, having touched my lotus-hand,
the glorious one of infinite forms will act.
By men whose every sin is destroyed by the touch of her fingers, unsurpassed perfection is attained;
likewise [is she] led by Aśvin, Rudra, Indra, and Vasu.
The gods, greatly rejoiced, grant him a boon:
by him who strikes down the lord of the Daityas with his discus, the corners of the eyes of the Daitya women have been taken away.
Where Bali, having offered water with his mind alone while remaining on the surface of the earth, obtained enjoyments;
likewise did the Lord of the Immortals obtain sovereignty over the thirty gods.
Śakra completed a full manvantara; then, O Lord,
you took me into Kaṃsa's service, though I was free from fault and had become an object of blame for him.

"Fie upon the creator who has bestowed the mind upon me! Fie on that mind by which I have been excluded from the virtuous, for it belongs to the entire mass of sentient beings whose nature is knowledge. (BrP 191.31c–191.32a)
For one whose faults have been turned away and who is ever manifest,
what in this world remains unknown to him who dwells within the hearts of all men?
Therefore, with my body bowed in devotion,
I go to the Lord of all lords,
who is an incarnate portion of Puruṣottama.
"Reflecting thus upon Govinda, who is without beginning, middle, or end, that Yādava approached Viṣṇu, the Unborn. Vyāsa said:
Thinking, "I am Akrūra," he bowed his head at the feet of Hari.
He too, having touched him with a hand marked by the signs of the banner, the thunderbolt, and the lotus,
drew him near and embraced him very firmly with affection.
Having exchanged greetings with him in the proper manner, Balarāma and Keśava then suddenly entered their own palace, taking him along.
Then, together with those two, Akrūra performed the customary salutations and other rites; having eaten his meal according to the rules, he subsequently related everything to them.
Just as Ānakadundubhi was reviled by that Kaṃsa,
and just as Queen Devakī was [reviled] by the evil-minded Dānava.
O Ugrasena, [tell me] how that evil-souled Kaṃsa conducts himself,
and for what purpose he was dispatched by Kaṃsa.
Having heard all that in detail, the Blessed One, the slayer of Keśin, said: "O lord of gifts, all of this has indeed been known by me."
"O illustrious one, I shall do whatever is deemed appropriate in this matter;
you should not think otherwise of this—know that Kaṃsa has been slain by me."
"Tomorrow Rama and I shall go to Mathurā together with you;
the elder cowherds will also go, taking many offerings."
"O hero, let this night pass; you should not give way to anxiety. Within three nights, I shall slay Kaṃsa along with his followers."
Vyāsa said:
Having then given instructions to the cowherds, Akrūra, along with Keśava,
went to the house of Nanda the cowherd, and Balabhadra also fell asleep there.
Then, at the clear dawn, the two of great strength, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
prepared together with Akrūra to go to the city of Mathurā.
Seeing him, the cowherd women, with tears in their eyes and bracelets slipping from their arms,
sighed, afflicted by extreme grief, and spoke thus to one another:
Having reached Mathurā, how will Govinda return to Gokula? How will he drink with his ears the honey of the artful conversations of the city women?
How can his mind, which has taken its abode among the playful utterances of city-dwelling women, ever turn toward rustic cowherds and cowherdesses?
By that merciless and evil-minded one, who according to the prescribed rite carried off Hari— the very essence of the entire cowherd settlement— a blow was dealt to the cowherd women.
A smile pregnant with inner feeling, speech, a gait graceful with charm—
these belong exceedingly to the women of the city, yet it is their very side-long glance that is truly so.
Since this rustic Hari has been bound by the fetters of their charms,
by what means will he come again to your side?
For here is Keśava, having mounted his chariot, proceeding toward Mathurā,
deceived by the cruel Akrūra who was himself driven by despair.
Does this cruel man not know that we are devoted to him with affection,
since he leads Hari away from us to another place, depriving us of the joy of his presence?
"This utterly merciless Govinda is proceeding together with Rāma, having mounted his chariot; let haste be made to restrain him."
"Why do you say that it is not permissible for us to speak in the presence of our gurus?
What can the gurus do to those who have been consumed by the fire of separation?"
The cowherds, headed by Nandagopa, are all prepared to depart;
not one of them makes an effort to turn Govinda back.
Today the night has dawned beautifully for the women residing in Mathurā,
whose eyes, like bees, enjoy the lotus-face of Acyuta.
Blessed are those on the road who, unimpeded, shall behold Kṛṣṇa departing from here and carry him in their sight with their own bodies bristling with horripilation.
Today there will be a great festival for the eyes of the citizens of the city of Mathurā,
arising from the sight of Govinda’s face.
What dream must have been seen by those fortunate women regarding Adhokṣaja,
they whose wide-eyed glances will behold him without obstruction?
"Aha! Today, after showing this great treasure to the cowherd women, the pitiless Creator has plucked out their eyes."
As Hari’s grip on us loosens through his affection,
even the bracelets upon his wrists quickly begin to slip.
"Akrūra, cruel-hearted, swiftly urged on the horses;
who would not feel compassion for women in such distress?"
"Ha! Ha! Kṛṣṇa, look at the high dust raised by the chariot;
even that dust by which Hari was cast far away is no longer visible!"
Thus, gazed upon by the cowherd women with exceeding affection,
Keśava, together with Rāma, abandoned the region of Vraja.
Traveling by chariot drawn by swift horses,
Rāma, Akrūra, and Janārdana reached the banks of the Yamunā at the time of midday.
Then Akrūra said to Kṛṣṇa, "Please remain here for a moment while I perform my daily ablutions in the waters of the Kālindī."
When "So be it" was said, O Brahmins, that high-minded one, having bathed and performed the ritual sipping of water, entered the waters of the Yamunā and meditated upon the supreme Brahman.
He beheld Balabhadra, adorned with a garland of a thousand hoods,
his body as pure as a kunda flower, and his eyes as broad as the petals of a blooming lotus.
He was surrounded by a multitude of great serpent offspring, air-eaters (nāgas),
being praised [by them], fragrant, and adorned with forest garlands.
Wearing dark garments,
adorned with beautiful earrings and a lovely crest-ornament, he stood intoxicated within the depths of the water.
On his lap [he saw] one dark as a rain-cloud, with large copper-colored eyes,
four arms, noble limbs, and adorned with weapons such as the discus.
Wearing yellow garments and adorned with variegated garlands,
he was like a rain-cloud made beautiful by the rainbow and streaks of lightning.
He beheld the untiring Kṛṣṇa, whose chest bore the Śrīvatsa mark, who was radiant with beautiful armlets and a crown, and who wore a lotus as an ear-ornament.
It was being meditated upon mentally by Sanandana and other sages, perfected yogis free from stain, with their eyes fixed on the tip of the nose.
Then Akrūra, recognizing Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa, was struck with wonder and thought quickly: "How have they come here?"
Janārdana paralyzed the speech of him who desired to speak;
then, emerging from the water, he returned once more to his chariot.
And there he beheld both Rāma and Kṛṣṇa standing upon the chariot, just as before, endowed with human bodies.
And having plunged once more into the water, he beheld those two exactly as before,
being praised by Gandharvas, sages, Siddhas, and great serpents.
Then, having realized his true nature, that lord of donors praised the imperishable Lord, who consists of all knowledge.
Akrūra said:
Salutations again and again to the Supreme Self, who consists of the subtle elements, whose majesty is inconceivable, who is all-pervading, and whose singular true nature is manifold yet one.
Salutations to you whose form is sound; salutations to you who have become the inconceivable oblation.
Salutations to you whose form is consciousness, the supreme beyond primordial nature, O Lord!

You, the single one, abide in five forms: as the self of the elements, the self of the senses, the self of primordial matter (pradhāna), the individual self (ātman), and the supreme self (paramātman).
Be gracious, O Soul of all dharmas, O Great Lord of the perishable and the imperishable,
who art proclaimed through such conceptualizations as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others!
O You whose essential nature is ineffable, O You whose purpose is ineffable,
O Supreme Lord whose very name is ineffable, I bow to You.
O Protector, that wherein conceptual constructions such as name, genus, and so forth do not exist—that is the supreme, eternal, and unchanging Brahman; you are that Unborn One.
Since there is no apprehension of any object apart from conceptual construction,
you are praised by the names Kṛṣṇa, Acyuta, Ananta, and Viṣṇu.
O Soul of All, O Unborn One, you are [defined] by these conceptual constructions;
you are the gods, you are the entire world, you alone are the universe. O Soul of the Universe, you are devoid of the distinctions of transformation.
For there is nothing whatsoever other than you in all existence;
you are Brahmā, Paśupati, Aryaman, and Vidhātṛ;
you are Dhātṛ, the Lord of the Thirty-three, Vāyu, and Agni.
You alone are the lord of waters, the lord of wealth, and the Ender; though your nature is one, you protect the world through diverse powers.
You create and destroy the universe in the form of the sun's rays.

O Unborn One, this entire manifold universe is composed of Your qualities; I bow to that Supreme Being, the imperishable, who is denoted by the word "Sat," and whose nature is consciousness, both being and non-being.
Oṃ, salutation to Vāsudeva; salutation to Saṃkarṣaṇa as well;
salutation to you, Pradyumna; salutation to you, Aniruddha.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus praised Kṛṣṇa within the water, that Yādava honored the Lord of All with mental offerings of incense and flowers.
Having abandoned all other objects and fixed his mind thereon,
he remained for a long time established in Brahman and then desisted from his meditative absorption.
O best of the twice-born, considering himself as one who had accomplished his purpose,
he emerged from the waters of the Yamunā and returned once more to his chariot.
Then Kṛṣṇa beheld Rāma and himself standing just as they had been before;
and to Akrūra, whose eyes were wide with amazement, Kṛṣṇa then spoke.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Akrūra, what wonder have you seen in the waters of the Yamunā,
since you are observed with eyes wide open in amazement?"
Akrūra said:
"O Acyuta, that wonder which was seen by me there within the water,
I now behold right here before me in embodied form."
O Kṛṣṇa, I have been united with you, that Great Soul by whom this world—which is of such wondrous form—is created; indeed, you are devoted to wonders.
"So what of it? Let us go to Mathurā, O Madhusūdana!
I am afraid of Kaṃsa; fie on the life of one who subsists on the food of others!"
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, he urged on those horses, swift as the wind;
and by evening, Akrūra had reached the city of Mathurā.
Beholding Mathurā, Kṛṣṇa, and Rāma, that Yādava said:
Akrūra said:
"O you two of great heroism, you have gone on foot while I am entering by chariot;
therefore, you two must go to the house of Vasudeva."
For it is for your sake that this old man is being cast out by Kaṃsa.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, Akrūra entered the city of Mathurā;
meanwhile, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, having entered, arrived at the royal highway.
Beheld with joyful eyes by women and men,
the two heroes proceeded with grace like young elephants that have reached their destination.
Seeing the washerman, a dyer of cloth, wandering about, the two of them begged him for their own forms— namely,
beautiful garments.
Then Kaṃsa’s washerman, his pride mounted by the favor he had received,
spoke many insulting words loudly to Rāma and Keśava.
Then, with a blow of his palm, Kṛṣṇa, out of anger, struck off the head of that wicked-souled washerman and cast it to the ground.
Then, having killed [the gardener] and taken the garments, Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, dressed in yellow and blue robes, went joyfully to the house of the florist.
With his pair of eyes wide open, the garland-maker was utterly amazed;
he then wondered in his mind, "To whom do these two belong, and from where have they come?"
Seeing those two, wearing yellow and blue garments and exceedingly beautiful,
he then reflected that two gods had arrived upon the earth.
Requested for flowers by those two, whose lotus-faces were in full bloom,
he supported himself upon the earth with his hands and touched the ground with his head.
"The two Lords, with faces bright with favor, have come to my house; I am blessed! I shall worship them," said the garland-maker to them. (BrP 192.78)
Then, with a joyful countenance, he offered them lovely flowers, saying "these" and "those," as he sought to entice them according to their desire.
Bowing down again and again, that most excellent garland-maker gave them beautiful,
fragrant, and stainless flowers.
Kṛṣṇa, being pleased with the garland-maker, granted him a boon:
"O blessed one, Śrī, taking refuge in you, shall never forsake you."
O gentle one, there shall be no loss of strength for you, nor any loss of wealth;
and as long as the earth and the sun endure, so shall your lineage of sons and grandsons continue.
And having enjoyed vast pleasures, at the end, through my grace and by recollecting me, you shall attain the divine world.
O auspicious one, your mind shall always be fixed upon the Dharma;
those born in your lineage shall possess long lives.
O highly fortunate one, no affliction such as calamities shall befall one born of your lineage for as long as the sun shall exist.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, O best of sages, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Baladeva and honored by the garland-maker, departed from that house.
Vyāsa said:
Then, on the royal highway, Kṛṣṇa saw a hunchbacked woman approaching, carrying a vessel of ointment and in the prime of her youth.
Kṛṣṇa spoke to her playfully: "O lotus-eyed one, tell me truly, whose unguent is this that you are carrying?"
Desiring Hari with passion and full of affection for him,
that hunchbacked woman spoke playfully and then looked at him with force.
The hunchback said: "O beloved, why do you not know that I have been appointed even by Kaṃsa as the one renowned as Naikavakrā in the art of anointing?"
Indeed, no paste ground by anyone else brings such pleasure to Kaṃsa;
for I am the recipient of his supreme wealth of favor.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O lady of beautiful countenance, let this fragrant, delightful unguent, worthy of a king and suited to our bodies, be given to us."
Vyāsa said:
Having heard him, she respectfully said to Kṛṣṇa, "Please accept it," and then she gave both of them unguents suitable for their bodies.
Then those two bulls among men, their limbs smeared with streaks of unguents,
shone resplendent like white and black clouds adorned with Indra’s bow.
Then Śauri,
who was skilled in the art of lifting, lifted her by the chin and weighed her with two fingers of his right hand.
Then Keśava pulled her with his feet and brought her to straightness;
having attained that straightness, she became the most excellent among women.
Holding Govinda by his garment, she spoke with playful grace, languid from the weight of her overflowing love: "Come to my house in Vraja."
"I shall come to your house," Keśava said to her;
looking at Rāma's face, he dismissed her and laughed aloud.
With their limbs smeared with streaks of colored paste and both dressed in blue and yellow garments,
they then went to the bow-hall, adorned with variegated garlands.
And having taken up the jewel of a bow while the guards asked him about it,
Kṛṣṇa suddenly seized it and drew it to its full extent.
Then, as he drew the bow with force until it snapped,
it produced an immense sound, and by that sound Mathurā was filled.
Then, when their bows were broken by the guards,
those two, intent on their purpose, cut through the army of guards and emerged from the abode of archers.
Having learned the news of Akrūra’s arrival and hearing that the bow had been broken, Kaṃsa then spoke to Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika.
Kaṃsa said:
"Those two cowherd boys have arrived before you;
they must be slain by wrestling, for they are the ones who have taken away my life."
"O you of great strength, I have indeed been gratified by you both through that destruction in wrestling; I shall grant your desired wishes, for it cannot be otherwise."
Whether by right means or by wrong means, those two have been made my enemies by you;
they must be slain, for upon their death, the kingdom shall become common to you all.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus instructed those two wrestlers, he then summoned the elephant-keeper and spoke aloud:
"By you, at the entrance of the assembly, an intoxicated elephant [must be stationed] before me."
Kuvalayāpīḍa was stationed there by him; those two cowherd boys were to be slain when they arrived at the entrance of the arena for the wrestling match.
Having given those orders and seeing that all the platforms had been brought forward,
Kaṃsa, whose death was imminent, awaited the rising of the sun.
Then all those citizens ascended the platforms,
as did the kings with their attendants upon the royal platforms.
And Kaṃsa had the assembly of wrestlers and judges stationed nearby in the middle of the arena;
Kaṃsa himself, however, was seated upon a lofty dais.
There were couches prepared for the women of the inner apartments,
others for the chief courtesans, and still others for the women of the city.
The cowherds, headed by Nanda, were seated on other couches,
while Akrūra and Vasudeva were stationed at the edge of the couch.
In the midst of the women of the city, Devakī, longing for her son,
remained standing even at the hour of death, thinking, "I shall see my son's face."
While the musical instruments were being played, as Cāṇūra leaped about excessively, the people raised cries of "Alas! Alas! while Muṣṭika slapped his arms.
Having slain Kuvalayāpīḍa, who had been urged on by his elephant-driver,
the two of them— whose limbs were smeared with ichor and blood and whose excellent weapons were the tusks of an elephant— [stood there].
Like two lions among a herd of deer, gazing with prideful playfulness,
Baladeva and Janārdana entered the vast arena.
Immediately thereafter, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose throughout all the arenas from the wonder of the people, who exclaimed, "This is Kṛṣṇa! This is Balabhadra!"
He is the one by whom that terrible night-stalking demoness Pūtanā was slain,
by whom the wagon was overturned, and by whom the twin Yamalārjuna trees were shattered.
This is he who, as a mere child, danced upon the serpent Kāliya,
and by whom the great mountain Govardhana was held up for seven nights.
By whom Ariṣṭa, Dhenuka, and the wicked Keśin were slain with mere ease— that very Acyuta is seen here.
And here before him goes his elder brother, the mighty-armed Baladeva,
who proceeds with playful grace, delighting the minds and eyes of women.
This is what is described by the wise who perceive the meaning of the Purāṇas:
that Gopāla shall lift up the submerged lineage of the Yādavas.
This is that very portion of Viṣṇu, the soul of all beings and the source of all births, who has descended to the earth as the bearer of the world's burden.
When Rāma and Kṛṣṇa had been thus described by the citizens, at that very moment Devakī’s chest was warmed by her breasts, which were flowing with milk out of affection.
Beholding his two sons as if witnessing a great festival,
Vasudeva cast off the old age that had come upon him and became like a youth again.
With their pairs of eyes wide open, the women of the king's inner apartments and the throngs of city women never ceased gazing upon the two of them.
The women said:
"Friends, behold the lotus-eyed face of Kṛṣṇa,
adorned with droplets of perspiration from the exertion of the elephant battle."
Like a blooming lotus in a lake sprinkled by the water of dew,
let this birth— whose syllables have been surpassed [by your presence]— be made fruitful for your sight.
O beautiful lady, behold this chest of the Child, marked with the Śrīvatsa and the abode of the universe, which destroys all adversaries; and behold his pair of arms as well.
Behold how Balabhadra is made to laugh by Muṣṭika as he leaps about, and likewise by Cāṇūra and others. BrP 193.45.
"Friends, look! This Hari approaches Cāṇūra for the sake of wrestling.
Are there no elders here who act with propriety?"
Where is Hari, whose body is so delicate and who has just begun to reach youth;
and where is this great asura, whose expansive body is as hard as a diamond?
"These two, in the prime of their youth, move with great grace upon the arena;
whereas the Daitya wrestlers, headed by Cāṇūra, are exceedingly fierce."
This is a great transgression on the part of the judges of wrestling,
that they should look on with indifference as a battle takes place between one who is a child and one who is strong.
Vyāsa said:
While the women of the city were speaking thus, making the earth tremble,
the Blessed Lord Hari rained down an abundance of joy upon the people.
And when Balabhadra, having slapped his arms, leaped gracefully step by step, it was a marvel that the earth did not shatter.
Then Kṛṣṇa, of immeasurable prowess, fought with Cāṇūra,
while the Daitya Muṣṭika, skilled in wrestling, fought with Baladeva.
And Hari engaged in close combat with Cāṇūra,
striking him with throws, fists, and blows like the falling of stakes and thunderbolts.
A great battle took place between the two of them with blows struck from their feet;
that battle between them was weaponless, exceedingly terrible, and most dreadful.
To the extent that Cāṇūra fought with Hari in the presence of the assembly festival, he performed deeds achievable only through his own strength and vital power.
To the extent that he suffered the loss of his supreme vital breaths,
Kṛṣṇa, who pervades the universe, fought with him as if in mere play.
Out of weariness and anger, he moved his hand from his own remaining hand,
having observed the loss of strength and the increasing prowess of Cāṇūra and Kṛṣṇa.
Kaṃsa, overcome with rage, silenced the musical instruments;
at that very moment, the drums and other musical instruments were forbidden from sounding.
Divine musical instruments were sounded repeatedly and in harmony:
"Victory to Govinda! Slay the Dānava Cāṇūra, O Keśava!"
Thus the gods, having vanished, praised him with great joy;
and Madhusūdana, after sporting for a long time with Cāṇūra, [departed].
Making an effort to slay him, the conqueror of enemies uprooted the Daitya wrestler and whirled him around; having whirled him a hundred times, he [prepared to strike].
He dashed the lifeless Cāṇūra against the ground;
struck by him upon the earth, Cāṇūra was shattered into a hundred pieces.
At that time, the mighty Baladeva caused the earth to become a great mire of flowing blood with Muṣṭika.
He fought with the Daitya wrestler Cāṇūra as Hari did;
he too struck him on the head, the chest, and with his knee using his fist.
Having thrown him to the surface of the earth,
Kṛṣṇa further crushed the lifeless Tośalaka, the mighty king of wrestlers.
With a blow from his left fist, he cast him down to the ground;
when the wrestler Cāṇūra was slain and Muṣṭika was struck down, [the others fled].
When the Tośalaka host had been destroyed, all the Mallas fled;
meanwhile, both Kṛṣṇa and Saṃkarṣaṇa danced upon the arena.
Having forcibly dragged away the cowherds of equal age,
Kaṃsa, his eyes red with rage, spoke loudly to the tall men who were delighted.
"Let these two cowherds be forcibly driven out from here along with the throngs of the assembly;
let the wicked Nanda also be seized and quickly bound with fetters."
Let Vasudeva also be executed with a punishment not fit for an elder;
and as for these cowherds who are again leaping about together with Kṛṣṇa.
"Let their cows be seized, and whatever wealth they possess!"—
at him who was thus commanding, Madhusūdana laughed.
Leaping up and mounting that dais, he swiftly seized Kaṃsa by the hair,
pulling him down to the surface of the earth with his crown slipping off.
He caused Kaṃsa to fall, and he himself fell upon him;
for he was falling upon one who was heavy with being the support of the entire world.
The king, the son of Ugrasena, was made to give up his life by Kṛṣṇa;
then Madhusūdana, seizing him by the hair as he lay dead, [dragged him].
The immensely powerful one dragged Kaṃsa’s body into the middle of the arena by means of his extreme weight as he was being pulled down.
When Kaṃsa had been seized by Kṛṣṇa, his brother, impelled by the body of the high-souled Kaṃsa, approached in a rage.
Sunāman was struck down by Balabhadra with effortless ease;
thereupon, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the entire arena.
Seeing the Lord of Mathurā slain by Kṛṣṇa out of contempt,
Kṛṣṇa also quickly grasped the feet of Vasudeva.
And Vasudeva, the mighty-armed one, together with Baladeva as his companion,
having raised up Janārdana from Devakī,
stood bowing before those two who had remembered their birth and spoken these words.
Vasudeva said:
"Be gracious, O Lord of the gods of gods, O foremost of deities, O Master!
By your grace, O Keśava, you have thus effected our deliverance."
Since the Blessed One, having been propitiated, descended into my house for the purpose of destroying the wicked, our lineage has been purified by him.
You are within all beings, abiding in all beings; O Soul of All, the past and the future proceed from you.
O inconceivable Acyuta, you are worshipped in the sacrifice as the embodiment of all the gods;
you alone are the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and the supreme lord of sacrifices.
O son of Devakī, that this mind of mine, which conceals its true nature, should feel such affection for you is an utter mockery.
You are the creator of all beings, existing without beginning or end;
where then will this human tongue of mine say, "He is my son"?
O Lord of the World, since this entire world has arisen from you,
by what logic could you have come into being from us without the power of *māyā*?
How can he, in whom the entire world— both the stationary and the moving— is established,
be born from a human being as one who sleeps upon his mother’s lap?
Therefore, O Supreme Lord, be gracious and protect the universe;
you are not my son by virtue of taking on partial incarnations. O Lord, this entire world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is yours.
O Supreme Lord, Soul of all beings, why do you delude my mind with the vision of Māyā, thinking "this is my son"? Indeed,
I have acted with extreme severity out of fear of Kaṃsa.
"You were led to Gokula when it was agitated by the fear of enemies; you have grown in prosperity for me and for my cows, O Lord of Cows.
[You possess] the deeds of Rudra, the Maruts, the Aśvins, and Indra."
Those things which were not accomplished and were not even observed— you, Viṣṇu, have arrived for the sake of benefiting the lords of the worlds; our supreme delusion has been dispelled.
Vyāsa said:
Having witnessed the deeds of the Blessed One, those two, Devakī and Vasudeva, attained spiritual insight; and Hari, seeing them, again displayed his illusory power (māyā).
To delude the circle of the gods, he indeed spread out his Vaiṣṇava illusion and said, "O Mother!
O Father! I have long been filled with longing."
"O you two, Saṃkarṣaṇa, who is afraid of Kaṃsa, has seen you;
the time for performing the worship of one's mother and father is passing away."
Indeed, he who causes vain affliction toward the virtuous, as well as toward his teachers, gods, the twice-born, and his mother and father, [is born as such]. (BrP 194.4)
"O father, for a living being who acts [righteously], birth becomes fruitful;
therefore, O father, all this transgression committed by us must be forgiven,
for we were under the control of Kaṃsa’s strength and prowess."
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, both of them then bowed in due order to the elders of the Yadu clan and,
with affectionate prostrations at their feet, won over the hearts of the citizens.
Then Kaṃsa’s wives and his mothers, overwhelmed by grief and sorrow, surrounded him as he lay slain upon the ground and wailed aloud.
Hari himself, his eyes clouded with tears, consoled those women who were in various states of distress and afflicted by remorse.
Then Madhusūdana released Ugrasena from his bonds and likewise consecrated him in his own kingdom, even though his son had been slain.
Consecrated in the kingdom by Kṛṣṇa, that lion of the Yadus performed the funeral rites for his son and for the others who had been slain there.
When he had performed the funeral rites for him and was seated upon the lion throne, Hari said to him:
"O Lord, command without hesitation what task is to be done."
"Due to the curse of Yayāti, this lineage is currently unworthy of sovereignty;
yet, while I stand as your servant, O gods, why should you issue commands through kings?"
Having spoken thus to Ugrasena,
the blessed Keśava, acting in human form, addressed Vāyu in human speech.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Vāyu, go and speak to Indra: 'Enough with your pride, O Vāsava!
Let the Sudharmā assembly hall be given by you to Ugrasena.'"
Kṛṣṇa says: "This unsurpassed jewel, worthy of a king, is called the Sudharmā assembly hall; it is fitting for the Yadus to sit within it."
Vyāsa said:
Having been thus addressed, Pavana went and told everything to the Lord of Śacī; Purandara, for his part, gave the assembly hall named Sudharmā to Vāyu.
And those bulls among the Yadus, taking refuge in the arms of Govinda, enjoyed that divine assembly hall, rich in all kinds of jewels, which had been brought by the wind.
Though they had mastered all branches of knowledge and were composed of universal wisdom,
those two heroes, the best of the Yadus, demonstrated the traditional succession of disciple and teacher.
Then the two heroes, Baladeva and Janārdana, went to Sāndīpani Kāśya, a resident of the city of Avanti, for the sake of learning weapons.
Having entered into discipleship under him, those two heroes, devoted to the conduct due to a teacher, displayed their proper behavior to all people.
O twice-born ones, he studied the science of archery along with its secret doctrines and compendiums; in sixty-four days and nights, that marvelous feat was accomplished.
Reflecting upon their superhuman deed, which was beyond all belief, Sāndīpani then thought that the moon and the sun had arrived there.
Having acquired the entire collection of weapons as soon as it was mentioned, the two of them said,
"Choose whatever guru’s fee (dakṣiṇā) you wish to be given to us."
Having perceived their super-sensory deed,
that high-minded one requested back his dead son from Prabhāsa on the salt ocean.
Then, having taken up their weapons and gone to that salt ocean, the two said to the sea,
"Give us the son of our preceptor."
Then, O best of the twice-born, the Ocean, with palms joined in reverence, said to them:
"I have not carried off the son of Sāndīpani."
O slayer of asuras, that Daitya named Pañcajana, in the form of a conch, seized the boy within my very waters.
Having been addressed thus, Kṛṣṇa went into the water, slew Pañcajana, and took from him that supreme conch shell produced from his bones.
By whose sound the strength of the Daityas is diminished,
the splendor of the gods increases, and unrighteousness goes to its destruction.
Having filled that Pāñcajanya conch and gone to the city of Yama,
Hari and the powerful Baladeva conquered Vaivasvata Yama.
Kṛṣṇa and Bala, the best among the strong, restored that boy— who was situated in torment— to his former body and gave him back to his father.
And Rāma and Janārdana both returned once more to Mathurā, which was protected by Ugrasena, while the men and women there were filled with joy.
Vyāsa said:
O brahmins, the mighty Kaṃsa married the two daughters of Jarāsaṃdha, Asti and Prāpti; yet Hari became the slayer of those two husbands.
Surrounded by a great army, the powerful Jarāsaṃdha, lord of Magadha, advanced in anger to slay [the Yadavas] along with the Yādavas.
Then, having approached Mathurā, the Lord of Magadha besieged it,
surrounded by twenty-three akṣauhiṇīs of his army.
Having gone forth with only a small retinue, both Rāma and Janārdana,
being powerful, fought equally against his mighty soldiers.
Then, O best of sages, Bala and the mighty Kṛṣṇa resolved to take up their ancient weapons.
Immediately thereafter, the discus and the Śārṅga bow, as well as two quivers with inexhaustible arrows, arrived from the sky; then the two heroes appeared, along with the mace Kaumodakī.
O brahmins, the plowshare of Balabhadra and the mace Sunanda, which was dear to Balarāma, descended from the sky.
Then, having defeated the lord of Magadha and his army in battle,
both heroes, Rāma and Janārdana, entered the city.
O best of the twice-born, when that most wicked Jarāsaṃdha had been defeated but remained alive and departed from there, Kṛṣṇa did not consider him truly conquered.
O best of the twice-born, Jarāsaṃdha, accompanied by his army, arrived once again after having been defeated by Rāma and Kṛṣṇa and having done them harm.
Thus, the King of Magadha, who was exceedingly arrogant, fought eighteen battles with the Yadus, led by Kṛṣṇa.
In all those battles, Jarāsandha, though superior in strength, was defeated by the Yadus with only a small force and fled.
That strength of the Yādavas, which has indeed been protected many times over,
is truly due to the majesty of the presence of Viṣṇu, the wielder of the discus, who is their partial incarnation (aṃśa).
That is but the play of the Lord of the universe, who abides in the nature of a human being,
that he hurls weapons of manifold forms against his enemies.
For him who effects the creation and destruction of the universe by his mind alone,
what need is there for extensive effort in the subduing of his enemies?
Nevertheless, such is the duty of men that they follow it;
thus, while making peace with the powerful, he wages war against the weak.
Employing conciliation, bribery, and likewise sowing dissension, he inflicts punishment and sometimes even resorts to flight.
The activity of those possessing human bodies proceeds in this manner;
it is the sport of that Lord of the World, proceeding according to His will.
Vyāsa said:
O twice-born ones, in the cow-pen, a brother-in-law told Gārgya, "You are a eunuch," in the presence of all the Yadus; then all the Yādavas laughed.
Then, overcome with anger, he went to the Deccan and performed austerities,
desiring a son who would bring fear to the Yadu dynasty.
Worshipping Mahādeva, he consumed that powder;
and at the end of twelve years, Hara, being pleased, granted him a boon.
That lord of the Yavanas indeed honored him as his own son;
and from his union with that woman, a son was born to him who possessed the luster of a bee.
Having consecrated that Kālayavana, whose chest was as hard as the tip of a thunderbolt, in his own kingdom, the lord of the Yavanas departed for the forest.
Intoxicated by the pride of his own prowess, he inquired about the powerful kings on earth; and Nārada told him of the Yādavas.
Surrounded by thousands upon thousands of millions of Mlecchas,
he also made a supreme effort, equipped with elephants, horses, and chariots.
O sages, filled with indignation toward the Yādavas, he proceeded day by day toward the city of Mathurā with uninterrupted marches.
Kṛṣṇa also reflected: "Having seen the Yādava army destroyed by the Yavana, the King of Magadha will advance."
The strength of the Magadhan king has been exhausted; that powerful Kālayavana shall be his slayer.
Thus, this twofold calamity has come upon the Yadus.
Therefore, I shall construct a fortress that will be exceedingly difficult for the Yadus to conquer—
a place where even women could fight, let alone the Vṛṣṇis and Yādavas.
Whether I am intoxicated, negligent, asleep, or even away on a journey,
let not the wicked enemies inflict excessive harm upon the Yādavas.
Having reflected thus, Govinda requested twelve yojanas of land from the great ocean; there he constructed the city of Dvārakā.
With its great gardens, its massive ramparts, adorned with hundreds of lakes,
and crowded with hundreds of walls, it was like Indra’s Amarāvatī.
Having brought the people residing in Mathurā there, Janārdana himself went to Mathurā while Kālayavana was nearby.
When the army had encamped outside Mathurā, Govinda went out unarmed;
and the Yavana saw him.
Having recognized him as Vāsudeva, that king, whose weapon was his arms, pursued him—
he who cannot be reached even by the minds of great yogis.
Followed by him, Kṛṣṇa also entered the great cave where the highly heroic King Mucukunda was lying asleep.
That Yavana, having entered, saw a man lying on a bed;
mistaking him for Kṛṣṇa, that evil-minded one struck him with his foot.
O sages, as soon as that Yavana was seen by him, he blazed with the fire born of his wrath and was reduced to ashes in that very instant.
For he, having gone to the war between the gods and asuras and having conquered the great asuras,
being afflicted by sleep, chose from the gods as a boon a very long period of slumber.
And it was declared by the gods: "He who shall awaken you while you are fast asleep will instantly be reduced to ashes by the fire born from your own body."
Having thus burned that wicked one and beheld Madhusūdana, he asked, "Who are you? and he replied, "I am born in the lineage of the Moon."
Mucukunda, the son of Vasudeva born of the Yadu lineage,
having heard this and remembering the words of the aged Gārgya, [acted accordingly].
Having recollected and prostrated before that Hari, the Lord of All, he said:
"O Supreme Lord, you are known; you are a portion of Viṣṇu."
Formerly, it was told by Gārgya that in the twenty-eighth yuga,
at the end of the Dvāpara age, the birth of Hari will take place in the lineage of Yadu.
"You have arrived, there is no doubt, as a benefactor to mortals;
for indeed, I am not able to endure your exceedingly great splendor."
Then, with a voice even more profound than the roar of a vast ocean, he spoke these words to him who had been so tenderly cherished by his feet: "Br̥hatkatha said: (BrP 196.28).
In the great war between the gods and the asuras, even the Daityas, those most mighty warriors, were unable to withstand that great splendor; I, however, cannot endure that splendor.
For a living being fallen into saṃsāra, you alone are the supreme refuge; be gracious, O remover of the distress of those who have sought your protection, and take away my inauspiciousness.
You are the oceans, the mountains, the rivers, and the forests;
you are the earth, the sky, the wind, the waters, and fire, as well as the Supreme Spirit (puruṣa).
Beyond the Puruṣa is the All-pervading, which is free from birth and conceptualization,
devoid of sound and other sense-objects, undecaying, and exempt from growth and decay.
From you come the immortals, the ancestors, the yakṣas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas;
from you come the siddhas, the apsarases, humans, domestic animals, and birds.
All reptiles, wild animals, and trees proceed from you;
and whatever being exists here, whether past or future, among the moving and the unmoving.
Whether formless or formed, gross or likewise most subtle—all that is You, O Creator of the world; there is nothing whatsoever apart from You.
O Blessed One, as I have always wandered in this wheel of saṃsāra,
overcome by the threefold suffering, I have never attained peace anywhere.
"O Lord, I mistook sufferings for pleasures, like a pool of water in a mirage; those things I grasped have resulted only in my torment."
O Lord, [there are] the kingdom, the earth, the army, the treasury, as well as the faction of friends, one's sons,
the wife, the servants, and the objects of the senses such as sound and the rest.
"O Imperishable One, O Lord of Gods, I grasped all this with the notion that it was happiness; yet in its ultimate consequence, it became for me a source of suffering."
O Lord, even the host of gods who have attained the celestial realm became desirous of my assistance; where, then, is eternal liberation?
O Supreme Lord, without propitiating you— the source and abode of all the worlds—
who could ever attain eternal bliss?
Those whose minds are deluded by your māyā, having encountered the evils of birth, death, old age, and so forth,
behold the King of the Pretas in the intermediate state.
Then, bound by hundreds of nooses, they experience great and most terrible suffering in the hells— this manifold form of yours.
O Supreme Lord, I am utterly addicted to sense-objects and deluded by Your Māyā; I wander within the bottomless pit of the notion of "mine-ness."

Thus, with a mind scorched by the exhaustion and torment of saṃsāra, I have come to you for refuge— you who are the shoreless Lord, the one worthy of praise, from whom nothing higher exists, the supreme state.

When he was thus praised by the wise Mucukunda— who was weary of worldly existence, whose splendor had matured, and who was full of longing— Vyāsa said: "At that time, [the Lord] was thus extolled by that intelligent Mucukunda."
Hari, the Lord of all beings, who is without beginning or end, spoke.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O lord of men, go to the divine worlds as you desire,
with your supreme sovereignty unimpeded and augmented by my grace.
Having enjoyed divine and great pleasures, you will be born into a noble family;
through my grace, you will remember your past lives and thereafter attain liberation.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus, the king prostrated before the Lord, the Acyuta of the worlds,
and emerging from the mouth of the cave, he beheld men who were small in stature.
Then, knowing that the Kali Yuga had arrived, the king went to Gandhamādana, the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, in order to perform austerities.
Kṛṣṇa, too, having caused that enemy's army to be destroyed by a stratagem,
went to Mathurā and seized it, resplendent with elephants, horses, and chariots.
Having brought him to Dvāravatī, he presented him to Ugrasena;
and the clan of Yadu became free from fear of defeat by enemies.
O best of Brahmins, Baladeva also, with all his conflicts completely stilled and longing to see his kinsmen, departed for Nanda’s cowherd settlement.
Then, O conqueror of enemies, he greeted the cowherds and cowherdesses with affection and great respect, just as he had done before.
Embraced by some, he in turn embraced others;
likewise, he laughed together with certain cowherds and cowherdesses.
There, the cowherds spoke many pleasant words to Halāyudha,
while the cowherd women, joyful with love, spoke, and others spoke with jealousy.
Other gopīs asked:
"Is Kṛṣṇa, who is beloved by the women of the city, dwelling happily, though he is overwhelmed by the surging essence of love?"
Does the mockery of our actions not perhaps increase the excessive pride in their own good fortune among the city women, whose friendship lasts but a moment?
Does Kṛṣṇa remember that we followed him with songs?
Will he perhaps come even once to see his mother?
Or rather, what is the use of those conversations? Let other stories be told; for without him we shall exist, and without us he shall exist.
Father, mother, brother, husband, and kinsmen—who among these has not been abandoned by us for his sake? Therefore, he is indeed ungrateful.
Nevertheless, please tell me the nectar of your words: does Kṛṣṇa intend to come here and take up residence?
This Dāmodara, this Govinda, whose mind is attached to the women of the city, has lost his affection for us; he appears to us as one difficult to behold.
Vyāsa said:
Addressed as "Kṛṣṇa" and again as "Dāmodara," the gopīs,
their hearts captivated by Hari, laughed with beautiful voices.
The cowherd women were comforted by Rāma with Kṛṣṇa’s messages, which were gentle and sweet, filled with love, free from pride, and uttered in a voice as honeyed as his own.
And in the lands of Vraja, Rāma engaged in conversations with the cowherds as before— conversations charming with humor— and he did so with affection toward them.
Vyāsa said:
While that high-souled Śeṣa, the upholder of the earth, was sporting in the forest with the cowherds in the guise of a human form, [the following occurred].
To him who had accomplished his great task and descended [to earth] for that very purpose,
Varuṇa spoke the Vāruṇī [liquor] excessively for the sake of enjoyment.
Varuṇa said:
"O Madirā, you shall always be the beloved of that one of great majesty;
go, O auspicious one, for the enjoyment and delight of that infinite being."
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by him, Vāruṇī then made her presence known within the hollow of a kadamba tree growing on the bank of Vṛndāvana.
While wandering about, Baladeva also smelled the intense fragrance of wine and then experienced that ancient exhilaration of intoxication.
Then, O sages, seeing a stream of liquor suddenly falling from the Kadamba tree, that wielder of the plow attained supreme joy.
Accompanied by cowherds and cowherdesses, he drank [the milk] filled with joy,
while being serenaded with charming songs by those skilled in singing and instrumental music.
Shimmering with pearl-like droplets of sweat from extreme exertion, he spoke in distress:
"Come, Yamunā, for I wish to bathe."
But that river, disregarding the words spoken by him as if they were those of a madman, did not come;
thereupon the wielder of the plow, filled with rage, seized his plow.
Seizing her by the very bank, he dragged her along, overwhelmed by intoxication:
"O sinful woman, you will not come? You will not come? Go elsewhere as you please!"
Suddenly dragged by him,
that river abandoned its course and flooded that forest where Baladeva was staying.
Then, having approached him in bodily form with eyes agitated by terror, she said to Rāma, "Be gracious! O wielder of the mace, release me!"
He said: "If you disregard my valor and strength, then I shall send you in a thousand pieces with a stroke of my plow."
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus, Balarāma, greatly terrified by that river, was appeased by her;
and since the land there had been flooded, he released the Yamunā.
Then, as he had bathed in the great forest, splendor came to him,
bringing a beautiful lotus for an ear-ornament and a single earring.
And Lakṣmī gave him a garland of unfading lotuses sent by Varuṇa,
as well as two blue garments worthy of the ocean.
Adorned with an ear-ornament and decorated with beautiful earrings,
wearing blue garments and garlands, he shone, endowed with radiant beauty.
Thus adorned, Rāma then took his pleasure there in Vraja;
after two months had passed, he returned once more to the city of Mathurā.
And Bala married Revatī, the daughter of King Raivata; from her were born Niśaṭha and Ulmuka.
Vyāsa said:
O twice-born ones, King Bhīṣmaka reigned in Kuṇḍina, in the region of Vidarbha;
his daughter was Rukmiṇī, and his son was Rukmin.
Kṛṣṇa desired Rukmiṇī, and she of the lovely smile desired him;
yet Rukmin, out of hatred, did not give her to the wielder of the discus even when he entreated her.
Urged by Jarāsandha,
that king of great prowess, Bhīṣmaka, gave Rukmiṇī to Śiśupāla along with Rukmin.
Then, for the sake of the marriage, all the kings headed by Jarāsaṃdha,
as well as Śiśupāla, went to Kuṇḍina, the city of Bhīṣmaka.
Kṛṣṇa also, surrounded by the Yadus led by Balabhadra,
set out for Kuṇḍina to witness the marriage of the King of Cedi.
When the wedding was to take place on the following day, Hari abducted that maiden,
having adopted an adversarial stance toward his kinsmen, Rāma and the others.
And then there were the illustrious Pauṇḍraka, Dantavakra, Vidūratha,
Śiśupāla, Jarāsandha, and kings such as Śālva and others.
Enraged, they made a supreme effort to slay Hari,
but having come together, they were defeated by Rāma and the other bulls among the Yadus.
"I will not enter Kuṇḍina without having slain Keśava in battle";
having made this vow, Rukmin rushed toward Kṛṣṇa to kill him.
Having destroyed that army crowded with elephants, horses, foot-soldiers,
and chariots, he was conquered and cast down to the earth by the wielder of the discus with effortless ease.
Having completely defeated Rukmin,
Madhusūdana, having arrived there, duly married Rukmiṇī according to the Rākṣasa rite.
And from her was born the heroic Pradyumna, a portion of Madana;
he was indeed the one whom Śambara abducted, and he was the one who slew Śambara.
The sages said:
"How was the hero Pradyumna recovered by Śambara?
And how was the immensely powerful Śambara slain by Pradyumna?"
Vyāsa said:
O twice-born ones, on the sixth day after he was born, Kālaśambara seized Pradyumna from the maternity chamber, thinking, "This one is the slayer of mine."
Having led him there, the crocodile cast him into the front of the salt ocean,
into that most terrible abode of sea-monsters filled with whirlpools generated by the surging waves.
And there, one fish swallowed the fallen boy;
yet he did not die, even though scorched by the fire within its belly.
O twice-born ones, that fish was killed by fishermen along with other fish and presented to Śambara, the foremost of the asuras.
His blameless wife, named Māyāvatī, who was the mistress of the entire household,
exercised authority over the cooks.
When the belly of the fish was torn open, there was seen a most beautiful youth,
like the first sprout of the tree of Love that had been consumed by fire.
"Who is this? How has she come to be within the belly of a fish?
To that slender woman, thus overcome with curiosity, Nārada spoke.
Nārada said: This son of Kṛṣṇa has been carried away from the lying-in chamber by Śambara, the one who effects the creation and destruction of all the worlds.
"Cast into the ocean, swallowed by a fish, and brought under its power—
O fair-browed one, protect this jewel among men with confidence."
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by Nārada, she protected that infant;
from childhood itself, she was infatuated with him by an excessive passion, deluded by his extraordinary beauty.
O best of the twice-born, when he was adorned with the fullness of youth,
she, who moved with the gait of an elephant, then became filled with desire for him.
Māyāvatī bestowed all her magical powers upon that great-souled Pradyumna, who was as dear to her as her own life, for her heart and eyes were fixed entirely upon him;
but as she remained clinging to him, that lotus-eyed son of Kṛṣṇa spoke to her.
Pradyumna said:
Why do you behave otherwise, having completely abandoned the disposition of a mother?
Vyāsa said:
And she said to him, "You are certainly not my son;
this Kālaśambara has carried you away from Viṣṇu as his own offspring."
Cast into the ocean, I was obtained by a fish from its belly;
yet your mother, so exceedingly affectionate, weeps for you even now, my beloved.
Vyāsa said:
Thus addressed, the mighty Pradyumna challenged Śambara to battle;
with a mind agitated by anger, he fought.
Having utterly destroyed that Daitya’s army, the son of Mādhavī bypassed his seven illusions and employed the eighth illusion.
With that illusory power, she struck down the Daitya Kālaśambara,
and having leapt up, she returned with him to her father’s city.
Seeing him fallen in the inner apartments together with Māyāvatī,
the wives of Kṛṣṇa became joyful in their intentions;
and the blameless Rukmiṇī, her gaze fixed upon him with love, spoke out of affection.
Rukmiṇī said:
"Blessed indeed is she whose son exists in the bloom of youth;
if only my own son Pradyumna were alive at this same age."
"O child, some mother has been truly blessed by being adorned with you as her son.
Or rather, considering the nature of my affection and the likeness of your body,
it is quite evident, my child, that you must be the offspring of Hari."
Vyāsa said:
In the meantime, Nārada arrived together with Kṛṣṇa and,
filled with joy, spoke to the queen Rukmiṇī, the foremost lady of the inner apartments.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O fair-browed one, here is your son who has returned after slaying Śambara;
he is the one by whom your son was previously carried away from the maternity chamber.
This wife of yours, Māyāvatī, is virtuous;
she is not the wife of Śambara. Hear now the reason for this.
When Manmatha had met his destruction,
