O Rukmiṇī, she who was devoted to his manifestation deluded Śambara by means of a magical form.
During the enjoyment of their wedding and other festivities, she— this woman with intoxicating eyes— manifested a beautiful form composed of illusion before that Daitya.
"Kāma has descended as your son; this Rati is his beloved.
You should have no doubt in this matter; she is your beautiful daughter-in-law."
Vyāsa said:
Then Rukmiṇī and Keśava were filled with joy, and that entire city exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! (BrP 200.29).
Then, seeing Rukmiṇī reunited with her son who had been lost for so long,
all the people in Dvāravatī were struck with wonder.
Vyāsa said:
Cārudeṣṇa, Sudeṣṇa, the beautiful Cārudeha, Suṣeṇa, Cārugupta, and another, Bhadracāru.
Rukmiṇī gave birth to sons— Cāruvinda, Sucāru, and Cāru, the best among the strong— as well as a daughter, Cārumatī.
Kṛṣṇa also had seven other beautiful wives: Kālindī, Mitravindā, Satyā, and likewise Nāgnajitī; [and further] Śaibyā, Bhadrā, and Lakṣmaṇā.
Queen Jāmbavatī was always contented, as was Rohiṇī; and there was another, the daughter of the King of Madra, Suśīlā, who was a circle of virtuous conduct.
Satyabhāmā, the daughter of Satrājit, and Lakṣmaṇā of the lovely smile— these,
along with sixteen thousand other women, belonged to the wielder of the discus.
The immensely powerful Pradyumna also took the auspicious daughter of Rukmin at her svayaṃvara; she, too, chose that son of Hari.
From her was born to him a son of great strength and prowess,
Aniruddha, who was irresistible in battle, an ocean of valor, and a subduer of his enemies.
Keśava also chose the granddaughter of that Rukmin as his bride;
and although Rukmin was competing with Śauri, he gave her to his grandson.
O twice-born ones, for her wedding, Rāma and the other Yādavas, together with Hari,
went to the city of Rukmin named Bhojakaṭa.

When that marriage of the high-souled Pradyumna had been concluded, the kings headed by the King of Kaliṅga spoke these words to Rukmin: BrP_201.10: "When that marriage of the high-souled Pradyumna had been concluded, the kings headed by the King of Kaliṅga spoke these words to Rukmin."
The Kaliṅgas and others said:
"O one of great splendor, the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) is unskilled at dice and possesses a great addiction to gambling;
therefore, let us lead his army away by means of a game of dice itself."
Vyāsa said:
"So be it," Rukmī, endowed with great strength, said to those kings;
and then, together with Rāma, he engaged in a game of dice in the assembly hall.
On the first day, Balarāma was defeated by Rukmin with one thousand gold coins;
on the second day, he was likewise defeated by Rukmin with another thousand.
Then Rukmin, the best among those skilled in gambling, accepted a wager of ten thousand gold coins from Balabhadra.
Then, O twice-born ones, the foolish lord of Kaliṅga abandoned his strength;
showing his teeth, the arrogant Rukmī spoke.
Rukmin said:
"In this great gambling match, this Balabhadra was defeated while ignorant of the game; it was all in vain that he, out of pride in his skill with dice, considered himself an expert at dice."
Upon seeing the King of Kaliṅga with his teeth bared in a snarl,
and Rukmin as well speaking such wicked words, Halāyudha was filled with rage.
Vyāsa said:
Then Halāyudha, his soul overcome with anger,
took up ten million gold pieces as the stake, and Rukmī likewise cast the dice.
Then Baladeva conquered him and said loudly, "He has been defeated by me! Rukmin, however, cried out loudly, "He is mine! Enough of this false talk, O Bala!"
"This stake proposed by you is true; it was not approved by me.
If it has been won by you in this manner, how can it be said that it was won by me?"
Then, a voice resounded loudly and deeply from the sky,
increasing the anger of the high-souled Baladeva.
Ākāśavāc said:
"Baladeva has indeed conquered; what was spoken by Rukmin is false.
Without uttering a single word, the deed has been accomplished through action alone."
Vyāsa said:
Then the mighty Bala, rising up with eyes bloodshot with rage,
struck Rukmin with his very dice-board (aṣṭāpada).
And seizing the King of Kaliṅga as he struggled with force, the powerful Balarāma,
enraged, broke the teeth with which he had laughed aloud.
And having pulled up a great pillar made of gold, the powerful Bala,
filled with rage, struck down those kings who were on that side.
Then, O twice-born ones, when that army was enraged, the entire circle of kings cried out "Alas! Alas! and became intent on flight.
Having heard that Rukmin had been slain by Bala, Madhusūdana did not say anything at all, out of fear for Rukmiṇī and Bala.
Then, O best of the twice-born, having taken Aniruddha after his marriage was performed,
the host of Yadus together with Keśava returned to Dvārakā.
Vyāsa said:
Then, O sages, Śakra, the lord of the three worlds, arrived at Dvāravatī upon the back of his intoxicated Airāvata to see Śauri.
Then, having entered Dvārakā and approached Hari,
he related the deeds of the Daitya Naraka.
Indra said:
"O Madhusūdana, with you as their protector— even while remaining in human form— all the sufferings of the gods have been brought to pacification."
For the protection of the ascetics, Ariṣṭa, Dhenuka,
as well as Pralamba and the others, and Keśin— all of them have been slain by you.
Kaṃsa, Kuvalayāpīḍa, Pūtanā the slayer of infants,
and all others who were harbingers of calamity to the world— every one of them has been brought to destruction by you.
When the three worlds have been protected by the awakening power of your staff-like arms,
the gods attain satisfaction by consuming the sacrificial oblations at the sacrifice.
O Janārdana, having heard the reason for which I have now come,
you ought to make an effort to provide a remedy for it.
O subduer of enemies, this lord of Prāgjyotiṣapura, named Bhauma Nāraka, inflicts injury upon all living beings.
O Janārdana, having slain the gods, siddhas, suras, and kings, that asura confined the maidens in his own palace.
He seized the water-dripping parasol of Varuṇa,
and likewise he carried off the peak of Mount Mandara, the mountain of jewels.
That asura seized my mother’s two divine nectar-dripping earrings,
for he desired the elephant Airāvata.
"O Govinda, this was ill-advised that I said to you;
let that which must be done in this matter be considered by yourself."
Vyāsa said:
Having heard this and smiling, the Blessed One, the son of Devakī,
took Vāsava by the hand and rose from his excellent seat.
Having mounted his well-considered Garuḍa, who travels through the sky,
and having placed Satyabhāmā upon him, he went to the city of Prāgjyotiṣa.
Then Śakra, having mounted the elephant Airāvata, departed for the abode of the thirty gods with a joyful mind, even as the inhabitants of Dvārakā looked on.
For a hundred yojanas all around this city of Prāgjyotiṣapura,
it was covered with terrifying nooses for the purpose of warding off enemy armies.
Hari cut those nooses asunder by hurling his Sudarśana discus;
then Mura rose up, and Keśava struck him down.
Then Hari reduced those seven thousand sons of Mura to ashes with the fire of his discus's edge, like moths.
O twice-born ones, having slain Mura, Hayagrīva, and likewise Pañcajana,
the wise one swiftly rushed toward the city of Prāgjyotiṣa.
There, Kṛṣṇa Govinda engaged in battle with Naraka’s great army, wherein he slew the Daityas by the thousands.
The powerful wielder of the discus, the slayer of the hosts of Daityas, hurled his discus and split in two Bhauma Naraka as he was discharging a rain of weapons and missiles.
Then, having seized the earth together with Ādi and Kuṇḍala, Hāṭaka appeared before the Lord of the World and spoke these words: BrP_202.22 //
Dharaṇī said:
"O Lord, when I was uplifted by you in the form of a boar,
this son, born from your touch, was then produced within me."
"This very man was given to me by you alone, and by you alone he has been struck down.
Take these two earrings and protect his lineage."
O Lord, O gracious and benevolent Master, it was for the sake of removing my very burden that you, the Blessed One, came to this world with a portion of yourself.
You are the creator, the transformer, and the destroyer; you are the source, the imperishable, and that which is the very nature of the world. O Acyuta, what can be praised by me of you?
The Lord is always all-pervading and the pervaded, the action, the agent, and the effect;
since You are the Self of the Self that has become the self of all beings, O Acyuta, how can You be praised by me?
Since you are the Supreme Self, the individual self, and the imperishable self of all beings, there is no praise possible; for what purpose, then, should it proceed?
Be gracious, O Soul of all beings! Whatever has been done by Naraka, let that be forgiven so that there may be no fault; he was struck down because he was my son.
Vyāsa said:
Having replied "So be it" to the Earth, O best of sages, the Blessed One, the creator of all beings, took the jewels from the abode of Naraka.
O best of the twice-born, in the maidens' quarters, he of incomparable prowess beheld more than sixteen hundred maidens.
He beheld six thousand fierce elephants with four tusks each,
as well as twenty-one hundred thousand horses from Kamboja.
And Govinda, by means of Naraka’s servants, immediately brought those maidens, as well as those nāgas and horses, to the city of Dvārakā.
Hari beheld the umbrella of Varuṇa as well as the mountain of jewels;
he then placed them upon Garuḍa, the lord of birds.
And having ascended it himself, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Satyabhāmā,
went to the abode of the gods in order to give the earrings of Aditi.
Vyāsa said:
Carrying the umbrella of Varuṇa as well as the mountain of jewels,
Garuḍa proceeded with ease, bearing Hṛṣīkeśa together with his wife.
Then, having blown his conch shell, Hari went to the gateway of heaven;
thereupon the gods approached Janārdana bearing vessels of *arghya*.
Worshipped by the gods, Kṛṣṇa entered the residence of the mother of the gods,
which resembled the peak of a white cloud, and beheld Aditi.
Having bowed to her, Janārdana, together with Śakra, gave her those two excellent earrings and announced to her the destruction of Naraka.
Then Aditi, the mother of the world, being pleased, composed her mind with single-minded devotion and praised Hari, the sustainer of the worlds, who remained unperturbed.
Aditi said:
Homage to you, O lotus-eyed one, who grants fearlessness to your devotees;
O eternal Self, Self of all beings, Universal Self, creator of all creatures!
O guide of the mind, intellect, and senses, whose nature consists of the qualities,
you who are entirely free from conceptual constructions such as "white" or "long."
Untouched by birth and other such states, free from dreams and the like,
[he is] twilight, night, day, earth, sky, wind, and water.
O Acyuta, you are the sacrificial fire, the mind, the intellect, and the source of the elements;
you are the creator of creation, preservation, and destruction, and the Lord of all agents.
Through his own forms known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva,
the Lord pervades this entire world of moving and unmoving beings by means of his powers of illusion (māyās).
O Janārdana, that cognition of a self in what is not-self is your illusion (māyā),
by which the notion of "I" and "mine" arises therein.
O Lord, this is the play of your illusion within the midst of saṃsāra,
by which you have been propitiated by those men who are devoted to their own duty.
For the sake of their own liberation, all these— Brahmā and the other gods, as well as humans and animals— cross over this entire illusion.
Enveloped by the blinding darkness of delusion within the great whirlpool of Viṣṇu’s Māyā,
they worship you so that their desires may be fulfilled at the end of their own existence.
"O Blessed One, those men were bound at your feet by your illusory power;
I, desiring a son and for the destruction of the enemy faction, [bound you]."
Even when propitiated, that does not lead to liberation, for it is merely a play of illusion;
for even from the wish-fulfilling tree, one's desire is limited to obtaining only a loincloth and clothing.
That which arises for those devoid of merit is an offense born of one's own fault;
therefore, be gracious, O Imperishable One who creates the delusion of Māyā for the entire world!
O Lord of beings, destroy this ignorance which is the very essence of [false] knowledge;
salutations to You who hold the discus in hand, and salutations to You who hold the Śārṅga bow in hand.
O Viṣṇu, salutations to you who hold a mace in your hand, salutations to you who hold a conch in your hand.
I behold this form of yours, adorned with gross attributes;
I do not know that which is beyond it. Be gracious, O Supreme Lord!
Vyāsa said:
Thus praised by Aditi, Viṣṇu smiled and spoke to the source of the gods.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Goddess, you are our mother; be gracious and grant us boons.
Aditi said:
"Let it be so, according to your wish; O tiger among men, you shall be invincible by all the gods and asuras without exception in the world of mortals."
Vyāsa said:
Immediately thereafter, Satyabhāmā bowed down before Diti, who was accompanied by Śakrāṇī, and said to her again and again, "Be gracious."
Aditi said:
"By my grace, O fair-browed one, neither old age nor deformity shall befall you;
O lady of faultless limbs, you shall have all your desires fulfilled."
Vyāsa said:
Having received permission from Aditi, the king of the gods duly honored Janārdana with great respect.
Then, O best of men, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Satyabhāmā, beheld all the celestial gardens, such as Nandana and the others.
And he beheld a divine tree, rich in fragrance, bearing clusters of blossoms,
providing cool refreshment, and adorned with copper-colored shoots.

O best of the twice-born, while the nectar was being churned, the Pārijāta tree— possessing a luster equal to gold— was produced; seeing it, Satyabhāmā spoke to Govinda, the Lord of the World and slayer of Keśin.
Satyabhāmā said:
"Why is this tree not being taken to Dvārakā by Kṛṣṇa?
If that word of yours is true—that Satyā is exceedingly dear to you—then let it be so."
"Let this tree be taken to my house for the purpose of a pleasure garden;
neither Jāmbavatī nor Rukmiṇī is as dear to me as she."
"Regarding truth, you have repeatedly spoken what is pleasing to Kṛṣṇa, saying 'As you are, so [is she],' O Govinda; if those words were true and not merely a figure of speech."
"Let this Pārijāta tree be the ornament of my home; I desire that,
wearing a cluster of Pārijāta blossoms in my mass of hair,
I may shine in the midst of my co-wives."
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus, Hari laughed and placed that Pārijāta tree upon Garuḍa; then the guardians of the grove spoke to him.
The forest guards said:
"O Govinda, Śacī is the queen of the king of the gods; you ought not to take away the Pārijāta tree, which is her possession."
This was produced by the gods during the churning for the nectar of immortality for the sake of adorning Śacī;
it is not safe, so you shall not depart having taken it.
Out of folly you seek this; who, being secure, would go taking him?
O Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Gods will certainly undergo a transformation because of him.

The immortals will follow Śakra as he raises his vajra in hand; therefore, O Acyuta, enough with all these gods and this conflict of yours! The wise do not praise that karma which is bitter in its ripening.
Vyāsa said:
When they had spoken thus, Satyabhāmā, becoming exceedingly angry, spoke to them.
Satyabhāmā said:
Who is Śacī, and who is Śakra, the lord of the gods, regarding the Pārijāta tree?
If this tree was common to all the worlds during the churning for the nectar of immortality.
Why was it that, in the past, Vāsava alone took possession [of her] as soon as she was born,
just as the gods, the moon, Śrī, and the forest-protectors did?
Furthermore, Śacī obstructed this Pārijāta tree, which is common to all the world,
by means of the great pride of her husband’s arm.
Therefore, go quickly and tell Paulomī my words;
Satyabhāmā speaks thus, in words haughty with pride in her husband.
"If you are the beloved of your husband, and if you are indeed dear to him,
then cause my husband's tree, which is being taken away, to be stopped."
I know your husband to be Śakra; I know him to be the lord of the thirty-three gods.
Nevertheless, as a mere mortal woman, I shall take this Pārijāta tree from you.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus, the guards went and spoke loudly exactly as they had been told;
and Śacī encouraged her husband, the lord of the thirty gods.
Then, O twice-born ones, Indra, surrounded by the armies of all the gods, set out to fight Hari for the sake of the Pārijāta tree.
Then, while Śakra stood with the thunderbolt in his hand, the gods became ready for battle, bearing weapons such as iron clubs, swords, maces, and spears.
Then Govinda beheld Śakra, accompanied by his retinue of gods, standing upon the king of serpents and prepared for battle.
Filling the quarters with the sound,
he blew his conch shell and released a multitude of arrows numbering in the tens of thousands.
Then, seeing the quarters and the sky covered with hundreds of arrows,
all the gods released their weapons and missiles many times over.
The Lord Madhusūdana, the master of the worlds, effortlessly cut into a thousand pieces each missile and weapon discharged by the gods.
Having dragged the noose of the Lord of Waters, the devourer of serpents moved along,
tearing it into pieces like the body of a young snake.
The Blessed One, the son of Devakī, caused the staff sent by Yama to fall upon the earth, having shattered it with his mace.
The omnipresent Śauri reduced the palanquin of the Lord of Wealth to pieces as small as sesame seeds with his discus,
while the sun and moon had their power destroyed by the mere fall of his glance.
The fire was led away by hundreds of arrows, the Vasus were driven in all directions,
and the Rudras, their spear-tips shattered by his discus, were cast down upon the earth.
The Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas,
and the Maruts were all driven by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow with his arrows into the sky like the down of a silk-cotton tree.
And Garuḍa, that bird, constantly struck and devoured the gods and the Dānavas with his beak, his two wings, and his sharp talons.
Then, with a thousand arrows, Devendra and Madhusūdana showered each other like two rain-clouds with torrents of water.
In that tumultuous conflict, Garuḍa fought with Airāvata;
and Janārdana fought with Śakra and all the assembled gods.
When his weapons and missiles were shattered and broken, Vāsava quickly seized his thunderbolt and Kṛṣṇa took up his Sudarśana discus.

Then, upon seeing the king of gods and Janārdana wielding the thunderbolt and the discus, the entire triple world, including all things mobile and immobile, broke out into cries of "Alas! Alas! (hāhākṛta).
Then the Blessed Lord Hari caught the thunderbolt hurled by Indra;
he did not release his discus at that time, but said, "Stay! Stay! (BrP 203.62).
To the lord of gods, whose vajra was lost and whose vehicle had been wounded by Garuḍa,
who was intent on flight, Satyabhāmā spoke these words:
Satyabhāmā said:
"O Lord of the three worlds, it is not fitting for the husband of Śacī to flee;
Śacī herself will attend upon you with the full splendor of a garland of *pārijāta* flowers."
"O Lord, what kind of kingdom is this for you, who do not see Śacī as she did before— radiant with a garland of *pārijāta* flowers and come to you out of affection?"
"Enough of this effort, Śakra; you ought not to feel shame.
Let this Pārijāta tree be taken away, and let the gods be free from their distress."
Due to the arrogance and pride born of her husband’s status,
Śacī did not receive me with honor or proper hospitality when I arrived at her home.
"O Śakra, because I am a woman, my mind was not heavy [with pride], and I was intent on praising my own husband; therefore, I entered into a dispute with you."
Therefore, enough with the Pārijāta tree, or with stolen property;
what woman would not be proud of her own beauty and fame? (BrP 203.69)
Vyāsa said:
O twice-born ones, when this had been said, the king of the gods desisted from her;
and he said to her, "Enough, O fierce one, friend; enough with these excessive lamentations."
Furthermore, I feel no shame before him who is the creator of the creation, destruction, and maintenance of everything, for I have been conquered by that one whose form is the universe.

In whom this entire world exists without beginning or middle, from whom it arises, and into whom it shall cease to be as the soul of all beings— by that cause of creation, dissolution, and preservation;

O Goddess, how can there be shame for one who has been rejected? He whose form is the entirety of the worlds, who is subtle and exceedingly minute, and who is known by those who have mastered all the Vedas, but not by others— how can he feel shame?
Who is capable of conquering that unborn, uncreated Lord, the eternal and primordial benefactor of the world, who acts by his own will? Vyāsa said:
O best of the twice-born, having been thus praised by the king of the gods, Keśava smiled and spoke these words with profound sincerity.
The Blessed One said:
"O Lord of the World, you are Indra, the king of the gods, while we are mortals;
therefore, this offense committed by me must be forgiven by you alone."
"And let this Pārijāta tree be taken to its proper place;
O Śakra, it was accepted by me for the sake of making Satyabhāmā’s word come true."
"And take this vajra; it has been sent by you to be used as a weapon.
O Śakra, this is your very own missile for rending your enemies."
Śakra said: "O Lord, why do you delude me by saying, 'I am a mortal'?
We know you to be the Blessed One, the knower of infinite bliss."
"Whoever you may be, O Lord of the World, you remain established in worldly activity;
O Destroyer of Asuras, you extract the thorn from the world."
"O Kṛṣṇa, let this Pārijāta tree be taken to the city of Dvāravatī;
once you have departed from the world of mortals, it shall no longer remain upon the earth."
Vyāsa said:
Having said, "So be it," Hari came to the earth before the lord of the gods,
being praised by Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Rishis who had assembled for that purpose.
Kṛṣṇa suddenly departed, taking that excellent tree with him;
then, standing above Dvārakā, he blew his conch shell.
O twice-born ones, having descended from Garuḍa accompanied by Satyabhāmā, he produced great joy among the inhabitants of Dvārakā.
He established the great Pārijāta tree in his pleasure garden;
by approaching it, every person remembers their former birth.
The earth for three yojanas was perfumed by the fragrance of whose flowers;
from that [tree], all those Yādavas [received] divine, superhuman scents.
As they looked up at that tree,
they beheld wealth consisting of elephants, horses, and other riches brought forward by the *kiṃkaras*.
And Kṛṣṇa took those women from the possession of Naraka;
then, when an auspicious time had arrived, Janārdana married them.
O best of the twice-born, Govinda brought together in a single place all those maidens who had been gathered from every part of the abode of hell by means of his power.
In accordance with his own dharma, he took the hands of sixteen thousand one hundred women as wives, each in her own body, according to the prescribed rites.
The Blessed One Madhusūdana assumed as many forms,
and each of those maidens perceived Madhusūdana individually.
"Govinda has taken my very hand," [they thought]. O brahmins, during the nights, Keśava Hari, the creator of the world, dwelt in the houses of all those women, assuming his universal form.
Vyāsa said:
O twice-born ones, Pradyumna and the others are declared to be the sons of Hari born of Rukmiṇī;
and Satyabhāmā gave birth to Bhānu and his other sons.
Prapakṣa and others, the sons of Rohiṇī, were radiant followers of Hari;
and from Jāmbavatī were born Sāmba and others, who were possessed of mighty arms.
Bhadravinda and others were the sons of great strength born to Nāgnajiti;
while Saṃgrāmajit and others were the sons born to Śaibyā.
Mādrī, however, bore sons beginning with Gātravat,
while Lakṣmaṇā obtained sons such as Kālindya, Śruta, and others.
And from his other wives as well,
one hundred and eighty thousand sons were born to the wielder of the discus.
Pradyumna was the foremost among them, the son of Rukmiṇī;
from Pradyumna was born Aniruddha, and from him Vajra was born.
O best of the twice-born, the mighty Aniruddha, though obstructed in battle by Bali’s grandson, married Bāṇa’s daughter, Ūṣā.
There occurred a great and terrible battle between Hari and Śaṅkara,
wherein the thousand arms of Bāṇa were severed by the wielder of the discus.
The sages said:
O Brahmin, how did the battle between Hara and Kṛṣṇa for the sake of Uṣā take place?
And how did Hari bring about the destruction of Bāṇa’s arms?
O illustrious one, you ought to tell us all of this in its entirety;
a great curiosity has arisen in us to hear this auspicious narrative.
Vyāsa said:
O brahmins, having observed Pārvatī sporting with Śambhu, Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa,
then felt a great longing for it herself.
Then Gaurī, who knows the minds of all, spoke to that beautiful woman.
Gaurī said:
Enough with this remorse; you too shall take delight with your husband.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus, she then turned her mind to the thought, "When [will this happen]? or "Who will be my husband? To her, Pārvatī spoke again:
Pārvatī said:
"O princess, he who shall overcome you in a dream on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha will become your husband."
Vyāsa said:
On that lunar day, just as she had been instructed by the Goddess in her dream,
the man overcame her, and she felt passion for him there.
Then, having awakened and not seeing that man, she became anxious for him.
Uṣā said:
"Where have you gone? Thus the shameless woman spoke to her friend.
Bāṇa’s minister was Kumbhāṇḍa, and Citralekhā was his daughter.
She had a female friend, and she asked her, "Who is this being spoken of by you?
When she was overcome with shame and did not tell her friend, that friend spoke.

Then, having inspired confidence, she related everything exactly as it had been told by the goddess; and once it was understood, Uṣā spoke to her again: "Employ that very means which has been described for the attainment of him."
Vyāsa said: Then Citralekhā, having painted upon a canvas the gods, Daityas, Gandharvas, and humans according to their preeminence, showed it to him.
Having set aside the Gandharvas, as well as the Uragas, Suras, and Asuras,
she fixed her gaze upon men, and even among them, upon the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis.
O brahmins, upon seeing Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, the fair-browed woman’s eyes became filled with shame; then, at the sight of Pradyumna, she cast her gaze down in modesty.
Having seen Aniruddha, her shame was cast aside somewhere; when she said, "This is he! This is he! He is mine! that friend who travels by yoga departed for Dvāravatī after having comforted Ūṣā.
Vyāsa said:
Bāṇa also, having prostrated himself before him, then spoke to the Three-eyed One.
Bāṇa said:
"O Lord, I am weary of these thousand arms without battle;
will there be a war that shall bring fruitfulness to these arms of mine?"
If it shall come to pass without battle, what use are my arms as a burden?
Śaṃkara said: "O Bāṇa, when the breaking of your peacock-banner occurs,
you shall then attain a battle that brings joy to the flesh-eaters."
Vyāsa said:
Then, having bowed to Śambhu, he returned home delighted;
and seeing the banner broken, he was thrilled and attained supreme joy.
At that very time, however, her excellent friend Citralekhā brought Aniruddha there by the power of the science of yoga.
Having learned that he was sporting with Uṣā in the midst of the maiden's inner apartments,
the guards went and reported it to the Daitya king.
Taking up an iron club, that slayer of enemy heroes struck the army of servants commanded by that high-souled one.
When those arrows were exhausted, Bāṇa, remaining on his chariot and intent on slaying him,
fought to the best of his ability until he was defeated by the hero.
Then, impelled by mantras, he fought with him using illusion;
and thereafter, he bound the joy of the Yadus with the serpent-weapon (*pannagāstra*).
To the Yadus who were lamenting in Dvāravatī, "Where has Aniruddha gone?",
Nārada announced that he had been bound by Bāṇa.
Having heard that he had been led away to Śoṇitapura by a woman skilled in magic, the Yādavas believed that his death was certain.
Then Hari, having mounted Garuḍa— who arrived as soon as he was thought of—
together with Bala and Pradyumna, set out for the city of Bāṇa.
Upon entering the city, there was a battle with the mighty Pramathas;
Hari led them to their destruction and proceeded to the vicinity of Bāṇa’s city.
Then the great fever of Maheśvara, three-legged and three-headed,
fought most fiercely with the wielder of the Śārṅga bow for the sake of protecting Bāṇa.
Even Baladeva experienced the burning sensation produced by the touch of those ashes through contact with Kṛṣṇa’s body, as he closed his eyes in pain.
Then, while fighting with the divine wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
he was swiftly cast out from Kṛṣṇa’s body by the Vaiṣṇava fever.
Seeing him overwhelmed by the crushing blow from Nārāyaṇa’s arm, the divine Grandfather said, "Let this be forgiven for him."
Then, saying "It is forgiven," the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana caused that Vaiṣṇava fever to dissolve into himself alone.
"Those men who shall remember my battle with you will be free from all feverish distress," having said this to him, Hari departed.
Then the Blessed One, having conquered and likewise brought to destruction the five fires,
Viṣṇu effortlessly crushed the army of the Dānavas.
Then, with his entire army, Bali’s son fought against Śaṅkara, as well as Kārttikeya and Śauri.
The battle between Hari and Śaṅkara was exceedingly terrible;
all the worlds were agitated, afflicted in many ways by their weapons and missiles.
While that great battle was raging, the gods thought, "Surely this dissolution of the entire world has arrived."
With the Jṛmbhaṇa weapon, Govinda caused Śaṅkara to yawn;
thereupon the Daityas and the Pramathas fled in every direction.
Overcome by yawning, Hara sat down on the seat of his chariot;
he was then unable to fight with Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless.
With his arm wounded by Garuḍa and tormented by Pradyumna’s weapon,
Guha— his spear shaken off by Kṛṣṇa’s roar of "Huṃ"— departed.
When Śaṃkara had yawned and vanished, when the army of the Daityas was destroyed, when Guha was conquered, and when the host of Pramathas was brought to ruin by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
Mounted upon a great chariot whose horses were guided by Nandīśa,
Bāṇa arrived there to fight against the forces of Kṛṣṇa, Pradyumna, and Balarāma.
The immensely powerful Balabhadra pierced Bāṇa’s army in many ways with his arrows, while Pradyumna retreated in accordance with the rules of dharma.
Bāṇa beheld his own army dragged by the tip of the wielder's plow, crushed by his mace, and struck down by the power of the Discus-bearer’s arrows.
Then, in brief, there was a battle between Kṛṣṇa and Bāṇa,
in which they fiercely discharged at one another arrows that pierced both bodies and armor.
Kṛṣṇa cut down those arrows discharged by Bāṇa with his own shafts;
Bāṇa pierced Keśava, while the wielder of the discus struck Bāṇa.
O twice-born ones, Bāṇa and Kṛṣṇa then discharged missiles at one another in their desire for victory, intent on wounding each other, and likewise hurled iron clubs.
When all his weapons and missiles had been completely cut down and were failing him,
Hari then set his mind upon killing Bāṇa by means of a great abundance of arrows.
Then Hari, the enemy of the host of Daityas, seized the Sudarśana discus, whose splendor was equal to the brilliance produced by a hundred suns.
As the enemy of Madhu was discharging that discus for the destruction of Bāṇa,
the naked Koṭarī, a magical power of the Daityas, appeared before Hari.
Seeing her before him, Hari closed his eyes and released the Sudarśana [discus],
aiming it at the enemy's forest of arms in order to cut them down.
Then, as the Asura Bāṇa swiftly discharged his weapons and missiles, Acyuta quickly and gradually cut off his arms.
When that forest of arms was severed, Madhusūdana,
desiring to release it for the destruction of Bāṇa, was recognized by the enemy of Tripura.
Having looked upon Bāṇa, who was raining down streams of blood from the severed trunks of his arms, the Lord of Umā leaped up and spoke to Govinda with conciliatory words.
Rudra said:
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the World, I know you to be the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama),
the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self, without beginning or end, the Transcendent.
Among gods, animals, and humans, this assumption of bodies is indeed your sport, characterized by the slaying of the Daityas.
Therefore, O Lord, be gracious; this assurance of safety has been granted by me to Bāṇa.
Consequently, you must not render false the word that has been spoken by me.
"O Imperishable One, this Daitya has grown through our protection;
he has received a boon from me, and therefore I beg your forgiveness."
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus, Govinda, with a serene countenance and his anger toward the asura subsided, spoke to the trident-bearing Lord of Umā.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Śaṅkara, let this Bāṇa live, for he has been granted a boon by you;
out of respect for your word, I have withdrawn this discus."
"O Śaṅkara, that fearlessness which was granted by you has been granted by me as well; you ought to perceive yourself as non-different from me."
I am you, and this world with its gods, asuras, and humans;
it is only men whose selves are deluded by ignorance who perceive things as distinct.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa departed for where Pradyumna’s son was staying;
the serpents that bound him perished, dried up by the wind from Garuḍa.
Then, having placed Aniruddha along with his wife upon Garuḍa,
Rāma, Kārṣṇi, and Dāmodara returned to the city of Dvārakā.
The sages said:
Śauri performed great deeds while assuming a human body;
he conquered Śakra, Śarva, and all the gods with ease.
O best of sages, tell us what other deeds he performed that obstructed divine activities; for our curiosity is indeed great.
Vyāsa said:
O best of sages, listen with respect to this as I relate how Vārāṇasī was consumed by fire by Kṛṣṇa during his incarnation as a man.
And Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva became known on earth as "Vāsudeva," being addressed by people deluded by ignorance as "You have descended [as the Lord]."
He thought, "I am Vāsudeva descended upon the surface of the earth," and with his memory thus lost, he then caused all the emblems of Viṣṇu to be made;
and, O best of the twice-born, he dispatched a messenger to Kṛṣṇa.
The messenger said:
"O fool, having abandoned my own name and the marks such as the discus, and having completely relinquished everything without exception that consists of Vāsudeva..."
And for the sake of my own life, likewise, come to me with prostration.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus, Janārdana laughed and spoke to the messenger.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O messenger, having gone there, you must speak these words of mine to Pauṇḍraka: 'I shall indeed bestow my own emblem, the discus, upon you.'"
Having understood the true meaning of your words, let that which must be done be performed;
having taken my token, I shall come to your city.
"And I shall undoubtedly release for you my own insignia, the discus, in accordance with your command that it should come here. (BrP 207.11)
"I shall accomplish that for you tomorrow;
moreover, O King, having come to you for refuge, I will act so that no further fear whatsoever shall arise from you."
Vyāsa said: When the messenger had spoken thus and departed, Hari, remembering that [the sage] had arrived,
mounted Garuḍa and went swiftly to that city.
Then, having heard of Keśava’s exertion, the Lord of Kāśī,
surrounded by his entire army, approached as a rear-guard ally.
Then, with a great force and the army of the King of Kāśī,
that Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva marched toward Keśava.
From afar, Hari beheld him standing in a magnificent chariot,
holding a discus, a conch, and a mace in his hands, while grasping a lotus with one hand.
Hari beheld him wearing a garland, holding a Śārṅga bow, with a banner fashioned in the likeness of Garuḍa, and the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest.
Seeing him wearing a crown and earrings, clad in yellow garments,
and profound in his inner disposition, Madhusūdana laughed.
And he fought with his army, O twice-born ones—an army powerful with elephants and horses, and resplendent with swords, spears, maces, tridents, javelins, and bows. (BrP 207.19)
In an instant, he destroyed that army with arrows released from the Śārṅga bow that were capable of rending fire,
and by the violent blows of his mace and discus.
Having brought the army of the King of Kāśī to destruction,
Janārdana spoke to the foolish Pauṇḍraka, who was marked by his own [false] insignia.
The Blessed Lord said:
"That which was spoken by Pauṇḍraka to me through the mouth of your messenger—
to cast off his insignia— that I shall now fulfill for you."
This discus has been released; this mace has been hurled at you;
and this Garuḍa has been designated—let him mount your banner.
Having uttered this, he was torn apart by the released discus;
crushed by the mace, he was broken, and Garuḍa was likewise struck down by the son of Vinatā.
Then, while the world raised cries of "Alas!", the lord of the Kāśīs,
remaining steadfast in his devotion to his friend, fought with Vāsudeva.
Then, having severed his head with arrows released from the Śārṅga bow,
he hurled it into the city of Kāśī, causing wonder among the people.
Having slain Pauṇḍraka and the King of Kāśī along with his followers, Śauri returned to Dvāravatī and rejoiced like an immortal who has ascended to heaven.
Seeing that head fallen there in the city of the Lord of Kāśī, the people, utterly amazed, said, "What is this? and "By whom was it done? (BrP 207.28).
Having learned that he had been slain by Vāsudeva, his son,
accompanied by his family priest, then propitiated Śaṅkara.
In the great field of Avimukta, Śaṅkara was gratified by him;
he then said to that prince, "Choose a boon."
"O Blessed One, O Maheśvara, by your grace, let a *kṛtyā* arise for the sake of slaying Kṛṣṇa, the killer of my father. (BrP 207.31)
Vyāsa said:
When it was said, "It shall be so," immediately after the southern fire (dakṣiṇāgni),
a great Kṛtyā rose up from that very hearth of his.
Then, with a mouth formidable with flames and a mass of hair ablaze, she cried out "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! in her anger and went to Dvāravatī.
Beholding her, who was fierce with distorted eyes,
all the people went for refuge to Madhusūdana, the protector of the worlds.
The people said:
"This Mahākṛtyā was produced by the son of the King of Kāśī, after he had propitiated the Bull-bannered Lord, for the sake of slaying you, O wielder of the discus."
"Where [is] this fierce Kṛtyā, whose matted locks are a mass of flames of fire?"
Vyāsa said:
The discus, released as a mere plaything by one addicted to dice,
was matted with garlands of fire and terrifying with its outbursts of flames.
The Sudarśana, the discus of Viṣṇu, swiftly pursued the Kṛtyā;
then that Kṛtyā of Maheśvara was destroyed by the discus.
She departed with great speed, and that *kṛtyā* followed her;
filled with haste, she entered Vārāṇasī itself.
O best of sages, their power having been thwarted by Viṣṇu’s discus,
the vast army of Kāśī as well as the force of the Pramathas [were defeated].
Accompanied by all manner of weapons and missiles, he advanced toward the discus;
having consumed that army, which was intent on discharging many weapons and missiles, by his own splendor.
Having rendered that entire city of Vārāṇasī—
populated by many servants and citizens, along with its horses, elephants, and men— unsafe, he departed.
It had every difficult chamber without exception, and was difficult even for the gods to behold;
all its houses, walls, and gateways were completely surrounded by flames.
The discus quickly consumed that entire city;
with its indignation undiminished and indifferent to the accomplishment of such a trivial task,
that discus, flashing with radiant light, returned to the hand of Viṣṇu.
The sages said:
"O sage, we wish to hear further of the prowess and heroism of the wise Balabhadra; it behooves you to explain that to us."
"O highly fortunate one, we have indeed heard here of the dragging of the Yamunā and other deeds; tell us, therefore, what else Balarāma performed."
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O sages, to the deed which was performed by Rāma—
the infinite, immeasurable Śeṣa, the upholder of the earth.
The hero Samba, son of Jambavati, forcibly took the daughter of Duryodhana, who was waiting for her svayaṃvara.
Then Karna, Duryodhana, and the others, as well as Bhishma, Drona, and their followers— possessing great heroism and filled with rage— bound him, having conquered him in battle.
Having heard that, all the Yādavas directed their anger toward Duryodhana and the others,
and the sages likewise resolved to thwart their great undertaking.
Having restrained them, Balarāma spoke with words faltering from the agitation of intoxication:
"They shall release you at my command; I alone will go to the Kauravas."
Then Baladeva went to the city named after the serpent (Hastināpura) and stayed in the midst of the outer grove; he did not enter that city.
Perceiving that his strength had returned, Duryodhana and the others then presented Rāma with a cow, the guest-offering (argha), and water;
having accepted everything according to the prescribed rites, he then spoke to those Kauravas.
Baladeva said:
"Ugrasena commands that you release Sāmba immediately."
Vyāsa said: Then,
O best of the twice-born, having heard those words, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the others, as well as Karṇa, Duryodhana, and their followers, were filled with rage.
And all the kings, led by Bāhlīka, spoke in anger,
looking upon the wielder of the mace, who was unworthy of the lineage of Yadu.
The Kauravas said:
"O sir, what is this speech uttered by you, O Balabhadra?
What Yādava shall issue commands to those born of the Kuru lineage?"
If Ugrasena also gives his command to the Kauravas,
then enough with those white umbrellas, adorned and fit for kings!
Therefore go, O Balabhadra; we shall release Sāmba for his unjust conduct, neither by your command nor by that of Ugrasena.
The prostration that was made by the Kukuras and Andhakas toward us, who are worthy of honor—that indeed has not been performed; for what kind of command is this from a servant to a master?
"You have been elevated to pride by being given equal seats and meals;
what fault is there in your conduct, since policy pleases even when it is disregarded?"
"This one whom you have presented as a candidate for strength is to be honored by us;
yet it is not out of mere affection that we say this, for he is not of our lineage, but is fit for your own family."
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, all the Kurus did not release the son of Hari;
having reached a single-minded resolve, they all entered the city called Gajasāhvaya.
Then, reeling from intoxication and the anger born of that insult,
Halāyudha rose up and struck the earth with his heel.
Then the earth was torn asunder by the heel-strikes of the Great-souled One;
he then slapped his arms, filling the quarters with the sound.
With eyes exceedingly copper-red and a face contorted by a frown, he spoke:
Baladeva said:
"Aha! This is the great arrogance of these worthless and evil-minded Kauravas; they claim that our sovereignty over them was born of Time."
Even those who do not respect the command of Ugrasena, which is never to be transgressed,
shall receive that command in accordance with dharma, together with the gods and the Lord of Śacī.
Ugrasena constantly occupies that Sudharmā hall of the Lord of Śacī;
fie upon these kings who find satisfaction in a royal throne that is the leavings of hundreds of men!
Even that king, whose female attendants wear clusters of blossoms from the Pārijāta tree,
is not their sovereign.
"Let Ugrasena remain as the lord of all kings;
today, having rendered the earth devoid of Kauravas, I shall go to that city."
Today [I shall slay] Karṇa, Duryodhana, Droṇa, Bhīṣma along with Bāhlika,
Duḥśāsana and the others, as well as Bhūri and Bhūriśravas.
I would slay Somadatta, Śala, Bhīma, Arjuna, along with Yudhiṣṭhira, the twin sons of Yama, and the other Kauravas, together with their horses, chariots, and elephants.
Then, taking that hero Sāmba along with his wife,
I shall go to the city of Dvārakā and visit Ugrasena and my other kinsmen.
Or else, urged by the King of the Gods for the swift removal of the earth's burden, he [will go] together with all the Kurus, including the Kauravas and others.
I shall quickly cast the city named after the Naga into the Bhāgīrathī.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the one marked with the palm tree, his eyes red with anger,
placed his plow with its head downward upon the rampart and drew it, wielding the club as his weapon.
Seeing Hastināpura suddenly reeling,
all the Kauravas, their hearts agitated, cried out in distress.
The Kauravas said:
"O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one, forgive us, forgive us! Let your anger be withdrawn; be gracious, O wielder of the mace!"
O Balarāma, here is Sāmba together with his wife, returned to you;
please forgive these offenders whose power was not recognized.
Vyāsa said:
Then, O best of sages, having quickly departed from their own city, the Kauravas brought Sāmba back, accompanied by his wife.
Having bowed to Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the others who were speaking pleasant words, Bala,
the best among the strong, said, "I have indeed forgiven them."
Even today, O twice-born ones, that city appears as if it were reeling;
such is the power of Rāma, who possesses strength and heroism, O twice-born ones.
Then the Kauravas, having honored Sāmba along with Balarāma,
sent him away accompanied by his wife and the wealth for the wedding.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, all you sages, to the deeds of the mighty Bala;
O twice-born ones, hear also of another extraordinary thing that occurred.
The monkey named Dvivida, possessed of great heroism, became the friend of Narakāsura, the lord of the Asuras who was opposed to the side of the gods.
That powerful one established a persistent enmity toward the gods.
Dvivida said:
"Kṛṣṇa has slain Naraka, who was endowed with the pride of strength;
therefore, I shall carry out retribution against all the gods."
Vyāsa said:
Causing the destruction of sacrifices and likewise the ruin of the world of mortals, he,
deluded by ignorance, then went on to destroy the sacrificial rites.
He violated the boundaries of the virtuous, brought about the destruction of embodied beings,
and, being fickle, burned the countryside along with cities, villages, and the lands between them.
In some places, by hurling mountains, he completely pulverized villages and other settlements;
likewise, uprooting mountains, he cast them into the waters of the ocean.
Furthermore, standing in the midst of the ocean, he agitated the sea;
O twice-born ones, by that excessive agitation, the ocean overflowed its shores.
Flowing with great velocity, it inundated the villages and cities situated on its banks,
assuming a vast form at will and submerging the crops in countless numbers.
By rolling, wandering, and crowding about, the monkey crushes everything;
thus this entire world is oppressed by that evil-minded one.
Deprived of Vedic recitation and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, the twice-born were deeply distressed;
once, in the Raivata garden, Halāyudha drank wine.
And the highly fortunate Revatī, as well as other excellent women,
sang aloud as he stood in the midst of the crowns of those sporting damsels.
The best of the Yadu chiefs sported there like Kubera on Mount Mandara;
then that monkey approached and seized the plow of Sīrin.
And he held a pestle directly in front of him as a mockery;
likewise, the monkey laughed right in the faces of those women.
Then, striking him, he indeed threw water-jars filled with liquid;
thereafter, his soul overcome with anger, he reviled that Bala.
Nevertheless, disregarding him, he let out a roar of "kilakila";
then Bala, rising up, seized a club in his rage.
That best of monkeys also seized a formidable mountain rock and hurled it;
but as it was thrown, he shattered it into a thousand pieces with his mace.
The best of the Yadavas split it, and it fell upon the surface of the earth;
then that monkey leaped over the club and alighted.
Drawing him forward with speed and fury, he struck him on the chest with his strength;
then, with force and rage, he was struck on the head with a fist.
Vomiting blood, Dvivida fell with his life spent;
by his falling body, the mountain peak was shattered.
Like a hundredfold strike by the thunderbolt of the wielder of the bolt, the sages were thus struck;
thereafter, the gods showered a rain of flowers upon Rāma.
Approaching him, they then praised him, saying: "Excellent! This great deed has been accomplished by you.
O hero, by this wicked monkey who assisted the faction of the Daityas, the world was cast into peril; fortunately, he has now met his destruction."
Vyāsa said:
Such are the many, immeasurable deeds of the wise Baladeva, who is Śeṣa, the upholder of the earth.
Vyāsa said:
Thus, with Baladeva as his companion, Kṛṣṇa brought about the destruction of the Daityas and likewise of the wicked rulers of the earth for the sake of the world.
And the omnipresent Lord Hari, together with Phalguna, caused the burden of the earth to be removed by the slaughter of all the akṣauhiṇīs.
Having relieved the burden of the earth and slain all the kings,
he brought about the destruction of his own lineage under the pretext of a Brahmins' curse.
Having abandoned Dvārakā, Kṛṣṇa— the self-born one who is a portion of Viṣṇu— cast off his human form and entered again his own abode consisting of Viṣṇu.
The sages said:
How did he destroy his own lineage under the pretext of a brahmin’s curse,
and how did Janārdana cast off his human body?
Vyāsa said:
Viśvāmitra, Kaṇva, and the great sage Nārada were seen by the young princes of the Yadu clan at the great holy site of Piṇḍāraka.
Then those men, intoxicated by youth and impelled by their future destiny,
dressed Sāmba— the son of Jāmbavatī— in the manner of a woman and,
having prostrated before them, spoke to those sages.
The princes said:
"O Lord, what will this woman, who desires a son, give birth to?"
Vyāsa said:
Endowed with divine knowledge, those brahmins of firm vows were then deceived by the boys; they pronounced a curse for their destruction.
The sages, being enraged, said: "He shall produce a pestle by which the total destruction of the entire lineage of the Yādavas will come to pass."
Thus addressed by them, those princes related the matter exactly as it had happened:
how the club was born from Ugrasena and from the womb of Sāmba.
Then Ugrasena had that club ground into iron powder;
that powder, known as *cairaka*, was indeed cast into the great ocean.
Then, O twice-born ones, the Andhakas were unable to pulverize even a fragment of that iron mace, which was shaped like a javelin, though they had already ground it down.
That too was thrown into the ocean and swallowed by a fish caught in the nets; when the fish was killed, a hunter took it from its belly, and an old man seized that [jar] from him.
Although the Blessed One Madhusūdana had realized the ultimate truth,
he did not wish to alter that which had been brought about by destiny.
And a messenger dispatched by the gods, having prostrated before Keśava, spoke thus in private: "O Blessed One, I have been sent as a messenger by the deities."
Together with the Vasus, Aśvins, Maruts, Ādityas, Rudras, Sādhyas, and others, Śakra makes this representation to you; O Lord, let it be heard.
The gods said:
"For the sake of relieving the burden [of the earth], the Blessed One, having been entreated by the thirty deities, has descended here for more than a hundred years."
The wicked Daityas have been slain and the burden of the earth has been removed by you;
let the gods, now having you as their protector, ascend to the sovereignty of the third heaven.
O Lord of the World, more than a hundred years have passed since then;
if it pleases you, please proceed now to heaven.
When the gods had thus petitioned him, the Lord replied: "If your pleasure lies in this very place, then you may remain for as long as you wish; your dependents must report [this matter] to me."
The Blessed One said:
"O messenger, all that you have said I already know;
indeed, the destruction of the Yādavas has already been set in motion by me."
"This burden of the earth is too great as long as the Yādavas have not been destroyed;
I shall swiftly take an incarnation to remove it within seven nights."
Having taken [him] from the ocean exactly as he was seized and returning to Dvārakā,
I shall withdraw the Yādavas and go once more to the abode of the gods.
Having cast off this human body, I am to be considered as already attained [my goal] by the Lord of the Gods and likewise by the deities, for I have Saṃkarṣaṇa as my companion.
Jarāsaṃdha and others who were slain as burdens upon the earth—
the burden from them was indeed transferred to the Yadus.
"Having thus relieved this very great burden of the earth, I shall go for the protection of the world of the immortals; speak to them [thus]."
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by Vāsudeva, O twice-born ones, the messenger of the gods bowed to him and departed for the presence of the king of the gods by means of his divine gait.
Then the Blessed One also beheld divine portents occurring on earth, in the atmosphere, and in the sky,
day and night, foreboding the destruction of the city of Dvārakā.
Seeing them, he said to the Yādavas: "Behold these most dreadful great portents! Let us go to Prabhāsa without delay to pacify them."
Vyāsa said:
The great devotee Uddhava, having prostrated himself, spoke to Hari.
Uddhava said:
"O Blessed One, please command now what must be done by me.
I believe that the Blessed One will withdraw this entire lineage."
O Acyuta, I perceive the omens that portend the destruction of this family.
The Blessed One said:
"Go by means of the divine gait arising from my grace to the holy hermitage of Badarī on Mount Gandhamādana."
In that place of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, which has sanctified the surface of the earth,
you shall attain perfection there by fixing your mind on me through my grace.
"I shall go to heaven after withdrawing my lineage;
the ocean will submerge Dvārakā once it has been abandoned by me."
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus, Uddhava, with the permission of Keśava, prostrated before him and departed for the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Then, O twice-born ones, all those Yādavas, having mounted swift-moving chariots, set out for Prabhāsa together with Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and the others.
Having reached Prabhāsa, those Kukkurāndhakas, purified and joyful,
drank liquor there with the approval of Vāsudeva.
As they were drinking there, a fire of strife arose among those Yādavas through their mutual rivalry, bringing about their destruction.
Driven by the power of destiny, they struck one another with weapons;
but when their weapons were exhausted, they seized the nearby eraka grass.
The *erakā* grass, once grasped by them, appeared as if it were made of adamant;
with it, they struck one another with most dreadful blows.
Pradyumna, Sāmba, and others led by them, as well as Kṛtavarman, Sātyaki, Aniruddha and the rest, Pṛthu, and Vipṛthu; BrP_210.42 //
Cāruvarman, Sucāru, and likewise the twice-born Akrūra and others,
struck one another with thunderbolts in the form of *eraka* grass.
Hari tried to restrain them, as did the other Yādavas, but they regarded the arrived Keśava as an adversary; they struck one another down.
Kṛṣṇa, also enraged, took up a handful of *erakā* grass;
for their slaughter, that handful then became an iron mace.
With that [weapon], that assailant slaughtered the Yādavas without exception;
and others, having suddenly approached, likewise slew one another.
Then, O best of the twice-born, while Dāruka looked on, that victorious chariot of the wheel-turning king was swiftly carried across the middle of the ocean by the horses.
Then, having circumambulated the discus, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, the two quivers, the conch, and the sword, they departed by way of the sun's path.
O best of the twice-born, in a mere instant, the destruction of the Yādavas occurred there, with the exception of the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa and Dāruka.
While they were walking about, the two of them beheld Rāma seated at the foot of a tree,
and saw a great serpent emerging from his mouth.
Having emerged from his mouth, that serpent of great majesty departed for the ocean,
being honored by the Siddhas as well as by the Uragas.
Then, taking that water of honor (*arghya*), the Ocean went out to meet him and, honored by the best of the *pannagas*, entered its waters.
Having witnessed Bala’s departure, Keśava spoke to Dāruka: *BrP 210.52*
The Blessed Lord said:
"Relate all of this to Vasudeva and Ugrasena:
the departure of Baladeva and likewise the destruction of the Yādavas."
Abiding in yoga, I too shall cast off this body;
and you must inform all the people residing in Dvārakā, as well as Āhuka, of this.
"Since the ocean will submerge this entire city,
you must await the arrival of Arjuna with your chariots well-prepared."
"One must not remain within Dvārakā once the Pāṇḍava has departed;
one should go along with him wherever that Kaurava goes."
And having gone, speak these words of mine to Arjuna, the son of Kuntī:
"This person, who is my own charge, must be protected by you to the best of your ability."
Thus, accompanied by Arjuna, may you take the people from Dvāravatī and depart; and Vajra shall become the king of the Yadus.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus, Dāruka prostrated himself before Kṛṣṇa again and again,
and after circumambulating him many times, he departed as instructed.
Having gone there, he acted accordingly; likewise, he brought Arjuna of great intelligence from Dvārakā and installed Vajra as king.
The Blessed One Govinda also, having established the supreme Brahman, whose essence is Vāsudeva, within his own self, maintained it in all beings.
Honoring the words that Durvāsas had spoken,
O best of beings, he became absorbed in yoga, placing one foot upon his knee.
Then, at that place, a hunter named Jarā arrived,
carrying an excellent arrow made from the remaining iron of a pestle.
Having observed that foot standing there in the form of a deer,
O best of the twice-born, he then pierced it with that very same lance.
Having gone there, he beheld a man bearing four arms;
having prostrated before him, he said to him again and again, "Be gracious!"
"This was done by me unknowingly, under the suspicion that it was a deer;
let it be forgiven. You ought not to burn me, who am already consumed by my own sin."
Vyāsa said:
Then the Blessed One said to him, "There is not even the slightest fear for you;
go, O hunter, by my grace to the abode of the Lord of Heaven."
Vyāsa said:
Immediately upon those words, a celestial chariot arrived;
having ascended it by the grace of that [sage], the hunter departed for heaven.
When he had departed, the Blessed One, having united himself with the Self—
that which has become Brahman, imperishable, inconceivable, consisting of Vāsudeva, and stainless— [remained there].
Having abandoned his human body, he attained the threefold state within that which is unborn, undecaying, indestructible, immeasurable, and the self of all.
Vyāsa said:
Then Arjuna, having searched for them, caused the funeral rites to be performed for the bodies of Kṛṣṇa and Rāma,
as well as for the others in due order.
The eight principal queens, headed by Rukmiṇī, who have been mentioned,
entered the fire after embracing the body of Hari.
And Revatī, O best of men, having embraced the body of Rāma,
entered the blazing fire, which was cooled by the joy of union with him.
But having heard that, Ugrasena as well as Ānakadundubhi,
Devakī, and Rohiṇī entered the fire.
Then Arjuna, having performed their funeral rites according to the prescribed rule,
emerged taking all the people and Vajra with him.
The thousands of wives of Kṛṣṇa departed from Dvāravatī;
and the son of Kuntī, protecting both Vajra and the people, proceeded slowly.
O brahmins, the assembly hall Sudharmā was brought by Kṛṣṇa to the world of mortals; however, the celestial tree Pārijāta returned to heaven.
On the very day that Hari departed from the earth for heaven,
it is said that this Kali, whose body is Time, descended here.
The great ocean submerged that empty Dvārakā,
yet the sea did not submerge the single dwelling of the best of the Yadus.
O brahmins, even today the great ocean does not overstep its bounds there,
because the Blessed Lord Keśava is eternally present in that place.
That place, endowed with the divine play of Viṣṇu, is exceedingly meritorious and the destroyer of all sins; by seeing it, one is liberated from evil.
O best of sages, Pārtha made his dwelling in the land of Pañcanada, which was endowed with abundant grain and wealth, for the sake of all people.
Then greed arose because of that lone archer Pārtha,
upon seeing the women being led away, their lords having been slain by the bandits.
Then those Ābhīras, performers of evil deeds whose minds were struck by greed and who were exceedingly arrogant, gathered together and took counsel.
The Ābhīras said:
"This lone archer Arjuna is leading away the women whose lords have been slain, bypassing us! Fie on this! Let our army be mobilized! (BrP 212.15)
Having slain Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Jayadratha, Karṇa, and the others, he was filled with pride and no longer recognized the strength of those who dwell in the villages.
He disregards all other men, especially those who are superior in strength and even those of the village; what is the use of further words to you?
Vyāsa said:
Then thousands of robbers, armed with sticks and seizing clods of earth, rushed toward those people whose lord had been slain.
Then, having turned back, the son of Kuntī spoke to the Ābhīras as if laughing:
Arjuna said:
Turn back, O you who are ignorant of dharma, if it is not that you wish to die here.
Vyāsa said:
Disregarding his words, they then seized that wealth,
as well as the women who were under the protection of Viṣvaksena from the son of Kuntī.
Then the heroic Arjuna began to string the divine bow Gāṇḍīva, which does not age in battle, but he was unable to do so.
He made ready his weapons with great effort, yet they became slack again;
even as he reflected upon them, the Pāṇḍava could not recall his missiles.
And Pārtha, filled with joy, released the remaining arrows at them;
yet those discharged by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva did not cause them any further injury.
The inexhaustible arrows given by Agni were also exhausted;
as he fought with the cowherds, Arjuna’s own resources came to an end.
But the son of Kuntī reflected: "Indeed, that strength by which I conquered the kings along with their armies through volleys of arrows was the very strength of Kṛṣṇa."
Then, while the son of Pāṇḍu looked on, those most excellent women were dragged away by the Ābhīras,
and others departed of their own accord out of desire.
Then, when his arrows were exhausted, Dhanañjaya struck the bandits with the tip of his bow;
and those bandits, O twice-born ones, laughed at his blows.
O best of sages, even as Pārtha looked on, those Mlecchas went away in all directions, taking with them the women of the Vṛṣṇi and Andhaka clans.
Then Jishnu, distressed, crying out "Alas!
Alas!", wept indeed, saying, "Oh, I have been released by that Blessed One!"
Arjuna said: That bow, those weapons, that chariot, and those horses—
all were lost in an instant, like a gift given to one who has not mastered the Vedas.
"Alas! How great is the power of destiny without that Great-Souled One, since I, rendered powerless, have been led low into defeat! (BrP 212.31)
Those two arms, that fist, that position, and I myself, O Arjuna—
I have become all insubstantial, like everything lost without that merit.
"Arjuna’s status as Arjuna and Bhīma’s status as Bhīma were surely established by him;
otherwise, how could I have been defeated by the Ābhīras without him? (BrP 212.33)
Vyāsa said:
Speaking thus, Jiṣṇu went to Indraprastha, the most excellent of cities;
there he installed Vajra, the joy of the Yādavas, as king.
Then Phālguna beheld Vyāsa, who was dwelling in the forest;
approaching that illustrious one, he saluted him with humility.
Beholding him bowing at his feet with a very resolute mind, [the sage], appearing dejected, said to Pārtha: "How is it that you have become so utterly pale?"
Have you followed the dust of a woman who has not yet given birth, or have you committed the murder of a Brahmin?
Or perhaps, suffering from the pain of shattered hopes for victory, your splendor has now vanished.
Or perhaps those seeking gifts from you were rejected;
or else, you have lost your luster because of your passion for a woman who should not be approached.
Or did you eat that single sweet dish after giving it to the brahmins,
O Arjuna, or were the riches of the wretched seized by you?
O Arjuna, has he perhaps come within the range of the sun's rays, or has he been struck by an evil eye? For how else could he be so devoid of splendor?
Whether you have been touched by water from fingernails or even sprinkled with water from a jar,
you have become exceedingly lusterless because of that, or perhaps you were defeated in battle by those inferior to you.
Vyāsa said:
Then Pārtha, having sighed, said, "O Blessed One, let it be heard," and as he was thus addressed,
O Brahmins, he related his own defeat exactly as it had happened.
Arjuna said:
That strength which was ours, as well as our splendor, our heroism, and our prowess;
that fortune and our very shadow—Hari has departed, leaving all these behind us.
O Sage, we have become as if made of straw, deprived of that other great one who always speaks with a smile.
That Supreme Person has departed— he who was the personified essence of my missiles, my arrows, and likewise of the Gāṇḍīva bow.
That Govinda, by the mere sight of whom prosperity, victory, wealth, and exaltation never left us— that Blessed One has departed, leaving us behind.
He by whose power Bhīṣma, Droṇa, the King of Aṅga, and others, as well as Duryodhana and his followers, were utterly consumed— that Kṛṣṇa has abandoned the earth.
"O father, deprived of its youth and its splendor, my earth appears like one whose luster has vanished;
I do not shine alone in the absence of that wielder of the discus."
"By whose power Bhīṣma and the others acted like moths in the fire that was I;
without that Kṛṣṇa, I have today been defeated by cowherds."
The Gāṇḍīva bow is renowned throughout the three worlds by virtue of its power;
yet, without it, I have been humiliated by the cowherds with their mere clubs.
O Great Sage, many thousands of women who were indeed unprotected have been carried off by bandits armed with clubs, even as I was striving [to protect them].
The entire retinue of Kṛṣṇa’s women, being brought away by the Ābhīras,
was seized after they overcame my army with their staff-weaponry.
"It is no wonder that I am bereft of splendor; that I still live is the marvel. O Grandfather, I am shameless, marked by the mire of the insults of the lowly."
Vyāsa said:
O best of the twice-born, having heard those words of that great-souled Pāṇḍava, who was distressed and miserable, I spoke.
Enough of your shame, O Pārtha; you ought not to grieve.
Know that such is the course of Time among all living beings.
O Pāṇḍava, time leads to the existence of beings and to their non-existence;
knowing that this world has time as its root, therefore, O Arjuna, maintain your steadfastness.
The rivers, the oceans, the mountains, and the entire earth;
gods, humans, animals, trees, and reptiles.
Created again and again by time, they shall once more go to their destruction;
knowing that all this is of the nature of time, attain peace.
O Dhanañjaya, it is exactly as you have said regarding the greatness of Kṛṣṇa;
he descended to the earth for the purpose of removing its burden.
In former times, the earth, oppressed by its burden, went into the presence of the gods;
for that purpose, Janārdana, who can assume any form at will, descended.
And that task has been accomplished: all the kings have been slain, and likewise the entire clan of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas has been brought to an end by Pārtha.
"O Arjuna, nothing else remains to be done by him on this earth;
therefore, that Blessed One, having accomplished his purpose, departed according to his will."
This God of gods performs creation during the period of creation, maintenance during the period of maintenance,
and at the end, he is capable of bringing about dissolution, just as he has done now.
Therefore, O Pārtha, you should not feel distress because of this defeat;
for men's prowess manifests itself during times of crisis.
"O Arjuna, since kings such as Bhīṣma and Droṇa were slain by you alone, was that not their subjugation by Time, arising in its due season?"
Just as their defeat occurred through the power of that Viṣṇu,
so too will your own destruction at the end come from the bandits, arising from you yourself.
That god, the Lord of the World, having entered other bodies,
maintains the stability of the world and brings about the destruction of all beings at its end.
O son of Kuntī, Janārdana shall be your ally in the arising of existence;
but at the end of existence, those who are your adversaries have been looked upon by Keśava.
Who would believe that you could slay all the Kauravas along with Bhīṣma?
And who would believe in your defeat at the hands of the Ābhīras?
O Pārtha, all this is the playful activity of Hari among all beings:
that the Kauravas were destroyed by you, and that you were defeated by the Ābhīras.
And as for those women who were seized by bandits and protected by you—
that too I shall relate to you exactly as it happened, O Arjuna.
In ancient times, O Pārtha, the brahmin Aṣṭāvakra was devoted to living in the water for many series of years, chanting the eternal Brahman.
When the hosts of asuras had been defeated, a great festival took place on the summit of Mount Meru;
going there, the celestial women beheld it.
And Rambhā, Tilottamā, and others by the hundreds and thousands praised and extolled that great-souled one, O Pāṇḍava.
Bowing low with humility and intent upon offering hymns of praise, they prostrated before the sage, who was submerged up to his neck in water and bearing a mass of matted locks.
O best of the Kauravas, as he became increasingly serene, all those women praised him— the most excellent among the twice-born— in that same measure.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"O illustrious ladies, I am pleased with you; whatever you desire may be chosen from me, for I shall grant it all, even that which is difficult to obtain."
Vyāsa said:
Rambhā, Tilottamā, and the other divine apsarases spoke:
The Apsarases said:
"O twice-born ones, since you are pleased with us, what could we possibly lack? (BrP 212.79)
But the others said, "O Brahmin, if the Blessed One is pleased,
then we wish to obtain Puruṣottama as our husband, O best of Brahmins."
Vyāsa said:
Having said, "It shall be so," the sage emerged from the waters.
And they saw him, having emerged, deformed and with eight faces.
O descendant of Kuru, seeing them concealing it, their laughter became manifest;
the sage, overcome with anger, cursed them.
Aṣṭāvakra said: "Since you have treated me with laughter and contempt, considering me to be deformed in appearance,
therefore I pronounce this curse upon you."
"Having obtained Puruṣottama as your husband by my grace,
you shall all, however, fall victim to the curse of my [son] and come into the hands of bandits."
Vyāsa said:
Having heard what was thus spoken and being propitiated by them, the sage spoke again:
"You shall indeed go once more to the world of the Lord of the Gods."
Thus, due to the curse of that sage Aṣṭāvakra, those excellent women, having obtained Keśava as their husband, fell into the hands of bandits.
Therefore, O Pāṇḍava, you should not feel even the slightest grief in this matter;
for all that has been withdrawn by Him alone, the Lord of All.
By him, as he was bringing about your own withdrawal,
your strength, splendor, heroism, and majesty were likewise withdrawn.
For one who is born, death is certain; likewise, there is a falling from that which has risen. Union ends in separation, and accumulation results in depletion.
Those wise ones who, having understood this, do not fall into grief or joy—
they alone, and others who train themselves in their conduct, become like them.
Therefore, O best of men, having understood this along with your brothers,
you must renounce the entire kingdom and go to the forest for asceticism.
Therefore, go and report these words of mine to Dharmarāja:
"O hero, act so that tomorrow you may attain your destination together with your brothers."
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus, he approached the King of Dharma and spoke accordingly; everything that had been seen or experienced was related by him in its entirety.
Having heard the words of Vyāsa as they were spoken by Arjuna,
and having installed Parīkṣit upon the throne, all those sons of Pāṇḍu departed for the forest.
Thus, O best of sages, I have related to you in detail the deeds of Vāsudeva, who was born in the lineage of Yadu.
The sages said:
"O best of sages, oh, how wonderful and superhuman is the majesty of Kṛṣṇa and Rāma that you have described, which is so difficult to find on this earth!"
We do not reach satiety while hearing the discourse of the Blessed One;
therefore, O highly fortunate one, tell us once more of the deeds of the God.
We have heard from the mouths of the virtuous as they were recounting it in the Purāṇas that there was an appearance of Viṣṇu, of immeasurable splendor, known as the Boar (Varāha).
We do not know his conduct, nor his ritual procedure, nor its extent; we do not know the true nature of his actions and qualities, nor his intended causality.
Of what nature was that Boar? What was his form and what was his deity? What was the power of his conduct, or what did he do at that time?
While the twice-born were assembled for the sake of sacrifice and looking on,
[he related] the life of Mahāvarāha, which brings happiness to all the worlds.
O Brahmin, just as Nārāyaṇa, the crusher of enemies, having assumed the form of a boar, lifted up the earth with his tusk when it was submerged in the ocean; ||| BrP_213.7 |||
Our intellects are not inclined to hear in detail all the deeds of the wise Hari-Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of his enemies.
O All-pervading One, O Brahman, you ought to explain the sequence of karmas, their manifestations, and whatever his fundamental nature may be.
Vyāsa said:
This great burden of questions has been set forth by you;
I shall speak according to my ability—listen indeed to the glory of Viṣṇu.
By good fortune, your minds have been awakened to hear of the power of Viṣṇu;
therefore, listen indeed to all his various manifestations.
To that god who has a thousand faces, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet,
a thousand heads, a thousand hands, and is imperishable;
The Lord with a thousand tongues, radiant, wearing a thousand crowns, the giver of thousands, the source of thousands, possessing a thousand arms, and immutable.
The oblation, the libation, the hotṛ priest, and the sacrificial offering;
the vessels, the purifiers, the altar, the initiation, the fuel-stick, and the sacrificial ladle.
The *sruk* ladle, the moon, the sun, the pestle, the *prokṣaṇī* water-vessel, the southern solstice,
the *adhvaryu* priest, the singer of the Sāmans, the learned sage, the member of the assembly, the seat, and the assembly hall.
The sacrificial post, the wheel, the *dhruvā* ladle, the *darvī* ladle, the cooking pots, and the mortars;
the eastern hall, the sacrificial ground, the *hotṛ* priest, and whatever else [is required].
Short and very long, stationary and moving;
likewise, expiations, water-offerings, sacrificial altars, and sacred grasses.
He is the fire that carries the sacrifice of mantras, the one who conveys the portions, the one who receives the portions,
the eater of the first offering, the consumer of Soma, whose flame is the oblation, and whose weapon is raised high.
The Brahmins learned in the Vedas speak of him as the eternal Lord in sacrifice—
of that wise Viṣṇu, the sovereign of the gods, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark.
"Thousands of manifestations have passed away many times over, and yet more will surely come to be; so indeed has the Grandfather spoken."
O highly fortunate ones, you have asked about this divine and meritorious narrative concerning the manifestation of Viṣṇu, which removes all sins and is auspicious.
Listen to that, O highly fortunate ones, with your inner selves directed toward it;
O sinless ones, I shall explain in due order that which you have asked of me.
The majesty and the life-story of Vāsudeva, the one of great intelligence,
[are told] for the benefit of gods and mortals and for the prosperity of the worlds.
The heroic Soul of all beings manifests many times;
and I shall describe his manifestations, which are meritorious, divine, and endowed with excellent qualities.
Having slept for a thousand yugas,
the God of gods, the Lord of the world, manifests for the sake of his purpose once that thousand yugas have been completed.
Brahmā, Kapila, Tryambaka, as well as the thirty gods,
the deities, the seven seers, the nāgas, and likewise the apsarases.
The high-souled Sanatkumāra,
the illustrious Manu, the progenitor of creatures,
and the ancient God then constructed the cities.
He whose splendor is equal to a blazing fire, who stands in the midst of the ocean when all things mobile and immobile have perished,
when gods, asuras, and humans have vanished, and when serpents and rākṣasas have been destroyed.
Those two, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, both invincible and desirous of battle,
were slain by that Blessed One after he had granted them an immeasurable boon.
Long ago, while the lotus-navelled Lord was sleeping upon the waters of the ocean,
the gods along with the hosts of sages were born there within that lotus.
This is the manifestation of the Great-Souled One known as Pauṣkaraka,
in which the ancient account, composed of divine revelation, is narrated.
The manifestation of the Great-Souled One as the Boar was the first to be heard;
therein Viṣṇu, the best of gods, assumed the form of a boar.
The Vedas are his feet, the sacrificial posts his fangs, the sacrifices his teeth, and the layers of the altar his mouth;
fire is his tongue, the darbha grass his hair, and the Veda his head—such is he of great ascetic power.
Divine, with day and night as his eyes, the Vedāṅgas as his limbs, and the Śruti as his ornament;
having clarified butter for his nose, the sacrificial ladle for his snout, and the great sound of the Sāmaveda as his voice.
