Consisting of truth and dharma, glorious, honored by his successive strides,
he had penance for his claws, was formidable, with knees like sacrificial animals and a face of terrifying form.

With entrails protruding, having the sacrificial fire as his phallus, possessing seeds, medicinal herbs, and great fruit, with musical instruments for his inner self, the mantra for his buttocks, deformed, and having the Soma-juice for his blood; BrP_213.36 //
The altar was his shoulder, the fragrance of the oblation his scent, and he possessed the great momentum of offerings to gods and ancestors;
the eastern hall was his body, radiant and endowed with various initiations.
The yogi has the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as his heart; he is the great one consisting of the great sacrifice (mahāsattra);
he shines with the eight upākarma rites as his crest-jewels, and is adorned by the revolving pravargya ceremonies.
He, whose path of movement consists of various meters, who sits upon the secret Upanishads,
and who is accompanied by his consort Chāyā, stands forth like a peak of jewels.
The Lord, having entered the single ocean, beheld the earth— bounded by the sea and including its mountains, groves, and forests— submerged in the waters of that single vast expanse.
He who, with his fang, having uprooted [the earth] out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
became the thousand-headed origin of the worlds and established the universe once again.
Thus, in ancient times, having become the Sacrificial Boar and desiring the welfare of all beings, the divine Earth, who bears the waters of the ocean, was lifted up by him.
O twice-born ones, this Vārāha incarnation has been described; after that, the Nārasiṃha, in which Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by the King of Beasts (the Man-lion).
Formerly, in the Kṛta age, the enemy of the gods, arrogant in his strength,
the primordial being of the Daityas, performed very great ascetic penance.
Devoted to the practice of recitation and fasting, he remained established in the vow of silence for ten thousand years and fifteen hundred years.
Then, indeed, he became pleased with him because of his tranquility and self-restraint, as well as his celibacy, his austerity, and his observance of rules.
O twice-born ones, the Blessed Lord Svayambhū himself came there in person,
traveling in a radiant celestial chariot, sun-colored and drawn by swans.
Together with the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Maruts, as well as the deities,
the Rudras along with the Viśvedevas, and the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Kiṃnaras.
With the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions, with the rivers and the oceans,
as well as with the lunar mansions, the auspicious moments, and the great planets moving through the sky.
By divine sages whose asceticism was matured, by perfected beings and scholars,
by most holy royal sages, and by hosts of gandharvas and apsaras;

The glorious Brahmā, the teacher of all that moves and is stationary, surrounded by all the gods and the best among the knowers of Brahman, spoke these words to the Daitya: BrP_213.51: "The glorious Brahmā, the teacher of all that moves and is stationary, surrounded by all the gods and the best among the knowers of Brahman, spoke these words to the Daitya."
Brahmā said:
"I am pleased with this austerity of yours, O you of noble vows, my devotee.
Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—and obtain whatever desire you wish."
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"Neither gods, asuras, nor gandharvas; neither yakṣas, uragas, nor rākṣasas; nor even the ṛṣis, though enraged with curses, can harm me, O Grandfather of the World. (Brahmapurāṇa 213.53)
"Endowed with ascetic power, they shall curse me; this is the boon chosen by me:
that I am not to be slain by weapon, nor by missile, nor by mountain, nor by tree."
Neither with something dry nor with something wet, neither upwards nor downwards—
with a single blow of his hand, he [struck] him along with his servants, army, and vehicles.
He who is capable of destroying me shall become my death;
I myself shall become the sun, the moon, the wind, and the fire.
I am the water and the atmosphere, and indeed the sky in every way; I am anger and desire, Varuṇa, Vāsava, and Yama;
I am Dhanada, the lord of wealth, the Yakṣa, and the sovereign of the Kiṃpuruṣas.
Brahmā said:
"O dear one, these divine and wonderful boons have been granted to you by me;
you shall obtain all these desires, O dear one, without a doubt."
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the blessed Grandfather quickly departed for the Vairāja abode of Brahmā, which is frequented by hosts of brahminical sages.
Then the gods, the nāgas, the gandharvas, and likewise the sages,
having heard of the granting of the boon, approached the Grandfather.
The gods said:
"O Blessed One, by this boon that asura will oppress us.
Therefore, be gracious quickly, O Blessed One; let his slaughter also be considered."
O Blessed One, you are the self-existent, the first creator, and the lord of all beings;
you are the maker of the offerings to gods and ancestors, the unmanifest, the primordial nature, and the eternal.
Vyāsa said:
Then, having heard those words for the benefit of the world, the blessed Lord Prajāpati spoke these words to all the hosts of gods.
Brahmā said:
O gods, he must necessarily obtain the fruit of his asceticism;
and at the conclusion of his penance, the Lord Viṣṇu will bring about his death.
Vyāsa said: Having heard these words of the lotus-born one, all the gods,
filled with joy, departed for their own divine abodes.
As soon as he had obtained the boon,
the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, emboldened by the granting of that boon, oppressed all living beings.
At that time, he likewise assaulted the highly fortunate sages in their hermitages— those of firm vows, devoted to truth and righteousness, and self-controlled.
Having likewise defeated the gods dwelling in the third heaven and having brought the three worlds under his control, that mighty asura dwells in heaven.
When the Dānava, intoxicated by the pride of his boon, wandered upon the earth,
he made the Daityas worthy of sacrifice and the deities unworthy of sacrifice.
The Ādityas, the Vasus, the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and likewise the Maruts,
approached the mighty Viṣṇu for refuge, he who is the worthy protector.

We have gone for refuge to the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa, the deity who is worthy of seeking shelter; he who consists of gods and Brahman, the sacrifice, the eternal Brahman-god; the past, the present, and the future; the Lord adored by the worlds.
The gods said:
"Save us today, O Lord of Gods, from the fear of Hiraṇyakaśipu;
for you are our supreme god, and you are our supreme teacher."
For you indeed are our supreme creator, O best of gods, beginning with Brahmā;
you whose eyes are like blossoming, stainless lotus petals, the destroyer of the faction of enemies!
For the destruction of the lineage of Diti, please become our refuge.
Vāsudeva said:
"O immortals, cast away your fear; I grant you freedom from fear.
In that same way, O gods, you shall regain the third heaven without delay."
"Here I am; I shall slay that lord of the Dānavas, the Daitya who is arrogant because of the granting of the boon and who is unslayable by the lords of the immortals, together with his host."
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus and dismissed the lords of the thirty gods,
the blessed one of great strength went to the abode of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Having made half of his body human and half of his body that of a lion, the Lord,
with his Nārasiṃha form, touched [Hiraṇyakaśipu’s] hand with his own hand.
Resembling a dense rain-cloud, with a voice like a thundercloud,
possessing the radiant power of a dense rain-cloud, he was as swift as a cloud.
Seeing that exceedingly powerful Daitya protected by haughty hosts of Daityas, he, possessing the prowess of a proud tiger, struck him down with a single hand.
This Nṛsiṃha has been described; furthermore, this is the supreme Vāmana, in whom he assumed the form of Vāmana for the destruction of the Daityas.
In ancient times, at the sacrifice of Bali, those unshakeable great asuras were shaken by the powerful Viṣṇu with his three strides.
Vipracitti, Śiva, Śaṅku, and likewise Ayaḥśaṅku;
Ayaḥśiras, Aśvaśiras, and the heroic Hayagrīva.
Vegavān, Ketumān, Ugra, the great asura Ugravyagra,
Puṣkara, Puṣkala, Śāśva, and Aśvapati.
Prahlāda, Aśvapati, Kumbha, Saṃhrāda, Gamanapriya,
Anuhrāda, Harihaya, Vārāha, and the youngest, Saṃhara.
Śarabha, Śalabha, Kupatha, Krodhana,
Kratha, Bṛhatkīrti, Mahājihva, Śaṅkukarṇa, and Mahāsvana.
Flaming-tongued, sun-eyed, deer-footed, lover of deer;
Vāyu, the most heavy, Namuci, Śambara, the great Viskara.
Candrahantṛ, Krodhahantṛ, and Krodhavardhana;
Kālaka, Kālakopa, Vṛtra, Krodha, and Virocana.
Gariṣṭha and Variṣṭha, both Pralamba and Naraka, Indratāpana and Vātāpi, Ketumān, and Baladarpita; ||| BrP_213.88 |||
Asiloman and Puloman, Bāṣkala, Pramada, Mada,
Svamiśra, Kālavadana, Karāla, and Keśin.
Ekākṣa, Candramas, Rāhu, Saṃhrāda, Saṃbara, and Svana;
they held śataghnīs and discuses in their hands, as well as maces.
Equipped with horse-mechanisms and weapons, as well as slings; with spears and mortars in their hands, and likewise bearing battle-axes.
And the Dānavas had nooses and mallets in their hands, as well as iron clubs;
they wielded great boulders as weapons and held spears in their hands.
Bearing various terrible weapons, wearing diverse garbs, and possessed of great strength,
they had the faces of tortoises and cocks, as well as the faces of hares and owls.
Some had faces like those of donkeys and camels, others had faces like boars; some had faces like cats and peacocks, while others had enormous mouths.

The Dānavas had faces like those of cranes, were heroic, and had faces like those of cattle, goats, sheep, and buffaloes; some had the faces of iguanas and monitor lizards, while others had the faces of jackals.
And there were terrible Dānavas with faces like mice and frogs, as well as those with faces like wolves,
fearsome ones with faces like crocodiles, and others with faces like curlews.
Some had the faces of horses, some the faces of donkeys, and others the faces of peacocks;
some were clothed in the skins of lordly elephants, while others wore garments of black antelope skin.
The asuras had their bodies covered with rags, were dressed in blue garments,
and wore turbans, crowns, and earrings.
Wearing crowns and long topknots, with necks like conch shells and great splendor,
those Daityas wore various garments and were adorned with diverse garlands and unguents.
Seizing their own weapons, which blazed with splendor,
they surrounded Hṛṣīkeśa from all sides as he was advancing.
Having crushed all the Daityas with the soles of his feet and the palms of his hands,
the Lord assumed a most terrifying form and swiftly seized the earth.
As he strode across the earth, the sun and moon were situated between his breasts;
and as he traversed the sky, they were likewise said to have been positioned at his navel.
The twice-born speak thus regarding Viṣṇu of immeasurable prowess as he was advancing: "Two [mountains] were stationed at the level of his knees."
Having seized the entire earth and having slain the foremost of the Asuras,
Viṣṇu, the best among the powerful, gave the earth to Śakra.
This is the manifestation known as Vāmana of the Great-Souled One;
this glory of Viṣṇu is indeed recounted by the twice-born who are learned in the Vedas.
Furthermore, there was a manifestation of the high-souled Viṣṇu, the self of all beings,
known as Dattātreya, who was endowed with supreme forbearance.
When the Vedas had been lost, as well as the ritual manuals and sacrifices, when the fourfold social order had become confused and dharma had fallen into laxity; ||| BrP_213.107 |||
When unrighteousness increases, truth is lost, and falsehood prevails;
when the subjects are wasting away and righteousness has fallen into disorder.
Indeed, by him the Vedas, along with their sacrifices and ritual practices, were truly recovered;
and by that high-souled one, the fourfold order of society was made free from confusion.
Therefore, a boon was granted to the wise Kārtavīrya, king of the Haihayas, by the wise Dattātreya, the giver of boons.
"O King, these two arms of yours shall become one hundred arms for my sake; of this there is no doubt. (BrP 213.111)
And you shall protect the entire earth, O Lord of the Earth;
and when standing in battle, you will be difficult for hosts of enemies to behold.
This was your glorious, wonderful, and auspicious manifestation as Vaiṣṇava;
and furthermore, this was the manifestation of the high-souled one as the son of Jamadagni.
There, the powerful Lord Rāma slew King Arjuna, who stood in his army and was difficult for enemies to conquer in battle with his thousand arms.
Having struck King Arjuna down from his chariot to the ground,
Rāma overpowered him as he cried out like a thundering cloud.
And the descendant of Bhṛgu cut off his entire thousand arms with a blazing battle-axe, even as he was accompanied by his kinsmen.
Covered with millions of Kṣatriyas, the earth— adorned by Meru and Mandara—
was rendered devoid of Kṣatriyas twenty-one times by him.
Having rid this earth of the Kṣatriyas, the highly illustrious Bhārgava performed a horse sacrifice for the destruction of all his sins.
In that sacrifice of great giving, the descendant of Bhṛgu,
being pleased, bestowed the earth as a sacrificial fee upon Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci.
The lord of the earth, the best among chariot-warriors, [bestowed] elephants, white horses, and chariots;
as well as inexhaustible gold, cows, and lordly elephants.
In that great horse-sacrifice,
the highly illustrious descendant of Bhṛgu gave [these gifts] even today for the welfare of the worlds.
The powerful and illustrious son of Jamadagni, having performed severe austerities,
dwells once again like a god on Mahendra, the best of mountains.
This is the manifestation of the high-souled Viṣṇu, the eternal and immutable lord of the gods, who is renowned as the son of Jamadagni.
Furthermore, in the twenty-fourth yuga, there was born to Daśaratha a lotus-eyed son, preceded by Viśvāmitra.
Having divided himself fourfold, the mighty-armed Lord and Master became renowned in the world as Rāma, equal to the sun in splendor.
For the sake of pleasing the world, for the subduing of the Rākṣasas,
and for the increase of Dharma, the highly illustrious one was born there.
They also call him a lord of men who is devoted to the welfare of all beings—
he who, knowing all dharmas, dwelt for fourteen years in the forest.
Accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma, the descendant of Raghu, who is devoted to the welfare of all beings,
performed austerities in the forest for fourteen years.
Beside him stood his wife, known among people as Sītā,
who was that previously mentioned Lakṣmī who follows her husband.
Dwelling in Janasthāna, that bull among men performed the work of the gods; meanwhile, [Rāvaṇa] was the cruel descendant of Pulastya who had wronged him.
Seeking the tracks of Sītā,
the highly illustrious one struck down [the demons] among the hosts of gods and asuras, as well as the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and bhogins.
There [he saw] Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, who was invulnerable and difficult to defeat in battle,
accompanied by tens of millions of Rākṣasas and resembling a mass of black collyrium.
The cruel Rāvaṇa, lord of the Rākṣasas, who causes the three worlds to tremble,
is difficult to conquer, difficult to restrain, arrogant, and possesses the prowess of a tiger.
He slew Rāvaṇa in battle, along with his ministers and his army— the one who was difficult for the hosts of gods to behold and who had become arrogant through the granting of boons.
In ancient times, Rāma, the Lord of Beings, swiftly slew Rāvaṇa, who resembled a great mass of clouds, possessed a massive body, and was endowed with great strength.
By him, for the sake of Sugrīva, the mighty lord of monkeys,
Vālī, was slain in battle and Sugrīva was consecrated.
And the son of Madhu, the arrogant Dānava named Lavaṇa,
that heroic and great Asura intoxicated by his boons, was slain in the Madhuvana forest.
By him, Mārīca and Subāhu— the two foremost among the strong— were slain by their might, for they had caused obstacles to the sacrifices of the sages whose souls were purified.
Slain and rendered hopeless by that high-souled one,
who was skilled in battle, other rākṣasas likewise were struck down in the encounter.
That tiger among men slew the two Rākṣasas, Virādha and Kabandha, who possessed terrible prowess; they were actually Gandharvas deluded by a curse.
With arrows possessing the brilliance of fire, the sun’s rays, and lightning, with variegated shafts of refined gold,
and with a strength equal to the thunderbolt and lightning of great Indra;
That Rāma slew his enemies in battle;
for him the wise Viśvāmitra had bestowed weapons for the sake of slaying the enemies of the gods, who were unassailable even by the deities themselves.
By whom, in the past, while the sacrifice of the high-souled Janaka was underway,
the bow of Maheśvara was broken as he sported with ease.
Having performed these deeds, Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma,
celebrated ten unimpeded Jārūthya horse-sacrifices.
While Rāma ruled the kingdom, no evil words were heard, the wind did not blow turbulently, and there was no plundering of wealth.
Widows did not lament, nor did misfortunes ever occur;
everything there was auspicious while Rāma ruled the kingdom.
Living beings had no fear arising from water, fire, or wind,
nor did the elderly perform funeral rites for children.
The Kṣatriya class is devoted to the highest celibacy (brahmacarya), while the Vaiśyas take delight in the Kṣatriya;
and indeed, the Śūdras, free from egoism, serve these three castes.
Wives did not transgress against their husbands, nor did husbands transgress against their wives;
the entire world was self-controlled, and the earth was free from robbers.
Rāma alone was the lord; Rāma became the protector.
There were thousands of years, and likewise [there were kings] possessing thousands of sons.
While Rāma was ruling the kingdom, all living beings— of gods, sages, and humans alike— were free from disease.
While Rāma was ruling the kingdom, there was universal concord upon the earth;
even those people who are knowers of the Purāṇas sing this verse regarding it: *BrP_213.152*
With their true purpose fixed upon Rāma, they [extol] the majesty of that wise one:
"He is dark-complexioned, youthful, with reddish eyes, a radiant countenance, and measured in his speech."
With arms reaching to his knees, a handsome face, lion-like shoulders, and mighty arms,
Rāma ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years.

In that kingdom, the sound of the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus Vedas, as well as the twang of the great-souled king’s bowstring, never ceased; it was constantly proclaimed: "Let there be giving! Let there be eating!"
Endowed with courage, perfected in virtue, and blazing with his own splendor,
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, shone forth, surpassing both the moon and the sun.
The mighty Rāghava, having performed hundreds of meritorious sacrifices accompanied by excellent sacrificial fees, abandoned Ayodhyā and ascended to heaven.
In this very manner, the mighty-armed and powerful lord, the delighter of the Ikṣvāku dynasty,
having slain Rāvaṇa along with his hosts, ascended to heaven.
This is another manifestation of the high-souled Keśava,
renowned in the Māthura-kalpa, truly for the welfare of all the worlds.
There [he slew] Śālva, the King of Cedi, Kaṃsa, and Dvivida;
as well as Ariṣṭa, Vṛṣabha, Keśin, and Pūtanā, the daughter of the Daityas.
The heroic one destroyed the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa, as well as Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika— those demons in human bodies.
The thousand arms of Bāṇa, the performer of wondrous deeds, were severed;
Naraka was slain in battle, as was the exceedingly powerful Yavana.
By his splendor, he seized all the jewels of the kings,
and those monarchs on the face of the earth who were of wicked conduct were subdued.
This manifestation of the Great-Souled One for the sake of the welfare of the world is Kalkī, named Viṣṇuyaśas, born in the village of Śambhala.
For the sake of the welfare of the entire world, the highly illustrious god appeared once more,
along with these and many other divine beings surrounded by hosts of gods.
The manifestations [of the Lord] are sung of in the Purāṇas by those who discourse on Brahman;
at the recitation of these manifestations, even the gods become bewildered.
In this Purāṇa, which is established in accordance with the Vedic revelation,
there is a recitation of the manifestations [of the Lord] by way of a mere summary.
The glory of the all-pervading Lord, the teacher of all worlds who is worthy of praise, has been proclaimed;
by this recitation of his manifestations, his ancestors are gratified.
He who, with palms joined in reverence, listens to [the glory] of Viṣṇu of immeasurable heroism, [attains liberation].
Having heard of these yogic powers (yoga-māyās) of the Lord of Yoga, a person is liberated from all sins and attains prosperity,
abundance, and vast enjoyments.

One attains [this] quickly through the grace of the Blessed One. Thus, O best of sages, have I proclaimed the meritorious manifestations of Viṣṇu, who possesses immeasurable splendor, which remove all sins.
The sages said:
"O Sage, we do not reach satiety from this nectar of meritorious dharma sung from your mouth; indeed, our curiosity remains great."
O Sage, you know the origin and dissolution of beings, as well as the course of their actions; because of that, we question you, the one of great intelligence.
It is heard that the path to the world of Yama is extremely difficult to traverse;
it constantly causes suffering and affliction, and brings fear to all living beings.
O best among speakers, tell us how men travel by that path to the abode of Yama, and what the measure of that path is.
O Sage, O Omniscient One, we ask you: tell us everything without exception—how is it that men do not encounter the sufferings of hell? O Sage! BrP_214.5 //
By what means—through generosity, righteousness, or self-restraint—is there a difference between the world of humans and that of Yama? To what extent does it differ? (BrP 214.6)
And how do they go to the heavenly realm, and by what karma to hell?
How many are the abodes of heaven, and how many are the hells?
How do those who have performed good deeds travel, and how do those who have committed evil deeds travel?
What is the form, what is the size, and what is the color of both when the living being is being led to the world of Yama? Tell us this.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O tigers among sages, you of virtuous vows,
as I speak of the wheel of worldly existence (*saṃsāra-cakra*), which is undecaying and whose stability does not exist.
Therefore, I shall declare to you the entire determination of the path of Yama,
beginning from the moment of the soul's departure, in a manner that no other will speak.
O best of beings, you ask me about the very nature of the path,
the road to the realm of Yama, and the interval between that and the human world.
The distance between them is eighty-six thousand yojanas;
that path is described as being like molten copper, yet not heated by the sun.
For those living beings known as "souls" must inevitably go there:
the meritorious go to the realms of merit, while the base evildoers go to the realms of sin.
And twenty-two hells are situated within the domain of Yama,
wherein those who have performed evil deeds undergo their retribution individually.
The hells are Raurava, Raudra, Śūkara, and Tāla,
as well as the most terrible Kumbhīpāka, Śālmala, and Vimohana.
There are those who eat insects, those who devour worms, those who subsist on lotus stalks, as well as those who wander about;
there are other rivers flowing with pus, and likewise others with blood for their waters.
The fiercely terrible Agnijvāla, Sandaṃśa, Śunabhojana, the horrific Vaitaraṇī, and likewise Asipattravana; BrP_214.17 //
There was no shade of trees there, nor were there ponds or lakes;
neither were there step-wells, oblong pools, nor wells, water-stations, or assembly halls.
On that path, there was no pavilion, no temple, no rivers, and no mountains; not a single hermitage site was to be found there.
That great path upon which a man, exhausted and utterly worn out, must necessarily rest— that very path must be traversed by all.
But when the time arrives, having abandoned friends, kinsmen, wealth, and so forth—
whether they be born from a womb, from an egg, from sweat, or from a sprout— BrP 214.21.
Both the moving and the unmoving shall go upon the great path,
along with gods, asuras, and humans, all subject to the power of Vaivasvata.
By women, men, and eunuchs alike—by all those designated as living beings upon this earth—at the forenoon, the afternoon, or likewise at midday; ||| BrP_214.23 |||
Whether at the time of twilight, at midnight, or when dawn has arrived—
whether by the elderly, the middle-aged, or likewise those established in youth— BrP 214.24.
Whether in the womb, in childhood, while living abroad, as a householder, on a mountain, or even on dry land— that great path must be traversed.
Whether they are situated in a field, or in water, or likewise within a house; whether sitting, or standing, or likewise lying upon a bed.
Whether they are awake or asleep, that great path must be traversed by the living being themselves,
once the lifespan ordained for this world has been experienced.
And at its conclusion, even if he is unwilling, he is released from his own life-breaths by water,
fire, poison, weapons, hunger, disease, or falling from a mountain.
Having encountered some sign, the embodied being is released from the vital breaths,
leaving behind the entire, very great body composed of the five elements.
He takes on another body born of his own karma, a body fit for torment;
he obtains a firm body for the experience of pleasure and pain.
Therefore, that man who commits evil suffers great hardships,
while the righteous person, joyful, is led here to the abode of Yama and experiences happiness.
The heat (ūṣman), provoked within the body and impelled by a violent wind,
blazes without fuel and shatters the vital points (marmasthāna).
The vital air named udāna moves upward from there;
it prevents the downward movement of the water and food that has been consumed.
Therefore, he who has given gifts of water and likewise the essence of food,
obtains joy in that calamity.
He by whom food has been given with a mind purified by faith attains satisfaction even then, even without food.
He who has not spoken falsehoods, nor caused a breach of affection,
and who is a believer and full of faith, attains a happy death.
Those men who are devoted to the worship of gods and Brahmins, who are free from malice,
pure, generous, and modest, meet with a happy death.
He who would not abandon the Dharma out of desire, nor out of passion, nor out of hatred,
and who acts according to what has been taught and is gentle— he attains a death in happiness.
Those men who give water to the thirsty and provide food to the hungry attain,
at the time of death, a passing endowed with happiness.
The givers of wealth conquer cold; the givers of sandalwood conquer heat;
and those who bear the distress of others conquer painful, life-threatening agony.
Those who bestow knowledge dispel delusion, and likewise, those who give lamps dispel darkness;
however, a false witness, a liar, and a teacher who does not provide instruction [lead to darkness].
All those who revile the Vedas are likewise subject to death through delusion;
they are terrifying, foul-smelling, and carry deceptive mallets in their hands.
Likewise, the evil-minded messengers of Yama approach;
when they come within the range of his vision, trembling arises within him.
Then he cries out incessantly for his brothers, mother, and father;
yet, O brahmins, that speech is perceived as indistinct and monosyllabic.
His vision becomes bewildered from terror, and his face is covered by coughing and vomiting;
then, overcome by pain, he abandons that body.
Moving at the forefront of the wind, he attains another body of that same form;
it is for the purpose of undergoing the torments of his own karma, and does not arise from a mother and father.
Suffering is experienced according to one's size, age, state, and physical form;
thereafter, Yama’s messenger binds them with terrible nooses.
For a living being whose time has arrived, who is intensely afflicted by pain,
whose body has been abandoned by the elements, and whose breath has reached the throat;
Once the life-force has been expelled from the body, it cries out most piteously;
having departed, it becomes like the wind within the six-sheathed physical frame.
On this earth, he is abandoned by mothers and fathers, as well as by brothers, maternal uncles, wives, sons, friends, and teachers.
And being beheld by those miserable ones with eyes filled with tears,
he abandons his own body and departs, having become like the wind.
It is a boundless darkness, most terrible and shrouded in gloom;
it bestows both pleasure and pain, and is difficult to traverse for those of evil deeds.
It is unbearable, endless, difficult to behold, and hard to approach;
it is unattainable, exceedingly difficult to traverse, and always brings harm to the most wicked.
Dragged by those beings and bound with the nooses of Yama,
and being struck with mallets, they are led along that great path.
Beholding a living being whose life-span is exhausted at the time of death,
the terrifying messengers of Yama arrive, desiring to lead him away.
At the time of their departure, some were mounted upon bears, tigers, and donkeys;
others upon camels, monkeys, scorpions, and wolves.
Others had owls, snakes, and cats as their mounts;
likewise, there were those mounted on hawks and jackals, or riding upon bees and herons.
Others had the faces of boars, beasts, vetālas, and buffaloes;
assuming various forms, they were terrible and struck fear into all living beings.
They had long testicles, terrifying mouths, crooked noses, and three eyes;
they possessed large jaws, cheeks, and faces, with pendulous lips.
With protruding, misshapen fangs resembling sprouts,
their limbs were smeared with flesh and blood, and they were exceedingly formidable with their sharp tusks.
With mouths resembling the netherworld, terrifying with flaming tongues, and eyes of a distorted form, flickering and glowing tawny-red; BrP_214.61 //
With eyes resembling fire— upraised like those of a cat, an owl, a firefly, or a *śakragopa* insect, squinting, crowded, and fixed— he stared at him.
They were adorned with many terrifying ornaments bound upon them like serpents,
their limbs were reddish and straight, and they were decorated with garlands of severed heads.
With black serpents coiled around their necks, terrifying with the sound of their hissing,
and with hair resembling flames of fire— stiff, coarse, and fearsome.
They were covered with tawny, reddish-brown, and flickering beards of dark brown,
and possessed great, most terrible, long-reaching staff-like arms resembling iron clubs.
Some there had two arms, others likewise had four;
some had sixteen arms, and others likewise had ten or twenty.
Others had innumerable arms, while some possessed thousands of arms,
equipped with weapons of deformed shapes that were blazing and terrifying.
The mighty ones, terrifying [the enemy] with various weapons such as spears, javelins, and discuses that were brilliantly aflame, as well as nooses, chains, and staffs.
When the lifespan of mortals has reached its end, the exceedingly fierce messengers of Yama arrive,
as well as all those who carry out his commands, in order to seize living beings.
That body born of one's own karma, which is to be subjected to torment,
is led by that living being toward the abode of Yama.
Bound with the nooses of Time and with fetters and adamantine chains,
and having been severely beaten by the enraged servants of Yama, he is led away.
Stumbling and weeping, crying out again and again, "O father! O mother! O son!"—thus did he speak, defiled by his own karma.
He was being threatened with great roars by those who, individually and filled with intense rage, were striking him from all sides with thunderbolts and spears.
Fainting, afflicted by suffering, and tormented here and there,
that creature is dragged and led along the path by those who are most terrifying.
[He falls] upon thorns, Kuśa grass, anthills, stakes, stones, and pebbles;
likewise, into a blazing fire, fierce with hundreds of caustic substances and thunderbolts.
Scorched by the rays of the blazing sun and burned by its beams,
he is dragged away by the messengers of Yama, who are terrifying with the howling of jackals.
Dragged by those terrible beings and devoured by hundreds of jackals,
the evildoer proceeds along the dreadful path to the abode of Yama.
On that great path, one must travel sometimes with fear, sometimes with terror, stumbling here and there, and crying out in distress.
Being reviled, agitated, fleeing, and overwhelmed by fear,
those known as living beings must go with their bodies trembling.
Men who are devoid of the gift of alms must travel along paths strewn with thorns and heated sand, while being scorched by them.
Those who take life must travel amidst the foul stench of fat and blood, surrounded by goats with mangled limbs and heaps of burnt and cracked skins.
Those who take the lives of living beings must go [to their destination] while moaning, crying out, shrieking discordantly, and being afflicted by intense agony.
Those who take life must travel [to their destination] pierced by spears, slings, swords, javelins,
arrows, and the sharp points of pikes.
And the sinners are being devoured by dogs, tigers, wolves, and herons.
Those who eat flesh must go [there], being cut by blows from saws and being pierced on all sides by the tips of the horns of buffaloes and bulls.
And one must travel in swarms with boars that tear at [the flesh], with meat-eaters,
and with needles, bees, ravens, and flies.
And those most wicked slayers of honey-makers must travel while being devoured by [beasts],
as must he who would kill a trusting master, a friend, or a woman.
Men who are clever must proceed even while being cut by weapons;
likewise, those who cause living beings to be killed or who strike the innocent [must go to their destination].
Those men who steal the excellent garments and coverings of other women go along the path of Yama while being devoured by Rākṣasas.
Naked and like departed spirits, they flee in haste to the abode of Yama, [having lost] their clothing,
grain, gold, or even their house and field.
Those evil-minded, most wicked evildoers who carry them away are themselves battered and shattered by being struck with stones, clubs, and staffs.
Carrying much blood,
those men who here on earth seize the property of a Brahmin, being fearless of hell, must go to the abode of Yama.
Those lowest of men beat the Brahmins and revile them;
they are bound to dry wood, their ears, eyes, and noses cut off.
Smeared with pus and blood, they are beaten by black vultures and jackals,
and by terrifying, fierce, and cruel servants.
Crying out in lamentation, those sinners go to the abode of Yama along that most difficult path,
which is blazing with light.
Raurava is described as difficult and treacherous for a human being;
it has the appearance of molten copper and is filled with sparks from the flames of fire.
It was strewn with *kuraṇṭaka* thorns, filled with broad and formidable blows,
crowded with spears and thunderbolts, radiant, and possessed of sharp thorns.
It was mixed with glowing coals and sand, impassable due to fire-breathing insects,
filled with garlands of flames, terrible, and scorched by the rays of the sun.
The embodied being is led along the path, dragged by those who are extremely cruel;
whenever the creature, afflicted by suffering, falls somewhere, it cries out.
At that very moment, he is struck with all kinds of weapons by the servants of Yama;
thus is beaten the greedy man who was unrighteous in his sins.
Helpless, a living being is led away by the irresistible servants of Yama;
for everyone must travel that path which is so difficult to traverse.
Led with contempt by various terrible messengers of Yama,
the servant of Yama leads the living being along an extremely dreadful path.
O twice-born ones, he is led into a terrible city made of copper and iron;
that city is vast in form, extending for a hundred thousand yojanas.
It is described as being square, auspicious, and possessing four gates;
its golden walls are ten thousand yojanas high.
Adorned with sapphires, great blue gems,
and rubies, that city was filled with various throngs of terrible and fearsome beings.
The auspicious eastern gate of that [city], adorned with hundreds of banners, was guarded by gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas.
It was adorned with diamonds, sapphires, lapis lazuli, and pearls,
and was filled with hosts of gandharvas and apsarases engaged in song and dance.
By that [path], there is the entrance for gods, sages, and yogins,
as well as for gandharvas, siddhas, yakṣas, vidyādharas, and serpents.
The northern city gate was adorned with bells and yak-tail fans,
arranged with parasols and chowries, and decorated with various jewels.
It was filled with throngs of sages and resounded with the delightful sounds of lutes, auspicious songs, and the chanting of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
By this path enter those who know the Dharma and are devoted to the vow of truth,
as well as those men who provide water in the heat of summer and provide fire in the cold of winter.
Those who escort the weary, those who delight in speaking kindly, those who are devoted to giving, those who are brave, and those who are devoted to their mother and father; BrP_214.113 //
Those who are constantly engaged in the service of the twice-born and are ever-honoring guests [reside there].
Furthermore, the western great gate of the city is adorned with jewels.
It had stairs made of variegated jewels, was adorned with javelins,
and resounded with the booming of kettledrums and clay drums, as well as the blare of conchs and trumpets.
It was constantly resounded with auspicious hymns by throngs of joyful Siddhas;
it was an entrance for those men who were delighted and possessed devotion to Śiva.

Those who have bathed in all the sacred fords, those who are attendants of the five fires, those heroes who died while setting out on a journey, and those who died on Mount Kālañjara; [all these attain the same state].

Those heroes who perished in fire, those by whom fasting unto death was accomplished, and those who were slain for the sake of their masters, friends, and kin, or in the tumult of seizing cattle; [they all attain these worlds].
Those brave men, rich in asceticism, enter through the western gate of that city,
which is most terrible and causes fear to all living beings.
Such was the southern gate, filled with cries of "Alas!
Alas!", enveloped in darkness, and crowded with those possessing sharp horns.
[The path was] impassable due to thorns, scorpions, snakes, and diamond-insects;
it was being ravaged by wolves, tigers, bears, lions, and jackals.
And by that [gate], there is always the entrance for all malevolent beings, with mouths like those of dogs, cats, and vultures, filled with flaming morsels.

Those who cause the slaughter of Brahmins, cows, children, the elderly, or the sick; or those who kill one who has come for refuge, one who is trusting, a woman, a friend, or one who is unarmed—[they go to hell].
Those fools who approach women who should not be approached, those who steal the property of others, those who misappropriate deposits, and those who administer poison or fire; BrP 214.124.
Those who seize the lands, houses, beds, clothes, and ornaments of others;
those who are cruel toward the vulnerabilities of others; and those who are always speakers of falsehood.
Those who give false testimony and those who sell their daughters cause great suffering in villages, kingdoms, cities, and settlements.
Those who delight in eating forbidden food, those who approach their daughter or daughter-in-law, and those who speak harshly to their mother or father go [to hell]. BrP 214.127.
Furthermore, all others who have been designated as perpetrators of great sins (mahāpātaka) indeed enter through the southern gate.
The sages said:
"O sage, we do not reach satiety from the nectar of meritorious dharma sung from your mouth; indeed, our curiosity remains great."
O Sage, you know the origin and dissolution of beings, as well as the course of their actions; therefore, we question you, the one of great intelligence.
It is heard that the path to the world of Yama is extremely difficult to traverse;
it constantly causes suffering and affliction, and brings fear to all living beings.
O best of speakers, tell us how men travel by that path to the abode of Yama, and what the measure of that path is.
O Sage, O Omniscient One, we ask you: tell us everything without exception—how is it that men do not undergo the sufferings of hell? O Sage!
By what means—through generosity, righteousness, and self-restraint—is there a difference between the world of humans and that of Yama? To what extent does it differ?
And how do they go to the heavenly realm, and by what karma to hell?
How many are the abodes of heaven, and how many are the hells?

How do those who have performed good deeds go, and how do those who have committed evil deeds go? What is the form, what is the size, and what is the color of both when the living being is being led to the world of Yama? Tell us this.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O tigers among sages, you of virtuous vows,
as I speak of the wheel of worldly existence, which is undecaying and whose stability does not exist.
Therefore, I shall declare to you the entire determination of the path of Yama,
beginning from the moment of the soul's departure, in a manner that no other will speak.
O best of beings, you ask me about the very nature of the path,
as well as the road to the realm of Yama and the distance between it and the human world.
The distance between them is eighty-six thousand yojanas;
that path is described as being like molten copper, yet not heated.
For those living beings known as "souls" must inevitably go [to their respective realms]:
the doers of merit go to meritorious places, while the base doers of evil go to sinful ones.
And twenty-two hells are situated within the domain of Yama,
wherein those who have performed evil deeds undergo their retribution individually.
The hells are Raurava, Raudra, Śūkara, and Tāla;
Kumbhīpāka, which is most terrible, as well as Śālmalī and Vimohana.
They are the Kīṭāda, the Kṛmibhakṣa, the Nālābhakṣa, and likewise the Bhrama;
there are other rivers flowing with pus, and likewise those with water of blood.
The fiercely terrible Agnijvāla, Saṃdaṃśa, Śunabhojana, the dreadful Vaitaraṇī, and likewise Asipattravana; BrP_214*.17 //
There was no shade of trees there, nor were there ponds or lakes;
neither were there large oblong ponds, nor wells, nor water-stations, nor assembly halls.
On that path, there was no pavilion, no sanctuary, no rivers, and no mountains; not a single hermitage site was to be found there.
That great path upon which a man, exhausted and utterly worn out, comes to rest— that very path must necessarily be traversed by all.
But when the time arrives, having abandoned friends, kinsmen, wealth, and the like—
whether they be born from a womb, from an egg, from sweat, or from a sprout— BrP 214.21.
Both the moving and the unmoving shall go upon the great path,
along with gods, asuras, and humans, all subject to the power of Vaivasvata.
By women, men, and neuter beings known as living souls upon this earth—
whether in the forenoon, the afternoon, or likewise at midday— BrP_214.23.
Whether at the time of twilight, at midnight, or when dawn has arrived,
[this should be done] by the elderly, the middle-aged, or likewise by those in their youth.
Whether in the womb, in childhood, while living abroad, as householders, on mountains, or even on dry land— that great path must be traversed.
Whether they are situated on dry land, in water, or within a house; whether they are sitting, standing, or likewise lying down on a bed.
Whether they are awake or fast asleep, that great path must be traversed by a living being who has himself experienced the allotted lifespan here in this world.
And at its conclusion, one is released from life itself, even against one's will,
by water, fire, poison, weapons, hunger, disease, or falling from a mountain.
Having encountered some sign, the embodied being is released from the vital breaths,
leaving behind the entire, very great body composed of the five elements.
He takes on another body produced by his own karma, a body fit for torment;
he obtains a firm body for the experience of pleasure and pain.
Because of that, the man who has committed evil experiences great hardships,
while the righteous person, joyful, is led here to the abode of Yama and enjoys pleasures.
The heat, provoked within the body and impelled by a violent wind,
blazes forth without fuel and pierces the vital points (marmas).
The vital air called udāna moves upward from there;
it prevents the downward movement of water and food that have been consumed.
Therefore, he who has given gifts of water and likewise provided the essence of food,
obtains joy in that time of adversity.
He by whom food has been given with a mind purified by faith attains satisfaction even then, even without food.
He who has not spoken falsehoods, nor caused a breach of affection,
and who is a believer and full of faith, attains a happy death.
Those men who are devoted to the worship of gods and Brahmins, who are free from malice,
pure, generous, and modest, meet their death in happiness.
He who would not abandon the Dharma out of desire, nor out of passion, nor out of hatred,
but acts according to what has been taught and is gentle— he attains a happy death.
Those men who give water to the thirsty and provide food to the hungry attain,
at the time of death, a passing endowed with happiness.
The givers of wealth conquer cold; the givers of sandalwood conquer heat; and those who bear the distress of others conquer the agonizing pain that destroys life.
Those who bestow knowledge dispel delusion, and likewise, those who give lamps dispel darkness;
however, a false witness, a liar, and one who does not provide instruction as a teacher [bring about the opposite].
All those who revile the Vedas likewise have delusion as their death;
they are terrifying, foul-smelling, and carry deceptive mallets in their hands.
Likewise, the evil-minded messengers of Yama approach;
when they come within the range of his vision, trembling arises within him.
Then that being cries out incessantly for its brothers, mother, and father;
yet, O Brahmins, that speech is perceived as indistinct and consisting of a single sound.
His vision becomes bewildered by terror, and his face is covered by coughing and vomiting;
then, overcome by pain, he abandons that body.
Moving at the forefront of the wind, he attains another body of that same nature;
it is for the purpose of undergoing the torments of his own karma, and not born from a mother and father.
Suffering is experienced according to one's size, age, stage of life, and physical form;
thereafter, the messenger of Yama binds [the person] with terrible nooses.
For a living being whose time has arrived, who is intensely afflicted by pain,
whose body has been abandoned by the elements, and whose breath has reached the throat;
The life-force, cast out from the body, wails most piteously;
having departed, it becomes like the wind within the six-sheathed physical frame.
On this earth, he is abandoned by mothers, fathers, brothers, maternal uncles, as well as by wives, sons, friends, and teachers.
And being gazed upon intensely by those wretched ones with eyes filled with tears,
he abandons his own body and departs, having become like the wind.
It is a shoreless darkness, most terrible and shrouded in gloom,
bestowing both pleasure and pain, and difficult to traverse for those of evil deeds.
It is unbearable, endless, difficult to behold, and hard to approach;
it is unattainable, exceedingly difficult to traverse, and always brings harm to the most wicked.
Dragged by those beings and bound with the nooses of Yama,
and being beaten with mallets, they are led along that great path.
Beholding a living being whose life has been exhausted at the end of its lifespan,
the terrifying messengers of Yama arrive, desiring to lead him away.
At the time of their departure, they mounted upon bears, tigers, and donkeys;
others [mounted] upon camels, monkeys, scorpions, and wolves.
Others had owls, snakes, and cats as their mounts;
some were mounted on vultures, hawks, and jackals, while others had honey-bees and herons for their vehicles.
Others had the faces of boars, beasts, vetālas, and buffaloes;
they assumed various forms, were terrible, and struck fear into all living beings.
They had long testicles, terrifying mouths, crooked noses, and three eyes;
they possessed large jaws and cheeks, and their lips hung down low.
With protruding, deformed fangs resembling sprouts,
their limbs were smeared with flesh and blood, and they were rendered exceedingly fierce by their formidable tusks.
With mouths resembling the netherworld, terrifying with flaming tongues,
and eyes of flickering, blazing tawny hue and extremely distorted shape.
With eyes like those of a cat, an owl, a firefly, or an indragopa insect— upraised, squinting, crowded together, and fixed, resembling flames.
They were adorned with many terrifying ornaments fastened like serpents,
their limbs were straight and red, and they were decorated with garlands of severed heads.
With black snakes coiled around their necks, terrifying with the sound of their hissing,
and with hair resembling flames of fire— stiff, coarse, and fearsome.
They were covered with tawny, reddish-brown, and flickering dark-brown beards,
and possessed great, most terrible, long-reaching arms like iron clubs.
Some there had two arms, others likewise had four;
some had sixteen arms, and others had ten or twenty.
Others had innumerable arms, and some possessed thousands of arms,
equipped with weapons of deformed shapes that were blazing and terrifying.
The mighty ones, terrifying [the enemy] with various weapons such as spears, javelins, and discs, all blazing brightly, as well as nooses, chains, and staffs; BrP 214.68.
When the lifespan of mortals has come to an end, the exceedingly fierce ones and likewise the executors of Yama's commands arrive to seize all living beings.
That body which one takes up, born of one's own karma and subject to torment—
that very body of the creature is led toward the abode of Yama.
Bound with nooses of Time and with fetters and adamantine chains,
and beaten severely by the enraged servants of Yama, he is led away.
Stumbling and weeping, crying out again and again, "O father! O mother! O son!"—thus did he speak, defiled by his own karma.
Having struck them with sharpened spears, sharp mallets, and heavy clubs,
and with blows from swords and javelins, as well as most dreadful thunderbolt-staves;
He was being threatened with loud roars by those who, each one individually and intensely enraged, were striking him from all sides with thunderbolts and spears.
Fainting, afflicted by suffering, and burning with heat here and there,
that creature is dragged and led along the path by those who inspire great terror.
In places filled with *kuśa* grass, thorns, anthills, stakes, stones, and pebbles, as well as in blazing fires fierce with hundreds of caustic substances and thunderbolts; ||| BrP_214*.76 |||
Scorched by the rays of the blazing sun and consumed by its beams,
he is dragged away by the messengers of Yama, who are terrifying with the howling of jackals.
Dragged along by those terrible beings and devoured by hundreds of jackals,
the evildoer proceeds upon the dreadful path to the abode of Yama.
On that great path, one must travel sometimes terrified, sometimes trembling, stumbling here and there, and crying out in agony.
Being reviled, agitated, fleeing, and overwhelmed by fear,
those known as living beings must go with their bodies trembling.
Men devoid of the gift must travel along paths strewn with thorns and heated sands while being scorched by them.
Those who kill living beings must travel in groups with their bodies smelling foul of fat and blood, like the carcasses of goats, and covered in burnt and cracked skin.
Those who take the lives of living beings must travel while making moaning sounds, crying out, and shrieking discordantly, afflicted by intense agony.
Those who take life must go [to their destination] pierced by spears, slings, swords, javelins, arrows,
and the sharp points of pikes.
And the sinners are being devoured by dogs, tigers, wolves, and herons.
Those who eat flesh must go there, being cut by blows from saws and being pierced on all sides by the tips of the horns of buffaloes and bulls.
And one must travel with boars that tear at [the flesh], with meat-eaters,
and with swarms of needles, bees, ravens, and flies.
And those most wicked honey-killers must proceed while being devoured by [beasts],
as must he who would slay a trusting master, a friend, or a woman.
And men who are clever must proceed even while being cut by weapons;
likewise, those who cause living beings to be killed or who strike the innocent [must go there].
Those men who steal the excellent garments and coverings of other women go along the path of Yama while being devoured by Rākṣasas.
Naked and like departed spirits, they flee in haste to the abode of Yama, [having stolen] clothing,
grain, gold, or even houses and fields.
Those evil-minded, most wicked evildoers who carry them off [are themselves] shattered by being beaten with stones, clubs, and staffs.
Carrying abundant blood, those men who here on earth seize the property of a Brahmin and are fearless of hell must go to the abode of Yama.
Those lowest of men beat the Brahmins and revile them;
they are bound to dry wood, their ears, eyes, and noses cut off.
Smeared with pus and blood, they are beaten by black vultures and jackals,
and by terrifying, fierce, and cruel servants.
Crying out in lamentation, those sinners go to the abode of Yama along that most difficult path which has the brilliance of blazing fire.
The Raurava hell is described as difficult and treacherous for a human being;
it has the appearance of molten copper and is filled with sparks from blazing flames.
It was strewn with *kuraṇṭaka* thorns, filled with broad and formidable blows,
crowded with spears and thunderbolts, radiant, and possessed of fierce thorns.
It is strewn with glowing coals and sand, impassable due to fire-breathing insects,
filled with garlands of flames, terrible, and scorched by the rays of the sun.
The embodied being is led along the path, dragged by extremely cruel [beings];
whenever the creature, afflicted by suffering, falls somewhere, he cries out.
At that very moment, he is struck with all kinds of weapons by the servants of Yama;
thus is beaten the greedy one who was unrighteous in his sins.
Helpless, a living being is led away by the irresistible servants of Yama;
for everyone must travel that path which is so difficult to traverse.
Led with contempt by various terrifying messengers of Yama,
the servant of Yama leads the living being along a most dreadful path.
O twice-born ones, he is led into a terrible city made of copper and iron;
that city is vast in form, extending for a hundred thousand yojanas.
It is described as being square, auspicious, and possessing four gates;
its golden ramparts are ten thousand yojanas high.
Adorned with sapphire, great sapphire, and ruby,
that city was filled with various multitudes, both formidable and terrifying.
Its auspicious eastern gate, adorned with hundreds of banners, was frequented by gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas.
Adorned with diamonds, sapphires, lapis lazuli, and pearls,
it was filled with the songs and dances of hosts of gandharvas and apsarases.
Through that [path], there is entry for the gods, the sages, and likewise for the yogins,
as well as for the gandharvas, siddhas, yakṣas, vidyādharas, and serpents.
The northern city gate was adorned with bells and chowries,
arranged with parasols and fly-whisks, and decorated with various jewels.
It was filled with throngs of sages, resonant with the delightful sounds of lutes and the chanting of auspicious songs, and echoing with the recitation of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
By this path enter those who know the Dharma and are devoted to the vow of truth,
as well as those men who provide water in the heat of summer and provide fire in the cold of winter.
Those who escort the weary, those who delight in speaking kindly, those who are devoted to giving, those who are brave, and those who are dedicated to their mother and father; ||| BrP_214*.113 |||
Those who are constantly engaged in the service of the twice-born and are perpetual worshippers of guests [reside there].
Furthermore, the western great gate of the city is adorned with jewels.
It had stairways made of variegated jewels, was adorned with javelins,
and resounded with the booming of kettledrums and clay drums, as well as the blare of conchs and trumpets.
It was constantly resounded with auspicious hymns by throngs of joyful perfected beings (siddhas);
through it, there was the entrance for those joyful men who possessed devotion to Śiva.

Those who have bathed in all the sacred fords, those who are attendants of the five fires, those heroes who died while setting out on a journey, and those who died on Mount Kālañjara; [all these attain the same state].

Those heroes who perished in fire, those by whom fasting unto death was accomplished, and those who were slain for the sake of their masters, friends, or kin, or in the tumultuous seizure of cattle; [all these attain the worlds of the virtuous].
Those heroic men, rich in asceticism, enter through the western gate into that city,
which is most terrible and causes fear to all living beings.
Such was the southern gate: resounded with cries of "Alas!
Alas!", enveloped in darkness, and filled with creatures possessing sharp horns.
[The path was] impassable due to thorns, scorpions, snakes, and diamond-insects;
it was being plundered by wolves, tigers, bears, lions, and jackals.
And by that [gate], there is always the entry for all those who do harm, with their mouths full of flaming morsels like dogs, cats, and vultures.

Those who cause the death of Brahmins, cows, children, the elderly, or likewise the sick; or those who kill one who has come for refuge, one who trusts them, a woman, a friend, or one who is unarmed—[they go to hell].
Those fools who approach women who should not be approached, those who steal the property of others,
those who misappropriate deposits, and those who administer poison or fire;
Those who seize the lands, houses, beds, clothes, and ornaments of others;
those who are cruel toward the vulnerabilities of others; and those who are always speakers of falsehood.
Indeed, those who provide false testimony and those who sell their daughters cause great suffering in villages, kingdoms, cities, and dwellings.
Those who delight in eating forbidden food, those who approach their daughter or daughter-in-law,
and those who speak harshly to their mother or father go there.
Furthermore, all others who have been designated as perpetrators of great sins (mahāpātaka) indeed enter through the southern gate.
The sages said:
"How do the sinners enter the city by way of the southern path?
O rich in asceticism, we wish to hear that; tell us in detail."
Vyāsa said:
I shall describe that most terrible, exceedingly dreadful, and fearsome gateway,
crowded with various beasts of prey and resounding with the howling of hundreds of jackals.
It was filled with the sound of "phetkāra" cries, inaccessible and hair-raising,
surrounded by bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and other rākṣasas.
Having seen the door at the very far end in this manner, those who have committed evil deeds suddenly fall into delusion and lament out of terror.
Then, having bound them with chains and nooses, they drag them about fearlessly;
they strike them with clubs and revile them again and again.
Then, having regained consciousness, drenched in blood,
they indeed went toward the southern gate, stumbling at every step.
It was filled with sharp thorns and strewn with gravel,
and covered with sharp stones resembling the edges of razors.
In some places it was covered with mud and impassable pits;
in other places it was strewn here and there with teeth resembling iron needles.
Distressed, they travel along a path filled with glowing embers, past mountains made treacherous by precipitous cliffs and crowded with trees.
In some places with uneven pits, in others with very slippery clods of earth,
with scorching sands, and likewise with sharp spikes;
In some places it was filled with heated iron spikes, in some places joined with forest fires,
in some places with heated rocks, and in some places pervaded by snow.
In some places it was covered with sand reaching up to the neck,
in some places it was filled with foul water, and in others again by the fire of a forest conflagration.
In some places there were lions, wolves, tigers, and dreadful ten-legged insects;
in some places there were great leeches, and in others, moreover, pythons.
In some places there were fierce flies, in others serpents with virulent poison,
and in yet other places wicked elephants, intoxicated by their strength and intent on destruction.
And with great bulls whose sharp horns were goring the path,
with buffaloes possessing massive horns, with camels, and with rutting wild asses;
Oppressed by fierce ḍākinīs, by terrifying rākṣasas,
and by most dreadful diseases, they go forth.
Being struck by a fierce wind mixed with great dust and by a rain of massive stones, they were left without refuge.
In some places they go forth being split apart by the falling of lightning,
and in others they are pierced on all sides by a great rain of arrows.
Scorched by falling thunderclaps, by most dreadful falls of meteors,
and by a rain of blazing coals, they enter [the hells].
Being filled by a great rain of dust, they weep,
and they are repeatedly terrified by the most dreadful roars of clouds.
Completely pulverized on all sides by a rain of arrows and drenched by streams of great caustic water, they pass away.
Torn apart on all sides by a great, cold wind that is both harsh and rough,
they wither and shrink away.
Thus, by this path— devoid of provisions, without support, difficult to traverse, and entirely lacking water— the men [proceeded].
All embodied beings who are deluded and performers of evil deeds are led with great exhaustion toward the abode of Yama.
Then, by the most terrible messengers of Yama who carry out his commands,
they are forcibly [taken] while alone, dependent on others, and deprived of friends and kinsmen.
Lamenting their own deeds, they weep again and again;
having become ghosts, they are forbidden [from food], with their throats, lips, and palates parched.
Emaciated in body and trembling with fear, they were being consumed by the fire of hunger;
some were bound with iron chains, while others had their feet tied upward.
Being parched, men are dragged by the exceedingly powerful messengers of Yama;
others, with their faces turned downward, are dragged along in great misery.
Deprived of food and drink, begging again and again, they spoke with voices choked with tears, saying, "Give! Give! (BrP 215.29).
With palms joined in reverence, wretched and tormented by hunger and thirst,
they beheld various kinds of foods, both high and low, as well as abundant things to be eaten and drunk.
Seeing them repeatedly begging for substances mixed with fragrant incense,
as well as boiled rice mixed with curd, milk, and ghee;
To those who were begging for fragrant drinks and cool waters,
the messengers of Yama— terrible beings with eyes red at the corners from rage— then spoke these harsh words while threatening them.
The messengers of Yama said: "You did not offer oblations at the proper time, nor did you give gifts to the brahmins;
and when gifts were being given, you forcibly obstructed them among the twice-born."
And the fruit of that sin has come upon you;
it was not consumed by fire, nor lost in water, nor stolen by kings or thieves.
O Brahmin, from where could such [a result] come now for those lowest of men by whom no gifts were given in the past,
whereas virtuous people of a sattvic nature have indeed bestowed their gifts?
For them, these imagined mountains of food appear,
consisting of various kinds of solid foods, soft foods, drinks, things to be licked, and things to be sucked.
You shall not attain [the goal], nor shall anything ever be given by you;
however, those by whom gifts have been given, oblations offered, sacrifices performed, and Brahmins honored—[by them it shall be attained].
"O denizens of hell, their food is always brought here and deposited for us; how could we possibly give away another's property? (BrP 215.38)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words of the servants, those who were free from desire yet afflicted by hunger and thirst were then tormented by the cruel weapons of Yama’s messengers.
With mallets and iron clubs, with spears, javelins, and sharp-edged spears,
with iron bars, slings, maces, axes, and arrows.
While being struck from behind by the utterly merciless messengers of Yama,
the evildoers are devoured from the front by lions, tigers, and other beasts.
Afflicted by their own karma, these wretched and most dreadful sinners, crying out in lamentation, find themselves unable to enter or to exit, suffering intensely.
There, having been severely crushed by the servants of Yama,
the sinners are led into the entrance where Yama himself resides.
Yama, the god who is righteous-souled, the performer of dharma, and the restrainer of all—
thus do men reach the city of the departed by such an exceedingly painful path.
Then, having been pointed out by the messengers, they are led before Yama;
thereafter, those of evil deeds behold him in his terrifying form.
Their eyes were pierced by evil, their own intellects were perverted,
and [they beheld him] with a face made terrible by fangs and eyes curved by knitted brows.
With hair standing erect and a great beard, his upper and lower lips quivering,
possessing eighteen arms, wrathful, and resembling a mass of black collyrium.
With hands raised holding all kinds of weapons, joined with a fierce staff,
mounted upon a great buffalo, and possessing eyes like blazing fire.
Wearing red garlands and garments, towering like a great cloud,
with a roar like the clouds at the end of an aeon, he seemed as if drinking up the great ocean.
He saw as if devouring the three worlds and vomiting forth fire,
and standing near him was Death, possessing a radiance like the fire of cosmic destruction.
Mārīcī, Ugrā, Mahāmārī, and the terrible Kālarātri— [each] resembling the fire of universal dissolution and as fearsome as Death itself.
Various painful diseases of many forms and terrifying nature appeared,
bearing spears, tridents, and goads, and holding nooses, discs, and swords.
Wielding adamantine staffs, they are fierce, bearing razors, quivers, and bows;
they are innumerable, possessed of great heroism, cruel, and have the luster of collyrium.
The terrifying messengers of Yama, their hands raised with all kinds of weapons,
surrounded him with this most formidable retinue.
The most wicked see Yama and the terrifying Citragupta;
and Yama rebukes those evildoers excessively.
But the venerable Citragupta, awakening him with words of dharma, said:
Citragupta said:
"O you of evil deeds, stealers of others' property,
arrogant because of your beauty and prowess, violators of the wives of others!"
Whatever action is performed by oneself is experienced again by oneself;
why then have you committed this evil deed for the sake of destroying yourselves?
Now, why do you grieve while being tormented by your own actions?
Experience your own sufferings; for there is no fault in anyone else.
"These rulers of the earth who have arrived in my presence are of wicked intellect and arrogant in their strength, due to their own terrible deeds."
O kings of wicked conduct, you who bring destruction upon your subjects!
For the sake of a kingdom lasting but a short time, why have you committed such evil deeds?
O kings, now reap the fruit of that [karma] for which you punished the subjects by force, through injustice, out of greed for sovereignty, or out of delusion.
Whence comes the kingdom and the wife for whose sake evil was committed?
Having abandoned all that, you now remain here alone.
We do not see that entire power by which all subjects were destroyed;
what kind of fruit is this, now that they are being torn apart by the messengers of Yama?
Vyāsa said:
Thus rebuked by Yama with many kinds of words,
those kings, grieving over their own deeds, remained silent.
Having thus personally assigned the duties of kings, the King of Dharma himself spoke these words for the sake of purifying their transgressions.
Yama said:
"O Caṇḍa, O Mahācaṇḍa, seize these kings and purify them from their sins, step by step, in the fires of hell."
Vyāsa said:
Then, rising up quickly, he seized the kings by their feet,
whirled them around with great force, and having thrown them upward, he caught them again.
In proportion to the measure of each respective sin, the messengers of Yama violently strike them upon a stone surface, as if striking a great tree with a thunderbolt.
Then, being shattered, blood flows from his channels;
at that time, the embodied soul becomes unconscious and motionless.
Then, touched by the wind, he slowly revives again;
thereafter, for the sake of purifying his sins, they cast him into the ocean of hell.
And then, O best of Brahmins, those messengers report other men who delight in evil deeds— those who are intensely afflicted by suffering— to Yama.
The messengers of Yama said: "O Lord, by your command, this man— who is utterly deluded, averse to dharma, and constantly devoted to supreme wickedness— has been brought here by us."
This man is greedy, of evil conduct, and possessed of great sins; he commits minor offenses, is always devoted to violence, and is impure.
One who approaches those who should not be approached, one of wicked soul, a stealer of another's property,
a buyer of a maiden, a false witness, an ungrateful person, and a deceiver of friends.
By this evil-souled one, intoxicated with pride, dharma was constantly reviled and sinful deeds were committed in the world of mortals.
O Lord of Gods, tell us now of his restraint and favor; are you the master in the application of these actions, or are we the ones who stand in opposition?
Vyāsa said:
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods and having placed the evildoer before him,
[he spoke] regarding the thousands of hells, numbering hundreds of millions and tens of millions.
Then those servants go forth to seize other men once the transgression has been committed; indeed, Yama is the master of evildoers.
He commanded those terrible servants of his for the purpose of suppression,
according to the specific punishment that had been ordained for each by Vasiṣṭha and the others.
Greatly enraged, the servants of Yama inflict those punishments upon the sinner with goads,
mallets, clubs, saws, spears, and javelins.
And by the falling of swords and spears, evildoers are torn asunder within thousands of hells, numbering hundreds of millions and tens of millions.
They are tormented by the servants of Yama due to the faults earned by their own actions;
listen now to the terrifying nature of the hells.
The names and the measurements by which men go there—
that hell is renowned as Mahāvācī, drenched in blood.
There, mixed with vajra-thorns and extending for ten thousand yojanas,
he is crushed as he sinks down and is pierced by those vajra-thorns.
For one hundred thousand years, a man who has killed a cow dwells in the most terrible hell;
he remains for a hundred thousand yojanas in the exceedingly dreadful Kumbhīpāka.
Blazing like a copper pot filled with sand and covered with glowing coals,
it awaits the slayer of a Brahmin, the usurper of land, and the stealer of deposits.
There they are burned, confined until the dissolution of all beings;
Raurava is surrounded by blazing iron bolts tipped with diamonds.
In that hell, which measures sixty thousand yojanas in length and breadth, men are pierced by iron arrows accompanied by flames.
Those men who are false witnesses are crushed there like sugarcane;
that hell is known as the blazing iron chest.
Those who have been made captives and thrown there are burned;
such is the hell called Apratiṣṭhā, filled with pus, urine, and excrement.
There, the oppressor of a Brahmin shall fall headlong into the terrible hell called Vilepaka, which is smeared with boiling lac.
O best of the twice-born, those who are immersed there in the drinking of intoxicants are burned in the hell called Mahāprabhā, which is characterized by towering, blazing spikes.
There, those who cause dissension between husband and wife are split with pikes;
they go to the most terrible hell and the iron slab known as Jayantī.
And by that [sin], the wicked man who consorts with another's wife is driven to the hell named Śālmalī, which is filled with blazing and formidable thorns.
Afflicted by suffering, that woman, who has approached many men,
embraces him who always speaks the truth and cuts away the vital secrets of others.
The tongues of those who gaze upon another's wife with lustful glances are pulled out by the attendants of Yama present in that assembly.
Their eyes are pierced with iron arrows by the servants of Yama.
Even those who go to their mother, sister, daughter, or daughter-in-law,
and those who kill women, children, or the elderly— even up to fourteen Indras—
fall into the fierce hell known as Mahāraurava, which is filled with garlands of flames.
He who sets fire to a city, a field, a house, or a village with flames shall fall into hell for fourteen thousand yojanas.
There that fool is burned for as long as the duration of a kalpa;
it is known as Tāmisra, extending for a hundred thousand yojanas.
Constantly struck by falling swords, spears, and mallets,
the thieves cast there are beaten by the servants of Yama.
For as long as three hundred kalpas, one is tormented with pikes, spears, maces, and swords;
that which is known as Mahātāmisra is said to be twice the duration of Tāmisra.
Filled with leeches and snakes, devoid of light, and extremely painful— there [the killer of a mother,
the killer of a father, and the betrayer of a friend must go].
They remain there being sawn apart for as long as the earth endures,
in the hell named Asipattravana, which bestows manifold suffering.
Extending for ten thousand yojanas and crowded with flaming swords,
he was struck there by those swords and shattered into a hundred pieces.
The betrayer of a friend is tormented until the dissolution of all beings,
in the hell named Karambhavālukā, which extends for ten thousand yojanas.
Surrounded by pits shaped like wells and filled with blazing sand, coals, and thorns,
one is burned and split apart for three hundred thousand times ten thousand years.
By which people are constantly burned through most cruel and false means,
[they go] to the hell named Kākola, which is overflowing with worms and pus.
There, that evil-minded man who eats delicacies alone is cast into the hell named Kuḍmala, which is filled with feces, urine, and blood.
Men who have neglected the performance of the five sacrifices are indeed cast there,
into that place which is foul-smelling, most terrifying, and filled with flesh and blood.
Those lowest of men who take pleasure here in food that is unfit to be eaten fall into a great banyan tree filled with worms and insects and strewn with corpses.
There, the man who sells his daughter shall fall headfirst;
that terrible hell is known by the name Tilapāka.
Those who delight in inflicting pain upon others are crushed there like sesame seeds;
they go to the hell called Tailapāka, which is a blazing flood of oil covering the earth.
There, the betrayer of friends and the slayer of those who have sought refuge are cooked;
it is known by the name Vajrakapāṭa, and is equipped with adamantine chains.
Those who have engaged in the sale of milk are mercilessly tormented there;
that place is called Nirucchvāsa, a blind darkness devoid of wind.
There, motionless, one is cast into that hell called Aṅgāropacaya, which blazes with glowing embers and obstructs the giving of gifts.
He who has not offered a gift to a Brahmin is burned there;
he is called a "great sinner" and goes to a hell extending for a hundred thousand yojanas.
Those who always speak falsehood are cast headlong into that hell called Mahājvālā, which is terrifying with its blazing radiance.
The man who directs his intellect toward evil is burned there for a very long time;
indeed, men are tormented in that hell known as Krakaca.

Those who take pleasure in approaching women who should not be approached are cast into the hell called Guḍapāka, which is filled with pits of glowing molasses and tormented by fierce saws made of diamond.
A man who causes the mixing of castes is cast into that [hell] and is burned there;
[he falls into] the Kṣuradhārā hell, which is covered with sharp razors.
There, for the duration of an eon, men who seize the lands of Brahmins are cut to pieces;
they go to the hell named Ambarīṣa, which is set ablaze by the fire of universal destruction.
There, for a hundred million eons, the stealer of gold is burned in the hell named Vajrakuṭhāra, which is filled with thunderbolts.
There, the evildoers who cut down trees are themselves cut down;
they go to the hell named Paritāpa, which is set ablaze by the fire of universal destruction.
The poisoner and the stealer of honey, that evildoer, is cooked there in the Kālasūtra hell, which is fashioned with adamantine threads.
Wandering there, those who plunder the crops of others are cut to pieces;
this is the hell named Kaśmala, covered with phlegm and snot.
In that regard, a man who always has a craving for meat is briefly reborn in the hell known as Ugragandha, which is filled with saliva, urine, and excrement.
Those who fail to offer funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) to their ancestors are cast into that hell named Durdhara,
which is swarming with leeches and scorpions.
There, the one who consumes bribes remains for ten thousand years;
and there is the hell fashioned of thunderbolts, which is the great torment of the thunderbolt.
Having been cast there, those who seize the wealth, grain, or gold belonging to others are burned and tormented by the servants of Yama.
And those thieves,
having killed living beings, who foolishly devour them like crows and vultures, are cut into pieces by the messengers of Yama with razors.
And those who seize the seat, bed, or clothing belonging to another shall be made to eat their own flesh by the servants of Yama until the end of the eon.
