And those fools, by whom the fruit or even the leaf of men was seized through their evil intent, are torn apart by the messengers of Yama with spears and javelins.
And by the wrathful messengers of Yama, those men who are always evil-minded regarding the property and wives of others are burned as if by grass fires.
Into the hearts of those men who are averse to dharma through their actions, thoughts, or speech, the messengers of Yama drive a flaming stake.
In the world of Yama, those terrible ones undergo torments;
thus for hundreds of thousands, and even hundreds of millions of crores.
In those hells, hell-beings who have committed evil deeds suffer;
even by performing a very small action of an unwholesome nature here in this world, a man [reaps the consequences].
Such a person undergoes torment in the terrible hells within the realms of Yama;
for deluded men do not listen to the Dharma as it has been well-spoken.
"By whom was it seen?"— thus do they reply with a direct denial,
even as those men who commit evil by day and by night with great effort.
For those who, deluded by negligence, do not practice the Dharma—
even while enjoying the fruits of their actions in this very world— are turned away from the hereafter.
Those lowest of men fall into most terrible hells;
dwelling in hell is agonizing, whereas dwelling in heaven bestows happiness. Men attain those states there by performing auspicious and inauspicious actions.
The sages said:
"O best of beings, what you have described regarding the path of Yama is exceedingly painful and terrible—
the horrific hells and the gateway of Yama."
"O Brahmin, is there or is there not a means on the exceedingly terrifying path to Yama?
Tell us that by which men may go to the abode of Yama with ease."
Vyāsa said:
Those men here who are endowed with righteousness, devoted to non-violence, intent on serving their gurus, and worshippers of the gods and Brahmins; BrP_216.3 //
I shall tell you how those people of the world of men, along with their wives and sons, travel upon that path. BrP_216.4 //
In various divine celestial chariots adorned with golden banners,
they proceed to the city of Dharmarāja, attended by hosts of apsarases.
Those who, out of devotion, bestow various kinds of gifts upon the Brahmins,
travel with ease indeed upon the great path.
But those who bestow well-prepared food upon Brahmins, especially upon those learned in the Vedas, being endowed with supreme devotion; ||| BrP_216.7 |||
Attended with great care by young and excellent women,
they proceed to the city of Dharmarāja in well-adorned celestial chariots.
And those who speak the truth, being pure both outwardly and inwardly,
they too— resembling the immortals— go to the abode of Yama by means of celestial chariots.
Those who know the Dharma bestow pure gifts of cows upon virtuous persons who are emaciated and living in poverty, dedicating them to Viṣṇu.
They go to the city of the King of Dharma in celestial palaces, radiant with divine colors, adorned with jewels, and attended by hosts of Apsarases.
Those who bestow a pair of sandals, an umbrella, a bed, or even a seat, as well as garments and ornaments; ||| BrP_216.12 |||
Adorned with horses, chariots, and elephants,
they go to the divine city of Dharmarāja, accompanied by umbrellas made of gold and silver.
And those who, with devotion and a purified inner self, offer consecrated molasses-drink and cooked rice to the foremost of the twice-born;
They go to the abode of Yama in various golden vehicles,
being served again and again at their pleasure by excellent women.
And those who diligently offer milk, ghee, curd, molasses, and honey to Brahmins— prepared with purity and well-refined— [attain great merit].
And in golden celestial chariots drawn by ruddy geese,
they go to the abode of Yama, attended by the musical instruments of the Gandharvas.
Those men who bestow fruits and fragrant flowers travel to the City of Dharma in celestial chariots drawn by swans.
Those who, endowed with faith, bestow sesame seeds, or a cow made of sesame, or even a cow made of ghee, upon Vedic scholars and Brahmins; ||| BrP_216.19 |||
They travel in stainless vehicles resembling the orb of the moon,
and they are sung of by Gandharvas in the city of Vaivasvata.
Those who possess large wells, small wells, tanks, lakes, oblong ponds, lotus-pools, and cool reservoirs of water; ||| BrP_216.21 |||
With vehicles resembling golden moons and resounding with the bells of the divine,
those beings of great splendor were fanned with fans and palm-leaf whisks.
Those whose temples and shrines here are variegated, shimmering with jewels, and beautiful and auspicious; ||| BrP_216.23 |||
They go by means of celestial chariots, swift as the wind,
to the divine city of Dharmarāja, which is crowded with various kinds of people.
Those who give water, the sustenance upon which all living beings depend,
proceed free from thirst and with ease along that great path in celestial chariots.
Those by whom wooden sandals, vehicles, stools,
and seats have been given to the twice-born indeed travel the road with ease.
Placing their feet upon excellent seats made of gold and jewels,
they travel in celestial chariots adorned by hosts of Apsarases.
In this world, men who act for the benefit of others plant various groves rich in flowers and abundant in fruit.
Well-adorned, they proceed while being entertained by the songs and instrumental music of excellent women amidst delightful and cool shades of trees.
Those who bestow gold, silver, coral, or likewise pearls,
travel in celestial chariots resplendent with gold.
Bestowers of land, they shine resplendently, satisfied with all their desires,
traveling in celestial chariots that resemble the rising sun and resound with loud music.
But those who bestow a maiden as a gift for a Brahmin, adorned with ornaments,
go to the abode of Yama in celestial chariots surrounded by divine maidens.
O best of the twice-born, endowed with supreme devotion, they offer fragrant aloe-wood, camphor, flowers, and incense to the members of the twice-born.
Fragrant, well-attired, radiant, and beautifully adorned, they proceed to the City of Dharma in various, highly decorated vehicles.
Those who give lamps travel in celestial vehicles, illuminating the ten directions;
they proceed in chariots resembling the sun, shining like fires.
Those men who give houses and dwellings go to the abode of Dharmarāja in houses adorned with gold, resembling the rising sun.
Those who give water vessels and offer water-pots and jars go,
honored by apsarases, upon proud, great elephants.
Those who provide Brahmins with oil for massaging the feet, oil for massaging the head, as well as water for bathing and drinking, go to the abode of Yama on horseback.
Those who provide rest for Brahmins who are exhausted and worn out on the road travel happily by means of a vehicle drawn by ruddy geese.
The brahmin who honors another with a welcome and a seat travels that path happily, supremely at peace.
He who greets Hari with the words "Salutation to the God who is the Friend of Brahman," and addresses a cow as "O Remover of Sin," proceeds happily along that path.
And those who eat only what remains after others have eaten, and who are free from hypocrisy and falsehood—
they too go upon that path by means of vehicles joined with cranes.
For those who subsist on a single meal a day, free from deceit and hypocrisy,
travel happily to the abode of Yama in celestial chariots drawn by swans.
Those who have conquered their senses and subsist on food once every fourth day go to the City of Dharma in vehicles yoked with peacocks.
Those who, firm in their vows, eat on the third day,
they too go to that state by means of divine elephant-chariots and celestial vehicles.
He who, in the sixth [month], eats only food, is constant in purity, and has his senses subdued,
goes seated upon an elephant like Śacīpati himself.
The divine city of Dharmarāja was adorned with various jewels, endowed with diverse sounds, and filled with the resonant cries of "Victory! (Jaya).
Those who fast for a fortnight go by means of vehicles yoked with tigers to that city of the King of Dharma, being attended upon by gods and asuras.
And those who, with their senses restrained, observe the month-long fast,
they too go to the abode of Yama in vehicles blazing like the sun.
He who sets out on the Great Departure with one-pointed mind and firm vows goes to the abode of Yama in celestial vehicles, attended by Gandharvas.
He who disciplines his body with a mind devoted to Viṣṇu goes from here to the abode of the Thirty-three Gods in a chariot the color of fire.
He who, being devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa, enters the fire,
goes to the abode of Yama in a celestial chariot radiant as fire.
The mortal man who gives up his life-breaths while remembering the eternal Viṣṇu goes to the City of Dharma by means of a vehicle as radiant as the sun.
The man who enters the water and gives up his life there indeed travels happily by a vehicle resembling the orb of the moon.
For that Vaiṣṇava who offers his own body to the vultures goes to the abode of Yama by means of a preeminent golden chariot.
He who meets death in battle while seizing women or seizing cattle goes forth with the radiance of the sun, being served by celestial maidens.
Those Vaiṣṇavas who, having conquered their senses, undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords,
travel along that formidable path adorned with comfortable vehicles.
Those best of the twice-born who worship with sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees,
travel happily in celestial chariots resembling molten gold.
Those who do not cause suffering to others and provide for their dependents with food and other necessities attain happiness, traveling in celestial chariots radiant with gold.
Those who are patient toward all beings, granting fearlessness to living creatures, who are completely freed from anger and delusion, devoid of pride, and have their senses restrained; BrP_216.60 //
Possessing great splendor, they travel to the city of Vaivasvata in celestial chariots as radiant as the full moon, attended by gods and gandharvas.
Those who worship Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Tryambaka, and Ravi as being one in essence,
indeed travel by means of celestial chariots possessing the brilliance of the sun.
And those men who do not eat meat, being endowed with truthfulness and purity,
they too go with ease to the city of the King of Dharma.
Among all kinds of food and edibles, there is nothing sweeter than meat;
therefore, one should not eat meat, for no happiness arises from sweet things.
"He who gives a thousand cows and he who does not eat meat—
these two are equal," so Brahmā, the best among those who know the Vedas, declared of old.
O Brahmins, whatever merit is found in all sacred fords and whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices, that same fruit is equal to abstaining from eating meat.
In this way, those righteous ones,
devoted to the vow of charity, go happily to the world of Yama by means of celestial vehicles to where the Sun’s son, the god [Yama], resides.
Upon seeing those righteous ones, Lord Yama himself shall honor them with a welcome,
the offering of a seat, water for the feet, and the respectful arghya, as well as with pleasant words.
Blessed are you, O great-souled ones, who act for your own benefit,
since you have performed meritorious deeds for the sake of divine happiness.
Having ascended this celestial chariot, adorned with the enjoyments of divine women,
go to the incomparable heaven that is endowed with all objects of desire.
Having enjoyed great pleasures there, at the end, when your merit is exhausted,
you shall experience here whatever small amount of inauspicious fruit remains.
But those men who, through the power of their merit, behold that King of Dharma with a gentle mind, as if he were their own father; ||| BrP_216.72 |||
Therefore, one should always practice Dharma, which bestows the fruit of liberation;
from Dharma, it is proclaimed that wealth, pleasure, and even liberation arise.
Dharma is mother, father, and brother; Dharma is protector and likewise friend;
Dharma is master, companion, guardian, as well as creator and nourisher.
From dharma comes wealth, from wealth comes desire, from desire come enjoyments and pleasures;
from dharma comes sovereignty and one-pointedness of mind, and from dharma comes the supreme state of heaven.
But dharma, when practiced, O brahmins, protects one from great fear;
and through dharma, one undoubtedly attains both divinity and the status of the twice-born.
And when the previously accumulated evil of men is exhausted,
O best of the twice-born, then their intellect turns toward dharma in this world.
Having attained the rare human state after thousands of other births,
he who indeed does not practice Dharma is truly a victim of deception.
Those who are contemptible, poor, deformed, diseased,
servants of others, and foolish should be known as those devoid of dharma.
For those who are long-lived, heroic, wise, wealthy, purposeful, healthy, and handsome— it is because they have practiced the Dharma in the past.
Thus, brahmins devoted to the Dharma go to the highest state;
but those who practice unrighteousness go to the womb of an animal.
Those men who are devoted to Vāsudeva, the destroyer of hell,
do not see Yama or the hells even in their dreams.
Those men who constantly bow before the God who is without beginning or end, and who is the destroyer of Daityas and Dānavas, do not behold Yama.
Those who have gone for refuge to Acyuta by deed, mind, and speech—Yama has no power over them; they are partakers of the fruit of liberation.
O twice-born ones, those people who always bow to Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the worlds,
never go anywhere other than the abode of Viṣṇu.
Having bowed to Viṣṇu, they do not see those messengers, nor that path, nor Yama, nor that city, nor the hells in any way whatsoever.
Even after committing many sins, men who are possessed by delusion do not go to hell if they bow down to Hari, the remover of all sins.
Even those people who constantly remember Janārdana with deceit,
they too, upon casting off the body, go to the stainless world of Viṣṇu.
Even one who is excessively addicted to anger may sometimes chant the praises of Hari;
through the destruction of his faults, he too shall obtain liberation, just like the Lord of Cedi.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Having thus heard about the path of Yama and the torments in the hells,
those best of sages again questioned Vyāsa regarding their doubts.
The sages said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, proficient in all scriptures,
who indeed is the companion of a mortal— is it the father, the mother, the son, or the teacher?"
Having abandoned their circle of kinsmen and relatives, as well as their circle of friends,
and leaving behind their home and body like pieces of wood or clods of earth,
people indeed go to the other world; who then follows them?
Vyāsa said: O Brahmins, one alone is born, and indeed one alone perishes;
one alone crosses over difficulties, and one alone goes to a miserable state.
The father, mother, brother, son, and teacher are without assistance;
likewise are the circle of kinsmen and relatives, as well as the circle of friends.
Having abandoned the dead body, which is like a piece of wood or a clod of earth,
people weep for but a moment and then turn away and depart.
When that body has been cast off by them, Dharma alone follows;
therefore, Dharma should always be cultivated as a companion by men.
A living being endowed with righteousness shall go to the supreme state of heaven;
likewise, one joined with unrighteousness falls into hell.
Therefore, a wise person should not be attached to objects acquired through evil means;
Dharma alone is proclaimed as the companion for human beings.
Out of greed, delusion, compassion, or even fear, a man of great learning may perform improper acts when, deluded by greed, he acts for the sake of another.
Dharma, artha, and kāma—these three are the fruits of living;
these three should be attained while avoiding unrighteousness.
The sages said:
"We have heard the words of the Blessed One, which are endowed with dharma and supremely beneficial;
yet our intellects are now directed toward understanding the accumulation of the body."
For when the dead body of men has become subtle and unmanifest,
having reached a state beyond the range of sight, how does dharma follow it?
Vyāsa said:
Earth, wind, space, water, light, the mind,
the intellect, and the self— these together constantly perceive dharma.
Acting as witnesses day and night for all living beings here,
it is indeed with these that Dharma follows that living soul.
O best of the twice-born, skin, bone, flesh, semen, and blood—
these abandon the body when it is deprived of life.
Then that living being, endowed with righteousness, prospers in happiness both in this world and in the next; what more shall I say to you?
The sages said:
"That has been shown by the Blessed One how dharma follows;
but we wish to know this: how does semen come into being?"
Vyāsa said:
O best of the twice-born, those deities who reside within the body— earth, wind, ether, water, light, and likewise the mind— consume the food.
Then, O Brahmins, when those five elements with the mind as the sixth have been satisfied, the pure-souled one becomes the great semen.
From that, O twice-born ones, the embryo arises from the union of the male and female fluids.
All this has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?
The sages said: "O Blessed One, you have explained to us how the embryo is formed;
now let it be told how the person, once born, proceeds."
Vyāsa said:
When the person is merely present, he is overwhelmed by those elements;
but when separated from those elements, he goes again to another state of existence.
Joined with the elements, he indeed attains the vital breath (jīva);
then the deities residing within the five elements behold his karma, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious. What more do you wish to hear?
The sages said: "O Blessed One,
having cast off skin, bone, and flesh, and being devoid of those elements,
where does that living soul abide when it experiences pleasure and pain?"
Vyāsa said:
O twice-born ones, the individual soul (jīva), joined with karma, quickly enters the semen; then, having reached the menses of women, it develops in due time.
Through the messengers of Yama comes affliction; through the messengers of Yama comes slaughter;
and a man experiences suffering, the wheel of saṃsāra, and torment.
In this world, O twice-born ones, that living being indeed experiences well-performed action from birth onwards, relying upon the fruit of dharma.
If, having fully applied himself to Dharma, he practices it from birth onwards,
then that person, having become [perfected], shall enjoy happiness eternally.
Then, when one practices both dharma and adharma intermittently,
that living being experiences suffering immediately following happiness.
One who is joined with unrighteousness, having gone to the realm of Yama and encountered great suffering, is born in the womb of an animal.
Listen now to me as I explain by which specific actions a living being, joined with delusion, is born into this or that womb in this world.
That which is described in the scriptures, along with the histories and the Vedas,
as the terrible domain of Yama, proceeds from the world of mortals.
"O twice-born ones, there are here holy places equal to the gods,
which surpass the animal realm and provide a destination in every respect."
In the divine abode of Yama, which is equal to the world of Brahmā in its qualities,
a living being, bound by the constraints of their own past actions, undergoes sufferings.
Indeed, by whatever disposition and by whatever action a person goes to a terrible state of existence, I shall explain that hereafter.
Having studied the four Vedas, a twice-born man who is possessed by delusion and then accepts a gift from an outcast is reborn in the womb of a donkey.
O twice-born ones, a donkey lives for fifteen years;
once dead, that donkey becomes a bull and lives for seven years.
Even a bull that has died is born as a Brahmarākṣasa;
after being a Brahmarākṣasa for three months, he is then born as a Brāhmaṇa.
Having officiated at a sacrifice for one who has fallen from his caste, O twice-born ones, he is born in the womb of a worm;
there he lives for fifteen years.
Released from the state of a worm, he is then born as a donkey;
the donkey remains for five years, and for five years he is a pig.
He becomes a cock for five years, a jackal for five years, and a dog for one year; after that, he is born as a human being.
The foolish disciple who commits an evil act against his preceptor undoubtedly undergoes three births here in this cycle of existence.
O Brahmins, first he becomes a dog, then a flesh-eating beast, and then a donkey;
after passing away among those who are afflicted, he is later born as a Brahmin.
That sinful disciple who, even in his mind, approaches the wife of his guru,
goes to fierce transmigrations by virtue of his unrighteous mind in this world.
Having been born in the womb of a dog, he lives for three years;
having met his death even there, he is reborn in the womb of a worm.
Having attained the state of a worm, he lives for one year;
then, meeting his death, he is born into a Brahmin womb.
If a teacher should strike a disciple who is like a son without cause,
acting out of his own caprice, he too becomes a perpetrator of violence.
O Brahmins, that son who treats his father and mother with contempt shall,
after death, first be born as a donkey.
Having attained the state of a donkey, he lives for ten years;
then, after one year, he is born as a crocodile, and thereafter as a human being.
He whose mother and father are both angry with him because of his ill-will toward his guru shall, upon death, be born as a donkey.
The donkey lives for ten or even fourteen months;
the cat for seven months, after which he is born as a human being.
O twice-born ones, by reviling one's mother and father, one is reborn as a sarīka bird;
but by striking them, one is born as a tortoise.
For ten years he is a tortoise, for three years a porcupine;
having become a serpent for six months, he is thereafter born as a human being.
One who consumes the food provided by his master yet serves those things hostile to the king,
being possessed by delusion, shall be born as a monkey after death.
Having been a monkey for ten years and a mouse for seven years,
and having become a dog for six months, he is thereafter born as a human being.
But the man who steals a deposit, having gone to the realm of Yama and passed through a hundred transmigrations, is born in the womb of a worm.
There, O twice-born ones, he lives for fifteen years;
having exhausted his evil deeds, he is thereafter born as a human being.
Furthermore, a man who is envious is born after death as a śārṅgaka bird;
and a foolish man who betrays trust is born as a fish.
Having been a fish for eight years, O twice-born ones, he is born as a deer;
after being a deer for four months, he is then born as a goat.
But having reached death as a goat, after a full year has passed, that creature is born as an insect; thereafter, it is born as a human being.
Grains such as barley, sesame, mung beans, kulattha, mustard, chickpeas, peas, then kidney beans, wheat, and likewise linseed; BrP 217.62.
O best of sages, that senseless mortal who, out of delusion, steals other crops is reborn as a shameless mouse.
Then, O best of sages, after dying and passing away, he is born as a pig;
and as soon as he is born as a pig, he dies again from disease.
Then that man is born as a mute dog because of that karma;
having been a dog for five years, he is thereafter born as a human being.
But having committed the violation of another's wife, one will indeed be born as a wolf;
then as a dog, a jackal, a vulture, a serpent, a heron, and likewise a crane.
O twice-born ones, that evil-souled man who, deluded by passion, violates his brother’s wife, becomes a male cuckoo for one year.
Having violated the wife of a friend, the wife of a teacher, or likewise the wife of a king,
one who is driven by lust will be born as a pig after death.
He becomes a boar for five years, a crane for ten years,
an ant for three months, and a worm for exactly one month.
Having undergone these transmigrations, one is born in the womb of a worm;
there, in the womb of a worm, one lives for fourteen months.
Having exhausted his demerit, that man is thereafter born as a human;
yet he who, having previously given away his daughter, desires to give her to a second [suitor], [is likewise reborn].
O Brahmins, that creature having died is born in the womb of a worm;
there it lives for thirteen years, O best of the twice-born.
When his unrighteousness has been exhausted, he is liberated from there and is then born as a human;
yet this applies even if he has failed to perform the rites for the gods or the rites for the ancestors.
Without having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, one dies and is born as a crow;
after being a crow for a hundred years, one is then born as a cock.
Furthermore, he who treats with contempt his eldest brother, who is like a father, is born as a *vyālaka* for one month, and thereafter becomes human.
Having met his death there as well, he is born in the womb of a crane;
as a crane he lives for ten years, and then he is born as a jīvaka.
From that he meets his end and shall attain the state of a human;
yet a low-caste man who has approached a Brahmin woman is born from a womb of worms.
Then, having met his death, he is born again as a boar;
O twice-born ones, as soon as he is born as a boar, he dies of disease.
O twice-born ones, by that karma he is born as a foolish dog;
having been a dog and having performed his allotted deeds, he is thereafter born as a human.
Having procreated offspring there, one who dies will be born as a mouse;
but an ungrateful man, O Brahmins, having died and gone to the realm of Yama, [suffers there].
Bound by cruel means in the realm of Yama, he undergoes agony from the staff,
the mallet, the stake, and the dreadful fire-staff.
The terrible forest of sword-leaves, the sand, and the thorny śālmalī tree—
having gone to the realm of Yama, they encounter these and many other such places.
O twice-born ones, having undergone those terrible torments,
he then enters the wheel of saṃsāra and is born in the womb of a worm.
O twice-born ones, he becomes a worm for fifteen years;
thereafter, having entered a womb, the man dies right there.
Then, having passed through many births in the cycle of existence, that creature enters into hundreds of wombs in manifold ways; thereafter, it is born as an animal.
Then, having experienced suffering for many groups of years,
he is again joined to rebirth and is subsequently born as a tortoise.
Having stolen curd, one becomes a crane; having stolen unprepared fish, a water-fowl; and having committed theft, the evil-minded person is born as a gadfly that stings for honey.
Having stolen fruit or a radish, or even a cake,
or having stolen beans, one is born as a fruit-mouse.
By stealing milk-rice (pāyasa), one attains the state of a partridge;
by stealing a cake made of flour, one is born as a screech-owl.
Having stolen water, a man of evil intellect is born as a crow;
having stolen bell-metal, a man of evil intellect is born as a green parrot.
Having stolen a silver vessel, one is born as a pigeon;
but having stolen a golden vessel, one is born in the womb of a worm.
Having stolen silk cloth, one attains the state of a kuraṅga bird;
and having stolen a silkworm cocoon, a man is born as a dancer.
Having stolen fine cloth, a human is born as a parrot;
having stolen silk, one is born as a swan after death.
O twice-born ones, having stolen cotton cloth, a man dies and is born as a curlew; likewise, having stolen silk or woolen cloth, he is reborn as a human.
Having stolen linen cloth, a person is born as a rabbit;
but having stolen powdered incense, a man, upon death, is born as a peacock.
Having stolen dyed garments, a man is born as a jīvajīvaka bird;
likewise, by stealing pigments and perfumes in this world, he becomes one such.
A Brahmin who is devoted to greed attains the state of a porcupine;
there he lives for fifteen years.
Having brought about the destruction of unrighteousness, a human being is then reborn;
moreover, by stealing milk, one is born as a crane.
But that man who, possessed by delusion, steals oil,
O brahmins, is born as a creature that drinks oil after he has died.
Having slain an unarmed man while himself armed— whether for the sake of wealth or out of enmity— that lowest of men shall be reborn as a donkey upon death.
He lives as a donkey for two years, after which he is killed by a weapon;
having died, he is born in the womb of a deer, constantly filled with anxiety.
Then, after a year has passed, the deer would be pierced by a weapon;
thereafter the deer is killed, and then the fish is also caught in a net.
When the fourth month has arrived, he is born as a beast of prey;
he remains a beast of prey for ten years and a leopard for five years.
Then, impelled by the passage of time, he meets his death;
having brought about the destruction of his unrighteousness, he attains human status once more.
A man who steals musical instruments is born with body hair;
likewise, the man who steals food mixed with oil-cake [is born as such].
O best of the twice-born, that man is born as a fierce, brown-haired rat; being evil-minded, he constantly bites human beings.
Having stolen clarified butter, the evil-minded person is reborn as a water-crow;
likewise, having stolen fish or meat, a human is born as a crow.
Having stolen salt, one is born as a *cirikāka* bird;
and that man who denies a deposit entrusted to him in trust [is likewise reborn].
When his lifespan has ended, that man is born in the womb of a fish;
having entered the womb of a fish and died, he is born as a human being.
Having attained human status, one is born with a diminished lifespan;
moreover, O twice-born ones, having committed sins, a man is born as an animal.
Nor does one’s own authority know anything of dharma for those men who,
having committed sins, always seek to cast them off through vows.
Endowed with both pleasure and pain, they become afflicted by disease;
they are born unclothed, and there is no doubt that they will even become barbarians.
Men who are of sinful conduct and possessed by greed and delusion [do not attain this],
whereas those men who have avoided sins from birth onwards [attain it].
They become healthy, handsome, and wealthy;
even women, by performing [this rite] according to this same method, shall obtain [these benefits], though having committed sin.
They become the wives of these very same wicked men;
generally, all the faults associated with abduction have been proclaimed.
O best of the twice-born, this has indeed been told to you only in brief;
O brahmins, you shall hear it again in another discourse.
O highly fortunate ones, this was heard by me in the past as Brahmā was speaking in the midst of the celestial sages; I have related it exactly as it was asked.
I have also described this to you in its entirety and exactly as it is;
having heard this, O best of sages, fix your minds upon Dharma.
The sages said:
"O sinless one, O Brahmin, the course of unrighteousness has been described by you to us.
Now we wish to hear about the course of righteousness, O best among speakers."
Having committed sinful deeds, how do they go to an inauspicious state?
And by what deed performed here do they go to an auspicious state?
Vyāsa said:
Having performed sinful deeds and having fallen under the sway of unrighteousness,
one who possesses a perverted mind goes to hell.
He who, having committed an unrighteous act out of delusion, later feels remorse and is joined with mental concentration, shall not practice evil again.
If the Brahmins who speak according to the Dharma declare it,
then one is quickly released from the offense committed through unrighteousness.
To the very extent that a person correctly speaks of unrighteousness with a concentrated mind, to that same extent he is liberated.
To the extent that his mind reviles the evil deed he has committed,
to that same extent his body is liberated from that unrighteousness.
Having bestowed various gifts upon a Brahmin with a concentrated mind, he casts off those former enjoyments just as a serpent sheds its sloughs.
Endowed with mental concentration, one attains a heavenly rebirth;
O best of the twice-born, I shall now describe those gifts which, when given, lead to this.
Even after committing improper acts, a man is subsequently joined with righteousness;
among all gifts, food is declared to be the best.
All food should be given by one who is upright and desires righteousness;
for food is the life-breath of human beings, and from it a living being is born.
The worlds are established upon food; therefore, food is praised.
Gods, sages, ancestors, and humans all praise food alone.
For by the gift of food, a human being attains heaven;
therefore, excellent food acquired through righteous means should be given to the twice-born.
With a joyful inner self, one should offer food to those who are devoted to their own Vedic study;
for when ten Brahmins eat his food even once, [the merit is great].
O best of the twice-born, one who has given food with a joyful mind to ten thousand Brahmins shall not be reborn in the animal realm.
A man who is always devoted to sinful acts may be liberated from unrighteousness by a Brahmin who, placing the Veda at the forefront, has gathered food through alms.
By giving to a brahmin devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas, one prospers in happiness here;
likewise, by not harming the property of brahmins and by protecting it according to justice.
That Kṣatriya who, being self-restrained and well-composed, bestows upon the foremost of the twice-born food obtained by his own prowess; ||| BrP_218.18 |||
Therefore, O twice-born ones, that righteous soul wipes away his evil deeds and acquires a sixth part of the harvest as a pure share of agriculture.
A Vaiśya who gives to the twice-born is liberated from sins,
even after having obtained a precarious state of life earned through harsh labor.
By giving food to the twice-born, a Śūdra is liberated from sin;
likewise, one who acquires food through his own physical strength and is free from violence [is freed].
The man who, filled with joy, bestows upon brahmins food acquired through righteous means, does not encounter difficulties.
By giving to the twice-born who are advanced in Vedic knowledge, one is liberated from sin;
by giving food that provides vigor in this world, a man becomes vigorous.
By blocking the path of the virtuous, one is liberated from all sins;
this is the path established by those who know the rules of giving, along which the wise travel.
Among those [virtues], the giving of food is the eternal dharma;
food acquired by a man through righteous means in every circumstance [should be given].
For food obtained through righteous means is always the supreme refuge;
indeed, by the gift of food, a man attains the highest state.
Endowed with all his desires, he enjoys happiness even after death;
thus, a man joined with merit is liberated from sins.
Therefore, food should be given that is free from injustice;
for the householder who always eats his food preceded by the offering to the vital breaths (prāṇāhuti), [attains merit].
A man should make each day fruitful by giving food;
he who constantly feeds a hundred of the best among those who know the Vedas, [attains great merit].
One who knows logic, knows the Dharma, and likewise knows history does not go to a terrible hell, nor does he undergo the cycle of worldly existence.
Endowed with all desires, he enjoys happiness even after death;
thus, joined with his actions, he rejoices, free from all feverish distress.
One is born endowed with beauty, fame, and wealth;
all this, O twice-born ones, has been told to you regarding the great fruit of giving food. Indeed, this is the very root of all virtues and of all gifts.
The sages said:
"But for those who have gone to the other world and dwell in the abodes corresponding to their own karma,
how is the śrāddha rite to be understood by their sons and other kinsmen?"
Vyāsa said:
Having paid homage to the Lord of the World, the Boar-form incarnation who brings prosperity to the worlds,
listen as I shall fully declare the ritual for the Śrāddha ceremony exactly as it has been taught.
O best of the twice-born, in ancient times the omnipresent Lord rescued his ancestors who were submerged in the waters of the Koka river after performing a śrāddha ceremony there.
The sages said:
"O best of the twice-born, for what reason were those ancestors submerged in the waters of the Kokā river, and how indeed were they raised up by him in the form of a boar?"
In that holy place of Kokāmukha, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, we wish to hear; please speak, for our curiosity is great.
Vyāsa said:
At the junction of the Tretā and Dvāpara ages, the divine and human ancestors formerly stood upon the ridge of Mount Meru together with all the gods.
While those ancestors were seated together, a divine maiden of radiant beauty, born of Soma, stood before them with her palms joined in reverence;
the divine ancestors who had assembled there spoke to her.
The ancestors said:
"Who are you, O blessed lady? Who is your lord? You ought to tell us."
Vyāsa said:
She spoke to the ancestors and the gods, saying, "I am indeed a digit of the moon;
if you so desire, I choose your sovereignty alone."
"First there was the name Ūrjā, and immediately after that, Svadhā;
and today you have bestowed upon her the name Kokā, which has been conceived by you."
For having heard her words, those ancestors, both divine and human,
gazed upon her face and found no satiety.

And the Viśvedevas, having recognized them as gazing upon the face of the maiden, saw that they had fallen from their yoga; having observed this, they abandoned them and departed for the third heaven.
The Blessed One, the Moon of great renown, did not see his daughter Ūrjā; with a troubled mind, he reflected, "Where has she gone?"
Then Soma perceived that she had been obtained by the ancestors according to their desire,
and that she had been looked upon with affection by them and accepted through the power of their asceticism.
Then, O twice-born ones, the moon, his soul overcome by anger, cursed the ancestors:
"You shall fall down, deprived of yoga and devoid of consciousness."
"Since you, O utter fools, desire my daughter who has not been given away,
and since she, though under her father's protection, has taken these men as her husbands."
Therefore, having independently abandoned her dharma, let her become a river known in the world as Kokā, taking refuge in the Śiśira mountain.
Thus cursed by the Moon, the Pitṛs, both divine and human,
fell from their yoga and descended to the ground at the foot of the Himavat.
There, upon the vast plateau of the king of mountains, Ūrjā fell,
having reached the excellent Saptasāmudra Tīrtha.
Then there was a river named Kokā, crowded with hundreds of holy fords;
flooding the mountain peak, it is known as a river because of its gliding flow.
Then those wise ancestors, being devoid of yoga, beheld the great river of cool waters, yet they did not recognize it as Sulocanā.
Then the king of mountains, seeing those ancestors afflicted by hunger,
commanded them to take the jujube fruit and a single cow that flowed with honey.
Milk, honey, that divine water of the Kokā river, and the fruit of the Badarī tree—
these have been assigned by the best of mountains for their nourishment.
O best of sages, as the ancestors lived according to that mode of life,
ten thousand years passed for them like a single day.
Thus, when the world was bereft of fathers and likewise devoid of the svadhā offerings,
the Daityas became powerful, as did the Yātudhānas and Rākṣasas.
Then those Daityas and Yātudhānas, acting with great speed, rushed from all sides toward those hosts of Pitṛs who were bereft of the Viśvedevas.
O twice-born ones, seeing the Daityas and Yātudhānas rushing toward them,
they seized in fury a lofty rock situated on the bank of the Kokā.
But when the rock had been seized, the impetuous Kokā covered her ancestors with water, flooding the Himālaya mountain.
Seeing the Pitṛs vanished, the Daityas and Rākṣasas likewise climbed a Vibhītaka tree and remained there, fasting and hidden from sight.
Distressed by the water and afflicted by hunger and exhaustion,
the ancestors, dwelling within that body of water, beheld their own wretched state and sought refuge with Lord Hari, Janārdana, singing his praises.
The ancestors said:
"Be victorious, O Govinda, abode of the universe!
May victory be ours, O Keśava, through your grace."
O Janārdana, O Lord of sinless majesty, you ought to lift us up from within the waters,
for we are surrounded by night-stalkers of terrible appearance, O Master.
O most excellent Vaikuṇṭha, Varāha, Viṣṇu,
Nārāyaṇa, Lord of all great lords!
Go forth, O Padmanābha, and conquer those who are afraid!
O Upendra, O Yogi, O slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha! O Viṣṇu, O Ananta, O Acyuta, O Vāsudeva!
O Lord whose hands hold the glorious Śārṅga bow, the discus, the lotus, and the conch!
"O Lord of Gods, protect us from the Rākṣasas!
O Śambhu, you are the father of the world; no one else is capable of repelling this terrifying host of night-stalkers. Therefore, we have come to you for refuge."
O Viṣṇu, by the mere chanting of your name, the night-stalkers flee, the spirits depart, and likewise the enemies go to their destruction this very moment.
"In this world, Dharma and the like are the primary truth.
Vyāsa said:
"Thus praised by the ancestors, that upholder of the earth—"
Then, his divine form revealed, the gratified Lord beheld the host of ancestors submerged in the waters at Kokāmukha, carrying a stone upon their heads.
Seeing him submerged in the water, Viṣṇu Janārdana, in the form of a boar,
resolved to lift up the terrified host of the ancestors.
Striking the rock with the tip of his tusk, the Boar hurled it;
and the Lord, taking the ancestors with him, lifted them up from the surface of the rock.
The ancestors, brilliant as gold, were caught upon the tusks of the Boar;
by the god Viṣṇu, they were rendered fearless at Kokāmukha.
And having raised up the ancestors at Viṣṇutīrtha, the divine Boar,
being fully composed, gave water to them at Lohārgala.
Then Keśava, taking kuśa grass produced from his own body hair and sesame seeds born from his sweat, fashioned an excellent firebrand.
Having made the light of the sun his lamp, and the sacred ford his desired vessel,
he remained beneath the Koṭivaṭa tree with the pure water of the Gaṅgā as his support.
Having taken from Tuṅgakūṭa the juices of sacrificial herbs,
the essences of honey and milk, perfumes, flowers, incense, and unguents;
Having taken the cow from Lake Saras and having taken jewels from the ocean,
he scraped the earth with his tusks and sprinkled it with water.
Having smeared it with the rising heat [of the fire], having scraped it again with *kuśa* grass, having carried it around with a flaming torch, and having sprinkled it repeatedly; ||| BrP_219.45 |||
Taking up *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing eastward and placing it within the pores of his skin,
he summoned the sages and asked, "I shall perform the libation for the ancestors."
When they replied, "Do so," the omnipresent Lord then summoned the Viśvedevas by means of mantras and, as their master, offered them seats.
Having summoned them with mantras according to the rites prescribed in the Vedas, Hari,
the wielder of the discus and mace, performed the protection of those deities with unbroken grains (akṣata).
The unbroken grains and medicinal herbs, originating from portions of all the gods, protect all directions; indeed, they were created for the purpose of protection.
Indeed, among the gods, dānavas, daityas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas,
as well as among all things mobile and immobile, no one at all is able to bring about their destruction.
Since they were not created by anyone, they have indeed been made invulnerable;
for in ancient times, they were appointed by Viṣṇu for the protection of the gods.
Having prepared an *arghya* offering with *kuśa* grass, fragrant scents, barley, and flowers, Śūkara then addressed those [gods] with the mantra, "To the Viśvedevas."
"I shall invoke the ancestors, both those who are divine and those who are human.
Being thus addressed by them with the words "Invoke them!", he, being pure, should perform the invocation.
The knower of the Vedas, having placed upon his knees darbha grass whose roots and tips were joined together along with sesame seeds,
offered him a seat with his left hand.
In the same manner, with one hand placed upon his knee, the Boar addressed those ancestors of the Brahmin forefathers, saying, "May they come to us."
He uttered "Apahata" for protection, keeping his sacred thread over the right shoulder (apassavya),
and performed the invocation of the ancestors by their names and lineages.
Uttering, "O ancestors, come with the speed of thought," and then saying,
"With the years [of the cycle]," he should then offer the *arghya* water to them.
"Those immortal words which remain, and that which has come down from father to father—that my grandfather gave as the *arghya* offering," thus [he spoke] to his grandfather. *Br̥hat-Purāṇa* 219.58.
And with the words "To my great-grandfather," he offered [the oblation] to the great-grandfather,
mixed with kusha grass, fragrance, sesame seeds, and flowers, while keeping his sacred thread over the right shoulder.
In the same manner, Janārdana performed the rite for his maternal grandfathers;
having honored them again with perfumes and other offerings, he offered incense with devotion.
Having uttered "The Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras," the Lord of the World then took up food mixed with clarified butter, sesame seeds, and kuśa grass.
Having placed that very [remnant] in a vessel, he then questioned the sages;
being urged by them with the words, "Offer it in the fire," he replied, "I shall do so."
One should offer three oblations to Soma, Agni, and Yama,
and one should recite the seven infallible Yajus verses beginning with "ye māmakāḥ."
And he gave what remained from the oblation, accompanied by the names and lineages,
three times for each individual ancestor, O twice-born ones.
Therefore, he should place whatever food remains in his alms-bowl;
then he gave delicious, flavorful food, beginning with milk-rice.
Fresh, sometimes steamed,
never stale, excellent, with little leafy vegetable and many fruits, possessing the six flavors, it was like nectar.
Whatever he gave to the brahmins in their alms-bowls, as well as to the ancestors—
food for the ancestors accompanied by Vedic mantras, drenched in clarified butter and sprinkled with honey.
He recited the three verses beginning with "madhu vātā" while consecrating [the food] with the mantra "pṛthivī," and he indeed muttered that quintet of mantras while the Brahmins were eating.
He recited to him the *Trimadhu*, the *Trisuparṇa*, and likewise the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, beginning from the section he had already started and not exceeding it.
He indeed recited for them the prayers to be recited—the Saura Sukta and the Puruṣa Sukta—and after the Brahmins had eaten, he asked, "Are you satisfied? (BrP 219.70).
"We are satisfied," he said once, thereby releasing her from her vow of silence;
then, taking the alms-bowl, he gave it to Chāyā.
Having divided that food into two parts, she then made each of them threefold;
then, having dug up the ground with her boar-form and covered it with *kuśa* grass, she concealed it.
Having arranged the kuśa grass with its tips pointing southward, he should prepare a seat upon them;
his resting place should indeed be on kuśa grass that has roots and contains sesame seeds.
Having prepared perfumes, flowers, and so forth, he then offered the funeral cake (piṇḍa) with devotion,
saying, "The earth is the vessel," and then presented the cake.
"So be it," replied the grandfathers and great-grandfathers from the intermediate space;
in that same manner, that boar offered funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to the maternal grandfathers as well.
He gave the food remaining from the offering of the funeral cakes to those who feed on smears,
saying with devotion, "This for you, O Fathers," and he bestowed garments upon them.
Having offered fragrant flowers and other such items to white garments that are two finger-breadths wide, washed, and new, and having performed circumambulations of them; BrP_219.77.
Having sipped water for purification, one should first cause the Brahmins representing the ancestors to sip water, and then those representing the gods;
thereafter, having sprinkled that ground with water, one should offer flowers and unhusked grain.
Having first given water with sesame seeds to the ancestors, and water with unbroken rice grains to the gods,
[he should say] "May it be inexhaustible for us" to the ancestors, and "May the deities be pleased" to the gods.
Having gratified [the ancestors] and turned away, one should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times; then, having returned, one should recite while uttering: "That which is my name... (yan me nāma).
"O ancestors, grant us houses filled with wealth and grain,
along with vessels for the *arghya* offering and sacred grass-blades (*pavitraka*) placed between the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*)."
He muttered the mantra: "Carrying away the strength that has been cast in," and he offered libations to the ancestors with snow, milk, honey, and sesame seeds.
When the word "Svasti" was uttered by the ancestors,
the god Gadādhara, having offered silver as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), gratified the brahmins with libations during the afternoon.
O best of the twice-born, he gave a portion to human beings, saying "Svadha," and when someone said, "It is prepared," he was answered by them in return.
"May you enjoy yourselves," he said; they replied, "We are indeed delighted.
Then, urged by those dear ones, he asked about the remaining food.
Then, taking those Brahmins by the hand, he should follow after them,
reciting "vāja-vāje," having gone outside the sacrificial altar.
Sprinkling himself with the water from Koṭitīrtha while moving counter-clockwise,
he requested a blessing for his abundant, unclipped locks of hair.
"May our donors prosper," [he said], and they replied, "So be it.
Having circumambulated them and performed a salutation at their feet, he departed.
The boar gave them seats and covered them;
then, after they had entered and rested, he took the middle morsel of food.
The Lord gave a funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his shadow-form wife, Mahī;
saying, "May the ancestors conceive a fetus," she too assumed a physical form.
Having received the rice-ball offerings from the brahmins, the boar performed the salutation of their feet;
he then desired to perform the ritual dismissal of the ancestors.
Kokā and the Pitṛs spoke words intended for their own benefit:
"O Blessed One, we were previously cursed by Himabhānu while we were dwelling in heaven."
"You shall all fall away from yoga and descend from heaven;
thus you have been saved by me as you enter the subterranean realm."
Even the Lords of the Universe, the protectors of yoga, have abandoned those who have fallen from yoga;
therefore, may all the Viśvedevas always protect us once again.
O Lord, O Boar, by your grace we shall go to heaven;
and may Soma, the presiding deity, remain our lord, O Acyuta, you who uphold yoga.
Likewise, Soma, the support of yoga, never protects us;
let our dwelling always be in heaven and on earth through the power of yoga.
And may there be nourishment for us in the atmosphere for a month;
for this Urjā is our wife, renowned by the name Svadhā.
"Let this very Khecarī be rich in yoga and the mother of yoga.
Thus was Vārāha, the creator of beings, addressed by his ancestors.
Then Viṣṇu spoke to the ancestors and to that great river, the Kokā:
"Everything that has been said by you to me shall come to pass."
Yama is declared to be your presiding deity (adhideva), Soma your sacred study (svādhyāya), and likewise Agni your presiding sacrifice (adhiyajña); such is your conceptualization.
"Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya shall indeed be your abodes;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra shall be your presiding lords."
"May these forms of yours be the Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras;
may you be yogins with bodies of yoga, sustainers of yoga, and observers of excellent vows."
"You shall wander at will among all living beings, bestowing fruits upon those dwelling in heaven, those dwelling in hell, and those on earth— both the moving and the unmoving."
"O supreme ones, you shall nourish yourselves by the power of your own yoga alone;
this is the daughter of the Moon, whose form consists of nectar and honey."
"The highly fortunate Svadhā shall become the daughter of Dakṣa;
there, this fair-faced woman will become your wife."
The river known as Kokānadī, which rests upon the king of mountains,
is immensely meritorious with ten million sacred fords and is protected by my own form.
"From this day forward, I shall indeed dwell here, effecting the destruction of sins;
the sight of the Boar is meritorious, and its worship bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
Drinking the water of the Kokā destroys great sins;
bathing at sacred fords is meritorious, and fasting bestows heaven.
It is declared that a gift given on the new moon day in the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha is inexhaustible and removes birth, death, and old age; this you should observe.
Having arrived at Kokāmukha, one should remain there for five days;
for whoever shall perform a śrāddha for the ancestors at that time, [his ancestors will be satisfied].
He shall undoubtedly partake of the fruits previously described;
I must always remain here on the eleventh and twelfth lunar days.
The wise person who fasts there shall obtain the fruit previously described;
therefore, O highly fortunate ones, go to that desired place as you please.
Having said, "I too shall dwell here," he vanished;
and when the boar had gone, the Pitṛs took leave of Kokā and departed.
The Kokā river also remains on the king of mountains together with the sacred fords;
she is the shadow consisting of the earth, the mother of crocodiles, nourished by the consumption of funeral cakes.
Having conceived a child with faith, that beautiful woman bore the son of Vārāha;
from her was born the son Bhauma, namely the Asura Naraka,
and the city of Prāgjyotiṣa was granted to him by Viṣṇu.
Thus have I spoken: having heard of the divine Boar-form of Viṣṇu, the bestower of boons, at Kokāmukha, a man is freed from impurity and becomes sinless.
One would obtain the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
[The sages said:
"O Blessed One, please explain the ritual for the *śrāddha* once more in great detail."
How, where, when, in whom, and by whom was that [attained]? Tell me that, O one rich in asceticism.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O tigers among sages, to the ritual procedure for the śrāddha in great detail;
I shall tell you how, where, when, by whom, and with which substances it is performed.
The Śrāddha rite, as prescribed by their own choice, should be performed with the recitation of mantras by Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas who observe the traditional laws of their families.
By women, by Śūdras of lower castes, and by the instruction of Brahmins,
[the rite] was performed according to the rules but without mantras and devoid of the fire-sacrifice.
O twice-born ones, [they dwell] at sacred fords such as Puṣkara, in holy shrines,
on the peaks of the great mountains, and in auspicious regions.
In rivers with holy waters, in streams and lakes,
at the confluences of rivers, and in the seven oceans;
In their own houses well-anointed, and in those permitted [for use],
at the roots of celestial trees, and in sacrificial lakes.
The śrāddha should be offered in these places, and those in which it should be avoided are now declared:
among the Kirātas, the Kaliṅgas, the Koṅkaṇas, and also among the Kṛmis.
In the Daśārṇas, the Kumāryas, the Taṅgaṇas, and also the Krathas;
on the northern banks of the Sindhu and on the southern bank of the Narmadā.
It is said that in the regions to the east of the Karatoyā, the śrāddha should not be offered;
however, one should offer the śrāddha here every month at the waning of the moon, as desired.
The Śrāddha on the full moon days should be performed during the transit of the lunar mansions;
the daily Śrāddha, which is without a deity, is proclaimed by men as being for the ancestors together with humans.
The occasional rites (naimittika) are performed together with the gods, as are the daily ones;
other optional (kāmya) śrāddhas are performed by the twice-born every year.
A *vṛddhi-śrāddha* should also be performed for birth ceremonies and other such rites;
in that regard, the twice-born say that even-numbered brahmins should be invited, preceded by the recitation of mantras.
When the sun has entered Virgo, for fifteen days,
the Śrāddha is prescribed there according to the very same procedure as mentioned before.
The first [day] leads to the acquisition of wealth; the second bestows bipeds;
the third is for one desiring sons; and the fourth destroys enemies.
On the fifth day one attains prosperity; on the sixth, a man becomes worthy of worship;
on the seventh, lordship over the Gaṇas; and on the eighth, supreme intelligence.
On the ninth day he obtains women; on the tenth, the fulfillment of his desires;
and on the eleventh, one devoted to ritual action attains all the Vedas.
On the twelfth day, the one who worships the ancestors obtains victory and gain,
as well as increase in progeny, cattle, intelligence, independence, and supreme nourishment.
Performing a śrāddha on the thirteenth lunar day while endowed with faith, one attains either long life or sovereignty; of this there is no doubt.
Endowed with faith, one should perform a *śrāddha* with whatever food is available for those whose young ancestors died or were slain by weapons.
Therefore, a pure man desiring their satisfaction should perform the śrāddha rite with effort on the fourteenth day or on the new moon day.
He obtains all desires and enjoys infinite heaven;
beyond this, O best of sages, listen as I speak.
Whatever is to be given there for the pleasure of the ancestors by one who desires to please them,
the satisfaction of the ancestors lasts for a month through offerings of sacrificial food (haviṣyānna).
The ancestors attain satisfaction for two months with the flesh of fish;
the flesh of the deer is to be known as providing satisfaction to the ancestors for three months.
The flesh of a hare nourishes the ancestors for four months;
that of a bird for five months indeed; and the meat of a boar for six months.
The meat of the chāgala goat provides satisfaction for seven months, that of the deer (aiṇeya) for eight months, and the meat of the ruru deer for nine months; of this there is no doubt.
Beef provides satisfaction to the ancestors for ten months;
likewise, mutton grants satisfaction to the ancestors for eleven months.
Likewise, for one year, he should consume cow's milk, milk-rice (pāyasa),
the meat of the vādhrīṇa, red iron, kālaśāka, and honey.
Meat from the rohita fish and food offered by those born of one's own family indeed bestow infinite satisfaction as well as sons.
O twice-born ones, there is no doubt in this matter regarding the śrāddha for the ancestors;
he who offers sesame seeds mixed with jaggery during the śrāddha rite [obtains great merit].
Whether it be honey or honey mixed with [other substances], all that indeed becomes inexhaustible.
May there be someone born in our family who shall offer us even a handful of water.
One should offer milk-rice mixed with honey during the rainy season under the Maghā asterism;
one should desire many sons, so that even if only one among them goes to Gayā.
Or he may marry a fair-complexioned maiden, or he may set free a dark-colored bull;
by worshipping the ancestors under the Kṛttikās, a man attains heaven.
One desiring offspring shall obtain them under Rohiṇī; under Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), one obtains brilliance;
under Ārdrā, one attains heroism; and under Punarvasu, one acquires fields.
Under Puṣya, one obtains inexhaustible wealth; under Āśleṣā, supreme longevity;
under Maghā, progeny and prosperity; and under the Phālgunīs, good fortune.
A man who bestows the śrāddha offering under the Uttarās becomes preeminent in character, blessed with offspring, and attains excellence in the sacred scriptures.
Under Citrā, one obtains beauty, splendor, and likewise offspring;
Svātī bestows profit from trade, and Viśākhā grants the desire for sons.
Those who perform [the rites] under Anurādhā shall attain the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin);
under Jyeṣṭhā, sovereignty; and under Mūla, supreme health.
Under the Āṣāḍhās one attains fame; under the Uttarās, freedom from sorrow;
through Śravaṇa, auspicious worlds; and under Dhaniṣṭhā, great wealth.
One gains knowledge of the Vedas under Abhijit, success as a physician under Śravaṇa,
goats and sheep under Proṣṭhapadā, and likewise cattle under the following (Uttarā) one.
Likewise, by performing a śrāddha under the Revatī asterisms, one obtains base metals; under the Aśvinīs, horses; and under the Bharaṇīs, one attains supreme longevity.
Thus does the knower of reality obtain the fruit during these lunar mansions;
therefore, O twice-born ones, the śrāddha rites for specific desires should be offered according to the prescribed rule.
When the sun has entered the zodiac sign of Virgo, one who desires the ultimate fruit should contemplate whatever desires he may have while the sun is situated in the sign of Virgo.
When humans perform the śrāddha for those [ancestors], they obtain their respective desires;
it should be performed for the Nāndīmukhas when the sun has entered the zodiac sign of Virgo.
This should be performed on the full moon day, according to the words of Varāha:
"The divine, terrestrial, and atmospheric beings, both the stationary and the moving."
The ancestors desire the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) when the sun has entered the zodiac sign of Virgo;
indeed, those sixteen days while the sun is situated in Virgo [are sacred].
The Lord Nārāyaṇa has declared that these are equal to sacrificial rites;
for one who desires a fruit difficult to attain, there is nothing superior to the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
One may worship the ancestors even with water, vegetables, roots, and so forth, when the daughter of the Sun (the Moon) has entered Virgo,
while the garlanded one with sharp rays (the Sun) has reached the constellations Uttarāphalgunī or Hastā.
He who worships his ancestors with devotion shall dwell in the triple heaven,
by the command of the King of the Ancestors, when the sun has entered the constellation of Hasta.
The city of the ancestors remains empty only as long as the scorpion is seen;
once the scorpion has passed away, the ancestors join with the gods.
Sighing and having uttered a most unbearable curse, they depart;
indeed, the Śrāddha should be performed on the Aṣṭakā days and during the Manvantaras.
On the Anvaṣṭakā days, it is prescribed that the rites should be performed in order, beginning with the mother;
likewise on the occasion of an eclipse, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, and at the conjunction of the sun and moon.
On one's birth star, during planetary affliction, and likewise during the two solstices and the two equinoxes, the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha is prescribed.
On the days of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), one should perform the most excellent śrāddha according to the prescribed rules;
on these occasions, O twice-born ones, the śrāddha should be performed except for the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa).
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha and on the ninth day of Kārttika,
men should perform the Śrāddha rite according to the rules for a solar transit (saṃkrānti).
On the thirteenth day of the month of Bhādrapada and of Māgha, on the day of the moon's waning,
a śrāddha should be performed with milk-rice (pāyasa), and it is to be conducted like that of the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana).
And when a learned Vedic scholar who knows the Vedas and maintains the sacred fires comes to one's house,
one should perform the most excellent Śrāddha rite according to the rules in his company alone.
When the acquisition of materials for a śrāddha is approved by the virtuous,
the twice-born should perform the śrāddha according to the pārvaṇa rite.
Every year, on the anniversary of the day of their death, one should perform the rites for one's mother and father,
as well as for a childless paternal uncle and for an elder brother.
The Pārvaṇa rite should be preceded by offerings to the gods, while the Ekoddiṣṭa rite is performed without the gods.
One should invite two Brahmins for the rite to the gods and three for the ancestral rite, or one for each of the two.
In this same manner, everything for the maternal grandfathers is proclaimed by analogy;
likewise, one should always offer a funeral cake (piṇḍa) and water on the ground for one who has become a preta.
One should offer sesame seeds and kuśa grass outside, near water;
and on the third day, the collection of the deceased's bones must be performed by the twice-born.
A Brāhmaṇa becomes pure in ten days, a Kṣatriya in twelve days,
a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified in a month.
At the end of the period of impurity, they prescribe a *śrāddha* for a single ancestor (*ekoddiṣṭa*) in the home;
this is performed on the twelfth day, at the end of the month, after three fortnights, and thereafter.
O twice-born ones, this should be performed month after month for as long as a year;
thereafter, the sapindikarana rite must be performed in due order.
Once the sapindikarana has been performed, the parvana rite is prescribed once again;
from that point forward, they are released from the state of being a preta and have attained the status of ancestors (pitṛs).
The ancestors are remembered as being of two kinds: formless and embodied.
The *nāndīmukha* ancestors are formless, while those of the *pārvaṇa* rites are embodied;
the *preta* ancestors who partake of the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite constitute the third—such is the threefold determination regarding the ancestors.
The sages said:
"O best of the twice-born, O foremost of speakers, tell us how the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for one who has become a *preta* should be performed according to the rules."
Vyāsa said:
O Brahmins, listen as I describe the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite;
it is performed without [the presence of] the gods and involves a single *argha* offering and a single *pavitraka*.
In that case, there is no offering into the fire, and that rite is devoid of the invocation;
furthermore, even there, one should feed an odd number of twice-born brahmins with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya).
Furthermore, there is another specific detail regarding the monthly rites and so forth;
listen with one-pointed attention as I describe it to you, O best of the twice-born.
O twice-born ones, one should prepare four vessels there, joined with sesame seeds, fragrant water, and so forth: three for the ancestors and one for the deceased.
One should pour the *argha* water from the vessel of the deceased into the three vessels while reciting "ye samānāḥ," and should perform the remaining rites as previously described.
For women as well, it should be exactly thus; the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite has been prescribed for them.
However, in the absence of a son, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite does not exist for them.
Men should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for a woman every year;
that same rite, as prescribed by the sacred law, should also be performed on the anniversary of death for the ancestors.
In the absence of a son, the sapindas shall perform this rite; in their absence, the uterine brothers;
and in the absence of these, the sons of the son shall duly perform it.
Likewise, the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā) should perform [the rites] for his maternal grandfathers;
those known as *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇas* [should perform them] for both their maternal and paternal grandfathers.
They should perform worship according to the rules, even with occasional *śrāddha* rites;
in the absence of all [male relatives], women should perform [the rite] for their own husbands without the recitation of mantras.

And in their absence, the king shall cause all activities, such as the maintenance of draft animals and so forth, to be properly carried out by men of that same caste on behalf of those who have no family.
Since the king is the kinsman of all social classes (varṇas),
O Brahmins, these rites— both regular and occasional— have thus been described to you.
I shall describe another rite based on the *śrāddha*, which is both regular and occasional;
therein, one should know that the new moon (*darśa*), characterized by the waning of the moon, is the occasion.
But that time is fixed as eternal; one should perform [the rite] for the father's great-grandfather after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, exactly as prescribed.
But he who is excluded from the ancestral rice-ball (piṇḍa) becomes a partaker of the smearing (lepa);
for among them, whoever is the fourth or another [descendant] shall indeed be a partaker of the smearing.
He too, along with his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, undergoes a degraded state of enjoyment as a consequence of that connection.
For these three types of men are to be known as those connected by the offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍa),
while others, starting from the great-grandfather, are connected by the smearing of the remains (lepa).
"Starting from these three [ancestors], the sacrificer is the seventh;
thus have the sages declared this seven-generational relationship."
Starting from the sacrificer and extending upwards, those who enjoy the ointment are likewise [included];
beyond them are all his ancestors and all others who dwell in hell.
Those who have fallen into the state of animals, and those who exist as spirits and the like—
the sacrificer indeed offers all of them [a share] when performing the śrāddha according to the rule.
O Brahmins, he is nourished by whatever I describe;
furthermore, that scattering of food which is performed on the earth by human beings [also nourishes him].
O twice-born ones, even those who have attained the state of piśācas find satisfaction through that water which falls upon the ground from the bathing garments.
By that, satisfaction arises for those who have reached the state of being trees;
and as for those droplets of fragrant water that fall upon the surface of the earth, [they likewise bring satisfaction].
Through those [offerings], there is nourishment for them, and for those who have gone to their family line, there is divinity;
furthermore, when the rice-balls have been lifted, whatever drops of water remain on the ground—
Through these [offerings], there is nourishment for those among them who have entered the state of animals within the family,
as well as for those children in the family who are toothless and excluded from ritual practices.

But those who have failed in their duties are disqualified; they should subsist on water that has been strained, and having eaten, they should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), as well as using the water produced from washing the feet.
In the same way, others likewise attain satisfaction for the Brahmins;
thus it is for the sacrificer and for those twice-born ones as well.
If someone throws water or food— whether pure or even defiled—
with that food, those in that family who have gone to another state of birth [are also benefited].
The Brahmins of those who perform the śrāddha rites correctly attain nourishment;
however, that śrāddha which is performed by men with wealth acquired through unjust means [does not].
They are not satisfied in births such as those of Caṇḍālas or Pulkasas;
thus, O Brahmins, nourishment [from offerings] is provided by many kinsmen alone.
For those performing a *śrāddha* here, [merit] arises from the scattering of water;
therefore, a man should perform the *śrāddha* with devotion according to the rules, even if it be only with vegetables.
One should perform the śrāddha; for one who performs it, no one in the family perishes.
The śrāddha should be offered to Brahmins who are self-controlled and maintainers of the sacred fire (agnihotrins).
Especially among pure, learned, and Vedic scholars—
one who has mastered the three Nāciketa fires, the three Madhu verses, the Trisuparṇa hymn, and the six Vedāṅgas.
One who is devoted to his parents, a sister’s son, one who knows the Sāmaveda,
as well as the officiating priest, the family priest, the teacher, and the sub-teacher— one should feed these.
A maternal uncle, a father-in-law, a brother-in-law, a relative, a teacher of the *Droṇa* [Veda],
a village priest (*maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa*), and one who is proficient in the meaning of the *Purāṇas*.
One who is free from ritualistic pride, content with whatever rites are performed, and who has renounced the acceptance of gifts—
such Brahmins should be appointed at a *śrāddha* ceremony as purifiers of the assembly.
On the day before, one should invite the aforementioned best of the twice-born for the rites dedicated to the gods and the ancestors; one should prepare them accordingly for those two purposes.
Those who perform the śrāddha must be self-restrained;
for he who, having given and having eaten at a śrāddha, engages in sexual intercourse, [incurs a fault].
For one month, the ancestors indeed lie within that semen of him who,
having gone to a woman during a *śrāddha*, either eats there or engages in sexual intercourse.
During that month, the ancestors of those two subsist on food made of feces and urine;
therefore, a wise person should first extend an invitation [to a guest].
On that day, or even when [the food] has not yet been obtained, one should avoid those who are attached to women;
likewise, one should avoid ascetics (*yatīn*) who have come at the proper time for the sake of alms and are self-restrained.
With a restrained mind, one should please them through prostrations and other such acts and feed them;
at that time, the wise man should also feed the yogins at the śrāddha.
For the ancestors are the foundation of yoga; therefore, one should always honor them.
Even if there were thousands of Brahmins, a single yogi would be superior.

It carries across the sacrificer and the enjoyers like a boat upon the water; likewise, a verse of the ancestors is sung here by those who discourse on Brahman: BrP_220.112: "Just as a boat carries people across the water, so does this gift carry the donor and the recipient across the ocean of existence. Thus is the song of the ancestors chanted here by the exponents of the Veda.
O lord of the earth, that which was sung by the ancestors long ago concerning Aila, the king:
"When shall there be born in our lineage a preeminent son? BrP_220.113.
He who shall offer on the ground the morsels of food remaining from what has been eaten by the yogis, or else an offering of rhinoceros meat and oblation at Gayā; ||| BrP_220.114 |||
Black śāka-vegetables, sesame seeds with clarified butter, and kṛsara-rice are for our satisfaction;
the Vaiśvadeva offering, the Soma-offering, and the meat of the rhinoceros are the supreme oblations.
We invoke blessings from the head down to the feet, excluding the tusks;
one should offer the śrāddha on the thirteenth lunar day under the Maghā asterism according to the prescribed rite.
During the southern solstice, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with honey and ghee;
therefore, a man should worship his ancestors according to the prescribed rites with devotion.
Desiring all objects of desire, liberation of the self from evil, as well as the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, and the lunar mansions, planets, and stars; BrP_220.118.
The ancestors, when gratified by the śrāddha rite, bring satisfaction to human beings,
bestowing longevity, progeny, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, and happiness.
In that same way, the ancestors, when gratified by the śrāddha, bestow a kingdom;
likewise, the afternoon excels the forenoon for the ancestors.
Having honored these twice-born guests who have arrived at his home with a welcome, he—
holding the *pavitra* grass in his hand and having offered water for sipping (*ācamana*)— should seat them upon their seats.
Having performed the śrāddha according to the prescribed rule and having fed the best of the twice-born,
one should dismiss them after speaking pleasant words and bowing down with devotion.
He should follow [the guest] as far as the door and return once he has expressed his approval;
thereafter, he should perform his daily rites and likewise feed the guests.
Some excellent men desire the daily rite for the ancestors;
others do not [desire it] for the ancestors in that same way; one should perform the remainder as previously prescribed.
Some others speak of it as being distinct, and some say it is like the previous [offering].
Then, that man should eat that food together with his servants and attendants.
Thus should one who knows the Dharma, being composed, perform the ancestral Śrāddha rite,
so that complete satisfaction arises among the foremost of the Brahmins.
Now I shall fully describe those lowest of the twice-born who are to be avoided:
one who betrays a friend, one with deformed nails, a eunuch, one afflicted with consumption, one with white leprosy, and a merchant.
Furthermore, he may have black teeth, or be bald, one-eyed, blind, deaf, or dull-witted;
he may be mute, lame, withered in limb, impotent, afflicted with skin disease, deformed, or squint-eyed.
One who is leprous, red-eyed, humpbacked, dwarf, deformed, or lazy;
one who treats friends as enemies, of low birth, a cattle-herder, or of repulsive appearance.

A man who has been superseded in marriage, one who supersedes his brother in marriage, the son of a woman superseded in marriage, a husband of a Śūdra woman, and the son of such a man— these twice-born men shall not partake in the śrāddha feast.

One who performs the sacraments for the son of a *vṛṣalī*, one who is unmarried yet acts as a husband to his brother's widow (*didhiṣūpati*), one who teaches for a fee, and one who has been taught by a teacher for a fee; // BrP 220.131 //
One who subsists on food from a birth-impurity, a hunter, a seller of Soma, one accused of a crime, a thief, an outcast, a usurer, and a rogue; BrP 220.132.
A slanderer, one who abandons the Vedas, one who neglects giving and the sacred fire, one who is cruel,
a king’s domestic priest, a servant devoid of learning, and furthermore, one who is envious— [these fall].
One who hates elders, one who is difficult to restrain, one who is cruel, one who is deluded, a temple-priest (devalaka),
an astrologer, and a maker of festive occasions are likewise censured.
One who officiates at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, a eunuch, and those who are censured or base—these should not be appointed at a śrāddha; seeing them defiles the row of guests.
Where there is the support of the wicked and the humiliation of the virtuous,
a terrible divine punishment falls instantly upon that place.
