But the fool who, abandoning the well-established scripture and discarding the primordial Dharma, should feed [others],
that donor perishes therein.
But he who, having abandoned a dependent twice-born man, brings another and feeds him,
that giver perishes there, consumed by the fire of the latter's sighs.
In the absence of clothing, there is no ritual action, nor sacrifice, nor Veda, nor ascetic penance;
therefore, garments should be given, especially at the time of a śrāddha.
Whoever gives these at a śrāddha— silk, linen, cotton, and likewise unwashed fine cloth— attains the highest desires.
Just as a calf finds its mother among a large herd of cows,
so does a living being find food for the Brahmins wherever it resides.
Even those who have met their death do not go [to the ancestors] if the name, the lineage, and the mantras are not provided, nor if the food is not given; yet satisfaction attends them nonetheless.
"Salutations to the deities, to the ancestors, and to the great yogis; may [these offerings] always be for Svāhā and Svadhā. (BrP 220.143)
At the beginning and at the end of the Śrāddha, one should then recite it three times;
likewise, during the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍas), one should recite it with a concentrated mind.
The ancestors arrive quickly and the rākṣasas flee;
they are gratified throughout the three worlds, for this mantra indeed delivers them.
One should provide new linen thread, as well as flaxen or cotton;
one should avoid silk thread, woven silk, and silkworm silk.
A wise man should avoid the tenth [day], even if it be unobstructed;
for these [days] do not please [the ancestors], and there would be misfortune for the donor as well.
A funeral ball (piṇḍa) should not be offered to an ancestor who is still living;
rather, one should feed him according to the prescribed rule with the desired food and edibles.
A man desiring enjoyment should always offer a ball of food (piṇḍa) into the fire;
one desiring offspring should offer the middle one to his wife, preceded by the recitation of the mantra.
Seeking supreme splendor, one should offer a ball of food to cows;
for wisdom, fame, and renown, one should present it to the waters.
Seeking long life, he gives [the offering] to the crows;
seeking a hall for his children, he gives it to the cocks.
Furthermore, some Brahmins said: "The extraction of the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) should be done first;
once permitted by those Brahmins, saying 'Let it be extracted at will,' [it may proceed]."
Therefore, the śrāddha should be performed exactly as it was described by the sages of old;
otherwise, a fault would arise and it would not reach the ancestors.
One should satisfy the ancestors with barley, rice, sesame, mung beans, wheat, chickpeas, as well as green gram, śyāmāka grain, and mustard juices.
One should honor [the ancestors] with wild rice, *hasti-śyāmāka*, and *priyaṅgu*;
likewise, a wise man should offer *prasātikā* and *satūlikā* in the śrāddha rite.
Mango, hog-plum, wood-apple, pomegranate, citron,
emblic myrobalan, milk, coconut, and jujube.
The orange, along with the date, the grape, the blue wood-apple,
the patola, the priyāla, and the karkandhu and badara fruits.
Vikaṅkata, vatsaka, karṇārū, and vāraka—
these varieties of fruit should be offered with diligence at a śrāddha ceremony.
Molasses, sugar, candied sugar, thickened juice, and parched grain; cow’s milk, curd, clarified butter, and oil produced from sesame seeds should be given.
One should offer rock salt, sea salt, and likewise lake salt,
as well as pure fragrances such as sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron.
One should offer kālaśāka, taṇḍulīya, vāstuka, and likewise mūlaka;
one may also give forest-grown vegetables and these flowers.
The *jāti*, *campaka*, and *lodhra* flowers, as well as *mallikā*, *bāṇa*, and *barbarī*; the stalks of *aśoka* and *āṭarūṣa*, and likewise *tulasī* and *tilaka*.
The pāvantī, the śatapattra, and the fragrant śephālikā,
as well as the kubjaka, the tagara, the mṛga, and the wild ketakī.
O twice-born ones, one should diligently offer jasmine and atimukta, as well as the lotus, kumuda, padma, and puṇḍarīka, which are suitable for acts of faith.
One should employ the blue lotus, the red lotus, and the white water lily;
as well as costus, spikenard, vetiver, cock’s-foot lily, and clove.
Nalika, uśīra, musta, granthiparṇī, and sundarī—
these and others like them are said to be suitable for perfumes.
Guggulu, sandalwood, śrīvāsa, and likewise aguru—
these are the incenses suitable for the ancestors, as is ṛṣiguggulu.
One should avoid rājamāṣa beans, chickpeas, lentils, koradūṣaka grains, vipruṣa, markaṭa, and kodrava millet.
One should avoid buffalo, yak, deer, sheep, and one-hoofed animal products; likewise, one should renounce curd, milk, and ghee produced from females, as well as those from camels and sheep.
One should avoid the tāla, varuṇa, and kākola fruits, as well as the fruit of the bahupattrā and arjunī, the jambīra, the red bilva, and also the fruit of the śāla tree.
Fish, pigs, and tortoises, as well as cows, should be especially avoided;
likewise, putika, musk, gorocana, and red sandalwood.
One should also avoid kāleyaka, which has a pungent odor, as well as turuṣka,
pālaṅka, kumārī, kirāta, and piṇḍamūlaka.
Gṛñjana, cukrikā, cukra, varuṇa, canapattrikā,
jīva, śatapuṣpā, nālikā, and gandhaśūkara— [these should not be eaten].
One should avoid the halabhṛtya, mustard, onion, and garlic;
as well as the mānakanda, viṣakanda, vajrakanda, and gadāsthika.
In the performance of the Śrāddha rite, one should avoid the puruṣālu, the sapiṇḍālu,
the alābu, the tiktaparṇī, the kūṣmāṇḍa, and the three pungent spices (kaṭukatraya).
The eggplant, the śivajāta, the hairy figs (vaṭa),
the kālīya, the red-bamboo, the crane, and likewise the lakuca.
In the performance of ancestral rites (śrāddha), one should avoid the fruit of the *vibhītaka* tree,
as well as fermented gruel (*āranāla*), sour liquids (*śukta*), anything that has decayed, and likewise anything that has been kept overnight.
O best of beings, one should also offer substances with a pungent odor, such as the *kovidāra* and *śigru*,
as well as those that are extremely sour, slimy, fine-textured, and stale.

One should not give food that has lost its flavor, nor that which has the smell of liquor, nor that which has the pungent scent of asafoetida, nor that containing *phaṇiśa*, *bhūnimba*, *nimba*, or *rājika*.
One should avoid kustumburu from Kaliṅga, amlavetasa,
pomegranate, māgadhī, ginger, fresh ginger, and tittiḍī.
One should devotedly offer āmrātaka, jīvaka, and tumburu,
as well as milk-rice, śālmalī, mung beans, sweetmeats, and other such foods.
O twice-born ones, one should offer a beverage, mango juice, and cow’s milk, as well as whatever foods there may be that are savory and unctuous.
In the performance of a śrāddha rite, only those foods that are slightly sour or slightly pungent should be offered;
however, those that are excessively sour, excessively salty, or excessively pungent must be avoided.
One should avoid from afar those foods here that are fit for Asuras— those which are rich, glossy, and slightly pungent or sour.
One should employ these delicious foods fit for the gods in the śrāddha ceremony:
goat meat, the meat of the common quail, the meat of the partridge, and the flesh of the hare.
One should employ the meat of the śivāla, the avaka, and the rājīva fish at a śrāddha,
as well as the vāghrīṇasa, the red śiva, and the scaled loha fish.
It is likewise stated that the lion-mouthed fish and the rhinoceros should be employed at a śrāddha;
for it has also been said by Manu regarding the rohita fish that one should employ it [at such rites].
It should be employed in offerings to the gods and ancestors, and likewise one should not separate it;
thus has it been spoken by me, O Brahmins, as observed by Vārāha.
One who eats what has been forbidden by me shall go to the Raurava hell;
and these things have been forbidden by Vārāha, O you whose wealth is asceticism.
Things that are unfit to be eaten by the twice-born should not be offered even to the ancestors;
one should avoid the Rohita fish, the boar, the tortoise, the monitor lizard, and the swan.
The ruddy goose, the water-hen, scaleless fish, the osprey,
boneless fish, and chickens that have been kept for a night.
Kalaviṅkas, peacocks, bhāradvājas, śārṅgakas, mongooses, owls, cats, lopās, and other creatures that are very difficult to capture; ||| BrP_220.192 |||
That evil-minded person who devours these and other such corrupted creatures— ṭiṭṭibha birds, jackals, tigers, bears, and hyenas— is lost.
But that perpetrator of great evil, that sinful soul who gives these despicable meats to his ancestors, shall go to the Raurava hell.
He will cast even his ancestors dwelling in heaven into hell by [eating] kusumbha greens, the citron fruit, drumstick, and kovidāra.
Oil-cake, droplets [of oil], lentils, garlic, hemp, kodrava grain, kokilākṣa, sour gruel, kambuka, and padmaka; BrP 220.196.
By eating the flesh of the cakora and the hawk, the fruit of the round gourd (alābu),
and the fruit of the palmyra trees, one goes to hell.
Having given [food] to the ancestors, a man shall go with them to the pus-filled river;
therefore, a wise person should not take it by all possible means.
O sages, Varāha himself has out of respect prohibited [these meats] for the sake of the ancestors;
indeed, he considered the eating of one's own flesh to be preferable.
For indeed, O twice-born ones, men should never take up these prohibited things with zeal, whether out of ignorance or through negligence, even if only once.
If one has consumed forbidden things,
one should then perform an expiation by means of fruits, roots, curd, milk, buttermilk, cow’s urine, and barley gruel.
In the case of eating food that is either permissible or forbidden, [the penance lasts] for seven days each;
likewise, this applies even if a prohibited act is committed by twice-born men only once.
The body should be purified, especially by those devoted to Viṣṇu;
and one should avoid prohibited substances, O best of the twice-born, as they have been described.
Then, having gathered [the necessary materials], one should perform the *śrāddha* according to one's own capacity.
By performing the *śrāddha* in this manner, in accordance with the prescribed rules and suited to one’s wealth,
a person gratifies the entire world from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
The sages said:
"If the father is living, but both fathers of the father have died, how indeed should the śrāddha be performed? Tell this in detail."
Vyāsa said: To whomsoever the father should offer the śrāddha, to him the son himself should offer it;
in this way, neither worldly nor Vedic dharma is lost.
The sages said:
"O Brahmin, how indeed should one whose father is dead but whose grandfather is still living perform the *śrāddha*? You ought to explain this to us."
Vyāsa said:
One should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to the father and feed the grandfather;
indeed, one should [offer] the cake to the great-grandfather—this is the settled rule in the scriptures.
When [the ancestors] have died, the rice-ball (piṇḍa) should be offered; while they are still living, one should feed them.
For them, the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite does not exist, nor is the Pārvaṇa rite prescribed.
That man who practices the conduct based on the Pitṛmedha rites will quickly increase in lifespan, wealth, and sons; of this there is no doubt.
O twice-born ones, the ancestors of that person who recites this chapter on the Pitṛmedha at the times of Śrāddha feasts shall eat his food for three yugas.
Thus has the ritual for the ancestral offerings (pitṛmedhakalpa) been described by me;
it removes sin and increases merit,
and it should be heard by men who are self-restrained.
And one should likewise recite [this] during ancestral rites (*śrāddha*).
Vyāsa said:
Thus, by a householder acting correctly, the deities as well as the ancestors [are honored].
Guests and kinsmen should be honored with offerings to the gods and ancestors, and with food.
All beings— servants, beasts, birds, and even ants— as well as mendicants seeking alms and whatever other travelers were in the house.
Brahmins devoted to virtuous conduct who neglect their daily and occasional rites become like householders and partake in sin.
The sages said:
"O Brahmin, you have described that which is constant and occasional;
human action is threefold: constant, occasional, and optional."
O Sage, we wish to hear from you as you speak about right conduct—
that by practicing which a human being attains happiness both in this world and in the hereafter.
Vyāsa said:
A householder must always maintain the observance of proper conduct;
for one devoid of proper conduct, there is no well-being either in this world or in the next.
In this world, sacrifice, charity, and austerity do not lead to a person's welfare if they proceed by transgressing the conduct of the virtuous.
For a man of evil conduct does not attain a long life in this world;
dharma must always be practiced through good conduct, for such is the very definition of conduct.
O twice-born ones, I shall describe the nature of that virtuous conduct;
having become single-minded with the self, one should likewise preserve it.
A householder must exert effort in accomplishing the three aims of life;
for upon their complete fulfillment, the householder achieves success both in this world and the next.
A self-possessed man should devote one quarter of his wealth to the welfare of the hereafter,
half to his own maintenance, and [the remainder] to the performance of obligatory and occasional rites.
Nevertheless, one should cause its very root to increase by means of the foot alone;
for a Brahmin who practices in this way, his purpose attains fulfillment.

In the same way, for the sake of preventing evil, the wise man should practice dharma; likewise, another kind of dharma which yields its fruit in this very life should be practiced for the sake of the next world.
Desire arising from fear of transgression, as well as another kind that is non-contradictory—
desire is thus fashioned in two ways so as not to conflict with the three aims of life.
O best of the twice-born, you should reflect upon all these as being mutually connected, and you must understand those that are contrary connections.
Dharma has the purpose of following after further dharma; dharma does not cause pain to one's own self-interest.
Desire is of two kinds according to both of these, and therefore those two are again twofold.
One should wake during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and reflect upon dharma and artha;
having risen, sipped water for purification (*ācamana*), bathed, and become self-controlled and pure.

One should worship the morning twilight while the stars are still visible and the evening twilight while the sun is still present, according to the prescribed rule; one should not abandon this practice except in times of distress.
O twice-born ones, one should avoid idle chatter, falsehood, and harshness of speech; likewise, one should avoid false scriptures, fallacious arguments, and the service of the wicked.
One who has restrained the self should perform the fire-oblation (homa) both in the evening and in the morning;
likewise, one should not gaze at the sun at its rising or its setting.
Grooming the hair, looking in a mirror, cleaning the teeth, applying collyrium,
and the libation to the deities are activities to be performed specifically in the forenoon.
One should not void excrement or urine on the road, nor in a village, a dwelling, a sacred bathing place, a field, or a cow-pen, nor on ploughed land.
One should not look at another man’s naked wife, nor should one look at one’s own excrement; likewise, one should avoid seeing or touching a woman in her courses, as well as conversing with her.
One should not discharge urine, feces, or engage in sexual intercourse in water;
nor should one stand upon excrement, urine, hair, ashes, or dregs.
A wise person should not step upon husks, charcoal, scattered items such as ropes or clothes, nor indeed upon garments on the road or on the ground.
Having performed the worship of the ancestors, the gods, humans, and likewise of all beings according to his means, the householder may then eat.
Facing either east or north, having sipped water for purification, restrained in speech, and pure,
a man should always eat his food with his mind focused on it, keeping his hands within his knees.
A wise person should not point out defects in food unless there has been an actual injury to it;
one should avoid food that contains visible salt, as well as food that is leavings.
A self-controlled person should not discharge feces or urine while walking or standing;
likewise, he should not consume even the slightest bit of food while impure from eating.
Being impure from remnants of food, one should not speak anything nor abandon one's private Vedic recitation;
nor should one look at the sun, the moon, or the stars out of desire.
One should avoid sharing a seat, a bed, or a vessel with them;
one should offer a seat to one's gurus, honoring them by rising from one's own seat and other such marks of respect.
A wise person should engage in conversation that is agreeable; one should follow along with that and should not act in opposition.
One should not eat wearing only a single garment, nor should one perform the worship of the deities;
a wise man should not invite the twice-born [for a feast], but should perform the fire-oblation (homa).
A man should never bathe naked, nor should he ever sleep naked;
likewise, he should not scratch his head with both hands at once.
The wise should not bathe their heads frequently without a specific reason;
and having bathed one's head, one should not touch any part of the body with oil.
One should avoid Vedic study during all periods forbidden for study; furthermore, one should never show disrespect toward Brahmins, fire, cows, or the sun.
During the day, one should discharge urine and feces facing north; at night, facing south;
or, in cases of distress, one may do so as desired.
One should not speak of the teacher's misdeeds, and one should appease him if he is angry;
one should not listen to slander, even when others are uttering it.
The way must be yielded to Brahmins, to a king, to one afflicted by suffering,
to one superior in learning, to a pregnant woman, to one tormented by disease, and to a person of high status.
And for those who are mute, blind, or deaf, as well as for the intoxicated and the insane;
likewise, [one should avoid] a temple, a tree sacred to Caidya (Śiśupāla), and a crossroads.
A wise person should circumambulate a teacher who is superior in knowledge;
one should not wear shoes, garments, garlands, or other items that have been worn by others.
On the fourteenth, the eighth, and the fifteenth days— the sacred festival days—
one should avoid oil massages, sensual enjoyments, and women.
A wise person should never stand with his arms or shanks raised;
he should not swing his feet about, nor should he cross one foot over the other.
One should avoid striking the vital points, verbal abuse, and backbiting directed at a harlot, one who has accomplished his purpose, a child, or an outcaste.
A wise person should not practice hypocrisy, arrogance,
or harshness toward fools, the insane, those addicted to vices, or even those who are deformed.
One should not mock or revile those who are deficient in limb or those who are destitute;
nor should one wield a rod against another, except for the purpose of instructing a disciple or a son.
Likewise, a wise man should not sit down after dragging his seat with his foot;
nor should he prepare saṃyāva, kṛśara, or meat for his own sake alone.
Having performed the worship of guests, one should eat in the evening and in the morning;
facing either the east or the north, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth while remaining silent.
O Brahmins, one should always act thus and avoid plants that are forbidden;
a man should never sleep with his head toward the north, nor should he ever sleep with his head toward the west.
Having placed his head toward the direction of Agastya, he should then sleep facing Puraṃdarī;
however, he should not sleep in waters containing fragrance, nor likewise at dawn.
Except for the day of an eclipse, bathing is declared to be supreme;
one should not wipe the limbs with the ends of one's garments or with hands and clothes.
A wise man should never shake out his hair nor wring out his garments;
he should never apply ointment without having first bathed.
Nor should he wear dyed garments, nor those that are variegated or black;
nor should he engage in the exchange of his clothes, nor of his ornaments.
One should avoid a garment that has been bitten by a rat, one that is excessively worn out,
one infested with insects or hair, and likewise one that has been looked upon by dogs.
One should avoid meat licked by a dog, meat defiled by the extraction of its essence, meat from the back, meat not intended for sacrifice (vṛthāmāṃsa), and meat that is forbidden.
A man should never eat salt directly;
O Brahmins, that which has been kept for a long time, as well as what is dried or stale, must be avoided.
O best of the twice-born, preparations made from flour, vegetables, sugarcane,
and milk, as well as preparations of meat, are not to be avoided even if they have been kept for a long time.
At the rising and setting of the sun, one should avoid lying down;
likewise, a man should not study while unclean, nor while reclining, nor with his mind distracted by something else.
One should never eat while lying down, nor while seated on the ground, nor while making noise; furthermore, one should never eat without first giving portions to the servants.
A man, having bathed, should eat in the evening and in the morning according to the prescribed rule;
a wise man must not approach the wife of another.
For men, approaching the wives of others destroys their merit from sacrifices and charitable works, as well as their lifespan;
indeed, nothing exists in this world so detrimental to longevity.
Just as a man's violation of another's wife in this world [is a grave offense],
so too are the rites for the gods, the fires, and the ancestors, as well as the salutation of one's teacher.
Having sipped water properly, one should likewise perform the act of eating food with care,
using clear water that is free from foam, noise, and foul odor.
One should sip water in that same manner while facing either the east or the north,
[avoiding water] from within a body of water, from a dwelling, from an anthill, or from the burrow of a mouse.
One should avoid using the five types of earth remaining after purification;
having washed both hands and feet and sprinkled oneself with water, one should remain composed.
A man should likewise sip water three or even four times with his hands between his knees;
then, having wiped his mouth twice, he should touch the sense- openings and his head.
Having sipped water properly, one who is pure should indeed perform the ritual action after sneezing, tasting [something],
passing wind, or spitting and so forth.
Upon touching [an impure object], one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana); or, if one has not been touched, one should look at the sun;
and one should also touch the right ear.
For this [offering] should be performed according to one's means; in the absence of the former, the latter follows.
It is not accepted that the subsequent [offering] may be undertaken while the previously mentioned [one] is available.
One should not grind one's teeth nor strike one's own body;
likewise, while sleeping, traveling, or eating, one should avoid the recitation of sacred texts.
One should also engage in sexual intercourse during the twilight, as well as set out on a journey;
likewise, one should perform the libation for the ancestors with faith in the afternoon.
One should perform the ritual bathing of the head for the sake of the gods and the ancestors;
one should also have the work of shaving performed while facing either the east or the north.
One should avoid a girl who has physical defects, even if she is of noble birth and free from disease;
likewise, one should marry a girl who is at least the seventh generation on the father's side and the fifth on the mother's side.
One should protect one's wife, abandon envy, as well as sleeping and sexual intercourse during the day,
and always avoid actions that cause distress to others or inflict suffering upon living beings.
A woman in her courses must be avoided by all castes for four nights;
one should also avoid her on the fifth day in order to prevent the birth of a female child.
Then, on the sixth night, during the nights of the Jyeṣṭhā conjunctions, one should go;
for sons are born from union on even nights, and daughters on uneven nights.
Those who follow heterodox paths are indeed eunuchs during the twilight hours on the first days of the lunar fortnights;
therefore, a wise man should avoid shaving on the *riktā* lunar days.
One should never listen to those who speak without discipline,
nor should one respectfully offer an exalted seat to one who is not exalted.
O twice-born ones, after undergoing the rite of shaving, at the conclusion of a ritual, after sexual intercourse with a woman,
and upon entering a cremation ground, a wise man who possesses clothes should bathe.
[He is the refuge] of gods, Vedas, and the twice-born; of the virtuous, the truthful, and the high-souled;
of gurus, devoted wives, those dedicated to the Brahma-sacrifice, and ascetics.
O twice-born ones, one should not engage in slander or jesting;
one should be clothed in white garments and adorned with white flowers.
A wise man should always wear auspicious attire and never adopt anything inauspicious; he should not associate with those who are arrogant, intoxicated, deluded, or ill-mannered.
One should cultivate loving-kindness toward those who lack moral discipline, as well as toward those defiled by age or birth,
but not toward men who are excessively wasteful, nor indeed toward enemies.
Nor with those incapable of action, nor with the censurable, nor indeed with those who associate with parasites,
nor with the destitute, nor with men solely intent on debate, nor with other such base persons.

One should rise to greet friends, consecrated kings, those who have completed their vows (snātakas), and fathers-in-law; and when they have come to one's house, one should honor them according to one's means.

O Brahmins, having performed the proper worship in their homes according to their means, for those who have stayed each year in succession, they should honor them in due order according to their respective places.
In that manner, one should worship in the fire and offer oblations in sequence:
first, one should offer to Brahmā, and after that, to Prajāpati.
One should offer the third [portion] to the household deities, and likewise another to Kaśyapa;
thereafter, one should give to Anumati, and then offer the *bahubali* (the many-offering).
O twice-born ones, listen as I speak: after performing the ritual action previously described by me in the procedure for the daily rite, one should then perform the Vaiśvadeva offering.
Having designated the gods individually according to their respective positions,
one should indeed offer three [libations] at the water-jar for Parjanya, the waters, and the earth.
And to Vāyu, to each of the directions, and to the quarters starting from the East in sequence;
and to Brahmā, to the intermediate space (antarikṣa), and to Sūrya, respectively.
And to all the gods, to all beings,
to Uṣas, and to the Lord of Beings, one who is pure should offer [the oblation] to the north.
Having uttered "Svadhā" and "Namaḥ" for the ancestors toward the south,
and having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), he should speak toward the northwest, saying, "O Yakṣman, this [is for you]."
One should duly offer water mixed with the remnants of the food;
thereafter, one should perform salutations to the gods and to the Brahmins.
The line on the right hand that runs upward from the thumb is known as the *brāhma* tīrtha, intended indeed for sipping water (*ācamana*).
The space between the forefinger and the thumb is declared to be the ancestral (pitrya) tīrtha;
with that one should offer water to the ancestors, except for those who are "joyful-faced" (nāndīmukha).
Likewise, the divine (daiva) [tīrtha] is at the tip of the finger; by that, the ritual procedures for divine acts are performed.
The sacred ford (tīrtha) at the base of the little finger belongs to Prajāpati; it is the bodily [tīrtha].
Thus, one should always perform the prescribed rites together with the ancestors at these sacred fords; never at any other ford.
Sipping water (ācamana) with the *brāhma* tīrtha is recommended; it is always done with the *paitrya* tīrtha for rites concerning the ancestors;
for the gods, it is done with the *daivata* tīrtha; and the *prājāpatya* is performed with the *jita* tīrtha.
A wise man should perform the offering of rice-balls and water for the Nāndīmukhas using the Prājāpatya tīrtha, as well as whatever else belongs to Prajāpati.
A wise man should not simultaneously hold water and fire;
nor should he stretch out his feet toward his gurus, the gods, the ancestors, or Brahmins.
One should not point out a cow suckling her calf; one should not drink water with cupped hands;
at all times for purification, whether the teachers be many or few, a wise man should not delay; nor should he blow upon a fire with his mouth.
O Brahmins, one should not dwell in a place where these four things are not found:
a lender of loans, a physician, a learned Vedic scholar, and a river with water.
Where the king has conquered his servants, is powerful, and devoted to dharma, there a wise man should always dwell; for where is there happiness under a bad king?
Where the citizens are well-united, always acting with justice,
and where the people are peaceful and free from envy, there residence brings about happiness.
In that kingdom where the farmers are generally not overly arrogant,
and where all medicinal herbs are found, there a wise man should dwell.
O Brahmins, one should not dwell in a place where these three are always present:
a person desiring victory, a person harboring ancient enmity, and a people constantly engaged in festivities.
A wise man should always dwell among virtuous companions where the king is invincible and the earth yields abundant crops.
Thus has this been told to you, O Brahmins, out of my desire for your welfare;
hereafter I shall proclaim the rules and procedures regarding what is to be eaten and what is to be consumed.
Food that has been kept overnight is fit to be eaten if it is mixed with oil or fat and has been stored for a long time;
likewise, preparations of wheat, barley, and cow's milk are edible even if they lack oil or fat.
The hare, the tortoise, the monitor lizard, the porcupine, the fish, and the scaly ant-eater—these may be eaten; likewise, the village pig and the domestic cock are to be avoided.

One does not incur fault by eating meat that remains from offerings to the ancestors, gods, and others at a śrāddha ceremony, or that which was offered at the request of a brahmin, or that which has been consecrated for medicinal purposes.
Of conch-shells, stones, gold, silver, ropes, or garments;
of vegetables, roots, fruits, as well as split bamboo and leather.
For gems, garments, corals, as well as pearls,
bowls, and sacrificial cups, purification by water is prescribed.
Likewise, the purification of stone vessels is by water and by rubbing with stones;
and for oily vessels, purification is by hot water.
By sprinkling winnowing baskets, skins, pestles,
mortars, and heaps of gathered clothes, [one is purified].
For all types of bark garments, purification by water and earth is prescribed;
the same is prescribed for all woolen cloths and for hair.
Furthermore, by means of a paste of white mustard seeds or a paste of sesame seeds,
there is always purification for those things that have been damaged.
Likewise, the purification of cotton products should be performed with water and ashes;
for wood, ivory, bone, and horn, purification is held to be by means of planing.
Furthermore, earthen vessels become pure through baking;
alms-food, the hand of an artisan, merchandise, and likewise the mouth of a woman, are pure.
The knowledge of traveling on the road, refined by the circle of servants,
previously praised, long past, separated by many intervals, and light.
The interior of a house, an abundance of food, a child, the movements within a house occupied by the elderly, the workshops, the storehouse, and the two breasts of a pure woman; BrP_221.122.
Likewise, pure waters flow free from odor;
the earth is purified by time, by burning, by sweeping, and by the herds of cows.
By plastering, scraping, sprinkling, sweeping the house and so forth, and by removing hair and insects, or when it has been smelled by a cow or infested with flies; BrP 221.124.
For the sake of purification, earth, water, and ashes should be thrown into food;
likewise, for copper, tin, and lead, one should use sour water or water infused with udumbara fruit.
Bell-metal is purified by ashes and water; liquids are purified by overflowing;
and that which has been smeared with impurities is purified by earth and water, along with the removal of the odor.
One should also take away the color and fragrance of other substances;
however, meat that is pure may be taken even if it has been killed by Cāṇḍālas or carnivorous beasts.
Oil and other substances found on a public road are pure; milk that satisfies a cow is pure; dust, fire, the shadow of a horse or a cow, rays of light, wind, and the earth [are also pure].
Sparks from a fire and flies and the like become faultless through contact with something impure;
likewise, the mouth of a goat, a horse, and a calf is pure.
The flow from a mother's breast is pure; so too is a bird when it causes fruit to fall, as well as a seat, a bed, a vehicle, and the grass on the banks of a river.
Those [garments] are purified like merchandise by the rays of the moon and sun and by wind,
as well as by bathing after walking on a road, and during the acts of sneezing and drinking.
One should sip water according to the rule when putting on a garment,
or when touched by those who have been touched, or after walking through a street, mud, or water.
And structures built of baked bricks are pure because they are reached by the wind;
from food that has been largely defiled, one should remove and discard the first portion.
One should perform the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) of the remainder with water and likewise with clay after sipping water;
furthermore, one who eats contaminated food shall undergo a fast for three nights.
But in the case of ignorance—or when preceded by knowledge—there is no cessation of that fault;
likewise for one who has touched a menstruating woman, a woman recently delivered, or an outcaste.
Having touched [a corpse], one should bathe for the sake of purification; likewise for those who carry the dead.
Having touched a human bone that still has grease on it, a Brahmin becomes pure by bathing.
Having sipped water for purification, one should touch a cow without oil on it or gaze at the sun;
likewise, one should not step over saliva or the remnants of ointments.
One should throw out of the house the remnants of food, feces, urine, and the water used for washing the feet;
one should not bathe in another's water without first removing five lumps of earth.
A wise man should bathe in natural pools, in the depths of the Gaṅgā, and in rivers; he should never stay in gardens or similar places during improper times.
One should not converse with those who are hated by the people, nor with women devoid of heroic virtue,
nor with those who revile the deities, the ancestors, the true scriptures, the sacrificers, or the renunciants.
Having engaged in physical contact or conversation with these, one becomes pure by looking at the sun;
likewise, having looked upon a woman in her courses, an outcast, or a corpse.
Those who follow unrighteous paths, those born of adultery, eunuchs, the naked, outcastes, corpse-bearers, and those who take pleasure in the wives of others; BrP 221.142.
For this alone must be done by the wise for the purification of themselves:
[the avoidance of] food from those who are unfit to be fed, mendicants, heretics, cats, donkeys, and cocks.
One who knows the Dharma becomes pure by bathing after touching outcasts, those who have been cast away, Cāṇḍālas, those who eat the food of the dead, a menstruating woman, or a village pig.
And likewise, two men defiled by the impurity of childbirth,
as well as one in whose house there is a daily decline in the performance of obligatory rites.
And that lowest of men who, abandoned by the Brahmins and subsisting on impure food,
should never cause the omission of his obligatory duty.
I shall now describe its non-performance solely in the cases of death and birth:
for ten days, a Brāhmaṇa should remain abstaining from giving gifts and performing fire-sacrifices.
A Kṣatriya shall remain abstaining from his own duties for twelve days, a Vaiśya for half a month, and a Śūdra for a full month.
Thereafter, all should perform their own respective duties as is appropriate;
having gone outside, water should be offered for the deceased by those of his lineage.
On the first day, the fourth, the seventh, and likewise the ninth,
the collection of his bones should be performed by the members of the lineage on the fourth day.
After the collection of their bones, the touching of their limbs is prescribed;
however, all other rites must be performed by the kinsmen after the collection.
On the day of death, there is contact (sparśa) for the sapinda relatives of both [the deceased and the survivor];
likewise, according to their wish, it occurs when death is caused by weapons, hanging, or fire.

Even in the case of death by poison, heat, and so forth, as well as by fasting or starvation, and likewise when a child, one residing in another country, or one who has gone forth (a renunciant) has died; ||| BrP_221.153 |||

Immediate purification is prescribed for humans; however, it is said that impurity lasts for three days for sapindas if another dies while they are already in a state of impurity due to a previous death.
The purification for the deceased has been fully described; the daily rites should be performed therein.
Indeed, this same rule is seen to apply to birth-impurity as well.
When a son is born, a bath with one's clothes on is prescribed for the father among his sapindas and sodakas according to the rule.
Even in that case, or if one has followed another [path] beyond that,
purification for one who possesses a previous birth is declared to occur through days.
When ten, twelve, or six months and half-months have passed,
all social classes (varṇas) shall perform their respective ritual duties according to the prescribed rule.
Henceforth, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite should be performed for the sake of the deceased;
likewise, wise men should bestow gifts upon the Brahmins.
Whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is dear to one in one's home,
that very thing should be given to a virtuous person by one who desires that it become inexhaustible.
When the days are complete, having touched water with their vehicles and weapons,
and having offered the funeral rice-balls (piṇḍas) for the deceased, all the castes have performed the required rites.
Being pure and united, they should act for the sake of prosperity both in this world and the next;
the Triple Veda (Trayī) must be studied constantly, and one must become wise.
O twice-born ones, wealth should be acquired in accordance with the Dharma and used with effort for sacrifice, so that one's own self, when provoked, does not fall into self-contempt.

O Brahmins, that which should not be concealed by great men must be performed without hesitation; for a man who lives in the house and conducts himself in this manner, [there is no fear].*BrP_221.164*
Having attained virtue, wealth, and pleasure— both auspicious in this world and the next—
this secret [teaching] bestows long life, brings prosperity, and increases the intellect.
It removes all sins, is meritorious, bestows prosperity, nourishment, and health, and is auspicious;
it grants fame and renown to men, and increases their splendor and strength.
O best of sages, this supreme means for attaining heaven should always be practiced by men— by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras alike.
Those who desire the highest good should understand this correctly with great effort;
for only by knowing it can one indeed perform the practice at all times.
Freed from all evil, he is glorified in the heavenly world;
O best of the twice-born, this which has been declared is the most essential of all essentials.
O twice-born ones, the Dharma proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti should not be given to just anyone;
it must not be given to an atheist, nor to one of wicked intellect,
nor to a hypocrite, nor to a fool, nor to one who prattles with fallacious reasoning.
The sages said:

"O Brahmin, O best of the twice-born, we wish to hear specifically about the duties of the social classes (varṇadharma) and the duties of the four stages of life (caturāśramadharma); please speak of them."
Vyāsa said:
Listen with self-restraint, in due order, to the duties of the castes as they are proclaimed by me for the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.

A Brahmin should be devoted to charity, compassion, austerity, sacrifice to the gods, and the study of his own Veda; he should be one who constantly performs water-libations and should maintain the sacred fires.
O twice-born ones, for the sake of subsistence, one may officiate at sacrifices for others, likewise teach them,
and knowingly accept gifts for the purpose of performing sacrifices.
O twice-born ones, one should act for the welfare of the entire world and never for the harm of anyone;
loving-kindness toward all beings is the supreme wealth of a Brahmin.
O twice-born ones, he should maintain an equal mind toward both a cow and the wealth of another;
O twice-born ones, approaching his wife during her season is praised for him.
O twice-born ones, even a Kṣatriya may indeed give gifts to the twice-born according to his desire;
he should also sacrifice with various sacrifices and study the Vedas.
Living by the sword and protecting the earth is his foremost means of livelihood;
even for him, the protection of the earth was practiced in the first eon.
O King, by the mere protection of the earth, rulers have fulfilled their duty,
since the protection [of subjects] constitutes the performance of sacrifices and other rites.
By punishing the wicked and protecting the virtuous,
the king who establishes the social order attains the worlds he desires.
O best of sages, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, granted cattle-rearing, trade, and agriculture as the means of livelihood for the Vaiśya.
For him as well, study, sacrifice, giving, and righteousness are praised,
as is the performance of obligatory and occasional rites and other such actions.
Action that relies upon the twice-born for its purpose, and their maintenance by means of wealth acquired through buying and selling or from the labor of artisans; ||| BrP_222.13 |||
Even a Śūdra may give gifts and perform the *pākayajña* sacrifices;
indeed, a Śūdra should perform all rites pertaining to the ancestors (*pitrya*) and so forth by means of these.
O best of the twice-born, all possessions are for the sake of maintaining servants and others, and approaching one's own wife during her fertile period.
Compassion toward all beings, forbearance, freedom from pride, truthfulness, purity, lack of exertion, auspiciousness, and pleasant speech; BrP_222.16 //
Likewise, O best of the twice-born, benevolence, lack of covetousness, absence of miserliness,
and freedom from envy are said to be qualities common to all social classes.
O twice-born ones, these are the common characteristics of all the stages of life (āśramas), as well as the qualities and secondary duties of the Brahmins and the other [twice-born] classes.
The duties of a Kṣatriya are prescribed for a twice-born man in times of distress, as are the duties of a Vaiśya;
and for a Rājanya, the duties of a Vaiśya and the duties of a Śūdra are likewise prescribed.
O twice-born ones, when one possesses the capacity, both [the husband and wife] must renounce it;
however, in times of distress, that very [act] may be performed, provided one does not cause a confusion of duties.
Thus, O Brahmins, these duties of the social classes have been declared by me today;
now listen as I correctly explain the duties of those belonging to the stages of life.
O Brahmins, the boy who has undergone the initiation ceremony and is intent on acquiring the Vedas, dwelling in the house of his guru as a celibate student (brahmacārī) with a concentrated mind.
Devoted to purity and right conduct, he should perform service to his guru;
and while observing the vows, he should acquire the Veda with a disciplined mind.
With a concentrated mind, the Brahmins should worship both twilights, as well as the sun and the fire;
likewise, they should perform the salutation to their guru.

O best of the twice-born, when the teacher stands, the disciple should stand; when he walks, he should walk; when he sits low, he should sit; and when he is silent, he should remain silent; furthermore, he should avoid all that is disagreeable to his guru.
He should recite the Veda with that very [mind], standing before [the teacher] with no other thought;
then he should eat the food obtained as alms, having been permitted by the guru.
He should first immerse himself in the water where his teacher has already immersed;
and he should bring him fuel, water, and other necessities every single morning.
And having mastered what is to be grasped, and having obtained permission from him,
the wise man, having fulfilled his obligations to the guru, should enter the householder stage of life.
O Brahmins, having obtained a wife according to the prescribed rites and having acquired wealth through his own efforts, he should perform all the duties of a householder to the best of his ability.
Having honored the ancestors with funeral offerings, the gods with sacrifices, and guests likewise;
having honored the sages with food and Prajāpati with Vedic study and offspring.
Through the *balikarman* one attains the spirits, through truthfulness of speech the entire world,
and a person reaches those worlds acquired by their own deeds.
And whatever wandering mendicants or celibate students there may be, they too find their support here; therefore, the householder's life is indeed supreme.
O twice-born ones, for the purpose of fetching the Vedas, for bathing at sacred fords,
and for seeing the earth, the Brahmins wander across the world.
For those who are homeless and without food, yet take their home in the evening,
the householder is said to be their constant support and source.
One should always speak sweet words of welcome to them;
and to those who have come to one's home, one should provide a bed, a seat, and food.
If a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated,
he departs having transferred his own misdeeds to that person and taking away their merit.
For one who remains at home, contempt, egoism, and hypocrisy,
as well as slander, injury, and harshness, are not praised.
And the householder who correctly practices this supreme rule,
being liberated from all bonds, attains the highest worlds.
O Brahmins, when his age has advanced, a householder who has fulfilled his duties should entrust his wife to his sons and go to the forest, either alone or together with her.
O twice-born ones, the sage there should subsist on leaves, roots, and fruits; he should wear his hair and beard in matted locks, sleep upon the ground, and be a guest to all.
O best of the twice-born, he should make his lower garment and upper robe from leather, kāśa, and kuśa grass; likewise, bathing three times a day is prescribed for him.
The worship of deities, burnt offerings (homa), honoring all guests,
alms-giving, and the presentation of oblations (bali) are prescribed for him and are highly commended.
Anointing the limbs with forest oils is also recommended for him;
O best of Brahmins, his asceticism consists in enduring cold, heat, and other such hardships.
But that sage who, as a forest-dweller, should practice these observances with self-restraint,
burns away his defects like fire and conquers the eternal worlds.
O best of beings, understand from me as I describe the true nature of that which is called the fourth stage of life for a mendicant by the wise.
O best of the twice-born, one should abandon attachment to sons, wealth, and wife;
having shaken off envy, one should proceed to the fourth stage of life.
O best of the twice-born, he should abandon all undertakings involving the three social classes;
he should be friendly toward all living beings, maintaining equanimity toward friends and others alike.

One who is disciplined should never commit an act of malice toward beings born from a womb, from an egg, and so forth, through speech, mind, or physical actions; furthermore, one should renounce all attachments.
Staying for one night in a village and five nights in a city— likewise,
neither attachment nor aversion arises in him toward animals.

And for the sake of sustaining life, seeking alms at the proper time, he should wander among the houses of those of commendable appearance when the embers have been extinguished and the people have not yet eaten.

One should not be despondent in the absence of gain, nor should one rejoice in its presence; one should possess only what is necessary for the maintenance of life, being free from attachment to material requisites.
One should despise gains that are excessively honored from all sides;
for even a liberated ascetic is bound by gains that are excessively honored.
Having abandoned those defects— namely desire, anger, pride, greed, delusion, and the like— the wandering mendicant should become free from the sense of "mine."
For one who wanders the earth having granted fearlessness to all beings,
no fear arises anywhere once he is liberated from the body.
Having established the Agnihotra within his own body,
the Brahmin indeed offers the bodily fire with oblations obtained through alms into his own mouth.
By means of the funeral pyre fire,
he goes to those worlds who practices the stage of liberation as prescribed— pure, possessed of a resolute intellect, and disciplined.
Like a flame without fuel, he becomes utterly tranquil;
that twice-born man goes to the world of Brahmā.
[The sages said:]
O illustrious one, you are omniscient and devoted to the welfare of all beings;
O Sage, there is nothing—past, present, or future—that is unknown to you.
"By what action, O Great-Minded One, does the lowest state arise for the castes, and by what does the highest state come to be? Tell us this."
By what action does a Śūdra attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa? We wish to hear by what means a Brāhmaṇa might fall into the state of a Śūdra. (BrP 223.3)
Vyāsa said:
On a delightful peak of the Himavat, adorned with various minerals,
filled with diverse trees and creepers, and endowed with many wonders.
There, the goddess Śailarājasutā, having prostrated before the three-eyed Mahādeva, the destroyer of Tripura and lord of the gods, who was seated there—
Long ago, O Brahmins, a beautiful-eyed woman asked this question;
I shall explain it to you fully, so listen to me, O best of beings.
Umā said:
"O Blessed One, destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, crusher of Pūṣan’s teeth,
three-eyed one who destroyed Dakṣa’s sacrifice, this great doubt of mine exists."
The fourfold varṇa system was created in the beginning by the Blessed Self-existent One;
by what ripening of karma does a Vaiśya descend to the state of a Śūdra?
By what means can a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya become a twice-born [Brāhmaṇa], or how can a Brāhmaṇa become a Kṣatriya?
O Lord, how is it possible to turn back the dharma that has been reversed?
By what action, O Brahmin, is one born from a Śūdra womb?
Or by what action, O Lord, does a Kṣatriya attain the state of a Śūdra?
O God, O sinless Lord of Beings, resolve this doubt of mine:
how may these three castes, by their very nature in this world, attain the status of Brahmins?
Śiva said:
"O Goddess, O auspicious one, brahminhood is difficult to attain;
by nature one is a brahmin, or a kṣatriya, a vaiśya, or a śūdra—this is my conviction."
By means of evil action performed here, that twice-born man falls from his station;
even after attaining a superior caste, he is cast down from it once again.
Abiding by the dharma of a Brahmin, he lives his life as a Brahmin;
whether he be a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, he attains the state of Brahman.
And he who, having abandoned the status of a Brahmin, devotes himself to the duties of a Kṣatriya,
falls away from his Brahminhood and is born into a Kṣatriya womb.
And that Brahmin of small intellect who, having attained the rare status of Brahminhood, always performs the work of a Vaiśya out of greed and delusion; BrP_223.16.
That twice-born man attains the status of a Vaiśya, or a Vaiśya may descend to the status of a Śūdra;
a Brahmin who has fallen from his own duty then attains the state of a Śūdra.
Having fallen from the world of Brahmā, he reaches that hell, deprived of his caste and cast out; fallen from the Brahmanic state, he is born into the womb of a Śūdra.
O illustrious lady who practices dharma, whether a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya,
having abandoned his own duties, he devotes himself to the work of a Śūdra.
Fallen from his own station and having entered into a mixture of castes,
such a person— whether a Brahmin, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya— attains the state of a Śūdra.
But that Śūdra who, through his own duty, possesses knowledge and realization, is pure,
knows the Dharma, and is devoted to the Dharma— he enjoys the fruit of the Dharma.
And this other [teaching], O Goddess, was proclaimed by Brahmā:
the ultimate perfection regarding the inner self (adhyātma) is practiced by those who desire dharma.

O Goddess, food from a fierce person is censured; so too is food from a group, food from a funeral rite, food from one in a state of impurity, proclaimed food, and food from a Śūdra, which should never be eaten under any circumstances.
"O Goddess, the food of a Śūdra is always censured by the gods and the high-souled ones;
it was issued from the mouth of the Grandfather (Brahmā), and this is my conviction as to what constitutes authority."
If a twice-born man dies with the remains of a Śūdra’s food in his stomach,
even if he has maintained the sacred fires and performed sacrifices, he shall share the destiny of a Śūdra.
By that remnant of a Śūdra’s food, a Brahmin is expelled from his status as a Brahmin and attains the state of a Śūdra; there is no doubt about this.
If a twice-born man dies with the undigested food of another still in his stomach,
that Brahmin shall enter the very womb of the one whose food he subsisted upon.
He who, having attained the state of a Brahmin which is difficult to obtain,
treats it with contempt or eats food that should not be eaten, shall indeed fall from his status as a twice-born.

A drinker of spirituous liquor, a slayer of a Brahmin, a thief, a robber, one who has broken his vows, one who is impure, one who has abandoned the private recitation of the Vedas, a sinner, one who is greedy, one who is deceitful, and one who is treacherous; BrP 223.29.
A Brahmin who is without vows, the husband of a Śūdra woman, one who eats from a *kuṇḍa* vessel, a seller of Soma,
or a servant of the low-born, indeed falls from his Brahmanic birth.
One who violates the teacher’s bed, one who hates the teacher, one who delights in reviling the teacher,
or even one who hates the Veda— a Brahmin falls from his status as a Brahmin.
But by performing these auspicious deeds in such a manner, O Goddess,
a Śūdra may attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Vaiśya may reach the status of a Kṣatriya.
The Śūdra, performing all his duties according to what is right and according to the prescribed rules,
should attend to the hospitality of all guests and eat only the remnants of the food.
He who, being foremost and always established on the path of the righteous, performs service and attendance toward those of the superior caste with diligence and an undistracted mind, is excellent.
He honors the gods and the twice-born, observes the vow of hospitality toward all guests,
approaches his wife only during her fertile season, remains self-restrained, and is moderate in his diet.
Diligent and seeking the company of the virtuous, eating only the remnants of food, he should not consume meat prepared in vain; such a Śūdra indeed attains the status of a Vaiśya.
Truthful in speech, free from egoism, beyond the pairs of opposites, and skilled in conciliation,
he is pure and devoted to the study of the Vedas, performing the eternal sacrifices.
Self-controlled, honoring Brahmins, and free from malice toward all social classes,
he should observe the vows of a householder and eat his meals only twice a day.
Eating only what remains, having conquered his appetite, free from desire and devoid of the sense of "I," he attended to the sacred fire and offered oblations according to the prescribed rule.
By attending to all guests and eating only the remnants of food,
a Vaiśya becomes a twice-born (dvija) who is ordained by the three sacred fires alone.
That Vaiśya is born pure in a great Kṣatriya family;
having been born as a Kṣatriya, that Vaiśya is consecrated from birth onwards.
Having been initiated and devoted to his vows, the twice-born becomes consecrated;
he gives gifts and performs sacrifices with abundant wealth and ample sacrificial fees.
Having studied the Vedas, seeking heaven, always taking refuge in the three sacred fires, constantly giving with moistened hands, and protecting his subjects according to dharma; BrP_223.43 //
He who perceives purity always makes his truths come true;
scorched by the rod of dharma, he accomplishes the goals of dharma, desire, and wealth.
Restrained by his organs of action and characterized by the sixfold division [of duties],
one who is skilled in the goal should not indulge in vulgar pleasures according to his own will.
The righteous-souled man should always approach his wife during her fertile period;
he should be constantly fasting, self-restrained, devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas, and pure.
He always sleeps within his own house, never staying outside;
he is ever cheerful, providing hospitality for all guests and pursuing the three goals of life.
To Śūdras who desire food, he should always say, "It is ready";
whether for his own sake or out of compassion, he should not expect anything in return.
Whatever means of subsistence he prepares for the sake of the ancestors, the gods, and guests,
and whatever alms he consumes in his own home according to the rule, [he offers that].
Performing the Agnihotra sacrifice twice a day according to the prescribed rule,
he was slain in battle while facing the enemy for the sake of the welfare of cows and Brahmins.
Having entered [the body] purified by the mantras of the three sacred fires, he becomes a twice-born,
endowed with knowledge and realization, consecrated, and one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
A Vaiśya becomes righteous-souled through his own duty, and a Kṣatriya likewise;
O Goddess, by these fruits of their actions, one born of a low caste or family [attains such status].
Even a Śūdra who is perfected through sacred tradition becomes a twice-born man once consecrated;
whereas even a Brāhmaṇa of wicked conduct, who eats all kinds of impure food, remains [merely a Brāhmaṇa in name].
Having completely abandoned his status as a Brahmin, he becomes such a Śūdra;
yet, O Goddess, through pure deeds, he is one whose self is purified and whose senses are conquered.
"Brahmā himself declared that even a Śūdra is to be served like a twice-born man wherever a Śūdra presides by virtue of his own nature and karma."
It is my conviction that he alone is to be known as pure among the twice-born;
neither birth, nor sacramental rites, nor sacred learning, nor lineage [determines purity].
The causes for being twice-born are indeed conduct alone;
everyone in this world is designated a Brahmin by virtue of their conduct.
Even a Śūdra, by abiding in his proper conduct, attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa;
for, O lady of beautiful hips, it is my view that the nature of Brahman is equal everywhere.
O Goddess, that twice-born one in whom the qualityless and stainless Brahman abides— these, O Goddess, are the pure ones who demonstrate the nature of the sacred places.
And she herself was told by Brahmā, the giver of boons, while he was creating living beings:
"For you are the great field of Brahmā; you move through the world like a foot."
Whatever seed is sown there, that will become one's harvest after death;
therefore, one should always be contented and always rely upon the path of the righteous.
One who desires prosperity should walk upon the path of Brahman;
as a householder living in the home, he should be one who studies the *saṃhitās*.
He should be constantly engaged in the private recitation of the Vedas, but not one who lives by teaching;
for such is the Brahmin who remains perpetually established on the path of the righteous.
One who maintains the sacred fires and studies the Veda is fit for becoming Brahman;
having attained the state of a Brahmin, O Goddess, it must be protected by one with a self-controlled mind.
O lady of pure smiles, through the acceptance of gifts from [low] wombs and through certain actions,
this secret has been told to you: how a Śūdra may become a twice-born,
or how a Brāhmaṇa, fallen from dharma, may attain the state of a Śūdra.
Umā said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, saluted by gods and asuras;
O God, O All-pervading Lord, explain to me my doubt regarding the dharma and adharma of human beings."
By what bonds are embodied beings always bound through the three means of action—by deed, mind, and speech—or how are they liberated? Tell me.
O Lord, by what kind of conduct, by what sort of action,
by what practices, or by what virtues do men here go to heaven?
Śiva said: O Goddess Umā, who always knows the true essence of dharma and purpose, who is eternally devoted to dharma—
listen to this question which is beneficial for all living beings and increases the intellect.
Delighting in truth and righteousness, peaceful, and free from all external marks,
those whose doubts have been severed are bound neither by unrighteousness nor by righteousness.
Those persons who know the reality of dissolution and origination, who are all-knowing and all-seeing,
and who are free from passion, are liberated from the bonds of karma.
Those who do not cause harm to anything by deed, thought, or speech,
and who do not become immersed in anything, are not bound by their actions.
Those who abstain from taking life, who possess virtuous conduct and are endowed with compassion,
who treat the hateful and the beloved alike, and who are self-controlled, are liberated from the bonds of karma.
Those men who possess compassion for all beings, who are trustworthy toward all creatures,
and who have abandoned violent conduct, go to heaven.
Those men who are always free from the sense of ownership over others' property, who avoid the wives of others,
and who enjoy wealth acquired through righteous means, go to heaven.
Those men who always behave toward the wives of others as they would toward their own mother, sister, or daughter, go to heaven.
Those men who are devoted to their own wives, who approach them only during the proper season,
and who enjoy refined pleasures rather than vulgar ones, go to heaven.
Those men who constantly refrain from theft, who are content with their own wealth,
and who live upon their own fortune, go to heaven.
Those men who always keep their eyes shielded by good conduct regarding the wives of others,
who have conquered their senses and are devoted to moral discipline, go to heaven.
This path created by the gods should always be followed by men;
likewise, the path free from passion should always be followed by the wise.

The path characterized by non-frivolity, and endowed with the practice of charity, ritual action, and austerity, as well as moral conduct, purity, and compassion, should always be followed by the wise.
Those desiring the path to heaven should not follow any other than this.
Umā said:
"O God, O Lord of Beings, O Sinless One, tell me those actions by which one is bound by speech, or indeed by which one is liberated."
Śiva said: Those men who do not speak falsehoods in this world, whether for their own sake, for the sake of others, or even when relying on unrighteousness, go to heaven.
Those men who do not speak untruth for the sake of livelihood, for the sake of dharma, or likewise out of desire, go to heaven.
Those men who speak with words that are gentle, clear in syllable, sweet, and free from evil,
addressing others with such inner disposition, go to heaven.
Those virtuous men who do not speak harsh, bitter, or cruel words,
and who do not delight in backbiting, go to heaven.
Those men who do not speak slanderously, nor cause the breach of friendships,
and who do not inflict suffering upon others, go to heaven.
Those men who avoid harshness and malice toward others,
who are self-controlled and impartial toward all beings, go to heaven.
Those men who abstain from deceitful speech, who avoid what is discordant,
and who always speak with gentleness, go to heaven.
Those men who do not utter words that rend the heart out of anger,
and who find peace even when provoked to wrath, go to heaven.
O Goddess, this Dharma established by Vāṇī should always be practiced by men;
falsehood must always be avoided by the wise through their auspicious, truthful qualities.
Umā said:
O illustrious one, O God of gods, wielder of the Pināka bow, tell me that action by which a person is always bound by the mind.
Maheśvara said:
O auspicious lady, men who are always endowed with mental dharma go to heaven; listen as I proclaim this to you.
O fair-faced one, listen to that by which a man is bound here: by a poorly directed mind, he assumes a poorly directed internal form.
When they see another's property left in a lonely forest,
those men who do not take it even in their minds are destined for heaven.
In the same way, those men who do not even mentally harm the wives of others when they are alone and acting out of lust, go to heaven.
Those men who always treat both enemy and friend with an equal mind,
and who practice loving-kindness upon meeting them, are destined for heaven.
Those men who are learned in the scriptures, compassionate, pure, true to their promises,
and fully content with their own lot, go to heaven.
Those men who are free from enmity, free from exertion, always delighting in a mind of loving-kindness,
and possessing compassion for all living beings, go to heaven.
Those men who possess knowledge, who perform their duties, who are patient, who are dear to their friends,
and who always discern between dharma and adharma, go to heaven.
O Goddess, those men who are free from longing for the accumulation of the fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious actions go to heaven.
Those men who are devoted to the gods and the twice-born always avoid those possessed of evil;
having attained such an elevation, they go to heaven.
"O Goddess, these paths leading to heaven, which result from auspicious deeds, have been proclaimed by me to you; what more do you wish to hear here?"
Umā said: "O Maheśvara, I have a certain great doubt concerning mortals;
therefore, you ought to explain it to me skillfully today."
"By what action, O Lord, does a person obtain long life?
Or by what austerity, O God of gods, does one obtain a great lifespan?"
"By what karma does a human being on earth have a short lifespan?
O irreproachable Lord, you ought to explain the ripening of such actions."
Furthermore, some are highly fortunate while others are unfortunate; likewise, some are of low birth while others are of noble birth.
Some men appear difficult to look upon, as if they were made of wood;
yet others are pleasant to behold, simply by the sight of them.
Some appear to be of poor wisdom, some appear to be learned,
and others likewise possess great wisdom, being endowed with both knowledge and discernment.
O God, some men are seen to have little speech while others have much; therefore, you ought to explain this.
Śiva said:
"Behold, O Goddess, I shall explain to you the arising of the fruits of action,
by which every man in the world of mortals experiences his own result."
A lord of yogis who takes life is always a man with a staff in his hand;
such a man, with weapon perpetually raised, slays hosts of living beings.
He was merciless toward all living beings, constantly causing them agitation;
he was utterly pitiless and offered no refuge even to insects and moths.
O Goddess, a man who has become such as this goes to hell;
but one whose nature is contrary to this, being righteous, is born in his true form.
For one who is violent in nature goes to hell, while the non-violent goes to heaven;
such a man undergoes fierce and agonizing torment in hell.
Whoever ever emerges from that hell may obtain human birth,
yet is born there with a short lifespan.
O Goddess, because one is joined with sinful actions such as violence and the like,
being harmful to all beings, one is born with a short lifespan.
O Goddess, by virtue of his auspicious karma, he has abstained from killing living beings; O Goddess, through that auspicious karma,
having laid down his weapons and being free from punishment, he never harms anyone at any time.
He does not cause others to kill, nor does he kill; he does not even approve of one who kills.
He is full of affection for all beings, regarding others just as he regards himself.
O Goddess, such a person always attains divinity;
filled with joy, he eternally enjoys the pleasures of happiness that have come to him.
If, however, one is ever born again in the world of humans,
this is the path of those long-lived ones who are well-conducted and perform good deeds;
it was proclaimed by Brahmā as the means for liberation from the injury of living beings.
Umā said:
With what character, with what conduct, and by what actions— or by what kind of gift— does a man attain heaven?

Maheśvara said: "The high-minded one is a donor who honors Brahmins and shows compassion toward the wretched, the afflicted, the destitute, and others, providing them with various kinds of food, edibles, meals, drinks, and garments."
He should construct shelters, assembly halls, water-stations, and lotus-pools;
being restrained and pure, he performs his daily duties and other rites.
Seats, beds, vehicles, houses, jewels, wealth, as well as all kinds of grain together with their fields, and women; BrP 225.4.
O Goddess, that man who always gives with a perfectly tranquil mind is born in the world of the gods.
Having dwelt there for a very long time, having enjoyed unsurpassed pleasures,
and having sported joyfully with the apsarases in the Nandana groves and other such places;
Falling from there, O Great Goddess, he is born among humans in a family of great fortune, O Goddess, one filled with wealth and grain.
There, endowed with all the qualities of sensual pleasure and filled with joy,
that man becomes wealthy, possessing great resources and great enjoyments.
O Goddess, these highly fortunate beings who are characterized by generosity were indeed declared of old by Brahmā to be pleasing to behold for all.
O Goddess, there are other men who are twice-born but miserly regarding gifts;
they are of little intelligence and do not bestow food, even though it is available.
Seeing the wretched, the blind, the miserable, mendicants, and even guests,
those possessed by the greed of the tongue turn away when they are entreated.
They never bestow wealth, nor garments, nor enjoyments, nor gold;
nor cows, nor various preparations of food.
O Goddess, those who are greedy though appearing non-greedy, and atheists who have abandoned the practice of giving—
such ignorant men go to hell.
When, through the revolution of time, those of small intellect indeed attain human status, they take birth in a family destitute of wealth.
Overcome by hunger and thirst, excluded from all the world,
and hopeless regarding all enjoyments, they live a life of unrighteousness.
Born into families of meager means, men who delight in meager enjoyments—
by this karma, O Goddess, men become destitute.
Others are constantly deceitful, arrogant, and devoted to the interests of others;
being small-minded, they do not offer a seat to one who deserves a seat.
And those of dull intellect who do not grant the path to one who deserves the path, nor honor with the prescribed rites those worthy of honor; BrP 225.18.

Those who, though possessing discernment, do not affectionately offer water for the feet or water for sipping, nor that which is auspicious and desired, nor address their teacher with reverence; (BrP 225.19)
Abiding together with greed increased by arrogance,
they dishonor those worthy of respect and treat the elders with contempt.
O Goddess, all such men as these go to hell; yet, if those men should ever emerge from that hell, [they remain in a wretched state].
Then, after many series of years, they take birth in a contemptible family among such low-minded and despised people as Śvapākas and Pulkasas.
They are born into families that cause distress to their elders;
they are neither hypocritical nor arrogant, being devoted to the worship of deities and guests.
Worthy of worship by the world, he was born as one who offers salutations; he spoke sweet words, performed all deeds with kindness, and was always beloved by all beings.
Free from hatred, pleasant-faced, gentle, and always bestowing kind words, he is non-violent toward all beings and always greets them with a welcome.
He remains honoring [the guest] according to their merit, preceded by hospitable rites;
he always honors his guru, giving way to one worthy of the path.
One who is devoted to receiving guests and likewise honors those who arrive,
such a person, O Goddess, attains the heavenly realm.
Then, having attained human birth, he shall be born into a distinguished family;
there, endowed with all kinds of jewels, he shall possess abundant enjoyments.
Giving as is appropriate to those who are worthy, he should be devoted to the practice of Dharma;
esteemed by all beings, he shall be honored by the entire world.
A man always experiences the fruit of his own actions by himself;
this is the dharma proclaimed by me, as uttered by the Creator himself.
But he whose conduct is fierce and who causes fear to all beings, whether with his hands or his feet, or again with a rope or a staff; ||| BrP_225.31 |||
O beautiful one, he who is intent on harm and skilled in the knowledge of atonement might afflict living beings with clods of earth, pillars, or various means, and indeed cause them great agitation.
He always causes distress to living beings and assails them;
one whose conduct and behavior are such as this goes to hell.
If, after the lapse of time, he should attain human status,
he is born into a low family afflicted by many ailments.
O Goddess, among men, this lowest of beings, who is hated by the world due to the fruits of his own actions,
should be recognized as such even among his kinsmen and relatives.
Another, full of compassion, regards all beings with a friendly gaze; equal toward his father, free from enmity, and with senses restrained.
Devoted to compassion, he does not alarm living beings nor does he harm them;
with his hands and feet restrained, he is trusted by all creatures.
One who performs auspicious deeds and is devoted to compassion does not terrify living beings with a rope, nor with a staff, nor with clods of earth, nor with weapons.
Thus, through the practice of virtuous conduct, one is born in heaven;
there, in a divine mansion, he dwells with joy like a god.
If that mortal, upon the exhaustion of his merit in heaven, is reborn among humans,
he is born with little exertion and free from affliction, and he prospers in happiness.
A man who partakes of happiness is free from exertion and always free from anxiety;
O Goddess, this is the path of the virtuous, wherein no affliction is found.
Umā said:
These men are seen to be skilled in reasoning and refutation,
endowed with knowledge and discernment, possessed of wisdom, and experts in the meaning [of things].
And others, O Lord, are of poor intellect, devoid of knowledge and discernment;
by what ripening of karma does a person become possessed of wisdom? (BrP 225.43)
O Virūpākṣa, how does a human being become one of little wisdom?
O best among all upholders of the Dharma, dispel this doubt of mine.
"O Lord, other men are seen who are blind from birth, as well as others afflicted by disease, and even those who are impotent; please tell us the cause of that."
Maheśvara said:
They constantly inquire day after day of the Brahmins— who are learned in the Vedas, perfected beings, and likewise knowers of dharma— regarding what is auspicious and what is inauspicious.
Avoiding unwholesome action and likewise practicing what is wholesome,
they constantly attain a heavenly rebirth and experience happiness in this world as well.
If he returns to the human state, he is born there as an intelligent man,
for whom auspiciousness arises through learning that follows the path of sacrifice.
And those who direct their corrupt gaze toward the wives of others,
by virtue of that corrupt disposition, they indeed become blind from birth.
Those men who, with a corrupted mind, look upon a naked woman,
become afflicted by disease in this world, for they are doers of evil deeds.
But those fools of wicked conduct who take pleasure in sexual intercourse with animals,
and those of very poor intelligence who do so with men, fall into the state of eunuchs.
Those who indeed bind animals, those who violate the bed of their teacher,
and those who engage in promiscuous sexual intercourse, are born as eunuchs.
Umā said:
"O best of gods, what indeed is blameworthy action, and likewise what is blameless? By performing what does a human being attain the highest good?"
Maheśvara said:
He who always inquires of the twice-born seeking the path to the highest good,
searching for dharma and desiring its virtues, attains heaven.
O Goddess, if he should ever attain human birth,
he is born there as one who is intelligent, endowed with retentive memory, and wise.
O Goddess, this is the duty of the virtuous, which leads to prosperity;
it has been thus proclaimed by me always for the benefit of human beings.
Umā said:
Other men, possessing very little knowledge and being haters of dharma,
do not wish to approach Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas.
Some men are observant of vows, devoted to faith and self-restraint;
others are without vows, fallen from their rules, and resemble Rākṣasas.
Tell me, by what ripening of karma do some become performers of sacrifice, while others likewise become free from delusion? BrP_225.59.
Maheśvara said:
