The boundaries of the worldly dharmas established by the scriptures follow authoritative standards;
indeed, those of firm vows are seen to abide by them.
Those who, fallen under the power of delusion, declare unrighteousness to be righteousness—
men who lack vows and have destroyed the boundaries of conduct— are Brahmarākṣasas.
Those men who, due to efforts made at the wrong time, are born here as humans without performing fire offerings or uttering the vaṣaṭ-call, they become the lowest of men.
O Goddess, this ocean of Dharma, which pertains to the wholesome and unwholesome actions of men, has been explained by me to you for the purpose of cutting through all doubts.
Vyāsa said:
O twice-born ones, upon hearing these words of her husband from the beginning, the Mother of the World then became joyful, well-pleased, and filled with wonder.
Those excellent sages who were there in the presence of Tripurāri,
O twice-born ones, had gone to that mountain on the occasion of a pilgrimage.
Having fully honored that god who holds the trident in his hand and having bowed down to him,
they also asked about their doubt out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
The sages said:
"O Three-eyed One, O destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, salutations be unto you!
O Lord of the World, we ask you about a doubt residing in our hearts."
In this most terrible, fearsome, and hair-raising cycle of existence,
men of little intelligence wander for a very long time.
Tell us the means by which people are liberated from the bondage of birth and saṃsāra; we wish to hear it, for our curiosity is great.
Maheśvara said:
O twice-born ones, for men bound by the fetters of karma and partaking in suffering, I see no other means of salvation superior to Vāsudeva.
Those who properly worship that God, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace,
through speech, mind, and action, attain the supreme goal.
Of what use is life here for those whose minds are not inclined toward Vāsudeva, who pervades the entire world, nor is their conduct like that of cattle?
The sages said:
O wielder of the Pināka bow, destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, you who are honored by all the worlds,
O Śaṅkara, we wish to hear the majesty of Vāsudeva.
Maheśvara said: Hari, the eternal Puruṣa, is superior even to the Grandfather;
Kṛṣṇa, with the luster of refined gold, is like the sun risen in a cloudless sky.
He has ten arms and great splendor; he is the destroyer of the enemies of the gods, marked with the Śrīvatsa, the lord of the senses (Hṛṣīkeśa), and the leader of all the hosts of deities.
Brahmā was born from his belly, and I was born from his head;
the luminaries arose from the hairs of his head, and the gods and asuras from the hairs of his body.
The sages were born from his body, as were the eternal worlds;
he is the manifest abode of the Grandfather and the dwelling place of all the gods.
He is the creator of this entire earth, the Lord of the three worlds,
and the destroyer of all beings, both stationary and moving.
For he is indeed the God of gods, the manifest Lord of the gods, the scorcher of foes;
the omniscient creator of all, omnipresent, with faces on every side.
There is nothing more supreme than that Being in the three worlds;
he is the eternal, illustrious one renowned as Govinda.
That bestower of honor, having manifested for the sake of the gods' mission and assumed a human form, will slay all the kings in battle.
Indeed, the hosts of gods, deprived of Trivikrama,
are not capable of performing the works of the gods in the world, just as those who are bereft of a leader.
The leader of all beings, who is saluted by all beings—
[I shall tell] of this lord of gods and of his supreme task.
In the body of one who has become eternally Brahman and who takes refuge in the Brahman-sages,
Brahmā dwells situated in the navel, and I am likewise established there.
And all the deities residing within his body were established in happiness;
that lotus-eyed god has Śrī as his inner essence and dwells together with Śrī.
Armed with the Śārṅga bow and the discus, bearing a sword, and having the enemy of all serpents as his banner;
he was endowed with supreme virtue, good character, purity, and self-restraint.
By his prowess, by his vigor, by his form, and by his appearance;
by his height and proportions, and by his vigor and perfection of uprightness.
He was endowed with compassion, beauty, and strength,
and possessed all divine weapons of wondrous appearance.
Possessing the thousand eyes of yogic illusion, Virūpākṣa was high-minded;
he praised his friends with his speech and was beloved by his kinsmen and relatives.
Patient and free from egoistic speech, that god is the bestower of Brahman;
he is the remover of fear for those afflicted by fear, and the one who increases the joy of his friends.
He was a refuge for all beings, devoted to protecting the distressed;
he was learned in the scriptures, endowed with every excellence, and honored by all creatures.
He was a benefactor to those who sought his protection and likewise a source of fear to his enemies;
he was knowledgeable in policy, perfected in statecraft, a proponent of the Veda, and one who had conquered his senses.
Endowed with the highest intelligence, he acted solely for the sake of the gods' welfare upon the auspicious path of Prajāpati, which is refined by the dharma of Manu.
Govinda will arise in the lineage of the high-souled Manu;
for Manu’s son shall be named Aṃśa, and after him Antardhāman.
O twice-born ones, from Antardhāman shall come the blameless Prajāpati Havirdhāman; Havirdhāman’s son will be Prācīnabarhis.
His ten sons will have Pracetas as their chief;
likewise, that Prācetasa shall become Dakṣa, the lord of progeny (Prajāpati) here on earth.
Likewise, from Dakṣāyaṇī was born Āditya, and from Āditya came Manu;
and from the lineage of Manu shall arise Ilā and Sudyumna.
From Budha, Purūravas shall arise; from him, Āyu will be born;
from him, Nahuṣa will be; and Yayāti shall be his son.
From him shall come the Mahāsattva Yadu; from him, Kroṣṭu will arise; and the great son of Kroṣṭu will be Vṛjinīvān.
And from Vṛjinīvat shall come Uṣaṅgu, who will be unconquered;
and from Uṣaṅgu there shall be a son, Śūra Citraratha.
But his youngest son shall be named Śūra;
he will belong to those of renowned valor who are endowed with the virtues of good conduct.
O best of Brahmins, that Śūra was born in the lineage of pure sacrificers;
he was the most excellent of Kṣatriyas, possessed of great heroism and great fame.
He will beget a son renowned as Vasudeva, known as Ānakadundubhi, who bestows honor and expands his own lineage.
His son will be the four-armed Vāsudeva,
a giver, a worshiper of Brahmins, one who has become Brahman, and a lover of the twice-born.
That Yādava will indeed liberate all the kings bound by King Jarāsaṃdha after defeating that monarch in his mountain cave.
That heroic one shall be enriched with all the jewels of the earth,
and he shall be unopposed on earth even by his own valor.
Endowed with valor, the lord of all kings,
a hero of firm frame, that sovereign dwelt in Dvārakā.
Having utterly defeated those of evil intent, he will protect the goddess Earth;
therefore, having approached him, you should honor him with excellent offerings worthy of Brahmins.
Let them worship me according to the prescribed rule, as if worshipping the eternal Brahmā; for whoever desires to see me and also the Grandfather Brahmā [should do so].
The powerful Lord Vāsudeva must be seen by him;
when He is seen, I am seen—of this I have no doubt.
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, know that Vāsudeva is the Grandfather (Pitāmaha).
He, the lotus-eyed one, will be filled with affection for whomever [he chooses]."
The host of gods, headed by Brahmā, will be pleased with that man in this world who takes refuge in Keśava.
He shall possess fame, glory, and even heaven;
he shall be a direct teacher of the dharmas and one who possesses the Dharma.
That Lord of gods, the infallible Acyuta, should always be saluted by those who know the Dharma;
for when this omnipresent Lord is worshipped, the Dharma itself shall indeed ever prevail.
For that god of great splendor, O tiger among men, desiring to act for the welfare of all creatures, created ten million sages for the sake of dharma.
Created by him according to that rite on Mount Gandhamādana,
they remain there, led by Sanatkumāra, endowed with ascetic power.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, he who is eloquent and knows the Dharma is worthy of homage;
for when he is saluted, he should salute in return, and when honored, he should honor in turn.

O best of the twice-born, that deity whom one has seen should be beheld day after day; one who has taken refuge in him should take refuge [in him] again; and one who has been worshipped should always worship [him] in turn.
Thus, such was the supreme austerity of that great Ādideva Viṣṇu, who is beyond reproach and whose conduct is always practiced by the virtuous.
Eternally worshipped in this world even by the gods,
they, following his vow, approached him with appropriate fearlessness.
Through action, mind, and speech, he is always to be honored by the twice-born;
having approached with diligence, the son of Devakī is to be beheld.
O best of sages, this path has indeed been ordained by me;
having seen that Lord of all gods, one shall have seen the most excellent of the deities.
And I myself always pay homage to that god Mahāvarāha, the grandfather of all the worlds and the lord of the universe.
And there, a triad will undoubtedly be seen;
for we gods all together dwell within his body.
And his elder brother, possessing the luster of a mass of white mountains,
shall become a sustainer of the earth, renowned as Halī and Bala.
The three-headed one was seen by that lordly god as Ananta;
he is the powerful Suparṇa, the son of Kaśyapa, by whose valor [the world is sustained].
He was unable to see the end of that divine Supreme Self;
and Śeṣa wandered about, filled with supreme joy.
He who dwells within, embracing the earth with his coils,
is this very Viṣṇu, the Lord Ananta, the upholder of the world.
He who is Rāma is Hṛṣīkeśa, the infallible upholder of the entire earth;
both of them are tigers among men, divine and possessed of divine prowess.
Those who bear the discus and the plow are to be seen and honored;
this is the favor I have declared for you, O ascetics rich in merit.
Therefore, you should diligently worship the best of the Yadus.
The sages said:
Oh, the wonderful majesty of Kṛṣṇa has been heard by us—
meritorious, auspicious, the destroyer of all sins, and the annihilator of worldly existence!
O great sage, having worshipped Vāsudeva according to the rules with devotion,
what destination do those men go who are intent upon the worship of Vāsudeva?
O Great Sage, do they attain liberation, or heaven,
or else, O best of sages, do they obtain both fruits?
O Omniscient One, you ought to sever the doubt residing in our hearts;
O best of sages, there is no one else in this world besides you who can do so.
Vyāsa said:
"Excellent, excellent, O best of sages, that which has been uttered by you!
Listen now in due order to that which brings happiness to the Vaiṣṇavas."
By the mere act of initiation into Kṛṣṇa, men indeed attain liberation;
how much more so, O twice-born ones, those who always worship Acyuta with devotion?
O best of sages, heaven and liberation are not difficult for them to attain;
indeed, the Vaiṣṇavas obtain whatever desires they wish for, even those that are hard to achieve.
O tigers among sages, just as a man might ascend a mountain of jewels and take whatever gem he desires, so too does one obtain his heart's wishes from Kṛṣṇa.
O Brahmins, just as a person, having approached a wish-fulfilling tree, takes fruits according to his own desire, so too does he obtain his heart's desires from Kṛṣṇa.
By worshipping Vāsudeva, the teacher of the world, according to the rules with faith,
men obtain the fruit of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Having propitiated that Lord of the World with a pure inner self,
men obtain their desires, even those difficult for the gods to attain.
For those who always worship with devotion the imperishable one named Vāsudeva,
nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain within the three worlds.
Blessed are those men in the world who always worship Hari,
the God who removes all sins and bestows the fruits of all desires.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, Śūdras, and those of the lowest castes—
by worshipping that best of gods, they attain the supreme goal.
Therefore, listen, O sinless sages, to that which you ask me;
I shall explain in brief the destiny of those great-souled ones.
Having abandoned the human body— which is unstable, a locus of disease,
joined with old age and death, and resembling a bubble on the water—
Foul-smelling with flesh and blood, joined with excrement, urine, and the like,
it is impure, having bones for its pillars, and is bound together by sinews, skin, and veins.
By means of a celestial chariot that moves at will, resounding with divine music and fragrances, possessing the hue of the rising sun, and adorned with garlands of tinkling bells; BrP_227.18 //
Being sung to by Gandharvas and adorned by Apsarases,
they go to the respective abodes of the world-protectors.
Having enjoyed their respective worlds, adorned with all objects of enjoyment, for a duration equal to a manvantara each, they remain there individually.
Then those twice-born ones go to the atmospheric world (*antarikṣaloka*), which bestows all happiness;
having enjoyed excellent pleasures there for ten *manvantaras*, O brahmins.
Therefore, those Vaiṣṇava twice-born ones indeed go to the world of the Gandharvas;
having enjoyed delightful things there for a period of twenty manvantaras.
From there, being well-honored, they go to the world of the Sun;
having enjoyed divine pleasures there for thirty manvantaras, they proceed further.
Therefore, those brahmins go to the world of the Moon, which bestows happiness;
there they remain for forty manvantaras, endowed with all virtues.
Having enjoyed auspicious pleasures for a long time, free from old age and death,
they then proceed to the world of the stars, which is beautifully adorned with celestial chariots.
Adorned with all virtues, those best of sages proceed on,
having enjoyed their desired pleasures for fifty manvantaras.
Therefore, those brahmins go to the world of the gods, which is very difficult to attain;
having enjoyed there for sixty manvantaras that which is so hard to obtain, they depart.
O Brahmins, endowed with various kinds of enjoyments and the eightfold collection of Rigvedic verses,
they go from there again to the world of Śakra, honored by the gods.
Having enjoyed there for seventy manvantaras,
he partook of various divine pleasures that increase the delight of the mind.
Therefore, they go to the unsurpassed world of Prajāpati;
having enjoyed there their desired pleasures, endowed with all qualities of desire.
For a period of eighty manvantaras, which bestows all happiness,
those Vaiṣṇava twice-born ones indeed go to that world of Brahmā.
Having sported there happily for ninety manvantaras,
he then returns here once more to a preeminent family of brahmins.
Brahmins who are practitioners of yoga and masters of the meaning of the Vedas and Śāstras are born;
thus, having enjoyed all desired pleasures in all the worlds, [they attain liberation].
Having come here, those best of the twice-born go again, one after another in succession; in each successive birth, they live for a hundred years.
Having enjoyed desired pleasures, they then depart for another world;
when ten births have been completed by them in this very sequence, [they attain liberation].
Then they go from the world of Brahmā to the divine realm of Hari;
having gone there, they enjoy inexhaustible pleasures endowed with all excellent qualities.
O best of the twice-born, for as long as a hundred manvantaras, being freed from birth and death, they go thereafter to the world of Varāha.
O best of Brahmins, possessing divine bodies, wearing earrings, with massive forms and great strength,
they sport there, having assumed four-armed forms.
O best of the twice-born, they remain in that eternal state for ten thousand times ten million years, honored by all the gods.
Then those wise twice-born ones go to the abode of Narasiṃha;
there they sport joyfully for tens of thousands of millions of years.
At the end of that, they go to the city of Viṣṇu, which is frequented by the Siddhas;
there they sport in happiness for ten thousand years.
Furthermore, O Brahmins, the most excellent practitioners go to the world of Brahmā;
staying there for a long time, for many hundreds of millions of years.
Then those lords of practitioners go to the city of Nārāyaṇa,
having enjoyed various pleasures for billions of crores of years.
Thereafter, those excellent practitioners— possessing divine forms and great strength— proceed to the city of Aniruddha while being praised by gods and asuras.
There, for fourteen thousand crores of years,
the devotees of Viṣṇu indeed remain, free from old age and death.
Afterwards, free from all feverish distress, they go to the city of Pradyumna;
there those brahmins remain for three hundred quadrillion years.
Moving according to their own will, joyful and endowed with strength and power,
the yogins afterwards go where the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa resides.
Having dwelt there for a long time and enjoyed thousands of pleasures,
they enter the stainless Virūpākṣa, who is Vāsudeva.
Released into the supreme reality, which is devoid of old age and death, having gone there, they shall become liberated; of this there is no doubt.
In this manner, O tigers among sages, those wise ones who are devoted to the worship of Vāsudeva gradually attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Vyāsa said:
On the eleventh day of both fortnights, having fasted, being composed in mind, having bathed according to the proper ritual, wearing clean garments, and with his senses subdued; BrP_228.1 //
Having worshipped Viṣṇu according to the prescribed rites with faith and a well-composed mind, using flowers, perfumes, lamps, incense, and food offerings; ||| BrP_228.2 |||
With various kinds of offerings, recitations, burnt oblations, circumambulations, diverse divine hymns, and captivating songs and instrumental music; BrP_228.3 //
Having thus worshipped according to the rules with prostrations like a staff, with shouts of "Victory!", and with other supreme hymns, one should keep a vigil throughout the night.
Or, by singing a story or a song of Viṣṇu with Viṣṇu as his supreme goal, a man goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu; there is no doubt about this.
The sages said:
O great sage, tell us the fruit of singing the hymn to Viṣṇu during the vigil;
we wish to hear it, for our curiosity is indeed great.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O tigers among sages, for I shall describe in due order the fruit of the song of Viṣṇu as it has been proclaimed in relation to the vigil.
There was a city on earth renowned as Avantī;
there dwells the Blessed Viṣṇu, the bearer of the conch, the discus, and the mace.
On the outskirts of that city lived a Cāṇḍāla, skilled in song,
who had acquired wealth through honest means and was devoted to supporting his dependents.
That Cāṇḍāla, a devotee of Viṣṇu firm in his vows,
would come every month on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) and, having fasted, would then sing.
The songs are marked with the names of Viṣṇu’s incarnations and are based on the musical scales of Gāndhāra, Ṣaḍja, Niṣāda, Pañcama, and Dhaivata.
During the night vigil, he sings praises to Viṣṇu with hymns;
and at dawn on the twelfth day, having bowed to the Lord and returned home, he continues his observance.
O best of the twice-born, having fed his sons-in-law and nephews along with their daughters, he then eats afterwards together with his attendants.
Thus, while he remained there performing the propitiation of Viṣṇu,
much of his life passed away in the company of various songs.
Once, during the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Caitra,
he went to an unsurpassed forest for the purpose of serving Viṣṇu.
Intent on devotion, he went to the bank of the Kṣiprā in the great forest beneath a Vibhītaka tree to gather wild flowers.
Then he was seen by the rākṣasa and seized to be eaten;
the caṇḍāla then said to him, "Indeed, you must not eat me today."
"O auspicious one, you shall eat tomorrow; I will surely return again.
Today I have a great task to attend to, therefore release me, O Rākṣasa."
"Tomorrow I shall meet with the truth, and then you shall eat me.
"For the sake of serving Viṣṇu, I must keep a vigil through the night;
you ought not, O Rākṣasa, to cause an obstacle to my vow."
Vyāsa said:
The Rākṣasa replied to him: "O elephant, I have had no food for ten nights;
today you have been found by me."
"I shall not be released; I will devour you, for I am severely oppressed by hunger.
Having heard the words of the night-stalker, the Mātaṅga spoke to him, consoling him with gentle speech and firm words of truth.
Mātaṅga said:
"O Brahmarākṣasa, hear this: the entire world has truth as its foundation.
By means of truth I shall curse you, so that you may return once more."
The sun, the moon, fire, wind, earth, heaven, water, and the mind;
day and night, Yama, and the two twilights—they know these to be the activities of men.

Whatever sin lies in those who commit adultery with another's wife, whatever in those who steal the property of others, and whatever sin lies in the killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, or the violator of the Guru’s bed— [all that is incurred by one who fails to protect the cow].

Whatever sin belongs to the husband of a barren woman, whatever sin belongs to the husband of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī), whatever sin belongs to one who maintains a shrine-keeper (devalaka), and whatever sin belongs to an eater of fish and meat; [all that is removed by this].
Whatever [sin] belongs to those who eat the flesh of boars, and whatever to those who eat the flesh of tortoises;
whatever to those who eat meat in vain, and whatever to those who eat the flesh from the back.
Whatever sin belongs to the ungrateful, the betrayer of friends, or the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is unmarried;
whatever sin belongs to one in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka), and whatever sin belongs to the perpetrator of cruel deeds—[may [he] be freed from all that].
Whatever sin belongs to a miser, and whatever [sin] belongs even to one who has failed a guest,
[is incurred on] the new moon day, the eighth, the sixth, and the fourteenth days of both the dark and the bright fortnights.
Regarding those [women], whatever sin a Brahmin incurs by approaching a woman who is menstruating,
he likewise incurs after having performed a śrāddha and then approached a woman.

Whatever sin there is in eating the food of those who have bathed after a funeral, or in eating impure food, and whatever sin there is for those who go to the wife of a friend, as well as for the slanderer; [all that is removed by this].
Whatever sin belongs to the slayer of honey who is devoted to deceit and guile, and whatever sin belongs to one who has promised something to a Brahmin but does not give it— [that sin he incurs].

Whatever sin lies in lying about a maiden, whatever sin in lying about cows or mules, whatever sin belongs to the killer of a woman or a child, and whatever sin belongs to one who speaks falsely; [all these are incurred by one who gives false testimony].

The sin incurred by those who revile the gods, the Vedas, the twice-born, kings, sons, friends, and virtuous wives, as well as the sin from improper conduct toward one's guru— [all these are removed].

Whatever sin exists among those who abandon the sacred fires, whatever among those who set fire to forests, whatever in the downfall of domestic sacrifices, whatever in the killing of a cow, and whatever in the lowest of the twice-born; [all that is removed by this].
Whatever sin belongs to one who has been superseded in marriage, whatever sin belongs to the one who supersedes,
and whatever sin belongs to both the giver and the receiver, as well as that of the killer of an embryo— [all these are incurred].
Moreover, O Rākṣasa, what is the use of these many oaths spoken by you?
Listen to a formidable oath, which I shall speak even though it is difficult to utter.
The sin of one who lives off his own daughter, the sin of witnesses who conceal the truth,
the sin of one who officiates at sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice, and the sin of a base eunuch in hearing [the sacred texts].
And whatever sin lies in one who has abandoned the life of renunciation, or in a lustful student of sacred knowledge—
by these sins may I be tainted if I do not come into your presence.
Vyāsa said: Having heard the words of the Mātaṅga, the Brahmarākṣasa was struck with wonder and said,
"Go, and keep your promise in truth."
Thus addressed by Kuṇapāśa, the Śvapāka took the flowers and went to the abode of Viṣṇu.
He gave those [fruits] to a brahmin; he too, having washed them with water and worshipped Viṣṇu, went to his home, O ascetics.
That heir of Mātaṅga, too, having observed a fast for that night,
remained awake on the outer grounds while singing.
When the night had turned to dawn, having bathed and paid homage to the god,
he set out toward where the Rākṣasa was, in order to make his promise true.
As he was walking along the road, a man said to him, "Noble sir, where are you going?
He told him everything, and the other spoke to him again:
Since the body is the means for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa,
the wise person should protect the body with great effort.
In this way, a man attains life, virtue, wealth, and happiness, as well as the supreme state of liberation;
while living, he also acquires renown.
"What talk can there be regarding one who is dead in this world? Having heard those words, Mātaṅga then replied with a reasoned argument.
Mātaṅga said:
"O noble one, placing truth before me, I go; oaths have been made."
Vyāsa said:
He then replied to him once more: "O virtuous one, why are you so dull-witted?
Have you not heard what was proclaimed by Manu?"
For the sake of protecting cows, women, and the twice-born; at the time of marriage; during sexual union;
when life is at stake; and when all one's wealth is being seized.

They say that five kinds of falsehoods are not sinful: a statement for the sake of dharma, [falsehood] toward women, likewise at a wedding, in the face of an enemy, and in deception regarding the loss of wealth; likewise, falsehood is permissible in the event of one's own destruction.
Having heard those words, Mātaṅga replied.
Mātaṅga said:
Do not speak thus; may you be blessed! Truth is honored in all the worlds.
Through truth, whatever happiness exists within the world is attained.
By truth the sun shines; by truth the waters consist of essence;
by truth the fire blazes, and by truth the wind blows.
The attainment of virtue, wealth, and pleasure, as well as the attainment of liberation, are difficult to achieve;
they arise for men through truth. Therefore, one should not abandon truth.
Truth is the supreme Brahman in the world; truth is the highest among sacrifices;
truth has arrived as heaven itself; therefore, one should never abandon truth.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, that Mātaṅga then cast down that best of men and went to where the Brahmarākṣasa, the slayer of living beings, resided.
Seeing that Caṇḍāla arrived, the Brahmarākṣasa,
his eyes wide with wonder, shook his head and said to him:
The Brahmarākṣasa said:
"Excellent, excellent, O illustrious one, you who uphold truthful speech!
I do not consider you to be a Mātaṅga, for you possess the characteristics of truth."
"By this deed, I consider you to be a pure and imperishable Brahmin.
O gentle-faced one, whatever concerning the dharma I shall speak to you, tell me:
what did you do there in the temple of Viṣṇu during the night?"
Vyāsa said:
The Mātaṅga addressed him: "Listen; I shall tell you exactly what was done by me in the house of Viṣṇu during the portion of the night."
Standing below the temple of Viṣṇu with his body bowed in reverence,
he kept a vigil throughout the night, singing a hymn in praise of Viṣṇu.
The Brahmarākṣasa said to him: "Tell me, for how long was this vigil performed with devotion in the temple of Viṣṇu? Speak."

Laughing, he said to him: "O Rākṣasa, twenty years have passed since you performed the night-vigil (prajāgara) on the Ekādaśī day month after month. Having heard the words of Mātaṅga, the Brahmarākṣasa replied.
The Brahmarākṣasa said:
"O virtuous one, you ought to grant me that which I shall now declare to you: the vigil kept by me for a single night."
"In this way I shall liberate you; I shall liberate you, and not otherwise.
By my truth, O illustrious one," having said this three times, he indeed became silent.
Vyāsa said:
Then the Mātaṅga spoke to him: "O night-stalker, I have already offered myself to you;
what is the use of further words? Eat me as you please!"
The Rākṣasa spoke to him again: "Grant me a two-watch vigil accompanied by song; you ought to show me mercy."
Mātaṅga said to the Rākṣasa, "Why do you speak such nonsense?
Eat me as you please; I will not surrender my Prajāgara. Hearing Mātaṅga's words, the Brahmarākṣasa spoke to him.
The Brahmarākṣasa said:
"What person of wicked mind and dull intellect would dare to look upon you,
who are protected by righteous deeds, or to assault or afflict you?"
For the wretched, the one seized by sin, the one deluded by sense-objects,
the one suffering in hell, and the fool— toward these, the virtuous should be filled with compassion.
Therefore, O illustrious one, having shown compassion, grant me the watch of a single night while I keep vigil, or else go to your own abode.
Vyāsa said:
The Cāṇḍāla spoke to him again: "I will not go to my own home, nor will I ever grant you the privilege of keeping watch over the night."
Then, laughing at that Cāṇḍāla, the Brahmarākṣasa spoke to him.
The brahmarākṣasa said:
"Give me the fruit of that song which was sung at the end of the night as a source of curiosity; save me and deliver me from this sin."
Vyāsa said:
When this had been uttered by him, Mātaṅga spoke to him.
Mātaṅga said:
What perverse deed did you previously commit so directly that,
through the resulting mass of faults, you were born as a brahmarākṣasa?
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of his, the Brahmarākṣasa,
tormented by grief, remembered his own past deeds and spoke to the Mātaṅga.
The Brahmarākṣasa said:
Listen to who I was in the past and what I did,
by the doing of which I entered this sinful rākṣasa womb.
Formerly, I was a twice-born man known as Somaśarman,
the son of the sacrificer Devaśarman, who was devoted to Vedic study.
For a certain king who was devoted to ritual action and excluded from the Sūtras and Mantras, he was thoroughly established in the work of the sacrificial post.
Afflicted by greed and delusion, he performed the duties of the Āgnīdhra priest at the sacrifice;
and when that was completed, out of folly, he practiced hypocrisy.
"I had begun to perform the great twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha),
but while it was underway, a sharp pain arose in my belly."
When ten nights were fully completed, yet the sacrifice was not yet concluded,
at that moment of the Rakshasa, as the oblation for Virupaksha was being offered.
"Because of that fault, I died and was reborn as a brahmarākṣasa;
for I was foolish and lacked the mantra, and [the recitation] was devoid of the proper thread and tone."
Because he performed sacrifices and officiated at sacrifices without knowing the science of sacrifice,
through the ripening of that karma he was born as a Brahmarākṣasa.
Therefore, lift me up who am submerged in the great ocean of sin;
you ought to grant me the final single verse for the night vigil.
Vyāsa said:
Then the Caṇḍāla said to him, "If you desist from the slaughter of living beings, I shall then give you my final song."
"So be it," he replied; and then that Mātaṅga also gave him the fruit of his song, having invited him to stay awake for half a muhūrta.
When that fruit of his song had been granted, the Brahmarākṣasa bowed to the Mātaṅga and departed joyfully for Pṛthūdaka, the most excellent of sacred fords.
There, O twice-born ones, having resolved upon fasting unto death, he gave up his life;
liberated from the state of a *rākṣasa*, he was strengthened by the fruit of his songs.
And by the power of Pṛthūdaka, he then dwelt for ten thousand years in the world of Brahmā, which is difficult to attain, free from all affliction.
At its conclusion, a Brahmin was born who was mindful and self-controlled;
O twice-born ones, I shall relate his life story to you once more.
Listen as I relate the remainder of Mātaṅga’s story:
when the Rākṣasa had departed, the wise and self-controlled man returned home.
Remembering those wicked deeds, he became despondent; though pure himself, he entrusted his wife to his sons and performed the circumambulation of the earth.
Starting from Kokāmukha as far as the sight of Skanda,
he went to see Skanda and also performed a circumambulation at Dhārācakra.
Then, O twice-born ones, having reached the excellent mountain Vindhya with its lofty peaks, he arrived at the sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Pāpapramocana.
That man born of a Cāṇḍāla lineage performed a bath that removes sin;
freed from sin, he remembered his many previous births.
In a previous birth, he was a monk who had restrained his speech and mind;
he was wise, disciplined in body, and a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
Once, while the cows were being driven from the city by thieves,
that mendicant was released by them because he had been covered in dust.
Due to that fault of unrighteousness, he entered the womb of a Caṇḍāla;
having bathed at Pāpapramocana, he died on the bank of the Narmadā.
O twice-born ones, there was an excellent Brahmin who was a fool in Vārāṇasī;
while he was living there for thirty years, a perfected being (siddhapūruṣa) [appeared].
Assuming various forms and endowed with the power of a garland of yogas, he wandered about;
seeing him, [the other] greeted him with a smile and spoke.
"O virtuous perfected man, from where have you come?"
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed in this way by him, and thinking, "I have been recognized," he who was worthy of worship, having arrived from the heavenly world, then replied to him.
To that perfected one, the fool said: "What do you know of Urvaśī, the most excellent of apsarases, who was born from the thigh of Nārāyaṇa in the triple heaven?"
The Siddha said to him, "I know her— Urvaśī, who was born of the virtuous, the primary ornament of heaven, and the bearer of Indra’s fly-whisk."
Then the brahmin, who had strayed from the straight path, said to his friend: "O friend, out of respect for me, please inquire after Urvaśī."
"And what she may say to you must be told; you shall be informed [by her].
"Very well," the perfected one replied, and that brahmin was filled with joy.
Having become a perfected being (siddha), he went to the summit of Meru, the abode of the gods;
having approached Urvaśī, he spoke to her what he had been told by the twice-born brahmin.
She said to that excellent Siddha, "I do not know the brahmin who is the lord of Kāśī;
what you have spoken is true, for he does not abide in my mind."
Having been addressed thus, he departed; and after a long time, that perfected one went again to Vārāṇasī, where he was once more seen by the fool.
"Having been seen and questioned again, he said, 'What did Urvaśī say to you?
Siddha replied, 'I do not know; Urvaśī herself spoke to me.'"
Then, having heard the words of the Siddha, with his lips parted by a smile, he spoke again:
"How do you know this? Thus must Urvaśī be addressed by you."
Having said, "Very well, I shall do so," the Siddha departed for heaven;
there he beheld Urvaśī emerging from the abode of Śakra.
The best of perfected beings spoke to her, and she in turn said to that perfected being:
"Let this most excellent of the twice-born observe some kind of religious vow."
"O Siddha, I know that by which karma [this was achieved] and not otherwise"; having approached those words of Urvaśī, he spoke them to that foolish brahmin.
The perfected one spoke, and he too declared this rule:
"O perfected man, this rule has been established by me in your presence."
"From this day forward, I shall indeed not eat the cart; this is the truth I have spoken.
Having said this, the Siddha departed for heaven, where he then beheld Urvaśī.
He said, "I shall eat no cart-vegetables from this day forward, never again.
To him, once he was prepared, Urvaśī said, "Now I have finally recognized him."
"Because he took those vows, this fool intends to mock me," saying this, the daughter of Nārāyaṇa departed quickly for her dwelling.
Even though he had attained perfection, he wandered the surface of the earth at will; and Urvaśī, of beautiful form, having gone to the city of Vārāṇasī, [remained there].
Assuming a divine form, she performed her ablutions in the waters of the Matsyodarī;
but that fool, O Sage, likewise went to the river Matsyodarī.
Then he went there and beheld Urvaśī as she was bathing;
seeing her, the god of love, which causes great agitation, grew strong within him.
The fool performed various antics, and Urvaśī herself recognized him;
knowing him to be the fool described by the Siddhas, she spoke to him with a smile.
Urvaśī said:
"O illustrious one, tell me quickly here what you desire from me;
I shall carry out your word, and you may act with full confidence."
The foolish Brahmin said:
"O lady of pure smiles, protect my life by giving yourself to me."
Vyāsa said:
Then Urvaśī spoke to that brahmin, "I am currently observing a vow;
wait for a moment and await my return."
"I am staying here," the Brahmin replied; she, too, went to heaven.
After only a month, she returned and saw that emaciated twice-born man.
Having remained on the riverbank for a month without food, a celestial maiden,
seeing him steadfast in his resolve, then assumed the form of an old woman.
She prepared a cart covered with sugar on the riverbank,
and having gone to the Matsyodarī river, she [prepared it] with ghee and honey.
Then, having bathed and dwelling upon the ground, Sulocanā summoned that Brahmin and spoke these words concerning the cart according to the facts.
Urvaśī said:
"O Brahmin, I have observed a severe vow for the sake of obtaining good fortune.
At the conclusion of the vow, I shall offer a gift of atonement; please accept it, O twice-born one."
Vyāsa said:
He asked, "What is this that is being given here in the world, covered with sugar?
My throat is parched with hunger; I ask you, O auspicious lady, please explain it well."
She said, "O Brahmin, Śakaṭa is here with sugar-cake flour;
taking this, satisfy your life-force without delay. (BrP 228.133)
Having heard that and remembering [his vow], even though he was tormented by hunger, he said:
"O blessed lady, I do not accept it, for a religious observance has been undertaken by me."
"I shall not eat the cart in front of the assembly of Siddhas";
for the sake of Urvaśī’s recognition, give it to someone else.
She said, "O gentle one, a rule was made by you regarding one made of wood;
this one is not made of wood, so eat, for you are greatly tormented by hunger."
The Brahmin replied to her: "O blessed lady, I did not make that specific restriction;
rather, I made my vow in a general sense."
That slender woman spoke to him again: "O Brahmin, if you will not eat, then take your household and go; your family will eat."
He said to her, "O lady of beautiful teeth, I shall not go home yet;
for you, O woman of lovely form, have arrived here, surpassing even those in the three worlds by your virtues."
Afflicted by love, I entreated her and was comforted by her;
she said, "Stay for a moment," and I replied, "I shall stay."
O virtuous lady of firm vows, for her who has been gone for only a month, and for me who remain here devoted to the truth, let there be a reunion.
Having heard his words and assuming her own supreme form,
Urvaśī laughed with profound emotion and spoke to that twice-born man.
Urvaśī said:
"O Brahmin, it is well that you have accomplished this vow with a resolute mind,
even by force, out of a desire for a sight of me."
"O Brahmin, I am indeed Urvaśī, who has come here for the purpose of testing you;
you have been examined and proven to be a sage of true austerity."
"Go to the region of Śūkaravoda, renowned as Rūpatīrtha;
there you shall attain perfection, O best of Brahmins, and from there you will find me."
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, O twice-born ones, Urvaśī flew up into the sky and departed;
and that brahmin Satyatapas went to Rūpatīrtha.
There, devoted to peace, pure, and observant of restraints and vows,
he departed for the highest Gāndharva world upon the casting off of his body.
Having truly enjoyed pleasures there for a hundred manvantaras,
he was born into a noble family as a king devoted to pleasing his subjects.
Having performed various sacrifices with excellent sacrificial fees,
that performer of rites entrusted the kingdom to his sons and returned once more to Śaukarava.
Having died at Rūpatīrtha, he returned once more to the world of Śakra;
having enjoyed pleasures there for a hundred manvantaras, he eventually descended from that state.
O you whose wealth is asceticism, in that most excellent city of Pratiṣṭhāna, Purūravas, the son of Budha, lived there for the sake of union with Urvaśī.
Thus, in former times, the twice-born Satyatapas,
having propitiated Viṣṇu at the famous sacred ford known as Rūpa and having worshipped him there in that birth—
"Having obtained enjoyments, one then attains liberation.
[The sages said:
"We have heard the fruit of this song during the excellent vigil."
By means of Kṛṣṇa, that Cāṇḍāla attained the supreme goal.
O high-minded one, tell us how devotion toward Viṣṇu may arise;
we now wish to hear by what austerity or by what action this may be attained.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O tigers among sages, for I shall explain in due order how devotion toward Kṛṣṇa may arise in a person, yielding great fruit.
In this most terrible saṃsāra, which brings fear to all beings,
which causes great delusion for men, and which is crowded with hundreds of various sufferings.
O twice-born ones, being born again and again among thousands of animal wombs, an embodied being somehow or other attains a human birth.
Even in human existence, one must attain the status of a Brahmin; even as a Brahmin, one must possess discernment.
From discernment arises the understanding of Dharma, and through that understanding comes the grasping of the highest goods.
As long as the accumulated evil of men has not been exhausted through their births,
so long does devotion to Vāsudeva, who pervades the universe, not arise.
Therefore, O Brahmins, I shall explain how devotion to Kṛṣṇa may arise,
as well as that devotion to other deities which is born here in this world for a person.
O best of sages, through action, mind, and speech, and with his inner self absorbed in that, he shall possess devotion toward the sacrifice.
Then, O Brahmins, being composed in mind, he practices devotion to Agni;
when the Fire-god is satisfied, his devotion becomes fixed upon the Sun.
O twice-born ones, he constantly performs worship of the Sun;
consequently, when the Sun is pleased, his devotion turns toward Śaṅkara.
He performs the worship of Śambhu with diligence according to the prescribed rules;
when the Three-eyed Lord is pleased, his devotion is directed toward Keśava.
Having worshipped that Lord of the World, the imperishable one named Vāsudeva,
he then attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation, O best of the twice-born.
The sages said:
O great sage, as for those men who are seen not to be devotees of Viṣṇu, why do they not worship Viṣṇu? Tell us the reason for that, O twice-born one.
Vyāsa said:
O best of sages, two types of creation of beings are renowned in this world:
the demonic and the divine, which were created of old by the Self-born One.
Having attained a divine nature, men worship Acyuta;
but having fallen into a demonic womb, they defile Hari.
O brahmins, those lowest of men whose consciousness has been destroyed by the māyā of Viṣṇu fail to reach that Hari and consequently go to the lowest state.
His is that profound illusion, difficult to be discerned even by gods and asuras;
it causes great delusion for men and is hard to cross for those who have not disciplined their selves.
The sages said:
"O knower of dharma, we wish to know that great illusion (mahāmāyā) of Viṣṇu, which is so difficult to cross; you ought to speak of it, for our curiosity is great."
Vyāsa said:
That illusion (māyā), which resembles a dream or a magician’s trick and which enthralls the world—
who, other than Keśava, is able to understand that illusion of Hari?
O Brahmins, listen as I relate that deception which was practiced by Nārada for the sake of Māyā against the Brahmin. BrP_229.21.
Formerly there was a glorious king renowned as Āgnīdhra;
his son, born in the city of Kāmadamana, was the pure-souled [Kāmadamano].
Delighting in the Dharma, possessing a nature of forbearance, devoted to the service of his father,
pleasing to his subjects, skillful, and having exerted himself in the study of the Vedas and the Shastras.
His father made an effort for his marriage, but he did not desire it;
his father said to him, "Why do you not wish to take a wife?"
"Indeed, it is said that all human beings desire this for the sake of happiness;
for wives are the very root of happiness, therefore, you should act accordingly."
Having heard his father’s words, he remained silent out of respect;
and O twice-born ones, his father urged him again and again.
Then he said to his father, "Father,
I have clearly relied upon and fully maintained the Vaiṣṇavī [power] that is consistent with my name."
Having approached him, the father said: "My son, this is not the dharma;
a wise man should not maintain such a practice."
"O son, do as I say; I am your father and your lord.
Do not let my lineage sink into hell through the extinction of our progeny."
Having heard that command of his father, the self-controlled son,
being pleased and recollecting the ancient variety of worldly existence, spoke.
The son said:
"Listen, father, to my words, which are truthful and supported by reason; O King, one's name must be made consistent with one's reality."
Throughout thousands of births, I have experienced hundreds of old ages and deaths,
as well as every kind of union with and separation from a spouse.
Grasses, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, reptiles, deer, birds,
cattle, women, men, and so forth— I have encountered these hundreds of times.
The Gaṇas, Kiṃnaras, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Mahoragas;
the Yakṣas, Guhyakas, Rākṣasas, Dānavas, Apsarases, and Suras.
And, O dear one, a thousand Nadīśvaras have been attained by me again and again;
indeed, I have been created many times in the act of creation and likewise withdrawn during the dissolution.
"O father, for one joined with the union of marriage, such is my mockery;
hear now what occurred in my third birth from this point,
which arose from the majesty of the sacred ford (tīrtha), which I shall relate to you in brief."
Having passed through many births, O dear one,
among men, gods, gandharvas, and great serpents, among the vidyādharas, birds, and kiṃnaras—
For he was born into a lineage of great sages who had performed intense austerities;
consequently, his devotion toward Janārdana, the Lord of the World and slayer of Madhu, became firm and unshakable.
Satisfied by various vows, fasts, and devotion,
the high-souled one who bears the discus, mace, and weapons approached the Lord of Birds in his gratification.
Viṣṇu, having mounted [his vehicle], the bestower of boons upon me, spoke in a loud voice: "O twice-born one, let a boon be chosen;
whatever boon you desire, I shall grant it."
Then I said to Hari, the Lord:
"O Keśava, if you are pleased, I choose that which is indeed your supreme *māyā*."
"I, Janārdana, desire to know that," [I said].
Then the enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha replied to me:
"O Brahmin, what use have you for that māyā?"
"I shall grant you dharma, artha, and kāma,
as well as excellent sons and freedom from disease.
Then I spoke again to Murāri:
Since this desire for wealth, dharma,
and victory is merely an illusion, O lotus-eyed one, I wish to understand this Māyā of yours; show it to me today.
Then the Lord Viṣṇu, the illustrious Śrīśa, the foremost among men-lions, spoke these words to me:
[Viṣṇu said:]
No one indeed knows my māyā, nor will anyone ever know it;
formerly, O twice-born one, there was a celestial sage named Nārada. (BrP 229.43c–229.44a)
He was born as the son of Brahmā, endowed with devotion to me; for he, being full of devotion, satisfied me just as you previously did.
I went away after the boon had been granted,
and he chose this very same boon; though I tried to dissuade him, he persisted out of extreme delusion.
"Since you have thus chosen this boon,
O Nārada, I then said to you: 'Once you have submerged yourself in my waters, you shall indeed come to know my Māyā.'"
Then, having submerged himself in the water, that Nārada emerged;
there appeared Suśīlā, the daughter of the Lord of Kāśī,
rich in youth and endowed with beautiful virtues, whom he [gave] to Cārudharman.
He gave her to the son of the king of Vidarbha, Svadharman; and he, the great seer, united with her, enjoyed incomparable pleasures.
When his father had gone to heaven, that powerful king, having joyfully obtained the kingdom that had descended to him by succession,
protected the realm of Vidarbha.
Surrounded by many sons and grandsons,
there then occurred a great battle between King Sudharman and the Lord of Kāśī.
There, having met their destruction in battle along with their sons and grandsons— the King of Vidarbha and the Lord of Kāśī—
Suśīlā then [saw] her father together with his son.
Having learned that her husband, along with his sons and grandsons,
had departed from the city and gone to the field of battle,
Suśīlā beheld the great carnage.
Overwhelmed with grief at the loss of her husband’s strength and her father’s strength, she lamented for a very long time and,
appearing deeply distressed, went to her mother.
Taking her brothers, sons, nephews, and grandsons,
as well as her husband and father,
she [prepared] a great funeral pyre in the great cremation ground.
Having prepared the fire, he himself offered [the oblation];
when the consumer of oblations had become fully kindled,
then Suśīlā entered it with speed.
Then, crying out "O son! O son!
she became the sage Nārada once more;
and that fire also became as pure as crystal.
Then the lake became full,
and Keśava, the best of gods, emerged from it;
smiling, he spoke to the divine sage Nārada.
"Tell me, O Great Sage, who is your son?
Whom do you grieve for as dead, you whose intellect is lost?
At that, Nārada became filled with shame.
Then I spoke to him once again:
"O Nārada, such is my Māyā, which is difficult to perceive even for those seated upon the lotus and others."
"She cannot be known even by those equal to Indra and Rudra;
how then will you know her, who is so difficult to conceive?
Having heard these words, that great maharṣi...
He said: "O Viṣṇu, grant me devotion;
likewise, when the time comes, grant me remembrance of you, and may there always be your vision, O Lord."
O Keśava, may that place where I, afflicted, have today ascended the funeral pyre be a sacred ford (tīrtha) eternally presided over by You, the destroyer of sins, O Acyuta.
Together with you, who were born from a lotus,
O twice-born one, I then said to that Nārada:
"Let the Sitodā be your place of cremation."
And I, Viṣṇu, shall always remain here;
Maheśvara shall remain to the north when the three-eyed one [appears] from the mouth of Viriñca.
When he utters this harsh speech against me,
then, for the sake of releasing his skull,
he shall come to this sacred ford of yours.
When the skull of the Destroyer of Tripura falls upon the surface of the earth at that sacred bathing place (tīrtha),
it shall thereafter be known as Kapālamocana.
It shall become renowned upon the earth;
from that time forward, he whose vehicle is the clouds will not leave that most meritorious and excellent sacred site.
And they do not declare that field to be so formidable, O twice-born one, as long as the slayer of the enemies of the immortals does not release the Brahman-slayer. (BrP 229.62c–63a)
That preeminent field is great and has attained merit; at that time, it was called Vimuktā by the gods— a secret,
praised holy site that bestows merit and is known as the Imperishable (Avyaya).
Even if a man has committed great sins, once he has entered there, pure and vigilant,
when he meditates upon me, he becomes purified.
Through the grace of the Blessed One, he attains liberation;
having become known as a Rudra-piśāca within that state,
he experiences suffering in another womb.
Having been freed from evil after many series of years,
he will attain birth in the house of a Brahmin;
thereafter, at the time of his end, he will be pure and self-controlled.
"O best of the twice-born, having spoken thus to Nārada, 'Rudra shall proclaim what is beneficial and liberating for him,' I went to the Ocean of Milk, my own abode."
And that brahmin also traveled to the third heaven,
being honored by the king of the Gandharvas;
this has indeed been told to you for the sake of awakening.
My illusion cannot be understood;
if you desire to know it, then this very day,
test it thus in water, by which means you may perceive it.
Thus enlightened by Hari, O dear one, that twice-born man submerged himself in the waters at Kokāmukha due to the force of his destined fate; and from there, indeed, a daughter was born.
He became a twice-born man in the house of a Cāṇḍāla; she, endowed with beauty and possessed of virtuous qualities,
reached and attained her youth.
Even though she was married to Subāhu, the son of a *caṇḍāla* who was devoid of beauty,
he did not truly become her husband.
She became his beloved;
he had two sons who were blind,
and later another daughter who was likewise deaf.
Her husband was poor, and she too, being simple-minded,
would weep there constantly whenever she went to the river;
once, having taken her water-jar, she departed.
Then, having entered the water to bathe,
that twice-born man once again became one who was devoted to the practice of ritual action and possessed of excellent character.
Then her husband, thinking she had been gone for a long time, went to that most meritorious river to look for her;
he saw the water-jar, but not her standing on the bank.
Then, out of extreme sorrow, she wept aloud, making a great noise;
thereupon, that pair of blind men and the deaf maiden, overcome with grief, approached her.
Seeing their father weeping, they too, overcome with grief and deeply afflicted, wept aloud;
then he questioned those standing on the riverbank.
"If you have seen a certain woman running toward the water, O twice-born ones,
tell me"; they said to him, "She has entered [the lake]."
He did not cross the river again;
"this alone is our desired goal here," he said,
having heard those most terrible words.
He wept, his eyes overflowing with tears of grief;
seeing him weeping along with his son and his daughter, I became exceedingly distressed.
Then, O lord of the earth, both distress and remembrance came upon me: "I am a Caṇḍāla woman," O King;
then I spoke to that Mataṅga.
Why indeed do you weep in distress?
Because of your extreme folly, she will not be recovered;
for what is the use of your lamenting here in vain?
He said to me: "I have two sons who are blind, and this daughter is likewise deaf; O twice-born one, how then can I now support these afflicted ones?"
"I shall console you, and I shall also nourish you"—
having spoken thus, he wept, blowing his breath repeatedly, together with his sons.
The more that outcaste dog-cooker wept, the more my heart was indeed moved; then, having restrained him who was thus afflicted, I—
Then he related the history of his own lineage;
thereafter, filled with grief and accompanied by his sons, he entered Kokāmukha in a state of great distress.
As soon as Mataṅga entered the water,
he was liberated from sin through the power of the sacred ford (tīrtha) and ascended a celestial chariot (vimāna) radiant as the moon.
He went to heaven, O dear one, while I was looking on;
when he had entered the water and died, I was overcome by an anguish that caused extreme delusion.
Then, O best of kings, having entered the waters of the Kokā— a place of great merit— he went to the third heaven;
yet once more, afflicted by distress, I was born into a Vaiśya family.
Having become a rememberer of past births through the grace of that most excellent sacred site,
I then went to Kokāmukha with a deeply disenchanted mind, my speech and thoughts fully restrained.
Having undertaken a vow and withered his own body, he ascended to heaven;
falling from there, he was born in your abode.
"O dear one, by the grace of Hari I am a rememberer of my past births;
having propitiated the god Murāri at Kokāmukha, I have renounced all desire for both auspicious and inauspicious [results]."
Having spoken thus and bowed to his father,
he went to Kokāmukha, the foremost of tīrthas,
and worshipped Viṣṇu in the form of the Boar.
That bull among men attained perfection;
thus did Kāmadamana, together with his sons and grandsons,
[attain it] at Kokāmukha, the most meritorious and excellent of sacred fords.
Having cast off that body composed of defects,
he then went to heaven in celestial chariots equal to the sun;
thus has the [glory] of the Supreme Lord been described by me.
O brahmins, Māyā, which is as difficult for even the gods to conceive and is comparable to a dream or a magician’s trick, is that by which the world falls into delusion regarding Murāri.
The sages said:
"O Vyāsa, we have heard from you that which has been proclaimed—
the meritorious account concerning the manifestations [of Viṣṇu], and the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, which is difficult to comprehend."
O great sage, we wish to hear from you correctly about the dissolution known as the great pralaya and that which occurs at the end of a kalpa.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O best of sages, to how the withdrawal occurs exactly as it happens at the end of a kalpa and during the elemental dissolution (prākṛta-pralaya).

O best of the twice-born, one month of the ancestors is a single day and night for them, while a year of the inhabitants of heaven is their day and night; and four thousand such cycles of the four yugas constitute a single day of Brahmā.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali constitute the four yugas;
these are said by the gods to consist of twelve thousand years.
O sages, all the four yugas are identical in their essential nature;
the first is called the Kṛta-yuga, and likewise the last is the Kali-yuga.
Since creation is performed by Brahmā in the first Kṛta Yuga,
so too is the withdrawal [of the world] performed at the end, in the Kali Yuga.
The sages said:
"O Blessed One, you ought to describe in detail the true nature of Kali,
in whom the four-footed Dharma, the Blessed One, suffers impairment."
Vyāsa said:
O sinless brahmins, listen briefly to the nature of Kali about which you ask me, and how that most powerful one prevails.
In the Kali age, the conduct of men does not follow the rules of the castes and stages of life,
nor is it motivated by the mastery of the Sāma, Ṛg, and Yajur Vedas.
In the Kali age, there are no marriages that conform to dharma, nor disciples who remain devoted to their gurus;
there are no sons who are righteous, nor is there the proper sequence for fire-rituals.
In the Kali age, a man born in any family whatsoever who is powerful and the lord of all may live off the daughters of men from all the social classes.
By whatever means a twice-born man is initiated in the Kali age, by that very same means it is done; O best of Brahmins, such indeed is the performance of expiatory rites in the Kali age.
O twice-born ones, in the Kali age, every scripture is indeed whatever word anyone utters;
all beings are deities in the Kali age, and everyone belongs to every stage of life.
In the Kali age, fasting, physical exertion,
and the distribution of wealth are practiced as dharma through observances performed according to one's own inclinations.
In the Kali age, men will become intoxicated by even a very small amount of wealth,
and women will become intoxicated by their own beauty and their hair alone.
When gold, gems, jewels, and even clothing have fallen into decay,
then in the Kali age women will be adorned only by their hair.
In the Kali age, women will likewise abandon a husband who is destitute of wealth;
indeed, for women, the husband will be one who possesses riches alone.
Whoever gives abundantly at that time shall be the master of men; then, the relationship of mastership shall be based on the cause of giving, and lineage shall be determined by that.
In that Kali age, accumulations of wealth will end with the household, the intellect will likewise end with material objects, and purposes will end with mere sensory enjoyments.
In the Kali age, women will become wanton and full of longing for pleasure;
they will be covetous of men who have acquired wealth through unjust means.
O twice-born ones, even when entreated by a friend, a man will then suffer the loss of his own interest even at a stake of half a half-measure.
O Brahmin, at that time in the Kali age, the mind will always be possessed of manliness,
and respect toward cows will shine forth as being connected with the giving of milk.
Due to the fear of drought, the people will for the most part be distressed by the fear of hunger;
at that time, they will all have their gaze fixed upon the sky.
Like ascetics subsisting on roots, leaves, and fruits, those men,
afflicted by that drought, will bring about their own destruction.
In the Kali age, due to their negligence, men will constantly and perpetually encounter famine, affliction, and lack of sovereignty, as well as the obstruction of all happiness.

When the Kali age has arrived, those who eat without bathing will no longer perform the worship of the fire, the deities, or guests, nor will they perform the rites of offering funeral cakes and water.
In the Kali age, women will be greedy, short of stature, intent on eating large quantities of food, prolific, and possessed of little fortune.
Then, scratching their heads with both hands, women, being unrestrained, will disobey the commands of their elders and husbands.
In the Kali age, women will be intent on nourishing themselves alone, prone to anger, devoid of bodily refinement, and speakers of harsh falsehoods.
Women of noble family will become immoral and of evil conduct, constantly longing for men of wicked character.
Mares will likewise take up the Veda according to its rules,
while householders will neither offer oblations nor give even what is appropriate.
Indeed, those living in the forest might become attached to the consumption of village food;
even monks may become sons, bound by the machinery of affection and kinship.
When the Kali age has arrived, kings will not be protectors but plunderers under the pretext of taxes, seizing the wealth of the people.
In the Kali age, whoever possesses horses, chariots, and elephants shall become a king;
and whoever is weak shall all become a servant.
The Vaiśyas, having abandoned their own duties such as agriculture and trade,
will come to live by the livelihood of Śūdras, subsisting through the work of artisans.

Likewise, Śūdras who have taken the vow of begging for alms, base individuals wearing the marks of renunciation, and those who are unrefined by sacraments will resort to a livelihood dependent on heretical sects.
Greatly oppressed by famine and the burden of taxes, the people,
filled with suffering, will flee to regions where wheat, rice, barley, and other grains abound.
When the path of the Vedas has vanished and the people are then filled with heresy,
the lifespan of living beings will become short due to the increase of unrighteousness.
While men perform terrible austerities not ordained by the scriptures,
child mortality will arise due to the fault of the king.
In the Kali age, the birth of women will occur at five, six, or seven years of age;
likewise for men, it will occur at nine, eight, or ten years of age.
And at that time, the appearance of grey hair will occur at twelve years of age;
indeed, in the Kali age, no one shall live for twenty years.
In the Kali age, men of little wisdom, wearing false signs and possessing wicked hearts,
perish in a short time because of that very reason.
Whenever a life of heresy is observed here,
then and there the increase of the Kali age is to be inferred by the wise.
Whenever there is a decline of the virtuous who follow the path of the Vedas,
at that very time the increase of the Kali age is to be inferred by the wise.
O Brahmins, when the undertakings of men who practice dharma come to naught, then the preeminence of the Kali age should be inferred by the discerning.
Whenever the Supreme Person, the Lord of sacrifices,
is not worshipped by men with sacrifices, then the power of the Kali age is to be known.
O best of the twice-born, when there is no delight in the declarations of the Vedas and an attachment to heretical doctrines, then the increase of the Kali age is to be inferred by the wise.
O Brahmins, in the Kali age, men afflicted by heresy will not worship Viṣṇu, the Lord of the world, the Creator of all, and the Supreme Sovereign.
"What is the use of gods? What is the use of twice-born brahmins or the Vedas? What is the use of purification or talk of water?"—thus will men corrupted by heresy prattle.
When the Kali age has arrived, O Brahmins, the rain-clouds will produce little rain, the fruit of the crops will likewise be meager, and even that fruit will be lacking in essence.
In the Kali age, garments will reach only to the knees, trees will mostly be of the *śamī* variety, and likewise, the social orders (*varṇas*) will consist mostly of *śūdras*.
When the Kali age has arrived, grains will consist mostly of small seeds, milk will consist mostly of clarified butter, and the only ointment will be that made from uśīra root.

O best of sages, in the Kali age, for men, mothers-in-law and fathers-in-law are the primary elders; wives are those who carry away the grain from the threshing floor and other such places; and friends are merely those who take food from one's house.
"Whose mother is he, whose father is he, since man is composed of his own karma?"—
thus will men follow after their fathers-in-law and proclaim.
Overcome again and again by the defects born of speech, mind, and body,
men of little intelligence will commit sins day after day.
O twice-born ones, whatever brings suffering to those who are devoid of truth, impure, and shameless— all that shall come to pass in the Kali age.
Devoid of Vedic study and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, and bereft of *svadhā* and *svāhā*,
there will then be only a very few brahmins remaining in the world.
In that [Kṛta Yuga], one performs an unsurpassed mass of merit in a very short time,
which is indeed accomplished through austerity alone in the Kṛta Yuga.
The sages said:
At what time does even a small amount of dharma yield a very great fruit?
You ought to explain this in its entirety; a desire to hear it has arisen within us.
Vyāsa said:
O Brahmins, in the blessed Kali age, great fruit may be obtained with little effort;
likewise, women and Śūdras shall become blessed—learn further concerning this.
That which is accomplished in ten years during the Kṛta age is achieved in a single year during the Tretā;
that same result in the Dvāpara is attained in a month, and in the Kali age, it is attained in a single day and night.
O twice-born ones, because a man obtains the fruit of austerity, celibacy, recitation,
and so forth, it is right to say that the Kali age is excellent.
What one attains by meditating in the Kṛta age, by sacrificing with rituals in the Tretā, and by worshipping in the Dvāpara,
that one attains in the Kali age simply by chanting the praises of Keśava.
In this Kali age, a person attains an extraordinary excellence of dharma with very little effort; O knowers of dharma, for that reason I am pleased with the Kali age.
First, the Vedas must be mastered by the twice-born who are devoted to the practice of vows;
thereafter, having attained righteousness, they should perform sacrifices according to the rules with their wealth.
For the twice-born, idle talk, idle food, and idle wealth lead to their downfall; likewise, they must remain restrained in the company of women.
O twice-born ones, there are faults in all their undertakings when performed improperly; furthermore, food, drink, and other such things do not come to them by their own will.
Therefore, because they are dependent in all their undertakings,
those who are endowed with discipline worship the worlds with great hardship.
By the mere service of the twice-born, a Śūdra becomes entitled to perform the *pākayajña* sacrifices;
he thus conquers his own world and is therefore more blessed than them.
"O tigers among sages, since there is no desire for them regarding what may or may not be eaten, nor regarding sinful acts, therefore that restraint has been called 'good'."
Wealth should always be acquired by men without violating their own dharma; it should be bestowed upon worthy recipients and offered in sacrifice according to the prescribed rules.
O best of the twice-born, there is great hardship in its acquisition and in its protection;
likewise, it should be understood that for men, its proper application is profound and difficult.
O best of the twice-born, by these and other such afflictions,
men indeed conquer their own worlds, beginning with those of Prajāpati, in due order.
O twice-born ones, by serving her husband through action, mind, and speech, a woman attains this very realm, and from that, the same world as him (sālokya).
Just as a man [obtains] those very things without excessive great effort,
so too did I, that woman, say "Excellent" to the third utterance of his.
O brahmins, I have told you this for which purpose you have come here; ask whatever you desire, and I shall explain it clearly to you.
In the Kali age, indeed, dharma is accomplished with very little effort by men whose every sin has been washed away by the waters of their own virtues.
O best of sages, [this is attained] by Śūdras who are intent on serving the twice-born,
and likewise by women through the effortless service of their husbands alone.
Therefore, I consider even this triad to be most auspicious for me;
for the twice-born, there is hardship in the practice of dharma during the Kṛta and subsequent ages.
Likewise, O best of sages, at the end of the age, men shall attain perfection through even slight austerity; blessed indeed, they shall practice righteousness.
"O twice-born ones who know the Dharma, that which was intended by you has been told by me, even though unasked; what else should be done? (BrP 230.82)
The sages said:
"Whether it be near or far, if we do not know the time,
then we long for the end of the age, the destruction of the Dvāpara Yuga."
For we have reached this time because of this thirst for the Dharma;
may we grasp the supreme Dharma with ease through little effort.
O Knower of Dharma, you ought to explain by means of omens that the end of the age has arrived, producing terror and agitation, and that the Dharma has been destroyed.
Vyāsa said:
At the end of the Yuga, kings will arise who do not protect their subjects but seize their share of the tribute, being solely intent on protecting themselves.
At the end of the age, there will be kings who are not kṣatriyas, brahmins who live by the service of śūdras, and śūdras who adopt the conduct of brahmins.

O best of sages, at the end of the Yuga, those learned in the Vedas and those who carry arrows on their backs (warriors), though devoid of ritual action and sacrificial offerings, will eat together in a single row.
At the end of the age, those lowest of men— unrefined, intent on wealth, and fond of liquor and meat— will take pleasure with the wives of their friends.
At the end of the age, thieves will abide by the conduct of kings, kings will have the character of thieves, and servants indeed will enjoy wealth that has not been assigned to them.
At the end of the age, wealth will be praiseworthy while the conduct of the virtuous is unhonored,
and there will be no censure for the fallen.
Men with lost noses, disheveled hair, and deformed features,
as well as women who give birth before reaching sixteen years of age, shall come into being.
At the end of the age, the countryside will have its pillars of justice ruined, crossroads will be infested with jackals, and women will have their hair as their only ornament.
All the twice-born Vājasaneyikas shall profess Brahman;
even those who speak like Śūdras and Brāhmaṇas dwelling among the lowest castes shall do so.
With white teeth, their senses conquered, shaven-headed and clad in saffron robes,
Śūdras will preach the Dharma, living by means of deceitful intellects.
One should know that when the age has reached its end, there will be an abundance of beasts of prey, a total depletion of cattle, and the displacement of the virtuous.

At the end of the Yuga, those from the lowest castes will dwell among the middle classes, while those from the middle classes will live among the lowest; all people will be devoid of shame and utterly ruined.
At the end of the Yuga, the best of the twice-born will become sellers of the fruits of asceticism and sacrifice,
and the seasons will become inverted.
Likewise, in the Kali age, when the Yuga has declined, two-year-old draft animals will carry the plow,
and the rain-cloud will pour down rain in streaks.
For all those born into families of heroes indeed become lords through forbearance;
yet at the end of the age, all subjects will become as lowly as the ground.
When the age has passed away, sons will likewise be given as gifts by their fathers,
and men will no longer practice righteousness.
At the end of the age, the earth will abound in saline soil, the roads will be infested with thieves, and all merchants indeed will become such.
In the same way, sons divide the paternal inheritance given to them;
even though they strive to seize it, they become adversaries through greed and other such motives.
When delicacy, beauty, and even precious jewels have come to ruin,
at the end of the Yuga, women will be adorned only by their hair.
When the end of the age has arrived, the householder who lacks vigor will find his delight therein; there is no other pleasure equal to that of a wife.
Abounding in the unvirtuous and the ignoble, endowed with false appearances, with few men and many women— these are the characteristics of the end of the age.
The world will be full of many beggars and will not give to one another;
impoverished by kings, thieves, fire, punishment, and the like, it will go to ruin.
At the end of the age, crops will be fruitless, the young will possess the character of the old, and those lacking virtue will be happy in the world.
In the rainy season, harsh winds will blow downward, raining down gravel;
and the next world will become uncertain at the end of the Yuga.
At the onset of the Yuga, Kṣatriyas will first become like Vaiśyas, subsisting on wealth and grain, and they will no longer be true kinsmen.
In the declining age, oaths and pledges will be seen as non-binding,
and debts will be repaid only after the loss of one's modesty.
At the end of the age, the joy of men will be fruitless, while their anger will bear fruit;
even goats will be slaughtered for the sake of milk.
In this very way, a sacrifice not ordained by the scriptures will come to pass; men who consider themselves wise will treat it as authoritative.
Without a doubt, there will be those who do not expound what is taught in the scriptures;
for indeed, everyone knows everything without having served their elders. (BrP 231.32)
When the end of the age has arrived, there will be no one called "unskilled";
the stars will not be separated from their paths, nor will the twice-born deviate from their duties.
When the end of the age has arrived, kings will be mostly thieves;
they will be like eunuchs, deceitful, drinkers of liquor, yet claim to be expounders of the Veda.
At the end of the age, the best of the twice-born will perform horse sacrifices;
they will officiate for those unworthy of such rites and consume what is forbidden as food.
When the end of the age has arrived, brahmins afflicted by thirst for wealth will utter the word "bhoḥ," and no one at all will recite [the Vedas].
The women had but a single ear-ornament and were clad in garments of gavedhuka grass;
the stars have lost their luster, and the ten directions are overturned.
At the end of the Yuga, the twilight glow will be like a limb scorched by fire;
sons will send their fathers away, and daughters-in-law will send their mothers-in-law to perform their own tasks.
In this way, women and men alike will dwell during the ages;
likewise, the twice-born will eat without having first performed their preliminary rites, and they will fail to offer oblations into the sacred fires.
Without having given alms or offerings, men will eat by themselves;
and women, having deceived their sleeping husbands, will go elsewhere.

In this degenerate age, there will be no one who is ill, nor one who is deformed, nor one who is industrious, nor one who is envious; nor will there be anyone who returns a favor for what has been done.
The sages said:
"When dharma has been thus delayed, where will human beings dwell, oppressed by taxes, and what shall be their food and their way of life?"
What will be their duties, what will they strive for, what will be their stature, and what will be their lifespan? And reaching what limit will they attain the Kṛta Yuga?
Vyāsa said:
After this, when dharma has declined and the people are likewise devoid of virtue,
they will encounter the ruin of their character and suffer a decrease in lifespan.
From the loss of lifespan comes the loss of strength; from the loss of strength comes discoloration;
from discoloration comes the affliction of disease; and from the affliction of disease comes despondency.
Through world-weariness comes self-awakening; from awakening comes the nature of righteousness.
Having thus reached the highest pinnacle, they shall attain the Kṛta Yuga.
In brief, some were devoted to righteousness, some had attained a state of neutrality,
some wondered what their duty was, and some were filled with curiosity.
"Direct perception and inference are the means of valid cognition"—this is what some have determined; yet other people will declare everything to be invalid. (BrP 231.48)
Moreover, there will be certain deluded men who are devoted to nihilism, destroyers of the Dharma, and brahmins who consider themselves learned.
At that time, those men will be devoid of knowledge, excluded from the understanding of the scriptures, hypocritical, and relying solely on what is to be believed based on immediate circumstances.
