Likewise, when the Dharma has fallen into disorder, people who honor the most excellent [teachings] will practice what is auspicious, being devoted to generosity and ethical conduct.
Eating everything, self-indulgent, pitiless, and shameless—they will become so in that world; such is the characteristic of that degenerate age (kaṣāya).
In this age of affliction by the passions, which destroys steadfastness in knowledge,
those who remain unadorned by worldly attachments will attain perfection in a short time.
O Brahmins, when people take recourse to the eternal livelihood of the Brahmins among those of lower castes, that is a sign of the age of degeneration (kaṣāya).
In the waning age, there will be great warfare, heavy rain, violent winds, and intense heat; that is the characteristic of the degenerate era (kaṣāya).
When the end of the age has arrived, Yakṣas in the form of Brahmins and kings who pierce the ears [of others] will enjoy the earth.
Devoid of Vedic study and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, these false leaders are full of pride;
they are flesh-eaters in the guise of Brahmins, devouring all things while their vows are in vain.
They will be fools, intent on wealth, greedy, base, and possessed of base retinues; they will be engaged in worldly transactions and fallen from the eternal Dharma.
They were stealers of others' jewels, violators of others' wives,
slaves to their desires, evil-minded, deceitful, and fond of rash acts.
And while those people are prevailing in every way,
there will arise sages of manifold forms who do not exist [now].
In the Kali age, those who are the principal persons born shall all be worshipped by human beings through the medium of their stories.
There will be thieves of grain as well as stealers of clothing;
they will seize both food and the things to be eaten, and they will carry off baskets.
Thieves shall be the plunderers of thieves, and the slayer shall be the slayer of the slayer;
and when the destruction of thieves has been accomplished by means of thieves, there will be security.
In this essence-less and turbulent age, when all activity has ceased and things remain stagnant,
men, oppressed by the burden of taxes, will take refuge in the forest.
When the sacrificial rites have ceased, demons, beasts of prey,
insects, mice, and serpents will assail human beings.
At the end of the age, men will become excellent in their learning; they will find security, abundance, health, and harmony among their kinsmen.
Acting as their own protectors yet being their own thieves, and equipped with rafts and provisions,
they will arise in various circles in every land, each separately.
At that time, due to the exhaustion of the age, all men will be deprived of their own countries, rendered destitute, and separated from their kinsmen.
Then, taking their children with them, all those men, tormented by the fear of hunger, will flee in terror and cross the Kauśikī river.
Men will take refuge in Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, Kāśmīra, and Kośala,
as well as in the mountain valleys at the edge of the Ṛṣika forest.
And the entire slope of the Himalayas and the shore of the salt ocean,
along with various withered leaves, bark garments, and animal skins.
Having built them themselves, they will dwell in them when that end of the age has arrived;
and men will live in the forests together with hosts of Mlecchas.
The earth will neither be empty nor will it be devoid of forests; moreover, rulers of men who were not protectors will become protectors.
Human beings will subsist on deer, fish, birds, beasts of prey, snakes, and insects, as well as on honey, vegetables, fruits, and roots.
Subsisting on withered leaves and fruits, and wearing garments of bark and skins,
they will dwell just like the community of sages, having prepared these things for themselves.
Without having prepared the soil for seeds and striking them with wooden stakes,
they will constantly tend to goats, sheep, donkeys, and camels.
Those dwelling on the banks will block the currents of the rivers for the sake of water,
bartering with one another through the trade of cooked food.
Those who possess body hair that has grown in its natural state, yet is accumulated with internal impurities,
will have many offspring but be devoid of progeny, and be bereft of noble lineage and virtuous conduct.
Thus at that time, men will live by unrighteousness;
being base, the people will likewise follow a base dharma.
And there the maximum lifespan of mortals will be thirty years;
they will be weak, exhausted by sensory objects, and overwhelmed by old age and sorrow.
Then, due to diseases, there will be a decay of their sense faculties;
because of the obstruction of the conditions for life, they will turn away from sense objects.
They will become desirous of hearing [the teachings], delighting in the sight of the virtuous,
and they will practice truthfulness as worldly affairs diminish.
And due to the non-attainment of their desires, those who are virtuous in nature will perform ritual exertion,
being themselves afflicted by decay.
Thus, for those who are intent on service, generosity, truthfulness, and the protection of living beings,
prosperity shall descend upon them once they have set foot upon the path of Dharma.
For those who have gained inferential knowledge and are revolving within the qualities,
having discerned what is truly sweet, only the Dharma is seen.
Just as they had reached the sequence of decline, so too did they attain the sequence of prosperity;
then, when the Dharma was firmly upheld, they beheld the Kṛta Yuga.
In the Kṛta age, there is virtuous conduct; in the Age of Deterioration (Kaṣāya), decline is said to occur.
Yet this time is actually one and the same, like the moon appearing diminished in color.
Just as the moon is obscured by darkness, so is the Kali Yuga;
and just as the moon is freed from darkness, so too is that Kṛta Yuga.
They know that the Supreme Brahman is the true meaning of the Veda;
yet here, an undiscriminated and uncomprehended inheritance is being maintained.
Austerity is indeed called the speech of one’s desire, for austerity makes one venerable;
the accomplishment of action occurs through qualities, and qualities are purified by action.
But a blessing, conforming to place and time, is uttered by the sages for each person according to the requirements of each age and at the appropriate moment.
The fulfillment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as for the gods;
auspicious and meritorious blessings, and likewise long life in age after age.
Likewise, the revolutions of the ages have been proceeding for a long time by the very nature of destiny; the world of living beings does not remain still for even a moment.
Vyāsa said: "Undergoing transformation through destruction and emergence,
the dissolution of all beings is threefold."
It is considered to be occasional, natural, and likewise absolute.
The dissolution at the end of their kalpa is the occasional (naimittika) Brahma-dissolution;
absolute liberation (mokṣa) is the primordial (prākṛta) dissolution occurring at the end of two parārdhas.
The sages said:
"O Blessed One, please explain the number of a parārdha as it has been described;
for it is known that the dissolution of the material world (prākṛta-pratisaṃcara) is twice that duration."
Vyāsa said:
O twice-born ones, each successive place is counted as ten times the value of the preceding one;
thus, at the eighteenth stage, it is designated as a *parārdha*.
O twice-born ones, when that period of a parārdha is doubled, that is the primary dissolution (prākṛtalaya);
at that time, the entire manifest universe indeed goes to dissolution along with its cause in the unmanifest.
This human blink, measured by its mere duration, constitutes one mātrā;
fifteen of those make a kāṣṭhā, and thirty kāṣṭhās likewise make a kalā.
A *nāḍikā* is by measure fifteen *kalās*;
by weight of water, it is twelve and a half *palas*.
A vessel made with four gold māṣas as its perforations, each measuring four finger-breadths according to the Māgadha standard, is traditionally defined as a prastha of water.
O best of the twice-born, two nāḍikās make one muhūrta;
thirty muhūrtas make a day and night; and likewise, thirty days make a month.
Twelve months constitute a day and night in heaven;
three hundred and sixty such years constitute a year for the enemies of the Asuras.
Twelve thousand of those [years] are declared to be a cycle of four ages (caturyuga);
a thousand cycles of four ages, however, is said to be a single day of Brahmā.
O best of the twice-born, fourteen Manus exist there during that kalpa;
and at its conclusion, O brahmins, occurs the occasional dissolution of Brahmā (brahmanaimittika-laya).
O best of the twice-born, listen as I describe his exceedingly fierce essential nature; thereafter, I shall further explain the dissolution of the primordial matter (prakṛti).
At the end of a thousand cycles of the four yugas, when the surface of the earth has almost entirely perished,
an exceedingly fierce drought occurs that lasts for a hundred years.
Then, O best of sages, those beings who possess little essence perish in great numbers due to the excessive oppression of the earth.
Then that Blessed One Kṛṣṇa, the imperishable one who has assumed the form of Rudra,
strives to bring about the destruction of all creatures who abide within himself.
Then, O best of sages, that Blessed Viṣṇu, stationed within the seven rays of the sun, drinks up all waters without exception.
Having indeed drunk all the waters contained within living beings and creatures,
O brahmins, he brings the entire surface of the earth to desiccation.
It brings to exhaustion all the oceans, rivers, mountains, mountain springs,
and whatever water exists within the netherworlds.
Then, due to the disappearance of that [water] as well,
seven suns, the thousand-rayed ones, are born there, nourished by their intake of water.
Then, O twice-born ones, seven blazing suns appear below and above,
burning the entire triple world together with the subterranean realms of Pātāla.
But as the three worlds— including the expanse of mountains, forests, and oceans— are being consumed by those blazing fires resembling radiant suns, they become devoid of moisture.
Then, O twice-born ones, the entire three worlds become devoid of trees and water,
and this earth takes on an appearance resembling the back of a tortoise.
Then that Hara, the Rudra of the fire of time who destroys the creation of beings,
burns the netherworlds below from the heat of the sighs of the serpent Śeṣa.
Having burned all the netherworlds,
that great fire reached the earth and consumed the entire surface of the world.
Then, that terrible one, possessing great whirlpools of garlands of flames, revolves right there throughout the entire world of Bhuva and the world of Svarga.
Then the entire triple world appeared like a frying pan,
surrounded by a whirling mass of flames, as their strength was utterly exhausted.
Then, O twice-born ones, the inhabitants of both worlds, overcome by heat and deprived of their space, go to Maharloka.
Therefore, the worlds scorched by that great heat go beyond that to Janaloka; seeking the highest, they proceed there after ten cycles.
Then, O best of sages, Janārdana, having assumed the form of Rudra and having burnt the entire world,
produces clouds born from the breath of his mouth.
Then, resembling herds of elephants, thundering and flashing with lightning,
the terrible Saṃvartaka clouds arise in the sky.
Some clouds resembled collyrium, some were like white water-lilies;
some were smoke-colored and thick, while others were yellow.
Some had the appearance of the color of turmeric, and others were like the juice of lac;
some resembled beryl, and others were like sapphire.
Others resemble conch shells and jasmine flowers; likewise, some resemble *jātī* flowers and *kunda* blossoms; some resemble the *indragopa* insect, and others resemble realgar.
Some thick clouds rise up resembling lotus petals;
some have the form of great cities, and others resemble mountains.
Others resemble gabled palaces, while some are dense masses like solid ground;
possessing massive bodies and a great roar, they fill the expanse of the sky.
O Brahmins, raining down great torrents, they extinguish that most terrifying fire which has spread throughout the three worlds.
And when the fire has been extinguished, O best of sages, those clouds also rain for more than a hundred years, flooding the entire world.
Having flooded the entire earth with torrents as thick as axles,
O twice-born ones, they likewise flood the world of Bhuva and the world above, reaching up to heaven.
When the world has been turned to darkness and all things mobile and immobile have perished,
those great clouds rain down for more than a hundred years.
Vyāsa said:
O best of the twice-born, when the waters have risen and reached the abode of the Seven Sages,
this entire triple-world then becomes a single ocean.
Then, O brahmins, the wind born from the breath of Viṣṇu brings those clouds to destruction after more than a hundred years of rain.
The Blessed One, who consists of all beings, is inconceivable and the creator of beings;
he is the beginningless origin of the universe, having drunk the wind entirely.
Then, in that single ocean,
the Lord Hari, the primordial creator, the Blessed One, assuming the form of Brahmā, lies upon the bed of Śeṣa.
He was praised by the Siddhas, such as Sanaka and others, who had gone to Janaloka,
and was meditated upon by those seeking liberation who had gone to Brahmaloka.
The Supreme Lord, having entered into his divine yogic sleep consisting of his own creative power (māyā),
meditated upon himself under the name of Vāsudeva.
O best of Brahmins, this is the dissolution known as the occasional (naimittika);
the "occasion" therein is Hari, who lies there assuming the form of Brahmā.
When the Soul of All awakens, then this world moves;
when Acyuta rests upon the bed of Māyā, all this closes its eyes.
That which is a day for the Lotus-born [Brahmā], consisting of a thousand cycles of four yugas,
is said to be his night when the world has become a single ocean.
Then, having awakened at the end of the night, the Unborn One, Viṣṇu, assuming the form of Brahmā, effects creation again, just as was previously told to you.
Thus, O twice-born ones, this dissolution of the kalpa—the occasional dissolution—has been described to you; now hear about the supreme elemental dissolution.
O twice-born ones, when the dwelling for the bed has been properly prepared by means of [protection against] drought, fire, and other such dangers,
throughout all the worlds and indeed in all the nether regions (pātālas), [the Lord remains there].
When that dissolution, brought about by the will of Kṛṣṇa, has set in— the withdrawal of the modifications beginning with Mahat into their source— there occurs the re-absorption into the particular.
Water indeed first swallows the quality of smell and the others belonging to earth;
then, its smell having been taken away, the earth becomes fit for dissolution.
When the subtle element of smell has perished, the earth becomes of the nature of water;
then the waters set forth, impetuous and with a great roar.
Filling this entire world, they remain and move about;
by means of their surging waters alone, they encompass the Lokāloka mountain on all sides.
That quality which belongs to water is consumed by light;
and when thoroughly heated, the waters perish due to the destruction of the subtle element of taste.
Then the waters, possessing the essence of nectar, indeed attain the state of light;
for when the water is in the state of fire, it is enveloped on all sides by radiance.
Then that fire, having pervaded everything, consumes that water;
and as it gradually fills all this world, it envelops it on every side.
When that [fire] is spread with rays horizontally, upwards, and likewise downwards,
the wind devours even the supreme form of light, the maker of radiance.
Then, when that [element] has dissolved and become the wind-nature pervading all things,
and the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra) has perished, the fire has completed its manifestation.
Then the light subsides and the great wind blows violently;
at that time, the world is without light and the fire is established within the wind.
Then, having reached the dissolution arising from the wind within himself,
the wind blows violently upward and across the ten directions.
Then space swallows the quality of wind, which is touch;
thereupon the wind becomes quiescent, while space remains unobstructed.
Formless, without taste or touch, odorless and incorporeal,
it shines forth as something exceedingly great, completely filling everything.
That space, characterized by sound, is spherical;
as mere sound, it thus exists pervading everything.
Then the source of the elements (bhūtādi) again swallows its quality, sound;
for when the elements and the senses have simultaneously merged into the source of the elements, indeed.
For this Bhūtādi, consisting of self-conceit and characterized by tamas, is so described;
and the great intellect, being discerning, swallows even that Bhūtādi.
The Earth is vast and great at the edge of the world, as well as within and without;
likewise, the seven primordial natures (prakṛtis) are thus arranged in sequence by the one of great intelligence.
Through the processes of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), however, all those [elements] enter into one another,
whereby this entire egg is enveloped and dissolves into the waters.
The seven worlds, including the mountains and extending to the oceans at the edge of the seven continents,
are indeed obstructed by water here, yet that water is consumed by light.
Light dissolves into the wind, the wind dissolves into space, and the origin of the elements (bhūtādi) swallows that space; likewise, the Great One (mahat) swallows it.

O twice-born ones, O best of the twice-born, Prakṛti swallows the Great One (Mahat) along with these [elements], when it is in a state of equilibrium among its qualities (guṇas), being neither excessive nor deficient.
It is declared that *prakṛti* is the cause, the *pradhāna*, the supreme instrument;
such is this entire *prakṛti*, whose nature consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
O Brahmins, the manifest form dissolves into that unmanifest;
it is again one, pure, imperishable, eternal, and all-pervading.
O best of the twice-born, even that portion of the Supreme Self, which is present in all beings,
is where all conceptualizations of name, caste, and so forth cease to exist.
When the object of knowledge consists of pure existence, being of the nature of consciousness, and is the supreme Self of the self—
that is Brahman, that is the supreme abode, the Supreme Self, and the Supreme Lord.
That Viṣṇu is indeed all this, from which one does not return again;
he is the primordial nature (prakṛti) which I have described, whose form consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
Both of these, the individual soul (puruṣa) and the intellect, dissolve into the Supreme Self;
and the Supreme Self is the support of all, the Supreme Lord.
He is celebrated under the name Viṣṇu in the Vedas and in the Vedāntas;
Vedic action is of two kinds: that which leads to worldly involvement and that which leads to renunciation.
By both of those [paths], that embodiment of sacrifice is worshipped by men;
indeed, he is worshipped through the paths of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas as they proceed.
The Lord of Sacrifice, the Person of Sacrifice, the Supreme Person among men,
whose self is knowledge— he, the embodiment of knowledge, is worshipped through the yoga of knowledge.
And through the paths of yoga when they have ceased, Viṣṇu is the bestower of the fruit of liberation;
whatever object whatsoever is denoted by short, long, or protracted [vowels], [it is he].
And whatever is beyond the scope of speech, all that is the imperishable Viṣṇu;
he alone is both the manifest and the unmanifest, he alone is the imperishable Puruṣa.
The Supreme Self, the Soul of the Universe, Hari who assumes the form of the universe—
in Him, that primordial nature (prakṛti), consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest, is dissolved.
And as for that Puruṣa, O Brahmins, who exists within that unmanifest self—
the period of time consisting of two parārdhas which I have described, O twice-born ones— BrP_233.46.
O best of Brahmins, that day of Viṣṇu, the Lord,
is said to occur when the manifest world has dissolved into primordial nature (prakṛti), and likewise when primordial nature has dissolved into the Puruṣa.
O ascetics, while he remains there, his night is of that same duration;
for that eternal Supreme Self, there is neither day nor night.
Nevertheless, this is spoken of as belonging to that Lord by way of metaphorical designation;
thus, O tigers among sages, has the dissolution of the primordial nature (prākṛta-laya) been described.
Vyāsa said:
O brahmins, having understood the threefold suffering— beginning with that which is internal— the wise man,
possessing the knowledge and dispassion that have arisen, attains ultimate dissolution.
The internal [suffering] is also twofold: physical and likewise mental. The physical is divided into many varieties; listen now to that.
By means of various ailments such as diseases of the head, catarrh, fever, colic, fistula-in-ano, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, swelling, asthma, vomiting, and so forth; (BrP 234.3)
In that way, the suffering born of the body is divided into those known as eye diseases, dysentery, leprosy, and bodily ailments;
you should now hear about the mental [suffering].
Born of desire, anger, fear, hatred, greed, delusion, and despondency, as well as grief, envy, contempt, jealousy, avarice, and humiliation; (BrP 234.5)
O best of the twice-born, mental suffering also occurs in many ways;
through such various distinctions as these, suffering is indeed remembered as being internal (ādhyātmika).
The *ādhibhautika* [suffering] of humans is produced by wild animals, birds, humans, and the like, as well as by *piśācas*, serpents, *rākṣasas*, reptiles, and so forth.
O best of the foremost twice-born, that suffering arising from cold, heat, wind, rain, water, lightning, and so forth, is called *ādhibhautika* (supernatural). BrP_234.8 //
O best of sages, suffering arising from the womb, birth, old age, ignorance, death, and likewise from hell, is divided into thousands of varieties.
Within the womb, the creature— possessing a delicate body— is enveloped by the placenta and covered with much impurity,
its collection of bones in the back and neck being bent.
Afflicted by excessive pain, he is tormented by his mother’s food that is extremely bitter, pungent, sharp, hot, and salty, and by those who consume it with great intensity.
Though he was the master of himself regarding the extension and contraction [of his limbs] and other such actions,
he lay in the great mire of excrement and urine, oppressed in every way.
Then, breathless yet conscious, remembering hundreds of previous births,
he remains in the womb in extreme suffering, bound by his own karma.
Being born with a face defiled by feces, blood, urine, and semen,
his skeletal frame is tormented by the *prājāpatya* wind.
Turned head-downwards by those powerful winds of birth,
the afflicted one emerges from the mother’s womb with great suffering.
Having fallen into a great swoon and being touched by the external air,
O best of sages, he undergoes a loss of consciousness once he is born again.
With his limbs pierced as if by thorns and torn as if by saws,
he fell upon the earth like a worm from a putrid sore.
Incapable even of scratching himself and powerless even to turn over,
he receives nourishment such as the drinking of breast milk only through the will of another.
Lying upon a bed of impurity, even while being bitten by insects, gadflies, and the like,
he is simply not capable of warding them off.
One encounters many sufferings of birth immediately following birth,
as well as those arising from external beings and so forth, during the state of childhood.
Enveloped by the darkness of ignorance, with a deluded inner faculty, a man does not know: from whence [he came], who he is, where he will go, or what his true nature is.
By what bond am I bound? What is the cause and what is not the cause?
What is to be done and what is not to be done? What should be spoken and what should not be spoken?
What is dharma and what is adharma? How indeed does one abide in it? What is to be done and what is not to be done, or what possesses virtue and what possesses fault?
Thus, great suffering born of ignorance is experienced by men who are like beasts, deluded, devoted solely to their genitals and bellies.
Ignorance is a state of darkness (tamas); from it, O twice-born ones, the activities of undertaking actions proceed for the ignorant, and from that follows the neglect of prescribed duties.
The great seers have declared that hell is the fruit resulting from the neglect of one's duties;
therefore, for the ignorant, there is supreme suffering both in this world and in the next.
And a man whose body is worn out by old age, with limbs grown flaccid, with loose and decayed teeth, covered in wrinkles, sinews, and veins; 234.27.
With his eyes lost at a distance, with stars appearing within his sky-like mouth,
with clusters of hair protruding from the openings of his nostrils, his body was trembling.
With the entire collection of bones in his back bent forward as all his strength became manifest,
his digestive fire having been extinguished, he took little food and remained with minimal activity.
His movements—walking, rising, lying down, and sitting—are performed with great difficulty;
his hearing and sight grow dim, and his face is fouled by trickling saliva.
With all his faculties no longer under his control and facing death,
he is unable to remember at that very moment even those things experienced just prior.
When the sentence was uttered but once, he experienced great exhaustion;
he suffered from insomnia brought on by the distress of labored breathing, coughing, and illness.
The aged man is raised up by one person and likewise laid down by another;
he is treated with contempt and humiliation by his servants, his own sons, and his wife.
With all his purity exhausted, longing for recreation and food,
he became an object of ridicule even to his attendants, while all his kinsmen were despondent.
Recollecting his own past actions as if experienced in another birth,
he sighs deeply in his youth, greatly tormented.
Having experienced such sufferings as these in old age,
hear now also of those sufferings which one encounters at death.
Then the man, with his neck, feet, and hands slackened, was overcome by trembling;
at times he was utterly exhausted, and at times he was endowed with the strength of consciousness.
"Regarding gold, grain, sons, wife, servants, houses,
and so forth— how will these fare?"— thus he was exceedingly agitated by the sense of "mine."
With his bone-joints being severed by great diseases that know the vital spots— terrible as saws and fierce as the arrows of Death— he is torn apart.
With his eyes rolling, repeatedly tossing his hands and feet,
and with his palate, lips, and throat completely parched, he makes a gurgling sound.
Though his throat was constricted, he was oppressed by gasping breath;
he was pervaded by great heat, as well as by thirst and hunger.
Afflicted by the servants of Yama, he undergoes departure from his body due to affliction;
and thereafter, through suffering, he assumes a body for torment.
These and other terrible sufferings men endure at the time of death;
now hear those which are experienced by deceased persons in hell.
The seizing by the nooses and other instruments of Yama’s servants, the flogging with rods,
the sight of Yama himself, and the gazing upon the terrifying path.
O best of the twice-born, in that place terrifying with pits of parched grain, sand, fire, machines, weapons, and so forth, there are various individual torments and further instruments of torture.
Of those being crushed by saws, blown into the *mṛṣā* fire, split apart with axes, and even buried in the ground; ||| BrP_234.46 |||
May they be impaled upon stakes, cast into the mouths of tigers,
devoured by vultures, and consumed by leopards.
They are boiled in oil, drenched in a mire of alkaline salt,
cast down from heights, and hurled by throwing machines.
O Brahmins, there is no known limit to the number of sufferings arising from sinful causes that are experienced by those in hell.
O best of the twice-born, the path of suffering exists not only in hell;
even in heaven, there is no peace for one who fears a fall and whose merit is subject to decay.
Furthermore, a man becomes an embryo and is born again;
he dissolves back into the womb once more, and as he is being born, he goes to his end.
One dies as soon as born, whether in childhood or in youth;
O Brahmins, whatever object arises that brings pleasure to men—
That very thing becomes the seed of the tree of suffering through [attachment to] wife,
sons, friends, and so forth, as well as house, field, wealth, and the like.
"Abundant happiness is not produced for men in the same way as that which is [true] happiness," so it is said for those whose minds are scorched by the heat of the sun of the suffering of saṃsāra.
Where else can there be happiness for human beings except in the shade of the tree of liberation?
Therefore, [this] threefold class of suffering has been [described] by the wise.
For one who is destined for the states of conception, birth, old age,
and so forth, there exists that which is characterized solely by the nature of bliss, wherein all surpassing delight has been cast aside.
The attainment of the Blessed One is considered the sole and ultimate medicine;
therefore, wise men should exert effort to attain him.
O best of the twice-born, knowledge and action are said to be the causes for attaining that [liberation].
Likewise, knowledge is said to be twofold: that arising from scripture and that arising from discrimination.
The Supreme Brahman arises from discernment and consists of the scripture of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahma);
whereas ignorance is like blinding darkness, and that which arises from the senses is like a lamp.
O best of sages, just as the sun is, so indeed is that knowledge born of discernment which Manu also declared after recollecting the meaning of the Vedas.
Therefore, listen to this as I speak regarding this connection:
two Brahmans are to be known—the Brahman of Sound (śabdabrahman) and that which is the Supreme Brahman.
"One who is proficient in the Śabdabrahman attains the Supreme Brahman;
'Two types of knowledge indeed are to be known,' so says the Atharvaṇa Śruti. (BrP 234.62)
For the attainment of the Imperishable is the higher [path], while the lower consists of the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas;
that which is unmanifest, undecaying, inconceivable, unborn, and immutable.
Ineffable and formless, devoid of hands, feet, and the like,
know it to be all-pervading, eternal, the source of all beings, and without cause.
Since all that is to be pervaded is indeed pervaded by it, the wise behold that;
that is Brahman, the supreme abode, and that is what should be meditated upon by those desiring liberation.
That subtle, supreme abode of Viṣṇu, proclaimed by the words of the Vedas,
[reveals] the origin and dissolution, as well as the coming and going of all beings.
He who knows both knowledge and ignorance is to be called the Blessed One (Bhagavān),
for he possesses in their entirety wisdom, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor.
All beings dwell there within that Supreme Self, which is denoted by the word "Bhagavat," except for those qualities and attributes that are to be abandoned.
And because he is the self of all beings, Vāsudeva is therefore remembered as such;
in ancient times, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), being questioned by the great seers, spoke this.
This is the true etymological explanation of the name Vāsudeva of Ananta:
because he dwells within all beings, and because all beings dwell within him,
Vāsudeva is therefore the Lord, the creator and ordainer of the worlds.
He is the primordial nature of all beings; having transcended all qualities and defects, he is indeed endowed with [divine] attributes; he has passed beyond all veils and is the Self of all.
By him the intermediate space between the worlds was pervaded;
for he, whose self consists of all auspicious qualities,
has brought about the creation of beings by a mere fragment of his own power.

He whose vast body is assumed at will according to his own desire, who has accomplished the welfare of the entire world, and who possesses a great treasury of splendor, strength, and sovereignty; BrP 234.72c–73a.

He is the singular mass of qualities such as his own vigor and power; he is the supreme among the supreme, in whom no afflictions or other defects exist, he who is the Lord of both the high and the low.
He is the Lord, whose nature is both individual and collective; his form is unmanifest and yet manifest;
he is the Lord of all, the seer of all, and the knower of all.
That by which the one possessing all powers, known as the Supreme Lord, is designated— that which is free from defects,
pure, supreme, stainless, and of a single form— BrP_234.75ab.
"That which is either perceived or that which is traversed is knowledge; what is other than this is said to be ignorance.
The sages said:
Now tell us of that Yoga, the medicine for the union with suffering,
by knowing which we may apply ourselves there to the Imperishable Puruṣottama.
Having heard their words, Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana,
the yogi and best among those who know yoga, then spoke with great delight.
Vyāsa said:
O brahmins, listen as I shall describe the yoga that destroys worldly existence;
by practicing which, a yogi may attain liberation, which is exceedingly difficult to reach.
Having first studied the treatises on yoga and having propitiated the guru with devotion,
the wise man should likewise study the Itihāsas, the Purāṇas, and the Vedas.
Having understood the food, the defects of yoga, and the proper place and time, the wise one—
free from dualities and without possessions— should practice yoga.
Consuming roasted barley flour, gruel, buttermilk, roots, fruits, milk,
barley-meal, broken grains, and oil-cake— such food is the means for accomplishing yoga.
Not when the mind is impaired, nor when one is puffed up with pride, nor when exhausted, nor likewise when hungry;
not during a dual affliction, nor in cold, nor in heat, nor in conditions characterized by wind.
One should not study near water that makes a sound, in a dilapidated cow-pen, at a crossroads, where reptiles dwell, in a cremation ground, on the bank of a river, or in the vicinity of fire.
One should never practice yoga at a shrine, nor on an anthill, nor in a place of danger, nor near a well, nor upon a heap of dry leaves.
I shall declare the defects that arise as obstacles for one who, out of delusion, applies himself [to yoga] while disregarding these regions.
Deafness, dullness, loss of memory, muteness, blindness, and fever arise instantly; likewise, ignorance arises in the same manner.
Therefore, a knower of yoga must always protect [the body] with all his effort,
since the body is the means for achieving dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
In a secluded hermitage, a hidden place, a silent and fearless mountain, in a clean and beautiful empty house, or in a solitary temple of the gods; BrP_235.13 //
Well-composed during the final watch of the night and the first watch of the day,
as well as during the forenoon and midday, he should be moderate in food and have his senses conquered.
Seated upon a beautiful, comfortable, and steady seat, neither too low nor too high, facing the east, free from desire, truthful in speech, and pure; BrP 235.15.
Moderate in sleep, having conquered anger, devoted to the welfare of all beings,
enduring all dualities, steadfast, with body, feet, and head held upright and even.
Placing both hands at the navel, seated peacefully in the lotus posture, fixing his gaze on the tip of the nose, and restraining his breath while remaining silent; BrP 235.17.
Having withdrawn the collection of senses into the heart by means of the mind, the sage,
with mouth closed and perfectly motionless, should utter the long *praṇava*.
Having veiled the activity of *tamas* with *rajas*, and likewise that of *rajas* with *sattva*,
he remained in the stainless and peaceful state, his eyes closed.
The yogi should constantly meditate upon the Supreme Person, who is all-pervading, stainless, and dissolved within the hollow of the heart-lotus, for he bestows liberation.
One should first place the elements that constitute the organs of action within the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña);
then the Knower of the Field is to be joined to the Supreme; thereafter, the knower of yoga performs the union.
For him whose flickering mind reaches its end within the Supreme Self after completely abandoning sense objects, the perfection of yoga is revealed.
When the mind, devoid of objects, dissolves into the supreme Brahman during meditative absorption for one disciplined in yoga, then he attains the highest state.
When the yogi’s mind becomes unattached to all actions,
having attained bliss, then he reaches nirvāṇa.
Having attained through the power of yoga the pure Supreme Person, known as the Fourth (turya), which transcends the three states, the yogi is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Free from desire for all objects of longing, seeing with affection toward all,
and possessing the realization of impermanence everywhere— such a yogi shall be liberated, and not otherwise.
The knower of yoga should not indulge the senses, but through detachment and constant application of practice, he is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Yoga does not consist in sitting in the lotus posture, nor in gazing at the tip of the nose;
rather, the union of the mind and the senses is called yoga.
Thus, O best of sages, has this Yoga been proclaimed by me, which grants liberation and is the cause of release from saṃsāra. What else do you wish to hear?
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Having heard his words, they exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!
and, having praised and honored Vyāsa, they prepared to ask him again.
The sages said:
O sage, O best of the twice-born, as we drink this nectar consisting of speech produced from the ocean of your mouth, no satiety is seen here.
Therefore, O Sage, best among bipeds, please explain in detail the Yoga that grants liberation, as well as the Sāṃkhya; we wish to hear them.
O Brahmin, how does one who is wise, learned in the Vedas, a performer of sacrifices, renowned, intelligent, free from malice, and whose mind is fixed on truth and dharma, attain the Brahman?
"Through austerity, celibacy, total renunciation, and wisdom—
whether through Sāṃkhya or Yoga— answer this which we have asked you."
You ought to explain that means by which a person attains one-pointedness of both the mind and the senses.
Vyāsa said:
No one attains perfection through anything other than knowledge and austerity, nor through anything other than restraint of the senses,
nor through anything other than the renunciation of everything.
All the great elements were created by the Self-Existent One at the beginning of creation;
they are most abundantly established within embodied beings in the multitude of living creatures.
The body of embodied beings arises from earth, moisture from water, the eyes are said to come from light,
wind is the support of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, and the space within the belly is from ether.
In his stride he is Viṣṇu, in his strength Śakra; in his stomach he is Agni when he desires to eat;
in his ears are the quarters of space, and in his sense of hearing Sarasvatī as Speech resides in his tongue.
The ears, the skin, the eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth—
these ten are called the senses, the gateways for the accomplishment of food.
One should always know sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth— these objects of the senses— as distinct from the senses themselves.
The mind yokes the senses as a charioteer yokes untrained horses;
and the inner self, residing in the heart, always yokes the mind as well.
Likewise, among all these sense organs, the mind is their sovereign;
and so too is the self of the elements the sovereign over the mind in both its restraint and its release.
The sense organs and their objects, inherent nature, consciousness, the mind,
inhalation and exhalation, and the individual soul are eternally present within the bodies of embodied beings.
There is no substratum for a being, nor are there qualities or conscious intentions;
for it is Being alone that creates fire, and never indeed the qualities.
O Brahmins, in this way the wise man, with his mind, perceives the seventeenth body— enveloped by the sixteen qualities— the Self within the self.
For this Great Self is not visible to the eye, nor indeed to all the sense organs; rather, it shines forth through the illumined mind.
One should perceive that which is without sound, touch, or form, devoid of taste and smell, immutable, bodiless within its own body, and lacking sense organs.
He who perceives that which is unmanifest and most highly honored within all mortal bodies is, after departing this life, fit for becoming Brahman.
The wise perceive with an equal vision a Brahmin endowed with knowledge and humility, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and even an outcaste.
For that one Great Self dwells within all beings, both moving and stationary, by whom all this is pervaded.
When the self of all beings sees the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self, then that soul of all beings attains Brahman.
As great as the knowing Self is within oneself, so great is the Self in the Supreme Self;
he who knows this constantly is fit for immortality.
Even the gods are bewildered on the path of one who has become the self of all beings, who seeks the welfare of all beings, and who is trackless while others seek his footprints.
Just as the movement of birds in the sky or of fish in the water cannot be seen, so too is the movement of those who possess knowledge.
Time ripens all beings by means of itself within itself;
but no one here knows that in which Time itself is ripened.
It does not receive anything above, nor across, nor below, nor again and again;
it receives nothing in the middle, nor indeed anything at all, nor anyone whatsoever.
All these worlds are situated within that; there is nothing external to them.
Even if one were to come before them, it would be like an arrow released from a bowstring.
Even if one possessed the speed of thought, one could never reach the end of the Cause;
therefore, there is nothing subtler than that, nor is there anything grosser.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces on all sides,
and with ears everywhere in the world, it stands pervading everything.
That very same [Self] is subtler than the subtle and greater than the great;
though it dwells eternally within all beings, it is not perceived.
This nature of the Self is twofold: the imperishable (akṣara) and the perishable (kṣara). The perishable exists within all beings, while the divine is the immortal imperishable.
Having made the city of nine gates his abode, the Haṃsa (the Swan), disciplined and self-controlled, dwells thus within every being, both the stationary and the moving.
Through the abandonment of conceptual constructions and by the accumulation of bodies, those who perceive the further shore declare that the Unborn attains the state of a swan.
That which was spoken by Haṃsa is both the perishable and that which is the immutable peak; having attained that imperishable state, the wise man abandons both life and birth.
Vyāsa said:
O Brahmins, since you have asked, I have here described according to the facts and in accordance with reality this Sāṃkhya, which is conjoined with knowledge.
But now, O brahmins, I shall proclaim the practice of yoga,
which consists of the complete unification of the intellect, the mind, and all the senses.
Knowledge of the all-pervading Self is this unsurpassed knowledge;
it is attained by one who is tranquil, self-controlled, and devoted to the practice of the inner self.
The wise, having completely severed the five defects of yoga, should realize that which is to be known by the Buddha who delights in the self and performs pure deeds.
One should conquer lust, anger, greed, fear, and sleep as the fifth;
one conquers anger through tranquility and lust by abandoning volitional thoughts.
By associating with virtuous beings, the wise man should strive to eliminate sleep;
he should guard his genitals and stomach through fortitude, and his hands and feet through his sight.
One should abandon fear through vigilance regarding the eye, the ear, and the mind, as well as speech and action; one should abandon hypocrisy by attending upon the wise.
Thus, one should always conquer these defects of yoga with constant vigilance;
furthermore, one should always pay homage to the fires, the Brahmins, and the deities.
One should avoid arrogant speech that is conducive to violence, even if it is pleasing to the mind;
for his seed consists of the splendor of Brahman, from which this entire world has arisen.
Of this Being of beings, the visible world of the stationary and the moving is seen;
as are meditation, study, charity, truth, modesty, straightforwardness, and forbearance.
Purity consists of the purification of the self and the restraint of the senses;
by these, one's vital energy increases and evil is cast away.
Being equal toward all beings, subsisting on whatever is obtained or not obtained,
he is cleansed of evil, radiant, moderate in diet, and has conquered his senses.
Having brought desire and anger under control, and having achieved one-pointedness of mind and the senses, he, being composed, should devote himself to the state of Brahman.
During the first and last watches of the night, one should fix the mind of this living being with its five senses upon the Self, even if only a single sense-organ remains moist with life.
Then his wisdom flows forth like water from the foot of a mountain;
he should first take hold of it with his mind, just as a fisherman seizes tortoises.
Then the knower of yoga [should restrain] the ear, then the eye, the tongue, and the nose;
having restrained these, he should establish them in the mind.
In that very way, having cast aside all volitional constructions, one should indeed fix the mind upon the Self;
if one should establish the five senses within the mind at the heart.
When these six, with the mind as the sixth, abide within the Self and become serene in that state of composure, then Brahman shines forth.
Like a smokeless fire with blazing flames, like the radiant sun,
or like the lightning-fire in the sky, they behold the Self within the self.
Everything indeed is seen there, because it pervades everywhere; those high-souled Brahmins who are wise perceive that [Brahman].
Possessing fortitude and great wisdom, devoted to the welfare of all beings,
one who is firm in his vows practices in this manner for a limited period of time.
For sitting alone in a secluded place, one may attain identity with the Imperishable;
[therein arise] delusion, wandering, whirling, as well as smelling, hearing, and seeing.
Having mastered through yoga the wonders of taste, touch, and the forms of cold, heat, and wind, as well as inspired insights and obstacles.
Disregarding those [worldly objects], the knower of reality should withdraw them through equanimity alone;
the disciplined sage should cultivate familiarity with yoga throughout the three worlds.
Likewise, he should apply himself on a mountain peak, at a shrine, or at the roots of trees,
restraining the collection of his senses as one whose mind is fixed on a vessel within a storehouse.
One should constantly contemplate with one-pointed focus so that the mind does not become agitated by yoga;
by whatever means possible, one should strive to restrain the flickering mind.
There, he should practice with diligence and never deviate from that;
moreover, with one-pointed mind, he should resort to empty dwellings for the sake of residence.
One should not transgress against another through speech, action, or even thought;
remaining equanimous, restrained in diet, one should be the same whether obtaining or not obtaining.
Whether someone should rejoice in him or whether someone should salute him,
one should regard both of them equally and not dwell upon their good or bad qualities.
One should not rejoice in gains, nor dwell upon losses;
being equal toward all beings, one possesses the same nature as the wind.
Thus, for the virtuous man who is established in his own self and perceives equality everywhere,
the Brahman of Sound manifests after six months of constant discipline.
Having seen others afflicted by pain, one who regards a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal—
thus devoted to the path— should not desist, being free from delusion.
Even one of inferior caste, or a woman desiring dharma,
those two also shall go to the supreme goal by this path.
O twice-born ones, having beheld this unborn, ancient, undecaying, and eternal [Self], which transcends the senses and is beyond the range of perception, one attains equality with the Supreme Lord.
The wise proceed to the state from which there is no return.
{The sages said:} If such is the word of the Veda, both "perform action" and "renounce action," [how is this so?]
To which direction do they go by means of knowledge, and to which do they go by means of action?
We truly wish to hear this; may your lordship explain it to us:
how is it that this mutual incompatibility persists in such an adverse manner?
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O tigers among sages, to that which you ask; I shall explain in brief both the perishable and the imperishable, consisting of action and knowledge.
O Brahmins, listen now to that direction which they go to by means of knowledge and which they reach through their actions; for this further matter is profound.
It is logical to say that "Dharma exists," but it would be improper for one to say regarding that very same thing, "This is like a yakṣa" or "This belongs to a yakṣa. (BrP 237.5)
Now, there are these two paths upon which the Vedas are established:
dharma characterized by worldly engagement (pravṛtti) and that which is described as withdrawal (nivṛtti).
A living being is bound by action and liberated by knowledge;
therefore, ascetics who have seen the further shore do not perform ritual action.
Through action, one is born after death as a embodied being consisting of sixteen elements;
through knowledge, however, one is eternally born as the unmanifest, which is of the nature of the imperishable.
But some men, devoted to limited intelligence, praise karma;
by means of it, they take delight in and remain attached to that web of bodies.
But those who have attained supreme understanding and perceive the subtleties of dharma do not praise ritual action, just as one drinking from a river does not praise a well.
One obtains the fruit of actions—happiness and suffering, existence and non-existence;
through knowledge one attains that state, having gone to which one does not grieve.
Wherever one goes, one does not die; wherever one goes, one is not born;
wherever one goes, one does not decay; and wherever one goes, one does not increase.
Therein dwells that supreme Brahman, unmanifest, immovable, eternal, undifferentiated, without extension, and immortal— so knows the master of yoga.
There, they are not afflicted by dualities nor by mental action;
they are equanimous toward all things, friendly, and devoted to the welfare of all beings.
O twice-born ones, one person consists of knowledge, while another consists of action;
O brahmins, he who has a touch like that of the moon abides by means of a subtle portion.
This very matter has been proclaimed by the Seer and is now being sung in detail;
it cannot be described or seen, like a thread of a wheel in the sky.

O Brahmins, one should know that he consists of the eleven transformations, is composed of a collection of *kalās*, possesses a physical form, and is characterized by the qualities of action (*karma-guṇa*).
One should know that divine being who has taken refuge therein like the moon of the intellect in a lotus—
the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), whose self is eternally conquered through yoga.
Tamas, rajas, and sattva should be known as having the individual soul (jīva) as their essential quality;
one should know the individual soul as having the self (ātman) as its quality, and the self as belonging to the Supreme Self (paramātman).
They say that consciousness is the quality of the individual soul (jīva),
and it is that which impels all the qualities of the soul;
beyond that, they who know the field (kṣetra) speak.
"Arranging the seven worlds.
Vyāsa said:
"Those who are the transformations of primordial nature (prakṛti) are known as the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas)."
They do not recognize him, nor does he recognize them.
And with these very senses, of which the mind is the sixth, he performs his work here,
just as a firm charioteer controls excellent horses that are well-tamed.
For the objects are superior to the senses, and the mind is superior to the objects;
the intellect is superior to the mind, and the Great Self is superior to the intellect.
Beyond the Great is the Unmanifest; beyond the Unmanifest is the Immortal.
There is nothing higher than the Immortal; that is the ultimate limit, the supreme goal.
Thus, the Self hidden within all beings does not manifest;
however, it is seen by those who perceive the subtle, through a sharp and subtle intellect.
Having dissolved the senses, with the mind as the sixth, along with their objects, into the inner self by means of wisdom,
he should not think of the manifold mind through the senses.
Having made meditation supreme and having perfected the mind through knowledge,
one who is no longer subject to the lord [of the senses] and whose self is tranquil shall thereafter go to the highest state.
But a mortal whose self is under the control of all the senses and whose mindfulness has wavered, through surrendering himself to them, encounters death.
Having destroyed all conceptual constructions, one should settle the mind upon pure being (*sattva*);
having caused the mind to enter into pure being, one then becomes like Mount Kālañjara.
Through clarity of mind, the ascetic here abandons both the auspicious and the inauspicious;
with a serene self, abiding in the Self, he enjoys ultimate happiness.
The characteristic of serenity is like the happiness experienced in a dream,
or like a lamp burning in a windless place that does not flicker.
Thus, yoking the self by means of the self during the first and last watches of the night,
one who is moderate in diet and pure in soul beholds the Self within the self.
This instruction for my son is the secret of all the Vedas; it is not based on mere tradition nor derived from external scripture, but is a teaching that brings realization within one's own self.
In all the discourses on Dharma and all the discourses on Truth, that wealth which was extracted like nectar after churning for ten thousand years— [that has been obtained].
Just as butter is extracted from curd, and just as fire is produced from wood,
even so has the knowledge of the wise been drawn forth for the sake of liberation.
This scripture, an instruction for one's sons, is to be spoken to those who have completed their Vedic studies;
yet this must not be given to one who is not tranquil, nor to one who is not self-controlled, even if he be an ascetic.
It should not be spoken to one who does not know the Vedas, nor to one who has not followed [the discipline],
nor to one who is envious, nor to one who is not upright, nor to one who does not act according to what has been instructed.
It is not for one consumed by the science of logic, nor likewise for a slanderer;
it is for the praiseworthy, for one who is worthy of praise, for the tranquil, and for the ascetic.
This secret dharma should be spoken to a beloved son or to a devoted disciple, but never to anyone else under any circumstances.
Even if a man were to give this entire earth filled with jewels,
the knower of reality would consider this [gift of the Dharma] alone to be superior to that.
Therefore, that which is more secret than the secret, pertaining to the inner self and transcending human nature—
what was seen by the great seers and sung in the Vedāntas— is this.
Therefore, O best of beings, I shall grant you that which you ask of me;
whatever dwells in my mind and whatever doubt exists in your hearts—all that has been heard by you. What else shall I tell you?
The sages said:
"O Blessed One, O best of seers, please explain to us once again in detail the nature of the inner self (adhyātma), so that we may understand what the inner self is and how it exists."
Vyāsa said:
O brahmins, regarding this spiritual science (adhyātma) which is recited here concerning the person, I shall tell it to you; let its exposition be attended to.
Earth, water, as well as fire, wind, and space—
these are the great elements (mahābhūta), as is he who is the creator of beings within all beings.
The sages said:
How can one describe that which consists of space and the other elements within bodies, when its form is not perceived by one who does not see the body?
What are the qualities of the senses, and how might one perceive them?
Vyāsa said:
I shall describe this to you exactly as it is revealed;
listen here with one-pointed attention, according to its true nature and just as it is.
Sound, the sense of hearing, and the bodily cavities—these three are characterized by space (ākāśa).
Vital breath, physical movement, and touch—these three are the qualities of wind (vāyu).
Form, the eye, and its maturation—light is ordained as these three;
likewise, taste, the tongue, and perspiration—these three qualities belong to the waters.
The olfactory sense, the act of smelling, and the body—these three are the qualities of earth.
Thus far has this collection of sense organs, composed of the five elements, been explained.
Touch is said to belong to wind, taste to water, and form to light;
sound is born from space, and smell is remembered as the quality of earth.
The mind, the intellect, and the primal nature—these qualities are born from their own source;
they transcend the qualities and are considered superior to them.
Just as a tortoise extends its limbs and then withdraws them,
even so does one whose intellect is preeminent restrain the collection of the senses.
Whatever one sees above the soles of the feet and below the crown of the head,
that supreme intellect functions solely for this very purpose.

The intellect is led by the qualities (guṇas), and the intellect likewise leads all the senses, including the mind as the sixth; since they all exist through the intellect, from where could the qualities [independently] come?
The five senses are possessed by men; the sixth is said to be the mind (manas);
they call the seventh intellect (buddhi), and know the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) as the eighth.
The eye is for seeing alone; the mind creates doubt;
the intellect is for determination; the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is called the witness.
Passion, darkness, and goodness—these three are born from their own source;
they exist equally in all beings, and one should observe these qualities.
In that state, whatever one perceives within oneself as conjoined with joy,
like something tranquil and composed, one should understand that to be the quality of *sattva*.
Furthermore, whatever is associated with distress, whether occurring in the body or in the mind,
one should recognize that as the activity of *rajas*.
But that which is joined with delusion, unmanifest, uneven,
inconceivable, and unknowable— one should understand that to be *tamas*.
Exultation, joy, bliss, mastery, and a state of mind that is healthy and self-abiding—
they call these the qualities of sattva, whether they arise without cause or from some cause.
Arrogance, false speech, greed, delusion, and likewise intolerance—
these are the marks of *rajas*, which function according to their causal reality.
Likewise, delusion, negligence, lassitude, and unawakened sleep arise in some way; these are to be known as the qualities of tamas.
The mind projects existence; the intellect is determinative;
and the heart is indeed what is dear here—this is the threefold impetus to action.
For the objects are higher than the senses, and the mind is higher than the objects;
the intellect is higher than the mind, and the Self is traditionally held to be higher than the intellect.
The intellect is the self of man; the intellect alone is the leader of the self.
When it undergoes a transformation of state, it then becomes the mind.
Following the distinct states of the sense organs, the intellect indeed undergoes transformation:
when hearing, it becomes the ear; when touching, it is called the sense of touch.
Seeing becomes the faculty of sight, and tasting becomes the tongue;
smelling becomes the sense of smell, while the intellect undergoes various transformations.
They call those the senses; by their activity, the intellect (buddhi) functions within the person, established in the state of the intellect.
Sometimes he attains joy, and sometimes he grieves;
yet here, he is never bewildered by either pleasure or pain.
Inhering in its own essential nature, it transcends these three states of being,
just as the ocean, the lord of rivers, overflows its great shore with its waves.
When it desires something, then it becomes the mind (manas);
one should indeed contemplate these as distinct within their respective substrates by means of the intellect (buddhi).
And the senses, which are pure, must be examined in their entirety,
one by one in due order, whenever and however each is prescribed.
The intellect (buddhi), whose nature is non-differentiation, abides as a state within the mind;
yet when it is active, it transcends both rajas and sattva.
Those who indeed abide with true devotion toward all these three [goals] proceed in accordance with their purposes,
just as spokes follow the rim of a chariot wheel.
One should employ the mind as a lamp by means of the senses, which are the best forms of intelligence,
as they emerge according to their proper application, remaining indifferent and spontaneous.
Having realized that "this world is of such a nature," one is not deluded;
neither grieving nor exulting, one remains eternally free from envy.
For the self cannot be seen by means of the senses whose domain is desire,
which operate in manifold ways, are difficult to restrain, and belong to those who have not disciplined themselves.
But when one properly restrains their rays with the mind,
then the Self shines forth like a form illuminated by a lamp.
Just as everything becomes illuminated for all living beings when darkness has departed, so too should this be understood.
Just as a water-dwelling bird is not smeared while moving through the water,
so too the yogi whose self is liberated is not smeared by the qualities or defects [of the gunas].
In this very way, one who has perfected wisdom, while moving among sense objects,
is not defiled in any way, remaining unattached amidst all things.
Having abandoned previously performed karma, he whose delight is always in the Self,
who has become the self of all beings, yet remains attached through association with the qualities (guṇas).
The Self itself produces [itself] even within the qualities at times;
the qualities do not know the Self, but it knows the qualities at all times.
He would perceive the qualities exactly as they are;
thus a man should discern the distinction between the *sattva* and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).
One creates the qualities, while the other does not create the qualities;
though these two are distinct by nature, they are always joined together.
Just as gold is joined with stone, so too are those two;
or likewise, they are joined together like a gnat and an udumbara fruit.
Just as the reed exists both separately and together within the Muñja grass,
even so these two exist together, each established within the other.
Vyāsa said:
Sattva creates the qualities, while the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) presides over them;
the Lord remains like one indifferent toward all the qualities as they undergo transformation.
All that which creates these qualities is endowed with its own inherent nature;
just as a spider emits thread, so does it emit those qualities.
"Once set in motion, they do not return; no further activity is perceived.
Thus some conclude, while others maintain that there is cessation.
Having thoroughly considered both of these, one should reach a conclusion according to one's own intelligence;
for by this very method, a great doubt indeed arises.
For the Self is indeed without beginning or end; having realized that, a person should live without anger, without exultation, and always free from envy.
Thus, with all doubts severed, he sat within his heart— firmly established in the thought of the intellect, impermanent, joyful, and beyond grief.
Just as men cross a river that has overflowed its banks by plunging into it,
so too should the wise Brahmins cross over this flickering world.
But the wise one who knows the truth does not suffer; he moves upon dry land.
Having thus reflected upon the self as pure knowledge belonging to the self, [he is not afflicted].
But having understood that creation of beings, their coming and going,
and being properly composed in his actions, a man indeed attains supreme peace.
This is the complete equipment of a twice-born man, especially for a Brahmin;
it is sufficient for the affection that is equal to self-knowledge, and it is his ultimate refuge.
Having realized that reality, one becomes a Buddha; what other characteristic of a Buddha could there be?
Having understood this, the wise, having accomplished all that was to be done, are liberated.
For the wise, there is no great fear—
that which is a source of very great fear for the ignorant in the next world— for there is no higher destination for anyone.
For that which is eternal for the wise exists; the man who finds fault with his mother in this world grieves there, not having beheld the Divine.
In that regard, one who is skilled does not grieve,
for those who know both that which is done and that which is left undone;
he performs whatever action without prior intention.
And he censures that which was done in the past;
whether it be pleasant or unpleasant,
both of those produce their results for him as he acts in this world.
The sages said:
"Please tell us that dharma from which no other dharma superior to it exists here, and which is more distinguished than all beings."
Vyāsa said:
O best of sages, listen as I shall fully proclaim that ancient dharma praised by the seers, which is superior to all other dharmas.
Having restrained the turbulent senses, which spread out in all directions here, by means of the intellect according to reality, as a father restrains his young children.
The one-pointed concentration of the mind and the senses is the supreme austerity;
it should be known that among all dharmas, this is called the highest dharma.
Having withdrawn all those [senses], with the mind as the sixth, by means of his intelligence,
he remained satisfied in the Self alone, no longer thinking of that which is manifoldly thought.
When the senses have withdrawn from their objects and abide within the self,
then you shall behold the eternal Supreme Self by means of the self.
The wise Brahmins behold that Great Soul, the Self of all, like a smokeless fire.
Just as a great tree with many branches, endowed with flowers and fruit, does not itself know, "Where is my flower? Where is my fruit? (BrP 238.22).
In this way, the self does not know: "Where shall I go? Whence am I?
For there is another inner self within it, which perceives everything.
With the blazing lamp of knowledge, one sees the Self by means of the self;
having thus seen the Self, O twice-born ones, become free from passion.
Freed from all evils like snakes that have cast off their skins,
having attained supreme wisdom in this world, they are free from anxiety and devoid of feverish distress.
[Cross] the terrible river that flows everywhere, which carries the world along,
possessing the crocodiles of the five senses and the banks of mental constructions.
This excellent river is covered by the grass of greed and delusion, infested with the reptiles of desire and anger,
agitated by the waves of untruth at its landing-place of truth, and mired in the mud of wrath.
Cross over with your intellect this river, which originates from the unmanifest, flows swiftly, is agitated by desire and anger, and is difficult for those of undisciplined souls to traverse.
That [ocean] flows through the sea of saṃsāra, difficult to cross due to the abysses of the various wombs;
it arises from one's own birth and is hard to approach because of the whirlpools of the tongue.
Having crossed that which those of perfected wisdom, the steadfast, and the wise cross over,
he— liberated from all sides, with his self shaken free, self-possessed, and pure— is one who has transcended.
Resorting to the highest wisdom, one becomes fit for becoming Brahman;
having transcended all afflictions, with a serene self and free from stain.
Having observed that almost all beings in every state were neither angry nor pleased, he likewise remained free from cruelty of mind.
Then you shall behold the origin and dissolution of all beings;
for the wise consider this to be superior to all other dharmas.

"O best among the upholders of dharma, the sages who perceive the truth declare that the self is all-pervading and that the brahmins are the sons [of the Self]; such is the instruction to their sons."
This great secret of self-knowledge, the most secret of all secrets, should be imparted to one who is disciplined, who seeks his welfare, and who is devoted. BrP_238.35 //
O brahmins, I have spoken directly according to my own realization:
it is neither female, nor male, nor indeed is it neuter.
Brahman is neither suffering nor happiness, and it is the essence of the past, the future, and the present;
having known this, neither man nor woman shall undergo rebirth.
O Brahmins, just as all doctrines are held, so too have these been described by me— both as they exist and as they do not exist.

Having seen what was beneficial for that purpose, he— filled with affection for him, endowed with virtues, possessed of a son who is a true son and full of compassion, and with a joyful mind— [acted].
The sages said:
"O Grandfather, it has been stated here by your son that liberation is attained through means, not without means."
O Sage, we wish to hear that method according to the proper rule.
Vyāsa said:
O highly wise ones, it is fitting for you— being ever sinless— to seek all goals through skillful means, as you possess subtle insight.

The intellect is considered to be directed toward the production of a jar through its instrumental causes, not toward the jar's actual arising; likewise, it is directed toward the means for attaining dharma and so forth, and is not the cause for other dharmas.
The path that leads to the eastern ocean does not go to the western one;
for there is but one path to liberation—listen to that from me, O sinless ones.
One should eradicate anger through forgiveness; desire, by abandoning mental constructions;
and the steadfast man ought to eliminate sleep by attending to living beings.
One should guard against fear through heedfulness, and protect one's field as well as one's discernment;
one should turn back desire, hatred, and lust through fortitude.
Through the practice of knowledge, the knower of reality overcomes both sleep and mental distraction;
likewise, through eating wholesome, digested, and moderate food, the yogi overcomes afflictions.
One should conquer greed and delusion through contentment, sense-objects through the vision of reality,
unrighteousness through compassion, and [attachment to] dharma through equanimity.
Furthermore, in the future, the wise man should conquer hope by abandoning attachment,
affection through the contemplation of impermanence, and hunger through the practice of yoga.
One should conquer the self by means of compassion, and craving through contentment;
one should conquer sloth through exertion, and discursive thought through certainty.
One should conquer excessive speech through silence, and fear through courage;
one should restrain speech and mind with the intellect, and restrain that intellect with the eye of knowledge.
The Great Self is knowledge; one should restrain that [mind], and one should restrain it through the tranquility of the self. This must be realized by one who is peaceful and whose actions are pure.
Having completely severed the five defects of yoga known by the wise— namely,
desire, anger, greed, fear, and sleep as the fifth.
Having abandoned [worldly attachments], one should properly practice the means of yoga:
meditation, study, charity, truthfulness, modesty, straightforwardness, and forbearance.
Purity through right conduct, cleanliness, and the restraint of the senses—
by these one's vital energy increases and one destroys evil.
His intentions are fulfilled and his higher knowledge proceeds;
he is cleansed of sin, radiant, moderate in diet, and has conquered his senses.
Having brought desire and anger under control, one should enter the state of Brahman;
this consists of freedom from delusion, non-attachment, and the total abandonment of desire and anger.

Freedom from dejection, absence of arrogance, lack of agitation, and steadfastness—this indeed is the path to liberation; it is serene, stainless, and pure. Likewise, there are the imperishable restraints of speech, body, and mind, undertaken according to one's desire.
The sages said: "O Brahmin, you ought to tell us the distinction between Sāṃkhya and Yoga;
for everything is known to you, O knower of dharma, O best of sages."
Vyāsa said:
The followers of Sāṃkhya praise Sāṃkhya, and the best among the knowers of Yoga praise Yoga; they indeed speak with superior arguments for the sake of establishing their own respective positions.
"O best of sages, how can one who lacks self-mastery be liberated?"—
thus do the wise declare Yoga to be the supreme means through its various causal factors.
The twice-born rightly declare the Veda to be the cause,
having understood all the destinies in this world, he who is dispassionate toward sense-objects.
"After the departure of the body, he shall clearly be liberated; it cannot be otherwise. This, indeed, the highly wise call the Sāṃkhya, the vision of liberation."

One should accept the valid reason for one's own position, speech that is effective and beneficial, and indeed the opinion of the learned; for you, who are esteemed by the learned, must accept what is approved by the learned.
O best of the twice-born, both these systems— the Yoga of direct perception as its cause and the Sāṃkhya of the determination of the scriptures— are united in the truth.
O lords of sages, both these doctrines, when understood and practiced according to the scriptures as approved by the learned, lead to the supreme goal.
O sinless ones, their purity is equal, as is their compassion toward all beings;
their observance of vows is equal, yet their philosophical perspectives are different.
The sages said:
"O great sage, O best of the twice-born, if the vow, purity, and compassion here are equal [to those of others], why then is their vision equal? Tell us that."
Vyāsa said: Attachment, delusion, as well as affection, desire, and anger—
these five defects arising from instability in yoga, they encounter.
Just as fish, having cut through a coarse net, reach the water once again,
so too do those free from defilement attain that state through yoga.
In the same way, having severed the snare, just as powerful deer reach the stainless path, so too shall they be liberated from all bonds.
Likewise, O Brahmins, those endowed with strength, having severed the bonds born of greed through yoga,
proceed upon the supreme path, which is stainless and auspicious.
But some brahmins are unsteady and turbid, while others are like those caught in snares;
they perish without a doubt, just so, unless they possess the power of yoga.
O best of Brahmins, those who are devoid of strength are like birds caught in a net;
they fall into bondage, whereas those sinless ones who possess yoga are exceedingly rare.
And just as birds, O subduer of enemies, upon encountering a fine net, perish there if they lack the strength, but are liberated if they possess power; so it is with men.
Bound by the fetters born of karma, even so, O twice-born ones, those devoted to yoga who are weak are not liberated; yet those endowed with strength are liberated.
Just as a small and weak fire, O Brahmins,
is extinguished when overwhelmed by thick fuel, so too is the power of yoga said to be.
And at that time, O Brahmins, that very fire, having regained its strength and being driven by the wind,
would swiftly burn this entire earth.
The yogi, empowered by the knowledge of reality, blazing with splendor and possessed of great strength,
may dry up the entire world like the sun at the time of the end.
Just as a weak man, O Brahmins, is carried away by a current,
so too is a yogi devoid of strength carried away by the objects of the senses.
Just as an elephant blocks a flowing stream,
even so, having attained the power of yoga, one should not be carried away by sense objects.
Or else, endowed with the power of yoga, they enter by their will or through yoga all the Prajāpatis, all the Manus, and the great elements as lords.
Neither Yama, nor the wrathful Antaka, nor Death of terrifying prowess—
none of these enter that [state] of the twice-born who possess the immeasurable splendor of yoga.
O best of the twice-born, having acquired power through yoga, he may create many thousands of selves and wander the earth with them all.
O Brahmins, someone might enjoy sense objects and then again perform fierce austerity,
and then contract them once more, just as the sun withdraws its qualities of radiance.
O best of sages, for the sake of strengthening a yoga that has already become firm,
one should undoubtedly approach Viṣṇu, who is the source of liberation.
"O best of the twice-born, these powers have been described by me according to the Yoga teachings;
O twice-born ones, I shall further describe the subtle ones for the sake of illustration."
O twice-born ones, O best of sages, listen now to the subtle illustrations regarding the concentration of the self or with respect to *dhāraṇā*.
Just as a careful archer, being fully concentrated, hits the target,
so too the yogi who is properly disciplined attains liberation without a doubt.
Just as a man, having fixed his mind steadily upon a vessel full of oil,
might ascend a staircase with a disciplined and composed mind, so too should one proceed.
Likewise, this liberated self makes itself perfectly steady through yoga;
it renders the self stainless, appearing like the sun.
And just as a focused helmsman, O best of Brahmins,
