would swiftly lead a ship situated upon the great ocean to its port, so too [should he lead you], O Brahmins.
In the same way, O twice-born ones, the practitioner who knows yoga, being disciplined through yoga, attains that difficult-to-reach state after casting off this body by means of self-concentration.
And just as a well-trained charioteer, with great composure, quickly leads the excellent horses to the desired destination, so does he lead the archer, that bull among men.
In the same way, O twice-born ones, a yogi who is concentrated in the dhāraṇās quickly attains the supreme state, like an arrow released at its target.
He who, having entered the self within the self, remains steadfast, is immovable;
like a fish that has destroyed its net, he attains the ageless state.
The one of immeasurable valor [should be worshipped] at the navel, the head, the belly, the heart, the chest, the two sides,
as well as in the eyes, the ears, and the nose.
O best of the twice-born, the yogi who is concentrated in the great vow unites the subtle self with the Self in these locations in a proper manner.
Having swiftly burned away both auspicious and inauspicious karma— which is as immovable as a mountain—
by resorting to the supreme yoga, he who so desires is liberated.
The sages said:
O best of beings, by consuming what kinds of food and by conquering what [obstacles], does a yogin attain power? You ought to explain that to us.
Vyāsa said:
O twice-born ones, the yogi who is intent on eating grains and oil-cakes,
and intent on avoiding oily substances, shall attain strength.
O best of the twice-born, by eating coarse barley gruel for a long period,
taking but a single meal a day, the yogi of purified soul shall attain strength.
Moving through the fortnights, months, and various seasons, as well as through caves,
the yogi who drinks water mixed with milk shall attain strength.
Or, O best of sages, by fasting continuously for an entire month,
the yogi of perfectly purified soul shall attain strength.
Having thus conquered desire as well as anger, cold and heat, and even rain;
likewise fear, grief, sleep, and the objects of human sense-experience.
O twice-born ones, having seen Discontent which is difficult to conquer and terrible, as well as Touch, Sleep, and likewise Sloth, which are hard to overcome, O best of sages; (BrP 239.48)
Free from passion and possessed of great wisdom, they illuminate the subtle Self by means of the self through the perfection of meditation and study.
O bulls among sages, this path of wise Brahmins is considered difficult; yet whoever travels it quickly proceeds with safety.
Just as if someone were to enter a terrible forest, abounding with many snakes and reptiles, full of pits, devoid of water, difficult to traverse, and thick with thorns.
Just as one would safely traverse a path that is devoid of food, mostly wilderness, with its trees scorched by forest fires, and infested with robbers; so too [should one proceed].
Any twice-born man who, having attained the path of yoga, proceeds along it,
may reach the end of the path in safety, even if he is considered to be full of many faults.
O best of the twice-born, that concentration of yoga must be maintained as if upon sharpened razor-edges; it is difficult to be mastered by those who have not disciplined their selves.
O Brahmins, those whose concentration (dhāraṇā) is uneven do not indeed attain an auspicious state,
just as boats without a helmsman fail to carry men across, O twice-born ones.
But he who remains steadfast in the primary stage of yoga through the dhāraṇās according to the rule,
is distinguished by being free from death, the suffering of birth, and [mere] worldly happiness.
This supreme path of yoga, which is established in various scriptures and practiced by various sages, has been definitively determined among the twice-born.
For that supreme [reality] consists of Brahman, O lords of sages;
it is Brahmā, the Lord, Viṣṇu the giver of boons,
Bhava, and the high-souled Dharma.
That which consists of the sons of Brahmā of great majesty,
and the terrible darkness (tamas), the great passion (rajas),
and the pure goodness (sattva), as well as primordial nature (prakṛti) and the supreme [Self].
And Siddhi, the goddess and wife of Varuṇa;
and all splendor and very great fortitude;
and the lord of stars, Sutāra, stainless in the sky.
And all the gods, the serpents, and the ancestors;
all the mountains and the immovable oceans; all the rivers, along with the mountains and the nāgas.
Having encountered one another— the Sadhyas, the hosts of Yakṣas, the quarters of the sky, the Gandharvas, the Siddhas, men, and women— that great-souled one became truly great.
The yogi, being liberated, shall enter [that state] before long. And this auspicious discourse, O best of brahmins, which is devoted to the divine one of great heroic intellect— BrP_239.62ab.
Having experienced all those yogas, mortals swiftly attain that Nārāyaṇa.
[The sages said:]
O best of Brahmins, this correct practice, approved by the learned,
has been described here according to the rules of the path of yoga by one desiring the welfare of his disciple.
Now, however, explain in accordance with reality the rule of dharma according to Sāṃkhya;
for all that knowledge which exists in the three worlds is indeed known to you.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O sages, to this entire narrative concerning those who have realized the Self,
as it was set forth by the ancient masters and lords, such as Kapila and others, who were practitioners of self-restraint.
In whom some excellent sages perceive great spiritual confusion,
yet in whom there are many virtues and the absolute elimination of all defects.

O twice-born ones, having thoroughly discerned through knowledge that all human objects of the senses and likewise those of the Piśācas are entirely fraught with defects and difficult to conquer; ||| BrP_240.5 |||

O twice-born ones, having understood the realms of the serpents, as well as the realms of the Gandharvas, and having understood the realms of the ancestors and those who wander among the animals; ||| BrP_240.6 |||
Having understood the domains of the Suparṇas, as well as the domains of the Maruts,
the domains of the great ṛṣis, and likewise the domains of the royal ṛṣis;
Having understood the domains of the Asuras as well as those of the Vaiśvadevas, and having understood the domains of the divine sages as well as the supreme states of the yogis; BrP_240.8 //
Having understood in truth the objects of the means of knowledge, as well as the objects of Brahman, and the supreme duration of life according to the worlds; ||| BrP_240.9 |||
And having understood the supreme duration of happiness, O best of sages, as well as the suffering that awaits at the proper time for those who fall while seeking sense objects; BrP_240.10 //
O Brahmins, likewise for those falling into the state of animals or into the hells;
O twice-born ones, having understood all the virtues and defects of heaven, [one should strive for liberation].
Whatever faults there are in the doctrines of the Vedas, and whatever virtues belong to the Vedic way;
whatever faults there are in the yoga of knowledge, and whatever virtues there are in the yoga of knowledge.
O twice-born ones, having understood the defects and likewise the merits in the knowledge of Sāṃkhya— knowing that *sattva* has ten qualities and *rajas* likewise has nine qualities— BrP_240.13.
Having understood that darkness (tamas) has eight qualities, and likewise that intellect (buddhi) has seven qualities;
having known that space (nabhas) has six qualities, and that the great darkness (mahat-tamas) has three qualities.
Having recognized that rajas is twofold and sattva is once again singlefold, and having understood the path in its true essence through the contemplation of dissolution; ||| BrP_240.15 |||
Endowed with both knowledge and discernment, those who have cultivated their selves through the [proper] causes attain auspicious liberation, just as subtle [beings] reach the highest ether.
The eye is conjoined with form, the nose with the quality of odor,
the ear is likewise grasped by sound, and the tongue with the quality of taste.
The skin, touch, and likewise the wind which depends upon it;
delusion conjoined with darkness, and greed residing within delusions.
Viṣṇu is stationed in movement, Śakra in strength, and likewise Anala (Fire) is attached to the stomach;
the Goddess (Earth) is joined with the waters, and the waters are dependent upon fire.
Fire is conjoined with wind, and wind is supported by space;
space is conjoined with the Great Principle (mahat), and darkness is situated within the Great Principle.
Rajas is attached to sattva, and sattva is likewise attached to the self;
the self is attached to the Lord, and likewise to the divine Nārāyaṇa.

Having understood the Lord as joined with liberation, yet liberation itself as existing nowhere at all, and having known the body—which possesses the quality of being a sentient being—as enveloped by sixteen qualities; ||| BrP_240.22 |||
Having understood both intrinsic nature and mental cultivation as being dependent upon the body,
one should regard the self as if it were neutral— that is, as that in which no evil exists.
O best of Brahmins, having understood the second type of karma of those who seek sense-objects,
[one should know] all the senses and the objects of the senses as being centered within the self.
Having understood, according to the sacred scriptures, the difficulty of attaining liberation, as well as the true nature of prāṇa, apāna, samāna, vyāna, and udāna; ||| BrP_240.25 |||
Having understood the first wind and again the source of the wind,
one should likewise [understand] those remaining sevenfold winds, each again sevenfold, according to the rule.
Having known the Prajāpatis and the Ṛṣis, as well as very many excellent creations, the many Saptarṣis, and the royal sages who are subduers of their enemies; ||| BrP_240.27 |||
O twice-born ones, having seen the celestial rishis, the Maruts, and other Brahman-rishis who resembled the sun, fallen from their sovereignty after a long period of time; BrP_240.28.
O twice-born ones, having heard of the destruction of the great hosts of beings,
and having understood the auspicious course of speech, [you realize that] even those of sinful deeds are worthy of worship.
And the suffering of those who have fallen into the Vaitaraṇī river in the abode of Yama, as well as the impure transmigrations through various wombs; ||| BrP_240.30 |||
And he dwells in the foul belly, a vessel of blood and water,
filled with phlegm, urine, and excrement, and possessed of a pungent stench.
Then, indeed, within this city of nine gates, which is a mass of semen and blood, held together by marrow and sinews, and strewn with hundreds of veins; BrP_240.32.

O twice-born ones, having understood the self that is beneficial and the various types of yoga, as well as the nature of those beings who are characterized by darkness (tāmasa) and whose souls delight in the false; BrP_240.33.
O best of sages, that which is contemptible for beings of a sattvic nature is censured for the sake of the great ones— the Sāṃkhyas who have realized the Self.
Likewise, having seen terrible eclipses of the moon and its brilliance, the falling of the stars, and the shifting of the constellations;
O twice-born ones, having understood the miserable separation of pairs,
and having seen the inauspicious mutual devouring of beings, [one should practice renunciation].
Having understood the delusion in childhood and the impurity of the body's wings,
he perceived passion and delusion arising in some beings who had taken refuge in existence.
Among thousands of men, perhaps one rare individual takes refuge in the intellect of liberation,
having understood through sacred revelation the extreme difficulty of attaining liberation.

O twice-born ones, having recognized the wickedness of sense objects, one should feel great respect for those not yet attained, maintain equanimity toward those already obtained, and again [reflect upon their nature).
And having pierced through the auspicious bodies of beings whose life-force has departed,
he dwells among the families of living creatures who are resolved upon death.

O twice-born ones, having understood the suffering of sentient beings characterized by sattva, and having known the most dreadful fate of those who have fallen, such as the slayers of Brahmins; ||| BrP_240.41 |||
And having understood the inauspicious destiny of those evil-minded Brahmins who are addicted to drinking liquor and those who are attached to the wives of their gurus.
And by which those best of the twice-born conduct themselves properly toward their mothers,
and by which human beings conduct themselves among the worlds including the gods.
Having understood through that knowledge the destiny of those who perform unwholesome deeds,
and having discerned individually the various rebirths of those who have entered the animal realm;
Likewise, he [perceived] the various declarations of the Vedas, the revolutions of the seasons,
the passing away of years, and the passing away of months.
Having likewise observed the waning of the lunar fortnights and the passing away of the days,
and having directly perceived the waning and waxing of the moon;
Having seen the increase of the oceans and likewise their subsequent decrease, and having seen the loss of wealth and likewise its subsequent increase; ||| BrP_240.47 |||
Having thus observed the conjunctions [of time] and especially the various ages (yugas), and having correctly understood, according to reality, the frailty of the body; ||| BrP_240.48 |||
Having recognized all the faults of one's own self residing within oneself,
and likewise having recognized the foul odors arising from one's own body.
The sages said:
"O best among the knowers of Brahman, what faults arising from portents do you perceive?
You ought to explain this entire doubt of ours in its entirety."
Vyāsa said:
O best of sages, listen; the wise followers of Kapila, the Sāṃkhyas who know the path, declare that there are five defects in the body, O twice-born ones.
Lust, anger, fear, sleep, and the fifth is said to be breath;
these defects are seen in the bodies of all embodied beings.
One cuts off anger through forbearance, desire by abandoning mental constructions,
sleep by associating with virtuous beings, and likewise fear through heedfulness.
The twice-born cut off the fifth breath by means of eating little food,
having understood virtues through hundreds of virtues and faults through hundreds of faults.
Having understood in truth, through hundreds of diverse causes, the various causes themselves;
and having seen the world as resembling the foam upon the waters, created by the hundreds of Māyās of Viṣṇu.
Seeing it as resembling a painted wall, with Nala as its only substance yet devoid of meaning, and agitated by darkness like a bubble in the rain; ||| BrP_240.56 |||
It provides pleasure that is destined for destruction, followed by great fear after its end;
it is like an elephant helplessly submerged in the mud of passion and darkness.

O twice-born ones, the highly wise Sāṃkhya brāhmaṇas, having abandoned affection for their offspring through the vast and all-pervading Sāṃkhya system consisting of knowledge and the object of knowledge, [attain liberation].
[He experiences] foul odors born of passion (rājasa), as well as those of a similar nature born of darkness (tāmasa),
and meritorious odors born of goodness (sāttvika), all arising from touch and residing in the body.
O best of beings, having severed [the bonds] with the weapon of self-knowledge and the staff of austerity,
one [crosses] that terrible lake of suffering and the like, which consists of the great depths of anxiety and grief.
Moreover, by means of wisdom, they cross over the great and most terrible serpent of disease and death, which has darkness for its tortoise and passion for its fish.

O best of the twice-born, the wise remain established upon this island of touch, which has affection for its mud, old age for its difficult terrain, action for its bottomless depths, truth for its shore, and is sustained by vows.
It possesses a great surge of joy and a multitude of diverse flavors;
it contains the great jewels of manifold delights, yet it is stirred by the fever of suffering.
O best of the twice-born, it has the great whirlpools of grief and thirst, the great pain of sharp diseases, the friction of the massed collection of bones, and the application of phlegm.
It is a formidable mine of pearls that is generosity, with coral formed from the spitting of blood;
it resounds with the noise of laughter and shouts, and is exceedingly difficult to achieve through various forms of knowledge.
Having obtained this city of sons and kinsmen, which is the world of birth, where one is devoted to attachment and union, and which is tainted by the salt-water of weeping tears; BrP_240.66.
Non-violence, truth, and moral restraint are its life-force; it is the union of the two arms of yoga; it follows the path of the Vṛnda forest; it is the milk that churns the ocean of all beings.
The sinless ascetics and perfected ones cross over this ocean of worldly existence— which is difficult to escape and devoid of true happiness— by means of the yoga of knowledge.
Having crossed over birth, which is difficult to traverse, they enter the stainless sky;
then, recognizing them as doers of good deeds, the Sun carries them by means of his rays.
O twice-born ones, O sinless ones, having entered like the fibers of a lotus stalk and carrying the sense objects,
the Pravaha wind receives them there.

O twice-born ones, [a wind] that is subtle, cool, fragrant, and pleasant to the touch [arises from] those ascetics who are free from passion, perfected, endowed with vigor, and whose wealth is their austerity.
O best of Brahmins, he who goes to the auspicious worlds as the foremost of the seven Maruts carries them to the supreme goal beyond the sky.
O lords of the world, the sky carries the dust to its highest state;
O best of Brahmins, the dust carries the quality of goodness (sattva) to its highest state.
The pure-souled *sattva* carries the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa;
the pure-souled Lord carries the Supreme Self by means of his own self.
Having attained the Supreme Self, the stainless ascetics who have become one with it are fit for immortality and do not return, O twice-born ones.
O brahmins, that is the supreme goal of the great-souled ones who are free from the pairs of opposites,
who delight in truth and uprightness, and who possess compassion for all living beings.
The sages said:
Having reached this supreme abode, do those of steadfast vows delight there from birth until death, or not?
O best of beings, you ought to tell us truly and accurately what is the reality in this matter; for, O most excellent one, we ought not to ask anyone other than you, a human being.
This is a great defect in liberation, if other ascetics, having attained perfection and reached the sages,
should remain fixed in that very same state of consciousness.
"O twice-born one, we see that the dharma characterized by worldly activity is supreme;
for one who is immersed in higher knowledge, there would indeed be another form of suffering."
Vyāsa said:
O best of sages, this question you have asked is indeed difficult and appropriate;
even for the wise, O most excellent of munis, there is confusion regarding this inquiry.
In this regard as well, listen to my words concerning the supreme reality,
wherein lies the ultimate wisdom of the high-souled Kapilas.
O twice-born ones, the senses also perceive their own bodies for embodied beings;
they are the instruments of the Self, and through them, the Self perceives the subtle.
Deprived of their own selves, they are like wood or a wall;
they perish without a doubt, like the tides in the great ocean.
O best of the twice-born, while the embodied being is asleep along with the senses,
the subtle self moves everywhere like the wind in the sky.
O sinless twice-born ones, remembering according to the proper method, he perceives and touches everything here in its entirety, awakening just as before.
Indeed, all the sense organs, being powerless in their respective places according to the rule,
dissolve away like snakes deprived of their venom.
Having completely occupied all the subtle pathways within their respective locations, the self undoubtedly dwells there; of this there is no doubt.
O best of men, [he understands] all the qualities of *sattva*, and again the qualities of *rajas*,
all the qualities of *tamas*, and the qualities of the intellect (*buddhi*).
The omniscient ones [know] the qualities of the mind and likewise the qualities of space,
as well as the qualities of wind and again the qualities born of moisture.
O twice-born ones, the Self, as the Knower of the Field, moves through auspicious and inauspicious actions,
while the senses follow that Great Soul like disciples.
Having transcended even primordial nature (prakṛti), he is pure, subtle, higher than the highest,
the great-souled Nārāyaṇa, changeless, and beyond the supreme.
O best of beings, he is liberated from all evils, has entered the state free from affliction,
the supreme self, devoid of qualities, and perfectly tranquil.
O brahmins, O twice-born ones, the mind is the most excellent among them, and the senses likewise come at the proper time, carrying out the instructions of the guru.
"O best of Brahmins, it is possible to attain peace as well as virtues in a short time through this Sāṃkhya-yoga which leads to liberation, as thus described. (BrP 240.96)
O best of Brahmins, the highly wise Sāṃkhya scholars attain the supreme goal through this knowledge;
no knowledge equal to it is found.
Let there be no doubt among you regarding this: the Sāṃkhya knowledge is considered supreme;
it has been declared to be the imperishable, the eternal, the ancient Brahman.
Those whose nature is tranquility speak of that which is without beginning, middle, or end; free from duality; the agent; eternal; immovable, and indeed perpetual.
"Since all transformations of creation and dissolution proceed from this,
so do the great seers, the teachers, proclaim in the scriptures."
All the Brahmins, the Vedas, and likewise those people who know the Sāman chants [proclaim] the supreme god devoted to the Brahman— the infinite, supreme, and infallible one.
And seeking him, those Brahmins, whose intellects are focused on his qualities, speak thus;
likewise do the Yogas and the Sāṃkhyas of immeasurable vision when they have been correctly instructed.
"O best of Brahmins, his formless aspect is Sāṃkhya;
such is the Vedic revelation," said those most excellent sages, "and they speak of his great superknowledges."
For there are two kinds of beings on earth, O best of the twice-born: those designated as "unapproachable" and "approachable"; among these, the approachable is superior.
O Brahmins, that which is indeed the great knowledge found in the Vedas, in the Sāṃkhya systems, and likewise in Yoga, as well as that which is seen according to rule in the Purāṇas— BrP_240.105a–c.
O lords of sages, all that which is found in the Sāṃkhya, whatever is seen in the great Itihāsas, and whatever is specifically observed in the authoritative treatises on reality— [all that is here].
And whatever knowledge exists here in this world, O great lords of sages, that has been attained through Sāṃkhya;
it is the supreme strength perceived by all.
Knowledge and liberation have been explained exactly as they are; likewise,
O brahmins, the subtle austerities have been duly prescribed in the Sāṃkhya.
The Sāṃkhyas always proceed with ease toward that which is the constant opposite of this [world], which is beneficial;
and having supported them as well, they are then fulfilled.
They fall again into the abodes of the Brahmins;
and having abandoned the body, they enter into liberation—
both the celestial dwellers and those who follow Yoga and Sāṃkhya.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, you take even greater delight here in this Sāṃkhya, which is worthy of great esteem and practiced by the disciplined;
for it is observed that those who do not [follow it] undergo rebirth among the animals.
There is no downward path for those who have committed evil; nor are even those twice-born ones inferior who,
as sages, are not attached to this knowledge.
The Sāṃkhya is vast, supreme, and ancient; it is like a great ocean, stainless and noble in its beauty. Indeed, the high-souled sages have mastered this entire Sāṃkhya system.
By meditating upon Nārāyaṇa, one attains the immeasurable;
this supreme reality has been declared by me. From Nārāyaṇa, this ancient universe arose.
"At the time of creation he brings about creation, and at the time of dissolution he withdraws it once again.
[The Sages said:]
What is that which is called the Imperishable (akṣara), from which one does not return again? And what is that which is called the Perishable (kṣara), from which one returns again?
O great sage, O best of sages, O bull among munis, we ask you about the manifestation of the imperishable and the perishable, so that we may understand it in its true essence.
For you are proclaimed by those who have mastered the Vedas as the foremost among the knowers of wisdom,
as well as by the highly fortunate seers and the great-souled ascetics.
O high-minded one, we desire to hear all of this from you;
we do not reach satiety while hearing this supreme nectar.
Vyāsa said:
In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history,
the conversation between Vasiṣṭha and Karāla Janaka.
King Janaka questioned Vasiṣṭha— the most excellent among sages, seated and possessing the splendor of the sun— regarding the supreme knowledge that leads to ultimate liberation.
Having saluted with joined palms Maitrāvaruṇi, who was seated and skilled in the determination of the inner course regarding the Supreme Self, [he spoke].
In former times, King Karālajanaka questioned the best of sages with words that were spontaneous, well-composed, sweet, and not harsh.
Karālajanaka said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the supreme, eternal Brahman,
in which the wise no longer undergo rebirth."
That which is called the perishable (*kṣara*), wherein this world dissolves,
and that which is declared the imperishable (*akṣara*)— auspicious, secure, and free from affliction.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O protector of the earth, to how this world dissolves,
where it dissolves, by what means, and for how long a time.
Know that a cycle of four ages (caturyuga) consists of twelve thousand years;
a day of Brahmā is said to consist of one thousand such cycles of ten kalpas.
O King, the night is of such a duration that at its conclusion he awakens and creates the Great Being, the first-born, who performs endless deeds.
O best of kings, I shall describe from the very root the origin of the universe, wherein Śambhu— the self-existent one whose nature is formless— manifests as the embodied one.
The powers of atomization (aṇimā), levitation (laghimā), and attainment (prāpti); the sovereign, imperishable light;
having hands and feet extending everywhere, with eyes, heads, and mouths on all sides.
Possessing ears everywhere in the world, he stands pervading everything;
this Lord Hiraṇyagarbha is traditionally known as the intellect (buddhi).
In the Yoga systems he is called "The Great One" (Mahān), and also as Viriñci;
furthermore, in the Sāṃkhya scripture, he who consists of many names is recited by various appellations.
He who possesses manifold forms, the soul of the universe, is remembered as the Single Syllable (Ekākṣara);
by him, through his own self, the entire triple world is sustained as a single essence.
Likewise, because he possesses manifold forms, he is celebrated as Viśvarūpa;
having indeed undergone transformation, he creates himself by means of himself.
From the conjunction with that Pradhāna, the one of great splendor produced the vast city of Ahaṃkāra, which is saluted by Prajāpati.
They call that manifestation from the unmanifest the "creation of knowledge" (vidyāsarga),
and likewise, the Great One and the ego (ahaṃkāra) are indeed the "creation of ignorance" (avidyāsarga).
Both the inactive and the active have likewise arisen from one source;
they are known as ignorance and knowledge by those who contemplate the Vedas and the scriptures.
O King, know that the third creation is that of the elements from the ego;
O Lord of Men, know that the fourth is the modified (vaikṛta) among the types of ego.
Wind, light, and then space, water, and likewise earth;
as well as sound and touch, form, taste, and likewise smell.
Know, O Indra among kings, that this fifth creation, consisting of ten groups produced simultaneously, is undoubtedly the elemental creation (bhautika) which accomplishes all purposes.
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth;
likewise, speech, the two hands, the two feet, the anus, and the generative organ.
These organs of perception and likewise the organs of action,
O King, were produced here simultaneously with the mind.
This twenty-fourfold reality, which manifests in all forms,
is that which the Brahmins who perceive the truth do not grieve over once they have known it.
Thus, O best of men, this supreme triple world has arisen; it should always be understood as being within the ocean of hell.
Together with yakṣas, bhūtas, and gandharvas, along with kinnaras and great serpents,
as well as cāraṇas, piśācas, gods, ṛṣis, and night-stalkers.
[He dwells] among gadflies, insects, and mosquitoes; with putrid worms and rats;
with dogs and outcaste dog-cookers; with deer, as well as with Cāṇḍālas and Pulkasas.
Whether it be in an elephant, a horse, a donkey, a tiger, a wolf, or even a cow—
whatever form there may be, this is the illustration for all of them.
"In water, on earth, and likewise in the sky, but nowhere else—this was the certainty regarding the abode of embodied beings; thus indeed have we heard."
O dear one, day after day, the entire self of beings known as the manifest (vyakta) flows away; that which is traditionally called the Imperishable (akṣara) likewise [flows]. (BrP 241.34)
Therefore, that is called the perishable (kṣara), for this world perishes;
and they say the world, which is of the nature of delusion, arises from the unmanifest as that which is known as the manifest.
And this great, eternal, imperishable state is free from all that is transitory;
it has been described to you, O Great King, because from it one does not return again.
The twenty-fifth principle is formless, eternal, and designated as *tattva*;
because it takes refuge in *sattva*, the wise call *tattva* "sattva."
That which is formless creates the manifest; it presides over that which possesses form.
For the twenty-fourth principle is the manifest, while the twenty-fifth is indeed formless.
He alone, the self-possessed one, dwells within the heart in all forms;
the eternal conscious being, though formless himself, is the animator of all that has form.
By virtue of the nature of creation and dissolution, he consists of creation and dissolution;
though eternally devoid of qualities, he constantly abides within the sphere of objects and is designated as possessing qualities.

Thus, this Great-Souled One, though undergoing transformations through millions of creations and dissolutions and possessing the power of nature (prakṛti), being wise, does not conceive of himself as an agent.
Endowed with the qualities of darkness, goodness, and passion, he is dissolved into various wombs here in this world due to his lack of awakening and because of his service to unenlightened people.
Due to dwelling together with latent impressions (*vāsanā*), one thinks "I am a fool";
yet, when told "That which I was is no longer I," one follows only the qualities (*guṇa*).
Through *tamas* one encounters various *tāmasa* states;
through *rajas*, the *rājasa* states; and by resorting to *sattva*, the *sāttvika* states.
These three forms— white, red, and black—
are all indeed to be known as belonging to primordial nature (prakṛti).
Those characterized by tamas go to hell; those characterized by rajas go to the world of humans;
and those characterized by sattva, partaking of happiness, go to the realm of the gods.
Through exclusively evil one attains the womb of an animal;
through both merit and evil one attains human status; and through merit alone one becomes a deity.
Thus the wise declare that liberation has the unmanifest as its object;
this which is the twenty-fifth [principle] proceeds from knowledge alone.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, due to a lack of awakening, one follows along with the unawakened;
from one body to thousands of bodies, he is not thereby divided.
Through the application of austerity, one is born among the thousands of animal wombs or even among the gods, together with virtues, until those virtues are exhausted.
From the state of humanity, a god goes to heaven and returns to the human realm;
from the human realm, he enters the abode of the place of hell.

Just as a silkworm, though itself devoid of qualities, constantly encloses itself with the threads of its own silk-filaments, so too does this [soul], though inherently without qualities, bind itself with qualities.
Though free from dualities, he encounters them here in various wombs;
[he suffers] from diseases of the head, diseases of the eyes, toothaches, and throat-obstructions.
In cases of dropsy, diarrhea, scrofula, and eczema;
in leucoderma, skin diseases, burns from fire, as well as in ringworm and epilepsy.
And whatever other various pairs of opposites arise for embodied beings that are natural to them, it is precisely those that one identifies with as the self.
Likewise, he should abandon arrogance and excessive pride, as well as his meritorious deeds;
he should wear a single garment or four garments, and always sleep on the ground.
Likewise, he sleeps like a frog, or remains in the heroic posture (vīrāsana);
the heroic posture is performed in the air, as is the act of lying down there.
He should likewise sleep on a bed of bricks, a bed of wheels, or a bed of ashes; he should lie upon the bare ground and smear himself with earth.
He should sleep on a plank during the digestion of water in the posture of a hero,
and likewise on various beds provided with planks and supports.
In the garden, however, he was clad in coarse hempen cloth and a black antelope skin;
he wore a garment of fine wool and was covered with a tiger skin.
He is clothed in a lion’s skin and likewise in silken garments;
he wears a wooden plank as a lower garment and similarly bears a garment made of bark.
The wise man, having likewise considered various other garments— such as one made of a single mat, or one of rags, or many other types of clothing— [chose his attire].
Various kinds of foods and diverse types of jewels,
as well as eating only once every night and the practice of eating at a single time of day.
He who eats at the fourth and eighth times, as well as at the sixth time; he who eats only once every six nights, and likewise he who eats only once every eight days.
One who fasts for a month, one who subsists on roots, likewise one who eats fruits, one who feeds on air, and one whose food consists of oil-cake, curd, and cow-dung; BrP_242.17 //
Subsisting on cow urine, as well as eating kāśa flowers, subsisting on śaivāla moss, or likewise maintaining oneself by other means; BrP_242.18 //
Subsisting on withered leaves and scattered fruits,
he performs various austerities out of a desire for spiritual perfection.
He [perceived] the Cāndrāyaṇa fasts according to rule, various ritual emblems,
those associated with the four stages of life, and even those based on dharma and adharma.
He also visited various other hermitages belonging to different sects,
as well as secluded shaded rocks and mountain springs.
Solitary sandbanks and various forests,
as well as secluded mountain caves within the woods.
He also [performed] various observances and diverse austerities,
as well as sacrifices of manifold forms and various branches of knowledge.
He established trade routes, as well as the duties of the twice-born, the kṣatriyas, the vaiśyas, and the śūdras;
and he distributed various kinds of gifts to the poor, the blind, the wretched, and others.
In that same way, one should strive to unite with various qualities:
sattva, rajas, and tamas, as well as dharma, artha, and kama.
Indeed, the Self itself, by its very nature,
thus differentiates itself into the utterances of *svāhā* and *vaṣaṭ*, as well as *svadhā* and salutation (*namaskriyā*).
They say that sacrificing, studying, giving, and likewise receiving gifts, as well as officiating at sacrifices and teaching, and even other such things [are duties]. BrP 242.27.
Through the process of birth and death, as well as through slaughter,
they say that all this— consisting of the auspicious, the inauspicious, and fear— is eternal.
The Goddess Prakṛti brings about both fear and dissolution;
at the end of the day, having transcended these qualities, he alone remains.
Just as the sun withdraws its web of rays at that time,
even so he regards all of that as being for the sake of sport.
Thus performing these various qualities of his own form, which are dear to the heart,
he [creates] this [world] characterized by the nature of creation and dissolution.
Attached to the path of action, he is the master of the three qualities and possesses those three qualities;
endowed with both action and the path of non-action, he likewise regards it as such.
O All-pervading Lord, by its very nature this entire world is blinded;
it is pervaded in manifold ways by both passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas).
In this way, these pairs of opposites have passed away and continue to arise from me eternally;
they are born from me and, at the time of dissolution, they go back into me as well.
O lord of men, because of his partisan intellect, he thinks that all these [sins] must be overcome, and likewise [he thinks the same] regarding meritorious deeds as well. (BrP 242.35)
"These [deeds] are indeed to be experienced by me when I have gone to the world of the gods;
and right here as well, I shall experience the arising of the fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious actions."
Thus, this must be done for my own happiness; having performed it once, may there be happiness for me in birth after birth, as long as I exist.
"I shall have no endless suffering here for what I have done;
for human happiness and sorrow are the same as sinking even into hell."
In time, I shall again come from hell to human birth;
and from the state of humanity to the state of a god, and from the state of a god back to the state of a man.
And from the state of humanity, he goes in turn to hell;
such is the self of the twice-born, indeed enveloped by the qualities (guṇas).
Because of that, one is reborn among gods and humans or in hell;
constantly enveloped by the sense of "mine," one revolves right there.
Throughout thousands of millions of creations, within bodies that end in death,
he alone performs such actions as consist of the fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious deeds.
Thus he attains the fruit embodied within the three worlds;
nature performs the action consisting of auspicious and inauspicious results.
And Prakṛti likewise attains movement at will throughout the three worlds—
in the animal realm, among human beings, and likewise in the world of the gods.
One should know that these three states are indeed natural;
and because they possess a nature that is without gender, they are inferred even by means of gendered signs.
In that very same way, one indeed infers the male organ through inference;
having reached another sign, it is the natural, unblemished organ.
Presiding over the openings of the wounds, one imagines actions within oneself;
these are all the five organs of action, beginning with the ears.
In this world, passion and the other qualities proceed together with the sense-objects;
[the ignorant think], "I am indeed performing these actions, and these senses are mine."
For he might think himself devoid of senses though he has a wound, or consider himself free from wounds;
he might regard himself as without marks when he has marks, or as being at the wrong time when it is his own appointed time.
He perceives non-existence as existence, himself as the self, the immortal as mortal for himself,
deathlessness as death, and the immovable as moving for himself.
He regards the non-field as the field, the selfless as the attachment of the self,
the unreal as the reality of the self, and non-existence as the existence of the self.
Indeed, due to a lack of awakening, one considers the imperishable Self to be perishable;
likewise, due to a lack of realization and from associating with unawakened people.
Thousands of millions of creations pass away ending in dissolution;
thousands of other births pass away ending in death.
In the state of animals, among humans, and likewise in the world of the gods,
he appears there by the thousands, like the moon reflected in many vessels of water.
In this very way, one possessed of evil intellect is led away due to a lack of awakening;
that fifteenth digit is the womb, which is recited as "the abode" (dhāma).
Know that Soma is indeed eternal; through sixteen parts, the unintelligent one is born perpetually again and again by means of a *kalā*.
O King, he does not become wise in this manner;
rather, it is the sixteenth digit that is subtle—one should understand that to be Soma.
But he is not employed by the gods; rather, he employs even the gods.
Having destroyed the sense of "mine-ness," O best of kings, he is born again;
indeed, he becomes possessed of the three qualities of *prakṛti* which consists of the three qualities.
Janaka said:
This relationship between the two—the imperishable and the perishable—is desired;
or it is like the relationship between a woman and a man, and that [imperishable] is indeed called Puruṣa.
Without the male, a female here does not bear a fetus;
likewise, without the female, the form of a male is not produced.
Through their mutual connection and by relying on each other's qualities, these [elements] produce form; thus it occurs in all wombs.

Through excessive union for the sake of pleasure, and by mutual reliance on each other's qualities, the form [of the embryo] is produced during the fertile period; I shall explain that with an illustration.
O twice-born one, we know that the qualities of a person here— namely the bones, the sinews, and the marrow— as well as those which belong to the mother, are derived from the father.
"We have heard that skin, flesh, and blood are derived from the mother;
thus it is recited in the Vedic scriptures, O best of the twice-born. (BrP 243.6)
Whatever is declared in the Vedas and whatever is recited as taught in the Śāstras—
that authority of the Vedas and Śāstras is the eternal authority.
In this very way, O Blessed One, primordial nature (prakṛti) and the spirit (puruṣa) are eternally connected; and because of that, the dharma of liberation does not exist.
Alternatively, tell me in truth some recent illustration; for you are always directly perceived by me.
We too, desiring liberation, long for that which is free from affliction,
invincible, undecaying, eternal, beyond the senses, and independent of a lord.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"That which has been stated by you as the illustration from the Vedic scriptures is indeed so, just as I shall explain it, since you are one who grasps the essential truth."
For you uphold the texts of both the Vedas and the Śāstras,
yet you do not know the true reality of those texts as it truly is, O Lord of Men.
For he who is intent on memorizing the texts of the Vedas and the Shastras,
yet does not know the true meaning of those texts, his memorization is in vain.
He who does not understand the meaning of that book merely carries its burden;
however, for him who knows the true essence of the book's meaning, the acquisition of the book is not in vain.
When questioned about the meaning of the book, one such as I ought to speak;
for by approaching the matter according to reality, he shall find its true significance.
How can one who is not at all eager for the meaning of the text, being of dull intellect and possessing feeble understanding, explain the text with certainty?
The man who engages in debate without knowing the true principles of the scriptures—
whether out of greed or out of hypocrisy— is a sinner and shall go to hell.
Furthermore, that man of defective character will not state the decision according to the truth;
for even though he knows the true meaning of this matter here, he is certainly not self-possessed.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, listen to how this is perceived according to its true nature among the Sāṃkhyas and among the high-souled practitioners of Yoga.
That which the practitioners of Yoga perceive is followed by the followers of Sāṃkhya;
he who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one is wise.
Skin, flesh, blood, fat, bile, marrow, bone, and sinew—
this, my dear, is that which consists of the senses, about which you have thus spoken to me.
From substance arises substance, and likewise from sense organ, sense organ;
one obtains body from body, and just so, seed from seed.
How can there be qualities for the embodied one who is without sense-faculties, without seed, and without substance, since the Great Self is devoid of qualities?
Qualities arise from qualities and cease within them;
thus, the qualities born of primordial nature (prakṛti) arise and pass away.
Skin, flesh, blood, fat, bile, marrow, bone, and sinew—
know these eight to be indeed produced from the primordial semen.
The masculine and the non-masculine are known as the feminine gender, which is primordial matter (prakṛti).
This wind is indeed masculine and is designated as "rasa" (essence/flavor).

The unmanifest primordial nature (prakṛti), though itself devoid of marks, is perceived through its own offspring which possess marks; just as the formless [elements] are always known through their manifested forms, such as flowers and fruits.
Thus, O dear one, he is perceived through inference by means of his marks; the twenty-fifth principle has a fixed nature within those marks.
Without beginning or end, infinite, and the sole seer of all,
he is nevertheless called a "quality" among qualities only because of his sense of self-identification with them.
Qualities belong to that which possesses qualities; how could there be qualities for that which is devoid of qualities?
Therefore, those people who perceive qualities understand it in this way.
But when he identifies with these qualities born of nature,
then, being possessed of those qualities, he perceives the various distinctions among the qualities.

That which the wise describe as entirely beyond the intellect— both Sāṃkhya and Yoga— is the state of being awakened, due to the total relinquishing of that which is [merely] being perceived by the intellect.
They say that the manifest, when unawakened by its own qualities, is the Lord;
yet the Lord is also eternally devoid of qualities and is the presiding controller.
The wise, seeking the supreme, who are skilled in Sāṃkhya and Yoga, perceive the twenty-five principles: primordial nature (prakṛti) and its twenty-four qualities (guṇas).
When the unmanifest has awakened and become free from its state of stillness, they do not perceive it as awakening; rather, they understand it then as being equal [to itself].
O subduer of enemies, this is a correct illustration, not an incorrect one;
those who understand it awaken through these two distinct [means].
This illustration of the perishable and the imperishable has been stated by each other:
they say that oneness is the imperishable, while multiplicity is called the perishable.
When this [system] culminates in the twenty-five principles, it is then correctly described;
for it consists of both the vision of its unity and the vision of its diversity.
This is the illustration of the distinction between the knower of reality and the two realities themselves;
the wise say that reality consists of twenty-five principles.
The wise declare that which is beyond the twenty-fifth principle to be the supreme reality;
it is the eternal reality, the practice to be avoided by that which is to be avoided, and the reality that transcends all principles.
Karālajanaka said:
"O best of the twice-born, you have spoken of this multiplicity and unity;
yet for one who observes them, the illustration of these two remains indeed doubtful."
Likewise, O sinless one, I do not perceive this reality through my gross intellect—neither by means of the awakened Buddhas nor by that which is being awakened; of this there is no doubt.
O sinless one, although you have stated the reason for the imperishable and the perishable, even that has, as it were, vanished from my mind due to its instability.
Therefore, I desire to hear this teaching on the vision of multiplicity and unity, as well as the pairs of opposites, the unobstructed, and the awakening, according to their true nature.
O Blessed One, you have fully understood, both individually and in their distinctness, knowledge and ignorance, the imperishable and the perishable, as well as Sāṃkhya and Yoga. BrP 243.45.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Ah, I shall explain to you that which you ask;
O Great King, listen to me as I describe the practice of yoga in its distinct details."
The duty of yogins is indeed yoga, and meditation alone is their supreme strength;
moreover, those who know the truth say that this meditation is of two kinds.
One-pointedness of mind and likewise breath control (prāṇāyāma);
breath control is both with attributes (saguṇa) and without attributes (nirguṇa), as is that which is mental.
O lord of men, after voiding urine or excrement, or after eating, one should not consume food for two periods of time; thereafter, being intent on it, one may eat.
Having withdrawn the senses from the objects of the senses by means of the mind, the sage [should focus] on that which is beyond the ten,
the twelve, or even the twenty-four.
Then that wise one should not urge himself with exhortations;
rather, he should abide in that which is ageless, as it has been described by the sages.
"The Universal Soul is to be known constantly; thus indeed have we heard.
For one whose mind is undiminished, this is the firm conclusion: that it is not otherwise."
Freed from all attachments, moderate in diet, and having conquered the senses,
one should fix the mind within the heart during both the first and last watches of the night.
O Lord of Mithilā, having steadied the collection of senses with the mind,
and having made the mind steady by means of the intellect, remain motionless like a stone.
One should be as unshakable as a pillar and as motionless as a block of wood;
one who knows the application of the rules through their intellect is therefore said to be disciplined.
He does not hear, nor does he smell, nor does he see anything;
he does not perceive touch, nor does the mind form any volition.
When one does not think anything at all and is as if unconscious, like a log of wood,
then the wise say that he has attained his true nature and is disciplined.
For just as a lamp does not shine [without oil], so too is it seen;
being without marks, he may attain a downward, upward, or horizontal course.
Then, O dear one, that which is attained therein and which is described when it is perceived—
the knower who resides within the heart as the inner self— should be known by those like me.
Like a smokeless seven-flamed fire, like the sun with its rays,
or like lightning-fire in the sky, one beholds the Self within the self.
That which the high-souled, steadfast, and wise Brahmins— established in the womb of Brahman— behold is indeed unborn, immortal in nature, and free from a source.
They say that very same [Self] is subtler than the subtle and greater than the great;
though it stands eternally everywhere within all beings, it is not seen.

O dear one, the Creator of the worlds, standing on the far shore of the great darkness, is not himself subject to darkness, for he perceives by means of the visible substance of the intellect, which serves as a lamp for the mind.
He is called "far beyond darkness" by the knowers of reality who have reached the further shore of the Vedas;
he is stainless, free from doubt, without marks, and designated as the markless.
For this indeed is the yoga of the worlds; what other characteristic of yoga could there be?
Seeing thus, one should perceive the supreme, undecaying Self.
Thus far, the Yoga philosophy has been declared by me to you in its true essence;
now I shall proclaim the knowledge of Sāṃkhya, which is the teaching of thorough enumeration.
They say that the unmanifest (avyakta), which is the manifestation of the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti) of the self, is the first;
from that, O best of kings, the second principle, the Great One (mahat), was produced.
We have heard that egoism (ahaṃkāra) is the third [evolute] from the Great One (mahat);
those who perceive the self according to the Sāṃkhya system say that the five elements arise from egoism.
These eight are the primary natures (prakṛtis), and there are also sixteen modifications (vikāras),
as well as the five specific objects (viśeṣas) and the five sense organs.
The wise, who know the rules of Sāṃkhya and are ever established on the path of Sāṃkhya, declare that this alone is the enumeration (sāṃkhya) of the principles.
For whatever is born from something, that very thing dissolves back into it;
the elements dissolve in reverse order and are grasped by the inner self.
The qualities are constantly born in accordance with their sequence and dissolve in reverse order, like the waves of the ocean.
O best of kings, such is the extent of the creation and dissolution of Prakṛti;
it exists in a state of unity during dissolution, and likewise in a state of multiplicity during creation.
In this very same way, O Indra among kings, it should be understood by those skilled in knowledge that the Unmanifest is the presiding controller; this too is an illustration of that.
The knower of reality understands both the unity and the multiplicity of primordial nature (prakṛti):
its unity at the time of dissolution and its multiplicity through the process of manifestation.
The Self should make manifold its nature, which is characterized by procreation;
and the Great Self, the twenty-fifth principle, presides over that field.
"O Indra among kings, he is called the Adhiṣṭhātṛ (the Presider) by the best of ascetics;
we have heard that he is the Adhiṣṭhātṛ because he presides over the fields."
He knows the field (kṣetra) which is unmanifest, and thus he is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña);
he dwells in the city of the unmanifest, and thus he is called the Person (puruṣa).
The field is indeed one thing, and the Knower of the Field is said to be another;
the field is called the Unmanifest, while the Knower is the twenty-fifth principle.
Knowledge is indeed one thing, and the object of knowledge is said to be another;
knowledge is called the Unmanifest, while the object of knowledge is the twenty-fifth principle.
The unmanifest is called the field (kṣetra), as well as the sentient being (sattva) and likewise the Lord (īśvara).
That which is without a lord and not the ultimate principle—that twenty-fifth principle is the true reality.
The Sāṃkhya philosophy is enumerated to this extent;
it establishes enumeration and shall also proclaim the primordial nature (prakṛti).
Having truly reckoned forty and twenty-four,
the number of thousands of functions is indeed twenty-five, yet it is devoid of reality.
The twenty-fifth principle is known as the awakened self (prabuddhātman) and the one who is awakening;
when it awakens to itself, then it becomes solitary (kevala).
Thus has right vision been described to you according to its true nature;
those who understand it in this way indeed attain equanimity.
Direct perception is indeed the correct demonstration of the nature of primordial matter;
just as these [effects] possess qualities, so too would they arise from that which is devoid of qualities.
But for those who act in this manner, there is no further return;
nor does the state of perishability exist, for they are mutually imperishable.
O subduer of enemies, those whose intellects do not perceive correctly, and in whom there is no right vision, undergo manifestation again and again.
Knowing all this, they will become manifest not by awakening everyone,
but by following that which is already manifest.
It is said that everything is unmanifest, yet the twenty-fifth principle is not "everything.
For those who understand this thus, no fear exists.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O best of kings, this much of the Sāṃkhya philosophy has been told to you;
now, learn from me about knowledge and ignorance in their proper sequence.
Those who possess the nature of creation and dissolution call the Unmanifest (avyakta) indivisible;
"creation and dissolution" has been mentioned, as well as knowledge and ignorance—this constitutes the group of twenty.
Understand now, my dear, that very science of one another’s relationship in its proper sequence,
as it was declared by the sages— a preeminent illustration of Sāṃkhya.

It has been heard by us that for all the organs of action, the organ of intellect (buddhīndriya) is known as their presiding knowledge; and likewise, for the organs of intellect, it is the specific objects (viśeṣa). BrP 244.4.
The wise declare that the objects of the senses are the knowledge of those [senses];
they declare that the five elements are the knowledge of the mind.
The ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) of the five elements is beyond doubt in this matter;
likewise, O lord of men, the ego-sense is knowledge (vidyā), and knowledge is the intellect (buddhi).
O best of men, *prakṛti* is to be known as *buddhi*, the unmanifest (*avyakta*), the supreme lord of the principles (*tattva*), *vidyā*, and is likewise remembered as the supreme *vidhi*.
They say that the Unmanifest is the lower [nature], while the twenty-fifth principle is indeed Knowledge;
he who has reached the further shore of both the object of knowledge and knowledge itself is said to be "the All of the All."
Knowledge is said to be unmanifest, while the object of knowledge is indeed the twenty-fifth principle;
likewise, knowledge is unmanifest, and the knower is the twenty-fifth.
I have indeed explained knowledge and ignorance in their true nature with particular detail;
now learn from me that which was described as the imperishable and the perishable.
Both of these are said to be perishable, and both of these are said to be imperishable;
however, I shall explain the reason according to my knowledge, based on true understanding.
Both of these are considered to be without beginning or end, and both are regarded as lords;
those who contemplate knowledge declare that both are designated as the ultimate reality (tattva).

Because it possesses the nature of creation and dissolution, they call the unmanifest (avyakta) imperishable; yet this very [unmanifest], undergoing transformation again and again for the sake of the creation of the qualities (guṇas), [is subject to change].
The mutual production of the qualities, beginning with Mahat, has as its presiding ground the Field; this indeed they call the twenty-fifth principle.
That web of qualities which exists within should be withdrawn into the manifest self;
that "I" [the ego] then dissolves into the twenty-fifth principle along with those qualities.
The qualities dissolve into the qualities; then there remains that single primordial nature (prakṛti).
At that time, even the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is designated as the Knower of the Field.
When the syllable, which is primordial nature (prakṛti), enters that which is designated as the qualities (guṇa)— that is,
when it attains a state devoid of qualities within the body through the transformation of the qualities— [then liberation occurs].
In this very way, through the complete destruction of knowledge regarding the field, the knower of the field becomes free from qualities by its very nature; thus indeed have we heard.
When this [self] becomes subject to change through the qualities within the qualities,
it then knows its own nature and likewise the qualitylessness of the Self.
In this way, one becomes purified by abandoning the primordial nature (prakṛti), when the wise person realizes: "I am one, and she is another."
Then this [element] attains a state free from distress and does not undergo mixture;
yet, O Indra among kings, by its very nature, one element is seen to be mixed with another.
But when he feels aversion for that net of qualities born of Prakṛti,
and beholding the Supreme, sees it, then, truly seeing, he shall no longer be joined to transmigratory existence.
"What have I done that I am thus submerged in time, like a fish that follows the water because of its familiarity with it? (BrP 244.23)
For it was I alone who, through delusion,
followed one person after another in this world, just as a fish follows [its prey] due to its perception of water.
Due to ignorance, the fish does not perceive itself as distinct from the water;
likewise, because of that lack of knowledge, I do not know myself as other than [the body]. (BrP 244.25)
Fie upon me, a wretched fool, who, having sunk [in this ocean],
has again out of delusion followed after one person after another from birth to birth!
This kinsman shall experience destruction along with me;
having attained equality and oneness with him, I am exactly as he is.
"I perceive equality here; indeed, I am truly like him.
For he is clearly stainless, and at that time, I was just such as he."
I, who through the delusion of ignorance and by means of my lack of knowledge have been active,
have remained for all this time due to association and excessive attachment.
Thus, having attained such mastery, I did not realize this time;
how could I have dwelt amidst those who are superior, inferior, and middling?
"How can I dwell here together with one who possesses such deceptive illusion?
Since you have not yet realized the state of awakening, remain firm in this place for now."
I shall not go to live together with her for this duration of time, because of her deception; for I have been deceived by her, who is subject to change, while I remained free from change.
That is not his fault; rather, this is my own fault, that I remained attached here even though he had turned away.
Then, while he remained there in many forms, both embodied and unembodied,
the formless one whose nature is formless was overcome by the sense of "mine-ness."
And by that very nature, through the sense of "mine" toward those various wombs here, he who is naturally free from possessiveness becomes distorted in each of them.
Existing within wombs with a mind whose discernment was lost,
I did not establish any sense of equanimity regarding the ego-sense.
"Having divided himself into many forms, he has joined me with them once again;
now I have awakened, free from possessiveness and free from ego."
Having forever abandoned this clinging sense of "mine-ness," which is produced by the mind and rooted in egoism, I shall take refuge in that which is free from affliction.
"I shall attain equality with this [universe], not with this mindless one;
my security lies with this, and never alone with that one."
Thus, through supreme perfect awakening, the twenty-fifth has awakened after [the others] and,
having abandoned the perishable, attains the imperishable state that is free from affliction.

O King of Mithilā, having first perceived the Unmanifest— which possesses the attributes of the manifest, as well as qualities and the absence of qualities— as being devoid of qualities, one becomes like that.
This illustration of the imperishable and the perishable has been declared by me here for you,
endowed with knowledge, according to the evidence of the Vedas.
I shall speak to you once more of that which is beyond doubt, subtle, pure, and stainless; listen to it as it was heard by me.
Sāṃkhya and Yoga have been proclaimed by me through the presentation of these two systems of scripture;
that which is declared in the Sāṃkhya scripture is indeed the very same as the Yoga philosophy.
O Lord of the Earth, the knowledge of the Sāṃkhyas, which is intent upon awakening,
is clearly proclaimed therein out of a desire for the welfare of their disciples.
And wise people say that this scripture is indeed extensive;
and in this scripture, regarding the yogis, [the process] beginning with rebirth is described.
O lord of men, the principle beyond the twenty-fifth is also recited;
thus has the supreme principle of the Sāṃkhyas been described exactly as it is.
They declare that, according to the teaching of Yoga, the Buddha, the unawakened, and the one awakening in reality, as well as the act of awakening and Buddhahood itself, are one.
Vasiṣṭha said: Furthermore, this unawakened and unmanifest one, which is always a storehouse of the qualities (guṇas),
brings forth and likewise withdraws the reality that sustains those qualities.
For the Unborn One, O King, having undergone transformation through play,
made himself manifold and appeared as if diverse.
Thus transforming in this way, though awakening, he does not truly awaken;
for he practices according to the qualities (guṇas), and likewise creates and withdraws them.
And because it awakens the unmanifest, they also call it "the awakening one";
yet the unmanifest, O dear one, does not awaken in that way, whether it possesses qualities or is devoid of qualities.
Indeed, they say that this is sometimes called "the awakened," if one awakens to this unmanifest twenty-fifth principle.
Awakening, he is known as "this is my self," according to the scriptures;
through mutual awakening, they speak of the unmanifest and imperishable.
And because it awakens the unmanifest, they call the twenty-fifth principle the "Awakening One," the Great-Souled One; yet even he does not perceive [it].
He awakens to the twenty-sixth, the stainless Buddha, the immeasurable and eternal;
yet he constantly perceives the twenty-fifth and the twenty-fourth as well.
O you of great splendor, that Brahman, which is both manifest and unmanifest and permeates all things visible and invisible as their very nature, is understood, my dear, as the absolute alone.
When one perceives the twenty-fifth as the twenty-fourth self,
being awakened, one thinks, "I am another."
Then he becomes possessed of his true nature, with his vision unclouded; he perceives the supreme intellect, which is pure and stainless.
O tiger among kings, when the twenty-sixth [tattva] has then been made into a Buddha, he departs;
thereafter, he abandons that unmanifest [principle], which is subject to the nature of creation and dissolution.
He knows that primordial nature (prakṛti) is devoid of qualities, yet joined with qualities and insentient;
consequently, through the vision of the unmanifest, he becomes one whose dharma is absolute.
Having attained union through this alone, one may reach the liberated self;
they say that this is the reality (tattva), which is beyond all categories (nistattva) and free from old age and death.
O King, by the mere hearing of the principles, one becomes a knower of reality;
the wise proclaim that there are twenty-five principles.
And one who possesses the truth, my dear, does not sink into the cycles of worldly existence;
for he attains the reality of these things—quickly understand their defining characteristic.
When the wise one perceives this twenty-sixth principle as being free from old age and death,
he undoubtedly attains equality through its power alone.
Though awakening through the twenty-sixth [principle], one who is being awakened yet lacks true understanding—
this is called "diversity" (nānātva), according to the illustration of the Sāṃkhya scriptures.
When that which consists of twenty-five principles, endowed with volition,
perceives through the intellect, it indeed becomes one.
O King of Men, O Lord of Mithilā, when he who is awakened attains equality with the Buddha,
this one whose nature was attached becomes a self free from attachment.
Having attained the unattached Self, they know the twenty-sixth principle to be born of karma;
and when he awakens to this, the all-pervading Lord abandons the unmanifest.
The twenty-fourth is unfathomable due to the awakening of the twenty-sixth; for this one, O sinless one, is both unawakened and in the process of awakening.
And the Buddha has been described according to his true nature based on the teachings as they were heard:
just as there is a difference between a gnat and an udumbara fruit, so it is between these two.
Just as in the case of fish and water, so too is their distinctness perceived;
in this very way, one should understand the multiplicity and unity of these two.
This much is declared to be liberation, known as theoretical knowledge (jñāna) and realized wisdom (vijñāna),
which quickly operates within the body of the twenty-fifth principle.
"This one must be liberated from the realm of the unmanifest"—thus they say;
"he shall be liberated in this very way and not otherwise," such is the certainty.
Indeed, by uniting with one who is pure, the wise man becomes another's self and another's dharma; he becomes one whose nature is purified, and not by uniting with one who is impure.
O bull among men, having encountered the Buddha whose nature is liberation,
one who is subject to separation indeed becomes liberated in soul.
Through liberation, liberation likewise comes to be attained here;
one becomes pure in action, truly pure, and possessed of immeasurable intelligence.
One becomes pure by uniting with the pure-souled; likewise, one becomes absolute by uniting with the absolute. And by uniting with the independent, independence is attained.
Thus much has been told by me to you, O Great King, the truth according to the reality of things; you,
being free from envy, should accept this with your intellect.
O King, this eternal, pure, and primordial Brahman should be imparted by you as the supreme gift to those people who are established in the Vedas.

This instruction, which causes awakening, should not be given to one who desires to perform [the rite] while remaining ignorant of its cause, nor to one who is prostrate before you but whose soul is as false as untruth.

It should not be given to one who is deceitful, to one who is impotent, nor to one of crooked intellect; likewise, it should not be given to one who harms others through the knowledge of the learned, but rather for the sake of awakening the disciple.
To one endowed with faith, possessed of virtue, constantly refraining from slandering others, and who is pure in yoga and wise; BrP 245.34abc.
To one who is compassionate, patient, and intent on the welfare of others; to one whose character is solitary, who delights in the prescribed rules,
who is free from dispute, and who is deeply learned.
This very secret should always be given only to one who is modestly dressed, who is not motivated by worldly causes, and who possesses these qualities;
it must not be given to one who is utterly devoid of such virtues.
They say this is the supreme, pure Brahman; what is done for the sake of spiritual welfare will not be joined with such merit if it is given to an unworthy recipient who merely preaches the Dharma.
One might give this entire earth filled with jewels, yet this which is not to be given should be bestowed upon one who has conquered his senses and is disciplined, even if he is without vows.
O King Karāla, this supreme reality should be given to one who knows the truth;
you have no fear whatsoever.
Today you have heard this supreme Brahman.
Thus has been declared that which is supremely pure,
free from sorrow, entirely without beginning or middle, unfathomable, and ageless and immortal.
Having perceived that which is free from disease, devoid of fear, and auspicious, and having understood this true meaning of it, one should abandon delusion known as the doctrines of others.
For this was indeed obtained in ancient times from the eternal Hiraṇyagarbha, O lord of men,
after he had been propitiated with effort by that one of fierce splendor.
O lord of men, just as you have asked about this eternal Brahman,
so has this been told by me to you, and nothing else.
"O King, this great knowledge, which is the ultimate refuge for those who know liberation, was obtained by me from Brahmā just as it was received.
Vyāsa said:
O best of sages, this which was spoken by Vasiṣṭha in former times is the supreme Brahman, from which one does not return again; it is the twenty-fifth principle.
One attains the supreme, imperishable knowledge; understanding it according to its true nature, one realizes that which is ageless and immortal, and does not undergo rebirth.
O brahmins, O twice-born ones, this supreme knowledge which brings about the highest good has been told by me in its true essence, having heard it from the divine sage.
This was collected by the seer Vasiṣṭha from Hiraṇyagarbha;
from Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, the tiger among seers, obtained this.
This eternal truth was known to me through Nārada;
having heard this supreme state, O best of sages, do not grieve.
For one by whom the perishable and the imperishable are distinguished, no fear exists;
but for him who does not know this in its true essence, fear indeed exists.
And due to lack of discernment, the deluded soul repeatedly undergoes calamities after death,
experiencing thousands of births that end in death.
Likewise, one experiences the world of the gods, as well as the realms of animals and humans;
or else, one is liberated from that ocean of ignorance.
O twice-born ones, in this terrible ocean of ignorance, which is said to be unmanifest and bottomless, living beings sink day after day.
Therefore, from that unfathomable, unmanifest, and eternal source which has been exhausted,
you have become free from passion and free from darkness, O twice-born ones!
Thus, O best of sages, I have declared this supreme liberation, the most essential of essentials, knowing which one does not return.
O Brahmins, this should never be given to an atheist, nor to one who lacks devotion,
nor to one of wicked mind, nor to one who is averse to faith.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
O twice-born ones, in ancient times Vyāsa thus spoke to the sages concerning the Purāṇa with gentle speech, using words that were most essential and free from the eighteen defects.
It is filled with pure collections of various scriptures free from blemish,
endowed with purity of lineage, and adorned with excellent words.
Having caused [the doctrine] to be heard according to the proper method, complete with the statement of the prima facie view and the final conclusion, the one of great intelligence ceased speaking.
Having heard that ancient account, which is equal to the Vedas, beginning with the one called Brāhma, and which bestows the fruit of all desires, those best of sages likewise [listened].
They became joyful, well-pleased, and filled with wonder again and again;
they then praised the sage Vyāsa Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.
The sages said:
"O best of sages, oh! By you has been told this supreme Purāṇa, which is equal to the Vedas, which grants all desired fruits, and which removes all sins."
We have heard what has been proclaimed by you in various words and syllables;
O Lord, there is indeed nothing in the three worlds that is unknown to you.
"O highly fortunate one, you are omniscient like Bṛhaspati among the gods;
we pay homage to you, the great sage of supreme wisdom, who is most devoted to Brahman."
O great sage, who is able to describe all your virtues, by whom the meanings of the Vedas have been revealed within the Mahābhārata?
Salutations to that Soul of Knowledge, who, having studied the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs and the grammars, composed the Bhārata scripture.
Homage be to you, O Vyāsa of vast intellect,
whose eyes are like the broad petals of a full-blown lotus;
by you, [this work] filled with the oil of the Bhārata [has been composed].
The lamp consisting of wisdom has been ignited for those blinded by the darkness of ignorance and led astray by false views;
and by you, the eyes have been opened with the collyrium-stick of knowledge.
Having spoken thus and having honored Vyāsa, they too were honored;
then, having accomplished their purpose, they all returned to their own hermitages from whence they had come.
Thus, O best of sages, I have indeed related this eternal Purāṇa,
which is exceedingly meritorious and the destroyer of all sins.
O best of the twice-born, just as I was questioned by you regarding this inquiry,
all of that has been fully proclaimed by me through the grace of Vyāsa.
This should be heard by householders, ascetics, and students;
it bestows wealth and happiness upon men, and is purifying and destructive of sin.
Likewise, it should be listened to with great effort and proper discipline by Brahmins devoted to the Supreme, by those beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, and by all who desire their own ultimate welfare.
A Brahmin attains knowledge, a Kṣatriya victory in battle,
a Vaiśya inexhaustible wealth, and a Śūdra shall obtain happiness.
Whatever desire a pure man hears while meditating upon it, that very desire he attains; there is no doubt about this.
This Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa indeed destroys all sins;
it is superior to all scriptures and brings about the goals of human existence.
This ancient narrative, equal to the Vedas, which I have recounted to you—
upon hearing it, the heap of sins arising from all defects is utterly destroyed.
Whatever a man obtains by fasting at Prayāga, Puṣkara, Kurukṣetra, and Arbuda, that he attains simply by hearing this.
O Brahmins, that fruit consisting of great merit which one does not obtain from a well-performed Agnihotra sacrifice for a year is attained by hearing this [account] but once.

Whatever fruit a person obtains by bathing in the waters of the Yamunā on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha and beholding Hari in Mathurā— [that same fruit one obtains here].
O Brahmins, he who has dedicated his mind to Keśava obtains that fruit perfectly through the recitation of this Purāṇa with concentrated devotion.
Whatever fruit a man may obtain by performing a ritual after observing its result,
he who reads or even hears this obtains that very same fruit.
That mortal who constantly reads or hears this ancient Purāṇa, which is equal to the Vedas, with faith, goes to the realm of Hari.
That Brahmin who, always self-restrained, causes [this] to be heard on the festival days,
especially on the eleventh and twelfth lunar days, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
This [account] bestows fame and long life, grants happiness and increases renown;
it provides strength and nourishment for men, brings fortune, and destroys evil dreams.
The wise person who, being well-composed and full of faith, recites this most excellent narrative at the three junctions of the day, shall obtain everything desired.
One afflicted by disease is freed from disease; one who is bound is released from bondage;
the frightened is liberated from fear; and one fallen into calamity is delivered from calamity.
A man obtains the memory of his past lives, knowledge, sons, intelligence, cattle, fortitude,
as well as virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
Whatever desires one may have in mind while reciting with a disciplined mind, a person attains all of them; there is no doubt in this matter.

And that person who, having bowed with a single-minded heart and purified by devotion to Viṣṇu, the teacher of the worlds and the giver of boons, constantly hears this which bestows heaven and liberation,
shall experience happiness here on earth with all impurities cast off, and divine bliss in heaven.
Thereafter, liberated from the qualities of material nature, he goes to the utterly stainless abode of Hari.
Therefore, the best of Brahmins, devoted to their own duties and desiring the sole path to liberation,
as well as the foremost of Kṣatriyas, should always remain self-restrained and seek the highest good.

This supreme [work], which yields great fruit and bestows dharma, artha, and mokṣa, should be heard daily by Vaiśyas born of pure lineage, as well as by righteous Śūdras. O best of men, may your minds be fixed upon dharma.
For that alone is the kinsman for one who has gone to the next world;
wealth and women, even when attended to by the skillful,
never attain power nor do they possess stability.
Through righteousness a man obtains a kingdom;
through righteousness a man goes to heaven; and through righteousness he gains long life, fame, austerity, and merit.
Through dharma a human being attains liberation;
here on earth, dharma is one's mother and father;
and in this world as well as in the next, dharma is one's friend.
Dharma is indeed your protector here and the giver of liberation;
yet there is nothing whatsoever apart from Dharma.
This is the most excellent secret, ancient, and equal to the Vedas.
It should not be given to one of wicked mind, and especially not to an atheist.
This supreme, ancient [account] has been spoken by me; it removes evil and increases righteousness. You have heard this most excellent secret.
"Command me, O sages; I am departing."
